Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Abhidhammāvatāra-purāṇaṭīkā

The Old Commentary on the Introduction to the Abhidhamma.

1. Paṭhamo paricchedo

1. The First Chapter.

Cittaniddesavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Exposition of Consciousness.

8. Tattha [M 0.0001][V 1.0001] tesu catubbidhesu paramatthesu, jātiniddhāraṇaṃ. Cittanti cittaṃ nāma. Vijānātīti vijānanaṃ, visayānaṃ vijānanaṃ visayavijānanaṃ. Cittasarūpaparidīpanamidaṃ vacanaṃ. Tassa pana cittassa ko vacanattho ko saddattho. Vuccate ācariyena. Sabbasaṅgāhakavasena sabbesaṃ cittānaṃ saṅgāhakanayavasena. Ārammaṇaṃ cinteti jānātīti cittaṃ, tadā sabbaṃ cittaṃ adhippetaṃ. Javanavīthivasena attasantānaṃ cinotīti cittaṃ, tadā kusalākusalamahākiriyācittaṃ adhippetaṃ. Aññesaṃ javanānaṃ aggahaṇaṃ kāmāvacarajavanāni eva yebhuyyavasena sattakkhattuṃ javantīti ñāpanatthaṃ.

8. Therein, among those fourfold ultimate realities, is the determination of their nature. 'Citta' is its name. It cognizes, thus it is cognition; the cognition of objects is object-cognition. This statement elucidates the nature of consciousness. Now, what is the etymological meaning of 'citta', and what is its verbal meaning? It is said by the teacher: By way of encompassing all, in the manner of gathering all consciousnesses, 'It thinks of and knows the object, thus it is citta'—here, all consciousness is meant. By way of the impulsion process, 'It accumulates its own continuum, thus it is citta'—here, wholesome, unwholesome, and great functional consciousnesses are meant. The non-inclusion of other impulsions is for the purpose of making it known that it is primarily sensuous-sphere impulsions that run for seven moments.

9. Vicittaṃ [V 1.0002] karaṇaṃ yassa taṃ vicittakaraṇaṃ, tassa bhāvo vicittakaraṇā. “Imassa rūpassa uddhaṃ idaṃ hotu, heṭṭhā idaṃ hotu, ubhayapasse ida”nti cintetvā yathācintitena kamena sesacittarūpanipphādanaṃ hoti, evaṃ yaṃ kiñci loke vicittaṃ sippajātaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ citteneva karīyati. Evaṃ vicittakaraṇatāya cittaṃ. Tadā karaṇatāya cittaṃ karotīti cittaṃ. Idaṃ taddhitapadaṃ. Vā ayaṃ añño nayo[M 0.0002]. Taṃ attano cittatāya aññadeva sarāgaṃ cittaṃ, aññaṃ sadosaṃ, aññaṃ samohaṃ. Aññaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ, aññaṃ rūpāvacarādibhedaṃ. Aññaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ, aññaṃ saddādiārammaṇaṃ. Rūpārammaṇesupi aññaṃ nīlārammaṇaṃ, aññaṃ pītādiārammaṇaṃ. Saddādiārammaṇesupi eseva nayo. Sabbesupi tesu aññaṃ hīnaṃ, aññaṃ majjhimaṃ, aññaṃ paṇītaṃ. Hīnādīsupi aññaṃ chandādhipateyyaṃ, aññaṃ cittādhipateyyaṃ, aññaṃ vīriyādhipateyyaṃ, aññaṃ vīmaṃsādhipateyyaṃ, tasmā yassa imesaṃ sampayuttabhūmiārammaṇahīnamajjhimapaṇītādhipatīnaṃ vasena attano cittatāya cittaṃ. Citto etasmiṃ atthīti cittaṃ. Tadā sabbaṃ cittaṃ. Paññattiyampi viññāṇe vicitte cittassa kammaṃ cittakammaṃ, cittakammameva cittakammakaṃ, cittakammake vicitte idha imasmiṃ adhikāre cittasammuti cittasaddo viññāṇe citte viññunā daṭṭhabbo.

9. That whose making is varied is 'vicittakaraṇa'; its state is 'vicittakaraṇatā'. Having thought, 'For this form, let this be above, this below, and this on both sides,' the remaining consciousness-born forms are produced according to the intended sequence. Thus, whatever varied craftsmanship exists in the world, all of it is done by consciousness alone. In this way, it is 'citta' due to its varied making. Then, because it makes, it is 'citta'; this is a derivative term. Or, this is another method: Due to its own varied nature, one consciousness is with lust, another with hatred, another with delusion. One is of the sensuous sphere, another is of the form sphere and other divisions. One has a form as its object, another has sound, etc., as its object. Among form-objects, one has blue as its object, another has yellow, etc., as its object. The same method applies to sound and other objects. Among all these, one is inferior, another is middling, and another is superior. Among the inferior and so on, one is governed by desire, another by consciousness, another by energy, and another by investigation. Therefore, because of its own varied nature according to associated states, grounds, objects, inferiority, middlingness, superiority, and dominant factors, it is 'citta'. 'Variety is in it, thus it is citta.' In that case, all consciousness is meant. Even in conventional designation, in varied consciousness, the work of consciousness is 'cittakamma'; 'cittakamma' itself is 'cittakammaka'. In this varied 'cittakammaka', in this context, the conventional term 'citta' should be understood by the wise as referring to consciousness.

Taṃ pana sabbasaṅgāhakavasena cintetītiādinā vuttappakāraṃ cittaṃ. Sārammaṇato sārammaṇabhāvena ekavidhaṃ. Savipākāvipākato savipākāvipākavasena duvidhaṃ. Tattha tasmiṃ duvidhe citte savipākaṃ nāma cittaṃ kusalākusalaṃ, avipākaṃ abyākataṃ, kusalākusalabhāvena akathitanti attho. Kusalajāti akusalajāti abyākatajātīti jātibhedato tividhaṃ.

Now, that consciousness, of the kind described by 'it thinks,' etc., in an all-encompassing way, is onefold by way of having an object. By way of having a result or not having a result, it is twofold. Therein, in that twofold division, consciousness that has a result is wholesome and unwholesome; consciousness that does not have a result is indeterminate, meaning it is not spoken of as wholesome or unwholesome. By distinction of class, it is threefold: the wholesome class, the unwholesome class, and the indeterminate class.

Tattha tasmiṃ vacane “kusala”nti etassa saddassa pana ko vacanattho.

Therein, in that statement, what is the meaning of the word 'kusala'?

10. Kucchitānaṃ salanato pāpakānaṃ dhammānaṃ kampanato viddhaṃsanato. Kucchitenākārena sayantīti kusā, kusānaṃ akusalasaṅkhātānaṃ lavanena chindanato. Kucchite sāti tanuṃ karotīti kusaṃ, kusena ñāṇena lātabbattā gahetabbattā. Vā ayaṃ añño nayo.

10. Because it shakes, trembles, and destroys despicable, evil states. Because they lie down in a despicable manner, they are 'kusā'; because it cuts off these 'kusā', which are designated as unwholesome states. Because it makes despicable things thin, it is 'kusa'; because it is to be obtained or grasped by that knowledge called 'kusa'. Or, this is another method.

11. Kusalasaddoyaṃ [M 0.0003] ayaṃ kusalasaddo cheke atthe ārogyatthe anavajjatthe iṭṭhavipāke atthepi diṭṭho amhehi. Idha imasmiṃ adhikāre anavajjādike atthe diṭṭho. Ādi-saddena ārogyatthaiṭṭhavipākatthā [V 1.0003] gahetabbā. Diṭṭho yasmā, tasmā anavajjaiṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ kusalaṃ. Natthi avajjaṃ kilesāvajjaṃ kilesadoso kilesadaratho etassāti anavajjaṃ, kammena vipaccīyateti vipāko, iṭṭhāniṭṭhādiārammaṇānubhavanavasena, attano sabhāvena ca iṭṭho vipāko etassāti iṭṭhavipākaṃ, anavajjameva iṭṭhavipākaṃ, taṃ lakkhīyati anena aviññātaṃ lakkhitabbaṃ kusalanti lakkhaṇaṃ, anavajjaiṭṭhavipākaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti anavajjaiṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ. Anavajjaiṭṭhavipākameva kusalaṃ. Nanu kathaṃ sayameva attano lakkhaṇaṃ bhaveyyāti codanā bhaveyya viññātāviññātasaddatthabhāvena lakkhaṇalakkhitabbabhāvayuttito. Kusalasaddatthavasena hi aviññātaṃ apākaṭaṃ kusalaṃ lakkhitabbaṃ hoti. Anavajjaiṭṭhavipākasaddatthavasena viññātaṃ pākaṭaṃ kusalaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ hoti. Akusalaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ akusalānaṃ viddhaṃsanaṃ akusalaviddhaṃsanaṃ, taṃ raso kiccametassāti akusalaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ, akusalaviddhaṃsanakiccaṃ. Vodānabhāvena paccupaṭṭhātīti vodānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, vodānaupaṭṭhānākāraṃ vodānagayhākāraṃ. Vā ayaṃ añño nayo. Vajjapaṭipakkhattā anavajjalakkhaṇameva kusalaṃ, vajjapaṭipakkhalakkhaṇaṃ kusalanti attho. Vodānabhāvarasaṃ vodānabhāvasampattikaṃ. Iṭṭhavipākapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ iṭṭhavipākaphalaṃ. Yonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ padañca taṃ ṭhānañcāti padaṭṭhānaṃ, ubho kāraṇatthādhivacanaṃ, tasmā āsannakāraṇanti attho, itarathā punaruttidoso siyā, yonisomanasikāro padaṭṭhānaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ etassāti yonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

11. This word 'kusala' is seen by us in the senses of skillful, healthy, blameless, and having a desirable result. Here, in this context, it is seen in the sense of blamelessness and so on. By the word 'and so on,' the senses of health and having a desirable result should be understood. Since it is seen thus, the wholesome is characterized by blamelessness and having a desirable result. There is no blame—no defilement-blame, no defilement-fault, no defilement-torment—in it, thus it is blameless. It ripens through action, thus it is a result. It has a desirable result because its result is desirable by its own nature and by way of experiencing desirable, undesirable, and other objects; thus it has a desirable result. The blameless itself has a desirable result. That which is characterized by blamelessness and a desirable result is the characteristic by which the unknown 'wholesome' is to be characterized. Blamelessness and having a desirable result are themselves the wholesome. 'But how can something be its own characteristic?'—such an objection might arise. This is resolved because the relationship between the characteristic and that which is to be characterized is based on the known and unknown meanings of the words. For, through the meaning of the word 'wholesome,' the unknown, unmanifest wholesome is what is to be characterized. Through the meaning of the words 'blameless' and 'desirable result,' the known, manifest wholesome is the characteristic. Its function is the destruction of the unwholesome. Its manifestation is purity. Or, this is another method: Because it is the opposite of what is blameworthy, the wholesome has the characteristic of blamelessness. Its function is the state of purity. Its manifestation is a desirable result. Its proximate cause is wise attention; 'pada' and 'ṭhāna' both mean cause, hence 'proximate cause' is the meaning, otherwise there would be the fault of redundancy. Wise attention is its proximate cause.

Sāvajjāniṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ [M 0.0004] akusalaṃ. Tadubhayaviparītaṃ tehi ubhayehi kusalākusalehi viparītaṃ avipākalakkhaṇaṃ etassāti tadubhayaviparītalakkhaṇaṃ abyākataṃ. Vā ayaṃ añño nayo. Avipākārahaṃ vipākassa ananucchavikaṃ.

The unwholesome is characterized by being blameworthy and by having an undesirable result. The indeterminate is that which is the opposite of both of these—opposite to both the wholesome and the unwholesome; it is characterized as not producing a result, thus it has the characteristic of being opposite to both. Or, this is another method: it is not capable of producing a result, not suitable for a consequence.

Savatthukāvatthukabhedatoti savatthukaṃ hadayavatthukaṃ, avatthukaṃ hadayavatthuvirahitaṃ.

By the distinction between having a physical basis and not having a physical basis: that which has a physical basis has the heart-basis; that which does not have a physical basis is devoid of the heart-basis.

12. Uddānato saṅkhepavasena kilesavatthuvasena duve kāmā honti. Chandarāgova kileso, tebhūmake pavattaṃ vaṭṭasahitaṃ vatthu, vasati kileso etthāti vatthu.

12. In brief, by way of defilement and its object, there are two kinds of sensual desire. Desire-passion itself is the defilement-desire; the objects occurring in the three planes, which are included in the round of existence, are the object-desire. 'Defilements dwell herein,' thus it is an object.

13. Kilesakāmo vatthuṃ kāmeti icchati, vatthu kilesakāmena kāmīyati icchīyatīti kattukārakakammakārakadvaye sādhanadvaye esa eso duvidhopi kāmo sijjhati.

13. The defilement-desire desires an object, longs for it; an object is desired, longed for by the defilement-desire. Thus, in both the active construction and the passive construction, this twofold desire is established.

14-5. So [V 1.0004] ayaṃ duvidhopi kāmo yasmiṃ padese sampattīnaṃ vasena avacarati, iti tasmā kāraṇā so pana padeso catupāyānaṃ channaṃ devānaṃ manussānaṃ vasena eva ekādasavidho hoti.

And these two kinds of sensual desire operate in a certain region by way of their presence. Therefore, that region is elevenfold, namely: the four woeful states, the six deva realms, and the human realm.

16. Kāmovacaratīti ettha etasmiṃ ekādasavidhe padese kāmo avacarati, iti tasmā kāraṇā so padeso assa kāmassa anena kāmena abhilakkhitattā kāmāvacarasaññito. Abhilakkhitasaddappayoge tatiyatthe “assā”ti chaṭṭhī hotīti saddasatthavidū paṭhanti. Sasatthāvacaro padeso viya satte sasanti hiṃsanti tehīti satthā, saha satthehīti sasatthā, sasatthā purisā avacaranti etthāti sasatthāvacaro. Yathā hi yasmiṃ padese sasatthā purisā avacaranti, so padeso vijjamānesupi [M 0.0005] aññesu dvipadacatuppadesu avacarantesu tesaṃ upalakkhitattā “sasatthāvacaro”tveva vuccati, evaṃ vijjamānesupi aññesu rūpāvacarādīsu tattha avacarantesu tesaṃ abhilakkhitattā ayaṃ padeso “kāmāvacaro”tveva vuccati.

16. The phrase 'sensual desire operates' means that in this elevenfold region, sensual desire operates. Therefore, that region is designated as the 'sensual sphere' because it is characterized by this sensual desire. In the usage of the word 'characterized,' the genitive case 'assa' is used in the sense of the instrumental, so say the experts in grammar. Just as a region where armed men roam is called 'frequented by armed men'—because they kill and harm beings, they are 'satthā' (weapons); 'with weapons' is 'sasatthā'; armed men roam here, thus 'sasatthāvacaro'—so too, even though other bipeds and quadrupeds may roam there, it is called 'frequented by armed men' due to being characterized by them. Similarly, even though other things, such as those of the form sphere, etc., also operate there, this region is called the 'sensual sphere' because it is characterized by sensual desire.

17. Yathā rūpabhavo uttarapadassa lopaṃ katvā rūpanti vutto, evaṃ tathā svāyaṃ so ayaṃ eso kāmāvacaro uttarapadassa lopaṃ katvā kāmo iti saññito kāmo nāma udīrito paṇḍitena kathito.

17. Just as 'rūpabhava' (form existence) is called 'rūpa' by eliding the latter word, so too this 'kāmāvacara' (sensual sphere) is designated 'kāma' (sensual desire) by eliding the latter word—this term 'kāma' is spoken and declared by the wise.

18. Tasmiṃ kāme idaṃ cittaṃ tasmiṃ kāmāvacare sadā avacarati, iti tasmā kāraṇā kāmāvacaraṃ iti evaṃ kāmaghātinā kāmānaṃ vināsakena buddhena kathitaṃ. Kiñcāpi etaṃ rūpārūpabhavesupi avacarati, yathā pana saṅgāme yebhuyyena avacaraṇato “saṅgāmāvacaro”ti laddhanāmo nāgo nagare carantopi “saṅgāmāvacaro”tveva vuccati, thalacarajalacarā pāṇino athale ajale ṭhitāpi “thalacarajalacarā”tveva vuccanti, evaṃ idaṃ aññattha avacarantampi kāmāvacaramevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena vā ettha kāmo avacaratītipi kāmāvacaraṃ. Kāmañcesa rūpārūpāvacaresupi avacarati, yathā pana vadatīti vaccho, mahiyaṃ setīti mahiṃsoti vutte na yattakā vadanti, mahiyaṃ vā senti, sabbesaṃ taṃ nāmaṃ hoti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

18. Because this mind always wanders in the sensual sphere with regard to sensual pleasure, for that reason it is called 'of the sensual sphere.' Thus it was spoken by the Buddha, the slayer of sensual pleasures, the destroyer of sensual pleasures. Although this mind also wanders in the form and formless existences, it should be understood as being of the sensual sphere even when wandering elsewhere. Just as an elephant that has obtained the name 'battlefield-wanderer' from wandering mostly on the battlefield is still called a 'battlefield-wanderer' even when moving about in a city, and just as land-dwelling and water-dwelling creatures are still called 'land-dwellers' and 'water-dwellers' even when they are not on land or in water, so it should be understood that this mind is indeed of the sensual sphere even when wandering elsewhere. Or, because sensual pleasure operates here by way of taking an object, it is called 'of the sensual sphere.' And although sensual pleasure also operates in the form and formless spheres, this should be understood as follows: just as when it is said, 'one who speaks is a calf (vaccho),' or 'one who lies on the earth is a buffalo (mahiṃso),' it is not the case that this name belongs to all who speak or lie on the earth; so too should this matter be understood.

19. Paṭisandhiṃ bhave kāme kāmabhavasaṅkhāte kāme paṭisandhiṃ avacārayati, iti tasmā kāmāvacaraṃ[V 1.0005]. Iti evaṃ vā ayaṃ añño nayo. Tatra tasmiṃ kāmāvacare pariyāpannaṃ antogadhaṃ, iti tasmā kāmāvacaraṃ.

19. It causes rebirth-linking to occur in sensual existence, in what is designated as sensual existence; therefore, it is called 'of the sensual sphere.' Or, this is another method. Because it is included and contained within that sensual sphere, for that reason, it is called 'of the sensual sphere.'

20. Aṭṭhavidhaṃ cittaṃ kāmāvacarasaññitaṃ idaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ cittaṃ. Dasapuññakiriyavatthuvaseneva puññakiriyā eva tesaṃ tesaṃ phalānisaṃsānaṃ [M 0.0006] vatthūni kāraṇānīti puññakiriyavatthūni, tesaṃ vaso, tena pavattati.

20. This eightfold mind is designated as belonging to the sensual sphere. It functions by the power of the ten grounds for meritorious action. Meritorious actions are the very grounds, the causes, for their respective fruits and benefits, thus they are called 'grounds for meritorious action'; it is by their power that this mind proceeds.

21. Dānaṃ sīlaṃ bhāvanā pattidānaṃ veyyāvaccaṃ dhammadesanā anumodanā diṭṭhijubhāvo saṃsuti dhammassavanañca apacāyo apacāyanaṃ, evaṃ iminā mayā vuttappakārena puññāni eva vatthūni puññavatthūni, tesaṃ pabhedo puññavatthuppabhedo ñeyyo paṇḍitena jānitabbo.

21. Giving, morality, mental development, transference of merit, service, teaching the Dhamma, rejoicing in merit, straightening of views, listening to the Dhamma, and reverence. In this way, as stated, these meritorious actions are the grounds of merit. Their distinction, the distinction among the grounds of merit, should be known by the wise.

22-3. Gacchanti saṅgahaṃ dāne pattidānānumodanā dāne saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, veyyāvaccāpacāyanā sīlamaye puññe saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, dhammadesanā dhammassavanaṃ diṭṭhiujukā bhāvanāmaye puññe saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, dasa puññakiriyāpi ca tīṇi eva sambhonti.

Transference of merit and rejoicing in merit are included under giving. Service and reverence are included under the merit consisting of morality. Teaching the Dhamma, listening to the Dhamma, and straightening of views are included under the merit consisting of mental development. Thus the ten meritorious actions are comprised in just three.

24. Sabbānussatipuññañca pasaṃsā saraṇattayaṃ ratanattayaguṇapasaṃsā ca ete diṭṭhijukammamhi saṅgayhanti, tasmiṃ saṅgahapāpuṇe saṃsayo sandeho natthi.

24. The merit of all recollections, praise, the threefold refuge, and praise of the qualities of the Triple Gem—these are included in the straightening of views. Regarding this inclusion, there is no doubt or uncertainty.

25. Purimā cetanā tato pubbabhāge pavattā cetanā, muñcacetanā paccuppannā cetanā, paracetanā pacchākāle pavattā cetanā, tissopi cetanā dānamaye puññe honti. Evanti yathā tissopi cetanā dānamaye puññe honti, evaṃ tathā dānamayapuññato sesesupi sīlamayabhāvanāmayesu tisso cetanā paṇḍito dīpaye katheyya.

25. The prior volition is the volition that occurs beforehand; the volition at the time of giving is the present volition; the subsequent volition is the volition that occurs afterward. All three volitions are present in the merit consisting of giving. Thus, just as all three volitions are present in the merit consisting of giving, so too a wise person should explain the three volitions in relation to the remaining types of merit, namely, that based on morality and that based on mental development.

Hi saccaṃ yadā pana yo puggalo deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakādisampattiṃ āgamma paṭicca. Paṭiggāhakādisampattinti ettha ādi-saddena desakālakalyāṇamittādayo gahitā. Aññaṃ vā somanassahetunti añña-ggahaṇena saddhābahulatāvisuddhidiṭṭhitākusalakiriyānisaṃsadassitāsomanassapaṭisandhikatādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Atthi dinnaṃ dānassa phalaṃ atthi. Ādi-saddena [M 0.0007] atthihutādayo gahitā. Purakkhatvāti purato katvā. Parehi anussāhito acodito dānādīni puññāni [V 1.0006] karoti. Dānādīnīti vacanena deyyadhammaṃ nissāya pavattadānacetanā gahetabbā. Tadā assa puggalassa. Saṅkharaṇaṃ saṅkhāro, natthi saṅkhāro etassāti asaṅkhāro, taṃ eva asaṅkhārikaṃ, appayoganti attho. Vuttanayenāti vuttanayo nāma “deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakādisampatti”nti vacanaṃ. Imasmiṃ panatthe saṅkharotīti saṅkhāro nāma attano vā pavattassa pubbappayogassa adhivacanaṃ, parassa vā pavattapubbappayogassa adhivacanaṃ. Ayamassa adhippāyo – yadā yo “dānādīni karissāmī”ti cittaṃ samuppādetvā nākāsi, pacchā attano pubbacetanāya ussāhito karoti, tadā sasaṅkhārikaṃ hoti, attano pubbappayogena saha pavattatīti attho. Paṭipattidassanena paṭipajjitabbā sīlādīhi paṭipajjanti jānanti gacchanti vā nibbānaṃ etāyāti paṭipatti, tāya dassanaṃ paṭipattidassanaṃ, tena. Jāto paricayo etesanti jātaparicayā. Sahasāti vegena. Catūsupi vikappesu dasseyya.

Indeed, this is true. When a person, relying on the excellence of the gift, the recipient, etc.—here, by 'etc.' are included suitable place and time, good friends, and so on. Or due to another cause for joy—by 'another' is included an abundance of faith, purity of view, seeing the benefit of wholesome actions, joy connected with rebirth, and so on. 'There is what is given, there is a fruit of giving'—here, by 'etc.' is included 'there is what is offered.' 'Having placed foremost' means having prioritized. Without being urged or prompted by others, one performs meritorious deeds such as giving. By 'such as giving,' the volition of giving that arises depending on the gift to be given should be understood. Then, for that person... 'Prompting' (saṅkharaṇaṃ) is a 'prompt' (saṅkhāro). 'There is no prompt for it' is 'unprompted' (asaṅkhāro); that itself is 'unprompted' (asaṅkhārikaṃ), meaning 'without instigation' (appayoga). 'By the stated method' refers to the statement 'excellence of the gift, the recipient, etc.' In this sense, however, a 'prompt' (saṅkhāro) is a term for one's own prior instigation or for another's prior instigation. This is the intended meaning: when someone, having generated the thought, 'I will perform acts of giving, etc.,' did not do so, but later does so, urged on by their own prior volition, then it is 'prompted' (sasaṅkhārikaṃ), meaning it occurs together with one's own prior instigation. 'By the vision of the practice': 'practice' (paṭipatti) is so called because by it one practices morality, etc., and knows or goes to Nibbāna; the vision of that is 'the vision of the practice.' 'Those who have acquired familiarity' (jātaparicayā): those for whom familiarity has arisen. 'Suddenly' (sahasā) means 'quickly' (vegena). One should show this in all four alternatives.

26. Dasapuññakriyādīnaṃ vasena ca bahūnipi bhavanti etāni pana cittāni dasapuññakiriyādīnaṃ vasenapi bahūnipi bhavanti iti evaṃ pakāsaye bhagavā pakāseyya.

26. And by way of the ten meritorious actions, etc., these minds also become numerous. Thus the Blessed One would explain that these minds also become numerous by way of the ten meritorious actions, etc.

27.

27.

Sattarasa sahassāni, dve satāni asīti ca;

Kāmāvacarapuññāni, bhavantīti viniddiseti. –

Seventeen thousand, two hundred and eighty: so many, it is declared, are the sensual-sphere merits.

Kāmāvacarapuññāni sattarasa sahassāni ca dve satāni ca asīti ca bhavanti, iti vacanaṃ viniddise ācariyo katheyya.

The sensual-sphere merits are seventeen thousand, two hundred, and eighty. Thus the teacher should point out, or should say, this statement.

Dasapuññakriyāvatthu, chadvārādhipatīhi ca;

Kāyādīhi ca tīheva, hīnādīhi ca tīhi tu.

The ten grounds of meritorious action; and by the six doors and by the controlling faculties; and by the three beginning with body; and indeed by the three beginning with inferior.

Dvīsu [M 0.0008] bhavesu kāmabhavarūpabhavesu. Paṭipadādibhedato dukkhāpaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññaṃ, dukkhāpaṭipadaṃ khippābhiññaṃ, sukhāpaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññaṃ, sukhāpaṭipadaṃ khippābhiññaṃ. Rūpāvacarabhāvanāpuññavasappavattaṃ rūpāvacare pavattassa bhāvanāpuññassa vasena pavattaṃ rūpāvacarūpapattinipphādakaṃ rūpāvacare upapattiyā paṭisandhiyā nipphādakaṃ hoti.

In two existences: the sensual existence and the form existence. By way of the distinction of practice, etc.: painful practice with slow direct knowledge, painful practice with quick direct knowledge, pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, and pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge. Arising by the power of the merit of form-sphere mental development: arising by the power of the merit of mental development that occurs in the form sphere, it produces rebirth in the form sphere; it is the producer of rebirth-linking in the form sphere.

Savatthukāvatthukabhedatoti [V 1.0007] arūpāvacaraṃ yadā kāmarūpe jāyati, tadā hadayavatthuṃ nissāya jāyati, iti tasmā savatthukaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Yadā arūpe jāyati, tadā hadayavatthuṃ anissāya jāyati, iti tasmā avatthukaṃ nāma jātaṃ.

By the distinction of 'with a basis' and 'without a basis': when formless-sphere consciousness arises in the sensuous or form sphere, it arises in dependence on the heart-basis; therefore, it is said to be 'with a basis.' When it arises in the formless sphere, it arises without dependence on the heart-basis; therefore, it is said to be 'without a basis.'

Ākāsānañcāyatanassa kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Viññāṇañcāyatanassa tattha pavattaviññāṇaṃ, tasmiṃ kasiṇugghāṭimākāse pavattaṃ viññāṇaṃ cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Ākiñcaññāyatanassa tassa apagamo tassa ākāsānañcāyatanassa apagamo abhāvo vohāro ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanassa ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti.

The object of the base of infinite space is the space from which the kasiṇa has been removed. The object of the base of infinite consciousness is the consciousness that arose there; that is, the consciousness, the mind, that arose with that space (from which the kasiṇa was removed) as its object. The object of the base of nothingness is the passing away of that—the passing away, the absence, the concept of the consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness. The object of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the consciousness of the base of nothingness.

Rūpe saññā rūpasaññā. Saññāsīsena cittampi gahitaṃ. Samatikkamā kasiṇugghāṭimākāsasamatikkamanena. Paṭighe dvārārammaṇānaṃ saṅghaṭṭane pavattā saññā paṭighasaññā. Dvipañcaviññāṇānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tāsaṃ paṭighasaññānaṃ dvipañcaviññāṇānaṃ atthaṅgamā atthaṅgamena. Nānā attā sabhāvo etassāti nānattaṃ, ārammaṇaṃ, nānatte nānāsabhāve pavattā saññā nānattasaññā, nānā attā sabhāvo etissāti vā nānattā, sāyeva saññā nānattasaññā, kāmāvacarasaññāti attho. Tāsaṃ nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā amanasikārena.

'Perception of form' (rūpasaññā) is perception in regard to form. With perception as the heading, mind is also included. 'By transcending': by means of removing the kasiṇa and transcending space. 'Perception of resistance' (paṭighasaññā) is perception that occurs in resistance, that is, in the impact of sense door and object. This is a designation for the two sets of five consciousnesses. 'From the cessation': by means of the cessation of those perceptions of resistance, that is, the two sets of five consciousnesses. 'Diversity' (nānattaṃ) is so called because 'diverse is its own nature'; this is the object. 'Perception of diversity' (nānattasaññā) is perception that occurs in diversity, in diverse natures. Or, 'diverse' (nānattā) is so called because 'diverse is its own nature'; that very perception is 'perception of diversity.' The meaning is sensuous-sphere perception. 'From non-attention': by means of non-attention to those perceptions of diversity.

Niyatāniyatavatthukabhedatoti [M 0.0009] sotāpattimaggo niyatavatthuko. Kasmā? Kāmarūpesuyeva hadayavatthuṃ nissāya uppajjanato. Itare pana tayo maggā aniyatavatthukā. Kasmā? Kāmarūpesu hadayavatthuṃ nissāya jāyanti, arūpe hadayavatthuṃ anissāya jāyanti, tasmā aniyatavatthukā. Tīhi vimokkhamukhehīti suññataanimittaappaṇihitasaṅkhātehi tīhi vimokkhamukhehi.

By the distinction of fixed and unfixed basis: The path of stream-entry has a fixed basis. Why? Because it arises only in the sensuous and form spheres, in dependence on the heart-basis. The other three paths, however, have an unfixed basis. Why? Because in the sensuous and form spheres they arise in dependence on the heart-basis, but in the formless sphere they arise without depending on the heart-basis; therefore they have an unfixed basis. 'By the three gateways to liberation': by the three gateways to liberation designated as emptiness, the signless, and the desireless.

Yassa saṃvijjanti, taṃ puggalaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃ saṃyojenti bandhantīti saṃyojanā. Sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsāyeva saṃyojanā sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojanā, tesaṃ pahānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojanappahānaṃ, taṃ karotīti sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojanappahānakaraṃ, sotāpattimaggacittaṃ. Mānopi ekadesato apāyagāmikoyeva pahiyyate. Sotāpattimaggena nissesato na pahiyyate. Sesakilesesupi [V 1.0008] eseva nayo. Uddhaccaṃ pana ekadesatopi apāyagāmikampi na pahiyyati. Sakadāgāmimaggacittaṃ rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttakaraṃ. Sotāpattimaggena nāsitasaṃyojanānaṃ pahānaṃ kasmā na vuttanti ce? Paṭhamamaggato dutiyamaggassa mahantattā paṭhamamaggena nāsitā saṃyojanā dutiyamaggena nāsitāti paññāyati, iti yasmā, tasmā na vuttaṃ. Tatiyacatutthamaggesupi eseva nayo. Ettha etasmiṃ lokuttaracitte. Ekekanti vicchāvasena vuttaṃ. Maggānurūpanti vacanaṃ paṭhamamaggassa paṭhamaphalañca anurūpanti viññāpanatthaṃ.

They are called 'fetters' (saṃyojanā) because, for the person in whom they exist, they connect (saṃyojenti) and bind (bandhanti) that person in the round of existence. Identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and observances are the fetters. The abandoning of these is the abandoning of the fetters of identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and observances. That which accomplishes this is the path consciousness of stream-entry. Conceit, too, is partially abandoned only in so far as it leads to the plane of misery; it is not completely abandoned by the path of stream-entry. The same principle applies to the remaining defilements. Restlessness, however, is not abandoned even partially, not even that which leads to the plane of misery. The path consciousness of the once-returner attenuates lust, hatred, and delusion. If it is asked why the abandoning of the fetters destroyed by the stream-entry path is not mentioned for the higher paths, it is because the second path is greater than the first, so the fetters destroyed by the first path are understood to be destroyed by the second. That is why it is not mentioned. The same principle applies to the third and fourth paths. Here, in this supramundane consciousness, ‘each one’ is stated by way of separation. The phrase 'in accordance with the path' is stated to make it known that the first fruit is in conformity with the first path.

28. Kāme aṭṭheva kāmāvacare aṭṭha eva cittāni, rūpe rūpabhave pañca cittāni, arūpisu cattāri cittāni, anuttarāni lokuttaracittāni cattāri, evaṃ iminā mayā vuttappakārena kusalāni cittāni ekavīsati honti.

28. In the sense sphere, there are just eight consciousnesses; in the fine-material sphere, five consciousnesses; in the immaterial spheres, four consciousnesses; and the unsurpassed, supramundane consciousnesses are four. Thus, in the way I have explained, there are twenty-one wholesome consciousnesses.

29. Kusalākusalāpagatena [M 0.0010] satā muninā kusalato, akusalato ca apagatena satā satisampannena kusale kusalena chekena vasinā pañcavasīhi samannāgatena yaṃ kusalacittaṃ catubhūmigataṃ catūsu bhūmīsu pavattaṃ sakalaṃ sabbaṃ lapitaṃ kathitaṃ, taṃ kusalacittaṃ mayāpi buddhadattācariyena lapitaṃ kathitaṃ.

29. By the mindful sage who is free from wholesome and unwholesome, endowed with mindfulness, skilled and expert in the wholesome, a master endowed with the five masteries—whatever wholesome consciousness pertaining to the four planes, occurring in the four planes, has been entirely spoken of and declared by him, that wholesome consciousness has also been spoken of and declared by me, the teacher Buddhadatta.

Niyatāniyatavatthuvasenāti paṭighasampayuttadvayaṃ kāmeyeva hadayavatthuṃ nissāya jāyati, aññabhūmīsu na jāyati, tasmā niyatavatthukaṃ hoti. Itarāni pana akusalāni kāmarūpesu uppajjanakāle hadayavatthuṃ nissāya jāyanti, arūpe hadayavatthuṃ anissāya jāyanti, tasmā aniyatavatthukāni, tena. Paṭisandhijanakājanakavasena cāti uddhaccasahagataṃ paṭisandhiṃ na janeti. Yadi paṭisandhiṃ janeyya, apāyesuyeva janeyya. Kasmā? Sotāpattimaggena ekadesato apāyagāmikampi na jahitaṃ, sabbaṃ na jahitanti attho. Sopi maggo apāyagāmī na hoti. Aññe pana kilesā ekadesavasena apāyagāmikā jahitā, tena paṭhamamaggenāti tasmā na janeti. Ekādasavidhaṃ pana paṭisandhiṃ janeti, tena.

By way of fixed and unfixed physical basis: the two consciousnesses associated with aversion arise only in the sense sphere, depending on the heart-basis, and do not arise in other planes; therefore, they have a fixed physical basis. The other unwholesome consciousnesses, when arising in the sense-sphere and fine-material spheres, arise depending on the heart-basis, but in the immaterial sphere, they arise without depending on the heart-basis; therefore, they have an unfixed physical basis. And by way of producing or not producing rebirth-linking: the consciousness accompanied by restlessness does not produce rebirth-linking. If it were to produce rebirth-linking, it would do so only in the planes of misery. Why? Because by the path of stream-entry, not even a part of what leads to the planes of misery is abandoned in the case of restlessness; the meaning is that it is not abandoned at all. That path itself does not lead to the planes of misery. But other defilements, in so far as they lead to the planes of misery, are partially abandoned by that first path; therefore, it, the restlessness-consciousness, does not produce such a rebirth-linking. The other eleven unwholesome consciousnesses, however, do produce rebirth-linking.

Diṭṭhamaṅgalādīnīti ādi-saddena sutamaṅgalādīni gahitāni. Sārato uttamato pacceti saddahati. Sabhāvatikkhena sabhāvo tikkho etassāti sabhāvatikkhaṃ, tena sabhāvatikkhena.

On 'seen auspicious signs, etc.': by the word 'etc.', heard auspicious signs and so on are included. 'As the essence, as the highest': one is convinced of it and has faith in it. 'By that which is keen in nature': one whose nature is keen is 'keen-natured'; by means of that keen nature.

Assa [V 1.0009] pana paṭighasampayuttassa pāṇātipātādīsu akusalakammesu tikkhappavattikāle asaṅkhārikassa uppatti, mandappavattikāle sasaṅkhārikassa uppatti veditabbā.

But in the case of this consciousness associated with aversion, it should be understood that when it proceeds keenly in unwholesome kammas such as the destruction of life, the unprompted type arises; and when it proceeds weakly, the prompted type arises.

Tassa momūhassa.

Of that utterly deluded one.

Dukkhavisesassa dukkhanānattassa.

Of specific suffering, that is, of the diversity of suffering.

30. Lobhamūlavasena [M 0.0011] aṭṭha cittāni, dosamūlavasā duve cittāni, mohamūlavasena dve cittāni. Evaṃ iminā mayā vuttappakārena akusalāni dvādasappakārāni siyuṃ bhaveyyuṃ.

30. By way of the root of greed, there are eight consciousnesses; by way of the root of aversion, two consciousnesses; and by way of the root of delusion, two consciousnesses. Thus, in the way I have explained, there are twelve kinds of unwholesome consciousnesses.

31. Yaṃ pāpamānasaṃ yaṃ akusalacittaṃ pāpāpāpesu pāpaapāpesu kusalākusalesu apāpena appavattena pāpāpāpappahīnena vuttaṃ īritaṃ kathitaṃ, taṃ pāpamānasaṃ taṃ akusalacittaṃ mayā samudāhaṭaṃ kathitaṃ.

31. Whatever evil-mindedness, whatever unwholesome consciousness in what is evil and not evil, in what is wholesome and unwholesome, has been spoken, uttered, and declared by the one who is without evil, who does not engage in it, who has abandoned evil and non-evil—that evil-mindedness, that unwholesome consciousness, has been expounded and declared by me.

Yathā panassa yathā pana assa vipākassa kusalaṃ dānādivasena dānādīnaṃ dasapuññakiriyavatthūnaṃ vasena chasu ārammaṇesu pavattati, idaṃ vipākacittaṃ tathā na pavattati. Hi saccaṃ idaṃ vipākaṃ paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutitadārammaṇavasena parittadhammapariyāpannesu kāmāvacaradhammantogadhesu chasu ārammaṇesu pavattati. Sampayuttadhammānañca visese asatipi kusalasampayuttadhammato assa vipākassa, sampayuttadhammānañca nānatte asatipi idaṃ vipākaṃ ādāsatalādīsu dhammajātesu mukhanimittaṃ viya nirussāhaṃ. Ayamassādhippāyo – yathā ādāsatale mukhanimittaṃ mukhe calite calati, acalite na calati, mukhassa kāraṇaṃ vinā mukhanimittassa viya kāraṇaṃ natthi, evaṃ kusalakāraṇā vipākassa aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ natthi, nirussāhaṃ vipākaṃ.

Just as wholesome consciousness operates in regard to the six objects by way of giving, etc.—that is, by way of the ten grounds for meritorious action—this resultant consciousness does not operate in that way. Indeed, this resultant consciousness operates in regard to the six objects—which are included among limited phenomena and comprised within sense-sphere phenomena—by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death, and registering. And although there is no specific difference in its associated states from the states associated with wholesome consciousness, and although there is no variety in its associated states, this resultant consciousness is effortless, like the reflection of a face on the surface of a mirror and so on, which are naturally arisen phenomena. This is the intended meaning: just as the reflection of a face on the surface of a mirror moves when the face moves and does not move when it is still, and just as the reflection has no cause apart from the face, so too the resultant has no other cause than the wholesome kamma; the resultant is effortless.

32. Kāmāvacaradevānaṃ manussānaṃ ime aṭṭha mahāvipākā duhetukatihetukānaṃ kāmāvacaradevānaṃ, manussānañca paṭisandhiyo bhavanti.

32. For the sense-sphere devas and for human beings, these eight great resultants become the rebirth-linking consciousnesses for two-rooted and three-rooted sense-sphere devas and human beings.

33-4. Tato paraṃ pavattiyaṃ yāvatāyukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ hutvā balavārammaṇe atimahantavibhūtārammaṇe [V 1.0010] tadārammaṇañca hutvā tato paraṃ maraṇakālasmiṃ cuti hutvā pavattanti[M 0.0012], evaṃ iminā mayā vuttappakārena catūsu ṭhānesu vipaccanti vipākabhāvena jāyanti.

33–4. Thereafter, during the course of life, they function as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); and when the object is strong or very distinct, they function as registering consciousness (tadārammaṇa); and then, at the time of death, they function as the death consciousness (cuti). Thus, in the way I have explained, they ripen in four instances, arising by way of result.

35. Sabhūmikusaleheva mahāpākā samā vinā mahāpākā kammadvāraṃ kammakāraṇaṃ vinā, kammañca mahāpuññānaṃ kiriyavatthukaṃ vinā vajjetvā sabhūmikusaleheva attano bhūmiyaṃ pavattehi kusalehi eva samā sadisā. Kammadvāraṃ nāma kāyaviññattikammadvāraṃ, vacīviññattikammadvāraṃ, bhavaṅgasaṅkhātaṃ manodvāraṃ, iti tividhaṃ kammadvāraṃ kammakāraṇaṃ. Kammaṃ nāma aṭṭhakāmāvacarakusalacetanā idha adhippetā.

35. The great resultants are similar to the wholesome consciousnesses of their own plane, except that they are without the door of kamma, the cause of kamma, and kamma itself, which is the basis of action for great merit. They are similar only to the wholesome consciousnesses occurring in their own plane. The door of kamma, the cause of kamma, is threefold: the door of bodily intimation, the door of verbal intimation, and the mind-door designated as the life-continuum. By 'kamma' here is meant the eight sense-sphere wholesome volitions.

36. Pākā kusalavipākā aviññattijanattā ca viññatti ca viññatti ca viññattiviññattiyoti vattabbe sarūpekasesaṃ katvā “viññattī”ti vuttaṃ, tā janentīti viññattijanā, na viññattijanā aviññattijanā, tesaṃ bhāvo aviññattijanattaṃ. Tasmā aviññattijanattā kāyaviññattivacīviññattisaṅkhātānaṃ kammadvārānaṃ ajanakattā manodvārasaṅkhātassa kammadvārassa vasena ca appavattanato avipākasabhāvato ca akammabhāvato ca appavattanato ceva puññakiriyavatthuvasena appavattanato ceva puññehi no samā asadisā.

36. The resultants—the wholesome resultants—are not similar to meritorious deeds because they do not generate intimations. Therefore, because they do not generate intimations—that is, because they do not generate the doors of kamma known as bodily and verbal intimation and do not operate by way of the mind-door—and because of their nature as resultants and non-kamma, and because they do not function as a ground for meritorious action, they are not equal to, not similar to, meritorious deeds.

37-9. Parittārammaṇattā hi tesamekantato tesaṃ vipākānaṃ ekantato parittārammaṇattā kāmāvacarārammaṇattā tesu vipākesu sattapaññattikārammaṇā karuṇāmuditā kadāci kismiñci kāle na jāyanti, tathā evaṃ tisso pana viratiyo etesu vipākesu na jāyanti, hi kasmā kāraṇā na jāyanti, pañca sikkhāpadā kusalāti kusalā nāmāti satthunā vuttā yasmā kāraṇā, tasmā na jāyanti. Tathādhipatinopettha tathā evameva cattāro adhipatinopi etesu vipākesu na santi. Kasmā[M 0.0013]? Chandādīni dhammajātāni puretaraṃ katvā anuppajjanato na santi, iti vacanaṃ viniddise ācariyo katheyya.

37–9. Indeed, because their object is limited—because the object of those resultants is exclusively limited and pertains to the sense sphere—compassion and appreciative joy, which have a being as their conceptual object, never arise in those resultants at any time. Similarly, the three abstinences also do not arise in these resultants. For what reason do they not arise? Because the five training rules have been declared by the Teacher to be wholesome by name; for that reason, they do not arise. Likewise, the four dominants are also not present in these resultants. Why? Because they do not arise by making states such as zeal foremost. Thus the teacher would explain, analyzing the statement.

40. Asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāravidhānaṃ pana puññato vipākesu asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāravidhānaṃ puññato kusalato āgamanavasena ñeyyaṃ. Tattha ekaccānaṃ ācariyānaṃ matena mukhe calite ādāsatale mukhanimittacalanaṃ viya asaṅkhārassa kusalassa vipāko asaṅkhāro hoti, sasaṅkhārassa kusalassa vipāko sasaṅkhāro hoti, evaṃ āgamanavasena ñeyyaṃ. Paccayato ceva ñeyyaṃ tattha ekaccānaṃ [V 1.0011] ācariyānaṃ matena balavantehi vibhūtehi paccayehi kammādīhi uppanno asaṅkhāro dubbalehi sasaṅkhāroti evaṃ paccayavasena viññeyyaṃ jānitabbaṃ.

40. The distinction between unprompted and prompted in the case of resultants should be understood by way of derivation from the meritorious wholesome kamma. Here, according to the view of some teachers, just as the reflection of a face on the surface of a mirror moves when the face moves, the resultant of an unprompted wholesome kamma is unprompted, and the resultant of a prompted wholesome kamma is prompted. Thus it should be understood by way of derivation. And it should also be understood by way of conditions. Here, according to the view of some teachers, what arises from strong, distinct conditions—kamma, etc.—is unprompted, while what arises from weak conditions is prompted. Thus it should be known by way of conditions.

41-2. Hīnādīnaṃ puññānaṃ vipākattā hīnādayo vipākā puññavādinā jinena paridīpitā bhavanti, iti evaṃ iminā vuttappakārena pavattaṃ idaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ cittaṃ ekantena savatthukaṃ kāmalokasmiṃ jāyate, aññattha pana aññāsu bhūmīsu na jāyate.

41–42. Because they are the results of inferior and other kinds of meritorious deeds, inferior and other kinds of results are expounded by the Conqueror, the advocate of merit. Thus, in the manner stated, this eightfold consciousness arises exclusively with a physical basis in the sense-sphere world; but it does not arise elsewhere, in other planes.

Viññāṇapañcakaṃ niyatārammaṇanti cakkhuviññāṇassa rūpameva ārammaṇaṃ, na saddādayo. Sesattayaṃ yadā cakkhuviññāṇena gahitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, tadāssa rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Yadā sotaviññāṇena gahitaṃ, tadāssa saddo ārammaṇo hoti. Yadā ghānajivhākāyaviññāṇehi gahitāni ārammaṇāni karonti, tadāssa gandharasaphoṭṭhabbārammaṇāni honti. Manoviññāṇadhātudvayaṃ yadā tadārammaṇaṃ hoti, tadā chaārammaṇaṃ hoti, evaṃ aniyatārammaṇaṃ hoti.

The pentad of consciousness has a fixed object: for eye-consciousness, the object is only form, not sounds, etc. When the remaining triad of mind-elements takes as its object what was grasped by eye-consciousness, its object is form. When it takes what was grasped by ear-consciousness, its object is sound. When they take as objects what were grasped by nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, their objects are smells, tastes, and tactile objects respectively. When the duad of mind-consciousness-element functions as registering consciousness, it takes any of the six kinds of objects; thus it has an unfixed object.

Rūpārammaṇāya kiriyāmanodhātuyā apagamo padaṭṭhānaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ etassāti apagamapadaṭṭhānaṃ, tāya āvajjanaṃ [M 0.0014] katvā ṭhitāya cakkhuviññāṇena dassanakiccaṃ karīyatīti attho. Tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ sampaṭicchanabhāvena gayhākāraṃ. Santīraṇādirasā somanassayuttā manoviññāṇadhātusantīraṇatadārammaṇarasā, upekkhāyuttā pana santīraṇatadārammaṇapaṭisandhibhavaṅgacutirasā, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā santīraṇādibhāvena gayhākāraṃ.

Its proximate cause is the cessation of the functional mind-element that has form as its object; hence it has cessation as its proximate cause. The meaning is that the function of seeing is performed by the eye-consciousness after that mind-element has adverted and ceased. Its manifestation is the mode of grasping in the manner of receiving. The functions of investigating and so on, when accompanied by joy, are the functions of the mind-consciousness-element: investigating and registering. However, when accompanied by equanimity, their functions are investigating, registering, rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death. Their manifestation is the mode of grasping in the manner of investigating and so on.

43. Kāmāvacarapuññassa kāmāvacarakusalassa soḷasa vipākā honti. Iti yaṃ vacanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ vacanaṃ tihetukapuññassa ukkaṭṭhassa vasena ācariyo paridīpaye. Ayamettha attho – chandādhipateyyādīnaṃ vasena ukkaṭṭhatihetukakusalaṃ kāmasugatiyaṃ tihetukapaṭisandhiṃ datvā pavatte aṭṭha ahetukakusalavipākāni, aṭṭha mahākusalavipākānīti soḷasa pākāni nipphādeti.

43. For sense-sphere merit, that is, sense-sphere wholesome kamma, there are sixteen results. The statement that was made is explained by the teacher with reference to superior, three-rooted merit. The meaning here is this: on account of the predominance of zeal and other factors, superior three-rooted wholesome kamma, having given a three-rooted rebirth-linking in a happy sense-sphere destination, produces during the course of existence sixteen results: eight rootless wholesome-resultant cittas and eight great wholesome-resultant cittas.

44. Kusalānugataṃ katvā bhājitaṃ kiṃ mahaggataṃ vipākacittaṃ kusalānugataṃ kusalaṃ anugataṃ katvā mahaggatakusalacittena samānaṃ katvā bhagavatā bhājitaṃ desitaṃ. Kiṃ kena kāraṇena? Kāmāvacarapuññaṃva kāmāvacarakusalaṃ iva asamānaphalaṃ natthi yato yasmā kāraṇā, tasmā [V 1.0012] vipākaṃ kusalānugataṃ katvā bhagavatā bhājitaṃ desitaṃ. Kāmāvacarapuññaṃvāti yathā aṭṭhavidhesu kāmāvacarakusalesu ukkaṭṭhatihetukakusalaṃ kāmasugatiyaṃ tihetukapaṭisandhiṃ datvā pavatte soḷasa kusalavipākāni nipphādeti, tihetukaomakañca duhetukaukkaṭṭhañca kāmasugatiyaṃ duhetukapaṭisandhiṃ datvā pavatte tihetukavirahitāni ahetukaduhetukasaṅkhātāni vipākāni nipphādeti, duhetukaomakaṃ pana kāmasugatiyaṃ ahetukapaṭisandhiṃ datvā pavatte aṭṭha ahetukavipākāni nipphādeti, evaṃ kāmāvacarapuññaṃ asamānaphalaṃva hoti.

44. Why is the exalted resultant consciousness taught as 'conforming to the wholesome'? Because it is made to follow the wholesome, made similar to the exalted wholesome consciousness, it is so taught and explained by the Blessed One. For what reason? Because unlike sense-sphere merit, it does not have a dissimilar result; that is why the resultant is taught by the Blessed One as conforming to the wholesome. As to 'unlike sense-sphere merit': just as, among the eight kinds of sense-sphere wholesome kammas, superior three-rooted wholesome kamma gives a three-rooted rebirth-linking in a happy sense-sphere destination and produces during the course of existence sixteen wholesome results; and inferior three-rooted and superior two-rooted wholesome kamma give a two-rooted rebirth-linking in a happy sense-sphere destination and produce during the course of existence results devoid of the three-rooted resultants, designated as rootless and two-rooted results; and inferior two-rooted wholesome kamma gives a rootless rebirth-linking in a happy sense-sphere destination and produces during the course of existence the eight rootless results. Thus sense-sphere merit has dissimilar results.

45. Gajādīnaṃ [M 0.0015] chāyā gajādisadisā hoti yathā, evaṃ mahaggatavipākaṃ sabbathā sabbapakārena attano kusaleheva samānaṃ hoti.

45. Just as the shadow of an elephant and so on is similar to the elephant and so on, so too the exalted resultant is in every way and in all respects similar to its own wholesome kamma.

46-7. Kāmāvacarapuññaṃva nāparāpariyavedanaṃ idaṃ mahaggatakusalaṃ kāmāvacarapuññaṃva aparāpariyavedanaṃ aparasmiṃ bhave phaladāyakaṃ na hoti, jhānā aparihīnassa bhavagāmino paṭisandhigāmino sattassa kusalānantaraṃyeva phalaṃ uppajjati, iti ca ñāpanatthaṃ etassa mahaggatavipākassa kusalānugataṃ kusalānugamanaṃ bhagavatā kataṃ.

46–47. 'Unlike sense-sphere merit, it is not to be experienced in a subsequent lifetime.' This exalted wholesome kamma, unlike sense-sphere merit which can be experienced in a subsequent lifetime (i.e., give its fruit in another existence), is not of that nature. For a being bound for a new existence, bound for rebirth, who has not fallen away from jhāna, the result arises immediately after the wholesome kamma. And it is to make this known that the Blessed One has described this exalted resultant as 'conforming to the wholesome'.

48. Ettha etasmiṃ mahaggatavipāke paṭipadākkamo tesañca hīnādīnaṃ bhedato jhānāgamanato mahaggatakusalajhānassa āgamanavasena vibhāvinā paṇḍitena veditabbo.

48. Herein, concerning this exalted resultant, the order of the path should be understood by a discerning wise person according to the distinction of the inferior and so forth, according to the attainment of jhāna, and by way of the attainment of the exalted wholesome jhāna.

49. Ettha vipāke chandādiadhipatīnaṃ abhāvo, ayameva visesato kusalato ayaṃ eva viseso, sesaṃ sabbapakāraṃ avisesena kusalena samaṃ mataṃ kathitaṃ bhagavatā.

49. Herein, in the resultant, there is an absence of predominance by zeal and other factors. This very thing is the specific distinction from the wholesome; the rest is considered equal in all aspects to the wholesome, as taught by the Blessed One.

50. Suññataṃ animittanti, tathāpaṇihitantipi suññataṃ anattā, animittaṃ aniccaṃ, appaṇihitaṃ dukkhaṃ iti etāni tīṇi nāmāni maggassa anantare catubbidhassa maggassa anantare catubbidhe phale honti.

50. Emptiness, signlessness, and the undirected: emptiness is non-self, signlessness is impermanence, and the undirected is suffering. These three names thus apply to the fourfold fruit that arises immediately after the fourfold path.

51. Labbhanti parabhāgasmiṃ maggānantare pavattaphalato aññasmiṃ kāle vaḷañjanaphalesu phalasamāpattisamāpajjanakālesu etāni tīṇi nāmāni na labbhante, phalehi vipassanāvaseneva anattaaniccadukkhasaṅkhātānaṃ [V 1.0013] tiṇṇaṃ vipassanānaṃ vasena eva tāni tīṇi nāmāni labbhare phalehi labbhante.

51. In the subsequent period, at a time other than the fruit that occurs immediately after the path—that is, during the times of entering fruition attainment for enjoyment—these three names are not obtained. They are obtained in relation to the fruits only by way of insight, that is, by way of the three insights into what are designated as non-self, impermanence, and suffering; thus they are obtained in relation to the fruits.

52. Honti [M 0.0016] sādhipatīneva lokuttaraphalāni tu ekantato sādhipatīni eva honti, lokuttaraphalāni ṭhapetvā aññasmiṃ vipāke adhipatī natthi.

52. The supramundane fruits, however, are indeed accompanied by predominance; they are exclusively so. Apart from the supramundane fruits, there is no predominance in any other resultant.

53. Maggo attano maggabhāvena maggo nāma vuccate bhagavatā. Phalaṃ maggaṃ upādāya aṭṭhaṅgikamaggaṃ nissayaṃ katvā maggo nāma iti vacanaṃ vuccate bhagavatā.

53. The path is called 'path' by the Blessed One because of its own nature as a path. The fruit, because it is based on the path, relying on the eightfold path, is also called 'path' by the Blessed One.

54. Ime satta akusalavipākā. Gāvo caranti etthāti gocaro, tassadisattā gocaro ārammaṇanti attho, aniṭṭho ca aniṭṭhamajjhatto ca aniṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhattā, teyeva gocaro aniṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhattagocaro, tasmiṃ aniṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhattagocare vattare vattanti. Sukhādittayayuttā te te aṭṭha ahetukakusalavipākā sukhādittayayuttā sukhasomanassaupekkhāvedanāhi sahagatā. Dukkhupekkhāyutā ime ime satta ahetukaakusalavipākā dukkhupekkhāvedanāhi sahagatā.

54. These are the seven unwholesome resultants. 'Pasture' (gocara) is where cows roam; because of its similarity to that, 'pasture' means object. The object is undesirable and moderately undesirable; in such an object they occur. Those eight rootless wholesome resultants are associated with the triad beginning with pleasure, that is, they are accompanied by feelings of pleasure, joy, and equanimity. These seven rootless unwholesome resultants are associated with feelings of pain and equanimity.

55. Evaṃ chattiṃsadhā pākaṃ pākasāsanapūjito sugato. Kiṃ visiṭṭho? Pākaṃ nāma asuraṃ, taṃ sāsati, pākena attano puññaphalena deve anusāsatīti vā pākasāsano, ko so? Sakko. Tena pākasāsanena pūjito savipākāvipākesu kusalavipākakiriyesu kusalo cheko evaṃ iminā mayā vuttappakārena pākaṃ cittaṃ chattiṃsappakāraṃ abrvi avoca.

55. Thus in thirty-six ways the Sugata, honored by the Subduer of Pāka, spoke of the resultant. How is he distinguished? 'Pākasāsana' (Subduer of Pāka): Pāka is the name of an asura, and he (Sakka) subdues him; or, he instructs the gods by the ripening of his own merit. Who is he? Sakka. Honored by this Subduer of Pāka, and skilled and expert in consciousness with and without resultant—in wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousness—the Sugata, in the manner I have stated, thus spoke, thus declared the resultant consciousness to be of thirty-six kinds.

Anuḷāresūti khuddakesu. Tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā chaḷārammaṇavijānanagayhākārā. Sabbaññutaññāṇassa gati viya gati etissāti sabbaññutaññāṇagatikā.

`Anuḷāresu` means 'in minor matters.' Its manifestation is its nature as such, having the mode of grasping and knowing the six kinds of objects. Its course is like the course of the Omniscient One's knowledge; therefore it is said to have the course of the Omniscient One's knowledge.

56. Somanassayuttānaṭṭha[M 0.0017], kusalākusalāni ca somanassayuttāni aṭṭha kusalākusalāni ca, kriyato pana pañca evaṃ iminā mayā vuttappakārena hāsacittāni terasa.

56. There are eight wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses associated with joy, and five from the functional side. Thus, in the manner stated, there are thirteen consciousnesses that produce a smile.

57. Puthujjanā hasantettha ettha etesu terasacittesu puthujjanā pana aṭṭhahi cittehi hasanti[V 1.0014]. Sekhā satta ariyā chahi cittehi hasanti. Asekhā khīṇāsavā pañcahi cittehi hasanti.

57. Among these thirteen consciousnesses, worldlings smile with eight consciousnesses. Learners—the seven kinds of noble ones—smile with six consciousnesses. Those beyond training—the arahants whose taints are destroyed—smile with five consciousnesses.

Kusalāni pana rūpārūpakusalāni sekhaputhujjanānaṃ uppajjanti. Imāni rūpārūpakiriyāni khīṇāsavānaṃ bhāvanāyeva kāro bhāvanākāro, tassa vaso bhāvanākāravaso, tena pavattāni. Tāni rūpārūpakusalāni bhāvanāpuññavasappavattāni bhāvanākusalavasena pavattāni. Imesaṃ rūpārūpakiriyānaṃ tesañca rūpārūpakusalānaṃ ayameva viseso.

The fine-material and immaterial-sphere wholesome states, however, arise for learners and worldlings. These fine-material and immaterial-sphere functional states of those whose taints are destroyed are simply the act of meditation, the mode of meditation; they proceed by its power, the power of the mode of meditation. Those wholesome states proceed by the power of the merit of meditation, by way of wholesome meditation. This alone is the distinction between these functional states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres and those wholesome states.

58-9. Yā puthujjanakālasmiṃ, abhinibbattitā pana puthujjanakālasmiṃ puthujjanabhāvaṭṭhitena yoginā abhinibbattitā yā rūpārūpasamāpatti, sā rūpārūpasamāpatti so yogī khīṇāsavo bhikkhu hutvā naṃ rūpārūpasamāpattiṃ yāva yattakaṃ kālaṃ na samāpajjate, tāva tattakena kālena tassa khīṇāsavabhikkhuno kusalā eva rūpārūpakusalā eva hoti. Khīṇāsavena sā rūpārūpasamāpatti sace yadi samāpannā samāpajjitā, kriyā rūpārūpakiriyā hoti.

58–59. An attainment of the fine-material or immaterial sphere that was produced by a yogin while established in the state of a worldling: if that yogin, having become a bhikkhu with taints destroyed, does not enter that attainment, for as long as he does not enter it, that attainment remains for him simply a wholesome state of the fine-material or immaterial sphere. If that attainment is entered by him when his taints are destroyed, it becomes a functional state of the fine-material or immaterial sphere.

60. Ekādasavidhaṃ kāme kāmāvacare kiriyacittaṃ ekādasavidhaṃ, rūpe rūpāvacare pañca, arūpisu cattāri iti sabbāni kriyacittāni vīsati.

60. Functional consciousness in the sense sphere is of eleven kinds. In the fine-material sphere, there are five, and in the immaterial spheres, four. Thus, there are twenty functional consciousnesses in all.

61. Lokuttarakriyacittaṃ, pana kasmā na vijjati? Maggassa ekacittakkhaṇikattā na vijjati. Ayamettha adhippāyo – catumaggaṭṭho [M 0.0018] khīṇāsavo nāma na hoti, maggānantarameva phalaṃ uppajjati, maggopi ekacittakkhaṇiko yadi cittaṃ bahucittakkhaṇikaṃ, phalasamaṅgino khīṇāsavassapi maggacittaṃ bhaveyya, evaṃ sati lokuttarakiriyacittaṃ bhaveyyāti adhippāyo.

61. But why is there no supramundane functional consciousness? Because the path consists of a single mind-moment, it does not exist. This is the meaning here: one standing in the fourfold path is not called one whose taints are destroyed; immediately after the path, fruition arises. The path, too, consists of a single mind-moment. If consciousness were of many mind-moments, then even one whose taints are destroyed and is endowed with fruition would have path-consciousness. In that case, there would be supramundane functional consciousness—this is the intended meaning.

62. Kriyākriyāpattivibhāgadesako karaṇaṃ kriyaṃ, kriyaṃ nāma vinayapariyāyena akattabbassa karaṇaṃ, na karaṇaṃ akriyaṃ, akriyaṃ nāma vinayapariyāyena kattabbassa akaraṇaṃ, āpajjanaṃ āpatti, kriyāya karaṇena āpatti kriyāpatti, akriyāya akaraṇena āpatti akriyāpatti, kriyāpatti ca akriyāpatti ca kriyāpatyākriyāpattiyo, ekassa āpatti-saddassa lopaṃ katvā “kriyākriyāpattiyo”ti vuttaṃ, tāsaṃ vibhāgo kriyākriyāpattivibhāgo, desetīti desako, tassa desako kriyākriyāpattivibhāgadesako. Ṇvu-tu-paccayesu paresu kammatthe chaṭṭhī hotīti [V 1.0015] vadanti. Jino kiṃ visiṭṭho? Kriyākriyāpattivibhāgadesako hitāhitānaṃ sakriyākriyārato hitassa sakriyāya rato, ahitassa akriyāya rato, yaṃ kriyākriyaṃ, kriyaṃ nāma kriyacittaṃ, akriyaṃ nāma kusalākusalavipākacittaṃ icchanti eke. Taṃ na. Kasmā? Kusalādhikāre “kusalaṃ muninā lapitaṃ” akusalādhikāre “pāpamānasaṃ pāpāpāpesvapāpena vuttaṃ” vipākādhikāre “pākaṃ sugato abravī”ti vatvā puna kriyādhikāre “kusalākusalavipākāni avocā”ti vacanassa vattabbābhāvato. Tena vāssa kriyākriyaṃ etassāti kriyākriyaṃ, kriyākriyasabhāvanti attho. Ayameva sārato paccetabbo. Yaṃ kriyākriyaṃ cittaṃ kriyākriyāsabhāvaṃ avoca desesi, taṃ kriyākriyaṃ kriyākriyasabhāvaṃ mayā samīritaṃ, sammā pakārena īritaṃ kathitaṃ.

62. The teacher who explains the analysis of action-and-inaction-offenses: 'Doing' (karaṇa) is 'action' (kriya). 'Action' means, according to the Vinaya method, doing what should not be done. 'Not doing' (na karaṇa) is 'inaction' (akriya). 'Inaction' means, according to the Vinaya method, not doing what should be done. 'Falling into' is an 'offense' (āpatti). An offense by means of action, by doing, is an 'action-offense' (kriyāpatti). An offense by means of inaction, by not doing, is an 'inaction-offense' (akriyāpatti). Both an action-offense and an inaction-offense are 'action-and-inaction-offenses' (kriyāpatyākriyāpattiyo); having elided one word 'offense' (āpatti), it is stated as 'kriyākriyāpattiyo.' The analysis of these is the 'analysis of action-and-inaction-offenses' (kriyākriyāpattivibhāgo). One who teaches is a 'teacher' (desako). The teacher of that is the 'teacher who explains the analysis of action-and-inaction-offenses' (kriyākriyāpattivibhāgadesako). They say that when the suffixes ṇvu, tu, etc., follow, the sixth case (genitive) is used in the sense of the object. How is the Victor distinguished? As the teacher who explains the analysis of action-and-inaction-offenses, delighting in his own action and inaction regarding the beneficial and the unbeneficial; that is, delighting in his own action regarding the beneficial, and delighting in his inaction regarding the unbeneficial. Some hold that 'action' (kriya) means functional consciousness, while 'inaction' (akriya) means wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant consciousness. That is not so. Why? Because in the section on the wholesome it is said, 'The wholesome was spoken by the sage'; in the section on the unwholesome, 'evil consciousness was spoken of by the Sinless One in regard to sins and non-sins'; and in the section on the resultant, 'The Sugata spoke of the resultant.' Then, in the section on the functional, to say, 'He spoke of the wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant,' would be baseless. Therefore, 'action-and-inaction' (kriyākriyaṃ) means 'of this,' that is, having the nature of action and inaction. This itself should be understood as the essence. That consciousness which is 'action-and-inaction,' which he taught and explained as having the nature of action and inaction—that 'action-and-inaction' having the nature of action and inaction has been set forth by me, rightly declared and spoken.

64. Ekūnanavuti [M 0.0019] sabbe, cittuppādā mahesinā lokuttare aṭṭha katvā ekūnanavuti sabbe cittuppādā mahesinā tathāgatena samāsato saṅkhepato niddiṭṭhā.

64. In all, eighty-nine arisings of consciousness were taught by the Great Sage; having counted the supramundane as eight, all eighty-nine arisings of consciousness were expounded in brief, concisely, by the Great Sage, the Tathāgata.

65. Piṭake abhidhammasmiṃ, ye bhikkhū pāṭavatthino abhidhammapiṭake paṭuno bhāvo pāṭavaṃ, tena attho pāṭavattho, so etesaṃ atthīti pāṭavatthino, chekabhāvatthikā ye bhikkhū, tehi bhikkhūhi ayaṃ abhidhammāvatāro uggahetabbo sikkhitabbo punappunaṃ cintitabbo.

65. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, regarding those monks who are proficient: proficiency (pāṭavaṃ) is the state of being skilled in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; one who has need of that is a 'pāṭavattho'; because that proficiency exists for them, they are 'pāṭavatthino'. By those monks who desire skillfulness, this Abhidhammāvatāra should be learned, studied, and repeatedly reflected upon.

66. Ye janā tassaṅkāsena taṃsannibhena abhidhammāvatārena abhidhammamahodadhiṃ mahāsāgarasannibhaṃ abhidhammaṃ taranti, te imaṃ lokaṃ paralokañca taranti. Itīti parisamāpane.

66. Those people who, by means of this Abhidhammāvatāra, cross over the great ocean of Abhidhamma, which resembles the great sea—they cross over this world and the next. The word 'iti' is used to mark the conclusion.

Iti abhidhammāvatāraṭīkāya

Here ends the Subcommentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Cittaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition of consciousness is finished.

Paṭhamo paricchedo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyo paricchedo

2. The Second Chapter.

Cetasikaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of Mental Factors.

67. Cittānantaramuddiṭṭhā[V 1.0016], ye ca cetasikā mayā ye ca cetasikā cittānantaraṃ mayā uddiṭṭhā, ito paraṃ idāni tesaṃ cetasikānaṃ vibhājanaṃ karissāmi ahaṃ.

67. Those mental factors that were pointed out by me after consciousness—now, hereafter, I will provide an analysis of those mental factors.

Imesu pana karuṇāmuditāvasena bhāvanākāle karuṇāpubbabhāgo vā, appanāpattāya karuṇāya pubbabhāgo, tasmiṃ pubbabhāge, karuṇāto pubbabhāge kāmāvacaracitteti attho. Ekā karuṇā uppajjati. Muditāpubbabhāge vā appanāpattāya muditāya pubbabhāge ekā muditā [M 0.0020] uppajjati. Iminā kāmāvacaracittena yogī micchākammantādīhi dhammehi viramati. Ramu-dhātu kīḷāyaṃ, vi-saddo viramaṇattho.

But among these, at the time of development by way of compassion and appreciative joy, there is the preliminary stage of compassion, which is the preliminary stage for compassion that has reached absorption. In that preliminary stage, the stage before that compassion, the meaning is that it is a sense-sphere consciousness. A single compassion arises. Or, in the preliminary stage of appreciative joy, the preliminary stage for appreciative joy that has reached absorption, a single appreciative joy arises. With this sense-sphere consciousness, the yogi abstains from states such as wrong action. The root 'ram' is in the sense of 'delighting,' and the prefix 'vi' has the meaning of abstaining.

68. Ādinā puññacittena, tettiṃsa niyatā matā ādinā puññacittena paṭhamamahākusalacittena saha niyatā tettiṃsa cetasikā bhagavatā matāti, atha vā karuṇāmuditā aniyatā ekena dhammena saha catuttiṃsa dhammā bhavanti.

68. With the first meritorious consciousness, thirty-three are considered fixed. This means: with the first meritorious consciousness, that is, with the first great wholesome consciousness, thirty-three mental factors are considered fixed by the Blessed One. Alternatively, compassion and appreciative joy are unfixed; with one of these factors, there are thirty-four factors.

69. Kasmā panettha mettā ca, upekkhā ca na uddhaṭā ettha etesu yevāpanakadhammesu, niddhāraṇaṃ, mettā ca upekkhā ca dhammarājena satthunā na uddhaṭā na vuttā kasmā kāraṇā.

69. Why here are loving-kindness and equanimity not singled out? Here, among these incidental factors—this is a specification—why were loving-kindness and equanimity not singled out, not mentioned, by the Teacher, the King of the Dhamma? For what reason?

70. Abyāpādena mettāpi abyāpādena mettā gahitā, upekkhāti tatramajjhattatāya ca gahitā yasmā kāraṇā, tasmā ubhopetā bhagavatā na gahitā.

70. Because loving-kindness is included under non-ill will, and equanimity is included under specific neutrality, for that reason both were not taken up separately by the Blessed One.

71. Kasmā yevāpanā dhammā, buddhenādiccabandhunā sabbe te yevāpanā dhammā yevāpananāmakā pāḷiyaṃ sarūpena eva. Bandhati snehena etasminti bandhu, ādiccassa bandhu ādiccabandhu, tena ādiccabandhunā buddhena na ca uddhaṭā na desitā.

71. Why were the incidental factors not singled out by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun? All those incidental factors are named 'incidental' in the Pāli canon by their very nature. 'One who binds with affection' is a 'kinsman' (bandhu). The kinsman of the sun is the 'Kinsman of the Sun' (ādiccabandhu). By that Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, they were not singled out, not taught separately.

72. Kasmā [V 1.0017] kāraṇā? Yasmā aniyatā keci yevāpanakā aniyatā, yasmā kāraṇā rāsiṃ dukavaggādirāsiṃ na bhajanti na sevanti, yasmā kāraṇā keci yevāpanakā dubbalā, tasmā pāḷiyaṃ bhagavatā na vuttā.

72. For what reason? Because some incidental factors are unfixed; because they do not belong to a collection, such as a group of two, etc.; and because some incidental factors are weak. Therefore they were not mentioned separately by the Blessed One in the Pāli canon.

73. Chandādhimokkhamuditā manasi ca kāro,

73. Zeal, decision, appreciative joy, and attention,

Majjhattatā ca karuṇā viratittayañca;

Puññesu tena niyatāniyatā ca sabbe,

Yevāpanā munivarena na ceva vuttā.

and neutrality, compassion, and the triad of abstinences; therefore, in meritorious states, all these incidental factors, both fixed and unfixed, were not mentioned separately by the Best of Sages.

Chandādhimokkho [M 0.0021] muditā manasikāro majjhattatā karuṇā viratittayañca puññesukusalesu niyatā cattāro aniyatā pañca sabbe yevāpanā na ca eva tena munivarena vuttā.

Zeal, decision, appreciative joy, attention, neutrality, compassion, and the triad of abstinences—in meritorious and wholesome states, four are fixed and five are unfixed. All are incidental factors, and they were not mentioned separately by that Best of Sages.

74-80. Kasmā panettha phassova, paṭhamaṃ samudīrito ettha etesu cetasikesu, jātiniddhāraṇaṃ, phassova paṭhamaṃ samudīrito kathito. Kasmā kāraṇā? Kira mayā sutaṃ, ārammaṇe cittassa paṭhamaṃ abhinipātattā phasso paṭhamaṃ samudīrito, phusitvā pana phassena phassena ārammaṇaṃ phusitvā yogino vedanāya ārammaṇaṃ vedaye, saññāya sañjānāti, cetanāya ārammaṇaṃ cetaye. Sahajātānaṃ cetasikānaṃ phassova idha imasmiṃ citte mahesinā paṭhamaṃ vutto. Hi kasmā kāraṇā? Yasmā balavapaccayattā, tasmā vutto. Akāraṇamidaṃ sabbaṃ, cittānaṃ tu saheva ca “paṭhamābhinipātattā”ti ca “balavapaccayattā”ti ca idaṃ sabbaṃ vacanaṃ akāraṇaṃ ahetukaṃ ayuttaṃ, kasmā kāraṇā? Cittajānaṃ cittehi sahappavattānaṃ cetasikānaṃ ekuppādādibhāvena samānuppādasamānanirodhasamānālambaṇasamānavatthukabhāvena pavattito akāraṇaṃ ayuttaṃ. Ayaṃ tu paṭhamuppanno, ayaṃ pacchāti natthidaṃ ayaṃ dhammo paṭhamuppanno, ayaṃ dhammo pacchākāle uppanno iti idaṃ vacanaṃ natthi. Balavapaccayattepi kāraṇaṃ na ca dissati. Desanākkamato ceva paṭhamaṃ samudīrito iccevaṃ iti evaṃ iti iminā mayā vuttappakārena phassassa paṭhamaṃ samudīritataṃ viññunā vibhāvinā viññeyyaṃ, visesato visesena aññathā na viññeyyaṃ. Na ca pariyesitabboyaṃ, tasmā pubbāparakkamo yasmā kāraṇā ayaṃ pubbāparakkamo viññunā na ca pariyesitabbo na gavesitabbo, dhammā eva vacanatthalakkhaṇādīhi vijānatā paṇḍitena pariyesitabbā.

74-80. Why is contact mentioned first? Here, among these mental factors—this is a specification—contact is mentioned and spoken of first. For what reason? The tradition is that because contact is the mind's first impact upon the object, it is mentioned first. Having contacted the object with contact, the yogi feels the object with feeling, perceives it with perception, and wills towards the object with volition. Among the co-nascent mental factors, contact is spoken of first by the Great Sage in this consciousness. For what reason? Because it is a strong condition. All this is without reason. That is, both the statement 'because it is the first impact' and 'because it is a strong condition' are without reason, without cause, and inappropriate. Why? Because the mental factors born of consciousness proceed together with consciousness, having the same arising, the same cessation, the same object, and the same basis, it is without reason and inappropriate. There is no such thing as 'this one arose first, this one later.' The statement 'this phenomenon arose first, this phenomenon arose at a later time' does not exist. Nor is any reason seen for its being a strong condition. It is mentioned first simply from the order of the teaching. Thus, in this way, in the manner I have stated, the fact that contact is mentioned first should be understood by the wise, the discerning one; it should not be understood otherwise, in a special way. And this sequence of priority should not be investigated. For this reason, this sequence of before and after should not be sought or investigated by a wise person. Only the phenomena themselves should be investigated by the pandit who understands them through their verbal meaning, characteristics, and so on.

Iṭṭhākārānubhavanarasā [M 0.0022][V 1.0018] iṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanakiccā subhojanarasaṃ anubhavanto rājā viya. Cetasikaassādapaccupaṭṭhānā cetasikapassaddhipadaṭṭhānā.

Its characteristic is experiencing the agreeable aspect; its function is experiencing agreeable objects, like a king enjoying the taste of fine food. Its manifestation is the enjoyment of mental factors. Its proximate cause is the tranquility of mental factors.

Paccābhiññāṇakaraṇarasā paṭijānanakiccā vaḍḍhakissa abhiññāṇakaraṇamiva vaḍḍhakino sakiṃ sañjānitvāpi dāruharesu suttassa paṭipasāraṇaṃ viyāti adhippāyo. Yathāgahitanimittavasenāti yathāpavattitanimittassa vasena. Manasi abhinivesakaraṇaṃ gayhākārā.

Its characteristic is making a recognition; its function is recognizing, like a carpenter's marking. The meaning is that it is like a carpenter, having once recognized them, stretching a string over pieces of wood. 'By way of the sign as grasped' means by way of the sign as it has occurred. Its manifestation is the firm settling of the mind on the feature to be apprehended.

Āyūhanarasā pavattanakiccasādhakā. Mahāvaḍḍhakiādayo viya yathā mahāvaḍḍhakī sayampi dāruṃ tacchati, parepi dāruṃ tacchāpeti, evaṃ sayampi ārammaṇe sandahati, sampayuttadhammepi abhisandahāpeti.

Its characteristic is accumulation; its function is to set things in motion. It is like a master carpenter and his assistants: just as a master carpenter hews the timber himself and has others hew it, so volition itself directs itself to the object and directs its associated states as well.

Āhananaṃ bhuso hananaṃ, pariyāhananaṃ samantā hananaṃ, taṃ raso etassāti āhananapariyāhananaraso.

Forceful striking is `āhanana`; striking all around is `pariyāhanana`. Its function is that of striking and striking all around.

Ārammaṇānumajjanalakkhaṇo ārammaṇaparimaddanalakkhaṇo.

It has the characteristic of stroking the object and the characteristic of massaging the object.

Pinayatīti pīti, sahajātadhamme ārammaṇe pinayatīti attho. Kāyacittapharaṇarasā. Udaggassa cittassa bhāvo odagyaṃ, taṃ paccupaṭṭhānaṃ etassāti odagyapaccupaṭṭhānā.

It gladdens, thus it is rapture (pīti); the meaning is that it gladdens the co-nascent states and the object. Its function is to pervade the body and mind. Elation is the state of an uplifted mind; that is its manifestation.

Saddahanti vatthuttayaṃ saddahanti. Akālusiyapaccupaṭṭhānā anāvilabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Saddheyyavatthupadaṭṭhānā saddahitabbavatthuttayāsannakāraṇā.

They have faith; they have faith in the threefold object. Its manifestation is non-turbidity, an unclouded state. Its proximate cause is an object of faith, that is, the threefold object in which faith should be placed.

Araññagatasudesako viya araññe gato maggasudesako viya.

Like a good guide for one gone to the forest; like a good guide to the path for one gone into the forest.

Attanā avinibbhuttānaṃ dhammānanti avigatānaṃ cetasikānaṃ. Tesanti tesaṃ cetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Santepi ca tesaṃ [M 0.0023] cetasikānaṃ anupālanalakkhaṇādimhi [V 1.0019] vidhāne atthikkhaṇeyeva taṃ tesaṃ pāletabbānaṃ cetasikānaṃ pavattakkhaṇeyeva taṃ jīvitaṃ te dhamme pāletabbe cetasike anupāleti. Udakaṃ viyāti yathā udakaṃ attani uppalādīni anupāleti, tathā anupālanalakkhaṇādimhi vidhāne santepi tesaṃ atthikkhaṇeyeva anupāleti, vijjamānakkhaṇeva anupāletīti adhippāyo. Paccayuppannepi ca dhamme anupāleti, dhāti viya kumāraṃ aññāya janitaṃ kumāraṃ rakkhantī dhāti viya, parassa puttaṃ aṅkādinā dhāretīti dhāti. Sayaṃpavattitadhammasambandheneva pavattati attanā pavattitehi dhammehi sampavattati. Niyāmako viya yathā niyāmako ekanāvāya vutthehi janehi saha pavattati, bhaṅgato uddhaṃ taṃ jīvitaṃ na pavattayati, attano ca abhāvā ṭhapayitabbānaṃ cetasikānañca abhāvā, bhaṅgakkhaṇe cetasike na ṭhapeti sayaṃ bhijjamānattā, vaṭṭisneho khīyamāno padīpasikhaṃ na karoti yathā.

‘Of states not separate from itself’ means of mental factors that have not departed. ‘Of them’ means of those mental factors. Although its characteristic, etc., is to maintain these mental factors, it is only at the very moment of their existence, at the very moment of their occurrence, that life maintains those mental factors that are to be maintained. Just as water maintains lotuses and so on within itself, so too it maintains them only at the moment of their existence; the intention is that it maintains them only while they are present. It also maintains states that have arisen from conditions, like a wet-nurse who protects a child born to another; a ‘dhāti’ (wet-nurse) is one who holds another's child in her lap. It proceeds only in connection with states set in motion by itself; it proceeds together with the states it has set in motion. It is like a pilot: just as a pilot proceeds together with the people aboard a single boat, life does not proceed beyond dissolution. Due to its own absence and the absence of the mental factors to be established, at the moment of dissolution it does not establish the mental factors, as it is itself dissolving—just as the oil in the wick, when exhausted, does not produce a lamp flame.

Sommabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānoti mudubhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, sītalabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno vā.

Its manifestation is a state of gentleness, that is, a manifestation of softness, or a manifestation of coolness.

Kāyoti cettha vedanādayo tayo khandhā vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho ime khandhā gahitā.

Here, by ‘kāya’ (body), the three aggregates beginning with feeling are taken: the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, and the formations aggregate. These are the aggregates that are taken.

Nimmaddanarasāti nimmaddanakiccā. Kāyacittānaṃ avūpasamatāuddhaccādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti ādiggahaṇena kukkuccaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Its function is subduing; its task is to subdue. It is the opponent of defilements such as restlessness, which are the non-pacification of body and mind; by the word ‘ādi’ (etc.), worry should be included.

Iti abhidhammāvatāraṭīkāya

Thus in the Subcommentary to the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Cetasikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of Mental Factors is concluded.

Dutiyo paricchedo.

The Second Chapter.

3. Tatiyo paricchedo

3. The Third Chapter.

Cetasikavibhāganiddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Division of Mental Factors.

89. Sabbe [M 0.0024] cetasikā vuttā, buddhenādiccabandhunā ye sabbe cetasikā ādiccabandhunā buddhena [V 1.0020] vuttā, te sabbe cetasikā nāmasāmaññato nāmasamānabhāvena dvepaññāsabhavanti te, anottappapariyosānā dvipaññāsa bhavanti.

89. All mental factors have been taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun. All those mental factors taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, become fifty-two by virtue of their commonality as ‘name,’ by their shared nature as ‘name.’ They are fifty-two, ending with lack of moral dread (anottappa).

90-92. Catupaññāsadhā kāme, rūpe pañcadaseritā kāme kāmāvacare catupaññāsa cittāni īritā. Rūpe rūpāvacare pañcadasa cittāni īritā bhavanti. Dvādasārūpe arūpāvacare dvādasa cittāni bhavanti. Cattālīsa manāsavā lokuttaracittāni cattālīsa bhavanti, ekavīsasataṃ sabbe cittuppādā samāsato saṅkhepato ekavīsasataṃ hoti. Etesu tesamuppattiṃ ito paraṃ etesu mayā vuttesu cittesu tesaṃ phassādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ uppattiṃ ekaṃ ekaṃ uddharitvā cittacetasikesu bhikkhūnaṃ pāṭavatthāya ahaṃ pavakkhāmi desissāmi.

90-92. Fifty-four in the sense sphere, fifteen are stated in the form sphere. In the sense sphere, that is, the sense-sphere plane, fifty-four consciousnesses are stated. In the form sphere, that is, the form-sphere plane, fifteen consciousnesses are stated to arise. Twelve in the formless sphere; in the formless-sphere plane, twelve consciousnesses arise.
