Bhagavato thomanena ca svākkhātatādayo dhammaguṇā, suppaṭipannatādayo saṅghaguṇā ca dassitā honti tappabhavassa anaññathābhāvatoti na tesaṃ visuṃ thomanā katā. Adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe puggale yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne ca apāyadukkhesu ceva vaṭṭadukkhesu ca apatamāne katvā dhāretīti dhammo, so catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ, catunnañca sāmaññaphalānaṃ, nibbānassa, pariyattidhammassa ca vasena dasavidho. Vuttañhetaṃ chattavimāne –

Having thus paid homage to the Jewel of the Buddha, preceded by praise, now, beginning the homage to the remaining jewels, he says: 'and to the Dhamma and the goodly Community.' Through the praise of the Blessed One, the qualities of the Dhamma—such as being well-proclaimed—and the qualities of the Sangha—such as being of good practice—are also shown, for since they originate from him they cannot be otherwise; therefore, separate praise for them is not made. The Dhamma is so called because it upholds (dhāreti) a person who has attained the path and realized cessation and is practicing as instructed, preventing them from falling into the suffering of the planes of misery and the suffering of the round of rebirth. This Dhamma is tenfold, comprising the four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, Nibbāna, and the scriptural Dhamma. For it is said in the Chatta Vimāna:

“Rāgavirāgamanejamasokaṃ,

Dhammamasaṅkhatamappaṭikūlaṃ;

Madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ,

Dhammamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti. (vi. va. 887);

The fading of lust, unshaken, sorrowless,

The Dhamma unconditioned, agreeable;

Sweet is this Dhamma, perfect, well-expounded,

To this Dhamma go for refuge.

Ettha hi kāmarāgādibhedo sabbopi rāgo virajjati etenāti “rāgavirāgo”ti maggo kathito. Ejāsaṅkhātāya taṇhāya, antonijjhānalakkhaṇassa ca sokassa taduppattiyaṃ sabbaso parikkhīṇattā “anejamasoka”nti phalaṃ kathitaṃ. Kenaci paccayena asaṅkhatattā “dhammamasaṅkhata”nti nibbānaṃ vuttaṃ. Avirodhadīpanato pana atthabyañjanassa sampannatāya, pakaṭṭhaguṇavibhāvanato suṭṭhu vibhajitattā ca “appaṭikūla”ntiādinā sabbopi pariyattidhammo kathito. Tattha ariyamagganibbānāni nippariyāyeneva apāyādito dhāraṇato dhammo, phalapariyattiyo [V 1.0126] pana pariyāyena. Tathā hettha dhāraṇaṃ nāma apāyādinibbattakakilesaviddhaṃsanaṃ. Iti ariyamaggassa kilesasamucchedakatāya, nibbānassa ca ālambaṇabhāvena tassa tadatthasiddhihetutāyapi ubhinnampi [M 1.0150] nippariyāyato labbhati. Itaresu pana ariyaphalassa maggena samucchinnakilesānaṃ paṭipassaddhakiccatāya, maggānukūlappavattito pariyattidhammassa ca tadadhigamahetutāyāti ubhinnampi pariyāyatova labbhatīti.

Herein, because all kinds of lust, such as sensual lust, fade away by means of it, the path is called 'the fading of lust.' Because craving, which is called agitation, and sorrow, which is characterized by inner torment, are utterly destroyed at its arising, the fruit is called 'unagitated and sorrowless.' Because it is not conditioned by any cause, Nibbāna is called 'the unconditioned Dhamma.' Further, because it reveals non-contradiction, is complete in meaning and phrasing, expounds excellent qualities, and is well-analyzed, the entire scriptural teaching is described by such terms as 'unopposed.' Here, the noble path and Nibbāna are Dhamma in the primary sense because they uphold one by protecting from the planes of misery and so on; but the fruits and the scriptures are so in a secondary sense. For here, 'upholding' means the demolition of the defilements that generate birth in the planes of misery. Thus, since the noble path extirpates the defilements, and since Nibbāna is a cause for accomplishing that aim by serving as its object, both are designated as Dhamma in the primary sense. As for the others, since the noble fruit has the function of tranquillizing the defilements extirpated by the path, and since the scriptural Dhamma is a cause for attaining the path, both are designated as Dhamma only in a secondary sense.

Attahitaparahitaṃ sādhentīti sādhū, tesaṃ gaṇo samudāyoti sādhugaṇo, sādhu cāyaṃ gaṇo cāti vā sādhugaṇo, sādhuno vā sammāsambuddhassa āyatto gaṇo tassa orasaputtabhāvatoti sādhugaṇo. So pana catunnaṃ ariyamaggasamaṅgīnaṃ, catunnañca phalasamaṅgīnaṃ vasena aṭṭhavidho ariyasaṅgho, taṃ sādhugaṇaṃ. Picāti nipātasamudāyo, eko vā nipāto, tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ vandanakiriyāya sampiṇḍanattho. Keci “gaṇo”ti idha pakaraṇatova ariyagaṇapuggalova labbhatīti sādhūti bhāvanapuṃsakavasena “vanditvā”ti iminā saha yojenti, tadā pana sādhūti bhayalābhādivirahena sakkaccaṃ ādaranti attho.

Those who accomplish what is beneficial for themselves and for others are called 'good people'; their group or assembly is the 'community of the good.' Or, it is a 'good community' because it is good and it is a community. Or, it is the community dependent on the Good One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, because they are his legitimate children; hence it is the 'community of the Good One.' This is the noble Sangha, which is eightfold, comprising the four kinds of persons endowed with the noble paths and the four kinds of persons endowed with the fruits. This is that 'goodly community.' The word 'pi' is a particle, or a collection of particles, used for the purpose of grouping together the act of veneration of the Three Jewels. Some, however, say that since in this context 'gaṇa' can only be understood as the community of noble persons, the word 'sādhu' should be construed with 'vanditvā' as a neuter adverb. In that case, 'sādhu' means 'well,' that is, respectfully and attentively, free from fear, desire for gain, and so on.

2. Evaṃ pakaraṇārambhe yathādhippetaṃ ratanattayappaṇāmaṃ katvā idāni yattha pāṭavatthāya idaṃ pakaraṇaṃ paṭṭhapīyati, taṃ saddhiṃ desakadesapaṭiggāhakasampattīhi vibhāvetvā dassento āha “paṇḍukambalanāmāyā”tiādi. Tattha devarājassa paṇḍukambalanāmāya silāya vimale sītale tale nisinno atulavikkamo devadevehi pūjito devadevo devapurakkhato devānaṃ devalokasmiṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ desesīti sambandho.

2. Thus, at the beginning of the treatise, having paid homage to the Triple Gem as intended, the author now indicates the setting in which this treatise was established for the purpose of recitation, clarifying it along with the perfections of the speaker, the place, and the audience. He says: 'On the stone named Paṇḍukambala,' and so on. The connection of the words there is as follows: Seated on the pure, cool surface of the stone named Paṇḍukambala, which belongs to the king of the gods, the one of incomparable prowess, the God of gods, worshipped by the foremost gods, placed at the fore by the gods, taught the Dhamma to the gods in the world of the gods.

Ayaṃ panettha attho – paṇḍukambalasarikkhavaṇṇatāya “paṇḍukambala”nti nāmaṃ samaññā etissāti paṇḍukambalanāmā. Sā hi sakkassa tādisapuññānubhāvena nibbattā paṇḍukambalajayasumanapupphasamānena vaṇṇena sabbakālaṃ virocati[M 1.0151], pamāṇato pana saṭṭhiyojanāyāmā, paññāsayojanavitthārā, pannarasayojanubbedhā ca hoti. Silāyāti avayavasambandhe sāmivacanaṃ. Tulāya sammito tulyo, na tulyo atulyo, atulyo vikkamo balaṃ etassāti atulyavikkamo. Sammāsambuddhassa hi paramapāramitānubhāvasaṃsiddhena hatthigaṇanāya koṭisahassahatthīnaṃ, purisagaṇanāya dasakoṭisahassapurisānaṃ balehi samappamāṇena kāyabalena, appamāṇena ca ñāṇabalena na kassaci devabrahmādīsu aññatarassa balatulanāya upanetabbaṃ atthi[V 1.0127]. Atha vā anaññasādhāraṇattā atulyo parakkamasaṅkhāto aparimāṇaguṇavisesāvahena anaññasādhāraṇena sammappadhānena samannāgatattā vā atulyo sammappadhānasaṅkhāto vikkamo imassāti atulyavikkamo. “Atulyavikkamo”ti ca vattabbe gāthābandhavasena ya-kāralopaṃ katvā “atulavikkamo”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā sammitatthe a-kārapaccayassāpi sambhavato atulo vikkamo assāti “atulavikkamo”ti vuttaṃ.

This is the meaning here. Because its color resembles a pale woollen blanket, its name is 'Paṇḍukambala.' For it, having arisen through the power of such merit of Sakka's, shines at all times with a color like that of the paṇḍukambala flower or the jayasumana flower. In size, it is sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas thick. The word 'silāya' is in the genitive case, denoting a part-whole relationship. 'Tulya' means 'equal,' that is, measured with a balance; 'atulya' means 'not equal.' One whose prowess or strength is unequal is 'Atulyavikkama,' of unequal prowess. For the Fully Enlightened One is endowed with a bodily strength equal in measure to the strength of a thousand koṭis of elephants or ten thousand koṭis of men, a strength perfected through the power of the supreme perfections, and he is endowed with immeasurable knowledge-strength. His strength cannot be brought into comparison with that of any other being among the gods, brahmās, and so on. Alternatively, because his effort is unique and not shared by others, or because he is endowed with the unique right effort that brings immeasurable excellent qualities, his effort, known as right effort, is unequal; hence he is 'Atulyavikkama.' And though the form should be 'Atulyavikkamo,' the 'ya' has been elided due to the meter of the verse, so it is said as 'Atulavikkamo.' Or, since the suffix '-a' can also have the sense of 'possessing,' it is said as 'Atulavikkamo,' meaning 'he whose prowess is unequal.'

Dibbantīti devā, pañcakāmaguṇādīhi kīḷanti, tesu vā viharanti, vijayasamatthatāyogena bāhirabbhantarike paccatthike vijetuṃ icchanti, issariyadhanādisakkāradānaggahaṇaṃ, taṃtaṃatthānusāsanañca karontā voharanti, puññañāṇānubhāvappattāya jutiyā jotenti, yathādhippetañca visayaṃ appaṭighātena gacchanti, yathicchitanipphādane ca sakkontīti attho. Atha vā devanīyā taṃtaṃbyasananittharaṇatthikehi “saraṇaṃ parāyaṇa”nti gamanīyā, abhitthavanīyā sobhāvisesayogena kamanīyāti vā devā, te tividhā – sammutidevā upapattidevā visuddhidevāti. Tattha sammutidevā nāma mahāsammatādayo khattiyā. Upapattidevā nāma [M 1.0152] cātumahārājike upādāya taduttaridevā. Visuddhidevā nāma khīṇāsavā. Idha pana upapattidevā daṭṭhabbā. No ca kho tepi avisesena, ṭhapetvā pana yāmādike cātumahārājikatāvatiṃsavāsinova adhippetā. Tesaṃ catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi rañjanato rājā, devānaṃ rājā issaro devarājā, tassa devarājassa, “sakkassa devarañño”ti adhippāyo. Na hi aññesaṃ devalokesu nisinno bhagavā abhidhammapiṭakaṃ desesīti.

They are called 'devas' because they sport with the five cords of sensual pleasure and dwell in them; or they wish to conquer external and internal adversaries through their power of victory; or they conduct themselves by bestowing honors such as sovereignty and wealth, and by instructing according to various purposes; or they shine with the radiance attained through the power of merit and knowledge; or they move unimpeded through desired realms; or they are capable of fulfilling their wishes—this is the meaning. Alternatively, they are called 'devas' because they are worthy of being approached by those seeking to escape from various calamities, as 'refuge and ultimate resort,' are worthy of praise, or are desirable due to their special beauty. Devas are of three kinds: conventional devas, rebirth devas, and purified devas. Among these, conventional devas are great appointed rulers such as Mahāsammata and other khattiyas. Rebirth devas include those from the Cātumahārājika realm and upwards to higher deva realms. Purified devas are the taint-destroyers. Here, however, the rebirth devas are to be understood—but not all of them indiscriminately. Rather, only those dwelling in the Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa realms are intended, excluding those from the Yāma realm and above. Because he pleases them with the four bases of sympathy, he is a 'king.' As he is the king and lord of the devas, he is the 'deva-king.' The intention here is 'Sakka, the king of devas,' for the Blessed One did not sit and teach the Abhidhamma Piṭaka in any other deva realm.

3. Yanti aniyamaniddeso, tassa pana “tatthā”ti iminā niyamanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yathāvuttānaṃ tiṇṇampi devānaṃ uttamo devo tehi sabbehi adhikataraṃ kīḷanādiyogatoti devadevo, bhagavā. So hi niratisayāya abhiññākīḷāya uttamehi dibbabrahmaariyavihārehi saparasantānasiddhāya pañcavidhamāravijayicchānibbattiyā cittissariyasattadhanādisammāpaṭipattiaveccappasādasakkāradānaggahaṇasaṅkhātena, yathāparādhayathānulomayathādhammānusāsanasaṅkhātena ca vohārātisayena paramāya paññāya ca sarīrappabhāsaṅkhātāya jutiyā anupamāya ñāṇasarīragatiyā māravijayasabbaññutaññāṇaparahitanipphādanesu appaṭihatāya sattiyā ca samannāgatattā sadevakena vā lokena “saraṇa”nti gamanīyato, abhitthavanīyato, bhattivasena kamanīyato ca sabbe te deve tehi tehi guṇehi abhibhuyya ṭhitoti sabbadevehi pūjanīyataro devo[V 1.0128], visuddhidevabhāvasaṅkhātassa vā sabbaññuguṇālaṅkārassa adhigatattā aññesañca devānaṃ atisayena devoti devadevo. Devānanti tadā dhammapaṭiggāhakānaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷādhivāsīnaṃ mātudevaputtappamukhānaṃ upapattidevānaṃ. Visuddhidevānampettha gahaṇanti vadanti. Te pana upapattidevesveva saṅgahitā manussaarahantānaṃ tattha abhāvato[M 1.0153]. Devadevehīti visuddhidevehi. Visuddhidevā hi vuttanayena itaradevehi sātisayaṃ kīḷanādiyogato idha “devadevā”ti adhippetā, tehi. Pūjitoti pūjitabbo, pūjituṃ arahoti attho. Etena visuddhidevesupi bhagavato aggapuggalataṃ dīpeti. Desesīti madhurakaravīkasaddasadisaṃ brahmassaraṃ nicchārento pakāsesi. Devalokasminti tāvatiṃsadevaloke. Sabhāvasāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ dhāretīti dhammo, kusalādibhedo abhidhammo, idha pana tappakāsakaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ “dhamma”nti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “piṭakuttame”ti. Devapurakkhatoti dasasahassacakkavāḷavāsidibbabrahmehi purakkhato, parivāritoti attho.

3. The non-restriction of 'they go' (yanti) should be understood as being restricted by 'therein' (tatthā). The foremost among the three types of devas mentioned is the Deva of Devas, the Blessed One, because He surpasses all of them due to his connection with divine sport and so forth. For He is endowed with unparalleled mastery in the sport of higher knowledge; with supreme divine, Brahmā, and noble abodes; with the accomplishment of the desire for the fivefold conquest of Māra, which is perfected in his own and others' continuities; by means of right conduct such as sovereignty over mind, the seven treasures, etc., unwavering faith, respectful homage, giving, and acceptance; and by means of exceptional communication, consisting of instruction according to the offense, according to what is agreeable, and according to the Dhamma. He is endowed with the highest wisdom; with radiance, which is the effulgence of his body; with the incomparable movement of his knowledge-body; and with unobstructed power in accomplishing the welfare of others through the conquest of Māra and omniscience. Therefore, He is to be approached as a refuge, praised, and sought out of devotion by the entire world, including the devas. Surpassing all those devas in these various qualities, He is the most worthy of worship among all devas. Alternatively, because He has attained the state of a purified deva, adorned with the qualities of omniscience, He is called the 'Deva of Devas' in an extraordinary sense compared to other devas. 'Among the devas' refers to those devas who were present at the reception of the Dhamma, the ten-thousand world-system dwellers, led by the deva Mātudevaputta—the devas by rebirth. Some say that purified devas are also included here. However, they are included within the devas by rebirth, as human arahants are not present there. 'By the Deva of Devas' means by the purified devas. The purified devas, as described, surpass other devas in divine sport and so forth, and are thus intended here as 'Devas of Devas'; by them. 'Worshipped' means worthy of worship, deserving of honor. This clarifies the Blessed One’s supreme status even among purified devas. 'He taught' means He proclaimed, emitting a Brahmā's voice like the sweet call of the karavīka bird. 'In the deva world' refers to the Tāvatiṃsa deva realm. 'Dhamma' is that which bears its own nature and common characteristics; Abhidhamma is that distinguished by wholesome states and so on. Here, however, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which reveals it, is called 'Dhamma.' As it will be said, 'in the supreme Piṭaka.' 'Preceded by devas' means surrounded by divine Brahmās dwelling in the ten-thousand world-systems.

Nanu ca “devāna”nti vacaneneva devapurakkhatabhāvo siddhoti kiṃ “devapurakkhato”ti vacanena? Nāyaṃ doso. Bhagavā hi kadāci cūḷapanthakattherādīnaṃ viya parammukhepi nisīditvā obhāsaṃ vissajjetvā sattānaṃ sammukhe nisinnaṃ viya dassento dhammaṃ deseti, kadācipi pārāyanikabrāhmaṇādīnaṃ viya sammukhepi nisīditvā aññehi ca parivuto aññesampi dhammaṃ deseti, idha pana na tathā, devehiyeva parivuto devānaṃ desetīti dassanatthaṃ “devapurakkhato”tipi vattabbamevāti.

But is not the state of being preceded by devas established by the very word 'of the devas' (devānaṃ)? Why then use the phrase 'preceded by devas' (devapurakkhato)? This is not a fault. For the Blessed One sometimes teaches the Dhamma, as in the case of Elder Cūḷapanthaka and others, even while sitting with his back turned, emitting light and making it appear as if he were sitting face-to-face with beings. At other times, as in the case of the Pārāyanika brahmins and others, he teaches the Dhamma while sitting face-to-face, surrounded by others, and teaches the Dhamma to others as well. Here, however, it is not so; to show that he teaches the devas while being surrounded solely by devas, the phrase 'preceded by devas' is also certainly to be stated.

4. Evametasmiṃ pakaraṇe gāravajananatthaṃ tena sampādetabbapāṭavavisayaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ desakādisampattīhi saha vibhāvetvā idāni yathādhippetapakaraṇārambhapayojanābhidhānābhidheyyasotujanasamussāhanakaraṇappakārāni ca vibhāvetuṃ “tatthāha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “pāṭavatthāyā”ti iminā pakaraṇārambhapayojanaṃ vuttaṃ. “Abhidhammāvatāra”nti iminā abhidhānābhidheyyāni. “Madhura”ntiādīhi pakaraṇaṃ viseseti. “Samāsenā”ti ca iminā sotujanasamussāhanakaraṇappakārānīti [M 1.0154] daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Aha”nti kattubhūtaṃ attānaṃ niddisati. Tathā hi yo paro na hoti, so niyakajjhattasaṅkhāto attā “aha”nti vuccati.

4. Thus, in this treatise, for the purpose of generating reverence, having explained the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—the subject matter of mastery to be accomplished by him—along with the accomplishments of the teacher and so forth, now, to explain the intended purpose of beginning the treatise, its name and what is named, and the ways of encouraging the audience, the phrase 'therein I...' (tatthāhaṃ) and so forth is stated. Herein, 'for the sake of mastery' (pāṭavatthāya) indicates the purpose of beginning the treatise. 'Introduction to the Abhidhamma' (Abhidhammāvatāra) indicates the name and the named. 'Sweet' (madhura) and so forth qualify the treatise. 'In brief' (samāsenā) and so forth should be understood as the ways of encouraging the audience. 'I' (ahaṃ) refers to oneself as the agent. For that which is not another, that self, designated as one's own inner self, is called 'I.'

Paṭuno bhāvo pāṭavaṃ, taṃyeva attho payojanaṭṭhenāti pāṭavattho, tadatthāya. Taṃ sandhāya vividhanayaggahaṇasamatthassa [V 1.0129] sutamayañāṇassa uppādanatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhanti, bhindanti vā pāpake akusale dhammeti bhikkhū, tesaṃ. Piṭakañca taṃ uttamañcāti piṭakuttamaṃ, tasmiṃ piṭakuttame, abhidhammapiṭaketi adhippāyo. Tañhi pariyattibhājanatthato piṭakaṃ, tīsu piṭakesu visiṭṭhabhāvato uttamañcāti piṭakuttamaṃ. Tattha pariyattibhājanatthatoti pariyattiatthena ceva bhājanatthena ca. Tathā hi “mā piṭakasampadānenā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) pariyatti piṭakanti vuccati. “Atha puriso āgaccheyya kudālapiṭaka”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.228; a. ni. 3.70) yaṃ kiñci bhājanampi. Tasmā idampi pariyāpuṇitabbaṭṭhena pariyatti, abhidhammatthānamādhāraṇatthena bhājanañcāti pariyattibhājanatthato piṭakanti vuccati. Tenevāhu –

The state of being skilled is mastery (pāṭavaṃ); that very meaning, in the sense of purpose, is 'for the sake of mastery' (pāṭavattho), meaning for that purpose. It is said to be for the purpose of generating knowledge based on learning (sutamayañāṇa) capable of grasping various methods. 'Monks' (bhikkhū) are those who see danger (bhayaṃ) in saṃsāra or who destroy (bhindanti) evil, unwholesome states; for them. The supreme Piṭaka (piṭakuttamaṃ) is that which is both a Piṭaka and supreme; in that supreme Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka is intended. For it is a Piṭaka (piṭakaṃ) in the sense of being a receptacle for the scriptures (pariyatti) and supreme (uttamaṃ) among the three Piṭakas due to its distinguished nature. Herein, 'in the sense of being a receptacle for the scriptures' (pariyattibhājanatthato) means both in the sense of scripture (pariyattiatthena) and in the sense of a receptacle (bhājanatthena). For in passages like 'not by the perfection of the Piṭaka' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.66), the scriptures are called a Piṭaka. In passages like 'then a man might come with a spade and a basket' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.228; Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.70), any container whatsoever is also called a piṭaka. Therefore, this too is called a Piṭaka in the sense of being what is to be learned (pariyatti) and a receptacle (bhājana) as the foundation for the meanings of the Abhidhamma; hence, it is a Piṭaka in the sense of being a receptacle for the scriptures. For this reason they said:

“Piṭakaṃ piṭakatthavidū,

Pariyattibbhājanatthato āhu;

Tena samodhānetvā,

Tayopi vinayādayo ñeyyā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā; pārā. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā; dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā);

"The experts in the Piṭaka say 'Piṭaka' in the sense of being a receptacle for the scriptures; by applying this, the three—Vinaya and the rest—should also be understood." (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1. First Great Council Discussion; Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1. First Great Council Discussion; Dha. Sa. Aṭṭha. Introduction).

Visiṭṭhabhāvo panassa lokavohāramatikkamma yathāsabhāvavasena desanato, visiṭṭhadhammakkhandhavibhāvanato ca veditabbo. Ettha hi “satto puggalo bhikkhū”tiādikaṃ lokavohāramatikkamma “khandhadhātuāyatana”ntiādinā yathādhammavaseneva bāhulladesanā pavattā, na itaresu viya [M 1.0155] yathāvuttavohāravasena, yato idaṃ yathādhammasāsananti vuccati. Sabbasaṅkhatadhammavisiṭṭho cettha paññākkhandho visesato vibhāvito, tasmā tiṇṇampi piṭakānaṃ buddhavacanabhāvepi yathāsabhāvānatikkamadesanādito idameva tīsu piṭakesu visiṭṭhanti yuttaṃ. Apica dhammātirekadhammavisesabhāvato cassa visiṭṭhabhāvo veditabbo. Abhidhamme hi nippadesato khandhāyatanādidhammānaṃ vibhattattā itaradvayato atirekatarā, visiṭṭhā ca pāḷi hoti, tasmā atirekassa, visiṭṭhassa ca pāḷidhammassa vasena idameva tīsu piṭakesu uttamanti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Yathāvuttavisiṭṭhabhāvayogatoyeva cetaṃ “abhidhammapiṭaka”nti vuccati abhi-saddassa visiṭṭhabhāvajotanato[V 1.0130]. Apica vuḍḍhimantādidhammānaṃ ettha vuttattā cetaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ. Yathāhu porāṇā –

Its distinctive nature should be understood from its teaching according to its own nature, transcending conventional speech, and from its exposition of distinctive aggregates of phenomena. Here, indeed, expressions like 'being,' 'person,' 'monk,' etc., are transcended, and the teaching proceeds abundantly in terms of 'aggregates,' 'elements,' 'sense bases,' etc., according to the true nature of phenomena, not in the conventional manner as in the other Piṭakas. Because of this, it is called the teaching according to the Dhamma. Herein, the aggregate of wisdom, distinctive among all conditioned phenomena, is especially expounded. Therefore, even though all three Piṭakas are the word of the Buddha, due to the teaching that does not deviate from its own nature and so forth, this alone is rightly considered distinctive among the three Piṭakas. Furthermore, its distinctive nature should be understood from its being a surpassing Dhamma and a special Dhamma. For in the Abhidhamma, the phenomena of aggregates, sense bases, etc., are analyzed without remainder, making its Pāḷi more comprehensive and distinctive than the other two. Thus, because of its comprehensive and distinctive Pāḷi and Dhamma, it is fitting to declare this as the highest among the three Piṭakas. This is called the 'Abhidhamma Piṭaka' precisely because it is connected with the aforementioned distinctive nature, and because the prefix 'abhi-' signifies a distinctive nature. Moreover, since phenomena such as 'growth' (vuḍḍhi) and 'possessor' (manta) are explained here, this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. As the ancients have said:

“Yaṃ ettha vuḍḍhimanto, salakkhaṇā pūjitā paricchinnā;

Vuttādhikā ca dhammā, abhidhammo tena akkhāto”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā; pārā. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā; dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā);

Herein, those dhammas that are extensive, characterized, honored, and well-defined, and those dhammas that are superior to what has been stated—for that reason, it is called Abhidhamma.

Tathā hettha “rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti, mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 160 ādayo) vuḍḍhimantopi dhammā vuttā, “rūpārammaṇaṃ vā saddārammaṇaṃ vā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1) nayena ārammaṇādīhi lakkhitabbattā salakkhaṇāpi “sekkhā dhammā asekkhā dhammā, lokuttarā dhammā”tiādinā nayena pūjitā pūjārahāpi “phasso hoti, vedanā hotī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1) nayena sabhāvaparicchinnattā paricchinnāpi “mahaggatā dhammā appamāṇā dhammā (dha. sa. tikamātikā 12, dukamātikā 99), anuttarā dhammā”tiādinā nayena adhikā visiṭṭhāpi dhammā vuttā, tasmā abhi-saddassa vuḍḍhiādiatthesupi pavattanato “vuḍḍhimanto dhammā etthā”tiādinā nibbacanena idaṃ piṭakaṃ [M 1.0156] “abhidhamma”nti vuccati. Abhidhammaṃ otaranti anenāti abhidhammāvatāraṃ nāma pakaraṇaṃ. Iminā panassa atthānugatamabhidhānaṃ dasseti. Tu-saddo padapūraṇe. Ācariyena hi gāthāpadapūraṇatthaṃ yebhuyyena tattha tattha nipātā vuccanti. Yattha pana nesaṃ payojanaviseso dissati, tattheva tamatthaṃ vakkhāma. Madhuranti nippariyāyato madhura-saddoyaṃ jivhāviññeyye rasavisese vattati, idha pana iṭṭhabhāvasāmaññena atthabyañjanasampatti madhurasaddena vuttā. Bhavati hi taṃsadisassa taṃ-saddenābhidhānaṃ yathā “aggimāṇavo”ti. Tena pana madhurena yogato idampi madhuraṃ yathā nīlaguṇayogato nīluppalanti. Nipuṇagambhīrāya byañjanasampattiyā ceva atthasampattiyā ca abhidhammavisayaṃ matiṃ vaḍḍhetīti mativaḍḍhanaṃ. Atha vā byañjanasampattiyā “madhura”nti vuttaṃ, atthasampattiyā “mativaḍḍhana”nti.

Thus, here too, dhammas that are extensive are stated, beginning with “he develops the path for the attainment of form, he dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness,” etc. (Dhs. 160 ff.). Also, they are characterized, being distinguishable by object, etc., by the method beginning with “with form as object, or sound as object,” etc. (Dhs. 1). Also, they are honored and worthy of honor by the method beginning with “trainable dhammas, untrainable dhammas, supramundane dhammas,” etc. Also, they are well-defined, being defined by their intrinsic nature by the method beginning with “contact exists, feeling exists,” etc. (Dhs. 1). Also, dhammas that are superior and distinguished are stated by the method beginning with “great dhammas, immeasurable dhammas (Dhs. Tikamātikā 12, Dukamātikā 99), unsurpassable dhammas,” etc. Therefore, because the word ‘abhi-’ functions in the meanings of extensiveness, etc., this collection is called “Abhidhamma” by the explanation: “Herein are the extensive dhammas,” etc. A treatise is called “Abhidhammāvatāra” because one enters into the Abhidhamma by it. Moreover, by this, he shows the designation conforming to the meaning. The particle “tu” is for filling the line. For the teacher often uses particles here and there for the purpose of filling the verse. But wherever a specific purpose of these is seen, there we will explain that meaning. “Madhura” (sweet): this word, in its primary sense, refers to the specific taste knowable by the tongue; but here the accomplishment of meaning and expression by way of shared pleasantness is stated by the word “madhura.” For the designation of something similar by that word occurs, as in “aggimāṇavo.” And by association with that sweetness, this too is “madhura,” just as a blue lotus is “blue” due to its blue quality. Because it increases understanding regarding the Abhidhamma subject matter by the accomplishment of subtle and profound expression, and by the accomplishment of meaning, it is “mativaḍḍhana” (increasing understanding). Or alternatively, by the accomplishment of expression, it is said to be “madhura,” and by the accomplishment of meaning, it is “mativaḍḍhana.”

5. Tāḷanti kuñcikaṃ, kuñcikāsadisanti attho. Muyhanti tenāti moho, avijjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, mohoyeva abhidhammamahāpuraṃ pavisantānaṃ pavesananivāraṇattā kavāṭabhūtoti [V 1.0131] mohakavāṭaṃ, tassa. Vighāṭeti, vighāṭīyati anenāti vā vighāṭanaṃ. Nanu ca avijjākavāṭaṃ paññāya ugghāṭīyati. Sā hi tassā ujuvipaccanīkabhūtāti? Saccaṃ, idampi tassā kāraṇabhāvena “mohakavāṭavighāṭanakara”nti vuttaṃ. Kāraṇakāraṇampi hi kāraṇavasena vuccati yathā “corehi gāmo daḍḍho, tiṇehi bhattaṃ siddha”nti.

5. “Tāḷa” means a key; the meaning is that it is similar to a key. One is deluded by it, hence ‘delusion’ (moha); this is a term for ignorance. Because delusion itself is like a door, preventing the entrance of those entering the great city of the Abhidhamma, it is called the “door of delusion” (mohakavāṭa). “Vighāṭeti” means it opens, or that by which it is opened—thus, an opener. But is not the door of ignorance opened by wisdom? For that is its direct opposite. It is true, even this, because of its causal function, is called “the opener of the door of delusion” (mohakavāṭavighāṭanakara). For even the cause of a cause is spoken of in terms of the cause, just as it is said, “The village was burned by thieves,” or “The meal was cooked with fuel.”

6. Suduttaranti dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhasaṅkhātacatugambhīrabhāvapaṭisaṃyuttatāya mandabuddhīhi tarituṃ asakkuṇeyyattā atiduttaraṃ, teneva cedaṃ mahodadhisamānattā “mahodadhī”ti vuttaṃ. Mahaṇṇavopi hi caturāsītiyojanasahassagambhīro na sakkā aññatra sinerupabbatarājato kenaci patiṭṭhaṃ laddhuṃ, evamidampi catugambhīratāpaṭisaṃyuttaṃ aññatra tathāgatā [M 1.0157] na kenaci patiṭṭhaṃ laddhuṃ sakkāti. Tarantānanti atthaggahaṇavasena uttaritukāmānaṃ. Ettha ca “taraṃvā”ti adhikāravasena vattabbaṃ, vakkhamānaṃ vā ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tarantānanti paratīrasampāpuṇanatthaṃ uttarantānaṃ. Taraṃvāti uḷumpaṃ viya, taṃsamānanti attho. Makarā nāma macchajātikā, tesaṃ ākaro nivāsabhūmīti makarākaro, taṃ.

6. “Suduttara” means extremely difficult to cross because it is associated with the four profound states designated as Dhamma, meaning, exposition, and penetration, which are beyond the capacity of those with weak intellect to traverse. Therefore, it is called “Mahodadhi” (the great ocean) due to its being similar to the great ocean. Just as the great ocean, eighty-four thousand leagues deep, cannot have a firm foundation found by anyone other than Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, so too this Dhamma, being connected with its fourfold profundity, cannot have a firm foundation found by anyone other than the Tathāgata. “Tarantānaṃ” refers to those who wish to cross over by way of understanding the meaning. Here, it should be understood as “taraṃvā” (like a raft) by way of context, or it should be brought in and connected with what is about to be said. “Tarantānaṃ” means those who are crossing over to reach the other shore. “Taraṃvā” is like a raft; the meaning is that it is similar to that. “Makarā” refers to a kind of sea-creature, and “makarākaro” is their dwelling place, the abode of such creatures.

7. Abhidhamme niyuttā ābhidhammikā, tesaṃ. Hatthasāraṃ viyāti hatthasāraṃ. Yathā hi manussānaṃ bahūsu ratanādīsu vijjamānesupi āpadāsu ca sukhaparibhogatthaṃ hatthe kayiramānaṃ sāraratanādikaṃ “hatthasāra”nti vuccati, evamidampi satipi mahante abhidhammapiṭake tassa sabbaso vittiṇṇatāya pariharituṃ asakkuṇeyyattā tadatthasārasampiṇḍanavasena kayiramānaṃ ābhidhammikabhikkhūnaṃ sukhapariharaṇatthāya sampajjatīti hatthasārasadisattā “hatthasāra”nti vuttaṃ. Pavakkhāmīti pakārena kathessāmi, anāgatavacanañcetaṃ, vattamānasamīpattā vā anāgate vattamānūpacārato vattamānavacanaṃ, paṭiññānantarameva vakkhatīti. Atthavasena pakārena kathentopi saddavasena saṅkhipitvā kathessāmīti dassento āha “samāsenā”ti. Samasanaṃ saṃkhipanaṃ samāso, tena samāsena, na byāsavasenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettāvatā ca payojanābhidhānābhidheyyasotujanasamussāhanakaraṇappakārāni dassetvā idāni yasmā sotujanasamussāhanaṃ nāma tesaṃ sakkaccasavane niyuñjanaṃ, tasmā te tattha niyojento āha “taṃ suṇātha samāhitā”ti. Sakkaccasavanapaṭibaddhā hi sammāpaṭipattīti. Tattha tanti taṃ mayā vakkhamānaṃ abhidhammāvatāraṃ suṇātha nisāmayatha. Samāhitā sammā āhitā, avikkhittacittāti attho.

7. Those devoted to the Abhidhamma are the ābhidhammikas; of them. Hatthasāraṃ is like a handful of essence. For just as among the many jewels and other precious things people possess, a choice jewel held in the hand for comfort and enjoyment in times of adversity is called a ‘handful of essence’ (hatthasāra), so too this work, although the Abhidhamma Piṭaka is vast, is prepared as a condensation of its essential meaning for the easy handling of the Abhidhamma bhikkhus, since it is impossible to master it in its entirety. Thus, because it is like a handful of essence, it is called hatthasāra. ‘I will explain’ (pavakkhāmi) means I will speak in detail; this is a future tense verb. Or, because of its proximity to the present, it is a present tense verb used metaphorically for the future, meaning he will speak immediately after the promise. To show that while speaking in detail in terms of meaning, he will speak concisely in terms of words, he says ‘in brief’ (samāsena). Condensing is samāsa; thus, samāsena means ‘in brief,’ not in an expanded way. Having thus shown the purpose, title, subject matter, encouragement of the audience, and method of composition, now, since encouraging the audience means engaging them in attentive listening, in order to engage them in it, he says: ‘Listen to it attentively’ (taṃ suṇātha samāhitā). For right practice is connected to attentive listening. Therein, taṃ means ‘that Abhidhammāvatāra which I am about to explain’; suṇātha means ‘listen, pay heed.’ Samāhitā means ‘well-composed,’ that is, with undistracted minds.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the introduction to the book is finished.

1. Paṭhamo paricchedo

1. The First Chapter

Cittaniddeso

Exposition of Consciousness

Kāmāvacarakusalavaṇṇanā

Explanation of Sense-Sphere Wholesome Consciousness

8. Evaṃ [M 1.0158][V 1.0132] tāva ratanattayappaṇāmādikaṃ dassetvā idāni yathāraddhappakaraṇassa atthasarīrabhūtamabhidhammaṃ saṅkhepato uddisanto āha “cittaṃ cetasika”ntiādi. Tattha cittasaddassa tāva vacanatthaṃ sayameva anantaraṃ vipañceti. “Cetasika”ntiādīsu pana avippayogībhāvena cetasi citte niyuttaṃ, tattha vā bhavaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti cetasikaṃ, vedanādikkhandhattayassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ruppati, rūpīyatīti vā rūpaṃ, sītuṇhādīhi vikāramāpajjati, āpādīyatīti attho, catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ, catuvīsatiupādārūpānañca vasena aṭṭhavīsatividhassa rūpakkhandhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Bhavābhavaṃ vinanato saṃsibbanato vānaṃ vuccati taṇhā, na vijjati sā ettha, tato vā nikkhantaṃ etanti nibbānaṃ, amataṃ asaṅkhataṃ vatthu. Iti-saddo nidassane. Natthi etassa uttaritaroti niruttaro. Atha vā catuvesārajjavihārattā natthi etassa uttaraṃ paccanīkavacananti niruttaro. Ñāṇappahānaantarāyaniyyānikesu hi sadevake loke na koci satthu sahadhammikaṃ uttaraṃ vacanaṃ kathetuṃ samattho atthīti. Tatra bhagavā utrāsābhāvato visāradova hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

8. Having thus first shown the homage to the Triple Gem and so on, now, briefly indicating the Abhidhamma, which is the very substance of the treatise undertaken, he says, ‘consciousness, mental factors,’ and so on. Therein, he first immediately explains the etymological meaning of the word ‘consciousness’ in detail. As for ‘mental factors’ (cetasika) and so on: because of its inseparability, it is associated with consciousness; or because it occurs therein, its existence being dependent on it, it is a mental factor. This is a designation for the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations. ‘Matter’ (rūpa) is so called because ‘it is afflicted’ (ruppati) or ‘it is deformed’ (rūpīyati); it undergoes alteration by cold, heat, and so on—this is the meaning. It is a designation for the aggregate of matter, which consists of twenty-eight kinds: the four great elements and the twenty-four kinds of derived matter. Craving (taṇhā) is called vāna because it weaves or stitches one to existence after existence. That vāna does not exist here, or this has departed from it, thus it is Nibbāna, the deathless, unconditioned state. The word iti is for the purpose of illustration. There is none higher than this, thus he is ‘unsurpassed’ (niruttaro). Or, because he abides in the four kinds of fearlessness, there is no opposing statement that can surpass his, thus he is ‘unsurpassed.’ For in the world with its devas, no one is able to make a justifiable statement surpassing the Teacher’s regarding the things obstructive to knowledge and relinquishment, and the path of deliverance. Therein the Blessed One is indeed fearless, being without trepidation. This has been said by the Blessed One:

“‘Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ime dhammā anabhisambuddhāti tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena paṭicodessatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi, etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

‘Sāriputta, I do not see any ground on which any ascetic or brahmin or deva or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could justly challenge me, saying: “While you claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One, these things have not been fully awakened to by you.” Not seeing any such ground, Sāriputta, I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.’

“Khīṇāsavassa [M 1.0159] te paṭijānato ime āsavā aparikkhīṇāti tatra vata maṃ…pe… viharāmi.

‘“While you claim to be one whose taints are destroyed, these taints of yours are not completely destroyed”: Sāriputta, I do not see any ground... I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.’

“Ye [V 1.0133] ca kho pana te antarāyikā dhammā vuttā, te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyāti tatra vata maṃ…pe… viharāmi.

‘“Those things you have declared to be obstructions are incapable of obstructing one who indulges in them”: Sāriputta, I do not see any ground... I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.’

“Yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desito, so na niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyāti tatra vata maṃ…pe… viharāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.150).

‘“The Dhamma taught by you for a certain purpose does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering”: Sāriputta, I do not see any ground... I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.’ (MN 12)

Cattāri ariyasaccāni pakāsetīti catusaccappakāsano. Dukkhasamudayanirodhamaggavasena hi cattāri ariyasaccāni. Yathāha, “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, ariyasaccāni. Katamāni cattāri? Dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasacca”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1083). Tattha tebhūmakā dhammā anekupaddavādhiṭṭhānatāya dhuvasubhādivirahena, kucchitatucchaṭṭhena ca dukkhaṃ nāma. Kammādivisesapaccayasamavāye dukkhuppattikāraṇabhāvena taṇhā samudayo nāma “samecca udeti dukkhaṃ imasmā”ti katvā. Dukkhassa anuppādanirodhapaccayattā dukkhanirodho nibbānaṃ. Taṃ pana dukkhanirodhaṃ ālambaṇakaraṇavasena gamanato pāpuṇanato, tadadhigamāya paṭipadābhāvato cāti “dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti lokuttaramaggo vuccati. Saccaṭṭho pana tesaṃ tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvato veditabbo. Vuttañhi “‘idaṃ dukkhanti, bhikkhave, tathametaṃ avitathametaṃ anaññathameta”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1090) vitthāro. Ettha pana catunnaṃ ariyaphalānaṃ, ariyamaggasampayuttānañca saccavinissaṭabhāvepi idha magganibbānappakāsanatāvacaneneva tappakāsanatthampi vuttaṃ hoti, anāsavabhāvena [M 1.0160] ekalakkhaṇattā taṃtaṃhetukavisayabhāvato cāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

He proclaims the Four Noble Truths; hence, he is the Proclaimer of the Four Truths (Catusaccappakāsano). For the Four Noble Truths are in terms of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. As it is said: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these Four Noble Truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering’ (SN 56.11). Herein, the phenomena of the three planes are called suffering because they are the basis for many afflictions, are devoid of permanence, pleasure, etc., and have a contemptible and empty nature. Craving is called the origin because, through the convergence of specific conditions such as kamma, it is the cause for the arising of suffering, as it is said: ‘From this, suffering arises after coming together.’ The cessation of suffering is Nibbāna, as it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering. The supramundane path is called ‘the way leading to the cessation of suffering’ because one proceeds towards that cessation of suffering by way of making it an object and reaching it, and because it is the path for its attainment. The truth-nature of these should be understood from their being real, not unreal, and not otherwise. For it was said: ‘“This is suffering,” bhikkhus, this is real, this is not unreal, this is not otherwise’ (SN 56.20), and so on in detail. Here, although the four noble fruits and the factors associated with the noble path are distinct from the truths, by the very statement proclaiming the path and Nibbāna, the purpose of proclaiming them is also stated. This should be understood as being because they have a single characteristic in being untainted, and because they have their respective causes and objects.

Ettha ca “niruttaro catusaccappakāsano”ti imehi bhagavato cittādicatubbidhadhammadesanānukūlaguṇavisesaṃ dasseti atathāvidhassa taṃdesanāsāmatthiyāyogato. Atha vā “niruttaro”ti vacanena catubbidhadhammassa anaññathattaṃ dīpeti. “Catusaccappakāsano”ti pana iminā ye te dhammā bhagavatā vineyyaparipācanatthaṃ desitā, na te idha adhippetā. Ye pana paripācitehi tehi abhisametabbavasena dukkhādayo catubbidhā vuttā, teyeva uddisitabbatthena adhippetāti dasseti.

Here, by the phrase ‘the Unsurpassed Proclaimer of the Four Truths,’ he shows the Blessed One’s special quality that is conducive to teaching the fourfold Dhamma of consciousness, etc., since one who is not of such a nature would be incapable of teaching it. Alternatively, by the word ‘Unsurpassed,’ he indicates the unalterable nature of the fourfold Dhamma. By the phrase ‘Proclaimer of the Four Truths,’ however, he shows that the teachings given by the Blessed One for the sake of maturing the trainees are not intended here. Rather, what is intended are only those fourfold things beginning with suffering, which are said to be realizable by those who have been matured, as they are the things to be pointed out.

Evaṃ [V 1.0134] saṅkhepato cattāro dhamme uddisitvā idāni uddeso nāma niddesatthāya hotīti yathāuddiṭṭhadhamme niddisituṃ “tattha citta”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu cittādīsu dhammesu. Visayavijānanaṃ cittanti yaṃ visayasaṅkhātassa ārammaṇassa vijānanaṃ upaladdhi, taṃ cittanti attho. Iminā pana cittassa ārammaṇapaṭibaddhavuttitaṃ, aniccataṃ, akārakatañca dīpeti. “Visayavijānana”nti hi ārammaṇena cittaṃ upalakkhento tassa tadāyattavuttitaṃ, taṃdīpanena ca tadabhimukhakāleyeva uppattidīpanato aniccabhāvañca dīpeti. Bhāvaniddesena pana vijānanamattadīpanato akārakabhāvaṃ. Yathāpaccayañhi pavattimattamevetaṃ, yadidaṃ sabhāvadhammo nāmāti. Evañca katvā sabbesampi cittacetasikadhammānaṃ bhāvasādhanameva nippariyāyato labbhati. Yaṃ pana “cintetīti cittaṃ, tena cittaṃ vicaratīti vicāro”tiādinā kattukaraṇavasena nibbacanaṃ vuccati, taṃ pariyāyakathananti veditabbaṃ. Sakasakakiccesu hi dhammānaṃ attappadhānatāsamāropanena kattubhāvo, tadanukūlabhāvena taṃsampayuttadhammasamūhe kattubhāvasamāropanena karaṇattañca pariyāyatova [M 1.0161] labbhatīti. Tathā nidassanaṃ pana dhammasabhāvato aññassa kattādino abhāvaparidīpanatthanti veditabbaṃ.

Having thus briefly enumerated the four dhammas, now, since an enumeration is for the purpose of an exposition, the section beginning ‘Therein, consciousness...’ etc., is commenced in order to expound the dhammas as enumerated. ‘Therein’ (tattha) means among those dhammas, consciousness, etc. The knowing of an object is consciousness; that is, the knowing, the cognizing of what is called an object, is consciousness—this is the meaning. By this he shows that consciousness has a nature dependent on an object, that it is impermanent, and that it is not an agent. For by characterizing consciousness as ‘the knowing of an object,’ he indicates that its occurrence is dependent on that object, and by this indication, he also shows its impermanent nature since it arises only at the time it confronts the object. And by the abstract noun formulation, by showing it is mere knowing, he demonstrates its non-agentive nature. For this, which is called a phenomenon with its own nature, is merely an occurrence in accordance with conditions. Thus, the abstract derivation (bhāvasādhana) for all phenomena of consciousness and mental factors is obtained directly, not figuratively. As for the etymology given in terms of agent and instrument, such as ‘it thinks (cinteti), thus it is consciousness (cittaṃ); with it one examines (vicarati), thus it is examination (vicāro)’, this should be understood as a figurative expression. For the state of being an agent is arrived at by superimposing self-dominance upon phenomena in their respective functions, and the state of being an instrument is arrived at only figuratively by superimposing the state of being an agent upon the group of associated phenomena that are conducive to it. Such an illustration, however, should be understood as being for the purpose of showing the absence of any agent, etc., other than the intrinsic nature of the phenomena.

“Visayavijānana”nti ca etena cittassa ārammaṇūpaladdhilakkhaṇatā vuttāti idānissa rasādīni vuccanti. Pubbaṅgamarasañhi cittaṃ sandhānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ nāmarūpapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Dvāraṃ patvā tadārammaṇañhi vibhāvanaṭṭhena cittaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ purecārikaṃ. Tathā hi cakkhudvārena daṭṭhabbaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ citteneva jānāti…pe… manodvārena viññātabbaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ citteneva jānāti. Yathā hi nagaraguttiko nagaramajjhe siṅghāṭake nisīditvā “ayaṃ nevāsiko, ayaṃ āgantuko”ti āgatāgataṃ janaṃ upadhāreti, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tasmā dvāraṃ patvā tadārammaṇaṃ vibhāvanaṭṭhena purecārikanti pubbaṅgamarasaṃ. Pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ uppajjamānaṃ purimaṃ purimaṃ nirantaraṃ katvā sandahamānamiva upaṭṭhāti, gahaṇabhāvaṃ gacchatīti sandhānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Pañcavokāre panassa niyamato nāmarūpaṃ, catuvokārabhave nāmameva padaṭṭhānanti nāmarūpapadaṭṭhānañca hoti. Nānattaṃ pana lakkhaṇādīnaṃ upari vakkhamānanayena veditabbaṃ. Vakkhati hi rūpaparicchede –

By 'cognizing the object,' its characteristic of apprehending an object is stated. Now its function and so on are stated. For the mind has the function of being a forerunner, its manifestation is connecting, and its proximate cause is name-and-form. Having reached a door, the mind is a forerunner, a precursor, in the sense of discerning that object. Thus, through the eye-door, it is by the mind itself that a visible object to be seen is known... through the mind-door, it is by the mind itself that a mental object to be cognized is known. For just as a city guard sitting at a crossroads in the middle of the city investigates the people who come and go, thinking, 'This is a resident, this is a visitor,' so should this point be understood. Therefore, having reached a door, it is a forerunner in the sense of discerning that object; thus its function is that of being a forerunner. It manifests as if connecting, making what arises later continuous with what arose earlier; it comes to a state of grasping, thus its manifestation is connecting. In the five-constituent existence, its proximate cause is invariably name-and-form; in the four-constituent existence, its proximate cause is name alone; thus its proximate cause is name-and-form. The diversity of the characteristics, etc., should be understood according to the method to be explained further on. For it will be said in the chapter on the analysis of form:

“Sāmaññaṃ vā sabhāvo vā, dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ mataṃ;

Kiccaṃ vā tassa sampatti, rasoti paridīpito.

The general or intrinsic nature of phenomena is considered their characteristic; their task or accomplishment is declared to be their function.

“Phalaṃ [V 1.0135] vā paccupaṭṭhānaṃ, upaṭṭhānanayopi vā;

Āsannakāraṇaṃ yaṃ tu, taṃ padaṭṭhānasaññita”nti. (abhidha. 633-634);

Its manifestation is its result or its mode of appearance; and whatever is its immediate cause is designated its proximate cause.

Yattha yattha pana lakkhaṇādīni vuccanti, tattha tattha imināva nayena tesaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Wherever characteristics and so on are mentioned, their diversity should be understood in this very way.

Vacanatthavijānanena viditacittasāmaññassa uttari cittavibhāgo vuccamāno sobheyyāti vacanatthavijānanameva tāva [M 1.0162] ādimhi yuttataranti taṃ tāva kathetukamyatāya pucchati “tassa pana ko vacanattho”ti. Pañcavidhā hi pucchā – (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.449; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.1; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.170) adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā vimaticchedanāpucchā anumatipucchā kathetukamyatāpucchāti. Tattha yaṃ aññātaṃ adiṭṭhaṃ, tassa ñāṇāya dassanāya pañhākaraṇaṃ adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā nāma. Yaṃ pana ñātaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, tassa aññehi paṇḍitehi saṃsandanatthāya pañhākaraṇaṃ diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā nāma. Pakatiyā pana saṃsayapakkhandanassa attano saṃsayasamugghāṭanatthaṃ pañhākaraṇaṃ vimaticchedanāpucchā nāma. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vāti? Aniccaṃ, bhante. Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.79; mahāva. 21) anumatiggahaṇatthaṃ pañhākaraṇaṃ anumatipucchā nāma. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.373; saṃ. ni. 5.402-404) pana taṃtaṃdhammānaṃ desanādhippāyena pañhākaraṇaṃ kathetukamyatāpucchā nāma.

Since a further analysis of mind would be fitting for one who has understood the general nature of mind by understanding the meaning of the word, understanding the meaning of the word is most appropriate at the beginning. Thus, out of a desire to teach, one asks: 'But what is the meaning of the word for it?' For there are five kinds of questions: the question illuminating the unseen, the question for comparing what has been seen, the question for cutting off doubt, the question for approval, and the question out of a desire to teach. Therein: asking a question to know and see what is unknown and unseen is called 'the question illuminating the unseen.' Asking a question to compare what is known and seen with other wise persons is called 'the question for comparing what has been seen.' Asking a question to dispel one's own doubt, for one who is prone to uncertainty, is called 'the question for cutting off doubt.' Asking a question to gain approval, such as: 'What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, venerable sir. But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?' and so on, is called 'the question for approval.' Asking a question with the intention of teaching various dhammas, such as: 'Monks, there are these four establishments of mindfulness. What four?' and so on, is called 'the question out of a desire to teach.'

Tāsu purimā tisso ācariyānaṃ na sambhavanti. Na hi te ganthakaraṇatthāya ārabhitvā idāni adiṭṭhaṃ jotenti, diṭṭhaṃ saṃsandenti, saṃsayaṃ vā pakkhandanti tabbisodhanapubbakameva ganthakaraṇe abhinivesanato. Itarā pana dve sambhavanti. Tāsu ayaṃ kathetukamyatāpucchā. Apica codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpentā ācariyā aññaṃ codakaṃ parikappetvā tassa vacanavasena samuṭṭhāpentīti taṃvasenettha adiṭṭhajotanāvimaticchedanāpucchāpi labbhantevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tassāti tassa citta-saddassa. Citte hi adhigate tassa vācako saddopi sahacariyato adhigatova hotīti tassa idha ta-saddena pariggaho. Keci pana “tassa cittassā”ti atthaṃ vadanti, taṃ “tassa [V 1.0136] ko vacanattho”ti iminā na sameti. Na hi cittassa “ko vacanattho”ti pucchā sambhavatīti.

Among these, the first three are not possible for the authors. For having undertaken the composition of the work, they do not now illuminate what is unseen, compare what has been seen, or dispel doubt, since their devotion to composing the work is preceded by the purification of the subject matter. But the other two are possible. Of these, this is a question out of a desire to teach. Moreover, when the authors raise an objection, they do so by positing another objector and raising it in his words. Therefore, it should be understood that by this means, questions illuminating the unseen and cutting off doubt are also obtained here. 'Of it' (tassa) means: of the word 'citta'. For when the mind is understood, the word that expresses it is also understood through association; hence it is included here by the word 'that' (ta). Some, however, say the meaning is 'of that mind,' but that does not agree with the phrase 'what is the meaning of the word for it?'. For a question 'what is the meaning of the word?' is not possible in regard to the mind itself.

Idāni [M 1.0163] yathāpucchitamatthaṃ vissajjetuṃ “vuccate”ti tāva paṭiññaṃ katvā “sabbasaṅgāhakavasenā”tiādinā vissajjanamāraddhaṃ. Tattha sabbasaṅgāhakavasenāti heṭṭhimantato cakkhuviññāṇādayo upādāya sabbesaṃ ārammaṇavijānanasabhāvattā tesaṃ sabbesameva saṅgāhakavasena, na pana vakkhamānanibbacanesu viya yathālābhavasenāti attho. Cintetīti vijānāti. Cintenti tena gocaranti vā cittaṃ. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ kattutāsamāropanena hissa karaṇabhāvo labbhati. Sabbasaṅgāhakavasena tāva atthaṃ dassetvā idāni yathālābhavasenapi dassetuṃ “attasantānaṃ vā cinotītipī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbacittasādhāraṇattā hi citta-saddassa yattha yattha yathā yathā attho labbhati, tattha tattha tathā tathā gahetabbo. Yassa pana cittassa yathāvuttaatthaviseso na labbhati, taṃ ruḷhīvasena cittanti veditabbaṃ. Yathā kilañjādīhi katampi tālapaṇṇehi katasarikkhakatāya ruḷhīsaddena “tālavaṇṭa”ntveva vuccatīti. Attasantānanti sakasantānaṃ, javanasantānanti attho. Atta-saddassa hi parapaccanīkavacanattā attano santānoti sadisavasena uppajjamāno javanasantāno vuccati. Taṃ cinoti rāsiṃ karotīti ayamattho sāsevanakānaṃ javanacittānaṃ vasena daṭṭhabbo. Tāni hi purejātāni pacchājātānaṃ āsevanapaccayā hutvā attano javanasantānassa paguṇabalavabhāvakaraṇena taṃ cinanti nāma. Vā-saddo asabbasaṅgāhakatthavikappane. Pi-saddo kiriyāsampiṇḍanatthe. Atha vā “sabbasaṅgāhakavasenā”ti imassa idhāpi sambandho hotīti idampi sabbasaṅgāhakavasena vuttanti gayhamāne attasantānanti viññāṇavacanassa atta-saddassa sakatthavuttittāyeva taṃvasena cittasantānanti attho. Anantarādipaccayavasena hi cittasantānassa abbocchinnappavattikaraṇato sabbameva cittajātaṃ cittasantānaṃ cinoti nāma. Imasmiṃ panatthe [M 1.0164] vā-saddo kiriyāvikappanattho. Pi-saddo “citta”nti imassa ākaḍḍhanatthoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Purimapakkhe pana cittanti adhikāratova gahetabbaṃ.

Now, to answer the question asked, having first made the promise 'It is said,' the answer is begun with 'by way of a comprehensive statement,' etc. Herein, 'by way of a comprehensive statement' means by way of including all of them, from eye-consciousness downwards, because they all have the nature of cognizing an object; it does not mean, as in the definitions to be stated, by way of specific application. 'It thinks' (cinteti), that is, it cognizes. Or, 'they think by means of it' or 'they experience an object by means of it'; thus it is mind (citta). For its instrumental nature is obtained by ascribing the agent's role to the associated states. Having first shown the meaning by way of a comprehensive statement, it is now said, 'Or, it accumulates its own continuum,' etc., in order to show it also by way of specific application. For since the word 'mind' is common to all consciousness, in whatever way a meaning is obtained for it, it should be taken in that way. But when a particular meaning as stated is not obtained for a certain mind, it should be understood as 'mind' by convention, just as something made with reeds, etc., is called a 'palm-leaf fan' by convention because it is made similar to one made of palm leaves. 'Its own continuum' (attasantāna) means one's own continuum, that is, the continuum of impulsion (javana). For since the word 'atta' (self) is used in opposition to 'other,' the continuum of impulsion, arising in a similar way, is called 'one's own continuum.' 'It accumulates it' means it makes a collection. This meaning should be seen by way of the impulsion-moments of consciousness accompanied by repetition. For by being a repetition condition for the later-born moments, the earlier-born moments make their own continuum of impulsion proficient and strong, and thus they are said to 'accumulate' it. The particle 'or' (vā) indicates an alternative meaning that is not comprehensive. The particle 'also' (pi) is for the purpose of summing up the action. Or, if the phrase 'by way of a comprehensive statement' is connected here too, then this too is said comprehensively. In that case, 'its own continuum' (attasantāna) means 'the continuum of mind' (cittasantāna), because the word 'atta', which can express consciousness, has the meaning of 'own'. For by causing the uninterrupted flow of the continuum of mind by means of the contiguity condition, etc., the entire class of mind is said to 'accumulate' the continuum of mind. In this meaning, the particle 'or' serves to indicate an alternative action. The particle 'also' should be seen as drawing in the word 'mind.' In the first alternative, however, 'mind' should be taken from the context.

9. Vicittaṃ karoti, vicittassa vā karaṇanti vicittakaraṇaṃ, tato vicittakaraṇā, vicittacittakammādīnaṃ karaṇatoti attho. Lokasmiñhi yaṃ kiñci cittakammādibhedaṃ vicittaṃ sippajātaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ citteneva cintetvā karīyatīti. Tenāha bhagavā – “diṭṭhaṃ vo, bhikkhave[V 1.0137], caraṇaṃ nāma cittanti? Evaṃ, bhante. Tampi kho, bhikkhave, caraṇaṃ nāma cittaṃ citteneva cintita”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.100). Svāyamattho saviññattikānaṃ bāttiṃsacittānamupalabbhati. Sāsavakusalākusalaṃ vā vicittagatiādikaraṇato vā vicittakaraṇaṭṭhena cittaṃ. Nanu ca vicittagatiādayo kammavasena nipphajjanti. Yathāha –

9. It makes things variegated, or it is the making of the variegated, thus it is 'variegated-making.' From that, 'because of making variegated.' The meaning is that it is the cause of variegated works of art, etc. For in the world, whatever kind of variegated craft there is, all that is done after having been devised by the mind. Thus the Blessed One said: 'Monks, have you seen the painting called "The Show"? ' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'Monks, that painting called "The Show" was devised by the mind.' This meaning is found in the thirty-two minds accompanied by intimation. Or, mind that is wholesome or unwholesome and connected with the taints is 'mind' in the sense of making things variegated because it creates variegated destinations, etc. But are not variegated destinations and so on produced by means of kamma? As it is said:

“Kammanānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca sattānaṃ gatiyā nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati apadā dvipadā catuppadā bahuppadā rūpino arūpino saññino asaññino nevasaññīnāsaññino, kammanānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca sattānaṃ upapattiyā nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati uccanīcatā hīnapaṇītatā sugataduggatatā, kammanānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca sattānaṃ attabhāve nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇatā sujātadujjātatā susaṇṭhitadussaṇṭhitatā, kammanānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca sattānaṃ lokadhamme nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati lābhālābhe yasāyase nindāpasaṃsāyaṃ sukhadukkhe”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1).

Dependent on the diversity of kamma, a diversity in the destination of beings is discerned: footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed; with form, without form; percipient, non-percipient, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. Dependent on the diversity of kamma, a diversity in the rebirth of beings is discerned: high and low, base and superior, good and bad destinations. Dependent on the diversity of kamma, a diversity in the individual existence of beings is discerned: beauty and ugliness, good birth and bad birth, being well-formed and ill-formed. Dependent on the diversity of kamma, a diversity in the worldly conditions of beings is discerned: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.

Tasmā kammabhedanibbattattā gatiādīnaṃ cittatā. Kammanti ca cetasikadhammabhūtā cetanā, abhijjhādayo ca vuccanti, na cittanti. Kathaṃ cittassa vicittagatiādikaraṇanti? Vuccate [M 1.0165] – kammassa cittasannissitattā tannipphāditampi citteneva kataṃ hoti, yathā rājayodhena parājito satturaññā jitoti vuccati. Vicittaṃ karaṇamassāti vā vicittakaraṇaṃ. Tato ekaṭṭhānikavajjitañhi cittaṃ paccekaṃ paṭisandhādivicittakiriyavantatāya, sabbameva vā cittaṃ āvajjanādiaññamaññavisadisakiriyavantatāya vicittakaraṇaṃ yuttanti. Sabbavikappesupi “rūpabhavo rūpa”ntiādīsu viya uttarapadalopo cittapariyāyena ca vicitta-saddena vā viggaho vi-saddalopo vā daṭṭhabbo. Atha vā “vicittakaraṇā”ti idaṃ cittavicittabhāvassa ñāpakahetunidassanaṃ. Tena yasmā idaṃ vicittakaraṇaṃ, tasmā tassa vicittassa nipphādakaṃ sayampi tatheva vicittanti viññātabbanti evaṃ karaṇavicittatāya vicittattā cittanti attho. Ṭhapetvā taṃ karaṇavicittatāya vicittabhāvaṃ attano eva jātibhūmisampayogādivasena vicittatāya cittanti dassento āha “attano cittatāya vā”ti. Tattha yasmā aññadeva kusalaṃ, aññaṃ akusalaṃ, aññaṃ abyākataṃ, aññaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ, aññaṃ rūpāvacarādibhedaṃ, aññaṃ sarāgaṃ, aññaṃ vītarāgaṃ, aññaṃ sadosaṃ, aññaṃ vītadosaṃ, aññaṃ samohaṃ, aññaṃ vītamohaṃ, aññaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ, aññaṃ saddādiārammaṇaṃ, rūpārammaṇesu ca aññaṃ nīlārammaṇaṃ, aññaṃ [V 1.0138] pītādiārammaṇaṃ. Evaṃ saddārammaṇādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ. Sabbesu ceva tesu aññaṃ hīnaṃ, aññaṃ majjhimaṃ, aññaṃ paṇītaṃ, hīnādīsu ca aññaṃ chandādhipateyyaṃ, aññaṃ cittādhipateyyaṃ, aññaṃ vīriyādhipateyyaṃ, aññaṃ vīmaṃsādhipateyyanti evamādinā jātibhūmisampayuttaārammaṇahīnamajjhimapaṇītaadhipatiādīnaṃ vasena vicittamanekappakāraṃ, tasmā imāya attavicittatāya vā cittanti vuccatīti.

Therefore, because of the diversity of kamma producing the variegatedness of destinies and so on, it is called 'citta' (mind). And 'kamma' refers to volition (cetanā), which is a mental factor, as well as covetousness and so on, not the mind itself. How then does the mind create variegated destinations and so on? It is said—because kamma is dependent on the mind, what is produced by it is also done by the mind, just as an enemy defeated by a king's soldier is said to have been defeated by the king. Or, 'vicittakaraṇaṃ' means diverse functioning. Since the mind, being devoid of a single state, individually performs diverse functions such as rebirth-linking and so on, or because all minds engage in distinct functions like adverting (āvajjanā) and others, it is appropriate to call it 'vicittakaraṇaṃ' (diverse functioning). And in all such derivations, like "form-existence is form" etc., the elision of the latter word, or the derivation by a synonym for 'citta' or by the word 'vicitta' with the elision of the prefix 'vi-', should be understood. Alternatively, 'because of making variegated' here exemplifies the cause revealing the diverse nature of the mind. Therefore, because this makes things variegated, the mind itself, being the producer of that diversity, is likewise diverse. Thus, it is called 'citta' due to being variegated through its function. Setting aside that variegatedness due to its function, the mind is also called 'citta' due to its own diverse nature arising from class, plane, association, etc. Hence, it is said: "or due to its own diverse nature." Here, one is wholesome, another unwholesome, another indeterminate; one belongs to the sense-sphere, another to the form-sphere, etc.; one is with lust, another without lust; one is with hatred, another without hatred; one is with delusion, another without delusion; one has a form as object, another has sound, etc., as object. Among form-objects, one has blue as object, another yellow, etc. Similarly, among sound-objects, etc., as appropriate. Among all these, one is inferior, another middling, another superior. Among the inferior, etc., one is with zeal as dominant, another with mind as dominant, another with energy as dominant, another with investigation as dominant, and so on. Thus, due to class, plane, association, object, inferiority, middlingness, superiority, dominance, etc., the mind is manifoldly diverse. Therefore, it is called 'citta' due to this intrinsic diversity.

Kāmañcettha ekameva cittaṃ evaṃ vicittaṃ nāma na hoti, vicittānaṃ pana antogadhattā etesu yaṃ kiñci ekampi vicittatāya [M 1.0166] cittanti vattuṃ vaṭṭati samudāyavohārena avayavassāpi vohariyamānattā yathā pabbatanadīsamuddādīnamekadesā diṭṭhā pabbatādayo diṭṭhāti, yathā ca ekekacittasampayuttāpi vedanādayo rāsaṭṭhena khandhavohārena “vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho”tiādinā vuccanti. Apicettha vipākaviññāṇaṃ kammakilesehi citanti cittaṃ, taṃ kilesasahāyena kammunā phalabhāvena nibbattitaṃ tehi citaṃ nāma hoti. Hotu tāvidaṃ lokiyavipākaṃ sandhāya, lokuttaraṃ pana patvā kathanti? Vuccate – “katame dhammā kusalā, yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti…pe… tasmiṃ samaye avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā ariyamaggacetanāyapi avijjūpanissayabhāvassa pakāsitattā lokuttarakusalassāpi anusayā upanissayā hontīti tannibbattitassa vipākassa kammakilesasañcitatāpariyāyo labbhatīti. Citaṃ tāyatīti vā cittaṃ. Kammādisañcitopi hi attabhāvo viññāṇūparame matoti vuccati. Yathāha –

Indeed, here a single mind is not thus variegated. However, because of being included within variegated states, any single one of them can be spoken of as "variegated mind," due to the use of conventional collective speech, just as parts are also spoken of conventionally. For example, when a part of a mountain, river, or ocean is seen, it is said that the mountain, etc., is seen. Similarly, even feelings and other states associated with a single mind are referred to collectively by way of aggregate as "the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception," and so on. Moreover, here, resultant consciousness is called "mind" because it is accumulated (citaṃ) by kamma and defilements. That which is produced as a result by kamma accompanied by defilements, is said to be accumulated by them. So be it with mundane results. But having attained the supramundane, how is it then? It is said: "Which states are wholesome? At the time when a supramundane wholesome mind arises... conditioned by ignorance, formations," etc. Because even the noble path volition reveals dependence on ignorance as its strong support, even the supramundane wholesome states have latent tendencies as their strong supports. Thus, the way the resultant produced by them is accumulated by kamma and defilements can be understood. Alternatively, "mind" (citta) is so called because it protects what has been accumulated. For even the individual existence accumulated by kamma and so on is said to be dead when consciousness ceases. As it is said—

“Āyu usmā ca viññāṇaṃ, yadā kāyaṃ jahantimaṃ;

Appaviddho tadā seti, niratthaṃva kaliṅgara”nti. (saṃ. ni. 3.95);

Life, heat, and consciousness, when they abandon this body, it lies discarded, like a useless log.

So panāyaṃ citta-saddo kiñcāpi anekatthesu dissati. Tathā hesa “citto ca gahapatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 2.133; 4.176) paññattiyaṃ āgato. “Sabbo loko paracittena acitto”tiādīsu viññāṇe. “Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekanikāyampi samanupassāmi, evaṃ citta”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.100) vicitte, nānappakāreti attho. “Caraṇaṃ nāma citta”ntiādīsu cittakammake. Idha pana catubbidhadhamme niddesato pakaraṇavasena yathāvuttavacanatthayutto viññāṇavacanova daṭṭhabboti imamatthaṃ dassento āha “paññattiyampī”tiādi[V 1.0139]. Paññāpīyati etāyāti [M 1.0167] paññatti, tassaṃ nāmapaññattiyanti attho. Cittoti hi ekassa gahapatino nāmaṃ. Pi-saddo vakkhamānasampiṇḍanattho. Viññāṇeti savipākāvipākabhede citte. Tañhi vijānanaṭṭhena “viññāṇa”nti vuccati. Yathāha – “vijānātīti kho, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṃ, tasmā viññāṇanti vuccatī”ti. Cittasammutīti cittavohāro. Daṭṭhabbāti viññātabbā. Idhāti imasmiṃ catubbidhadhammaniddesaṭṭhāne. Viññunāti vijānatā, ābhidhammikenāti attho.

This term “citta,” indeed, is found in various contexts. For example, in expressions like “Citto the householder,” it refers to a designation. In phrases such as “The whole world is without a mind of its own,” it denotes consciousness. In statements like “Monks, I do not perceive even one single group so variegated,” it signifies variety, meaning multiplicity. In contexts like “The painting called 'Caraṇa',” it pertains to a work of art. Here, however, in the description of the fourfold Dhamma, it should be understood in the sense of consciousness, according to the meaning of the words spoken in context. To clarify this meaning, it is stated, “even in designation,” etc. “Designation” (paññatti) means that by which something is designated; here, it refers to name-designation. For instance, “Citto” is the name of a certain householder. The particle “pi” has the meaning of collecting what is to be stated. “Consciousness” (viññāṇa) refers to citta in the distinction of resultant and non-resultant types. It is called “viññāṇa” because of its characteristic of cognizing, as stated: “Monks, it cognizes, therefore it is called consciousness.” “Conventional usage of citta” (cittasammuti) means the common expression for citta. “Should be seen” means should be understood. “Here” refers to this place of describing the fourfold Dhamma. “By the wise” means by one who understands, that is, by an Abhidhamma scholar.

Vibhāgavantānaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvavibhāvanaṃ vibhāgena vinā na hotīti cittassa vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “sārammaṇato”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ālambanti taṃ nissāya pavattantīti ārammaṇaṃ, paccayo, gocaro ca. Tathā hi “labhati māro ārammaṇaṃ, labhati māro otāra”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.80) paccayo “ārammaṇa”nti vuccati. “Nimittaṃ assāsapassāsā, anārammaṇamekacittassā”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.159) gocaro. Idha pana ubhayampi vaṭṭati sabbasseva cittassa sappaccayasagocarattā. Saha ārammaṇena vattati tadavinābhāvatoti sārammaṇaṃ. Bhāvappadhānaniddesavasena cettha sārammaṇabhāvo sārammaṇa-saddena vutto yathā “idampi buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ (khu. pā. 6.3). Cakkhu suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.85) ratanaattattaniyādibhāvo ratanādīhi saddehīti, tato sārammaṇabhāvatoti attho. Evamaññatthāpi yathānurūpaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ekavidhanti ekappakāraṃ, ekakoṭṭhāsanti attho.

The clarification of the intrinsic nature of phenomena that have divisions cannot occur without division. Therefore, to show the division of consciousness, terms such as ‘with an object’ and so on are introduced. Herein, ‘object’ (ārammaṇa) refers to that upon which the mind relies and operates in dependence—it is a condition (paccayo) and a sphere (gocaro). For instance, in passages like ‘Māra gains an object, Māra gains an opening’ (Dīgha Nikāya 3.80), the term ‘object’ is used to denote a condition. In phrases such as ‘The sign is in-breath and out-breath, without an object for a single mind’ (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.159), it refers to a sphere. Here, however, both meanings are applicable, since all consciousness operates with conditions and within a sphere. ‘With an object’ (sārammaṇa) means that it functions together with an object, being inseparable from it. In this context, the state of having an object (sārammaṇabhāvo) is conveyed by the term ‘sārammaṇa’ by way of a designation where the state is primary, just as in passages like ‘This too is the sublime jewel in the Buddha’ (Khp 6.3) and ‘The eye is empty of self or what belongs to self’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.85), the state of being a jewel, self, or belonging to self is expressed by the words ‘jewel,’ ‘self,’ etc. Thus, the meaning here is ‘from the state of having an object.’ Similarly, in other cases, the meaning should be understood accordingly. ‘Onefold’ (ekavidhaṃ) means of one kind; the meaning is ‘of one category’ (ekakoṭṭhāsaṃ).

Savipākāvipākatoti vipākuppādanasabhāvassa vijjamānāvijjamānabhāvato. Vipāka-saddo hi dvīsu atthesu pavattati. Katthaci vipakkabhāvamāpannesu arūpadhammesu, katthaci vipākuppādanasabhāve[M 1.0168]. Tathā hesa “vipākā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. tikamātikā 3) vipakkabhāvamāpannesu arūpadhammesu pavattati. “Vipākadhammadhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. tikamātikā 3) vipākuppādanasabhāve. Idha pana vipākuppādanasabhāvo daṭṭhabbo. Itarathā hi abhiññākusalādīnaṃ savipāka-pade asaṅgahitabhāvāpatti siyā. Tathā hi yadi vipakkabhāvamāpannā eva dhammā idha gahitā siyuṃ, te yassa santi, taṃ savipākamitaramavipākanti abhiññākusalassa ceva kadāci avipākassa diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādikammassa bhāvanāyapahātabbākusalassa ca vipākuppattiyā abhāvato avipāka-padasaṅgaho siyā, evañca [V 1.0140] sati “avipākaṃ abyākata”nti vakkhamānattā nesaṃ abyākatabhāvo āpajjati, na cetamiṭṭhaṃ kusalākusalaniddeseyeva tesaṃ niddesato. Vipākuppādanasabhāve pana gahite taṃsabhāvo nāma anupacchinnāvijjamānataṇhānusayasmiṃ santāne sabyāpārappavatti evāti tassā tesupi atthitāya asatipi vipākuppādane savipāka-padasaṅgaho siddhoti na koci iṭṭhavighāto āpajjati. Yena pana kāraṇena abhiññākusalādikamavipākaṃ, yo cettha vattabbo vinicchayo, taṃ sabbaṃ tassa tassa āgataṭṭhāneyeva dassayissāma.

Having a result and being resultless is due to the presence or absence of the nature of producing a result. For the term ‘vipāka’ operates in two senses: sometimes with regard to non-material states that have reached the state of being a result, and sometimes with regard to the nature of producing a result. Thus, in phrases like ‘resultant states,’ it operates with regard to non-material states that have reached the state of being a result. In phrases like ‘states that produce resultant states,’ it operates with regard to the nature of producing a result. Here, however, the nature of producing a result should be understood. Otherwise, the fault would arise that things like the wholesome states of direct knowledge would not be included under the term ‘having a result.’ For if only states that have reached the state of being a result were taken here, then whatever has them would be ‘having a result,’ and the rest would be ‘resultless.’ Thus, the wholesome states of direct knowledge, the kamma to be experienced in this very life which is sometimes resultless, and the unwholesome states to be abandoned by development—since they lack the production of a result—would be included under the term ‘resultless.’ And this being so, since it will be said that ‘the resultless is indeterminate,’ their indeterminate nature would follow, which is not desirable, since their designation is precisely as wholesome and unwholesome. But when the nature of producing a result is taken, that nature is indeed an active occurrence in a continuum where the latent tendency of craving is present and has not been cut off. Since this nature exists in them too, even when a result is not being produced, their inclusion under the term ‘having a result’ is established, and thus no undesirable consequence arises. As for the reason why the wholesome states of direct knowledge, etc., are resultless, and the judgment to be made here, we will explain all that in its respective place.

Katamaṃ panettha savipākaṃ, katamamavipākanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “tattha savipāka”ntiādi. Abyākatanti vipākakiriyāvasena duvidhamabyākataṃ. Tesu vipākacittaṃ tāva ādāsatale mukhanimittaṃ viya nirussāhattā vipākuppādane asamatthaṃ. Kiriyacittesu ca yadetaṃ khīṇāsavasantāneyeva niyatamaṭṭhārasavidhaṃ viññāṇaṃ, taṃ upacchinnabhavamūlāya santatiyaṃ pavattatīti samucchinnamūlāya latāya pupphaṃ [M 1.0169] viya phaladāyī na hoti. Āvajjanadvayaṃ pana anupacchinnabhavamūlepi santāne pavattamānaṃ anāsevanabhāvena dubbalattā moghapupphamiva bījabhāve asamatthaṃ aphalameva. Iti sabbametaṃ abyākataṃ vipākārahatābhāvato avipākanti vuttaṃ “avipākaṃ abyākata”nti. Jāyanti ettha asadisāpi sadisākārāti jāti, samānākāro, kusalākusalābyākatānaṃ jāti kusalākusalābyākatajāti, tassā bhedato tividhaṃ kusalaṃ akusalaṃ abyākatanti. Vacanatthapucchāya payojanaṃ vuttameva.

In reference to the question, “Herein, what is with result, and what is without result?” the text states, “Therein, with result,” etc. The indeterminate is twofold by way of resultant and functional. Among these, resultant consciousness, like the reflection of a face on a mirror’s surface, is incapable of producing a result because of its lack of initiative. As for functional consciousness, the eighteen types of consciousness that are fixed only in the continuum of those whose taints are destroyed—these occur in a continuity whose root of existence is severed. Like a flower on a vine whose root is cut, they do not bear fruit. The two adverting consciousnesses, though occurring in a continuity whose root of existence is not severed, are weak due to not being cultivated. Like a barren flower, they are incapable of being a seed and thus yield no fruit. Therefore, all this indeterminate is called ‘resultless’ due to its inability to produce a result; hence it is said, “the resultless is indeterminate.” Here, ‘jāti’ (class) means that even dissimilar things arise with a similar appearance, hence ‘jāti,’ meaning a similar appearance. The ‘class’ of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate is the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate ‘class’; and by its division, it is threefold: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. The purpose in questioning the meaning of the words has already been stated.

10. “Kucchitāna”ntiādi vissajjanaṃ. Tattha kucchitānanti ninditānaṃ, asuci viya nāgarikehi viññūhi garahitabbānaṃ pāpadhammānanti attho. Salanatoti hiṃsanato, apanayanato vā. Kusalañhi yathānurūpaṃ tadaṅgādivasena akusaladhamme pajahantaṃ te hiṃsati, apanayatīti vā vuccati. Atha vā salanato saṃvaraṇato, pidahanatoti attho. Kusaladhammavasena hi akusalappavattinivāraṇena, appavattidhammatāpādanena ca manacchaṭṭhesu dvāresu appavattiyā saṃvutā pihitā honti. Kusānanti rāgādiasucisampayogena nānāvidhadukkhahetutāya ca kucchitenākārena appahīnabhāvena santāne sayanti pavattantīti kusā, pāpadhammā. Atha vā kucchitānaṃ pāṇātipātādīnaṃ sāvajjadhammānaṃ sānato nisānato tejanato kusā, dosalobhādayo. Dosādīnañhi vasena cetanāya tikkhabhāvappattiyā pāṇātipātādīnaṃ mahāsāvajjatāti. Tesaṃ lavanena chindanena yathānurūpaṃ pajahanenāti attho. Kusenāti kucchitānaṃ sānato tanukaraṇato, osānakaraṇato [V 1.0141] vā “kusā”ti laddhanāmena ñāṇena. Lātabbattāti ādātabbattā, sahajātaupanissayabhāvena santāne pavattetabbattā. Ñāṇañhi tihetukakusalaṃ sahajātabhāvena [M 1.0170] ceva upanissayabhāvena ca, duhetukakusalaṃ upanissayabhāveneva santāne pavatteti. Evañca katvā kosallasambhūtaṭṭho kusalaṭṭhoti sabbakusalānaṃ sādhāraṇavasena attho vuccati. Atha vā kusenāti jātisaddatāya ekavacananiddeso, kusehīti pana attho. Puññakiriyāvasena hi pavattāni saddhādīni indriyāni yathāvuttanayena “kusānī”ti vuccanti, tehi lātabbattā vuttanayena pavattetabbattā. Apicettha –

10. The explanation begins with ‘kucchitānaṃ.’ Here, ‘kucchitānaṃ’ means of the blameworthy, that is, of evil states that are to be censured by the discerning, like impure things by city dwellers. ‘Salanato’ means from injuring or from removing. For the wholesome, in accordance with its nature, by way of its factors and so on, in abandoning unwholesome states, is said to injure or remove them. Alternatively, ‘salanato’ means from restraining or from concealing.
