For by means of wholesome states, through preventing the arising of unwholesome states and bringing about their non-arising, those unwholesome states are restrained and closed off in the six doors, with the mind as the sixth. ‘Kusā’ are evil states because they lie (sayanti) and proceed in the continuum, not being abandoned, in a blameworthy (kucchita) manner, due to their association with defilements like greed and being the cause of various sufferings. Alternatively, ‘kusā’ are hate, greed, etc., because they sharpen (sānato, nisānato, tejanato) blameworthy (kucchita) states like killing, etc. For through the intensity of volition influenced by hate, etc., acts like killing become greatly blameworthy. ‘Lavanena’ means by their cutting off, by their abandoning according to suitability. ‘Kusena’ means by the knowledge (ñāṇa) that has obtained the name ‘kusa’ because it sharpens (sānato), i.e., diminishes or brings to an end, the blameworthy states. ‘Lātabbattā’ means because it is fit to be taken up, fit to be established in the continuity through co-nascence and decisive support. For three-rooted wholesome states are established in the continuity both through co-nascence and decisive support, while two-rooted wholesome states are established only through decisive support. And having done so, the meaning of ‘kusala’ as ‘arisen from skill’ (kosallasambhūta) is stated as the common meaning for all wholesome states. Alternatively, ‘kusena’ is a singular expression of the generic word ‘kusa,’ but the meaning is ‘by the kusas.’ For the faculties like faith, etc., which arise through meritorious activity, are called ‘kusāni’ in the way stated—because they are fit to be brought forth (lātabbattā) by them (tehi) in the manner described. Moreover, here—

“Kuso viya lunātīti, kusā viya lunāti vā;

Kusalaṃ kuṃ saletīti, lunāti kusamiccapī”ti.

“It cuts like kusa grass, or it cuts the evil states (kusā); it removes evil, or it cuts evil—thus it is called kusala.”

Tattha yathā kuso gahito ubhayabhāgagataṃ hatthapadesaṃ lunāti, evamidampi uppannānuppannavasena ubhayabhāgagataṃ kilesapakkhaṃ lunāti chindati, seyyathāpi – “anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, uppannānaṃ…pe… pahānāyā”ti āgataṃ sammappadhānaṃ. Tasmā kuso viya lunātīti kusalaṃ. Kusā viya lunātīti ettha “ku”iti bhūmi vuccati, dhammānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhāvena taṃsadisatāya idha rūpārūpakkhandho vutto. Attano nissayabhūtassa tassa etarahi, āyatiñca anudahanato vināsanato kuṃ sāyantīti kusā, rāgādayo, te viya attano nissayaṃ lunāti chindatīti kusalaṃ. Payogasampāditā hi kusaladhammā accantameva rūpārūpadhamme appavattikaraṇena samucchindanti anupādisesanibbānadhātupāpanatoti. Vuttanayena pana “ku”nti laddhanāmassa rūpārūpakkhandhassa salanato apanayanato kuṃ saletīti kusalaṃ. Kusaṃ lunātīti pana kucchitā ettha sayantīti kuso, kāyo, taṃ lunāti yathāvuttavasenevāti kusalaṃ.

Here, just as a blade of kusa grass, when grasped, cuts the hand on both sides, so too does this cut and sever the defilements on both sides—those arisen and unarisen—just as it is said: "One generates desire, makes effort, for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, for the abandoning of arisen ones..." Thus, it is called 'wholesome' (kusala) because it cuts like kusa grass (kusa). In the phrase 'it cuts like kusā,' 'ku' refers to the earth, called so because it serves as the foundation for things, and here it denotes the form and formless aggregates due to their similar nature. Lust and so on are called 'kusā' because they presently and in the future wear away and destroy the 'ku' which is their own foundation. Like them, this wholesome state cuts and severs its own foundation, and is therefore called 'kusala'. Indeed, wholesome states, when fully developed, utterly destroy form and formless phenomena by preventing their recurrence, leading to the attainment of the Nibbāna element without residue. Alternatively, in the way described, the form and formless aggregate, which has acquired the name 'ku,' is called 'wholesome' (kusala) because it removes and strips away (salana) the 'ku.' Moreover, 'cutting the kusa grass' (kusaṃ lunāti) here refers to the body, called 'kusa' because wretched things (kucchitā) lie (sayanti) in it. It is cut in the manner described, hence it is called 'wholesome' (kusala).

11. Idāni [M 1.0171] kusala-saddassa atthuddhāradassanatthamāha “cheke kusala-saddoya”ntiādi. Tattha “kusalo tvaṃ rathassa aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ (ma. ni. 2.87), kusalānaccagītassa, sikkhitā cāturitthiyo”tiādīsu (jā. 2.22.94) cheke diṭṭho, chekapariyāyo pavīṇatthoti attho. “Kacci nu bhoto kusalaṃ, kacci bhoto anāmaya”ntiādīsu (jā. 1.15.146; 2.20.129) ārogye. “Katamo pana, bhante, kāyasamācāro kusalo? Yo kho, mahārāja, kāyasamācāro [V 1.0142] anavajjo”ti (ma. ni. 2.361) ca “aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti kusalesu dhammesū”ti (dī. ni. 3.145) ca evamādīsu anavajje. “Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samādānahetu evamidaṃ puññaṃ vaḍḍhati (dī. ni. 3.80), kusalassa kammassa katattā upacitattā”ti (dha. sa. 431) ca ādīsu iṭṭhavipāke. Anavajjādiketi anavajjaiṭṭhavipāke, “anavajjādike”ti ca attanā vakkhamānalakkhaṇassa anurūpattā vuttaṃ, na pana ārogyatthassa asambhavato. Kilesarogassa hi abhāvato kusalaṃ ārogyaṃ hoti.

11. Now, to clarify the meaning of the word "kusala," it is said: "cheke kusala-saddoya" and so on. Here, in phrases like "you are skilled in the parts and accessories of the chariot" (Majjhima Nikāya 2.87), "skilled in dancing and singing," and "the four women were trained" (Jātaka 2.22.94), it is seen in the sense of 'skilled' (cheka), meaning that 'skilled' is a synonym for 'proficient.' In expressions like "I hope you are well, sir, I hope you are free from illness" (Jātaka 1.15.146; 2.20.129), it refers to health. In passages such as "What, venerable sir, is skillful bodily conduct? Great king, bodily conduct that is blameless" (Majjhima Nikāya 2.361) and "Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed—how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding skillful qualities" (Dīgha Nikāya 3.145), it denotes blamelessness. In statements like "Because of undertaking skillful qualities, this merit grows" (Dīgha Nikāya 3.80) and "due to having done and accumulated skillful deeds" (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 431), it refers to desirable results. Thus, 'in the sense of blameless, etc.' means in the sense of blamelessness and desirable results. And 'in the sense of blameless, etc.' is said because it is suitable for the characteristic about to be stated, not because the meaning of health is impossible. For the absence of the disease of defilements is itself the health of what is skillful.

Vajjā rāgādayo, te yassa na santi, taṃ anavajjaṃ, iṭṭho vipāko catukkhandhasaṅkhāto yassa, taṃ iṭṭhavipākaṃ, iṭṭhavipākatā cassa taṃsabhāvavantatāya daṭṭhabbā, na tassa avassaṃ iṭṭhavipākasambhavatoyeva, lakkhīyati anenāti lakkhaṇaṃ, anavajjañca taṃ iṭṭhavipākañcāti anavajjaiṭṭhavipākaṃ. Taṃ lakkhaṇamassāti anavajjaiṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ.

Faults are lust and the like; that in which these are not present is blameless. That which has a desirable result, reckoned as the four aggregates, is 'that with a desirable result'. The state of having a desirable result should be regarded as its inherent nature, not merely as invariably producing a desirable result. A mark by which something is characterized is a characteristic. That which is blameless and has a desirable result is 'blameless-with-desirable-result.' Its characteristic is 'the characteristic of being blameless and having a desirable result'.

Nanu ca kusalameva anavajjaiṭṭhavipākaṃ, vuttaniyāmena pana anavajjaiṭṭhavipākato aññaṃ kusalaṃ siyā. Na hi sayameva attano lakkhaṇanti sakkā vattunti? Nāyaṃ doso pariññātāpariññātavacanatthabhāvabhede [M 1.0172] ekassāpi lakkhitabbalakkhaṇabhāvaparikappanato. “Anavajjaiṭṭhavipāka”nti hi pariññātavacanatthaṃ. “Kusala”nti apariññātavacanatthaṃ. Evañca yena sabhāvena pariññātavacanatthassa saddassa attho hoti, yena ca apariññātavacanatthassa, tesaṃ pariññātāpariññātavacanatthasabhāvānaṃ bhedena taṃsamaṅgissa kusalassa ekassāpi bhedo parikappīyati yathā “pure bhavaṃ paṭu āsi, paṭutaro etarahī”ti guṇabhedena, vatthubhedena ca parikappīyati, tasmā pariññātavacanatthabhāvena lakkhaṇaṃ, apariññātavacanatthabhāvena lakkhitabbanti evaṃ parikappitabhede pariggayhamāne na koci doso āpajjati.

Is it not so that the wholesome itself is that which is blameless and has a desirable result? But according to the stated rule, the wholesome would be something other than that which is blameless and has a desirable result. For can it be said that something is its own characteristic? This is not a fault, because of the distinction between the state of a term having a fully known meaning and a not fully known meaning, the state of being the characteristic and the thing-to-be-characterized can be conceived even for a single thing. For 'blameless-with-desirable-result' is a term with a fully known meaning. 'Wholesome' is a term with a not fully known meaning. And thus, by whatever nature the meaning of the term with a fully known meaning exists, and by whatever nature the meaning of the term with a not fully known meaning exists, due to the distinction between the natures of these terms with fully known and not fully known meanings, a distinction is conceived even in a single wholesome state which possesses both—just as one might say, 'formerly the venerable one was sharp, now he is sharper,' distinguishing by quality, or distinguishing by substance. Therefore, the characteristic is by the nature of the term with a fully known meaning, and the characterized is by the nature of the term with a not fully known meaning. When the distinction conceived in this way is grasped, no fault is incurred.

Atha vā lakkhīyatīti lakkhaṇaṃ, anavajjaiṭṭhavipākañca taṃ lakkhaṇañcāti anavajjaiṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ, yaṃ anavajjaiṭṭhavipākaṃ hutvā lakkhīyati, taṃ kusalanti attho. Atha vā anavajja-saddena anavajjabhāvo vutto, iṭṭhavipākasaddena iṭṭhavipākabhāvo, tasmā anavajjo ca iṭṭhavipāko ca anavajjaiṭṭhavipākaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇametassāti karaṇatthe, kammatthe vā lakkhaṇa-saddena anavajjaiṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇanti anavajjaiṭṭhavipākasabhāvavantaṃ, anavajjaiṭṭhavipākabhāvena [V 1.0143] lakkhitabbaṃ vāti attho. Kiṃ panettha kāraṇaṃ padadvayapariggahena, nanu ekeneva padena adhippetatthasiddhi siyā. Kiñcāpi hi “anavajjalakkhaṇa”nti vutte “aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti kusalesu dhammesū”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.145) viya vajjarahitattā abyākatassāpi pasaṅgo siyāti iṭṭhavipāka-padaṃ vattabbameva, “iṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇa”nti pana vutte itaraṃ na vattabbaṃ abyākatassa vipākārahabhāvena iṭṭhavipākatāpasaṅgabhāvato? Saccametaṃ, anavajja-padena kusalassa pavattisukhataṃ, iṭṭhavipāka-padena ca vipākasukhataṃ dassetuṃ [M 1.0173] padadvayaṃ vuttaṃ. Anavajjapadañhi attano pavattisabhāvavasena lakkhaṇavacanaṃ, itaraṃ kālantare vipākuppādanasamatthatāvasenāti. Atha vā kusalassa atthavisuddhiṃ dassetuṃ purimapadaṃ vuttaṃ, parisuddhavipākataṃ dassetuṃ pacchimaṃ. Purimaṃ vā kusalassa akusalasabhāvato nivattanaṃ, pacchimaṃ abyākatasabhāvatoti alamatipapañcena. Ettha ca “anavajja…pe… lakkhaṇa”nti vacanena kusalassa sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ anavajjaiṭṭhavipākasabhāvassa kusalajātiyā sādhāraṇattā. Akusalādīnamasādhāraṇabhāvena sabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ vāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Alternatively, it is a characteristic (lakkhaṇa) because it is characterized (lakkhīyati). And 'a characteristic of being faultless and having a desirable result' means that which, being faultless and having a desirable result, is characterized as wholesome. Or, by the term 'faultless,' the state of being faultless is meant; by the term 'desirable result,' the state of having a desirable result. Therefore, 'faultless and having a desirable result' is 'anavajjaiṭṭhavipākaṃ.' 'That whose characteristic it is' (taṃ lakkhaṇametassāti) is 'anavajjaiṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ.' Here the word 'characteristic' can be taken in the instrumental or objective sense, meaning 'possessing the nature of being faultless and having a desirable result,' or 'to be characterized by the state of being faultless and having a desirable result.' What is the reason here for using two terms? Would the intended meaning not be achieved with just one term? For although if one said 'faultless characteristic,' the inclusion of the indeterminate might follow because it is without fault—as in passages such as, 'Moreover, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed, how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning wholesome states'—thus the term 'desirable result' must be stated. But if one said 'characteristic of having a desirable result,' the other term would not need to be stated, because for the indeterminate, since it is not capable of yielding a result, there is no possibility of its having a desirable result. This is true. The two terms are stated to show the pleasantness of the wholesome in its occurrence (through 'faultless') and the pleasantness in its result (through 'desirable result'). For the term 'faultless' describes the characteristic in the sense of its own nature of occurrence, while the other describes it in the sense of its capacity to produce a result at a later time. Alternatively, the first term is stated to show the purity of the wholesome in its meaning, and the latter to show the purity of its result. Or the first signifies its turning away from the nature of the unwholesome, and the latter from the nature of the indeterminate. But enough of this excessive proliferation. Here, by the statement 'faultless... characteristic,' the general characteristic of the wholesome is stated, because the nature of being faultless and having a desirable result is common to the class of the wholesome. Or it should be understood as its individual characteristic because it is not shared by the unwholesome and so on.

Akusalaviddhaṃsanarasanti yathānurūpaṃ akusalappajahanakiccaṃ. Kusalañhi parittamahaggatalokuttarabhedabhinnaṃ yathākkamaṃ tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedappahānavasena akusalapakkhaṃ pajahati. Atha tadaṅgādippahānānaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇanti? Vuccate – dānādipuññakiriyavatthugatena tena tena kusalaṅgena tassa tassa maccherādiakusalaṅgassa pahānaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ, taṃ dīpālokena andhakāraviddhaṃsanaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ, kāmāvacarakusalānaṃ parittānubhāvatāya tehi attano ṭhitikkhaṇe viddhaṃsitānamakusalānaṃ tadapagame sati puna āgamena vottharaṇato. Tesaṃ tesaṃ nīvaraṇadhammānaṃ vikkhambhanasaṅkhātaṃ pavattinivāraṇavasena pahānaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ, taṃ ghaṭappahārena jalatale sevālaviyūhanaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā hi balavatā ghaṭappahārena dūrīkataṃ sevālaṃ tasmiṃ apanītepi taṃpahāravegena sahasā na ottharati, evameva upacārappanābhedena jhānena vikkhambhitā kāmacchandādayo tadappavattikālepi tassa balena sahasā na ottharantīti. Anuppattidhammatāpādanasaṅkhātaṃ sammā ucchedavasena pahānaṃ samucchedappahānaṃ, taṃ pana asanisampātena rukkhādīnaṃ samūlaviddhaṃsanaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi ariyamaggena [M 1.0174] samucchinnakilesā anusayamattakenāpi santāne pavattanti. Yathā pana ekavārappavattenapi indagginā saha mūlehi viddhaṃsitā rukkhādayo na puna viruhanti, evamevaṃ ekacittakkhaṇikenapi [V 1.0144] tena attano uppādamatteneva anusayamattaṭṭhāyinopi kilesā sabbena sabbaṃ viddhaṃsitāyeva honti.

Its function is destroying the unwholesome, which is the task of abandoning the unwholesome as is appropriate. For the wholesome, differentiated into the limited, the exalted, and the supramundane, abandons the unwholesome side respectively by way of abandonment by substitution, abandonment by suppression, and abandonment by cutting off. Now, what is the difference between abandonment by substitution and the others? It is said: The abandonment of a particular unwholesome factor such as stinginess by a particular wholesome factor included in the grounds for meritorious action such as giving is abandonment by substitution. This should be seen as the destruction of darkness by the light of a lamp; for because of the limited power of sense-sphere wholesome states, when they cease, the unwholesome states destroyed at the moment of their presence can arise again and overwhelm the mind. Abandonment by suppression is the abandonment that consists in preventing the occurrence of the hindrances. This should be seen as the parting of water-moss on the surface of the water by a blow with a pot. For just as water-moss pushed far away by a strong blow with a pot does not immediately cover the surface again because of the force of that blow even when the pot is removed, so too, when sensual desire and other hindrances have been suppressed by jhāna differentiated as access and absorption, they do not immediately overwhelm the mind even when the jhāna is not occurring, because of its power. Abandonment by cutting off is abandonment by way of complete extirpation, which is called the rendering of them unable to arise again. This should be seen as the destruction of trees and so on, down to their roots, by the strike of a thunderbolt. For defilements cut off by the noble path do not arise in the mental continuum even as a latent tendency. Just as trees destroyed with their roots by a single flash of lightning do not grow again, so too, by that path-consciousness, which lasts for only a single mind-moment, by its mere arising, the defilements, even those remaining only as latent tendencies, are utterly and completely destroyed.

Vodānaṃ visuddhi, saṃkilesamalavimuttīti attho, tathā hutvā paccupaṭṭhānamassāti vodānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, parisuddhākārena yogino ñāṇassa upaṭṭhātīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Cleansing is purity, meaning release from the stain of defilements. Its manifestation is cleansing, appearing as such. The meaning is that it appears to the yogi's knowledge in a purified aspect.

Evaṃ kusalassa vajjarahitaiṭṭhavipākasabhāvehi lakkhaṇaṃ, kiccaupaṭṭhānākāravasena ca rasapaccupaṭṭhānāni vatvā puna vajjapaṭipakkhabhāvavasena ca lakkhaṇaṃ, sampattiphalavasena ca rasādikaṃ dassetuṃ “vajjapaṭipakkhattā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vajjānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvo vajjapaṭipakkhattaṃ, tato. Etena “anavajjalakkhaṇa”nti ettha a-kāro paṭipakkhatthoti dasseti, tena panassa abyākatato nivattanaṃ kataṃ. Itarathā hi nāssa vajjaṃ, vajjato aññaṃ vā anavajjanti abyākatassāpi taṃlakkhaṇatāpasaṅgo siyā. “Vajjapaṭipakkhattā”ti pana vutte yasmā kusalākusalānameva pahāyakappahātabbabhāvena ālokandhakārānaṃ viya aññamaññaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhāvo, tasmā kusalameva vajjapaṭipakkhattā anavajjalakkhaṇaṃ, na aññanti ayamattho siddho hoti. Vodānabhāvarasanti vodānabhāvasampattikaṃ, kilesamalehi asaṃkiliṭṭhabhāvena sampajjanakanti attho. Paccupaṭṭhāpīyati upanīyati kāraṇena, attano vā kāraṇaṃ paṭicca, tappaṭibaddhabhāvena paṭimukhaṃ vā upaṭṭhātīti paccupaṭṭhānaṃ, iṭṭho vipāko paccupaṭṭhānamassāti iṭṭhavipākapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

Having thus stated the characteristic of the wholesome by its nature of being faultless and having a desirable result, and its function and manifestation by way of its task and mode of appearance, the passage beginning 'because of being the opposite of what is faulty' is stated in order to show again its characteristic by way of its being the opposite of what is faulty, and its function and so on by way of its accomplishment and fruit. Therein, 'because of being the opposite of what is faulty' (vajjapaṭipakkhattā) is because of the state of being the opposite of faults. By this it is shown that in the phrase 'faultless characteristic' (anavajjalakkhaṇa), the prefix 'a-' has the sense of opposition. By this, its exclusion from the indeterminate is effected. Otherwise, if 'faultless' meant 'not a fault' or 'other than a fault,' the inclusion of the indeterminate in that characteristic would follow. But when it is said 'because of being the opposite of what is faulty,' since the wholesome and the unwholesome are in direct opposition to each other, like light and darkness, in their relationship of abandoner and to-be-abandoned, this meaning is established: only the wholesome has the characteristic of being faultless because it is the opposite of what is faulty, and nothing else. Its function is the state of cleansing means its accomplishment is the state of cleansing; the meaning is that it is accomplished by way of being unstained by the defiling taints. A manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) is what is made to appear, what is brought near by a cause, or what appears facing its own cause in dependence on it, because of its connection to it. Its manifestation is a desirable result means that a desirable result is its manifestation.

Asati [M 1.0175] yonisomanasikāre kusalassa anuppajjanato, sati ca tasmiṃ uppajjanato tassa so āsannakāraṇanti āha “yonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhāna”nti. Tattha yoniso pathena upāyena manasikāro yonisomanasikāro, atthato pana sānusayasantānavato channaṃ dvārānamāpāthagatesvārammaṇesu patirūpadesavāsādisampattiyā kusaladhammānaṃ paccayabhāvena bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭetvā uppannamāvajjanaṃ yonisomanasikāro nāma. Vuttapaṭipakkhavasena ayonisomanasikāropi daṭṭhabbo. Yaṃ pana niranusayasantānasamaṅgissa kiriyacittānaṃ paccayabhāvena uppannaṃ, taṃ ṭhapetvā niravajjadhammaṃ sāvajjadhammassa kassaci paccayabhāvānupagamanato yonisomanasikārapakkhaṃ vā bhajeyya. Khīṇāsavasantānagatattā yonisoayonisobhāvamanapekkhitvā āpāthagatārammaṇesu uppattimattaṃ [V 1.0145] vinā na kassaci kusalākusalabhāvassa paccayo hotīti tadubhayavasena navattabbattā abyākatamanasikāroti vā saṅkhaṃ gaccheyyāti.

Because the wholesome does not arise when there is no wise attention, and because it does arise when there is, it is said that 'its proximate cause is wise attention.' Herein, wise attention (yonisomanasikāro) is attention (manasikāro) in a wise way (yoniso), that is, by the right method or means. In meaning, however, wise attention is the adverting consciousness that arises, having turned the life-continuum, towards objects that have come into the range of the six doors for one with a mental continuum containing latent tendencies, due to the accomplishment of suitable residence, etc., which is a condition for wholesome states. Unwise attention should be understood in the way opposite to what has been said. But as to that attention which arises as a condition for the functional consciousness of one who possesses a mental continuum free from latent tendencies, one might assign it to the side of wise attention, since, being a faultless state, it does not become a condition for any faulty state. Or, because it belongs to the mental continuum of one whose taints are destroyed, without regard to whether it is wise or unwise, apart from its mere arising towards an object that has come into range, it is not a condition for any state to be wholesome or unwholesome; therefore, because it cannot be spoken of in terms of those two, it should be reckoned as indeterminate attention.

Sāvajjāniṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇamakusalanti etthāpi “vajjā rāgādayo, te yassa santi, taṃ sāvajjaṃ, aniṭṭho vipāko yassa, taṃ aniṭṭhavipāka”ntiādinā vuttanayānusārena paṭipakkhayojanā daṭṭhabbā. Rasādito panetaṃ anatthajananarasaṃ, saṃkilesapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Atha vā gārayhabhāvato sāvajjalakkhaṇameva, saṃkilesabhāvarasaṃ, aniṭṭhavipākapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Vacanatthato pana na kusalanti akusalaṃ, kusalapaṭipakkhanti attho. Paṭipakkhatthe hi ayaṃ akāro, na pana aññatthe, nāpi abhāve. Itarathā hi tikaṃ na siyā, dukaṃ, catukkaṃ vā āpajjeyya. Tathā hi yadi kusalato aññamakusalaṃ siyā[M 1.0176], tadā abyākatassāpi tato aññabhāvena akusala-saddasaṅgahoti kusalākusalajātibhedato duvidhanti dukaṃ vattabbaṃ. Yadi ca kusalābhāvo akusalaṃ, tena na kāci jāti gayhatīti kusalābyākatajātibhedato dukameva vattabbaṃ. Atha siyā “abhāvopi visuṃ gahetabbo”ti, evaṃ sati tassa jātiyā abhāvato jāti-saddena saha sambandho na siyā. Vijjamānassa hi jāti nāma hoti. Yatheva vā kusalassa abhāvo, evaṃ abyākatassāpi abhāvo atthīti anabyākatajātipi vattabbāti catukkaṃ āpajjeyya. Na cetamiṭṭhaṃ kusalādivasena tividhajātiyā eva icchitattā, pāḷiyañca “kusalā dhammā akusalā dhammā abyākatā dhammā”ti tikavaseneva vuttattā “kusalapaṭipakkha”nti pana vuccamāne mittapaṭipakkho amitto viya, lobhapaṭipakkho alobho viya ca yaṃ dhammajātaṃ kusalassa ujuvipaccanīkabhūtaṃ, taṃ akusalanti tassa vasena tikaṃ upapannaṃ hoti, ujuvipaccanīkatā cassa sāvajjāniṭṭhavipākattā, tena pahātabbabhāvato ca veditabbā, na pana kusalavināsanato. Na hi akusalena kusalaṃ pahīyati, mahābalattā pana kusalameva taṃ pajahati. Kusalañhi mahābalaṃ, akusalaṃ dubbalaṃ. Tenevāha “abalā naṃ balīyanti, maddantenaṃ parissayā”ti (su. ni. 776), tasmā kusalameva yathāvuttanayena akusalassa pahāyakaṃ, nākusalaṃ itarassāti veditabbaṃ.

Unwholesome has the characteristic of being blameworthy and of having an undesirable result. Here too, the opposition should be understood according to the method stated: 'Faults are such things as greed; that which possesses them is blameworthy. That which has an undesirable result is of undesirable result.' In terms of function, etc., it has the function of generating what is unbeneficial, and its manifestation is defilement. Alternatively, because it is reprehensible, its characteristic is simply blameworthiness; its function is the state of defilement; its manifestation is an undesirable result; and its proximate cause is unwise attention. In terms of its etymological meaning, 'not wholesome' (na kusalaṃ) is unwholesome (akusalaṃ); the meaning is 'the opposite of wholesome.' For here the prefix 'a-' is in the sense of opposition, not in another sense, nor in the sense of absence. Otherwise, there would not be a triad; it would result in a dyad or a tetrad. For if the unwholesome were something other than the wholesome, then since the indeterminate is also other than the wholesome, it would be included under the term 'unwholesome'; thus a dyad should be stated, a division into the two classes of wholesome and unwholesome. And if the unwholesome were the absence of the wholesome, then since no class of phenomena is thereby apprehended, a dyad should be stated, a division into the two classes of wholesome and indeterminate. If it be said, 'Absence should be taken separately,' in that case, since it is an absence of a class, it would have no connection with the word 'class.' For what is called a class is something that exists. And just as there is an absence of the wholesome, so there is an absence of the indeterminate; thus an 'un-indeterminate' class would have to be stated, and this would result in a tetrad. But this is not desirable, for a threefold classification by way of wholesome, etc., is intended, and in the Pāli it is stated by way of a triad: 'wholesome states, unwholesome states, indeterminate states.' However, when it is said to be 'the opposite of the wholesome'—just as an enemy is the opposite of a friend and non-greed is the opposite of greed—that class of phenomena that is the direct contrary of the wholesome is the unwholesome. On this basis, the triad is established. Its direct contrariety should be understood from its being blameworthy and having an undesirable result, and from its being something to be abandoned, but not from its destroying the wholesome. For the wholesome is not abandoned by the unwholesome; rather, because of its great strength, the wholesome abandons the unwholesome. For the wholesome is powerful, the unwholesome is weak. Thus it is said: 'The weak are oppressed by the strong; dangers crush them' (Snp 776). Therefore, it should be understood that it is the wholesome that abandons the unwholesome in the way stated, not the unwholesome that abandons the other.

Tadubhaya…pe… abyākatanti yaṃ dhammajātaṃ kusalaṃ viya na anavajjaiṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ, nāpi akusalaṃ viya sāvajjāniṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ, atha kho avipākattā [V 1.0146] tadubhayaviparītalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ abyākatanti attho. Nanu ca “tadubhayaviparītalakkhaṇa”nti vutte sukhadukkhavedanānaṃ viparītā upekkhāvedanā [M 1.0177] viya iṭṭhāniṭṭhavipākānaṃ viparīto añño koci vipāko yassa atthi, taṃ abyākatanti āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati tathā asambhavato. Yathā hi ālokandhakārānaṃ viparīto añño koci natthi, evamiṭṭhāniṭṭhavipākānaṃ viparīto na koci vipāko atthīti. Atha vā taṃ-saddo idha iṭṭhāniṭṭhavipākanirapekkhaṃ kusalākusalamattameva paccāmasatīti kusalākusalānaṃ savipākattā tadubhayaviparītalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ avipākalakkhaṇanti atthoti alamettha anuyogena. Kusalākusalabhāvena na byākatanti abyākataṃ. Kusalākusalañhi vatvā abyākatassa vuttattā kusalākusalabhāveneva avuttattāti viññāyati, na pakārantarena. Tathā avacanañca tassa tadubhayaviparītalakkhaṇattāyeva, na pana avattabbattāmattenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā vi-saddo virodhivacano. Ā-saddo abhimukhabhāvappakāsano, tasmā attano paccayehi aññamaññaṃ virodhābhimukhataṃ kataṃ lakkhaṇavirodhato pahāyakappahātabbabhāvato vāti byākataṃ, kusalākusalaṃ. Tato aññaṃ abyākataṃ. Tañhi lakkhaṇato aññamaññaṃ kusalākusalaṃ viya na tassa viruddhaṃ. Na hi avipākataṃ aniṭṭhavipākatā viya, iṭṭhavipākatāya iṭṭhavipākatā viya ca aniṭṭhavipākatāya iṭṭhāniṭṭhavipākatāhi virujjhati, na cāpi abyākataṃ kusalākusalesu kiñci pajahati, na ca kenaci pahātabbanti. “Tadubhayaviparītalakkhaṇamabyākata”nti viññāyamāne ahosi kammaṃ, nāhosi kammavipāko, natthi kammavipāko, na bhavissati kammavipākoti iminā tikena saṅgahitassa gatiupadhikālappayogavipattīhi avipākassa diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādikammassa bhāvanāyapahātabbassa akusalassa ca abhiññākusalassa ca vipākuppādanābhāvato “siyā nu kho abyākatabhāvo vā”ti kadāci koci cinteyyāti tannivāraṇatthamāha “avipākārahaṃ vā”ti, vipākaṃ [M 1.0178] dātuṃ nārahati tattha sāmatthiyābhāvatoti avipākārahaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādayo tāva paccayavekallādīhi kāraṇehi avipākā, sace panete tabbidūrā assu, tadā vipākadāne samatthatāya vipākārahāyeva, taṃ pana na tathā, atha kho yena kenaci ākārena vipākadāne asamatthatāyeva vipākārahaṃ na hoti, taṃ abyākataṃ nāmāti.

Indeterminate is that which is the opposite of both... That is, whatever class of phenomena is not, like the wholesome, characterized by being blameless and having a desirable result, nor, like the unwholesome, characterized by being blameworthy and having an undesirable result, but rather, because it is without result, is characterized as the opposite of both—that is the meaning of 'indeterminate.' Now, when it is said 'characterized as the opposite of both,' does it not follow that just as neutral feeling is the opposite of pleasant and painful feelings, so there must be some other kind of result that is the opposite of desirable and undesirable results, and that which has this is the indeterminate? It does not follow, because that is impossible. For just as there is no other thing that is the opposite of light and darkness, so there is no result that is the opposite of desirable and undesirable results. Alternatively, the word 'both' here refers back only to the wholesome and unwholesome themselves, without regard to their desirable and undesirable results. Since the wholesome and unwholesome have results, that which is characterized as the opposite of both is characterized as being without result. This is the meaning. Enough with this inquiry. It is 'indeterminate' (abyākata) because it is not 'determined' (byākata) as wholesome or unwholesome. For since the indeterminate is spoken of after the wholesome and the unwholesome have been spoken of, it is understood that it is unstated only in terms of being wholesome or unwholesome, not in any other way. And it should be seen that its being unstated is due to its having the characteristic of being the opposite of both, not merely because it is inexpressible. Alternatively, the prefix vi- has the meaning of opposition; the prefix ā- indicates facing towards. Therefore, the wholesome and the unwholesome are 'determined' (byākata) because they are made to face each other in opposition by their respective conditions, either due to the opposition of their characteristics or because one is the abandoner and the other is to be abandoned. What is other than these is the indeterminate (abyākata). For in terms of characteristic, it is not opposed to them as the wholesome and unwholesome are to each other. For being without result is not opposed to having a desirable result in the way having an undesirable result is, nor is it opposed to having an undesirable result in the way having a desirable result is. Nor does the indeterminate abandon anything among the wholesome and unwholesome states, nor is it to be abandoned by anything. When it is understood that 'the indeterminate is characterized as the opposite of both,' someone might sometimes think: 'Could it be that kamma that was, but had no result; that has no result; that will have no result'—kamma included in this triad, such as kamma to be experienced in this very life which is resultless due to defects in destination, substratum of rebirth, time, or means of application, and unwholesome kamma to be abandoned by development, and wholesome kamma of direct knowledge, which do not produce a result—is indeterminate?' To prevent this, it is said: 'or it is not capable of yielding a result.' It is 'not capable of yielding a result' because it is not fit to give a result, owing to an absence of capacity for that. This is what is meant: Kamma to be experienced in this very life and so on is resultless for such reasons as deficiency in conditions. But if these were free from such deficiencies, then because of their capacity to give a result, they would be capable of yielding a result. But that which is indeterminate is not so. Rather, that which is incapable of giving a result in any way whatsoever, which is not capable of yielding a result, is what is called indeterminate.

Idāni evaṃ tikavasena niddiṭṭhesu kusalādīsu paṭhamaṃ tāva kusalacittaṃ vibhajanto “tattha kusalacitta”ntiādinā tassa gaṇanaparicchedaṃ dasseti. Ekavīsatividhanti aṭṭha kāmāvacarāni[V 1.0147], pañca rūpāvacarāni, cattāri arūpāvacarāni, cattāri lokuttarānīti evaṃ saṅkhepato ekavīsatividhaṃ. Bhūmito catubbidhanti kāmarūpārūpalokuttarabhūmisaṅkhātānaṃ catunnaṃ bhūmīnaṃ vasena tattha pavattamānaṃ cittampi catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha bhavanti etthāti bhūmi, ṭhānaṃ, avatthā ca. Avatthāpi hi avatthavantānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānaṃ viya gayhati. Evañhi nesaṃ sukhaggahaṇaṃ hoti. Avatthāti cettha dhammānaṃ kāmataṇhādīhi paricchinnāparicchinnabhāvo. Tattha purimā tisso bhūmiyo ubhayavasena veditabbā, itarā avatthāvaseneva. Na hi lokuttaradhammānaṃ kāmabhavādito aññaṃ ṭhānamupalabbhatīti.

Now, among the wholesome states, etc., that have been pointed out by way of the triad, first, when analyzing wholesome consciousness, he indicates its numerical determination with the words 'Therein, wholesome consciousness,' etc. Twenty-onefold: eight are sense-sphere, five are fine-material-sphere, four are immaterial-sphere, and four are supramundane. Thus in brief, it is twenty-onefold. Fourfold by plane: by way of the four planes designated as the sense-sphere plane, the fine-material-sphere plane, the immaterial-sphere plane, and the supramundane plane, the consciousness occurring in them is also fourfold. Herein, 'they are in this' (bhavanti ettha), thus it is a 'plane' (bhūmi); it is also a ground (ṭhāna) and a state (avatthā). For a state is apprehended as if it were the ground of occurrence for the things that are in that state. In this way, they are easily apprehended. Here, 'state' is the defined or undefined condition of phenomena due to sensual craving and so on. Among these, the first three planes should be understood in both ways (as ground and state), the other only by way of state. For no ground other than the planes of sensual existence, etc., is found for the supramundane states.

Aññattha pavattamānassāpi vakkhamānanayena kāmabhūmipariyāpannattā bhūmito ekavidhanti. Savatthukāvatthukabhedatoti cakkhādīni pañca, hadayañcāti cha vatthūni. Kusalassa pana cakkhādinissitattābhāvato hadayavatthu idha vatthūti adhippetaṃ. Tena sahitaṃ ekantena tannissitappavattitoti savatthukaṃ, kāmarūpadhātuyaṃ pavattamānaviññāṇaṃ. Tattha hi arūpassa rūpapaṭibandhappavatti, arūpadhātuyaṃ pana rūpābhāvato vatthuvirahitameva pavattatīti tattha pavattamānaṃ [M 1.0179] avatthukaṃ. Hīna…pe… tividhanti ettha paccayato, phalato ca majjhimapaṇītehi nihīnaṃ, tesaṃ vā guṇehi parihīnanti hīnaṃ, attano paccayehi padhānabhāvaṃ nītanti paṇītaṃ, ubhinnaṃ vemajjhe bhavaṃ majjhimaṃ. Tattha hīnena chandena cittena vīriyena vīmaṃsāya vā pavattitaṃ hīnaṃ, majjhimehi chandādīhi pavattitaṃ majjhimaṃ, paṇītehi paṇītaṃ. Chandādīnaṃ pana hīnādibhāvo adhimuttivasena daṭṭhabbo. Hīnādhimuttivasena hi nesaṃ hīnatā, paṇītādhimuttivasena paṇītatā, tadubhayavemajjhavasena majjhimatā. Yasakāmatāya vā kataṃ kusalaṃ hīnaṃ, puññaphalakāmatāya majjhimaṃ, “puññaṃ nāmetaṃ sādhūhi kattabbamevā”ti evaṃ ariyabhāvaṃ nissāya kataṃ paṇītaṃ. “Ahamasmi dānapati, ime panaññe dānadāsādayo”tiādinā attukkaṃsanaparavambhanāhi upakkiliṭṭhaṃ pavattitaṃ vā hīnaṃ, tathā anupakkiliṭṭhaṃ majjhimaṃ, maggaphalapadaṭṭhānaṃ paṇītaṃ. Bhavabhogasampattinimittaṃ vā kataṃ hīnaṃ, sāvakapaccekabodhipāramitāvasena attano vimokkhatthāya kataṃ majjhimaṃ, sammāsambodhipāramitāvasena sabbesaṃ vimokkhatthāya kataṃ paṇītanti.

Even when occurring elsewhere, because it pertains to the sense-sphere plane, it is onefold by way of plane, according to the method about to be explained. By the division into having a basis and lacking a basis: there are six bases, namely the five, the eye, etc., and the heart-base. However, since the wholesome is not dependent on the eye, etc., here the heart-base is intended as the 'basis'. That which occurs entirely dependent on it is 'with a basis'—that is, consciousness occurring in the sense-sphere and form-sphere. For there, the immaterial occurs bound to the material; but in the formless sphere, due to the absence of matter, it occurs entirely without a basis. Thus, what occurs there is 'without a basis.' Inferior... etc... threefold: here, that which is lower than the middling and superior in cause and in fruit, or is deficient in their qualities, is 'inferior'. That which is brought to prominence by its own causes is 'superior'. That which is in the middle of the two is 'middling'. Herein, that which is performed with inferior zeal, consciousness, energy, or investigation is 'inferior'; that performed with middling zeal, etc., is 'middling'; and that with superior is 'superior'. The inferior, etc., nature of zeal, etc., should be understood by way of resolve. For their inferiority is due to inferior resolve, their superiority to superior resolve, and their middling nature to being in between those two. Or, wholesome action done out of a desire for fame is 'inferior'; done for the sake of the fruit of merit, it is 'middling'; and done relying on the noble state, with the thought, 'This merit should indeed be done by the good,' it is 'superior'. Or, that which is performed defiled by self-exaltation and disparagement of others—such as, 'I am a master of giving, but these others are slaves of giving, etc.'—is 'inferior'. That which is similarly undefiled is 'middling', and that which is a proximate cause for the path and fruit is 'superior'. Or, what is done for the sake of attaining existence and wealth is 'inferior'; what is done for one’s own liberation by way of the perfections of a disciple or a paccekabuddha is 'middling'; and what is done for the liberation of all beings by way of the perfections of a Sammāsambuddha is 'superior'.

Somanassu…pe… bhedatoti bheda-saddo paccekaṃ sambandhitabbo “somanassupekkhābhedato ñāṇabhedato payogabhedato”ti. Tattha payogabhedatoti saṅkhārabhedatoti attho. Nanu ca somanassupekkhābhedo [V 1.0148] tāva yutto tesaṃ bhinnasabhāvattā. Ñāṇappayogabhedo pana kathanti? Vuccate – ñāṇappayogakato bhedo ñāṇappayogabhedo tesaṃ bhāvābhāvamupādāya pavattattā. Idāni tameva somanassupekkhādibhedaṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “seyyathida”nti pucchitvā “somanassasahagata”ntiādinā vissajjeti. Tattha seyyathidanti taṃ katamaṃ, taṃ kathanti vā attho.

Joy... etc... by the division of: the word 'division' should be connected with each term, as: 'by the division of joy and equanimity, by the division of knowledge, and by the division of prompting.' Here, 'by the division of prompting' means 'by the division of formations.' Now, the division of joy and equanimity is indeed fitting, since their natures are different. But how is there a division of knowledge and prompting? It is said: the division of knowledge and prompting is a division made by knowledge and prompting, because it occurs on account of their presence or absence. Now, to show that very division of joy, equanimity, and so on, in detail, having asked, 'That is to say?' (seyyathidaṃ), it is answered with 'accompanied by joy,' and so on. Here, 'seyyathidaṃ' means 'which is that?' or 'how is that?'

Sobhanaṃ [M 1.0180] mano, sobhanaṃ vā mano etassāti sumano, tassa bhāvo somanassaṃ, mānasikasukhavedanāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, somanassena uppādato yāva nirodhā sahagataṃ pavattaṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ sampayuttanti attho. Atha vā somanassena saha ekuppādādibhāvaṃ gatanti somanassasahagataṃ. Jānāti yathāsabhāvaṃ paṭivijjhatīti ñāṇaṃ, tena samaṃ ekuppādādīhi pakārehi yuttanti ñāṇasampayuttaṃ. Nāssa saṅkhāro atthīti asaṅkhāraṃ, asaṅkhārameva asaṅkhārikaṃ. Saha saṅkhārena pavattamānaṃ sasaṅkhāraṃ, tadeva sasaṅkhārikaṃ. Saṅkhāroti cettha attano, parassa vā pubbappayogo “saṅkharoti tikkhabhāvasaṅkhātena maṇḍanavisesena sajjeti, saṅkharīyati vā sajjīyati cittaṃ etenā”ti katvā. Tattha dānādipuññakaraṇakāle maccheramalathinamiddhādīhi upakkilesehi saṃsīdamāne citte upakkilesavūpasamavasena, cittassa ca ussāhajananavasena tīsu dvāresu pavatto sammāvāyāmo attano payogo nāma. Kusalakaraṇe nirussāhassa pana “ambho, sappurisa, kusalakaraṇaṃ nāma paṇḍitehi āsevitamaggo, tattha tayāpi paṭipajjituṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā dānaṃ dehi, sīlaṃ rakkha, tañhi te atthāya hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”tiādinā kusalakaraṇatthāya ussāhajananavasena paresaṃ kāyavacīdvāresu pavattā āṇatti parappayogo nāma. Tesu pana purimo pubbabhāgappavattacittasantāne, pacchimo paresaṃ cittasantāneyeva sambhavatīti tannibbattito cittassa tikkhabhāvasaṅkhāto viseso idha upacārato saṅkhāroti veditabbo. Tenāhu ācariyā –

A beautiful mind, or one has a beautiful mind—thus, 'sumano' (good-minded). The state of that is 'somanassa' (joy), which is a designation for pleasant mental feeling. It is associated with joy from its arising until its cessation, meaning it is connected, mixed, and conjoined. Alternatively, it has attained a state of single arising, etc., together with joy, thus it is 'accompanied by joy'. It knows, it penetrates according to its true nature—this is 'knowledge'. It is conjoined with that in the same ways, such as single arising, etc.; thus, it is 'conjoined with knowledge'. It has no prompting, thus it is 'unprompted'; the unprompted itself is 'asaṅkhārikaṃ'. Occurring with prompting, it is 'prompted'; that itself is 'sasaṅkhārikaṃ'. Here, 'prompting' refers to one's own or another's prior effort, because 'it prompts,' that is, it prepares with a special adornment known as sharpness; or the mind is prompted, that is, prepared, by it. In this context, when the mind is sinking due to defilements like the stain of stinginess, sloth, and torpor during the performance of meritorious actions such as giving, the right effort that arises in the three doors for the purpose of pacifying those defilements and generating energy in the mind—this is called 'one's own prompting'. For one lacking energy in performing wholesome deeds, the command occurring in the bodily and verbal doors of others for the purpose of generating energy for performing wholesome deeds—by saying, 'Friend, good person, performing wholesome deeds is the path frequented by the wise; you too should undertake it. Therefore, give gifts, uphold virtue—for this will be for your welfare, benefit, and happiness'—is called 'another's prompting'. Among these, the former occurs in the mental continuum of a preceding moment, while the latter occurs only in the mental continuum of others. Therefore, the special quality known as sharpness of mind produced by that should be understood here figuratively as 'prompting'. Thus, the teachers have said:

“Pubbappayogasambhūto, viseso cittasambhavī;

Saṅkhāro iti saṅkhāra-sabhāvaññūhi kittito”ti.

“Born of prior endeavor, a special quality arising in the mind; it is proclaimed as ‘prompting’ by those who know the nature of prompting.”

Atha [M 1.0181] vā “sasaṅkhārikamasaṅkhārika”nti ca etaṃ kevalaṃ saṅkhārassa bhāvābhāvamattāpekkhāya vuttaṃ, na tassa sahappavattisabbhāvābhāvatoti bhinnasantānappavattinopi saṅkhārassa idamatthitāya taṃvasena nibbattaṃ cittaṃ saṅkhāro assa atthīti sasaṅkhārikaṃ saha-saddassa vijjamānatthaparidīpanato [V 1.0149] “salomako sapakkhako”tiādīsu viya. Tabbiparītaṃ pana tadabhāvato yathāvuttavaseneva asaṅkhārikaṃ. Atha vā saṅkharaṇaṃ, saṅkharīyati vā etena āgantukasambhūtena cittasaṃsīdanasabhāvāpanayanavaseneva sajjīyati, saṅkharoti vā taṃ yathāvuttavasenevāti saṅkhāroti ujukameva pubbappayogajanito tikkhabhāvo vuccati, tadabhāvato asaṅkhārikaṃ, sabhāvatikkhanti attho. Taṃsahagatāya sasaṅkhārikaṃ, atha vā maccheramalādīhi saṅkharīyatīti saṅkhāro, cittassa saṃsīdanasabhāvo, so yassa natthīti asaṅkhārikaṃ, itaraṃ sasaṅkhārikaṃ. Paṇītautubhojanādiko vā balavapaccayo saṅkhāro “saṅkharoti cittaṃ tikkhabhāvena, saṅkharīyati vā taṃ etenā”ti katvā. A-kārassa vuḍḍhatthavuttitāya vuḍḍhippatto saṅkhāro assāti asaṅkhārikaṃ, balavapaccayavantanti attho. Vuḍḍhiparidīpakena pana a-kārena avisesitattā sasaṅkhārikaṃ sappaccayaṃ dubbalapaccayanti adhippāyo. Ñāṇena vippayuttaṃ virahitanti ñāṇavippayuttaṃ.

Alternatively, the terms 'prompted' and 'unprompted' are said merely with reference to the presence or absence of prompting, not to the real presence or absence of its simultaneous occurrence. Therefore, even if a prompting occurs in a different continuum, a consciousness produced through its influence is 'prompted' because 'it has a prompting', since the word 'saha' indicates the meaning of 'existing', as in 'hairy' or 'winged'. The opposite of that, due to its absence, is 'unprompted' in the way already explained. Alternatively, 'prompting' is the preparing of the mind by what has arisen adventitiously, by way of removing the nature of mental sinking; or it prompts it in the way already explained. Thus, 'prompting' is directly said to be the sharpness born of prior effort. Due to its absence, it is 'unprompted', meaning naturally sharp. Because of being accompanied by that, it is 'prompted'. Alternatively, 'prompting' is the nature of the mind's sinking, because it is prompted by the stain of stinginess and so on. When this is absent, it is 'unprompted'; otherwise, it is 'prompted'. Alternatively, a strong condition such as superior season, food, etc., is 'prompting', because 'it prompts the mind with sharpness, or the mind is prompted by this'. Because the letter 'a' can have the meaning of 'growth', 'unprompted' means 'it has a prompting that has reached growth', the meaning being 'possessing a strong condition'. But since it is not specified by the letter 'a' which indicates growth, 'prompted' is intended to mean 'with a condition', that is, 'with a weak condition'. 'Dissociated from knowledge' means devoid of or lacking knowledge.

Upekkhatīti upekkhā, vediyamānāpi ārammaṇaṃ ajjhupekkhati, majjhattākārasaṇṭhitiyāti attho. Atha vā iṭṭhe, aniṭṭhe ca ārammaṇe pakkhapātābhāvena upapattito yuttito ikkhati anubhavatīti upekkhā. Atha vā upetā sukhadukkhānaṃ aviruddhā ikkhā anubhavananti upekkhā. Aviruddhattāyeva hesā tesaṃ anantarampi pavattati. Sukhadukkhavedanā pana visuṃ visuṃ viruddhasabhāvattā nāññamaññaṃ anantaraṃ pavattanti[M 1.0182]. Teneva hi paṭṭhāne somanassassa anantaraṃ domanassassa, domanassassa anantaraṃ somanassassa ca uppatti paṭisiddhā. Ayañca attho lobhasahagatacittasampayuttavedanāyapi labbhati, purimā pana dve na tathā. Na hi lobhasahagatādīnaṃ majjhattākārena ajjhupekkhanaṃ, upapattito ikkhanaṃ vā atthīti. Upekkhāsahagatanti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

It is equanimity (upekkhā) because it looks on (upekkhati); even while being felt, it looks upon the object with neutrality, maintaining a balanced state—this is the meaning. Alternatively, it is upekkhā because it observes and experiences the object without partiality, whether it is desirable or undesirable, in a fitting and appropriate manner. Or, it is upekkhā because it is an experience endowed with non-opposition to pleasure and pain. Due to its non-opposing nature, it can arise immediately after them. However, feelings of pleasure and pain, being of mutually opposing natures, do not arise immediately after one another. For this reason, in the Paṭṭhāna, the arising of displeasure immediately after joy, or joy immediately after displeasure, is prohibited. This meaning also applies to the feeling associated with a mind accompanied by greed, but the previous two explanations do not. For states accompanied by greed and so on do not involve looking on with neutrality or observing in a fitting manner. “Accompanied by equanimity”—all this is in the same way as explained above.

Nanu ca aññepi phassādayo sampayuttadhammā atthīti somanassādīnaṃ vaseneva pana aṭṭhavidhatā kasmā gahitāti? Bhedakarabhāvato. Phassādīnañhi sabbacittasādhāraṇattā, saddhādīnañca sabbakusalasādhāraṇattā na tehi cittassa vibhāgo, somanassādayo pana katthaci citte honti, katthaci na hontīti pākaṭova tehi cittassa vibhāgoti. Kasmā panete katthaci citte honti, katthaci na hontīti? Kāraṇassa sannihitāsannihitabhāvato. Kiṃ pana nesaṃ kāraṇanti? Vuccate – tattha somanassasahagatabhāvo tāva ārammaṇavasena hoti. Iṭṭhārammaṇasmiñhi [V 1.0150] somanassasahagatacittamuppajjati. Nanu ca iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ lobhassa vatthu rajjanīyattāti kathaṃ tattha kusalaṃ uppajjatīti? Nayidamekantikaṃ iṭṭhepi ārammaṇe niyamitādivasena kusalassa uppajjanato. Yassa hi “kusalameva mayā kattabba”nti kusalakaraṇeyeva cittaṃ niyamitaṃ hoti, akusalappavattitova nivattetvā kusalakaraṇeyeva pariṇāmitaṃ, abhiṇhakaraṇena ca kusalaṃ samudāciṇṇaṃ, paṭirūpadesavāsasaddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayapubbekatapuññatāsaṅkhātacatucakkūpanissayavasena, yoniso ca ābhogo pavattati, tassa iṭṭhepi ārammaṇe alobhasampayuttameva cittamuppajjati, na lobhasampayuttaṃ. Hoti cettha –

But are there not other associated states such as contact and so on? Why then is the eightfold classification established only on the basis of joy and the rest? Because of their differentiating quality. For since contact and the like are common to all consciousness, and faith and the like are common to all wholesome consciousness, consciousness is not differentiated by them. But joy and the rest are present in some types of consciousness and absent in others, so the differentiation of consciousness by them is clear. And why are they present in some types of consciousness and absent in others? Because of the presence or absence of their cause. What, now, is their cause? It is said: Here, being accompanied by joy occurs, in the first place, on account of the object, for consciousness accompanied by joy arises in regard to an agreeable object. But is not an agreeable object a basis for greed, since it is enticing? How then can wholesome consciousness arise in relation to it? This is not invariably so, for wholesome consciousness can arise even in regard to an agreeable object on account of such factors as regulation. For in the case of one whose mind is regulated by the thought, 'I must do only what is wholesome'; who has turned his mind away from the unwholesome and inclined it only toward the wholesome; who has cultivated the wholesome by repeated practice; who is supported by the fourfold wheel—living in a suitable place, hearing the good Dhamma, associating with superior persons, and merit made in the past—and whose attention proceeds wisely, for such a one, even in regard to an agreeable object, consciousness associated with non-greed arises, not consciousness associated with greed. And on this it is said:

“Niyāmapariṇāmehi[M 1.0183], samudāciṇṇatāya ca;

Ñāṇapubbaṅgamābhogā, iṭṭhepi kusalaṃ siyā”ti.

By regulation and inclination, and by accumulated practice, and by attention preceded by knowledge, the wholesome can arise even toward a desirable object.

Apica saddhābahulatādīhi ca kāraṇehi cittassa somanassasahagatatā veditabbā. Assaddhānaṃ, hi micchādiṭṭhikānañca ekantamiṭṭhārammaṇabhūtaṃ tathāgatarūpampi disvā somanassaṃ na uppajjati. Ye ca kusalappavattiyaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ na passanti, tesaṃ parehi ussāhitānaṃ kusalaṃ karontānampi somanassaṃ na uppajjati, tasmā saddhābahulatā visuddhidiṭṭhitā ānisaṃsadassāvitāti imehipi kāraṇehi cittassa somanassasahagatatā hoti.

Moreover, being accompanied by joy should be understood to occur through such causes as an abundance of faith. For in those without faith and in those with wrong view, joy does not arise even when they see the form of the Tathāgata, which is an exclusively agreeable object. And for those who do not see the benefit in the practice of the wholesome, joy does not arise even when they perform wholesome deeds urged on by others. Therefore, being accompanied by joy occurs for these reasons: abundance of faith, purity of view, and seeing the benefit.

Apica ye te ekādasa dhammā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti. Seyyathidaṃ – buddhānussati dhammānussati saṃghānussati sīlānussati cāgānussati devatānussati upasamānussati lūkhapuggalaparivajjanaṃ siniddhapuggalasevanā pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇā tadadhimuttatāti imehipi kāraṇehi cittassa somanassasahagatabhāvo veditabbo. Buddhādiguṇe anussarantassa hi yāva upacāruppādā sakalasarīraṃ pharamānā pīti uppajjati. Tathā dīgharattaṃ akkhaṇḍatādivasena attanā rakkhitaṃ catupārisuddhisīlaṃ paccavekkhantassa, gihino dasasīlaṃ pañcasīlaṃ paccavekkhantassa, dubbhikkhabhayādīsu paṇītaṃ bhojanaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ datvā “evaṃnāma dānaṃ adāsi”nti attanocāgaṃ paccavekkhantassa, gihinopi tathārūpe kāle sīlavantānaṃ dinnadānaṃ paccavekkhantassa, yehi guṇehi samannāgatā devā devattaṃ gatā, tathārūpānaṃ guṇānaṃ attani atthitaṃ paccavekkhantassa, samathavipassanāhi vikkhambhitakilese saṭṭhipi [V 1.0151] sattatipi vassāni asamudācarante disvā “aho mayhaṃ kilesā na samudācarantī”ti cintentassa, cetiyadassanatheradassanesu asakkaccakiriyāya saṃsucitalūkhabhāvena buddhādīsu pasādasinehābhāvena gadrabhapiṭṭhe rajasadise lūkhapuggale [M 1.0184] parivajjantassa, buddhādīsu pasādabahule muducitte siniddhapuggale paṭisevantassa, ratanattayaguṇaparidīpake pasādanīyasuttante paccavekkhantassa, ṭhānanisajjādīsupi pītiuppādanatthaṃ tanninnatādivasena pavattentassa yebhuyyena pīti uppajjati. Pītiyā ca somanassena saha avinābhāvato taduppattiyā tassāpi uppatti niyatāti evaṃ pītikāraṇānipi somanassakāraṇānīti daṭṭhabbāni. Kiñca – agambhīrapakatitā, somanassapaṭisandhikatāti imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi somanassasahagatatā hoti. Yo hi agambhīrapakatiko hoti, appamattakepi hitopakaraṇe tussati, yo ca somanassapaṭisandhiko appasannesu ārammaṇesupi appaṭikkūladassāvī, tassa yebhuyyena somanassasahagatacittaṃ uppajjati. Yathāvuttānaṃ pana somanassakāraṇānamabhāvena majjhattārammaṇatāya ca upekkhāsahagatatā veditabbā.

Moreover, there are these eleven things that lead to the arising of the rapture factor of enlightenment. Namely: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities, recollection of peace; avoiding coarse persons, associating with amiable persons; reflecting on inspiring discourses, and being inclined toward that. On account of these causes, too, being accompanied by joy should be understood. For one who recollects the qualities of the Buddha and so on, rapture arises, suffusing the entire body up to the arising of access concentration. Likewise, rapture generally arises for one reflecting on the fourfold purity of virtue one has long protected; for a householder reflecting on the ten or five precepts; for one reflecting on one's own generosity after giving to spiritual companions in a time of need; for a householder reflecting on gifts given to the virtuous; for one reflecting on the presence in oneself of the qualities by which deities attained their state; for one reflecting on how one's defilements, suppressed by serenity and insight, have not been active for sixty or seventy years; for one who avoids coarse persons and associates with amiable persons; for one who reflects on inspiring discourses that illuminate the qualities of the Three Jewels; and for one who is inclined toward that, acting with the aim of arousing rapture. Since rapture is inseparable from joy, with the arising of the former, the arising of the latter is certain. Thus, the causes of rapture should also be seen as causes of joy. Furthermore, being accompanied by joy occurs for two other reasons: having a shallow nature and having a joyful rebirth-linking. For one who has a shallow nature is pleased even by a slight favor, and one with a joyful rebirth-linking sees even unpleasing objects as not repulsive; for such a person, consciousness accompanied by joy usually arises. However, through the absence of the aforesaid causes of joy and because the object is neutral, being accompanied by equanimity should be understood.

Ñāṇasampayuttassa pana kammato upapattito indriyaparipākato kilesadūrībhāvatoti imehi kāraṇehi hoti. Yo hi paresaṃ hitajjhāsayena dhammaṃ deseti hīnukkaṭṭhādīni ca naḷakāramuddāgaṇanādīni sippāyatanāni, vaḍḍhakīkasivāṇijjādīni ca kammāyatanāni, visaharaṇādīni ca vijjāyatanānīti evaṃ niravajjasippāyatanādīni sikkhāpeti, sayaṃ vā sikkhati, dhammakathikassa sakkāraṃ katvā dhammaṃ kathāpeti, “āyatiṃ paññavā bhavissāmī”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nānappakāraṃ puññakammaṃ karoti, tassevaṃ nānappakāraṃ paññāsaṃvattanikakammaṃ sampādentassa taṃ kammaṃ upanissāya uppajjamānaṃ kusalaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ uppajjati. Tathā abyāpajje loke uppannassa uppajjamānaṃ kusalaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Being associated with knowledge occurs for these reasons: because of action, because of rebirth, because of the maturity of the faculties, and because of being far from the defilements. For one who, with the intention of benefiting others, teaches the Dhamma; or teaches or learns such blameless fields of craft, occupations, and sciences as reed-work, accounting, counting, carpentry, agriculture, trade, and toxicology; or who, after honoring a Dhamma teacher, has the Dhamma taught; or who, having made the aspiration, 'May I be wise in the future,' performs various kinds of meritorious deeds—for one who thus accomplishes various kinds of kamma conducive to wisdom, wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge arises in dependence on that kamma. Similarly, for one reborn in a world free from affliction, the wholesome consciousness that arises is associated with knowledge. For it is said:

“Tassa [M 1.0185] tattha sukhino dhammapadāni pilavanti, dandho, bhikkhave, satuppādo, atha so satto khippameva visesabhāgī hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.191).

“For him, being happy there, the teachings float to the surface. Slow, monks, is the arising of mindfulness, but then that being quickly partakes of distinction.”

Tathā paññādasakaṃ sampattassa indriyaparipākaṃ nissāya uppajjamānaṃ kusalaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ hoti. Yena pana samathavipassanābhāvanāhi kilesā vikkhambhitā, tassa kilesadūrībhāvaṃ nissāya uppajjamānaṃ cittaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ uppajjati. Yathāha –

Similarly, for one who has reached the second decade of life, wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge arises in dependence on the maturity of the faculties. And for one by whom the defilements have been suppressed through the development of serenity and insight, consciousness associated with knowledge arises in dependence on being far from the defilements. As it is said:

“Yogā [V 1.0152] ve jāyate bhūri, ayogā bhūrisaṅkhayo”ti. (Dha. pa. 282).

“From striving springs wisdom; from non-striving, wisdom’s loss.”

Apica ye te dhammā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti. Seyyathidaṃ – paripucchakatā vatthuvisadakiriyā indriyasamattapaṭipādanā duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā paññavantapuggalasevanā gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā tadadhimuttatāti imehi kāraṇehi ñāṇasampayuttabhāvo hoti. Tathā hi yo paññavante upasaṅkamma khandhadhātuāyatanaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaṅgasamathavipassanādīnaṃ paripucchābahulo hoti, tassa taṃvasena uppannaṃ sutamayañāṇaṃ ādiṃ katvā uppajjamānaṃ cittaṃ ñāṇasahagataṃ hoti. Yena pana nakhakesacīvarasenāsanādīni ajjhattikabāhiravatthūni pubbe avisadāni chedanamalaharaṇādinā visadāni katāni, tassevaṃ visadavatthukassa uppannesu cittacetasikesu visadaṃ ñāṇaṃ hoti parisuddhāni dīpakapallakādīni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Yassa ca saddhindriyādīsu aññataraṃ balavaṃ hoti, itarāni mandāni, tato tāni sakasakakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkonti, tasmā so tassa bojjhaṅgavibhaṅge āgatanayena tena tena ākārena samattaṃ paṭipādeti, tassevaṃ indriyānaṃ samattaṃ paṭipādentassa vipassanāñāṇādīnaṃ vasena [M 1.0186] cittaṃ ñāṇasahagataṃ hoti. Yo pana duppaññapuggale parivajjeti, paññavantapuggale vā payirupāsati, khandhādīsu ogāḷhaṃ bhagavato gambhīrañāṇacariyaṃ vā paccavekkhati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu tadadhimuttacitto vā viharati, imesampi uppajjamānaṃ kusalaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ hoti. Apica buddhādiguṇānussaraṇenapi cittaṃ ñāṇasahagataṃ hoti. Yathāha –

Furthermore, there are those things that conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena. Namely: frequent questioning, making the basis clear, balancing the spiritual faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reflecting on the profound sphere of knowledge, and being resolved upon that. For these reasons, there is the state of being associated with knowledge. Indeed, for one who frequently approaches the wise and inquires about the aggregates, elements, sense bases, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, path factors, jhāna factors, serenity, and insight, the mind that arises for him on that account, beginning with the knowledge born of learning, is accompanied by knowledge. Moreover, for one who has made internal and external bases such as nails, hair, robes, and lodgings—previously unclear—clear by cutting, removing dirt, and so forth, for such a person with a clear basis, the knowledge that arises in the mind and mental factors is clear, just like the light of a lamp flame that has arisen depending on a purified wick and oil vessel. For one in whom one of the spiritual faculties, such as faith, is strong while the others are weak, those others cannot perform their respective functions. Therefore, one establishes balance in them in the manner described in the Analysis of the Enlightenment Factors. When one thus establishes balance in the faculties, the mind becomes accompanied by knowledge by way of insight knowledge and the like. Furthermore, for one who avoids unwise persons, associates with wise persons, reflects deeply on the Blessed One’s profound conduct of knowledge regarding the aggregates and so forth, or dwells with a mind resolved upon that in standing, sitting, and so forth—for such a person, the wholesome consciousness that arises is associated with knowledge. Moreover, even through the recollection of the qualities of the Buddha and so forth, the mind becomes accompanied by knowledge. As it is said:

“Yasmiṃ, mahānāma, samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti tathāgataṃ ārabbha. Ujugatacitto kho pana, mahānāma, ariyasāvako labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11).

“Mahānāma, at a time when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, his mind is not overwhelmed by lust, nor by hatred, nor by delusion. At that time his mind is directed straight, with the Tathāgata as its object. With a mind directed straight, Mahānāma, the noble disciple gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is gladdened, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, one experiences happiness. The mind of a happy person becomes concentrated. One who is concentrated understands things as they really are.”

Evaṃ buddhānussatiādayopi rāgādimalavisodhanena ñāṇuppattihetukāyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiñca [V 1.0153] – tihetukapaṭisandhikatā ñāṇuppattikāraṇaṃ. Paṭisandhipaññā hi ādito paṭṭhāya bhavaṅgasantativasena bahulaṃ pavattamānā santānaparibhāvanena ñāṇuppattiyā savisesaupanissayo hoti. Asaṅkhārikattaṃ pana sappāyautubhojanaāvāsādipaccayehi hotīti. Honti cettha –

Thus, the recollection of the Buddha and so on should be seen as causes for the arising of knowledge through the purification of such defilements as lust. Furthermore, having a three-rooted rebirth-linking is a cause for the arising of knowledge. For the wisdom at rebirth-linking, occurring frequently from the outset by way of the continuity of the life-continuum, becomes a special decisive support condition for the arising of knowledge through the cultivation of the mental continuum. The unprompted state, however, occurs because of such favorable conditions as suitable climate, food, and lodging. Herein, there are these verses:

“Iṭṭhārammaṇatā saddhābāhulyaṃ diṭṭhisuddhi ca;

Phaladassāvitā ceva, pītibojjhaṅgahetuyo.

“Desirability of the object, abundance of faith, and purity of view, and also seeing the fruit: these are the causes of the enlightenment factor of rapture.

“Ekādasa [M 1.0187] tathā dhammā, agambhīrasabhāvatā;

Somanassayuttā sandhi, iccete sukhahetuyo.

“Thus eleven phenomena, a nature that is not profound, and a rebirth-linking associated with mental happiness—these are the causes of happiness.

“Abhāvo sukhahetūnaṃ, majjhattārammaṇanti ca;

Upekkhuppattihetu ca, evaṃ ñeyyā vibhāvinā.

“The absence of the causes of happiness and a neutral object are the cause for the arising of equanimity; thus it should be understood by the discerning one.

“Kammūpapattito ceva, tathā indriyapākato;

Kilesūpasamā dhamma-vicayassa ca hetuhi.

“From kamma and rebirth, and from the ripening of the faculties; from the calming of the defilements, and from the causes of the investigation of phenomena;

“Sattadhammehi buddhādi-guṇānussaraṇena ca;

Sappaññasandhito ceva, cittaṃ ñāṇayutaṃ siyā.

“Through the seven phenomena, and by recollecting the qualities of the Buddha and so on, and from a rebirth-linking with wisdom, the mind may be associated with knowledge.

“Utubhojanaāvāsa-sappāyādīhi hetuhi;

Asaṅkhārikabhāvopi, viññātabbo vibhāvinā”ti.

“By such causes as suitable climate, food, and lodging, the state of being unprompted should also be understood by the discerning one.”

Evaṃ vedanāñāṇappayogabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ kāmāvacaracittaṃ niddisitvā idāni taṃ nigamento āha “idaṃ…pe… nāmā”ti.

Having thus indicated the eight kinds of sense-sphere consciousness by way of the distinctions of feeling, knowledge, and prompting, now, concluding, he says: “This… is the name.”

12. Yena panatthena idaṃ “kāmāvacara”nti vuccati, taṃ dāni dassetuṃ “uddānato”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha uddānatoti uddesato, saṅkhepatoti attho. Kiñcāpi avasiṭṭhakilesādayo viya kilesakāmopi assādetabbatāya vatthukāme saṅgahito ñāṇaṃ viya ñeyyeti [V 1.0154] saṅkhepato ekoyeva kāmo siyā, tathāpi kilesakāmo vatthukāmabhāvaṃ gacchanto kāmanīyaṭṭhena gacchati, na kāmanavasena. Kāmanavasena ca pana kilesakāmova hoti, na pana vatthukāmoti āha “klesavatthuvasā”tiādi. Ko panettha vatthukāmo, ko kilesakāmoti codanaṃ manasi nidhāya “chando kāmo, rāgo kāmo, chandarāgo kāmo, saṅkappo kāmo, rāgo kāmo, saṅkapparāgo kāmo”ti (mahāni. 1) evaṃ niddesapāḷiyaṃ āgatā niddiṭṭhā [M 1.0188] kāmataṇhāva idha kilesakāmo. Vatthukāmoti ca “manāpikā rūpā…pe… manāpikā phoṭṭhabbā…pe… sabbepi kāmāvacarā dhammā…pe… sabbepi rūpāvacarā…pe… sabbepi arūpāvacarā…pe… kāmā”ti (mahāni. 1) tattheva niddiṭṭhā saviññāṇāviññāṇappabhedā tebhūmakadhammāti dassento āha “kileso…pe… vaṭṭaka”nti. “Chandarāgovā”ti avadhāraṇena kilesabhāvena niruḷhesu lobhadosamohādīsu dasasu dosamohādayo nava kilese paṭikkhipati. Kāmarūpārūpataṇhāya vatthu patiṭṭhānaṃ, kāraṇabhūtanti vā vatthu.

12. Now, to show for what reason this is called the ‘sense sphere,’ the section beginning ‘in summary’ has been started. Here, ‘in summary’ means by way of a heading, that is, concisely. Although, just like the remaining defilements, sensuality as defilement might be included under sensuality as object on the grounds that it is to be savored, just as knowledge is included under the knowable, so in brief there would be only one kind of sensuality. Nevertheless, when sensuality as defilement becomes sensuality as object, it does so in the sense of being desirable, not through the act of desiring. And through the act of desiring, there is only sensuality as defilement, not sensuality as object. Thus he says, ‘by way of defilement and object,’ etc. Keeping in mind the question, ‘What here is sensuality as object, and what is sensuality as defilement?’, he says that sensual craving, which has come down in the Niddesa passage—‘Desire is sensuality, lust is sensuality, desire-lust is sensuality; intention is sensuality, lust is sensuality, intention-lust is sensuality’ (Mahāni. 1)—is here sensuality as defilement. And showing that sensuality as object is the phenomena of the three planes, divided into animate and inanimate, which are pointed out in the same text—‘Agreeable forms… agreeable tangible objects… all sense-sphere phenomena… all fine-material-sphere phenomena… all immaterial-sphere phenomena… are sensuality’ (Mahāni. 1)—he says: ‘defilement… the round.’ By the specification ‘desire-lust,’ from among the ten defilements established as such—greed, hatred, delusion, etc.—he rejects the nine defilements, hatred, delusion, and so on. The object (vatthu) is the basis for the craving for the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere, or it is what has become the cause.

13. Kathaṃ pana kilesakāmo nāma, kathañca vatthukāmoti āha “kilesakāmo”tiādi. Kāmetīti vatthukāmaṃ pattheti. Kāmīyatīti kilesakāmena patthīyati. Iti-saddo “tasmā”ti imassa atthe. Ca-saddo eva-kāratthe, tena yasmā kilesakāmo kāmetīti kāmo, vatthukāmo ca kāmīyatīti, tasmā eva kilesakāmo, vatthukāmo cāti duvidhopi esa kāmo kārakadvaye kattari, kammani ca sijjhati, kattubhāvaṃ, kammabhāvañca paccanubhotīti attho. Atha vā duvidhoti dvinnaṃ kāmānaṃ vācakato duvidho. “Kāmo”ti ayaṃ saddo kārakadvaye sijjhati yathāvuttakārakayugaḷe nipphajjati, kattari, kammani ca “kāmo”ti padasambhavo hotīti attho. Vo-kāro pana nipātamattaṃ “evaṃ vo kālāmā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) viya. Atha vā vokārakadvayeti khandhadvayeti attho. Kilesakāmo hi saṅkhārasabhāvattā saṅkhārakkhandhe, vatthukāmo ca vakkhamānanayena pañcakāmaguṇabhūto rūpasabhāvattā rūpakkhandheti evaṃ duvidhopesa kāmo khandhadvaye sijjhati nipphajjati, antobhāvaṃ gacchatīti.

13. But how is it called ‘sensuality as defilement,’ and how ‘sensuality as object’? He says: ‘sensuality as defilement,’ etc. ‘He desires’ (kāmeti): he longs for sensuality as object. ‘It is desired’ (kāmīyati): it is longed for by sensuality as defilement. The word iti has the meaning of ‘therefore.’ The word ca has the meaning of the emphatic particle eva. Thus, because sensuality as defilement is ‘sensuality’ (kāma) since it desires, and sensuality as object is ‘sensuality’ since it is desired, therefore this twofold sensuality is accomplished in the two agentive roles, the agent and the object; that is, it experiences the state of being an agent and the state of being an object. Or, it is twofold because it is expressive of two kinds of sensuality. The word ‘sensuality’ is accomplished in the two agentive roles; that is, the word ‘sensuality’ can be formed in the aforesaid pair of agentive roles, the agent and the object. The particle vo, however, is a mere expletive, as in such passages as ‘Thus, Kālāmas, you…’ (AN 3.66). Or, vokārakadvaye means in the two aggregates. For sensuality as defilement, being of the nature of formations, is accomplished in the aggregate of formations; and sensuality as object, being the five cords of sensual pleasure in the way to be described, is of the nature of form and thus is accomplished in the aggregate of form. In this way this twofold sensuality is accomplished in, that is, is included within, the two aggregates.

14. Sampajjanāni [M 1.0189] sampattiyo, tāsaṃ vasena visayavisayībhāvena aññamaññaṃ samosaraṇavasena, sampāpuṇanavasenāti attho. Iminā pana idaṃ dīpeti – yattha duvidhopi kāmo visayavisayībhāvena sahito pavattati, soyeva ekādasavidho padeso kāmāvacarasaññito[V 1.0155]. Yattha pana rūpārūpadhātuyaṃ kevalaṃ vatthukāmova pavattati, na so padeso kāmāvacaro nāmāti. Nanu ca duvidhopi sahito rūpārūpadhātūsu pavattati, rūpārūpāvacaradhammānaṃ vatthukāmattā, tadārammaṇabhūtānañca rūpārūpataṇhānaṃ taṃyogena kilesakāmabhāvasiddhitoti? Nayidamevaṃ orambhāgiyabhūtassa bahalakilesasseva kāmarāgassa idha kilesakāmabhāvena adhippetattā. “Uddānato duve kāmā”ti sabbe kāme uddisitvāpi hi “padeso catupāyāna”ntiādinā visayaniyamanena “duvidhopi aya”nti ettha kāmekadesabhūto nīvaraṇāvatthāya kathito kāmarāgo kilesakāmabhāvena, tabbatthukāyeva dhammā vatthukāmabhāvena gahitā, na rūpārūpataṇhā, tabbatthukadhammā cāti ñāpīyati. Evañca katvā upari vakkhamānā sasatthāvacarūpamā upapannā hoti, yathāvuttānameva kāmānaṃ idha adhippetattā rūpārūpadhātūsu vimānakapparukkhavatthālaṅkāraparittakusalādibhedesu kāmāvacaradhammesu pavatto chandarāgo kilesakāmo nāma na hoti, na ca tabbatthubhūtaṃ vimānakapparukkhādiparittadhammajātaṃ vatthukāmo nāmāti siddhaṃ. Tenevāha “kāmo vā kāmasaññā vā brahmaloke na vijjatī”ti. Kāmāvacarasattasantānagatataṇhāya visayabhāve sati pana taṃyogena rūpārūpadhātūsupi pavattamāno parittadhammo vatthukāmoyevāti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā niddese āgatanayena niravaseso kilesakāmo kāmataṇhābhavataṇhāvibhavataṇhānirodhataṇhāpabhedo idha pavattati. Vatthukāmesupi [M 1.0190] appakaṃ rūpārūpavipākamattaṃ ṭhapetvā sabboyeva idha pavattatīti anavasesappavattiṃ sandhāya “kāmoyaṃ duvidhopi cā”ti vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi evaṃ vuttaṃ, tesu pana bahalakilesakāmabhūto bahalakāmarāgo ca tabbatthukā pañca kāmaguṇā ca idha gahitāti dassanatthaṃ “sampattīnaṃ vasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Sampajjanavasena, samijjhanavasenāti attho. Avacaratīti pavattati. Iti-saddo hetumhi, yasmā duvidhopi ayaṃ kāmo avacarati, tasmā kāmo ettha avacaratīti kāmāvacarasaññitoti attho.

14. Occurrences (sampajjanāni) are accomplishments (sampattiyo); the meaning is by way of converging upon each other through the relationship of object and subject, and by way of reaching attainment. By this it is shown that wherever the twofold sensuality operates together through the relationship of object and subject, that very elevenfold sphere is designated as the sense-sphere. But where in the form and formless realms only sensuality as object operates, that sphere is not called the sense-sphere. But might one not object that the twofold sensuality operates together in the form and formless realms too, since the phenomena of the form and formless realms are sensuality as object, and since craving for form and formlessness, which are their objects, are established as having the nature of sensuality as defilement through connection with them? This is not so, because what is intended here as sensuality as defilement is only the gross sensual lust, which is a defilement belonging to the lower fetters. For although all sensualities are indicated by the summary statement, 'In summary, there are two sensualities,' by the restriction of the domain in the passage beginning, 'the sphere of the four planes of misery,' it is shown that here 'this twofold sensuality' refers to a part of sensuality—namely, sensual lust in the state of a hindrance—which is spoken of as sensuality as defilement, and the phenomena that are its basis are taken as sensuality as object, not craving for form and formlessness and the phenomena that are their basis. And when this is done, the simile of the domain of armed men, to be mentioned below, becomes appropriate. Because only the aforesaid sensualities are intended here, the desire and lust that operates in the form and formless realms in regard to sense-sphere phenomena of various kinds—such as celestial mansions, wishing trees, ornaments, and minor wholesome states—is not called sensuality as defilement; nor is the collection of minor phenomena that are its basis, such as celestial mansions and wishing trees, called sensuality as object. Thus it is established. For this reason it is said: 'Sensuality or the perception of sensuality does not exist in the Brahma-world.' However, it should be understood that when there is an object for the craving that has entered the continuity of a sense-sphere being, then the minor phenomena that operate even in the form and formless realms through connection with it are indeed sensuality as object. Alternatively, according to the method that comes in the Exposition, the entire sensuality as defilement—differentiated as sensual craving, craving for existence, craving for non-existence, and craving for cessation—operates here. As for sensuality as object, except for a small amount which is merely the resultants of the form and formless realms, all of it operates here. Thus, with reference to its complete operation, it is said: 'This sensuality is twofold.' Although it is stated thus, to show that among them what is taken here is the gross sensuality as defilement, that is, gross sensual lust, and the five cords of sensual pleasure that are its basis, it is said: 'by way of accomplishments.' The meaning is: by way of occurring, by way of being fulfilled. 'Operates' (avacarati) means it proceeds. The word 'iti' is in the sense of reason. The meaning is: since this twofold sensuality operates here, therefore it is designated as the sense-sphere because sensuality operates here.

15. Saggamokkhahetubhūtā puññasammatā ayā yebhuyyena apetāti apāyā. Nirayādivasena cattāro apāyā catupāyā. Channanti cātumahārājikatāvatiṃsayāmātusitānimmānaratiparanimmitavasavattisaṅkhātānaṃ channaṃ devalokānaṃ. Merupādavāsino pana asurā tāvatiṃsesuyeva saṅgayhantīti na tehi saddhiṃ sattannanti vuttaṃ. Manaso ussannatāya manussā, satisūrabhāvabrahmacariyayogyatādiguṇavasena upacitamānasatāya ukkaṭṭhaguṇacittatāyāti attho, te pana nippariyāyato jambudīpavāsino veditabbā. Yathāha –

15. Because they are for the most part (yebhuyyena) devoid (apetā) of that which is considered merit (puññasammatā ayā), the cause for heaven and liberation, they are called 'planes of deprivation' (apāyā). The four planes of woe (catupāyā) are the four apāyas, namely, hell and so on. 'The six' refers to the six deva worlds, enumerated as the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa, the Yāma, the Tusita, the Nimmānarati, and the Paranimmitavasavatti. But since the asuras who dwell at the foot of Mount Meru are included right within the Tāvatiṃsa, it is not said that there are seven including them. Humans (manussā) are so called because of the loftiness (ussannatā) of their minds (manaso); the meaning is that their minds possess superior qualities (ukkaṭṭhaguṇacittatā) and are developed (upacitamānasatā) on account of such qualities as mindfulness, heroism, and suitability for the holy life. And they are to be understood as being, in the primary sense, the inhabitants of Jambudīpa. As it is said:

“Tīhi[V 1.0156], bhikkhave, ṭhānehi jambudīpakā manussā uttarakuruke ca manusse adhiggaṇhanti deve ca tāvatiṃse. Katamehi tīhi? Sūrā satimanto idha brahmacariyavāso”ti (a. ni. 9.21).
