“Bhikkhus, on three grounds the human beings of Jambudīpa surpass the human beings of Uttarakuru and the Tāvatiṃsa devas. What three? They are heroic, they are mindful, and the holy life is lived here.”

Tehi pana samānarūpāditāya saddhiṃ parittadīpavāsīhi itaramahādīpavāsinopi “manussā”icceva paññāyiṃsu. Lokiyā pana manuno apaccabhāveneva “manussā”ti vadanti[M 1.0191]. Ekādasavidhoti caturāpāyesu tiracchānapettivisayānaṃ visuṃ paricchinnassa okāsassa abhāvepi yattha te araññasamuddapabbatapādādike nibaddhavāsaṃ vasanti, tādisassa ṭhānassa gahitattā ekādasavidho.

But because of their similarity in form and so on, the inhabitants of the other great continents, along with the inhabitants of the minor continents, were also known simply as 'humans.' Worldly people, however, call them 'humans' simply because they are the offspring of Manu. As to the elevenfold division: in the four planes of woe, although there is no separately defined region for animals and the sphere of afflicted spirits, since such places where they dwell permanently—such as forests, oceans, and the foothills of mountains—are included, it is called elevenfold.

16. Nanu cettha aññesampi dhammānaṃ pavattisambhavato kāmasseva avacaraṇavasena kathaṃ nāmalābhoti āha “assābhilakkhitattā”tiādi. Tattha assāti imassa duvidhassa kāmassa. Abhilakkhitattāti ekādasavidhe padese pākaṭattā. Atha vā assāti karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ, tasmā anena duvidhena kāmena ekādasavidhassa padesassa abhilakkhitattā, paññāpitattāti attho. Atha vā upayogatthe sāmivacanavasena assa ekādasavidhassa padesassa tena duvidhena abhilakkhitattāti attho. Saha satthehīti sasatthā, yattha te avacaranti, so sasatthāvacaro, padeso. So viya. Yathā hi yasmiṃ padese sasatthā purisā avacaranti, so vijjamānesupi aññesu dvipadacatuppadādīsu avacarantesu tesaṃ tattha pākaṭattā, tehi vā abhilakkhitattā “sasatthāvacaro”tveva paññāyati, evaṃ vijjamānesupi aññesu rūpāvacarādīsu avacarantesu abhilakkhaṇavasena ayaṃ padeso “kāmāvacaro”tveva saññitoti. Esa nayo rūpārūpāvacaresu.

16. But since it is possible for other phenomena to operate here too, how does it get its name just on account of the operation of sensual pleasure? He says: 'Because it is characterized by it,' etc. Therein, 'by it' (assa) refers to this twofold sensual pleasure. 'Because it is characterized' means because it is prominent in the elevenfold sphere. Alternatively, 'assa' is a genitive used in the instrumental sense; therefore, the meaning is: because the elevenfold sphere is characterized, that is, designated, by this twofold sensual pleasure. Or, with the genitive in the sense of relation, the meaning is: because this elevenfold sphere is characterized by that twofold sensual pleasure. 'With weapons' (saha satthehi) is sasatthā; the sphere where they operate is a 'domain of armed men' (sasatthāvacaro). It is like this: just as a sphere where armed men operate is known as a 'domain of armed men'—even though other bipeds, quadrupeds, etc., also operate there—because those armed men are prominent there or because it is characterized by them, so too this sphere is designated as the 'sense-sphere' on account of this characterization, even though other phenomena, such as those of the form sphere, also operate there. This same method applies to the form and formless spheres.

17-8. Nanu ca cittaṃ kāmāvacaranti vuttaṃ, yathāvuttanayena pana padesassa gahitattā kathaṃ tattha avacarantaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ nāmāti āha “svāya”ntiādi. So ayaṃ kāmāvacaro “kāmo”ti saññitoti sambandho. Rūpabhavo rūpanti yathā rūpabhavo rūpaṃ. Avuttopi hi yathāsaddo evaṃ-saddasanniṭṭhānato labbhati. Yathā “rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāvetī”ti ettha “rūpabhavūpapattiyā”ti vattabbe rūpabhavo [M 1.0192] “rūpa”nti saññitoti ayamettha attho. Kathaṃ panesa evaṃ saññitoti āha “uttarassā”tiādi. Atha vā yathā uttarassa padassa lopaṃ katvā [V 1.0157] udīrito esa rūpabhavo “rūpa”nti saññito, evaṃ svāyaṃ kāmāvacaro kāmoti sambandho. Tasmiṃ kāmeti tasmiṃ uttarapadalopavasena kāmasaññite padese. Idanti idaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ cittaṃ. Adhikāravasena pana tassa gahaṇepi sabbesameva parittacittānamayamattho labbhati sabbesampi kāme avacaraṇato. Sadāti sabbakālaṃ, bāhulyenāti adhippāyo. Iminā pana idaṃ dīpeti – yathā saṅgāme yebhuyyena avacaranto “saṅgāmāvacaro”ti laddhanāmo hatthī aññattha avacarantopi bāhullappavattivasena “saṅgāmāvacaro”tveva paññāyati, evamidaṃ aññattha avacarantampi kāmaloke bāhullavuttito “kāmāvacara”micceva vuttanti. Tena pana nanu cetaṃ rūpārūpabhavesupi avacaraṇato rūpāvacarādināmampi labheyyāti idaṃ codanaṃ pariharati. Hoti cettha –

17-8. But has it not been said that consciousness is of the sense-sphere? Since, according to the method stated, it is the region that is taken, how can that which operates therein be called 'of the sense-sphere'? He says: 'This very…,' etc. The connection is: this sense-sphere consciousness is designated as 'kāma.' Just as form-existence is 'form.' For even though unstated, the word 'yathā' (just as) is obtained from its proximity to the word 'evaṃ' (so). For example, in the phrase 'he develops the path for rebirth in the form realm,' when one should say 'for rebirth in the form-existence,' the form-existence is designated as 'form'—this is the meaning here. But how is it so designated? He says: 'of the latter…,' etc. Alternatively, just as this form-existence, spoken of with the elision of the latter word, is designated as 'form,' so this sense-sphere consciousness is designated as 'kāma.' 'In that "kāma"' means: in that region designated as 'kāma' by way of eliding the latter word. 'This' means this eightfold consciousness. But although this is taken up by force of the context, this meaning is obtained for all limited consciousnesses, since they all operate in the sensual realm. 'Always' means at all times; the intention is 'for the most part.' By this he shows this: just as an elephant that gets the name 'battle-dweller' because it operates for the most part in battle is known as a 'battle-dweller' even when it operates elsewhere, on account of its predominant activity, so this consciousness, even when operating elsewhere, is called 'of the sense-sphere' because of its predominant occurrence in the sensual world. By this he refutes the objection: 'But since this also operates in the form and formless existences, should it not also get the names "of the form-sphere," etc.?' Here there is this verse:

“Kāmevacaratītyetaṃ, kāmāvacarasaññitaṃ;

Sese avacarantampi, saṅgāmāvacaro yathā”ti.

“Because it operates in the sensual realm, it is designated 'of the sense-sphere'; though it operates in the remaining spheres too, it is like the battle-dweller.”

Iti-saddo hetumhi. Ca-saddo vattabbantarasamuccaye. Tena yasmā uttarapadalopena kāmāvacaro “kāmo”ti saññito, yasmā ca tasmiṃ kāme idaṃ cittaṃ sadā avacarati, tasmā “kāmāvacara”micceva kathitaṃ, na pana kāmāvacarāvacaraṃ, nāpi rūpārūpāvacaranti vāti adhippāyo. Kāmaghātināti desanāñāṇena vineyyasantānagatassa kilesakāmassa hananasīlena sammāsambuddhena.

The word 'iti' is in the sense of reason. The word 'ca' serves to combine another statement. The intention is this: because the sense-sphere consciousness (`kāmāvacaro`) is designated 'kāma' by the elision of the latter word, and because this consciousness always operates in that 'kāma,' it is therefore spoken of simply as 'of the sense-sphere' (`kāmāvacara`), and not as 'operating in that which is of the sense-sphere' (`kāmāvacarāvacara`), nor as 'of the form-sphere' or 'of the formless-sphere.' 'By the Slayer of Kāma' (`Kāmaghātinā`) refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One, who by nature destroys, with the knowledge of teaching, the defilement of sensual pleasure in the mental continuity of those who can be trained.

19. Paṭisandhiṃ [M 1.0193] …pe… avacārayatīti vāti atha vā yasmā yattha katthaci uppannampi kāme bhaveyeva paṭisandhiṃ avacārayati, tasmā idaṃ kāme avacārayatīti “kāmāvacara”nti kathitaṃ cā-saddassa rassattaṃ katvāti attho. Evaṃ uttarapadalopavasena padasambhavaṃ dassetvā idāni vināpi uttarapadalopaṃ kāmāvacara-saddassa sambhavaṃ dassetuṃ “pariyāpannanti tatra vā”ti vuttaṃ. Tatrāti tasmiṃ kāmabhave. Pariyāpannanti antogadhaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo –

19. It is called 'of the sense-sphere' because it causes rebirth-linking to enter [the sensual realm]... or alternatively, because wherever it arises, it causes rebirth-linking to enter only into sensual existence, therefore it is called 'of the sense-sphere' (`kāmāvacara`) from the phrase 'it causes to enter the sensual realm' (`kāme avacārayati`), with the shortening of the syllable 'cā'—this is the meaning. Having thus shown the formation of the term through the elision of the subsequent word, now, to show the formation of the term 'of the sense-sphere' even without the elision of the subsequent word, it is said: 'or included therein.' 'Therein' means in that sensual existence. 'Included' means contained within. This is the intention here—

“Katame dhammā kāmāvacarā? Heṭṭhato avīcinirayaṃ pariyantaṃ katvā uparito paranimmitavasavattī deve antokaritvā yaṃ etasmiṃ antare etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannā khandhadhātuāyatanā [V 1.0158] rūpaṃ vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇaṃ. Ime dhammā kāmāvacarā”ti (dha. sa. 1287) –

“What are the things that belong to the sense-sphere? From below, having the Avīci hell as its limit, and from above, including the Paranimmitavasavattī gods, whatever aggregates, elements, and sense bases are within this range, belonging here, included here: form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. These things belong to the sense-sphere.” (Dhs. 1287)

Vuttattā yathā manussitthiyā kucchismiṃ nibbattopi tiracchānagatiko tiracchānayoniyameva pariyāpannattā “tiracchāno”tveva vuccati, evamidaṃ rūpārūpabhavesu uppannampi kāmabhavapariyāpannattā “kāmāvacara”micceva kathitanti. Tappariyāpannatā cassa avīciparanimmitaparicchinnokāsaninnāya kāmataṇhāya visayabhāvatoti veditabbā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ ācariyadhammapālattherena nikkhepakaṇḍepi “‘etthāvacarā’ti vacanaṃ avīciparanimmitaparicchinnokāsāya kāmataṇhāya visayabhāvaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti. Padasambhavo panettha evaṃ veditabbo – kāmataṇhā kāmo, so ettha ārammaṇakaraṇavasena avacaratīti kāmāvacaranti. Nanu cettha katamā kāmataṇhā, yā kāmāvacaradhammārammaṇā taṇhā. Katame kāmāvacaradhammā, ye kāmataṇhāvisayāti evaṃ itarītaranissayatādoso āpajjatīti[M 1.0194]? Nāpajjati, avīciādiekādasokāsaninnatāya yaṃkiñci taṇhaṃ kāmataṇhābhāvena gahetvā taṃsabhāvāya taṇhāya visayabhāvena kāmāvacaradhammānaṃ upalakkhetabbabhāvato. Atha vā kilesavatthuvasena duvidhopi kāmo yathārahaṃ sahajātavasena ettha avacaratīti kāmāvacaraṃ, ārammaṇakaraṇavasena vā duvidhepi kāme etaṃ avacaratīti kāmāvacaraṃ. Atha vā mañcanissitakesu ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontesu nissayanissitānaṃ abhedassa buddhiyā gahitattā nissitakesu nissayūpacāravasena “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti vuccati, evametampi kāmāvacarabhave pavattanavasena tannissitattā nissayavohārena “kāmāvacara”nti vuccati. Hoti cettha –

Because it has been said that just as a being destined for the animal realm, even when born in the womb of a human woman, is still included in the animal realm and is thus called an 'animal,' so too this consciousness, even when arising in the realms of form or formlessness, is called simply 'of the sense-sphere' because it is included in the sensual existence. It should be understood that its inclusion is due to its being the objective field of sensual craving, which is inclined towards the space delimited by Avīci and Paranimmita-vasavattī. As the Venerable Ācariya Dhammapāla stated in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa: 'The term “operating here” is used with reference to its being the objective field of sensual craving, which is inclined towards the space delimited by Avīci and Paranimmita-vasavattī.' The derivation of the term here should be understood as follows: sensual craving is 'kāma,' and because this operates here by way of taking an object, it is called 'of the sense-sphere' (`kāmāvacara`). Now, one might ask: 'What is sensual craving here? It is craving that takes sense-sphere phenomena as its object. And what are sense-sphere phenomena? They are the objects of sensual craving.' Thus, the fault of mutual dependence arises. But this is not a fault, because any craving inclined toward the eleven realms beginning with Avīci is taken as sensual craving by nature, and the phenomena of the sense-sphere are to be recognized as being the objects of that craving. Alternatively, both kinds of sensuality—by way of defilement and object—operate here appropriately, either through co-nascence, or this consciousness operates in both kinds of sensuality by way of taking them as object, hence it is called 'of the sense-sphere.' Or, just as when people are shouting on a bed, because the non-distinction between the support and the supported is perceived, it is said, 'the beds are shouting,' by way of metaphorical usage regarding the support—so too, this consciousness is called 'of the sense-sphere' by a conventional term for its support, because it occurs in dependence on the sensual existence. Here there is this verse—

“Kāmovacaratītyettha, kāmevacaratīti vā;

Ṭhānūpacārato vāpi, taṃ kāmāvacaraṃ bhave”ti.

“Here, because sensuality operates, or because it operates in the sensual realm; or also by way of metaphorical usage regarding the place, it would be 'of the sense-sphere'.”

20. Pujjaphalanibbattanato, attasantānaṃ punanato ca puññāni, kattabbatāya kiriyā, tesaṃ tesaṃ ānisaṃsānaṃ vatthutāya vatthūni cāti puññakiriyavatthūni. Gaṇanato dasaparimāṇattā dasa ca tāni puññakiriyavatthūni cāti dasa puññakiriyavatthūni, tesaṃ vasenāti dasapuññakriyavatthuvasena, dasapuññakiriyavatthubhāvena taṃmayaṃ hutvāti attho. Eva-kārena pana rūpārūpalokuttaraṃ [V 1.0159] viya na kevalaṃ bhāvanāvasenevāti dasseti. Atha vā dasapuññakiriyavatthuvaseneva pavattati, na pana parehi parikappitaparapasaṃsādipuññakiriyavatthuvasenāti eva-saddena avadhāraṇaṃ. Yato vakkhati “sabbānussatipuññañcā”tiādi.

20. Because they bring about a venerable fruit, because they purify one's own continuum, and because they are actions to be done which are the basis of various benefits, they are called 'bases of meritorious action.' Being ten in number, they are the ten bases of meritorious action. By means of these ten bases of meritorious action, or by becoming identical with them, is the meaning. The particle `eva` shows that it is not only by way of development, as with the form, formless, and supramundane spheres. Alternatively, the emphasis by the word `eva` is that it proceeds solely by means of the ten bases of meritorious action, and not by way of bases of meritorious action imagined by others, such as praising others. For it will be said, 'All recollections and merit...,' etc.

21. Kāni pana tāni dasapuññakiriyavatthūni, yesaṃ vasena idaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ cittaṃ pavattatīti vuttanti imaṃ anuyogaṃ sandhāya tāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “dānaṃ sīla”ntiādi vuttaṃ[M 1.0195]. Tattha diyyati etenāti dānaṃ, pariccāgacetanā. Idha pana cittādhikāravasena taṃsampayuttaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Tathā “sīlā”dīsupi. Sīlatīti sīlaṃ, kāyavacīkammāni samādahatīti attho. Susilyavasena hi kāyakammādīni avippakiṇṇāni sampati, āyatiñca hitasukhāvahāni sammā ṭhapitāni samāhitāni honti, sīlayati upadhāretīti vā sīlaṃ. Upadhāraṇaṃ panettha kusalānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhāvo. Bhāveti kusaladhamme āsevati vaḍḍheti etāyāti bhāvanā. Attano santāne nipphannā patti diyyati etenāti pattidānaṃ. Taṃtaṃkiccakaraṇe byāvaṭassa bhāvo veyyāvaccaṃ. Deseti etāyāti desanā. Pattiṃ anumodati etenāti pattānumodo. Pubbapadalopena pana “anumodo”ti vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhiyā ujubhāvo diṭṭhijuttaṃ, sammādiṭṭhiyā ujukaraṇanti attho. Attano, parassa vā hitajjhāsayavasena sammā suṇanti etāyāti saṃsuti. Pūjāvasena apacāyati sāmīciṃ karoti etenāti apacāyo. Puññakiriyavatthūnaṃ pabhedo puññakiriyavatthuppabhedo. Majjhapadalopavasena pana “puññavatthuppabhedo”ti vuttaṃ yathā ājaññayutto ratho “ājaññaratho”ti. Ayaṃ tāvettha padavicāro.

21. Now, what are these ten bases of meritorious action, by means of which this eightfold mind arises, as has been said? To address this inquiry, they are presented in their essential form as 'giving, virtue,' etc. Herein, 'giving' (dāna) is that by which one gives—the volition of relinquishment. Here, however, since mind is the primary topic, it should be understood as that which is associated with it. Similarly for 'virtue' (sīla) and the rest. 'Virtue' (sīla) is that which establishes; it means properly establishing bodily and verbal actions. For through good conduct, bodily actions and so forth are unscattered in the present, and in the future, bringing benefit and happiness, they are well-placed and composed. Or, 'virtue' is that which supports; here, supporting is the state of being a foundation for wholesome qualities. 'Development' (bhāvanā) is that by which one cultivates, practices, and increases wholesome qualities. 'Sharing of merit' (pattidāna) is that by which one gives the merit produced in one's own continuity. 'Service' (veyyāvacca) is the state of being engaged in performing various tasks. 'Teaching' (desanā) is that by which one teaches. 'Rejoicing in merit' (pattānumodo) is that by which one rejoices in merit. 'Anumodo' (rejoicing) is said by eliding the first word. 'Straightening of view' (diṭṭhujukamma) is the straightness of view; it means making straight by means of right view. 'Listening' (suti) is that by which one listens properly with the intention of benefiting oneself or others. 'Reverence' (apacāyana) is that by which one reveres and acts respectfully. The classification of the bases of meritorious action is 'puññakiriyavatthuppabhedo.' By eliding the middle word, however, it is called 'puññavatthuppabhedo,' just as a chariot yoked with thoroughbreds is called a 'thoroughbred chariot.' This, then, is the analysis of the terms here.

Ayaṃ pana vinicchayo – tattha sekhaputhujjanānaṃ paraṃ uddissa pūjānuggahakāmatāya attano vijjamānavatthupariccajanavasena pavattā cetanā dānamayapuññakiriyavatthu nāma. Khīṇāsavānampi tathā pavattā dānameva, sā pana puññakiriyā nāma na hotīti na idha adhippetā. Pujjaphalanibbattanato, hi attasantānaṃ punanato ca puññaṃ, na ca khīṇāsavasantāne pavattā phalanibbattikā hoti, na ca taṃ punāti visuddhasantānappavattattāti. Evaṃ sesesupi.

This, however, is the determination: Here, for trainees and worldlings, the volition that arises through relinquishing one’s own existing possessions for the sake of honoring and helping others is called the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving. For those whose cankers are destroyed, too, giving that occurs in such a way is still giving, but it is not called a meritorious action; thus, it is not intended here. For merit (puñña) is so called because it produces a venerable fruit and because it purifies one's own continuity. But that which occurs in the continuity of one whose cankers are destroyed does not produce a fruit, nor does it purify, because it occurs in a purified continuity. So too with the rest.

Yā pana niccasīlauposathasīlādivasena pañcasīlaṃ aṭṭhasīlaṃ dasasīlaṃ samādiyantassa, asamādiyantassapi kulacārittavasena [M 1.0196] sampattakāyaduccaritādīhi viramantassa, upasampadamāḷake saṃvaraṃ samādiyantassa, pātimokkhaṃ paripūrentassa, āpāthagatavisayesu cakkhādīni indriyāni thakentassa[V 1.0160], cīvarādike ca paccaye paccavekkhantassa, kuhanādivatthuto ājīvaṃ parisodhentassa pavattā cetanā, ayaṃ sīlamayapuññakiriyavatthunāma. Etthāha – “dānaṃ nāmetaṃ mayhaṃ kulavaṃso kulacāritta”nti evaṃ cārittasīle ṭhatvā dentassa pavattā dānamayapuññakiriyavatthu kiṃ, udāhu sīlamayanti? Sīlamayameva cārittasīlabhāvato. Deyyadhammapariccāgavasena pavattāpi hesā pubbābhisaṅkhārassa aparabhāge cetanāya ca tathā pavattattā sīlamayameva puññakiriyavatthu, na dānamayaṃ. Pūjānuggahakāmatāya hi dinnaṃ dānamayanti.

The volition that arises for one who undertakes the five precepts, eight precepts, or ten precepts by way of habitual virtue or observance-day virtue; or for one who, even without formally undertaking them, refrains from bodily misconduct and the like due to family tradition; or for one who undertakes restraint in the ordination hall; or for one who fulfills the monastic code; or for one who restrains the sense faculties such as the eye when objects come into range; or for one who reflects on requisites such as robes; or for one who purifies their livelihood by avoiding deceitful means and so forth—this is called the basis of meritorious action consisting of virtue. Here one might ask: “This giving is my family lineage, my family practice.” For one who gives while established in such customary virtue, is this the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, or of virtue? It is solely of virtue, because it is customary virtue. For although it arises by way of relinquishing a gift, because the volition in the subsequent phase of the prior formation also arises in that way, it is the basis of meritorious action consisting of virtue, not of giving. For what is given out of a desire to honor and help is called giving.

“Cakkhu anicca”ntiādinā pana cakkhādike tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā sammasantassa pavattā gotrabhuvodānapariyosānā vipassanācetanā, kasiṇādīsu ārammaṇesu appanaṃ appattā gotrabhupariyosānā parikammacetanā cāti ayaṃ bhāvanāmayapuññakiriyavatthu nāma. Appanāppattāpi bhāvanāyeva, sā pana na kāmāvacarāti idha na gahitā. Niravajjavijjāyatanakammāyatanasippāyatanānaṃ sikkhanacetanāpi bhāvanāmayeyeva samodhānaṃ gacchatīti ācariyā. Yā cettha deyyadhammaṃ khayato vayato sammasitvā dadato pavattā, sāpi pubbe viya ubhayabhāge cetanānaṃ tathā pavattattā bhāvanāmayapuññakiriyavatthuyevāti veditabbaṃ.

The insight volition that arises for one who contemplates the eye and so forth by attributing the three characteristics—'the eye is impermanent,' etc.—culminating in change-of-lineage and purification, and the preliminary volition culminating in change-of-lineage that has not attained absorption in objects such as kasinas—this is called the basis of meritorious action consisting of development. Even that which has attained absorption is development, but since it is not of the sense sphere, it is not included here. The volition to train in blameless fields of knowledge, fields of work, and fields of craft is also included under development, according to the teachers. And here, the volition that arises for one who gives after contemplating the gift as subject to destruction and disappearance should be understood as the basis of meritorious action consisting of development, because, as before, the volitions in both phases arise in that way.

Dānādikaṃ yaṃ kiñci sucaritakammaṃ katvā “asukassa ca nāma patti hotu, sabbasattānaṃ vā hotū”ti evaṃ attanā katassa parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ paccāsīsanavasena pavattā pattidānamayapuññakiriyavatthu nāma. Kiṃ panevaṃ pattiṃ dadato puññakkhayo hotīti? Na hoti, yathā pana ekaṃ dīpaṃ jāletvā tato dīpasahassaṃ jālentassa paṭhamadīpo khīṇoti [M 1.0197] na vattabbo, purimālokena pana saddhiṃ pacchimālokassa ekībhāve atimahāva hoti, evameva pattiṃ dadato parihāni nāma na hoti, vuḍḍhiyeva pana hotīti daṭṭhabbā. Kathaṃ panesā dinnā nāma hotīti? “Idaṃ me puññakammaṃ sabbasattānaṃ, asukassa vā pariṇamatū”ti evaṃ pubbabhāge, pacchāpi vā vacībhedaṃ karontena manasā eva vā cintentena dinnā nāma hoti. Keci pana “yaṃ mayā kataṃ sucaritaṃ, tassa phalaṃ ‘dammī’ti vuttepi patti dinnāva hotī”ti vadanti. Kusalakammādhikārattā pana parehi ca kammasseva anumoditabbattā kammameva dātabbaṃ, anumodentenapi kammameva anumoditabbanti idamettha ācariyānaṃ sanniṭṭhānaṃ.

When one has done some good deed, such as giving, the volition that arises by way of aspiring to make what one has done common to others, thinking, 'May the merit accrue to so-and-so,' or 'to all beings'—this is called the basis of meritorious action consisting of the sharing of merit. But for one who gives merit, does the merit decrease? No, it does not. Just as when one lights a single lamp and from it lights a thousand other lamps, the first lamp is not said to be diminished—rather, the later light becomes immensely great by merging with the earlier light—so too, for one who gives merit there is no loss; instead, it should be seen that there is only an increase. And how is this considered given? It is considered given when, either beforehand or afterwards, one makes the verbal expression, 'May this meritorious deed of mine accrue to all beings, or to so-and-so,' or when one just thinks this in one's mind. Some, however, say that the merit is given even if one merely states, 'I give the fruit of whatever wholesome deed I have done.' But since wholesome action is the primary concern, and since it is the action itself that is to be rejoiced in by others, it is the action itself that should be given. When rejoicing, too, one should rejoice in the action itself. This is the conclusion of the teachers in this matter.

Cīvarādīsu [V 1.0161] paccāsārahitassa asaṃkiliṭṭhena ajjhāsayena samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ vattapaṭivattakaraṇavasena, gilānupaṭṭhānavasena ca pavattā veyyāvaccamayapuññakiriyavatthu nāma.

The volition that arises for one who, with an undefiled disposition and without expectation regarding robes and other requisites, performs duties and reciprocal duties for ascetics and brahmins and attends to the sick—this is called the basis of meritorious action consisting of service.

Āmisakiñcakkhādinirapekkhacittassa attano paguṇaṃ dhammaṃ vimuttāyatanasīse ṭhatvā desentassa, tatheva niravajjavijjāyatanādikaṃ upadisantassa ca pavattā desanāmayapuññakiriyavatthu nāma. Parehi kataṃ yaṃ kiñci sucaritakammaṃ dinnamadinnampi vā issāmaccheramalaṃ pahāya “sādhu suṭṭhū”ti anumodantassa pavattā anumodanapuññakiriyavatthu nāma, “atthi dinna”ntiādinā kammassakatāñāṇavasena diṭṭhiṃ ujuṃ karontassa pavattā diṭṭhijukammapuññakiriyavatthu nāma. Yadi evaṃ ñāṇavippayuttacittassa diṭṭhijukammapuññakiriyatā na labbhatīti? No na labbhati purimapacchimacetanānampi taṃtaṃpuññakiriyāsveva saṅgaṇhanato. Tathā hi vakkhati –

The volition that arises for one with a mind free from desire for material gain and so forth, who, standing on the ground of liberation, teaches the Dhamma in which one is proficient, and similarly instructs others in the blameless fields of knowledge and so forth—this is called the basis of meritorious action consisting of teaching. The volition that arises for one who, having abandoned the stains of envy and avarice, rejoices with 'Good! Excellent!' in any good deed done by others, whether a share has been given or not—this is called the basis of meritorious action consisting of rejoicing. The volition that arises for one who makes one's view straight through the knowledge of kamma as one's own property, with such thoughts as, 'There is what is given'—this is called the basis of meritorious action consisting of straightening one's view. If so, is the meritorious action of straightening one's view not obtained by one with a mind dissociated from knowledge? No, it is not unobtainable, because the prior and subsequent volitions are also included in those very meritorious actions. For so it will be said:

“Purimā muñcanā ceva, parā tissopi cetanā;

Hoti dānamayaṃ puññaṃ, evaṃ sesesu dīpaye”ti.

The prior volition of relinquishing and the subsequent volition constitute the merit consisting of giving. Thus it should be explained for the remaining cases.

Tasmā [M 1.0198] kiñcāpi ujukaraṇavelāyaṃ ñāṇasampayuttameva cittaṃ hoti, purimapacchābhāge pana ñāṇavippayuttampi hotīti tassāpi diṭṭhijukammapuññakiriyabhāvo uppajjati.

Therefore, although at the moment of straightening the view the mind is associated with knowledge, in the phases before and after it may be dissociated from knowledge. Thus for such a mind, too, the state of a meritorious action of straightening one's view arises.

Apare panāhu – viññāṇapaññāṇavasena dassanaṃ diṭṭhi, cittaṃ paññā ca. Diṭṭhiyā ujubhāvo diṭṭhijuttaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Kusalañca viññāṇaṃ kammassakatāñāṇādi ca sammādassanaṃ. Tattha kusalaviññāṇena ñāṇuppādepi attano sucaritānussaraṇaparaguṇapasaṃsāsaraṇagamanānaṃ saṅgaho, kammassakatāñāṇena kammapathasammādiṭṭhiyāti. Dānādisampayuttaṃ pana ñāṇaṃ dānādīsveva antogadhanti veditabbaṃ. “Evamimaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā tattha vuttanayena paṭipajjanto lokiyalokuttaraguṇavisesaṃ adhigamissāmi, bahussuto vā hutvā pare dhammadesanāya anuggaṇhissāmī”ti evaṃ attano, paresaṃ vā vimuttāyatanasīsena saddhammaṃ suṇantassa pavattā savanamayapuññakiriyavatthu nāma. Niravajjavijjāyatanādisavanacetanāpi ettheva saṅgayhati. Pūjārahe, garuṭṭhāniye, mahallake ca disvā āsanā vuṭṭhahantassa pattacīvarapaṭiggahaṇamaggadānaabhivādanaañjalikammakaraṇaāsanapupphagandhādiabhihāraṃ karontassa ca pavattā bahumānacetanā apacitisahagatapuññakiriyavatthu [V 1.0162] nāma. Veyyāvaccāpacāyanānañhi ayaṃ viseso – vayasā, guṇena ca jeṭṭhānaṃ, gilānānañca taṃtaṃkiccakaraṇaṃ veyyāvaccaṃ, sāmīcikiriyā apacāyananti.

But others say: 'View is seeing by way of consciousness and discernment; it is mind and wisdom. The straightening of view is what is right in view. What is that? Wholesome consciousness and knowledge such as the knowledge of kamma as one's own property—this is right view. Herein, wholesome consciousness includes the recollection of one's own good conduct, praising others' virtues, and going for refuge. The knowledge of kamma as one's own property is right view regarding the path of kamma. The knowledge associated with giving and so forth, however, should be understood as being included within those very acts of giving and so on.' 'Having heard this Dhamma, by practicing according to the method stated therein, I will attain the special mundane and supramundane qualities; or, having become learned, I will assist others with the teaching of the Dhamma.' Thus, for one who listens to the good Dhamma for one's own sake or for others' sake, with the sphere of liberation as the chief aim, there arises the basis for meritorious action consisting of listening. The volition to listen to the faultless bases of knowledge and so on is also included here. When one sees those worthy of offerings, those in a position of respect, and elders, and rises from one's seat, takes their bowl and robes, makes way for them, pays homage, performs the gesture of reverence with joined palms, offers a seat, flowers, perfume, and so on—the volition of reverence that arises is the basis for meritorious action accompanied by deference. For this is the difference between service and deference: performing the respective duties for those senior in age and virtue and for the sick is service; courteous conduct is deference.

22-3. Evaṃ aṭṭhakathāya āgatanayena dasapuññakiriyavatthūni dassetvā idāni sutte āgatanayena dānaṃ sīlaṃ bhāvanāti tīṇiyeva dassetuṃ tesu itaresampi saṅgahaṃ dīpento āha “gacchanti saṅgaha”ntiādi. Tattha pattidānānumodanā dāne saṅgahaṃ gacchanti taṃsabhāvattā. Dānampi hi issāmaccherānaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ, etepi, tasmā samānapaṭipakkhatāya [M 1.0199] dānena saha ekalakkhaṇattā ete dānamayapuññakiriyavatthumhi saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Veyyāvaccāpacāyanā sīlamaye puññe saṅgahaṃ gacchanti cārittasīlasabhāvattā. Desanāsavanadiṭṭhiujukā pana kusaladhammāsevanato bhāvanato bhāvanāmaye saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Keci pana “desento, suṇanto ca desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā lakkhaṇaṃ paṭivijjha deseti, suṇāti ca, tāni ca desanāsavanāni paṭivedhameva āharantīti desanāsavanaṃ bhāvanāmaye saṅgahaṃ gacchatī”ti vadanti. Dhammadānabhāvato “desanā dānamaye saṅgahaṃ gacchatī”tipi sakkā vattuṃ. Tathā diṭṭhijukammaṃ sabbatthāpi sabbesaṃ niyamanalakkhaṇattāti. Dānādīsu hi yaṃ kiñci “atthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattāya sammādiṭṭhiyāva visodhitaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsanti. Evañca katvā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “diṭṭhijukammaṃ pana sabbesaṃ niyamanalakkhaṇa”nti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.305) vuttaṃ. Mahāsaṃghiyā pana abhayagirivāsino ca diṭṭhijukammaṃ visuṃ puññakiriyabhāvena na gaṇhanti. Tathā hi te dānaṃ sīlaṃ bhāvanā saṃsuti desanānussatimodanaṃ veyyāvaccapūjāsaraṇappattipasaṃsā cāti attanā katapuññānussaraṇaṃ buddhādīsu saraṇagamanaṃ paraguṇapasaṃsāti imāni tīṇi pakkhipitvā diṭṭhijukammaṃ aggahetvā dvādasa puññakiriyavatthūni paññāpenti. Puna tīṇevāti paṭhamaṃ dasāpi samānā puna saṅkhepato tīṇeva sambhonti.

22-3. Having thus shown the ten bases for meritorious action according to the method of the commentaries, now, in order to show just the three—giving, virtue, and development—according to the method of the suttas, the author indicates the inclusion of the others within these, saying: 'they are included,' and so on. Herein, transference of merit and rejoicing in merit are included under giving because they are of the same nature. For giving is the opponent of envy and avarice, and so are these two. Therefore, because they are the same kind of opponent and have a single characteristic in common with giving, they are included in the basis for meritorious action consisting of giving. Service and deference are included under the merit of virtue because they are of the nature of virtuous conduct. Teaching, listening, and straightening one's view, however, are included under development because they are the cultivation of wholesome states. Some, however, say: 'When teaching and listening, one directs one's knowledge according to the teaching, penetrates the characteristics, and thus teaches and listens; and since that teaching and listening bring about penetration itself, teaching and listening are included under development.' It can also be said that teaching is included under giving because it is the gift of the Dhamma. Similarly, straightening one's view has the characteristic of regulating all of them everywhere. For among giving and the other meritorious actions, whatever is purified by right view—which proceeds according to the principle 'There is what is given,' and so on—becomes greatly fruitful and of great benefit. Thus it is said in the commentary to the Dīgha Nikāya: 'Straightening one's view, however, has the characteristic of regulating all of them' (DN-a 3.305). However, the Mahāsaṅghikas and the Abhayagirivāsins do not count straightening one's view separately as a basis for meritorious action. Instead, they add three items—recollection of the merit one has done, going for refuge to the Buddha and so on, and praising the virtues of others—and, omitting straightening one's view, they set forth twelve bases for meritorious action. 'Again, just three' means that although at first there are ten, in brief they become just three.

24. Idāni parehi niddisiyamānānaṃ puññānussaraṇādīnaṃ attanā niddiṭṭhesveva samodhānaṃ dassetuṃ “sabbānussatipuññañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sabbasseva attanā katasucaritassa anussaraṇaṃ sabbānussatipuññaṃ nāma. Pasaṃsāti parehi katāya puññakiriyāya, sammāpaṭipattiyā ca vippasannacittena [M 1.0200] pasaṃsanaṃ, santussananti attho. Saraṇattayanti ettha saranti hiṃsantīti saraṇāni, buddhādīni tīṇi ratanāni. Tāni hi saraṇagatānaṃ teneva saraṇagamanena bhayaṃ santāsaṃ duggatiparikkilesaṃ hiṃsanti vināsenti. Tayo avayavā assāti tayaṃ, tīhi avayavehi [V 1.0163] yuttasamudāyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, saraṇānaṃ tayaṃ saraṇattayaṃ, tīṇi saraṇānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Na hi avayavavinimutto samudāyo nāma koci atthīti. Idha pana saraṇattayaggahaṇena upacārato, uttarapadalopato vā saraṇagamanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Na hi saraṇattayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu nāma hoti. Atthato panetaṃ “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā, svākkhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṃgho”tiādinā buddhādīsu pasādapaṭilābhavasena pavattā cetanā diṭṭhijukammasmiṃ saṅgahaṃ yanti taṃvaseneva tesaṃ ijjhato. Na hi viparītadiṭṭhikassa imāni tīṇi sambhavanti, tasmā te ekantena diṭṭhijukammapuññakiriyavatthusmiṃ saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, na visuṃ puññakiriyabhāvena gahetabbāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “natthi saṃsayo”ti. Diṭṭhijukammassa bhāvanāmayasaṅgahepi saṅkhepanayena bhāvanāmaye saṅgayhanti, vitthāranayena pana “kattha nu kho”ti saṃsayo siyāti imesaṃ bhāvanāmayasaṅgaho na vutto. Diṭṭhijukammassa vā sabbesaṃ mahapphalabhāvaniyāmakattena mūlabhūtattā tassa padhānabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ visuṃ tattha saṅgayhantīti vuttaṃ. Apare pana “saṅgaṇhanto saṅgaṇhāti, gaṇhanto ‘muñcatī’ti vacanato saraṇagamanassa sīlasamādāne viya gahaṇaṃ sambhavatīti sīlamaye saṅgayhatī”ti vadanti. “Saraṇagamanaṃ paṇipātabhāvato apacitisahagate saṅgayhatī”ti keci.

24. Now, to show the inclusion of the recollection of merit and other such things indicated by others within those indicated by oneself, it is said: 'And all recollection of merit,' etc. Herein, the recollection of all the good conduct one has performed is called 'all recollection of merit.' 'Praise' is praising, with a confident mind, the meritorious deeds and right practice performed by others; the meaning is being content. 'The triple refuge': here, 'refuges' (saraṇāni) are so called because they harm (saranti); they are the three jewels: the Buddha, and so on. For by the very act of going for refuge, they harm and destroy the fear, terror, and defilements of a bad destination for those who have gone for refuge. 'Triple' (tayaṃ) means having three components; this is a term for a collection connected with three components. 'The triple refuge' (saraṇattayaṃ) means the three refuges, for there is no collection apart from its components. Here, however, by the taking up of the 'triple refuge,' what is intended is the act of going for refuge, either metaphorically or by elision of the latter word. For the triple refuge is not, as such, a basis for meritorious action. In meaning, however, this is the volition that arises through acquiring confidence in the Buddha and the others, by thinking: 'Indeed, the Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened one, the Dhamma is well expounded, the Sangha is practicing the good way,' etc. This volition is included in the straightening of views, since it is accomplished by means of that. For these three do not arise for one with wrong view; therefore, they are definitely included in the basis of meritorious action that is the straightening of views and are not to be taken as a separate kind of meritorious action. This is the intention. Hence he says: 'There is no doubt.' Although the straightening of views is included in the category of development, it is included there in a concise way. But in a detailed way, the doubt 'Where, indeed?' might arise, so the inclusion of these things in the category of development is not stated. Or, since the straightening of views is the root of all, being the determinant for their great fruitfulness, it is said that they are included in it separately to show its pre-eminent status. Others, however, say: 'Since the taking up of the going for refuge is possible, just as in undertaking the precepts, it is included in the category of virtue.' Some say: 'The going for refuge is included in what is associated with reverence, because it is an act of prostration.'

25. Idāni yathāvuttapuññakiriyavatthūnaṃ purimapacchimabhāgavasena pavattamānāpi cetanā tattha tattheva saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti [M 1.0201] dassetuṃ “purimā muñcanā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha purimāti dānatthāya deyyadhammaṃ dhammena samena uppādentassa, uppannaṃ “pariccajissāmī”ti cintentassa, dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesantassa ca yāva vatthuno paṭiggāhakassa hatthe vissajjanaṃ, pariṇāmanaṃ vā, tāva pavattā pubbabhāgacetanā. Paṭiggāhakassa pana hatthe vissajjanacetanā, pariṇāmanacetanā vā muñcanacetanā nāma. Sāyeva niggahītalopena “mucanā”ti vuttā. “Muñcanā”itiyeva vā pāṭho. Parāti attanā vissaṭṭhavatthumhi ālayaṃ akatvā “sādhu suṭṭhu aggaṃ dānaṃ me dinna”nti somanassacittena paccavekkhantassa uppannā aparabhāgacetanā. Tissopi cetanāti iti ayañca purimā cetanā, ayañca muñcanacetanā, ayañca aparacetanāti tissopi cetanā ekato hutvā dānamayaṃ puññaṃ hoti, dānamayapuññakiriyavatthu nāma hotīti attho. “Puñña”nti padaṃ apekkhitvā “hotī”ti ekavacananiddeso. Idāni yathāvuttamatthaṃ sesesupi atidisanto āha “evaṃ sesesu dīpaye”ti. Sesesūti sīlādīsu puññakiriyavatthūsu evaṃ yathāvuttanayena “sīlaṃ ‘rakkhissāmī’ti cintentassa, ‘pabbajissāmī’ti vihāraṃ gacchantassa pavattā purimacetanā, sīlaṃ [V 1.0164] samādiyantassa, pabbajantassa, sīlaṃ paripūrentassa uppannā majjhimacetanā, ‘pūritaṃ me’ti paccavekkhantassa uppannā aparacetanāti evaṃ tissopi cetanā ekato hutvā sīlamayapuññakiriyavatthu nāmā”tiādinā dīpaye, pakāseyyāti attho. Nanu ca attanā katapuññānussaraṇacetanā diṭṭhijukammasaṅgahitā, ayañca aparacetanā sāyevāti kathamassā tattha saṅgahoti? Nāyaṃ doso, visayabhedena ubhinnampi visesasabbhāvato. Puññānussaraṇañhi attanā katapuññavisayameva. Ayaṃ pana tabbatthuvisayāti pākaṭoyeva dvinnaṃ visesoti.

25. Now, to show that the volition occurring in the preliminary and subsequent phases of the aforementioned bases of meritorious action is also included therein, it is said: 'The preliminary, the relinquishing,' etc. Herein, 'the preliminary' is the preliminary-phase volition that occurs for one who, for the sake of giving, produces a gift righteously and justly, who thinks, 'I will relinquish it,' and who seeks a worthy recipient, up to the point of placing the object in the recipient’s hand or dedicating it. The volition of placing it in the recipient’s hand or the volition of dedicating it is called the 'relinquishing volition.' This is called 'relinquishing' (mucanā) by elision of the nasal consonant; or the reading may be 'relinquishing' (muñcanā). 'Subsequent' is the later-phase volition that arises for one who, without forming an attachment to the object relinquished, reflects with a joyful mind: 'Good! Excellent! A supreme gift has been given by me.' 'These three volitions' means: this preliminary volition, this relinquishing volition, and this subsequent volition—these three volitions together become merit consisting of giving; they are called the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving. This is the meaning. With reference to the word 'merit,' the singular verb 'becomes' (hoti) is used. Now, extending the meaning as stated to the remaining cases, he says: 'Thus one should explain in the remaining cases.' 'In the remaining cases' means that in the remaining bases of meritorious action, such as virtue, etc., one should explain in the same way: 'For one who thinks, "I will keep the precepts," or who goes to a monastery thinking, "I will go forth," there is the preliminary volition. For one undertaking the precepts, going forth, or fulfilling the precepts, there is the middle volition. For one reflecting, "It has been fulfilled by me," there is the subsequent volition. Thus these three volitions together are called the basis of meritorious action consisting of virtue,' and so on. This is the meaning. But is not the volition in recollecting one's own merit included in the straightening of views? And is not this subsequent volition the very same? How then is it included there? This is not a fault, because there is a distinction between the two due to a difference in their object. For the recollection of merit has as its object only the merit one has done. But this subsequent volition has that very object of the act as its object. Thus the distinction between the two is clear.

Ettāvatā [M 1.0202] ca yaṃ vuttaṃ “dasapuññakiriyavatthuvaseneva pavattatī”ti, tattha dasapuññakiriyavatthūni sarūpato, saṅgahato ca niddisitvā idāni tathāpavattamānassa cassa pāṭekkaṃ pavattākāravisayaṃ dassetuṃ “idānī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ayanti vakkhamānanidassanaṃ. Dātabbo dhammo deyyadhammo, annādidasavidhaṃ vatthu. Vuttañhi –

Thus far, with reference to the statement, 'It proceeds by way of the ten bases of meritorious action,' the ten bases of meritorious action have been indicated in terms of their individual nature and their inclusion. Now, to show the specific manner and object of its proceeding in each case when it occurs thus, the passage beginning 'Now...' is started. Herein, 'this' refers to the example that will be stated. A thing to be given is a gift, that is, the ten kinds of items such as food. For it is said:

“Annaṃ pānaṃ vatthaṃ yānaṃ, mālāgandhavilepanaṃ;

Seyyāvasathapadīpeyyaṃ, dānavatthū dasāvime”ti.

Food, drink, clothing, and vehicles; garlands, scents, and ointments; lodging, dwellings, and lamplight—these are the ten objects of giving.

Paṭiggāhako ādi yesaṃ desakālamittādīnaṃ te paṭiggāhakādayo, deyyadhammassa, paṭiggāhakādīnañca sampatti sampannatā deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakādisampatti. Tattha deyyadhammassa paṇītamanāpabhāvo dhammena samena uppannabhāvo deyyadhammasampatti. Paṭiggāhakānaṃ aggadakkhiṇeyyabhāvo paṭiggāhakasampatti. Dullabhaannapānādiko deso desasampatti. Tādisova kālo kālasampatti. Dullabhaannapānādike hi dese, kāle vā dinnaṃ ajjhāsayassa balavatāya mahapphalaṃ, somanassahetukañca hoti, tasmā te dānassa sampattivasena vuttā. Mittasampatti pana kalyāṇamittabhāvo. Kalyāṇamittañhi nissāya dānādīsu cittaṃ odagyappattaṃ hoti. Paricārikasampatti pana anāṇattiyāpi taṃtaṃkiccasampādane appamattassa paricārikajanassa paṭilābho. Aññaṃ vā somanassahetunti saddhābahulatāvisuddhidiṭṭhitādibhedaṃ aññaṃ somanassakāraṇaṃ vā. Āgammāti upāgamma, paṭiccāti attho. Haṭṭhapahaṭṭhoti somanassavasena haṭṭho ceva pahaṭṭho ca. Ubhayenapi adhikasomanassaṃ vuttaṃ. Atthi…pe… pavattanti “atthi dinnaṃ, atthi yiṭṭhaṃ, atthi hutaṃ, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, atthi ayaṃ loko, atthi paro loko, atthi mātā, atthi pitā, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi loke [V 1.0165] samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā [M 1.0203] sammāpaṭipannā, ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.441) evaṃ pavattaṃ dasavidhaṃ sammādiṭṭhivatthuvasena ceva dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyādīnaṃ vasena ca pavattaṃ. Ādi-saddena hi na kevalaṃ navannaṃyeva sammādiṭṭhivatthūnaṃ gahaṇaṃ, atha kho dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyānampi saṅgaho. Sammā ñāyena pavattā diṭṭhi, pasatthā vā diṭṭhīti sammādiṭṭhi, taṃ. Purakkhatvāti pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā. Tañca kho sahajātapubbaṅgamavasena “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 1-2) viya sampayogassa adhippetattā.

'Recipients, etc.' refers to those beginning with the recipient, such as the place, time, and friends. The 'excellence of the gift, recipients, etc.' is the excellence, the perfection, of the gift and of the recipients and so on. Herein, the excellence of the gift is its being refined, pleasing, and acquired righteously and justly. The excellence of the recipients is their being supreme recipients of offerings. The excellence of place is a place where food and drink are difficult to obtain. The excellence of time is a similar kind of time. For a gift given in a place or at a time when food and drink are scarce becomes of great fruit and a cause for joy because of the strength of the donor’s disposition. Therefore, these are spoken of as excellences of giving. The excellence of friends is having spiritual friends, for by relying on spiritual friends the mind becomes uplifted towards giving and other wholesome acts. The excellence of attendants is the acquisition of a diligent attendant who accomplishes the various tasks even without being commanded. 'Or another cause of joy' means another reason for joy, distinguished as abundance of faith, purity of view, and so on. 'Having approached' means having come up to, that is, depending on. 'Joyful and elated' means being joyful and elated on account of gladness; by both terms an abundance of joy is expressed. 'There is... proceeds': it proceeds based on the tenfold object of right view and on the grounds for the enlightenment factor of investigation of dhammas, as in: 'There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the next world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings who are reborn spontaneously; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who are faring rightly and practicing rightly, who, having realized this world and the next world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known.' For by the word 'etc.' is meant the inclusion not only of the nine objects of right view but also of the grounds for the enlightenment factor of investigation of dhammas. 'Right view' is the view that proceeds in the right way, or the praised view. 'Having placed at the forefront' means having made it the forerunner. And this is intended in the sense of a co-arisen forerunner, as in such passages as 'Mind is the forerunner of all states,' because association is intended.

Anussāhitoti lobhamacchariyādivasena puññakiriyāya saṅkocaṃ anāpajjanato attanā, parena vā kenaci anussāhito hutvā. Sabhāvato hi puññappavattidassanamidaṃ. Parehīti pana parapākaṭussāhadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Paṭhamanti desanākkamena, idha niddiṭṭhakkamena vā paṭhamaṃ. Mahākusalacittanti somanassasahagatatādiaṅgapāripūriyā mahantaṃ kusalacittaṃ. Atha vā pacchimabhavikabodhisattānaṃ paṭisandhiākaḍḍhanato mahantaṃ pūjitaṃ kusalacittanti mahākusalacittaṃ. Sabbesampi hi sabbaññubodhisattānaṃ paṭisandhi mettāpubbaṅgamassa tihetukasomanassamayassa asaṅkhārikacittassa vipākoti vuttaṃ. Ettha “deyyadhamma…pe… haṭṭhapahaṭṭho”ti ettāvatā imassa somanassasahagatabhāvamāha, “sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā”ti ñāṇasampayuttabhāvaṃ, “anussāhito”ti pana iminā asaṅkhārikabhāvanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Unprompted” means not shrinking back from meritorious deeds on account of greed, avarice, and so on, being unprompted by oneself or by anyone else. For this is a manifestation of the natural arising of merit. The words “by others,” however, are said in the sense of seeing the manifest prompting by another. “First” means first in the order of exposition, or in the order specified here. “Great wholesome consciousness” means a great wholesome consciousness on account of its completeness with factors such as being accompanied by joy. Or, it is a “great wholesome consciousness” because it is a great, revered wholesome consciousness that draws the rebirth-linking of Bodhisattas in their final existence. For it is said that the rebirth-linking of all Omniscient Bodhisattas is the result of an unprompted, triple-rooted consciousness accompanied by joy, which is preceded by loving-kindness. Herein, by the words “a gift … joyful and elated,” he states its nature of being accompanied by joy; by “having placed right view at the forefront,” its nature of being associated with knowledge; and by “unprompted,” it should be understood that he indicates its unprompted nature.

Vuttanayenevāti “deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakādisampattiṃ, aññaṃ vā somanassakāraṇaṃ āgammā”ti evaṃ vuttanayena. Ussāhitoti deyyadhamme sāpekkhāditāya, sīlasampadādīsu anadhimuttatādīhi ca puññakiriyāya saṅkocāpajjanato attanā, parena vā kenaci ussāhito. Parehīti [M 1.0204] pana vuttanayameva. Karoti dānādīni puññānīti sambandho. Tamevāti somanassasahagatādinā taṃsadisatāya vuttaṃ. Hoti hi taṃsadisepi taṃvohāro yathā ca “sāyeva tittirī, tāniyeva osadhānī”ti. Ettha pana “ussāhito”ti iminā sasaṅkhārikataṃ dasseti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Imasmiṃ panattheti imasmiṃ sasaṅkhārikasaddābhidheyye, ussāhitabbacittasaṅkhāte atthe taṃvisayeti attho. Pubbappayogassāti puññakiriyāya saṅkoce jāyamāne tato vivecetvā samussāhanavasena pavattassa cittappayogassa. Pubba-ggahaṇaṃ panettha tathāpavattapubbābhisaṅkhāravasena [V 1.0166] so payogo hotīti katvā vuttaṃ, na tassa pubbakālikatāyāti vuttovāyamattho.

“In the way already stated” means in the way stated thus: “relying on the attainment of suitable gifts, recipients, etc., or on another cause for joy.” “Prompted” (ussāhito) means: because of falling into hesitation in performing a meritorious action due to attachment to the gift to be given, or due to lack of resolve in virtues such as moral perfection, etc., one is prompted by oneself or by someone else. “By others” is in the way already stated. The connection is: “He performs meritorious deeds such as giving.” “That very one” (tameva) is said because of its similarity to the one accompanied by joy, etc. For that designation is used even for what is similar to it, as in “that very partridge, those very herbs.” Here, however, by “prompted” it indicates the prompted nature (sasaṅkhārika). The rest is as already stated. “In this meaning”: in this meaning which is denoted by the word “prompted,” which is designated as a mind that should be prompted; this is the meaning of “in that subject.” “Of the prior application”: when hesitation in performing a meritorious action arises, it is the application of mind that proceeds by way of encouragement, having separated it from that hesitation. The taking of “prior” here is stated because that application occurs by means of a prior volition that has arisen in such a way, not because it is prior in time. This is the meaning stated.

Paṭipattidassanenāti bhikkhū disvā deyyadhammapariccajanavandanādipaṭipattidassanena. Balanti anantīti bālā, assāsitapassāsitamatteneva jīvanti, na paññājīvitenāti adhippāyo. Bālāyeva bālakā. Te pana idha “atthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattāya sammādiṭṭhiyā abhāvena asañjātabuddhino dārakā. Pākaṭavasena cettha bālaka-ggahaṇaṃ. Sahasā karaṇādikāle pana itaresampi ñāṇavippayuttaṃ hotīti. Somanassaṃ jātaṃ etesanti somanassajātā, jātasomanassāti attho. Sahasāti sīghaṃ sīghaṃ dātukāmatāya uppattisamakālameva.

“By seeing the practice” means: by seeing the monks and by seeing the practice of relinquishing offerings, paying homage, and so on. “Fools” (bālā): they do not breathe (anantīti), meaning they live merely by in-and-out breathing, not by the life of wisdom; this is the intended meaning. Fools are just children (bālakā). But here they are children whose wisdom has not arisen because of the absence of right view that proceeds in the manner of “There is what is given,” etc. And here the taking of “children” is in the sense of what is manifest. But at the time of acting hastily, for others too the consciousness is dissociated from knowledge. “Those in whom joy has arisen” (somanassajātā) means joy has arisen in them; this is the meaning. “Hastily” (sahasā) means: just at the time of its arising, due to the desire to give very quickly.

Ettha ca “paṭipattidassanenā”ti iminā paresaṃ payogābhāvamāha, “jātaparicayā”ti attano payogābhāvaṃ. Ubhayenāpi imassa asaṅkhārikabhāvaṃ dīpeti. “Bālakā, sahasā”ti ca imehi ñāṇavippayuttabhāvamāha, “bhikkhū…pe… jātā”ti somanassasahagatabhāvaṃ. Atha vā “paṭipatti…pe… paricayā”ti iminā asaṅkhārikabhāvassa “bālakā bhikkhū…pe… jātā”ti [M 1.0205] ca imehi ñāṇavippayuttasomanassasahagatabhāvassa ca dīpitattā “sahasā”ti vacanena yathāvuttameva ñāṇavippayuttaasaṅkhārikabhāvaṃ pakāseti. Evaṃ sati paṭilomato somanassasahagatādibhāvo dassito hoti. Anulomato pana “somanassajātā”ti iminā somanassasahagatabhāvaṃ, sahasā-ggahaṇena ñāṇavippayuttāsaṅkhārikabhāvaṃ dīpeti. “Paṭipatti…pe… disvā”ti ettāvatā pana somanassasahagatādibhāvassa kāraṇaṃ vuttanti. Teti te ñātakā, te bālakāti vā attho. “Somanassahetūnaṃ abhāvaṃ āgammā”ti idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Majjhattārammaṇaṃ tathārūpe cetobhisaṅkhārādayopi hi upekkhāsahagatatāya kāraṇamevāti. Cittassa somanassābhāve puggalassapi somanassarahitatā hotīti “catūsupi…pe… hontī”ti puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā vuttaṃ, somanassarahitā honti puññaṃ karontāti adhippāyo. “Eva”ntiādi nigamanaṃ.

And here, by “by seeing the practice” he states the absence of prompting by others; by “arisen familiarity,” the absence of prompting by oneself. By both he illuminates its unprompted nature. And by “children, hastily” he states its nature of being dissociated from knowledge; by “monks … arisen,” its nature of being accompanied by gladness. Alternatively, since by “practice … familiarity” its unprompted nature is illuminated, and by “children, monks … arisen” its nature of being dissociated from knowledge and accompanied by gladness is illuminated, by the word “hastily” he clarifies its already stated nature of being dissociated from knowledge and unprompted. This being so, the state of being accompanied by gladness, etc., is shown in reverse order. In the direct order, however, by “in whom gladness has arisen” he illuminates the state of being accompanied by gladness; by the taking of “hastily,” the state of being dissociated from knowledge and unprompted. By the phrase “having seen the practice…” the reason for the state of being accompanied by gladness, etc., is stated. “They” means those relatives, or those children. “Relying on the absence of causes for gladness”—this should be seen as a mere indication. For mental formations, etc., concerning a neutral object are also a cause for the state of being accompanied by equanimity. When there is an absence of gladness in the mind, the person too is devoid of gladness. Thus, “in all four … they are” is stated with the person as the basis, the intention being: those who perform merit are devoid of gladness. “Thus,” etc., is the conclusion.

Imesu pana aṭṭhasu viññāṇesu somanassasahagatato upekkhāsahagataṃ balavataraṃ, ñāṇavippayuttato ñāṇasampayuttaṃ, sasaṅkhārikato asaṅkhārikaṃ sadisaṃ balavataraṃ. Visadisaṃ pana vedanāñāṇappayogavasena balavaṃ, dubbalañca hoti. Somanassasahagatatihetukaasaṅkhārikato hi upekkhāsahagatatihetukasasaṅkhārikaṃ [V 1.0167] balavataraṃ, upekkhāsahagataduhetukaasaṅkhārikato somanassasahagatatihetukaasaṅkhārikaṃ balavataraṃ. Iti catutthacittato tatiyacittaṃ balavataraṃ, tato aṭṭhamacittaṃ, tato sattamacittaṃ, tato dutiyacittaṃ, tato paṭhamacittaṃ, tato chaṭṭhacittaṃ, tato pañcamacittanti evamimesaṃ balavabalavatarabhāvo veditabbo.

Now, among these eight consciousnesses, when the factors are similar, the one accompanied by equanimity is stronger than the one accompanied by joy; the one associated with knowledge is stronger than the one dissociated from knowledge; and the unprompted is stronger than the prompted. But when they are dissimilar in terms of feeling, knowledge, and prompting, one is strong and one is weak. For the prompted, triple-rooted consciousness accompanied by equanimity is stronger than the unprompted, triple-rooted consciousness accompanied by joy. And the unprompted, triple-rooted consciousness accompanied by joy is stronger than the unprompted, double-rooted consciousness accompanied by equanimity. Thus, the third consciousness is stronger than the fourth; stronger than that is the eighth; stronger than that, the seventh; stronger than that, the second; stronger than that, the first; stronger than that, the sixth; and stronger than that, the fifth. In this way, their relative strength should be understood.

26. Evaṃ [M 1.0206] pāḷiyaṃ āgatanayena vedanāñāṇappayogabhedato aṭṭhavidhataṃ niddisitvā idāni aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatapuññakiriyādīnaṃ vasenapi pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ “dasa puññakriyādīna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena channaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ, catunnaṃ adhipatīnaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ, hīnādibhedassa ca saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tenevāhu –

26. Having thus indicated the eightfold nature based on the divisions of feeling, knowledge, and prompting according to the method that has come down in the Pāli, now, in order to show the classification also by way of the meritorious actions, etc., that have come down in the Commentary, the words “Ten meritorious actions, etc.” are stated. By the word “etc.” the inclusion of the six objects, the four dominants, the three kammas, and the division into inferior, etc., should be understood. For that reason they have said:

“Kamena puññavatthūhi, gocarādhipatīhi ca;

Kammahīnādito cāpi, gaṇeyya nayakovido”ti.

One skilled in the method should count in sequence by the grounds of merit, by objects and dominants, and also by kamma and by inferior and so on.

27. Idāni tathāpavattamānassa tassa yo yo tesaṃ tesaṃ vasena labbhamāno gaṇanaparicchedo, taṃ sampiṇḍitvā dassetuṃ “sattarasa sahassānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthevaṃ gaṇanā veditabbā – imāni tāva aṭṭha viññāṇāni dasannaṃ puññakiriyavatthūnaṃ vasena pavattanato paccekaṃ dasa dasāti katvā asīti cittāni honti, tāni ca chasu ārammaṇesu pavattanato chagguṇitāni sāsītikāni cattāri satāni honti, tāni catunnaṃ adhipatīnaṃ sahayogavasena catugguṇitāni sahassaṃ, vīsādhikāni ca nava satāni honti, tāni ca kāyavacīmanosaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ vasena tiguṇitāni sasaṭṭhisattasatādhikāni pañca sahassāni honti, tāni ca hīnamajjhimapaṇītabhedato tiguṇitāni sāsītikadvisatādhikāni sattarasa sahassāni hontīti. Nanu ca ñāṇavippayuttacittānaṃ vīmaṃsādhipatisahayogābhāvato adhipativasena sahassaṃ, sāsītikāni ca cha satāni hontīti tāni kammādīnaṃ vasena sampiṇḍitāni vīsasatādhikāni pannarasa sahassāni bhavantīti? Saccametaṃ, sotapatitavasena pana taṃ anādiyitvā adhipatigaṇanā gahitāti na tassa vasena gaṇanahāni katāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

27. Now, to show in summary the numerical determination that is obtained by way of each of these as they occur, the words “seventeen thousand,” etc., are stated. There, the counting should be understood as follows: First, these eight consciousnesses, because they arise by way of the ten grounds of meritorious action, become eighty consciousnesses, taking each as ten. And these, because they arise in the six objects, become four hundred and eighty when multiplied by six. And these, by way of co-arising with the four dominants, become one thousand nine hundred and twenty when multiplied by four. And these, by way of the three kammas designated as bodily, verbal, and mental, become five thousand seven hundred and sixty when multiplied by three. And these, by way of the division into inferior, medium, and superior, become seventeen thousand two hundred and eighty when multiplied by three. But is it not the case that since the consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge lack co-arising with the dominant of investigation, by way of dominants they would be one thousand six hundred and eighty? And these, summed up by way of kamma, etc., would be fifteen thousand one hundred and twenty? This is true. But it should be seen that, having taken the counting of the dominants without taking that distinction into account, following the traditional way it is heard, no reduction in the count has been made on that basis.

Nanu [M 1.0207] ca “savipākaṃ kusala”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ pana kathaṃ, kuhiṃ, kiṃ phalatīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “taṃ panā”tiādi. Yasmā tihetukaṃ kusalaṃ tihetukaṃ vā duhetukaṃ vā paṭisandhiṃ deti[V 1.0168], nāhetukaṃ paṭisandhiṃ deti. Yadā ca tihetukaṃ paṭisandhiṃ janeti, tadā pavatte soḷasa vipākāni abhinipphādeti. Yadā dvihetukaṃ, tadā dvādasa. Duhetukaṃ pana duhetukamahetukañca paṭisandhiṃ janeti, na tihetukaṃ. Yadā ca duhetukaṃ janeti, tadā pavattiyaṃ dvādasa. Yadā ahetukaṃ, tadā aṭṭha. Ye pana āgamanato vipākassa saṅkhārabhedamicchanti, tesaṃ matena tihetukaṃ dvādasa, dasa vā vipaccati, duhetukaṃ dasa, aṭṭha vā, tasmā vuttaṃ “yathānurūpa”nti. Nānāvidhasampattiṭṭhānabhāvato sobhanā, gantabbato gati cāti sugati, kāmāvacarabhavova sugati kāmāvacarasugati. Tassaṃ kāmāvacarasugatiyaṃ. Bhavabhogasampattinti ettha ca bhavatīti bhavo, upapattibhavasaṅkhātānaṃ vipākakkhandhakaṭattārūpānametaṃ gahaṇaṃ, bhuñjitabbato bhogo, pavattiyaṃ paṭilabhitabbasampatti, bhavoti vā paṭisandhi, bhogo sesavipākakaṭattārūpehi saha pavattiyaṃ paṭilabhitabbā sampatti, bhavo ca bhogo ca bhavabhogo, teyeva sampannabhāvato sampatti, tesaṃ vā sampatti bhavabhogasampatti, taṃ abhinipphādeti, janakavasena ca upanissayavasena ca sādhetīti attho. Ettha ca bhavabhogasampattīnaṃ niravasesato labbhamānaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya “kāmāvacarasugatiya”nti vuttaṃ. Sahetukavipākavajjaṃ pana pavattivipākakaṭattārūpasabhāvaṃ bhavasampattiṃ, ekaccabhogasampattiñca, bhogasampadameva vā avisesena sugatiyaṃ duggatiyampi abhinipphādetiyeva. Nāgasupaṇṇādīnampi hissa devasampattisadisaṃ manuññaṃ bhogajātaṃ, tabbisayāni ca vipākacittāni, suvaṇṇatāsussaratādi ca taṃ sabbaṃ kāmāvacarakusalasseva phalaṃ. Na hi akusalassa iṭṭhaphalaṃ atthi. Vuttañhetaṃ [M 1.0208] – “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ akusalassa iṭṭho kanto vipāko saṃvijjatī”ti.

Was it not said, 'Wholesome action is with result'? How, where, and what result does it bear? With reference to that inquiry, it is said, 'That, however...' and so on. Because a three-rooted wholesome action gives rise to either a three-rooted or a two-rooted rebirth-linking, but not a rootless rebirth-linking. And when it generates a three-rooted rebirth-linking, then in the course of existence it brings about sixteen resultant states. When it generates a two-rooted one, then twelve. A two-rooted action, however, generates a two-rooted or a rootless rebirth-linking, but not a three-rooted one. And when it generates a two-rooted one, then in the course of existence, twelve resultants. When it generates a rootless one, then eight. But for those who, according to the texts, desire a distinction in the result based on the type of formations, in their opinion, a three-rooted action ripens into twelve or ten results, and a two-rooted action into ten or eight. Therefore, it is said, 'as is appropriate.' Because it is beautiful, being the location of various kinds of accomplishment, and because it is a destination to be gone to, it is a 'happy destination' (sugati). The sense-sphere existence itself is the happy destination, the sense-sphere happy destination. In that sense-sphere happy destination. And here, in 'accomplishment of existence and enjoyment' (bhavabhogasampatti), 'existence' (bhava) means becoming; this is a reference to the resultant aggregates and kamma-produced matter designated as rebirth-existence. 'Enjoyment' (bhoga) means what is to be enjoyed; it refers to the accomplishment to be obtained in the course of existence. Or, 'existence' means rebirth-linking, and 'enjoyment' means the accomplishment to be obtained in the course of existence together with the remaining resultant states and kamma-produced matter. 'Existence and enjoyment' are existence and enjoyment; and because they are endowed with accomplishment, they are 'accomplishment,' or it is the accomplishment of them. It brings this about; that is, it accomplishes it by way of being a generator and by way of being a decisive support condition. And here, 'happy destination in the sense sphere' is said with reference to the place where the accomplishment of existence and enjoyment is obtained without remainder. However, excluding the resultant states with roots, it produces the accomplishment of existence—which has the nature of resultant states and kamma-produced matter in the course of existence—and a certain accomplishment of enjoyment, or simply the accomplishment of enjoyment, indiscriminately in both happy and unhappy destinations. For even the delightful wealth of nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others, which is like divine prosperity, and the resultant consciousnesses related to those objects, and such things as a golden complexion and a sweet voice—all that is the fruit of wholesome kamma in the sense sphere. For there is no desirable result for unwholesome kamma. As it is said: 'This is impossible, there is no occasion for it, that a desirable, pleasant result should arise from unwholesome kamma.'

Kāmāvacarakusalavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the sense-sphere wholesome is completed.

Rūpāvacarakusalavaṇṇanā

Description of Wholesome Fine-Material-Sphere States

Idāni yasmā kāmāvacarakusalānantaraṃ uddiṭṭhassa rūpāvacarakusalassa niddesāvakāso anuppatto, tasmā taṃ dassanatthaṃ “itaresū”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha itaresūti yathāvuttakāmāvacarakusalato itaresu, rūpāvacarādīsūti attho. Savatthukato ekavidhaṃ ekantena vatthusannissitattā[V 1.0169]. Na hi arūpadhātuyaṃ rūpāvacaradhammā labbhanti rūpavirāgabhāvanāya nibbattattā puna rūpāvacarajjhānasamāpattiyā abhāvato.

Now, since the occasion has arrived for the exposition of the wholesome fine-material-sphere states, which were mentioned after the wholesome sense-sphere states, therefore, to explain this, the passage beginning with 'in the others' is commenced. Herein, 'in the others' means in those other than the aforementioned wholesome sense-sphere states, that is, in the fine-material sphere and so on. With respect to having a physical basis, it is of one kind, because it is entirely dependent on a physical basis. For fine-material-sphere states are not found in the immaterial sphere, since beings there are reborn through the development of dispassion towards form, and furthermore, because there is no attainment of fine-material-sphere jhānas there.

Hīnamajjhimapaṇītabhedatoti ettha pubbe viya adhipatīnaṃ hīnādibhāvehi jhānassa hīnādibhāvo yojetabbo. Atha vā paṭiladdhamattamanāsevitaṃ hīnaṃ paridubbalabhāvato, nātisubhāvitaṃ aparipuṇṇavasibhāvaṃ majjhimaṃ, ativiya subhāvitaṃ pana sabbaso paripuṇṇavasibhāvaṃ paṇītaṃ. Tathā uḷārapuññaphalakāmatāvasena pavattitaṃ hīnaṃ, lokiyābhiññatthāya pavattitaṃ majjhimaṃ, vivekakāmatāya ariyabhāve ṭhitena pavattitaṃ paṇītaṃ. Attahitāya vā pavattitaṃ hīnaṃ, kevalaṃ alobhajjhāsayena pavattitaṃ majjhimaṃ, parahitāya pavattitaṃ paṇītaṃ. Vaṭṭajjhāsayena vā pavattitaṃ hīnaṃ, vivekajjhāsayena pavattitaṃ majjhimaṃ, vivaṭṭajjhāsayena lokuttarapādakatthaṃ pavattitaṃ paṇītaṃ.

As for the division into inferior, medium, and superior, here, as before, the inferior, medium, and superior nature of the jhāna should be connected with the inferior, etc., states of the predominants. Alternatively, what is merely attained but not cultivated is inferior due to its very weak condition; what is not very well developed, lacking complete mastery, is medium; what is extremely well developed, with completely perfected mastery, is superior. Similarly, what is undertaken due to a desire for great meritorious results is inferior; what is undertaken for the sake of mundane higher knowledge is medium; what is undertaken by one established in the noble state with a desire for seclusion is superior. Or, what is undertaken for one's own benefit is inferior; what is undertaken merely with an intention of non-greed is medium; what is undertaken for the benefit of others is superior. Or, what is undertaken with an intention for the round of existence is inferior; what is undertaken with an intention for seclusion is medium; what is undertaken with an intention for deliverance, as a basis for the supramundane, is superior.

Paṭipadādibhedatoti dukkhapaṭipadādandhābhiññādīnaṃ paṭipadābhiññānaṃ bhedena. Paṭipadāvacaneneva vā tadavinābhāvato abhiññāpi labbhati. Tathā hettha paṭipadācatukkanti voharantīti [M 1.0209] ādi-saddena adhipatiādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo, tasmā paṭipadādibhedatoti paṭipadābhedato, adhipatibhedato, ārammaṇabhedato, hānabhāgiyādibhedatoti attho. Tattha paṭipadābhedato tāva dukkhapaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññaṃ, dukkhapaṭipadaṃ khippābhiññaṃ, sukhapaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññaṃ, sukhapaṭipadaṃ khippābhiññanti evaṃ catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha dukkhā paṭipadā assāti dukkhapaṭipadaṃ. Dandhā abhiññā assāti dandhābhiññaṃ. Esa nayo “dukkhapaṭipadaṃ khippābhiñña”ntiādīsupi.

As for the division by path, etc.: by the division of the paths and higher knowledges, such as the painful path and slow higher knowledge. Or, by the mere mention of the path, the higher knowledge is also obtained because of its inseparability. Thus here, the fourfold path is spoken of, etc., and by the word 'etc.' the inclusion of the predominants, etc., should be understood. Therefore, 'by the division of the path, etc.' means by the division of the path, by the division of the predominants, by the division of the object, and by the division of the factors of decline, etc. Herein, first, by the division of the path, it is fourfold: the painful path with slow higher knowledge, the painful path with quick higher knowledge, the pleasant path with slow higher knowledge, and the pleasant path with quick higher knowledge. Herein, 'dukkhapaṭipadaṃ' means one whose path is painful. 'Dandhābhiññaṃ' means one whose higher knowledge is slow. The same method applies to 'dukkhapaṭipadaṃ khippābhiññaṃ,' etc.

Tattha appahīnanīvaraṇassa, avikkhambhitajhānanikantikassa ca ñāṇakiccassa aparibyattatāya pariniṭṭhitasakalapubbakiccassa “pathavī pathavī”ti vā “āpo āpo”ti vā evaṃ pavattapaṭhamasamannāhārato paṭṭhāya yāva tassa tassa jhānassa upacāruppattiyā nīvaraṇappahānaṃ, nikantivikkhambhanañca hoti, tāva pavattā pubbabhāgabhāvanā paṭipadā nāma “paṭipajjati jhānaṃ etāyā”ti katvā. Pahīnanīvaraṇassa, pana vikkhambhitajhānanikantikassa ca ñāṇakiccassa paribyattabhāvato upacārajjhānaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva appanāya uppatti, tāva pavattā paññā pubbabhāgapaññāya visiṭṭhabhāvato abhiññā nāma, tasmā yo ādito kilese jhānanikantiñca [V 1.0170] vikkhambhento dukkhena sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilamanto vikkhambheti, vikkhambhitakilesajhānanikanti ca appanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena aṅgapātubhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti, tassa dukkhapaṭipadaṃ, dandhābhiññañca jhānaṃ hoti. Yo pana sasaṅkhārena kilesādike vikkhambhetvā na cirena aṅgapātubhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti, tassa dukkhapaṭipadaṃ, khippābhiññañca. Yo kilesādike vikkhambhento sukhena akilamanto vikkhambheti, appanāparivāsaṃ pana cirāyati, tassa sukhapaṭipadaṃ, dandhābhiññaṃ. Yo pana sukheneva kilesādike vikkhambhetvā [M 1.0210] sīghameva appanaṃ pāpuṇāti, tassa sukhapaṭipadaṃ, khippābhiññanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, for one whose hindrances are not abandoned, whose delight in jhāna is not suppressed, for whom the function of knowledge is unmanifest, and for whom all preliminary tasks have been completed, the preliminary development that occurs from the first application of mind with 'earth, earth' or 'water, water,' and so on, up until the abandoning of the hindrances and the suppression of delight occurs with the arising of access to that particular jhāna, is called the 'path' (paṭipadā), because it is said, 'one progresses to jhāna by means of this.' But for one whose hindrances are abandoned and whose delight in jhāna is suppressed, due to the manifested state of the function of knowledge, the wisdom that occurs from the beginning of access jhāna up to the arising of absorption is called 'higher knowledge' (abhiññā) because of its distinction from the preliminary wisdom. Therefore, for one who from the beginning suppresses defilements and delight in jhāna with difficulty, with effort, and with application, becoming weary as they suppress them, and who, having suppressed the defilements and delight in jhāna, dwells in the vicinity of absorption for a long time before attaining the manifestation of the factors—for such a one, the jhāna is of painful practice and slow higher knowledge. But for one who suppresses defilements and the like with effort and does not take long to attain the manifestation of the factors—for such a one, the jhāna is of painful practice and quick higher knowledge. For one who suppresses defilements and the like with ease, without becoming weary, but is slow in the vicinity of absorption—for such a one, the jhāna is of pleasant practice and slow higher knowledge. But for one who suppresses defilements and the like with ease and quickly attains absorption—for such a one, the jhāna is of pleasant practice and quick higher knowledge. This should be understood.

So panāyaṃ paṭipadābhiññānaṃ bhedo kilesindriyādhikāravasena veditabbo. Yassa hi rāgādayo kilesā tibbā honti, saddhāpañcamakāni ca indriyāni mudūni. Yo ca samathavipassanāsu akatādhikāro, tassa pavattajhānaṃ dukkhapaṭipadaṃ, dandhābhiññañca hoti. Tassa hi kilesasamudācāratibbatāya nīvaraṇavikkhambhanassa kicchena kasirena samijjhanato paṭipadā dukkhā asukhā, tasseva saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ mudutāya abhiññāpi dandhā mandā asīghappavattinī hoti. Bhavantare vā samathe akatādhikārattā paṭipadā dukkhā, vipassanāya akatādhikārattā abhiññāpi dandhā. Yo pana vuttaviparīto hoti, tassa kilesānaṃ atibbasamudācāratāya, indriyānañca tikhīṇatāya samathavipassanāsu katādhikāratāya yathākkamaṃ sukhapaṭipadā, khippābhiññā ca hoti. Bhavantare kataparicayassa hi yathā paguṇaṃ katvā vissaṭṭhagantho appamattakena payogena suppavatti vācuggato ca hoti, evaṃ bhāvanā appakasireneva ijjhatīti. Svāyaṃ akato, kato ca adhikāro samathanissito paṭipadāyaṃ vutto samādhippadhānattā paṭipadāya. Vipassanānissito abhiññāya ñāṇappadhānattā appanāyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

This distinction between the path and direct-knowledge should be understood according to the predominance of defilements and faculties. For one whose defilements, such as lust, are strong, and whose five faculties beginning with faith are weak, and who has not made a foundation in serenity and insight, the arising jhāna is of painful progress and slow direct-knowledge. For such a person, because the suppression of the hindrances is accomplished with difficulty and hardship due to the intense arising of defilements, the path is painful and unpleasant. And for that same person, due to the weakness of the faculties such as faith, direct-knowledge is slow, dull, and does not arise quickly. Or, in another existence, due to not having made a foundation in serenity, the path is painful; and due to not having made a foundation in insight, direct-knowledge is also slow. But for one who is the opposite of what has been described—for whom the arising of defilements is not intense, whose faculties are sharp, and who has made a foundation in serenity and insight—the path is, respectively, of pleasant progress, and direct-knowledge is swift. For one who has developed familiarity in another existence, just as a text that has been made fluent and its difficulties unraveled is recited with little effort and proceeds smoothly from the mouth, so too does meditation succeed with little hardship. Thus, this foundation, whether made or not made, should be understood as follows: that which is based on serenity is spoken of in relation to the path, because the path is chiefly concerned with concentration; that which is based on insight is in relation to direct-knowledge, because absorption is chiefly concerned with wisdom.

Yo pana tibbakileso tikkhindriyo vipassanāyameva vā katādhikāro hoti, tassa vuttanayena dukkhā paṭipadā, khippā pana abhiññā hoti, tabbiparītassa sukhapaṭipadā dandhābhiññāti. Tasmā kilesānaṃ tibbamandabhāvato, indriyānaṃ tikhiṇamudubhāvato, pubbaparicayassa ca sambhavāsambhavavasenāti evaṃ kilesindriyādhikāravasena imāsaṃ bhedo veditabbo.

But for one who has intense defilements and keen faculties, or who has made a foundation in insight only, for him, by the method stated, the path is painful, but direct-knowledge is swift. For one who is the opposite, the path is pleasant and direct-knowledge is slow. Therefore, this distinction should be understood according to the intensity or mildness of the defilements, the keenness or dullness of the faculties, and the presence or absence of prior familiarity—thus, according to the predominance of defilements, faculties, and foundation.

Apica [M 1.0211] yāni parato sappāyāsappāyāni, palibodhupacchedādīni pubbakiccāni, appanākosallāni [V 1.0171] ca āgamissanti, tesu yo upacārādhigamato pubbe, pacchā ca asappāyasevī hoti, tassa dukkhā paṭipadā, dandhā ca abhiññā hoti. Ubhayattha sappāyasevino sukhā paṭipadā, khippā ca abhiññā. Yo pana tato pubbabhāge asappāyaṃ sevitvā aparabhāge sappāyasevī hoti, tassa dukkhā paṭipadā, khippā abhiññā. Tabbiparītassa sukhā paṭipadā, dandhā abhiññā ca veditabbā.

Furthermore, with regard to the suitable and unsuitable things, the preliminary duties such as the cutting off of impediments, and the skills in absorption that will be discussed hereafter: for one who, both before and after attaining access concentration, engages in what is unsuitable, the path is painful and direct-knowledge is slow. For one who engages in what is suitable in both instances, the path is pleasant and direct-knowledge is swift. But for one who, having engaged in the unsuitable in the earlier part, engages in the suitable in the later part, the path is painful, but direct-knowledge is swift. The opposite of this should be understood as a pleasant path and slow direct-knowledge.

Tathā palibodhupacchedādipubbakiccaṃ asampādetvā bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa saparipanthatāya dukkhā paṭipadā, vipariyāyena aparipanthatāya sukhā. Appanākosallāni asampādentassa ñāṇassa avisadatāya dandhā abhiññā hoti, sampādentassa vipariyāyato khippā abhiññāti. Kiñca – taṇhāvijjātibhavanavasena etāsaṃ bhedo veditabbo. Taṇhābhibhūtassa hi dukkhā paṭipadā hoti tassā samādhissa ujupaṭipakkhattā samathapaṭipadāya paripanthakabhāvato, anabhibhūtassa tadabhāvato sukhā.
