Avijjābhibhūtassa ca tassā paññāya ujupaṭipakkhabhāvato dandhā abhiññā, itarassa khippā abhiññāti. So panāyaṃ paṭipadābhedo kevalaṃ samathabhāvanāvasena paṭiladdhajjhānassa, maggādhigamavasena paṭiladdhajjhānassa pana natthi dukkhapaṭipadādibhedo. Keci pana maggavaseneva tassa paṭipadādibhedaṃ vaṇṇenti “maggassa hi dukkhapaṭipadādibhāve tasmiṃ dukkhapaṭipadādika”nti.

Likewise, for one who engages in meditation without completing the preliminary duties, such as the cutting off of impediments, the path is painful because it is obstructed; conversely, because it is unobstructed, it is pleasant. For one who does not accomplish the skills in absorption, direct-knowledge is slow due to the lack of clarity in wisdom; for one who does accomplish them, conversely, direct-knowledge is swift. Furthermore, this distinction should be understood in terms of craving and ignorance. For one overcome by craving, the path is painful, because craving is the direct opposite of concentration and is an obstacle to the path of serenity; for one not overcome, due to the absence of that, it is pleasant. And for one overcome by ignorance, direct-knowledge is slow, because ignorance is the direct opposite of wisdom; for the other, direct-knowledge is swift. However, this distinction in the path applies only to one who has attained jhāna by means of serenity meditation; for one who has attained jhāna by means of the attainment of the path, there is no such distinction of painful progress and so on. Some, however, explain this distinction of path and so on by way of the path itself, saying: 'For when the path is of painful progress, etc., then that jhāna is of painful progress, etc.'

Adhipatibhedādīsu pana chandādhipateyyaṃ cittādhipateyyaṃ vīriyādhipateyyaṃ vīmaṃsādhipateyyanti evaṃ adhipatibhedato, parittaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ, parittaṃ appamāṇārammaṇaṃ, appamāṇaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ[M 1.0212], appamāṇaṃ appamāṇārammaṇanti evaṃ ārammaṇabhedato, hānabhāgiyaṃ ṭhitibhāgiyaṃ visesabhāgiyaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyanti evaṃ hānabhāgiyādibhedato ca catubbidhatā veditabbā. Tattha “chandavato ce jhānaṃ nibbattissati, mayhampi nibbattissatī”ti evaṃ chandaṃ dhuraṃ katvā uppannaṃ chandādhipateyyaṃ. Esa nayo “cittādhipateyyā”dīsupi. Appaguṇaṃ pana uparijhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ asakkontaṃ parittaṃ, suppasarāvamattesu avaḍḍhitārammaṇesu nibbattaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ. Vuttapaṭipakkhato pana yathākkamaṃ appamāṇārammaṇādīni veditabbāni. Hānabhāgiyādivisesaṃ sayameva vakkhati.

However, in the divisions of predominances and so on, a fourfold nature should be understood: thus, from the division of predominances, as predominance by zeal, predominance by mind, predominance by energy, and predominance by investigation; thus, from the division of objects, as limited with a limited object, limited with an immeasurable object, immeasurable with a limited object, and immeasurable with an immeasurable object; and thus, from the division of what pertains to decline and so on, as pertaining to decline, pertaining to stability, pertaining to distinction, and pertaining to penetration. Herein, that which has arisen having made zeal the principal factor, with the thought, 'If a jhāna will arise for one with zeal, it will arise for me too,' is predominance by zeal. This method also applies to 'predominance by mind' and so on. 'Limited' is that which is of little quality and unable to become a condition for a higher jhāna. 'With a limited object' is that which has arisen in unexpanded objects that are merely within easy reach. From the opposite of what has been stated, 'immeasurable,' 'with an immeasurable object,' and so on should be understood in due order. He himself will explain the distinctions of what pertains to decline and so on.

Jhānaṅgayogabhedatoti katthaci pañca jhānaṅgāni, katthaci cattāri, katthaci tīṇi, katthaci dve[V 1.0172], katthaci aparāni dveti evaṃ jhānaṅgānaṃ sampayogabhedato. Nanu cettha kāmāvacarakusale viya saṅkhārabhedo kasmā na gahito. Idampi hi kevalaṃ samathānuyogavasena paṭiladdhaṃ sasaṅkhāraṃ, maggādhigamavasena paṭiladdhamasaṅkhāraṃ, tasmā “jhānaṅgasaṅkhārayogabhedato dasavidha”nti vattabbanti? Nayidamevaṃ, maggādhigamavasena sattito paṭiladdhassāpi aparabhāge parikammavaseneva uppajjanato, tasmā sabbassapi jhānassa parikammasaṅkhātapubbābhisaṅkhārena vinā kevalaṃ adhikāravasena anuppajjanato “asaṅkhāra”ntipi vattuṃ na sakkā, adhikārena ca vinā kevalaṃ parikammābhisaṅkhāreneva anuppajjanato “sasaṅkhāra”ntipi vattuṃ na sakkāti jhānaṅgayogabhedato pañcavidhatā ca vuttāti.

From the division by the combination of jhāna factors: in some cases there are five jhāna factors, in some four, in some three, in some two, and in some another two. Thus, it is from the division by the combination of jhāna factors. Now, why is the distinction of prompting not included here, as it is in the case of wholesome sense-sphere states? For this jhāna, too, when attained by way of the practice of serenity, is 'with prompting,' and when attained by way of the attainment of the path, is 'without prompting.' Therefore, should it not be said that it is tenfold, from the division by the combination of jhāna factors and prompting? This is not so. For even that which is attained by the power of the attainment of the path arises in a subsequent part only by way of preparatory effort. Therefore, since no jhāna arises solely by way of a foundation without the prior formation known as preparatory effort, it cannot be called 'without prompting.' And since it does not arise solely by the preparatory formation without a foundation, it cannot be called 'with prompting.' Thus, the fivefold classification from the division by the combination of jhāna factors is stated.

Kāmacchando byāpādo thinamiddhaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ vicikicchāti imāni pañca nīvaraṇāni vippahīnāni etassāti kāmacchanda…pe… vippahīnaṃ. “Agyāhito”ti ettha āhita-saddassa viya vippahīna-saddassettha paravacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāmacchandādīhi vā vippahīnaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ tesaṃ pahāyakabhāvenāti kāmacchanda…pe… vippahīnaṃ. Tattha kāmetīti kāmo, chandanaṭṭhena chando cāti [M 1.0213] kāmacchando, bahalakāmarāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Byāpādādīnamatthaṃ vakkhati. Yasmā kāmacchandādīsu appahīnesu jhānaṃ nuppajjati, tasmā tānissa pahānaṅgānīti veditabbāni. Nanu aññepi akusalā dhammā iminā jhānena pahīyanti, atha kasmā pañceva pahānaṅgavasena vuttānīti? Visesena jhānantarāyakarattā. Kāmacchandavasena hi nānāvisayapalobhitaṃ cittaṃ na ekattārammaṇe samādhiyati. Kāmacchandābhibhūtaṃ vā nānāvisayasamupabyūḷhāya kāmadhātuyā pahānapaṭipadaṃ na paṭipajjati, byāpādena ca ārammaṇe paṭihaññamānaṃ na samāhitaṃ pavattati, thinamiddhābhibhūtaṃ akammaññaṃ hoti, uddhaccakukkuccaparetaṃ avūpasantameva hutvā paribbhamati, vicikicchāupahataṃ jhānādhigamapaṭipadaṃ nārohati “sammāsambuddho nu kho, na nu kho, pathavī pathavī”tiādinā pavattamanasikārena “jhānaṃ siyā nu kho, na nu kho”tiādinā vicikicchantassa jhānādhigamapaṭipadāya asaṃsijjhanato. Yato vakkhati –

Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt—these five hindrances are abandoned for this one; thus, sensual desire... is abandoned. Here, in the phrase 'Agyāhito' (not seized), the word 'vippahīna' (abandoned) should be understood as a contrary term to the word 'āhita' (placed upon). Or, it is abandoned, disconnected from sensual desire and the others, by way of their being the things to be abandoned. Here, 'kāma' is that which desires, and 'chanda' is in the sense of willing; thus, 'kāmacchanda.' This is a designation for strong sensual lust. The meaning of ill will and the others will be explained. Since jhāna does not arise when sensual desire and the others are unabandoned, they should be understood as its factors of abandonment. But are not other unwholesome states also abandoned by this jhāna? Why, then, are only these five mentioned as factors of abandonment? Because they are especially obstructive to jhāna. For a mind allured by various objects through sensual desire does not become concentrated on a single object. Or, overpowered by sensual desire, it does not undertake the path of abandoning the sense-sphere, which is crowded with various objects. And being struck by ill will at an object, it does not proceed in a concentrated way. Overcome by sloth and torpor, it becomes unfit for work. Beset by restlessness and remorse, it remains uncalmed and wanders about. Afflicted by doubt, it does not ascend the path to the attainment of jhāna, because for one who doubts with such mental application as, 'Is he a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, or not? Is it earth, is it earth?' or, 'Could there be jhāna or not?' the path to the attainment of jhāna does not succeed. Wherefore it will be said:

“Bhāgī assamahaṃ addhā, imāya paṭipattiyā;

Pavivekasukhassāti, katvā ussāhamuttama”nti.

"'Surely I would be a partaker of this practice, of the bliss of seclusion,' thus having made the supreme effort."

Tasmā [V 1.0173] samādhiādīnaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhāvena visesena jhānādhigamassa antarāyakaraṇato etāneva pahānaṅgānīti vuttāni. Hoti cettha –

Therefore, because these, by being directly opposed to concentration and the like, especially obstruct the attainment of jhāna, they alone are called the factors of abandonment. And here there is this:

“Paccanīkā yato pañca, samādhādīnamettha hi;

Jhānantarāyikā tasmā, pahānaṅge niyāmitā”ti.

"Since the five are here opposed to concentration and so on, and are therefore obstructive to jhāna, they are designated as factors of abandonment."

Evamidaṃ pahānaṅgavasena dassetvā idāni sampayogaṅgavasena dassetuṃ “vitakka…pe… sampayutta”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha vitakkādayo vacanatthalakkhaṇādivasena upari āgamissanti. Yasmā pana imesu uppannesu jhānaṃ uppannaṃ nāma hoti, tenassa imāni sampayogaṅgānīti veditabbāni, tasmā na etehi [M 1.0214] samannāgataṃ aññadeva jhānaṃ nāma atthīti gahetabbaṃ. Yathā pana nemiādiaṅgasamudāye rathādivohāro hoti, evaṃ jhānaṅgasamudāye jhānavohāro. Vuttampi hetaṃ vibhaṅge “jhānanti vitakko vicāro pīti sukhaṃ cittassekaggatā”ti (vibha. 569). Kasmā pana aññesupi phassādīsu sampayuttadhammesu vijjamānesu imāniyeva pañca jhānaṅgavasena vuttānīti? Vuccate – upanijjhānakiccavantatāya, kāmacchandādīnaṃ ujupaṭipakkhabhāvato ca. Vitakko hi ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropeti, vicāro anubandhati. Evaṃ jhānādhigamassa visesapaccayabhūtehi tehi avikkhepāya samādahitapayogassa cetaso payogasampattisamuṭṭhānā pīti pīṇanaṃ, sukhañca upabrūhanaṃ karoti. Atha naṃ sasampayuttadhammaṃ etehi abhiniropanānubandhanapīṇanaupabrūhanehi anuggahitā ekaggatā samādhānakiccena attānaṃ anuvattāpentī ekattārammaṇe samaṃ, sammā ca ādhiyati, indriyasamatāvasena samaṃ, paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ dūrībhāvena līnuddhaccābhāvena sammā ca ṭhapetīti evametesameva upanijjhānakiccaṃ āveṇikaṃ. Kāmacchandādipaṭipakkhabhāvena pana sayameva vakkhati. Evaṃ upanijjhānakiccavantatāya, kāmacchandādīnaṃ ujupaṭipakkhabhāvato ca imeyeva pañca jhānaṅgabhāvena vavatthitāti. Yathāhu –

Having shown this by way of the factors of abandonment, now to show it by way of the factors of association, it is said: 'associated with initial application...' Herein, initial application and the rest will be explained later with their characteristics, functions, and so on. Since jhāna is said to have arisen when these arise, they should be understood as its factors of association. Therefore, it should not be assumed that there is some other thing called jhāna apart from being endowed with these. Just as the assemblage of parts like the rim results in the designation 'chariot,' so the assemblage of jhāna factors results in the designation 'jhāna.' For this was said in the Vibhaṅga: 'Jhāna means initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind' (Vibh. 569). But why, when other associated phenomena like contact are also present, are only these five mentioned as jhāna factors? It is said: because of their function relating to absorption and because they are the direct opposites of sensual desire and so on. For initial application directs the mind onto the object, and sustained application keeps it engaged there. Thus, through these, which are special conditions for attaining jhāna, rapture—arising from the successful application of the mind that has made the effort to avoid distraction—causes exhilaration, and happiness causes it to grow. Then, one-pointedness, supported by this directing, engaging, exhilarating, and growth, conforming itself by performing the function of concentration, settles the mind evenly and rightly on a single object; evenly through the balance of the faculties, and rightly through the absence of sluggishness and restlessness because opposing states are kept at a distance. Thus, these alone have the unique function relating to absorption. Moreover, that they are direct opposites of sensual desire and so on, he himself will state. Therefore, because of their function relating to absorption and because they are the direct opposites of sensual desire and so on, these five alone are established as jhāna factors. As it is said:

“Upanijjhānakiccattā, kāmādipaṭipakkhato;

Santesupi ca aññesu, pañceva jhānasaññitā”ti.

"Because they have the function of absorption, and because they are opposed to sensual desire and so on, only these five are designated as jhāna [factors], even though other [associated states] exist."

Desanākkamato, mahaggatadhammesu paṭhamaṃ adhigantabbato ca paṭhamaṃ, paṭhamaṃ samāpajjitabbantipi [V 1.0174] paṭhamanti vadanti. Taṃ pana na ekantalakkhaṇaṃ jhānapaṭilomādivasena samāpajjane asambhavato.

They call it the 'first' due to the order of the teaching, because it is the first to be attained among the exalted states, and also because it is the first to be entered. However, this is not its exclusive characteristic, since this does not apply in the case of entering [the jhānas] in ways such as the reverse order of the jhānas.

Purimapacchimacittesu uppajjamānassāpi appanākkhaṇe anuppajjanato vitakko vippahīno etassa, tato vā etaṃ vippahīnanti [M 1.0215] vitakkavippahīnaṃ. Bhāvanāya hi pahīnattā vitakko jhānakkhaṇe nuppajjati. Asaṃkiliṭṭhasabhāvattā pana upacārabhāvanāya ca taṃ pahātuṃ asamatthabhāvato purimabhāge, pacchābhāge ca apaccanīkacittappavattito uppajjatiyevāti.

Although initial application arises in the preceding and succeeding consciousnesses, since it does not arise at the moment of absorption, initial application is abandoned for this [jhāna]; or, this [jhāna] is abandoned of it, thus it is 'abandoned of initial application.' For, because it is abandoned by means of cultivation, initial application does not arise at the moment of jhāna. However, because its nature is undefiled, because of the inability to abandon it by means of access cultivation, and because in the succeeding stage consciousness proceeds without opposition, it arises in the preceding stage and in the succeeding stage.

Nanu ca “asaṃkiliṭṭhasabhāvattā”ti vuttaṃ, atha kathaṃ jhānena esa pahīyati? Na hi kusalehi asaṃkiliṭṭhadhammassa pahānaṃ atthi rāgādisaṃkiliṭṭhānaṃ pāpadhammānametassa ujupaṭipakkhabhāvatoti? Vuccate – asaṃkiliṭṭhasabhāvassāpi etassa oḷārikatāya dubbalabhāvato jhānakkhaṇe anuppattisabhāvāpādanatthaṃ tattha nikantivikkhambhanavasena dutiyajjhānabhāvanā hotīti tassā balena taṃ jhānakkhaṇe anuppajjantaṃ nikantivikkhambhanavasena vā vikkhambhitaṃ pahīnaṃ nāma hoti. Yadi evaṃ upacārenapi nikanti vikkhambhīyatīti tatthapissa pahānaṃ siyā, yathā paṭhamajjhānassa upacāre nīvaraṇānīti? Nayidamevaṃ, nīvaraṇappahānassa viya vitakkārammaṇikanikanti vikkhambhanassa upacārena sātisayaṃ anipphajjanato. Sātisayañhi tattha nikantippahānaṃ appanāya eva hoti, tasmā yadavocumhā “upacārabhāvanāya ca taṃ pahātuṃ asamatthabhāvato”ti, taṃ suṭṭhu upaparikkhitvā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Vicāravippahīna”ntiādīsupi vuttanayānusārena attho daṭṭhabbo. Dutiyajjhāneyeva pahīnassa vitakkassa idha appavattimattadassanatthaṃ “vitakkavicāravippahīna”nti vitakka-ggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Evaṃ “vitakkavicārapītivippahīna”ntiādīsupi.

But was it not said, "due to its undefiled nature"? Then how is it abandoned by jhāna? For wholesome states do not abandon an undefiled state; they abandon evil states defiled by lust and so on, of which this [jhāna] is the direct opposite. It is said: Even though this [initial application] is undefiled in nature, due to its coarseness and weakness, the development of the second jhāna occurs through the suppression of delight in it in order to bring about its non-arising at the moment of jhāna. By the power of that [development], since it does not arise at the moment of jhāna, it is called 'abandoned' by way of suppression, or suppression of delight. If so, since delight is also suppressed in the access stage, would its abandonment not occur there too, as with the hindrances in the access stage of the first jhāna? This is not so, because, unlike the abandoning of the hindrances, the suppression of delight in the object of initial application is not fully accomplished by access. For the complete abandoning of delight occurs only in absorption. Therefore, what we said—"because of the inability to abandon it by means of access cultivation"—should be understood as having been stated after careful examination. The meaning in "abandoned of sustained application" and so on should be understood according to the method stated. Although initial application is abandoned in the second jhāna itself, the mention of initial application in the phrase "abandoned of initial application and sustained application" is made merely to show its non-occurrence here. Likewise in "abandoned of initial application, sustained application, and rapture," and so on.

Yathāsambhavanti pathavīkasiṇādīsu yaṃ yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ yassa yassa sambhavati, tadanatikkamato. Kasiṇānāpānesu hi pañceva jhānāni pavattanti, asubhakāyagatāsatīsu paṭhamajjhānaṃ, anupekkhābrahmavihāresu pañcamajjhānavajjāni, upekkhābrahmavihāre pañcamajjhānanti.

"As is possible" means: without transgressing, in the case of the earth kasiṇa and so on, whichever object is possible for whichever [jhāna]. For in the kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing, all five jhānas occur; in the [meditations on] foulness and mindfulness directed to the body, the first jhāna; in the brahmavihāras apart from equanimity, the jhānas excluding the fifth; and in the brahmavihāra of equanimity, the fifth jhāna.

Pathavīkasiṇādīsūti [M 1.0216][V 1.0175] ettha ādi-ggahaṇena kevalaṃ āpokasiṇādīnameva, atha kho asubhādīnampi appanāvahakammaṭṭhānānaṃ saṅgahoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca abhibhāyatanavimokkhajhānāni pavattākāramattato bhinnāni, ārammaṇato pana kasiṇāyatanāneva hontīti kasiṇāyatanajhāneheva tāni saṅgahitāni. “Yathāsambhavaṃ…pe… anekavidha”nti vā vacanena rūpāvacarajjhāne sabbopi labbhamānakabhedo saṅgahitoti abhibhāyatanavimokkhajhānāni visuṃ na vuttāni, tāni pana sarūpato evaṃ veditabbāni.

In the phrase 'earth kasiṇa, etc.,' the word 'etc.' should be understood to include not only the water kasiṇa and so on, but also meditation subjects that lead to absorption, such as the unattractive. Here, the absorptions of the bases of mastery and the liberations differ only in their mode of occurrence, but since their object is simply the kasiṇa bases, they are included under the kasiṇa-based absorptions. By the statement 'as appropriate... in various ways,' all possible distinctions of the form-sphere absorptions are included, so the absorptions of the bases of mastery and the liberations are not separately mentioned. However, they should be understood thus in their own nature.

Tattha ñāṇuttarassa yogāvacarassa pathavīkasiṇādiārammaṇaṃ abhibhavitvā “na mettha appanānibbattane bhāro”ti paṭipannassa nimittuppattito uddhaṃ dutiyatatiyavīthiyaṃ, catutthapañcamavīthiyaṃ vā paṭiladdhaṃ jhānaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ nāma. Tañhi ārammaṇaṃ abhibhavatīti abhibhū, yogino sukhavisesānaṃ adhiṭṭhānatāya, manāyatanadhammāyatanapariyāpannatāya vā āyatananti abhibhāyatanaṃ, abhibhavitabbaṃ vā abhibhū, ālambaṇaṃ, taṃ āyatanamassāti abhibhāyatanaṃ. Atha vā ālambaṇābhibhavanatoyeva abhibhū, parikammaṃ, ñāṇaṃ vā, taṃ āyatanaṃ kāraṇamassāti abhibhāyatanaṃ. Parikammaṃ, ñāṇaṃ vā ālambaṇaṃ abhibhavitvā pavattamānaṃ upacāruppattito pañcamavīthimanatikkamitvā appanaṃ nibbatteti. Pañcamavīthito paraṃ nibbattaṃ pana abhibhavitukāmatāya nibbattitampi abhibhāyatanaṃ nāma na hoti. Sāmaññagatiyā pana kasiṇāyatanameva hoti. Imameva hi sīghatarappavattiṃ sandhāya aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tāni abhibhavitvā samāpajjati, saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ nibbattetī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 204) vuttaṃ. Nanu ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ yathārutavaseneva attho kasmā na gayhati. “Saha nimittuppādenevā”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 204) hi vuttattā nimittuppattiyā sahuppannaṃ jhānamabhibhāyatananti [M 1.0217] viññāyatīti? Nayidamevaṃ, nimittuppādena saha appanāya asambhavato. Nimittuppādoti hi idha paṭibhāganimittassa uppatti tadārammaṇassa vā upacārajjhānassa, kiṃ tāva paṭibhāganimittuppattiyā saha appanāya nibbatti upacārajjhāne asati tassā asambhavato, nāpi upacārajjhānena saha ekavīthiyaṃ nibbatti tassā upacārabhāvanāpabandhasevitabbabhāvena tadā asambhavato, tasmā nāticirāyanappavattidassanatthaṃ samīpimhi samīpakārīyūpacārena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tathā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yadi nimittuppattito nāticirappavattamabhibhāyatanaṃ, kathaṃ tassa dandhābhiññākhippābhiññābhedo pāḷiyaṃ vuttoti? Vuccate – catutthapañcamajavanavīthiyaṃ uppannaṃ cirakālanibbattitāya dandhābhiññaṃ, dutiyatatiyavīthiyaṃ [V 1.0176] uppannaṃ tabbiparītalakkhaṇatāya khippābhiññanti. Keci pana “abhibhāyatanaṃ nāma vasibhāvappattameva, netara”nti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ, vasibhāvappattiyā nimittuppattito dūratarabhāvena “saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ nibbattetī”ti aṭṭhakathāvacanena saha virujjhanato.

Here, for the meditator endowed with supreme knowledge, having mastered the object of the earth kasiṇa or another, and who undertakes the practice thinking, 'There is no burden for me in attaining absorption,' the absorption attained from the arising of the sign onwards—whether in the second or third cognitive process, or the fourth or fifth—is called the base of mastery. For it masters the object, it is 'mastering' (abhibhū); and because it is a foundation for the yogi's special bliss, or because it is included in the mind-base and the dhamma-base, it is a 'base' (āyatana); thus it is a 'mastering-base' (abhibhāyatana). Or, the object to be mastered is the 'mastering' (abhibhū), and that is its base (āyatana); thus 'mastering-base'. Or alternatively, 'mastering' (abhibhū) is the preparatory work or the knowledge, precisely because it masters the object; that is its base (āyatana) or cause, thus 'mastering-base'. The preparatory work or knowledge, having mastered the object and proceeding, gives rise to absorption without surpassing the fifth cognitive process from the arising of access. However, an absorption arising after the fifth process, though produced with the desire to master, is not called the base of mastery. In a general sense, it is simply a kasiṇa-base. Indeed, referring to this swifter progression, the commentary states: 'Having mastered those, one attains absorption; here, absorption arises simultaneously with the appearance of the sign.' But why is the meaning in the commentary not taken literally? Since it is said, 'simultaneously with the appearance of the sign,' should it not be understood that the absorption arising together with the sign is the mastering base? This is not so, because absorption cannot arise simultaneously with the appearance of the sign. Here, 'appearance of the sign' refers to the arising of the counterpart sign or the access absorption with that as its object. Firstly, absorption cannot arise simultaneously with the appearance of the counterpart sign, because without access absorption it is impossible. Nor can it arise in the same cognitive process as access absorption, because at that time it is impossible, since access must be cultivated through continuous practice. Therefore, it should be understood that the commentary speaks thus, using a figure of speech based on proximity, to show that the progression is not too prolonged. If the mastering base arises not long after the appearance of the sign, how is the distinction between slow and quick direct knowledge stated in the Pāli text explained? It is said: That which arises in the fourth or fifth impulsion cognitive process, being produced after a long time, is 'slow direct knowledge.' That which arises in the second or third process, having the opposite characteristic, is 'quick direct knowledge.' Some, however, say, 'The mastering base is only that which has attained mastery, not the other.' That is merely their opinion, for the attainment of mastery is far removed from the appearance of the sign, and thus contradicts the commentary’s statement: 'Here, absorption arises simultaneously with the appearance of the sign.'

Apica vasibhāvappattaṃ jhānaṃ abhibhavanakāraṇanirapekkhaṃ vasibhāvabaleneva sakkaccaṃ samāpajjituṃ na sakkāti na taṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ nāma hoti, tasmā appattavasibhāvā paṭhamuppannāyeva abhibhāyatananti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ “appamāṇaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ, appamāṇaṃ appamāṇārammaṇa”nti (dha. sa. 212-213) abhibhāyatanadesanāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Vasibhāvappattañhi jhānaṃ appamāṇanti vuccati. Idañca uppannamattattā parittamevāti? Nāyaṃ doso. Paṭhamaṃ abhibhāyatanavasena paṭiladdhajjhānaṃ pacchā vasibhāvappattampi abhibhāyatananāmameva labhatīti vasibhāvappattamabhibhāyatanaṃ appamāṇaṃ, itaraṃ parittaṃ.

Moreover, an absorption that has attained mastery cannot be carefully entered into simply by the power of mastery itself, without regard for the cause of mastering; thus, it is not called a base of mastery. Therefore, one should conclude here that the base of mastery is precisely the first-arisen absorption before attaining mastery. If so, how is it said in the teaching on the bases of mastery: ‘The immeasurable with a limited object, the immeasurable with an immeasurable object’ (Dhs. 212-213)? For an absorption that has attained mastery is called immeasurable. But this first-arisen absorption, being merely newly arisen, is limited, is it not? This is not a fault. The absorption first obtained as a base of mastery, even when it later has attained mastery, still retains the name 'base of mastery'. Thus, the base of mastery that has attained mastery is immeasurable, while the other is limited.

Atha [M 1.0218] vā vasibhāvappattaṃ appamāṇanti ukkaṃsagatipariggahavasena vuccati. Taṃ pana yaṃ balavataraṃ, taṃ appamāṇanti imassa atthassa upalakkhaṇaṃ katvā vadanti. Balavabhāvanibandhanaṃ appamāṇattaṃ. Balavabhāvo ca paṭhamaappanāvārato pacchimapacchimaappanāvārānaṃ balavatāya avasitāpattepi jhāne sambhavatīti balavantaṃ appamāṇaṃ, itaraṃ parittanti evaṃ avasitāpattepi jhāne appamāṇādibhāvo veditabbo. Atha vā appanāya balavabhāvo nāma upacārassa balavatāya sati hoti. Upacārañca taṃ balavaṃ, yaṃ sahasā appanaṃ uppādetuṃ sakkuṇeyya, tasmā khippābhiññānaṃ dvinnaṃ abhibhāyatanajhānānaṃ upacāravīthiyā anantaraṃ dutiyavīthiyaṃ uppannaṃ upacārajjhānassa balavatāya sayampi balavataranti appamāṇaṃ nāma hoti. Dutiyavīthimatikkamitvā tatiyavīthiyaṃ uppannaṃ taditarasabhāvatāya parittaṃ. Tathā dandhābhiññānaṃ catutthavīthiyaṃ uppannaṃ appamāṇaṃ. Pañcamavīthiyaṃ uppannaṃ parittanti. Atha vā yattha katthaci appanāvīthiyaṃ pañcamaṃ uppajjanakaappanāto catutthaṃ uppajjamānāya balavabhāvoti taṃvasenāpettha parittaappamāṇatā veditabbā.

Alternatively, an absorption that has attained mastery is called 'immeasurable' in the sense of encompassing the highest degree. But they say this, taking it as an indication of this meaning: that which is stronger is 'immeasurable'. Immeasurability is dependent on strength. And since strength arises from the first absorption occasion onwards, with later and later absorption occasions being stronger, even in an absorption that has not yet attained mastery, the strong one is 'immeasurable' and the other is 'limited'. In this way, the state of being immeasurable and so forth should be understood even in an absorption that has not yet attained mastery. Alternatively, the strength of absorption exists when the access is strong. And that access is strong which is able to produce absorption quickly. Therefore, for those of quick direct knowledge, the base-of-mastery absorption arising in the second cognitive process immediately after the access cognitive process is itself stronger due to the strength of the access absorption, and is thus called 'immeasurable'. That which arises in the third cognitive process, having surpassed the second, is 'limited' due to its different nature. Similarly, for those of slow direct knowledge, that which arises in the fourth cognitive process is 'immeasurable', and that which arises in the fifth cognitive process is 'limited'. Alternatively, wherever in an absorption cognitive process, the absorption arising fourth is stronger than the absorption arising fifth, by that means too, the limited and immeasurable nature should be understood.

Taṃ panetaṃ gaṇanato aṭṭhavidhaṃ hoti. Yathāha –

Now, this is eightfold by way of enumeration. As it is said:

“Ajjhattaṃ [V 1.0177] arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni. Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni. Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmi. Nīlāni nīlavaṇṇāni nīlanidassanāni nīlanibhāsāni, tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmi. Pītāni pītavaṇṇāni pītanidassanāni pītanibhāsāni. Lohitāni lohitavaṇṇāni lohitanidassanāni [M 1.0219] lohitanibhāsāni. Odātāni odātavaṇṇāni odātanidassanāni odātanibhāsāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hotī”ti (dī. ni. 2.173; 3.338; ma. ni. 2.249; a. ni. 1.427-434; 8.65).

“Being inwardly without perception of form, one sees external forms that are limited, and one is percipient thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ Being inwardly without perception of form, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly. Being inwardly without perception of form, one sees external forms that are immeasurable. Being inwardly without perception of form, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, I know, I see. Blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance; having mastered them, I know, I see. Yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance. Red, red in color, red in appearance, red in radiance. White, white in color, white in appearance, white in radiance; one is percipient thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’”

Tattha ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti alābhitāya vā anatthikatāya vā ajjhattesu kesādīsu parikammaappanāsaññāvirahito. Bahiddhā rūpāni passatīti bahiddhā aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu, catūsu bhūtakasiṇesu eva vā kataparikammakatāya parikammavasena ceva appanāvasena ca tāni bahiddhā aṭṭha, cattāri vā kasiṇarūpāni passati. Parittānīti amahantāni. Abhibhuyyāti yathā mahagghaso sampannagahaṇiko puriso kaṭacchumattaṃ bhattaṃ labhitvā “kiṃ ettha bhuñjitabbaṃ bhattaṃ atthī”ti saṅkaḍḍhitvā sabbaṃ ekakabaḷameva karoti, evameva ñāṇuttariko puggalo visadañāṇo “kiṃ ettha parittake ārammaṇe samāpajjitabbaṃ atthi, nāyaṃ mama bhāro”ti tāni rūpāni parikammena, ñāṇena vā abhibhavitvā samāpajjati. Heṭṭhā vuttanayena sīghaṃ appanaṃ nibbatteti. “Jānāmi passāmī”ti iminā panassa pubbābhogo kathito, tadāgamanato ca antosamāpattiyaṃ cittābhisaṅkhāro. Itarathā anena ābhogamatte kathite tena sādhitabbaṃ jhānaṃ na vuttaṃ hoti, abhibhāyatanadesanāvāyaṃ jhānavisayāti. Āgamaṭṭhakathāsu pana samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa pubbabhāgabhāvanāvasena jhānakkhaṇe pavattamabhibhavanākāraṃ gahetvā pavattamābhogaṃ sandhāya –

Here, ‘being inwardly without perception of form’ means being devoid of the perception of preparation and absorption regarding internal things such as hair, due to not having attained it or due to a lack of interest. ‘One sees external forms’ means that having performed the preparatory work on the eight external kasiṇas or on the four element kasiṇas, one sees those eight or four external kasiṇa-forms by way of both preparation and absorption. ‘Limited’ means not large. ‘Having mastered’ (abhibhuyya) is like a great eater skilled in taking, who, having obtained a mere spoonful of rice, thinks, ‘What rice is there to eat here?’ and gathering it all up, makes it into a single mouthful. Similarly, a person of superior knowledge, with clear knowledge, thinking, ‘What is there to attain in this limited object? This is no burden for me,’ masters those forms by means of preparation or knowledge and enters the attainment. One quickly produces the absorption in the manner stated below. By ‘I know and see,’ this one's preliminary attention is stated, and from its arising, the mental formation within the attainment. Otherwise, if only this attention were stated, the jhāna to be accomplished by it would not be mentioned, for this teaching on the spheres of mastery is a matter of jhāna. However, in the commentaries on the Āgamas, with reference to the attention that occurs by taking up the mode of mastery at the moment of jhāna—which occurs by way of preliminary development for one who has emerged from the attainment—it is said:

“Iminā panassa ābhogo kathito. So ca kho samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa, na antosamāpattiya”nti [V 1.0178] (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.173; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.249; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.8.65) vuttaṃ.

“By this, this one's attention is stated. And that is for one who has emerged from the attainment, not for one who is within the attainment.”

Dutiye [M 1.0220] suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānīti parisuddhāparisuddhavaṇṇāni. Parisuddhāni hi nīlādīni suvaṇṇāni, aparisuddhāni dubbaṇṇānīti idha adhippetāni.

In the second, ‘of beautiful and ugly color’ means of pure and impure color. For here, pure colors like blue, etc., are intended as ‘beautiful,’ and impure ones as ‘ugly.’

Tatiye appamāṇānīti vuddhippamāṇāni vipulāni khalamaṇḍalādīni. Vaḍḍhanavasena panettha appamāṇatā na gahitā kasiṇavaḍḍhanassa idha asambhavato. Kasiṇassa hi dve vaḍḍhanabhūmiyo upacārabhūmi, appanābhūmi vā. Tattha na tāva idha upacārabhūmiyaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ sambhavati. Nimittuppattiyā samakālaṃ viya uppajjamāne jhāne kuto tassa okāsoti, nāpi appanābhūmiyaṃ. Vaḍḍhitassa paṭhamuppannajhānārammaṇatā na yujjati, tasmā sabhāvamahantāneva ālambaṇāni idha appamāṇānīti adhippetāni. Keci pana “vaḍḍhitavaseneva appamāṇānīti gahetvā paṭhamaṃ abhibhavanicchāya abhāvena vaḍḍhetvā pacchā abhibhavanicchāya sati abhibhavanākārena pavatto tasmiṃ appanaṃ nibbattetīti appanaṃ paṭilabhitvā vaḍḍhitanimittesu idaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ vutta”nti vadanti.

In the third, ‘immeasurable’ means vast and extensive things like a threshing-floor circle, etc. Here, immeasurability is not taken in the sense of expansion, since the expansion of a kasiṇa is impossible in this context. For a kasiṇa has two stages of expansion: the access stage or the absorption stage. Now, expansion is not possible here in the access stage. How could there be an opportunity for it when the jhāna arises, as it were, simultaneously with the appearance of the sign? Nor is it possible in the absorption stage. It is not fitting for what has been expanded to be the object of the first-arisen jhāna. Therefore, here, ‘immeasurable’ is intended to mean objects that are naturally large. Some, however, taking ‘immeasurable’ in the sense of having been expanded, say that first, due to the absence of the desire for mastery, one expands it, and later, when the desire for mastery arises, one produces absorption in it by proceeding in the mode of mastery. Thus, after attaining absorption, this sphere of mastery is said to occur in relation to the expanded sign.

Catutthe abhibhuyyāti abhibhavitvā. Yathā nāma sampannagahaṇiko mahagghaso puriso ekaṃ bhattavaḍḍhitakaṃ labhitvā “‘aññopi hotu, aññopi hotū’ti kiṃ esa mayhaṃ karissatī”ti na taṃ mahantato passati, evameva ñāṇuttaro visadañāṇo puggalo “‘kiṃ ettha samāpajjitabbaṃ, nayidaṃ appamāṇa’nti mayhaṃ cittekaggatākaraṇe bhāro”ti abhibhavitvā samāpajjati. Vuttanayeneva appanaṃ nibbatteti.

In the fourth, ‘having mastered’ (abhibhuyya) means having mastered. Just as a great eater skilled in taking, having obtained a single serving of rice, thinks, ‘What will this do for me? Let there be more, let there be more,’ and does not regard it as large, so too a person of superior knowledge, with clear knowledge, masters it, thinking, ‘What is there to attain here? This is not immeasurable, nor is it a burden for me to make my mind one-pointed,’ and then enters the attainment. One produces the absorption in the manner already stated.

Pañcame nīlāni…pe… nīlanibhāsānīti etāni pariyāyanāmānīti tattha “nīlānī”ti sabbasaṅgāhakavasena vuttaṃ. Ettakeyeva pana vutte taṃyogato tabbohārena guṇayuttepi pasaṅgo siyāti tannivāraṇatthaṃ “nīlavaṇṇānī”ti vaṇṇavasena vuttaṃ. Evampi hi bahubbīhivasena guṇopi pasaṅgo hotīti “nīlanidassanānī”ti nidassanavasena vuttaṃ[M 1.0221]. Nidassitabbañhi nidassanaṃ, cakkhunā daṭṭhabbaṃ rūpaṃ. Tato setādinivāraṇatthaṃ nīla-saddena saha samāso katoti apaññāyamānacīvarāni asambhinnavaṇṇāni ekanīlāneva hutvā dissamānānīti [V 1.0179] vuttaṃ hoti. “Nīlanibhāsānī”ti idaṃ pana obhāsavasena vuttaṃ, nīlobhāsāni nīlappabhāyuttānīti attho. Etena tesaṃ suvisuddhattaṃ dasseti. ‘Pītānī”tiādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Aṭṭhasu cetesu purimaṃ abhibhavanākārena vaṇṇābhogarahitāni aṭṭhapi kasiṇāni parittāni ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tatiyaṃ tathā appamāṇāni. Dutiyacatutthāniyeva dve vaṇṇābhogasahitāni ārabbha uppannaṃ, na pana vaṇṇakasiṇavasena uppannaṃ tassa visuṃ vakkhamānattā.

In the fifth, ‘blue’... and so on... ‘of blue radiance’—these are synonymous terms. Here, ‘blue’ is stated in the sense of general inclusion. However, if only this much were stated, due to its connection, there might be an application even to things possessing that quality. To prevent that, ‘of blue color’ is stated in terms of color. Even so, a quality might still be implied by way of a bahubbīhi compound, so ‘of blue appearance’ is stated in terms of appearance. For an appearance is what is to be seen, a form to be seen with the eye. Then, to exclude white, etc., a compound is made with the word ‘blue,’ meaning that they appear as uniformly blue, with unmixed color, their texture not being discernible. ‘Of blue radiance’ is stated here in terms of luster, meaning possessed of blue luster and blue effulgence. By this, their complete purity is shown. The meaning in ‘yellow,’ etc., should also be understood in this same way. Among these eight, the first is stated with reference to what has arisen by taking as its object the eight limited kasiṇas, devoid of attention to color, in the mode of mastery. The third is likewise with the immeasurable ones. Only the second and fourth have arisen in dependence on the two that are accompanied by attention to color, but not as having arisen by way of the color kasiṇas, since that will be spoken of separately.

Pañcamādīni pana tesu katādhikāre sandhāya suvisuddhavaṇṇavaseneva desitāni. Na hi tesaṃ abhibhavanassa parittatā, appamāṇatā vā kāraṇaṃ, atha kho suvisuddhanīlādibhāvo. Tattha hi te katādhikārāti. Nanu ca āgamaṭṭhakathāsu “suvaṇṇāni vā hontu dubbaṇṇāni vā, parittaappamāṇavaseneva imāni abhibhāyatanāni desitānī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.173; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.249; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.8.65) vuttanti? Saccaṃ, taṃ pana āgame abhibhāyatanānaṃ aññathā āgatattā vuttaṃ. Tattha hi –

However, the five beginning with ‘blue’ are taught with reference to those who have made their foundation in them, only by way of perfectly pure color. For the reason for their mastery is not their limitedness or immeasurability, but rather their state of being perfectly pure blue, etc. For in that they have made their foundation. But is it not said in the commentaries on the Āgamas: ‘Whether they are of beautiful color or ugly color, these spheres of mastery are taught only by way of limitedness and immeasurability’? True, but that is stated because the spheres of mastery have come down differently in the Āgama. For there—

“Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti (dī. ni. 2.173; 3.338; ma. ni. 2.249; a. ni. 1.427-434; 8.65) –

“‘One who is inwardly percipient of form sees external forms: limited, of beautiful or ugly color; and immeasurable, of beautiful or ugly color. One who is inwardly without perception of form sees external forms: limited, of beautiful or ugly color; and immeasurable, of beautiful or ugly color.’”

Evaṃ cattāriyeva abhibhāyatanāni āgatāni, tasmā tadaṭṭhakathāsu vaṇṇābhoge vijjamāne avijjamānepi parittaappamāṇatāvaseneva [M 1.0222] imesaṃ desitabhāvo vutto. Parittaappamāṇatā hi imesu catūsu abhibhavanassa kāraṇaṃ vaṇṇābhoge vijjamāne avijjamānepīti. Nanu ca sabbattha “suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti vacanato vaṇṇābhogasahitāniyeva tattha gahitānīti? Taṃ na, vaṇṇābhogarahitāni, sahitāni ca sabbāni parittāni ekato katvā “parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti vuttāni, tathā “appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ visiṭṭhānaṃ vaṇṇābhogarahitānaṃ, sahitānañca ekajjhaṃ manasikāro, na ekajjhaṃ, visuṃyeva tesaṃ manasikāro. Yadi evaṃ visuṃ kathamekattanti? Parittabhāvasāmaññato. Yadi evaṃ suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇa-ggahaṇamatiriccati [V 1.0180] avasiṭṭhoti? Nātiriccati pariyāyadesanābhāvato. Atthi hi esa pariyāyo, yadidaṃ vaṇṇābhogajanitājanitaṃ visesaṃ aggahetvā parittabhāvasāmaññena ekattaṃ netvā “parittāni abhibhuyyā”ti vatvā puna tadantogadhameva pabhedaṃ vineyyavasena dassetuṃ tāni ca kadāci vaṇṇavasena āvajjitāni honti, “suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni abhibhuyyā”ti vattabbatāya vaṇṇābhogarahitāni, sahitāni ca visuṃ manasi katvā ubhayatthāpi vaṇṇābhogarahitaparittābhibhavane, taṃsahitaparittābhibhavane ca parittābhibhavanasāmaññaṃ gahetvā ekattaṃ katanti. Abhidhamme pana nippariyāyadesanattā vaṇṇābhogarahitāni, sahitāni ca visuṃ vuttāni. Atthi hi ubhayatthābhibhavanavisesoti. Hotu tāva, evaṃ suttābhidhammapāṭhavisesato aṭṭhakathāya pāṭhabhede pana ko adhippāyoti? Vuccate – suttante hi paṭhamavimokkhaṃ dvedhā bhinditvā paṭhamadutiyaabhibhāyatanāni vuttāni, pariyāyadesanattā vimokkhānampi abhibhavanapariyāyo vijjatīti “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī”ti abhibhāyatanadvayaṃ vuttaṃ.

Thus, only these four bases of mastery are presented, and therefore, in their commentaries, it is said that they are taught simply on account of their limited or boundless nature, whether an advertence to color is present or not. For in these four, the reason for mastery is their limited or boundless nature, whether an advertence to color is present or not. But is it not the case that everywhere, from the phrase 'fair and foul,' only those with an advertence to color are included there? That is not so. Those without an advertence to color and those with it, all the limited ones, are grouped together and spoken of as 'limited, fair and foul,' and similarly, 'boundless, fair and foul.' If so, how is there a single advertence to the distinct ones—those without an advertence to color and those with it? It is not a single advertence; their advertence is separate. If so, being separate, how is there unity? Through the commonality of their limited nature. If so, does the inclusion of 'fair and foul' become superfluous and redundant? It is not superfluous, because it is a figurative teaching. For there is this figurative method: without grasping the distinction of whether it is generated by an advertence to color or not, one brings them to unity through the commonality of their limited nature, saying, 'having mastered the limited.' Then, to show the division included within that for the sake of those to be trained, and because they are at times adverted to by way of color, in order to say 'having mastered the fair and foul,' those without an advertence to color and those with it are attended to separately. In both cases—in the mastery of the limited without an advertence to color and in the mastery of the limited with it—the commonality of mastering the limited is taken, and they are made one. In the Abhidhamma, however, because the teaching is not figurative, those without an advertence to color and those with it are stated separately. For there is a distinction in mastery in both cases. So be it. Given the difference in the texts of the Sutta and Abhidhamma, what is the intention behind the difference in the commentary's text? It is said: In the Suttanta, the first liberation is divided into two, and the first and second bases of mastery are stated. Because the teaching is figurative, a figurative method of mastery also exists for the liberations; hence, the two bases of mastery, 'perceiving form internally,' are mentioned.

Tatiyacatutthaabhibhāyatanesu [M 1.0223] dutiyavimokkho, vaṇṇābhibhāyatanesu tatiyavimokkho ca abhibhavanappavattito saṅgahito, idha pana nippariyāyadesanattā vimokkhābhibhāyatanāni asaṅkarato dassetuṃ vimokkhe vajjetvā abhibhāyatanāni kathitāni. Sabbāni ca vimokkhakiccāni vimokkhadesanāya vuttāni, tadetaṃ “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī”ti sutte āgatassa abhibhāyatanadvayassa abhidhamme avacanato “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīnañca sabbavimokkhakiccasādhāraṇavacanabhāvato vavatthānaṃ katanti viññāyati. Avassañcetaṃ eva sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, na sampaṭicchantehi suttābhidhammapāṭhabhede aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ vattabbaṃ. Atha kimettha vattabbaṃ, nanu aṭṭhakathāyameva “kasmā pana yathā suttante ‘ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittānī’tiādi vuttaṃ, evaṃ avatvā idha catūsupi abhibhāyatanesu ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññitāva vuttā”ti vatvā “ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyato”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttanti? Na taṃ tassa kāraṇavacanaṃ, atha kho katthaci “ajjhattaṃ rūpāni passatī”ti avatvā sabbattha yaṃ vuttaṃ “bahiddhā rūpāni passatī”ti, tassa ca kāraṇavacanaṃ. Teneva hi tattha vā idha vā “bahiddhā rūpāniyeva abhibhavitabbānī”ti tattheva vuttaṃ, anabhibhavanīyatā ca ajjhattarūpānaṃ bahiddhā rūpāni viya avibhūtattā. Na hi suṭṭhu vibhūtabhāvamantarena ñāṇuttarānaṃ ārammaṇābhibhavanaṃ sambhavatīti. Nanu ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pāṭhadvayavisesassa desanāvilāso kāraṇabhāvena vuttoti? Saccaṃ vutto, so ca yathāvuttavavatthānavaseneva veditabbo[V 1.0181]. Desanāvilāso hi nāma vineyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vijjamānasseva pariyāyassa vibhāvanaṃ, na yassa kassacīti. Evaṃ tāva abhibhāyatanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In the third and fourth bases of mastery, the second liberation is included, and in the bases of mastery related to color, the third liberation is included, due to their proceeding by way of mastery. Here, however, because the teaching is not figurative, in order to show the liberations and the bases of mastery unmixed, the bases of mastery are spoken of, having excluded the liberations. And all the functions of the liberations are stated in the teaching on the liberations. Thus, it is understood that a distinction has been made because the two bases of mastery that come in the Sutta as 'perceiving form internally' are not mentioned in the Abhidhamma, and because phrases like 'one with form sees forms' are general statements applicable to the function of all liberations. This must certainly be accepted thus. Those who do not accept it must state another reason for the difference in the texts of the Sutta and the Abhidhamma. Now, what is to be said here? Is it not the case that in the commentary itself, having asked, 'But why, just as it is said in the Suttanta, "Perceiving form internally, one sees external forms that are limited," and so on, is it not said thus here, but instead, in all four bases of mastery, only perception of formlessness internally is mentioned?' the reason given is, 'Because internal forms are not to be mastered'? That is not the reason for that. Rather, it is the reason why, in some places, instead of saying 'one sees internal forms,' it is said everywhere 'one sees external forms.' For that very reason, it is stated right there, whether there or here, 'only external forms are to be mastered.' And the unmasterable nature of internal forms is due to their not being manifest, like external forms. For mastery of an object by superior knowledge is not possible without it being very manifest. But is it not said in the commentary that the skillful style of the teaching is given as the reason for the difference between the two texts? Truly, it is said, and that should be understood only by way of the distinction stated above. For a skillful style of teaching is the clarification of an existing figurative method in a way that is suitable to the disposition of those to be trained, not just any method whatsoever. Thus, for now, the base of mastery should be understood.

Tattha [M 1.0224] vimokkhoti paṭiladdhajjhānassa jhānaṃ samāpajjitukāmatāvasappavattajavanavīthisamanantarameva pituaṅke vissaṭṭhaaṅgapaccaṅgassa viya dārakassa ārammaṇe nirāsaṅkameva hutvā paṭhamakappanā viya ca lahuṃ avuṭṭhahitvā antamaso catupañcacittakkhaṇato anosakkitvā ārammaṇe abhirativasena pavattassa vasibhāvappattassa jhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tañhi kasiṇāyatanavasena vā abhibhāyatanavasena vā uppannaṃ paccanīkadhammehi suṭṭhu vimuttattā, ārammaṇe adhimuttatāya ca “vimokkho”ti vuccati. Vuttampi cetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

Therein, 'liberation' is a designation for that jhāna which has attained mastery, which proceeds by way of delight in the object, not receding for at least four or five thought-moments, not emerging quickly as in the initial application, and having become free from hesitation regarding the object—like a child with limbs relaxed in its father’s lap—immediately after the stream of impulsion that proceeds by the power of the desire to enter a jhāna that has been attained. For that, having arisen by way of a kasiṇa-base or a base of mastery, is called 'liberation' because it is well freed from opposing states and because of its firm resolve upon the object. And this is also stated in the commentary:

“Kenaṭṭhena pana vimokkho veditabboti? Adhimuccanaṭṭhena. Ko ayaṃ adhimuccanaṭṭho nāma? Paccanīkadhammehi ca suṭṭhu vimuccanaṭṭho, ārammaṇe ca abhirativasena suṭṭhu adhimuccanaṭṭho”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 248).

'By what meaning, then, should 'liberation' be understood? By the meaning of resolution. And what is this meaning of resolution? It is the meaning of thorough liberation from opposing states and the meaning of thorough resolution through delight in the object.'

Yadi vasibhāvappattameva vimokkho, kathamassa ārammaṇacatukke parittatā pāḷiyaṃ vuttā. Avasitāpattañhi jhānaṃ parittanti vuccatīti? Nāyaṃ doso, paripuṇṇavasibhāvappattaṃ sandhāya aparipuṇṇavasibhāvappattassa parittabhāvena tattha adhippetattā, tasmā vasibhāvappattameva jhānaṃ vimokkho nāma, na itaraṃ. Itaraṃ pana yadi kasiṇāyatanavasena uppannaṃ, kasiṇāyatanaṃ. Atha abhibhāyatanavasena, abhibhāyatanamevāti. Keci pana “paṭhamaappanāto pacchimapacchimāya paṭipakkhato suṭṭhu vimuttattā kasiṇāyatanavasena, abhibhāyatanavasena ca uppannaṃ paṭhamakappanaṃ ṭhapetvā sesaṃ vimokkhoyevā”ti vadanti.

If 'liberation' is only the jhāna that has attained mastery, how is its limitedness in the fourfold object stated in the Pāli? For a jhāna that has not attained mastery is said to be limited. This is not a fault, because the limited nature there is intended for that which has incompletely attained mastery in relation to that which has perfectly attained mastery. Therefore, only a jhāna that has attained mastery is called 'liberation,' not another. As for the other, if it has arisen by way of a kasiṇa-base, it is a kasiṇa-base; if by way of a base of mastery, it is only a base of mastery. Some, however, say: 'Because from the first absorption onwards there is thorough liberation from each successive opposing factor, whatever arises by way of a kasiṇa-base or by way of a base of mastery—excluding the initial application—the rest is indeed liberation.'

Taṃ panetaṃ gaṇanato tividhaṃ. Yathāha –

This, however, is threefold by way of enumeration. As it is said:

“Rūpī [M 1.0225] rūpāni passati, ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati, subhanteva adhimutto hotī”ti (dī. ni. 2.174; 3.339; paṭi. ma. 1.209).

'One with form sees forms; not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally; one is resolved only on the beautiful.'

Tattha [V 1.0182] rūpīti ajjhattaṃ kesādīsu uppāditaṃ rūpajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ, tadassa atthīti rūpī. Rūpāni passatīti bahiddhāpi nīlakasiṇādirūpāni jhānacakkhunā passati. Iminā ajjhattabahiddhavatthukesu kasiṇesu jhānapaṭilābho dassito. Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti ajjhattaṃ narūpasaññī, attano kesādīsu anuppāditarūpāvacarajjhānoti attho. Iminā bahiddhā parikammaṃ katvā bahiddhāva paṭiladdhajjhānatā dassitā. “Subha”nti iminā suvisuddhesu nīlādīsu vaṇṇakasiṇesu jhānāni dassitāni. Tattha kiñcāpi antoappanāyaṃ “subha”nti ābhogo natthi, yo pana suvisuddhaṃ subhakasiṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā viharati, so yasmā “subha”nti adhimuccanavasena paṭhamajjhānaṃ upasampajjitvā viharati, tathā dutiyādīni, tasmā evaṃ desanā katāti. Paṭisambhidāmagge pana “idha bhikkhu mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.212) brahmavihāravasena subhavimokkho vutto. Dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ pana brahmavihārānaṃ visuṃyeva āgatattā taṃ nayaṃ paṭikkhipitvā sunīlakādivaseneva subhavimokkho aṭṭhakathāyaṃ anuññātoti idhāpi tattha vuttanayeneva vavatthānaṃ katanti evaṃ tāva vimokkhajhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Here, 'one with form' means the form-sphere jhāna, which is form, that has been produced internally in regard to hair, etc. It is called 'one with form' because that exists for him. 'He sees forms' means he sees external forms such as the blue kasiṇa, etc., with the jhāna eye. By this, the attainment of jhāna in regard to internal and external objects like the kasiṇas is shown. 'Internally not perceiving form' means internally not perceiving form—that is, the form-sphere jhāna has not been produced in regard to one's own hair, etc. By this, it is shown that after preparing externally, the jhāna is attained externally. 'Fair' indicates the jhānas attained in regard to the very pure color kasiṇas like blue, etc. Although in the case of absorption, there is no advertence as 'fair,' one who dwells taking the very pure fair kasiṇa as the object, because he enters and dwells in the first jhāna through the resolution 'fair,' and similarly for the second, etc., thus the teaching is given in this way. However, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the 'liberation of the fair' is explained through the divine abidings, as in: 'Here, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,' etc. (Paṭis. 1.212). But in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, since the divine abidings are treated separately, that method is rejected, and the 'liberation of the fair' is approved in the commentary only through the method of the very pure blue, etc. Therefore, here too, the distinction should be made according to the method stated there. Thus, for now, the jhāna of liberation should be understood.

Yathānurūpanti hīnādianurūpaṃ. Paṭhamajjhānañhi hīnaṃ kappassa tatiyabhāgāyuke brahmapārisajje upapattiṃ nipphādeti, majjhimaṃ upaḍḍhakappāyuke brahmapurohite, paṇītaṃ ekakappāyuke mahābrahme. Tathā dutiyajjhānaṃ, tatiyajjhānañca hīnaṃ dvikappāyuke parittābhe, majjhimaṃ catukappāyuke appamāṇābhe, paṇītaṃ aṭṭhakappāyuke ābhassare. Catutthajjhānaṃ hīnaṃ [M 1.0226] soḷasakappāyuke parittāsubhe, majjhimaṃ dvattiṃsakappāyuke appamāṇasubhe, paṇītaṃ catusaṭṭhikappāyuke subhakiṇhe. Pañcamajjhānaṃ pana tividhampi pañcakappasatāyuke vehapphale upapattiṃ nipphādeti, tadeva titthiyehi saññāvirāgavasena bhāvitaṃ pañcakappasatāyukeyeva asaññasatte. Anāgāmīhi pana puthujjanādikāle pacchāpi bhāvitaṃ saddhādiindriyādhimuttatānukkamena yathākkamaṃ sahassadvisahassacatusahassaaṭṭhasahassasoḷasasahassakappāyukesu avihāatappāsudassāsudassīakaniṭṭhanāmakesu pañcasuddhāvāsesu upapattiṃ nipphādetīti evametaṃ yathānurūpaṃ soḷasarūpāvacarabrahmalokūpapattinipphādakanti āha “yathānurūpaṃ…pe… hotī”ti.

According to their suitability means corresponding to what is suitable for the inferior, etc. For the first jhāna, the inferior produces rebirth among the Brahmā’s Retinue with a lifespan of a third of an eon; the middling, among the Brahmā’s Ministers with a lifespan of half an eon; the superior, among the Great Brahmās with a lifespan of a full eon. Similarly, the second jhāna and the third jhāna: the inferior produces rebirth among the Minor Luster with a lifespan of two eons; the middling, among the Immeasurable Luster with a lifespan of four eons; the superior, among the Radiant with a lifespan of eight eons. The fourth jhāna: the inferior produces rebirth among the Minor Aura with a lifespan of sixteen eons; the middling, among the Immeasurable Aura with a lifespan of thirty-two eons; the superior, among the Beautiful Aura with a lifespan of sixty-four eons. The fifth jhāna, however, produces rebirth in the Vehapphala with a lifespan of five hundred eons in all three grades. The same, when developed by non-Buddhists through dispassion towards perception, produces rebirth among the Non-Perceptive Beings with a lifespan of five hundred eons. But when developed by non-returners, whether during their time as ordinary people or afterwards, it produces rebirth in the five Pure Abodes—Aviha, Atappa, Sudassa, Sudassī, and Akaniṭṭha—with lifespans of one thousand, two thousand, four thousand, eight thousand, and sixteen thousand eons respectively, according to the gradual predominance of faculties like faith, etc. Thus, it is said: "According to their suitability... it produces rebirth in the sixteen realms of the fine-material Brahmā worlds."

Yasmā pana rūpabhavepi pavattiyaṃ labhitabbā upabhogasampatti kāmāvacarasseva phalaṃ, tasmā [V 1.0183] idha “bhavabhogasampattiṃ nipphādetī”ti avatvā upapattinipphādanameva vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca dutiyajjhānabhūmiṃ upādāya sabbattha paripuṇṇassa mahākappassa vasena paricchedo daṭṭhabbo, paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ pana asaṅkhyeyyakappavasena. Na hi tattha itaravasena paricchedo sambhavati ekakappepi avināsābhāvena mahākappassa catutthabhāgeyeva tassa saṇṭhahanato.

However, since even in the form-existence the prosperity of enjoyment that can be obtained in the course of existence is a result of the sense-sphere alone, it should be understood that here only the production of rebirth is stated, not 'it produces the prosperity of existence.' And here, reckoning should be understood in terms of a full great eon everywhere beginning with the second jhāna plane; but in the first jhāna plane, in terms of an incalculable eon. For there, a reckoning in other terms is not possible, because it is not destroyed even within a single eon, since it lasts for only the fourth part of a great eon.

Rūpāvacarakusalavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of wholesome fine-material consciousness is concluded.

Arūpāvacarakusalavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Wholesome Immaterial-Sphere Consciousness

Idāni arūpāvacarakusalassa niddesāvakāso anuppattoti tanniddesatthamāha “sesesu panā”tiādi. Ākāsakasiṇavajjitassa yassa kassaci kasiṇassa ugghāṭanato laddhamākāsaṃ kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ. Tattha pavattaṃ viññāṇanti ākāsānañcāyatanamāha. Tañhi dutiyāruppassa [M 1.0227] ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Sabbasoti sabbākārena, rūpanimittadaṇḍādānasambhavadassanādinā sabbena rūpadhammesu, pathavīkasiṇādirūpanimittesu tadārammaṇajjhānesu ca dosadassanākārena, tesu eva vā rūpanimittesu nikantippahānaasamāpajjitukāmatādinā ākārenāti attho. Atha vā sabbasoti sabbāsaṃ, kusalādibhedena anavasesānanti attho. Rūpasaññānanti saññāsīsena vuttarūpāvacarajjhānānañceva tadārammaṇānañca. Rūpāvacarajjhānampi hi “rūpa”nti vuccati uttarapadalopena “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīsu viya. Tadārammaṇampi kasiṇarūpaṃ purimapadalopena “devena dattoti, bahiddhā rūpāni passatī”tiādīsu viya, tasmā idha rūpe rūpajjhāne taṃsahagatasaññā rūpasaññāti gahitā, saññāsīsena vuttarūpāvacarajjhānānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. “Rūpa”nti saññā assāti rūpasaññaṃ, rūpanāmavantanti attho. Taṃgahitena pathavīkasiṇādibhedassa tadārammaṇassa cetaṃ nāmanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Rūpasaññāna”nti hi sarūpekasesavasena niddeso kato. Samatikkamāti virāgā, nirodhā ca. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Etāsaṃ kusalavipākakiriyāvasena pañcadasannaṃ jhānasaṅkhātānaṃ rūpasaññānaṃ, etesañca pathavīkasiṇādivasena navannaṃ ārammaṇasaṅkhātānaṃ rūpasaññānaṃ anavasesānaṃ sabbākārena ca, tesu eva vā nikantippahānaasamāpajjitukāmatādinā ākārena [V 1.0184] virāgā, nirodhā ca jigucchanato ceva tappaṭibandhachandarāgavikkhambhanato ca nibbattaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāya sahagataṃ arūpāvacarakusalacittaṃ. Na hi sakkā sabbaso anatikkantarūpasaññena taṃ nibbattetunti.

Now, the opportunity has arisen for the exposition of the immaterial-sphere wholesome consciousness, and for the purpose of that exposition, it is said, "As for the rest," etc. The space attained by removing any kasiṇa except the space kasiṇa is called "space from kasiṇa-removal." The consciousness occurring there, he says, is the base of infinite space. For that serves as the object for the second immaterial attainment. "Completely" means in every way: in the manner of seeing faults in all material phenomena, such as by seeing the possibility of taking up a stick against the material sign, etc., and in the material signs like the earth kasiṇa, and in the jhānas that take them as objects; or in those very material signs in the manner of abandoning attachment, unwillingness to attain them, and so on. Alternatively, "completely" means of all, without remainder, classified as wholesome, etc. "Perceptions of form" refers to the form-sphere jhānas and their objects, spoken of under the heading of perception. For even a form-sphere jhāna is called "form" by eliding the subsequent word, as in phrases like "one with form sees forms." Its object, a kasiṇa-form, is also called "form" by eliding the prior word, as in phrases like "given by a deity" or "one sees external forms." Therefore, here, the perception associated with form or form-jhāna is taken as "perception of form"; this is a designation for the form-sphere jhānas mentioned under the heading of perception. "Perception of form" means that which has the name "form." By this, it should be understood that this is the name for the various objects such as the earth kasiṇa. For the exposition "perceptions of form" is given by way of sarūpekasesa, where one term stands for all similar cases. "Transcending" means through dispassion and cessation. What is being said? The immaterial-sphere wholesome consciousness, accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space, is generated from the dispassion towards and cessation of these fifteen perceptions of form reckoned as jhānas (in terms of wholesome, resultant, and functional) and these nine perceptions of form reckoned as objects (like the earth kasiṇa), without remainder and in every way—or in the manner of abandoning attachment and unwillingness to attain them—and from disgust and the suppression of the desire and lust connected with them. For it is impossible for one who has not completely transcended perceptions of form to generate that state.

Na kevalaṃ etāsaṃyeva samatikkamanato idaṃ nibbattaṃ, atha kho paṭighasaññādīnamatthaṅgamāditopīti āha “paṭighasaññāna”ntiādi. Tattha cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ, rūpādīnañca ārammaṇānaṃ [M 1.0228] paṭighātena aññamaññasamodhānasaṅkhātena paṭihananena uppannā saññā paṭighasaññā, rūpasaññādidvipañcasaññānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathāha –

Not only is this generated from the mere transcendence of these, but also from the cessation of perceptions of resistance and so forth, as it is said: "perceptions of resistance," etc. Here, the perception that arises from the impingement—a striking designated as a mutual encounter—of the bases like the eye, etc., and the objects like forms, etc., is the perception of resistance. This is a designation for the group of five perceptions beginning with form-perception, etc. As it is said:

“Tattha katamā paṭighasaññā? Rūpasaññā saddasaññā gandhasaññā rasasaññā phoṭṭhabbasaññā, imā vuccanti paṭighasaññāyo”ti (vibha. 603).

"Herein, what is perception of resistance? Perception of form, perception of sound, perception of smell, perception of taste, perception of touch—these are called perceptions of resistance." (Vibhaṅga 603).

Tāsaṃ kusalākusalavipākabhūtānaṃ atthaṅgamā pahānā asamuppādā appavattikaraṇenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nanu ca etā rūpāvacarajjhānasamāpannassāpi na santi. Na hi paṭhamajjhānādisamāpannakāle pañcadvāravasena cittaṃ pavattatīti? Saccametaṃ, yathā pana “sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti ettha pasaṃsāvasena aññattha pahīnānampi sukhadukkhānaṃ catutthajjhāne, “sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchānaṃ pahānā rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā sakadāgāmimaggaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti ettha paṭhamamaggeyeva pahīnānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhādīnaṃ dutiyamagge ca vacanaṃ, evameva imasmiṃ jhāne paṭipajjanakānaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ imassa jhānassa pasaṃsāvasena etāsaṃ ettha vacananti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā kiñcāpi tā rūpāvacarasamāpannassāpi na santi, na pana pahīnattā na santi. Kiñcarahi paccayābhāvena. Na hi rūpāvacarabhāvanā rūpavirāgāya saṃvattati, rūpāyattā eva tāsaṃ pavattīti. Arūpabhāvanā pana rūpavirāgāya saṃvattati, tasmā “tā ettha pahīnā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Tathā hi etāsaṃ ito pubbe appahīnattāyeva “paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpannassa saddo kaṇṭako”ti vutto bhagavatā. Idha ca pahīnattā eva arūpasamāpattīnaṃ āneñjābhisaṅkhāravacanādīhi, “ye te santā vimokkhā atikkamma rūpe [M 1.0229] arūpā”tiādinā ca āneñjatā, santavimokkhatā ca vuttā.

Regarding these, which are wholesome, unwholesome, or resultant, it is said that this is by their setting, abandoning, non-arising, and being rendered non-occurrent. But do these not also fail to exist for one who has attained the form-sphere jhānas? For at the time of attaining the first jhāna and so forth, consciousness does not occur by way of the five sense-doors. This is true. However, just as in the statement, 'With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness,' pleasure and pain, though abandoned elsewhere, are mentioned in the fourth jhāna by way of praise. And in the statement, 'With the abandoning of identity view and doubt, and with the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion, he enters and dwells in the path of the once-returner,' identity view and so forth, though abandoned in the very first path, are mentioned in the second path. So too, it should be understood that these are mentioned here by way of praise for this jhāna, for the purpose of generating zeal in those who practice it. Alternatively, although these do not exist for one who has attained the form-sphere, they are not absent because they are abandoned, but rather because of the absence of a condition. For the development of the form-sphere does not lead to dispassion for form; their occurrence is dependent on form. But the development of the formless leads to dispassion for form. Therefore, it is fitting to say, 'Here, they are abandoned.' Indeed, because these were not abandoned before this, the Blessed One said, 'For one who has attained the first jhāna, sound is a thorn.' Here, however, they are abandoned, as indicated by statements about the imperturbable formations of the formless attainments, and by such phrases as, 'Those peaceful liberations that, transcending forms, are formless,' which describe imperturbability and peaceful liberation.

Nānattasaññānanti [V 1.0185] nānatte gocare pavattānaṃ, nānattānaṃ vā saññānaṃ, vuttāvasesānaṃ catucattālīsakāmāvacarasaññānanti attho. Etā eva hi –

'Perceptions of diversity' means perceptions occurring with diverse objects as their range, or diverse perceptions themselves—that is, the remaining forty-four sense-sphere perceptions that have been mentioned. For these indeed are:

“Tattha katamā nānattasaññā? Asamāpannassa manodhātusamaṅgissa vā manoviññāṇadhātusamaṅgissa vā saññā sañjānanā sañjānitattaṃ, imā vuccanti nānattasaññāyo”ti (vibha. 604) –

"Therein, what are the perceptions of diversity? For one who is not attained in absorption, who is endowed with the mind-element or with the mind-consciousness-element, the perception, the act of perceiving, the state of having perceived—these are called the perceptions of diversity." (Vibhaṅga 604).

Evaṃ vibhaṅge vibhajitvā vuttā. Tā pana yasmā rūpasaddādibhede nānatte nānāsabhāve ārammaṇe pavattanti, yasmā ca aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalasaññā, dvādasa akusalasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakusalavipākasaññā, dve akusalavipākasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakiriyasaññāti evaṃ catucattālīsappabhedā nānāsabhāvā, aññamaññaṃ asadisā, tasmā “nānattasaññā”ti vuccanti. Amanasikārāti sabbaso anāvajjanā asamannāhārā apaccavekkhaṇahetu javanapaṭipādakena vā bhavaṅgacittassa anto akaraṇā ṭhapetvā kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ nānārammaṇe cittassa asaṅkharaṇatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Iminā hi nānattasaññāmanasikārahetūnaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ samatikkamopi vutto, rūpajjhāne pana tadabhāvato “nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā”ti na vuttaṃ. Atha samatikkamādīnaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇanti? Vuccate – yasmā rūpasaññā, paṭighasaññā ca iminā jhānena nibbattitabhavepi na vijjanti, arūpasaññāya bhāvanāya abhāve cutito uddhaṃ uppattirahānaṃ rūpasaññāpaṭighasaññānaṃ yāva attano [M 1.0230] vipākuppatti, tāva anuppattidhammataṃ āpādiyamānattā, pageva pana imaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannakāle, tasmā “samatikkamā, atthaṅgamā”ti ubhayathāpi tāsaṃ abhāvoyeva dassito. Nānattasaññāsu pana yā tasmiṃ bhave na uppajjanti ekantarūpanissitattā, tā anokāsatāya na uppajjanti, na arūpabhāvanāya nivāritattā, anivāritattā ca kāci uppajjanti, tasmā tāsaṃ amanasikāro anāvajjanaṃ apaccavekkhaṇaṃ javanapaṭipādakena vā bhavaṅgamanassa anto akaraṇaṃ appavesanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatra pavattamānānampi hi jhānaṃ samāpannassa tāsaṃ amanasikāroyeva itarathā jhānasamāpattiyā abhāvato. Iti saṅkhepato “rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā”ti iminā sabbarūpāvacaradhammānaṃ pahānaṃ vuttaṃ, “paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā”ti sabbesaṃ kāmāvacaracittacetasikānaṃ pahānaṃ, amanasikāro ca vutto, tīhi panetehi samādhissa thirabhāvo kathitoti.

Thus they are stated in the Vibhaṅga, having been analyzed. Now, because they occur with regard to diverse objects with their distinctions of form, sound, and so on, which have diverse intrinsic natures; and because they are of forty-four kinds with diverse intrinsic natures, dissimilar to one another—namely, eight wholesome sense-sphere perceptions, twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven wholesome-resultant sense-sphere perceptions, two unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and eleven functional sense-sphere perceptions—they are called 'perceptions of diversity.' 'Non-attention' means complete non-adverting, non-contemplation, and non-reviewing; or, it is said to be the non-concocting of the mind towards diverse objects—excluding the space from the removal of the kasiṇa—by not placing them within the life-continuum consciousness by means of the producer of impulsion. By this is also stated the transcending of the material phenomena that are the causes for attention to perceptions of diversity. In the form-sphere jhānas, however, because of their absence, it is not said, 'through the non-attention to perceptions of diversity.' Now, what is the distinction between transcending and so on? It is said: Because form-perceptions and resistance-perceptions do not exist even in an existence produced by this jhāna—since, due to the development of formless perception, form-perceptions and resistance-perceptions, which are devoid of arising after death, are brought to a state of non-arising until their own result arises—how much more so at the time of attaining this jhāna. Therefore, their absence is shown in both ways, as 'transcending' and 'setting.' As for perceptions of diversity, those that do not arise in that existence, being dependent solely on form, do not arise for lack of opportunity, not because they are prevented by the development of the formless. And some do arise because they are not prevented. Therefore, for them, 'non-attention' is stated, meaning non-adverting, non-reviewing, or not placing them within the life-continuum mind by the producer of impulsion, not allowing them entry. For even when they are occurring, for one who has attained the jhāna there is only non-attention to them, otherwise there would be no attainment of jhāna. Thus, in brief: by 'the transcending of form-perceptions,' the abandoning of all form-sphere phenomena is stated. By 'the setting of resistance-perceptions and the non-attention to perceptions of diversity,' the abandoning of all sense-sphere consciousness and mental factors, and non-attention, are stated. And by these three, the stability of concentration is described.

Ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāsahagatanti [V 1.0186] ettha pana nāssa antoti anantaṃ, anantaṃ ākāsaṃ ākāsānantaṃ, kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ, anantatā pana uppādavayantābhāvato anantamanasikāravasena vā veditabbā. Na hi etassa uppādanto, vayanto vā paññāyati asabhāvadhammattā. Sabhāvadhammo hi ahutvā sambhavanato, hutvā ca vinassanato uppādavayantaparicchinno, netaro. Na ca panetaṃ manasi karonto yogāvacaro tassa paricchedasaṅkhātamantaṃ gaṇhāti, atha kho rūpavivekamattasseva gahaṇena anantapharaṇākāreneva manasikāraṃ pavatteti, tasmā uppādavayantavirahato manasikāravasena vā etamanantanti veditabbaṃ. “Anantākāsa”nti ca vattabbe ananta-saddassa paranipātavasena “ākāsānanta”nti vuccati. Ākāsānantameva ākāsānañcaṃ [M 1.0231] saṃyogaparassa ta-kārassa ca-kāraṃ katvā, tadeva āyatanaṃ sasampayuttadhammassa jhānassa ārammaṇabhāvato adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena devāyatanaṃ viyāti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, tasmiṃ appanāpattā saññā ākāsānañcāyatanasaññā, tāya sahagataṃ viññāṇaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ. Atha vā ākāsānañcaṃ āyatanamassā sasampayuttadhammāya saññāyāti ākāsānañcāyatanā, sāyeva saññā, tāya jhānaṃ sahagatanti ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ.

Regarding 'associated with the perception of the base of infinite space': here, 'it has no end (na assa anto), thus it is infinite (anantaṃ).' Infinite space (ākāsānantaṃ) is the space from the removal of the kasiṇa. Its infinitude should be understood either from the absence of arising and passing away or by way of attention to the infinite. For of this, no end in arising or end in passing away is discerned, because it is not a phenomenon with an intrinsic nature. A phenomenon with an intrinsic nature, by arising where it was not and perishing after it has been, is defined by arising and passing away; the other is not. And when the meditator attends to this, they do not grasp its limit, which is called a boundary; rather, by grasping only the seclusion from form, they direct their attention in the mode of boundless pervasion. Therefore, it should be understood as infinite either due to the absence of arising and passing away or by way of attention. And while one should say 'anantākāsa,' it is called 'ākāsānanta' by way of post-position of the word 'ananta.' 'Ākāsānanta' itself becomes 'ākāsānañca' by making the 't' following the conjunct into a 'c.' That same thing is a 'base' (āyatana) because it is an object for the jhāna with its associated states and because it is a foundation, like a divine abode. Thus, it is the 'base of infinite space' (ākāsānañcāyatana). The perception that has attained absorption therein is the 'perception of the base of infinite space.' The consciousness associated with that is 'associated with the perception of the base of infinite space.' Alternatively, the base of infinite space is the base (āyatana) for this perception with its associated states, thus 'ākāsānañcāyatanā.' That is the perception itself. The jhāna is associated with it, thus 'associated with the perception of the base of infinite space'.

Viññāṇa…pe… sahagatanti yadetaṃ paṭhamāruppaviññāṇaṃ, taṃsabhāvadhammattā uppādādiantavantampi ārammaṇakaraṇavasena anantākāse pharaṇato attānaṃ ārabbha antassa aggahaṇavasena pavattamanasikārato vā anantaṃ viññāṇanti viññāṇānantaṃ, “viññāṇānañca”nti vattabbe viññāṇañca-saddo tadatthe nirūḷho ā-kāra na-kāralopoti vā katvā “viññāṇañca”micceva vuttaṃ. Evañca katvā vakkhati –

Consciousness... and so on... associated: That which is the first formless consciousness, although it has an end such as arising, etc., due to being a phenomenon with its own intrinsic nature, is called 'infinite consciousness' (viññāṇānanta) because it pervades infinite space by way of making it an object, or because of the attention that proceeds by way of not grasping an end with respect to itself. And while 'viññāṇānañca' should be said, the word 'viññāṇañca' is used instead, either because the word 'viññāṇañca' is established in that meaning, or by making a deletion of the letters 'ā' and 'na'. And having done so, it will be said:

“Viññāṇānantamiccevaṃ, vattabbaṃ panidaṃ siyā”ti.

"'Infinite consciousness'—thus, indeed, should this be stated."

Atha vā dutiyāruppaviññāṇena añcitabbaṃ ārammaṇavasena pāpuṇitabbanti viññāṇañcaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

Alternatively, it is 'viññāṇañca' because it is to be honored and reached as an object by the second formless consciousness. The rest is the same as the preceding.

Ākiñcaññā…pe… sahagatanti nāssa paṭhamāruppaviññāṇassa kiñcananti akiñcanaṃ, antamaso bhaṅgamattampi avasiṭṭhaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sati hi bhaṅgamattepi tassa sakiñcanatā [V 1.0187] siyā. Akiñcanassa bhāvo ākiñcaññaṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanaviññāṇābhāvassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Nothingness... and so on... associated with it: there is nothing of the first formless consciousness, thus it is 'nothingness.' It is said that not even the slightest remnant remains. For if even the slightest remnant remained, it would possess something. The state of having nothing is 'nothingness'—this is a designation for the absence of the consciousness of the base of infinite space. The rest is as previously explained.

Nevasaññā…pe… sahagatanti heṭṭhimajhānesu viya oḷārikāya saññāya abhāvato nevassa saññā atthīti nevasaññaṃ, sukhumāya ca saññāya atthitāya nāssa saññā natthīti [M 1.0232] nāsaññaṃ, nevasaññañca taṃ nāsaññañceti nevasaññānāsaññaṃ, catutthāruppajjhānaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “nevasaññanāsañña”nti vattabbaṃ? Saccametaṃ. Vacanasobhanatthaṃ pana dīghaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Atha vā nevassa saññā nāsaññāti evaṃ ekajjhaṃ bahubbīhisamāsavasena “nevasaññānāsañña”nti vuttaṃ. Nevasaññānāsaññañca taṃ āyatanañca manāyatanadhammāyatanapariyāpannattāti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ, tena sampayuttaṃ saññāsahagataṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ. Atha vā saññāyeva paṭusaññākiccakaraṇe asamatthatāya nevasaññā, uṇhodake tejodhātu viya saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattiyā nāsaññāti nevasaññānāsaññā, sā eva sesadhammānaṃ nissayapaccayatāya, adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena dhammāyatanapariyāpannatāya eva vā āyatananti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanabhūtāya saññāya sahagatanti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ.

Neither perception...nor non-perception—associated with it: as in the lower jhānas, due to the absence of gross perception, it is not that it has perception, thus 'neither perception'; and due to the presence of subtle perception, it is not that it lacks perception, thus 'nor non-perception'; it is both neither perception and nor non-perception, thus 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception'—this is the fourth formless jhāna. If so, should it be called 'nevasaññanāsañña'? This is true. However, for the sake of elegant expression, it is stated with a long vowel. Alternatively, 'neither is its perception nor is it non-perception'—thus, as a single bahubbīhi compound, it is called 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' And that neither-perception-nor-non-perception, being included in the mind-base and the mental-phenomena-base, is also a base, thus 'the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' Associated with that, it is 'associated with the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.'
