Alternatively, perception itself, being incapable of performing the function of sharp perception, is 'neither perception'; and like the heat element in warm water, due to reaching a subtle state as a residual formation, it is 'nor non-perception'—thus 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' That very perception, by being a support condition for the remaining phenomena, or by being included in the mental-phenomena-base in the sense of a foundation, is a base, thus 'the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' Associated with the perception that has become the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is 'associated with the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception'.

Yathānurūpaṃ…pe… nipphādakanti “paṭhamāruppabhūmiyā paṭhamaṃ, dutiyāruppabhūmiyā dutiya”ntiādinā attano anurūpavasena catūsu arūpabhūmīsu upapattisādhakaṃ. Tāsu pana paṭhamā vīsatisahassakappāyukā hoti, dutiyā cattālīsasahassakappāyukā, tatiyā saṭṭhisahassakappāyukā, catutthā pana caturāsītisahassakappāyukāti veditabbaṃ.

According to suitability… and so on… accomplisher: it accomplishes rebirth in the four formless planes according to their respective suitability, in the manner of 'the first in the first formless plane, the second in the second formless plane,' and so on. Among these, the first has a lifespan of twenty thousand aeons' duration, the second forty thousand aeons' duration, the third sixty thousand aeons' duration, and the fourth is to be understood as having eighty-four thousand aeons' duration.

Arūpāvacarakusalavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the wholesome of the formless sphere is completed.

Lokuttarakusalavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Supramundane Wholesome

Evaṃ tividhampi lokiyakusalaṃ niddisitvā idāni lokuttarakusalaṃ niddisanto āha “itaraṃ [V 1.0188] panā”tiādi. Lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena [M 1.0233] loko, so tividho – saṅkhāraloko sattaloko bhājanalokoti. Tato idaṃ uttaratīti lokuttaraṃ. Cattāropi hi maggā upādānakkhandhasaṅkhātasaṅkhāralokato uttaranti anāsavabhāvena. Sattalokesu ca sotāpattimaggo anariyalokato uttarati, sakadāgāmimaggo sotāpannalokato, anāgāmimaggo sakadāgāmilokato, arahattamaggo anāgāmilokato uttarati. Bhājanalokesu pana paṭhamamaggo apāyalokato uttarati, sakadāgāmimaggo kāmalokekadesato, anāgāmimaggo sakalakāmalokato, arahattamaggo rūpārūpalokato uttarati. Iti catubbidhampi maggacittaṃ tividhalokato uttaratīti lokuttaraṃ, kucchitasalanādito pana kusalaṃ, cintanādito cittañcāti lokuttarakusalacittaṃ. Phalaṃ pana lokato uttiṇṇattā lokuttaraṃ, ubhayampi vā saha nibbānena upādānakkhandhasaṅkhātalokato uttaraṃ visiṭṭhataranti lokuttaraṃ. Yathāha “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ dhammānaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90).

Having thus explained the threefold mundane wholesome, now, explaining the supramundane wholesome, he says, "but the other" and so on. The world (loka) is so-called in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating. It is threefold: the world of formations, the world of beings, and the receptacle world. That which transcends this is called the supramundane. Indeed, the four paths transcend the world of formations, which consists of the aggregates of clinging, by being of a taintless nature. Among the worlds of beings, the path of stream-entry transcends the world of non-noble beings; the path of the once-returner transcends the world of stream-enterers; the path of the non-returner transcends the world of once-returners; and the path of arahantship transcends the world of non-returners. In the receptacle worlds, the first path transcends the world of the woeful realms; the path of the once-returner transcends a part of the sensual world; the path of the non-returner transcends the entire sensual world; and the path of arahantship transcends the worlds of form and formlessness. Thus, the fourfold path consciousness transcends the threefold world and is therefore called supramundane. Moreover, it is wholesome (kusala) because it shakes off what is contemptible, and it is consciousness (citta) because it thinks; hence, supramundane wholesome consciousness. The fruition, too, is called supramundane because it has transcended the world. Alternatively, both the path and fruition, together with Nibbāna, are called supramundane because they are superior, surpassing the world of formations consisting of the aggregates of clinging. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, as far as phenomena are conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the foremost among them" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.34; Itivuttaka 90).

Niyatāniyatavatthukabhedatoti sotāpattimaggassa paratoghosapaccayena vinā anuppajjanato arūpabhave sambhavo natthīti taṃ niyatavatthukaṃ, itaraṃ pana sattavidhampi paratoghosaṃ vināpi vipassanābaleneva nipphajjanato tatthāpi sambhavatīti aniyatavatthukaṃ.

Regarding the distinction between fixed and unfixed bases: the path of stream-entry has a fixed basis because it cannot arise without the condition of a voice from another; therefore, its occurrence in the formless existence is not possible. The other seven kinds, however, can arise even there solely through the power of insight, even without a voice from another; therefore, they have an unfixed basis.

Tīhi…pe… tividhanti lokuttaravimokkhānaṃ dvārabhāvato vimokkhamukhasaṅkhātāhi suññatānupassanādīhi tīhi vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāhi pattabbato idaṃ lokuttarakusalaṃ tividhaṃ suññataṃ animittaṃ appaṇihitanti. Katame pana [M 1.0234] te lokuttaravimokkhāti? Nava lokuttaradhammā. Yathāha “cattāro ca ariyamaggā cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni nibbānañca, ayaṃ anāsavo vimokkho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.213). Imāni hi saṃkilesadhammehi suṭṭhu vimuttattā vimokkhā nāma. Tāni pana paccekaṃ suññato vimokkho, animitto vimokkho, appaṇihito vimokkhoti tividhāni. Yathāha “tayome, bhikkhave, vimokkhā – suññato vimokkho, animitto vimokkho, appaṇihito vimokkho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.209). Idha pana kusalādhikārattā catumaggasaṅkhātāyeva lokuttaradhammā adhippetā.

By the three... and so on... threefold: this supramundane wholesome is threefold—emptiness, signless, and desireless—because it is to be attained by the three insights leading to emergence, namely, the contemplations of emptiness, signlessness, and desirelessness, which are designated the entrances to liberation as they are the gateway to the supramundane liberations. But what are those supramundane liberations? The nine supramundane states. As it is said: "The four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—this is taintless liberation" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.213). These are called liberations because they are thoroughly freed from defiling states. These, in turn, are individually threefold: the liberation of emptiness, the liberation of signlessness, and the liberation of desirelessness. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these three liberations—the liberation of emptiness, the liberation of signlessness, and the liberation of desirelessness" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.209). Here, however, on account of the topic being the wholesome, only the supramundane states designated as the four paths are intended.

Suññatādināmalābho ca nesaṃ āgamanato, saguṇato, ārammaṇato ca veditabbo. Tathā hi [V 1.0189] āgacchati maggo, phalañca etenāti āgamanaṃ. Tañhi duvidhaṃ maggāgamanaṃ, phalāgamanañca. Tesu vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā maggāgamanaṃ, ariyamaggo phalāgamanaṃ. Tattha maggassa āgataṭṭhāne maggāgamanaṃ gahetabbaṃ, phalassa āgataṭṭhāne phalāgamanaṃ. Idha pana maggassa āgatattā maggāgamanaṃ gahitanti. Tato āgamanato. Saguṇatoti sabhāvato. Ārammaṇatoti ārammaṇadhammato.

The acquisition of the names emptiness, etc., for them is to be understood from their mode of arrival, their intrinsic nature, and their object. For the path comes, and the fruit comes through this—this is 'arrival.' That arrival is twofold: the arrival of the path and the arrival of the fruit. Among these, insight leading to emergence is the arrival of the path, and the noble path is the arrival of the fruit. In that regard, the 'arrival of the path' is to be taken where the path has arrived, and the 'arrival of the fruit' where the fruit has arrived. In this case, the arrival of the path is taken because the path has arrived. Therefore, it is from the mode of arrival. 'By its intrinsic nature' means by its own nature. 'By its object' means by way of the object-phenomenon.

Yo hi sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ anattalakkhaṇapaṭivedhavasappavattāya anattānupassanāya vasena maggaṃ paṭilabhati, tassa sā anupassanā asuññattakarānaṃ attābhinivesapaccayānaṃ diṭṭhekaṭṭhakilesānaṃ vikkhambhitabhāvena tebhūmakadhammānaṃ attasuññatāya yāthāvato gahaṇato suññatānupassanā nāma hoti. Tāya pana paṭiladdhamaggo suññatāya āgatattā suññato nāma. Tenāha “anattato manasikaronto suññatavimokkhena vimuccatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.227).

One who attains the path by means of the contemplation of non-self, which operates by way of penetrating the characteristic of non-self in all formations—for that person, that contemplation is called the contemplation of emptiness because, by suppressing the defilements rooted in views, which are the cause of adherence to self and which make for non-emptiness, it correctly grasps, as it actually is, the emptiness of self in the phenomena of the three realms. Moreover, the path attained through this is called 'emptiness' because it has come about through emptiness. Therefore it is said: "By attending to non-self, one is liberated through the liberation of emptiness" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.227).

Yo [M 1.0235] pana sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ aniccalakkhaṇapaṭivedhavasappavattāya aniccānupassanāya maggaṃ paṭilabhati, tassa sā anupassanā niccanimittādigāhakarānaṃ kilesānaṃ vikkhambhitattā dhuvabhāvūpaṭṭhānasaṅkhātaniccanimittādino aggahaṇato animittānupassanā nāma. Tāya pana laddhamaggo animittāya āgatattā animitto nāma. Tenāha “aniccato manasikaronto animittavimokkhena vimuccatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.227).

One who attains the path by means of the insight into impermanence, which operates by way of penetrating the characteristic of impermanence in all formations—for that person, that insight is called the signless contemplation because, due to the suppression of defilements that grasp at the sign of permanence, etc., it does not apprehend the sign of permanence, etc., which is designated as the appearance of a stable nature. Moreover, the path attained through that signless contemplation is called 'signless' because it has come about through the signless. Hence it is said: "By attending to impermanence, one is liberated through the signless liberation" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.227).

Yo pana sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ dukkhalakkhaṇapaṭivedhavasappavattāya dukkhānupassanāya vasena maggaṃ paṭilabhati, tassa sā anupassanā taṇhāpaṇidhānassa vikkhambhanena paṇidhivirahitattā appaṇihitānupassanā nāma. Tāya pana laddhamaggo appaṇihitāya āgatattā appaṇihito nāma. Tenāha “dukkhato manasikaronto appaṇihitavimokkhena vimuccatī”ti. Ayaṃ tāvassa āgamanavasena nāmalābho.

One who attains the path through the contemplation of suffering, which operates by way of penetrating the characteristic of suffering in all conditioned phenomena—that contemplation is called the contemplation of the undirected because it is free from aspiration by suppressing the aspiration of craving. Moreover, the path attained through this is called the undirected because it is reached through the undirected. Hence it is said, "By attending to suffering, one is liberated through the undirected liberation." This, for now, is the designation it receives based on its mode of arrival.

Attano pana rāgādīhi suññatattā, niccanimittādivirahitattā, taṇhāpaṇidhiabhāvato ca saguṇato, rāgādisuññasseva, niccanimittādivirahitassa, paṇidhivippamuttassa ca nibbānassa ārammaṇakaraṇato ārammaṇato ca suññatādivimokkho nāma hotīti evamassa saguṇārammaṇehi nāmalābho daṭṭhabbo. So ca kho suttantapariyāyeneva, no abhidhammapariyāyena. Suttantakathā hi pariyāyadesanā, itarā nippariyāyadesanā, tasmā saguṇārammaṇato nāmassa sabbasādhāraṇabhāvena [V 1.0190] avavatthānakarattā pariyāyabhāvato suttantapariyāyeneva lābho, āgamanato pana abhidhammapariyāyenapi vavatthānakarabhāvena nippariyāyattā. Teneva hi ācariyena “tīhi vimokkhamukhehi pattabbato tividha”nti vimokkhamukhameva dhuraṃ katvā vuttaṃ, na “suññatādināmato tividha”nti. Animittanāmaṃ panettha [M 1.0236] āgamanatopi suttantapariyāyeneva labbhati abhidhamme maggaṃ pati animittanāmassa anuddhatattā. Anuddhaṭattaṃ pana na anuddharitabbatāmattena, atha kho nippariyāyato tassa magge alabbhanato. Kiñcāpi hi ayaṃ vipassanā niccanimittaṃ ugghāṭentī pavattati, saṅkhāranimittassa pana anissajjanato na nippariyāyato animittanāmaṃ labhati. Yaṃ panetaṃ sutte –

Moreover, because of its own emptiness of lust and so forth, its being devoid of signs of permanence and the like, and its freedom from craving and aspiration, it is called the liberation of emptiness, etc., since it takes as its object Nibbāna that is empty of lust and so forth, devoid of signs of permanence, and released from aspiration. Thus, its designation should be understood in terms of its own qualities and its object. This designation, however, is according to the Sutta method, not the Abhidhamma method. For the Sutta teachings are expounded with an indirect meaning, while the other (Abhidhamma) is expounded with a direct meaning. Therefore, the acquisition of the name from the perspective of its qualities and object is only by the Sutta method, because it has an indirect meaning, being common to all and not establishing a specific distinction. But from the perspective of its mode of arrival, it has a direct meaning, establishing a distinction even by the Abhidhamma method. Thus, the Teacher said, 'It is threefold because it is attainable through the three gateways to liberation,' making the gateways to liberation the primary focus—not 'threefold due to the names of emptiness, etc.' Here, the name 'signless' is obtained even from the perspective of its mode of arrival only by the Sutta method, because in the Abhidhamma, the name 'signless' is not brought up with respect to the path. The fact that it is not brought up, however, is not merely that it should not be brought up; rather, it is because that name cannot be obtained in a direct sense in relation to the path. For although this insight occurs by dismantling the sign of permanence, because it does not relinquish the sign of formations, it does not obtain the name 'signless' in a direct sense. But as it is said in the Sutta—

“Animittañca bhāvehi, mānānusayamujjaha;

Tato mānābhisamayā, upasanto carissasī”ti. (su. ni. 344) –

"Develop the signless, abandon the underlying tendency to conceit; then, with the full understanding of conceit, you will fare on in peace."

Maggassa animittabhāvavacanaṃ, taṃ yathāvuttapariyāyavasena labbhamānaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Abhidhamme pana yā sayampi nippariyāyato animittanāmaṃ na labhati, sā kathaṃ maggassa taṃ dadeyyāti maggassa animittanāmaṃ na uddhaṭaṃ. Yadi evaṃ suññatanāmenapi idaṃ samānaṃ. Anattānupassanāpi hi kiñcāpi puggalasuññataṃ gaṇhāti, dhammasuññataṃ pana na gaṇhātīti sayaṃ nippariyāyena suññatānupassanā nāma na hotīti suññatanāmampi maggassa na dadeyya. Atha puggalasuññatāggahaṇamattena sayaṃ suññatānupassanā hutvā maggassa taṃ dadeyya, aniccānupassanāpi saṅkhāranimittassa gahaṇepi niccanimittādiugghāṭanato sayaṃ animittānupassanā hutvā maggassa animittanāmaṃ dadeyyāti? Na idamevaṃ, niccādinimittugghāṭanena animittabhāvassa nippariyāyena magge alabbhanato niccādinimittugghāṭanassapi pariyāyabhāvato. Nanu idampi sabbattha samānaṃ. Suññataappaṇihitabhāvopi hi nippariyāyena amagge na labbhati puggalasuññataggahaṇassa, paṇidhisosanassa ca ujukaṃ maggeneva nipphajjanato, tasmā suññatānupassanāpi appaṇihitānupassanāpi pariyāyeneva taṃ taṃ nāmaṃ labhantīti maggassa nippariyāyato nāmaṃ na dentīti? Na, tato [M 1.0237] laddhaariyamaggassa nippariyāyato sampayuttadhammavaseneva suññataappaṇihitanāmasambhavato. Kathaṃ? Ṭhapetvā buddhuppādaṃ sarabhaṅgasatthārādikālepi dubbijānīyabhāvena sukhumassa anattalakkhaṇassa paññāya eva gocarabhāvato anattānupassanāya anupassanato [V 1.0191] maggakkhaṇe paññindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “anattato manasikaroto paññindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hotī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.221).

The statement that the path is signless is made by taking what is obtained by way of the aforementioned indirect method. However, in the Abhidhamma, if something does not itself obtain the name 'signless' in a direct sense, how could it then give that name to the path? Therefore, the name 'signless' is not brought up for the path. If so, this is also the same for the name 'emptiness.' For although the contemplation of non-self grasps the emptiness of a person, it does not grasp the emptiness of phenomena. Thus, it is not itself called the contemplation of emptiness in a direct sense, and so it would not give the name 'emptiness' to the path. But if, by merely grasping the emptiness of a person, it becomes the contemplation of emptiness itself and thereby gives that name to the path, then would not the contemplation of impermanence, even when grasping the sign of formations, by dismantling the signs of permanence, etc., become the contemplation of the signless itself and thereby give the name 'signless' to the path? This is not so, because the state of signlessness is not obtained on the path in a direct sense by the dismantling of signs like permanence, and the dismantling of such signs is itself of an indirect nature. Is not this also the same in all cases? For the states of emptiness and desirelessness are not obtained in a direct sense apart from the path, since the grasping of the emptiness of a person and the drying up of aspiration are accomplished directly only by the path itself. Therefore, would not the contemplation of emptiness and the contemplation of desirelessness obtain those names only in an indirect sense and thus not give those names to the path in a direct sense? No, because for the noble path obtained from that, the names 'emptiness' and 'desirelessness' are possible in a direct sense precisely by virtue of its associated states. How so? Except during the appearance of a Buddha, even in the times of teachers like Sarabhaṅga, because the subtle characteristic of non-self is hard to understand, it is the object of wisdom alone. Therefore, for one contemplating by means of the contemplation of non-self, at the moment of the path, the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant. As it is said: "When one attends to non-self, the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant."

Tañca pana sayaṃ attābhinivesasamugghāṭanato, ariyamaggapariyāpannattā ca nippariyāyatova suññatanāmaṃ labhati. Dukkhānupassanāya samādhivipaccanīkassa paṇidhisaṅkhātarāgassa sosanato tassā vasena anupassantassa maggakkhaṇe samādhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “dukkhato manasikaroto samādhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hotī”ti. Tañca pana sayaṃ paṇidhisosanato, ariyamaggapariyāpannattā ca nippariyāyatova appaṇihitanāmaṃ labhati. Sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ pana aniccabhāvaṃ āgamanato sutvā pacchā sayaṃ paccakkhato passato “aniccameva vata so bhagavā ‘anicca’nti āhā”ti bhagavati saddhābāhullapaṭilābhato aniccānupassanāya manasikaroto maggakkhaṇe saddhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “aniccato manasikaroto saddhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hotī”ti. Taṃ pana sayaṃ saṅkhāranimittato vuṭṭhahantampi ariyamaggapariyāpannaṃ na hotīti nippariyāyato animittanāmaṃ na labhati, tasmā yathā kāyakammādhikaṃ cittaṃ “kāyakamma”nti vuccati, evaṃ suññatasaṅkhātapaññindriyādhimatto maggo suññatanāmaṃ labhati, appaṇihitasaṅkhātasamādhindriyādhimatto appaṇihitanāmaṃ, saddhindriyādhimatto pana saddhāya animittanāmālābhato sayampi taṃ na labhati. Yadi sampayuttadhammavasena suññatādināmālābho, atha kathaṃ “āgamanato”ti [M 1.0238] vuttaṃ? Saccaṃ, āgamanato adhimattassa pana indriyassa vasena laddhanāmampi āgamanatova laddhaṃ hoti.

And that faculty of wisdom, because it uproots self-adherence by itself and is included in the noble path, unconditionally obtains the name 'emptiness.' Through the contemplation of suffering, by drying up craving—which is called 'aspiration' and is the opponent of concentration—the faculty of concentration becomes predominant at the moment of the path for one who contemplates in this way. As it is said: 'When one attends to suffering, the faculty of concentration becomes predominant.' And that faculty of concentration, because it dries up aspiration by itself and is included in the noble path, unconditionally obtains the name 'desireless.' However, having first heard from the textual tradition about the impermanence of all formations, and afterwards seeing it directly for oneself, thinking, 'Indeed, the Blessed One said “impermanent”!', due to obtaining an abundance of faith in the Blessed One, when one attends by way of the contemplation of impermanence, at the moment of the path, the faculty of faith becomes predominant. As it is said: 'When one attends to impermanence, the faculty of faith becomes predominant.' That faculty of faith, however, even though it emerges from the sign of formations, is not included in the noble path in such a way as to be called 'signless', and thus it does not unconditionally obtain the name 'signless.' Therefore, just as a mind where bodily action predominates is called 'bodily action,' so too the path where the faculty of wisdom, designated as emptiness, predominates obtains the name 'emptiness'; the path where the faculty of concentration, designated as desireless, predominates obtains the name 'desireless.' But the path where the faculty of faith predominates does not itself obtain that name, because faith does not obtain the name 'signless.' If the names 'emptiness,' etc., are obtained by virtue of associated factors, then why was it said that they are 'from the mode of arrival'? True, for a name obtained by virtue of a faculty that has become predominant through a mode of arrival is also obtained from that mode of arrival.

Atha vā abhidhammapariyāyenapi suññatabhāvo nāma puggalasuññatāyevāti puggalasuññataggāhitāya anattānupassanāya suññatanāmaṃ nippariyāyatova labbhati. Paṇidhi nāma rāgādikā evāti rāgādisositāya dukkhānupassanāya appaṇihitanāmampi nippariyāyatova labbhati.

Or else, even by the Abhidhamma method, the state of emptiness is simply the emptiness of a person; thus, the contemplation of non-self, which grasps the emptiness of a person, unconditionally obtains the name 'emptiness.' Aspiration is simply craving and the like; thus, the contemplation of suffering, which dries up craving and the like, unconditionally obtains the name 'desireless.'

Nimittanti pana ṭhapetvā suttantapariyāyaṃ abhidhammapariyāyena saṅkhāranimittaṃ hotīti saṅkhāranimittaggāhitāya aniccānupassanāya animittanāmaṃ nippariyāyato na labbhati, tasmā nippariyāyato suññataappaṇihitanāmikānaṃ anattadukkhānupassanānaṃ vasena paṭiladdhamaggo āgamanato suññataappaṇihitanāmaṃ labhati, animittanāmaṃ pana pariyāyatova labhati. Tena vuttaṃ [V 1.0192] – “animittanāmaṃ panettha āgamanatopi suttantapariyāyeneva labbhati abhidhamme maggaṃ pati animittanāmassa anuddhaṭattā”ti. Iti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vimokkhānaṃ pavesanadvārabhāvato suññatānupassanādināmikā anattānupassanādikā tisso anukkamena balavabhāvaṃ patvā vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanābhūtā tīṇi vimokkhamukhānīti veditabbāni. Vuttañhetaṃ –

However, as for 'sign,' setting aside the Suttanta method, by way of the Abhidhamma method, it is the sign of formations. Therefore, the contemplation of impermanence, which grasps the sign of formations, does not unconditionally obtain the name 'signless.' Therefore, the path obtained by way of the contemplations of non-self and suffering, which are unconditionally named 'emptiness' and 'desireless,' obtains the names 'emptiness' and 'desireless' by way of its approach. But the name 'signless' is obtained only provisionally. Hence it is said: 'Here, the name "signless" is obtained only through the Suttanta method, even from the standpoint of attainment, because in the Abhidhamma, the name "signless" is not directly applied to the path.' Thus, because they serve as doors of entry to these three liberations, the three contemplations—those named 'emptiness-contemplation' and so on, and those beginning with 'non-self-contemplation' and so on—having successively attained strength and become insight leading to emergence, should be understood as the three gateways to liberation. This is indeed said—

“Tīṇi kho panimāni vimokkhamukhāni lokaniyyānāya saṃvattanti, sabbasaṅkhāre paricchedaparivaṭumato samanupassanatāya animittāya ca dhātuyā cittasampakkhandanatāya, sabbasaṅkhāresu manosamuttejanatāya appaṇihitāya ca dhātuyā cittasampakkhandanatāya, sabbadhamme parato samanupassanatāya suññatāya ca dhātuyā [M 1.0239] cittasampakkhandanatāya, imāni tīṇi vimokkhamukhāni lokaniyyānāya saṃvattantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.219).

"These three gateways to liberation conduce to deliverance from the world: by attending to all conditioned things as delimited and bounded, and by the mind leaping into the signless element; by stirring the mind regarding all conditioned things, and by the mind leaping into the desireless element; and by attending to all phenomena as other, and by the mind leaping into the empty element. These three gateways to liberation conduce to deliverance from the world."

Ettha hi paricchedaparivaṭumatoti udayabbayavasena paricchedato ceva parivaṭumato ca. Aniccānupassanā hi “udayato pubbe saṅkhārā natthī”ti paricchinditvā tesaṃ gatiṃ samannesamānā vayato paraṃ na gacchanti, ettheva antaradhāyantīti parivaṭumato pariyantato samanupassati. Samanupassanatāyāti sammadeva anupassanatāya saṃvattantīti sambandho. Manosamuttejanatāyāti cittasaṃvejanatāya. Dukkhānupassanena hi saṅkhāresu cittaṃ saṃvijjati. Parato samanupassanatāyāti “nāhaṃ, na mama”nti evaṃ anattato samanupassanatāya. Iti imāni tīṇi padāni aniccānupassanādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vasena vuttānīti veditabbāni. Teneva ca tadanantare pañhāvissajjane –

Here, 'delimited and bounded' means delimited and bounded by way of rise and fall. For the contemplation of impermanence, having delimited with 'before the rise, formations did not exist,' and examining their course, it sees them as bounded by limits, in that they do not proceed beyond the fall but vanish right there. By 'attending to' (samanupassanatāya) is meant that it conduces to right attention. By 'stirring the mind' (manosamuttejanatāya) is meant by arousing mental agitation. For through the contemplation of suffering, the mind is agitated regarding formations. By 'attending to as other' (parato samanupassanatāya) is meant attending to as non-self, in the manner of 'not I, not mine.' Thus, these three phrases should be understood as spoken in relation to the three contemplations beginning with impermanence. And for that very reason, immediately following, in the answer to the question—

“Aniccato manasikaroto khayato saṅkhārā upaṭṭhahanti, dukkhato manasikaroto bhayato saṅkhārā upaṭṭhahanti, anattato manasikaroto suññato saṅkhārā upaṭṭhahantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.219) –

"When one attends to formations as impermanent, they appear as vanishing. When one attends to formations as suffering, they appear as fearful. When one attends to formations as not-self, they appear as empty."

Vuttaṃ. Nanu cettha abhidhammāvatārassa bhāsamānattā abhidhammapariyāyeneva vimokkhamukhāni ca vavatthapetuṃ yuttanti? Saccaṃ, aniccānupassanāyapi pana maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hotīti pakāsanatthaṃ suttantapariyāyenapi [V 1.0193] ekaṃ vavatthānaṃ kataṃ, tathā vuṭṭhito pana maggo abhidhammapariyāyena suddhikapaṭipadāyameva saṅgayhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

It has been said. Now, since the Abhidhammāvatāra is being explained here, is it not proper to determine the gateways to liberation only by the Abhidhamma method? True. However, to show that the arising of the path also occurs through the contemplation of impermanence, one determination has been made by the Suttanta method as well. But the path that has arisen in that way should be seen as included in the path of purification only by the Abhidhamma method.

Catumaggayogabhedatoti sotāpattiādīhi catūhi ariyamaggehi sampayogappabhedato. Ariyamaggānaṃ pana sammādiṭṭhādiaṭṭhaṅgasabhāvattā, tesañca sabbalokuttare atthitāya [M 1.0240] bhaṅgavasena abhedepi indriyānaṃ apāṭavapāṭavataratamabhāvena sacchikiriyāvisesato kilesānaṃ pahānabhedo hotīti taṃvasena catubbidhatā daṭṭhabbā. Tenevāha “sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchā”tiādi. Sati vijjamāne pañcakkhandhasaṅkhāte kāye diṭṭhi sakkāyadiṭṭhi, sayaṃ vā tattha sati diṭṭhi sakkāyadiṭṭhi, pañcasu khandhesu attattaniyābhinivesavasena pavattāya micchādiṭṭhiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sā pana ekekasmiṃ khandhe catudhā abhinivesanavasena vīsatividhā hoti. Tathā hi koci rūpaṃ attato samanupassati “yaṃ rūpaṃ, so attā, yo attā, taṃ rūpaṃ, yathā dīpassa vaṇṇoyeva acci, acciyeva vaṇṇo”ti. Rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ samanupassati, chāyāvantaṃ viya rukkhaṃ. Attani vā rūpaṃ, pupphe viya gandhaṃ. Rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ, samugge viya maṇi. Evaṃ vedanādīsupi “vedanaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādinā yojetabbaṃ. Tattha yo pañcavidho abyatirittaattābhiniveso, sā ucchedadiṭṭhi. Yo pana pannarasavidho byatirittaattābhiniveso, sā sassatadiṭṭhīti veditabbaṃ.

By the distinction of connection with the four paths: it is through the distinction of connection with the four noble paths, such as stream-entry. Moreover, since the noble paths have the nature of the eight factors beginning with right view, and since they exist in all supramundane states, even though there is no distinction in terms of their composition, a distinction in the abandonment of defilements arises due to the varying degrees of dullness or sharpness of the faculties and the special nature of the realization. Thus, their fourfold nature should be understood in that way. Therefore, he said: 'identity view, doubt,' and so on. A view regarding the existing body, which is designated as the five aggregates, is identity view. Or, a view of self regarding that which exists is identity view. This is a designation for the wrong view that arises through adherence to 'self' and 'what belongs to self' with regard to the five aggregates. This view, by adhering to each aggregate in four ways, becomes twentyfold. For instance, someone regards form as self: 'What is form, that is self; what is self, that is form,' just as the flame is the color of the lamp, and the color is the flame. Or, one regards the self as possessing form, like a tree possessing shade. Or, one regards form as in the self, like fragrance in a flower. Or, one regards the self as in form, like a gem in a box. Similarly, it should be applied to feeling and so on: 'One regards feeling as self,' and so forth. Herein, the fivefold adherence to an inseparable self is the annihilation view. The fifteenfold adherence to a separable self is to be understood as the eternalism view.

Sabhāvaṃ vicinanto tāya kicchati kilamatīti vicikicchā, tikicchituṃ dukkaratāya vā vigatā cikicchā ñāṇapatikāro imissāti vicikicchā. Sā pana –

One who examines the nature becomes distressed and wearied by it—that is doubt (vicikicchā). Or, because it is difficult to cure (tikicchituṃ), it is that from which remedy (cikicchā) by knowledge is absent (vigatā)—that is doubt. It is as follows:

“Satthari kaṅkhati vicikicchati, dhamme, saṅghe, sikkhāya, pubbante, aparante, pubbantāparante, idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu kaṅkhati vicikicchatī”ti (dha. sa. 1008 thokaṃ. visadisaṃ) –

"He doubts, he is perplexed about the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, the past, the future, both the past and the future, and about phenomena that are dependently arisen through specific conditionality."

Evaṃ buddhādīsu kaṅkhāvasena aṭṭhavatthukā,

Thus, it has eight bases by way of doubt regarding the Buddha and so on.

“Ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhānaṃ, na nu kho ahosiṃ, kiṃ nu kho ahosiṃ, kathaṃ nu kho ahosiṃ[M 1.0241], kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhānaṃ, bhavissāmi nu kho ahamanāgatamaddhānaṃ[V 1.0194], na nu kho bhavissāmi, kiṃ nu kho bhavissāmi, kathaṃ nu kho bhavissāmi, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ bhavissāmi nu kho ahamanāgatamaddhānaṃ, etarahi vā pana paccuppannamaddhānaṃ ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī hoti, ahaṃ nu khosmi, no nu khosmi, kiṃ nu khosmi, kathaṃ nu khosmi, ayaṃ nu kho satto kuto āgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) –

"Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past? Will I be in the future? Will I not be in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I become in the future? Or now, in the present, he is inwardly perplexed: Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? This being—where has it come from? Where will it go?"

Evaṃ pubbantādayo ārabbha pavattivasena soḷasavatthukā ca niddiṭṭhā.

Thus, it is also indicated as having sixteen bases by way of occurring with reference to the past and so on.

Tattha satthari kaṅkhanto tassa rūpakāyadhammakāyānaṃ vijjamānataṃ, avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati, dhamme kaṅkhanto tassa svākkhātadvākkhātabhāve kaṅkhati, saṅghe kaṅkhanto tassa suppaṭipannavippaṭipannatādibhāve kaṅkhati, sikkhāya kaṅkhanto tassā supaññattaduppaññattabhāvaṃ kaṅkhati, pubbante kaṅkhanto sassatākāraṃ, adhiccasamuppattiākārañca nissāya atīte attano vijjamānataṃ, avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati, aparante kaṅkhanto sassatākāraṃ, ucchedākārañca nissāya anāgate attano uppattiṃ, anuppattiñca kaṅkhati, pubbantāparante kaṅkhanto paccuppanne attano atthibhāvaṃ, natthibhāvañca kaṅkhati. Paccuppanno hi addhā pubbabhāgāparabhāgakoṭṭhāsavantatāya “pubbantāparanto”ti vuccati, yuttaṃ pana taṃ ārabbha kaṅkhājanananti? Yuttaṃ, ayuttanti kā ettha cintā. Ummattako viya hi bālaputhujjano. Tasmā so yaṃ kiñci kaṅkhatiyeva. Teneva ca soḷasavatthukavicikicchāniddese “etarahi vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ācariyā pana “pubbantāparantoti atītānāgate ekajjhaṃ gahetvā tadubhayamārabbha [M 1.0242] kaṅkhanto pubbantāparante kaṅkhatī”tipi vadanti. Idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu kaṅkhanto pana avijjādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ, saṅkhārādīnañca paccayuppannānaṃ hetuhetusamuppannabhāvassa sabbhāvāsabbhāvaṃ kaṅkhatīti evaṃ tāva aṭṭhavatthukakaṅkhāya pavatti veditabbā.

Here, one who doubts the Teacher doubts the existence or non-existence of his physical body and Dhamma body. One who doubts the Dhamma doubts whether it is well-proclaimed or ill-proclaimed. One who doubts the Saṅgha doubts whether it is practicing rightly or wrongly, and so on. One who doubts the training doubts whether it is well-enunciated or poorly enunciated. One who doubts the past, relying on the notion of permanence or the notion of chance origination, doubts whether one's self existed or did not exist in the past. One who doubts the future, relying on the notion of permanence or the notion of annihilation, doubts whether one's self will arise or not arise in the future. One who doubts both past and future doubts the existence or non-existence of one's self in the present. For the present is called "both past and future" because it possesses portions connected to the earlier and later phases. But is it appropriate for doubt to arise concerning this? It is appropriate—what need is there for deliberation here? Truly, the ignorant ordinary person is like a madman. Therefore, he doubts just about anything. Thus, in the exposition of the sixteen bases of doubt, it is stated, 'or now, however,' and so on. But some teachers also say: 'Doubting past and future means taking the past and future together and doubting concerning both.' Furthermore, one who doubts the phenomena of specific conditionality and dependent origination doubts the reality or unreality of the status of ignorance and so on as causes, and of formations and so on as causally arisen. Thus, the occurrence of doubt based on eight grounds should be understood in this way.

Soḷasavatthukā pana “ahosiṃ nu kho…pe… na nu kho ahosi”nti kaṅkhanto vuttanayeneva atīte attano vijjamānāvijjamānataṃ kaṅkhati. Kiṃ nu kho ahosinti jātiliṅgupapattiyo nissāya “khattiyo nu kho ahosiṃ, brāhmaṇādīsu gahaṭṭhādīsu devādīsu aññataro nu kho”ti kaṅkhati. Kathaṃ nu khoti saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya “dīgho nu kho ahosiṃ, rassaodātakāḷādīnañca aññataro”ti kaṅkhati. Issaranimmānādīni nissāya “kena [V 1.0195] nu kho pakārena ahosi”nti nibbattanākārato kaṅkhatīti vadanti. Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosinti jātiādīni nissāya “khattiyo hutvā nu kho brāhmaṇo ahosiṃ…pe… devo hutvā nu kho manusso ahosi”nti attano aparāparaṃ pavattiṃ kaṅkhati. Bhavissāmi nu kho, na nu khoti heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva anāgate attano vijjamānāvijjamānataṃ kaṅkhati. “Kiṃ nu kho bhavissāmī”tiādi vuttanayameva. Ahaṃ nu khosmi, na nu khosmīti idāni attano atthibhāvaṃ, natthibhāvañca kaṅkhati. Tattha kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Kiṃ nu khosmīti khattiyādikova samāno attano khattiyādibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Kathaṃ nu khosmīti “abbhantare jīvo nāma atthī”ti gahetvā tassa dīghādibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Paccuppannaṃ pana attano sarīrasaṇṭhānaṃ ajānanto nāma natthi. Kuto āgato, kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatīti attabhāvassa āgatagataṭṭhānāni kaṅkhatīti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding the sixteen bases of doubt: 'Was I or was I not?'—one doubts in the manner described about whether one existed or not in the past. 'What was I?'—one doubts based on birth, gender, and rebirth, thinking, 'Was I a noble, or one among brahmins, householders, gods, or others?' 'How was I?'—one doubts based on form and appearance, thinking, 'Was I tall, short, fair, dark, or something else?' Regarding divine creation and other causes, some say one doubts about the manner of arising, considering 'By what means was I?' 'Having been what, what did I become?'—one doubts based on birth and other factors, thinking, 'Having been a noble, did I become a brahmin?... Having been a god, did I become a human?'—thus doubting one's successive states of existence. 'Will I be or will I not be?'—one doubts in the manner described earlier about whether one will exist or not in the future. 'What will I be?' and so on, is in the same manner as stated. 'Am I or am I not?'—one doubts about one's present existence or non-existence. The reason for this has already been stated. 'What am I?'—even while being a noble or the like, one doubts whether one is a noble or something else. The same applies to the rest. 'How am I?'—grasping the idea, 'There is an inner life-principle,' one doubts whether it is tall, short, etc. However, there is no one who does not know the present form of their own body. 'Where have I come from? Where will I go?'—one should understand that one doubts about the place of origin and the future destination of one's being.

Sīlañca [M 1.0243] vatañca sīlabbataṃ, tattha gosīlādiasuddhimaggo samādānavasena sīlaṃ, avītikkamavasena vataṃ. Ubhayathāpi vā sīlaṃ, tapokammabhāvena gahitattā vataṃ. Gavādipakatibhāvato attano vā gavādibhāvādhiṭṭhānaṃ sīlaṃ, “gacchanto bhakkheti, tiṭṭhanto muttetī”tiādinā gavādikiriyāya karaṇaṃ vataṃ. Taṃtaṃakiccasammasato vā nivatti sīlaṃ, taṃsamādānavato vesabhojanakiccacaraṇādivisesapaṭipatti vataṃ. Sabhāvaṃ atikkamma parato āmasanaṃ gahaṇanti parāmāso, sīlabbatassa parāmāso sīlabbataparāmāso. Ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlena suddhi, vatena suddhi, sīlabbatena suddhīti evaṃ asuddhimagge “suddhimaggo”ti pavattassa micchābhinivesassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sakkāyadiṭṭhi ca vicikicchā ca sīlabbataparāmāso cāti sakkāya…pe… parāmāso, teyeva kammavipākesu, vaṭṭasmiṃ vā satte saṃyojenti bandhantīti saṃyojanāni, tesaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhiādīhi tadaṅgavasena pahīnānaṃ anuppattidhammatāpādanena accantasamucchedappahānaṃ karotīti sakkā…pe…ppahānakaraṃ.

Morality and vows (sīla and vata) are sīlabbata. Here, in the impure path of cow-morality and so on, morality is by way of undertaking, and vows are by way of non-transgression. Or, in both ways it is morality; and it is a vow because it is undertaken as an ascetic practice. Morality is the resolve to adopt cow-like behavior due to the nature of cows and so on, or the determination to become like cows and so on, while a vow is the actual performance of such actions, like 'while walking, it grazes; while standing, it urinates,' by engaging in cow-like actions. Or, morality is the cessation from various improper actions through consideration, while a vow is the special practice undertaken by one who undertakes that morality, such as avoiding certain foods or engaging in certain duties. Transgressing one's own nature and grasping something from another—that is clinging (parāmāsa). The clinging to precepts and practices is sīlabbataparāmāsa. Outside of this teaching, for ascetics and brahmins, 'purity through morality, purity through vows, purity through precepts and practices'—this is a designation for the wrong adherence that occurs when what is actually an impure path is called the 'pure path.' Identity view, doubt, and clinging to precepts and practices—these are the fetters because they bind beings to karmic results or to the round of rebirth. It effects the complete eradication of these—which are abandoned in part through the purification of view and so on—by bringing them to a state of non-arising.

Nibbānaṃ pati savanato sandanato soto vuccati ariyo aṭṭhaṅgikamaggo, tassa ādito pajjanaṃ sotāpatti, nibbānaṃ maggati, nibbānatthikehi maggīyati, kilese mārento gacchatīti vā maggo, sotāpatti eva maggo sotāpattimaggo. Atha vā sotaṃ ādito pajjati adhigacchatīti sotāpatti, paṭhamo ariyapuggalo, tassa maggo sotāpattimaggo, sammādiṭṭhiādīni aṭṭhaṅgāni, tena sampayuttaṃ cittaṃ sotāpattimaggacittaṃ.

The noble eightfold path is called the stream (sota) because it flows and streams towards Nibbāna. Its initial entering is stream-entry (sotāpatti). It seeks Nibbāna, it is sought by those desiring Nibbāna, or it is called the path (magga) because it goes while destroying the defilements. Thus, stream-entry itself is the path—the stream-entry path. Alternatively, one who first enters and attains the stream is a stream-attainer (sotāpatti), the first noble person; their path is the stream-entry path—the eight factors beginning with right view. The mind associated with this is the stream-entry path consciousness.

Rajjati [V 1.0196] abhisajjatīti rāgo, so idha pañcakāmavisayā, kāmabhavavisayā ca taṇhā. Dussatīti doso, dasavidhaāghātavatthupadaṭṭhāno [M 1.0244] byāpādo. Muyhatīti moho, dukkhādīsu aṭṭhasu aññāṇaṃ. Etesaṃ kilesānaṃ tanuttaṃ tanubhāvaṃ karotīti rāga…pe… tanuttakaraṃ. Tattha dvīhi kāraṇehi tanuttaṃ abhiṇhānuppattito, pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya cāti. Sakadāgāmissa hi vaṭṭānusārimahājanassa viya kilesā abhiṇhaṃ na uppajjanti, kadāci viraḷākārā hutvā uppajjanti, tathā uppajjantāpi maddantā chādentā andhakāraṃ karontā nuppajjanti. Dvīhi pana maggehi pahīnattā mandamandā tanukatanukā uppajjanti. Keci pana sakadāgāmissa kilesā cirena uppajjantāpi bahalāva uppajjanti. Tathā hissa puttadhītaro dissantīti vadanti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ, vatthupaṭisevanena vināpi gabbhaggahaṇasabbhāvato, tasmā vuttanayeneva dvīhi kāraṇehi nesaṃ tanubhāvo veditabbo. Kasmā panettha mohassa tanubhāvo vutto, nanu tatiyamaggavajjhānameva iminā tanuttakaraṇaṃ vattabbaṃ, itarathā heṭṭhā tīhipi maggehi uparimaggavajjhakilesānaṃ bahalābahalāvatthāya pahīyamānattā idha sabbesameva uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanānaṃ tanubhāvo vattabbo, teneva ca pāḷiyampi “kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ tanubhāvāya dutiyāya bhūmiyā pattiyā”ti vuttanti. Saccametaṃ, sutte pana uparimaggavajjhānaṃ tanubhāvapariyāyaṃ gahetvā “rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā sakadāgāmī hotī”ti hetuttayatanubhāvassa āgatattā idhāpi tadanulomena vuttaṃ. “Kāmarāgabyāpādāna”micceva vā pāṭho. Tathā hi ettheva upari dutiyamaggañāṇaniddese “byāpādakāmarāgānaṃ, tanubhāvaṃ tu sādhaya”nti (abhidha. 1353) vuttaṃ. Paṭisandhivasena sakideva imaṃ manussalokaṃ āgacchatīti sakadāgāmī, tassa maggo sakadāgāmimaggo. Kiñcāpi hi maggaṭṭhassa paṭisandhivasena āgamanāsambhavato [M 1.0245] phalaṭṭhoyeva sakadāgāmī nāma hoti, tassa pana āgamanabhūto maggo maggantarāvacchedanatthaṃ tadāyattabhāvūpanayanena sakadāgāmimaggoti vuccati, taṃsampayuttaṃ cittaṃ sakadāgāmimaggacittaṃ.

It colors, it attaches—thus, lust. Here, it is craving for the five cords of sensual pleasure and for sensual existence. It corrupts, it harms—thus, hatred; ill will, whose proximate cause is the ten bases of resentment. It deludes—thus, delusion; ignorance regarding the eight things beginning with suffering. It makes these defilements attenuated, makes them thin—thus, the attenuator of lust, hatred, and delusion. Herein, attenuation is due to two reasons: their infrequent arising and the weakness of their obsession. For in the case of a once-returner, defilements do not arise frequently, unlike those of ordinary worldlings; they arise only occasionally and in a scattered manner. Even when they do arise, they do not arise crushing, concealing, and darkening. But having been abandoned by the two paths, they arise very weakly, very thinly. Some, however, say that even if the defilements of a once-returner arise after a long time, they arise strongly. For instance, they say that his sons and daughters are seen. But that is not a valid reason, for conception is possible even without the enjoyment of an object. Therefore, their attenuation should be understood in the same way by the two reasons stated. But why is the attenuation of delusion mentioned here? Should not this attenuation be spoken of only in terms of what is to be abandoned by the third path? Otherwise, since the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths are abandoned in a grosser or subtler state by the three lower paths, the attenuation of all the higher fetters should be mentioned here. And indeed, in the Pāli text it is said, 'For the attenuation of sensual lust and ill will, one attains the second ground.' This is true. But in the Suttas, taking the attenuation of defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths as a manner of speaking, it is said, 'By the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, one becomes a once-returner.' Therefore, here too, it is mentioned in accordance with that. Alternatively, the reading might be 'of sensual lust and ill will' only. For indeed, further on in the exposition of the second path-knowledge, it is said, 'But achieve the attenuation of ill will and sensual lust.' He comes back to this human world only once by way of rebirth—thus, a once-returner. His path is the once-returner’s path. Although for one at the path stage, coming back by way of rebirth is not possible, and it is only the fruition-attainer who is called a once-returner, nevertheless, the path that is the basis for that coming back is called the once-returner’s path for the purpose of distinguishing it from other paths, by bringing about its dependence on that result. The consciousness associated with that path is the once-returner’s path-consciousness.

Pañcasu kāmaguṇesu, kāmabhave ca rāgo kāmarāgo. Byāpajjati tena cittanti byāpādo. Paṭisandhivasena imaṃ kāmadhātuṃ na āgacchatīti anāgāmī. Rūpabhave chandarāgo rūparāgo. Arūpabhave chandarāgo arūparāgo. Māno idha arahattādhigamaṃ paṭicca uṇṇatimattaṃ. Uddhaccampi “ko me bhāro kilesasamucchedane”ti evamākārappavattaṃ cittassa avūpasamamattaṃ. Avijjāpi asukhe sukhasaññāvipallāso. Ārakattā kilesehi, micchāpaṭipannehi vā, rāgādiarīnaṃ, saṃsāracakkassa arānañca hatattā, paccayādīnaṃ arahattā, rahopi pāpākaraṇena pāpakaraṇe [V 1.0197] rahassa abhāvā, rahitabbato jahitabbato “rahā”ti laddhanāmānaṃ vā pāpadhammānaṃ abhāvato, sādhūhi arahitabbato apariccajitabbato, rahasaṅkhātassa vā gamanassa saṃsāre abhāvato arahā, aṭṭhamo ariyapuggalo, tassa bhāvo arahattaṃ, aggaphalassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tañhi “arahā”ti abhidhānassa, buddhiyā ca pavattinibandhanattā arahato bhāvoti katvā “arahatta”nti vuccati, tassa āgamanabhūto maggo arahattamaggo, taṃsampayuttaṃ cittaṃ arahattamaggacittaṃ.

Lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure and for sensual existence is sensual lust. The mind is afflicted by it—thus, ill will. He does not come back to this sense-sphere realm by way of rebirth—thus, a non-returner. Desire-lust for the form realm is form-lust. Desire-lust for the formless realm is formless-lust. Conceit here is merely a slight elation in relation to the attainment of arahantship. Restlessness is merely the mind’s lack of calm, occurring in the form of the thought, 'What burden is there for me in the destruction of defilements?' Ignorance is the perversion of perception, perceiving happiness in what is not happiness. Because he is far from defilements, or from those who practice wrongly; because the enemies (lust, etc.) and the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra are destroyed; because the requisites, etc., are worthy of him; because there is no secret in doing evil, due to not doing evil; because evil qualities, called 'secret' (rahā) due to being abandoned or shunned, are absent; or because he is worthy of being honored and not to be relinquished by the virtuous; or because the going called 'secret' is absent in saṃsāra—thus, an arahant. He is the eighth noble person. His state is arahantship. This is a designation for the highest fruit. For it is called 'arahantship' because it is the state of an arahant, being the basis for the designation 'arahant' and for the arising of understanding. The path that is the basis for its attainment is the path of arahantship. The consciousness associated with that path is the path-consciousness of arahantship.

Jhānaṅgayogabhedatoti rūpāvacaraṃ viya pañcahi jhānaṅgehi sampayogabhedato. Kathaṃ panassa bhedoti? Ettha tāva aṭṭhakathāvādo, tayo ca theravādāti cattāro vādā honti. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tāva “saṅkhārupekkhābhāvaṃ patvā vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāmaggassa jhānaṅgaṃ niyametī”ti vuttaṃ. Tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero pana “maggāsannavipassanāya [M 1.0246] padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ pādakajjhānaṃ niyametī”ti āha. Moravāpivāsimahādattatthero “vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyamenti. Yañhi jhānaṃ sammasitvā vuṭṭhāti, taṃsadisova hotī”ti āha. Tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero pana “puggalajjhāsayo niyameti, ‘aho vata pañcaṅgikaṃ, caturaṅgikaṃ vā maggaṃ pāpuṇeyya’ntiādinā yathā yathāssa ajjhāsayo hoti, tathā tathā maggo hotī”ti āha.

The differentiation based on the connection with jhāna factors means that it is differentiated by its association with the five jhāna factors, like the form-sphere jhāna. But how is its differentiation made? Here, there is first the commentary’s view, and then three views of the elders, making four views in total. For instance, in the commentary it is said: 'Having reached the state of equanimity towards formations, it determines the jhāna factors for the insight path leading to emergence.' The elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, however, said: 'It determines the preliminary jhāna, which serves as the basis for insight approaching the path.' The elder Mahādatta of Moravāpi said: 'The aggregates that serve as the object of insight determine it. For whatever jhāna one emerges from after contemplating, the path is similar to that.' The elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, however, said: 'The individual’s inclination determines it. Depending on how one’s inclination is—thinking, "Oh, may I attain the five-factored path or the four-factored path," and so on—the path arises accordingly.'

Yasmā pana aṭṭhakathāvādo pamāṇaṃ, tayo ca therā paṇḍitā byattā, tasmā cattāropi vādā aññamaññaṃ appaṭibāhanavasena evaṃ veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Kāmāvacaradhamme tāva sammasitvā sukkhavipassakassa uppannamaggopi samāpattilābhino jhānaṃ pādakaṃ akatvā uppāditamaggopi vipassanāniyāmena paṭhamajjhānikāva honti. Sace pana kiñci jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā uppādito hoti, tassa vasena aṅgapariṇāmo hotīti taṃtaṃjhānasadiso hoti. Yasmā panettha kāmāvacarakkhandhe ārabbha pavattā vipassanā kāmāvacaradhammesu ca mahaggatadhammesu viya bhāvanāvisesato jhānaṅgaviseso natthi, tasmā “vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyamentī”ti evaṃ pavatto dutiyattheravādo imaṃ vādaṃ na pavisati. Jhānadhamme sammasitvā uppāditamaggo sace pādakajjhānaṃ natthi, sammasitajjhānaniyāmena taṃtaṃjhāniko hoti. Sace paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhāya dutiyādijhāne sammasitvā uppādito, puggalajjhāsayaniyāmena dvīsu aññatarajjhānasadiso hoti. Sace pana puggalassa tathāvidho ajjhāsayo natthi, tadā kathanti? Ettha tāva keci “nānāvajjanavīthiyameva nivattamānapādakajjhānato ekāvajjanavīthiyaṃ [V 1.0198] gotrabhubhāvaṃ patvā nivattamānāya vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhāyeva [M 1.0247] balavanto, tasmā sammasitakkhandhaniyāmena taṃsadiso maggo hotī”ti vadanti. Evañca sati “pādakajjhānaniyāmena hotī”ti evaṃ pavatto paṭhamattheravādo pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya kāmāvacarakkhandhe sammasitvā uppāditamaggameva sandhāya tiṭṭhatīti.

However, since the commentary’s view is authoritative, and the three elders are learned and skilled, all four views should be understood in such a way that they do not contradict each other. How so? First, even the path that arises for a dry-insight practitioner after contemplating sense-sphere phenomena, or the path that arises for an attainments-gainer without making jhāna the basis, is still of the first jhāna type by the rule of insight. If, however, it arises after making some jhāna the basis, then by virtue of that, there is a transformation of factors, and it becomes similar to that particular jhāna. Now, because for insight occurring with regard to the sense-sphere aggregates, there is no distinction in jhāna factors based on a distinction in development, as there is between sense-sphere and exalted phenomena, therefore the second elder’s view, which states, 'The aggregates that serve as the object of insight determine it,' does not apply to this view. If the path arises after contemplating jhāna phenomena, and there is no preliminary jhāna, then it is of that particular jhāna type by the rule of the contemplated jhāna. If, having emerged from the first jhāna, one contemplates the second or higher jhānas and the path arises, then by the rule of the individual’s inclination, it is similar to one of the two jhānas. But if the individual has no such inclination, what then? Here, some say: 'For the insight that, turning back from the preliminary jhāna in a multiple-adverting cognitive process, reaches the change-of-lineage moment in a single-adverting cognitive process, the aggregates that serve as its object are stronger. Therefore, the path is similar to that by the rule of the contemplated aggregates.' And if this is so, then the first elder’s view, which states, 'It is by the rule of the preliminary jhāna,' refers specifically to the path that arises after emerging from the preliminary jhāna and contemplating the sense-sphere aggregates.

Apare pana “pādakajjhānaṃ maggassa mūlakāraṇavasena paccayo hoti āsannakāraṇavasenapi, sammasitakkhandhā pana mūlakāraṇavaseneva paccayā honti, tasmā sammasitakkhandhato pādakajjhānameva balavataranti pādakajjhānasadiso maggo hotī”ti vadanti. Evaṃ sante pana “sammasitakkhandhaniyāmenā”ti evaṃ pavatto dutiyattheravādo samāpattiṃ pādakaṃ akatvā kevalaṃ jhānadhammeyeva sammasitvā uppāditamaggameva sandhāya tiṭṭhati. Yasmā pana heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimajjhānato uparūparijhānaṃ balappattaṃ hoti, tasmā heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimajjhānato vuṭṭhāya uparūparijhānadhamme vipassato uppannamaggo pādakajjhānaṃ anapekkhitvā sammasitajjhānavasena taṃtaṃjhāniko hoti. Uparūparijhānato pana vuṭṭhāya heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimajjhānadhamme sammasitvā uppāditamaggo sammasitajjhānaṃ anapekkhitvā pādakajjhānasadiso hotīti idamettha sārataraṃ. Evañhi sati dvinnampi therānaṃ vādā nippadesavisayā samaphalā honti.

Others, however, say: 'The base jhāna is a condition for the path both as a root cause and as a proximate cause, whereas the contemplated aggregates are a condition only as a root cause. Therefore, since the base jhāna is more powerful than the contemplated aggregates, the path is similar to the base jhāna.' If this is so, then the second elder’s view, which states, 'by the principle of the contemplated aggregates,' refers specifically to the path that arises solely from contemplating jhāna phenomena without making an attainment the basis. However, because each higher jhāna is stronger than the lower ones, when one emerges from a lower jhāna and practices insight into the phenomena of the higher jhānas, the path that arises, without depending on the base jhāna, is of that particular jhāna type by virtue of the contemplated jhāna. But when one emerges from a higher jhāna and contemplates the phenomena of the lower jhānas, the path that arises, without depending on the contemplated jhāna, is similar to the base jhāna. This is the more essential point here. Thus, when this is so, the views of both elders, being exhaustive in their respective domains, have equal results.

Tatiyattheravādo cettha pādakajjhānaṃ, sammasitajjhānaṃ vā vinā ajjhāsayamatteneva na ijjhati. Tīsupi vādesu ṭhapetvā sesajhānaṅgapariṇāmaṃ vedanāpariṇāmo vipassanāniyāmeneva hoti. Tayopi theravādā vipassanāniyāmena vinā na hontīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nanu ca vedanāpi jhānaṅgameva, tasmā tāyapi pādakajjhānaniyāmeneva bhavitabbanti? Taṃ na, vedanāyapi pādakajjhānaniyāmena pariṇāme sati vipassanāniyāmaṃ anapekkhitvā pādakajjhānaniyāmeneva maggakkhaṇe [M 1.0248] sesajhānaṅgāni pariṇāmaṭṭhāneyeva vedanāyapi pariṇāmo bhaveyya, tathā pana ahutvā ekāvajjanavīthiyā āditova pariṇāmanato maggavuṭṭhānavīthiyā āsannatarappavattāya vipassanāya vasena vedanāniyāmo hoti.

And here, in the third elder's view, it does not succeed merely by intention, without either the base jhāna or the contemplated jhāna. In all three views, apart from the transformation of the remaining jhāna factors, the transformation of feeling occurs solely by the principle of insight. It should be understood that the views of the three elders do not exist without the principle of insight. But is not feeling also a jhāna factor? Therefore, should it not also be determined by the principle of the base jhāna? That is not so. For if feeling also transformed by the principle of the base jhāna, then—without depending on the principle of insight—at the moment of the path, feeling would also transform in the same way as the remaining jhāna factors. But since this is not so, the principle for feeling is determined by insight, which occurs closer to the cognitive process of emergence from the path, because it transforms from the very beginning of the single adverting process.

Atha vā pādakajjhānasammasitajjhānānaṃ sambhave tesu anuppannā vedanā vipassanāya na hotīti pādakajjhānasammasitajjhānaniyāmena pariṇamatītipi na sakkā vattuṃ. Ettha siyā – yattha tāva pādakajjhānaṃ atthi, tattha taṃ niyameti. Yattha pana tikacatukkapādakajjhānaṃ natthi, tasmiṃ [V 1.0199] arūpabhave kiṃ niyametīti? Tatthāpi pādakajjhānameva niyameti. Yo hi bhikkhu aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī paṭhamajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā sotāpattimaggaphalāni nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā arūpabhave nibbatto paṭhamajjhānikāya sotāpattiphalasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā upari tīṇi maggaphalāni nibbatteti, tassa tāni paṭhamajjhānikāneva honti. Dutiyajjhānikādīsupi eseva nayo. Arūpepi hi lokuttaraṃ tikacatukkajjhānaṃ uppajjatīti evamettha ekekassa lokuttarakusalassa jhānaṅgayogabhedo veditabboti.

Alternatively, it cannot be said that when base jhānas and contemplated jhānas are possible, a feeling not arisen in them is not due to insight, nor that it transforms by the principle of the base and contemplated jhānas. Here, it might be asked: wherever a base jhāna exists, it establishes the principle. But where there is no base jhāna of the three- or four-factored type, such as in the formless existence, what establishes the principle? Even there, it is the base jhāna itself that establishes the principle. For a monk who has attained the eight attainments, having made the first jhāna the base, generates the path and fruit of stream-entry, and then, without having lost the jhāna, dies and is reborn in the formless existence. Having emerged from the fruition attainment of stream-entry associated with the first jhāna, he establishes insight and generates the three higher paths and fruits; for him, those are associated with the first jhāna. The same method applies to the second jhāna and so on. For even in the formless realm, the supramundane three- or four-factored jhāna arises. Thus, in this way, the distinction in the combination of jhāna factors for each supramundane wholesome state should be understood.

Maggā…pe… nipphādetīti tebhūmakakusalaṃ viya paṭisandhippavattīsu avipaccavantampi attano attano anurūpassa phalassa nipphādanena taṃtaṃphalappatte sotāpanno sakadāgāmī anāgāmī arahāti sāmaññato cattāro ariyapuggale abhinipphādetīti. Visesato pana sattakkhattuparamatādike anekepi sotāpannādayo nipphādeti.

The path… produces. Just as wholesome states pertaining to the three planes, though not ripening at that time, produce their own suitable fruits in rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, so too, by producing the respective fruits to be attained, it brings forth, in general, the four noble individuals: the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arahant. Specifically, however, it produces many kinds of stream-enterers and others, such as those with a maximum of seven rebirths.

Lokuttarakusalavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the supramundane wholesome is concluded.

Catubhūmakakusalavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Wholesome Pertaining to the Four Planes

28. Evaṃ [M 1.0249] catubhūmakakusalacittaṃ sarūpato niddisitvā idāni taṃ nigamento āha “kāme aṭṭhevā”tiādi. Tattha kāmeti kāmabhave. Tathā “rūpe”tiādīsu.

28. Having thus explained the wholesome consciousness pertaining to the four planes according to its nature, now, by way of conclusion, he says: 'In the sense sphere, there are eight,' and so on. Herein, 'in the sense sphere' means in the sense-sphere existence. Likewise for 'in the form sphere,' and so on.

29. Kusalākusalāpagatenāti kusalākusalakammato apagatena. Aggamaggassa hi uppannakālato paṭṭhāya arahato sabbāni kusalākusalakammāni pahīnāni nāma honti paccayavekallena paṭisandhidāne asamatthabhāvato. Yato ca ariyamaggañāṇaṃ “kammakkhayakara”nti vuccati. Atha vā ahetuapaccayavisujjhanassa abhāvato kilesasamucchedakena maggakusalena akusalehi apagatena. Kusale kusalenāti kucchitānaṃ salanādīhi [V 1.0200] kusalasaṅkhātāya paṭipattiyaṃ desanuppādanādīsu chekena. Munināti ubhayalokamunanakena aggaphalañāṇena, sabbaññutaññāṇena vā samannāgatattā muninā. Tenāha –

29. 'Gone beyond the wholesome and unwholesome' means gone beyond wholesome and unwholesome kamma. For from the moment the highest path arises, all wholesome and unwholesome kammas of an Arahant are said to be abandoned, being incapable of giving rebirth-linking due to a deficiency of conditions. Wherefore, the noble path-knowledge is called 'the destroyer of kamma.' Alternatively, it means gone beyond the unwholesome by means of the path-wholesome that eradicates the defilements, because there is no purification of conditions without a root. By 'skillful in the wholesome' is meant being adept in the practice called 'wholesome'—from shaking off the contemptible, etc.—and being skillful in teaching, generating, and so on. By 'sage' is meant one who is a sage because of being endowed with the knowledge that understands both worlds, that is, the knowledge of the highest fruit or the knowledge of omniscience. Hence it is said:

“Yo munāti ubho loke, muni tena pavuccatī”ti.

He who understands both worlds, is therefore called a sage.

Vasināti chaḷabhiññatāya paramena cittavasibhāvena samannāgatattā, jhānādīsu pañcavidhavasisabbhāvato ca vasibhūtena vasibhāvūpagatindriyena.

By 'masterful one' is meant one who is so called because he is endowed with supreme mastery of mind through the six higher knowledges, and because he possesses the fivefold mastery in jhāna and other states; one whose faculties have attained the state of mastery.

Catubhūmakakusalavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the wholesome pertaining to the four planes is concluded.

Akusalavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Unwholesome

Ettāvatā ca yaṃ “kusalākusalābyākatajātibhedato tividha”nti ettha vuttaṃ kusalaṃ, taṃ sarūpato niddisitvā idāni tadanantaruddiṭṭhaṃ akusalaṃ niddisanto āha “akusalaṃ panā”tiādi. “Bhūmito ekavidha”nti vuttamatthaṃ niyametvā dassento āha “kāmāvacaramevā”ti. Nikāyantarikā pana rūpārūpāvacarampi akusalaṃ icchantīti tesaṃ [M 1.0250] matinisedhanatthaṃ avadhāraṇaṃ kataṃ. Mahaggatabhūmiyaṃ uppajjantampi hetaṃ tattha rūpadhātuyaṃ pavattivipākaṃ dentampi ekantena kāmāvacaramevāti. Kuto panesa niyamoti? Kāmataṇhāvisayabhāvato. Kāmataṇhāvisayatā hi kāmāvacarabhāvassa kāraṇaṃ yathā rūpārūpataṇhāvisayatā rūpārūpabhāvassa. Ekaṃsena cetaṃ evaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Itarathā byāpitalakkhaṇaṃ na siyā. Yadi hi ālambitabbadhammavasena bhūmivavatthānaṃ kareyya, evaṃ sati anārammaṇānaṃ saṅgaho na siyā. Atha vipākadānavasena, evampi avipākānaṃ saṅgaho na siyā, tasmā ālambaṇadhammavaseneva pariyāpannānaṃ sā kātabbā. Apariyāpannānaṃ pana lokato uttiṇṇatāya lokuttaratā, uttaritarābhāvato anuttaratā ca veditabbāti.

Thus far, having explained according to its nature the wholesome, which was stated here as 'threefold by way of the distinction of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate classes,' now, explaining the unwholesome which was mentioned immediately after, he says: 'But the unwholesome,' and so on. To define and show the meaning of what was said, 'onefold by plane,' he says: 'only of the sense sphere.' However, those of other schools hold that the unwholesome also exists in the form and formless spheres; to refute their view, this emphasis is made. Even if it arises in a sublime sphere, and even if it gives its resultant activity in the form element there, it is exclusively of the sense sphere. But why this principle? Because of its being an object for craving for sensual pleasures. For being an object for craving for sensual pleasures is the reason for being of the sense sphere, just as being an object for craving for form and for the formless is the reason for being of the form and formless spheres. This should be accepted unequivocally. Otherwise, the characteristic of pervasiveness would not hold. For if one were to establish the planes based on the phenomena to be taken as object, then those without an object would not be included. If based on the giving of results, then even those that are without result would not be included. Therefore, for those that are included in the round, that classification should be made based on the objective field. As for those not included, their supramundane nature should be understood from their having transcended the world, and their unsurpassed nature from there being nothing superior.

Domanassassa anīvaraṇāvatthāya abhāvena taṃsahagatacittuppādo kāmabhūmiyaṃyeva pavattatīti so [V 1.0201] niyatavatthuko, itare arūpabhūmiyampi pavattanato aniyatavatthukāti āha “niyatā…pe… duvidha”nti. Vicikicchuddhaccasahagatānaṃ mohekahetukattā, itaresampi lobhamohadosamohavasena dvihetukattā āha “ekahetukaduhetukato”ti. Ādito ekādasannaṃ akusalacittānaṃ paṭisandhijananato, uddhaccasahagatassa tadabhāvato āha “paṭisandhijanakājanakato”ti. Uddhaccasahagatañhi pavattivipākaṃ dentampi paṭisandhiṃ nākaḍḍhati. Yato vakkhati –

Because dejection does not occur in a state free from the hindrances, the arising of consciousness accompanied by dejection occurs only in the sense-sphere realm; thus, it has a fixed basis, whereas the others, since they occur even in the formless realm, have unfixed bases—hence it is said, "fixed... twofold." Because consciousness accompanied by doubt and restlessness has delusion as its single root, and the others have two roots—greed-and-delusion and hatred-and-delusion—it is said, "with one root or two roots." Since the first eleven unwholesome consciousnesses produce rebirth-linking, but the one accompanied by restlessness does not, it is said, "producing rebirth-linking or not producing it." For the consciousness accompanied by restlessness, even though it gives rise to resultant states in the course of existence, does not bring about rebirth-linking. As it will be said:

“Ekādasavidhānaṃ tu, hitvā uddhaccamānasaṃ;

Ekādasavidhā ceva, bhavanti paṭisandhiyo”ti. (abhidha. 536);

Having excluded the mind accompanied by restlessness, the rebirth-linkings are indeed of eleven kinds.

Yena pana kāraṇena taṃ paṭisandhiṃ nākaḍḍhati, taṃ paṭisandhivinicchayakathāhi imissā gāthāya vaṇṇanāpadeseyeva vakkhāma[M 1.0251]. Tīhi vedanāhīti sukhadukkhopekkhāsaṅkhātāhi tīhi vedanāhi. Yathāha – “tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā dukkhā adukkhamasukhā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.249). Yaṃ pana katthaci sutte “dvemā, bhikkhave, vedanā sukhā dukkhā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.267) vacanaṃ, taṃ kusalapakkhikaṃ upekkhaṃ sukhe, akusalapakkhikañca dukkhe pakkhipitvā pariyāyena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Suppatiṭṭhitabhāvakāraṇattā mūlamivāti mūlaṃ, lobho mūlaṃ etassāti lobhamūlaṃ. Kiñcāpi hi mohopi lobhamūlesu atthi, so pana sabbākusalasādhāraṇattā vavatthānakaro na hotīti asādhāraṇadhammavasena “lobhamūla”ntveva vuttaṃ yathā “bherisaddo yavaṅkuro”ti. Tathā “dosamūla”nti etthāpi. Mūlantaravirahato moho eva mūlaṃ imassa, nāññanti mohamūlaṃ.

The reason why it does not bring about rebirth-linking, that we shall explain in the discussion on the determination of rebirth-linking, in the section of the commentary on this verse. By 'tīhi vedanāhi' (by three feelings) is meant the three feelings known as pleasant, painful, and neutral. As it is said: "Monks, there are these three feelings. Which three? Pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.249). However, where it is said in some sutta: "Monks, there are these two feelings: pleasant and painful" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.267), this should be understood as spoken figuratively, by including wholesome-aligned equanimity under the pleasant and unwholesome-aligned equanimity under the painful. 'Mūla' (root) is so called because it is the cause of being firmly established, like a root. 'Lobhamūla' (rooted in greed) means greed is the root of this. Although delusion is also present in the greed-rooted consciousnesses, because it is common to all unwholesome states, it is not a distinguishing factor. Therefore, it is simply called "rooted in greed" based on the non-common factor, just as "the sound of a drum" is called 'drum' or "a sprout of barley" is called 'barley'. The same applies to 'dosamūla' (rooted in hatred). Due to the absence of another root, delusion alone is the root of this, and no other; thus, 'mohamūla' (rooted in delusion).

Micchāvasena dassanaṃ diṭṭhi, diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhigataṃ yathā “ākāsagataṃ thāmagata”nti. Atha vā vipariyesaggāhikāya diṭṭhiyā gatameva, na ettha gantabbavatthu tathāsabhāvanti diṭṭhigataṃ, dvāsaṭṭhiyā vā diṭṭhīsu antogadhanti diṭṭhigataṃ, tena samaṃ pakārehi yuttanti diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ.

Seeing in a wrong way is view (diṭṭhi). View itself is 'diṭṭhigata' (gone to a view), just as 'ākāsagataṃ' means gone to the sky or 'thāmagataṃ' means gone to strength. Or else, it is what is gone to by the view that grasps perversely; here there is no object to be gone to that is of such a nature—thus it is 'diṭṭhigata.' Or it is included within the sixty-two views—thus it is 'diṭṭhigata.' Conjoined with it in various ways is 'diṭṭhigatasampayutta' (associated with view).

“Yadā hī”tiādi lobhamūlacittānaṃ pavattiākāradassanaṃ. Micchādiṭṭhinti ucchedadiṭṭhiādiṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ. Tāya hi vipallattacittā tāva kodhavisayo, yāva indriyagocaroti [V 1.0202] paralokaṃ paṭikkhipitvā “natthi kāmesu ādīnavo”ti gaṇhanti. Ādi-saddena –

'When indeed,' etc., shows the mode of occurrence of consciousnesses rooted in greed. 'Wrong view' means wrong view such as annihilationism. For those whose minds are perverted by that, the object of anger extends as far as the range of the senses; having rejected the next world, they take up the idea that 'There is no danger in sense pleasures.' By the word 'etc.,'

“Esa panthovitatho devayāne,

Yena yanti puttavanto visokā;

Taṃ passanti pasavo pakkhino ca,

Tena te mātaripi mithunaṃ carantī”ti. –

This is the false path, the divine vehicle, by which the sorrowless with children go. Beasts and birds see it, and by it they engage in intercourse even with their mothers.

Ādinā [M 1.0252] nayena puttamukhadassanaṃ saggamokkhamaggoti evamādikaṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Kāme vāti ettha vā-saddo aniyamattho. Tena “brāhmaṇānaṃ suvaṇṇaharaṇameva adinnādāne sāvajjaṃ, itaraṃ anavajjaṃ, gurūnaṃ, gunnaṃ, attano jīvitassa, vivāhassa ca atthāya musāvādo anavajjo, itaro sāvajjo, guruādīnaṃ atthāya pesuññakaraṇaṃ anavajjaṃ, itaraṃ sāvajjaṃ, bhāratayuddhasītāharaṇādikathā pāpavūpasamāya hotī”ti evamādike micchāgāhe saṅgaṇhāti. Diṭṭhamaṅgalādīnīti diṭṭhasutamutamaṅgalāni. Sārato paccetīti vuḍḍhiyā pubbanimittabhāvena aggahetvā “idameva vuḍḍhikāraṇa”nti evaṃ sāravasena gaṇhāti. Sabhāvatikkhenevāti lobhassa, micchābhinivesassa vā vasena saraseneva tikhiṇena kururena. Mandenāti dandhena atikhiṇena. Tādisaṃ pana attano, parassa vā samussāhanena pavattatīti āha “samussāhitenā”ti. Parassa bhaṇḍaṃ vā haratīti vā-saddena tathāpavattanakamusāvādādīnampi saṅgaho veditabbo. Kāmānaṃ vāti anubhuyyamānānaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ. Vā-saddena parasantakassa ayathādhippetatāya yaṃ laddhaṃ, taṃ gahetabbanti gahaṇādikaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

In this way, it includes wrong views such as 'seeing one's child's face is the path to heaven or liberation,' and so forth. Here, the word 'or' (vā) in 'in sensual pleasures' (kāme vā) implies no fixed rule. Thus, it encompasses wrong graspings such as: 'For brahmins, only the taking of gold is blameworthy in taking what is not given; other cases are blameless. For the sake of teachers, cows, one's own life, or marriage, lying is blameless; otherwise, it is blameworthy. Slander for the sake of teachers and others is blameless; otherwise, it is blameworthy. Tales like the Bharata war or the abduction of Sītā are for the pacification of evil.' By 'things seen, heard, or considered auspicious' (diṭṭhamaṅgalādīni) are meant auspicious signs that are seen, heard, or thought. 'Grasping the essence' means taking it not as a preliminary sign of growth, but grasping it as the essence, thinking, 'This alone is the cause of growth.' 'With intrinsic sharpness' (sabhāvatikkheneva) means by way of greed or wrong insistence, very sharply and cruelly, by its very nature. 'Slowly' (mandena) means sluggishly, without sharpness. Such action, however, occurs through one's own or another's exertion; hence it is said, 'through exertion' (samussāhitena). The word 'or' (vā) in 'or taking another's goods' (parassa bhaṇḍaṃ vā harati) should also be understood to include similar actions like lying that arise in such a way. 'Of sensual pleasures' (kāmānaṃ vā) refers to the sensual qualities being experienced. The word 'or' (vā) implies that whatever is obtained from another's belongings, even if not as intended, should be taken—thus including taking and similar acts.

Sampayuttadhammavasena bhedābhāvato dosamūlaṃ asaṅkhārikasasaṅkhārikabhedato duvidhaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā “domanassasahagataṃ paṭighasampayutta”nti vuttaṃ? Asādhāraṇadhammehi tassa cittassa upalakkhaṇatthaṃ. Pāṇassa atīva, atikkamitvā vā pātanaṃ pāṇātipāto. Ādi-saddena adinnādānamusāvādapesuññapharusasamphappalāpabyāpāde saṅgaṇhāti. Dasaakusalakammapathesu hi kāmesumicchācāraabhijjhāmicchādiṭṭhisaṅkhātā tayova kammapathā iminā na sijjhanti. Sabhāvatikkhaṃ hutvā pavattamānaṃ cittaṃ asaṅkhārameva hoti, itaraṃ sasaṅkhāranti adhippāyenāha “tikkhamandappavattikāle”ti. Mandaṃ [M 1.0253] pana hutvā pavattamānaṃ ekaṃsena sasaṅkhāramevāti na sakkāva [V 1.0203] viññātuṃ. Yaṃ sasaṅkhārena sappayogena pavattati, taṃ mandameva hotīti katvā tathā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Due to the absence of division based on associated states, the hatred-rooted consciousness is twofold, by way of unprompted (asaṅkhārika) and prompted (sasaṅkhārika) types. If so, why is it said, 'accompanied by displeasure and associated with aversion'? It is for the purpose of characterizing that consciousness by its unique qualities. The excessive or transgressing destruction of life is 'taking life' (pāṇātipāto). The word 'ādi' (etc.) includes taking what is not given, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, and ill-will. Indeed, among the ten unwholesome paths of action, only three paths of action—namely, wrong conduct in sensual pleasures, covetousness, and wrong view—are not accomplished by this. A mind that arises with intrinsic sharpness is unprompted; the other is prompted—this is the intended meaning in saying, 'at the time of sharp or slow occurrence' (tikkhamandappavattikāle). But it is not possible to know for certain that a mind arising slowly is invariably prompted. It should be understood that what occurs with prompting and effort is necessarily slow—thus it is said.

Mohamūlaṃ cittaṃ mūlantaravirahato atimūḷhaṃ vicikicchuddhaccayogato cañcalañcāti upekkhāsahagatameva hoti, na tassa kadācipi sabhāvatikkhatā atthi. Ārammaṇe hi saṃsappanavasena, vikkhipanavasena ca pavattamānassa cittadvayassa kiṃ tādise kicce sabhāvatikkhatāya, ussāhetabbatāya vā bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā na tattha saṅkhārabhedo atthi. Nanu ca uddhaccaṃ sabbākusalasādhāraṇaṃ, kasmā pana etameva tena visesetvā vuttaṃ “uddhaccasahagata”nti. Visesato balavabhāvato. Idañhi etasmiṃ citte balavaṃ, tasmā sampayuttadhammesu padhānaṃ hutvā pavattatīti idameva tena visesitabbaṃ. Teneva hi pāḷiyaṃ sesākusalesu uddhaccaṃ yevāpanakavasena āgataṃ, idha pana sarūpatoyeva niddiṭṭhaṃ. Evaṃ asādhāraṇappadhānadhammavasena mohamūlaṃ vicikicchāsampayuttaṃ uddhaccasampayuttanti duvidhaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asanniṭṭhānaṃ saṃsayo, vikkhepo avūpasamo, bhantatāti attho. Tattha vicikicchāsahagatassa asanniṭṭhānakāle, uddhaccasahagatassa vikkhepakāle ca pavatti veditabbā.

The delusion-rooted consciousness, being utterly deluded due to the absence of other roots, and being restless due to its connection with doubt and agitation, is thus only accompanied by equanimity. It never has intrinsic sharpness. Indeed, for the two types of consciousness that operate by slipping away from the object or by distraction, what need is there for intrinsic sharpness or for being prompted in such a function? Therefore, there is no division based on prompting there. Now, agitation is common to all unwholesome states. Why then is it specifically mentioned here as 'accompanied by agitation' (uddhaccasahagata)? Because of its particularly strong presence. Indeed, in this consciousness, it is strong; therefore, it becomes primary among the associated states, and thus it alone must be specifically noted. For this reason, in the Pāli Canon, agitation is mentioned in relation to other unwholesome states in a general way, but here it is explicitly described as being of its own nature. Thus, it should be understood that the delusion-rooted consciousness is said to be twofold—associated with doubt and associated with agitation—by way of its unique predominant factors. Indecisiveness is doubt; distraction is unsettledness; this is the meaning of 'bewilderment.' In this context, the occurrence of the consciousness accompanied by doubt is to be understood as at the time of indecision, while the consciousness accompanied by agitation is at the time of distraction.

Yathānurūpanti paṭisandhijanakājanakassa, kammapathabhāvappattāpattassa ca anurūpato. Atha vā yathānurūpanti yo yassa hetu, tadanurūpato. Yebhuyyena hi lobhamūlakena khuppipāsādinirantarapetavisaye uppajjanti, dosamūlakena doso viya caṇḍajātatāya taṃsarikkhake niraye, mohamūlakena niccasammūḷhāya tiracchānayoniyaṃ, tasmā lobhādihetuanurūpato tattha tattha apāye upapattiṃ nipphādetīti āha “yathānurūpaṃ…pe… upapattiyā”ti[M 1.0254]. Akusalavipākānaṃ dukkhappadhānatāya “dukkhavisesassā”ti vuttaṃ.

'According to what is suitable' (yathānurūpaṃ) means suitable to the generating and non-generating of rebirth-linking, and to the attainment and non-attainment of the state of a path of action. Alternatively, 'according to what is suitable' means according to what is the cause for whom, suitable to that.
