For the most part, due to greed-rooted causes, beings arise in the realm of petas, constantly afflicted by hunger, thirst, and so forth; due to hatred-rooted causes, in a hell resembling that hatred on account of its fierce nature, just like hatred itself; due to delusion-rooted causes, in the animal realm, in constant delusion. Therefore, it is said that according to the cause—whether greed, etc.—it produces rebirth in various miserable states: 'according to what is suitable... up to... for rebirth' (yathānurūpaṃ...pe... upapattiyā). Because unwholesome results are predominantly suffering, it is said, 'of a particular suffering' (dukkhavisesassa).

31. Apāpena alāmakena pāpāpāpappahīnena pāpāpāpesu mānasesu yaṃ pāpamānasaṃ vuttaṃ, pāpāpāpesu puggalesu apāpena pāpāpāpappahīnena yaṃ pāpamānasaṃ vuttanti vā sambandho. Atha vā pāpāpāpesu mānasesu pāpena pāpamānasena pāpavasena pāpāpāpappahīnena yaṃ pāpamānasaṃ vuttanti yojanā. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – asammāsambuddhena tāva dhammasabhāvassa dubbijānīyattā kusalampi akusalato, akusalampi kusalato vucceyya, bhagavato pana saha vāsanāhi [V 1.0204] viddhaṃsitākusalassa kammakkhayakarañāṇena paccayavekallato viddhaṃsitakusalakammassa ca sammāsambuddhabhāvato ekanteneva akusaladesanā akusaladhammavasenevāti.

31. The connection is: 'what was called the wicked mind among wicked and non-wicked minds' [was called so] by one who is not wicked, not base, who has abandoned both the wicked and the non-wicked; or, 'what was called the wicked mind among wicked and non-wicked individuals' [was called so] by one who is not wicked, who has abandoned both the wicked and the non-wicked. Alternatively, the construction is: 'what was called the wicked mind among wicked and non-wicked minds' [was called so] by the wicked, with a wicked mind, through the power of wickedness, by one who has abandoned both the wicked and the non-wicked. Here, however, the intended meaning is this: For one who is not a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, because the nature of phenomena is difficult to discern, even the wholesome might be called unwholesome, and the unwholesome might be called wholesome. But for the Blessed One, because his unwholesome states, together with their latent tendencies, have been destroyed by the knowledge that brings about the exhaustion of kamma, and because his wholesome kamma has been destroyed due to an absence of conditions, owing to his state of Perfect Self-Enlightenment, the teaching of the unwholesome is entirely and only by way of unwholesome states.

Akusalavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the unwholesome is concluded.

Abyākatavaṇṇanā

The exposition of the indeterminate.

Aññamaññavisiṭṭhānaṃ kusalākusalānaṃ pākanti vipākaṃ, vipakkabhāvamāpannānamarūpadhammānametamadhivacanaṃ. Yathā hi loke sālibījādīnaṃ phalāni taṃsadisāni nibbattāni vipakkāni nāma honti, vipākaniruttiñca labhanti, na mūlaṅkurapattadaṇḍanaḷādīni, evaṃ kusalākusalānaṃ phalāni arūpadhammabhāvena, sārammaṇabhāvena ca taṃsadisāni vipakkabhāvamāpannānīti vipākaniruttiṃ labhanti, na pana kammābhinibbattāpi rūpadhammā kammavisadisattā. Vipākameva cittaṃ vipākacittaṃ. Karaṇamattaṃ kiriyā phaladānāsambhavato. Yena pana kāraṇena tassa phaladānaṃ na sambhavati, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Kiriyā [M 1.0255] eva cittaṃ kiriyacittaṃ. Vipākassa kāmāvacarādibhāvo kusale vuttanayena yathāsambhavaṃ veditabbo. Alobhādisampayuttahetūhi saha vattanato sahetukaṃ. Tadabhāvato ahetukaṃ. Nibbattakahetuvasena sijjhamānampi hetaṃ sampayuttahetuvaseneva “sahetukamahetuka”nti vuccati, itarathā vavatthānābhāvato.

The ripening of wholesome and unwholesome states, which are mutually distinct, is called 'result' (vipāka). This is a designation for immaterial states that have attained the state of being ripened. Just as in the world, the fruits of rice seeds and the like, which arise resembling their cause, are called 'ripened' and receive the term 'result'—but not the roots, sprouts, leaves, stalks, or reeds—so too the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome states, by being immaterial and having an object, resemble their cause and thus receive the term 'result' when they attain the state of being ripened. However, material states, even though produced by kamma, do not receive this term because they are dissimilar to kamma. Consciousness that is simply a result is 'resultant consciousness.' Mere functioning is 'functional' (kiriyā), since the giving of a result is not possible for it. The reason why the giving of a result is not possible for it has already been stated below. Consciousness that is mere functioning is 'functional consciousness.' The classification of resultant consciousness into sense-sphere, etc., should be understood according to the method explained for the wholesome, as is applicable. Because it occurs together with roots such as non-greed, it is 'with roots.' Due to the absence of these, it is 'rootless.' Although it is accomplished by way of a generating cause, it is called 'with roots' or 'rootless' only on the basis of associated roots, since otherwise there would be no distinction.

Sakakusalaṃ viyāti attano janakaṃ kāmāvacarakusalaṃ viya. Janakajanitabbasambandhavasena hi taṃ taṃ kusalaṃ tassa tassa vipākassa sakaṃ nāmaṃ hoti.

'Like one's own wholesome' (sakakusalaṃ viya) means like the sense-sphere wholesome kamma that is its own generator. For through the relationship of generator and generated, each wholesome state becomes 'its own' by name for its corresponding result.

“Sakakusalaṃ viyā”ti vuttattā pavattākāraārammaṇādito cassa taṃsadisatā āpajjeyyāti taṃnivāraṇatthamāha “yathā panā”tiādi. Chasu ārammaṇesūti parittādiatītādiajjhattādibhedesu chasu rūpādiārammaṇesu. Bhavantarapaṭisandhānato paṭisandhi. Avicchedappavattihetubhāvena bhavassa aṅganti bhavaṅgaṃ. Nibbattitabhavato parigaññatāya cutihetutāya cuti. Parittadhammapariyāpannesūti kāmāvacaradhammapariyāpannesu. Kāmāvacaradhammā hi kilesavikkhambhanādīsu [V 1.0205] asamatthabhāvena parittānubhāvatāya, oḷārikāhi vā kāmataṇhādīhi parito gahitattā “parittā”ti vuccanti. Vipākassa saṅkappetvā ārammaṇaggahaṇābhāvato kammānurūpameva pavattatīti parittakammavipāko parittārammaṇeyeva pavattitumarahati, na mahaggataappamāṇārammaṇeti vuttaṃ “parittadhammapariyāpannesū”ti. Yadi evaṃ mahaggatavipākopi mahaggatārammaṇeyeva āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, saññāyattārammaṇassa samādhippadhānassa kammassa appanāpattassa tādiseneva vipākena bhavitabbattā. Vaṇṇalakkhaṇādikañhi aggahetvā lokasaññānurodheneva gahite pathavādike parikammasaññāya samuppāditaṃ [M 1.0256] paṭibhāganimittasaṅkhātamārammaṇaṃ saññāvasaṃ saññāyattaṃ hoti, tasmā tadārammaṇassa samādhippadhānassa appanāpattassa kammassa vipākena samādhippadhānaappanāpattehi viya saññāyattārammaṇatāya nibbiseseneva bhavitabbaṃ. Parittavipāko pana mahaggataappamāṇapaññattārammaṇakammanibbattopi hoti, so parato āgamissati.

Because it is said to be 'like one's own wholesome,' to prevent the inference that it would have a similar nature in terms of mode of occurrence, object, and so on, he states: 'But as for...' etc. 'Among the six objects' (chasu ārammaṇesu) means among the six objects such as form, etc., which are divided into limited, past, internal, and so on. 'Rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi) is so called from linking to another existence. 'Life-continuum' (bhavaṅga) is so called because it is a factor (aṅga) of existence (bhava) by being a cause for its unbroken continuity. 'Death' (cuti) is so called because it is the cause of passing away, marking the end of the produced existence. 'Encompassed by limited phenomena' (parittadhammapariyāpannesu) means encompassed by sense-sphere phenomena. For sense-sphere phenomena are called 'limited' (parittā) because of their limited power, being incapable of suppressing defilements, etc., or because they are thoroughly grasped by coarse sense-desires and so on. Since a result does not grasp an object by volition but proceeds only in accordance with the kamma, the result of a limited kamma is fit to occur only with a limited object, not a sublime or immeasurable one—this is what is meant by 'encompassed by limited phenomena.' If so, does a sublime result also necessarily take only a sublime object? It does not, because the kamma that attains absorption is predominant in concentration and has a perception-dependent object, and its result must be of a similar nature. For when the earth-kasiṇa, etc., is apprehended not by grasping its characteristics such as color, but simply in accordance with worldly perception, the object known as the counterpart sign, produced by the perception of preparation, is dependent on perception and under the control of perception. Therefore, the result of a kamma that attains absorption, is predominant in concentration, and has such an object must be without any difference from it, on account of its object being perception-dependent, just like the absorption-attaining states that are predominant in concentration. But a limited result can also be produced by a kamma that has a sublime, immeasurable, or conceptual object—this will be discussed later.

Mukhanimittaṃ viyāti mukhaṃ paṭicca uppannanimittaṃ viya. Yathā hi taṃ nirīhaṃ aparaṃ mukhanimittaṃ uppādetuṃ, aññaṃ vā kiñci attano balena kātuṃ na sakkoti, evametampi vipākuppādanādīsu na ussahati. Tenāha “nirussāha”nti. Ussāhoti cettha anupacchinnāvijjātaṇhāmānānusayasmiṃ santāne vipākuppādanasamatthatāsaṅkhāto, āsevanapaccayabhāvasaṅkhāto, viññattijanakatāsaṅkhāto ca byāpāro. So vipāke natthi kammavegukkhittattā patitaṃ viya hutvā pavattamānassa tassa ekantena dubbalabhāvatoti taṃ nirussāhaṃ.

'Like the reflection of a face' (mukhanimittaṃ viya) means like a sign that arises in dependence on the face. Just as that inert thing cannot produce another reflection of a face or accomplish anything by its own power, so too this resultant consciousness is incapable of producing a result and so on. Therefore, he says 'without striving' (nirussāhaṃ). Here, 'striving' (ussāha) refers to the activity in a continuum where the latent tendencies of ignorance, craving, and conceit are not cut off, which activity is reckoned as the ability to produce a result, as the state of being a repetition condition, and as the function of generating intimation. That striving is absent in a result because, having been cast forth by the force of kamma, it proceeds as if it has fallen and is thus extremely weak. Therefore, it is 'without striving.'

Vipaccanaṭṭhānanti vipaccanavasena pavattanaṭṭhānaṃ, paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutitadārammaṇavasena catukiccānametesaṃ pavattiokāsoti attho. Tattha cutibhavaṅgānaṃ antarāḷaṃ paṭisandhikiccānaṃ ṭhānaṃ, paṭisandhiāvajjanānaṃ, tadārammaṇāvajjanānaṃ, javanāvajjanānaṃ, voṭṭhabbanāvajjanānañca antarāḷaṃ bhavaṅgakiccānaṃ ṭhānaṃ, tadārammaṇapaṭisandhīnaṃ, javanapaṭisandhīnaṃ, bhavaṅgapaṭisandhīnaṃ vā antarāḷaṃ cutikiccānaṃ ṭhānaṃ, javanabhavaṅgānaṃ antarāḷaṃ tadārammaṇakiccānaṃ ṭhānanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmā panetaṃ ṭhānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃtaṃkiccavasena pākaṭaṃ hoti, tasmā ṭhānaṃ veditabbanti ṭhānaṃ uddharitvā pākaṭakiccavaseneva taṃ pakāsetuṃ “imāni hī”tiādi [M 1.0257] vuttaṃ. Atha vā kiccampi kiccavantānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānabhāvena gayhatīti ṭhānantipi kiccameva uddhaṭanti taṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ “imāni hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'The place of ripening' (vipaccanaṭṭhāna) is the place of occurrence by way of ripening; the meaning is that it is the occasion for the occurrence of these four functions: rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death, and registration (tadārammaṇa). Herein, the interval between death and life-continuum is the place for the function of rebirth-linking. The interval between rebirth-linking and adverting, between registration and adverting, between impulsion and adverting, and between determining and adverting is the place for the function of life-continuum. The interval between registration and rebirth-linking, between impulsion and rebirth-linking, or between life-continuum and rebirth-linking is the place for the function of death. The interval between impulsion and life-continuum is to be understood as the place for the function of registration. And since this 'place' for phenomena becomes manifest through their respective functions, therefore, having taken up the term 'place' in order to explain it by way of its manifest function, it is said, 'For these...,' etc., meaning 'the place is to be understood.' Alternatively, since function (kicca) is also understood as the place of occurrence for those that possess the function, by 'place' the function itself is set forth. To show this in its own nature, it is said, 'For these...,' etc.

32. Aṇḍajajalābujayonisambhavānaṃ [V 1.0206] manussānaṃ, vinipātikāsurānañca ahetukapaṭisandhiyāpi sabbhāvato āha “duhetukatihetūna”nti. Paṭisandhiviññāṇasampayuttā dve alobhādayo hetū yesaṃ te duhetukā. Esa nayo tihetukesupi. Tattha duhetukānaṃ ñāṇavippayuttāni cattāri, tihetukānaṃ ñāṇasampayuttāni cattāri paṭisandhiyo honti, tathā bhavaṅgacutiyopi. Yena yena hi cittena paṭisandhi hoti, taṃ tadeva bhavaṅgacutivasenapi pavattati. Tadārammaṇaṃ pana avisesena daṭṭhabbaṃ duhetukānampi tihetukatadārammaṇassa icchitattā. Nanu cetaṃ asamapekkhitābhidhānaṃ ācariyeneva imassa paṭisiddhattā. Tathā hi vakkhati –

32. For humans born from eggs or from the womb, and for the asuras of the lower realms, since there is also the existence of rootless rebirth-linking, he says 'of those with two roots or three roots' (duhetukatihetūnaṃ). Those whose rebirth-linking consciousness is associated with two roots, such as non-greed, are called 'two-rooted.' The same method applies to those with three roots. Herein, for the two-rooted, there are four rebirth-linking consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge, and for the three-rooted, there are four rebirth-linking consciousnesses associated with knowledge. Likewise for the life-continuum and death consciousnesses. For by whatever consciousness rebirth-linking occurs, that very same consciousness proceeds by way of life-continuum and death. However, registration (tadārammaṇa) should be seen as undifferentiated, because even for the two-rooted, a three-rooted registration is accepted. But is this not an unconsidered statement, since the teacher himself has refuted this? For thus he will say:

“Ahetupaṭisandhissa, na tadārammaṇaṃ bhave;

Duhetukaṃ tihetuṃ vā, duhetupaṭisandhino”ti. (abhidha. 443);

"For one with rootless rebirth-linking, there is no registration. For one with two-rooted rebirth-linking, it is two-rooted or three-rooted." (Abhidha. 443)

Nayidamasamapekkhitābhidhānaṃ paṭisandhijanakakammaṃ sandhāya tattha paṭisiddhattā. Yena hi kammena yā paṭisandhi ādinnā, na taṃ tato adhikataraṃ tadārammaṇaṃ pavatte abhinipphādeti. Yaṃ pana aññampi kiñci kammaṃ tadāladdhāvakāsaṃ siyā, na taṃ tattha tato adhikatarampi vipākaṃ na nibbattetīti atthi. “Sahetukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ ahetukassa bhavaṅgassa anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.1.102) hi paṭṭhānavacanena ahetukassāpi nānākammena sugatiyaṃ sahetukatadārammaṇamanuññātaṃ. Tenāhu ācariyā –

This is not an unconsidered statement, because it is refuted there with reference to the rebirth-generating kamma. For the kamma by which a rebirth-linking is given does not produce a registration greater than itself in the course of existence. However, if some other kamma gains an opportunity there, it can produce a result even greater than that. Indeed, by the statement in the Paṭṭhāna, 'A rooted life-continuum is a condition for a rootless life-continuum by way of contiguity condition' (Paṭṭhāna 3.1.102), a rooted registration by various kammas is permitted even for a rootless being in a fortunate existence. Therefore, the teachers have said—

“Hoti aññena kammena, sahetukaṃ ahetuna”nti.

"By another kamma, a rooted result arises for a rootless being."

Yathā [M 1.0258] ca ahetukassa sahetukaṃ, evaṃ duhetukassa tihetukampi icchanti. Ācariyajotipālatthero pana “sahetuka”nti avisesena vuttattā ahetukānampi tihetukatadārammaṇaṃ icchati. Vuttañhi tena “sahetuka”nti avisesopadesena duhetukaṃ, tihetukañca gahetabbaṃ. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ahetukassāpi tihetukatadārammaṇamabhihitaṃ, yañcarahi atthasamāse ahetukānaṃ tihetukaphalāni detī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ kathaṃ? So eva pucchitabbo, yo tassa kattāti. Apare pana “mūlasandhiyā jaḷattā tassa tihetukatadālambaṇaṃ na labbhatiyevā”ti vadanti.

Just as they accept a rooted result for a rootless being, so too do they accept a three-rooted result for a two-rooted being. However, the Elder Ācariya Jotipāla, because 'rooted' is stated without distinction, also accepts a three-rooted registration for rootless beings. For it was said by him: "Since 'rooted' is taught without distinction, both the two-rooted and the three-rooted should be understood." Indeed, in the commentary it is said: "Even for a rootless being, a three-rooted registration is mentioned; and when in the summary of meaning it gives three-rooted fruits to the rootless..." How is this? He himself, its author, should be asked. But others say: "Because of the dullness of the root-connection (mūlasandhi), its three-rooted registration is not obtained at all."

33-4. Tatoti [V 1.0207] paṭisandhito paraṃ, dutiyacittato paṭṭhāya. Satipi antarantarā vīthicittuppāde tadavasāne uppajjamānassa yāvatāyukaṃ anivattanato vuttaṃ “yāvatāyuka”nti. Balavārammaṇeti atimahantavibhūtārammaṇe. Pañcadvāre hi atimahantārammaṇe manodvāre vibhūtārammaṇe tadārammaṇamuppajjati, na aññesu. Ekārammaṇappavattiyā paṭisandhādīnaṃ tiṇṇampi ekaṭṭhāne dassanatthaṃ uddese tadārammaṇassa avasānakaraṇaṃ, idha pana pavattikkamavasena cutiyā avasānakaraṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

33-4. 'From that' (tato) means after rebirth-linking, starting from the second consciousness. Although cognitive process consciousnesses arise in between, it is said 'for as long as life lasts' (yāvatāyukaṃ) because the life-continuum, arising at the end of those processes, does not cease for the entire lifespan. 'With a strong object' (balavārammaṇe) means with a very great or distinct object. For registration (tadārammaṇa) arises with a very great object in the five sense-doors, and with a distinct object in the mind-door, not in other cases. In the summary, registration is placed at the end in order to show the occurrence of the three—rebirth-linking and the others—in a single place with a single object. Here, however, it should be understood that death is placed at the end, according to the order of occurrence.

35-6. Kammadvāranti kāyavacīkammadvārassa janakavasena na pavattantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha kāyoti kāyaviññatti. Kammanti taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā, kāyena kataṃ kammaṃ kāyakammaṃ. Kiñcāpi hi kāyo kammassa catuvīsatiyā paccayesu na kenaci paccayena paccayo hoti, tathāpi taṃsamuṭṭhānassa tassa sabbhāveyeva kāyakammādivohāroti taṃ tena katanti vuccati. Kāyakammassa pavattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ dvāraṃ kāyakammadvāraṃ. Yadi evaṃ kammadvāravavatthānaṃ na siyā[M 1.0259]. Kāyadvārena hi siddhaṃ kammaṃ “kāyakamma”nti vuccati. Taṃ pana “dvāre caranti kammānī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāyakammadvāra) vacanato vacīdvārepi sijjhatīti dvārena kammavavatthānaṃ na siyā, tathā vacīkammaṃ kāyadvārepi sijjhatīti kammena dvāravavatthānampi na siyāti? Taṃ na, tabbahulavuttiyā ceva yebhuyyena vuttiyā ca vavatthitattā. Kāyakammañhi kāyadvāreyeva bahulaṃ pavattati, appaṃ vacīdvāre, tasmā kāyadvāre bahulappavattanato etassa kāyakammabhāvo siddho vanacarakādīnaṃ vanacarakādibhāvo viya. Tathā kāyakammameva yebhuyyena kāyadvāre pavattati, na itaraṃ, tasmā kāyakammassa yebhuyyena ettheva pavattito assa kāyakammadvārabhāvo siddho brāhmaṇagāmādīnaṃ brāhmaṇagāmādibhāvo viyāti nettha kammadvāravavatthāne koci vibandhoti. Vacīkammadvārepi esa pabandho yathāsambhavaṃ daṭṭhabbo.

35-6. By 'kamma-door' it is meant that they (resultant consciousnesses) do not occur in the sense of generating through the bodily and verbal kamma-doors. Here, 'body' means bodily intimation. 'Kamma' is the volition that originates it; kamma done by the body is 'bodily kamma.' Although the body is not a condition for kamma by way of any of the twenty-four conditions, nevertheless, because of the existence of that (volition) which originates from it, the designation 'bodily kamma,' etc., is used, and so it is said to be 'done by that.' The door which is the basis for the occurrence of bodily kamma is the 'bodily kamma-door.' [Objection:] Kamma accomplished through the body-door is called 'bodily kamma.' But since that kamma is also accomplished through the speech-door—as stated, 'actions proceed through doors'—is a distinction of kamma by door not impossible? And since verbal kamma is also accomplished through the body-door, is a distinction of doors by kamma not also impossible? This is not so, because the distinction is established based on predominance and frequency. Bodily kamma occurs predominantly through the body-door, and rarely through the speech-door. Therefore, its nature as bodily kamma is established because it occurs mostly through the body-door, just as the nature of forest-dwellers is established for those who dwell mostly in the forest. Similarly, it is bodily kamma that occurs for the most part through the body-door, not the other. Hence, its nature as the bodily kamma-door is established because bodily kamma primarily occurs here, just as the nature of a Brahmin village is established for a village mostly inhabited by Brahmins. Thus, there is no obstacle to this distinction of kamma-doors. This same line of reasoning should be applied to the verbal kamma-door as is appropriate.

Manokammadvāraṃ pana sayaṃ manoyeva samānaṃ attanā sahagatacetanāanabhijjhādikammānaṃ pavattidvārabhāvena manodvārasaṅkhaṃ labhatīti na taṃ cittassa uppattidvāravasena gaṇhāti. Na hi sayaṃ attatova pavattati. Yadi pana cittasampayuttā kammadvārabhāvena adhippetā, tadā tesaṃ kammadvārabhāvo manasmiṃ na upacārīyatīti sampayuttadhammānaṃ cittādhipatibhāvo citte viyāti cittaṃ “manokammadvāra”nti vuccati. Sabhāvato pana kammadvāraṃ nāma sampayuttadhammāyevāti cittaṃ tato pavattanato manokammadvāravasena pavattati. Anantarapaccayabhūtassa pana manokammadvārabhāve vattabbameva [V 1.0208] natthi. Idha pana “aviññattijanattā”ti vacanena kāyavacīkammadvāravaseneva appavattiyā sādhitattā manokammadvāraṃ na gahitameva. Na hi “aviññattijanattā”ti kāraṇaṃ manokammadvāravasenapi appavattiṃ sādheti. Atha vā “avipākasabhāvato”ti [M 1.0260] vacanena manokammadvāravasenapi appavatti sādhitā hoti. “Kammadvāra”nti ettha kammaggahanena nānakkhaṇikakammassa adhippetattā tassāpi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Iti imesu kāyavacīkammadvārasaṅkhātesu dvīsu dvāresu, manokammadvārena saha tīsu eva vā yathā kusalaṃ pavattati, na evaṃ vipāko, yathā ca kusalaṃ kāyavacīmanokammassa āyūhanavasena dānādipuññakiriyavatthuvasena pavattati, na evamayaṃ. Ayaṃ pana neva kāyavacīkammadvāresu pavattati viññattisamuṭṭhāpakattābhāvato, na kammavasena, manokammadvāravasenāpi ca pavattati vipākuppādanabhāvābhāvato, na puññakiriyavasena pavattati dānādivasena appavattanatoti dassetuṃ “kammadvārañca…pe… no samā”ti vuttaṃ. Evanti dānādivasena.

As for the mental kamma-door, the mind itself, by serving as the door for the occurrence of kammas such as non-covetousness—that is, volitions associated with itself—obtains the designation 'mind-door.' It is not, however, taken as a door for the arising of consciousness, for consciousness does not proceed from itself. But if the factors associated with consciousness are intended as the kamma-door, their status as kamma-door is not metaphorically transferred to the mind; rather, just as the associated factors are dominant in the consciousness, so the consciousness is called the 'mental kamma-door.' By nature, however, what is called the kamma-door is just the associated factors, and since consciousness proceeds from them, it functions as the mental kamma-door. Moreover, regarding its being a mental kamma-door in the sense of an immediate condition, there is nothing to be said. Here, however, by the statement 'because it does not generate intimation,' non-occurrence is established only with respect to the bodily and verbal kamma-doors, and thus the mental kamma-door is not included. For the reason 'because it does not generate intimation' does not establish non-occurrence through the mental kamma-door as well. Alternatively, by the phrase 'due to its resultant nature,' non-occurrence through the mental kamma-door is also established. Here, in 'kamma-door,' by the word 'kamma,' kamma of different moments should be understood as intended. Thus, resultant consciousness does not occur in these two doors designated as the bodily and verbal kamma-doors—or in all three including the mental kamma-door—in the same way that wholesome consciousness does. And just as wholesome consciousness occurs by way of accumulating bodily, verbal, and mental kamma, and as the basis for meritorious deeds such as giving, this (resultant) does not. This (resultant) does not occur through the bodily or verbal kamma-doors, because it lacks the ability to originate intimation, nor does it occur by way of kamma. And it does not occur through the mental kamma-door, because it lacks the nature of producing a result, nor does it occur by way of meritorious deeds, because it does not proceed in the manner of giving, etc. To show this, it was said: 'And the kamma-door... etc. ... are not similar.' 'Thus' means in the manner of giving, etc.

37. “Parittārammaṇattā”tiādi sampayuttadhammavasena visesadassanaṃ. Yasmā ete parittārammaṇā, karuṇāmuditā ca paññattārammaṇā sattapaññattiyaṃ pavattanato, tasmā dvinnamālambaṇānaṃ ekacittassa visayabhāvānanugamanato na tesu karuṇāmuditā kadācipi jāyantīti ayamettha paṭhamagāthāya adhippāyo.

37. "Because their object is limited," etc.—this shows the distinction based on associated phenomena. Since these have a limited object, and compassion and gladness have a conceptual object, occurring in the conceptualization of beings, therefore, because the two objects do not fall within the range of a single consciousness, compassion and gladness never arise in them. This is the meaning intended in the first verse.

38. Dutiyagāthāya pana hi-saddo yasmāti imassa atthe. Yasmā “pañca sikkhāpadā kusalā”ti (vibha. 715) vuttā, tasmāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bhagavatā hi sikkhāpadavibhaṅge “pañca sikkhāpadā kusalā”ti (vibha. 715) evaṃ “pāṇātipātā veramaṇī”tiādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ kusalabhāvo vutto, te ca viratisabhāvā eva ādito tiṇṇaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ, pacchimassa ca sammākammante, itarassa sammāvācāyaṃ, pañcannampi micchājīvahetukapañcaduccaritato viramaṇavasena [M 1.0261] pavattānaṃ sammāājīve ca antobhāvato, tasmā tā ekantakusalabhūtānaṃ kadāci abyākate labhanti, itarathā saddhāsatiādayo viya “siyā kusalā, siyā abyākatā”ti vucceyyunti. Yadi evaṃ lokuttaraphalesu aṭṭha, satta vā maggaṅgā na labbhantīti? No na labbhanti lokiyaviratīnameva tattha ekantakusalabhāvassa vuttattā, lokuttaraviratiyo pana phalassa maggapaṭibimbabhūtattā maggasadisato aṭṭhaṅgikatāya, sattaṅgikatāya [V 1.0209] ca bhavitabbanti na ca ekantakusalabhāvena vavatthāpetuṃ yuttā. Evañca katvā upari lokuttaraphalesupi aṭṭhaṅgikatādibhedo maggo uddhaṭoti.

38. In the second verse, the word 'hi' is in the sense of 'because.' Because it is said, 'The five precepts are wholesome' (Vibh. 715), therefore, that is the meaning. This is what is meant: The Blessed One, in the analysis of the precepts, stated that 'the five precepts are wholesome' (Vibh. 715), thus declaring the wholesome nature of the five precepts, such as abstaining from killing living beings, etc. These, being of the nature of abstinences, are included thus: the first three precepts and the last in Right Action, and the other in Right Speech. Since all five, occurring as abstention from the five wrong conducts rooted in wrong livelihood, are included in right livelihood, therefore these, being exclusively wholesome, are never found among the indeterminate; otherwise, like faith, mindfulness, etc., they might be called 'sometimes wholesome, sometimes indeterminate.' If this is so, are the eight or seven path factors not attained in the supramundane fruits? It is not that they are not unattained, because the entirely wholesome nature is stated only of mundane abstinences. However, the supramundane abstinences, being reflections of the path in the fruit, must be considered eightfold or sevenfold like the path, and should not be definitively classified as exclusively wholesome. Thus, having established this, the eightfold distinction of the path, etc., is extended even to the supramundane fruits above.

39. “Tathādhipatino”tiādi adhipativasena visesadassanaṃ. Sabbesampi hi tebhūmakakusalānaṃ añño āyūhanakālo, añño vipaccanakālo, tasmā na tāni attano vipākehi adhipatiṃ gāhāpetuṃ sakkontīti na te chandādīni dhuraṃ katvā pavattanti. Lokuttarakusalāni ca pana āyūhanakālassa, vipaccanakālassa ca antarābhāvato attano chandādīnaṃ balassa avūpasantakāleyeva vipākaṃ nibbattentīti anantarapaccayā hutvā vipākehi adhipatiṃ gāhāpetuṃ sakkontīti. Evañca katvā upari lokuttaravipākānaṃ adhipatiyogaṃ vakkhati.

39. "Thus being dominant," etc., shows the distinction by way of dominance. For all wholesome states of the three planes, one is the time of accumulation, and another is the time of fruition. Therefore, they are unable to cause their results to take dominance. Thus, they do not occur taking zeal, etc., as their chief. However, supramundane wholesome states, because there is no interval between the time of accumulation and the time of fruition, produce their result while the strength of their zeal, etc., has not yet ceased. Therefore, being immediate conditions, they are able to cause their results to take dominance. And having done so, he will state the dominance connection for the supramundane results above.

40. Yasmā moravāpivāsimahādattattherena vipākānaṃ āgamanato asaṅkhārikasasaṅkhārikabhāvo icchito, tipiṭakacūḷanāgattherena paccayato, tasmā ubhinnampi matidassanatthamāha “asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāravidhāna”ntiādi. Purimatthero hi yathā mukhe calite ādāsatale mukhanimittaṃ calati[M 1.0262], evaṃ asaṅkhārikassa kusalassa vipāko asaṅkhāriko, sasaṅkhārikassa vipāko sasaṅkhārikoti āha, tasmā tassa matidassanatthaṃ “asaṅkhāra…pe… puññato”ti vuttaṃ. Dutiyatthero pana asaṅkhārikādīsu yena kenacipi cittena kamme āyūhite āsannamaraṇassa attano, paresaṃ vā payogena vinā asaṅkhārena appayogena kammakammanimittagatinimittapaccupaṭṭhāne paṭisandhi uppajjamānā asaṅkhārikā. Yassa kassaci sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kammādipaccupaṭṭhāne sasaṅkhārikā. Tathā bhavaṅgacutiyopi. Tadārammaṇañca paṇītāpaṇītautubhojanādipaccayavasena, anantaraniruddhakusalākusalassa vasena vā asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāranti evaṃ paccayato asaṅkhārikādividhānatamāha, tasmā tassa matidassanatthaṃ “ñeyyaṃ paccayato cevā”ti vuttaṃ. Idameva ca pana ācariyā pasaṃsanti.

40. Because the Venerable Mahādatta of Moravāpi wished for the spontaneous and prompted nature of results to be understood from their arising, and the Venerable Cūḷanāga of the Tipiṭaka from conditions, therefore, to show the views of both, it is said: 'The distinction between spontaneous and prompted,' and so on. For the first Venerable, just as when the face moves, the reflection in the mirror moves, so too, the result of spontaneous wholesome kamma is spontaneous, and the result of prompted wholesome kamma is prompted. Thus, to illustrate his view, it is said: 'Spontaneous... from merit.' The second Venerable, however, stated that when kamma is generated by any mind, spontaneous or otherwise, for one near death, rebirth-linking arises spontaneously—without one's own or others' effort, without prompting—through the presentation of the kamma, kamma-sign, or destiny-sign. For anyone whose kamma is prompted, rebirth-linking arises prompted, with effort, through the presentation of kamma, etc. Similarly, the life-continuum and death consciousness. Moreover, the registering consciousness is classified as spontaneous or prompted based on conditions such as superior or inferior climate, food, etc., or based on the immediately ceased wholesome or unwholesome state. Thus, he explained the classification of spontaneous and prompted in terms of conditions. Therefore, to illustrate his view, it is said: 'It should be known also from conditions.' Indeed, the teachers praise this very explanation.

41-2. Hīnādīnaṃ vipākattāti adhipatiyogābhāvepi hīnamajjhimapaṇītānaṃ kusalānaṃ vipākattā. Etena āgamanato hīnādibhāvaṃ vibhāveti. Vineyyasantānagatakilesamalavidhamanena tassa punanato puñño vādo vacīghoso etassa, vuttanayeneva puññaṃ vadatīti vā puññavādī, tena puññavādinā. “Ekantena savatthuka”nti vuttepi rūpaloke pavatti anivāritāti āha “kāmalokasmi”nti[V 1.0210]. “Na panaññattha jāyate”ti iminā pana byatirekato laddhamatthaṃ dassetīti.

41-2. 'Because it is the result of inferior, etc.': this means that even in the absence of a connection with dominance, it is the result of wholesome states that are inferior, middling, and excellent. By this, he distinguishes the characteristic of being inferior, etc., based on its origin. By the thorough destruction of the impurities of defilements in the continuum of those to be trained, his speech is meritorious due to his purification; or, because he speaks of merit in the manner stated, he is a 'speaker of merit'; by that speaker of merit. Even when 'exclusively with a basis' is stated, occurrence in the form realm is not prevented—therefore he says, 'in the sense-sphere world.' 'But it is not born elsewhere'—by this, through exclusion, he shows the meaning that has been obtained.

Evaṃ tāva sahetukavipāke niddisitvā idāni ahetuke niddisituṃ “ahetukavipākacittaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kasmā pana sahetukassa kammassa ahetukavipāko hotīti? Vuccate – cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ tāva pañcannaṃ ārammaṇābhinipātamattattā alobhādisampayogo na sambhavati, tathā mandatarakiccesu sampaṭicchanasantīraṇesūti [M 1.0263] evaṃ hetūnaṃ uppattiyā asambhavato ca nesaṃ ahetukatā daṭṭhabbā. Upekkhādiyoge pana cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ tāva catunnaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇepi pavattamānānaṃ vatthārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭanāya dubbalabhāvato upekkhāsahagatatā, kāyaviññāṇassa ca tāya balavabhāvato sukhasahagatatā hoti. Sampaṭicchanaṃ pana ārammaṇaghaṭṭanayogyabhāvena oḷārikattā, catucittakkhaṇātītavasena cirajātattā ca dubbalamattano nissayena saha asamānajātikañca cakkhādivatthuṃ nissāya uppannehi cakkhuviññāṇādīhi laddhānantarapaccayatāya, apubbanissayatāya ca ārammaṇarasassāde dubbalanti iṭṭhādīsu ārammaṇesu upekkhāsahagatameva. Santīraṇaṃ pana vuttaviparītato iṭṭhārammaṇe sukhasahagataṃ, iṭṭhamajjhatte ca upekkhāsahagatanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Manoviññāṇadhātu viya visiṭṭhamananakiccābhāvato manomattā nissattanijjīvādiatthehi dhātu cāti manodhātu. Sā hi satipi viññāṇabhāve manoviññāṇato sambhavassa visiṭṭhamananakiccassa akaraṇato mananamattāyeva hoti. Vuttalakkhaṇaviparītato pana mano ca taṃ viññāṇañcāti manoviññāṇaṃ, tadeva yathāvuttaṭṭhena dhātūti manoviññāṇadhātu.

Having thus explained the rooted resultant consciousness, now, to explain the rootless, it is said, 'But the rootless resultant consciousness...' But why does a rootless result arise from a kamma with roots? It is said: First, for the five sense-consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness, because they are merely the impact of the object, association with non-greed and other roots is not possible. Similarly for the weaker functions of receiving and investigating. Thus, their rootlessness should be understood from the impossibility of the arising of roots. Regarding the connection with equanimity, etc.: even when the four sense-consciousnesses—eye, ear, nose, and tongue—arise with pleasant objects, they are accompanied by equanimity due to their weakness caused by the collision between the physical base and the object. Body-consciousness, however, is accompanied by pleasure because that collision is strong. The receiving consciousness is weak because it is gross, being suited for the impact of the object, and because it arises late, after four thought-moments have passed. It is also weak in savouring the taste of the object because it receives immediately contiguous conditionality from the eye-consciousness and so forth—which have arisen relying on a dissimilar base like the eye-base—and because it is not a prior support. Thus, with pleasant, etc., objects, it is accompanied only by equanimity. The investigating consciousness, however, due to the opposite of what was said, should be understood as accompanied by pleasure with a pleasant object, and by equanimity with a pleasant-neutral object. Due to the absence of the function of distinct ideation, it is mere mind; and it is an element in the sense of being without a soul, without life, etc.—thus it is the mind-element. For it, even though it is a state of consciousness, because it does not perform the function of distinct ideation which is possible for mind-consciousness, it is mere ideation. But, in contrast to the stated characteristic, it is mind and it is that consciousness, thus it is mind-consciousness; and that itself, in the sense explained, is an element, thus it is the mind-consciousness-element.

Viññāṇapañcakaṃ niyatārammaṇaṃ yathākkamaṃ rūpādiekekasseva ārammaṇakaraṇato. Sesattayamaniyatārammaṇaṃ pañcārammaṇikachaḷārammaṇikabhāvato.

The fivefold consciousness has a fixed object, because each in due order takes only one object, such as form, and so on. The remaining three have an unfixed object, because they can take five objects or six objects.

Daṭṭhabbatāya diṭṭhaṃ, rūpāyatanaṃ. Sotabbatāya sutaṃ, saddāyatanaṃ. Munitabbatāya mutaṃ, sampattasseva gahetabbatāyāti attho, gandhādittayassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Cakkhādīhi vinā kevalaṃ manasā eva vijānitabbatāya viññātaṃ, dhammāyatanaṃ. Anāmaṭṭhakālavisesavacanattā ca nesaṃ atītānāgatāpi rūpādayo diṭṭhādisaddehi vuccanti. Teneva hi [M 1.0264] “daṭṭhabbatāyā”tiādinā kālasāmaññena [V 1.0211] nesaṃ nibbacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ yassa taṃ diṭṭhārammaṇaṃ. Evaṃ sutārammaṇādīsu.

The seen is that which is to be seen; the form base. The heard is that which is to be heard; the sound base. The sensed is that which is to be sensed—meaning, that which is to be grasped only upon contact; this is a name for the triad of smell, taste, and touch. The cognized is that which is to be cognized by the mind alone, without the eye and so on; the dhamma base. And because for these there is no specific mention of time, past and future forms and so on are also referred to by the terms 'seen' and so on. For that very reason, their derivation is stated with a general reference to time by the phrase 'because it is to be seen,' and so on. That which has the seen as its object is 'seen-object.' Likewise for 'heard-object' and so on.

Cakkhuto pavattanti cakkhudvāratova pavattaṃ sabbavākyānaṃ avadhāraṇaphalattā. Tena manodhātuādīnaṃ cakkhuviññāṇabhāvo nivārito hoti tesaṃ dvārantaratopi pavattisambhavato. Atha vā “cakkhuto pavatta”nti idaṃ sañjātippavattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na sañcaraṇappavattiṃ, tasmā yathā kuṇḍamukhato udakaṃ sañcaraṇavasena pavattati, na evaṃ pavattamidha gahitaṃ. Yathā pana candakantapāsāṇato udakaṃ sañjātivasena pavattati, evaṃ pavattameva cakkhuto pavattanti gahitaṃ. Yathā ca kiṃ? Yathā kucchito samuṭṭhitaṃ pittasemharuhirādi mukhato sandantampi “mukhassavo”ti na vuccati, mukhatoyeva pana samuṭṭhahitvā tato savantaṃ kheḷaṃ “mukhassavo”ti vuccati, evaṃ hadayavatthusannissayato samuṭṭhahitvā cakkhuto pavattamānaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ nāma na hoti. Cakkhutoyeva pana samuṭṭhahitvā tato pavattamānaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ nāmāti. Yo pana imamatthaṃ asallakkhetvā byañjanamattasseva abhinivisitvā taṃdvārappavattānaṃ sesānampi cakkhuviññāṇabhāvaṃ maññeyya, taṃ nivāretuṃ pakārantarenapi viggahaṃ dassento āha “cakkhumhi sannissita”nti. Yathā cakkhuto pavattaṃ, cakkhusannissitaṃ vā viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, evaṃ sotaviññāṇādīsupi “sotato pavattaṃ, sotasmiṃ sannissitaṃ vā viññāṇaṃ sotaviññāṇa”ntiādinā yojanaṃ atidisanto āha “tathā sotaviññāṇādīnī”ti.

They proceed from the eye, meaning they proceed only from the eye-door, due to the restrictive force of the statement. Thereby, the status of eye-consciousness is denied to the mind-element and others, since their proceeding through other doors is also possible. Alternatively, 'proceeding from the eye' is said with reference to proceeding as origination, not proceeding as movement. Therefore, just as water flows from the mouth of a pitcher by way of movement, that kind of proceeding is not taken here. But just as water arises from a moonstone by way of origination, so too is 'proceeding from the eye' to be understood. And how so? Just as bile, phlegm, and blood, having arisen from the stomach and flowing from the mouth, are not called 'mouth-discharge,' but saliva, having arisen from the mouth itself and flowing from there, is called 'mouth-discharge'; so too, consciousness that has arisen depending on the heart-base and is proceeding from the eye is not called eye-consciousness. But consciousness that has arisen from the eye itself and proceeds from there is called eye-consciousness. As for one who, not discerning this meaning and adhering only to the mere letter, might think that the other consciousnesses proceeding through that door are also eye-consciousness—to prevent this, showing the analysis in another way, the text states: 'dependent on the eye.' Just as consciousness proceeding from the eye, or dependent on the eye, is eye-consciousness, so too for ear-consciousness and so on. Extending the application with 'consciousness proceeding from the ear, or dependent on the ear, is ear-consciousness,' and so on, the text states: 'so too for ear-consciousness and the others.'

Cakkhusannissitaṃ hutvā rūpassa vijānanalakkhaṇametassāti cakkhusannissitarūpavijānanalakkhaṇaṃ. Tattha cakkhusannissitavacanena dibbacakkhādikaṃ aññaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ viññāṇaṃ nivatteti[M 1.0265]. Vijānana-ggahaṇena cakkhusannissite phassādidhamme nivatteti. Cakkhurūpa-ggahaṇena nissayato, ārammaṇato ca cittaṃ vibhāveti ubhayādhīnavuttikattā. Yadi hi cakkhu nāma na siyā, andhāpi rūpaṃ passeyyuṃ, na ca passanti. Yadi ca nīlādirūpaṃ nāma na siyā, desādiniyamena na bhavitabbaṃ, attheva ca niyamo. Ekantasārammaṇatā ca cittassa vuttāti ārammaṇena vinā nīlādiābhāsaṃ cittaṃ pavattatīti evaṃ pavatto vādo micchāvādoti gahetabbo. Tenāha bhagavā “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”ntiādi (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425; saṃ. ni. 4.60; kathā. 465). Ettha [V 1.0212] siyā – kiṃ panetaṃ cakkhu, rūpañca viññāṇassa paccayo hontaṃ ekameva paccayo hoti, udāhu anekanti? Cakkhu tāva ekampi, rūpaṃ pana anekameva saṅgataṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Paccayabhāvavisesato. Cakkhu hi cakkhuviññāṇassa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttapaccayehi paccayo hontaṃ atthibhāveneva hoti tasmiṃ sati tassa bhāvato, asati abhāvato. Yato taṃ atthiavigatapaccayehissa paccayoti vuttaṃ, svāyaṃ paccayabhāvo na ekasmiṃ na sambhavatīti ekampi cakkhuviññāṇassa paccayo hoti. Rūpaṃ pana yadipi cakkhu viya purejātaatthiavigatapaccayehi paccayo hoti puretaraṃ uppannaṃ hutvā vijjamānakkhaṇeyeva upakārakattā, tathāpi anekameva saṅgataṃ hutvā paccayo hoti ārammaṇabhāvato. Yañhi taṃ ārammaṇaṃ tassa yathā tathā upalabbhanīyavaseneva ārammaṇapaccayabhāvo, viññāṇassa ca indriyādhīnavuttikassa ārammaṇasabhāvūpaladdhi na ekadvikalāpagatavaṇṇavasena hoti, nāpi katipayakalāpagatavaṇṇavasena, atha kho ābhogānurūpaṃ āpāthagatavaṇṇavasenāti anekameva rūpaṃ saṃhaccakāritāya viññāṇassa paccayo hotīti. Amumeva [M 1.0266] hi visesaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe cā”ti (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425; saṃ. ni. 4.60; kathā. 465) pāḷiyaṃ vacanabhedo katoti. Evaṃ sotaviññāṇepi yathārahaṃ vattabbaṃ. Ghānaviññāṇādīnaṃ pana sampattaggāhatāya attano nissayena saha allīnasseva gahaṇato ekakalāpagatampi gandhādikaṃ tesaṃ uppattiyā paccayo hoti.

Its characteristic is the cognizing of form while being dependent on the eye. Herein, by the words 'dependent on the eye,' it excludes other consciousness that has form as its object, such as the divine eye. By the inclusion of 'cognizing,' it excludes dhammas such as contact that are dependent on the eye. By the inclusion of 'eye' and 'form,' it clarifies the mind in terms of support and object, because its occurrence is dependent on both. For if there were no such thing as the eye, even the blind would see form, but they do not. And if there were no such thing as form, like blue, etc., there would be no determination by way of location, etc., but such a determination does exist. And the mind has been said to be exclusively with an object; thus, the view that 'the mind proceeds as an appearance of blue, etc., without an object' should be understood as a wrong view. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Conditioned by the eye and by forms, eye-consciousness arises,' etc. Here it might be asked: Is this eye and form, in being a condition for consciousness, a single condition or multiple conditions? The eye is a single condition, but form is indeed multiple and combined. What is the reason? Because of the specific nature of their conditionality. For the eye is a condition for eye-consciousness by way of support, pre-nascence, faculty, dissociation, existence, and non-disappearance conditions, and it is so simply by its existence—when it exists, consciousness arises; when it does not, it does not arise. Since it is said to be a condition by way of existence and non-disappearance conditions, and this conditionality is not impossible in a single thing, the eye, though single, is a condition for eye-consciousness. Form, however, although it is a condition by way of pre-nascence, existence, and non-disappearance conditions like the eye—having arisen earlier and being helpful at the moment of its existence—is nevertheless a condition as multiple and combined, due to its nature as an object. For the object-conditionality of an object is precisely by way of its being apprehensible in such and such a way. For consciousness, whose occurrence is dependent on a faculty, the apprehension of the object's nature does not happen by way of the color of one or two particles, nor by way of the color of a few particles, but rather by way of the color that has come into range in accordance with the attention. Thus, multiple form, by its collective action, is a condition for consciousness. To clarify this very distinction, a difference in grammatical number was made in the Pāḷi text: 'conditioned by the eye (singular) and by forms (plural).' So it is said. In this way, it should be stated as appropriate for ear-consciousness as well. For nose-consciousness, etc., however, because they grasp what has come into contact, grasping it as adhering to their own support, even smell, etc., belonging to a single particle is a condition for their arising.

Rūpamattārammaṇarasanti rūpāyatanamattasseva ārammaṇakaraṇarasaṃ. Matta-saddena yathā ārammaṇantaraṃ nivatteti, evaṃ rūpāyatanepi labbhamāne ekacce visese nivatteti. Na hi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ vaṇṇamattato aññaṃ kiñci nīlādivisesaṃ tattha gahetuṃ sakkoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “pañcahi viññāṇehi na kiñci dhammaṃ paṭivijānāti aññatra abhinipātamattā”ti. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppajjamānaṃ rūpārammaṇe eva uppajjanato tadabhimukhabhāvena gaṇhātīti vuttaṃ “rūpābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāna”nti. Attano anantaraṃ uppajjamānānaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ samanantaravigatā arūpadhammā pavattiokāsadānena anantarasamanantaranatthivigatapaccayehi upakārakā, nissayārammaṇā dhammā viya āsannakāraṇāti dassento āha “rūpārammaṇāya kiriyāmanodhātuyā apagamapadaṭṭhāna”nti. Sotaviññāṇādīsupi vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Kiriyāmanodhātuyā ārammaṇabhedato bhinnasabhāvattā āha “kiriyāmanodhātūna”nti. Cakkhuviññāṇādīhi gahitaṃ rūpādiārammaṇaṃ tadanantarameva aparipatantaṃ [V 1.0213] katvā sampaṭicchantaṃ gaṇhantaṃ viya hotīti vuttaṃ “rūpādisampaṭicchanarasa”nti. Tathābhāvena sampaṭicchanabhāvena paccupaṭṭhātīti tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

The function of eye-consciousness is having mere form as its object; that is, its function is making only the form base its object. By the word 'mere,' just as it excludes other objects, so too, when the form base is present, it excludes certain particulars. For eye-consciousness is unable to grasp anything there other than mere color, any particular such as blue. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'With the five consciousnesses one does not discern any dhamma, apart from mere impact.' Its manifestation is 'facing the form object,' because eye-consciousness, when arising, arises only in a form object and thus grasps by way of facing it. Its proximate cause is its serving as the departing condition for the subsequent functional mind-element. This is to show that non-material dhammas that have ceased immediately before are a proximate cause for the non-material dhammas arising immediately after them, by giving an opportunity for their occurrence and being helpful by way of contiguity, immediate contiguity, absence, and disappearance conditions, like support and object dhammas. Now, concerning the functional mind-elements: because they have different natures due to the difference in their objects, the plural 'of the functional mind-elements' is used. The function of the receiving consciousness is 'receiving form, etc.,' because it is as if it receives the form object, etc., grasped by eye-consciousness, etc., immediately after, preventing it from perishing. Its manifestation is 'being so,' because it manifests with that nature, with the nature of receiving.

Chasu ārammaṇesu kadāci pañcannaṃ jaccandhādivasena tatopi ūnānaṃ, brahmaloke ca dvinnameva vijānanasabhāvāpi chaḷārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇā [M 1.0267] vuttā taṃsabhāvānativattanato, chasveva vā itaresaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ antogadhattā. Santīraṇādirasāti yathāsambhavaṃ santīraṇatadārammaṇādikiccā, santīraṇatadārammaṇapaṭisandhibhavaṅgacutikiccāti adhippāyo. “Hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānā”ti idaṃ imāsaṃ dvinnaṃ manoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ anibaddhaṭṭhānatāya nibaddhakāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Vuttanayena pana “taṃtaṃanantarātītaviññāṇāpagamapadaṭṭhāna”ntipi vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Ahetukacittānaṃ visuṃ visuṃ lakkhaṇādikassa dassitattā parisesato sahetukacittānaṃ ekasadisameva lakkhaṇādikanti viññāyati. Taṃ pana heṭṭhā vibhāvitameva.

Among the six objects, sometimes five are cognized, or even fewer, as in the case of the congenitally blind and so forth. In the Brahma world, although there is the nature of cognizing only two, the characteristic of cognizing six objects is stated because it does not transcend that inherent nature, or because the other objects are included within the six. Its function is investigating, etc.; that is, its functions are investigating, registering, and so on, as is possible. The intention is that its functions are investigating, registering, rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death. 'Having the heart-base as its proximate cause'—this is stated to show the fixed cause for these two mind-consciousness elements, as their physical basis is not fixed. However, in the manner stated, it is also appropriate to say, 'having as its proximate cause the cessation of the respective immediately preceding consciousness.' Because the characteristics and so on of the rootless consciousnesses have been shown individually, it is understood that, for what remains, the characteristics and so on of the rooted consciousnesses are all similar. But that has already been explained below.

Idāni imāsaṃ ārammaṇādito bhedaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha paṭhamā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekantamiṭṭhārammaṇeti ekanteneva iṭṭhārammaṇe, atiiṭṭhārammaṇeti attho. Pañcasu ṭhānesūti sahetukavipākānaṃ vuttesu catūsu, sampaṭicchanavoṭṭhabbanānaṃ antarāḷasaṅkhātasantīraṇaṭṭhāne cāti pañcasu ṭhānesu, pañcasu kiccesūti vā attho. Kiñcāpi somanassapaṭisandhikassa domanassajavanāvasāne tadārammaṇasambhave asati yaṃ kiñci paricitapubbaṃ parittārammaṇamārabbha upekkhāsahagatasantīraṇamuppajjatīti icchitaṃ, tathā pana uppajjamānassa kadāciyeva sambhavato yebhuyyappavattiṃ gahetvā cha ṭhānāni avatvā pañceva vuttāni. Atha vā taṃ uppajjamānaṃ tadārammaṇaṭṭhāneyeva nibbattatīti taṃvaseneva tassāpi ṭhānaṃ gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Acakkhusaṃvattanikakammanibbattatāya jātiyā andho jaccandho. Kiñcāpi hi jātikkhaṇe aṇḍajajalābujānaṃ sabbesampi cakkhu natthi, yassa bhāvābhāvato andhānandhavicāraṇā bhaveyya, tathāpi cakkhussa uppajjamānārahakālepi cakkhuvipattivibandhakena kammunā paṭihatasāmatthiyena paṭisandhidāyakena [M 1.0268] itarenāpi vā kammena tassa anupādiyamānattā satto “jaccandho”ti vuccati. Atha vā jaccandhoti pasūtiyaṃyeva andho, mātukucchiyaṃyeva andho hutvā nikkhantoti attho. Tena duhetukatihetukānaṃ mātukucchigatakālepi cakkhussa avipajjanaṃ siddhaṃ hoti, evaṃ jātibadhirādīsupi yathārahaṃ vattabbaṃ. Jaccajaḷoti jātiyā aññāṇako[V 1.0214]. Kiñcāpi duhetukapaṭisandhikopi jātiyaṃ aññāṇako, tassa pana pavattiyaṃ paññā sambhavatīti vuttanayena yebhuyyato pavattiyampi paññāyāsambhavato jaccajaḷo veditabbo. Jaccummattako surāmerayapānādiummattakabhāvasaṃvattanikakammaparibhāvitena kammena gahitapaṭisandhiko. Paṇḍakoti paradāragamanādikammaparibhāvitena kammunā gahitapaṭisandhiko. So pañcavidho āsittapaṇḍako usūyapaṇḍako pakkhapaṇḍako opakkamikapaṇḍako napuṃsakapaṇḍakoti. Idha pana opakkamikapaṇḍakassa sahetukassāpi bhāvato, napuṃsakassa ca visuṃ gahaṇato tayo paṇḍakā adhippetā. Ādi-saddena jātimūgajātipaṅgulamammanādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Keci pana “ekacce ahetukapaṭisandhikā avikalindriyā hutvā thokaṃ vicāraṇapakatikāpi honti, tasmā tādisānampi idha ādi-saddena saṅgaho”ti vadanti. Ettha ca jaccandhādīnameva ayaṃ paṭisandhīti na gahetabbā. Jaccandhādayo pana iminā paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantīti gahetabbaṃ.

Now, to explain the distinctions among these concerning objects and so on, the phrase 'Therein, the first...' and so on is stated. 'In an exclusively desirable object' means in an object that is exclusively desirable; the meaning is 'in an extremely desirable object.' 'In five places' refers to the five places: the four already mentioned for the rooted resultants, and the place of investigating, which is called the intermediate state between receiving and determining. Alternatively, it means 'in five functions.' Although it is held that for one reborn with joy, when there is no subsequent registering consciousness after a javana accompanied by displeasure, an investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity arises regarding any previously familiar minor object, yet since such an occurrence is rare, taking into account the majority of cases, only five places are mentioned instead of six. Alternatively, it should be understood that since that arising occurs in the place of the registering consciousness itself, its place is also included by virtue of that. One born blind (jaccandho) is one who is blind by birth, being produced by kamma that does not bring about the eye. For although at the moment of birth none of the egg-born or womb-born beings have an eye by the presence or absence of which one could distinguish between the blind and the non-blind, yet if the eye faculty, even at the time it is fit to arise, is not produced by the rebirth-giving kamma or by any other kamma—its capacity being obstructed by kamma that hinders the eye's development—such a being is called 'jaccandho' (congenitally blind). Alternatively, 'jaccandho' means one who is blind from birth, having come out from the mother's womb already blind. Thus, the non-impairment of the eye faculty while in the womb is established for those with two or three roots. The same applies, as appropriate, to those born deaf and so forth. A 'jaccajaḷo' is one who is ignorant by birth. Although even one reborn with two roots is ignorant at birth, wisdom may arise for them in the course of existence. However, in the manner stated, a 'jaccajaḷo' should be understood as one for whom wisdom generally does not arise even in the course of existence. A 'jaccummattako' is one who has taken rebirth through kamma conditioned by actions conducive to madness, such as drinking liquor and spirits. A 'paṇḍaka' is one who has taken rebirth through kamma conditioned by actions such as adultery. There are five types of paṇḍaka: the āsitta-paṇḍaka, the usūya-paṇḍaka, the pakkha-paṇḍaka, the opakkamika-paṇḍaka, and the napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka. Here, however, because the opakkamika-paṇḍaka can also be rooted, and because the napuṃsaka is mentioned separately, three types of paṇḍaka are intended. The word 'ādi' (and so forth) includes those born mute, lame, stammering, and so on. Some say that certain beings reborn without roots, though with unimpaired faculties, also have a slightly investigative nature, and thus such cases are also included here under 'ādi'. And here, it should not be understood that this rebirth-linking consciousness belongs exclusively to the congenitally blind and so forth. Rather, it should be understood that the congenitally blind and so forth take rebirth with this consciousness.

43. Tihetukapuññassāti tihetukassapi ukkaṭṭhapuññassa. Duhetukammassa pana sabbathāpi soḷasannaṃ vipākānaṃ asambhavato tappaṭikkhepaparattā cetanāya “tihetukapuññassā”ti avisesato vuttaṃ.

43. 'Of three-rooted merit' means of superior merit that is three-rooted. However, since for two-rooted kamma the sixteen kinds of resultants are in every way impossible, the phrase 'of three-rooted merit' is stated without distinction, with the intention of excluding that two-rooted kamma.

Kāmāvacaravipākavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the exposition of the sense-sphere resultants.

Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaravipākavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Form-Sphere and Formless-Sphere Resultants

Mahaggatavipākānaṃ [M 1.0269] taṃtaṃkusalāgamanavaseneva jhānaṅgahāni, na pana bhāvanāvisesenāti tesaṃ pahānaṅgāni anuddhaṭāni. Upapattiyanti upapattibhave.

For the exalted resultants, the abandoning of jhāna factors occurs only by virtue of the attainment of the respective wholesome jhāna, not by a distinction in development; thus their abandoning-factors are not specified. 'At rebirth' means in the rebirth-existence.

Arūpāvacaravipākacittāni vuccantīti sambandho.

The connection is that the formless-sphere resultant consciousnesses are spoken of.

44. Kusalānugataṃ katvāti kusalānurūpaṃ kusalasadisaṃ katvā. Yathā kāmāvacaravipākaṃ kusalato visadisampi katvā vibhattaṃ, evamakatvā kusalasadisameva katvāti atthaṃ vadanti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ [V 1.0215] pana kusalānantaraṃ katvā mahaggatavipākānaṃ bhājitapāḷiṃ sandhāya “kusalānugataṃ katvā bhājita”nti vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyañhi –

44. ‘Having made it follow the wholesome’ means having made it conform to, or resemble, the wholesome. They say the meaning is that, unlike the sense-sphere resultants which were analyzed as being dissimilar to the wholesome, these were not analyzed in that way but were made to resemble the wholesome. However, in the commentary, with reference to the Pāḷi passage where the exalted resultants are analyzed, it is said, ‘analyzed having been made to follow the wholesome,’ because they are placed immediately after the wholesome. For in the Pāḷi:

“Katame dhammā abyākatā? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacarassa kusalassa kammassa katattā upacitattā vipākaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppannaṃ hotī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 431) –

'Which states are indeterminate? At the time when, because sense-sphere wholesome kamma has been done and accumulated, resultant eye-consciousness has arisen...' and so on (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 431).

Kāmāvacaravipākaṃ vibhajitvā mahaggatavipākaṃ vibhajantena –

Having analyzed the sense-sphere resultants, when analyzing the exalted resultants:

“Katame dhammā abyākatā? Yasmiṃ samaye rūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti, vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati pathavīkasiṇaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hoti, ime dhammā kusalā, tasseva rūpāvacarassa kusalassa kammassa katattā upacitattā vipākaṃ vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati pathavīkasiṇaṃ…pe… ime dhammā abyākatā”ti (dha. sa. 498).

'Which states are indeterminate? At the time when one develops the path for attainment of the form realm, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... having entered the first jhāna, one abides in it, with the earth kasiṇa; at that time there is contact... there is non-distraction—these states are wholesome. Because that same form-sphere wholesome kamma has been done and accumulated, its resultant is: quite secluded from sensual pleasures... having entered the first jhāna, one abides in it, with the earth kasiṇa... these states are indeterminate' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 498).

Evaṃ kusalaṃ uddisitvā tadanantaraṃ katvā mahaggataṃ vipākaṃ vibhattaṃ, tasmā yathā kāmāvacaravipākaṃ, evaṃ avibhajitvā [M 1.0270] idaṃ kusalānantaraṃ katvā vibhattanti imamatthaṃ jotetuṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “kusalānugataṃ katvā”ti vuttaṃ. Imināpi ca ācariyena parihāramukhena vakkhamānaatthavisesavacanicchāya tattha vuttanayeneva codanā katā. Evañhi sati kusalānantaraṃyeva phalaṃ uppajjatīti ñāpanaṃ suṭṭhūpapannaṃ hotīti ayamettha amhākaṃ ācariyassa maggo.

Thus, having set forth the wholesome, the exalted resultant is analyzed by placing it immediately after. Therefore, to illuminate this meaning—that this is analyzed by placing it immediately after the wholesome, not analyzing it in the same way as the sense-sphere resultant—the commentary says, 'having made it follow the wholesome.' And by this teacher, too, a question was raised in the same way as stated there, by way of an alternative explanation, with the desire to state a specific distinction of meaning that will be explained. For when this is so, the demonstration that the fruit arises immediately after the wholesome becomes very fitting. This here is the path of our teacher.

Mahaggatanti mahaggatavipākaṃ. Tañhi idha adhigataṃ. Kāmā…pe… yatoti yasmā kāmāvacarakusalaṃ asamānaphalaṃ hoti tihetukassa duhetukāhetukavipākānaṃ, duhetukassa ca ahetukavipākānampi jananato, na evamidaṃ, idaṃ pana ekanteneva sadisavipākajananato samānaphalameva, tasmāti attho. Ettha ca “kusala”nti avuttepi kāmāvacarapuññaṃvāti upamitattā upameyyassapi kusalabhāvo viññāyati. Kasmā panetaṃ sadisavipākaṃ, na kāmāvacaraṃ viya visadisavipākampīti? Vuccate – kāmāvacarapuññañhi ācinanto rūpataṇhādinānāvatthukakāmataṇhūpanissayato [V 1.0216] ācinati, tasmā tadūpanissayakusalaṃ tadanurūpato nānāvatthukaṃ vipākaṃ janeti. Mahaggataṃ pana ācinanto ekavatthukāyeva bhavataṇhāya vasena ācinatīti tadanurūpato taṃ nānāvatthuṃ ajanetvā ekavatthumeva janetīti.

'Mahaggata' means the exalted resultant, for it is attained here. 'Sensual... yato' means because sense-sphere wholesome kamma produces dissimilar results, since a three-rooted wholesome kamma generates two-rooted and rootless resultants, and a two-rooted wholesome kamma also generates rootless resultants. This, however, is not so; this, on the other hand, invariably produces only similar resultants and thus has a similar fruit; therefore, this is the meaning. And here, even though 'wholesome' is not explicitly stated, because of the comparison with sense-sphere merit, the quality of being wholesome is also understood in the case of what is being compared. But why does this produce similar resultants, and not also dissimilar resultants like sense-sphere kamma? It is said: because when one accumulates sense-sphere merit, one accumulates it with the support of craving for sensual pleasures, which has diverse objects such as craving for forms, etc.; therefore, wholesome kamma dependent on that generates a resultant with diverse objects in accordance with it. But when one accumulates the exalted, one accumulates it by way of craving for existence, which has only a single object; and thus, in accordance with that, it generates a single object, not diverse objects.

45-6. Sabbathāti dhammato ārammaṇato paṭipadādito ca. Tathā hi ye phassādayo kusale ca labbhanti, te vipākepi labbhanti, yasmiñca ārammaṇe kusalaṃ pavattati, tattheva idaṃ vipākampi. Yāva paṭipadādayo kusalassa labbhanti, tāva imassa vipākassapīti. Kāmaṃ yassa kassaci chāyā taṃtaṃvatthusadisāva, mahantassa pana kusalavipākassa mahantāhiyeva upamāhi [M 1.0271] bhavitabbanti “gajādīna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Apare apare attabhāve bhavaṃ vedanamassāti aparāpariyavedanaṃ. Yadi aparāpariyavedanaṃ na hoti, kathañcarahi imassa phaluppattīti āha “jhānā aparihīnassā”tiādi.

45-6. 'From all sides' means from the standpoint of the states, the object, and the practice, etc. For indeed, those states such as contact that are obtained in the wholesome are also obtained in the resultant. And in whatever object the wholesome occurs, in that very same object this resultant also occurs. Insofar as the practice and other factors are obtained for the wholesome, so too are they for this resultant. Indeed, just as the shadow of any being whatsoever is similar to that very being, so for a great wholesome resultant, there must be great similes—hence 'elephants, etc.' and so on was said. The experiencing of existence in later and later existences is 'successive experiencing.' If there were no successive experiencing, how then could the fruit of this arise? Hence it is said, 'for one who has not declined from the jhānas,' and so on.

47. Kusalānantaranti kusalabhavānantaraṃ. Yasmiñhi bhave taṃ kusalaṃ kataṃ, so idha kusala-saddena upacārato gahito kammānantaraṃyeva phalassa asambhavato. Na hi taṃ lokuttarakusalaṃ viya anantaraphalanipphādakaṃ, atha kho ekaccakāmāvacarakusalaṃ viya aparāpariyavedanaṃ ahutvā satipi anekeyeva kāmāvacarakamme mahogho viya parittaṃ udakaṃ tamajjhottharitvā attanoyeva vipākadānena ekantena anantarabhaveyeva phalaṃ nibbatteti. Nanu ca aparihīnajjhānasseva kassaci nikantivasena kāmabhave paṭisandhi hoti. Tathā hi tissamahābrahmā uparibrahmalokūpapattiyā bhāvitamaggo bhikkhūhi yācito tato cavitvā moggalibrāhmaṇassa gehe paṭisandhiṃ aggahesīti vuttanti taṃ kathanti? Nikantibaleneva jhānaṃ parihāyatīti tato parihīnajjhāno nibbattatīti vadanti. Apare pana ācariyā “anīvaraṇāvatthāya nikantiyā jhānassa parihāni vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbā”ti vatvā “satipi mahaggatakammuno vipākaṃ paṭibāhanasamatthasseva parittakammassa abhāve ‘ijjhati, bhikkhave, sīlavato cetopaṇidhi visuddhattā’ti (a. ni. 8.35) vacanato kāmabhave cetopaṇidhi mahaggatakammassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā parittakammuno vipākassa okāsaṃ karotī”ti vadanti, taṃ yuttaṃ. Etassāti imassatthassa ñāpanatthanti sambandho.

47. 'Kusalānantara' means immediately following a wholesome existence. For in whatever existence that wholesome kamma was performed, that existence is here figuratively referred to by the term 'wholesome,' since the result cannot arise immediately after the kamma itself. For it is not like supramundane wholesome kamma, which produces its result immediately; nor is it like certain sense-sphere wholesome kammas that are to be experienced in some later life. Rather, even when many sense-sphere kammas exist, it overwhelms them like a great flood overwhelms a little water, and by its own power of giving result, it exclusively produces its fruit in the immediately following existence. But is it not the case that for someone who has not fallen away from jhāna, rebirth in the sense-sphere occurs due to attachment? For instance, it is said that Tissa, the great Brahmā, who had developed the path for rebirth in a higher brahma world, when asked by the monks, passed away from there and took rebirth in the household of the Brahmin Moggallāna—how is this explained? Some say that due to the power of attachment, the jhāna is lost, and thus one is reborn having fallen away from the jhāna. Other teachers, however, say: 'The loss of jhāna due to attachment should be investigated and understood to occur in a state free from the hindrances.' They state: 'Even when there is exalted kamma, in the absence of a lesser kamma capable of obstructing its result, in accordance with the saying, "Monks, the aspiration of a virtuous one succeeds because of its purity" (AN 8.35), an aspiration in the sense-sphere, having obstructed the result of the exalted kamma, creates an opportunity for the result of a lesser kamma.' This is reasonable. The phrase 'etassāti' connects to the purpose of explaining this meaning.

48-9. Evaṃ [M 1.0272] avisesena kusalasadisataṃ atidisitvā idāni visesaṃ dassetuṃ “paṭipadākkamo [V 1.0217] cevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathā hi dukkhapaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññaṃ jhānaṃ uppādetvā punappunaṃ samāpajjantassa taṃ jhānaṃ taṃpaṭipadameva hoti, evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ aparihīne tassa tassa vipāko nibbattamāno taṃtaṃpaṭipadova bhavituṃ arahati. Chandādhipateyyādibhāvo pana tasmiṃ khaṇe vijjamānānaṃ chandādīnaṃ adhipatipaccayabhāvena hoti, na āgamanavasena. Tathā hi ekameva jhānaṃ nānakkhaṇesu nānādhipateyyaṃ hoti, tasmā vipākassa āgamanavasena chandādhipateyyāditā na gahitā. Tenāha “abhāvodhipatīna”nti. Tadabhāvatova sarasato tassa hīnāditā na sambhavatīti sāpi jhānāgamanatova vuttā.

48-49. Having thus generally extended the analogy of similarity to the wholesome, now to show the specific differences, it is said: 'The order of practice, etc.' Just as for one who, having aroused a jhāna through painful practice and slow direct-knowledge, repeatedly enters that jhāna, that jhāna itself is of that same practice, so too for one who has not fallen away from that jhāna, when its resultant arises, it is fit to be of that same practice. The state of predominance by zeal, etc., however, occurs at that moment due to the predominance-condition of the existing zeal, etc., not by way of the source kamma. For even a single jhāna can have different predominating factors at different moments; therefore, for the resultant, predominance by zeal, etc., is not taken by way of its source. Hence it is said: 'the absence of predominating factors.' Precisely because of their absence, its inferiority, etc., is not possible by its own nature; so that too is stated only by way of the source jhāna.

Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaravipākavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Resultants Pertaining to the Form-Sphere and Formless-Sphere is concluded.

Lokuttaravipākavaṇṇanā

Exposition of Supramundane Resultants

Maggacittassa viya phalacittassa maggayogato bhedābhāvena “catumaggayogato”ti avatvā “catumaggasampayuttacittaphalattā”ti vuttaṃ, catūhi ariyamaggehi sampayuttakusalacittassa phalattā catubbidhasāmaññaphalasampayuttacittabhāvatoti attho. Sotāpattimaggassa phalaṃ cittaṃ sotāpattimaggaphalacittaṃ. Evaṃ sesesu. Maggavīthiyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ, tikkhattuṃ vā phalasamāpattiyā aparicchinnaparimāṇaṃ pavattamānampi dvīsveva ṭhānesu pavattiyā duvidhameva hotīti āha “maggavīthiphalasamāpattivasena pavattito duvidha”nti.

Because the fruit-consciousness, unlike the path-consciousness, does not have a 'connection with the path' (maggayoga), the phrase 'by connection with the four paths' is not used; instead, it is said, 'because it is the fruit of consciousness conjoined with the four paths.' The meaning is: because it is the fruit of wholesome consciousness conjoined with the four noble paths, it is consciousness conjoined with the four kinds of fruits of recluseship. The fruit-consciousness of the stream-entry path is the stream-entry-path-fruit-consciousness. Similarly for the rest. Even though it occurs twice or three times in the path-process, and for an immeasurable duration in fruit-attainment, because its occurrence is in only these two situations, it is only twofold. Thus it is said, 'It is twofold by way of occurring in the path-process and in fruit-attainment.'

50-1. Maggassānantare phale labbhanti maggāgamanatoti adhippāyo. Maggo hi āgamanato “suññato”ti laddhanāmo saguṇālambaṇavasena animittaappaṇihitanāmampi labhatīti phalassa nāmattayampi deti, tathā āgamanato appaṇihito [M 1.0273] maggo saguṇārammaṇavasena animittasuññataappaṇihitanāmakoti phalassa nāmattayampi deti. Evañca katvā abhidhamme ekekassa phalassa tīṇi tīṇi nāmāni vuttāni. Nanu ca abhidhamme “saguṇārammaṇato nāmaṃ anadhippeta”nti vuttaṃ? Saccaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pana nāmalābhaṃ sandhāya, na nāmadānaṃ. Tattha hi vavatthānakarattābhāvato tathā anadhippetaṃ, na alabbhanato. Idha pana ekekassa [V 1.0218] phalaṃ nāmattayampi labhatīti vavatthānappayojanābhāvato saguṇārammaṇehi laddhanāmadānassa adhippetattā tividhampi nāmaṃ deti. Ekantena cetaṃ evaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, itarathā vipassanāpi vipassato laddhanāmamaggassa taṃ na dadeyyāti. Parabhāgasminti aparabhāge. Vaḷañjanaphalesūti samāpajjanavasena anubhavitabbaphalesu. “Vaḷañjanaphalesu nā”ti maggāgamanaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhittanti āha “vipassanāvasenevā”tiādi. Vaḷañjanaphalañhi visuṃ vipassanāvaseneva nibbattatīti tassa taṃvasena nāmalābho. Yadi evaṃ maggassa viya animittanāmalābho na siyā? Taṃ na, yathā maggānantarassa phalassa viya vaḷañjanakaphalasamāpattiyāpi maggāgamanato ca jhānapaṭipadābhedo hoti, evaṃ animittanāmampi labbhatīti.

50-1. The meaning is that the fruits are obtained immediately after the path; the intention is that they come from the path. For the path, by its coming, acquires the name 'void,' and by way of its object having its own nature, it also obtains the names 'signless' and 'undirected.' Thus, it also gives the three names to the fruit. Similarly, the undirected path, by its coming, and by way of its object having its own nature, is named 'signless,' 'void,' and 'undirected,' and thus it also gives the three names to the fruit. And so, in the Abhidhamma, three names are stated for each fruit. But is it not said in the Abhidhamma that 'a name from its object having its own nature is not intended'? It is true that this is said, but that refers to the acquisition of a name, not the giving of a name. There, because there is no making of a distinction, it is not intended in that way—not because it cannot be obtained. Here, however, since each fruit obtains the three names, and because there is no purpose in making a distinction, the giving of a name acquired through its object having its own nature is intended, and thus it gives the threefold name. This should be accepted as being so in every way; otherwise, insight would not give to the path the name acquired from the one who has insight. 'In the later portion' means in the subsequent part. 'In the fruits of experience' means in the fruits to be experienced by way of attainment. The phrase 'not in the fruits of experience' is rejected with reference to the path's coming, and thus it is said, 'only by way of insight,' and so on. For the fruit of experience arises separately only by way of insight, and thus it obtains its name in that way. If so, would it not be that it does not obtain the name 'signless' as the path does? That is not so. For just as for the attainment of the fruit of experience, like the fruit immediately following the path, there is the coming from the path and a difference in the mode of practice of the jhānas, so too the name 'signless' is obtained.

52-3. Honti sādhipatīnevāti ettha kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Maggabhāvenāti soḷasahi ākārehi catusaccapaṭivedhakamaggabhāvena, kilesamāraṇavasena gamanasaṅkhātena, nibbānatthikehi maggitabbabhāvasaṅkhātena vā maggabhāvena. Phalaṃ…pe… vuccatīti sayaṃ phalabhāvampi maggassa phalattā, taṃsadisatāya vā tamupādāya maggoti vuccati “maggaṅgaṃ maggapariyāpanna”ntiādīsūti adhippāyo.

52-3. Here, the reason for 'they are always with predominance' has already been stated. 'By way of the nature of the path' means by the nature of the path that penetrates the four truths in sixteen aspects; by way of what is termed 'going' in the sense of destroying defilements; or by way of the state of being sought by those who desire Nibbāna. The meaning is that the fruit... is called 'path' because, although it is itself the state of fruit, it is the fruit of the path, or because of its similarity to it, or because it is based on it, as in such statements as 'a factor of the path,' 'included in the path,' and so on.

Lokuttaravipākavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of supramundane results is concluded.

Akusalavipākavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Unwholesome Results

Yathā [M 1.0274] atiiṭṭhe iṭṭhamajjhatte ca ārammaṇe vedanābhedasambhavato kusalavipākamanoviññāṇadhātu duvidhā hoti somanassasahagatā, upekkhāsahagatāti, evaṃ atianiṭṭhe aniṭṭhamajjhatte ca ārammaṇe vedanābhedo natthīti akusalavipākamanoviññāṇadhātu ekavidhāvāti “sattākusalavipākānī”ti vuttaṃ. Sati hi tattha vedanābhede atianiṭṭhe domanassena bhavitabbaṃ, na ca paṭighena vinā domanassaṃ uppajjatīti. Kāyaviññāṇassa dukkhasahagatā kusalavipāke vuttavipariyāyena veditabbā. Ettha ca akusalavipākesu labbhamānadukkhaṃ [V 1.0219] viya nātikaṭukāpi upekkhā ekantanihīnassa akusalassa vipākabhāvato dukkhasabhāvattā hīnā eva. Na hi akusalassa vipāko adukkho hoti, upekkhābhāvo panassa balavatā bādhiyamānassa paṭipaharituṃ asakkontassa dubbalapurisassa tena kariyamānabādhassa upekkhanā viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Imāni…pe… cittānīti imāni satta ekekassa akusalassa vipākacittāni, na pana kusalavipāke viya tihetukādipuññavisesena. Uddhaccasahagatassapi hi pavattiyaṃ satteva vipākā labbhanti. Kasmā panettha yathā kusalavipākaṃ sahetukampi uddhaṭaṃ, na evaṃ akusalavipākanti? Hetūnaṃ asambhavato. Lobhādīnañhi ekantasāvajjatāya ayonisomanasikārahetukānaṃ natthi vipākabhāvo, alobhādīnampi ekantamanavajjasabhāvānaṃ vā kāraṇassa tabbidūratāya nattheva akusalavipākabhāvo. Na hi alobhādīnaṃ paṭipakkhalobhādayo te abhinipphādenti, tasmā idaṃ sabbathā sahetuppavattiyā asambhavato ahetukamevāti.

Just as in the case of very desirable and moderately desirable objects, due to the possibility of different feelings, the wholesome resultant mind-consciousness element is twofold—accompanied by joy and accompanied by equanimity—so too, in the case of very undesirable and moderately undesirable objects, there is no difference in feeling. Therefore, the unwholesome resultant mind-consciousness element is of one kind only. Hence, it is said, 'There are seven unwholesome resultants.' For if there were a difference in feeling there, in the case of a very undesirable object, sorrow would have to arise, but sorrow does not arise without aversion. The bodily consciousness accompanied by pain should be understood in the opposite way to what was stated for the wholesome resultant. Here, even the equanimity found in unwholesome resultants, though not as intensely painful as the suffering that can be experienced, is still inferior, being the result of what is entirely base and having the nature of suffering. For the result of the unwholesome is not without suffering. The state of equanimity here should be seen as like the indifference of a weak man who, being oppressed by a stronger man and unable to retaliate, endures the harm being done by him. 'These... consciousnesses' means these seven are the resultant consciousnesses for each unwholesome state, but not, as in the case of wholesome resultants, distinguished by special merit such as being three-rooted, etc. For even in the case of that which is accompanied by restlessness, only seven resultants are obtained. Why is it that here, unlike the wholesome resultant, the unwholesome resultant is not specified as being with roots? Because of the impossibility of roots. For greed and so on, being entirely blameworthy and caused by unwise attention, have no resultant state. Likewise for non-greed and so on, being entirely blameless in nature, or because the cause is very far from such a thing, there is no state of unwholesome result with them as roots. For their opposites, greed and so on, do not produce them. Therefore, since it is entirely impossible for this to occur with roots, it is only rootless.

Kammakammanimittagatinimittesūti ettha atītabhave āyūhitaṃ aparāpariyavedanīyaṃ, upapajjavedanīyaṃ vā kammaṃ kammaṃ nāma[M 1.0275]. Kammakaraṇakāle cetanāya gahitamārammaṇaṃ kammanimittaṃ nāma. Upapajjitabbabhavapariyāpanno narakādīsu aggijālādivaṇṇo gatinimittaṃ nāma.

Here, regarding 'kamma, kamma-sign, and destiny-sign': 'kamma' refers to kamma accumulated in a past existence that is to be experienced in a subsequent life or upon rebirth. 'Kamma-sign' refers to the object grasped by volition at the time of performing the kamma. 'Destiny-sign' refers to a sign pertaining to the existence into which one is to be reborn, such as the appearance of flames and so on in hell.
