54. Imeti akusalavipākā. Tesaṃ aniṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhattavisayesu pavattivacanena tabbipariyāyena kusalavipākānaṃ iṭṭhaiṭṭhamajjhattavisayesu pavatti atthato āpannāti sā visuṃ na vuttā. Sukhādittayayuttāti sukhasomanassupekkhāyuttā.

54. 'These' means the unwholesome results. By the statement of their occurrence in undesirable and moderately undesirable spheres, the occurrence of wholesome results in desirable and moderately desirable spheres is understood by implication, so it is not stated separately. 'Connected with the threefold feeling' means associated with happiness, joy, and equanimity.

“Eva”ntiādi yathāvuttavipākānaṃ nigamanaṃ.

The word 'Thus,' and so on, is the conclusion for the results as stated.

Akusalavipākavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of unwholesome results is concluded.

Vipākacittavaṇṇanā

Exposition of Resultant Consciousness

55. Pākassa [V 1.0220] asurakaññānaṃ gabbhaparipākassa sāsanato vināsanato, pākasaṅkhātassa vā asurassa vināsanato pākasāsano vuccati sakko devarājā, tena pūjito pākasāsanapūjito. Pākaṃ vā paripakkaṃ sāsanametesūti pākasāsanā, khīṇāsavā, tehi pūjitoti pākasāsanapūjito.

55. Sakka, the king of the devas, is called Pākasāsana because he chastises and destroys the ripening of the wombs of the asura maidens of Pāka, or because he destroys the asura named Pāka. Honored by him, the Buddha is 'Pākasāsanapūjito.' Alternatively, 'Pākasāsanā' are those whose instruction is ripe, that is, fully mature, namely, the destroyers of the taints (arahants); honored by them, the Buddha is 'Pākasāsanapūjito.'

Vipākacittavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of resultant consciousness is concluded.

Dānādivasenāti pavattākāramattato dānādivasena, na pana puññakiriyavatthuvasena khīṇāsavasantānagatassa puññakiriyabhāvābhāvatoti vuttovāyamattho.

'By way of giving, etc.' means merely by way of the mode of occurrence as giving, etc., but not by way of a basis for meritorious action, because for one whose taints are destroyed, there is an absence of a state of meritorious action in his continuum. This is the meaning stated.

Āvajjatīti āvajjanaṃ, ābhuñjati oṇojeti pariṇāmeti vāretīti vā attho. Tañhi āpāthagataṃ ārammaṇaṃ paṭhamamābhuñjati, cakkhuviññāṇādīni vīthicittāni āpāthagatārammaṇābhimukhaṃ oṇojeti, cittasantānaṃ vā purimākārato aññathā pariṇāmeti, anuppabandhato pavattanakaṃ bhavaṅgacittasantānaṃ parato pavattituṃ adatvā āpāthagataṃ [M 1.0276] vā ārammaṇaṃ aññattha gantuṃ adatvā vāreti. Hasitaṃ uppajjati, uppādīyati vā etenāti hasituppādaṃ, tadeva cittanti hasituppādacittaṃ. Voṭṭhapetīti voṭṭhabbanaṃ. Kasmā panettha āvajjanavoṭṭhabbanāni upekkhāsahagatāni, hasituppādañca somanassasahagatanti? Vuccate – āvajjanaṃ tāva apubbārammaṇe sakideva ca pavattamānasantativicchedavasena pavattanato, dubbalabhavaṅgapaccayaṃ vā sabbathā visayarasamanubhavituṃ na sakkotīti iṭṭhādīsu sabbattha upekkhāyuttameva hoti. Voṭṭhabbanañca vuttavipariyāyena vedanābhedārahampi samānaṃ vipākappabandhaṃ vicchinditvā visadisacittappabandhassa nibbattanato santatipariṇāmaneyeva kiccantare byāvaṭattā vipākaṃ viya ārammaṇarasassāde asamatthamevāti sabbattha upekkhāsahagatameva. Hasituppādaṃ pana vuttaviparītato parihīnavipallāsānaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ santāne iṭṭhārammaṇeyeva uppajjanato sabbathā somanassasahagatamevāti.

“It adverts” means adverting; or the meaning is that it bends towards, directs, transforms, or prevents. For it first bends towards an object that has come into range, directs the process-consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness towards the object that has come into range, or transforms the stream of consciousness from its previous state into another, or it prevents the stream of life-continuum consciousness, which is proceeding uninterruptedly, from proceeding further, or prevents the object that has come into range from going elsewhere. “A smile arises” or “is caused to arise by this” means smile-producing; that very consciousness is the smile-producing consciousness. “It determines” means determining. But why here are adverting and determining accompanied by equanimity, while the smile-producing consciousness is accompanied by joy? It is said: First, adverting occurs only once towards a new object and arises by way of cutting off the continuity of the ongoing stream, or because, being conditioned by a weak life-continuum, it is entirely incapable of fully experiencing the taste of the object—thus, it is always associated with equanimity in all cases, whether the object is desirable or not. And determining, though capable of a difference in feeling contrary to what was stated, interrupts the continuity of resultant consciousness and gives rise to a dissimilar stream of consciousness. Since it is occupied with another function, namely, altering the continuity, it is, like a resultant consciousness, incapable of savoring the taste of the object—thus, it is always associated with equanimity. But the smile-producing consciousness, contrary to what was stated, arises only towards a desirable object in the continuum of those whose taints are destroyed and who are free from perversions—thus, it is always associated with joy.

Lakkhaṇādito panetāsu purimaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ purecaraṃ rūpādivijānanalakkhaṇaṃ, āvajjanarasaṃ[V 1.0221], tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, bhavaṅgavicchedapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Dutiyaṃ chaḷārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇaṃ, arahataṃ anoḷārikesu vatthūsu hasituppādarasaṃ, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ekantato hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ. Tatiyampi chaḷārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇaṃ, pañcadvāramanodvāresu voṭṭhabbanāvajjanarasaṃ, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ahetukavipākamanoviññāṇadhātubhavaṅgānaṃ aññatarāpagamapadaṭṭhānanti.

Moreover, regarding their characteristics and so forth, the first has the characteristic of cognizing a visible form, etc., as the forerunner to eye-consciousness, etc.; its function is adverting; its manifestation is the state of being so; its proximate cause is the cutting off of the life-continuum. The second has the characteristic of cognizing the six objects; its function is the production of a smile in arahants towards subtle objects; its manifestation is the state of being so; its proximate cause is exclusively the heart-base. The third also has the characteristic of cognizing the six objects; its function is determining at the five sense-doors and adverting at the mind-door; its manifestation is the state of being so; its proximate cause is the cessation of either a rootless resultant mind-consciousness-element or the life-continuum.

Bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭayamānāti bhavaṅgasantānaṃ āvaṭṭayantī viya. Sādhāraṇāti sekkhāsekkhaputhujjanānaṃ sādhāraṇā. Asādhāraṇāti asekkhānaṃyeva āveṇikā. Tenāha “khīṇāsavassā”ti. Chasu dvāresu…pe… ārammaṇesūti [M 1.0277] cakkhādīsu chasu dvāresu, padhānasāruppaṭṭhānādigatesu chasu rūpādiārammaṇesu. Padhānasāruppañhi ṭhānaṃ disvā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthāya “sāruppamidaṃ ṭhānaṃ mayā laddha”nti tusantassa cakkhudvāre rūpārammaṇe, bhaṇḍabhājanaṭṭhāne mahāsaddaṃ sutvā “evarūpā loluppataṇhā me pahīnā”ti tusantassa sotadvāre saddārammaṇe, gandhehi vā pupphehi vā cetiyapūjanakāle “evarūpena vata sugandhena bhagavantaṃ pūjemī”ti tusantassa ghānadvāre gandhārammaṇe, rasasampannaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ sabrahmacārīhi saha bhājetvā paribhuñjanakāle “sāraṇīyadhammo vata me pūrito”ti tusantassa jivhādvāre rasārammaṇe, ābhisamācārikavattapūraṇakāle “kāyena vattapaṭivattaṃ pūremī”ti tusantassa kāyadvāre phoṭṭhabbārammaṇeti evaṃ pañcadvāresu pañcārammaṇesu pavattati.

“Turning the bhavaṅga” means as if turning the continuum of bhavaṅga. “Common” means common to learners, non-learners, and ordinary people. “Uncommon” means unique to non-learners alone. Hence it is said, “of one whose taints are destroyed.” “At the six doors... and at the objects” means: at the six doors such as the eye, and at the six objects such as visible forms, etc., which are related to places suitable for striving and so forth. For instance, upon seeing a place suitable for striving, one delights, thinking, “I have found this suitable place for a pleasant abiding in this very life,” with a visible form as object at the eye-door; upon hearing a loud sound in a place for storing utensils, one delights, thinking, “Such greedy craving has been abandoned by me,” with a sound as object at the ear-door; when offering flowers or incense at a shrine, one delights, thinking, “Indeed, I honor the Blessed One with such a sweet fragrance,” with an odor as object at the nose-door; when sharing and consuming a meal rich in flavor with fellow monastics, one delights, thinking, “Indeed, the principle of cordiality has been fulfilled by me,” with a taste as object at the tongue-door; when fulfilling the duties of proper conduct, one delights, thinking, “I fulfill the duties and counter-duties with the body,” with a tangible object at the body-door. Thus, it occurs at the five sense-doors with their respective five objects.

Manodvāre pana yathāvuttesveva pañcasu paccuppannārammaṇesu ghaṭikārasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 2.282 ādayo) viya bhagavato pubbenivāsañāṇena pariññāte atītārammaṇe, “aṭṭhissaro nāma paccekabuddho bhavissatī”ti (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.16 devadattavatthu) āgataṭṭhānādīsu viya anāgataṃsañāṇena paricchinne anāgatārammaṇe cāti evaṃ chasvevārammaṇesu hasitaṃ uppādetīti veditabbaṃ. Nanu ca atītaṃsādīsu appaṭihatādīsu appaṭihatañāṇaṃ vatvā “imehi tīhi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivatta”nti vacanato vicāraṇapaññārahitāya etāya kathaṃ bhagavato uppatti yujjeyyāti? Hasituppādacittena pavattiyamānampi bhagavato sitakaraṇaṃ pubbenivāsaanāgataṃsasabbaññutaññāṇānaṃ anuvattakattā ñāṇānuparivattiyeva, evaṃ pana ñāṇānuparivattibhāve sati na koci pāḷivirodho. Evañca katvā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tesaṃ ñāṇānaṃ ciṇṇapariyante idaṃ [M 1.0278] cittaṃ uppajjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Avassañcetaṃ evaṃ icchitabbaṃ, itarathā aññassāpi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakassa ahetukacittassa bhagavato uppatti na [V 1.0222] yujjeyya. Na hi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakassa taṃsamuṭṭhitāya viññattiyā kāyakammādibhāvaṃ āpajjanabhāvo vibandhatīti. Evañca katvā pañcadvāre iminā cittena somanassuppādanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na hāsuppādanaṃ pañcadvārikacittānaṃ aviññattijanakattā. Manodvāre pana hāsuppādanaṃ. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pañcadvāre “somanassito hotī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 568) ettakameva vuttaṃ, manodvāre ca “hāsayamāna”nti. Idha pana “hasituppādakiccā”ti avisesavacanaṃ pañcadvāre somanassakaraṇavasena pavattassapi manodvāre hāsajananassa paccayabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Hasituppādakiccāti hasitasseva uppādanakiccā. Teneva hi taṃ “hasituppāda”nti vuccati, na pana aññesaṃ hasituppādacittānaṃ abhāvato. Tathā hi vakkhati “kusalato catūhī”tiādi.

At the mind-door, however, it should be understood that a smile is produced in relation to the six types of objects: in the five present objects as previously mentioned, such as in the Ghaṭikāra Sutta; in a past object fully understood through the Blessed One's knowledge of past lives; and in a future object discerned through the knowledge of the future, such as in passages like the statement, “There will be a Paccekabuddha named Aṭṭhissaro.” But is it not said that regarding past matters, etc., there is unobstructed knowledge, and that “for the Blessed One, the Buddha, endowed with these three qualities, all bodily action is preceded by knowledge and occurs in conformity with knowledge”? Given that this smile-producing consciousness is devoid of analytical wisdom, how could its arising in the Blessed One be justified? Even when the Blessed One's act of smiling occurs by means of the smile-producing consciousness, it still occurs in conformity with knowledge, as it is subsequent to the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of the future, and omniscient knowledge. Thus, when it occurs in conformity with knowledge, there is no contradiction with the Pāli canon. And so, the commentary states, “This consciousness arises at the completion of the exercise of those knowledges.” And this must necessarily be accepted as such, for otherwise, the arising in the Blessed One of any other rootless consciousness that produces intimation would not be justified. For the fact that a consciousness produces intimation does not preclude the intimation produced by it from becoming bodily action, and so on. And so, at the five sense-doors, only the production of joy by this consciousness should be understood, not the production of a smile, because five-door consciousnesses do not generate intimation. At the mind-door, however, a smile is produced. For this reason, the commentary mentions only “he is joyful” in the context of the five sense-doors, whereas at the mind-door, it says “smiling.” Here, however, the general statement “has the function of producing a smile” should be understood as referring to the fact that even though it occurs by way of producing joy at the five sense-doors, it is a condition for generating a smile at the mind-door. “Has the function of producing a smile” means it has the function of producing a smile itself. Hence, it is called “smile-producing,” not because other smile-producing consciousnesses are absent. As it will be said: “From the wholesome, four...” and so on.

Cha asādhāraṇañāṇānīti āsayānusayañāṇaṃ, indriyaparopariyañāṇaṃ, yamakapāṭihāriyañāṇaṃ, mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇaṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, anāvaraṇañāṇanti imāni cha paccekabuddhādīhi asādhāraṇāni ñāṇāni. Nanu ca sabbaññutaññāṇameva anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ, itarathā sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇānaṃ asabbaññutasāvaraṇañāṇatā ca āpajjeyya, tathā hi yadi sabbaññutaññāṇato aññamanāvaraṇañāṇaṃ siyā, tassa sāvaraṇattā sāvaraṇe ca visaye sabhāvapaṭivedhābhāvato sabbaññubhāvaṃ na sijjheyya, anāvaraṇañāṇassa ca asabbadhammārammaṇabhāvena yattha taṃ na pavattati, tatthāvaraṇasambhavato anāvaraṇabhāvopi na [M 1.0279] siyāti? Saccametaṃ, ekameva taṃ ñāṇaṃ anavasesasaṅkhatāsaṅkhatasammutidhammavisayattā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tattha ca āvaraṇābhāvato nissaṅgavāramupādāya anāvaraṇañāṇanti evaṃ visayapavattibhedena aññehi asādhāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ dvedhā vuttanti. Yathāha –

The six uncommon knowledges are: knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies, knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties, knowledge of the twin miracle, knowledge of the attainment of great compassion, omniscient knowledge, and unobstructed knowledge. These six knowledges are uncommon, not shared with Paccekabuddhas and others. But is not omniscient knowledge itself unobstructed knowledge? Otherwise, omniscient knowledge and unobstructed knowledge would become non-omniscient and obstructed knowledge respectively. For if unobstructed knowledge were different from omniscient knowledge, then due to the latter being obstructed, and because of the absence of direct penetration of an obstructed object, omniscience could not be achieved. And since unobstructed knowledge would not have all phenomena as its object, wherever it does not operate, obstruction would be possible, thus its unobstructed nature would not be possible. This is true. That knowledge is indeed one—omniscient knowledge—because its object encompasses all conditioned, unconditioned, and conventional phenomena without exception. And due to the absence of obstruction therein, and taking into account its freedom from barriers, it is called unobstructed knowledge. Thus, to show that it is uncommon in relation to others, it is spoken of as two based on the difference in its range of operation. As it is said—

“Sabbaṃ saṅkhatamasaṅkhataṃ anavasesaṃ jānātīti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tattha āvaraṇaṃ natthīti anāvaraṇañāṇa”ntiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.119).

"Knowing all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena without exception is the knowledge of omniscience. There is no obstruction in that—this is unobstructed knowledge," and so on (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.119).

Idha ṭhatvāti hasitassa uppādanato hasitassa uppādananti vuttacittassa āgataṭṭhāne ṭhatvā. Pariggaṇhitabbānīti paricchinditvā gaṇhitabbāni. Kiñcāpi rūpāvacarakiriyānaṃ jhānaṅgappahānaṃ vipāke viya āgamanato ahutvā kusale viya bhāvanāvisesena pavattākāramattaṃva [V 1.0223] hoti, paṭhamajjhānassa pana pahānaṅgasambhavābhāvato ekassa vaseneva niddisituṃ sesānampi pahānaṅgaṃ avatvā sampayogaṅgameva tesu dassitanti.

Here, 'standing' (ṭhatvā) means standing at the place of origin of the consciousness called 'the arising of laughter'. 'They should be grasped' (pariggaṇhitabbāni) means they should be discerned (paricchinditvā) and grasped (gaṇhitabbāni). Although the relinquishment of jhāna factors in form-sphere functional consciousness is merely a mode of occurrence by way of a distinction in development, as in wholesome consciousness, and not a coming into being as in resultants, yet because there is no possibility of factors to be abandoned in the first jhāna, in order to indicate it by way of one factor, and for the others, without mentioning factors of abandonment, only the associated factors are shown.

57. Yasmā pana bhāvanāvasena pavattākāramattaṃ vinā bhāvanāya kātabbassa nīvaraṇappahānādikiccassa abhāvato ujukaṃ bhāvanā nāma na hoti, tasmā “bhāvanākāravasappavattānī”ti ākāra-ggahaṇaṃ katanti.

57. But since, because there is no task to be performed by meditation—such as abandoning the hindrances—there is no such thing as direct meditation apart from its being merely a mode of occurrence by way of meditation, therefore the word 'mode' (ākāra) is included in the phrase 'occurring by way of the mode of meditation' (bhāvanākāravasappavattānī).

58-9. Nanti taṃ yathāvuttarūpārūpasamāpattiṃ. Samāpannā sace kriyāti ettha kiñcāpi sā eva samāpatti samāpajjituṃ na sakkā, niruddhānaṃ anuppannato, paṭiladdhasamāpattikasseva samāpajjitukāmatāya saddhiṃyeva samāpajjanato, paṭhamajjhānādikameva paṭilabhitvā dutiyajjhānādikaṃ samāpajjituṃ asakkuṇeyyabhāvato ca, pubbe paṭiladdhasamāpattisadisaṃ puna samāpajjanato puthujjanakālasmiṃ abhinibbattitasamāpattisadisā ettha sā eva tathā vuttā.

58-59. 'That' (naṃ) refers to that attainment of form and formless states as described. Here, in 'if, having attained, one performs an action' (samāpannā sace kriyā), although that same attainment cannot be attained again—because what has ceased does not arise, and because one attains it only when one has already obtained the attainment, together with the desire to attain it, and because it is impossible to attain the second jhāna and so on without having first attained the first jhāna and so on—yet because one attains again an attainment similar to what was previously attained, here it is spoken of as that very same attainment, similar to one that arose in the time of an ordinary person.

61. Ekacittakkhaṇattāti [M 1.0280] ekacittakkhaṇeyeva pavattanato. Yadi hi so punappunaṃ uppajjeyya, tadāssa arahato uppattiyā kiriyabhāvo icchitabbo siyā. Sakiṃyeva pana pavattati catusaccapaṭivedhakiccassa ekavāreneva pariniṭṭhānato, takkiccena ca vinā tassa anupalabbhanīyattā. Tenāha – “na pāraṃ diguṇaṃ yantī”ti (su. ni. 719), tasmā natthi lokuttaraṃ kiriyacittanti ayamettha adhippāyo.

61. 'Because of a single mind-moment' (ekacittakkhaṇattā) means because it occurs in just a single mind-moment. For if it were to arise repeatedly, then it would be necessary to accept that its arising for an Arahant is a functional state. But it occurs only once, because the function of penetrating the four truths is completed in a single instance, and because without that function it cannot be apprehended. Therefore it is said: 'They do not go to the further shore a second time' (Snp. 719). Therefore, there is no supramundane functional consciousness—this is the meaning here.

62. Kriyā…pe… desakoti yā āpattiyo kāyavācāhi akātabbaṃ katvā āpajjati, tā kiriyā, yā pana āpattiyo kāyavācāhi kātabbaṃ akaronto āpajjati, tā akiriyā, kiriyā ca akiriyā cāti kiriyākiriyā, kiriyākiriyā ca tā āpajjitabbato āpattiyo cāti kiriyākiriyāpattiyo, tāsaṃ vibhāgaṃ desetīti kiriyā…pe… desako. Atha vā kiriyājhānabhūtā samāpattiyo kiriyāpattiyo, kusalabhūtā pana samāpattiyo akiriyāpattiyo, tāsaṃ vibhāgaṃ desetīti kriyā…pe… desako. Yaṃ kiriyākiriyaṃ cittanti sambandho. Pañcannaṃ mārānaṃ jitattā jino. Hitāhitānanti atthānatthānaṃ. Sāti so jino. Kriyākriyāratoti sabbasattānaṃ hitassa karaṇe, ahitassa ca akaraṇe nirato. Atha vā ekantamiṭṭhavipākattā hitāti kusalānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ[V 1.0224]. Tappaṭipakkhattā ahitāti akusalānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathākkamaṃ tesaṃ kiriyāyaṃ, akiriyāyañca ratoti hitāhitānaṃ…pe… rato. Atha vā hitāhitāti kusalākusalā eva, tesaṃ kiriyākiriyāmattamavipākabhāvaṃ kātuṃ icchatīti hitāhitānaṃ…pe… rato. Atha vā hitāhitānaṃ puggalānaṃ sakiriyākiriyāya attano attano kiccassa idhalokaparalokanipphādanassa [M 1.0281] karaṇe rato abhiratoti hitāhitānaṃ…pe… rato.

62. Action... and so on... the expounder (desako): The offenses that one commits by doing with body or speech what should not be done are actions (kiriyā); whereas the offenses one commits by not doing with body or speech what should be done are inactions (akiriyā). Actions and inactions are action-inaction (kiriyākiriyā), and since they are offenses to be committed, they are action-inaction offenses (kiriyākiriyāpattiyo). One who explains their classification is the expounder of action... and so on. Alternatively, the attainments that are functional jhānas are action-attainments (kiriyāpattiyo); whereas the attainments that are wholesome are inaction-attainments (akiriyāpattiyo). One who explains their classification is the expounder of action... and so on. The connection is: 'Whatever is action-inaction consciousness.' The Conqueror (Jina) is so called because he has conquered the five Māras. 'Beneficial and harmful' (hitāhitānaṃ) means what is beneficial and what is not. 'That' (sā) refers to that Conqueror. 'Delighting in action and inaction' (kiriyākriyārato) means he delights in doing what is beneficial for all beings and not doing what is harmful. Alternatively, because it is entirely pleasant in result, 'beneficial' is a term for the wholesome. Its opposite, 'harmful,' is a term for the unwholesome. In order, he delights in their action and inaction respectively—thus, 'delighting in the beneficial and harmful'... and so on. Alternatively, 'beneficial and harmful' refers simply to the wholesome and unwholesome. He wishes to make their action and inaction a mere non-resultant state—thus, 'delighting in the beneficial and harmful'... and so on. Alternatively, he delights and rejoices in the action and inaction of beneficial and harmful individuals, each performing their own duties to accomplish the aims of this world and the next—thus, 'delighting in the beneficial and harmful'... and so on.

64-6. Sabbe lokuttare aṭṭha katvā ye ekūnanavuti cittuppādā vuttā, tāni cittāni mayā niddiṭṭhānīti sambandho. Pāṭavaṃ atthenti patthenti, pāṭavasaṅkhāto vā attho etesanti pāṭavatthino. Uggahetabboti savanapaṭipucchāvasena uggahitabbo, uggaṇhitvā pana na kevalaṃ uggahaṇamatteyeva ṭhātabbanti dassento āha “cintetabbo punappuna”nti, na hi sakkā uggahaṇamattenevettha sabbathā sanniṭṭhānaṃ gantunti adhippāyo. Abhidhammamahodadhinti dhammasaṅgaṇīādisattappakaraṇavasena ṭhitamabhidhammapiṭakamahaṇṇavaṃ, khandhāyatanādivasena ṭhitaṃ paramatthamahaṇṇavaṃ vā. Tarantīti atthaggahaṇavasena uttaranti, sutamayañāṇamūlakena vā bhāvanāñāṇena otarantīti attho. Imaṃ lokanti paccuppannabhavaṃ. Paraṃ lokanti anāgatabhavaṃ. Tarantīti atikkamanti. Idha lokasmiñhi chandarāgappahānavasena imaṃ lokaṃ taranti, āyatiṃ bhavūpapādakassa kammassa kammakkhayakarañāṇena vināsanato paralokaṃ taranti, anupādāparinibbānavasena parinibbāyantīti attho.

64-6. The connection is: 'Making all the supramundane types of consciousness eight, the eighty-nine productions of consciousness that have been mentioned—these states of mind have been explained by me.' 'They seek proficiency' (pāṭavaṃ atthenti), 'they desire it' (patthenti)—or, those for whom proficiency is the goal are 'intent on proficiency' (pāṭavatthino). 'It should be learned' (uggahetabbo) means it should be grasped through listening and questioning. But having grasped it, one should not stop at mere grasping—indicating this, he says, 'it should be reflected upon again and again.' For it is not possible here to reach complete certainty through mere grasping alone—this is the intention. 'The great ocean of Abhidhamma' (Abhidhammamahodadhiṃ) means the great ocean of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, established through the seven texts beginning with the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, or the great ocean of ultimate meaning, established through aggregates, sense-bases, and so on. 'They cross' (taranti) means they transcend by grasping the meaning, or they penetrate it through the knowledge of meditation which is rooted in the knowledge of learning—this is the meaning. 'This world' (imaṃ lokaṃ) means the present existence. 'The other world' (paraṃ lokaṃ) means future existence. 'They cross' (taranti) means they go beyond. For here in this world, they cross this world by abandoning desire and lust. They cross the other world by destroying the kamma that produces future rebirth by means of the knowledge that brings about the cessation of kamma—they attain final Nibbāna without clinging—this is the meaning.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus in the work named the Abhidhammattha-vikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the Commentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma,

Cittaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the commentary on the exposition of consciousness is completed.

2. Dutiyo paricchedo

2. The Second Chapter

Cetasikaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Mental Factors

67. Ettāvatā [V 1.0225] ca cittaṃ cetasikaṃ rūpaṃ nibbānanti evaṃ uddiṭṭhesu catūsu dhammesu cittaṃ tāva jātibhūmisampayogappavattākārādivasena vibhāgena niddisitvā idāni tadanantaraṃ uddiṭṭhe [M 1.0282] cetasikadhamme niddisituṃ “cittānantaramuddiṭṭhā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Vibhājananti jātibhūmiādivasena vibhāgaṃ, tesu tesu cittesu yathārahaṃ sampayogavasena visuṃ visuṃ bhājanañca.

67. Thus far, among the four phenomena mentioned—namely, mind, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna—having first delineated the mind by way of classification according to origin, plane, association, modes of occurrence, and other aspects, now, in order to delineate the mental factors mentioned immediately thereafter, the passage beginning "mentioned immediately following the mind" is introduced. "Classification" refers to the division by origin, plane, and so forth, as well as the distinct allocation of each according to its appropriate association with various types of consciousness.

Katame pana cetasikā, yesaṃ vibhājanaṃ vuccatīti te saha nibbacanena sarūpato dassetuṃ “tattha cittasampayuttā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “cittasampayuttā”ti idaṃ cetasikalakkhaṇadassanaṃ. Tena ye cittena saha sampayogalakkhaṇena yuttā, teyeva cetasikāti dasseti. Kiṃ pana taṃ sampayogalakkhaṇanti? Ekuppādaekanirodhaekavatthukaekārammaṇasaṅkhātā pakārā. Samaṃ pakārehi yuttāti hi sampayuttā. Tattha yadi ekuppādatāmatteneva ca sampayuttatā adhippetā, sahuppattikānaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ aññamaññasampayuttatā āpajjeyyāti ekanirodha-ggahaṇaṃ. Evampi avinibbhogarūpānaṃ aññamaññasampayuttatā āpajjeyyāti ekavatthuka-ggahaṇaṃ. Evampi “avinibbhogarūpesu ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ sesamahābhūtopādārūpānaṃ nissayapaccayo hotīti tasmā tāni ekavatthukānīti, cakkhādīnaṃ nissayabhūtāni vā bhūtāni ekaṃ vatthu etesu nissitanti ekavatthukānī”ti kappentassa tesaṃ sampayuttatāpatti siyāti tannivāraṇatthaṃ ekārammaṇa-ggahaṇaṃ.

And what are the mental factors, whose classification is being discussed? To show them together with their etymology and intrinsic nature, it is said, "Herein, those associated with consciousness," etc. Herein, "those associated with consciousness" is a statement showing the characteristic of mental factors. By this, it indicates that only those which are conjoined by the characteristic of association with consciousness are mental factors. But what is that characteristic of association? It is the modes designated as having a single arising, a single cessation, a single base, and a single object. For those conjoined by the same modes are indeed associated. Here, if association were intended as mere single arising, then co-arising material and immaterial phenomena would be associated with each other—hence the inclusion of single cessation. Even so, inseparable material phenomena would be associated with each other—hence the inclusion of single base. Even so, for one who imagines that "among inseparable material phenomena, one great element is the support condition for the other great elements and derived material phenomena; therefore, they have a single base," or that "the material bases, which serve as supports for the eye, etc., have a single base because these depend on them," there could be an attribution of association to them—hence the inclusion of single object to prevent that.

Paṭilomato vā “ekārammaṇā”ti vutte ekavīthiyaṃ pañcaviññāṇasampaṭicchanādīnaṃ, nānāvīthiyaṃ parasantāne ca ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe uppajjamānānaṃ bhinnavatthukānaṃ sampayuttatā āpajjeyyāti ekavatthuka-ggahaṇaṃ. Evampi maraṇāsannavīthiyaṃ sampaṭicchanasantīraṇādīnaṃ sampayuttatā āpajjeyyāti ekanirodha-ggahaṇaṃ. Kiṃ pana nānuppādāpi evaṃ tividhalakkhaṇā honti[V 1.0226], atha ekuppādā evāti vicāraṇāya ekuppādā [M 1.0283] eva evaṃ tividhalakkhaṇā hontīti dassanatthaṃ “ekuppādā”ti vuttaṃ. Iti imehi catūhi sampayogalakkhaṇehi ye cittasampayuttā, te cetasikā nāmāti evaṃ cetasikalakkhaṇaṃ ṭhapitaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ panete cetasikā nāmāti āha “citte bhavā”ti. “Cetasi bhavā cetasikā”ti vattabbe citta-saddassapi ceto-saddena saha samānatthatāya atthamattaṃ dassetuṃ “citte bhavā cetasikā”ti vuttaṃ.

Or, conversely, if it were stated as 'having a single object,' then in a single cognitive process, the five sense consciousnesses, the receiving consciousness, etc., and in different cognitive processes, those arising in another's mind-stream with a single object, could be considered associated even though their bases differ—thus, the inclusion of 'having a single basis.' Similarly, in the cognitive process near death, the receiving consciousness, the investigating consciousness, etc., could be considered associated—thus, the inclusion of 'having a single cessation.' But do phenomena with separate arisings also possess these three characteristics, or only those with a single arising? To show that only those with a single arising possess these three characteristics, it is stated, 'having a single arising.' Thus, through these four characteristics of association, whatever is associated with consciousness is called a mental factor; in this way, the characteristic of mental factors is established. But how are these called mental factors? It is said: 'Existing in consciousness.' Though it should be said, 'Existing in cetas, hence cetasikā (mental factors),' because the word citta shares the same meaning as the word ceto, to show the meaning alone, it is stated: 'Existing in consciousness, hence mental factors.'

Niyatāti niyatuppattikā, karuṇāmuditādayo viya kadāci anuppajjitvā yadā yadā taṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, tadā tadāva tena avinibhuttā hutvā jāyamānāti attho. Sarūpena āgatāti chandādayo viya “ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye aññepi atthi paṭiccasamuppannā arūpino dhammā”ti evaṃ yevāpanakavasena anāgantvā “phasso hoti, vedanā hotī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1) sarūpeneva pāḷiyaṃ āgatā. Yevāpanāti evaṃ desanā etesanti yevāpanakā. Ekūnatiṃsa dhammāti kiccabhedaṃ anāmasitvā kevalaṃ asambhinnadhammavaseneva ekenūnā tiṃsa dhammā. Pāḷiyaṃ pana cittena saha tiṃsa dhamme gahetvā tesaṃ kiccabhedato gahaṇena chappaññāsa dhammā vuttā. Seyyathidanti sarūpapucchā. Phasso…pe… cittujukatāti yathāpucchitānaṃ sarūpadassanaṃ. Iti-saddo parisamāpane, nidassane vā. Puna tettiṃsa hontīti sambandho. Tettiṃsa hontīti teyeva ekūnatiṃsa dhammāti adhippāyo.

'Fixed' means having a fixed arising; the meaning is that, unlike compassion, joy, and so on, which sometimes do not arise, these arise inseparably from that consciousness whenever it arises. 'Appearing in their own form' refers to those which, unlike desire, etc., do not appear by way of the inclusive phrase 'whatever other dependently arisen, immaterial phenomena there are at that time,' but appear in the Pāli in their own form, such as 'there is contact, there is feeling,' and so on. Yevāpanaka means 'those for whom the teaching is thus.' 'Twenty-nine phenomena' refers to twenty-nine phenomena counted without considering their functional differences, solely based on their undivided nature. In the Pāli, however, by taking thirty phenomena together with consciousness and considering their functional differences, fifty-six phenomena are stated. 'What are they?' is a question about their intrinsic nature. 'Contact... mental uprightness' shows the intrinsic nature of what was asked. The word iti serves for conclusion or for illustration. 'Again, they become thirty-three' is the connection. 'They become thirty-three' means those same twenty-nine phenomena are intended.

“Kadāci uppajjantī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ kathaṃ daṭṭhabbanti āha “imesū”tiādi. Karuṇāmuditāvasenāti paṭhamasamannāhārato paṭṭhāya gotrabhupariyosānappavattitakaruṇāmuditāparikammavasena. Karuṇāpubbabhāgoti karuṇāya [M 1.0284] pubbabhāgo, parikammappanāvasena pavattakaruṇābhāvanāya appanākoṭṭhāsato purimakoṭṭhāso, paṭhamasamannāhārato paṭṭhāya gotrabhupariyosānappavattaparikammakoṭṭhāso hutvāti attho. Evaṃ “muditāpubbabhāgo”ti etthāpi. Bhāga-saddassa drabyavuttitāya tappurisassa ca uttarapadatthappadhānatāya “karuṇāpubbabhāgo”tiādinā pulliṅgena vuttaṃ. Eta-saddassa pana guṇavuttitāya guṇavisesavati vattamāno tassa liṅgavasena pariṇamatīti karuṇāmuditāpekkhāya “etā”ti itthiliṅgavasena vuttanti. Na panekato uppajjanti, kiñcarahi visuṃ visuṃyevāti attho. Teneva hi “karuṇāpubbabhāgo vā muditāpubbabhāgo vā”ti vikappo vuttoti. Kasmā panetā dve ekato nuppajjantīti? Bhinnārammaṇattā. Karuṇā hi dukkhitasatte ārabbha tesaṃ dukkhāpanayanakāmatāvasena pavattati, muditā [V 1.0227] sukhitasatte ārabbha tesaṃ sukhānumodanavasena, tasmā ubhinnampi bhinnavisayattā na ekasmiṃ citte uppatti sambhavatīti. Micchākammantādīhīti ādi-saddena micchāvācāmicchājīvānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Sammākammantādīni paripūrentīti sammākammantasammāvācāsammāājīvāni paripūrenti. Ko viratīti tīsu ekā virati uppajjati, sammākammantaṃ pūrentī paṭhamā, sammāvācaṃ pūrentī dutiyā, sammāājīvaṃ pūrentī tatiyā virati uppajjatīti attho. Karuṇāmuditāhi saha na uppajjanti tāsaṃ paññattārammaṇattā, viratiyā ca ekantaparittārammaṇattā. Aññamaññena ca na uppajjanti aññamaññassapi bhinnavisayattā. Micchākammantādīnañhi ārammaṇāneva yathākkamaṃ sammākammantādīnaṃ ārammaṇāni tato viratibhāvato. Etesūti imesu pañcasu.

It is said, 'Sometimes they arise'—how should this be understood? It is explained with 'among these' and so on. 'By way of compassion and sympathetic joy' means by way of the preliminary work for compassion and sympathetic joy, occurring from the initial application up to the change-of-lineage. 'The preliminary part of compassion' means the part prior to compassion; it is the part prior to the absorption section in the development of compassion that proceeds by way of preliminary work and absorption; the meaning is that it is the preliminary work section occurring from the initial application up to the change-of-lineage. Similarly in the case of 'the preliminary part of sympathetic joy.' Because the word 'part' (bhāga) denotes a substance and a tappurisa compound emphasizes the meaning of the latter term, 'the preliminary part of compassion,' etc., is stated in the masculine gender. But since the word 'this' (eta) denotes a quality, when referring to something possessing a specific quality, it conforms to its gender; thus, with reference to compassion and sympathetic joy, 'these' (etā) is stated in the feminine gender. They do not, however, arise together; rather, the meaning is that they arise quite separately. For that very reason, the alternative 'either the preliminary part of compassion or the preliminary part of sympathetic joy' is stated. But why do these two not arise together? Because they have different objects. For compassion occurs with regard to suffering beings, by way of the desire to remove their suffering; sympathetic joy occurs with regard to happy beings, by way of rejoicing in their happiness. Therefore, since the objects of both are different, their arising in a single consciousness is not possible. 'From wrong conduct, etc.': by 'etc.' wrong speech and wrong livelihood are included. 'They perfect right conduct, etc.' means they perfect right conduct, right speech, and right livelihood. 'As to which abstinence': one of the three abstinences arises; the meaning is that the first abstinence arises, perfecting right conduct; the second arises, perfecting right speech; the third abstinence arises, perfecting right livelihood. They do not arise together with compassion and sympathetic joy because the latter have a concept as object, while an abstinence has an exclusively limited-sphere object. And they do not arise with one another because their objects are also different from one another. For the objects of wrong conduct, etc., are respectively the objects of right conduct, etc., due to the state of abstaining from them. 'Among these' means among these five.

68. Viratīnampi [M 1.0285] saṅgahaṇatthaṃ “karuṇāmuditādīsū”ti vattabbe gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ ādi-saddalopavasena “karuṇāmuditāsū”ti vuttaṃ. Evañca katvā vuttaṃ “ekenā”ti, itarathā “ekāyā”ti vattabbanti.

68. Although, for the sake of including the abstinences, it should be stated as karuṇāmuditādīsū, for the sake of metrical ease in the verse, it is stated as karuṇāmuditāsū by omitting the word ādi. And having done so, it is said ekenā; otherwise, it should be said ekāyā.

69-71. Kiṃ panettha kāraṇaṃ, catūsu brahmavihāresu dve idha niddiṭṭhā, na itarāti codento āha “kasmā panā”tiādi. Upekkhā ca na uddhaṭāti sambandho. Navahi lokuttaradhammehi janaṃ rañjetīti dhammarājā. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthehi sadevakaṃ lokaṃ anusāsatīti satthā. Abyāpādena mettā gahitā tasseva hitākārappavattikāle mettābhāvūpagamanato. Teneva hesa “mettā mettāyanā”tiādinā niddiṭṭho. Tatramajjhattatāya upekkhā gahitā tāyeva sattesu majjhattākārappavattāya upekkhābrahmavihārabhāvato. Ādiccena saha samānagottatāya, ariyasāvakabhāvena vā tassa bhagavato puttatāya ādicco bandhu imassa, ādiccassa vā bandhūti ādiccabandhu.

69-71. Raising an objection, one asks, 'What is the reason here that, among the four divine abodes, two are specified and not the others?' saying, 'But why?' and so on. The connection is: 'And equanimity is not excluded.' He delights beings with the nine supramundane states; therefore, he is the King of Dhamma. He instructs the world with its devas regarding benefits in this life and the next; therefore, he is the Teacher. Loving-kindness is included under non-ill will, because one attains the state of loving-kindness precisely when one acts for another's welfare. For that reason, it is indicated by 'loving-kindness, the practice of loving-kindness,' and so on. Equanimity is included under impartiality, because it is by acting impartially towards beings that it becomes the divine abode of equanimity. Because of sharing the same lineage as the sun, or because of being a noble disciple and thus a son of the Blessed One, the sun is his kinsman, or he is a kinsman of the sun; hence, he is the 'Kinsman of the Sun.'

72. Rāsinti phassapañcakādisattarasarāsiṃ. Paṭhamamahācittuppādavasena hi –

72. 'Heaps' means the seventeen heaps beginning with the fivefold group of contact. For, by way of the first great arising of consciousness—

“Phasso hoti, vedanā hoti, saññā hoti, cetanā hoti, cittaṃ hoti, vitakko hoti, vicāro hoti, pīti hoti, sukhaṃ hoti, cittassekaggatā hoti, saddhindriyaṃ hoti, vīriyindriyaṃ hoti, satindriyaṃ hoti, samādhindriyaṃ hoti, paññindriyaṃ [V 1.0228] hoti, manindriyaṃ hoti, somanassindriyaṃ hoti, jīvitindriyaṃ hoti, sammādiṭṭhi hoti, sammāsaṅkappo hoti, sammāvāyāmo hoti, sammāsati hoti, sammāsamādhi hoti, saddhābalaṃ hoti, vīriyabalaṃ hoti, satibalaṃ hoti[M 1.0286], samādhibalaṃ hoti, paññābalaṃ hoti, hiribalaṃ hoti, ottappabalaṃ hoti, alobho hoti, adoso hoti, amoho hoti, anabhijjhā hoti, abyāpādo hoti, sammādiṭṭhi hoti, hirī hoti, ottappaṃ hoti, kāyapassaddhi hoti, cittapassaddhi hoti, kāyalahutā hoti, cittalahutā hoti, kāyamudutā hoti, cittamudutā hoti, kāyakammaññatā hoti, cittakammaññatā hoti, kāyapāguññatā hoti, cittapāguññatā hoti, kāyujukatā hoti, cittujukatā hoti, sati hoti, sampajaññaṃ hoti, samatho hoti, vipassanā hoti, paggāho hoti, avikkhepo hotī”ti (dha. sa. 1) –

There is contact, there is feeling, there is perception, there is volition, there is consciousness, there is initial application, there is sustained application, there is rapture, there is happiness, there is one-pointedness of mind; there is the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of mind, the faculty of gladness, the faculty of life; there is right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration; there is the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, the power of wisdom, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread; there is non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, non-covetousness, non-ill will, right view; there is moral shame, moral dread; there is tranquility of body, tranquility of mind, lightness of body, lightness of mind, pliancy of body, pliancy of mind, wieldiness of body, wieldiness of mind, proficiency of body, proficiency of mind, rectitude of body, rectitude of mind; there is mindfulness, clear comprehension, calm, insight, exertion, non-distraction. (Dhs. 1)

Evaṃ dhammuddhāraṃ karontena bhagavatā phassādayo tiṃsa dhamme chappaññāsa katvā phassapañcakarāsi jhānapañcakarāsi indriyaṭṭhakarāsi maggapañcakarāsi balasattakarāsi hetuttikarāsi kammapathatikarāsi lokapāladukarāsi chayugaḷadukarāsi upakāradukarāsi yuganandhadukarāsi vīriyasamathadukarāsīti sattarasannaṃ rāsīnaṃ vasena vibhāgo kato.

Thus, as the Blessed One was summarizing the Dhamma, he made the thirty phenomena beginning with contact into fifty-six, making a division by way of seventeen groups: the fivefold group of contact, the fivefold group of jhāna factors, the eightfold group of faculties, the fivefold group of path factors, the sevenfold group of powers, the threefold group of roots, the threefold group of courses of action, the pair of world-guardians, the group of six pairs, the pair of helpful qualities, the pair of conjoint qualities, and the pair of exertion and non-distraction.

Kathaṃ? Etesupi cittaṃ tāva phassapañcakaṃ patvā “cittaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ, indriyāni patvā “manindriya”nti. Vitakko jhānaṅgāni patvā “vitakko hotī”ti vutto, maggaṅgāni patvā “sammāsaṅkappo”ti. Saddhā indriyāni patvā “saddhindriyaṃ hotī”ti vuttā, balāni patvā “saddhābala”nti. Hirī balāni patvā “hiribalaṃ hotī”ti vuttā, lokapāladukaṃ patvā “hirī”ti. Ottappepi eseva nayo. Alobho mūlaṃ patvā “alobho hotī”ti vutto, kammapathaṃ patvā “anabhijjhā”ti. Adoso mūlaṃ patvā [M 1.0287] “adoso hotī”ti vutto, kammapathaṃ patvā “abyāpādo”ti. Ime satta dvīsu ṭhānesu vibhattā. Vedanā pana phassapañcakaṃ patvā “vedanā hotī”ti vuttā, jhānaṅgāni patvā “sukha”nti, indriyāni patvā “somanassindriya”nti. Evamayaṃ eko dhammo tīsu ṭhānesu vibhatto. Vīriyaṃ pana indriyāni patvā “vīriyindriyaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ, maggaṅgāni patvā “sammāvāyāmo”ti, balāni patvā “vīriyabala”nti, vīriyasamathaṃ patvā “paggāho”ti. Satipi indriyāni patvā “satindriyaṃ hotī”ti vuttā, maggaṅgāni patvā “sammāsatī”ti, balāni patvā “satibala”nti, upakāradukaṃ patvā “sati hotī”ti[V 1.0229]. Evaṃ ime dve dhammā catūsu ṭhānesu vibhattā. Samādhi pana jhānaṅgāni patvā “cittassekaggatā hotī”ti vutto, indriyāni patvā “samādhindriya”nti, maggaṅgāni patvā “sammāsamādhī”ti, balāni patvā “samādhibala”nti, yuganandhadukaṃ patvā “samatho”ti, vīriyasamathaṃ patvā “avikkhepo hotī”ti. Evamayaṃ eko dhammo chasu ṭhānesu vibhatto. Paññā pana indriyāni patvā “paññindriyaṃ hotī”ti vuttā, maggaṅgāni patvā “sammādiṭṭhī”ti, balāni patvā “paññābala”nti, mūlāni patvā “amoho”ti, kammapathaṃ patvā “sammādiṭṭhī”ti, upakāradukaṃ patvā “sampajañña”nti, yuganandhadukaṃ patvā “vipassanā”ti. Evamayaṃ eko dhammo sattasu ṭhānesu vibhattoti evamete dvādasa dhammā indriyāditaṃtaṃkiccavantatāya dviṭṭhānikādibhedena sattarasasu rāsīsu vibhattā. Itare aṭṭhārasa kiccavasena bhedābhāvato ekaṭṭhānikāyevāti imesu sattarasasu rāsīsu yevāpanakadhammā ekarāsimpi na bhajanti taṃtaṃkiccabhāvatoti katvā vuttaṃ “rāsiṃ bhajanti nā”ti.

How? Among these, consciousness, having reached the fivefold group of contact, is stated as “consciousness”; having reached the faculties, as “the faculty of mind.” Initial application, having reached the jhāna factors, is stated as “initial application”; having reached the path factors, as “right intention.” Faith, having reached the faculties, is stated as “the faculty of faith”; having reached the powers, as “the power of faith.” Moral shame, having reached the powers, is stated as “the power of moral shame”; having reached the pair of world-guardians, as “moral shame.” The same method applies to moral dread. Non-greed, having reached the roots, is stated as “non-greed”; having reached the courses of action, as “non-covetousness.” Non-hatred, having reached the roots, is stated as “non-hatred”; having reached the courses of action, as “non-ill will.” These seven are classified in two places. Feeling, however, having reached the fivefold group of contact, is stated as “feeling”; having reached the jhāna factors, as “happiness”; having reached the faculties, as “the faculty of gladness.” Thus, this one phenomenon is classified in three places. Energy, however, having reached the faculties, is stated as “the faculty of energy”; having reached the path factors, as “right effort”; having reached the powers, as “the power of energy”; having reached the pair of exertion and non-distraction, as “exertion.” Mindfulness, too, having reached the faculties, is stated as “the faculty of mindfulness”; having reached the path factors, as “right mindfulness”; having reached the powers, as “the power of mindfulness”; having reached the pair of helpful qualities, as “mindfulness.” Thus, these two phenomena are classified in four places. Concentration, however, having reached the jhāna factors, is stated as “one-pointedness of mind”; having reached the faculties, as “the faculty of concentration”; having reached the path factors, as “right concentration”; having reached the powers, as “the power of concentration”; having reached the pair of conjoint qualities, as “calm”; having reached the pair of exertion and non-distraction, as “non-distraction.” Thus, this one phenomenon is classified in six places. Wisdom, however, having reached the faculties, is stated as “the faculty of wisdom”; having reached the path factors, as “right view”; having reached the powers, as “the power of wisdom”; having reached the roots, as “non-delusion”; having reached the courses of action, as “right view”; having reached the pair of helpful qualities, as “clear comprehension”; having reached the pair of conjoint qualities, as “insight.” Thus, this one phenomenon is classified in seven places. In this way, these twelve phenomena are classified into seventeen groups by way of their having various functions, such as faculties, and by way of divisions into two places and so on. The remaining eighteen, however, due to the absence of difference in function, belong only to one place. Among these seventeen groups, the ‘appropriating phenomena’ (yevāpanaka-dhammā) do not share even a single group because of their respective functions. Thus, it is said, “they do not share a group.”

Nanu cete kiñcāpi sesarāsayo na bhajanti tesaṃ sadisakiccasaṅgahavasena ṭhitattā. Phassapañcakarāsi pana khandhasaṅgahavaseneva [M 1.0288] ṭhapitoti cetanāya viya nesaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahato tattha samavarodho yuttoti? Taṃ na, khandhasaṅgahavasena ṭhapitopi hi phassapañcakarāsi sabbacittasādhāraṇadhamme saṅgahetvā ṭhapitoti chandādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pakiṇṇakavasena uppajjamānānaṃ sabbacittasādhāraṇatāya abhāvato, manasikārassa ca satipi sabbacittasādhāraṇatte nippariyāyato saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahābhāvato na etesaṃ phassapañcakarāsibhajanampi yuttanti. Kasmā pana manasikārassa nippariyāyato saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahābhāvoti? Vuccate – ṭhapetvā cetanaṃ sesadhammānaṃ sakasakakiccesupi parādhīnabhāvena pavattanato abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ nippariyāyato na labbhati. Yadi labheyya, cittekaggatājīvitindriyānaṃ sabbacittasādhāraṇattā vedanāviññāṇāni viya tāni phassapañcake vattabbāni siyuṃ, na panevaṃ vuttā, tasmā ṭhapetvā cetanaṃ sesadhammānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ nippariyāyato na labbhatīti na tesaṃ nippariyāyato khandhasaṅgaho labbhati. Cetanāyayeva pana sakiccaparakiccasādhanavasena pavattanato nippariyāyato abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇassa atthitāya khandhasaṅgaho labbhatīti. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ phasso phassapañcake vuttoti? “Phassapaccayā vedanā (vibha. 225), phuṭṭho vedeti, phuṭṭho sañjānātī”tiādivacanato (saṃ. ni. 4.93) vedanā saññā cetanā viññāṇanti imesaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ uddesaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā tesaṃ paccayassapi uddisitukāmatāya phasso tattha vutto[V 1.0230]. Dubbalāti sakavisayepi parāyattabhāveneva pavattanato dubbalā. Adhimokkho hi samādhissa paribyattabhāve paribyattabhāvato samādhāyattavutti, manasikāropi cetanāya paribyattabhāvato cetanāyattavuttīti parāyattāva te honti.

But is it not so that although these remaining groups do not partake, they are established by way of inclusion with similar functions? And since the fivefold group of contact is established solely by way of inclusion in the aggregates, is it not fitting that they are included there just as volition is included in the aggregate of formations? That is not so. For even though the fivefold group of contact is established by way of inclusion in the aggregates, it is established by gathering the mental factors common to all consciousness. Since the three factors—desire and so forth—arise as particulars and are not common to every consciousness, and because attention, even though common to all consciousnesses, is not invariably included in the aggregate of formations, it is not fitting for these to partake in the fivefold group of contact either. But why is attention not invariably included in the aggregate of formations? It is said: because, apart from volition, the remaining factors operate dependently on others even in their own functions, the characteristic of forming is not invariably found in them. If it were found, then factors like one-pointedness of mind and the life faculty—being common to every consciousness—would have to be stated in the fivefold group of contact, just as feeling and consciousness are. But they are not stated thus. Therefore, apart from volition, the remaining factors do not possess the characteristic of forming invariably, and thus their invariable inclusion in the aggregates is not found. For volition alone, however, because it operates by way of accomplishing its own and others' functions, the inclusion in the aggregates is found due to its invariable possession of the characteristic of forming. If so, how is contact mentioned in the fivefold group of contact? Because of statements such as, “Feeling is conditioned by contact” (Vibhaṅga 225), and “One feels when touched, one perceives when touched” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.93), and because of the desire to also designate the condition for these immaterial aggregates—feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness—which stand in the place of designation, contact is mentioned there. They are weak because they operate with dependence on others even in their own domain. For decision, its occurrence is dependent on concentration because its manifestation is in the manifestation of concentration; and for attention, its occurrence is dependent on volition because its manifestation is from the manifestation of volition. Thus, they are indeed dependent on others.

73. Manasī [M 1.0289] ca kāroti manasikāro ca. Manasikārasaddassa hi atthamattasandassanavasena gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ asamāsaniddeso, dīghakaraṇaṃ, majjhe ca ca-saddavacananti. Tena munivarenāti sambandho.

73. And 'making in the mind' is attention. Indeed, for the purpose of showing merely the meaning of the word “manasikāra,” and for the sake of ease in composing the verse, the explanation is given without a compound, with a lengthened vowel, and with the word “ca” placed in the middle. Therefore, the connection is with “by that excellent sage.”

74-80. Paṭhamābhinipātattāti ārammaṇe phusanavasena paṭhamameva abhinipatanato. Sabbepi cetasikā cittāyattā cittakiriyabhāvena vuccantīti “cittassā”ti vuttaṃ. Kirāti arucisūcanaṃ. Evaṃ mahāsaṃghikamataṃ dassetvā idāni tameva vitthāretuṃ “phusitvā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Mahāsaṃghikā hi “paṭhamaṃ phasso ārammaṇaṃ phusati, atha tena phuṭṭhaṃ dutiyaṃ vedanā vediyati, evaṃ etehi phuṭṭhaveditaṃ tatiyaṃ saññā sañjānāti, tehi pana phuṭṭhaveditasaññāte catutthaṃ cetanāya sampayuttadhamme abhisandahatī”tiādinā vadanti. Balavapaccayattāti yathā pāsādaṃ patvā thambhā sesadabbasambhārānaṃ balavapaccayā, evamesa yasmā sesasampayuttānaṃ balavapaccayo, tasmāti attho. Tasmāti hetunigamanaṃ.

74-80. “Because it is the first to fall upon” means because of its falling upon the object first by way of touching. All mental factors are dependent on consciousness and are called “of consciousness” because they are spoken of as the activity of consciousness. The word “kira” indicates displeasure. Having thus presented the Mahāsaṅghika view, now, in order to elaborate on that very view, the passage beginning “having touched, then...” is stated. For the Mahāsaṅghikas say, “First, contact touches the object; then, what has been touched by that, feeling feels second; similarly, what has been touched and felt by these, perception perceives third; then, what has been touched, felt, and perceived by these, volition connects the associated phenomena fourth,” and so on. “Because it is a strong condition” means that just as in a palace the pillars are a strong condition for the remaining materials and supplies, so too this is a strong condition for the remaining associated factors—that is the meaning. The word “therefore” is a conclusion of the reason.

Saheva cāti ca-saddo aṭṭhānappayutto, so “cittajāna”nti imassa anantaraṃ daṭṭhabbo. Kasmā? Cittānaṃ, cittajānañca ekuppādādibhāvena saheva pavattitoti evamettha padasambandho veditabbo. Idanti idaṃ yathāvuttavidhānaṃ, evaṃ “paṭhamābhinipātattā”ti kāraṇaṃ pariharitvā idāni “balavapaccayattā”ti idaṃ pariharanto āha “balava…pe… dissatī”ti. Ca-saddo avadhāraṇe, neva dissatīti attho. Sesadhammānampi hi sahajātapaccayabhāvassa sādhāraṇattā tasseva balavapaccayabhāve na kiñci kāraṇaṃ dissatīti. Yadi sabbamidamakāraṇaṃ, kathañcarahi phasso paṭhamaṃ vuttoti āha “desanākkamato”tiādi. “Vedanā hoti, phasso [M 1.0290] hoti, saññā hoti, phasso hoti, cetanā hoti, phasso hoti, cittaṃ hoti, phasso hoti, vedanā hoti, saññā hoti, cetanā hoti, vitakko hotī”tiādīhi āharitumpi vaṭṭeyya, desanāvārena pana phassova paṭhamaṃ vuttoti veditabbo. Yathā cettha, evaṃ sesadhammesupi pubbāparakkamo [V 1.0231] nāma na pariyesitabbo. Vacanatthalakkhaṇādīhīti vacanatthato ca lakkhaṇādito ca.

And in 'saheva ca', the word 'ca' is misplaced; it should be understood as immediately following 'cittajānaṃ'. Why? Because minds and mind-born states occur together due to their simultaneous arising, etc., the connection of words here should be understood in this way. By 'this' is meant this method as stated. Having thus refuted the reason 'because it is the first to fall upon,' he now refutes 'because it is a strong condition,' saying, 'strong…pe… is seen.' The word 'ca' is for emphasis, meaning 'it is not seen at all.' For since the state of being a co-nascent condition is common to the other phenomena as well, no reason is seen for why it alone should be a strong condition. If all this is not a reason, then how is it that contact is mentioned first? He says, 'due to the sequence of teaching,' etc. Though it would be possible to cite passages like, 'There is feeling, there is contact; there is perception, there is contact; there is volition, there is contact; there is consciousness, there is contact; there is feeling, there is perception, there is volition, there is thought,' etc., it should be understood that contact is mentioned first in the order of the teaching. As it is here, so too in the case of other phenomena—a sequence of earlier and later should not be sought. By 'from the meaning of the word, characteristics, etc.' is meant from the meaning of the word and from its characteristics, and so on.

Phusatīti kattuniddeso. Tattha kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva, phusanti etena vāti phasso. Sampayuttadhammā hi ārammaṇe pavattamānā taṃ phusanalakkhaṇena phassena phusantā viya honti, ārammaṇaphusanamattaṃ vā phassotipi sādhanattayampi yujjateva. Phusanaṃ lakkhaṇametassāti phusanalakkhaṇo, vedanāya paccayabhāvaṭṭhena ārammaṇaphusanalakkhaṇoti attho. Saṃghaṭṭanarasoti manodvāre cittārammaṇānaṃ saṃghaṭṭanato saṃghaṭṭanakicco. Ayañhi ārammaṇe anallīyamānopi rūpaṃ viya cakkhuṃ, saddo viya ca sotaṃ cittamārammaṇañca ghaṭṭeti. Pañcadvāresu vā vatthārammaṇasaṃghaṭṭanena sampajjatīti saṃghaṭṭanasampattiko phasso “saṃghaṭṭanaraso”ti vutto. Yathā “dve pāṇī vajjeyyu”ntiādīsu pāṇimhi ghaṭṭanaṃ tabbisesabhūtā rūpadhammā, evaṃ cittassa ārammaṇe saṃghaṭṭanaṃ tabbisesabhūto eko cetasikadhammo daṭṭhabbo. Tiṇṇaṃ sannipātasaṅkhātassa attano kāraṇassa vasena paveditattā sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno. “Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”ti (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425; saṃ. ni 2.4.60; kathā. 465) hi vacanato cakkhurūpaviññāṇādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sannipātavasena gahetabbatāya upaṭṭhānato sannipātasaṅkhātassa kāraṇassa vasena upaṭṭhānamassāti upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena paccupaṭṭhānena sannipātapaccupaṭṭhānatā [M 1.0291] vuttā. “Phassapaccayā vedanā”ti (vibha. 225) vacanato vedanā phalamassāti vedanāpaccupaṭṭhāno. Tajjasamannāhārena ceva indriyena ca parikkhate visaye anantarāyeneva uppajjanato āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhāno. Ayañhi tassa phassassa kāraṇabhūto tadanurūpabhūto samannāhāroti tajjasamannāhārasaṅkhātena āvajjanena ceva cakkhādiindriyena ca yathākkamaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇatadabhimukhabhāvavasena parikkhate abhisaṅkhāte āpāthagateyeva visaye ekantena uppajjanato āpāthagato visayo padaṭṭhānaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ imassāti āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhāno.

The word 'phusati' is an agentive designation. The reason for this has been stated previously: 'They touch by means of this,' hence it is contact. For associated phenomena, when occurring in relation to an object, are as if touching it by means of contact, which has the characteristic of touching. Alternatively, the mere touching of the object is also contact; thus all three derivations are indeed applicable. Its characteristic is touching, hence it is 'characterized by touching.' By way of being a condition for feeling, it means 'characterized by touching the object.' Its function is impacting. In the mind-door, its function is impacting due to the collision of the mind and its object. For even without adhering to the object, it impacts the mind and the object, just as form impacts the eye or sound impacts the ear. Alternatively, in the five sense-doors, it is accomplished by the impacting of the base and the object; thus contact, which is accomplished by impacting, is said to have the function of impacting. Just as in phrases like 'two hands might strike,' the striking on the hand is a distinct material phenomenon, so too the impacting of the mind upon the object should be seen as a distinct mental phenomenon. Its manifestation is the meeting of three, because it is declared to arise by virtue of its cause, which is called the meeting of three. For according to the statement, 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact,' its manifestation is by way of its cause, called the meeting of three, because the three—eye, form, and consciousness—are to be understood as a meeting. Thus, its having the meeting of three as its manifestation is stated. According to the phrase, 'Dependent on contact, feeling arises,' feeling is its result, hence its manifestation is feeling. Its proximate cause is the object that has entered the range of the senses, because it arises without obstruction in a field prepared by appropriate attention and the sense faculty. For by the adverting called 'appropriate attention'—which is the cause of that contact and conforms to it—and by the faculties of the eye, etc., the object is prepared in due order by way of making it an object and facing towards it. Since contact arises exclusively in an object that has thus entered the range, the object that has entered the range is its proximate cause. Hence, its proximate cause is the object that has entered the range of the senses.

Nanu cāyaṃ dhammo cetasiko, svāyaṃ arūpadhammo samāno kathaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo hotīti antolīnacodanaṃ manasi katvā tassā sodhanatthaṃ “arūpadhammopi samāno”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “phusanākāreneva pavattatī”ti iminā arūpassāpi sato tassa dhammassa ayaṃ sabhāvoti dasseti. Sā ca tassa phusanākārappavatti ambilaṃ ambapakkādiṃ khādantaṃ passantassa parassa kheḷuppattiparaṃ [V 1.0232] bādhiyamānaṃ disvā dayālukassa sarīrakampanaṃ, rukkhasākhagge duṭṭhitaṃ purisaṃ disvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitassa purisassa jaṅghacalanaṃ, pisācādibhāyitabbaṃ disvā ūrupatthambhoti evamādi viya daṭṭhabbā. Soti so yathāvuttalakkhaṇādiko phasso.

But isn’t this phenomenon a mental concomitant? And being an immaterial phenomenon, how can it have the characteristic of contact? Having considered this implicit objection, to clarify it, the words 'even though it is an immaterial phenomenon,' etc., are stated. Here, by 'it occurs in the mode of contact,' it is shown that this is the nature of that phenomenon, even though it is immaterial. And that occurrence in the mode of contact should be understood through such examples as: the production of saliva in another person who sees someone eating a sour unripe mango; the trembling of the body of a compassionate person on seeing another being tormented; the shaking of the legs of a person standing on the ground on seeing a person perched precariously on a tree branch; and the stiffening of the thighs on seeing something to be feared, like a ghost. That is the contact which has the characteristics, etc., as described.

Sundaranti sukhavedanāsampayuttattā pasatthaṃ. Manoti viññāṇaṃ. Sumanassa bhāvoti sumanasaṅkhātassa viññāṇassa bhāvo. Yvāyaṃ saddappavattinibandhano attho, so somanassaṃ. Somanassavedanāsampayuttattā hi sumana-saddo tasmiṃ viññāṇe pavattati. Vedena anubhavanākārena [M 1.0292] ayitaṃ pavattaṃ vedayitaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇamassāti vedayitalakkhaṇā. Iṭṭhassa iṭṭhākāratova anubhavanaṃ kiccamassāti iṭṭhākārānubhavanarasā. Sā hi sabhāvato iṭṭhamārammaṇaṃ iṭṭhavasena, itarañca iṭṭhākāreneva anubhavati, tattha iṭṭhākārānubhavanaṃ kusalākusalacittasampayuttavedanāya labbhati tassā aniṭṭhassapi kappanāvasena iṭṭhākārena gahaṇato, sabhāvato pana iṭṭhānubhavanaṃ abyākatacittasampayuttāyapi labbhati tassā vipallāsaggāhābhāvato. “Rājā viya subhojanarasa”nti iminā imaṃ dīpeti – phassassa phusanamattameva hoti, saññāya sañjānanamattameva, cetanāya sañcetanāmattameva, viññāṇassa vijānanamattameva, ekaṃsato pana issaravatāya sāmibhāvena vedanāva ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavati, rājā viya sūdakārena sampāditasubhojanarasanti. Assādīyatīti assādo, sukhavedanā. Tenāha bhagavā – “yaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhesu assādo”ti. Cetosannissitattā cetasi bhavo assādoti cetasikaassādo, tathā paccupaṭṭhātīti cetasikaassādapaccupaṭṭhānā. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vediyatīti āha “passaddhipadaṭṭhānā”ti. Idaṃ pana nirāmisasomanassavasena veditabbaṃ.

By 'pleasant' is meant praised because it is associated with pleasant feeling. By 'mind' is meant consciousness. By 'state of being glad' is meant the state of consciousness called 'glad.' The meaning connected with the occurrence of the term 'glad' is gladness. For the term 'sumana' (glad) occurs in that consciousness because it is associated with the feeling of gladness. That which has arisen, occurred, and been experienced by way of feeling is 'vedayita' (felt); its characteristic is being felt. Its function is to experience what is agreeable in an agreeable manner. For by nature, it experiences an agreeable object as agreeable, and it also experiences other things in an agreeable manner. The experiencing of what is agreeable is found in feelings associated with wholesome and unwholesome consciousness because even the disagreeable is apprehended in an agreeable manner through conceptualization. But by nature, the experiencing of what is agreeable is also found in feelings associated with indeterminate consciousness because it is free from distorted apprehension. By 'like a king enjoying the taste of delicious food,' this is illustrated: contact is merely the act of touching, perception is merely the act of perceiving, volition is merely the act of intending, and consciousness is merely the act of cognizing. But in an absolute sense, feeling alone experiences the taste of the object with mastery, like a king enjoying the delicious food prepared by a cook. It is called gratification (assāda) because it is enjoyed; it is pleasant feeling. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, whatever pleasure and gladness arise dependent on the five aggregates subject to clinging, this, monks, is called gratification in the five aggregates subject to clinging.' Because it depends on the mind, it is called mental gratification, being a gratification that exists in the mind. Thus, it is manifested as mental gratification. Because it is said, 'One with a tranquil body experiences happiness,' it has tranquility as its proximate cause. This, however, should be understood as referring to gladness devoid of sensual pleasure.

Nīlādibhedassa ārammaṇassa sañjānanaṃ tameva saññaṃ katvā jānanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti sañjānanalakkhaṇā. Paccābhiññāṇakaraṇarasāti pati abhiññāyati etenāti paccābhiññāṇaṃ, tadevetanti puna paccābhiññāṇanimittaṃ saṇṭhānādiko ākāro, tassa karaṇaraso kiccamassāti paccābhiññāṇakaraṇarasā. Sā hi uppajjamānā pacchā sañjānanassa kāraṇabhūtaṃ saṇṭhānādikaṃ ākāraṃ gahetvā [M 1.0293] uppajjatīti. Idañca nimittakārikāya nimittena sañjānantiyā ca sabbāya samānasaññāya yojetabbaṃ. Nimittena sañjānantīpi hi puna aparāya saññāya ca sañjānanassa nimittaṃ karotīti. Tañca kusalākusalakiriyājavanasaññaṃ dhuraṃ [V 1.0233] katvā veditabbaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ abhiññāṇakaraṇaṃ kathaṃ daṭṭhabbanti āha “vaḍḍhakissa abhiññāṇakaraṇamivā”ti. Yathā vaḍḍhakissa dārūsu “idaṃ uddhaṃ, idaṃ adho”ti evaṃ pacchā sañjānanapaccayabhūtassa saññāṇassa karaṇaṃ, evamassā puna sañjānanapaccayanimittakaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Hatthidassakaandho viya “idameva sacca”nti saññāya yathāgahitanimittavasena abhinivesakaraṇato yathā…pe… paccupaṭṭhānā. Etena saññāya ākāraggahaṇaṃ katvā ṭhitassa diṭṭhiādīnaṃ uppajjanato akusalasaññāya anurūpavasena phalapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Atha vā abhinivesakaraṇanti “idameva sacca”nti saññābhinivesamattameva, tasmā upaparikkhābhāvena yathāgahitanimittavasena abhinivesākārena upaṭṭhānato ākārapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Tiṇapurisakesu migapotakānaṃ “purisā”ti uppannasaññā viya avikappasabhāvattā yathāupaṭṭhitavisayapadaṭṭhānā. Ettha ca ñāṇavippayuttasaññāya ākāraggahaṇavasena uppajjanakāle cittaṃ abbohārikaṃ saññānugatikaṃ hoti. Ñāṇasampayutte citte pana sasambhārapathaviyā anugatā sesadhātuyo viya saññācittañca abbohārikaṃ ñāṇānugatikaṃ hoti.

It has the characteristic of perceiving, which is the knowing of an object distinguished by blue, etc., by making that very perception. Its function is to effect re-cognition. One re-cognizes by means of it, thus it is re-cognition. Its function is to effect re-cognition because its task is to make the sign for repeated recognition—that is, the appearance such as shape—of that very thing. For when it arises, perception grasps the appearance, such as shape, which later becomes the cause for recognition. This should be connected with every perception that makes a sign and perceives by a sign, and with every similar perception. For even when perceiving by a sign, it also makes a sign for another perception to perceive. This should be understood with reference to the perception in wholesome, unwholesome, and functional javanas. But how should this effecting of re-cognition be seen? It is said, 'Like a carpenter's effecting of re-cognition.' Just as a carpenter makes a mark on wood, thinking, 'This is the top, this is the bottom,' which becomes a condition for later recognition, so it is said that perception makes a sign that is a condition for subsequent recognition. Its manifestation is... like a blind man who has seen an elephant, through adherence based on the sign as grasped, thinking, 'This alone is true.' By this, it is shown that for one who abides having grasped an appearance by means of perception, due to the arising of views and so forth, there is a manifestation as a result corresponding to unwholesome perception. Alternatively, 'effecting adherence' is merely the adherence of perception that 'This alone is true.' Therefore, due to the absence of investigation, its manifestation is said to be an appearance in the form of adherence based on the sign as grasped. Its proximate cause is the object as it has appeared, due to its non-discriminative nature, like the perception 'these are men' that arises in young deer regarding scarecrows. Here, when a perception dissociated from knowledge arises by way of grasping an appearance, the mind is non-discursive and follows perception. But in a mind associated with knowledge, just as the remaining elements follow the earth element with its components, so too perception and mind, being non-discursive, follow knowledge.

Abhisandahatīti pabandhati pavatteti, “gaṇhatha gaṇhathā”ti vadantī viya sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇe payojeti, sakasakakicce ca paṭṭhapetīti attho. Cetayitalakkhaṇāti niddokkantassa pabuddhakkhaṇe sambhamappavatti viya cetaso ussāhatāva [M 1.0294] lakkhaṇā. Atha vā “abhisandahatī”ti vuttattā payojanalakkhaṇātveva attho. Āyūhanarasāti cetasikairiyanarasā, payogarasāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kusalākusalakiriyājavanasampayuttāyayeva panetaṃ labbhati. Saṃvidahanapaccupaṭṭhānāti “tvaṃ idaṃ karohī”ti vicārentī viya hotīti vicāraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā. Etāya hi pavattamānāya sabbepi sampayuttadhammā yathā sakiccapasutā honti, teneva hesā sakiccaparakiccasādhikā vuttā. Jeṭṭhasisso pare sajjhāyane uyyojento sayampi sajjhāyati. Tasmiñhi sajjhāyituṃ āraddhe sesasissāpi sajjhāyanti. Mahāvaḍḍhakismimpi vaḍḍhakikammaṃ kātuṃ āraddhe itarepi karonti yevāti āha “jeṭṭhasissamahāvaḍḍhakiādayo viyā”ti. Ādi-saddena jeṭṭhantevāsikādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ.

It urges, it initiates, it sets in motion—just as one saying, "Take it, take it," directs associated states toward an object and establishes them in their respective functions: such is the meaning. The characteristic of volition is the mind's exertion, like the arising of agitation in one awakening from deep sleep. Or, because it is said to "urge," the meaning is simply its characteristic of application. Its function is striving—the function of mental activity; this means the function of effort. However, this is found only in association with wholesome, unwholesome, or functional javanas. Its manifestation is prompting—like one considering, "You do this"; thus its manifestation is deliberation. For when this arises, all associated states become engaged in their respective tasks, which is why it is called "the accomplisher of one's own and others' work." Just as the senior student, while urging others to recite, also recites himself—for when he begins reciting, the other students recite as well—or as when the master carpenter begins his work, the others also do theirs—thus it is said: "like the senior student, the master carpenter, and so on." The word "and so on" includes the senior apprentice and others.

Yathāpaccayaṃ pavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ natthi kāci vasavattitāti vasavattibhāvanivāraṇatthaṃ “vitakkanaṃ vitakko”ti vuttaṃ. Ūhanaṃ ārammaṇassa parikappanaṃ, tasmiṃ abhiniropananti vā vuttaṃ hoti. Yasmā cittaṃ vitakkabalena ārammaṇaṃ abhiruḷhaṃ viya hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “ārammaṇe [V 1.0234] cittassa abhiniropanalakkhaṇo”ti. Yathā hi koci gāmavāsī puriso rājavallabhaṃ, taṃsambandhinaṃ mittaṃ vā nissāya rājagehaṃ ārohati anupavisati, evaṃ vitakkaṃ nissāya cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ārohati. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ avitakkacittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ārohati, na hi dvipañcaviññāṇadutiyajjhānādike vitakko upalabbhati, yassa balena taṃ ārammaṇaṃ ārohati, tasmā sabhāvato bhāvanābalena tattha anuppajjanako? Saccaṃ, tampi vitakkabalena ārohati. Yathā hi so puriso paricayena tena vināpi nirāsaṅko rājagehaṃ pavisati, evaṃ paricayena vitakkena vināpi avitakkacittaṃ [M 1.0295] ārammaṇaṃ ārohati. Paricayoti cettha santāne abhiṇhaṃ pavattacittabhāvanāsaṅkhāto paricayo. Vitakkassa hi santāne abhiṇhaṃ pavattassa vasena cittassa ārammaṇābhirohanaṃ ciraparicitaṃ, tena taṃ cittaṃ kadāci vitakkena vināpi tattha vattateva. Yathā taṃ ñāṇasahitaṃ hutvā sammasanavasena ciraparicitaṃ kadāci ñāṇarahitampi sammasanavasena pavattati, yathā vā kilesasahitaṃ hutvā pavattaṃ sabbaso kilesarahitampi paricayena kilesavāsanāvasena pavattati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

There is no control over phenomena as they proceed according to conditions. To refute the notion of control, it is said, 'thinking is thought.' Application is the pondering of the object, or it is said to be the directing of the mind onto it. Because the mind, through the power of thought, is as if mounted upon the object, it is said, 'its characteristic is the directing of the mind onto the object.' Just as a villager, relying on a royal favorite or a friend connected to him, ascends and enters the king’s house, so too the mind, relying on thought, ascends the object. If that is so, how does a consciousness without thought ascend the object? For in the two sets of five sense-consciousnesses and in the second jhāna and beyond, thought is not found, by whose power it might ascend the object. Is it therefore not produced there by its own nature or by the power of development? Truly, even that ascends through the power of thought. Just as that man, through familiarity, enters the king’s house without hesitation even without his patron, so too a consciousness without thought, through familiarity, ascends the object even without thought. Here, 'familiarity' refers to the repeated occurrence of mental development in the continuum. Due to the frequent occurrence of thought in the continuum, the mind’s ascent upon the object becomes well-practiced. Thus, that mind sometimes operates there even without thought. Just as that which, having been associated with knowledge, is long-practiced in the mode of comprehension, may sometimes proceed in the mode of comprehension even when devoid of knowledge; or as that which, having operated in association with defilements, proceeds by familiarity through the latent tendency of defilements even when entirely free of them—so should this matter be understood.

Atha vā dvipañcaviññāṇaṃ avitakkampi vatthārammaṇaghaṭṭanassa balavatāya, dutiyajjhānādīni ca heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimabhāvanāya balavatāya ārammaṇaṃ ārohatīti. Ādito, abhimukhaṃ vā hananaṃ paharaṇamattaṃ āhananaṃ, parito, parivattetvā vā hananaṃ visesena paharaṇaṃ pariyāhananaṃ, taṃ kiccamassāti āhananapariyāhananaraso. Tathā hi tena yogāvacaro ārammaṇaṃ vitakkāhataṃ vitakkapariyāhataṃ karotīti vuccati. Ānayanaṃ cittassa ārammaṇe upanayanaṃ, ākaḍḍhanaṃ vā, tathā hutvā paccupaṭṭhānamassāti ānayanapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Alternatively, even though the two sets of five sense-consciousnesses lack thought, the mind ascends the object due to the strong impact of the base and object, and because the second jhāna and higher states are strengthened by the cultivation of the immediately lower stages. Striking directly, or face-to-face, is merely hitting, an instance of striking; striking all around, or turning around and striking, is striking with distinction—thorough striking. That is its function: the function of striking and thorough striking. Thus, by it, the meditator makes the object struck by thought and thoroughly struck by thought, as it is said. Its manifestation is that of leading; it is the bringing of the mind to the object, or the drawing of it, and it manifests as such.

Tenāti tena vicārena karaṇabhūtena, hetubhūtena vā cittaṃ ārammaṇe vicarati anuvicarati, avicāracittassa pana avitakkacitte vuttānusārena pavatti veditabbā. Vicaraṇaṃ anusañcaraṇaṃ anuparigamanaṃ. Svāyaṃ viseso santānamhi labbhamāno javanasantāne pākaṭo hotīti daṭṭhabbo. Esa nayo sesesupi. Ārammaṇassa anumajjanaṃ anumasanaṃ parimajjanamassa lakkhaṇanti ārammaṇānumajjanalakkhaṇo. Tathā hi vicāro parimajjanahattho viya, saṃsaraṇahattho viyāti vuccati. Tatthāti ārammaṇe. Sahajātānaṃ [M 1.0296] anuyojanaṃ ārammaṇe anuvicaraṇasaṅkhātaanumajjanavasena veditabbaṃ. Dhammānañhi sabhāvavinimuttā kāci kiriyā nāma natthi. Tathāgahetabbākāro bodhaneyyajanānurodhena paramatthato ekasabhāvopi sabhāvadhammo pariyāyavacanehi [V 1.0235] visayasamāropitarūpehi bahūhi pakārehi pakāsīyati. Evañhi so suṭṭhu pakāsito hotīti. Anupabandhapaccupaṭṭhānoti ārammaṇe cittassa avicchinnassa viya pavattipaccupaṭṭhāno. Tathā hi so anusandhānatāti niddiṭṭho.

By that, by that sustained application which is the instrument or the cause, the mind moves and roams over the object. But the process of a mind without sustained application should be understood according to what was said regarding a mind without initial application. Sustained application is roaming along, wandering around, completely moving around. This distinction, obtainable in the continuum, should be seen as becoming clear in the javana continuum. This method applies to the rest as well. Its characteristic is the massaging, touching, or stroking of the object; hence, it is characterized by the massaging of the object. For sustained application is said to be like a massaging hand or a roaming hand. Therein—that is, regarding the object. The engagement of co-arisen states should be understood by way of the massaging known as roaming over the object. For truly, there is no action of phenomena that is separate from their own nature. Thus, a natural phenomenon, though ultimately of a single nature, is explained in many ways by means of synonyms and forms attributed to the object, in accordance with those who are to be instructed. For in this way it is well explained. Its manifestation is uninterrupted connection—it manifests as the seemingly uninterrupted process of the mind upon the object. Thus it is indicated as 'connection'.

Ettha ca vicārato oḷārikaṭṭhena tasseva pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena paṭhamaghaṇṭābhiravo viya cetaso paṭhamābhinipāto vitakko, anuravo viya anusañcaraṇaṃ vicāro. Yathā hi ghaṇṭābhighātajo paṭhamābhiravo anuravato oḷāriko, pubbaṅgamo ca hoti, evaṃ ārammaṇābhiropanaṭṭhena vitakko oḷāriko, pubbaṅgamo viya ca hoti. Tato sukhumaṭṭhena anumajjanasabhāvena ca ghaṇṭānuravo viya anupabandho vicāro. Vipphāravā cettha vitakko cittassa paṭhamuppattikāle cittassa paripphandanabhūto ākāse uppatitukāmassa sakuṇassa pakkhavikkhepo viya, padumābhimukhapāto viya ca gandhānubandhacetaso bhamarassa. Santavutti vicāro cittassa nātiparipphandanabhāvo, ākāse uppatitassa sakuṇassa pakkhappasāraṇaṃ viya, padumassa uparibhāge paribbhamanaṃ viya ca padumābhimukhapatitassa bhamarassa. Āgamaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vipariyāyena āgataṃ. Tathā ca vuttaṃ dukanipātaṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

Here, being coarser than sustained application and being its forerunner, initial application is the mind's initial impact, like the first striking of a bell; sustained application is the subsequent movement, like the reverberation.
