For just as the initial sound from striking a bell is coarser than the reverberation and is the forerunner, so too initial application, by way of placing the mind on the object, is coarse and like a forerunner. Then, being more subtle and having the nature of massaging, sustained application is the continuous process, like the reverberation of the bell. Herein, initial application is the agitated movement of the mind at its first arising, like the flapping of wings of a bird wishing to fly into the sky, or like the descent towards a lotus of a bee whose mind is intent on its fragrance. Sustained application is the calm activity of the mind, a state of not being overly agitated, like the spreading of wings of a bird that has flown into the sky, or like the hovering over a lotus of a bee that has descended upon it. However, in the Āgama commentary, it is given in the reverse. And so it is said in the commentary on the Dukanipāta:

“Ākāse gacchato mahāsakuṇassa ubhohi pakkhehi vātaṃ gahetvā pakkhe sannisīdāpetvā gamanaṃ viya ārammaṇe cetaso abhiniropanabhāvena pavatto [M 1.0297] vitakko, vātaggahaṇatthaṃ pakkhe phandāpayamānassa gamanaṃ viya anumajjanabhāvena pavatto vicāro”ti.

‘Initial application, which occurs by way of directing the mind onto the object, is like the movement of a great bird flying in the sky, which, having caught the wind with both wings, lets its wings settle and glides. Sustained application, which occurs by way of massaging, is like the movement of that bird when, in order to catch the wind, it makes its wings flutter.’

Tampi anupabandhena pavattiyaṃ yujjati. Tathā hi upacāre, appanāyaṃ vā santānena pavattiyaṃ vitakko niccalo hutvā ārammaṇaṃ anupavisitvā viya pavattati, na paṭhamābhinipāte viya pākaṭo hotīti.

This also is fitting in the case of continuous occurrence. For in access concentration or in absorption, during the continuous process, initial application, having become motionless, proceeds as if it has entered the object, and is not as manifest as in the initial impact.

Pinayatīti kāyacittaṃ appeti, vaḍḍheti vā. Sampiyāyanalakkhaṇāti ārammaṇaṃ kallato gahaṇalakkhaṇā. Pīṇanarasāti kāyacittānaṃ paribrūhanakiccā. Pharaṇarasāti paṇītarūpehi kāyassa byāpanarasā, attanā sampayuttacittasamuṭṭhānehi rūpehi sakalarūpakāyabyāpanaṃ [V 1.0236] karotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Na hi aññathā imissā pharaṇaṃ hoti, dhammānaṃ abyāpāratāya kesaggamattampi saṅkamanābhāvato. Udaggabhāvo odagyaṃ.

It gladdens; that is, it suffuses or increases body and mind. Its characteristic is delighting, that is, taking an object as agreeable. Its function is nourishing, that is, the task of augmenting body and mind. Its manifestation is pervading; that is, it pervades the body with sublime forms. This means that it is said to pervade the entire material body with material forms originated by the consciousness with which it is associated. For otherwise this pervading would not occur, since states, being non-operative, do not translocate even by a hair's tip. The state of being uplifted is elation.

Ekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ aggametassāti ekaggaṃ, cittaṃ, yena pana dhammena yogato taṃ ekaggaṃ nāma hoti, so ekaggabhāvo. So pana cittasseva hoti, na yassa kassacīti āha “cittassa ekaggabhāvo”ti, nivāte dīpasikhāya ṭhiti viya cittassa ṭhitīti vuttaṃ hoti. Visārassa byaggabhāvassa paṭipakkho sabhāvo avisāro, na visārābhāvamattaṃ, taṃ imassa lakkhaṇanti āha “avisāralakkhaṇo”ti. Avikkhepo sampayuttadhammānaṃ avikkhittatā, avisārāvikkhepānaṃ samādhānabhāvato atthato visesābhāvepi samukhena, sampayuttamukhena ca ubhayaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avūpasamalakkhaṇassa vikkhepassa paṭipakkhatāya cittassa upasamanākārena paccupaṭṭhātīti upasamapaccupaṭṭhāno. Visesatoti yebhuyyena. Sukhavirahitopi hi atthi samādhīti so yebhuyyena sukhapadaṭṭhāno hoti. Atha vā [M 1.0298] visesatoti atisayena. “Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyatī”ti (a. ni. 11.11) vacanato hi sukhaṃ samādhissa visesakāraṇaṃ sukhavirahitassapi tadupanissayeneva samijjhanato.

One object is supreme for it, thus it is one-pointed (ekaggaṃ), namely the mind. That state by which the mind becomes one-pointed is called one-pointedness (ekaggabhāvo). This, however, pertains only to the mind, not to just anything—hence it is said, 'one-pointedness of mind.' This means that the stability of the mind is like the steady flame of a lamp in a windless place. Its characteristic is non-scattering. The state of non-scattering is the natural opposite of scattering and agitation; it is not merely the absence of scattering. Its function is non-distraction, which is the undistractedness of associated states. Although there is no essential difference in meaning between non-scattering and non-distraction, as both constitute concentration, both are mentioned: one with respect to itself, and the other with respect to its associated states. It manifests as tranquility because, by being the opposite of distraction which is characterized by non-calm, it manifests as the calming of the mind. Its proximate cause is happiness, especially—that is, for the most part. For although there is concentration devoid of happiness, it for the most part has happiness as its proximate cause. Alternatively, 'especially' means exceedingly. For according to the saying, 'The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.11), happiness is a special cause of concentration, since even concentration devoid of happiness succeeds only through its support.

Saddahanti etāyāti kammaphalādisaddahanakiriyāya pavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ tattha ādhipaccabhāvena saddhāya paccayataṃ dasseti. Tassā hi dhammānaṃ tathā paccayabhāve sati taṃsamaṅgipuggalo “saddahatī”ti voharīyati. Saddahanaṃ saddheyyavatthuno pattiyāyanaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇametissāti saddahanalakkhaṇā. Kālusiyamalaṃ vidhametvā sampayuttānaṃ, puggalasseva vā pasādaṃ anāvilabhāvakāraṇaṃ kiccametissāti pasādanarasā. Yathā kathaṃ viyāti āha “udakappasādakamaṇi viyā”ti. Akālusiyapaccupaṭṭhānāti anāvilabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Ratanattayaṃ kammaṃ kammaphalañca saddheyyavatthu, taṃ imissā āsannakāraṇanti saddheyyavatthupadaṭṭhānā. Na hi saddhāya avatthubhūtesu titthiyādīsu sā uppajjati. Sā panāyaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ ādāne hattho viya, sabbasampattisampadāne vittaṃ viya, amatakasiphalaphalane bījaṃ viya ca daṭṭhabbā. “Saddhāhattho, mahānāma, ariyasāvako, saddhīdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭhaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 184), saddhā bījaṃ tapo vuṭṭhī”tiādivacanañhettha (saṃ. ni. 1.197; su. ni. 77) sādhakaṃ.

'One believes by means of this'—this shows that faith is a condition, by way of dominance, for those states that occur as the act of believing in karma, its results, and so on. For when it is a condition for such states, a person endowed with it is called 'one who believes.' Its characteristic is believing, that is, confidence in an object of faith. Its function is clarifying; that is, it dispels the stain of turbidity and causes clarity in associated states, or in the person. This is said to be like a water-purifying gem. Its manifestation is non-turbidity, that is, a state free from impurity. Its proximate cause is an object of faith; that is, the Triple Gem, karma, and the result of karma are the objects of faith that are its proximate cause. For faith does not arise in relation to what is not a proper object, such as heretics and so on. Furthermore, this faith should be seen as like a hand for taking up wholesome states, like wealth for obtaining all accomplishments, and like a seed for producing the fruit of the deathless. The following sayings are evidence for this: 'Faith is the hand, O Mahānāma, of the noble disciple'; 'Faith is here a person's best wealth' (SN 1.246; Snp 184); 'Faith is the seed, austerity the rain' (SN 1.197; Snp 77).

Saranti 237 etāyāti saraṇakiriyāya pavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ tattha ādhipaccabhāvena satiyā paccayataṃ dasseti. Tassā hi dhammānaṃ tathā paccayabhāve sati taṃsamaṅgipuggalo “saratī”ti voharīyati. Udake alābu viya pilavitvā gantuṃ adatvā pāsāṇassa viya niccalassa ārammaṇassa ṭhapanaṃ asammuṭṭhatākaraṇaṃ apilāpanaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇamassāti apilāpanalakkhaṇā. Sā hi ārammaṇe daḷhaṃ [M 1.0299] patiṭṭhitattā esikā viya vuccati. Sammosapaccanīkakiccaṃ asammosaraso, na sammosābhāvamattaṃ. “Satārakkhena cetasā viharatī”ti (a. ni. 10.20) vuttattā cetoguṇaratanahārakānaṃ kilesacorānaṃ nivāraṇato āha “ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti. Tathā hesā cakkhudvārādirakkhanato dovāriko viyāti vuccati. Paṭhamaṃ saññāya thiruppannabhāve pacchā satiyā patiṭṭhānabhāvato āha “thirasaññāpadaṭṭhānā”ti. Atha satisaññānaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇanti? Saññā tāva paṭhamaṃ aggahitanimittaṃ sañjānāti, gahitanimitte puna paccābhiññāṇapaccayanimittaṃ karoti, paṭhamaṃ aggahite pana saññākiccaṃ appadhānaṃ hoti, sati pana paṭhamaṃ aggahitanimittampi sarati gahitanimittampi, gahitanimitte pana satikiccaṃ guṇabhūtaṃ hotīti idameva tāsaṃ nānattaṃ.

They remember by means of this—this shows that mindfulness is a condition for phenomena occurring in the act of remembering by way of its dominance. For when phenomena are thus conditioned by it, the person endowed with it is called 'one who remembers.' Its characteristic is that of not floating away, which is the establishment of the object, making it immovable like a stone and not allowing it to float away like a gourd in water. Because it is firmly established on its object, it is called a pillar. Its function is non-confusion, which consists in opposing confusion; it is not merely the absence of confusion. As it is said, 'One dwells with a mind guarded by mindfulness' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.20), it is said to have protection as its manifestation because it wards off the defilement-thieves who steal the jewels of mental qualities. Moreover, because it guards the sense-doors, it is called a gatekeeper. Because perception first arises firmly, and afterwards mindfulness is established, it is said to have firm perception as its proximate cause. Now, what is the distinction between mindfulness and perception? Perception, for its part, first recognizes an unapprehended sign; with regard to an apprehended sign, it then creates a sign that is a condition for re-cognition. But with regard to what is first unapprehended, the function of perception is not prominent. Mindfulness, however, remembers both the initially unapprehended sign and the apprehended sign. But with regard to the apprehended sign, the function of mindfulness becomes subordinate—this is precisely their difference.

Vīrabhāvoti yena vīriyena vīro nāma hoti, so dhammo. Vīrānaṃ vā kammanti yena kammena vīro nāma hoti, taṃ vīrānaṃ kammaṃ nāma. Vīriyaṃ panassa sādhakabhāvato tathā vuttaṃ. Dhammavinimuttaṃ vā kiñci kammaṃ natthīti vīriyameva kammabhāvena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vidhinā īretabbaṃ pavattetabbanti vā vīriyaṃ. Ussāho taṃ taṃ kiccaṃ samārambho, parakkamo vā. Upatthambhanaṃ pana sampayuttadhammānaṃ kosajjapakkhe patituṃ adatvā dhāraṇaṃ anubalappadānaṃ. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ saṃsīdanabhāvanivārako dhammo, na saṃsīdanābhāvamattaṃ, asaṃsīdanabhāvena paccupaṭṭhātīti asaṃsīdanabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. “Saṃviggo yoniso padahatī”ti (a. ni. 4.113) vacanato saṃvegapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Saṃvegoti cettha saṃvegamayaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Asaṃvegapubbikāya pana kusalakiriyāya vīriyārambhavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha vīriyārambhavatthūni nāma –

'The state of a hero' is that energy by which one is called a hero; that is the state. Or, 'the action of heroes' is that action by which one is called a hero; that is the action of heroes. And energy is said to be so because of its accomplishing nature. Or, it should be understood that since there is no action devoid of states, energy itself is spoken of as action. It is to be methodically exerted, to be set in motion—that is energy. It is exertion, the undertaking of this and that task, or striving. Support, however, is the sustaining of associated states by not allowing them to fall into the sphere of laziness; it is the giving of support. It is the quality that prevents associated states from collapsing, not merely the absence of collapsing. As it manifests as a non-collapsing state, its manifestation is a non-collapsing state. From the statement, 'Being stirred, one strives with proper attention' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.113), it has spiritual urgency as its proximate cause. Here, spiritual urgency means knowledge consisting of spiritual urgency. But for wholesome activity not preceded by spiritual urgency, the bases for arousing energy are its proximate cause. Therein, the bases for arousing energy are:

“Maggo [M 1.0300] gantabbo hoti, maggo gato. Kammaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti, kammaṃ kataṃ. Appamattako ābādho uppanno hoti, gilānā vuṭṭhito hoti, aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā. Gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto na labhati, lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ labhati…pe… pāripūri”nti –

'The path is to be traveled; the path has been traveled. Work is to be done; work has been done. A slight illness has arisen; one has recovered from illness, recently recovered from sickness. While wandering for alms in a village or town, one does not obtain enough food; one obtains coarse or fine food to the extent of satisfaction… to satisfaction.'

Evaṃ [V 1.0238] vuttāni etāni anurūpapaccavekkhaṇasahitāni aṭṭha vīriyārambhavatthūni, tammūlakāni vā paccavekkhaṇāni. Ettha ca vitakko sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇaṃ āropeti. Cetanā te taṃtaṃkiccesu niyojeti. Vīriyaṃ pana te saṃsīdituṃ adatvā ussāhetīti ayaṃ vitakkacetanāvīriyānaṃ viseso.

Thus, these eight grounds for the arousal of energy, together with appropriate reflections, or reflections rooted in them, have been stated. Here, thought directs the associated mental states toward the object. Volition engages them in their respective functions. But energy, not allowing them to sink down, encourages them—this is the distinction between thought, volition, and energy.

Vijānanalakkhaṇāti visesena jānanalakkhaṇā, yathāsabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇāti attho. Visayassa ārammaṇassa obhāsanaṃ pakāsanaṃ tappaṭicchādakasammohandhakārassa vidhamanatoti visayobhāsanaṃ, taṃ kiccamassāti visayobhāsanarasā. Katthaci visaye asammuyhanākārena sammohapaṭipakkhatāya vā paccupaṭṭhānato sammohābhāvassa paccupaṭṭhānato vā asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā.

The characteristic of wisdom is knowing distinctly, meaning its characteristic is penetrating things as they truly are. Its function is the illumination of the object, revealing it and dispelling the darkness of delusion that obscures it. Its manifestation is non-delusion, manifesting as not being deluded about any object, or as being the opponent of delusion.

Attanā anupāletabbānaṃ sahajātadhammānaṃ anupālanaṃ jīvitassa byāpāro, tañca tesaṃ jīvananti taṃ tassa kāraṇabhāvaṃ purakkhatvā vuttaṃ “jīvanti tenā”ti. Rūpārūpajīvitindriyassa anurūpato lakkhaṇādikaṃ dassetuṃ “attanā avinibhuttāna”nti vuttaṃ. “Sampayuttāna”nti hi vuccamāne rūpadhammānaṃ sampayogābhāvato rūpajīvitindriyassa saṅgaho na siyā. “Avinibhuttāna”nti pana vuttattā yāni [M 1.0301] avinibbhogarūpāni rūpajīvitindriyena saddhiṃ avinibhuttāni avisaṃsaṭṭhāni. Ye ca arūpadhammā arūpajīvitindriyena sampayuttā, tesaṃ sabbesaṃ saṅgaho hotīti. Pavattanarasanti uppādato yāva bhaṅgā anupālanato antarā anivattanasabhāvasādhanena tesaṃ pavattanakiccaṃ. Keci pana “rūpajīvitindriyaṃ tesaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇato paṭṭhāya, arūpajīvitindriyaṃ uppādato paṭṭhāya pavattiyā paccayo”ti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ. Paṭṭhāne hi “abyākataṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca asaññasattānaṃ ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ paṭicca indriyapaccayaṃ kammapaccayasadisa”nti asaññasattānaṃ indriyapaccayo kammapaccayasadisaṃ katvā vutto, tasmā rūpajīvitindriyampi uppādato paṭṭhāya paccayo hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uppādato yāva bhaṅgā ṭhapanato ṭhapanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Anupālanavasena yāpayitabbā pavattetabbā dhammā padaṭṭhānamassāti yāpayitabbadhammapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Yadi evaṃ tesaṃ anupālanādisādhakaṃ, kathaṃ tesaṃ nirodho hoti. Evañhi sabbakālaṃ ṭhātabbanti āha “santepi cā”tiādi. Anupālanalakkhaṇādimhīti ādi-saddena pavattanarasādimeva saṅgaṇhāti. Atthikkhaṇeyevāti attanā anupāletabbānaṃ, attano vā atthikkhaṇeyeva. Udakanti taḷākagatajalaṃ, daṇḍagatajalaṃ vā[V 1.0239]. Tattha taḷākagataudakassa gahaṇe attanā anupāletabbadhammānaṃ atthikkhaṇe anupālanaṃ sādhitaṃ hoti, daṇḍagatajalassa pana gahaṇe attano atthikkhaṇe anupālanaṃ. Attanā anuppāditadhamme kathaṃ pāletīti āha “dhāti viya kumāra”nti. Yadi sesadhammānaṃ pavattikāraṇena kenaci bhavitabbaṃ, jīvitassa pana kiṃ pavattikāraṇanti āha “sayaṃ…pe… pavattatī”ti. Yathā kathaṃ viyāti āha “niyāmako viyā”ti. Sopi attanā pavattitanāvāsambandhena pavattati. Yadi dhammānaṃ pavatti jīvitindriyapaṭibaddhaṃ, bhaṅgato uddhampi kiṃ pana pavattetīti āha “na bhaṅgato uddha”nti. Kasmāti āha “attano [M 1.0302] ca pavattetabbānañca abhāvā”ti. Bhaṅgakkhaṇe pana kathanti āha “na bhaṅgakkhaṇe ṭhapetī”ti.

The function of life is to sustain the co-nascent phenomena that are to be sustained by it, and that is their life. Therefore, having made that its causal status, it is said, 'They live by that.' To show the characteristic, etc., appropriate to the material and immaterial life faculty, it is said, 'of those not separate from itself.' For if 'of those associated' were said, the material life faculty would not be included, since material phenomena lack association. But since 'of those not separate' is said, all inseparable material phenomena that are not separate from the material life faculty are included, as are all immaterial phenomena associated with the immaterial life faculty. Its function is to cause continuity, by sustaining them from arising until dissolution, thereby establishing their nature of not ceasing in the interim. Some, however, say, 'The material life faculty is a condition for their continuity from the moment of stability, and the immaterial life faculty from the moment of arising.' This is not correct. For in the Paṭṭhāna, the faculty condition for non-percipient beings is said to be similar to the kamma condition, as in the passage: 'Dependent on an indeterminate state, and for non-percipient beings dependent on one great element, there is a faculty condition similar to the kamma condition.' Therefore, it should be understood that the material life faculty is also a condition from the moment of arising. Its manifestation is establishing, as it establishes phenomena from arising until dissolution. Its proximate cause is the phenomena that are to be maintained and made to continue. If it is thus the means of sustaining them, how does their cessation occur? For then they should exist for all time. To this, it is said, 'even when they are present,' etc. In 'the characteristic of sustaining, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes the function of causing to continue and so on. 'At the very moment of existence' refers either to the moment of existence of those phenomena to be sustained by it, or to its own moment of existence. 'Water' refers either to the water in a lake or the water in a vessel. In the case of the water in a lake, the sustaining of those phenomena to be sustained by it at their moment of existence is established. But in the case of the water in a vessel, it is the sustaining at its own moment of existence. How does it sustain phenomena not produced by itself? It is said, 'like a nurse for a child.' If the continuity of other phenomena must have some cause, what then causes the continuity of life? It is said, 'it itself...continues.' How, like what? It is said, 'like a helmsman.' He too continues in connection with the boat that he himself causes to continue. If the continuity of phenomena is dependent on the life faculty, what then does it cause to continue after dissolution? It is said, 'not after dissolution.' Why? It is said, 'due to the absence of both itself and of that which is to be made to continue.' But at the moment of dissolution, what then? It is said, 'it does not establish at the moment of dissolution.'

Yasmā pana lobhapaṭipakkho alobho hoti, ye dhammā tena sampayuttā, taṃsamaṅgino vā sattā, te na lubbhanti, sayampi kadāci na lubbhateva, atthato vā alubbhanākāro eva ca so hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “na lubbhanti tenā”tiādi. Esa nayo “na dussanti tenā”tiādīsupi. Alaggabhāvo ārammaṇaṃ nissāya pavattantassapi tattha anāsattatā. Tenāha “kamaladale jalabindu viyā”ti. Apariggaho kassaci vatthuno mamattavasena asaṅgaho. Muttabhikkhu viyāti khīṇāsavabhikkhu viya. So hi muttarāgattā katthaci mamāyanarahito hoti. Anallīno bhāvo adhippāyo etassāti anallīnabhāvo. Evañhi “asucimhi patitapuriso viyā”ti upamāya sameti. Yathā hi tassa purisassa satipi kāyena allīyane bhāvo anallīno, evaṃ alobhopi ārammaṇakaraṇavasena gahitepi ārammaṇe alaggabhāvena anallīnabhāvo anallīnākāroyeva pavattati. Evaṃsabhāvo hi so dhammoti.

Since, however, non-greed is the opposite of greed, those mental states associated with it, or beings endowed with it, are not greedy. It itself is never greedy at all; or in meaning, it is simply the state of not being greedy. Therefore, it is said, 'They are not greedy by that,' and so on. This same method applies to 'They are not hateful by that,' and so forth. Non-adherence is non-attachment to an object, even while occurring in dependence on that object. Hence, it is said, 'Like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.' Non-appropriation is the non-grasping of any object with a sense of 'mine.' Like a liberated monk, that is, like a monk whose taints are destroyed. For he, being freed from passion, is devoid of any sense of 'mine' anywhere. Its meaning is the state of non-adhesion; thus, non-adhesion. For thus it accords with the simile, 'Like a man who has fallen into filth.' Just as that man, though his body is smeared, is mentally unadhering, so too non-greed, even when an object is taken as its object, persists by way of non-adherence as a state of non-adhesion. For such is the nature of this state.

Caṇḍikassa bhāvo caṇḍikkaṃ, pharusabhāvo, atthato pana kopoyeva, tappaṭipakkho apharusabhāvo acaṇḍikkaṃ. Avirodho aviggaho appaṭipakkho sabhāvo. Āghātavinayanarasoti ettha āghāto nāma parassa attānaṃ, attano paraṃ uddissa, parasseva ca paraṃ uddissa pavatto upanāho balavakopo. Tassa vinayanaraso apanayanaraso. Sommabhāvo majjanavasena hilādaniyatā sītalabhāvo. Tenāha “puṇṇacando viyā”ti.

The state of being fierce is fierceness, a harsh state; in meaning, it is simply anger. Its opposite is non-harshness, non-fierceness. Its nature is non-opposition, non-conflict, and non-hostility. Its function is the dispelling of resentment. Here, resentment means a grudge, a strong anger, that arises directed at another by oneself, at oneself by another, or at another by another. Its function of dispelling is the function of removal. Its manifestation is gentleness, a pleasant and cool state, by way of soothing. Hence, it is said, 'like the full moon.'

Kāyaduccarītādīhīti [M 1.0303] hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ. Hirīyati lajjanākārena jigucchiyati. Tehiyevāti kāyaduccaritādīhiyeva. Ottappatīti ubbijjati. Hirī pāpe gūthe viya passantī jigucchatīti [V 1.0240] āha “pāpato jigucchanalakkhaṇā hirī”ti. Ottappaṃ te uṇhaṃ viya passantaṃ tato uttasatīti vuttaṃ “uttāsalakkhaṇaṃ ottappa”nti. Ubhopi pāpānaṃ akaraṇarasāti lajjanākārena pāpānaṃ akaraṇarasā hirī, uttāsākārena ottappaṃ. Pāpato saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānāti vuttappakāreneva pāpato saṅkocanākārena paccupaṭṭhānā. Attagāravaparagāravapadaṭṭhānāti attagāravapadaṭṭhānā hirī ajjhattasamuṭṭhānatāya, attādhipatitāya ca. Paragāravapadaṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānatāya, lokādhipatitāya ca. Attānañhi garuṃ katvā hiriyā pāpaṃ pajahati kulavadhū viya. Paraṃ garuṃ katvā ottappena pāpaṃ pajahati vesiyā viya. Ajjhattasamuṭṭhānāditā ca nesaṃ tattha tattha pākaṭabhāvena veditabbā, na pana tesaṃ kadāci aññamaññaviyogato. Na hi lajjanaṃ nibbhayaṃ vā pāpabhayaṃ vā alajjanaṃ atthīti. Hiriyā balavabhāve pana ottappaṃ abbohārikaṃ hoti, ottappassa balavabhāve hirī abbohārikā. Ime ca dve dhammā “lokapālā”ti vuccanti. Yathāha –

The phrase 'by bodily misconduct, etc.' (Kāyaduccarītādīhīti) is in the instrumental case, denoting cause. 'To be ashamed' (Hirīyati) means to be disgusted in the manner of shame. 'By those very things' (Tehiyevāti) means by those very bodily misconducts, etc. 'To be afraid' (Ottappati) means to be agitated. Hiri, seeing evil as disgusting like excrement, is disgusted; hence it is said: 'Hiri has the characteristic of disgust at evil.' Ottappa, seeing evil as hot, is frightened by it; hence it is said: 'Ottappa has the characteristic of fear.' Both have the function of not doing evil: Hiri has the function of not doing evil by way of shame, and Ottappa by way of fear. Their manifestation is shrinking away from evil, in the manner described. Hiri has self-respect as its proximate cause, arising internally and being governed by oneself. Ottappa has respect for others as its proximate cause, arising externally and being governed by the world. For one abandons evil through Hiri by holding oneself in high esteem, like a woman of good family. One abandons evil through Ottappa by holding others in high esteem, like a courtesan. Their arising internally and so on should be understood according to their prominence in each case, not from their ever being separate from each other. For there is no shame that is fearless, nor fear of evil that is shameless. However, when Hiri is strong, Ottappa becomes inoperative; when Ottappa is strong, Hiri becomes inoperative. These two states are called the 'guardians of the world,' as it is said:

“Dveme, bhikkhave, sukkā dhammā lokaṃ pālenti. Katame dve? Hirī ca ottappañca, ime kho, bhikkhave, dve sukkā dhammā lokaṃ na pāleyyuṃ, nayidha paññāyetha ‘mātā’ti vā ‘mātucchā’ti vā ‘mātulānī’ti vā”tiādi (a. ni. 2.9).

"Monks, these two bright states protect the world. Which two? Moral shame and moral dread. If, monks, these two bright states did not protect the world, there would be no recognition here of 'mother,' or 'maternal aunt,' or 'maternal uncle’s wife,' and so on (A. Ni. 2.9)."

Passambhanaṃ darathavūpasamo, kāya-saddo samūhavacano. So cettha vedanādikkhandhattayaṃ. Vatticchāvasena hi saddo visiṭṭhavutti hotīti āha “kāyoti cetthā”tiādi. Vedanādayoti [M 1.0304] vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandhoti tayo khandhā. Tathā ca vuttaṃ tattha “katamā tasmiṃ samaye kāyapassaddhi hoti, yā tasmiṃ samaye vedanākkhandhassā”tiādi (dha. sa. 40). Daratho sārambho domanassapaccayānaṃ uddhaccādīnaṃ kilesānaṃ, tathā pavattānaṃ vā catunnaṃ khandhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tassa vūpasamaṃ lakkhaṇamassāti kāyacittadarathavūpasamalakkhaṇā. Kāyacitta…pe… rasāti yathāvuttānameva paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ abhibhavanarasā. Darathanimmaddanena pariḷāhaparipphandanavirahito sītibhāvo aparipphandanasītibhāvo. Avūpasamo paripphandanaṃ asantavuttitā. Uddhaccādikilesāti uddhaccappadhānā uddhaccādhikacittuppādasampayuttā kilesā. Tepi hi uddhaccavasena avūpasamakarā. Uddhaccaṃ vā ādiṃ katvā sabbeyeva kilesā uddhaccādikilesā. Evaṃ sesesupi.

Calming is the pacification of distress. The word 'body' is a collective term. Here it refers to the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling. For a word has a specific meaning according to the speaker's intention; thus it is said, 'Here, "body" means...' and so on. 'Feeling and so on' means the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations—these three aggregates. And so it is said there: 'What at that time is tranquility of body? That which at that time is tranquility of the aggregate of feeling...' and so on (Dhs. 40). Distress is agitation, a condition for displeasure, for defilements such as restlessness; or it is a designation for the four aggregates that have so arisen. The pacification of this distress is their characteristic; thus, they are characterized by the pacification of bodily and mental distress. Their function is the overcoming of the opposing states as stated. Their manifestation is a cool state without agitation, being free from burning and agitation through the crushing of distress. Non-pacification is agitation, an un-tranquil state. 'Defilements beginning with restlessness' are defilements associated with thought-moments in which restlessness is predominant or excessive. For these too cause non-pacification by way of restlessness. Or, taking restlessness as the beginning, all defilements are 'defilements beginning with restlessness.' The same applies in the remaining cases.

Garubhāvo [V 1.0241] dandhatā, thinamiddhādhikānaṃ tathā pavattānaṃ vā catunnaṃ khandhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Dandhatāya paṭipakkho adandhatā agarubhāvo.

Heaviness is sluggishness; this is a designation for the four aggregates in which sloth and torpor are predominant, or which have arisen in such a way. The opposite of sluggishness is non-sluggishness, which is lightness.

Thaddhabhāvo thambho. Diṭṭhimānādhikānaṃ, tappadhānānaṃ vā catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. Thaddhabhāvanimmaddanatoyeva katthaci ārammaṇe appaṭihatākārena paccupaṭṭhanti, sampayuttānaṃ vā tattha appaṭighātaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpentīti appaṭighātapaccupaṭṭhānā.

Stiffness is rigidity. This is a name for the four aggregates in which view and conceit are predominant, or in which they are primary. Precisely by crushing stiffness, they manifest towards an object in an unhindered manner, or they cause their associated states to manifest there without obstruction; thus, their manifestation is non-obstruction.

Kammani sādhu kammaññaṃ, na kammaññaṃ akammaññaṃ, tassa bhāvo akammaññabhāvo, dānasīlādipuññakiriyāya asamatthatā. Atthato kāmacchandādisaṃkilesadhammā, tappadhānā vā cattāro akusalakkhandhā. Akammaññabhāvanimmaddaneneva sampannākārena ārammaṇassa gahaṇaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇasampatti. Vuttāvasesā kāmacchandādayo, tadekaṭṭhā ca saṃkilesadhammā sesanīvaraṇādayo. Imā pana dve vinibandhanimmaddanena [M 1.0305] pasādanīyavatthūsu pasādāvahā, hitakiriyāsu viniyogakkhamabhāvāvahā suvaṇṇavisuddhi viyāti daṭṭhabbā.

That which is fit for action is 'workable'; that which is not workable is 'unworkable.' Its state is unworkability, the inability to perform meritorious actions such as giving and virtue. In meaning, it refers to defiling states such as sensual desire, or the four unwholesome aggregates predominated by them. Through the crushing of unworkability, there is the accomplishment of taking an object, the perfect grasping of the object. Its proximate cause is the remaining hindrances, such as sensual desire, and other defiling states that share their foundation. This pair of qualities, however, by crushing the bonds, brings about confidence in regard to confidence-inspiring objects and enables engagement in beneficial actions, like the purity of refined gold. Thus it should be understood.

Gelaññaṃ assaddhiyādayo, tadekaṭṭhā ca pāpadhammā, tappaṭipakkho agelaññabhāvo lakkhaṇaṃ etāsanti agelaññabhāvalakkhaṇā. Gelaññanimmaddaneneva natthi etāsaṃ ādīnavo doso upaddavo vā, na vā etā ādīnaṃ kapaṇaṃ vanti pavattantīti nirādīnavā, tenākārena paccupaṭṭhanti, taṃ vā sampayuttesu paccupaṭṭhāpentīti nirādīnavapaccupaṭṭhānā.

Illness is lack of faith and so on, and the evil states that share their foundation. Their opposite, the state of non-illness, is their characteristic; thus, they are characterized by the state of non-illness. Through the crushing of illness, there is no danger, fault, or affliction in them, nor do they proceed miserably or wretchedly; thus, they are without danger. They manifest in that way, or they cause their associated states to manifest it; thus, their manifestation is freedom from danger.

Kāyasambandhī, cittasambandhī ca ujubhāvoti lakkhitabbatāya kāyacittānaṃ ajjavalakkhaṇā. Kāyacittānaṃ naṅgalasīsacandakoṭigomuttavaṅkatāsaṅkhātānaṃ kuṭilabhāvānaṃ atthato māyāsāṭheyyādibhūtānaṃ nimmaddanato kāyacittānaṃ kuṭilabhāvanimmaddanarasā. Tatoyeva sabbathāpi ajimhabhāvena paccupaṭṭhanti, sampayuttānaṃ vā ajimhataṃ paccupaṭṭhāpentīti ajimhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā.

Bodily and mental uprightness has the characteristic of the straightness of body and mind, as it is to be marked as uprightness connected with body and mind. Its function is the crushing of crooked states in body and mind, which are designated as crookedness like a plowshare, the tip of the moon's crescent, or cow's urine—meaning deceit, fraud, and the like. For that very reason, they manifest in all ways as non-crookedness, or they cause associated states to manifest as non-crookedness; thus, they have non-crookedness as their manifestation.

Nanu ca kāyapassaddhiādīnaṃ dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ dhammānaṃ ekekapaṭipakkhattā darathanimmaddanādikiccaṃ ekekameva karoti. Kasmā pana dve dve dhammā vuttāti? Na kho panevaṃ cintitabbaṃ bhagavatāpi tatheva desitattā. Kasmā pana bhagavatā tathā desitā? Sabhāvadhammabhāvato. Na hi bhagavatā pubbe avijjamānā ete dhammā desanāvasena uppāditā, atha [V 1.0242] kho sabhāvato vijjamānāyeva sayambhuñāṇena sammā sacchikatvā yathāsabhāvā desitā, tasmā kathamettha bhagavatā sabhāvato vijjamānassa hāpanaṃ kātuṃ sakkā. Sabhāvato vijjamānatāya cettha bhagavato vacanameva pamāṇaṃ. Na hi bhagavā yathādhammasāsanādhikāre ayathādhammaṃ katheyyāti, yassa pana vijjamānassāpi akathanaṃ, taṃ aññahetukaṃ. Na cettha tādiso hetu upalabbhati, yena imesu [M 1.0306] ekekadhammassa akathananti. Yathā pana dvinnaṃ purisānaṃ ekoyeva veriko hoti, tassa te purisā otāraṃ disvā ekato hutvāva hananti, evameva dve dve dhammā ekato hutvā ekaṃ paṭipakkhadhammaṃ hananti, yathā ca panete visuṃ disvāpi taṃ veriṃ hananti, na evamete taṃ visuṃ hananti tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ avinābhāvatoti, tasmā ete paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ ekekabhāvepi dve dveyeva vuttāti, apica cittapassaddhiādīhi cittameva passaddhi lahu mudu kammaññaṃ paguṇaṃ ujuñca hoti. Kāyapassaddhiādīhi pana rūpakāyopīti tadatthadassanatthaṃ bhagavatā ettheva duvidhatā vuttā, na samādhiādīsu.

But do not bodily tranquility and the like, being two states each, perform the task of crushing distress and so forth by counteracting a single opposing state? Why then are two states mentioned? Indeed, it should not be thought thus, because the Blessed One has taught it in that very way. But why did the Blessed One teach it in that way? Due to their inherent nature as phenomena. For these states were not brought into existence by the Blessed One's teaching, having been non-existent before; rather, existing by their very nature, the Blessed One, having fully realized them with his self-awakened knowledge, taught them as they truly are. Therefore, how could the Blessed One possibly omit what exists by nature here? Since these things exist by nature, the Blessed One's words alone are the authority here. For the Blessed One would not speak contrary to the Dhamma in matters pertaining to the teaching. If something exists yet is not spoken of, that is due to another reason. But no such reason is found here that would justify not mentioning each state individually. Just as when two men have a single enemy, they see an opportunity and attack him together, so too do these pairs of states join forces to counteract a single opposing state. And whereas those men might strike their enemy even when acting separately, these states do not strike their opponent separately, due to their mutual inseparability. Therefore, even though each counteracting state relates to a single opposing state, they are spoken of in pairs. Moreover, through mental tranquility and the like, the mind itself becomes tranquil, light, malleable, workable, proficient, and upright. But through bodily tranquility and the like, the physical body also becomes so. To show this meaning, the Blessed One spoke of them here as twofold, but not in the case of concentration and the like.

Chandanaṃ chando, ārammaṇena atthikatā. “Chando kāmo”tiādīsu (mahāni. 1) pana taṇhāpi chandoti vuccati. “Chandaṃ janeti vāyamatī”tiādīsu vīriyampīti tato nivattanatthaṃ vuttaṃ “kattukamyatāyetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Kattukamyatā vuccati karaṇicchā. Cetasikassa dhammassa sārammaṇattā karaṇicchā nāma ārammaṇassa ālambitukāmatāmukheneva hotīti ārammaṇakaraṇicchālakkhaṇo chando “kattukamyatālakkhaṇo”ti vutto. Tenevāha “ārammaṇapariyesanaraso, ārammaṇena atthikatāpaccupaṭṭhāno”ti ca. Yadaggena panāyaṃ attano ārammaṇapariyesanaraso, tadaggena sampayuttadhammānampi hotiyeva ekārammaṇatāya. Tena tesaṃ ārammaṇaggahaṇe cetaso hatthappasāraṇaṃ viyāti vuccati. Kathaṃ pana dānavatthuvissajjanavasena pavattamānacetanāsampayutto chando ārammaṇena atthiko hotīti? Nanu avocumhā “ārammaṇakaraṇicchālakkhaṇo”ti, tasmā saṅgāmagataissāsassa khipitabbausūnaṃ gahaṇe atthikatā viya dānavatthuvissajjanavasena [M 1.0307] pavattacchandopi vissajjitabbena tena atthikoyevāti. Svāyaṃ kusalesu uppanno kusalacchando nāma hoti yonisomanasikārasamuṭṭhānattā. Tabbiparītato pana akusalesu uppanno akusalacchando.

Desire (chanda) is the act of desiring, an eagerness for an object. In phrases like 'desire is craving' (Mahaniddesa 1), craving is also called desire. In expressions such as 'one generates desire, one strives,' even energy is implied—hence, to distinguish it, it is said, 'this is a synonym for the wish to act.' The wish to act is called the desire to do. Because a mental state has an object, the desire to do is essentially a desire to take up the object; thus, desire is said to have 'the characteristic of the wish to act.' For this reason, it is also said, 'its function is seeking an object, its manifestation is eagerness for an object.' And in so far as it has the function of seeking its object, so too do its associated states, because they have a single object. Therefore, in grasping the object, it is said to be like the stretching forth of the mind's hand. But how can desire, associated with volition that arises in the act of giving or relinquishing, be eager for an object? Did we not say, 'it has the characteristic of the wish to act'? Thus, just as a warrior in battle is eager to seize arrows to be shot, so too is the desire that arises in the act of giving or relinquishing eager for that which is to be relinquished. When this arises in wholesome states, it is called wholesome desire because it originates from wise attention. Conversely, when it arises in unwholesome states, it is called unwholesome desire.

Adhimuccanaṃ ārammaṇe sanniṭṭhānavasena veditabbaṃ, na pasādanavasena. Tenāha “sanniṭṭhānalakkhaṇo”ti. Yathā tathā hi ārammaṇe nicchayanaṃ adhimuccanaṃ anadhimuccantassa pāṇātipātādīsu[V 1.0243], dānādīsu vā pavattiyā abhāvato, saddhā pana pasādanīyesu pasādādhimokkhoti ayametesaṃ viseso. Voṭṭhabbanaṃ pana yathā santīrite atthe nicchayanākārena pavattitvā parato pavattamānānaṃ tathā pavattiyā paccayo hoti. Yadi evaṃ vicikicchāsampayuttesu dhammesu kathanti? Tesampi ekaṃseneva saṃsappanākārassa paccayatāya daṭṭhabbaṃ, dārakassa viya ito cito ca saṃsappanassa “karissāmi, na karissāmī”ti anicchayassa paṭipakkhakiriyā asaṃsappanaṃ. Yesu cittuppādesu ayaṃ sanniṭṭhānalakkhaṇo adhimokkho, tesaṃ ārammaṇadhammoyeva sanniṭṭhātabbattā sanniṭṭheyyadhammo. So padaṭṭhānamassāti sanniṭṭheyyadhammapadaṭṭhāno. Indakhiloti esikāthambho vuccati.

Determination (adhimokkha) should be understood by way of resolving upon the object, not by way of confidence. Hence it is said, 'It has the characteristic of resolving.' For determination is deciding upon an object in one way or another, because for one who does not resolve, there is no engagement in killing living beings, etc., or in giving, etc. Faith, however, is resolving with confidence in what inspires confidence. This is the distinction between them. Moreover, deciding (voṭṭhabbana) functions as a condition for the occurrence of subsequent states by way of a decisive mode, having first occurred in the form of resolving regarding a well-considered matter. But how is it in the case of states associated with doubt? Even in those cases, it should be seen as functioning as a condition for the mode of wavering, like a child wavering back and forth, undecided between 'I will do it' and 'I will not do it'; its opposing action is non-wavering. In those thought-processes where this determination, which has the characteristic of resolving, occurs, the object-dharma itself is to be resolved upon; hence, it is the object-to-be-resolved-upon. That is its proximate cause; thus, its proximate cause is the object-to-be-resolved-upon. 'Indakhīla' means a city-gate post.

Tesu tesu dhammesūti yesu dhammesu sayaṃ uppannā, tesu attanā sampayuttesu cittacetasikadhammesu. Anārammaṇattepi hi tesu samappavattesu udāsīnabhāvo “tatramajjhattatā”ti vuccati. Samaṃ avisamaṃ vāhitaṃ attanā pavattitasampayuttānaṃ vā yathāsakakiccesu pavattanaṃ lakkhaṇametissāti samavāhitalakkhaṇā. Tattha samaṃ hutvā pavattanalakkhaṇāti atthe apakkhapatitabhāvo vutto hoti, avisamaṃ katvā pavattanalakkhaṇāti atthe ūnādhikatānivāraṇaṃ[M 1.0308]. Udāsīnabhāvena pavattamānāpi hi esā sampayuttadhamme samaṃ katvā yathāsakakiccesu pavatteti, yathā rājā tuṇhī nisinnopi adhikaraṇadhammaṭṭhe yathāsakakiccesu samaṃ appamatte pavatteti. Alīnānuddhatappavattipaccayānaṃ dhammānaṃ ūnādhikatāya līnuddhatabhāvassa nivāraṇakiccāti vuttaṃ “ūnādhikatānivāraṇarasā”ti. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ sahajātādhipatīnaṃ adhipatibhāvo. Ādhipaccañhi tesaṃ kiccato adhikabhāvoti? Nāyaṃ doso. Tampi tassa kiccameva, yaṃ sahajātadhammānaṃ adhipatibhāve pavattāpanaṃ. Yathā hi raṅgamaṇḍalaṃ gato naṭakācariyo te te naṭake yathāsakaṃ anurūpaṃ bhūmiyaṃ yojeti, evamesāpi attanā sampayuttadhammesu adhipatibhāve ṭhite adhipatibhāve yojeti, indriyatte ṭhite indriyatte, na pana sakasakakiccato ūnataṃ, adhikataṃ vā pattuṃ detīti. “Idaṃ nihīnakiccaṃ hotu, idaṃ atirekakicca”nti evaṃ pakkhapātavasena viya pavatti pakkhapāto. Taṃ upacchindantī viya hotīti pakkhapātupacchedanarasā. Sā cittacetasikānaṃ ajjhupekkhanena samappavattesu ājānīyesu sārathi viya daṭṭhabbā.

In whatever states—that is, in those states in which it itself arises, in those mental and mental concomitant phenomena associated with itself. For its state of impartiality towards those states as they proceed evenly, even without taking them as an object, is called 'equanimity.' Its characteristic is conveying evenly, that is, causing its associated states to proceed in their respective functions. Here, 'proceeding evenly' means the state of being without partiality; 'causing to proceed not unevenly' means the prevention of deficiency or excess. For even when it proceeds with impartiality, it causes the associated phenomena to proceed evenly in their respective functions, just as a king, though sitting silently, causes the legal officers to proceed evenly and diligently in their respective duties. Its function is said to be the prevention of deficiency and excess, that is, the task of preventing the states of slackness and agitation by balancing the causal conditions for non-slackness and non-agitation. If so, how can it be a dominant condition for co-arisen dominant factors? For dominance means that their function is of greater importance. There is no fault here. That too is its function—to cause co-arisen phenomena to proceed in a dominant state. Just as a master actor who has gone to the stage directs each actor to their appropriate role, so too does this equanimity, when associated phenomena are established in a dominant state, direct them to a dominant state; when established as a faculty, it directs them to a faculty state, without allowing them to attain deficiency or excess in their respective functions. Partiality is an inclination as if to say, 'Let this be an inferior function, let this be an excessive function.' Its function is to cut off such partiality. It should be seen like a charioteer overseeing thoroughbreds that proceed evenly, by overseeing the mind and mental factors.

Kiriyā kāroti kāra-saddassa bhāvasādhanataṃ āha. Tena kāroti nāññaṃ, kiriyāyevāti dīpitaṃ [V 1.0244] hoti. Manasmiṃ kāroti manasi ārammaṇassa karaṇaṃ. Yena hi mano ārammaṇe karīyati ārammaṇenassa saṃyojanato, tato eva tena ārammaṇampi manasi karīyatīti. Manasikāroti cettha aluttasamāso daṭṭhabbo. Purimamanatoti bhavaṅgamanato. Visadisaṃ mananti vīthijavanamanaṃ, taṃ karotīti manasikāro, manasikārasāmaññena vīthijavanapaṭipādake dasseti. Ettha pana upayogatthabhummavacane samāso daṭṭhabbo. Sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ sārento payojento viya hotīti manasikāro [M 1.0309] sāraṇalakkhaṇoti vutto. Saṃyojanarasoti payojanaraso. Vitakko sampayuttānaṃ ārammaṇe abhiniropanasabhāvattā ārammaṇe cittaṃ pakkhipanto viya hoti. Cetanā attano ārammaṇaṃ gaṇhantī sampayuttepi sakasakakiccaṃ kāretīti attanā karaṇena balaṃ niyojento balanāyako viya hoti. Manasikāro sampayutte ārammaṇe payojetīti ājānīyappayojanakasārathi viyāti ayametesaṃ viseso.

The phrase 'it does an action' (kiriyāṃ karoti) indicates that the word 'kāra' is formed as an abstract noun. Thus, it is clarified that 'it does' is nothing but action itself. 'Doing in the mind' (manasmiṃ kāroti) means the making of the object in the mind. For when the mind is made to be on the object, by its connection with the object, then by that very means the object is also made to be in the mind. Here, 'manasikāro' should be understood as a compound with an unelided case ending. 'From the former mind' means from the life-continuum mind. 'Dissimilar mind' refers to the mind of the cognitive-process impulsion. 'Doing that' (taṃ karotīti) is mental attention (manasikāro), which, by the general characteristic of attention, indicates that which establishes the cognitive-process impulsion. Here, however, the compound should be understood in the sense of the locative case with the meaning of instrumentality. Mental attention is said to have the characteristic of directing, as it is like guiding and applying associated states towards the object. Its function is connection, that is, its function is application. Initial application (vitakka), due to its nature of placing associated states upon the object, is like casting the mind upon the object. Volition (cetanā), while taking its own object, also causes associated states to perform their respective tasks. Thus, by its own action, it acts like a commander deploying strength. Mental attention applies associated states to the object, like a charioteer applying a thoroughbred horse. This is the distinction between them.

Ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānoti ārammaṇe saṃyojanavasena tadabhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. Ettha satiyā appamussanacchandatā visayābhimukhapaccupaṭṭhānatā, manasikārassa pana saṃyojanavasenāti ayametesaṃ viseso. Ārammaṇapaṭipādakassa saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannatāvacanaṃ itaramanasikārānaṃ viññāṇakkhandhapariyāpannataṃ dasseti. Mahisāsakā pana “āvajjanassa viññāṇabhāve sabbaññutaññāṇassa sabbavisayatā parihāyeyya, tasmā taṃ javanasampayuttasaṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannamevā”ti vadanti. Tesañhi ayamadhippāyo – yadi taṃ visuṃ cittasabhāvaṃ siyā, paccuppannacittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattassa tassa anantaraṃ uppajjamānajavanānaṃ paccuppannārammaṇatā na bhaveyya, aññadatthu atītārammaṇatāva siyā, evañca sati sabbaññutaññāṇassāpi paccuppannacittārammaṇatāya abhāvato asabbavisayatā āpajjeyya, yadaggena ca taṃ asabbavisayaṃ, tadaggena sāvaraṇampi hoti yattha na pavattati, tattha āvaraṇasambhavato, tasmāssa sakalalokasiddho sabbaññubhāvo, anāvaraṇabhāvo ca parihāyetha, javanasampayuttabhāve pana sati āvajjanassa nāyaṃ iṭṭhavighāto āpajjatīti. Tayidaṃ tesamabhinivesamattaṃ “āvajjanā kusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ, akusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantarapaccayena [M 1.0310] paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417) vacanena tassānantaraṃ kusalākusaluppattiyā dīpitattā. Sabbaññutaññāṇassa pana paccuppannacittārammaṇabhāvo evaṃ veditabbo – atītādivasena hi vibhāgamakatvā “imassa cittaṃ jānāmī”ti pavattassa āvajjanaṃ sāmaññena yaṃ kiñci abhimukhībhūtaṃ cittamāvajjati, tato javanānipi attano attano [V 1.0245] abhimukhībhūtaṃ cittamārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattanti, na cettha javanānaṃ bhinnārammaṇatā āsaṅkitabbā cittasāmaññena ārammaṇassa abhinnattā, tasmā sabbaññutaññāṇassa paccuppannacittārammaṇataṃ paṭicca na kāci vihesā anubhavitabbāti. Kiṃ vā etena yuttivādena, nanu vuttaṃ bhagavatā – “acinteyyo buddhavisayo”ti (a. ni. 4.77), tasmā aparimitapuññasambhārekaphalassa acinteyyasabhāvattā āvajjanena vināpi visayaggahaṇe vibandhanābhāvato yattha katthaci pavatti appaṭihatāyevāti. Keci panettha “āvajjanaṃ anāgatacittamārammaṇaṃ katvā nirujjhati, javanameva pana paccuppannamārammaṇaṃ gaṇhātī”ti vadanti. Yasmā pana “anāgatārammaṇā āvajjanā paccuppannārammaṇānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti pāḷi natthi, tasmā taṃ appamāṇaṃ.

Its manifestation as being directed towards the object is its manifestation as being directed towards the object by way of connection with the object. Here, for mindfulness, non-forgetfulness is its manifestation as being directed towards the object, but for mental attention, it is by way of connection—this is the distinction between them. The statement that the 'object-establishing' (ārammaṇapaṭipādaka) belongs to the aggregate of formations shows that other types of mental attention belong to the aggregate of consciousness. However, the Mahīsāsakas say, 'If advertence were of the nature of consciousness, the omniscience would lose its universality regarding all objects. Therefore, it is included only in the aggregate of formations associated with impulsion.' For their intention is this: If it were a separate mental nature, then for the impulsions arising immediately after it, which would have taken the present mind as their object, there would be no present object; rather, there would only be a past object. And if that were the case, omniscience too would lack a present mental object, leading to its non-universality. And to the extent that it is non-universal, to that extent it would also be obstructed wherever it does not occur, due to the possibility of obstruction there. Therefore, its universally acknowledged omniscience and unobstructed nature would decline. But if advertence is associated with impulsion, this undesirable consequence does not arise. This is merely their insistence, as the statement, 'Advertence is a condition for wholesome aggregates and unwholesome aggregates by way of contiguity condition' (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.417), indicates the immediate arising of wholesome and unwholesome states after it. As for omniscience having a present mental object, it should be understood thus: When advertence occurs without making a distinction such as past, etc., and thinks, 'I know this mind,' it generally attends to whatever mind is present. Then, the impulsions also take their respective present minds as objects. Here, there is no reason to assume that the impulsions have different objects, since the generality of the mind ensures the object’s non-differentiation. Therefore, no difficulty should be experienced regarding omniscience having a present mental object. Or, what is the use of this rational argument? Has it not been said by the Blessed One, 'The range of a Buddha is inconceivable' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.77)? Therefore, since the sole fruit of immeasurable stores of merit has an inconceivable nature, even without advertence, there is no obstruction to apprehending objects, and its occurrence is unimpeded anywhere. Some, however, say here, 'Advertence takes a future mind as its object and ceases, while impulsion takes a present object.' But since there is no scriptural statement that 'advertence with a future object is a contiguity condition for aggregates with a present object,' this is unfounded.

Karotīti karuṇā. Kiṃ karoti, kesaṃ kiṃ nimittanti āha “paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ hadayakampana”nti. Kampananti ca paresaṃ dukkhaṃ disvā tassa asahanākārena cittassa aññathattaṃ, tadidaṃ sappurisānaṃyeva hotīti āha “sādhūna”nti. Sappurisā hi attahitaparahitasādhanena “sādhū”ti vuccanti. “Kiṇātī”ti imassa atthamāha “vināsetī”ti, adassanaṃ gameti apanetīti attho. Tenāha “paradukkhāpanayanākārappavattilakkhaṇā”ti. Paresaṃ dukkhassa apanayanaṃ hotu vā, mā vā, so [M 1.0311] paradukkhāpanayanākāro, tathāpavattilakkhaṇāti para…pe… lakkhaṇā. Apanetukāmatāya paresaṃ dukkhassa asahanaṃ anadhivāsanaṃ paradukkhāsahanaṃ. Na vihiṃsā avihiṃsā, sattānaṃ aviheṭhanaṃ, taṃ paccupaṭṭhāpeti, vihiṃsāya vā paṭipakkhabhāvena paccupaṭṭhātīti avihiṃsāpaccupaṭṭhānā.

Compassion (karuṇā) is so called because it acts. What does it do? For whom? With what sign? It is said: 'It is the trembling of the hearts of the good at the suffering of others.' And trembling is the alteration of the mind due to the inability to bear the suffering of others upon seeing it; and this happens only to the virtuous—hence it is said 'of the good.' For the virtuous are called 'good' because they accomplish their own welfare and the welfare of others. The meaning of 'kiṇāti' is explained as 'it destroys,' meaning it causes to disappear, it removes. Therefore, it is said, 'Its characteristic is to proceed in the manner of removing the suffering of others.' Whether the removal of the suffering of others occurs or not, its characteristic is to proceed in that manner. The inability to bear, the intolerance of the suffering of others due to the desire to remove it—this is the non-endurance of the suffering of others. Non-harming (avihiṃsā) is the non-affliction of beings. It manifests as such, or it manifests as the opposite of harming—thus, its manifestation is non-harming.

Pamodanalakkhaṇāti parasampattiyā pamodanalakkhaṇā. Anissāyanarasāti issāyanassa usūyanassa paṭipakkhabhāvakiccā. Pantasenāsanesu, adhikusaladhammesu ca aramaṇaṃ arati. Sā atthato issādhikaṃ domanassasahagataṃ, thinamiddhādhikañca uddhaccaṃ. Tattha purimaṃ parasampattivisayaṃ, dutiyaṃ pantasenāsanādivisayanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aratiyā vihananākārena paccupaṭṭhāti, tassā vighātaṃ vā vūpasamaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetīti arativighātapaccupaṭṭhānā. “Aniyate icchantī”ti iminā cetasikantarabhāvena icchantīti dasseti.

Its characteristic is rejoicing, that is, the characteristic of delighting in the success of others. Its function is non-envy, that is, its task is to be the opposite of envy and jealousy. Discontent (arati) is non-delight regarding remote dwellings and superior wholesome states. In essence, it is grief accompanied by envy, and restlessness accompanied by sloth and torpor. Here, the former should be seen as having the success of others as its sphere, while the latter has remote dwellings and the like as its sphere. It manifests in the manner of eliminating discontent, or it presents the overcoming or stilling of it; thus, its manifestation is the overcoming of discontent. By the phrase 'desiring the undetermined,' it shows that it desires by way of being another mental factor.

Kāyaduccaritatoti vatthuvītikkamasaṅkhātaduccaritato. Kāyaduccaritādivatthūnanti parapāṇaparadhanaparaitthiādīnaṃ [V 1.0246] kāyaduccaritādīnamālambaṇabhūtānameva vatthūnaṃ. Avītikkamalakkhaṇāti amaddanalakkhaṇā. Kāyaduccaritādivatthuto saṅkocanakiriyāpadesena kāyaduccaritāditoyeva saṅkocanakiriyā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi viratiyo duccaritavatthuno akiriyapaccupaṭṭhānā yujjanti, atha kho duccaritasseva, viratīnañca soraccavasena saṅkocanaṃ, akiriyā ca hirottappānaṃ jigucchādivasenāti ayametesaṃ viseso. Saddhā…pe… padaṭṭhānāti ettha saddhādayo sabbeva dhammā kāyasucaritādīnaṃ padaṭṭhānāti eke. Apare pana “kammaṃ kammaphalaṃ saddahantassa kāyaduccaritādiakaraṇato, hirottappasampannassa musāvādādiakathanato, appicchasantuṭṭhīsallekhaguṇasamannāgatassa micchājīvavivajjanato ca saddhādayo [M 1.0312] tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ yathākkamena padaṭṭhānā”ti vadanti. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino. Imāsūti imāsu tīsu viratīsu. Ekekaṃ niyataṃ viratimicchantīti aññaṃ ekaṃ catutthaniyataviratimicchanti. Atha vā niddhāraṇatthe bhummavasena imāsaṃ antare ekaṃ niyataṃ viratimicchantīti attho. Ubhayathāpi pana tesaṃ icchā na yujjati aparāya viratiyā dhammasenāpatināpi adesitattā, visayassa ca sadā sannihitattābhāvena niyatāya eva ekissā abhāvato. Teneva hi abhayagirivāsinoyeva ca keci imāsaṃ tividhattaṃ aniyatattameva ca icchanti. Vuttañhi tehi –

"Bodily misconduct" means misconduct reckoned as transgression of the object. The objects of bodily misconduct, etc., are the very objects that serve as supports for bodily misconduct, etc., such as the lives of others, the wealth of others, and the wives of others. "Non-transgression" has the characteristic of non-violation. It should be understood that the act of restraint is described as restraint from bodily misconduct, etc., itself, by way of the function of contracting from the object of bodily misconduct, etc. For abstinences are not properly presented as having non-action as their manifestation in relation to the object of misconduct, but rather in relation to the misconduct itself; and the contraction of the abstinences is through gentleness, while non-action is through shame and fear of wrongdoing by way of disgust, etc.—this is their distinction. "Faith…etc.…as proximate cause": here, some say that all these qualities are the proximate causes for bodily good conduct, etc. But others say: "Because one who has faith in kamma and its result does not commit bodily misconduct, etc.; because one endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing does not speak falsehood, etc.; and because one possessing the qualities of fewness of wishes, contentment, and effacement avoids wrong livelihood; therefore faith and the other two are, in order, the proximate causes for the three things." Some—namely, the dwellers at Abhayagiri—say... "Among these" means among these three abstinences, "they desire a single, fixed abstinence." That is, they desire another, a fourth, fixed abstinence. Alternatively, it means that, with the meaning of specification understood in the locative sense, they desire a single, fixed abstinence from among these. In either case, however, their desire is not justifiable, because another abstinence was not taught even by the General of the Dhamma, and because the object is not always present, making a single, fixed abstinence impossible. Therefore, indeed, some of the dwellers at Abhayagiri themselves desire that these three are indefinite. For it was said by them...

“Karuṇāmuditā sammāvācākammantaājivā;

Yebhuyyato aniyatā, honti gocarabhedato”ti. –

"Compassion and sympathetic joy, right speech, right action, and right livelihood; for the most part, they are indefinite, owing to the difference in their objective fields."

Ettha pana “yebhuyyato”ti vacanaṃ lokuttaracittesu sabbadā ekatoyeva ca labbhamānataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Here, the term "for the most part" is stated with reference to their being always obtained together in supramundane consciousnesses.

Dutiyacittena sampayogaṃ gacchantīti sambandho. Yathā cittaṃ, evaṃ taṃsampayuttadhammāpīti dutiye sasaṅkhārā evāti āha “sasaṅkhārabhāvamattameva hettha viseso”ti. Tathāti yathā tatiye, tathā catutthepi pītiyā sukhapadaṭṭhānattā. Sukhassa cettha abhāvato āha “ṭhapetvā pīti”nti. Nanu ca “karuṇāmuditā upekkhāsahagate na sambhavantī”ti vadanti, tasmā yathā pītiyā, evaṃ tāsampi paṭikkhepo kātabboti? Na kātabbo, appanāpattito pubbe karuṇāmuditānaṃ upekkhāsahagatānampi sambhavato. Karuṇāmuditābhāvanākāle hi appanāvīthito pubbe upekkhāsahagatacittenāpi parikammaṃ hoti, appanāvīthiyaṃ pana somanassasahagatacitteneva ekāvajjanavīthiyā [V 1.0247] vedanāparivattanābhāvato, tasmā pubbabhāgavaseneva karuṇāmuditānampi [M 1.0313] upekkhāsahagatesu sambhavo hotīti ācariyā. Apare pana sabbadāpi tāsaṃ upekkhāsahagatesu sambhavaṃ na icchanti. “Avasesā pañcamena sampayogaṃ gacchantī”ti avisesena vuttattā idāni visesadassanatthamāha “somanassaṭṭhāne cā”tiādi.

The connection is that they are associated with the second consciousness. Just as the consciousness is, so too are the associated states; thus, in the second, they are only of the prompted kind. Hence, it is said, "The only distinction here is just the state of being prompted." Similarly, as in the third, so too in the fourth, because joy serves as the proximate cause for happiness. Since happiness is absent here, it is said, "except for joy." But do they not say, "Compassion and sympathetic joy do not arise accompanied by equanimity"? Therefore, just as with joy, should they also be excluded? They should not be, because before the attainment of absorption, compassion and sympathetic joy can arise even when accompanied by equanimity. For during the development of compassion and sympathetic joy, before the absorption process, preliminary work is done even with a consciousness accompanied by equanimity. However, in the absorption process itself, it is only with a consciousness accompanied by joy, since there is no alteration of feeling within a single cognitive process. Thus, the teachers say that by way of the preliminary stage, compassion and sympathetic joy can arise accompanied by equanimity. Others, however, do not accept that they can ever arise accompanied by equanimity. "The remaining ones are connected with the fifth," being stated generally, now to show the distinction, it is said, "and in the place of joy," etc.

81. Karuṇāmuditādayoti karuṇāmuditā ceva viratittayañca. Tenāha “pañcā”ti.

81. "Compassion, sympathetic joy, etc." means compassion and sympathetic joy, and the three abstinences. Hence it is said, "five."

Evaṃ kāmāvacarakusalacittasampayutte dassetvā idāni rūpāvacarakusalacittasampayuttadhamme dassetuṃ “avasesesu panā”tiādimāha. Tattha ṭhapetvā viratittayanti viratittayaṃ vajjetvā. Kasmā panettha viratittayaṃ pariccattanti? Vuccate – suvisuddhakāyakammādikassa cittasamādhānavasena rūpārūpāvacarakusalappavatti, na kāyakammādīnaṃ sodhanavasena, nāpi duccaritadurājīvānaṃ samucchindanavasena. Tathā hi nīvaraṇādidhammānaṃ avatthattayaṃ hoti vītikkamāvatthā pariyuṭṭhānāvatthā anusayāvatthāti. Tattha vītikkamāvatthāya paṭipakkhaṃ kāmāvacarakusalaṃ pariyuṭṭhānāvatthāya rūpārūpāvacaraṃ, anusayāvatthāya lokuttarakusalaṃ. Duccaritadurājīvānaṃ pana ṭhapetvā vītikkamāvatthaṃ, anusayāvatthañca vītikkamāvatthāya visuṃ pariyuṭṭhānāvatthā na upalabbhati. Yassā vipaccanīkaṃ rūpārūpāvacarakusalaṃ siyā, tasmā taṃ neva kāmāvacarakusalaṃ viya tesaṃ vītikkamāvatthaṃ sodheti, na ca lokuttaraṃ viya anusayāvatthaṃ samucchindati, paṭipassambheti vā. Sīlavisuddhiyaṃ sīlasodhanavasena kāmāvacarakusaleneva vigatavītikkamassa parisuddhakāyakammādikassa yogino cittasamādhānavasena pavattatīti mahaggatacittuppāde viratīnaṃ asambhavoyeva. Imameva hi atthaṃ sādhetuṃ “viratiyo panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tettiṃsa vā karuṇādijhānavasena pavattanakāle[M 1.0314]. Tatoti tato tatiye vuttacetasikato. Karuṇāmuditānaṃ appanāpattānamekantasomanassasahagatattā āha “pañcamena…pe… karuṇāmuditāvajjā”ti.

Having thus shown the states associated with wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense-sphere, now, to show the states associated with wholesome consciousness pertaining to the fine-material sphere, he begins with "But in the remaining…" Herein, "setting aside the three abstinences" means excluding the three abstinences. Why are the three abstinences excluded here? It is said: The arising of wholesome states pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres occurs through the concentration of mind of one whose bodily actions, etc., are thoroughly purified, not through the purification of bodily actions, etc., nor through the eradication of wrong conduct and wrong livelihood. For states such as the hindrances have three stages: the stage of transgression, the stage of obsession, and the stage of latent tendency. Herein, wholesome states of the sense-sphere are the counteractive for the stage of transgression; fine-material and immaterial states are for the stage of obsession; and supramundane wholesome states are for the stage of latent tendency. But for wrong conduct and wrong livelihood, apart from the stage of transgression and the stage of latent tendency, no separate stage of obsession is found for which fine-material and immaterial wholesome states would be the counteractive. Therefore, such a state neither purifies their stage of transgression like the wholesome states of the sense-sphere, nor eradicates their stage of latent tendency like the supramundane states, nor does it suppress it. In the purification of virtue, for a meditator whose bodily actions, etc., are purified and free from transgression by means of the wholesome states of the sense-sphere, the arising of lofty consciousness occurs through the concentration of mind; hence, the abstinences have no place in the arising of lofty consciousness. To establish this very meaning, the passage beginning with "But the abstinences…" is introduced. Or, there are thirty-three factors at the time of arising through the jhānas of compassion, etc. "From that" means from the mental factors mentioned in relation to the third jhāna. Because compassion and sympathetic joy, when reaching absorption, are invariably accompanied by joy, it is said: "With the fifth…excepting compassion and sympathetic joy."

Rūpāvacarapañcame vuttanayenāti tiṃsevāti adhippāyo. Yadi evaṃ rūpāvacarato ko visesoti āha “arūpāvacarabhāvovettha viseso”ti, pañcame rūpasaññābhāvato rūpāvacarabhāvo, idha pana rūpasaññāsamatikkamena pattabbattā arūpāvacarabhāvoti ayamevassa tato visesoti attho.

"In the manner stated for the fifth of the fine-material sphere" means that there are thirty factors. If so, what is the distinction from the fine-material sphere? He says, "The distinction here is its being a formless sphere." In the fifth, it is a fine-material sphere due to the absence of form perception; but here, because it is attainable through the transcendence of form perception, it is a formless sphere. This is its distinction from that.

Paṭhamajjhāniketi [V 1.0248] paṭhamajjhānavati. Maggacitteti catubbidhepi maggañāṇe. Dutiyajjhānikādibhedeti dutiyatatiyacatutthapañcamajjhānike. Vuttanayenāti “dutiyena vitakkavajjā”tiādinā vuttanayena. Kiṃ avisesenāti ce, noti āha “karuṇāmuditāna”ntiādi. Maggadhammesu pādakajjhānādivasena kadāci sammāsaṅkappaviraho siyā, na pana virativiraho, kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ samucchinnavaseneva ariyamaggassa pavattanatoti āha “niyataviratibhāvo”ti. Lokuttarabhāvoti chabbisuddhiparamparāya pattabbattā lokato uttaraṇabhāvo.

"One of the first jhāna" means one possessing the first jhāna. "Path-consciousness" means in the fourfold path-knowledge. "The distinction of the second jhāna and so on" means those possessing the second, third, fourth, and fifth jhānas. "By the method stated" means by the method stated thus, "with the second, without initial application of mind," etc. If it is asked, "Is this without distinction?" he says, "No," and begins the passage "of compassion and sympathetic joy..." In the path-factors, sometimes there might be an absence of right intention because of the basic jhāna and so on, but there is no absence of the abstinences, because the noble path occurs only by way of having completely cut off bodily misconduct and so on; thus he says "the state of fixed abstinence." "The supramundane state" is the state of transcending the world because it is attainable through the succession of the six purifications.

Evaṃ kusalacetasikānaṃ sampayogavacanatthalakkhaṇādīni dassetvā idāni akusalacetasikāni dassetuṃ “akusalā panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Cha yevāpanakāti kiñcāpi paṭhame aniyatayevāpanakā na labbhanti, akusalesu pana labbhamānakayevāpanadhamme ekattha dassetuṃ tesampi idheva vacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañca katvā upari dhammānaṃ uddesānantaraṃ “evaṃ yevāpanā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vicikicchāsahagate chandādhimokkhānaṃ, uddhaccasahagate chandassa ca abhāvato vuttaṃ “paṭipāṭiyā dasasu cittesū”ti.

Having thus shown the characteristics, the meaning of their association, and so on, of the wholesome mental factors, now, to show the unwholesome mental factors, the passage beginning 'But the unwholesome…' is introduced. Regarding 'Six invariably associated factors': Although in the first section on wholesome factors, invariably associated factors are not found, their mention is included here to show in one place the invariably associated factors that are found among the unwholesome states. Having done so, after the enumeration of the above factors, it is said, 'Thus are the invariably associated…' etc. Due to the absence of desire and resolution in consciousness accompanied by doubt, and of desire in consciousness accompanied by restlessness, it is said, 'in the ten consciousnesses in order…'

82. Niddiṭṭhāti [M 1.0315] nissesena dassitā. Hatā vihatā viddhastā pāpā apāyādidukkhapāpanato “pāpā”ti saṅkhātā akusaladhammā yena so bhagavā hatapāpo, tena. Lābho alābho, yaso ayaso, nindā pasaṃsā, sukhaṃ dukkhanti imesu aṭṭhasu lokadhammesu akampanaṭṭhena tādinā sammāsambuddhena. So hi lābhādīsu yādiso, alābhādīsupi tādisoyevāti “tādī”ti vuccati.

82. 'Niddiṭṭhā' means shown in detail. The unwholesome states, reckoned as 'evil' (pāpā) because they lead to suffering such as that of the lower realms, are destroyed, overthrown, and annihilated by him—therefore the Blessed One is 'hatapāpo,' the destroyer of evil. By the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who is 'tādī' (steadfast) by virtue of being unshaken by these eight worldly conditions: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. For he is the same in gain as in loss, etc.—thus he is called 'tādī.'

Na hirīyatīti na lajjati. Ahirikoti puggalo dhammasamūho vā. “Ahirikka”nti vattabbe ekassa ka-kārassa lopaṃ katvā “ahirika”nti vuttaṃ. Na ottappanti ottappassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ dhammamāha. Ajigucchanaṃ ahīḷanaṃ. Alajjanaṃ avilā. Ajigucchanalakkhaṇanti sabhāvavasena vuttaṃ, alajjanalakkhaṇanti kusalābyākatassa sādhāraṇāya hiriyā paṭipakkhavasena. Tehevāti kāyaduccaritādīhi eva. Asārajjanaṃ nibbhayatā. Anuttāso asambhamo. Rasādīni hiriottappesu vuttapaṭipakkhavasena gahetabbānīti na tāni idha vuttāni. Tesu hi alajjanākārena pāpānaṃ karaṇarasaṃ ahirikaṃ. Anuttāsākārena anottappaṃ[V 1.0249]. Vuttappakāreneva pāpato asaṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānāni. Attani, paresu ca agāravapadaṭṭhānāni. Gāmasūkarassa viya asucito kilesāsucito ajigucchanaṃ ahirikena hoti. Salabhassa viya aggito pāpato anuttāso anottappena hoti. Yathāhu porāṇā –

One does not feel shame; thus, one is shameless. 'Shamelessness' (ahirika) can refer to a person or a group of phenomena. When it should be called 'ahirikka,' the dropping of one 'ka'-syllable makes it 'ahirika.' 'Not fearing wrongdoing' refers to the phenomenon that is the opposite of moral dread. It is non-disgust, non-reproach, and non-shame. The characteristic of non-disgust is stated according to its intrinsic nature, while the characteristic of non-shame is stated as the opposite of the shame common to wholesome and indeterminate states. By those very things—such as bodily misconduct—there is non-embarrassment and fearlessness, non-terror and non-trembling. The function (rasa) and other aspects should be understood as the opposite of what was stated for shame and moral dread, so they are not mentioned here. For shamelessness (ahirika) has the function of committing evil with an attitude of non-shame; moral recklessness (anottappa), with an attitude of non-fear. As previously explained, their manifestation is non-shrinking from evil. Their proximate cause is disrespect toward oneself and others. Just as a village pig feels no disgust toward filth, so through shamelessness one feels no disgust toward the impurity of defilements. Like a moth before a flame, so through moral recklessness one feels no fear of evil. As the ancients have said—

“Jigucchati nāhiriko, pāpā gūthāva sūkaro;

Na bhāyati anottappo, salabho viya pāvakā”ti.

“The shameless one feels no disgust for evil, like a pig for filth; the morally reckless one fears not, like a moth before a flame.”

Ettha [M 1.0316] ca yathā hiriyā balavabhāve ottappaṃ abbohārikaṃ hoti, ottappassa balavabhāve hirī abbohārikā, evaṃ ahirikassa balavabhāve anottappaṃ abbohārikaṃ, anottappassa balavabhāve ahirikaṃ abbohārikaṃ hotīti keci, taṃ na yujjati. Yathā hi asucinā attānaṃ makkhento, sappamukhe hatthaṃ pavesento bāladārako tattha paṭikkūlabhāvassa, ādīnavassa ca anupaparikkhanato neva jigucchati, na ca uttasati, evamevaṃ dhammasabhāvassa aññāṇato moho pāpato neva jigucchati, na uttasati, tasmā taṃsampayuttacittuppāde ubhayampi balavataraṃ hotīti.

Here, some say that just as when moral shame (hirī) is strong, moral dread (ottappa) becomes inoperative, and when moral dread is strong, moral shame becomes inoperative, so too when shamelessness (ahirika) is strong, moral recklessness (anottappa) becomes inoperative, and when moral recklessness is strong, shamelessness becomes inoperative. But this is not correct. For just as a foolish child, smearing himself with filth or putting his hand into a snake's mouth, neither feels disgust nor fears, due to not considering the repulsiveness and danger therein, so too, due to ignorance of the nature of phenomena, the deluded mind neither feels disgust for evil nor fears it. Therefore, in a state of consciousness associated with delusion, both (shamelessness and moral recklessness) become stronger.

Lubbhantīti abhigijjhanti, allīyantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ārammaṇaggahaṇalakkhaṇoti ettha ārammaṇaggahaṇaṃ nāma “mama ida”nti taṇhābhinivesavasena abhiniviṭṭhassa ārammaṇassa avissajjanaṃ, na ārammaṇakaraṇamattaṃ. Abhisaṅgo atisayavatāya āsattiyā dummocanīyabhāvo. Apariccāgo avijahanaṃ. Telañjanarāgo viyāti dhovitvāpi pariccajituṃ asakkuṇeyyo telamakkhitaañjanarāgo viya. “Assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti vacanato vuttaṃ “assādadassanapadaṭṭhāno”ti. Tattha assādavasena dassanaṃ assādadassanaṃ. Nanu ca assādadassanampi atthato lobhoyevāti kathaṃ sayaṃ attano padaṭṭhānaṃ hotīti? Saccaṃ, paṭhamaṃ nātibalavalobhavasena assādadassano pacchā balavalobho hotīti tassa taṃpadaṭṭhānatā vuttā. Teneva ca “taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Apare pana “assādo nāma sukhavedanā, assādadassananti assādadiṭṭhī”ti vadanti. Sukhavedanāya vā kāraṇabhūtaṃ subhanimittaṃ assādo nāma, asubhe “subha”nti pavattā tayo vipallāsā assādadassanaṃ nāmāti keci.

'They are greedy' (lubbhanti) means they are excessively greedy; it means they cling. Its characteristic is grasping an object. Here, 'grasping an object' means the non-relinquishing of an object to which one is attached through the obsession of craving, thinking 'this is mine,' not merely the act of taking something as an object. Adhesion (abhisaṅga) is the state of being difficult to release due to excessive attachment. Non-relinquishment (apariccāga) is non-abandonment. It is like a stain of lampblack mixed with oil, which cannot be removed even by washing. From the saying, 'For one who dwells on enjoyment, craving increases,' it is said to have 'seeing enjoyment as its proximate cause.' There, seeing in terms of enjoyment is 'seeing enjoyment.' But is not 'seeing enjoyment' in essence just greed? How can it be a proximate cause for itself? It is true. Initially, 'seeing enjoyment' occurs due to greed that is not very strong, and later strong greed arises; therefore, it is said to be its proximate cause. For that reason it is said, 'Craving increases.' Others, however, say, 'Enjoyment is pleasant feeling, and "seeing enjoyment" is the wrong view concerning enjoyment.' Still others say, 'enjoyment' is either the pleasant feeling or the beautiful sign that is its cause, and the three perversions that perceive the unattractive as 'beautiful' are called 'seeing enjoyment.'

Muyhantīti [M 1.0317] na bujjhanti. Dhammasabhāvassa yāthāvato adassanaṃ cittassa andhabhāvo. Aññāṇaṃ [V 1.0250] ñāṇapaṭipakkho dhammo. Tattha purimalakkhaṇaṃ sabhāvavasena vuttaṃ, itaraṃ paṭipakkhavasena. Atha vā aññāṇalakkhaṇoti kiccavasena vuttaṃ. So hi asampaṭivedharasoti vutto. Dhammasabhāvaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ asamatthatā asampaṭivedho. Ārammaṇasabhāvacchādanarasoti yathā aññāṇaṃ, mohasamaṅgipuggalo vā ārammaṇasabhāvaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na labhati, mohassa tathā pavatti ārammaṇasabhāvacchādanaṃ. Ettha ca ñāṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ yathāsabhāvato jānāti, diṭṭhi yathāsabhāvaṃ vijahitvā ayāthāvato gaṇhāti, moho pana na kathañci vijānāti. Yadi evaṃ ārammaṇaggahaṇakālo kathaṃ tadā so ārammaṇaṃ jānātevāti? Tadāpi na jānāti. Yathā pana phassādayo phusanākārādimattavaseneva ārammaṇaṃ gaṇhanti, na jānanavasena, evamayaṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā uppajjamāno paṭicchādanākāreneva gaṇhāti, na pana jānanākārenāti. Yassa uppajjati, tassa andhakaraṇaṃ andhakāro, tathā paccupaṭṭhāti, taṃ vā paccupaṭṭhāpetīti andhakārapaccupaṭṭhāno.

'They are deluded' (muyhanti) means they do not understand. The blindness of the mind is the failure to see the true nature of phenomena as it really is. Ignorance is a state opposed to knowledge. Here, the first characteristic (blindness) is explained in terms of its intrinsic nature, while the other (ignorance) is explained in terms of opposition. Alternatively, the characteristic of ignorance is described in terms of its function. It is said to have the function of non-penetration. The inability to penetrate the true nature of phenomena is non-penetration. It has the function of concealing the object's true nature. For a person endowed with delusion cannot penetrate the object's true nature, as the operation of delusion is to conceal that nature. Here, knowledge understands the object as it truly is, while wrong view abandons the true nature and grasps it falsely. Delusion, however, does not understand it in any way. If that is so, how does it cognize an object when it arises? Even then, it does not understand. Just as contact and other mental factors grasp an object merely by way of touching, etc., and not by way of knowing, so too delusion arises, grasping the object only by way of concealing, not by way of knowing. For the one in whom it arises, it creates darkness. Its manifestation is like darkness, or it causes darkness to appear.

Micchā passantīti dhammasabhāvassa viparītavasena aniccādiṃ niccādivasena passanti. Ayoniso abhiniveso uppathābhiniveso. Dhammasabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā parato niccādito vā parappaccayato vā āmasanaṃ parāmāso, viparītaggāhavasena “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti abhinivesanaṃ micchābhiniveso. Ariyānaṃ adassanakāmatādīti ādi-saddena saddhammaasotukāmatādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

'Seeing wrongly' means perceiving the impermanent and so on as permanent and so on, contrary to the true nature of phenomena. 'Unwise adherence' is adherence to a wrong path. Misapprehension (parāmāsa) is grasping beyond the true nature of phenomena, either from ideas of permanence and so on, or from another's influence. Wrong adherence (micchābhinivesa) is clinging with a perverse grasp, with the conviction, 'This alone is true, all else is false.' 'Not wishing to see the noble ones, etc.': by the word 'etc.,' this includes not desiring to hear the true Dhamma and similar things.

Yassa dhammassa vasena uddhataṃ hoti cittaṃ, taṃsampayuttadhammā vā, so dhammo uddhaccaṃ. Tenāha “uddhatabhāvo”ti. Avūpasamoti asannisinnabhāvo. Vātā…pe… paṭākā viyāti [M 1.0318] yathā paṭākā yottabalena dhajayaṭṭhiṃ amuñcantīpi vātābhighātena ettha avaṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, evamidampi adhimokkhabalena ārammaṇaṃ amuñcantampi ayonisomanasikārabalena ārammaṇe acalaṃ avaṭṭhātuṃ na sakkotīti vātappahāreneva caladhajapaṭākā viya anavaṭṭhānakiccaṃ. Bhantattaṃ paribbhamanākāro. Uddhaccassa sabbākusalasādhāraṇattā, aññesañca akusalasādhāraṇānaṃ visuṃ padaṭṭhānassa labbhamānattā vuttaṃ “ayoniso…pe… padaṭṭhāna”nti. Yenākārena vā manasikaroto uddhaccaṃ uppajjati, tenākārena manasikaraṇaṃ idha ayonisomanasikāro. Atha vā uddhaccanimittassa ārammaṇassa manasikaraṇaṃ idha ayonisomanasikāro.

That state by which the mind is agitated, or the states associated therewith, is restlessness (uddhacca). Hence it is said, 'the state of being agitated.' 'Unsubdued' means the state of not being settled. Like a flag... or a banner—just as a banner, though not released from the flagpole by the strength of its cord, cannot remain steady due to the impact of the wind, so too this mind, though not releasing its object by the power of determination, cannot remain steadily fixed on the object due to the force of unwise attention. Thus, like a fluttering flag or banner struck by the wind, its function is instability. 'Distraction' is the characteristic of wandering about. Because restlessness is common to all unwholesome states, and because distinct proximate causes are obtainable for other common unwholesome states, it is said, 'unwise attention... is the proximate cause.'
