The manner of attending by which restlessness arises is here called unwise attention. Alternatively, attending to an object that is a sign of restlessness is here called unwise attention.

Maññatīti [V 1.0251] abhimaññati, ahaṃkāraṃ karotīti attho. Seyyādivasena uccato namanaṃ uṇṇati. Sampaggaharasoti uṇṇativaseneva attano, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā sampaggaṇhanakicco, na vīriyaṃ viya taṃtaṃkiccasādhanena. Abhibhussahanavasena hīnassa attānaṃ nīcaṃ katvā gahaṇampi paggaṇhanavasenevāti veditabbaṃ. Ketu…pe… paccupaṭṭhānoti ettha ketu vuccati accuggatadhajo, idha pana ketu viyāti ketu, uḷāratamādibhāvo, taṃ ketubhāvasaṅkhātaṃ ketuṃ kamyatīti ketukamyaṃ, yassa dhammassa vasena taṃ ketukamyaṃ, so ketukamyatā. “Aha”nti pavattanato mānassa diṭṭhisadisī pavattatīti diṭṭhimānā ekacittuppāde na pavattanti, dve kesarasīhā viya ekaguhāyaṃ, tasmā māno diṭṭhivippayuttacitte sabbadā anuppajjamānopi diṭṭhisampayuttacitte niyamena anuppajjanato diṭṭhivippayuttalobhapadaṭṭhāno. Māno dhammasamūhaggahaṇe balavaṃ hutvā attukkaṃsanabhāvena [M 1.0319] pavattati, diṭṭhi ekekadhammampi niccādiākārena gaṇhantī pavattati. Attasinehasannissayo vā māno, attakilamathānuyogasannissayā diṭṭhīti ayametesaṃ viseso.

'He conceives' (maññati) means he conceives with pride; the meaning is he engages in 'I-making.' Loftiness (uṇṇati) is a condescension from a high position, by way of being superior. Its characteristic is uplifting; its function is to uplift oneself or associated states by way of loftiness, not like energy which accomplishes various tasks. It should be understood that even taking oneself as inferior by way of disdainful endurance is also by way of uplifting. 'Its manifestation is like a banner...' Here, 'ketu' means a lofty banner. But in this context, 'like a ketu' signifies the state of being extremely exalted. Desiring that which is designated as the state of a banner is 'ketukamyaṃ'. The state by which one has this desire for a banner is 'ketukamyatā' (desire for prominence). Because conceit proceeds from 'I-ness,' its operation is similar to that of wrong view, yet wrong view and conceit do not arise in a single thought-moment, like two lions in one cave. Therefore, although conceit does not always arise in consciousness dissociated from wrong view, it necessarily does not arise in consciousness associated with wrong view, and its proximate cause is greed dissociated from wrong view. Conceit arises with a strong grasping of a group of phenomena, manifesting as self-exaltation, while wrong view arises by grasping even a single phenomenon as permanent, etc. Conceit is based on affection for self, while wrong view is based on the practice of self-mortification—this is their distinction.

Issatīti usūyati. Tatthevāti parasampattīsuyeva. Issāvasena parasampattīsu atussanato vuttaṃ “anabhiratirasā”ti. Tenevetaṃ vuccati –

'He is jealous' (issati) means he envies. 'Therein' means 'only in the success of others.' By way of jealousy, due to discontent with the success of others, its characteristic is said to be non-delight. Thus it is said—

“Issānalasikhā yesaṃ, hadaye jalatīdha te;

Neva vindanti pāmojjaṃ, sambuddhādīhi sevita”nti.

“Those in whose hearts the flame of the fire of envy blazes here, they find no joy, that joy experienced by the Buddhas and others.”

Maccharayogena maccharini pavattaṃ macchara-saddaṃ gahetvā āha “maccharabhāvo macchariya”nti. Niruttinayena pana “mā idaṃ acchariyaṃ aññesaṃ hotu, mayhaṃva hotū”ti macchariyanti porāṇā. Niguhaṇaṃ attano sampattiyā paresaṃ adassanaṃ. Saṅkocanaṃ attasampattīnaṃ parehi sādhāraṇabhāvakaraṇassa aruccanākārena paṭikuṭanaṃ. “Mā idaṃ parassa hotū”ti paresu paṭihananavasena attasantakassa ārammaṇakaraṇato maccheraṃ paṭighacittesveva labbhatīti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ ekasseva dhammassa aññattha paṭihaññitvā aññārammaṇabhāvappasaṅgato. Parehi sādhāraṇabhāve paṭihananavasena pana taṃ ārabbha pavattanato maccheraṃ paṭighacittesu uppajjatīti yuttaṃ. Attasampattīti āvāsādisampatti.

Taking the word 'macchara' (stingy), which applies to one who is stingy due to the yoke of stinginess, it is said: 'The state of being stingy is stinginess.' But according to the etymological method, the ancients say, 'May this excellence not be for others, may it be for me alone'—that is stinginess. Concealment is not showing one's own possessions to others. Restriction is recoiling, in the form of dislike, from making one’s own possessions common to others. Some say that stinginess is found only in minds of aversion because it involves, by way of obstructing others, making what belongs to oneself the object, thinking, 'May this not be for another.' But this is not fitting, since it would absurdly follow that one and the same phenomenon, being obstructive in one respect, would have a different object. It is fitting, however, to say that stinginess arises in minds of aversion because it arises with that possession as its object, by way of obstructing its being shared with others. One's own possessions are possessions such as dwellings and the like.

Kucchitaṃ katanti ettha katampi akatampi garahitabbattā kucchitaṃ kataṃ nāma hoti. Evañhi [V 1.0252] vattāro honti “yaṃ mayā na kataṃ, taṃ kukata”nti. Tathā hi vakkhati “katākatānusocanarasa”nti. Evaṃ katākataṃ duccaritaṃ sucaritampi kucchitaṃ kataṃ nāma. Sucaritampi hi garahantassa kucchitaṃ katanti hoti[M 1.0320]. Yathā pana pathavīkasiṇārammaṇaṃ jhānaṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ, evaṃ kukataṃ ārabbha vippaṭisāravasena pavattaṃ cittaṃ taṃsahacaritatāya idha kukatanti gahetabbaṃ. Atha vā katākataṃ ārabbha uppajjanakavippaṭisāracittaṃyeva garahitabbato “kucchitaṃ kataṃ kukata”nti vuccati. Yassa dhammassa vasena taṃ cittaṃ kukataṃ nāma hoti, so dhammo kukkuccaṃ. Tenāha “kukataṃ, tassa bhāvo”ti. Pacchā anutappanaṃ viheṭhanaṃ pacchānutāpo. Katākatānusocanaṃ katākatassa sucaritaduccaritassa anusocanaṃ, “akataṃ vata me kalyāṇa”ntiādinā anutappanaṃ, “akataṃ mayā pubbe kalyāṇakammaṃ, ito dāni paṭṭhāya karomī”ti pavattaṃ pana kusalapakkhikaṃ vīriyameva, na katākatānusocanaṃ, katākatākāravisiṭṭhassa sucaritaduccaritassa anusocanavasena virūpaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ vippaṭisāro. Katākatānusocanañhi avaḍḍhisampādanato virūpaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ, taṃ parāyattatāhetutāya dāsabyaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā hi dāsabye sati dāso parāyatto hoti, evaṃ kukkucce sati taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo. Na hi so attano dhammatāya kusale pavattituṃ sakkoti. Atha vā katākatakusalākusalānusocanavasena āyattatāya tadubhayavasena kukkuccena taṃsamaṅgī hotīti taṃ dāsabyaṃ viya hoti.

Here, 'kucchitaṃ kataṃ' (a blameworthy deed) means that both what is done and what is not done are blameworthy; hence it is called 'kucchitaṃ kataṃ.' For people say, 'What I have not done is badly done (kukata).' Thus it will be said, 'its characteristic is remorse over what is done and not done.' In this way, both misconduct that is done and good conduct that is not done are called 'kucchitaṃ kataṃ.' For even good conduct is called 'kucchitaṃ kataṃ' when one blames it. Just as the jhana that has the earth-kasiṇa as its object is called 'the earth-kasiṇa,' so too the mind that arises with regret concerning what is badly done should be understood here as 'kukata' due to its association with that. Alternatively, the regretful mind itself that arises concerning what is done and not done is called 'kucchitaṃ kataṃ kukata' because it is blameworthy. The state by which that mind is called 'kukata' is 'kukkucca' (remorse). Hence it is said, 'kukataṃ, its state.' Subsequent regret (pacchānutāpo) is later remorse, a torment. Its characteristic is lamenting over what is done and not done, that is, lamenting over good and bad deeds done and not done, repenting with thoughts such as, 'Alas, I did not do what is good.' However, the effort that arises with the thought, 'I did not do good deeds before, but from now on I will do them,' is simply wholesome energy, not lamenting over what is done and not done. Regret (vippaṭisāro) is a perverse refuge (virūpaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ), distinguished by lamenting over the good and bad deeds characterized by what was done and not done. For lamenting over what was done and not done is a perverse refuge because it leads to decline. It should be seen as akin to slavery because it is a cause of dependence. Just as a slave is dependent when in a state of slavery, so too is a person endowed with remorse. Such a person cannot engage in what is wholesome by their own nature. Alternatively, because of dependence through lamenting over wholesome and unwholesome deeds done and not done, one endowed with remorse through that twofold state is like a slave. Thus, it is akin to slavery.

Anussāhanāvasīdanavasena saṃhatabhāvo thinaṃ, tena yogato cittaṃ thinaṃ, tassa bhāvo thinatā. Tenāha “anussāhasaṃhananatā”ti. Asamatthatāvighātavasena akammaññatā middhaṃ. Tenāha “asattivighāto”ti. Yasmā middhavaseneva tena sampayuttadhammā medhitā vihatasāmatthiyā honti, tasmā “middhatā middha”nti vuttaṃ. Na vijjati ussāho assāti anussāhaṃ, tabbhāvopi anussāhaṃ. Anussāhasaṅkhāto saṃhananabhāvo anussāhasaṃsīdanatā, kusītabhāvoti [M 1.0321] vuttaṃ hoti. Asattivighātoti yasmā taṃ middhaṃ uppajjamānameva sattivināsavasena uppajjati, tasmā natthi etassa sattīti taṃ sampayuttacittaṃ asatti, tassa bhāvopi, asattiyeva vighātoti asattivighāto.

The state of being shrunken due to lack of exertion and sinking down is sloth (thinaṃ); because of its connection, the mind is sluggish, and that state is slothfulness (thinatā). Hence it is said, 'the state of being shrunken due to lack of exertion.' Unwieldiness, by way of obstructing capability, is torpor (middhaṃ). Hence it is said, 'the obstruction of capability.' Because the associated states are dulled and their capability is destroyed by the influence of torpor, it is said, 'the state of torpor is torpor.' There is no exertion in it—thus, anussāhaṃ. Its nature is also anussāhaṃ. The state of being shrunken, designated as the absence of exertion, is anussāhasaṃsīdanatā—this is called a state of laziness. Asattivighāto (obstruction of capability) is so called because that torpor, as soon as it arises, arises by way of destroying capability. Therefore, since there is no capability in it, the associated mind is without capability; its nature is also non-capability. Thus, it is the obstruction of capability.

Anussāhanalakkhaṇanti ussāhapaṭipakkhalakkhaṇaṃ. Vīriyassa vinodanaṃ khepanaṃ vīriyavinodanaṃ. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ saṃsīdanākārena paccupaṭṭhāti, tesaṃ vā saṃsīdanaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetīti [V 1.0253] saṃsīdanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Akammaññatālakkhaṇanti ettha kāmaṃ thinampi akammaññatāsabhāvameva, taṃ pana cittassa akammaññaṃ, middhaṃ vedanādikkhandhattayassāti ayamettha viseso. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ “tattha katamaṃ thinaṃ? Yā cittassa akallatā akammaññatā. Katamaṃ middhaṃ? Yā kāyassa akallatā akammaññatā”ti (dha. sa. 1162) ca ādinā imesaṃ niddeso pavatto. Oṇahanaṃ viññāṇadvārānaṃ pidahanaṃ, sampayuttānaṃ bandhanaṃ vā. Līnatā līnākāro, ārammaṇaggahaṇe saṅkoco. Yasmā thinena cittasseva saṃhananaṃ hoti, middhena pana vedanādikkhandhattayassa viya rūpakāyassapi, tasmā taṃ pacalāyikāniddaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetīti pacalāyikāniddāpaccupaṭṭhānantipi vaṭṭati. Pottharūpapaṭicchādakapaṭo viya ārammaṇasabhāvāvacchādako moho. Mukhe bandhapaṭo viya sampayuttadhamme pattharituṃ adentaṃ middhanti ayametesaṃ viseso.

Its characteristic is lack of exertion, meaning its characteristic is being the opposite of exertion. The removal or dispelling of energy is the dispelling of energy. It is manifest in the form of the sinking of associated states, or it causes their sinking—thus, its manifestation is sinking. The characteristic of unworkability: here, though sloth itself has the nature of unworkability, it is the unworkability of the mind, while torpor is that of the three aggregates beginning with feeling—this is the distinction here. Indeed, in the Pāli canon, the exposition of these proceeds thus: 'Therein, what is sloth? It is the unwieldiness, the unworkability of the mind. What is torpor? It is the unwieldiness, the unworkability of the body' (Dhs. 1162), and so on. It is a covering over, a closing of the doors of consciousness, or the binding of associated states. It is sluggishness, a sluggish state, a shrinking back in grasping the object. Because sloth causes the constriction of the mind alone, whereas torpor affects the three aggregates beginning with feeling as well as the material body, it therefore manifests as nodding sleep—thus, its manifestation is also said to be nodding sleep. Delusion covers the intrinsic nature of the object like a cloth covering a manuscript, while torpor is like a cloth tied over the mouth, preventing the associated states from spreading out—this is their distinction.

Sesāti idha lakkhaṇādivasena vuttāvasesā phassādayo. Kusalesu vuttanayenāti lakkhaṇādito vuttanayena. Na koci ettha viseso atthīti ce, no natthīti āha “ettha panā”tiādi, vitakkādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ yathākkamaṃ micchāsaṅkappādināmamattameva visesoti attho. Ekūnavīsatīti [M 1.0322] ṭhapetvā mānādayo cha aniyatayevāpanake sesā sarūpenāgatā pannarasa chandādayo ca cattāro niyatayevāpanakāti ime ekena ūnā vīsati cetasikā. Aniyatayevāpanakānaṃ pana idha alabhantānampi ettha vacane kāraṇaṃ vuttameva.

Here, 'the rest' refers to the remaining mental factors such as contact, etc., mentioned by way of characteristics, etc. 'By the method stated in the wholesome' means by the method stated from characteristics onwards. If it is said, 'Is there no distinction here?', it is not that there is none; thus it is said, 'But here,' etc. The meaning is that the distinction lies only in the mere names—wrong thought, etc.—for the three, initial thought, etc., respectively. 'Nineteen': excluding the six beginning with conceit, which are indeterminate adventitious factors, the remaining fifteen that have come in their own nature and the four determinate adventitious factors beginning with zeal—these are the nineteen mental factors. As for the indeterminate adventitious factors, even though they are not found here, the reason for their mention has already been stated.

Thinamiddhassa aniyatabhāvoti thinamiddhassa aniyatassa idha uppajjanakabhāvamāha, na pana paṭhame niyatabhāvaṃ tattha sabbasova anuppajjanato. Na hi sabhāvatikhiṇaṃ cittaṃ thinamiddhayogī hotīti. Tatiye mānassa aniyatassa sambhavepi niyatadhamme sandhāya “aṭṭhārasā”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “māno panettha aniyato”ti. Diṭṭhiyā saha na uppajjatīti ettha kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Catutthe avasesāti aṭṭhāraseva, pañcame ṭhapetvā pītiṃ diṭṭhiyā saha aṭṭhāraseva, tathā chaṭṭhepi. Sattame pītiyā, diṭṭhiyā ca abhāvato sattarasa, tathā aṭṭhamepi.

'The indeterminate nature of sloth and torpor' refers to the possibility of indeterminate sloth and torpor arising here, not to their determinate nature in the first case, since they do not arise there at all. For a mind that is naturally sharp is not associated with sloth and torpor. In the third case, although indeterminate conceit is possible, 'eighteen' is stated with reference to the determinate factors. Hence it is said, 'but conceit here is indeterminate.' The reason why it does not arise together with wrong view has already been stated. In the fourth case, the remaining factors are just eighteen. In the fifth case, excluding joy but together with wrong view, there are just eighteen, and likewise in the sixth case. In the seventh case, due to the absence of both joy and wrong view, there are seventeen, and similarly in the eighth case.

Etepi tayoti na kevalaṃ karuṇāmuditā eva, etepi tayo ekato na uppajjanti aññamaññaṃ visayabhedatoyeva. Tathā hi issā parasampattivisayā, macchariyaṃ attasampattiyā parehi [V 1.0254] sādhāraṇābhāvavisayaṃ, kukkuccaṃ katākatavisayanti, tasmā yaṃ abhayagirivāsino vadanti “issāmaccheraṃ yadicchāvasena ekatopi uppajjatī”ti, na taṃ gahetabbaṃ.

These three also—not only compassion and sympathetic joy—do not arise together, precisely because their objects are mutually distinct. For envy has the success of others as its object; stinginess has as its object the non-sharing of one's own success with others; and remorse has as its object what has been done and not done. Therefore, what the residents of Abhayagiri say—'envy and stinginess can arise together at will'—should not be accepted.

Sabhāvato, parikappanato vā aniṭṭhassa ārammaṇassa aniṭṭhākāraṃ vā ārammaṇassa anubhavanaṃ sambhuñjanaṃ aniṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇamassāti aniṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ. Tenāha “aniṭṭhākārasambhogarasa”nti, yathābhūtena vā ayathābhūtena vā aniṭṭhākārena ārammaṇassa sambhuñjanarasaṃ, paccānubhavanakiccanti attho. Titthiyādīnañhi sabhāvato iṭṭhe buddhādiārammaṇepi aniṭṭhākārato gahaṇavasena [M 1.0323] domanassaṃ uppajjati. Domanassassa ekantena kāmadhātuyaṃyeva pavattanato āha “hadayavatthupadaṭṭhāna”nti. Tassa hi anīvaraṇāvatthāya abhāvato rūpārūpadhātuyaṃ asambhavo.

The experiencing or enjoying of an undesirable object, or of the undesirable aspect of an object, whether by its own nature or by fabrication, is 'experiencing an undesirable object'; that is its characteristic, hence its characteristic is experiencing an undesirable object. Therefore it is said, 'its function is the enjoyment of an undesirable aspect,' the meaning of which is: its function is enjoying an object through its undesirable aspect, whether that aspect is actual or not, and its task is re-experiencing. For in the case of heretics and others, sorrow arises from grasping in an undesirable way even an object that is by nature desirable, such as the Buddha. Because sorrow occurs exclusively in the desire realm, it is said, 'the heart-base is its proximate cause.' For its absence in the form and formless realms is due to the state of non-hindrance that prevails there.

Attano pavattiākāravasena aniṭṭharūpasamuṭṭhāpanavasena vā virūpaṃ sappanaṃ visappanaṃ, aniṭṭharūpasamuṭṭhāpanavaseneva vā visappanaṃ sarīrakampanaṃ, taṃ raso kiccaṃ, sampatti vā assāti visappanaraso, nissayassa hadayavatthuno, sakalasseva vā kāyassa vijjhattabhāvāpādanato āha “attano nissayadahanaraso vā”ti, vijjhattabhāvāpādanatoti ca milātabhāvāpādanatoti attho. Yathā kathaṃ viyāti āha “dāvaggi viyā”ti. So hi vanaghaṭeyeva uppanno tameva dahati. Dussanapaccupaṭṭhānoti attano, parassa ca dūsanākārena paccupaṭṭhāno. So hi yassa santāne uppanno, taṃ ekantena antamaso virūpabhāvāpādanenapi dūseti, paraṃ pana dūsetu vā, mā vā hatthena gahitaasuci viya. “Anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādīni nava āghātavatthūni padaṭṭhānamassāti āghātavatthupadaṭṭhāno. So upayogaphalakālesu aniṭṭhattā visasaṃsaṭṭhapūtimuttaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo. Aṭṭhārasa vāti issādīsu aniyatesu ekena saddhiṃ aṭṭhārasa vā.

By way of its own mode of occurrence, or by way of producing undesirable forms, it is a deformed spreading, a poisonous spreading; or by way of producing undesirable forms alone, it is a poisonous spreading, a bodily trembling. That is its function, task, or accomplishment; hence its function is poisonous spreading. Because it brings about a state of being pierced for its support, the heart-base, or for the entire body, it is said, 'or its function is to burn its own support.' 'Bringing about a state of being pierced' means bringing about a state of withering. As to how, it is said, 'like a forest fire.' For having arisen in a forest grove, it burns that very grove. Its manifestation is corrupting: it is manifest in a way that corrupts oneself and others. For in whosesoever continuum it arises, it utterly corrupts them, at least by producing a deformed appearance, while it may or may not corrupt another, like filth held in the hand. The nine grounds of resentment, such as, 'They have done me harm,' are its proximate cause. At the times of its application and its result, because it is undesirable, it should be seen as like putrid urine mixed with poison. 'Or eighteen' means eighteen together with one of the indeterminate factors, such as envy.

Pavattiṭṭhitimattāti cetaso pavattisaṅkhātā ṭhitimattā, maggaṅgādibhāvaṃ na gacchati adhimokkhavirahatoti attho. Atha vā pavattiṭṭhitimattāti khaṇaṭṭhitimattā. “Nivāte dīpaccīnaṃ ṭhiti viyā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Cittaṭṭhiti viya santānaṭṭhitiyā paccayo bhavituṃ asamatthattā nicchayābhāvena asaṇṭhahanato cetaso pavattipaccayamattatāya pavattiṭṭhitimattā khaṇaṭṭhitimattā pavattipaccayamattā ṭhiti pavattiṭṭhitīti katvā. Vigatā cikicchāti nissakke paccattavacanaṃ “pisuṇā [V 1.0255] vācā paṭivirato”tiādīsu [M 1.0324] viya, vigatā tikicchāyāti attho. Ayameva vā pāṭho. “Vigatā cikicchā”ti cikicchituṃ dukkaratāya cetaṃ vuttaṃ, na sabbathā cikicchāya abhāvato. “Evaṃ nu kho, na nu kho”tiādinā saṃsappanavasena seti, samantato vā setīti saṃsayo. Kampanarasāti cittassa kampanakiccā. Uddhaccañhi attanā gahitākāreyeva ṭhatvā bhamatīti ekārammaṇasmiṃ eva vipphandanavasena pavattati, vicikicchā pana yadipi ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe uppajjati, tathāpi “evaṃ nu kho, na nu kho”ti aññaṃ gahetabbākāraṃ apekkhatīti nānārammaṇe kampanaṃ hoti. Anicchayākārena dveḷhakākārena paccupaṭṭhāti, anicchayaṃ vā paccupaṭṭhāpetīti anicchayapaccupaṭṭhānā.

'Merely stability in occurrence' means merely the stability designated as the occurrence of the mind; the meaning is that it does not attain the state of a path factor, etc., due to the lack of determination. Alternatively, 'merely stability in occurrence' means momentary stability. For it is said, 'Like the stability of a lamp flame in a windless place.' Because it is unable to be a condition for the stability of the continuity, as mental stability is, due to an absence of certainty and an inability to be firm, and because it is merely a condition for the mind's occurrence, it is called 'merely stability in occurrence'—momentary stability, a stability that is merely a condition for occurrence. 'Devoid of cure' (vigatā cikicchā): this is a reflexive expression in the sense of 'without,' as in phrases like 'abstaining from divisive speech,' meaning 'devoid of a cure for it.' Or this is the reading. 'Devoid of cure' is said because it is difficult to cure, not because a cure is entirely absent. 'Is it so, or is it not so?': it lies by way of creeping around, or it lies on all sides; thus it is 'doubt' (saṃsayo). 'Its function is trembling' means its task is to make the mind tremble. For restlessness, while remaining in the mode it has grasped, wanders about; it proceeds by way of agitation concerning a single object. Doubt, however, even if it arises regarding a single object, still looks for another mode to be grasped, thinking, 'Is it so, or is it not so?'; thus its trembling occurs with regard to various alternatives. It is manifest in the manner of indecision, in the manner of perplexity, or it causes indecision to be manifest; thus its manifestation is indecision.

Adhimokkhavicikicchānaṃ aññamaññaṃ viparītakiccatāya āha “vicikicchāya abhāvenā”ti. Samādhīti cittekaggatā. Sā hi ārammaṇe cittassa sammā ādhānato “samādhī”ti vuccati. Balavā hotīti balavamittena dinnapiṭṭhibalo puriso viya balavā hoti, balādibhāvaṃ gacchatīti adhippāyo.

Because determination and doubt have mutually opposite functions, it is said, ‘through the absence of doubt.’ Concentration (samādhi) is one-pointedness of mind. Indeed, it is called ‘concentration’ because of the proper fixing (ādhāna) of the mind on its object. ‘It becomes strong’ means it becomes strong like a man given support by a strong friend; the meaning is that it attains a state of strength, and so on.

Sattārammaṇattāti sattapaññattārammaṇattā. Nanu paññattārammaṇāpi vipākā hontīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “kāmāvacaravipākānaṃ ekantaparittārammaṇattā”ti. Kuto pana viratīnaṃ kusalattamevāti cāritanti āha “pañca sikkhāpadā kusalāti (vibha. 715) hi vutta”nti. Yadi evaṃ lokuttaravipākesu viratiyo na labbhantīti? No na labbhanti sikkhāpadavibhaṅge lokiyaviratiyoyeva sandhāya vuttattā. Tena lokiyavipākesuyeva viratiyo na sambhavantīti gahetabbaṃ.

‘Because it has beings as its object’ means it has the concept of beings as its object. But is it not so that mental states taking concepts as objects can also be results? Addressing this objection, it is said, ‘Because the results of the sense-sphere have exclusively limited objects.’ Then, why is it that abstinences are exclusively wholesome? In response to this, it is said, ‘For the five precepts are wholesome,’ as stated (Vibhaṅga 715). If that is so, are abstinences not found in supramundane results? No, it is not that they are not found, because in the analysis of the precepts, only mundane abstinences are referred to. Therefore, it should be understood that abstinences do not arise in mundane results.

Kāyapasādasannissitattā [M 1.0325] kāye bhavo sātabhāvo lakkhaṇamassāti kāyikasātalakkhaṇā. Cetasikasukhe vuttanayena paccupaṭṭhānādayo netabbāti āha “sesā vuttanayā evā”ti.

‘The characteristic of bodily pleasure’ means its characteristic is a pleasant state existing in the body, because it is dependent on the body’s sensitivity. Manifestation and so on should be understood according to the method stated for mental pleasure; therefore, it is said, ‘The rest are exactly as previously explained.’

84-6. Nanu ca iṭṭhe ārammaṇe sukhavedanā uppajjati, aniṭṭhe dukkhavedanā, iṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhatte upekkhāvedanā, cakkhuviññāṇādayo ca kusalavipākā iṭṭhe, iṭṭhamajjhatte vā ārammaṇe uppajjanti, tattha yutto tāva iṭṭhamajjhatte upekkhāvedanāyogo, na pana iṭṭhārammaṇe, na cāpi etaṃ sakkā vattuṃ parikappanāvasena iṭṭhārammaṇampi iṭṭhamajjhattato gaṇhanti yathā “kammaviññāṇa”nti vipākānaṃ avañcanīyabhāvato, tasmā kathaṃ iṭṭhe, iṭṭhamajjhatte ca uppajjamānesu [V 1.0256] cakkhusotaghānajivhāviññāṇesu upekkhāvedanāyeva sambhavati, na sukhavedanā, yato tesu upekkhāvedanā vuttāti imaṃ codanaṃ saṅkhepato dassetuṃ “iṭṭhārammaṇayogasmi”ntiādiṃ vatvā puna tassā sodhanatthaṃ “upādāya ca rūpenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhūtarūpaṃ upādāya nissāya pavattaṃ rūpaṃ upādāyarūpaṃ. “Upādāya ca rūpenā”ti pana “manasī ca kāro”ti ettha vuttanayameva. “Upādāyakarūpenā”ti vā pāṭho, cakkhuviññāṇassa vatthubhūtena cakkhupasādena, tathā sotaviññāṇādīnaṃ vatthubhūtena sotapasādādinā ca upādāyarūpenāti attho. Upādārūpake panāti ya-kāralopaṃ katvā niddeso “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso”tiādīsu viya, yathākkamaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ ārammaṇabhūte rūpasaddādike upādāyarūpeti attho. Saṃghaṭṭanānighaṃsassāti saṃghaṭṭanāsaṅkhātassa nighaṃsassa. Saṃghaṭṭanāyeva aññamaññavisayavisayībhāvassa anurūpadesuppattisaṅkhātanighaṃso viyāti nighaṃsoti vuccati. Atha vā sampattāsampattaggahaṇavasena saṃghaṭṭanāya nighaṃsassa cāti attho. Cakkhurūpasotasaddā hi [M 1.0326] aññamaññaṃ asampattāyeva anurūpadesuppattiyā aññamaññaṃ ghaṭṭanti nāma. Tato tesaṃ vasena ghaṭṭanākārabhūto aññamaññābhimukhabhāvo “saṃghaṭṭanā”ti vutto. Ghānagandhā, pana jivhārasā ca aññamaññaṃ sampattāyeva āsannataradese uppannā aññamaññaṃ nighaṃsenti āhacca tiṭṭhanti. Tato tesaṃ vasena nighaṃso vuttoti. Dubbalattāti adhikaraṇīmatthake picupiṇḍakaṃ ṭhapetvā picupiṇḍeneva pahatakāle viya phuṭṭhamattabhāvena dubbalattā. Dīpayeti evaṃ saṃghaṭṭanānighaṃsassa dubbalattā vedanā majjhattaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti upekkhāyogaṃ pakāseyya. Yadi evaṃ kāyaviññāṇepi idaṃ samānanti, noti āha “pasādaṃ panā”tiādi. Yathā hi adhikaraṇīmatthake kappāsapicupiṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā kūṭena paharantassa kūṭaṃ picupiṇḍamatikkamma adhikaraṇiṃ gaṇhāti, evamevaṃ kāyadvāre bahiddhā mahābhūtārammaṇaṃ ajjhattikakāyapasādaṃ ghaṭṭetvā taṃ atikkamma pasādapaccayesu mahābhūtesu paṭihaññati, nighaṃso balavā hoti, tasmā iṭṭhārammaṇe kāyaviññāṇasampayuttā sukhavedanā hoti, aniṭṭhārammaṇe pana vuttanayena dukkhavedanāti vuttaṃ hoti.

84-6. But is it not so that pleasant feeling arises with a desirable object, unpleasant feeling with an undesirable one, and neutral feeling with a neither-desirable-nor-undesirable object? And is it not also true that eye-consciousness and the like, being the result of wholesome kamma, arise in relation to a desirable or neutral object? In that case, neutral feeling is appropriate only for a neutral object, not for a desirable one. Nor can it be said that they consider a desirable object as neutral due to conceptualization, as in the case of ‘kamma-consciousness,’ because the results of kamma are unalterable. So how is it that in eye-, ear-, nose-, and tongue-consciousness arising in relation to desirable or neutral objects, only neutral feeling occurs, not pleasant feeling, since neutral feeling is said to arise in them? To briefly present this objection, it is stated: ‘In relation to a desirable object,’ etc. Then, to clarify this, it is further explained: ‘Dependent on material form,’ etc. The material form that arises dependent on and supported by the primary elements is called ‘derived material form.’ Here, the phrase ‘dependent on material form’ should be understood in the same way as ‘mental activity’ is explained elsewhere. Alternatively, the reading may be ‘dependent on derived material form,’ meaning that eye-consciousness depends on the eye-sensitivity, which serves as its basis, and similarly, ear-consciousness and the others depend on ear-sensitivity, etc., as their basis. Regarding ‘in derived material,’ the elision of the letter ‘ya’ is made for the sake of explanation, as in phrases like ‘reflects wisely.’ In order, it means that eye-consciousness and the others take their respective objects—visible form, sound, etc.—as derived material. ‘Of impact and pressure’ means of the pressure known as impact. Impact itself is called ‘pressure’ because it is like the pressure that arises from the appropriate occurrence of mutual interaction between sense objects and their faculties. Alternatively, it means both impact and pressure, depending on whether there is contact or not. For instance, the eye and visible form, and the ear and sound, though not actually coming into contact, are said to interact by appearing in appropriate locations relative to each other. Therefore, in their case, the mutual facing that constitutes the mode of interaction is called ‘impact.’ On the other hand, the nose and smell, and the tongue and taste, being in actual contact, press against each other when they arise in close proximity and remain in contact. Hence, in their case, it is called ‘pressure.’ ‘Due to weakness’ means due to its weakness, being merely touched, just as when a lump of cotton placed on an anvil is struck, it is only the cotton that is hit. It explains that thus, due to the weakness of impact and pressure, feeling remains in a neutral state, thereby manifesting the appropriateness of equanimity. If it is argued that the same should apply to body-consciousness, the reply is: ‘But the sensitivity...’ etc. Just as when a lump of cotton placed on an anvil is struck by a hammer, the hammer bypasses the cotton and hits the anvil, so too in the case of the body door, the external great elements as object strike the internal body-sensitivity and, bypassing it, collide with the primary elements conditioned by the sensitivity. Here, the pressure is strong. Therefore, in relation to a desirable object, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasant feeling, while in relation to an undesirable object, as explained, it is accompanied by unpleasant feeling. Thus it is said.

Manodhātunāti ettha kiñcāpi dhātu-saddo idha itthiliṅgeyeva dissati, imināyeva pana ācariyassa vacanena pulliṅgo atthīti siddhaṃ. Keci pana “sakkaṭavohārena vutta”nti vadanti. Sampayuttā dasa dhammāti sambandho. Tasmāvetthāti ettha va-kāro padasandhimattakaro.

Regarding ‘manodhātunā’ here—although the word ‘dhātu’ appears here only in the feminine gender—it is established by this very statement of the teacher that the masculine gender also exists. Some, however, say that ‘it is spoken according to Sanskrit usage.’ ‘Associated with ten phenomena’ is the connection. Therefore, in ‘tasmāvettha,’ the letter ‘va’ is merely a euphonic consonant.

Kāyaviññāṇe dukkhavedanāti kiñcāpi sukhādikanti ādi-saddena akusalavipākakāyaviññāṇassa [V 1.0257] dukkhavedanāsampayogo vutto, idha panassā lakkhaṇādidassanatthaṃ puna “kāyaviññāṇe dukkhavedanā”ti upaññāso kato, rasādayo [M 1.0327] panassa kusalavipāke sukhavedanāya vuttavipariyāyena yojetabbāti idha na vuttā. Sesāti sesacetasikā.

Regarding ‘painful feeling in body-consciousness’—although the association of painful feeling with unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness is stated by the word ‘etc.’ (in ‘pleasant, etc.’), here, however, the phrase ‘painful feeling in body-consciousness’ is repeated to show its characteristics, etc. But its function and so on should be applied to the wholesome resultant consciousness in the opposite way to that stated for pleasant feeling, and thus they are not mentioned here. ‘The rest’ refers to the remaining mental factors.

Balappattoti sesāhetukacittasampayuttasamādhito ayaṃ vīriyindriyayogena balavabhāvappatto, na pana balarāsippattoti attho. Yadi evaṃ kasmā cetasikavibhāganiddese “balāni dve dvicittesū”ti vuttaṃ? Tattha hi kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇayugaḷaṃ sandhāya tathā vuttaṃ. Sabbaṃ sesāhetukacittesu cittekaggatāya vibhaṅge –

‘Attained strength’ means that this, through its connection with the faculty of energy, has attained a state of strength greater than the concentration associated with the other rootless consciousnesses; but the meaning is not that it has attained the full measure of strength. If so, why is it said in the analysis of mental factors, ‘The two strengths are in two consciousnesses’? There, it is said thus with reference to the pair of functional rootless mind-consciousness. In the analysis of one-pointedness of mind in all the other rootless consciousnesses:

“Katamā tasmiṃ samaye cittassa ekaggatā hoti? Yā tasmiṃ samaye cittassa ṭhitī”ti (dha. sa. 11) –

‘What is the one-pointedness of mind at that time? Whatever at that time is the mind’s stability.’ (Dhs. 11)

Ettakameva vatvā kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātusampayuttāya ekaggatāya vibhaṅge –

Having said only this much, in the analysis of one-pointedness associated with the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element:

“Katamā tasmiṃ samaye cittassa ekaggatā hoti? Yā tasmiṃ samaye cittassa ṭhiti saṇṭhiti avaṭṭhiti avisāhāro avikkhepo avisāhaṭamānasatā samatho samādhindriyaṃ samādhibala”nti (dha. sa. 11) –

‘What is the one-pointedness of mind at that time? Whatever at that time is the mind’s stability, steadfastness, settledness, non-distraction, non-scattering, undistractedness of mind, tranquility, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration.’ (Dhs. 11)

Balapariyosānaṃ katvā vibhajitattā vīriyavibhaṅge ca –

Because it is analyzed by making strength its culmination, and in the analysis of energy:

“Katamaṃ tasmiṃ samaye vīriyindriyaṃ hoti? Yo tasmiṃ samaye cetasiko vīriyārambho nikkamo parakkamo uyyāmo vāyāmo ussāho ussoḷhī thāmo dhiti asithilaparakkamatā anikkhittachandatā anikkhittadhuratā dhurasampaggāho vīriyaṃ vīriyindriyaṃ vīriyabala”nti (dha. sa. 13) –

‘What is the faculty of energy at that time? Whatever at that time is mental effort, exertion, striving, endeavor, perseverance, enthusiasm, vigor, steadfastness, fortitude, unrelaxed effort, unabandoned desire, unabandoned burden, shouldering the burden, energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy.’ (Dhs. 13)

Balapariyosānaṃ [M 1.0328] katvā vibhajitattā vibhaṅgavāre āgataṃ samādhibalaṃ, vīriyabalañca sandhāya “balāni dve dvicittesū”ti vuttaṃ, na pana dhammuddesavāre balarāsiyaṃ āgatabalaṃ sandhāya sabbāhetukacittesu dhammuddesassa maggarāsito paṭṭhāya parihīnattā.

Having concluded the section on the powers, and because they have been analyzed, the statement 'two powers in two consciousnesses' is made with reference to the power of concentration and the power of energy, which are mentioned in the chapter on analysis (Vibhaṅga). It is not made, however, with reference to the powers included in the collection of powers in the chapter on the enumeration of dhammas, because the enumeration of dhammas is deficient in all rootless consciousnesses, starting from the path-aggregate.

87. Vipākakiriyāhadayehīti [V 1.0258] vipākakiriyacittehi. Hadayaṃ mano mānasaṃ cittanti hi pariyāyavacanaṃ. Sobhanaṃ gataṃ gamanamassāti sugato. Bhagavato hi vineyyajanūpasaṅkamanaṃ ekantena tesaṃ hitasukhanipphādanato sobhanaṃ, tathā lakkhaṇānubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitarūpakāyatāya dhutavilambitādidosarahitaṃ avahasitarājahaṃsavasabhavāraṇamigarājagamanaṃ kāyagamanaṃ, ñāṇagamanañca nimmalavipulakaruṇāsativīriyādiguṇavisesasamaṅgībhūtamabhinīhārato yāva mahābodhiṃ anavajjatāya sobhanamevāti. Atha vā sakalampi lokaṃ pariññābhisamayavasena sayambhuñāṇena parijānanto sammā gato avagatoti sugato, tathā lokasamudayaṃ pahānābhisamayavasena pajahanto anuppattidhammataṃ āpādento sammā gato atītoti sugato, lokanirodhasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena sammā gato adhigatoti sugato, lokanirodhagāminipaṭipadāsaṅkhātaṃ maggaṃ bhāvanābhisamayavasena sammā gato pattoti sugato. Atha vā sammā gadatīti sugato. Bhagavā hi bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ vineyyānaṃ yathārahaṃ kālayuttameva dhammaṃ bhāsati, tasmā sammā gadatīti da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā “sugato”ti vutto. Atha vā sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ, nibbānameva vā gatoti sugato, tena sugatena.

87. "Vipākakiriyāhadayehīti" means with resultant and functional consciousnesses. For 'hadaya,' 'mano,' 'mānasa,' and 'citta' are indeed synonyms. 'His going is excellent, thus he is the Well-Gone (sugato).' The Blessed One's approach to trainable persons is entirely for their welfare and happiness; thus, it is excellent. Similarly, his physical gait, adorned with the major and minor characteristics, free from faults like being too slow or too fast, surpasses the gait of a royal swan, a bull, an elephant, or a lion king; and his gait of knowledge, endowed with special qualities such as immaculate and vast compassion, mindfulness, and energy, is excellent up to his great enlightenment on account of his aspiration and faultlessness. Alternatively, he is the Well-Gone (sugato) because, having fully understood the entire world with his self-originated knowledge by way of the full understanding of comprehension, he has rightly gone and understood. Likewise, having abandoned the origin of the world by way of the full understanding of abandonment and brought it to a state of non-arising, he has rightly gone and passed beyond; thus he is the Well-Gone. Having realized Nibbāna, known as the cessation of the world, by way of the full understanding of realization, he has rightly gone and attained it; thus he is the Well-Gone. Having developed the path leading to the cessation of the world by way of the full understanding of development, he has rightly gone and reached it; thus he is the Well-Gone. Or, he is the Well-Spoken (sugato) because he speaks rightly. The Blessed One speaks the Dhamma that is true, factual, beneficial, and timely, as is suitable for those to be trained. Therefore, because he speaks rightly, he is called 'Sugato,' with the 'd' changed to a 't'. Or, he is the Well-Gone (sugato) because he has gone to the beautiful place—to perfect self-enlightenment or to Nibbāna itself. Hence, 'by that Sugata'.

88. “Avagacchatī”tiādīsu yo bhikkhu anūnaṃ atthato vā byañjanato vā anūnaṃ suparipuṇṇaṃ tatoyeva paramaṃ [M 1.0329] visiṭṭhaṃ imaṃ abhidhammāvatāraṃ nāma pakaraṇaṃ avagacchati avabujjhati, sammāuggahaṇadhāraṇādisampādanavasena ogāhitvā jānāti. Atha vā paramanayadīpanato paramaṃ imaṃ pakaraṇaṃ yo anūnaṃ katvā avagacchati jānāti, tassevaṃ avagacchato yathāsabhāvaṃ mananato matisaṅkhātā paññā durāsade maṃsacakkhunā paramāṇu viya lokiyañāṇena durāsade durādhigantabbe adhigantuṃ dukkaratare, atigambhīraṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā sinerupabbatarājānaṃ rāhuādīhi mahākāyehipi sabbena sabbaṃ ajjhogāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya mahāsamudde viya ṭhapetvā sammāsambuddhaṃ sāriputtādīhipi mahāñāṇehi sāvakehi sabbena sabbaṃ ajjhogāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyarūpe abhidhammanaye vijambhate hemantasālapanti viya pattharati, abhimukhābhimukheyeva dhamme pavattatīti vā attho.

88. In such passages as "one who comprehends," it means a monk who comprehends and understands this treatise called the "Abhidhammāvatāra" without deficiency in meaning or wording, completely, and for that very reason supreme and distinguished; he knows it by having penetrated it through accomplishing right grasping, retention, and so on. Or, one who, having made it complete, comprehends and knows this supreme treatise because of its exposition of the supreme method. For one who thus comprehends, the wisdom called intellect, which arises from reflecting according to its true nature, unfolds in the Abhidhamma method—which is difficult to approach, like an atom with the physical eye; difficult to approach with worldly knowledge, difficult to attain, and extremely hard to reach. It is in an exceedingly profound state, like the great ocean, of such a nature that, apart from the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, even great disciples with vast knowledge like Sāriputta are unable to completely penetrate it, just as the great ocean, setting aside Mount Sineru, cannot be completely fathomed even by great-bodied beings like Rāhu and others. This wisdom spreads out like a row of sal trees in winter, or the meaning is that it proceeds facing the dhammas directly.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus is the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

The Commentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma.

Cetasikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Designation of Mental Factors is concluded.

3. Tatiyo paricchedo

3. Chapter Three

Cetasikavibhāganiddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Classification of Mental Factors

89. Nāmasāmaññatoyeva [V 1.0259] dvepaññāsāti phassādināmasāmaññena dvīhi adhikā paṇṇāsa honti, sampayuttadhammabhedato pana ekūnanavuticittasampayutto phasso ekūnanavutividhoti evamādinā bahuvidhāpi hontīti attho.

89. "Just fifty-two in general terms of name": Because of the generality of the term 'name,' referring to contact and so on, there are fifty-two; but due to the distinctions among associated states, contact, being associated with eighty-nine types of consciousness, is of eighty-nine kinds, and so on, they are manifold in this way—this is the meaning.

Nanu ca phassādayo heṭṭhā pāḷikkamena dassitā, idha pana kasmā na tathā vuttāti? Ekekasabhāvavantānaṃ taṃtaṃsāmaññāpekkhāya [M 1.0330] ekasmiṃ ṭhāne niddisitukāmattā. Phassādayo hi manakkārāvasānā terasa kusalākusalābyākatasāmaññato ekato vuttā, majjhattādayo muditāvasānā pañcavīsati kusalābyākatasāmaññato, lobhādayo pana anottappāvasānā akusalabhāvasāmaññatoti evaṃ taṃtaṃsāmaññāpekkhāya samānasabhāvā dhammā ekato vuttāti.

But were not contact and the others shown earlier in the order of the Pāḷi? Why are they not stated here in the same way? It is because of the desire to indicate them in one place, in consideration of the respective commonalities of those that possess individual natures. For instance, contact and the others, ending with attention, are thirteen, stated together due to the commonality of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; the neutral states and the others, ending with sympathetic joy, are twenty-five, due to the commonality of wholesome and indeterminate; while greed and the others, ending with lack of moral dread, are due to the commonality of unwholesome states. Thus, states of similar nature are stated together in consideration of their respective commonalities.

90. Evaṃ phassādayo dhamme uddisitvā idāni “ettakesu ayaṃ dhammo samupalabbhatī”ti cittuppādesu tesaṃ payogaṃ dassetuṃ paṭhamaṃ tāva cittagaṇanaṃ dassento āha “catupaññāsadhā”tiādi. Kāmeti kāmāvacareti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ “rūpe arūpe”ti etthāpi. Āsavavisayattābhāvato na vijjanti etesu āsavāti anāsavā.

90. Having thus enumerated the states beginning with contact, now, to show their application in the arisings of consciousness by stating, "In how many of these does this state occur?" he first presents the enumeration of consciousness, saying, "Fifty-fourfold," etc. "Sensual" means pertaining to the sensual realm. Similarly, with "form" and "formless" here as well. Because they are not a domain for the taints, taints do not exist in them; hence, they are "untainted."

91-2. Samāsatoti vitthārāpekkhāya vuttaṃ, na itopi samāsassa abhāvato. Atisaṅkhepato pana ekūnanavuti cittuppādā honti. Etesūti imesu cittuppādesu. Tesaṃ phassādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ uppattiṃ ekekaṃ uddharitvā cittacetasikesu bhikkhūnaṃ pāṭavatthāya pavakkhāmīti sambandho. Ekakanti ekekaṃ, gāthābandhavasena e-kāralopo.

91–92. "In brief": This is said in relation to the detailed account, not because a briefer summary is impossible. But in extreme brevity, there are eighty-nine arisings of consciousness. "In these": in these arisings of consciousness. The connection is this: "Having taken up one by one the arising of those states beginning with contact, I will explain it for the monks as a subject of study concerning consciousness and mental factors." "Individually" (ekakaṃ): this stands for ekekaṃ (one by one); the elision of the vowel 'e' is for the sake of the meter.

93. Cetasikavibhāgaṃ vattukāmopi avinibbhogadhamme dassetuṃ cittena saha ekato katvā [V 1.0260] āha “phassapañcaka”nti. Ekato uppādo etesanti ekuppādā, saha khīyantīti sahakkhayā, ekato uppajjitvā ekato nirujjhanakāti attho.

93. Though intending to explain the classification of mental factors, in order to show the inseparable states, he combines them with consciousness and says, "the pentad beginning with contact." "Arising together" (ekuppādā): they have a single arising. "Perishing together" (sahakkhayā): they perish together. The meaning is that they arise together and cease together.

94. Sabbesveva ekavīsasatesu cittesu samupalabbhanato sabbasādhāraṇā. Kiñcāpi anantaragāthāya cittena [M 1.0331] saha ekuppādādibhāvakathaneneva imesaṃ sabbasādhāraṇatā vuttā, tattha pana ekuppādādimattakathanameva icchitaṃ, na sabbasādhāraṇatā. Vuttopi vāyamattho tattha apākaṭattā puna pākaṭaṃ katvā idha vuttoti.

94. "Common to all": Because they are found in all one hundred and twenty-one types of consciousness. Although their commonality to all is stated in the next verse by mentioning their simultaneous arising, etc., with consciousness, there the intention is only to mention their simultaneous arising, etc., not their commonality to all. Or, even if this meaning was stated there, it was unclear, and is therefore stated here to make it clear.

95-100. Dvipañcaviññāṇavajjitacatucattālīsakāmāvacaracittesu, lokiyalokuttaravasena ekādasasu paṭhamajjhānikacittesu cāti pañcapaññāsacittesu vitakkassa desitattā āha “vitakko…pe… samudīrito”ti. Vicāro pañcapaññāsasavitakkacittesu ceva ekādasasu dutiyajjhānikacittesu cāti chasaṭṭhicittesu uppajjatīti āha “cāro…pe… jāyate”ti.

95–100. Since initial thought is taught as occurring in the fifty-five types of consciousness—that is, in the forty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses excluding the two sets of five sense-consciousnesses, and in the eleven first-jhāna consciousnesses, both mundane and supramundane—he says, "initial thought... is stirred up." Since sustained thought arises in the sixty-six types of consciousness—that is, in the fifty-five consciousnesses accompanied by initial thought and in the eleven second-jhāna consciousnesses—he says, "sustained thought... is born."

Ekapaññāsacittesu pītīti kāyaviññāṇavajjitesu aṭṭhārasasu somanassasahagatakāmāvacaracittesu ceva catutthapañcamajjhānavajjitatettiṃsarūpajjhānikacittesu cāti ekapaññāsacittesu pīti jāyati. Tesaṭṭhiyā sukhanti ekapaṇṇāsasappītikacittesu ceva ekādasasu catutthajjhānikacittesu, kusalavipākakāyaviññāṇe cāti tesaṭṭhiyā cittesu sukhaṃ jāyati. Tesaṭṭhisukhasahagatacittāni ceva tīṇi ca dukkhasahagatānīti chasaṭṭhicitte vajjetvā avasesapañcapaṇṇāsacittesu upekkhā uppajjatīti āha “upekkhā pañcapaññāsacittesū”ti. Dukkhaṃ tīsūti dvīsu paṭighacittesu ceva akusalavipākakāyaviññāṇe cāti tīsu cittesu dukkhaṃ jāyati. Hoti…pe… somanassindriyanti tesaṭṭhiyā sukhasahagatacittesu ekameva kāyaviññāṇaṃ apanetvā avasesesu somanassindriyaṃ hoti. Akusalavipākakāyaviññāṇavasena ekameva dukkhindriyasahagataṃ, tathā kusalavipākakāyaviññāṇameva sukhindriyasampayuttanti āha “dukkhindriyaṃ…pe… sukhindriya”nti.

Rapture arises in fifty-one types of consciousness: in the eighteen types of sense-sphere consciousness accompanied by joy, excluding body-consciousness, and in the thirty-three types of form-sphere jhāna consciousness, excluding those of the fourth and fifth jhānas. Happiness arises in sixty-three types of consciousness: in the fifty-one types of consciousness accompanied by rapture, in the eleven types of fourth-jhāna consciousness, and in the wholesome-resultant body-consciousness. Excluding the sixty-six types of consciousness—the sixty-three accompanied by happiness and the three accompanied by pain—equanimity arises in the remaining fifty-five. Thus it is said: 'Equanimity in fifty-five types of consciousness.' Pain arises in three types of consciousness: in the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion and in the unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness. Of the sixty-three types of consciousness accompanied by happiness, the faculty of joy is present in all except for the single body-consciousness. The faculty of pain is associated with only one type—the unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness—and similarly, the faculty of happiness is associated only with the wholesome-resultant body-consciousness. Thus, it is said, 'The faculty of pain... the faculty of happiness.'

Ahetukavipākakiriyāmanodhātuvajjitesu [M 1.0332] majjhimagaṇanāya pañcādhikasataparimitesu kusalākusalavipākakiriyācittesu vīriyaṃ desitanti āha “pañcuttara…pe… āhā”ti. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthesu [V 1.0261] satte vineti, vigato vā nāyako imassa, visiṭṭho vā sabbalokassa nāyako sāmi, visesena vā vineyyasatte nibbānapuraṃ netīti vināyako. Samādhindriyaṃ vicikicchāvajjitavīriyasahagatacittesu vuttanti āha “catuttarasate”tiādi.

Energy is taught as occurring in the one hundred and five wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses according to the middle calculation, which excludes the rootless resultant and functional mind-elements. Thus it is said: 'One hundred and five....' He is the Guide (vināyako) because he guides beings for their welfare in this life and the next; or because the leader (nāyaka) has departed from this world; or because he is the distinguished leader (visiṭṭho nāyako) and lord of the whole world; or because he especially (visesena) leads beings to be trained to the city of Nibbāna. The faculty of concentration is said to be in the consciousnesses accompanied by energy, excluding the one accompanied by doubt. Thus it is said: 'One hundred and four,' and so on.

Aṭṭhārasa ahetukacittāni, dve ekahetukacittāni ca vajjetvā avasesaekuttarasate citte chando uppajjatīti dassetuṃ “sabbāhetukacittānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dasa viññāṇeti kusalākusalavipākavasena dviguṇite cakkhādike pañcaviññāṇe.

To show that desire arises in the remaining one hundred and one types of consciousness—excluding the eighteen rootless consciousnesses and the two single-rooted consciousnesses rooted in delusion—it is said, 'all rootless consciousnesses,' and so on. 'Ten consciousnesses' refers to the five sense-consciousnesses beginning with eye-consciousness, doubled to account for their wholesome and unwholesome results.

102-6. Niyatā na yevāpanakā viya kadācīti attho. Kathaṃ panete ekanavutiyā cittesveva jāyantīti āha “ahetukesū”tiādi. Ekūnāsītiyāti dvādasa ñāṇasampayuttakāmāvacarāni, pañcadasa rūpāvacarāni, dvādasa arūpāvacarāni, samacattālīsa lokuttaracittānīti evaṃ ekūnāsītiyā tihetukacittesu. Aṭṭhavīsatiyā citteti soḷasasu kāmāvacarakusalamahākiriyāsu, dvādasasu ca lokiyacatutthajjhānacittesu cāti aṭṭhavīsaticittesu. Sāṭṭhake cattālīsavidheti aṭṭhasahite cattālīsavidhe, aṭṭhacattālīsavidheti vuttaṃ hoti. Cha yugaḷānīti kāyapassaddhicittapassaddhādīni cha yugaḷāni. Kusalābyākatā cāti kusalacittasampayogato kusalā, abyākatacittasampayogato abyākatāti kusalenapakāsanavidhānesu chekena satthunā pakāsitā desitāti attho.

102–6. 'Fixed' (niyatā): this means they are not occasional like the yevāpanaka factors. 'How then do these arise only in the ninety-one types of consciousness?' He says, 'In the rootless,' and so on. 'In seventy-nine': this refers to the seventy-nine types of triple-rooted consciousness: twelve sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge, fifteen fine-material-sphere consciousnesses, twelve immaterial-sphere consciousnesses, and forty supramundane consciousnesses. 'In twenty-eight types of consciousness': this refers to the sixteen wholesome and great functional sense-sphere consciousnesses and the twelve mundane fourth-jhāna consciousnesses. 'In forty-eight types' (sāṭṭhake cattālīsavidhe): this means in forty types with eight added, that is, in forty-eight types. 'Six pairs': this refers to the six pairs beginning with tranquility of the mental body and tranquility of consciousness. 'Wholesome and indeterminate': they are wholesome when associated with wholesome consciousness and indeterminate when associated with indeterminate consciousness. Thus they have been explained and taught by the skillful Teacher in the section on the exposition of the wholesome.

108-111. Saṃsayoti [M 1.0333] vicikicchā. Sā hi saṃseti samantato seti, “evaṃ nu kho, no nu kho”ti parisappatīti saṃsayo. Mahante sīlakkhandhādike esati gavesatīti mahesī. Tena mahesinā sammāsambuddhena. Aṭṭhasūti aṭṭhalobhasahagatacittesu. Catūsūti tesveva diṭṭhisahagatacittesu. Diṭṭhiviyuttesu catūsūti sambandho. Dvīsvevāti dvīsu dosamūlakacittesu. Dvīsu jāyanti no sahāti dosamūlesveva dvīsu jāyanti, saha pana na uppajjanti, usūyanakāle issā, maccharaṇakāle maccherantiādinā nānā hutvāva uppajjanti. Pañcasūti pañcasu sasaṅkhārikacittesu.

108–111. 'Doubt' (saṃsayo) is uncertainty (vicikicchā). It is called doubt because it doubts (saṃseti), lies on all sides (samantato seti), and wanders around (parisappati) thinking, 'Is it so? Is it not so?' A 'great seer' (mahesī) is one who seeks (esati) and searches for (gavesati) great things (mahante) such as the aggregates of virtue. By that great seer, the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'In eight': in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. 'In four': in the four of those accompanied by wrong view. The connection for conceit is with the four dissociated from wrong view. 'In two only': in the two types of consciousness rooted in aversion. 'They arise in two, but not together': envy, avarice, and worry arise in the two consciousnesses rooted in aversion, but they do not arise simultaneously; envy (issā) arises at a time of jealousy (usūyanakāle), avarice (maccheraṃ) at a time of stinginess (maccharaṇakāle), and so on, arising separately. 'In five': in the five types of prompted unwholesome consciousness.

112. Cittassa cetasikattābhāvepi kusalākusalābyākatadhammānaṃ gaṇanaṭṭhānato “mano”ti cittampi vuttaṃ.

112. Although consciousness (citta) is not itself a mental factor (cetasika), it is also called 'mind' (mano) because it is the basis for enumerating wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states.

114-5. Ettāvatā [V 1.0262] cetasikavibhāgaṃ dassetvā idāni ekekasmiṃ cittuppāde labbhamānarāsīsu aṅgavibhāgadassanatthaṃ “ekūnatiṃsacittesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nanu ca phassapañcamakarāsi sabbapaṭhamaṃ āgatā, sā kasmā na vuttāti? Sabbasādhāraṇabhāvato. Na hi so cittuppādo atthi, yo phassapañcamakavinimuttoti. Ekādasa paṭhamajjhānikāni somanassasahagatāni, dvādasa sahetukakāmāvacarāni, tathā cattāri akusalāni, sukhasantīraṇahasituppādāni dveti ekūnatiṃsacittesu pañcaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ pañcakarāsisaṅkhātaṃ mataṃ. Catu…pe… niddiseti ekādasa dutiyajjhānikāni, kusalavipākakiriyāvasena dvādasa upekkhāsahagatasahetukakāmāvacarāni, upekkhādomanassasahagatāni aṭṭha akusalāni, dvipañcaviññāṇavajjitaupekkhāsahagatāni cha ahetukacittāni cāti imāni sattatiṃsa cittāni yathāyogaṃ catūhi jhānaṅgehi yuttāni. Ettha [M 1.0334] hi ekādasa dutiyajjhānikāni vicārapītisukhasamādhīhi sahagatāni, itarāni yathāyogaṃ upekkhādomanassesu ekekena vitakkavicārasamādhīhīti catūhi sampayuttāni.

114–15. Having thus shown the classification of mental factors, now, to demonstrate the division of components within the groups obtainable in each arising of consciousness, it is said, 'In twenty-nine types of consciousness,' etc. But why was the group of five beginning with contact not mentioned, since it comes first of all? Because it is common to all. There is no arising of consciousness that is free from the group of five beginning with contact. In twenty-nine types of consciousness—the eleven first-jhāna consciousnesses accompanied by joy, the twelve rooted sense-sphere consciousnesses accompanied by joy, the four unwholesome consciousnesses accompanied by joy, and the two consciousnesses of joyful investigating and smile-producing—the five-factored jhāna, considered as a group of five, is found. 'Four...' etc., is explained. The thirty-seven types of consciousness—the eleven second-jhāna consciousnesses, the twelve rooted sense-sphere consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity (as wholesome, resultant, or functional), the eight unwholesome consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity or displeasure, and the six rootless consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity (excluding the two sets of five sense-consciousnesses)—are associated with four jhāna factors as appropriate. Here, the eleven second-jhāna consciousnesses are accompanied by sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and concentration. The others are associated with four factors, as appropriate: with one of either equanimity or displeasure, and with initial thought, sustained thought, and concentration.

Ekādasavidhanti ekādasavidhaṃ tatiyajjhānikacittaṃ pītisukhacittekaggatāyogato tivaṅgikamudīritaṃ. Catuttiṃsa…pe… mudīritanti dvādasa arūpāvacaracittāni, dvāvīsati catutthapañcamajjhānikāni sāsavānāsavānīti catuttiṃsa cittāni yathāyogaṃ upekkhekaggatāyogato, sukhekaggatāyogato ca duvaṅgikamudīritaṃ. Catutthajjhānikāni hi ekādasa sukhekaggatāsahitāni, sesāni tevīsati upekkhekaggatāsahitāni.

The elevenfold refers to the elevenfold third-jhāna consciousness, which is proclaimed as threefold due to its association with rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness. Thirty-four... proclaimed are the twelve formless-sphere consciousnesses and the twenty-two fourth- and fifth-jhāna consciousnesses, with and without taints; thus, thirty-four consciousnesses. These are proclaimed as twofold according to their respective association with either equanimity and one-pointedness or with happiness and one-pointedness. For the eleven fourth-jhāna consciousnesses are accompanied by happiness and one-pointedness, while the remaining twenty-three are accompanied by equanimity and one-pointedness.

116. Sabhāvenāvitakkesūti dutiyajjhānādayo viya bhāvanābalena vinā sabhāveneva avitakkesu dvipañcaviññāṇesu. Tesu hi vijjamānānipi sesajhānaṅgāni vitakkavirahena upanijjhānakiccesu asamatthāni. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyampi “vitakkapacchimakañhi jhānaṅgaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Bhāvanāya avitakkabhāvappattāni pana bhāvanābaleneva upanijjhānakiccesu paṭutarā, tasmā sabhāvenāvitakkesu jhānaṅgāni na uddhareyya. “Na uddhaṭā”ti vā pāṭho, na uddhaṭānīti attho.

116. The phrase 'in those that are without initial application by their own nature' refers to the two sets of five consciousnesses, which are without initial application by their own nature, not by the power of development like the second jhāna and so on. In these, even though the other jhāna factors are present, they are incapable of the function of close examination because of the absence of initial application. For this reason, it is said in the commentary: 'For the jhāna factors are indeed those that follow initial application.' However, those states that attain the state of being without initial application through development are, by the power of development itself, more proficient in the function of close examination. Therefore, one should not extract the jhāna factors in the case of what is without initial application by its own nature. Or the reading is 'have not been extracted,' which means they are not extracted.

Yadi evaṃ kasmā dvipañcaviññāṇesu sarūpeneva cittekaggatā vuttā, nanu tassā vitakkavirahena jhānaṅgakicce asamatthatāya rāsibhajanābhāvato yevāpanakavasena vacanaṃ yuttanti[V 1.0263]? Vuccate – kusalākusalesu avijjamānadhammassa vipākesupi anupalabbhanato jhānaṅgakiccassa akaraṇepi kusalākusalesu desitaniyāmeneva sarūpena idhāpi vuttā. Hotu tāva etaṃ, jhānarāsiyaṃ vedanā kasmā vuttā. Sā hi sabbacittasādhāraṇabhāvato [M 1.0335] phassapañcakarāsimhi ceva, upekkhādiindriyabhāvato indriyarāsimhiyeva vattabbā, na itarattha tadabhāvatoti? Saccaṃ, vedanā pana sabbavedanānaṃ sāmaññasabhāvena phassapañcake āgatavedanā ca aparena visesavacanena tattha niddiṭṭhā, na tattha antokaraṇatthaṃ. Teneva hi dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ dvipañcaviññāṇesu saṅgahavāre jhānaṅgarāsi na uddhaṭāti rūpadhātuyaṃ tiṇṇaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ appaṭighabhāvepi kāmadhātuyaṃ sappaṭighamahābhūtehi samānabhāvato tatthāpi sappaṭighabhāvo viya dvipañcaviññāṇesu vedanācittekaggatānaṃ vitakkaviyogena jhānakiccākaraṇepi savitakkacittesu jhānacittasamaṅgīvedanādīhi samānattā jhānaṅgabhāvena vacanaṃ nāma yuttaṃ. Teneva ca nāmarūpasamāse “phassapañcakarāsijhānadukarāsiindriyattikarāsī”ti vuttanti. Atha vā kiṃ etāya yutticintāya, dhammasabhāvavedinā tathāgatena dhammasabhāvaṃ avirajjhitvā desitanti na ettha anuyogo kātabboti. Ahetukacittānaṃ ārammaṇe suppatiṭṭhitatābhāvena aniyyānikattā vuttaṃ “sabbā…pe… na uddhare”ti. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyampi “hetupacchimako maggo”ti.

If so, why is one-pointedness of mind mentioned in its own right in the two sets of five consciousnesses? Since it is incapable of performing the function of a jhāna factor due to the absence of initial application, and thus is not included in the group, would it not be fitting to speak of it in terms of its removal? It is said: Because a phenomenon that is non-existent in wholesome and unwholesome states is also not found in their results, even when the function of a jhāna factor is not performed, it is mentioned here in its own right in the same way as was taught for the wholesome and unwholesome states according to the rule. But let that be. Why is feeling mentioned in the jhāna group? Since it is common to all consciousness and is a faculty such as equanimity, it should be spoken of only in the contact-pentad and the group of faculties, not elsewhere, due to its absence there. True. But the feeling that comes in the contact-pentad is by way of its general nature common to all feelings; it is pointed out there [in the jhāna group] by a different, specific statement, not for the purpose of including it therein. For this reason, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in the section on inclusion, the group of jhāna factors is not extracted in the case of the two sets of five consciousnesses. Just as in the form sphere, though the three great elements are non-resistant, they are considered resistant because of their similarity to the resistant great elements in the sense-sphere, so too in the two sets of five consciousnesses, though feeling and one-pointedness of mind do not perform the function of jhāna due to the absence of initial application, it is fitting to call them jhāna factors because of their similarity to the feeling, etc., that are constituents of jhāna consciousness in states with initial application. And for that reason, in the summary of name-and-form, it is said: 'the group of the contact-pentad, the group of the jhāna-dyad, the group of the faculty-triad.' Or, what is the use of this reasoning? The Tathāgata, who knows the nature of phenomena, taught the nature of phenomena without distortion; therefore, no objection should be raised here. Because rootless consciousnesses are not emancipating due to their not being well-established on an object, it is said: 'All... should not extract.' And this is said in the commentary: 'The path has the root as its final component.'

117. Tīṇi soḷasacittesūti pannarasasu ahetukavipākacittesu ceva kiriyāmanodhātumhi cāti soḷasasu cittesu. Manindriyaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ vedanindriyesu labbhamānamekanti tīṇindriyāni honti. Imesupi kusalavipākakāyaviññāṇadhātuyaṃ manindriyasukhindriyajīvitindriyavasena tīṇindriyāni, akusalavipākakāyaviññāṇadhātuyaṃ dukkhindriyena saha tīṇi, sukhasantīraṇe somanassindriyena saha tīṇi, avasesaterasacittesu upekkhindriyena saha tīṇīti. Ettha cittanti sasampayuttadhammassa cittuppādassa adhippetattā manindriyassāpi ādhārabhāvo yujjeyya. Itarathā hi manindriyanti [M 1.0336] cittasseva gahaṇe tassa attano ca ādhārabhāvo na yujjatīti. Ekasmiṃ pana cattārīti ekasmiṃ vicikicchāsahagate vīriyindriyamanindriyajīvitindriyaupekkhindriyavasena cattāri. Pañca terasasūti ṭhapetvā vicikicchāsahagataṃ avasesāni ekādasa akusalacittāni, kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātudvayanti terasasu cittesu vīriyindriyādīni tīṇi, samādhindriyaṃ, vedanindriyesu labbhamānaṃ ekanti pañcindriyāni. Ettha hi dvīsu dosamūlesu vīriyindriyasamādhindriyamanindriyajīvitindriyadomanassindriyavasena [V 1.0264] pañca, pañcasu somanassasahagatesu purimāni cattāri somanassindriyena saddhiṃ pañca, sesesu upekkhindriyena saddhiṃ pañca honti.

117. Three in sixteen consciousnesses: that is, in the fifteen rootless resultant consciousnesses and the functional mind-element. There are three faculties: the mind faculty, the life faculty, and one obtainable from among the feeling faculties. Among these, in the wholesome-resultant body-consciousness element there are three faculties, namely, the mind faculty, the pleasure faculty, and the life faculty; in the unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness element, there are three along with the pain faculty; in the investigating consciousness accompanied by pleasure, there are three along with the joy faculty; in the remaining thirteen consciousnesses, there are three along with the equanimity faculty. Here, since 'consciousness' is intended to mean a moment of consciousness together with its associated states, it is fitting that the mind faculty also has the status of a basis. Otherwise, if the mind faculty were taken as consciousness itself, it would not be fitting for it to be its own basis. But in one there are four: in the one consciousness accompanied by doubt, there are four faculties, namely, the energy faculty, the mind faculty, the life faculty, and the equanimity faculty. Five in thirteen: that is, setting aside the consciousness accompanied by doubt, in the remaining eleven unwholesome consciousnesses and the two functional mind-consciousness elements. In these thirteen consciousnesses there are five faculties: the three beginning with the energy faculty, the concentration faculty, and one obtainable from among the feeling faculties. Here, in the two consciousnesses rooted in hatred, there are five, namely, the energy faculty, the concentration faculty, the mind faculty, the life faculty, and the displeasure faculty. In the five consciousnesses accompanied by joy, there are five: the preceding four along with the joy faculty. In the remaining ones, there are five along with the equanimity faculty.

118. Satta dvādasacittesūti dvādasasu ñāṇavippayuttacittesu saddhāsatisamādhivīriyajīvitamanindriyāni ca vedanindriyesu labbhamānamekanti satta indriyāni. Tattha hi chasu somanassasahagatesu saddhindriyādīni cha somanassindriyena saddhiṃ satta, itaresu chasu upekkhindriyena saddhiṃ satta honti. Ekenūnesu…pe… manesu cāti dvādasa ñāṇasampayuttāni kāmāvacarāni, sattavīsati lokiyajjhānacittāni cāti ekūnacattālīsavidhesu lokiyacittesu purimāni satta, paññindriyañcāti aṭṭheva indriyāni. Ettha hi somanassasahagatesu chasu kāmāvacaresu, dvādasasu rūpāvacaracatukkajjhānesu cāti aṭṭhārasacittesu somanassindriyena, sesesu ca upekkhindriyena saddhiṃ yojetvā aṭṭhindriyāni veditabbāni.

118. Seven in twelve consciousnesses: that is, in the twelve beautiful sense-sphere consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge, there are seven faculties: the faith faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, energy faculty, life faculty, mind faculty, and one obtainable from among the feeling faculties. Here, in the six consciousnesses accompanied by joy, there are the six faculties beginning with the faith faculty along with the joy faculty, making seven. In the other six, there are seven along with the equanimity faculty. Eight in thirty-nine consciousnesses: that is, in the thirty-nine kinds of mundane consciousnesses—namely, the twelve sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge and the twenty-seven mundane jhāna consciousnesses—there are the preceding seven faculties and the wisdom faculty, thus eight faculties. Here, the eight faculties should be understood by combining them with the joy faculty in the eighteen consciousnesses—that is, the six sense-sphere ones accompanied by joy and the twelve of the four form-sphere jhānas—and with the equanimity faculty in the remaining ones.

119. Cattālīsāya cittesu navakanti samacattālīsavidhesu lokuttaracittesu purimāni aṭṭhaindriyāni, anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ aññindriyaṃ aññātāvindriyanti imesu labbhamānamekanti indriyānaṃ navakā. Sotāpattimaggesu hi anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ [M 1.0337] labbhati. Sotāpattiphalato paṭṭhāya arahattamaggapariyosānesu taṃ na labbhati. Tassa ṭhāne aññindriyaṃ. Arahattaphale tampi na labbhati. Tassa ṭhāne aññātāvindriyaṃ tiṭṭhatīti. Evanti chahi indriyehi sampayuttassa abhāvato katthaci tīṇi, katthaci cattāri, katthaci pañca, katthaci satta, katthaci aṭṭha, katthaci navindriyānīti evaṃ chahi ākārehi indriyayogopi, na kevalaṃ jhānaṅgayogova, atha kho indriyehi saha cittuppādānaṃ sampayogopi veditabboti.

119. Nine in forty consciousnesses: that is, in the forty kinds of supramundane consciousnesses, there are groups of nine faculties, consisting of the preceding eight faculties and one obtainable from among these three: the faculty 'I shall know the unknown,' the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has final knowledge. For in the path of stream-entry, the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' is obtained. From the fruition of stream-entry up to the end of the path of arahantship, that is not obtained; in its place is the faculty of final knowledge. In the fruition of arahantship, that too is not obtained; in its place stands the faculty of one who has final knowledge. Thus, because of the absence of an association with six faculties, there are sometimes three, sometimes four, sometimes five, sometimes seven, sometimes eight, and sometimes nine faculties. In this way, the combination with faculties should be understood as occurring in six modes; not only the combination with jhāna factors, but also the association of the arisings of consciousness with the faculties should be understood.

120-3. Idāni maggaṅgasampayogaṃ dassento paṭhamaṃ tāva yesu cittesu maggaṅgāni na labbhanti, tāni dassetvā pacchā maggaṅgayogacittuppāde dassetuṃ “amaggaṅgānī”tiādimāha. Etthāti etasmiṃ ekavīsasatappabhede cittasmiṃ, imasmiṃ maggaṅgādhikāre vā. Viññāṇesu dvipañcasūti sabhāvāvitakkesu cakkhādīsu dvipañcaviññāṇesu. Kiñcāpi heṭṭhā dvipañcaviññāṇesu jhānaṅgābhāvo, ahetukesu ca maggaṅgābhāvo vuttova, ajhānaṅgāni pana tattha adhikāravasena vuttāni, idha pasaṅgāgatavasena. Amaggaṅgāni tattha pasaṅgāgatavasena, idha adhikāravasenāti na koci punaruttidoso.

Now, to show the association with path factors, first, having indicated those consciousnesses in which path factors are not found, he then says 'without path factors,' etc., to show the arisings of consciousness associated with path factors. 'Here' means in this consciousness with its one hundred and twenty-one divisions, or in this section on path factors. 'In the two sets of five consciousnesses' means in the two sets of five consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness, which are without initial application by their own nature. Although the absence of jhāna factors in the two sets of five consciousnesses and the absence of path factors in the rootless consciousnesses have already been stated previously, there the non-jhāna-factors were stated as the main topic, while here they are mentioned incidentally. There the non-path-factors were mentioned incidentally, while here they are stated as the main topic. Thus there is no fault of repetition.

Ekanti [V 1.0265] vicikicchāsampayuttaṃ cittaṃ. Tañhi micchāsaṅkappamicchāvāyāmayogato dve maggaṅgāni etthāti dumaggaṅgaṃ. Timaggaṅgāni sattasūti cattāri diṭṭhivippayuttāni, dve dosamūlāni, uddhaccasahagatacittanti sattasu micchāsaṅkappamicchāvāyāmamicchāsamādhiyogato timaggaṅgāni. Cattālīsa…pe… caturaṅgikoti dvādasa ñāṇavippayuttāni, cattāri diṭṭhisampayuttāni, paṭhamajjhānikavajjāni catuvīsati mahaggatacittānīti cattālīsacittesu yo maggo labbhati, so yathāyogaṃ sammāsaṅkappasammāvāyāmasammāsatisammāsamādhiyogato, micchādiṭṭhimicchāsaṅkappamicchāvāyāmamicchāsamādhiyogato, sammādiṭṭhisammāvāyāmasammāsatisammāsamādhiyogato [M 1.0338] ca caturaṅgiko mato. Tattha ñāṇavippayuttesu dvādasasu paṭhamāni cattāri, diṭṭhisampayuttesu majjhimāni, sesesu pacchimāni labbhanti.

The mind associated with doubt is one. Indeed, because of its connection with wrong thought and wrong effort, two path factors are present here; thus it has two path factors. Three path factors are in seven types of consciousness: in the four dissociated from view, the two rooted in aversion, and the mind accompanied by restlessness. Thus in these seven, due to their connection with wrong thought, wrong effort, and wrong concentration, there are three path factors. Forty… four-factored: in forty minds—namely, the twelve dissociated from knowledge, the four associated with view, and the twenty-four sublime minds excluding those of the first jhāna—the path that is obtained is considered four-factored as it is connected, as the case may be, with (1) right thought, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; (2) wrong view, wrong thought, wrong effort, and wrong concentration; and (3) right view, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Among these, in the twelve dissociated from knowledge, the first set of four is obtained; in those associated with view, the middle set; and in the rest, the last set.

Pañcaddasasu…pe… pañcaṅgikoti dvādasasu ñāṇasampayuttakāmāvacaresu ceva tīsu lokiyapaṭhamajjhānikesu cāti pannarasasu cittesu sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappasammāvāyāmasammāsatisammāsamādhivasena pañcaṅgiko maggo. Nanu ca sammāvācādayo kāmāvacaresu labbhantīti? Saccaṃ labbhanti, pāṭhe pana anāgatattā idha pariccattāti. Dvattiṃsacittesūti paṭhamajjhānikavajjesu dvattiṃsalokuttaracittesu. Sattaṅgikoti avitakkattā sammāsaṅkappo na labbhatīti taṃ pariccajitvā avasesasattamaggaṅgavasena sattaṅgiko vutto.

In fifteen… five-factored: in fifteen consciousnesses—that is, in the twelve sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge and in the three mundane first jhāna consciousnesses—the path is five-factored by way of right view, right thought, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. But are not right speech and the others obtained in the sense-sphere consciousnesses? Truly, they are obtained, but since they are not mentioned in the text, they are omitted here. In thirty-two consciousnesses: in the thirty-two supramundane consciousnesses, excluding those of the first jhāna. Seven-factored: because right thought is not obtained due to the absence of initial application of mind, it is omitted, and by way of the remaining seven path factors, it is called seven-factored.

Yattha pana sammāsaṅkappo labbhati, tattha tena saha aṭṭhaṅgikoti āha “maggo aṭṭhasū”tiādi. Tattha aṭṭhasu cittesūti paṭhamajjhānikesu aṭṭhasu lokuttaracittesu. Evanti chahi maggaṅgehi sampayuttassa abhāvato katthaci dve maggaṅgāni, katthaci tīṇi, katthaci cattāri, katthaci pañca, katthaci satta, katthaci aṭṭhāti evaṃ chahi pakārehi.

But where right thought is obtained, there, together with it, the path is eight-factored; thus he said, 'the path in eight,' etc. There, 'in eight consciousnesses' means in the eight supramundane consciousnesses of the first jhāna. Thus, because there is no consciousness associated with six path factors, in some cases there are two path factors, in some three, in some four, in some five, in some seven, and in some eight—thus in six ways.

124-6. Idāni balasampayogaṃ dassento āha “balāni dve”tiādi. Tattha vīriyabalasamādhibalavasena dve balāni kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātudvaye vibhaṅgavāre āgatāni vīriyabalasamādhibalāni paccekaṃ labbhantīti “dve dvicittesū”ti vuttaṃ. Ekasmiṃ tīṇīti ekasmiṃ vicikicchāsahagate vīriyabalaahirikabalaanottappabalavasena tīṇi balāni. Ekādasasu cattārīti vicikicchāsahagatavajjesu ekādasasu akusalacittesu samādhibalañceva pubbe [V 1.0266] vuttāni tīṇīti cattāribalāni. Cha dvādasasūti dvādasasu ñāṇavippayuttacittesu saddhāvīriyasatisamādhihiriottappavasena cha balāni.

124-6. Now, to show the association with the powers, he said, 'two powers,' etc. There, since the power of energy and the power of concentration are obtained individually in the two functional rootless mind-consciousness-elements, as mentioned in the section on the Vibhaṅga, it is said, 'Two in two consciousnesses.' In one, three: in the one consciousness accompanied by doubt, there are three powers by way of the power of energy, the power of moral shamelessness, and the power of moral recklessness. In eleven, four: in the eleven unwholesome consciousnesses, excluding the one accompanied by doubt, there are four powers: the power of concentration and the three previously mentioned. Six in twelve: in the twelve consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge, there are six powers by way of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, moral shame, and moral dread.

Ekūnāsītiyā [M 1.0339] sattāti dvādasasu ñāṇasampayuttakāmāvacaracittesu ceva sattavīsatimahaggatacittesu ca cattālīsāya lokuttaracittesu cāti ekūnāsītividhesu cittesu saddhāvīriyasatisamādhipaññāhiriottappavasena satta balāni. Soḷasevābalānīti pañcadasa ahetukavipākāni, kiriyāmanodhātuāvajjanañcāti soḷasa balavippayogato abalacittāni. Evanti pañcahi balehi sampayuttassa abhāvato katthaci dve, katthaci tīṇi, katthaci cattāri, katthaci cha, katthaci sattāti pañcahi ākārehi sabalaṃ, imesu ekassāpi abhāvato abalampi ca viññeyyaṃ, vijānitabbanti attho. Heturāsiādayo vinicchayabhāvato na vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Yesu cittesu yāni jhānaṅgamaggaṅgabalindriyāni jāyantīti sambandho. Gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ indriyānaṃ osānakaraṇaṃ.

In seventy-nine, seven: in seventy-nine kinds of consciousness—namely, the twelve sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge, the twenty-seven sublime consciousnesses, and the forty supramundane consciousnesses—there are seven powers by way of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, moral shame, and moral dread. Sixteen are without powers: the fifteen rootless resultant consciousnesses and the functional five-door-adverting consciousness. These sixteen are consciousnesses without powers due to being dissociated from the powers. Thus, because there is no consciousness associated with five powers, consciousness with powers is of five kinds: in some cases with two, in some with three, in some with four, in some with six, and in some with seven. And it should be understood that there is also consciousness without powers, due to the absence of any of these powers; this is the meaning of 'it should be known.' It should be understood that the aggregates of conditions, etc., are not mentioned because they are not a matter for determination here. The connection is: 'In which consciousnesses do which jhāna factors, path factors, powers, and faculties arise?' For the sake of metrical facility in the verse, the faculties are placed at the end.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the commentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma,

Cetasikavibhāganiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the exposition on the division of mental factors is finished.

4. Catuttho paricchedo

4. The Fourth Chapter

Ekavidhādiniddesavaṇṇanā
