Explanation of the Exposition of the Onefold and Other Modes

128-30. Vijānanasabhāvatoti ārammaṇavijānanasabhāvattā. Nanu ca heṭṭhā sārammaṇato ekavidhabhāvo vuttoti? Saccaṃ vutto, so pana cetasikānañca sādhāraṇoti idha tabbivajjanatthaṃ vijānanalakkhaṇatāva vuttā. Saṅkhepagaṇanavasena ca sahetukānaṃ ekasattatividhatā vuttā. Hetuvādināti kusalākusalābyākatahetūnaṃ byākaraṇakusalena[M 1.0340]. Atha vā “ye dhammā hetuppabhavā[V 1.0267], tesaṃ hetuṃ tathāgato āhā”ti (apa. thera 1.1.286; mahāva. 60) vacanato taṃtaṃpaccayuppannadhammānaṃ taṃtaṃpaccayavādinā.

128-30. 'Because of its nature of cognizing' means because it has the nature of cognizing an object. But was not its onefold nature stated previously with respect to its having an object? Truly, it was stated, but since that is also common to mental factors, here, in order to exclude that, only the characteristic of cognizing is stated. And by way of a concise enumeration, the seventy-one kinds of consciousness with roots are stated. 'By the proponent of causes' means by one skilled in the explanation of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate causes. Alternatively, from the statement, 'Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has told their cause,' it refers to one who states the respective conditions for phenomena that have arisen from those particular conditions.

131-4. Savatthukāvatthukatoti ekantena sabbavatthunissitabhāvato ceva tadabhāvato ca. Keci pana hadayavatthuvasena savatthukāvatthukataṃ vaṇṇenti, taṃ na yujjati savatthukaniddese “sabbo kāmavipāko”ti pasādanissitānampi saṅgahitattā. Ubhayavasenāti savatthukāvatthukavasena. Kānici hi cittāni ekantena savatthukāni, kānici avatthukāneva, kānici ubhayasabhāvāni. Tathā ceva niddisati “sabbo kāmavipāko cā”tiādi.

131-4. 'With and without a basis' means because of being exclusively dependent on a physical basis and because of the absence of that. Some, however, explain 'with and without a basis' by way of the heart-basis, but that is not correct, because in the exposition of 'with a basis,' those dependent on the sense faculties are also included by the phrase 'all sense-sphere results.' 'By way of both' means by way of being with a basis and without a basis. For some consciousnesses are exclusively with a basis, some are only without a basis, and some are of a dual nature. Thus he indicates this by 'all sense-sphere results, and so on.'

Sabbo kāmavipāko cāti sahetukāhetukabhinno sabbo tevīsatividho kāmāvacaravipāko ca. Ādimaggoti sotāpattimaggo. So hi sabbalokuttaresu ādito uppajjanato, aṭṭhasu ariyapuggalesu ādipuggalassa sambandhīti vā “ādimaggo”ti vuccati. Vinā vatthunti sakasakavatthuṃ vinā nuppajjanti. Teneva hetāni arūpabhave nuppajjanti tattha vatthūnaṃ abhāvato. “Nuppajjanti vinā vatthu”nti ca idaṃ antobhāvitakāraṇatthaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Tena yasmā vatthuṃ vinā nuppajjanti, tasmā ekantena savatthukāti vuttaṃ hoti.

'And all sense-sphere results' means all twenty-three kinds of sense-sphere results, whether with roots or without roots. 'The initial path' means the path of stream-entry. It is called the 'initial path' because it arises first among all supramundane states, or because it is related to the first individual among the eight noble persons. 'Without a basis' means they do not arise without their respective physical bases. For that very reason, these do not arise in the formless realm of existence, because of the absence of physical bases there. And the statement 'they do not arise without a basis' is made with an implied causal meaning. Therefore, since they do not arise without a basis, it is said that they are exclusively with a basis.

Ekantena avatthukā arūpabhaveyeva paṭisandhādivasena pavattanato. Kathaṃ pana rūpasannissayena vinā tattha arūpaṃ pavattati, kasmā na pavattati pañcavokāreti? Tathā adassanato. Yadi evaṃ kabaḷīkārāhārenapi vinā rūpadhātuyaṃ rūpena pavattitabbaṃ, kiṃ kāraṇā? Kāmadhātuyaṃ tathā adassanato. Api tu yassa cittasantānassa pavattikāraṇaṃ [M 1.0341] rūpe avigatataṇhaṃ, tassa saha rūpena pavatti. Yassa pana nibbattikāraṇaṃ rūpe vigatataṇhaṃ, tassa vinā rūpena pavatti kāraṇassa taṃvimukhatāyāti rūpasannissayena vinā tattha arūpaṃ pavattati. Dvecattālīsa sesānīti manodvārāvajjanaṃ kusalakiriyāvasena soḷasa kāmāvacarāni, tatheva aṭṭha arūpāvacarāni, paṭhamamaggavajjāni satta lokuttarāni, paṭighadvayavajjitadasaakusalāni ceti dvecattālīsa vuttāvasesacittāni.

[They are] exclusively without a basis because they occur only in the formless realm by way of rebirth-linking and so on. But how does the formless exist there without dependence on form, and why does it not exist in the five-constituent realm? Because it is not seen to be so. If so, then form should exist in the fine-material realm even without edible food. For what reason? Because it is not seen to be so in the sense-sphere realm. However, for that continuity of consciousness whose cause for continued existence is uneliminated craving for form, existence occurs together with form. But for that whose cause of generation is eliminated craving for form, existence occurs without form, because the cause is liberated from that. Thus the formless exists there without dependence on form. The forty-two remaining are: the mind-door-adverting consciousness; the sixteen sense-sphere consciousnesses by way of wholesome and functional; similarly the eight formless-sphere; the seven supramundane excluding the first path; and the ten unwholesome excluding the two connected with aversion—thus the forty-two remaining consciousnesses are mentioned.

135-7. Rūpādīsu ekekameva ārammaṇaṃ imassāti ekekārammaṇaṃ. Tassa tassa ārammaṇassa āpāthagatakāle taṃtaṃvijānanavasena pañcapi ārammaṇāni imassāti pañcārammaṇaṃ. Evampīti [V 1.0268] na kevalaṃ savatthukādivaseneva, atha kho ekekārammaṇāditopi. Abhiññāvajjitānaṃ sabbamahaggatānampi dhammārammaṇabhāvena ekārammaṇattā āha “sabbaṃ mahaggata”nti. Paṇṇattārammaṇato ekārammaṇanti keci. Taṃ arūpāvacaradutiyacatutthajjhānāni patvā na yujjati tesaṃ mahaggatārammaṇattā. Abhiññādvayassa chaḷārammaṇikabhāvena, tassa ca rūpāvacarapañcamajjhānato abhinnattā taṃ pahāya “tecattālīsā”ti vuttaṃ.

135-7. Because it has only one object from among forms and so on, it is called 'having a single object.' Because it has five objects by way of cognizing each respective object when that object comes into range, it is called 'having five objects.' Thus also: not only by way of being with a basis and so on, but also by way of having a single object and so on. Because all sublime consciousnesses, except for the direct knowledges, have a single object by virtue of having a mental object, he said, 'all sublime.' Some say it has a single object because it has a concept as its object. That is not correct with respect to the second and fourth formless-sphere jhānas, as their object is a sublime one. Because the two direct knowledges have six kinds of objects, and because they are not different from the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, excluding them, it is said 'forty-three.'

141. Puññavipākakiriyato kāme dvādasāti sambandho. Dhāti nipātamattaṃ. Puññavipākakriyatoti ñāṇavippayuttakusalavipākakiriyato.

141. The connection is: 'twelve in the sense sphere, from the wholesome, resultant, and functional.' 'Dhāti' is merely a particle. 'From the wholesome, resultant, and functional' means from the wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses that are dissociated from knowledge.

143-9. Iriyāya kāyikāya kiriyāya pavattipathabhāvato iriyāpatho, gamanādi. Atthato tadavatthā rūpappavatti. Kāmañcettha rūpavinimutto iriyāpatho, viññatti vā natthi, tathāpi sabbaṃ rūpasamuṭṭhāpakacittaṃ iriyāpathupatthambhakaṃ, viññattivikāruppādanañca hoti. Yaṃ pana cittaṃ viññattijanakaṃ[M 1.0342], taṃ ekaṃsato itaradvayassa janakaṃ avinābhāvato, tathā iriyāpathupatthambhakaṃ rūpassāti imassa visesassa dassanatthaṃ “rūpīriyāpathaviññatti-janakājanakādito”ti iriyāpathaviññattīnaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Janakājanakāditoti tiṇṇampi janakato, kassacipi ajanakato, dvinnaṃ ekassa ca janakato. Kānici hi cittāni rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti, iriyāpathaṃ kappenti, viññattiṃ janayanti. Kānici rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti, iriyāpathaṃ kappenti, viññattiṃ na janayanti. Kānici rūpameva samuṭṭhāpenti, itaradvayaṃ na karonti. Kānici tīṇi na karonteva. Tathā ceva dasseti “dvādasākusalā”tiādi. Evañcāpi hi taṃ cittanti na kevalaṃ ahetukāditova, evaṃ rūpādijanakāditopi taṃ catubbidhaṃ. “Evañcādimhi ta”ntipi likhanti. Tassa pana ādimhi nikkhittaṃ cittaṃ evañca catubbidhanti atthaṃ vadanti. Tatthāti tesu rūpajanakādīsu. Dasa kiriyāti manodhātuvajjā dasa kiriyā.

143-9. A posture (iriyāpatha) is so called because it is the path of occurrence for the bodily action of movement, such as walking. In meaning, it is the occurrence of material form in that state. Although a posture is distinct from material form, or there is no intimation, still, all consciousness that originates material form supports the posture and produces intimation and alteration. But the consciousness that produces intimation invariably produces the other two—material form and posture—due to their inseparability. To show this special point, that it supports the posture and material form, postures and intimations are mentioned separately in the phrase 'from being a generator or non-generator of material form, posture, and intimation.' 'From being a generator or non-generator, etc.' means: from being a generator of all three, from being a non-generator of any, and from being a generator of two or of one. For some consciousnesses originate material form, establish postures, and generate intimation. Some originate material form and establish postures but do not generate intimation. Some originate only material form and do not do the other two. Some do not do any of the three. This is shown similarly with 'the twelve unwholesome,' etc. Thus, that consciousness is not only classified as rootless, etc., but is also fourfold in this way, from being a generator of material form, etc. Some also write, 'Thus, etc., in this.' They explain its meaning as: 'The consciousness placed at the beginning is also fourfold in this way.' 'Therein' means among those that are generators of material form, etc. 'Ten functional' means the ten functional consciousnesses, excluding the mind-element.

Samuṭṭhāpenti rūpānīti attano uppādakkhaṇeyeva attanā janetabbarūpāni samuṭṭhāpenti. Kappentīti sannāmenti. Yathāpavattaṃ iriyāpathaṃ upatthambhenti. Yathā hi antarantarā uppajjamānehi vīthicittehi abbokiṇṇe bhavaṅge pavattamāne aṅgāni osīdanti, pavedhantā viya honti, na evaṃ dvattiṃsavidhesu vakkhamānesu ca chabbīsatividhesu jāgaraṇacittesu pavattamānesu. Tadā pana aṅgāni [V 1.0269] upatthaddhāni yathāpavattairiyāpathabhāveneva pavattanti. Janayanti ca viññattinti manodvāre pavattā eva viññattiṃ janayanti, na pana pañcadvāre pavattāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'They originate material forms' means that at the very moment of their own arising, they originate the material forms that are to be generated by them. 'They establish' means they arrange. They support the posture as it occurs. For when the life-continuum is occurring, interspersed with intermittently arising process consciousnesses, the limbs sink and seem to tremble; but it is not so when the thirty-two kinds and the twenty-six kinds of waking consciousnesses to be mentioned are occurring. Then, the limbs are firm and continue in the state of the posture as it occurs. 'And they generate intimation' should be understood to mean that they generate intimation only when occurring at the mind-door, not when occurring at the five sense-doors.

Dvipañcaviññāṇānaṃ jhānaṅgayogābhāvena rūpājanakattā āha “dvepañcaviññāṇā”ti. Jhānaṅgāni hi cittena saha rūpasamuṭṭhāpakāni, tesaṃ anubalappadāyakāni maggaṅgādīni tesu [M 1.0343] vijjamānesu savisesaṃ rūpappavattidassanato. Arūpavipākā pana rūpavirāgabhāvanāya nibbattattā hetuno taṃvimukhatāya rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpentīti āha “vipākā ca arūpisū”ti.

Because the two sets of fivefold consciousness do not generate material form owing to their lack of association with the jhāna factors, he says, 'the two sets of fivefold consciousness.' For the jhāna factors are originators of material form together with consciousness; and since path factors and so on, which give them additional strength, are present in them, a special occurrence of material form is seen. But since the formless resultants are produced through the development of dispassion towards material form, they do not originate material form because their cause is liberated from it; hence he says, 'and the resultants in the formless sphere.'

150. Sabbesaṃ sandhicittanti sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ paṭisandhicittaṃ. Tañhi vatthudubbalatāya, appatiṭṭhitatāya, paccayavekallato, āgantukatāya ca rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā hi paṭisandhiviññāṇena sahajātaṃ vatthu pacchājātapaccayarahitaṃ, āhārādīhi ca anupatthaddhaṃ dubbalaṃ, tassa ca dubbalattā tannissitaviññāṇampi dubbalanti. Yathā ca papāte patito aññassa nissayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ tampi bhinnasantatiyaṃ kammakkhittatāya papāte patitaṃ viya appatiṭṭhitaṃ na rūpasamuṭṭhāpane ussahati ca vatthuno ca attanā saha apacchā apure uppajjamānattā purejātapaccayassa alābhato. Yathā pana āgantuko puriso agatapubbaṃ desaṃ gato aññesaṃ “etha bho antogāme vo annapānagandhamālādīni dassāmī”ti vattuṃ na sakkoti attano avisayatāya, appahutāya ca, evamevaṃ paṭisandhicittampi āgantukanti. Evaṃ vatthudubbalatādīhi kāraṇehi rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti. Apica āhārindriyādivasena yehākārehi cittasamuṭṭhānarūpānaṃ cittacetasikā paccayā honti, tehi sabbehi paṭisandhiyaṃ cittacetasikā samatiṃsakammajarūpānaṃ yathāyogaṃ paccayā honti. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭṭhāne –

150. 'The linking consciousness of all' means the rebirth-linking consciousness of all beings. It does not originate material form because of the weakness of its physical basis, its unestablished nature, the deficiency of its conditions, and its being a newcomer. For the physical basis co-nascent with the rebirth-linking consciousness is weak because it is devoid of the postnascence condition and unsupported by nutriment, etc.; and because its basis is weak, the consciousness dependent on it is also weak. Just as one who has fallen into an abyss cannot be a support for another, so this consciousness, having been cast by kamma into a broken continuity, is like one fallen into an abyss, unestablished, and is not able to originate material form. And because its physical basis arises simultaneously with it, neither after nor before, it does not obtain the prenascence condition. Just as a newcomer who has gone to a country he has not been to before cannot say to others, 'Come, sirs, I will give you food, drink, perfumes, and garlands in the village,' because it is not his domain and he lacks resources, so the rebirth-linking consciousness is a newcomer. Thus, for reasons such as the weakness of its physical basis, it does not originate material form. Moreover, in all the ways that consciousness and mental factors are conditions for mind-originated material form—by way of nutriment, faculty, etc.—in those same ways the consciousness and mental factors at rebirth-linking are, as appropriate, conditions for the thirty kinds of kamma-originated material form. This is stated in the Paṭṭhāna:

“Paṭisandhikkhaṇe vipākābyākatā āhārā sampayuttānaṃ khandhānaṃ kaṭattā ca rūpānaṃ āhārapaccayena paccayo”tiādi (paṭṭhā. 1.1.429).

"At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant-indeterminate nutriment is a condition by way of nutriment condition for the associated aggregates and for the material form produced by kamma," etc. (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.429).

Tasmā [M 1.0344] samatiṃsakammajarūpāni cittasamuṭṭhānarūpānaṃ ṭhānaṃ gahetvā ṭhitānīti paṭisandhicittaṃ rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpetīti veditabbaṃ.

Therefore, it should be understood that the rebirth-linking consciousness does not originate material form because the thirty kinds of kamma-originated material form stand having taken the place of mind-originated material form.

Cuticittañcārahatoti ettha khīṇāsavassa cuticittaṃ upasantavaṭṭamūlasmiṃ santāne sātisayaṃ santavuttitāya [V 1.0270] rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti, anāgāmiādīnaṃ tadabhāvatoti vadanti. Ṭīkākāro pana ānandācariyo bhaṇati –

Regarding 'And the death-consciousness of an Arahant': Here, they say that the death-consciousness of an Arahant—one whose taints are destroyed—does not originate material form because of its exceedingly tranquil mode of occurrence in a continuum where the root of the round has been pacified; for non-returners and others this is not so, as that condition is absent. The subcommentator, the teacher Ānanda, however, says:

“Kāmāvacarānaṃ pacchimacittassa uppādakkhaṇe yassa cittassa anantarā kāmāvacarānaṃ pacchimacittaṃ uppajjissati, rūpāvacare, arūpāvacare pacchimabhavikānaṃ, ye ca rūpāvacaraṃ, arūpāvacaraṃ upapajjitvā parinibbāyissanti, tesaṃ cavantānaṃ, tesaṃ vacīsaṅkhāro nirujjhissati, no ca tesaṃ kāyasaṅkhāro nirujjhissatīti vacanato aññesampi cuticittaṃ rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpetī”ti.

Because of the statement—'At the arising moment of the final consciousness of sense-sphere beings, after which consciousness the final consciousness of sense-sphere beings will arise; for those in their final existence in the form sphere and the formless sphere; and for those who, having been reborn in the form sphere or the formless sphere, will attain final Nibbāna—for them, as they are passing away, verbal formation will cease, but bodily formation will not cease'—it is inferred that for others, too, the death-consciousness does not originate material form.

Ācariyassa hi ayamadhippāyo – “kāmāvacarānaṃ pacchimacittassā”ti etena avisesena kāmāvacarasattānaṃ cuticittassa, “ye ca rūpāvacaraṃ…pe… nirujjhissatī”ti iminā kāmabhavato cavitvā rūpārūpabhavūpapajjanakānaṃ kāmāvacaracuticittassāpi uppādakkhaṇato uddhaṃ vacīsaṅkhārassa nirodhaṃ vatvā kāyasaṅkhārassa tadabhāvavacanato cuticittassa kāyasaṅkhārāsamuṭṭhāpanaṃ siddhaṃ. Yadaggena ca taṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti, tadaggena taṃ sesarūpampi na janeti. Na hi rūpasamuṭṭhāpakassa gabbhagatatādivibandhābhāve kāyasaṅkhārāsamuṭṭhāpane kāraṇaṃ atthi. Na ca yuttaṃ cutito uddhaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānañcassa rūpaṃ pavattatīti, nāpi “cuticittaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetī”ti pāḷi atthi, na cāpi vaṭṭamūlānupasamo cuticittassa rūpuppādane [M 1.0345] kāraṇaṃ cuticittena na uppannānampi tato purimatarehi uppannānaṃ viya bhavantare anuppajjanato, tasmā sabbesampi cuticittaṃ rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpetīti. Yadi kāyasaṅkhārasamuṭṭhāpanameva rūpajananārahabhāvaṃ sādheti, tadā catutthajjhāne kathanti? Nāyaṃ doso, tassa bhāvanābalena sātisayaṃ santavuttitāya kāyasaṅkhārāsamuṭṭhāpanepi maraṇāsannacittānaṃ viya paridubbalattābhāvato rūpasamuṭṭhāpane vibandho natthīti. Kuto pana paṭṭhāya cittajarūpaṃ nuppajjatīti? Yato paṭṭhāya kāyasaṅkhāre nuppajjati. Kadā ca kāyasaṅkhāro nuppajjatīti? Cutito pubbe dvattiṃsamacittakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya nuppajjati, tettiṃsamacittakkhaṇe uppannaṃ pacchimasoḷasakato puretarameva nirujjhatīti vadanti. “Yassa kāyasaṅkhāro na nirujjhati, tassa cittasaṅkhāro na nirujjhissatī”ti (yama. 2.saṅkhārayamaka.113) pañhe “pacchimacittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe tesaṃ kāyasaṅkhāro ca na nirujjhati, cittasaṅkhāro ca na nirujjhissatī”ti pacchimacittasseva vajjitattā cutito dutiyatatiyacittenāpi saha nirujjhatīti apare. Yassa cittassa anantarā kāmāvacarānaṃ [V 1.0271] pacchimacittaṃ uppajjatīti ettha “yassā”ti kāmāvacaracuticittassa anantarapaccayabhūtaṃ cittaṃ sandhāya vuttanti tassa uppādatopi uddhaṃ kāyasaṅkhārābhāvavacanena heṭṭhimakoṭiyā cutito tatiyacitteneva saha nirujjhati. Dutiyacittaṃ na pāpuṇātīti eke.

For this is the teacher's intention: By the phrase 'the final consciousness of sense-sphere beings,' he refers without distinction to the death-consciousness of sense-sphere beings. By the phrase 'And for those who... will cease,' which states the cessation of verbal formation from the arising moment of the death-consciousness onwards even for those who pass away from the sense-sphere existence to be reborn in the form or formless existence, and by stating that bodily formation does not cease, it is established that the death-consciousness does not originate bodily formation. And from the point that it does not originate bodily formation, from that point it also does not generate the remaining material form. For in the absence of an impediment such as being in the womb, there is no reason for a generator of material form not to originate bodily formation. Nor is it right that material form originated by consciousness should continue after death, nor is there any Pāli text stating, 'the death-consciousness originates material form.' Nor is the non-pacification of the root of the round a reason for the death-consciousness to generate material form, for what is not generated by the death-consciousness does not arise in another existence, just like what was generated by earlier consciousnesses. Therefore, for all beings, the death-consciousness does not originate material form. If it is argued that only the origination of bodily formation establishes the capacity to generate material form, then what about the fourth jhāna? This is not a fault; for although it does not originate bodily formation because of its exceedingly tranquil mode of occurrence due to the power of development, there is no impediment to its originating material form since it is not extremely weak like the consciousnesses near death. From when, then, does mind-originated material form not arise? From when bodily formation does not arise. And when does bodily formation not arise? They say it does not arise starting from the thirty-second mind-moment before death; what arose at the thirty-third mind-moment before death ceases even before the last sixteen moments. In the question, 'For one for whom bodily formation is not ceasing, for him will mental formation not cease?' (Yamaka 2.Saṅkhārayamaka.113), the answer, 'At the dissolution moment of the final consciousness, for them bodily formation is not ceasing and mental formation will not cease,' excludes only the final consciousness. Therefore, others say it ceases along with the second or third consciousness before death. In the phrase 'after which consciousness the final consciousness of sense-sphere beings will arise,' 'which' is said referring to the consciousness that is the proximate condition for the death-consciousness of a sense-sphere being. Thus, by the statement of the absence of bodily formation from its arising onwards, the lower limit is that it ceases along with the third consciousness before death. Some say it does not reach the second consciousness before death.

151-7. Ekaṃ dve tīṇi cattāri ṭhānāni imassāti ekadviticatuṭṭhānaṃ, ekadviticatuṭṭhānattāti attho. Ṭhānanti ca idha kiccamadhippetaṃ. Tañhi tiṭṭhanti ettha dhammā avaṭṭhitā viya hontīti “ṭhāna”nti vuccati. Maṃsacakkhudibbacakkhuñāṇacakkhubuddhacakkhusamantacakkhuvasena pañca nimmalāni locanāni imassāti pañcanimmalalocano.

151-7. 'It has one, two, three, four places,' thus it is 'one-two-three-four-placed'; the meaning is 'because of having one, two, three, or four places.' Here, by 'place,' function is intended. For because phenomena stand here as if established, it is called a 'place.' Because he has five immaculate eyes—namely, the physical eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Buddha eye, and the all-seeing eye—he is 'one with five immaculate eyes.'

Nippapañcenāti [M 1.0346] rāgādipapañcarahitena. Rāgādayo hi saṃsāre papañcanato “papañcā”ti vuccanti.

'Without proliferation' means devoid of proliferations such as lust. For lust and so on are called 'proliferations' because they proliferate in saṃsāra.

Āvajjane paṭicchane ṭhāne manodhātuttikanti sambandho, kiriyāmanodhātu āvajjanaṭṭhāne, vipākadvayaṃ sampaṭicchanaṭṭhāneti attho.

The connection is: the mind-element triad is in the function of adverting and receiving. The meaning is: the functional mind-element is in the function of adverting; the resultant pair is in the function of receiving.

“Somanassayuttasantīraṇaṃ pañcadvāre santīraṇaṃ siyā”ti vattabbe “santīraṇa”nti adhikāratova labbhatīti gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ “somanassayuta”nti ettakameva vuttaṃ.

When it should be said, 'The investigating consciousness accompanied by joy might be investigating at the five doors,' only 'accompanied by joy' is stated for the sake of metrical ease, since 'investigating' is obtained from the context.

Balavārammaṇe satīti tadārammaṇakiccassa balavārammaṇeyeva labbhanato vuttaṃ, na imasseva āveṇikabhāvena sabbesampi tadārammaṇānaṃ balavārammaṇeyeva uppajjanato. Voṭṭhabbananti kiriyāmanoviññāṇadhātusaṅkhātaṃ voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ cittaṃ.

The phrase 'when the object is strong' is stated because the function of registration is obtained only with a strong object; this is not a special property of this one instance, for all registrations arise only with a strong object. 'Determining' is the consciousness with the function of determining, which is designated as the functional mind-consciousness-element.

158-9. Sabbesanti sabbesaṃ kāmarūpārūpabhavikasattānaṃ. Iminā idaṃ dasseti – pañcadvāresu voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ kesañcideva sattānaṃ arūpabhave sabbaso pañcadvārikacittappavattiyā, rūpabhave ca dvārattayappavattiyā abhāvato. Manodvāre āvajjanakiccaṃ pana sabbesameva sacittakasattānaṃ karotīti. Dviṭṭhānikaṃ nāma hotīti yathāvuttaṭṭhānadvayavantatāya dviṭṭhānikacittaṃ nāma hoti. Keci pana “somanassasahagatasantīraṇaṃ kāmasugatiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati[V 1.0272], tasmā taṃ pañcaṭṭhānika”nti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ paṭṭhāne tathā adīpitattā. Tattha hi –

158-9. 'For all' means for all beings in the sense-sphere, form-sphere, and formless-sphere existences. By this it is shown that the function of determining at the five doors pertains only to some beings—since in the formless existence there is a complete absence of the five-door cognitive process, and in the form existence there is an absence of the three-door process. The function of adverting at the mind door, however, it performs for all beings who possess consciousness. 'It is called two-functioned' means that because it has the two aforesaid functions, it is called a two-functioned consciousness. Some, however, say: 'The investigating consciousness accompanied by joy draws rebirth-linking in a happy sense-sphere destination; therefore it is five-functioned.' But that is merely their opinion, as it is not explained thus in the Paṭṭhāna. For there—

“Upekkhāsahagataṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca upekkhāsahagato dhammo uppajjati nahetupaccayā”ti ettha (paṭṭhā. 2.7.8) “ahetukaṃ upekkhāsahagataṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ paṭicca tayo khandhā, tayo khandhe paṭicca eko khandho, dve khandhe paṭicca dve khandhā[M 1.0347], ahetukapaṭisandhikkhaṇe upekkhāsahagataṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ paṭicca tayo khandhā, tayo khandhe paṭicca eko khandho, dve khandhe paṭicca dve khandhā”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.7.8) –

"Dependent on a state accompanied by equanimity, a state accompanied by equanimity arises by non-root condition." Here (Paṭṭhāna 2.7.8), this means: "Dependent on one rootless aggregate accompanied by equanimity, three aggregates arise; dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate arises; dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates arise. At the moment of rootless rebirth-linking, dependent on one aggregate accompanied by equanimity, three aggregates arise; dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate arises; dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates arise" (Paṭṭhāna 2.7.8).

Evaṃ upekkhāsahagata-padassa pavattipaṭisandhivasena paṭiccanayo uddhaṭo. Pītisahagatasukhasahagata-padānaṃ pana –

Thus, for the term 'accompanied by equanimity,' the method of conditionality has been extracted by way of occurrence and rebirth-linking. But for the terms 'accompanied by joy' and 'accompanied by happiness'—

“Pītisahagataṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca pītisahagato dhammo uppajjati nahetupaccayā. Ahetukaṃ pītisahagataṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ paṭicca tayo khandhā, tayo khandhe paṭicca eko khandho, dve khandhe paṭicca dve khandhā. Sukhasahagataṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca sukhasahagato dhammo uppajjati nahetupaccayā. Ahetukaṃ sukhasahagataṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ paṭicca tayo khandhā, tayo khandhe paṭicca eko khandho, dve khandhe paṭicca dve khandhā”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.7.6) –

"Dependent on a state accompanied by joy, a state accompanied by joy arises by non-root condition. Dependent on one rootless aggregate accompanied by joy, three aggregates arise; dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate arises; dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates arise. Dependent on a state accompanied by happiness, a state accompanied by happiness arises by non-root condition. Dependent on one rootless aggregate accompanied by happiness, three aggregates arise; dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate arises; dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates arise" (Paṭṭhāna 2.7.6).

Evaṃ pavattivaseneva uddhaṭo, na “ahetukapaṭisandhikkhaṇe”tiādinā paṭisandhivasena, tasmā yathādhammasāsane avacanampi abhāvameva dīpetīti na tassa paṭisandhidānaṃ atthīti dviṭṭhānikatāva vuttāti. Te mahaggatavipākā navāti sambandho.

Thus, it is extracted only by way of occurrence, not by way of rebirth-linking with the words 'at the moment of rootless rebirth-linking,' etc. Therefore, even the non-statement in the teaching of the Dhamma as it is indicates its absence. Hence, there is no giving of rebirth-linking for it, and thus its two-functioned nature is stated. The connection is: 'Those nine sublime resultant consciousnesses.'

162. Chadvārā eva chadvārikā. Atha vā chadvārikesūti chadvārikacittesūti attho.

162. The six doors themselves are 'the six-doored.' Or, 'in the six-doored' means 'in the consciousnesses pertaining to the six doors.'

164-6. “Pañcakicca”ntiādi yathāvuttānameva nigamanaṃ. Sesanti aṭṭhasaṭṭhividhaṃ cittaṃ. Ekakiccayogato, ekaṃ kiccamassāti vā ekaṃ, ekameva ekakaṃ. Sabbacittānaṃ kiccavasena niddesaṭṭhāneyeva kiccānaṃ paṭipāṭimpi dassetuṃ “bhavaṅgāvajjana”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya cutipariyosānaṃ vattabbanti? Saccaṃ, cutipaṭisandhīnaṃ pana pākaṭattā [V 1.0273] tathā [M 1.0348] na vuttaṃ. Bhavassa hi paṭisandhi ādi, cuti pariyosānanti pākaṭameva, tasmā pākaṭaṭṭhānaṃ pahāya apākaṭaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ bhavaṅgameva ādito vuttaṃ. Tadārammaṇaṃ pana kiñcāpi apākaṭaṃ, atha kho anekantikaṃ kismiñci bhave katthaci javanavīthiyaṃ alabbhanatoti ekantalabbhamānaparidīpanatthaṃ taṃ na vuttaṃ. Atha vā tadārammaṇacittampi yebhuyyena bhavaṅganāmaṃ labbhatīti purimajavanavīthiyaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ pacchimajavanavīthiyā āvajjanassa purecarabhūtaṃ bhavaṅga-ggahaṇeneva saṅgahitanti visuṃ na vuttaṃ. Keci pana “pañcadvāresu pavattivasena pañcavidhatāya dassanatthaṃ ‘bhavaṅgāvajjana’ntiādi vutta”nti vadanti, tattha pana appavattamānānaṃ kesañci sabbhāvato taṃ na yujjati, chadvārappavattivasena chabbidhattanayadassanatthanti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Yathā cettha “bhavaṅgāvajjana”ntiādinā cakkhudvāre vuttaṃ, evaṃ sotadvārādīsupi dassanādiṃ apanetvā savanādiṃ pakkhipitvā kiccappavatti yojetabbā. Manodvāre pana –

164-6. ‘The five functions’ and so on is a conclusion of what has been stated. The rest refers to the sixty-eight types of consciousness. From the perspective of having a single function, it is called ‘single’ (ekaṃ), meaning it has one function (kiccaṃ assa); or ‘single’ (ekakaṃ) means just one. To show the order of the functions in the place where the functions of all consciousnesses are indicated, ‘life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and advertence (āvajjana)’ and so on, were stated. If so, should it be stated as occurring from rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) to the end at death (cuti)? It is true, but rebirth-linking and death are obvious, so it was not stated that way. For rebirth-linking is the beginning of existence (bhava), and death is the end—this is obvious. Therefore, setting aside what is obvious, to show it starting from what is not obvious, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) alone was stated first. Although registering (tadārammaṇa) is not obvious, still it is uncertain; it is not obtained in any impulsion process (javanavīthi) in some existences, so to show what is invariably obtainable, that was not stated. Alternatively, the registering consciousness (tadārammaṇacitta) is mostly called life-continuum (bhavaṅga), so in the earlier impulsion process, the registering precedes the advertence (āvajjana) in the subsequent impulsion process, and thus it is included by the life-continuum—hence it was not stated separately. Some, however, say that ‘life-continuum, advertence,’ etc., were stated to show the fivefold division based on the process occurring at the five doors. But that is not appropriate, since some do not occur. It is fitting to say that it illustrates the sixfold division based on the process at the six doors. Just as here, ‘life-continuum, advertence,’ etc., were stated in relation to the eye-door, so too in the ear-door and other doors, removing seeing etc. and inserting hearing etc., the occurrence of the functions should be applied. As for the mind-door—

“Bhavaṅgaṃ paṭhamaṃ hoti, tato āvajjanaṃ mataṃ;

Dutiyaṃ tamatikkamma, javanaṃ tatiyaṃ siyā”ti. –

‘The life-continuum is first, then advertence is considered; having passed beyond that, impulsion would be the third.’

Yojanā daṭṭhabbā. Channaṃ viññāṇānanti cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ, manoviññāṇassa ca. Sattaviññāṇadhātūnanti cakkhuviññāṇadhātādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ, manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātudvayassāti sattannaṃ viññāṇadhātūnaṃ.

The application should be understood. Of the six consciousnesses—that is, the five beginning with eye-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. Of the seven consciousness elements—that is, the five beginning with the eye-consciousness element, along with the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element—thus, the seven consciousness elements.

169-71. Pañcābhiññāvivajjitanti –

169-71. ‘Devoid of the five higher knowledges’—

“Iddhividhaṃ dibbasoto, paracittavijānanā;

Pubbenivāsānussati, dibbacakkhūti pañcadhā”ti. –

‘The kinds are: psychic power, the divine ear, knowledge of others’ minds, recollection of past lives, and the divine eye.’

Evamāgatāhi pañcahi abhiññāhi yuttena rūpāvacarapañcamajjhānacittena vajjitaṃ. Dibbasotādīnaṃ ekekārammaṇattepi pañcannampi abhiññānaṃ ekasseva cittassa avatthābhedabhāvato vuttaṃ “pañcābhiññāvivajjita”nti[M 1.0349]. Keci pana “idha ekantena dhammārammaṇikacittānameva vacanato [V 1.0274] paracittavijānanaṃ vajjetvā anāgataṃsañāṇena saha pañcābhiññānaṃ paṭikkhepo”ti vadanti.

It is devoid of the fifth jhāna consciousness of the form realm, which is endowed with these five higher knowledges. Even though each of the divine ear and other knowledges has a single object, because the five higher knowledges are merely different states of a single consciousness, it is said, ‘devoid of the five higher knowledges.’ However, some say, ‘Here, since only consciousnesses with exclusively mental objects are spoken of, the rejection of the five higher knowledges applies along with the knowledge of the future, excluding the knowledge of others’ minds.’

Dvipañcaviññāṇānaṃ, manodhātuttayassa ca pariccāgena ekacattālīsa hontīti āha “cattālīsaṃ tathekaka”nti. Abhiññāni cāti ca-saddo aṭṭhānappayutto, so “cattālīsaṃ tathekaka”nti imassānantaraṃ daṭṭhabbo, tena pana abhiññācittadvayaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Atha vā abhiññā nāma heṭṭhā ekekārammaṇikesu vuttassa pañcamajjhānasseva avatthāvisesoti abhiññācittānaṃ chaḷārammaṇikesu aggahaṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By the exclusion of the twofold fivefold consciousness and the threefold mind-element, there remain forty-one. Hence it is said, ‘Forty and one likewise.’ The word ‘ca’ (and) in ‘abhiññāni ca’ is misplaced; it should be understood as following immediately after ‘Forty and one likewise.’ By it, the two higher knowledge consciousnesses are included. Alternatively, the term ‘higher knowledge’ refers to a specific state of the fifth jhāna, which was mentioned previously among those with a single object; therefore, it should be understood that the higher knowledge consciousnesses are not included among those with six kinds of objects.

172-3. Tidhā katvāti tidhā karaṇahetu. Hetvattho hi ayaṃ tvā-saddo yathā “sīhaṃ disvā bhayaṃ chambhitattaṃ uppajjati, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontī”ti. “Puññāpuññavasenā”tiādinā jātibhūmihetuvedanādivasena yāva chasattatividho bhedo, tāva manoviññāṇadhātuṃ bhinditvā taṃvasena cittavibhāgadassanatthaṃ nayadānaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ.

172-3. ‘Having divided into three’ means the reason for dividing into three. Indeed, this suffix ‘-tvā’ has the meaning of cause, just as in, ‘Seeing a lion, fear and trembling arise; but seeing it with wisdom, his taints are destroyed.’ It should be understood that by ‘by means of merit and demerit,’ and so on, up to a division into seventy-six kinds, the mind-consciousness element is broken down based on birth, plane, root, feeling, and so on, and by that means, this application of method is done to show the division of consciousness.

175. Tidhā katvāti paṭhamaṃ vipākadvayakiriyābhedato, dutiyaṃ kusalākusalāditoti evaṃ dhātudvayaṃ paccekaṃ tidhā katvā.

175. ‘Divided into three’ means: first, by the distinction of the two resultants and the functional; second, by wholesome, unwholesome, and so on. Thus, having divided the pair of elements, each into three.

180. Bhūmi…pe… vibhāvayeti tiṃsabhūmīnaṃ nānattavasena pavattito tiṃsavidhaṃ, tattheva tiṃsapuggalānaṃ nānattavasena pavattito ca tiṃsavidhantiādinā idaṃ yathāniddiṭṭhacittaṃ bahudhā hotīti ca vibhāveyyāti attho.

180. ‘Plane…etc.…he should discern’ means that this consciousness, as described, becomes manifold, being manifested as thirtyfold due to the diversity of the thirty planes, and also thirtyfold due to the diversity of the thirty individuals therein, and so on, and he should discern it thus.

181. Idhāti [M 1.0350] imasmiṃ sāsane. Hatthagatāmalakā viya hontīti yathā hatthagataṃ āmalakaṃ cakkhumato supākaṭaṃ hoti, evamimassa matimato bhikkhuno abhidhammapiṭakagatā atthā supākaṭā honti, āvajjitāvajjitakkhaṇe suvisadāva paññāyantīti attho.

181. Here: in this Dispensation. They are like a myrobalan fruit in the hand: just as a myrobalan fruit in the hand is perfectly clear to one with good sight, so too for this wise monk the meanings contained in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka are perfectly clear, appearing very distinctly to his wisdom at the very moment he directs his mind to them—this is the meaning.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the Commentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma,

Ekavidhādiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the commentary on the exposition of the single method, etc., is complete.

5. Pañcamo paricchedo

5. The Fifth Chapter

Bhūmipuggalacittuppattiniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Arising of Consciousness in Relation to Planes and Individuals

182-8. Buddhiyā [V 1.0275] vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ karotīti buddhivuddhikaraṃ. Yassa yassa nayassa kathanaṃ paṭiññātaṃ, taṃ taṃ dassento āha “cittānaṃ bhūmīsuppatti”nti. Taṃ vatvā bhūmīnaṃ ādhāravasena pasaṅgāgataṃ gatibhedaṃ, bhavabhedañca dassetuṃ “devā cevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Catassopāyabhūmiyo”ti vatvā asuragatiyā petagatiyaṃyeva saṅgahitattā “gatiyo pañcā”ti vuttanti vadanti. Mayaṃ pana “tissovāpāyabhūmiyo”ti pāṭhena bhavitabbanti maññāma. Na hi esa anākulavacano ācariyo īdisaṃ pubbāparaviruddhaṃ viya sammohajanakaṃ vacanaṃ bhāsati. Pāḷiyampi hi –

182-8. It brings about an increase and growth in wisdom: this is what makes for the growth of wisdom. Demonstrating whatever method of explanation has been promised, he says, “the arising of consciousness in the planes.” Having said that, in order to show the distinctions of destination and the distinctions of existence that arise incidentally on the basis of the planes, the passage beginning “both the devas” was stated. Some say that having stated “four planes of misery,” because the asura destination is included in the ghost destination, it is said “there are five destinations.” We, however, think that the reading should be “three planes of misery.” For this teacher, whose speech is not confused, would not utter such a statement that is bewildering and seemingly contradictory between what precedes and what follows. For in the Pāli canon too—

“Pañca kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyo. Katamā pañca? Nirayo tiracchānayoni pettivisayo manussā devā”ti (a. ni. 9.68) –

“Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. What five? Hell, the animal womb, the domain of ghosts, human beings, and devas.”

Evaṃ [M 1.0351] tiṇṇameva apāyānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Kāmarūpārūpavasena tayo bhavā. Tatthāti tesu tīsu bhavesu. Tiṃsevāti catasso apāyabhūmiyo, sattavidhā kāmasugatibhūmi, soḷasa rūpībrahmalokā, catasso arūpabhūmiyoti ekatiṃsabhūmīnamantare cittappavattiadhikārattā asaññabhūmiṃ apanetvā avasesā tiṃseva bhūmiyoti attho. Tāsu tiṃseva puggalāti tāsu bhūmīsu uppannā puggalā bhūmigaṇanavasena tiṃseva honti. Bhūmivasena tiṃsavidhāpi pana paṭisandhicittagaṇanāya ekūnavīsati hontīti dassento āha “bhūmīsvetāsū”tiādi.

Thus, it is stated with reference to just the three planes of misery. There are three kinds of existence: the sense-sphere existence, the form-sphere existence, and the formless-sphere existence. Therein means in those three kinds of existence. Thirty means: the four planes of misery, the sevenfold sense-sphere happy destination, the sixteen form-sphere brahmā worlds, and the four formless planes. Since the governing topic concerns the occurrence of consciousness among these thirty-one planes, when the plane of non-percipient beings is excluded, the remaining planes are just thirty—this is the meaning. In these there are thirty persons means that the persons born in those planes are thirty in number according to the count of the planes. But to show that although there are thirty types by way of planes, by the count of rebirth-linking consciousnesses there are nineteen, he says: “In these planes,” etc.

Paṭisandhikacittānanti dasa kāmāvacarapaṭisandhicittāni, pañca rūpāvacarapaṭisandhicittāni, cattāri arūpāvacarapaṭisandhicittānīti imesaṃ ekūnavīsatipaṭisandhicittānaṃ vasena. Asaññīnamacittakāti asaññasattānaṃ acittakā paṭisandhi. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Rebirth-linking consciousnesses means: by way of these nineteen rebirth-linking consciousnesses, namely, the ten sense-sphere rebirth-linking consciousnesses, the five form-sphere rebirth-linking consciousnesses, and the four formless-sphere rebirth-linking consciousnesses. The non-percipient are without consciousness means that the rebirth-linking of non-percipient beings is without consciousness. For this has been said:

“Asaññasattā [V 1.0276] devā ahetukā anāhārakā aphassakā avedanakā asaññakā acetanakā acittakā pātubhavantī”ti.

“Non-percipient beings, devas, arise without root-causes, without nutriment, without contact, without feeling, non-percipient, without volition, without consciousness.”

Yadi paṭisandhivasena vīsati puggalā, kathaṃ bhūmivasena tiṃsāti vuttā. Ekatiṃsāti hi vattabbanti āha “idhā”tiādi.

If there are twenty individuals by way of rebirth-linking, how is it said that there are thirty by way of planes? To the objection, “Indeed, thirty-one should be stated,” he replies with the passage beginning “Here,” etc.

Na vijjati hetu imesanti ahetū, duve, tīṇi ca hetū imesanti dvitihetū, paṭisandhivasena ahetukā, duhetukā, tihetukā cāti attho. Tattha ahetukā āpāyikā ca, ekacce bhūmadevā, manussesu jaccandhajaccabadhirajaccummattakanapuṃsakaubhatobyañjanakādayo ca. Vuttāvasesā kāmasugativāsinova duhetukā. Tihetukā pana kāmasugativāsinova. Ariyā pana aṭṭhāti catunnaṃ ariyamaggasamaṅgīnaṃ, catunnañca ariyaphalasamaṅgīnaṃ vasena aṭṭha ariyapuggalā[M 1.0352]. Nanu ca ariyāpi tihetukāyevāti? Saccaṃ, cittuppādaṃ pana patvā tesaṃ visesasabbhāvato visuṃyeva uddhaṭāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

No root-cause exists for them, so they are rootless; two or three root-causes exist for them, so they are two-rooted or three-rooted; that is, by way of rebirth-linking, they are rootless, two-rooted, and three-rooted—this is the meaning. Among them, the rootless ones are those in the woeful planes, some earth-devas, and among humans, those born blind, born deaf, born mad, eunuchs, hermaphrodites, etc. The remaining inhabitants of the sense-sphere happy destinations are two-rooted. The three-rooted, however, are also inhabitants of the sense-sphere happy destinations. The noble ones, however, are eight: that is, the eight noble persons by way of the four endowed with the noble path and the four endowed with the noble fruition. But are not the noble ones also three-rooted? True, but it should be understood that they are treated separately because of the special nature of their consciousness when it arises.

189-92. “Bhūmīsuppattiṃ bhaṇato me nibodhathā”ti sutvā codako “tiṃsabhūmīsū”tiādinā sabbesaṃ bhūmīnaṃ sādhāraṇacittāni pucchati, itaro “cuddasevā”ti vissajjeti. Tattha aṭṭha parittakusalāni, cattāri diṭṭhivippayuttāni, uddhaccasahagataṃ, manodvārāvajjanañcāti cuddaseva, na ūnāni nādhikāni, sabbāsu tiṃsabhūmīsu honti, sabbabhūmīnaṃ sādhāraṇānīti attho.

189-92. Having heard, “Understand from me as I explain the arising in the planes,” the questioner asks about the consciousnesses common to all planes with the phrase beginning “In the thirty planes,” and the other replies, “Only fourteen.” Herein, the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, the four dissociated from wrong view, the one accompanied by restlessness, and mind-door adverting—these fourteen only, no less and no more, occur in all thirty planes; this means they are common to all planes.

Sadā…pe… siyunti dve dosamūlāni, kusalavipākacakkhusotaviññāṇasampaṭicchanasantīraṇadvayavajjitāni aṭṭhārasa kāmāvacaravipākacittānīti vīsati cittāni sadā kāmeyeva bhave siyuṃ, na kadāci aññattha uppajjantīti attho. Nanu ca brahmūnampi akusalavipākāni uppajjantīti? Saccaṃ uppajjanti, tāni kāmabhave aniṭṭharūpādayo ārabbha uppajjanti brahmaloke tesaṃ abhāvatoti kāmabhaveyeva niyamitāni. Rūpāvacaravipākacittāni pañca rūpāvacarabhaveyeva siyuṃ, cattāro ca arūpāvacaravipākā arūpīsūti āha “pañca rūpabhave”tiādi.

Regarding the verse “Always… they would be”: the twenty consciousnesses that always arise only in the sense-sphere existence are the two rooted in hatred, the resultant nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses (six types), the three investigating consciousnesses, the eight great resultant consciousnesses, and the smile-producing consciousness. Thus these twenty consciousnesses always arise only in the sense-sphere existence, never elsewhere—this is the meaning. But do not unwholesome resultants also arise for the brahmās? True, they do arise, but they arise in the sense-sphere existence by taking undesirable forms, etc., as object, because these do not exist in the brahmā world; thus they are restricted to the sense-sphere existence. The five form-sphere resultant consciousnesses arise only in the form-sphere existence, and the four formless-sphere resultant consciousnesses in the formless realms—hence it is said, “five in the form-sphere,” etc.

Kāma [V 1.0277] …pe… bhavantīti rūpāvacarakusalakiriyacittāni ceva kusalavipākāni ca cakkhusotaviññāṇasampaṭicchanasantīraṇāni voṭṭhabbanavajjāni ca dve ahetukakiriyacittāni paṭhamamaggaviññāṇanti aṭṭhārasa cittāni kāmarūpabhaveyeva bhavanti, na arūpabhave. Tattha hi sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkantattā rūpāvacarakusalakiriyā nuppajjanti. Cakkhuviññāṇādīni vatthudvāravirahato, hasituppādo ekantavatthunissayattā, sotāpattimaggo paratoghosapaccayāyeva nibbattanato [M 1.0353] na uppajjati. Dvecattālīsāti aṭṭha parittakusalāni, cattāri arūpakusalāni, paṭhamamaggavajjāni satta lokuttaracittāni, paṭighadvayavajjitāni ca dasa akusalacittāni, pubbe vuttaahetukakiriyādvayavajjitāni nava kāmāvacarakiriyacittāni, cattāri arūpāvacarakiriyacittānīti evaṃ dvecattālīsa cittāni tīsu bhavesu honti.

Regarding the verse “In the sense-sphere…”: the eighteen types of consciousness—namely, the ten form-sphere wholesome and functional consciousnesses, the five wholesome-resultant rootless consciousnesses, the stream-entry path consciousness, and the two rootless functional consciousnesses (five-door adverting and smile-producing)—arise only in the sense-sphere and form-sphere existences, not in the formless-sphere existence. There, because all perceptions of form are completely transcended, the form-sphere wholesome and functional consciousnesses do not arise. Eye-consciousness and the like do not arise due to the absence of a physical base and sense doors; the smile-producing consciousness does not arise because it depends entirely on a physical base; the stream-entry path consciousness does not arise because it is produced solely by hearing the teachings from another. The forty-two types of consciousness—the eight sense-sphere wholesome, the four formless-sphere wholesome, the seven supramundane consciousnesses excluding the first path consciousness, the ten unwholesome consciousnesses excluding the two rooted in aversion, the nine sense-sphere functional consciousnesses excluding the two rootless functional consciousnesses previously mentioned, and the four formless-sphere functional consciousnesses—thus, these forty-two types of consciousness arise in the three kinds of existence.

193-204. Evaṃ bhavavasena cittuppattiṃ dassetvā idāni kālavasena dassento āha “ṭhapetvā panā”tiādi. Sabbāsanti niddhāraṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Aṭṭha mahākiriyā, arahattamaggaphalacittāni, anāgāmiphalaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakusalakiriyāti teraseva cittāni apāyarahitāsu chabbīsabhūmīsu honti apāyesu vipākāvaraṇasabbhāve etesaṃ anuppajjanato. Aparāni cha cittānīti sambandho. Tāni pana rūpabhavasādhāraṇānaṃ pañcaparittavipākānaṃ, kiriyamanodhātuyā ca vasena veditabbāni.

193-204. Having thus shown the arising of consciousness by way of existence, now, showing it by way of planes, he says, “But having set aside,” etc. “Of all” is a genitive of specification. Thirteen types of consciousness—the eight great functional consciousnesses, the path and fruition consciousness of arahantship, the fruition of non-returning, and the wholesome and functional consciousnesses of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—occur only in the twenty-six planes free from the woeful planes, since they do not arise in the woeful planes due to the presence of resultant-obstruction. The connection is to “the other six consciousnesses.” These should be understood as the five sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses common to the form sphere, and the functional mind-element.

Pañca cittānīti diṭṭhisampayuttavicikicchāvasena pañca cittāni. Tāni hi pañcasu suddhāvāsabhūmīsu na labbhanti. Tattha anāgāmikhīṇāsavānameva adhivutthattā, tesañca paṭhamamaggeneva imesaṃ pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ anuppādadhammataṃ āpāditattā.

Five consciousnesses: the five consciousnesses comprising those associated with wrong view and the one associated with doubt. These five are not found in the five Pure Abodes, since only non-returners and arahants dwell there, and because through the first path they have brought these five consciousnesses to a state of non-arising.

Aparāni duveti tatiyāruppakusalakiriyacittāni. Tāni hi nevasaññānāsaññāyatanesu atikkantārammaṇattā, apāyesu ca ahetukapaṭisandhikattā nuppajjanti. Catuvīsatībhūmisu dve cāti viññāṇañcāyatanakusalakiriyāvasena dve cittāni. Tevīsabhūmisu dveyevāti ākāsānañcāyatanakusalakiriyacittāni.

The other two are the wholesome and functional consciousnesses of the third formless attainment. For they do not arise in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception because their object has been transcended, nor in the woeful planes because rebirth-linking there is rootless. And two in twenty-four planes refers to the two consciousnesses, wholesome and functional, of the base of infinite consciousness. Just two in twenty-three planes refers to the wholesome and functional consciousnesses of the base of infinite space.

Ekādasavidhanti rūpāvacarakusalakiriyā hasituppādoti ekādasa. Sotāpattiphalaṃ yāva anāgāmimaggo cattāri ca cittāni suddhāvāsaapāyavajjāsu ekavīsatibhūmīsu bhavanti. Ekaṃ [M 1.0354][V 1.0278] sotāpattimaggacittaṃ suddhāvāsaapāyaarūpabhūmivajjesu sattarasasu bhūmīsu jāyati. Dve dosamūlāni, kusalavipākaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni, satta akusalavipākāti dvādasa cittāni mahaggatabhūmivajjāsu ekādasasu kāmabhūmīsu jāyanti. Aṭṭha mahāvipākacittāni kāmāvacaradevamanussavasena sattabhūmīsu jāyanti. Chasu bhūmisūti vehapphalasuddhāvāsasaṅkhātāsu chasu pañcamajjhānabhūmīsu.

Eleven kinds means the ten form-sphere wholesome and functional consciousnesses and the smile-producing consciousness. The four consciousnesses from the fruition of stream-entry up to the path of non-returning arise in the twenty-one planes, excluding the Pure Abodes and the woeful planes. The one stream-entry path consciousness arises in seventeen planes, excluding the Pure Abodes, the woeful planes, and the formless planes. The two rooted in hatred, the three wholesome-resultant nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses, and the seven unwholesome resultants—these twelve types of consciousness arise in the eleven sense-sphere planes, excluding the sublime planes. The eight great resultant consciousnesses arise in the seven planes of sense-sphere devas and humans. In six planes refers to the six fifth-jhāna planes, namely Vehapphala and the five Pure Abodes.

Cattāri…pe… bhūmisūti catutthajjhānavipāko parittasubhaappamāṇasubhasubhakiṇhavasena tīsu bhūmīsu jāyati, dutiyajjhānavipāko, tatiyajjhānavipāko ca parittābhāappamāṇābhāābhassaravasena tīsu bhūmīsu, paṭhamajjhānavipāko brahmapārisajjabrahmapurohitamahābrahmāvasena tīsu bhūmīsu hotīti evaṃ cattāri cittāni ekekavasena tīsu tīsu bhūmīsu jāyanti.

Four... and so on... in three planes. The fourth-jhāna resultant arises in three planes: the plane of Limited Glory, the plane of Immeasurable Glory, and the plane of Refulgent Glory. The second-jhāna resultant and the third-jhāna resultant arise in three planes: the plane of Limited Radiance, the plane of Immeasurable Radiance, and the plane of Streaming Radiance. The first-jhāna resultant arises in three planes: the plane of Brahmā's Retinue, the plane of Brahmā's Ministers, and the plane of the Great Brahmās. Thus, these four consciousnesses each arise in three planes.

206-9. Evaṃ ettakāneva cittāni ettakāsu bhūmīsu uppajjantīti cittaniyamavasena uppattiṃ dassetvā idāni ettakāsu eva bhūmīsu ettakāneva cittāni uppajjantīti bhūminiyamavasena dassetuṃ “kusalākusalā kāme”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kāme kusalākusalā vīsati, tesaṃ pannarasa ahetukā pākā, āvajjanadvayañcāti sattatiṃseva mānasā narakādīsu catūsupi apāyesu jāyare. Avasesāni pana sattarasa kāmāvacaravipākakiriyacittāni, pañcatiṃsa mahaggatalokuttarānīti dvepaññāsa mānasā kadācipi tesu nuppajjanti abhūmibhāvatoti attho.

206-9. Having thus shown the arising of consciousness according to the fixed order of consciousness by stating, 'Only this many consciousnesses arise in this many planes,' now, to show that 'only this many consciousnesses arise in this many planes' according to the fixed order of planes, the passage beginning 'Wholesome and unwholesome in the sense sphere...' is introduced. Herein, in the sense sphere there are twenty wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses, their fifteen rootless resultants, and the two advertings; thus thirty-seven mental states arise in the four woeful planes, such as hell. But the remaining seventeen sense-sphere resultant and functional consciousnesses, and the thirty-five sublime and supramundane consciousnesses—these fifty-two mental states never arise in them because it is not their plane. This is the meaning.

Asīti hadayāti vuttāvasesāni asīti cittāni. Ghānādiviññāṇattayanti kusalavipākaghānādiviññāṇattayaṃ. “Apuññajā pākā”ti akusalavipākānaṃ sabbesameva gahitattā ghānādiviññāṇattayaṃ aggahitavisesampi pārisesañāyena kusalavipākameva viññāyati.

'Eighty based on the heart' means the remaining eighty consciousnesses that have been mentioned. 'The triad of consciousnesses of smell, etc.' means the triad of wholesome-resultant consciousnesses of smell, etc. By 'resultants born of demerit,' since all unwholesome resultants are included, the triad of consciousnesses of smell, etc., though not specifically included, is understood by the method of remainder to be only the wholesome resultants.

213. Domanassanti [M 1.0355] domanassasahagataṃ. Kriyā ca dveti voṭṭhabbanavajjitā dve ahetukakiriyā.

213. 'Displeasure' means that which is accompanied by displeasure. 'And the two functional' means the two rootless functional consciousnesses, excluding the determining consciousness.

214. Bhūmivasenevāti puggale anāmasitvā kevalaṃ bhūmivasena. Puggalānaṃ vasena ca bhūmivasena ca cittuppattiṃ vibhāvayeti sambandho.

214. 'Solely by way of the plane' means without referring to persons, but only by way of the plane. The connection is that it explains the arising of consciousness both by way of persons and by way of planes.

216-8. Pañcabhūmisūti [V 1.0279] caturāpāyamanussavasena pañcabhūmīsu. Ahetukānaṃ paṭisandhisadisatadārammaṇavasena “sattatiṃsevā”ti vuttaṃ, aññakammena pana dvihetukatadārammaṇassāpi sambhavato ekacattālīsa honti. Ācariyajotipālattherassa adhippāyena tihetukavipākehipi saddhiṃ pañcacattālīsevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ahetukassa vuttehīti ahetukasattassa vuttehi sattatiṃsamānasehi saha. Nava kriyāti aṭṭha mahākiriyā, hasituppādo cāti imāni asādhāraṇakiriyacittāni nava.

216-8. 'In the five planes' means in the five planes consisting of the four woeful states and the human state. For rootless beings, it is said 'thirty-seven' on account of rebirth-linking and similar registration. But through other kamma, since two-rooted registration is also possible, there are forty-one. According to the opinion of the Elder Ācariya Jotipāla, it should be understood that there are forty-five along with the three-rooted resultants. 'With those mentioned for the rootless' means together with the thirty-seven mental states mentioned for a rootless being. 'Nine functional' means the eight great functional consciousnesses and the smile-producing consciousness; these are the nine unique functional consciousnesses.

220-1. “Catupaññāsa mānasā”ti vatvā tesaṃ sarūpato dassanatthaṃ āha “dvihetukassā”tiādi. Puna “catupaññāsā”tiādi pana nigamanaṃ.

220-1. Having stated 'fifty-four mental states,' to show their nature individually, the text states, 'for the two-rooted,' etc. The repetition of 'fifty-four,' etc., is the conclusion.

223-4. Paññāsevassa cittānīti tihetukassa puthujjanassa vuttacatupaññāsacittesu diṭṭhivicikicchāsahagatavajjāni ekūnapaññāsa, sotāpattiphalanti imāni paññāseva cittāni assa kāmāvacarassa sotāpannadehino jāyante. Navatiṃsevāti ekūnacattālīsacittāni. Paṭhamaṃ phalanti sotāpattiphalaṃ.

223-4. 'Fifty consciousnesses for him': These are the fifty consciousnesses that arise for a stream-enterer embodied in the sense sphere, namely, the forty-nine among the fifty-four consciousnesses mentioned for a three-rooted worldling, excluding those accompanied by wrong view and doubt, plus the stream-entry fruition. 'Navatiṃsa' means thirty-nine consciousnesses. 'The first fruition' means the stream-entry fruition.

225-8. Dutiyañca phalaṃ hitvāti sakadāgāmiphalaṃ hitvā. Ca-saddena sotāpattiphalañca hitvāti attho. Attano phalena [M 1.0356] saha yāni aṭṭhacattālīsa cittāni, tāni anāgāmissa sattassa jāyanti. Cattālīsañca cattārīti tevīsati kāmāvacaravipākacittāni, vīsati kiriyacittāni, arahattaphalañcāti catucattālīsa cittāni. Sakaṃ sakanti “sotāpannassa sotāpattimaggacittaṃ, sakadāgāmino sakadāgāmimaggacitta”ntiādinā attano attano maggacittaṃ. Kasmā pana tesaṃ ekekameva cittaṃ hotīti āha “ekacittakkhaṇāhi te”ti. Pañcatiṃsevāti sattarasa kāmarūpārūpakusalacittāni, paṭighadvayavajjāni dasa akusalāni, rūpabhave labbhamānakāni pañca ahetukavipākāni, āvajjanadvayaṃ, paṭhamajjhānavipāko cāti pañcatiṃsa cittāni tīsu paṭhamajjhānabhūmīsu puthujjanassa jāyanti.

225-8. 'And abandoning the second fruition' means abandoning the once-returner's fruition. By the word 'and,' the meaning is also abandoning the stream-entry fruition. For a non-returner being, forty-eight consciousnesses arise together with his own fruition. 'And forty-four': these are the forty-four consciousnesses, namely, twenty-three sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, twenty functional consciousnesses, and the arahantship fruition. 'Each one's own' means each one's own path-consciousness, as in 'for the stream-enterer, the stream-entry path-consciousness; for the once-returner, the once-returner's path-consciousness,' etc. Why do they have only one consciousness each? It is said, 'because they are of a single mind-moment.' 'Thirty-five': these are seventeen sense-sphere, form-sphere, and formless-sphere wholesome consciousnesses; ten unwholesome consciousnesses, excluding the two accompanied by aversion; five rootless resultant consciousnesses obtainable in the form sphere; the two advertings; and the first-jhāna resultant. These thirty-five consciousnesses arise for a worldling in the three first-jhāna planes.

232-5. Hitvā cāti ettha ca-saddena paṭhamaphalassa gahaṇaṃ dasseti. Tena apuññapañcakaṃ hitvā paṭhamaṃ phalaṃ gahetvā cāti attho. Apuññapañcakanti diṭṭhisampayuttavicikicchāsahagatavasena [V 1.0280] pañca akusalacittāni. Tatthāti tesu sotāpannassa vuttesu. Tatthevāti sakadāgāmissa vuttesu. Puññajaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ santīraṇadvayañcevāti sambandho.

232-5. In the phrase 'and abandoning,' the word 'and' here indicates the inclusion of the first fruition. Thus the meaning is: having abandoned the pentad of demerit and having taken up the first fruition. The 'pentad of demerit' means the five unwholesome consciousnesses accompanied by wrong view and doubt. 'Therein' means among those mentioned for the stream-enterer. 'Therein indeed' means among those mentioned for the once-returner. 'The wholesome-resultant receiving and the two investigating'—this is the connection.

237. Evaṃ paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ puthujjanasotāpannādivasena cittasambhavaṃ dassetvā idāni tesameva vasena dutiyajjhānabhūmiyaṃ dassetuṃ “puthujjanassā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Dutiyajjhānatatiyajjhānavipākānaṃ ekasattasseva asambhavepi dutiyajjhānatale nibbatte puthujjanādayo puthujjanādibhāvasāmaññena ekato gahetvā “dutiyajjhānatatiyajjhānapākato”ti vuttaṃ.

237. Having thus shown the possibility of consciousness in the first-jhāna plane by way of worldlings, stream-enterers, etc., now, in order to show the same for them in the second-jhāna plane, the passage beginning 'for a worldling...' is introduced. Although the resultants of the second and third jhānas cannot arise for a single being, worldlings and others born on the second-jhāna plane are taken together and referred to as 'from the resultant of the second and third jhānas' because of their common status as worldlings, etc.

242. Parittasubhādito paṭṭhāya yāva akaniṭṭhā tatiyacatutthajjhānabhūmīsu paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ vuttagaṇanāya cittappavatti veditabbā. Tenāha “parittakasubhādīna”ntiādi.

242. Starting from the plane of the Gods of Limited Glory up to the Akaniṭṭha plane, the process of consciousness in the third and fourth jhāna planes should be understood according to the calculation stated for the first-jhāna plane. Therefore it is said, 'Of those beginning with the Gods of Limited Glory,' etc.

247. Catuvīsati [M 1.0357] cittānīti aṭṭhaparittakusalāni, cattāri arūpakusalāni, paṭighadvayavajjitāni dasa akusalacittāni, paṭhamāruppavipāko, manodvārāvajjanañcāti catuvīsati cittāni paṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ puthujjanassa jāyanti.

247. 'Twenty-four consciousnesses': eight great wholesome consciousnesses, four formless wholesome consciousnesses, ten unwholesome consciousnesses excluding the two accompanied by aversion, the first formless resultant, and the mind-door-adverting consciousness—these twenty-four consciousnesses arise for a worldling in the first formless plane.

250-3. Dasa pañcāti aṭṭha mahākiriyā, catasso arūpakiriyā, manodvārāvajjanaṃ, paṭhamāruppavipāko, arahattaphalañcāti pannarasa cittāni paṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ arahato honti.

250-3. 'Fifteen': eight great functional consciousnesses, four formless functional consciousnesses, mind-door-adverting consciousness, the first formless resultant, and the arahantship fruition—these fifteen consciousnesses occur for an arahant in the first formless plane.

Tevīsāti paṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ puthujjanassa vuttesu catuvīsaticittesu ākāsānañcāyatanakusalavipākavajjā bāvīsati ca dutiyāruppavipāko cāti tevīsati dutiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ puthujjanassa honti. Tattheva tiṇṇaṃ phalaṭṭhasekhānaṃ puthujjanassa vuttesu akusalapañcakavajjāni aṭṭhārasa, taṃtaṃphalañcāti ekūnavīsati cittāni honti.

'Twenty-three': From the twenty-four consciousnesses mentioned for a worldling in the first formless plane, if the wholesome and resultant consciousnesses of the base of infinite space are excluded, twenty-two remain; with the addition of the second formless resultant, there are twenty-three. These arise for a worldling in the second formless plane. Therein, for the three noble trainees who have attained the fruition, there are nineteen consciousnesses: the eighteen that remain from those mentioned for a worldling when the pentad of unwholesome consciousnesses is excluded, plus their respective fruitions.

Kriyā dvādasāti aṭṭha mahākiriyā, ākāsānañcāyatanavajjitā tisso arūpakiriyā, manodvārāvajjananti dvādasa kiriyacittāni. Pākekoti eko arūpavipāko.

'Twelve functional': eight great functional consciousnesses; three formless functional consciousnesses, excluding that of the base of infinite space; and the mind-door-adverting consciousness—these are the twelve functional consciousnesses. 'One resultant' means the one formless resultant.

Dutiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ puthujjanassa vuttesu viññāṇañcāyatanakusalavipākavajjāni ekavīsati[V 1.0281], ākiñcaññāyatanavipāko cāti bāvīsati cittāni tatiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ puthujjanassa uppajjanti.

Among the consciousnesses mentioned for a worldling in the second formless plane, twenty-one remain when the wholesome and resultant consciousnesses of the base of infinite consciousness are excluded; with the addition of the resultant of the base of nothingness, twenty-two consciousnesses arise for a worldling in the third formless plane.

254-60. Puthujjanassa vuttesu apuññapañcakavajjāni sattarasa, paṭhamaphalañcāti aṭṭhārasa tatiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ sotāpannassa uppajjanti. Tānīti tāneva aṭṭhārasa cittāni. “Ṭhapetvā paṭhamaṃ phala”nti hi vacanato dutiyaphalaṃ pakkhipitvāti ayamattho avuttasiddho. Na hi sakadāgāmino sakadāgāmiphalañca nuppajjati[M 1.0358]. Evañca katvā vuttaṃ “ṭhapetvā dutiyaṃ phala”nti. Etthāpi anāgāmiphalaṃ pakaraṇasiddhamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aṭṭha mahākiriyā, dve tatiyacatutthāruppakiriyā, manodvārāvajjanaṃ, ākiñcaññāyatanavipāko, arahattaphalanti terasa cittāni tatiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ khīṇāsavassa jāyanti. Tatiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ puthujjanassa vuttesu dvāvīsaticittesu ākiñcaññāyatanakusalavipākavajjāti vīsati, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanavipākoti ekavīsati cittāni catutthāruppabhūmiyaṃ puthujjanassa jāyanti. Puthujjanassa vuttesu apuññapañcakavajjāni soḷasa, sotāpattiphalañcāti sattarasa tattheva sotāpannassa honti. Aṭṭha mahākiriyā, dve ca nevasaññānāsaññāyatanavipākakiriyā, manodvārāvajjanaṃ, arahattaphalañcāti dvādasa cittāni tattheva arahato uppajjanti.

254-60. Among the consciousnesses mentioned for a worldling, seventeen remain when the pentad of demerit is excluded; with the addition of the first fruition, eighteen arise for a stream-enterer in the third formless plane. 'These' means those same eighteen consciousnesses. Because of the statement 'excluding the first fruition,' the meaning 'having included the second fruition' is established without being stated. For the once-returner's fruition does not fail to arise for a once-returner. And so it is said, 'excluding the second fruition.' Here too, it should be understood that the non-returner's fruition is established by the context. Thirteen consciousnesses arise in the third formless plane for one whose taints are destroyed: the eight great functional consciousnesses, the two functional consciousnesses of the third and fourth formless planes, the mind-door-adverting consciousness, the resultant of the base of nothingness, and the arahantship fruition. Among the twenty-two consciousnesses mentioned for a worldling in the third formless plane, twenty remain when the wholesome and resultant of the base of nothingness are excluded; with the addition of the resultant of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, twenty-one consciousnesses arise for a worldling in the fourth formless plane. Among those mentioned for a worldling, sixteen remain when the pentad of demerit is excluded; with the addition of the stream-entry fruition, seventeen arise for a stream-enterer in that same plane. Twelve consciousnesses arise in that same plane for an arahant: the eight great functional consciousnesses, the two, the resultant and functional of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the mind-door-adverting consciousness, and the arahantship fruition.

261-3. Arūpakusalā ceva kiriyāpi ca uppajjanti, na pana vipākāti adhippāyo. Uddhamuddhamarūpīnanti viññāṇañcāyatanādīsu arūpīnaṃ. Heṭṭhimāti viññāṇañcāyatanikānaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanakusalavipākā nuppajjanti, ākiñcaññāyatanikānaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaviññāṇañcāyatanakusalavipākāti evamādinā heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimā arūpā nuppajjanti. Kasmāti āha “diṭṭhādīnavato kirā”ti. Kirāti anussutiyaṃ. Diṭṭhādīnavatoti ārammaṇe, jhāne ca diṭṭhadosattā. Kusalānuttarāti lokuttarakusalā.

261-3. The meaning is that immaterial wholesome and functional states arise, but not resultant states. 'Above and above among the immaterial' refers to the immaterial beings in the base of infinite consciousness and so on. 'Those below' means that for those in the base of infinite consciousness, the wholesome-resultant states of the base of infinite space do not arise; and for those in the base of nothingness, the wholesome-resultant states of the base of infinite space and the base of infinite consciousness do not arise. In this way, the successively lower immaterial states do not arise. Why is this so? He says, 'Because of the danger that has been seen, it is said.' 'It is said' is by way of tradition. 'Because of the danger that has been seen' means because the danger has been seen in the object and in the jhāna. 'The unsurpassed wholesome states' means the supramundane wholesome states.

266. Sabbo rūpo mahaggatoti sabbo rūpāvacaramahaggatacittuppādo. Manodhātūti kiriyāmanodhātuvipākamanodhātūnaṃ kāmavipāka-ggahaṇena gahitattā.

266. 'All form is exalted' means every exalted consciousness-arising of the fine-material sphere. 'Mind-element': because the functional mind-element and the resultant mind-element are included by the inclusion of sense-sphere resultant consciousness.

269-73. Evaṃ…pe… heṭṭhimanti dutiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ vuttesu dutiyāruppattayaṃ ṭhapetvā attano pākena saha tatiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ [M 1.0359] ekūnacattālīsa cittāni tatthavuttesu tatiyāruppattayaṃ ṭhapetvā [V 1.0282] attano pākena saha sattatiṃsāti evaṃ sesadvayepi heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimaṃ hitvā cittagaṇanā ñeyyā. Attano attanoti paṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ paṭhamāruppavipāko, dutiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ dutiyāruppavipākoti evaṃ attano attano vipākā cattāro ca anāsavā lokuttaravipākāti evaṃ catūsu arūpabhūmīsu ekekāya bhūmiyā pañca pañca vipākā jāyanti. Yā kiriyā teraseva siyuṃ, tā sabbapaṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ khīṇāsavassa jāyanteti sambandho. Dutiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ khīṇāsavassa paṭhamāruppakiriyacittaṃ vajjetvā dvādaseva kriyā honti. Tatiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ dutiyāruppakiriyacittaṃ vajjetvā ekādasa. Catutthāruppabhūmiyaṃ tatiyāruppakiriyacittaṃ vajjetvā daseva viññeyyā.

269-73. Thus… and so on… 'In the lower': among those mentioned for the second immaterial plane, setting aside the triad of the second immaterial sphere along with its own resultant, there are thirty-nine consciousnesses in the third immaterial plane. Among those mentioned there, setting aside the triad of the third immaterial sphere along with its own resultant, there are thirty-seven. In this way, in the remaining two as well, the count of consciousnesses should be known by omitting the successively lower ones. 'One's own' means: in the first immaterial plane, the first immaterial resultant; in the second immaterial plane, the second immaterial resultant, and so on. Thus, their own four resultants and the four taintless supramundane resultants. Thus, in each of the four immaterial planes, five resultants arise. The functional consciousnesses are just thirteen. The connection is that all of them arise in the first immaterial plane for an Arahant. For an Arahant in the second immaterial plane, excluding the functional consciousness of the first immaterial plane, there are just twelve functional consciousnesses. In the third immaterial plane, excluding the functional consciousness of the second immaterial plane, there are eleven. In the fourth immaterial plane, excluding the functional consciousness of the third immaterial plane, just ten should be understood.

274-5. Idāni kevalaṃ puggalavasena tesameva puggalānaṃ āveṇikacittaṃ dassetuṃ “arahato panā”tiādinā arahatoyeva uppajjanakacittaṃ dassetvā anāgāmiādīnaṃ pāṭipuggalikaṃ sakasakaphalacittaṃ pākaṭamevāti saṃkhittaṃ. Arahatoti khīṇāsavassa. Arahato bhāvo arahattaṃ, arahattaphalanti attho. Tañhi “arīnaṃ hatattā arahā”tiādinā arahanta-saddassa pavattinimittabhāvena “arahatta”nti vuccati. Idāni tesaṃ tesaṃ puggalānaṃ sādhāraṇacittāni dassetuṃ “catunnañca phalaṭṭhāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

274-5. Now, to show the unique consciousness of those same individuals solely in terms of persons, by showing with 'But for an Arahant…' etc. the consciousness that arises only for the Arahant, it is stated concisely that the respective individual fruition consciousnesses of the non-returner and others are manifest. 'Arahant' means one whose taints are destroyed. The state of an Arahant is Arahantship, which means the fruit of Arahantship. For it is called 'Arahantship' as it is the ground for the currency of the word 'Arahant,' which is derived from 'he has slain the foes,' etc. Now, to show the consciousnesses common to these various individuals, it is said: 'And for the four who abide in the fruit…,' etc.

290. Susāranti atthabyañjanavasena pariccajitabbassa pheggussa abhāvato suṭṭhu sāraṃ, sabbaso sāranti attho. Paranti susārattā eva paraṃ. Sattānaṃ idhalokaparalokahitapaṭicchādakassa avijjandhakārassa vidhamanato mohandhakārappadīpaṃ. Cintetīti atthavasena cinteti. Vācetīti byañjanavasena [M 1.0360] sajjhāyati. Rāgadosānaṃ mohena saha avinābhāvato tassa anupagamanaṃ atthasiddhamevāti “mohandhakārappadīpa”nti vatvāpi “naraṃ…pe… nopayantī”ti rāgadosānupagamanameva vuttaṃ. “Mohandhakārappadīpa”nti vā vacaneneva mohassa anupagamo vutto hotīti rāgadosānameva anupagamanaṃ vuttaṃ. Mūlabhūtānaṃ pana tiṇṇaṃ anupagamanavacanena sesakilesānampi anupagamanaṃ vuttamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

290. 'Excellent essence' means it is truly the essence because of the absence of worthless pith that should be discarded, in terms of meaning and phrasing; the meaning is, it is entirely essence. 'Supreme': it is supreme precisely because it is of excellent essence. 'A lamp for the darkness of delusion' because it dispels the darkness of ignorance that conceals the welfare of beings in this world and the next. 'He reflects' means he reflects on it in terms of meaning. 'He recites' means he recites it in terms of phrasing. Since greed and hatred are inseparable from delusion, their non-approach is established by implication. Thus, although it says 'a lamp for the darkness of delusion,' with 'a person... they do not approach,' it is the non-approach of greed and hatred that is stated. Or, by the very statement 'a lamp for the darkness of delusion,' the non-approach of delusion is stated, so the non-approach of greed and hatred alone is mentioned. However, it should be understood that by stating the non-approach of the three that are the roots, the non-approach of the remaining defilements is also stated.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus, in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the Commentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma,

Bhūmipuggalacittuppattiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the commentary on the exposition of the arising of consciousness according to plane and individual.

Paṭhamo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

Here ends the first part.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Abhidhammāvatāra-abhinavaṭīkā

The New Subcommentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma

(Dutiyo bhāgo)

(The Second Part)

6. Chaṭṭho paricchedo

6. The Sixth Chapter

Ārammaṇavibhāganiddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Analysis of Objects

291-3. Etesanti [M 2.0001][V 2.0001] yathāvuttappabhedānaṃ. Nanu ca “cittaṃ cetasika”ntiādinā cittādīniyeva uddiṭṭhānīti tāneva niddisitabbāni, ārammaṇaṃ pana appakataṃ, taṃ kasmā idha vuccatīti codanaṃ manasi karitvā āha “tena vinā natthi hi sambhavo”ti. Yasmā ārammaṇena vinā cittasambhavo natthi, na hi anārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ nāma atthi, tasmā “tayidaṃ cittaṃ kaṃ ārabbha uppajjatī”ti āsaṅkānivāraṇatthaṃ ito paraṃ ārammaṇaṃ dassayissāmīti attho[V 2.0002]. Katividhaṃ pana taṃ ārammaṇaṃ, kiṃ sarūpañcāti āha “rūpaṃ sadda”ntiādi. Vacanatthaṃ pana nesaṃ sayameva vakkhati. Chaḷārammaṇakovidāti channaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ byākaraṇakusalā buddhādayo.

291-3. 'These' means those of the kinds already stated. Now, having kept in mind the objection—'Since by “mind, mental factors,” etc., only mind and so on were indicated, only they should be expounded; but the object is not under discussion, so why is it mentioned here?'—he says: 'For without that, there is no arising.' The meaning is: because without an object there is no arising of consciousness, for there is no such thing as consciousness without an object, therefore, to ward off the query, 'Depending on what does this consciousness arise?' from this point on I will show the object. But of how many kinds is that object, and what is its nature? He says: 'Form, sound,' etc. But he himself will state the etymological meaning of these terms. 'Those skilled in the six objects' means the Buddhas and others, who are skilled in the analysis of the six objects.

Bhūteti cattāro mahābhūte. Upādāyāti nissāya. Catusamuṭṭhitoti kammādīhi catūhi paccayehi samuṭṭhito. Nidassitabbaṃ nidassanaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Daṭṭhabbabhāvo cakkhuviññāṇassa gocarabhāvo[M 2.0002], saha nidassanenāti sanidassano. Paṭihaññati, paṭihanananti vā paṭigho, yena byāpārādivikārapaccayantarasahitesu cakkhādīnaṃ nissayesu vikāruppatti, so sayaṃ nissayavasena ca sampattānaṃ, asampattānañca paṭimukhabhāvo aññamaññapatanaṃ paṭighoti attho. Tattha sayaṃ sampattiṃ phoṭṭhabbassa nissayavasena sampatti gandharasaghānajivhākāyānaṃ. Itaresaṃ ubhayathāpi asampatti, tasmā idha asampattānaṃ paṭimukhabhāvo “paṭigho”ti vuccati. Saha paṭighenāti sappaṭigho, sanidassano ca so sappaṭigho cāti sanidassanasappaṭigho. Etthāha – yassa daṭṭhabbabhāvo atthi, so sanidassano, cakkhuviññāṇagocarabhāvova daṭṭhabbabhāvo. Tassa ca rūpāyatanato anaññattā kathaṃ saha nidassanena sanidassanoti yujjatīti? Vuccate – anaññattepi tassa aññehi dhammehi rūpāyatanaṃ visesetuṃ aññaṃ viya katvā vuttaṃ “saha nidassanena sanidassana”nti. Dhammasabhāvasāmaññena hi ekībhūtesu dhammesu yo nānattakaro viseso, so aññaṃ viya katvā upacārituṃ yutto. Evañhi atthavisesāvabodho hoti. Rūpārammaṇasaññitoti ayaṃ evarūpo vaṇṇo rūpārammaṇanti saññito. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – cattāro mahābhūte upādāya te amuñcitvā pavattamāno kammasamuṭṭhāno cittasamuṭṭhāno utusamuṭṭhāno āhārasamuṭṭhāno ca nīlādivasena dissamāno indriyehi ghaṭṭento ca vaṇṇo rūpārammaṇaṃ nāmāti.

'Elements' means the four great elements. 'Depending on' means relying on. 'Of fourfold origin' means originated from the four conditions, kamma and so on. 'That which can be shown' is an indication.
