What is that? The state of being seeable, the domain of eye-consciousness. 'With indication' is sanidassana. 'It is struck,' or a 'striking,' is resistance (paṭigha). The meaning is that resistance is that by which an alteration arises in the physical bases of the eye, etc., along with other conditions for alteration such as activity; it is the mutual impact or facing of what has arrived and what has not arrived by way of the physical basis itself. Among these, there is arrival for smell, taste, and the tangible by way of their physical bases, and for the tangible itself. For the others, there is non-arrival in both ways. Therefore, here the facing of what has not arrived is called 'resistance.' 'With resistance' is sappaṭigha. It is with indication and with resistance, thus sanidassanasappaṭigha. Here it is said: That which has the state of being seeable is sanidassana; the state of being seeable is just the domain of eye-consciousness. Since this is not different from the form base, how is it tenable to say 'with indication, sanidassana'? It is said: Although it is not different, in order to distinguish the form base from other dhammas, it is spoken of as if it were something else, thus: 'with indication, sanidassana.' For when dhammas are unified by a common intrinsic nature, a distinction that creates diversity can be figuratively treated as something else. In this way, an understanding of the specific meaning comes about. 'Designated as the form-object': this kind of color is designated as the form-object. This is what is said: that color which, depending on the four great elements and not abandoning them, arises from kamma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment, is seen as blue, etc., and impinges on the sense faculties, is named the form-object.

294-7. Cittañca utu ca cittotu, tehi sambhavati, te vā sambhavā paccayā imassāti cittotusambhavo. Saha viññattisamuṭṭhāpakaviññāṇena pavatto saddo saviññāṇakasaddo, saviññāṇakasaddo pana na kevalaṃ saviññāṇakasantānappavattova kucchisaddādivasena tassa utusamuṭṭhitassāpi sambhavato.

Consciousness and temperature are 'consciousness-temperature.' 'Originated from consciousness and temperature' means it originates from them, or they are the conditions for its origin. Sound that occurs together with the consciousness that originates intimation is 'sound with consciousness.' But 'sound with consciousness' is not only that which occurs in a conscious continuity, since it can also arise from temperature, as in the case of sounds from the belly and so on.

Dharīyatīti [M 2.0003][V 2.0003] kalāpaparamparāya sandhārīyati. Sūcanatoti attano vatthussa supākaṭakaraṇato. Gandho hi “idaṃ sugandhaṃ, idaṃ duggandha”nti pakāseti, paṭicchannapupphaphalādīni “idamettha atthī”ti pesuññaṃ karontaṃ viya hotīti.

'It is carried' means it is sustained by a succession of material groups. 'Because it indicates' means because it makes its own basis clearly known. For smell reveals, 'This is fragrant, this is foul.' It is as if it were engaging in slander, revealing hidden flowers, fruits, and so on, by indicating, 'This is here.'

Rasamānāti assādavasena tussamānā. Rasantīti asanti, anubhavantīti attho. Ettha ra-kāro padasandhikaro. Evañhi “rasamānā naṃ asantīti raso”ti niruttinayo sundaro hoti. Itarathā “rasanti assādentī”ti vuccamāne “rasamānā”ti idaṃ niratthakameva siyā. Atha vā “rasamānā”ti ito ra-kāraṃ, “rasantī”ti ito sa-kārañca gahetvā “raso”ti niruttinayo daṭṭhabbo.

'Delighting' means being satisfied by way of savoring. 'They taste' (rasanti) means they eat (asanti), that is, they experience. Here, the letter 'ra' is for euphonic conjunction. For thus the etymology 'delighting in it, they eat it, hence taste (raso)' is elegant. Otherwise, if it were said 'they taste means they savor,' this word 'delighting' would be meaningless. Or, the etymology of 'taste' (raso) should be understood by taking the 'ra' from 'delighting' (rasamānā) and the 'sa' from 'they taste' (rasanti).

298. Phusīyatīti ghaṭṭīyati. Kiṃ taṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ nāmāti āha “pathavītejavāyavo”ti. Iminā dhātuttayameva kāyaviññāṇaviññeyyabhāvasaṅkhātaphoṭṭhabbaṃ nāma, na aññanti dasseti. Kasmā panettha āpodhātu na gahitā, nanu sītatā phusitvā gayhati, sā ca āpodhātu evāti? Saccaṃ gayhati, na pana āpodhātu, kiñcarahi tejodhātu eva. Mande hi uṇhabhāve sītavuddhi, na sītatā nāma koci guṇo atthi. Kevalaṃ pana uṇhabhāvassa mandatāya sītatābhimāno. Kathaṃ panetaṃ viññātabbanti ce? Sītavuddhiyā anavaṭṭhitabhāvato pārāpāre viya. Tathā hi ghammakāle ātape ṭhatvā chāyaṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ sītavuddhi hoti, tattheva pathavīgabbhato uṭṭhitānaṃ uṇhavuddhi ca. Kiñcarahi himapātasamayādīsu sītassa paripācakattadassanato ca tejodhātu eva sītatāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadi ca sītatā āpodhātu siyā, ekasmiṃ kalāpe uṇhabhāvena saddhiṃ upalabbheyya dvinnaṃ dhātūnaṃ avinibbhogappavattito, na ca panevaṃ upalabbhati, tasmā ñāyati “na āpodhātu sītatā”ti[M 2.0004]. Idaṃ catumahābhūtānaṃ avinibbhogavuttitaṃ icchantānaṃ uttaraṃ, anicchantānampi pana catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ ekasmiṃ kalāpe kiccadassanena sabhāgavuttitāya sādhitāya idameva uttaraṃ. Keci pana “vāyodhātu sītatā”ti vadanti, tesampi idameva uttaraṃ. Yadi vāyodhātu sītatā siyā, ekasmiṃ kalāpe uṇhabhāvena saddhiṃ upalabbheyya, na ca panevaṃ upalabbhati, tasmā viññāyati “na vāyodhātu sītatā”ti. Ye pana vadanti “dravatā āpodhātu, sā ca phusitvā gayhatī”ti, te vattabbā “dravabhāvopi nāma phusīyatīti idaṃ āyasmantānaṃ adhimānamattaṃ saṇṭhāne viyā”ti. Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi –

298. 'Is touched' means is struck. What is called the tangible? It is said: 'the earth, fire, and air elements.' By this it is shown that only these three elements are what is called the tangible, designated as the object of body-consciousness, and nothing else. Why is the water element not included here? Is it not that coolness is grasped by being touched, and that this is the water element? True, it is grasped, but it is not the water element; rather, it is the fire element. For when the quality of heat is weak, there is an increase of cold, but there exists no quality called 'coolness.' It is merely an assumption of coolness due to the weakness of the heat. And how is this to be understood? From the unstable nature of the increase of cold, like the near and far shores. For example, in the hot season, for those who have stood in the sun and then entered the shade, there is an increase of coolness; but in the same place, for those who have emerged from an underground chamber, there is an increase of heat. Furthermore, since during times of snowfall and so on the maturing quality of cold is seen, it should be understood that coolness is just the fire element. If coolness were the water element, it would be found together with heat in a single material group, owing to the inseparable occurrence of the two elements; but it is not found thus. Therefore, it is known that 'coolness is not the water element.' This is the answer for those who hold that the four great elements occur inseparably; and for those who do not, too, this is the answer, since their common nature is established by the fact that the function of the four great elements is seen in a single material group. Some, however, say, 'coolness is the air element'; for them, too, this is the answer. If coolness were the air element, it would be found together with heat in a single material group; but it is not found thus. Therefore, it is understood that 'coolness is not the air element.' As to those who say, 'fluidity is the water element, and it is grasped by being touched,' they should be told: 'This idea that fluidity is touched is a mere assumption on your part, like that about shape.' For this has been said by the ancients:

“Dravabhāsahavuttīni[V 2.0004], tīṇi bhūtāni samphusaṃ;

Dravataṃ samphusāmīti, lokoyamabhimaññati.

“Touching the three elements that occur together with the appearance of fluidity, this world conceives, ‘I am touching fluidity.’

“Bhūte phusitvā saṇṭhānaṃ, manasā gayhate yathā;

Paccakkhato phusāmīti, ñātabbā dravatā tathā”ti.

“Just as, having touched the elements, shape is grasped by the mind, so too should fluidity be understood, though one thinks, ‘I touch it directly.’”

299. Sabbaṃ nāmanti sabbaṃ cittacetasikanibbānasammataṃ nāmaṃ. Cittacetasikañhi ārammaṇaṃ pati namanato nāmaṃ. Nibbānaṃ pana cittacetasikassa attānaṃ pati nāmanato nāmaṃ. Rūpanti nipphannarūpaṃ. Kiṃ avisesenāti ce, noti āha “hitvā rūpādipañcaka”nti. Lakkhaṇānīti aniccādilakkhaṇāni. Paññattīti nāmupādāyavasena duvidhā paññatti.

299. 'All is name' means all that is considered name, that is, consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna. For consciousness and mental factors are 'name' (nāma) because they bend (namanti) towards an object. Nibbāna, however, is 'name' because it makes consciousness and mental factors bend towards itself. 'Form' means produced form. If it is asked, 'Is this without exception?' he says no, stating: 'excluding the pentad of form, etc.' 'Characteristics' means the characteristics of impermanence, etc. 'Concept' means concept is twofold, by way of its dependence on names.

300. Imāni pana chabbidhāni ārammaṇāni sabbāni sabbattha labbhanti, udāhu katthaci kānicīti āha “chaḷārammaṇānī”tiādi. Tīṇi rūpeti rūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ rūpasaddadhammavasena tīṇi ārammaṇāni labbhanti. Ghānādittayassa pana tattha abhāvato gandhārammaṇādīni dhammārammaṇato visuṃ na labbhanti. Arūpabhave pana sabbaso rūpānaṃ abhāvato ekaṃ dhammārammaṇameva labbhati, na aññanti āha “arūpe dhammārammaṇamekaka”nti[M 2.0005]. Nanu ca arūpabhavato cavitvā kāmabhave nibbattantānaṃ arūpabhaveyeva gatinimittavasena rūpārammaṇaṃ upaṭṭhātīti? Saccaṃ upaṭṭhāti, taṃ pana kāmabhaveyeva ārammaṇaṃ. Upapajjitabbabhavasmiñhi vaṇṇo gatinimittavasena upaṭṭhāti.

300. Now, are these six kinds of objects all obtainable everywhere, or are some obtainable only in certain places? He says, 'six objects,' etc. 'Three in the form realm' means that in the fine-material realm, three objects are obtainable: visible form, sound, and dhammas. However, because the triad of faculties beginning with the nose is absent there, the objects of smell, etc., are not obtainable separately from the dhamma-object. In the formless existence, due to the complete absence of forms, only one object, the dhamma-object, is obtainable, and no other; hence it is said, 'in the formless, a single dhamma-object.' But for those passing away from the formless existence and being reborn in the sense-sphere existence, does not a form-object arise as a sign of their destination while they are still in the formless existence? True, it does arise, but that object belongs to the sense-sphere existence. For it is a color belonging to the existence in which one is to be reborn that appears as the sign of destination.

301-2. Evaṃ cha ārammaṇāni sarūpato, pavattippabhedato ca dassetvā idāni tesu abhayagirivāsīnaṃ kiñci vippaṭipattiṃ dassetvā taṃ paṭikkhipituṃ “khaṇavatthuparittattā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha khaṇavatthuparittattāti khaṇassa ceva vatthuno ca parittattā. Ye rūpādayoti sambandho. Yesanti yesaṃ ācariyānaṃ laddhi. Yesanti vā dhammārammaṇena saha sambandhībhāvato, vuttaṃ vavatthāpakattā ca. Te hi dhammārammaṇaṃ vavatthāpento attanā saha taṃ sambandhenti, tasmā dhammārammaṇena saha sambandhībhāvāpekkhāya “yesa”nti sāmivacananti. Iminā pana idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ye rūpādayo pañca ārammaṇā santattaayoguḷe patitajalabindu viya parittakkhaṇikā, dibbacakkhunā asakkuṇeyyaggahaṇā paramāṇu viya parittavatthukā, tato ca sakasakaviññāṇānaṃ āpāthaṃ [V 2.0005] na gacchanti, kevalaṃ pana manoviññāṇasseva gocarā, te dhammārammaṇaṃ nāmāti yesaṃ laddhi, te yesaṃ vā dhammārammaṇaṃ nāmāti. Eteneva ca atītānāgatabhāvena atidūraaccāsannabhāvena, kuṭṭādiantaritābhāvena ca āpāthaṃ anāgacchantānampi rūpādīnaṃ saṅgaho kato hotīti. Evaṃladdhikā pana te –

301-2. Having thus shown the six objects in terms of their own nature and their different modes of occurrence, now, in order to point out a certain wrong view of the Abhayagirivāsins concerning them and to refute it, the passage beginning 'Because of the minuteness of the moment and the physical basis' was stated. Herein, 'Because of the minuteness of the moment and the physical basis' means because of the minuteness of both the moment and the physical basis. The connection is with 'those forms, etc.' 'Of which' (yesaṃ) refers to the doctrine of those teachers. Or, 'of which' is used because of the connection with the dhamma-object and because it serves to define what is stated. For in defining the dhamma-object, they connect it with themselves; therefore, with reference to the connection with the dhamma-object, 'of which' is a genitive. By this the following is stated: The five objects, forms, etc., which are of limited duration like a drop of water fallen on a red-hot iron ball, and which have a minute physical basis like an atom, ungraspable even by the divine eye, and which therefore do not come into the range of their respective consciousnesses but are the domain of mind-consciousness alone—that these are the dhamma-object is the doctrine of those teachers, or that these are their dhamma-object. And by this same method, the inclusion is made of forms, etc., that do not come into range because they are past or future, too distant or too near, or obstructed by a wall, etc. Such are the holders of this doctrine—

“Imesaṃ kho, āvuso, pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ nānāvisayānaṃ nānāgocarānaṃ na aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhontānaṃ mano paṭissaraṇaṃ, mano ca nesaṃ gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.455) –

“Friends, these five faculties have different fields, different domains, and do not experience each other’s field and domain; mind is their resort, and mind experiences their field and domain.”

Idaṃ [M 2.0006] suttaṃ āharitvā paṭikkhipitabbāti dassento āha “te paṭikkhipitabbāvā”tiādi. Tattha paṭikkhipitabbāvāti na anuvattitabbā. Aññamañña…pe… bhontānanti cakkhundriyaṃ sotindriyassa gocaraṃ na paccanubhoti, tathā “sotindriyaṃ cakkhundriyassā”tiādinā aññamaññassa ārammaṇaṃ neva paccanubhontānaṃ nānubhavantānaṃ na gaṇhantānaṃ. Tesanti tesaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ.

Showing that this sutta should be cited and then refuted, he says the passage beginning, 'they are to be refuted.' Herein, 'are to be refuted' means are not to be followed. '[They] do not experience each other’s… etc.' means that the eye faculty does not experience the domain of the ear faculty, and similarly, 'the ear faculty does not experience the domain of the eye faculty,' and so on. Thus they do not experience, partake of, or grasp each other’s object. 'Of these' means of these five faculties.

303. Tañca gocaraṃ mano paccanubhotīti sambandho. Taṃ rūpādipañcavidhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ca-saddena dhammārammaṇañca mano paccanubhoti, cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karotīti attho. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – yadi cakkhādīnamāpāthagatāni vinā avasesā dhammārammaṇā honti, tadā taṃvisayaṃ cittaṃ pañcindriyānaṃ visayaṃ paccanubhontaṃ nāma na hoti, attanoyeva pana visayaṃ paccanubhontaṃ nāma hoti. Evañca sati manova tesaṃ gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhotīti dupparihāriyaṃ bhaveyya, na ca taṃ suttavacanaṃ sakkā atikkametuṃ, tasmā vuttanayena cakkhādīnaṃ anāpāthagatāpi manogocarā rūpādayo rūpādiārammaṇāneva honti, na dhammārammaṇāti. Yadi rūpārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ attano visayaṃ nānubhoti, paravisayameva anubhoti, kathaṃ dassanādikiccaṃ na karoti? Taṃtaṃkiccānaṃ nissayabhūtassa vatthuno anissitattā. Kathañcarahi pañcindriyānaṃ visayaṃ paccanubhoti nāma? Dassanādikiccassa akaraṇepi cakkhuviññāṇādīhi diṭṭhādiākārasseva gahaṇato pañcindriyānaṃ visayaṃ paccanubhoti nāma. Yadi hi cakkhuviññāṇādīhi diṭṭhādiākāraṃ na gaṇhāti, rūpādīnaṃ nīlattādivasena jānanaṃ manoviññāṇameva karoti, na pañcaviññāṇānīti tathā jānanameva na hoti. Tassa pana atthitāyevetaṃ [V 2.0006] viññātabbaṃ – anāpāthagatarūpādārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ attano visayaṃ na paccanubhoti nāma. Atha kho [M 2.0007] pañcindriyānaṃ visayameva paccanubhotīti. Atha siyā, na mayaṃ cittassa pañcindriyavisayānubhavanaṃ paṭikkhipāma, tassa pana anubhavanaṃ dassanādikiccavirahena dhammārammaṇavasenevāti ce? Tampi na, sutte tathā āgataṭṭhānassa abhāvato. Yadi hi cittaṃ dassanādikiccavirahena pañcindriyavisayaṃ dhammārammaṇavaseneva paccanubhoti, pañcindriyānaṃ visayaṃ paccanubhavamānā manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātupi dhammārammaṇāyeva siyā, evañca sati “dhammāyatanaṃ manodhātuyā ca manoviññāṇadhātuyā ca taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti paṭṭhāne vattabbaṃ siyā, tathā pana avatvā –

303. The connection is: 'And mind experiences that domain.' That fivefold object of form, etc., and by the word 'and' also the dhamma-object, the mind experiences, which means it makes them its object. Here, this is the intended meaning: If, apart from those that have come into the range of the eye faculty, etc., the remaining objects are dhamma-objects, then the consciousness experiencing that object is not called 'one that experiences the sphere of the five sense faculties.' Rather, it is called 'one that experiences its own sphere.' In that case, the statement 'mind alone experiences their field and domain' would be difficult to maintain, and it would be impossible to transgress that statement from the suttas. Therefore, in the way stated, even forms, etc., that have not entered the range of the eye faculty, etc., but are within the domain of the mind, are still form-objects, etc., and not dhamma-objects. If a consciousness with a form-object does not experience its own sphere but only experiences another's sphere, how does it not perform the function of seeing, etc.? Because it is not dependent on the physical basis, which is the support for those respective functions. But then, how is it said to experience the sphere of the five sense faculties? Even if it does not perform the function of seeing, etc., it is still said to experience the sphere of the five sense faculties because it grasps the mode of the seen, etc., through eye-consciousness, etc. For if it does not grasp the mode of the seen, etc., through eye-consciousness, etc., but mind-consciousness alone knows forms, etc., as blue, etc., then the five consciousnesses do not know them, and in that case, such knowing would not exist. However, from its very existence this should be understood: a consciousness that takes an object of form, etc., not within the range of the senses, is not said to experience its own object. Rather, it is said to experience the sphere of the five sense faculties. But one might argue: 'We do not deny that a consciousness experiences the sphere of the five sense faculties, but its experience is only by way of a dhamma-object, since it lacks the function of seeing, etc.' That too is not correct, because there is no passage in the suttas that has come down that way. For if a consciousness experiences the sphere of the five sense faculties only by way of a dhamma-object, since it lacks the function of seeing, etc., then the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, while experiencing the sphere of the five sense faculties, would also have only dhamma-objects. In that case, in the Paṭṭhāna, it should have been stated: 'The dhamma-base is a condition for the mind-element and for the mind-consciousness-element, and for the associated states, by way of object condition.' But since it is not stated thus—

“Rūpāyatanaṃ saddāyatanaṃ gandhāyatanaṃ rasāyatanaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ manodhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.2),

'The form base, the sound base, the odor base, the taste base, and the tangible base are a condition for the mind-element and for the states associated with it by way of object condition' (Paṭṭh. 1.1.2),

“Rūpāyatanaṃ…pe… dhammāyatanaṃ manoviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti ca (paṭṭhā. 1.1.2) –

'and 'The form base ...pe... the dhamma-base is a condition for the mind-consciousness-element and for the states associated with it by way of object condition' (Paṭṭh. 1.1.2)—

Vuttattā pañcindriyānaṃ visayaṃ paccanubhontī manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātu taṃpañcindriyānaṃ visayavasena paccanubhoti, na dhammāyatanavasenāti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Since this has been stated, the conclusion to be drawn here is that the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element, when experiencing the sphere of the five sense faculties, experience it by way of the sphere of those five sense faculties, not by way of the dhamma-base.

304-5. Evaṃ ekenākārena paṭikkhepavidhiṃ dassetvā puna aparenapi kāraṇena dassento āha “dibbacakkhādī”tiādi. Ādi-ggahaṇena dibbasotañāṇaggahaṇaṃ. Itipi na yujjatīti na kevalaṃ pubbe vutteneva kāraṇena, atha kho imināpi kāraṇena na yujjatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yadipi cakkhādīnaṃ anāpāthagatarūpādīni dhammārammaṇā nāma honti, tadā [M 2.0008] dibbacakkhādīni rūpādiārammaṇāni na siyuṃ tesaṃ pasādavisayānaṃ rūpasaddānaṃ pariggaṇhanato, evañca sati suttesu dibbacakkhudibbasotānaṃ dhammārammaṇatāva vattabbā, na rūpādiārammaṇatā, vuttā ca sā, tasmā cakkhādīnaṃ avisayā rūpādayo rūpādārammaṇāneva, na dhammārammaṇāti. Teneva ca dhammasaṅgahepi –

304–5. Having thus shown the method of refutation in one way, he now shows it with another reason, saying, 'the divine eye, etc.' By 'etc.' the divine ear-knowledge is included. 'This too is not tenable' means that it is said to be untenable not only for the reason previously stated but also for this reason. If forms, etc., that have not come into the range of the eye faculty, etc., are called dhamma-objects, then the divine eye, etc., would not have forms, etc., as their objects, since they grasp forms and sounds that are the sphere of the sense faculties. This being so, in the suttas it should be said that the divine eye and divine ear have dhamma-objects, not form-objects, etc., as their objects—but the latter is stated. Therefore, forms, etc., that are not the sphere of the eye faculty, etc., are still form-objects, etc., not dhamma-objects. And for that same reason, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī too—

“Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ [V 2.0007] rūpārammaṇaṃ vā saddārammaṇaṃ vā gandhārammaṇaṃ vā rasārammaṇaṃ vā phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ vā dhammārammaṇaṃ vā, yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha, tasmiṃ samaye phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hotī”ti (dha. sa. 1) –

'On an occasion when a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, having a form-object, or a sound-object, or an odor-object, or a taste-object, or a tangible object, or a dhamma-object, or whatever it may be that it has taken as its object, on that occasion there is contact ...pe... there is non-distraction' (Dhs. 1)—

Vuttaṃ. Kiñca anāpāthagatānaṃ dhammārammaṇatte sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ rūpādiārammaṇaṃ na hotīti āpajjatīti. Evaṃ satīti yadi kadāci rūpādiārammaṇaṃ hutvā kadāci dhammārammaṇaṃ hoti, kadāci dhammārammaṇaṃ hutvā kadāci rūpādiārammaṇaṃ hoti, tadā tesaṃ rūpādiārammaṇānaṃ niyamopi kathaṃ bhave “idaṃ rūpādiārammaṇaṃ, idaṃ dhammārammaṇa”nti niyamo na bhaveyya, ārammaṇasaṅkaro bhaveyyāti attho.

It has been stated. Moreover, if things that have not come into range were mind-objects, it would follow that the knowledge of omniscience would not have form, etc., as its object. This being so, if at one time it has form, etc., as its object and at another time a mind-object, and at one time a mind-object and at another time form, etc., as its object, then how could there be a determination for those objects as form-objects, etc.? There would be no determination such as 'this is a form-object, etc., this is a mind-object'; the meaning is that there would be a confusion of objects.

306. Evaṃ chabbidhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ dassetvā idānissa anantarabhedaṃ parittārammaṇādittikavasena dassento āha “sabbaṃ ārammaṇa”ntiādi. Chabbidhaṃ parittattikādikaṃ taṃ etaṃ sabbaṃ ārammaṇanti sambandho. Parittattikādīnanti parittārammaṇattikādīnaṃ. Parittārammaṇattiko hi idha “parittattiko”ti vutto majjhapadalopavasena. Ādi-ggahaṇena maggārammaṇattiko [M 2.0009] atītārammaṇattiko ajjhattārammaṇattikoti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ tikānaṃ saṅgaho. Tattha “parittārammaṇā dhammā, mahaggatārammaṇā dhammā, appamāṇārammaṇā dhammā”ti evamāgato parittārammaṇattiko. Ādipadavasena “maggārammaṇā dhammā, maggahetukā dhammā, maggādhipatino dhammā”ti evamāgato maggārammaṇattiko. “Atītārammaṇā dhammā, anāgatārammaṇā dhammā, paccuppannārammaṇā dhammā”ti evamāgato atītārammaṇattiko. “Ajjhattārammaṇā dhammā, bahiddhārammaṇā dhammā, ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā dhammā”ti evamāgato ajjhattārammaṇattikoti veditabbaṃ.

306. Having thus shown the sixfold object, now, to show its subsequent division by way of the triad of limited objects, etc., he says, 'all that object,' etc. The connection is: That sixfold object, which consists of the limited triad and so on, is all this object. 'Of the limited triad, etc.' means of the triad of limited objects, etc. For here the triad of limited objects (parittārammaṇattiko) is called the 'limited triad' (parittattiko) by elision of the middle term. By the word 'etc.' these three triads are included: the path-object triad, the past-object triad, and the internal-object triad. Therein, the triad of limited objects is that which comes thus: 'states with limited objects, states with lofty objects, states with immeasurable objects.' By way of the word 'etc.', the path-object triad is that which comes thus: 'states with the path as object, states with the path as root-cause, states with the path as dominant influence.' The past-object triad is that which comes thus: 'states with past objects, states with future objects, states with present objects.' The internal-object triad is that which comes thus: 'states with internal objects, states with external objects, states with both internal and external objects.' This should be understood.

307-9. Kriyāhetudvayanti ahetukakiriyadvayaṃ hasituppādamanodhātu itarassa mahaggatādiārammaṇatāvasenāpi vakkhamānattā. “Iṭṭhādibhedā”tiādi parittārammaṇabhāvavibhāvanaṃ. Iṭṭhādibhedāti iṭṭhaiṭṭhamajjhattaaniṭṭhaaniṭṭhamajjhattabhedā. Paṭipāṭiyāti “rūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa, saddo sotaviññāṇassā”tiādinā anukkamato. Rūpādi…pe… ttayassa tūti kiriyāmanodhātuyā ceva kusalākusalavipākavibhāgavasena dvinnaṃ manodhātūnañca sabbaṃ rūpādipañcakagocaraṃ[V 2.0008]. Tā hi hadayavatthuṃ nissāya cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ purimapacchimā hutvā niyatā rūpādīneva ārabbha pavattanti.

307–9. The two functional without roots means the two rootless functional consciousnesses: the smile-producing consciousness and the mind-element, since for the other (i.e., the determining consciousness), having lofty objects, etc., will also be stated. 'Divided into desirable, etc.' is an explanation of the state of having a limited object. 'Divided into desirable, etc.' means divided into desirable, moderately desirable, undesirable, and moderately undesirable. 'In order' means in sequence, as in 'form for eye-consciousness, sound for ear-consciousness,' etc. As for the three ...pe... form, etc.: for the functional mind-element and for the two mind-elements divided as wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant, the entire fivefold resort of form, etc., is their object. For these, relying on the heart-basis, arise before and after eye-consciousness, etc., invariably taking only form, etc., as their object.

311. Kāmadhātuyanti kāmabhave. Tattha hi nesaṃ sabbesaṃ vatthārammaṇāni upalabbhanti. Cattārīti tesveva kiriyāmanodhātu, kusalavipākacakkhusotaviññāṇāni, tathā sampaṭicchananti imāni cattāri cittāni. Sesāni pana vatthārammaṇābhāvena tattha nuppajjanti. Neva kiñcīti vatthārammaṇānaṃ sabbaso abhāvato etesu kiñci na jāyati.

311. 'In the sense-sphere realm' means in sense-sphere existence. For it is there that the bases and objects for all of them are found. 'Four' means these four consciousnesses: among them, the functional mind-element, the wholesome-resultant eye- and ear-consciousnesses, and similarly the receiving consciousness. But the others do not arise there owing to the absence of bases and objects. 'Nothing at all' means that nothing at all arises among these owing to the complete absence of bases and objects.

312-3. “Mahāpākāna”ntiādi [M 2.0010] paṭhamaparicchede vuttatthameva. Paṭuppannāti paccuppannā.

312–3. 'Of the great resultants,' etc., has the meaning already stated in the first chapter. Paṭuppannā means present.

314. Evaṃ parittārammaṇe dassetvā idāni mahaggatārammaṇe appamāṇārammaṇe ca dassetuṃ “dutiyāruppacittañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dutiyāruppacittaṃ paṭhamāruppārammaṇato, catutthāruppaṃ tatiyāruppārammaṇato mahaggatārammaṇaṃ. Chabbidhanti kusalavipākakiriyāvasena paccekaṃ tividhatāya chappakāraṃ.

314. Having thus explained limited objects, now to explain lofty objects and immeasurable objects, it is said, 'and the second formless-sphere consciousness,' etc. Therein, the second formless-sphere consciousness has a lofty object because its object is the first formless-sphere attainment; the fourth formless-sphere consciousness has a lofty object because its object is the third formless-sphere attainment. 'Sixfold' means of six types because each is threefold by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional.

316-20. Ñāṇaṃ parihīnaṃ etesaṃ, ñāṇato parihīnāti vā ñāṇahīnā. Parittārammaṇā…pe… honti teti aṭṭha ñāṇavippayuttacittuppādā sekhaputhujjanakhīṇāsavānaṃ kadāci nirussukkabhāvena ādarākaraṇavasena akammaññasarīratāaññavihitatāhi vā asakkaccadānapaccavekkhaṇadhammassavanādīsu atipaguṇavipassanāya ca kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha pavattikāle parittārammaṇā. Atipaguṇānaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle mahaggatārammaṇā. Kasiṇanimittādipaññattipaccavekkhaṇakāle parittārammaṇādivasena navattabbā. Akusalesu cattāro diṭṭhisampayuttacittuppādā catupaññāsakāmāvacaradhammānaṃ, rūpassa ca “attā satto”ti parāmasanaassādanābhinandanakāle parittārammaṇā. Tenevākārena sattavīsatimahaggatadhamme ārabbha pavattakāle mahaggatārammaṇā. Paṇṇattidhamme ārabbha pavattanakāle siyā navattabbā parittārammaṇādivasena. Diṭṭhivippayuttāni teyeva dhamme ārabbha vinā parāmāsena assādanābhinandanavasena pavattiyaṃ, paṭighasampayuttāni domanassavasena pavattiyaṃ, vicikicchāsampayuttaṃ dveḷhakabhāvena, uddhaccasahagataṃ vikkhipanavasena, avūpasamavasena ca pavattiyaṃ parittamahaggatanavattabbārammaṇāti veditabbā. Kriyatopi ca tathāti kiriyacittatopi ñāṇasampayuttā [V 2.0009] cattāroti attho. Kriyāvoṭṭhabbananti [M 2.0011] sarūpakathanametaṃ, na pana kusalākusalavipākavoṭṭhabbanassa vijjamānattā.

316-20. Knowledge is deficient in these; or they are called 'deficient in knowledge' because they are deficient in knowledge. The eight cittas dissociated from knowledge—which arise in trainees, ordinary persons, and arahants, sometimes due to lack of enthusiasm, carelessness, bodily unwieldiness, being otherwise engaged, or inattentiveness in giving, reviewing, listening to the Dhamma, etc., or due to very mature insight—have limited objects when they occur in relation to sense-sphere phenomena. When reviewing the first jhānas, etc., of those with very mature qualities, they have sublime objects. When reviewing concepts like kasiṇa signs, etc., they are unclassifiable in terms of having limited objects, etc. Among the unwholesome states, the four cittas associated with wrong view have limited objects when misapprehending, savoring, and delighting in the fifty-four sense-sphere phenomena and form as 'a self' or 'a being.' In the same way, when occurring in relation to the twenty-seven sublime phenomena, they have sublime objects. When occurring in relation to conceptual phenomena, they may be unclassifiable in terms of having limited objects, etc. The cittas dissociated from wrong view, when they occur in relation to those same phenomena with savoring and delighting but without misapprehension; the cittas associated with aversion, when they occur through displeasure; the citta associated with doubt, through perplexity; and the citta accompanied by restlessness, through distraction and lack of calm—these should be understood as having limited, sublime, or unclassifiable objects. This is also the case with the functional cittas; that is, the four functional cittas associated with knowledge. The term 'functional determining' is a statement of its nature, and not because determining as wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant exists.

Tividho hoti gocaroti parittamahaggataappamāṇavasena tividhopi gocaro hoti. Kathaṃ? Kusalakiriyāvasena aṭṭha ñāṇasampayuttacittuppādā sekhaputhujjanakhīṇāsavānaṃ sakkaccadānapaccavekkhaṇadhammassavanavipassanādīsu kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha pavattakāle kāmāvacarārammaṇikaabhiññāya parikammānulomakāle ca parittārammaṇā. Paṭhamajjhānādipaccavekkhaṇakāle mahaggatārammaṇajhānādīnaṃ parikammakāle mahaggatadhamme ārabbha sammasanakāle ca mahaggatārammaṇā honti. Yathālābhaṃ gotrabhuvodānakāle pana lokuttaraṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle ca nibbānārammaṇābhiññāya parikammakāle ca appamāṇārammaṇā. Paṇṇattipaccavekkhaṇakāle paṇṇattārammaṇikajhānābhiññānaṃ parikammakāle ca navattabbā. Abhiññādvayassa parittādiārammaṇataṃ sattarasamaparicchede vakkhati. Kiriyāvoṭṭhabbanampi yathāvuttadhammānaṃ taṃtaṃārammaṇe pavattamānānaṃ purecaraṃ hutvā taṃ tadeva āvajjantaṃ pavattatīti parittādiārammaṇaṃ. Pañcadvāre voṭṭhabbanavasena pavattiyaṃ parittārammaṇameva.

'The range is threefold' means the range is threefold by way of limited, sublime, and immeasurable. How so? By way of wholesome and functional cittas, the eight cittas associated with knowledge of trainees, ordinary persons, and arahants have limited objects when engaged in careful giving, reviewing, listening to the Dhamma, insight, etc., regarding sense-sphere phenomena, and during the preliminary work and conformity moments for direct knowledge related to sense-sphere objects. At the time of reviewing the first jhāna and so on, or during the preliminary work for sublime jhānas, when contemplating sublime phenomena, their objects are sublime. At the moment of change-of-lineage and purification, according to what has been attained, or when reviewing the supramundane Dhamma, and during the preliminary work for direct knowledge with Nibbāna as object, their object is immeasurable. When reviewing concepts, or during the preliminary work for concept-based jhānas and direct knowledges, their objects are unclassifiable. The limited, sublime, and immeasurable objects of the two direct knowledges will be explained in the seventeenth chapter. The functional determining consciousness also, being a forerunner to those cittas that are occurring with their respective objects among the aforementioned phenomena, occurs adverting to that very same object; thus, its objects are limited, sublime, or unclassifiable. In the five-door process, when it functions as determining, it has only a limited object.

Vuttāvasesānīti yathāvuttehi avasiṭṭhāni pannarasa rūpāvacarāni paṭhamatatiyāni, cha arūpāvacarakusalavipākakiriyacittānīti ekavīsati cittāni. Navattabbārammaṇānīti parittādivasena navattabbassa kasiṇādinimittasattapaññattiākāsaviññāṇābhāvassa ārammaṇakaraṇato navattabbārammaṇāni.

The remaining ones are the fifteen fine-material-sphere cittas and the six immaterial-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional cittas—twenty-one cittas in total. They have unclassifiable objects because they take as their object that which is unclassifiable in terms of 'limited,' etc., namely: the kasiṇa sign, the concept of a being, and other concepts, as well as space, the base of infinite consciousness, and the base of nothingness.

Parittārammaṇattikaṃ samattaṃ.

The Triad on Limited Objects is concluded.

321-2. Evaṃ [M 2.0012] parittārammaṇattikavasena visayīvibhāgaṃ dassetvā idāni yasmā appamāṇārammaṇaniddeseneva maggārammaṇattikasaṅgahitopi visayīvibhāgo niddiṭṭho hoti, tasmā taṃ pahāya atītārammaṇattikavasena dassetuṃ “dutiyāruppacittañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dutiyāruppacittaṃ atītassa paṭhamāruppaviññāṇassa ārammaṇakaraṇato, catutthāruppaṃ tatiyāruppassa ārammaṇakaraṇato ekantaatītārammaṇaṃ. Paccuppannāva gocarāti rūpādimhi dharamāneyeva [V 2.0010] pañcadvārikacittānaṃ uppajjanato. Anāgatārammaṇaṃ pana niyataṃ kiñci natthi anāgataṃsañāṇassapi pañcamajjhānato abhinnattā.

321-2. Having thus shown the division of consciousnesses by way of the triad of limited objects, now, because the division of consciousnesses included in the path-object triad has also been indicated by the exposition of immeasurable objects, therefore, leaving that aside, in order to show the division by way of the triad of past objects, it is said, 'and the second immaterial citta,' and so on. Therein, the second immaterial citta is exclusively past-object because it takes the past first immaterial consciousness as its object; the fourth immaterial citta is so because it takes the third immaterial citta as its object. The range is only the present, because the five-door consciousnesses arise only while form, etc., are present. However, there is no citta that is exclusively future-object, since even the knowledge of the future is not different from the fifth jhāna.

324-6. Siyā…pe… nāgatagocarāti aṭṭha tāva mahāvipākā devamanussānaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇakāle kammaṃ vā kammanimittaṃ vā ārabbha pavattiyaṃ atītārammaṇā. Bhavaṅgacutikālepi eseva nayo. Gatinimittaṃ pana kadāci kammanimittañca ārabbha paṭisandhiggahaṇakāle, tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgakāle ca paccuppannārammaṇā, tathā pañcadvāre tadārammaṇavasena pavattiyaṃ. Manodvāre pana atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇānaṃ javanānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā pavattiyaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇā. Kusalākusalavipākāhetukaupekkhāsahagatamanoviññāṇadhātudvayepi eseva nayo. Kevalañhi tā yathākkamaṃ manussesu jaccandhādīnaṃ, apāyesu ca sabbesaṃ paṭisandhi honti. Pañcadvāre ca santīraṇakāle paccuppannārammaṇāva hontīti ayametesaṃ viseso. Somanassasahagatā pana pañcadvāre santīraṇavasena, tadārammaṇavasena ca pavattikāle paccuppannārammaṇā, manodvāre ca tadārammaṇakāle atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇāti veditabbā. Hasituppādacittaṃ pana [M 2.0013] khīṇāsavānaṃ pañcadvāre haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākāraṃ kurumānānaṃ paccuppannārammaṇaṃ hoti, manodvāre atītādibhede dhamme ārabbha hasituppādavasena pavattiyaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇaṃ. “Kusalākusalā”tiādīsu kusalesu tāva cattāro ñāṇasampayuttacittuppādā sekhaputhujjanānaṃ, atītādibhedāni khandhadhātuāyatanāni sammasanakāle, paccavekkhaṇakāle, atītādiārammaṇikaabhiññānaṃ parikammakāle ca atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇā. Paññattinibbānapaccavekkhaṇakāle, gotrabhuvodānakāle, paññattinibbānārammaṇikaabhiññānaṃ parikammādikāle ca navattabbārammaṇā. Paññattinibbānāni hi idha atītādikālavasena navattabbānīti tadārammaṇāni atītārammaṇādivasena navattabbāni. Tenāha “santapaññattikālepī”ti, yathāsambhavaṃ santassa nibbānassa, paññattiyā ca ārammaṇakaraṇakāleti attho. Potthakesu pana “sante paññattikālesū”ti likhanti, so apāṭho. Tassa pana apāṭhabhāvaṃ ajānantā atthahānimpi asallakkhetvā vacanavipallāsavasena paññattikālasmiṃ satīti atthaṃ likhanti. Ñāṇavippayuttānipi vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Kevalañhi tesaṃ maggaphalanibbānapaccavekkhaṇāni natthi. Ñāṇavirahena lokuttaradhammārammaṇe asamatthabhāvatoti ayameva viseso.

324-6. (The verse beginning:) 'It may have... a future object.' First, the eight great resultant cittas, when they arise at the time of rebirth-linking for devas and humans taking kamma or a kamma sign as object, have a past object. This is also the case at the time of the life-continuum and death. But when they take a destination sign or sometimes a kamma sign as object at the time of rebirth-linking, and during the life-continuum immediately after, they have a present object; so too when they occur as registering in the five doors. In the mind door, however, by taking the object of javanas that have past, future, or present objects, they have past, future, or present objects. This is also the case for the two mind-consciousness elements accompanied by equanimity that are rootless wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant. They simply become the rebirth-linking consciousness for those born blind, etc., among humans, and for all beings in the planes of misery, respectively. Their distinction is that in the five doors, at the time of investigating, they have only a present object. The joy-accompanied resultant, however, should be understood to have a present object when it occurs as investigating and as registering in the five doors, and to have past, future, or present objects at the time of registering in the mind door. The smile-producing citta of arahants, when they are making a happy and delighted expression in the five doors, has a present object; in the mind door, when it arises as smile-producing in relation to phenomena of past, future, or present time, it has a past, future, or present object. In the case of 'wholesome and unwholesome,' etc., first, among the wholesome, the four cittas associated with knowledge of trainees and ordinary persons have past, future, or present objects when they are contemplating the aggregates, elements, and bases of past, etc., time; when they are reviewing; and during the preliminary work for the direct knowledges that have past, etc., objects. When reviewing a concept or Nibbāna, at the time of change-of-lineage and purification, and during the preliminary work, etc., for the direct knowledges that have a concept or Nibbāna as object, they have a timeless object. For here concepts and Nibbāna are unclassifiable in terms of past, etc., time, so cittas that take them as object are unclassifiable in terms of having a past object, etc. Hence he said, 'even at the time of a peaceful concept,' which means, 'at the time of taking as object, as the case may be, Nibbāna, which is peaceful, and a concept.' But in the books they write 'at quiescent, conceptual times,' which is a wrong reading. Not knowing it is a wrong reading and not noticing the damage to the meaning, they write the meaning as 'when the time of the concept is present,' by a reversal of words. The cittas dissociated from knowledge should also be understood in the way stated. Their only distinction is that they do not have the reviewing of path, fruition, and Nibbāna, because of their inability to take supramundane phenomena as object due to the absence of knowledge.

Akusalesu [V 2.0011] cattāro diṭṭhisampayuttacittuppādā atītādibhedānaṃ tebhūmakadhammānaṃ assādanābhinandanaparāmasanakāle atītādiārammaṇā. Tatheva paññattiṃ ārabbha pavattikāle navattabbārammaṇā. Diṭṭhivippayuttesupi eseva nayo. Kevalañhi tattha parāmāsaggahaṇaṃ natthi. Dve paṭighasampayuttacittuppādā atītādibhede dhamme ārabbha dussanakāle atītādiārammaṇā, paṇṇattiṃ ārabbha dussanakāle navattabbārammaṇā. Vicikicchuddhaccasampayuttā tesu [M 2.0014] dhammesu aniṭṭhaṅgatabhāvena ca avūpasamavikkhepavasena ca pavattiyaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannanavattabbārammaṇā. Kiriyāsu aṭṭha sahetukacittuppādā kusalacittuppādagatikā eva. Tattha hi ñāṇasampayuttā kusalesu ñāṇasampayuttehi, ñāṇavippayuttā ñāṇavippayuttehi samānā. Kevalaṃ pana te sekhaputhujjanānaṃ uppajjanti, ime khīṇāsavānanti ayamevettha viseso. Kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu pana upekkhāsahagatā pañcadvāre voṭṭhabbanavasena pavattiyaṃ paccuppannārammaṇā, manodvāre atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇānañceva paññattinibbānārammaṇānañca javanānaṃ purecārikakāle atītānāgatapaccuppannanavattabbārammaṇā. Abhiññādvayassa atītādiārammaṇataṃ vakkhati. Navattabbā…pe… ādināti kasiṇanimittādipaññattārammaṇattā atītārammaṇādinā navattabbā.

In unwholesome states, the four consciousnesses associated with wrong view have past and so on as their objects when they occur with enjoyment, approval, and clinging to phenomena of the three planes classified as past and so on. Similarly, when they occur taking concepts as objects, they have neither-specified objects. The same principle applies to those dissociated from wrong view; only the grasping of clinging is absent there. The two consciousnesses associated with aversion have past and so on as their objects when they occur with displeasure regarding phenomena classified as past and so on; when they occur with displeasure regarding concepts, they have neither-specified objects. Those associated with doubt and restlessness have past, future, present, and neither-specified objects when they occur due to being undesirable regarding those phenomena and due to being unsettled through distraction. Among functional states, the eight rooted consciousnesses behave just like wholesome consciousnesses. There, those associated with knowledge are similar to wholesome states associated with knowledge, while those dissociated from knowledge are similar to those dissociated from knowledge. However, the former arise only in trainees and ordinary persons, while the latter arise in arahants—this is the distinction here. The rootless functional mind-consciousness element, accompanied by equanimity, has a present object when it occurs as the determining consciousness in the five-door process; in the mind-door, when it precedes the impulsion processes that have past, future, present, conceptual, and Nibbāna objects, it has past, future, present, and neither-specified objects. It will be stated that the two types of higher knowledge have past and so on as objects. ‘Neither-specified…etc.…and so on’ means that because they take concepts such as kasiṇa signs as their object, they are neither-specified in terms of having a past object, etc.

327. Kriyā pañcāti ñāṇasampayuttā catasso, ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātu upekkhāsahagatāti imā pañca kiriyā. Rūpato pañcamī kriyāti rūpāvacarapañcamajjhānasaṅkhātā kiriyābhiññā ca. Natthi kiñci agocaranti atītādibhedesu, kālavimuttesu ca agocaraṃ nāma kiñci natthi, sabbameva nesaṃ gocaraṃ hotīti attho.

327. ‘Five functional states’ means these five functional states: the four associated with knowledge, and the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity. ‘The fifth functional state from the form realm’ refers to the functional higher knowledge, which is reckoned as the fifth jhāna of the form realm. ‘There is nothing beyond their scope’ means that there is nothing whatsoever that is not an object for them, whether among phenomena classified as past and so on, or among those free from time; all is their object—this is the meaning.

Atītārammaṇattikaṃ.

The Triad on Past Objects.

Vuttanayānusāreneva ajjhattārammaṇattikasaṅgahitopi visayīvibhāgo sakkā viññātunti so visuṃ na uddhaṭo. Sarūpato panesa evaṃ veditabbo – viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti ime tāva kusalavipākakiriyāvasena cha cittuppādā attano santānasambandhaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ samāpattiṃ ārabbha pavattanato ajjhattārammaṇā. Rūpāvacaracatukkajjhānāni, paṭhamatatiyārūppāni, lokuttarakusalavipākāni ca niyakajjhattato [M 2.0015] bahibhāvena bahiddhābhūtāni pathavīkasiṇādīni ārabbha pavattito bahiddhārammaṇāni. Sabbeva kāmāvacarakusalākusalābyākatā [V 2.0012] dhammā rūpāvacarapañcamajjhānañca ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇāni. Tattha kāmāvacarakusalato cattāro ñāṇasampayuttacittuppādā attano khandhādīni paccavekkhantassa ajjhattārammaṇā, paresaṃ khandhādipaccavekkhaṇe, paṇṇattinibbānapaccavekkhaṇe ca bahiddhārammaṇā, tadubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā. Ñāṇavippayuttesupi eseva nayo. Kevalañhi tesaṃ nibbānapaccavekkhaṇā natthi. Akusalāpi attano khandhādīnaṃ assādanābhinandanaparāmāsādikāle ajjhattārammaṇā, parassa khandhādīsu ceva anindriyabaddharūpakasiṇādīsu ca tatheva pavattikāle bahiddhārammaṇā, tadubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā. Dvepañcaviññāṇāni, tisso ca manodhātuyoti ime terasa cittuppādā attano rūpādīni ārabbha pavattiyaṃ ajjhattārammaṇā, parassa rūpādīsu pavattā bahiddhārammaṇā, tadubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā, somanassasahagataṃ santīraṇaṃ pañcadvāre santīraṇatadārammaṇavasena attano pañcarūpādidhamme manodvāre tadārammaṇavasena aññepi ajjhattike kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha pavattiyaṃ ajjhattārammaṇā, paresaṃ dhammesu pavattamānā bahiddhārammaṇā, tadubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā. Upekkhāsahagatasantīraṇadvayepi eseva nayo.

Following the method already stated, the division of subjects can be understood even when included in the internal-object triad, so it is not separately extracted. However, it should be understood in this way according to its nature: the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these six types of consciousness, in terms of wholesome, resultant, and functional, arise by taking the lower meditative attainment connected with their own continuum as their object, thus having an internal object. The four fine-material jhānas, the first and third immaterial attainments, and the supramundane wholesome and resultant states, being external to one's own internal constitution, arise by taking external objects such as the earth kasiṇa, etc., thus having an external object. All wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states of the sense sphere, as well as the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, have both internal and external objects. Among them, the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge from the wholesome sense-sphere states have an internal object when reviewing their own aggregates, etc.; an external object when reviewing the aggregates of others or concepts and Nibbāna; and both internal and external objects by way of both. The same applies to those dissociated from knowledge, except that they do not review Nibbāna. Unwholesome states also have an internal object during the time of delighting in, rejoicing in, or clinging to their own aggregates, etc.; an external object during the time of engaging similarly with the aggregates of others or with non-faculty-bound material phenomena such as kasiṇas, etc.; and both internal and external objects by way of both. The two sets of fivefold consciousness and the three mind-elements—these thirteen types of consciousness have an internal object when they arise taking their own form, etc., as object; an external object when they occur in relation to the form, etc., of others; and both internal and external objects by way of both. The investigating consciousness accompanied by joy has an internal object when it arises in the five doors taking its own five kinds of material phenomena, etc., as object by way of investigating and registering, and in the mind-door taking other internal sense-sphere phenomena as object by way of registering; it has an external object when engaging with the phenomena of others; and both internal and external objects by way of both. The same applies to the two types of investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity.

Kevalaṃ pana taṃ sugatiduggatīsu paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasenāpi ajjhattādibhedesu kammādīsu pavattati. Aṭṭha mahāvipākāni paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutitadārammaṇavasena ajjhattādibhedesu dhammesu pavattanato ajjhattādiālambaṇāni. Hasituppādampi attano rūpādīni ārabbha pahaṭṭhākārakaraṇavasena pavattiyaṃ ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, parassa rūpādīsu pavattaṃ [M 2.0016] bahiddhārammaṇaṃ. Manodvārepi attano katakiriyapaccavekkhaṇena hasituppādane ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, paresaṃ katakiriyapaccavekkhaṇena bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, tadubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ. Manodvārāvajjanaṃ pana manodvāre āvajjanavasena, pañcadvāre ca voṭṭhabbanavasena pavattiyaṃ ajjhattādiārammaṇaṃ. Aṭṭha mahākiriyā kusalagatikāyeva. Kevalañhi tā khīṇāsavānaṃ uppajjanti, kusalāni sekhaputhujjanānanti ettakameva nānattaṃ. Rūpāvacarapañcamajjhānassa ajjhattādiārammaṇataṃ vakkhati.

However, that equanimous investigating consciousness also functions by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death in good and bad destinies, and occurs with objects such as kamma in the internal, etc., divisions. The eight great resultant consciousnesses, occurring in relation to internal, etc., phenomena by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death, and registering, thus have internal, etc., objects. The smile-producing consciousness, too, when it occurs by way of producing a delighted manner in dependence on one's own form, etc., has an internal object; when it occurs in relation to another's form, etc., it has an external object. At the mind-door as well, the arising of smiling consciousness through reviewing one's own actions has an internal object; through reviewing others' actions, it has an external object; through both, it has an internal and external object. Mind-door-adverting consciousness, however, occurring at the mind-door by way of adverting, and at the five sense-doors by way of determining, has an internal, etc., object. The eight great functional consciousnesses are of the same kind as the wholesome ones. For they arise only in those whose taints are destroyed, whereas wholesome consciousnesses arise in trainees and ordinary people—this is the only difference. The state of having internal, etc., objects for the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere will be stated.

329. “Phalaṃ, magga”nti ca sāmaññena pucchitattā āha “cattāro…pe… puññato”ti.

329. “Fruit, path”: because it was asked in general terms, he said, “four…pe… from merit.”

332-4. Arahattamaggaphalāni pana te jānituṃ na sakkonti, tathā kusalābhiññā ca[V 2.0013]. Tenāha “sabbesu panā”tiādi. Voṭṭhabbanassa āvajjanakiccasamayaṃ sandhāya gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ “voṭṭhabbanampi cā”ti vuttaṃ. “Cattāro…pe… puññato”ti idaṃ ñāṇasampayuttassāpi sekhaputhujjanasantānappavattassa aggamaggaphalajānane asamatthatāya nidassanamattaṃ. Kusalābhiññācittampi pana taṃ gocaraṃ kātumasamatthameva. Evañca katvā heṭṭhā “kriyābhiññā manodhātū”ti vuttaṃ.

332-4. However, they are unable to know the path and fruition of arahantship, as well as wholesome higher knowledge. Therefore, it is said: “But in all…” etc. With reference to the time when determining has the function of adverting, for the sake of metrical ease, it is stated: “And even determining…” etc. “Four… from merit”—this is merely an indication of the inability, even for one associated with knowledge occurring in the continuum of a trainee or an ordinary person, to know the highest path and fruition. Yet, even a mind of wholesome higher knowledge is quite incapable of making that its object. And so it was stated below: “functional higher knowledge and the mind-element.”

335-8. Kasmāti kāraṇapucchā. “Arahato”tiādi vissajjanaṃ. Hi-saddo “yasmā”ti imassa atthe. Yasmā puthujjanā vā sekhā vā arahato maggacittaṃ, phalamānasañca jānituṃ na sakkonti, tasmāti attho. Ayañca nesaṃ asamatthatā anadhigatattā anadhigate ca visaye sabbesampi moho atthevāti dassetuṃ “puthujjano na jānātī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sotāpannassa mānasanti sotāpannassa pāṭipuggalikaṃ maggaphalasaṅkhātalokuttaramānasaṃ. Evaṃ “sakadāgāmissa mānasa”ntiādīsupi. Lokiyamānasaṃ [M 2.0017] pana arahantassāpi jānāti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “atha kho māro pāpimā bhagavato cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāyā”ti. Vuttamevatthaṃ saṅkhipitvā dassento āha “heṭṭhimo heṭṭhimo”tiādi. Yatheva heṭṭhimo heṭṭhimo puggalo uparūpari cittaṃ na jānāti, evaṃ uparimo uparimopi heṭṭhimassa heṭṭhimassa cittaṃ na jānātīti ce? No na jānāti, so pana attanā adhigatavisayattā jānātiyevāti dassento āha “uparūparī”tiādi. Yathā “uparūparī”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ “heṭṭhimassa heṭṭhimassā”ti vattabbe ekaṃ heṭṭhima-saddaṃ ca-saddena saṅgahetvā “heṭṭhimassa ca mānasa”nti vuttaṃ.

335-8. “Why?” This is a question asking for the reason. The answer begins with “Of an arahant,” etc. The word hi is in the sense of yasmā (because). The meaning is: because ordinary people or trainees cannot know the path-consciousness or the fruit-consciousness of an arahant, therefore it is so. To show that this inability of theirs is due to their not having attained it, and that in regard to an unattained domain all are deluded, it is said: “An ordinary person does not know,” etc. “The mind of a stream-enterer” means the supramundane consciousness of a stream-enterer, designated as path and fruit, which is personal to the individual. Similarly in the phrases “the mind of a once-returner,” etc. However, one knows even the mundane mind of an arahant. For so it is said: “Then Māra the Evil One, having known with his own mind the reflection in the Blessed One’s mind…” To show the same meaning in brief, he says: “The lower, lower…” etc. If it is asked: “Just as the lower person does not know the mind of the higher person, so too the higher person does not know the mind of the lower person?” It is not that he does not know it. On the contrary, to show that he does indeed know it because it is a domain he himself has attained, he says: “The higher, higher…” etc. Just as it is said “the higher, higher,” so too, when it should be said “of the lower, lower,” one word “lower” is included by the word “and” (ca), and thus it is said: “and the mind of the lower.”

339-41. Evampi visayīpadhānavasena vibhāgaṃ dassetvā idāni visayappadhānavasena dassetuṃ “yo dhammo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kusalameva ārammaṇanti kusalārammaṇaṃ. Kāmeti padaṃ ubhayattha sambandhitabbaṃ “kāme kusalārammaṇaṃ kāme kusalākusalassā”ti. Kiñcāpi hi akusalassa ekantakāmāvacarattā na etassa visesitabbatā atthi, kusalaṃ pana visesitabbamevāti taṃ apekkhāya “kāme”ti uparipadena sambandhitabbameva. Atha vā akusalasahacariyato kusalampi kāmāvacarameva gayhatīti “kāme”ti idaṃ purimapadasseva visesanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

339-41. Having thus shown the classification by way of the predominance of the subject, now to show it by way of the predominance of the object, it is said, “Whatever state,” etc. “Having a wholesome object” means having only a wholesome state as object. The word “sensual” should be connected to both phrases, thus: “sensual with a wholesome object” and “sensual with a wholesome and unwholesome object.” For although the unwholesome is exclusively of the sensual sphere and thus does not need to be specified, the wholesome must indeed be specified. Therefore, with reference to that, the word “sensual” should be connected with the latter phrase. Alternatively, because the wholesome is also taken as being of the sensual sphere due to its association with the unwholesome, this word “sensual” should be seen as a qualifier of the former phrase.

Kāmāvacarapākassāti [V 2.0014] pañcaviññāṇasampaṭicchanānaṃ ekantena rūpakkhandhārammaṇattā tadavasesassa ekādasavidhassa kāmāvacaravipākassa. Kāmakriyassāti vuttanayeneva manodhātuvajjitassa dasavidhakāmāvacarakiriyacittassa. Etesaṃ…pe… ārammaṇaṃ siyāti ettha kusalassa tāva attanā katassa dānādikāmāvacarakusalassa pasannacittena anussaraṇakāle, tatheva parehi katassa anumodanakāle, tasseva duvidhassāpi aniccatādivasena paccavekkhaṇakāle[M 2.0018], cetopariyañāṇādīnaṃ parittakusalārammaṇikaabhiññānaṃ parikammādikāle ca ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Akusalesu ca catunnaṃ diṭṭhigatasampayuttānaṃ kāmāvacarakusalaṃ ārabbha assādanābhinandanaparāmasanakāle, diṭṭhivippayuttānaṃ kevalaṃ assādanādikāle ca dvinnaṃ paṭighasampayuttānaṃ attanā, parehi ca katakusalamārabbha vippaṭisāradussanakāle, vicikicchācittassa asanniṭṭhānakāle, uddhaccasahagatassa avūpasamavikkhepakāle ca ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Abhiññācittadvaye kusalassa sekhaputhujjanānaṃ attanā, parehi vā katakusalassa anussaraṇakāle, paracittavijānanakāle, “iminā puññakammena manussesu, kāmāvacaradevesu ca nibbattatī”ti jānanakāle, “anāgate dānādīni puññāni karomi, karissatī”ti jānanakāle ca kiriyacittassāpi khīṇāsavānaṃ attanā, parehi vā katakammānussaraṇakālādīsu ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Kāmāvacaravipākesu navannaṃ sugatipaṭisandhīnaṃ kammakammanimittārammaṇikapaṭisandhikāle, sabbesampi tadārammaṇānaṃ kāmāvacarakusalārammaṇikajavanānantaraṃ tadārammaṇakāle ca ārammaṇaṃ hotīti. Dasavidhakāmāvacarakiriyāsu ca aṭṭhannaṃ mahākiriyacittānaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ kāmāvacarakusalapaccavekkhaṇasammasanakāle, parittārammaṇikakiriyābhiññānaṃ parikammādikāle, hasituppādassa dānādiṃ paccavekkhitvā tussanakāle, manodvārāvajjanassa pana kāmāvacarakusalārammaṇikajavanānaṃ purecārikakāle ca ārammaṇaṃ hotīti evaṃ kāmāvacarakusalaṃ channaṃ rāsīnaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti.

By ‘sense-sphere resultant’ is meant the remaining eleven kinds of sense-sphere resultant consciousness, since the five sense consciousnesses and the receiving consciousness exclusively take the form aggregate as object. By ‘sense-sphere functional’ is meant the ten kinds of sense-sphere functional consciousness, excluding the mind-element, in the way already stated. For these… the object may be as follows: For the wholesome, it becomes an object at the time of recollecting with a serene mind sense-sphere wholesome kamma such as giving done by oneself; likewise, at the time of rejoicing in what was done by others; at the time of reviewing both kinds of deeds in terms of impermanence, etc.; and at the time of the preliminary work for the direct knowledges with a limited wholesome object, such as knowledge of others’ minds. For the unwholesome, it becomes an object for the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view at the time of savoring, delighting in, and adhering to sense-sphere wholesome kamma; for the two types dissociated from wrong view, at the time of merely savoring, etc.; for the two types associated with aversion, at the time of remorse and resentment regarding wholesome kamma done by oneself or others; for the consciousness of doubt, at the time of indecision; and for the consciousness accompanied by restlessness, at the time of non-tranquility and agitation. For the two consciousnesses of direct knowledge: for the wholesome one, it becomes an object for trainees and worldlings at the time of recollecting wholesome kamma done by oneself or others, at the time of knowing others’ minds, at the time of knowing, “By this meritorious kamma one is reborn among humans and in the sense-sphere heavens,” and at the time of knowing, “In the future I will do, or they will do, meritorious deeds such as giving”; for the functional one, it becomes an object for Arahants at the time of recollecting kamma done by oneself or others, etc. For the sense-sphere resultants: for the nine happy rebirth-linkings, it becomes an object at the time of rebirth-linking that takes kamma or a kamma-sign as its object; and for all the registering consciousnesses, it becomes an object at the time of registering, immediately following a javana process with a sense-sphere wholesome object. For the ten kinds of sense-sphere functional consciousness: for the eight great functional cittas, it becomes an object for Arahants at the time of reviewing and examining sense-sphere wholesome kamma; for the functional direct knowledges with a limited object, at the time of the preliminary work; for the smile-producing consciousness, at the time of delighting after reviewing giving, etc.; and for the mind-door adverting consciousness, at the time it precedes javanas with a sense-sphere wholesome object. Thus, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness serves as an object for six classes of consciousness.

342. Tatoti yathāvuttarāsito. Tenāha “pañcannaṃ pana rāsīna”nti. Ettha ca kiriyacittesu hasituppādo na sambhavati ekantaparittārammaṇattā. Tattha kāmāvacarakusalassa tāva [M 2.0019] sekhaputhujjanānaṃ jhānapaccavekkhaṇasammasanakāle, rūpāvacarakusalārammaṇikaabhiññānaṃ parikammādikāle, akusalassa vuttanayena parāmasanādikāle, abhiññāsu kusalābhiññāya sekhaputhujjanānaṃ attanā, parehi vā atītabhave uppāditajhānānussaraṇakāle, paresaṃ rūpāvacaracittaparicchindanakāle, “iminā kammena imasmiṃ brahmaloke nibbattissatī”ti jānanakāle ca “anāgate [V 2.0015] jhānaṃ bhāvessatī”ti vā jānanakāle, kiriyābhiññāya ca khīṇāsavānaṃ yathāvuttavasena pavattikāle ca navavidhassa pana kiriyacittassa khīṇāsavānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena rūpāvacarakusalapaccavekkhaṇakāleti evaṃ rūpāvacarakusalaṃ pañcannaṃ rāsīnaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti.

342. Thus, from the aforementioned class. Hence it is said, “of the five classes.” Here, among the functional cittas, the smile-producing consciousness does not occur because it has an exclusively limited object. In this regard: for sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, it becomes an object at the time when trainees and worldlings review and examine jhāna, and at the time of the preliminary work for the direct knowledges that take form-sphere wholesome kamma as object; for the unwholesome, in the way stated, at the time of adhering, etc.; for the direct knowledges: for the wholesome direct knowledge, it becomes an object when trainees and worldlings recollect a jhāna produced by themselves or others in a past existence, when they discern the form-sphere consciousness of others, when they know, “By this kamma one will be reborn in this brahma world,” or when they know, “In the future one will develop jhāna”; and for the functional direct knowledge, when it occurs for Arahants in the way stated; and for the ninefold functional consciousness, it becomes an object for Arahants at the time of reviewing form-sphere wholesome kamma in the way stated above. Thus form-sphere wholesome kamma becomes an object for five classes of consciousness.

343-7. Āruppakusalañcāpi ārammaṇapaccayo hotīti sambandho. Tebhūmakakusalassāti sabbassa kāmāvacarakusalassa, rūpāvacarakusalesu kusalābhiññāya, arūpāvacarakusalesu dutiyacatutthakusalassa cāti imassa tebhūmakakusalassa. Esa nayo “tebhūmakakriyassā”ti etthāpi. “Catutthadūna”nti vā “catutthadutiyāna”nti vā vattabbe gāthābandhavasena vibhattiyā, savibhattissa vā tiya-saddassa lopaṃ katvā “catutthadū”ti vuttaṃ. Imesaṃ…pe… paccayoti kāmāvacarakusalassa, tāva abhiññākusalassa ca rūpāvacarārammaṇesu vuttanayena dutiyacatutthāruppassa paṭhamatatiyavasenāti evaṃ tebhūmakakusalassa tathā sekhaputhujjanakāle attano santānagatassa, parasantānagatassa vā āruppakusalassa pajānanakāle kāmāvacararūpāvacarakiriyacittassa sekhaputhujjanakāleyeva attanā nibbattitaṃ paṭhamatatiyāruppaṃ ārabbha khīṇāsavakāle dutiyacatutthāruppanibbattane arūpakiriyacittassāti evaṃ tebhūmakakiriyassa heṭṭhā [M 2.0020] vuttanayeneva akusalassa, catutthadutiyānañca arūpāvacaravipākānanti evametesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ rāsīnaṃ arūpakusalamārammaṇaṃ hoti.

343-7. The connection is: “The formless-sphere wholesome also becomes an object-condition.” By ‘three-plane wholesome’ is meant all sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, the wholesome direct knowledge among the form-sphere wholesome states, and the second and fourth wholesome states among the formless-sphere wholesome states. This is the three-plane wholesome. The same method applies to ‘three-plane functional.’ Where it should be said `catutthadutiyānaṃ` (“of the fourth and second”), on account of the meter of the verse the word `catutthadū` is stated, by eliding the inflected word `dutiya`. For these… it is a condition as follows: For the three-plane wholesome, it becomes an object for sense-sphere wholesome consciousness and for the wholesome direct knowledge, in the manner stated concerning form-sphere objects, when the second and fourth formless attainments are taken as object by way of the first and third. Likewise, for the three-plane functional, it becomes an object for the sense-sphere and form-sphere functional consciousness of an Arahant when discerning the formless wholesome kamma in the continuity of a trainee or worldling (whether oneself in the past, or another); and for the formless functional consciousness at the time of an Arahant, when the second and fourth formless attainments are produced based on the first and third formless attainments produced by oneself. It also becomes an object for the unwholesome in the way stated above, and for the fourth and second formless-sphere resultants. Thus the formless wholesome kamma becomes an object for these eight classes of consciousness.

Paricchijja gāhikāya taṇhāya āpannanti pariyāpannaṃ, tebhūmakadhammajātaṃ, na pariyāpannanti apariyāpannaṃ, tadeva puññañcāti apariyāpannapuññaṃ. Kāmāvacaratopi kusalassa kiriyassāti sambandho. Rūpatoti rūpāvacarato. Catunnaṃ…pe… sadāti sekhānaṃ maggapaccavekkhaṇakāle maggārammaṇikakusalābhiññāya parikammādikāle ñāṇasampayuttakusalassa, khīṇāsavānaṃ maggapaccavekkhaṇakāle maggārammaṇikakiriyābhiññāya ca parikammakāle ñāṇasampayuttakiriyacittassa, tesaṃ tesaṃ javanānaṃ purecaravasena pavattikāle manodvārāvajjanassa, sekhānaṃ attano, paresaṃ vā maggajānanakāle abhiññādvayassāti evametesaṃ catunnaṃ rāsīnaṃ apariyāpannakusalamārammaṇaṃ hoti.

That which is included by the delimiting grasp of craving is ‘included’ (`pariyāpanna`), that is, the class of phenomena belonging to the three planes. What is not included is ‘unincluded’ (`apariyāpanna`); that very merit is ‘unincluded merit.’ The connection is with the wholesome and functional of the sense sphere. ‘From the form’ means from the form-sphere. ‘Of the four… always’: For trainees, it becomes an object for wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge at the time of reviewing the path and during the preliminary work for the wholesome direct knowledge that takes the path as object. For Arahants, it becomes an object for functional consciousness associated with knowledge at the time of reviewing the path and during the preliminary work for the functional direct knowledge that takes the path as object. It becomes an object for the mind-door adverting consciousness when it occurs preceding those respective javanas. It becomes an object for the two direct knowledges at the time of knowing the path of a trainee—whether one's own or another's. Thus the unincluded wholesome becomes an object for these four classes of consciousness.

Tathevākusalaṃ…pe… īritanti sekhānaṃ pahīnāvasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇakāle, sekhaputhujjanānaṃ attano, paresaṃ vā santānappavattākusalasammasanakāle, akusalārammaṇikakusalābhiññāya [V 2.0016] parikammādikāle kāmāvacarakusalassa, attano, paresaṃ vā pavattaakusalānussaraṇādīsu rūpāvacarakusalassa, khīṇāsavānaṃ pahīnakilesapaccavekkhaṇaaññasantānagataakusalasammasanādikāle, pahīnakilesapaccavekkhaṇena tussanakāle, sabbesampi taṃtaṃjavanānaṃ purecarakāle ca kāmāvacarakiriyacittassa, kusalābhiññāya vuttanayena rūpāvacarakiriyacittassa, parāmāsaassādanābhinandanādivasena pavattiyaṃ akusalassa, uddhaccarahitakammārammaṇavasena akusalavipākasantīraṇassa, kāmāvacarajavanānaṃ anussaraṇakāle sabbampi [M 2.0021] ekādasatadārammaṇavipākassāti evaṃ kāmāvacaravipākānanti evametesaṃ channaṃ rāsīnaṃ akusalamārammaṇaṃ hoti.

Likewise, the unwholesome… is declared: It becomes an object for sense-sphere wholesome consciousness for trainees at the time of reviewing the defilements abandoned and those remaining; for trainees and worldlings at the time of examining unwholesome states that have occurred in their own or in others’ continuities; and at the time of the preliminary work for the wholesome direct knowledge that takes an unwholesome state as object. It becomes an object for form-sphere wholesome consciousness at the time of recollecting, etc., unwholesome states that have occurred in oneself or in others. It becomes an object for sense-sphere functional consciousness for Arahants at the time of reviewing abandoned defilements and examining unwholesome states in another’s continuity; at the time of delighting in the reviewing of abandoned defilements; and at the time it precedes all those respective javanas. It becomes an object for form-sphere functional consciousness in the case of the wholesome direct knowledge in the way stated. It becomes an object for unwholesome consciousness when this occurs by way of adhering, savoring, delighting, etc. It becomes an object for the unwholesome-resultant investigating consciousness when this takes kamma as its object, free from restlessness. It becomes an object for all eleven resultant registering consciousnesses at the time of recollecting sense-sphere javanas. Thus it is an object for the sense-sphere resultants. In this way, the unwholesome becomes an object for these six classes of consciousness.

348-56. Vipākārammaṇaṃ…pe… paccayoti sekhaputhujjanānaṃ vipākasammasanādikāle kāmāvacarakusalassa, vipākakkhandhānussaraṇādīsu rūpāvacarakusalassa, vuttanayeneva khīṇāsavānaṃ vipākasammasanādikāle, puthujjanakāle aniṭṭhavipākābhāvaṃ ārabbha tussanakāle, yathāvuttajavanānaṃ purecarakāle kāmāvacarakiriyacittassa, kusalesu vuttanayeneva rūpāvacarakiriyacittassa, vipākaṃ ārabbha tadārammaṇappavattiyaṃ vipākārammaṇikakammunā paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantassa kammanimittavasena pavattiyañca kāmāvacaravipākassa, assādanābhinandanaparāmāsādivasena pavattiyaṃ akusalassāti evametesaṃ channaṃ rāsīnaṃ kāmāvacaravipākamārammaṇapaccayo hotīti. Rūpāvacaravipākārammaṇepi imināva nayena yojanā kātabbā. Kevalañhi taṃ kāmāvacaravipākānaṃ kiriyacittesu ca hasituppādassārammaṇaṃ na hotīti ayamettha viseso. Lokuttaravipākassa kāmāvacarakusalakiriyānamārammaṇakkamo appamāṇārammaṇaniddese vuttanayena veditabbo.

348-56. Result as object… and so on… as condition: For trainees and worldlings, at the time of reviewing results, the wholesome sense-sphere consciousness; when recollecting the result aggregates, etc., the wholesome form-sphere consciousness; in the same way for Arahants at the time of reviewing results; for worldlings at the time of being pleased concerning the absence of undesirable results; at the time of the precursor for the previously mentioned javanas, the functional sense-sphere consciousness; in the case of wholesome states, in the same way, the functional form-sphere consciousness; for sense-sphere resultant consciousness, when it occurs as a registering consciousness taking a result as its object, and when it occurs as a kamma-sign for one who takes rebirth-linking through a kamma that had a result as its object; and when unwholesome states arise due to relish, delight, or misapprehension—thus, for these six groups, the sense-sphere result serves as object-condition. The same method should be applied to the form-sphere result as object. The only difference here is that the form-sphere result does not serve as an object for sense-sphere resultants, functional consciousnesses, or the smile-producing consciousness. The sequence of the supramundane result as object for the wholesome and functional sense-sphere consciousnesses should be understood in the way explained in the section on boundless objects.

Kāmāvacarakiriyacittassa kāmāvacarakusalādīnaṃ channaṃ rāsīnamārammaṇakkamo kusalārammaṇe vuttasadisova. Kevalañhi ettha yadetaṃ khīṇāsavasantānasseva niyataṃ navavidhaṃ kiriyacittaṃ, taṃ parasantānappavattakusalākusalassa, sasantāneva sekhaputhujjanakāle anāgatārammaṇikaabhiññāya parikammādivasappavattakusalassa ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Vipākesu [M 2.0022] ca paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutisaṅkhātānaṃ vipākānaṃ kammārammaṇavasena ārammaṇaṃ na hotīti ayameva viseso.

The sequence of sense-sphere functional consciousness serving as an object for the six groups of consciousness beginning with sense-sphere wholesome states is similar to what was stated for the wholesome object. The only distinction here is that the ninefold functional consciousness, which is exclusively for the continuum of an Arahant, serves as an object for wholesome and unwholesome consciousness arising in another's continuum, and for wholesome consciousness arising in one's own continuum during the time of a trainee or worldling, which occurs during the preliminary work, etc., for the direct knowledge that has a future object. And among results, for the resultant consciousnesses designated as rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death, it does not become an object in the sense of a kamma-object. This is the only distinction.

Rūpāvacarakiriyacittassa pañcannaṃ rāsīnaṃ ārammaṇakkamo kusalārammaṇe vuttasadisova. Visesopi [V 2.0017] kāmāvacarakiriyārammaṇe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Āruppakiriyacittassāpi tesaṃ pañcannaṃ rāsīnaṃ gocarabhāvo vuttasadisova. Āruppakiriyassa pana paṭhamatatiyaṃ dutiyacatutthasseva gocaro hoti.

The sequence of form-sphere functional consciousness serving as an object for the five groups is similar to what was stated for the wholesome object. The distinction, too, should be understood in the same way as explained for the object of the sense-sphere functional consciousness. For the formless-sphere functional consciousness too, its being an object for those five groups is similar to what was stated. However, for the formless functional consciousness, the first and third jhānas are the object of the second and fourth jhānas, respectively.

357-8. Evaṃ rūpanibbānavajjitamārammaṇaṃ dassetvā idāni rūpārammaṇaṃ, nibbānārammaṇañca dassetuṃ “rūpaṃ catusamuṭṭhāna”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Rūpanti aṭṭhavīsatividho bhūtopādāyabhedabhinno rūpakkhandho. Kiñcāpi na sabbameva rūpaṃ paccekaṃ catusamuṭṭhānaṃ, samudito pana rūpakkhandho catūhi eva samuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhātīti katvā vuttaṃ “catusamuṭṭhāna”nti. Kāmapākakiriyassāti kāmāvacaravipākassa, kāmāvacarakiriyacittassa ca, tattha ca kāmāvacarakusalassa tāva vaṇṇadānādipuññakiriyakāle, vaṇṇādīnaṃ aniccādivasena sammasanakāle, abhiññāya parikammādikāle, akusalassa assādanābhinandanaparāmāsādikāle, abhiññādvayassa iddhividhabhūtassa suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇādirūpanimmānakāle, pubbenivāsānussatibhūtassa “purimabhave evaṃvaṇṇo ahosi”ntiādinā anussaraṇakāle, dibbacakkhubhūtassa cavamānaupapajjamānasattānaṃ vaṇṇadassanakāle, dibbasotabhūtassa saddasavanakāle, anāgataṃsañāṇabhūtassa “anāgate evaṃvaṇṇo bhavissāmī”tiādinā jānanakāle, kāmāvacaravipākesu dvipañcaviññāṇasampaṭicchanadvayassa yathāyogaṃ rūpādivijānanakāle, sukhasantīraṇassa santīraṇatadārammaṇakāle, upekkhāsantīraṇadvayassa santīraṇatadārammaṇakammanimittagatinimittārammaṇakāle[M 2.0023], sahetukavipākassa kammanimittagatinimittārammaṇakāle, tadārammaṇakāle ca, kāmāvacarakiriyāsu pana kusale vuttanayānusārena aṭṭhamahākiriyacittassa, “evarūpaṃ vaṇṇādimadāsi”nti tussanakāle hasituppādassa, pañcadvāramanodvāresu voṭṭhabbanāvajjanakāle manodvārāvajjanassa, pañcadvāre āvajjanakāle pañcadvārāvajjanassa ca ārammaṇaṃ hotīti evaṃ catusamuṭṭhānikaṃ rūpaṃ channaṃ rāsīnamārammaṇaṃ hoti.

357-8. Having thus shown the object excluding form and Nibbāna, now, to show the object of form and the object of Nibbāna, the passage beginning “Form is of four origins” is introduced. “Form” refers to the form aggregate, of twenty-eight kinds, distinguished as primary elements and derived form. Although not every single form arises from all four origins individually, the form aggregate as a whole arises from these four origins; hence it is said to be “of four origins.” “Of sense-sphere resultant and functional” refers to the sense-sphere resultant consciousness and the sense-sphere functional consciousness.
