In this context, form is an object: for wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, at the time of performing meritorious deeds like giving offerings, at the time of contemplating the impermanence, etc., of forms, and at the time of the preliminary work for direct knowledge; for unwholesome consciousness, at the time of relishing, delighting in, and misapprehending forms, etc.; for the two direct knowledges—that of psychic powers, at the time of creating forms such as golden or ugly ones, and that of recollection of past lives, at the time of recollecting, “In a past life, I had such a form,” etc.; for the divine eye, at the time of seeing the forms of beings passing away and being reborn; for the divine ear, at the time of hearing sounds; for the knowledge of the future, at the time of knowing, “In the future, I will have such a form,” etc.; for sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses—for the ten sense-door consciousnesses and the two receiving consciousnesses, at the time of cognizing forms, etc., as appropriate; for the pleasure-accompanied investigating consciousness, at the time of investigating or registering; for the two equanimity-accompanied investigating consciousnesses, at the time of investigating, registering, or when the object is a kamma-sign or destiny-sign; for the rooted resultant consciousness, when the object is a kamma-sign or destiny-sign, or at the time of registering; for sense-sphere functional consciousnesses—for the eight great functional consciousnesses, following the method described for the wholesome; for the smile-producing consciousness, at the time of rejoicing, thinking, “I gave such a form,” etc.; for the mind-door-adverting consciousness, when it performs the function of determining at the five sense-doors or adverting at the mind-door; and for the five-door-adverting consciousness, at the time of adverting at the five doors. Thus, form arising from four origins becomes the object of six groups.

359-60. Nibbānaṃ pana gotrabhuvodānakāle, nibbānārammaṇikaabhiññāya parikammādikāle ca kāmāvacaratihetukakusalassa, atītabhave sacchikatanirodhānussaraṇakaālādīsu rūpāvacarakusalassa, vuttanayeneva kāmarūpāvacarakiriyacittassa, maggaṭṭhānaṃ tadanantaraphalavaḷañjanaphalakālesu apariyāpannakusalavipākassa cāti evaṃ channaṃ rāsīnaṃ ārammaṇaṃ [V 2.0018] hotīti dassetuṃ “nibbānārammaṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ubhayassāti kāmāvacararūpāvacaravasena duvidhassa.

359-60. Nibbāna becomes the object for six groups: for the triple-rooted wholesome sense-sphere consciousness at the time of change-of-lineage and purification, and at the time of the preliminary work, etc., for the direct knowledge that has Nibbāna as its object; for the wholesome form-sphere consciousness at the time of recollecting the cessation realized in a past existence, etc.; for the functional consciousnesses of the sense-sphere and form-sphere in the manner previously explained; and for the supramundane wholesome (path) and resultant (fruition) consciousnesses at the moments of the path, the immediately following fruition, and the enjoyment of fruition. To indicate that it thus becomes the object for six groups, the passage beginning “having Nibbāna as its object” is stated. “For both” refers to the twofold division into sense-sphere and form-sphere.

361-2. Nānappakārakanti dvādasamaparicchede vakkhamānanayena nānāvidhappakāraṃ. Navannaṃ…pe… paccayoti kāmāvacarakusalassa, akusalassa, hasituppādamanodhātuvajjitakāmāvacarakiriyacittānañceva dvinnaṃ abhiññācittānañca sabbāpi paññatti, rūpāvacarakusalavipākakiriyānaṃ kasiṇanimittādikā, paṭhamāruppakusalavipākakiriyānaṃ ākāsapaññatti, tatiyāruppakusalādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ abhāvapaññattīti evaṃ paññatti navannaṃ rāsīnaṃ ārammaṇapaccayo hotīti.

361-2. “Various kinds” means of various different types, in the way to be described in the twelfth chapter. “Of the nine… as condition”: Concept serves as an object-condition for nine groups as follows: all concepts are objects for sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, unwholesome consciousness, and functional consciousnesses (excluding the smile-producing and the mind-element), and for the two direct-knowledge consciousnesses; the kasiṇa-sign, etc., are objects for form-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses; the concept of space is the object for the first formless-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses; and the concept of nothingness is the object for the three—wholesome, resultant, and functional—of the third formless sphere. Thus, concept serves as the object-condition for these nine groups.

363-5. Evaṃ yo dhammo yassa dhammassa ārammaṇaṃ hoti, taṃ ekekuddhāravasena dassetvā idāni sabbe catubhūmakacittuppāde [M 2.0024] chahi ārammaṇehi yojetvā dassetuṃ “rūpārammaṇikā dve”tiādi gāthāttayaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

363-5. Having thus shown individually which phenomenon serves as an object for which phenomenon, now, to show how all consciousnesses of the four planes are connected with the six objects, the three verses beginning, “Two have form as their object,” are stated. Their meaning is as explained before.

366-9. “Paṭhamāruppakusala”ntiādi pana heṭṭhā vuttanayampi arūpāvacarārammaṇesu arūpāvacaradhammānaṃ sekhāsekhavasena nānappakārato pavattiākāraṃ pakāsetuṃ vuttaṃ. Kusalassāti sekhaputhujjanānaṃ dutiyāruppakusalassa. Vipākassa pana khīṇāsavānaṃ pavattamānassāpi ārammaṇaṃ hoti tassa purimabhave kammanimittārammaṇattā. Arūpabhave atisantabhāvena pavattamānaṃ bhavaṅgacittaṃ na bhāvanāya parisuddhaṃ upaṭṭhātīti āha “paṭhamāruppapāko”tiādi. Paṭhamaṃ tu kiriyacittaṃ puññassa dutiyāruppacetaso ārammaṇaṃ na hoti, vipākassa dutiyāruppacetaso ārammaṇaṃ na hotīti sambandho. Tattha khīṇāsavakāle kassaci kusalassa abhāvato “na puññassā”ti vuttaṃ. Ākāsānañcāyatanakiriyāsamaṅgissa viññāṇañcāyatanavipākacittaṃ na pavattatīti “na pākassā”ti vuttaṃ. Khīṇāsavassa diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthaṃ, nirodhasamāpajjanatthañca samāpattiyo samāpajjantassa paṭhamāruppakiriyacittaṃ dutiyassa ārammaṇaṃ hotīti āha “paṭhamaṃ tu kriyācitta”ntiādi.

366-9. The phrases “first immaterial-sphere wholesome,” etc., are stated to clarify the various ways formless-sphere phenomena occur as objects for immaterial-sphere consciousness, distinguishing between trainees and Arahants, in accordance with the method stated before. “For the wholesome” refers to the second immaterial-sphere wholesome consciousness of trainees and worldlings. For the resultant, even when it occurs in Arahants, it serves as an object because it had a kamma-sign as its object in a previous existence. Because the life-continuum consciousness occurring in the immaterial realm is extremely subtle, it does not appear clearly through meditation—hence, the phrase “first immaterial-sphere resultant,” etc. However, the first functional consciousness is not an object for the wholesome consciousness of the second immaterial sphere, nor is it an object for the resultant consciousness of the second immaterial sphere—this is the connection. In that regard, because an Arahant has no wholesome consciousness, it is said, “not for the wholesome.” Because for one endowed with the functional consciousness of the base of infinite space, the resultant consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness does not occur, it is said, “not for the resultant.” For an Arahant who enters attainments for the sake of a pleasant abiding in this very life or for the attainment of cessation, the first immaterial-sphere functional consciousness becomes an object for the second—hence, the phrase “but the first functional consciousness,” etc.

370-3. “Dvidhā”ti ca vatvā tameva duvidhataṃ, tividhatañca dassetuṃ “kusalaṃ kusalassā”ti, “kriyassāpi kriyā hotī”ti ca ādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ vuttanayameva. Evameva [V 2.0019] …pe… siyāti paṭhamāruppacitte vuttanayena sekhaputhujjanānaṃ dvidhā, khīṇāsavānañca tidhā ārammaṇaṃ bhavatīti attho.

370-3. And having stated “twofold,” to show that same twofoldness and also threefoldness, the phrases “the wholesome for the wholesome,” “the functional also for the functional,” etc., are stated. The meaning is as previously explained. “Just as ... it may be” means: as explained in the case of the first immaterial-sphere consciousness, for trainees and worldlings it becomes an object in two ways, while for Arahants it becomes an object in three ways. This is the meaning.

374-5. Yaṃ yaṃ gocaraṃ ārabbhāti rūpārūpanibbānapaññattīsu yaṃ yaṃ gocaraṃ ārabbha. Ye yeti arūpadhammā. Yo [M 2.0025] naroti yo gahaṭṭho, pabbajito vā māṇavo. Kirāti anumatiyaṃ. Tassa “uttaratevā”ti iminā sambandho. Pāranti avasānaṃ. Taṃ imassa paramanipuṇagambhīranayasamaṅgitāya yāthāvato otarantehi akasirena tarituṃ asakkuṇeyyattā duppāpuṇeyyanti katvā āha “duttara”nti. Uttaranti uttamaṃ. Abhidhammāvatārassa hi uttamatāya tadekadesabhūtapārampi uttamameva hoti. Soti so samuttiṇṇābhidhammāvatārapāro naro. Uttarateva, na pana na sakkoti taṃ uttaritunti attho.

374-5. “Whatever sphere it concerns”: taking as object whatever sphere among form, the formless, Nibbāna, and concepts. “Those”: those that are immaterial states. “Whoever that person is”: whatever man, be he a householder or one gone forth. Kirā is a particle of assent. Its connection is with the phrase “he surely crosses over.” Pāraṃ means the end. Because it is difficult to attain (duppāpuṇeyyaṃ), since for those who are penetrating according to reality its nature endowed with a most subtle and profound method, it is impossible to cross without difficulty, he says it is “hard to cross” (duttara). Uttaraṃ means supreme. Since the Abhidhammāvatāra is supreme, even the “far shore” (pāraṃ), which is a part of it, is supreme. So means that person who has crossed over to the far shore of the Abhidhammāvatāra. “He surely crosses over”: the meaning is that it is not that he is unable to cross it.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the Commentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma,

Ārammaṇavibhāganiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the commentary on the exposition of the analysis of objects is concluded.

7. Sattamo paricchedo

7. The Seventh Section

Vipākacittappavattiniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition on the Occurrence of Resultant Consciousness

376. Anantañāṇenāti anantārammaṇe pavattañāṇena. Niraṅgaṇenāti ettha rāgādayo akusalā aṅganti etehi taṃsamaṅgino puggalā nihīnabhāvaṃ gacchantīti aṅgaṇāti vuccanti. Yathāha –

376. “By boundless knowledge” (anantañāṇena) means by knowledge that occurs in regard to limitless objects. “Stainless” (niraṅgaṇena): Here, unwholesome states such as lust are called “stains” (aṅgaṇa) because persons endowed with them fall into a low state. As it is said:

“Rāgo aṅgaṇaṃ, doso aṅgaṇaṃ, moho aṅgaṇaṃ, pāpakānaṃ kho, āvuso, akusalānaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ adhivacanaṃ yadidaṃ aṅgaṇa”nti ca ādi (vibha. 924).

“Lust is a stain, aversion is a stain, delusion is a stain. Friends, ‘stain’ is a designation for evil, unwholesome states that operate through desire.” (Vibh. §924)

Attano [V 2.0020] santāne sīlādiguṇe esī gavesīti guṇesī, tena guṇesinā. Karuṇāyaṃ niyutto, sā assa atthīti vā kāruṇiko, tena kāruṇikena. Ettha [M 2.0026] ca “anantañāṇenā”ti iminā bhagavato sabbaññubhāvamāha, “niraṅgaṇenā”ti khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ, “guṇesinā”ti pubbacariyaṃ, “kāruṇikenā”ti mahākaruṇāsamaṅgibhāvaṃ. Ettakena pana thomanena bhagavato vipākadesanāya niyyānikādibhāvaṃ dīpeti. Asabbaññunā hi desitaṃ aniyyānikaṃ hoti, akhīṇāsavena desitaṃ na pākaṭaṃ, apuññavatā desitaṃ nappatiṭṭhāti, akāruṇikena vuttaṃ sukhadāyakaṃ na hoti. Bhagavato pana sabbaññubhāvato tena desitaṃ niyyānikaṃ, khīṇāsavattā pākaṭaṃ, puññavantatāya patiṭṭhāti, mahākaruṇāsamaṅgitāya sukhadāyakanti. Cittappabhavanti vipākacittānaṃ uppattiṃ.

“One who seeks virtues” (guṇesī) means one who seeks virtues such as morality in his own continuum; by him who seeks virtues (guṇesinā). “Compassionate” (kāruṇiko) means one devoted to compassion, or one who possesses it; by him who is compassionate (kāruṇikena). Here, by “by boundless knowledge” (anantañāṇena) is stated the Blessed One's omniscience; by “stainless” (niraṅgaṇena) his state of being free from defilements (khīṇāsavabhāva); by “one who seeks virtues” (guṇesinā) his past conduct (pubbacariya); and by “compassionate” (kāruṇikena) his possession of great compassion (mahākaruṇāsamaṅgibhāva). By this much praise, the Blessed One's teaching on results is shown to be leading to liberation, etc. For if taught by one not omniscient, it would not lead to liberation; if taught by one not free from defilements, it would not be clear; if taught by one without merit, it would not be established; if spoken by one without compassion, it would not bring happiness. But because the Blessed One is omniscient, his teaching leads to liberation; because he is free from defilements, it is clear; because he is meritorious, it is established; and because he possesses great compassion, it brings happiness. “The arising of consciousness” (cittappabhava) means the arising of resultant consciousness (vipākacittānaṃ uppatti).

377-86. Idāni vipākakathāya mātikāvasena aṭṭhakathāya ṭhapite dasappakāre dassetuṃ “ekūnatiṃsa kammānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathāraddhāya vipākakathāya mūlakāraṇabhāvato “ekūnatiṃsa kammānī”ti paṭhamaṃ kammavavatthānaṃ kataṃ. Kamme pana kathite vipākakathāya adhiṭṭhānabhūtā vipākāpi kathetabbāti “pākā dvattiṃsa dassitā”ti dutiyaṃ vipākavavatthānaṃ kataṃ. Kammavipākānañca advāresu adissanato “tīsu…pe… dissare”ti tatiyaṃ kammadvāravipākadvārā vuttā. Kammavipākānaṃ vacanappasaṅgeyeva ekasseva kammassa taṃ taṃ paccayamāgamma anekaphalanipphādanaṃ dassetuṃ “kusalaṃ…pe… vividhaṃ phala”nti catutthaṃ kāmāvacarakusalassa pavattipaṭisandhīsu nānāphalanipphādanaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vutte pana pavattipaṭisandhīnaṃ labbhamānavipākavasena vuttabhāvaṃ ajānantā –

377-86. Now, to show the ten types established in the commentary by way of the outline of the discussion on results, it is said, beginning with “twenty-nine types of kamma,” etc. Therein, because kamma is the fundamental cause of the discussion on results that has been undertaken, the classification of kamma is made first. But when kamma has been discussed, the results, which are the basis for the discussion on results, must also be discussed. Thus, “thirty-two results are shown” is the second classification of results. And since kamma and its results are not seen apart from the doors, “in three... they are seen” is the third statement of the doors of kamma and the doors of results. In the context of speaking about kamma and its results, to show how a single kamma, by encountering that particular condition, produces diverse results, “wholesome... various fruits” is the fourth statement, showing how wholesome kamma in the sensuous realm produces diverse fruits in the course of existence and rebirth-linking. But having said this, those who do not understand that what has been said is in terms of the results obtainable in the course of existence and rebirth-linking—

“Tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesenā”ti;

“Ekaṃ pupphaṃ cajitvāna, asītikappakoṭiyo;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmī”ti. ca –

“By the remaining result of that very kamma,” and “Having offered one flower, for eighty crores of aeons, I do not experience a bad destination.”

Evamādivacanassa [M 2.0027] byañjanacchāyāya atthaṃ gahetvā dinnapaṭisandhikāyapi cetanāya puna paṭisandhidānaṃ maññeyyunti “ekāya…pe… pakāsitā”ti pañcamaṃ ekena kammena ekissāyeva paṭisandhiyā nibbattanaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekasmiṃ bhave nānākammassa vipākappavattiṃ suṇantā “disvā kumāraṃ satapuññalakkhaṇa”ntiādivacanassa atthaṃ ajānantā “nānākammena ekāva [V 2.0021] paṭisandhi hotī”ti cinteyyunti “nānā…pe… paṭisandhiyo”ti chaṭṭhaṃ nānākammassa nānāpaṭisandhidānaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā vipaccantassa ca ekassa kammassa soḷasa vipākāni dvādasamaggo ahetukaṭṭhakampīti ayaṃ vipākavibhāgo hetubhedavasena hotīti dassanatthaṃ “tihetukaṃ…pe… na ca hoti tihetukā”ti sattamaṃ aṭṭhakathāya āgatahetukittanaṃ dassitaṃ. Taṃ pana hetukittanaṃ ekekassa kammassa vipākavibhāgadassanatthanti. Idāni tipiṭakacūḷanāgattherassa, moravāpivāsimahādattattherassa, tipiṭakamahādhammarakkhitattherassāti tiṇṇaṃ therānaṃ vādesu “ekāya cetanāya dvādasa vipākāni ettheva dasakamaggo ahetukaṭṭhakampī”ti āgatassa dutiyattheravādassa, “ekāya cetanāya dasa vipākāni ettheva ahetukaṭṭhakampī”ti āgatassa tatiyattherassa vādassa ca na sammāpatiṭṭhitattā suppatiṭṭhitassa paṭhamattheravādassa vasena dassetuṃ vipākesu asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāravidhānaṃ paccayabalena hoti, no kammabalenāti dīpanatthaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ, “asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāra”ntiādinā kammena saha asamānampi katvā saṅkhārabhedo vutto. Kammassa somanassupekkhāsahagatabhāvepi ārammaṇavaseneva vipākavedanāya parivattanaṃ dassetuṃ “ārammaṇena…pe… parivattana”nti navamaṃ ārammaṇena vedanāparivattanaṃ vuttaṃ. Kammavasena ceva ārammaṇavasena ca aniyatassa tadārammaṇassa javanavasena niyamadassanatthaṃ “tadārammaṇa…pe… niyāmita”nti dasamaṃ javanena tadārammaṇaniyamo vuttoti.

By grasping the meaning of such statements through their wording and implication, one might think that even a volition that has already given rebirth-linking can again provide rebirth-linking. Therefore, the fifth section states that a single kamma produces only one rebirth-linking: "By one... as explained." Hearing that various kammas bear fruit in a single existence, and not understanding the meaning of statements like "seeing the young prince endowed with the marks of a hundred merits," one might think, "A single rebirth-linking arises from multiple kammas." To clarify this, the sixth section states that different kammas produce different rebirth-linkings: "By various... rebirth-linkings." Similarly, to show that this classification of results (vipāka) occurs based on the distinction of roots (hetu)—where a single ripening kamma can produce sixteen results, with the twelfth being the rootless eightfold result (ahetukaṭṭhaka)—the seventh section demonstrates the enumeration of roots that came down in the commentary: "Triple-rooted... and not triple-rooted." This enumeration of roots is intended to show the classification of results for each individual kamma. Now, regarding the views of three elders—Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga Thera, Moravāpivāsī Mahādatta Thera, and Tipiṭaka Mahādhammarakkhita Thera—the second elder’s view, "From a single volition, twelve results arise, including the tenfold kamma-path and the rootless eightfold result," and the third elder’s view, "From a single volition, ten results arise, including the rootless eightfold result," are not well-established. Therefore, to present the well-established view of the first elder, the eighth section explains that the distinction between unprompted (asaṅkhāra) and prompted (sasaṅkhāra) results occurs due to the power of conditions (paccaya), not the power of kamma. The eighth section, beginning with "unprompted (asaṅkhāra) and prompted (sasaṅkhāra)," states the distinction of promptedness, even though it is not the same as that of the kamma. Though kamma is accompanied by joy (somanassa) or equanimity (upekkhā), the resulting feeling (vipākavedanā) changes solely based on the object (ārammaṇa). Thus, the ninth section states: "By the object... the change occurs," showing how feeling transforms due to the object. To demonstrate the determination (niyama) of the registering consciousness (tadārammaṇa), which is undetermined by kamma and object, but determined by the impulsion (javana), the tenth section states: "The registering... is determined," explaining how the registering consciousness is regulated by the impulsion.

Ekūnatiṃsa [M 2.0028] kammānīti kusalākusalavasena vīsati parittāni, nava mahaggatānīti ekūnatiṃsa kammāni. Yasmā panesā vaṭṭavasena vipākakathā, tasmā lokuttarakusalaṃ vajjetvā ekūnatiṃseva kammāni vuttāni. Evaṃ “pākā dvattiṃsā”ti etthāpi tevīsati parittā, nava mahaggatāti pākā dvattiṃsa. Tīsu dvāresūti kāyavacīmanodvāravasena tīsu kammadvāresu. Kammadvāravavatthānaṃ heṭṭhā saṅkhepato dassitameva. Vitthārato panetaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāya (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāyakammadvāra), taṃsaṃvaṇṇanādito ca gahetabbaṃ. Kāmaṃ kammānipi chasu dvāresu pavattanti, pañcadvārappavattāni pana avipākāni, manodvāradvārattayavasena bhinnānaṃ vipākadāyakānameva saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ “tīsu dvāresū”ti vuttaṃ. Chasūti cakkhudvārādīni pañca, manodvārañcāti chasu vipākadvāresu.

"Twenty-nine types of kamma" (ekūnatiṃsa kammāni) means twenty sense-sphere (paritta) wholesome and unwholesome actions, and nine lofty (mahaggata) actions, making twenty-nine in total. Since this discussion of results (vipāka) concerns the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa), the supramundane (lokuttara) wholesome kamma is excluded, hence only twenty-nine types of kamma are mentioned. Thus, with "thirty-two results" (pākā dvattiṃsa), there are twenty-three sense-sphere (paritta) and nine lofty (mahaggata) results. "In three doors" (tīsu dvāresu) means in the three kamma doors: the doors of body, speech, and mind. A concise definition of kamma doors has already been provided below. But for a more detailed explanation, one should consult the Aṭṭhasālinī, the commentary to the Dhammasaṅgaṇī (DhsA. 1, Kāyakammadvāra), and its sub-commentary. Although kamma does occur in all six doors, what occurs through the five sense-doors is non-resultant; thus "in three doors" is said to include only those that give a result, namely, those occurring through the three doors of kamma: body, speech, and mind. "In six" (chasu) means in the six doors of result, that is, the five doors beginning with the eye-door, and the mind-door.

Taṃ taṃ paccayamāgammāti kālasampadādikaṃ taṃ taṃ paccayamāgamma. Tenāhu porāṇā –

"By encountering that particular condition" (taṃ taṃ paccayamāgamma) means by encountering that particular condition such as timely fulfillment (kālasampadādikaṃ). Therefore, the ancients said:

“Kālopadhippayogānaṃ[V 2.0022], gatiyā ca yathārahaṃ;

Sampattiñca vipattiñca, kammamāgamma paccatī”ti.

"Depending on time, basis, and application, and on destiny, as is proper, and on success and failure, the fruit of kamma ripens."

Atha vā taṃ taṃ paccayanti somanassādihetubhūtaṃ taṃ taṃ sahakāripaccayaṃ. Vividhaṃ phalanti somanassupekkhāsahagatasahetukāhetukaasaṅkhārasasaṅkhāravasena nānappakāraphalaṃ. Ekāya cetanāyāti upapajjavedanīyabhūtāya, aparāpariyavedanīyabhūtāya vā ekāya cetanāya. Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyabhūtā pana pavattivipākameva nibbatteti, no paṭisandhiṃ.

Alternatively, "that particular condition" (taṃ taṃ paccayaṃ) means that particular cooperative condition (sahakāripaccayaṃ) which is the cause of joy, etc. "Various fruits" (vividhaṃ phalaṃ) means various kinds of fruits, such as those accompanied by joy or equanimity, with roots or without roots (sahetuka or ahetuka), and unprompted or prompted (asaṅkhāra or sasaṅkhāra). "By a single volition" (ekāya cetanāya) means by a single volition that is either of the nature to be experienced in the next becoming (upapajjavedanīyabhūtā) or of the nature to be experienced in subsequent becomings (aparāpariyavedanīyabhūtā). However, a volition of the nature to be experienced in this very life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīyabhūtā) produces only results in the course of life (pavattivipāka), and not rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

Kiñcāpi “tihetuka”nti avisesena vuttaṃ, ukkaṭṭhameva pana tihetukakammaṃ tihetukavipākaṃ deti, tathā duhetukampi [M 2.0029] ukkaṭṭhameva duhetukavipākaṃ deti. Omakaṃ pana tihetukakammaṃ duhetukukkaṭṭhasadisaṃ, duhetukāhetukameva vipākaṃ deti. Tathā duhetukampi ahetukameva vipākaṃ detīti. Ukkaṭṭhomakavibhāgo ca panesa kusalākusalaparivāralābhato, āsevanavippaṭisārappavattiyā vā daṭṭhabbo. Yañhi kammaṃ attano pavattikāle purimapacchābhāgappavattehi kusaladhammehi parivāritaṃ, pacchā vā āsevanalābhena samudāciṇṇaṃ, taṃ ukkaṭṭhaṃ. Yaṃ pana karaṇakāle akusaladhammehi parivāritaṃ, pacchā vā “dukkaṭaṃ mayā”ti vippaṭisāruppādanena paribhāvitaṃ, taṃ omakaṃ nāma hoti.

Although "triple-rooted" (tihetuka) is stated generally, only a strong (ukkaṭṭha) triple-rooted kamma gives a triple-rooted result. Similarly, a strong double-rooted kamma gives a double-rooted result. A weak (omaka) triple-rooted kamma, however, being similar to a strong double-rooted one, gives a double-rooted or rootless result. Likewise, a weak double-rooted kamma gives only a rootless result. This distinction between strong and weak is to be understood by the acquisition of wholesome or unwholesome associated factors, or by the occurrence of repeated practice or remorse. For that kamma which, at the time of its occurrence, is surrounded by wholesome factors occurring before and after, or is later accumulated through repeated practice, is strong (ukkaṭṭha). But that which, at the time of doing, is surrounded by unwholesome factors, or is later impaired by the arising of remorse, thinking "I have done wrong," is called weak (omaka).

Athettha yathāvuttavidhānaṃ kiṃ paṭisandhipavattīnaṃ avisesena, udāhu pavattivasenevāti ce? Pavattivaseneva, paṭisandhiyaṃ pana ayaṃ visesoti dassento āha “tihetukenā”tiādi. Etthāpi tihetukukkaṭṭhakammeneva tihetukapaṭisandhi hoti, omakena pana duhetukukkaṭṭhena ca duhetukā paṭisandhi, duhetukomakena pana ahetukāvāti ayaṃ viseso veditabbo. Yasmā panettha ñāṇaṃ jaccandhādivipattinimittassa mohassa, sabbākusalassa vā paṭipakkhaṃ, tasmā taṃsampayuttaṃ kammaṃ jaccandhādivipattipaccayaṃ na hotīti tihetukaṃ atidubbalampi samānaṃ duhetukapaṭisandhimeva ākaḍḍhati, nāhetukanti āha “na ca hoti ahetukā”ti. Yasmā paṭisambhidāmagge sugatiyaṃ jaccandhabadhirādivipattiyā ahetukūpapattiṃ vajjetvā gatisampattiyā ahetukūpapattiṃ dassentena dhammasenāpatinā –

Here, is the aforementioned procedure without distinction between rebirth-linking and the course of life, or is it by way of the course of life alone? It is by way of the course of life alone. But regarding rebirth-linking, showing this distinction, it is said 'by the triple-rooted' and so on. Here too, this distinction should be understood: only by strong triple-rooted kamma does triple-rooted rebirth-linking occur; by weak triple-rooted and by strong double-rooted kamma, double-rooted rebirth-linking occurs; and by weak double-rooted kamma, rootless rebirth-linking occurs. Since knowledge here is the opposite of delusion—which is the cause of defects like congenital blindness—or the opposite of all unwholesome states, kamma associated with it does not become a condition for defects like congenital blindness. Thus, even when it is extremely weak, triple-rooted kamma still draws only a double-rooted rebirth-linking, not a rootless one. Hence it is said, 'nor does a rootless one occur.' Because in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the General of the Dhamma, having excluded rootless arising with defects like congenital blindness and deafness, and showing rootless arising with the attainment of a good destiny, said—

“Gatisampattiyā ñāṇasampayutte aṭṭhannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hoti, gatisampattiyā [V 2.0023] ñāṇasampayutte katamesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hoti? Kusalassa kammassa javanakkhaṇe tayo hetū kusalā tasmiṃ khaṇe jātacetanāya sahajātapaccayā [M 2.0030] honti, tena vuccati kusalamūlapaccayāpi saṅkhārā. Nikantikkhaṇe dve hetū akusalā tasmiṃ khaṇe jātacetanāya sahajātapaccayā honti, tena vuccati akusalamūlapaccayāpi saṅkhārā. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe tayo hetū abyākatā tasmiṃ khaṇe jātacetanāya sahajātapaccayā honti, tena vuccati nāmarūpapaccayāpi viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayāpi nāmarūpa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.231-232) –

“For a fortunate rebirth associated with knowledge, arising occurs conditioned by eight roots. For a fortunate rebirth associated with knowledge, conditioned by which eight roots does arising occur? At the moment of the impulsion of wholesome kamma, three wholesome roots are a conascent condition for the volition arising at that moment; therefore it is said that formations are conditioned by wholesome roots. At the moment of desire, two unwholesome roots are a conascent condition for the volition arising at that moment; therefore it is said that formations are conditioned by unwholesome roots. At the moment of rebirth-linking, three indeterminate roots are a conascent condition for the volition arising at that moment; therefore it is said that name-and-form conditions consciousness, and consciousness conditions name-and-form.” (Paṭi. Ma. 1.231-232)

Evaṃ javanakkhaṇe tiṇṇaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā ñāṇasampayuttavipākuppatti vuttā, na pana “javanakkhaṇe dvinnaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā”ti, tasmā tihetukakammeneva tihetukapaṭisandhi hoti, na duhetukenāti āha “duhetukena…pe… na ca hoti tihetukā”ti. Yadi hi duhetukakammena tihetukapaṭisandhi siyā, yathā “aṭṭhannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hotī”ti vatvā tassa vibhaṅgo kato, evaṃ “gatisampattiyā ñāṇasampayutte sattannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hoti. Gatisampattiyā ñāṇasampayutte katamesaṃ sattannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hoti? Kusalassa kammassa javanakkhaṇe dve hetū kusalā tasmiṃ khaṇe…pe… saṅkhārā, nikantikkhaṇe dve hetū akusalā tasmiṃ khaṇe…pe… saṅkhārā, paṭisandhikkhaṇe tayo hetū abyākatā tasmiṃ khaṇe…pe… nāmarūpa”nti sattannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā ñāṇasampayuttūpapattiṃ vatvā tassa vibhaṅgo kātabbo siyā, na ca panevaṃ atthi, tasmā viññāyati “duhetukakammena tihetukapaṭisandhi na hotī”ti.

Thus, the arising of a result associated with knowledge is stated as conditioned by three roots at the javana-moment, but not as 'conditioned by two roots at the javana-moment.' Therefore, only by three-rooted kamma does three-rooted rebirth-linking occur, not by two-rooted kamma. Hence it is said: 'By two-rooted... it is not three-rooted.' For if three-rooted rebirth-linking were to occur by two-rooted kamma, then just as it was said, 'Arising occurs conditioned by eight roots,' and its analysis was given, so too it would have to be said, 'In a fortunate destination associated with knowledge, arising occurs conditioned by seven roots. In a fortunate destination associated with knowledge, conditioned by which seven roots does arising occur? At the javana-moment of wholesome kamma, two wholesome roots at that moment... formations; at the moment of craving, two unwholesome roots at that moment... formations; at the moment of rebirth-linking, three indeterminate roots at that moment... name-and-form.' Having stated that arising associated with knowledge occurs conditioned by seven roots, its analysis would have to be given. But this is not the case. Therefore, it is understood: 'Three-rooted rebirth-linking does not occur by two-rooted kamma.'

Yadi evaṃ –

If so—

“Gatisampattiyā ñāṇavippayutte channaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hoti. Gatisampattiyā ñāṇavippayutte katamesaṃ…pe… [M 2.0031] hoti? Kusalassa kammassa javanakkhaṇe dve hetū kusalā tasmiṃ khaṇe…pe… saṅkhārā. Nikantikkhaṇe dve hetū akusalā tasmiṃ khaṇe…pe… saṅkhārā. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe dve hetū abyākatā tasmiṃ khaṇe…pe… nāmarūpa”nti –

“In a fortunate destination dissociated from knowledge, arising occurs conditioned by six roots. In a fortunate destination dissociated from knowledge, conditioned by which six roots does arising occur? At the javana-moment of wholesome kamma, two wholesome roots at that moment... formations. At the moment of craving, two unwholesome roots at that moment... formations. At the moment of rebirth-linking, two indeterminate roots at that moment... name-and-form.”

Evaṃ [V 2.0024] duhetukakammena duhetukūpapattiṃ uddharitvā “gatisampattiyā ñāṇavippayutte sattannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hoti. Gatisampattiyā ñāṇavippayutte katamesaṃ sattannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hoti? Kusalassa kammassa javanakkhaṇe tayo hetū kusalā tasmiṃ khaṇe…pe… saṅkhārā. Nikantikkhaṇe dve hetū akusalā tasmiṃ khaṇe…pe… saṅkhārā. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe dve hetū abyākatā tasmiṃ khaṇe…pe… nāmarūpa”nti evaṃ tihetukakammena duhetukapaṭisandhiyāpi anuddhaṭattā sāpi na hotīti ce? No na hoti, duhetukomakakammena ahetukapaṭisandhiyā viya tihetukomakena duhetukapaṭisandhiyāva dātabbattā, kammasarikkhakavipākadassanatthaṃ pana mahātherena pāṭho sāvaseso kato.

Thus, having set forth the two-rooted arising by two-rooted kamma, if it is asked: since a two-rooted rebirth-linking by three-rooted kamma has not been set forth—as in, 'In a fortunate destination dissociated from knowledge, arising occurs conditioned by seven roots. In a fortunate destination dissociated from knowledge, conditioned by which seven roots does arising occur? At the javana-moment of wholesome kamma, three wholesome roots at that moment... formations. At the moment of craving, two unwholesome roots at that moment... formations. At the moment of rebirth-linking, two indeterminate roots at that moment... name-and-form'—does this mean it also does not occur? No, it is not that it does not occur. For just as rootless rebirth-linking is to be accounted for by weak two-rooted kamma, so too two-rooted rebirth-linking is to be accounted for by weak three-rooted kamma. However, the Great Elder has left the text incomplete for the purpose of showing that the result is similar to the kamma.

Yadi evaṃ purimavuttehi idaṃ samānaṃ kammasarikkhakatābhāvatoti duhetukakammena tihetukapaṭisandhi na uddhaṭā, na pana alabbhanatoti? Taṃ na, akusalakammassa alobhasampayogābhāvato, alobhaphaluppādane viya ñāṇavippayuttassa ñāṇaphaluppādane asamatthabhāvato. Paññābalasampayogato hi taṃñāṇaphaluppādane samatthaṃ hoti.

If so, is it that three-rooted rebirth-linking by two-rooted kamma was not set forth because this case is similar to the previous ones—that is, due to the lack of similarity between the kamma and its result—and not because it is simply unobtainable? That is not so. It is because that which is dissociated from knowledge is incapable of producing a knowledge-result, just as unwholesome kamma is incapable of producing a result of non-greed due to its lack of association with non-greed. For it is only through association with the power of wisdom that it becomes capable of producing that knowledge-result.

Etthāha – kiṃ panetaṃ kammameva paṭisandhiṃ dentaṃ attanā sadisavedanameva deti, udāhu visadisavedanampīti? Duhetukomakameva visadisavedanaṃ deti, itaraṃ pana sadisavedanameva[M 2.0032]. Tathā hi papañcasūdaniyā majjhimaṭṭhakathāya mahākammavibhaṅgasutte sukhavedanīyādikammavaṇṇanāya –

Here it is asked: Does this kamma, when giving rebirth-linking, give rise only to a feeling similar to itself, or also to a dissimilar feeling? Only weak two-rooted kamma gives rise to a dissimilar feeling, while the other gives rise only to a similar feeling. Thus, in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, in the Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta, in the description of kamma to be experienced pleasantly and so on—

“Kāmāvacarakusalato somanassasahagatacittasampayuttā catasso cetanā, rūpāvacarakusalato catukkajjhānacetanāti evaṃ paṭisandhipavattesu sukhavedanāya jananato sukhavedanīyaṃ kammaṃ nāma. Kāmāvacarañcettha paṭisandhiyaṃyeva ekantena sukhaṃ janeti, pavatte pana iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇe adukkhamasukhampi.

“From wholesome sense-sphere kamma, four volitions associated with a mind accompanied by joy, and from wholesome form-sphere kamma, the volitions of the four jhānas—thus, because they generate pleasant feeling at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence, they are called ‘kamma to be experienced pleasantly.’ Herein, sense-sphere kamma generates exclusively pleasant feeling only at rebirth-linking, but during the course of existence, with a desirable or neutral object, it may also generate neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

“Akusalacetanā pavatte kāyadvārappavattadukkhassa jananato dukkhavedanīyaṃ kammaṃ nāma.

“Unwholesome volitions, because they generate suffering that occurs through the body-door during the course of existence, are called ‘kamma to be experienced painfully.’”

“Kāmāvacarakusalato pana upekkhāsahagatacittasampayuttā catasso cetanā, rūpāvacarakusalato catutthajjhānacetanāti evaṃ paṭisandhipavattesu tatiyavedanāya jananato adukkhamasukhavedanīyaṃ [V 2.0025] kammaṃ nāma. Ettha ca “kāmāvacaraṃ paṭisandhiyaṃyeva ekantena adukkhamasukhaṃ janeti, pavatte iṭṭhārammaṇe sukhampī”ti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.300) –

“From wholesome sense-sphere kamma, four volitions associated with a mind accompanied by equanimity, and from wholesome form-sphere kamma, the volition of the fourth jhāna—thus, because they generate the third feeling, that is, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence, they are called ‘kamma to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.’ And herein it is said: ‘Sense-sphere kamma generates exclusively neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling at rebirth-linking, but during the course of existence, with a desirable object, it may also produce pleasant feeling’” (Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 3.300).

Vuttaṃ. Nanu ca “ārammaṇena hoteva, vedanāparivattana”nti vacanato ārammaṇavasena vedanāniyamo hoti, na ca somanassasahagatakammena paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantassa iṭṭhārammaṇameva kammanimittādikamāpāthamāgacchatīti niyamo atthi, upekkhāsahagatakammena vā iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇanti na sakkā vattuṃ, tasmā kathaṃ kammavaseneva vedanāniyamoti? Vuccate – iṭṭhādiārammaṇampi āpāthamāgacchantaṃ kammabaleneva āgacchatīti somanassasahagatakammena paṭisandhiggahaṇakāle tassa balena iṭṭhārammaṇamāpāthamāgacchati, upekkhāsahagatakammena [M 2.0033] iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇanti na na sakkā vattuṃ, tasmā kammavasena paṭisandhiyā ārammaṇaniyamo, ārammaṇavasena vedanāniyamoti. Apica “ārammaṇena hoteva, vedanāparivattana”nti idaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttanti na tena paṭisandhiyā kammasarikkhakavedanābhāvo paṭikkhipituṃ sakkā, duhetukomakaṃ pana somanassasahagatampi attano nihīnatāya duhetukaphaluppādane asamatthattā, ahetukāya ca attanā sadisavedanāya paṭisandhiyā asambhavato upekkhāsahagatapaṭisandhiyā anurūpato iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇamupaṭṭhapetvā tadārammaṇaṃ upekkhāsahagatameva paṭisandhiṃ deti.

It has been said. But is it not stated, ‘The change of feeling is indeed due to the object,’ so that the determination of feeling is based on the object? And there is no rule that for one who takes rebirth-linking through kamma accompanied by joy, only a desirable object such as a kamma-sign comes into range; nor can it be said that for one with kamma accompanied by equanimity, a desirable or neutral object always appears. Therefore, how can the determination of feeling be based solely on kamma? It is replied: Even a desirable, etc., object comes into range only by the power of kamma. Thus, at the moment of taking rebirth-linking with kamma accompanied by joy, a desirable object comes into range due to that kamma's power. And it can indeed be said that for one with kamma accompanied by equanimity, a desirable or neutral object appears. Therefore, the determination of the object at rebirth-linking is based on kamma, and the determination of feeling is based on the object. Moreover, the statement, ‘The change of feeling is indeed due to the object,’ was said in reference to the registering consciousness (tadārammaṇa), and therefore it cannot be used to reject that the feeling at rebirth-linking is similar to the kamma. However, weak two-rooted kamma, even if accompanied by joy, is incapable of producing a two-rooted result due to its inferiority. And since a rebirth-linking with a feeling similar to itself is impossible for a rootless consciousness, it presents a desirable or neutral object suitable for a rebirth-linking accompanied by equanimity, and having that as its object, it gives rise to a rebirth-linking accompanied only by equanimity.

Nanu ca “pacchimabhavikamahābodhisattānaṃ mettāpubbabhāgaṃ somanassakammaṃ paṭisandhiṃ detī”ti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ, mahāsivatthero ca upekkhāsahagatañāṇasampayuttaasaṅkhārikavipākacittena paṭisandhiṃ icchati. Vuttañhi tena “somanassasahagatato upekkhāsahagataṃ balavataraṃ, tena paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanti, tena gahitapaṭisandhikā hi mahajjhāsayā honti tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero viyā”ti, tasmā somanassasahagatakusalato upekkhāsahagatapaṭisandhipi labbhati yathā ca, evaṃ tathā upekkhāsahagatato somanassasahagatāpīti kathaṃ kammasadisavedanā paṭisandhīti? Etthāpi ca kammampi upekkhāsahagatamevāti therassa adhippāyo siyāti sakkā vattuṃ. Apicāyaṃ vādo mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ paṭikkhittova. Tathā hi vuttaṃ saṅgahakārehi “aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ayaṃ therassa manoratho, natthi eta”nti paṭikkhipitvā sabbaññubodhisattānaṃ hitūpacāro balavā hoti, tasmā mettāpubbabhāgakāmāvacarakusalavipākasomanassasahagatatihetukaasaṅkhārikacittena paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantīti [V 2.0026] vuttanti, tasmā paṭikkhittavādaṃ [M 2.0034] gahetvā na sakkā aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ cāletunti sampaṭicchitabbamevetaṃ kammasadisavedanā paṭisandhīti. Asampaṭicchantehi vā aṭṭhakathāya adhippāyo sādhukaṃ kathetabboti.

Moreover, is it not stated in the commentaries that “for the great Bodhisattas in their final existence, a joyful kamma with a preliminary part of loving-kindness gives rebirth-linking”? Yet, the Elder Mahāsīva maintains that rebirth-linking occurs through an unprompted resultant consciousness accompanied by equanimity and conjoined with knowledge. For he said: “That which is accompanied by equanimity is stronger than that which is accompanied by joy, thus they take rebirth-linking with it. Those who are reborn with such rebirth-linking possess great resolve, like the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga.” Therefore, just as rebirth-linking accompanied by equanimity can be obtained from wholesome kamma accompanied by joy, so too, from kamma accompanied by equanimity, can that which is accompanied by joy be obtained. So how can rebirth-linking have a feeling similar to the kamma? Here, it may also be said that the Elder’s intention might be that the kamma itself was accompanied by equanimity. However, this view has been rejected in the Great Commentary. For the compilers, having rejected it, stated: “In the commentary, this is merely the Elder’s wishful thinking; this is not the case.” And they said: “The beneficial practice of the omniscient Bodhisattas is powerful. Therefore, they take rebirth-linking with a triple-rooted, unprompted, sense-sphere wholesome-resultant consciousness accompanied by joy, with a preliminary part of loving-kindness.” Thus, by taking up a rejected view, it is not possible to challenge the statement of the commentary, and this must be accepted: rebirth-linking has a feeling similar to the kamma. Or, for those who do not accept this, the intention of the commentary should be well explained.

Asaṅkhāranti asaṅkhārikakammaṃ. Asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhārampi phalaṃ detīti sambandho.

‘Unprompted’ means unprompted kamma. The connection is that unprompted kamma also gives a prompted result.

Ārammaṇenāti iṭṭhādiārammaṇena. Vedanāparivattananti tassa tassa ārammaṇassa anurūpato somanassādivedanāya parivattanaṃ, kusalavipākasantīraṇatadārammaṇāni sandhāya cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tāni hi iṭṭhārammaṇe somanassasahagatāni, iṭṭhamajjhatte upekkhāsahagatāni. Akusalavipākaṃ pana santīraṇatadārammaṇaṃ aniṭṭhe, aniṭṭhamajjhatte ca ārammaṇe upekkhāsahagatameva. Na hi tassa ārammaṇavasena vedanābhedo atthi, heṭṭhā vuttanayena dvīsupi upekkhāsahagatameva. Dvipañcaviññāṇasampaṭicchanesu ca ṭhapetvā kāyaviññāṇadvayaṃ sesāni iṭṭhādīsu sabbattha heṭṭhā vuttakāraṇavaseneva upekkhāsahagatāni, tathā kāyaviññāṇaṃ iṭṭhādīsu sukhasahagataṃ, aniṭṭhādīsu dukkhasahagatanti. Javanena niyamitaṃ aṭṭhakathāyanti adhippāyo. Hetuniyamanameva cettha javanavasena hoti vedanābhedassa ārammaṇeneva, saṅkhārabhedassa ca paccayavaseneva niyamitattā. Ettha ca akusalavipākānaṃ vibhāgābhāvato kusalavipākatadārammaṇānameva ārammaṇajavanapaccayavasena niyamanaṃ hoti. Taṃ pana sarūpato evaṃ veditabbaṃ – tihetukukkaṭṭhakammena hi tadārammaṇaṃ pavattamānaṃ kammavasena niyamābhāvato sabbesupi kusalavipākatadārammaṇesu sampattesu ārammaṇajavanapaccayavasena, ārammaṇajavanavaseneva vā niyataṃ ekameva uppajjati. Kathaṃ? Tadārammaṇesu hi ārammaṇavasena vedanāniyamo hoti, javanavasena hetuniyamo[M 2.0035], paccayavasena saṅkhāraniyamo. Ahetukesu pana saṅkhārabhedābhāvato paccayavasena niyamanaṃ natthi. Tattha ārammaṇena vedanāniyamanaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Javanavasena hetuniyamane pana kammasarikkhakahetuvasena tihetukāni duhetukāni ahetukānīti tīṇi javanāni veditabbāni. Tattha kammasarikkhakahetuvasena tihetukajavanāni nāma kāmāvacarakusalakiriyāsu ñāṇasampayuttajavanāni, duhetukajavanāni nāma ñāṇavippayuttajavanāni, ahetukāni nāma akusalajavanāni ceva kiriyāhetukajavanañca. Akusalajavanānipi hi kusalakammasarikkhakahetuvasena ahetukāni kusalahetūnaṃ tesu abhāvato.

By ‘object’ is meant a pleasant, etc., object. The ‘transformation of feeling’ means the transformation into joy or other feelings appropriate to that particular object. And this is said with reference to the wholesome-resultant investigating and registering consciousnesses. For these, when the object is pleasant, are accompanied by joy; when the object is neutral-pleasant, they are accompanied by equanimity. However, the unwholesome-resultant investigating and registering consciousness is accompanied only by equanimity when the object is unpleasant or neutral-unpleasant. Indeed, for it there is no variation of feeling based on the object; as explained earlier, in both cases, it is accompanied only by equanimity. And as for the two sets of five sense-consciousnesses and the receiving consciousnesses, except for the two types of body-consciousness, the rest are accompanied by equanimity in all cases of pleasant, etc., objects, for the reason stated earlier. Similarly, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure when the object is pleasant, etc., and by pain when the object is unpleasant, etc. The intention is that it is ‘determined by impulsion in the commentary.’ Here, the determination of roots is by way of impulsion, while the distinction of feeling is by way of the object, and the distinction of prompting is by way of condition. And here, since there is no division for unwholesome resultants, only the wholesome-resultant registering consciousnesses are determined by way of object, impulsion, and condition. That, however, should be understood in its own nature thus: When the registering consciousness arises due to a three-rooted excellent kamma, since there is no determination by way of kamma, among all wholesome-resultant registering consciousnesses that have been attained, only one, being determined, arises by way of object, impulsion, and condition, or by way of object and impulsion alone. How so? For in the registering consciousnesses, the determination of feeling is by way of object, the determination of roots is by way of impulsion, and the determination of prompting is by way of condition. However, in rootless consciousnesses, since there is no distinction of prompting, there is no determination by way of condition. Here, the determination of feeling by the object should be understood as explained earlier. As for the determination of roots by way of impulsion, three kinds of impulsions should be understood by way of roots similar to the kamma: three-rooted, two-rooted, and rootless. Among these, ‘three-rooted impulsions’ are those impulsions conjoined with knowledge in sense-sphere wholesome and functional consciousnesses. ‘Two-rooted impulsions’ are those dissociated from knowledge. ‘Rootless impulsions’ are unwholesome impulsions and the functional rootless impulsion. For unwholesome impulsions are also rootless by way of roots similar to wholesome kamma, because wholesome roots are absent in them.

Tattha [V 2.0027] kammassa javanasadisatadārammaṇābhinipphādanasāmatthiye sati tihetukajavane javite tihetukatadārammaṇaṃ hoti, duhetukajavane javite duhetukatadārammaṇaṃ, ahetukajavane javite ahetukatadārammaṇaṃ hotīti. Evaṃ javanavasena hetuniyamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kathaṃ paccayavasena saṅkhāraniyamoti? Kālasampadādīnaṃ, utusampadādīnañca paccayānaṃ balavabhāve sati asaṅkhārikatadārammaṇaṃ hoti, dubbalabhāve sasaṅkhārikaṃ. Ahetukatadārammaṇassa pana paccayavasena niyamo natthi, tasmā yadi iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ hoti, tadā upekkhāsahagataṃ tadārammaṇaṃ paṭibāhitvā somanassasahagatatadārammaṇameva hoti. Somanassasahagatatadārammaṇesupi aniyamena ārammaṇavasena sabbesu sampattesu javanassa tihetukabhāve duhetukāhetuke paṭibāhitvā tihetukameva tadārammaṇaṃ hoti. Tihetukatadārammaṇesupi aniyamena javanavasena sabbesu sampattesu paccayassa balavabhāve sati sasaṅkhārikatadārammaṇaṃ paṭibāhitvā asaṅkhārikameva [M 2.0036] tadārammaṇaṃ hoti. Eteneva nayena sesaṃ tadārammaṇampi taṃtaṃjavanānurūpato niyamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Therein, when the kamma has the capacity to produce a registering consciousness similar to the impulsion, then when a three-rooted impulsion has occurred, a three-rooted registering consciousness arises; when a two-rooted impulsion has occurred, a two-rooted registering consciousness arises; when a rootless impulsion has occurred, a rootless registering consciousness arises. Thus, the determination of roots should be understood by way of impulsion. How is the determination of prompting by way of condition? When conditions such as the excellence of time, the excellence of season, etc., are strong, the registering consciousness is unprompted; when they are weak, it is prompted. However, for a rootless registering consciousness, there is no determination by way of condition. Therefore, if the object is pleasant, then having suppressed the registering consciousness accompanied by equanimity, only the registering consciousness accompanied by joy arises. Even among registering consciousnesses accompanied by joy, when there is no determination by way of object, and among all that have been attained, when the impulsion is three-rooted, having suppressed the two-rooted and rootless, only the three-rooted registering consciousness arises. Even among three-rooted registering consciousnesses, when there is no determination by way of impulsion, and among all that have been attained, when the condition is strong, having suppressed the prompted registering consciousness, only the unprompted registering consciousness arises. By this same method, the determination of the remaining registering consciousnesses should also be understood in accordance with their respective impulsions.

Ahetukatadārammaṇaṃ pana paccayaṃ anapekkhitvā ārammaṇavasena ceva javanavasena ca niyamanaṃ hoti. Idamettha yebhuyyappavattivasena niyamanaṃ. Kadāci pana ārammaṇavasena, paccayavasena, paricitavasena ca tadārammaṇaniyamo hoti. Tattha ārammaṇavasena ceva paccayavasena ca niyamanaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Paricitavasena pana niyamane yebhuyyena tihetukakusalappavattiyā tesu paricitassa kadāci duhetuke, ahetuke vā javane javite paricayavasena tihetukatadārammaṇameva hoti. Yebhuyyena ca duhetukajavanappavattiyā tattha paricitassa kadāci tihetuke, ahetuke vā javane javite paricayavasena duhetukatadārammaṇameva hoti. Tatheva akusalesu paricitassa kadāci tihetukaduhetukesupi javanesu javitesu paricayavasena ahetukatadārammaṇameva hotīti. Evañca katvā paṭṭhāne –

However, the rootless registering consciousness is determined by way of object and by way of impulsion, without regard to condition. Here, this determination is by way of what mostly occurs. But sometimes, the determination of the registering consciousness occurs by way of object, by way of condition, and by way of familiarity. Therein, the determination by way of object and by way of condition is just as explained earlier. When determination occurs by way of familiarity, for one familiar with mostly three-rooted wholesome processes, sometimes even when a two-rooted or rootless impulsion has occurred, due to familiarity, only a three-rooted registering consciousness arises. Similarly, for one familiar with mostly two-rooted impulsion processes, sometimes even when a three-rooted or rootless impulsion has occurred, due to familiarity, only a two-rooted registering consciousness arises. In the same way, for one familiar with unwholesome states, sometimes even when three-rooted or two-rooted impulsions have occurred, due to familiarity, only a rootless registering consciousness arises. And having established this, in the Paṭṭhāna it is said—

“Kusalākusale niruddhe sahetuko vipāko tadārammaṇatā uppajjati, sahetuke khandhe aniccato dukkhato anattato vipassati, kusalākusale niruddhe ahetuko vipāko tadārammaṇatā uppajjatī”ti –

“When wholesome and unwholesome states have ceased, a rooted resultant registering consciousness arises. One contemplates the rooted aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. When wholesome and unwholesome states have ceased, a rootless resultant registering consciousness arises.”

Avisesena akusalajavanānantarampi sahetukatadārammaṇaṃ, tihetukajavanānantarañca ahetukatadārammaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tihetukomakena, pana duhetukukkaṭṭhena ca kammena tadārammaṇappavattiyaṃ [M 2.0037][V 2.0028] kammassa tihetukavipākadāne asamatthatāya tihetukajavanepi javite duhetukatadārammaṇameva hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Duhetukomakena pana kammena tadārammaṇappavattiyaṃ kammassa sahetukatadārammaṇanibbattane asamatthatāya sahetukajavanepi javite ahetukatadārammaṇameva hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Indiscriminately, it is stated that a rooted registering consciousness can arise even immediately after unwholesome impulsions, and a rootless registering consciousness immediately after triple-rooted impulsions. However, when a registering consciousness arises due to weak triple-rooted kamma or superior double-rooted kamma, since the kamma is incapable of yielding a triple-rooted resultant, even when a triple-rooted impulsion has occurred, the registering consciousness is only double-rooted. The rest is as has been stated. But when a registering consciousness arises due to weak double-rooted kamma, since the kamma is incapable of producing a rooted registering consciousness, even when a rooted impulsion has occurred, the registering consciousness is only rootless. The rest is as has been stated.

387-91. Tulyena pākacittenāti somanassasahagatañāṇasampayuttaasaṅkhārikena mahāvipākacittena. Balavārammaṇeti atimahantārammaṇe. Catubbidhañhi ārammaṇaṃ atimahantaṃ mahantaṃ parittaṃ atiparittanti. Vuttañca –

387–91. ‘With a similar resultant consciousness’ means with a great resultant consciousness that is accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted. ‘With a strong object’ means with an extremely large object. For an object is fourfold: extremely large, large, limited, and extremely limited. And it has been said:

“Tathā hi visayaṃ āhu, catudhā ettha paṇḍitā;

Mahantātimahantato, parittātiparittato”ti.

“For so the wise here declare the object to be fourfold: as large and extremely large, as limited and extremely limited.”

Atimahantādibhāvo cassa āpāthagatakāle uppajjanakacittakkhaṇavasena veditabbo. Tathā hi āpāthagatakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya yāva soḷasacittakkhaṇā, tāva vijjamānāyukaārammaṇaṃ atimahantaṃ nāma. Pannarasacuddasacittakkhaṇāyukaṃ mahantaṃ nāma. Terasacittakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya aṭṭhacittakkhaṇāyukaṃ parittaṃ nāma. Tato paraṃ atiparittaṃ nāma. Tattha atimahantārammaṇe tadārammaṇapariyosānāni vīthicittāni uppajjanti. Mahante javanapariyosānāni, natthi tadārammaṇuppādo. Paritte javanampi na uppajjati, santīraṇānantaraṃ voṭṭhabbanameva dvattikkhattuṃ pavattati. Atiparitte bhavaṅgacalanamattameva. Kathaṃ? Atimahante hi ārammaṇe pañcadvāresu yathānurūpaṃ aññatarasmiṃ dvāre āpāthagate pasādaghaṭṭanānubhāvena hadayavatthusannissitā bhavaṅgasantati vocchijjati, vocchijjamānā ca sahasā na occhijjati. Yathā pana vegena dhāvanto puriso antarā ṭhātukāmopi ekadvepadavāre atikkamitvāva ṭhātuṃ sakkoti, na pana ṭhātukāmatāya [M 2.0038] saddhiṃyeva, evameva dīpasikhā viya, gaṅgāsoto viya, vegena javamānā bhavaṅgasantati antarā occhijjamānāpi pasādaghaṭṭanato paraṃ dvattikkhattuṃ uppajjitvāva occhijjati. Tattha paṭhamacittaṃ bhavaṅgasantatiyā calanākārena uppajjanato bhavaṅgacalanaṃ nāma, dutiyaṃ upacchijjanavasena uppajjanato bhavaṅgupacchedo nāma. Calanañcettha visadisacittassa upanissayabhāvagamanaṃ. Vuttañca –

The state of an object as extremely large, etc., should be understood in terms of the number of consciousness-moments that can arise while it is in range. For an object whose life-span from the moment it comes into range lasts for up to sixteen consciousness-moments is called an ‘extremely large object.’ An object with a life-span of fifteen or fourteen consciousness-moments is called a ‘large object.’ An object with a life-span from thirteen down to eight consciousness-moments is called a ‘limited object.’ Beyond that, it is called an ‘extremely limited object.’ Therein, in the case of an extremely large object, cognitive processes arise that conclude with registering. In the case of a large object, they conclude with impulsion; there is no arising of registering. In the case of a limited object, not even impulsion arises; after investigating, only determining occurs two or three times. In the case of an extremely limited object, there is merely a vibration of the life-continuum. How so? When an extremely large object comes into range at one of the five sense doors, the stream of the life-continuum, which is dependent on the heart-base, is interrupted by the force of the impact on the sensitive matter. Though being interrupted, it does not cease abruptly. For just as a person running swiftly, even if they wish to stop midway, can only stop after overrunning one or two more steps, not at the very instant they wish to stop; so too, like a lamp flame or the current of the Ganges, the swiftly flowing stream of the life-continuum, though being interrupted midway, ceases only after arising two or three more times following the impact on the sensitive matter. Therein, the first consciousness, arising as a vibration of the life-continuum, is called ‘vibration of the life-continuum.’ The second, arising as the cutting off of the life-continuum, is called ‘arrest of the life-continuum.’ And here, ‘vibration’ means its becoming a decisive support condition for a dissimilar consciousness. As it has been said:

“Ārammaṇantarāpāthe[V 2.0029], dvikkhattuṃ calite mano;

Cittantarassa hetuttaṃ, yānaṃ calanamīrita”nti.

“When an object enters the avenue and the mind vibrates twice, its being a cause for another consciousness—that vehicle—is called vibration.”

Yadi evaṃ dutiyassapi taṃ atthīti tampi bhavaṅgacalanamicceva vattabbanti? Saccaṃ, bhavaṅgassa pana upacchijjanavasena pavattivisesaṃ gahetvā purimassa nāmato visadisanāmaṃ kātuṃ “bhavaṅgupacchedo”ti vuccatīti. Nanu ca rūpādīhi pasāde ghaṭṭite pasādanissitasseva calanaṃ yuttaṃ, kathaṃ pana hadayavatthusannissitāya bhavaṅgasantatiyā calananti? Santativasena ekābaddhattā. Yathā hi bheriyā ekasmiṃ tale ṭhitasakkharāya makkhikāya nipannāya aparasmiṃ tale daṇḍādinā pahaṭe anukkamena bhericammavarattādīnaṃ calanena sakkharāya calitāya makkhikāya palāyanaṃ hoti, evameva rūpādimhi pasāde ghaṭṭite tannissayesu mahābhūtesu calitesu anukkamena taṃsambandhānaṃ sesarūpānampi calanena hadayavatthumhi calite tannissitassa bhavaṅgassa calanākārena pavatti hoti. Vuttañca –

If so, since this is also true for the second moment, should it not also be called ‘vibration of the life-continuum’? True, but to distinguish it from the former by giving it a different name, taking the special mode of occurrence as the arresting of the life-continuum, it is called ‘arrest of the life-continuum.’ But when form, etc., strikes a sense faculty, is it not fitting that the vibration should be only in what is dependent on that faculty? How then is there vibration in the stream of the life-continuum, which is dependent on the heart-base? Because of their being bound together as one through continuity. For just as, when a fly is resting on a pebble placed on one side of a drum, and the other side is struck with a stick, the fly flees when the pebble is moved by the progressive vibration of the drum skin, straps, etc.; so too, when an object such as a form strikes a sense faculty, the great elements on which that faculty depends vibrate, and by the progressive vibration of the other material phenomena connected with them, the heart-base vibrates. When the heart-base vibrates, the life-continuum dependent on it occurs in the mode of vibration. And it has been said:

“Ghaṭṭite aññavatthumhi, aññanissitakampanaṃ;

Ekābaddhena hotīti, sakkharopamayā vade”ti. (sa. sa. 176);

“When one thing is struck, another dependent on it vibrates; this occurs because they are bound as one—so should one explain with the simile of the pebble.” (sa. sa. 176)

Evaṃ bhavaṅgacalanabhavaṅgupacchedesu uppajjitvā niruddhesu “kiṃ nāmeta”nti vadantī viya vīthicittāni ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ paṭipādentī [M 2.0039] kiriyāmanodhātu uppajjati, tassānantaraṃ yathārahaṃ dassanādikiccaṃ sādhayamānā pañcaviññāṇadhātūsu aññatarā uppajjati, tadanantaraṃ tāya gahitamevārammaṇaṃ sampaṭicchamānā vipākāhetukamanodhātu uppajjati, tadanantaraṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ santīrayamānā vipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu uppajjati, tadanantaraṃ tamevārammaṇaṃ vavatthāpayamānā kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu uppajjati, tadanantaraṃ kāmāvacarakusalākusalakiriyajavanesu yaṃ kiñci laddhapaccayaṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ ārabbha javanaṃ hutvā yebhuyyena sattakkhattuṃ javati, tadanantaraṃ ekādasatadārammaṇacittesu aññataraṃ kammaṃ ārammaṇaṃ javanaṃ paccayo paricitatāti imesaṃ anurūpavasena dvikkhattuṃ uppajjati, tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgapāto hoti.

Thus, when the vibration and arrest of the life-continuum have arisen and ceased, the functional mind-element arises, which sets the cognitive process in motion towards the object, as if saying, ‘What can this be?’ Immediately after that, one of the five sense-consciousness elements arises, accomplishing its respective function of seeing, etc. Following that, the resultant rootless mind-element arises, receiving that same object. Following that, the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element arises, investigating that same object. Following that, the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element arises, determining that same object. Following that, whatever sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, or functional impulsion has obtained its conditions runs, taking that very object, for the most part seven times. Following that, one of the eleven kinds of registering consciousness arises twice, in conformity with the kamma, the object, the impulsion, the conditions, and familiarity. After that, there is a lapse into the life-continuum.

Idha ṭhatvā imissā cittaparamparāya sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ ambopamā veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Eko kira puriso phalitambarukkhassa heṭṭhā sasīsaṃ pārupitvā nipanno niddāyati, athekaṃ ambapakkaṃ vaṇṭato [V 2.0030] muccitvā tassa kaṇṇasakkhaliṃ puñchamānaṃ viya “ṭha”nti bhūmiyaṃ patati, so tassa saddena pabujjhitvā sīsato vatthaṃ apanetvā cakkhuṃ ummīletvā olokesi, tato hatthaṃ pasāretvā phalaṃ gahetvā madditvā upasiṅghitvā pakkabhāvaṃ ñatvā paribhuñjitvā mukhagataṃ saha semhena assādetvā puna tatheva niddāyati. Tattha tassa purisassa ambarukkhamūle niddāyanakālo viya bhavaṅgasamaṅgikālo, ambapakkassa patitakālo viya ārammaṇassa pasādaghaṭṭanakālo, patanasaddena pabuddhakālo viya manodhātuyā bhavaṅgassa āvaṭṭitakālo, ummīletvā olokitakālo viya cakkhuviññāṇassa dassanakiccaṃ sādhanakālo, hatthaṃ pasāretvā gahitakālo viya vipākamanodhātuyā ārammaṇasampaṭicchanakālo, gahetvā madditakālo [M 2.0040] viya vipākamanoviññāṇadhātuyā ārammaṇassa santīritakālo, upasiṅghitakālo viya kiriyāmanoviññāṇadhātuyā vavatthāpitakālo, paribhuttakālo viya javanassa ārammaṇarasaanubhavitakālo, mukhagataṃ saha semhena assāditakālo viya tadārammaṇassa javanena anubhūtārammaṇaanubhavanakālo, puna niddāyanaṃ viya puna bhavaṅgakāloti evamettha upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

To facilitate the grasp of this sequence of consciousness, the simile of the mango should be understood. How? A certain man, it is said, covered his head and fell asleep at the foot of a mango tree laden with fruit. Then a ripe mango, detached from its stalk, fell to the ground with a ‘thud,’ as if brushing his ear. Awakened by the sound, he uncovered his head, opened his eyes, and looked. Then he stretched out his hand, took the fruit, squeezed it, sniffed it, and knowing it was ripe, he ate it. After savoring the taste in his mouth along with the saliva, he fell asleep again as before. Herein, the man's sleeping at the foot of the mango tree is like the time one is in the life-continuum. The falling of the ripe mango is like the object's striking a sense faculty. His awakening to the sound is like the mind-element's adverting from the life-continuum. His opening his eyes and looking is like the eye-consciousness's accomplishing the function of seeing. His stretching out his hand and taking the fruit is like the resultant mind-element's receiving the object. His squeezing it after taking it is like the resultant mind-consciousness-element's investigating the object. His sniffing it is like the functional mind-consciousness-element's determining the object. His eating it is like the impulsion's experiencing the taste of the object. His savoring the taste in his mouth along with the saliva is like the registering consciousness's experiencing the object that had been experienced by the impulsion. His falling asleep again is like the time of returning to the life-continuum. Thus the application of the simile should be understood.

Ayaṃ pana upamā kiṃ dīpeti? Ārammaṇassa pasādaghaṭṭanameva kiccaṃ, kiriyāmanodhātuyā bhavaṅgāvaṭṭanameva kiccaṃ, pañcaviññāṇadhātūnaṃ dassanādikameva kiccaṃ, vipākamanoviññāṇadhātuyā sampaṭicchanameva kiccaṃ, vipākamanoviññāṇadhātuyā santīraṇameva kiccaṃ, kiriyāmanoviññāṇadhātuyā vavatthāpanameva kiccaṃ, javanasseva pana ārammaṇarasānubhavanaṃ tadārammaṇassa etena anubhūtasseva anubhavananti evaṃ kiccavasena dhammānaṃ aññamaññāsaṃkiṇṇataṃ dīpeti, evaṃ pavattamānaṃ pana cittaṃ “tvaṃ āvajjanaṃ nāma hohi, tvaṃ dassanādīsu aññataraṃ, tvaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ nāmā”tiādinā niyuñjake kārake asatipi cittaniyāmavaseneva pavattatīti veditabbaṃ. Taṃ pana cittaniyāmaṃ saddhiṃ utuniyāmādīhi paricchedāvasāne vakkhati. Ayaṃ tāva atimahantārammaṇe cittappavattivibhāvanā.

Now, what does this simile illustrate? The function of the object is merely to impinge on the sense faculty; the function of the functional mind-element is merely to advert; the function of the five sense-consciousness elements is merely to see and so on; the function of the resultant mind-element is merely to receive; the function of the resultant mind-consciousness-element is merely to investigate; the function of the functional mind-consciousness-element is merely to determine; while the function of impulsion is to experience the taste of the object, and the function of registering consciousness is to experience what has already been experienced by it. Thus, it illustrates the non-intermixture of phenomena according to their functions. Moreover, it should be understood that this cognitive process occurs by its own law of consciousness, without any directing agent saying, “You be adverting,” “You be one of the seeings, etc.,” “You be receiving,” and so on. This law of consciousness, along with the law of temperature and so on, will be explained at the end of the chapter. This, for now, is the explanation of the cognitive process in regard to an extremely great object.

Mahantārammaṇe pana tadārammaṇuppādassa abhāvato tasmiṃ āpāthagate vuttanayena javanapariyosānesu vīthicittesu uppannesu bhavaṅgapātova hoti, ārammaṇassa pana parikkhīṇāyukattā ekacittakkhaṇikappamāṇepi vā āyumhi sati samāsannamaraṇo viya puriso dubbalabhāvato tadārammaṇaṃ nuppajjati. Apica tadārammaṇamuppajjantaṃ niyamato dvikkhattumeva uppajjati, na ekavāraṃ. Ekacittakkhaṇāvasiṭṭhe ca ārammaṇe ekasmiṃ tadārammaṇe uppannesu [M 2.0041] dutiyassa [V 2.0031] uppajjanakāle tassa niruddhattā nuppajjati. Na hi dvīsu tadārammaṇesu ekaṃ paccuppannārammaṇaṃ, ekaṃ atītārammaṇaṃ hoti, tasmā dutiyassa anuppattiyā paṭhamampi nuppajjatīti. Majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana sakimpi tadārammaṇassa pavatti vuttā. Paramatthavinicchayepi ca tameva vādaṃ sampaṭicchitvā “sakiṃ dve vā tadālamba”nti (parama. vi. 116) vuttaṃ. Abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “cittappavattigaṇanāyaṃ sabbavāresu dve eva cittavārāni āgatānī”ti vatvā taṃ na sampaṭicchitaṃ, tasmā mahantārammaṇe javanāvasāne bhavaṅgapātova hoti, natthi tadārammaṇuppādo, ayañca tadārammaṇehi tucchatāya “moghavāro”ti vuccati.

However, in the case of a great object, there is no arising of registering consciousness. When that object has come into range and the cognitive process has arisen ending with impulsion in the way described, there is only a lapse into the life-continuum. For, because the object’s lifespan is exhausted, it is too weak for registering consciousness to arise, like a person near death. Furthermore, when registering consciousness does arise, it arises as a rule exactly twice, not once. And when the object has a remaining duration of only one consciousness-moment, after one registering consciousness has arisen, the second does not arise because at the time for its arising the object has ceased. For it is not the case that of two registering consciousnesses, one has a present object and the other a past object. Therefore, because the second does not arise, the first does not arise either. In the Commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya, however, the occurrence of registering consciousness even once is mentioned. And in the Paramatthavinicchaya, accepting that same view, it is said: “Registering occurs once or twice.” But in the Commentary to the Abhidhamma this is not accepted; it is said: “In the counting of cognitive processes, in all cases two consciousness-moments have come down.” Therefore, in the case of a great object, at the end of the impulsion, there is only a lapse into the life-continuum; there is no arising of registering consciousness. And this, because of its being void of registering consciousness, is called a “vain process.”

Parittārammaṇe javanuppādassapi abhāvato santīraṇāvasānesu vīthicittesu uppannesu tadanantaraṃ voṭṭhabbanameva āsevanaṃ labhitvā javanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā dvikkhattuṃ pavattati, tato bhavaṅgapāto hoti. Voṭṭhabbanaṃ pana appatvā antarā cakkhuviññāṇādikaṃ patvā nivattissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Javanaṃ pana ārammaṇassa appāyukabhāvena paridubbalattā nuppajjati. Tañhi uppajjamānaṃ sattacittakkhaṇāyukeyeva uppajjati, katipayacittakkhaṇāyuke pana paṭhamajavanameva nuppajjati. Tadanuppattiyañhi itarānipi nuppajjanti, tasmā parittārammaṇe natthi javanuppādoti ayaṃ dutiyo moghavāro aṭṭhakathāya vutto. Ṭīkākāro pana tathā asampaṭicchitvā aññathā dutiyamoghavāraṃ pakappeti. Vuttañhi tena tīsu moghavāresu dutiyamoghavāro upaparikkhitvā gahetabbo.

In the case of a slight object, since there is no arising of impulsion, when the process-consciousnesses have arisen ending with investigating, immediately after that determining alone, having obtained repetition, occurs twice in the place of impulsion, and then there is a lapse into the life-continuum. There is no possibility that the process turns back midway, after reaching eye-consciousness and so on, without having reached determining. Impulsion, however, does not arise because the object is very weak due to its short lifespan. For when impulsion arises, it arises only when the object has a lifespan of seven consciousness-moments; but when the object has a lifespan of only a few consciousness-moments, even the first impulsion does not arise. And when that does not arise, the others do not arise either. Therefore, in the case of a slight object, there is no arising of impulsion. This is the second vain process as stated in the Commentary. The Subcommentator, however, not accepting this, construes the second vain process differently. For it is said by him that among the three vain processes, the second one is to be determined after examination.

Yadi hi anulome vedanāttike paṭiccavārādīsu “āsevanapaccayā na magge dve, namaggapaccayā āsevane dve”ti ca vuttaṃ siyā, sopi moghavāro labbheyya. Yadi ca voṭṭhabbanampi āsevanapaccayo [M 2.0042] siyā, kusalākusalānampi siyā. Na hi āsevanapaccayaṃ laddhuṃ yuttassa āsevanapaccayabhāvī dhammo āsevanapaccayo hotīti avutto atthi. Voṭṭhabbanassa pana kusalākusalānaṃ āsevanapaccayabhāvo na vutto. “Kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo uppajjati nāsevanapaccayā. Akusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca akusalo dhammo uppajjati nāsevanapaccayā”ti vacanato paṭikkhittova. Athāpi siyā “asamānavedanānaṃ vasenevaṃ vutta”nti, evampi yathā “āvajjanā kusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ, akusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417) vuttaṃ, evaṃ “āsevanapaccayena paccayo”tipi vattabbaṃ siyā. Jātibhedā na vuttanti ce, “bhūmibhinnassa kāmāvacarassa rūpāvacarādīnaṃ [V 2.0032] āsevanapaccayabhāvo viya jātibhinnassapi bhaveyyā”ti vattabbo eva siyā, abhinnajātikassa ca vasena yathā “āvajjanā sahetukānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ “āsevanapaccayena paccayo”tipi vattabbaṃ siyā, na tu vuttaṃ, tasmā vedanāttikepi saṃkhittāya gaṇanāya “āsevanapaccayā namagge ekaṃ, namaggapaccayā āsevane eka”nti evaṃ gaṇanāya niddhāriyamānāya voṭṭhabbanassa āsevanapaccayattābhāvā yathāvuttappakāro dutiyo moghavāro vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbo. Voṭṭhabbanaṃ pana vīthivipākasantatiyā āvaṭṭanato “āvajjanā”icceva vuttaṃ. Tato visadisassa javanassa karaṇato manasikāro ca. Evañca katvā paṭṭhāne “voṭṭhabbanaṃ kusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”tiādi na vuttaṃ, “āvajjanā”icceva vuttaṃ, tasmā voṭṭhabbanato catunnaṃ vā pañcannaṃ vā javanānaṃ ārammaṇapurejātaṃ bhavituṃ asakkontaṃ rūpādiāvajjanādīnaṃ paccayo [M 2.0043] bhavituṃ na sakkoti, ayametassa sabhāvoti javanāpāripūriyā dutiyo moghavāro dassetuṃ yutto siyāti.

For if, in the positive permutation of the feeling-triplet, in the Paṭiccavāra, etc., it were said: “By repetition condition, two are related to not-path; by not-path condition, two are related to repetition,” then that futile process would also be tenable. And if determining were a repetition condition, it would be so for wholesome and unwholesome states as well. For there is no unstated case where a state fit to receive the repetition condition and capable of being a repetition condition is not stated as being a repetition condition. But the status of determining as a repetition condition for wholesome and unwholesome states is not stated. Indeed, it is rejected by the statement: “Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises, not by repetition condition. Dependent on an unwholesome state, an unwholesome state arises, not by repetition condition.” And if it were said, “This is stated thus on account of dissimilar feelings,” even so, just as it is said, “Adverting is a condition for wholesome aggregates and for unwholesome aggregates by contiguity condition,” so too it should have been said, “by repetition condition.” If it is said, “It is not stated because of the difference in intrinsic nature,” then the reply should be: “Just as there is a repetition condition for a sense-sphere state with regard to form-sphere states, etc., which are different in plane, so too there could be one for a state different in intrinsic nature.” And with respect to states of the same intrinsic nature, just as it is said, “Adverting is a condition for rooted aggregates by contiguity condition,” so too it should have been said, “by repetition condition.” But it is not said. Therefore, since in the feeling-triplet, in the summary enumeration, the count is fixed as “by repetition condition, one to not-path; by not-path condition, one to repetition,” and because determining lacks the nature of being a repetition condition, the second futile process of the kind described above should be taken after investigation. Moreover, determining is called “adverting” because it adverts the continuity of the process-resultants. And because it produces a dissimilar impulsion, it is also attention. Thus, in the Paṭṭhāna it is not said, “Determining is a condition for wholesome aggregates by contiguity condition,” etc., but only “adverting” is stated. Therefore, an object such as form, being unable to be an object-prenascence condition for the four or five impulsions that follow determining, cannot be a condition for adverting and so on. This is its nature. Thus, it would be appropriate to show the second futile process as the non-completion of impulsion.

Ayañhi ācariyassa adhippāyo – yadi voṭṭhabbanampi āsevanapaccayo siyā, yathā “sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca sukhāya vedanāya sampayutto dhammo uppajjati āsevanapaccayā namaggapaccayā”ti anulomapaccaniye, paccaniyānulome ca “sukhā…pe… namaggapaccayā āsevanapaccayā”ti ca vuttaṃ hasituppādacittavasena, evampi voṭṭhabbanavasena “adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiccā”tiādinā pubbe vuttanayena pāṭho siyā. Tathā ca sati vāradvayavasena gaṇanāya “āsevanapaccayā namagge dve, namaggapaccayā āsevane dve”ti ca vattabbaṃ siyā, na pana vuttaṃ, “āsevanapaccayā namagge ekaṃ, namaggapaccayā āsevane eka”nticceva vuttaṃ. Apica yadi hi voṭṭhabbanampi āsevanapaccayo siyā, dutiyamoghavāro viya purimavāresupi siyā. Tathā ca sati attano viya kusalākusalānampi siyā. Na hi āsevanapaccayaṃ laddhuṃ yuttassa āsevanapaccayabhāvī dhammo āsevanapaccayo hotīti avutto atthi “purimā purimā kusalā khandhā”tiādinā anavasesato vuttattā, voṭṭhabbanassa pana avutto “abyākato dhammo kusalassa dhammassa āsevanapaccayena paccayo”tiādivacanassa abhāvato. Na kevalaṃ avuttova, atha kho “kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo uppajjati, akusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca akusalo dhammo uppajjatī”ti phassādikusalākusaladhamme paṭicca sahajātādipaccayavasena kusalākusalassa uppattiṃ [V 2.0033] vatvā paṭhamajavanassa voṭṭhabbanato āsevanapaccayālābhaṃ sandhāya “nāsevanapaccayā”ti paṭikkhittova.

For this is the teacher’s intention: If determining were also a repetition condition, then just as it is said in the positive-negative and negative-positive permutations, “Dependent on a state associated with pleasant feeling, a state associated with pleasant feeling arises by repetition condition, by not-path condition,” and “pleasant… by not-path condition, by repetition condition,” with reference to the smile-producing consciousness, so too, on account of determining, there would be a reading in the way previously stated, beginning: “Dependent on a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling….” And if that were so, in the count by way of two instances, it would have to be said: “By repetition condition, two to not-path; by not-path condition, two to repetition.” But it is not said so; it is only said: “By repetition condition, one to not-path; by not-path condition, one to repetition.” Moreover, if determining were a repetition condition, it would apply in the preceding processes just as in the second futile process. And if that were so, it would apply to its own kind as well as to wholesome and unwholesome states. For there is no unstated case where a state fit to receive the repetition condition and capable of being a repetition condition is not stated as such, since this is stated without remainder, beginning: “The preceding, preceding wholesome aggregates….” But for determining it is unstated, due to the absence of a statement such as: “An indeterminate state is a condition for a wholesome state by repetition condition.” Not only is it unstated, but in fact, after stating the arising of wholesome and unwholesome states dependent on wholesome and unwholesome phenomena such as contact by way of conascence condition, etc., it is explicitly rejected with the words “not by repetition condition,” with reference to the first impulsion’s not obtaining the repetition condition from determining.

Athāpettha [M 2.0044] samodhānaṃ siyā, samānavedanānaṃ eva āsevanapaccayabhāvassa dassanato voṭṭhabbanena asamānavedanānaṃ kusalākusalānaṃ vasenāyaṃ paṭikkhepo katoti. Evampi sati yathā “āvajjanā kusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ akusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ samānavedanāvasena “āsevanapaccayena paccayo”tipi vattabbaṃ siyā. Atha voṭṭhabbanassa kusalākusalehi bhinnajātikattā tassa tesaṃ āsevanapaccayabhāvo na vuttoti ce.
