Yañcettha paṇṇapuṭaṃ nidassitaṃ, taṃ nidassitabbena samānaṃ na hoti, nāvāpaṇṇapuṭānañhi nadīsotassa āvaṭṭanaṃ gati ca visadisīti nāvāyaṃ nadīsotassa anubandhanaṃ, paṇṇapuṭassa ananubandhanañca yujjati, idha pana kiriyājavanetarajavanānaṃ bhavaṅgasotassa āvaṭṭanaṃ gati ca sadisīti etassa ananubandhanaṃ, itarassa anubandhanañca na yujjati, tasmā vicāretabbameva ta”nti vadanti.

523–4. By 'states not of the sense sphere' are meant other states, namely, the sublime and supramundane states. 'It does not follow' means it does not ensue. 'Its generator... it follows': just as a young boy, having left home and wishing to go outside, follows his own father or another kinsman similar to his father who wishes him well, holding his finger, and not some other royal attendant, so too this, having the nature of wishing to emerge from the object of the life-continuum, follows only its own generator—the first wholesome impulsion, etc.—or a similar second wholesome, etc., sense-sphere impulsion, and not another sublime or supramundane state. This is the meaning here. 'Wholesome, unwholesome, etc.': by the word 'etc.' it includes the functional indeterminate. The teacher Ānanda, however, states in the Paṭṭhāna: 'When wholesome and unwholesome states have ceased, the resultant registration arises.' Thus it is said that registration occurs immediately only after wholesome and unwholesome states. For a powerful impulsion follows the life-continuum like a boat in a river's current, but a functional impulsion of tranquil occurrence possessing six-factored equanimity does not follow the river's current, like a leaf-basket. Therefore, he does not accept registration after a functional impulsion. The Elder Jotipāla and other teachers, however, say: 'Even when something is obtainable, its non-mention is sometimes seen due to some intention, just as in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in the exposition of the unwholesome, where the dominance condition, though obtainable, is not mentioned. Therefore, if registration were mentioned even after an indeterminate state, one might then suppose its occurrence even after determining. For this reason, registration after a functional impulsion is not mentioned, but not because it is unobtainable. And the leaf-basket shown here as an example is not similar to what is to be exemplified. For the turning and movement of a boat and a leaf-basket by a river's current are dissimilar; thus the following of the boat by the river's current and the non-following of the leaf-basket are plausible. But here, the turning and movement of a functional impulsion and other impulsions by the stream of the life-continuum are similar; thus the non-following of the one and the following of the other is not plausible. Therefore, this should indeed be investigated.'

525-6. Yathā cetaṃ mahaggatalokuttaradhamme nānuvattati, tathā yadā ete kāmāvacaradhammāpi mahaggatānuttaradhammārammaṇā hutvā pavattanti, tadā tepi nānubandhatīti āha “kāmāvacaradhammāpī”tiādi. Mahaggatā-ggahaṇena cettha lokuttarānampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Te cāpīti [V 2.0050] ca-saddena [M 2.0067] lokuttarārammaṇānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Kasmā nānubandhatīti āha “parittārammaṇattā”tiādi. Parittārammaṇattāti heṭṭhā vuttanayena kāmāvacaravipākānaṃ ekantena parittārammaṇattā. Tathāparicitattāti yathā javanaṃ, evaṃ aparicitattā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā hi so pitaraṃ, pitusadisaṃ vā kañci anubandhanto taruṇadārako gharadvārantaravīthicatukkādimhi pariciteyeva dese anugacchati, na araññaṃ vā rakkhasabhūmiṃ vā gacchantaṃ, evaṃ kāmāvacaradhamme anubandhantampi parittamhi pariciteyeva dese pavattamāne te dhamme anubandhati, na mahaggatalokuttaradhamme ārabbha pavattamānepi.

525–6. Just as this does not ensue in regard to the sublime and supramundane states, so too, when these sense-sphere states occur having sublime and supreme states as their object, they too do not follow. Hence it is said: 'even the sense-sphere states,' etc. Here, by the taking up of 'sublime,' the inclusion of the supramundane should also be understood. By the word ca in te cāpi ('they also'), the inclusion of those with supramundane objects is meant. Why do they not follow? It is said: 'because of having a limited object,' etc. 'Because of having a limited object' means because sense-sphere resultants exclusively have a limited object, in the way stated above. 'Because of not being familiar with it' means because of not being familiar with it in the same way as the impulsion is. This is what is meant: just as a young child, following his father or someone like his father, follows only in familiar places such as the house door, the inner street, or the crossroads, but not when his father is going into a forest or a land of ogres, so too, while following sense-sphere states, it follows those states only when they are occurring in a limited and familiar domain, not when they are occurring in relation to sublime or supramundane states.

527-32. Idāni kiṃ imāya yuttikathāya, aṭṭhakathāpamāṇato cetaṃ gahetabbanti dassento āha “kiṃ tenā”tiādi. Javaneti kāmāvacarajavane. Tadārammaṇacittāni “tadārammaṇa”nti laddhanāmāni cittāni tadārammaṇabhāvaṃ na gaṇhanti, tadārammaṇabhāvena na pavattantīti attho. Atha vā nāmagottaṃ ārabbha javane javite tadārammaṇaṃ tassa javanassa ārammaṇaṃ na gaṇhanti na labbhantīti attho. Rūpārūpabhavesu vāti vā-saddena “javane javitepi tadārammaṇaṃ na gaṇhantī”ti ākaḍḍhati. Paṇṇattiṃ ārabbhāti kāmabhavepi paṇṇattiṃ ārabbha. Lakkhaṇārammaṇāyāti aniccādilakkhaṇattayārammaṇāya, balavavipassanāyāti attho. “Tīṇi lakkhaṇāni, tisso ca paññattiyo kusalattike na labbhantī”ti aṭṭhakathāya vuttattā tiṇṇaṃ lakkhaṇānaṃ dhammato abhāvena taṃ ārabbha pavattāya vipassanāya tadārammaṇāni na labbhanti. Paṭṭhāne pana “sekhā vā puthujjanā vā kusalaṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato vipassanti, kusalākusale niruddhe vipāko tadārammaṇatā uppajjatī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.406) vacanato khandhārammaṇikavipassanāya tadārammaṇaṃ [M 2.0068] labbhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Micchattaniyatesūti “katame dhammā micchattaniyatā? Cattāro diṭṭhigatasampayuttacittuppādā”ti (dha. sa. 1426) evamāgatesu micchāgāhavasena pavattesu dhammesu javanaṃ hutvā javitesu. Kasmā pana tesu javitesu tadārammaṇaṃ na labbhatīti? Kāmāvacaravipākānañhi niyatamicchādiṭṭhi viya “attā occhijjatī”tiādinā attaparikappanāvasena appavattanato niyatamicchādiṭṭhivasappavattesu tesu javitesu tadanantaraṃ tadārammaṇāni na uppajjanti, aniyatamicchādiṭṭhivasappavattesu pana javitesu tadārammaṇaṃ nuppajjatīti natthi. Atha vā micchattaniyatesūti micchābhāvaniyatasabhāvesu taṃvisayesūti attho. Micchattaniyatadhammānaṃ dhammasabhāvaṃ aggahetvā micchattaniyatasabhāvasseva gahaṇato, tassa ca vipākānaṃ avibhūtattā micchattaniyatasabhāve ārabbha [V 2.0051] tadārammaṇā na labbhanti. Pi-saddena sammattaniyatesupīti sampiṇḍeti, “lokuttaradhamme ārabbhā”ti vā etena siddhattā na tesaṃ visuṃ uddharaṇaṃ kataṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana micchattaniyatasammattaniyatānaṃ aññamaññapaṭipakkhabhāvena balavabhāvato tadārammaṇassa avatthubhāvadassanatthaṃ micchattaniyatānantaraṃ sammattaniyatāpi uddhaṭā. Micchattaniyatasabhāvassa viya paṭisambhidāsabhāvassapi kāmāvacaravipākānaṃ avibhūtabhāvena paṭisambhidāñāṇāni ārabbha javane javite tadārammaṇaṃ na labbhatīti āha “paṭisambhidāñāṇānī”tiādi. Manodvārepīti na kevalaṃ pañcadvāresuyeva, atha kho manodvārepi. Sabbesanti ahetukaduhetukādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ. Anupubbatoti heṭṭhā vuttaanukkamato.

527–32. Now, showing that this should be understood on the authority of the commentary, he says: 'What is the use of that reasoning?' etc. 'In the impulsion' means in a sense-sphere impulsion. The registration cittas, which have obtained the name 'registration,' do not take on the state of registration; the meaning is that they do not occur as registration. Alternatively, the meaning is that when impulsion has run its course in relation to a name and clan, registration does not take the object of that impulsion; it is not obtained. 'Or in the form and formless planes of existence': by the word 'or' he draws in 'even when impulsion has run its course, they do not take on registration.' 'In relation to a concept' means in relation to a concept even in the sense-sphere existence. 'For one with the characteristics as object' means for one with the three characteristics of impermanence, etc., as object; the meaning is, for powerful insight. Because it is said in the commentary, 'The three characteristics and the three concepts are not found in the wholesome triad,' registration is not obtained for insight that occurs in relation to them, due to the absence of the three characteristics as actual dhammas. In the Paṭṭhāna, however, it is said: 'Trainees or worldlings contemplate the wholesome as impermanent, as suffering, as nonself; when the wholesome and unwholesome have ceased, the resultant registration arises.' From this it should be understood that registration is obtained for insight that has the aggregates as its object. 'In those fixed in wrongness': when impulsion has run its course on states that have occurred by way of wrong grasp, which are stated thus: 'What states are fixed in wrongness? The four cittas associated with wrong view.' But why is registration not obtained when impulsion has run its course on them? Because sense-sphere resultants do not occur by way of conceiving a self, such as 'the self is annihilated,' like a fixed wrong view, registration cittas do not arise afterwards when impulsion has run its course on those states that occur under the sway of fixed wrong view. But it is not the case that registration does not arise when impulsion has run its course on those states that occur under the sway of an unfixed wrong view. Alternatively, 'in those fixed in wrongness' means in those objects whose nature is fixed in wrongness. Because the nature of the states fixed in wrongness is not grasped, but only the nature of being fixed in wrongness is grasped, and because this is indistinct to the resultants, registration is not obtained in relation to the nature fixed in wrongness. By the word pi he includes 'also in those fixed in rightness.' Or, since this is established by the statement 'in relation to supramundane states,' they are not mentioned separately. In the commentary, however, to show the absence of a basis for registration due to the powerful nature of states fixed in wrongness and states fixed in rightness being mutually opposed, states fixed in rightness are also cited after states fixed in wrongness. Just as the nature of what is fixed in wrongness is indistinct to sense-sphere resultants, so too is the nature of the analytical knowledges. Therefore, when impulsion has run its course in relation to the analytical knowledges, registration is not obtained. Hence he says: 'the analytical knowledges,' etc. 'Even in the mind door' means not only in the five doors, but also in the mind door. 'Of all' means of all, such as the rootless, the two-rooted, etc. 'In sequence' means according to the sequence stated above.

533. Na vijjatīti manodvārassa appaṭighabhāvena na vijjati. Bhavaṅgatoti bhavaṅgasantānato, tassa ārammaṇato [M 2.0069] vā. Vuṭṭhānanti bhavaṅgasantāne, tassārammaṇe vā sati tassa vuṭṭhānaṃ.

533. 'It is not found': it is not found because of the non-impingent nature of the mind door. 'From the life-continuum' means from the continuum of the life-continuum, or from its object. 'Emergence' means its emergence when there is the continuum of the life-continuum or its object.

535-6. Satta sattāti ekekassa satta sattāti katvā. Pāpapākāti akusalavipākā. “Dvādasāpuññacittāna”nti vatvā “pāpapākā”ti vacanaṃ “tatridaṃ sugatassa sugatacīvarappamāṇa”ntiādīsu viya saññāsaddavasena vuttaṃ. Evaṃ pavattiyaṃ akusalavipākānaṃ pavattiṃ dassetvā idāni paṭisandhiyaṃ dassetuṃ “ekādasavidhāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Uddhaccacetanāya pavattivipākadānamattaṃ vinā paṭisandhidānābhāvato āha “hitvā uddhaccamānasa”nti. Kiṃ panettha kāraṇaṃ, adhimokkhavirahena sabbadubbalampi vicikicchāsahagataṃ paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati, adhimokkhasabhāvato tato balavatarampi uddhaccasahagataṃ nākaḍḍhatīti? Paṭisandhidānasabhāvābhāvato. “Balavaṃ ākaḍḍhati, dubbalaṃ nākaḍḍhatī”ti hi ayaṃ vicāraṇā paṭisandhidānasabhāvesuyeva. Yassa pana paṭisandhidānasabhāvo eva natthi, na tassa balavabhāvo paṭisandhiākaḍḍhane kāraṇanti.

535–6. 'Seven, seven' means taking it as seven for each one. 'Results of evil' means unwholesome resultants. Having said 'of the twelve demeritorious cittas,' the word 'results of evil' is spoken by way of a conventional term, as in such cases as 'Herein, this is the measure of the Sugata's robe.' Thus, having shown the occurrence of unwholesome resultants during the course of life, now to show their occurrence at rebirth-linking, it is said 'of eleven kinds,' etc. Because the consciousness accompanied by restlessness gives only resultants during the course of life, without giving rebirth-linking, it is said 'excluding the mind accompanied by restlessness.' What is the reason here that the consciousness accompanied by doubt, though the weakest of all because of its lack of resolution, draws rebirth-linking, while the consciousness accompanied by restlessness, though stronger than that because it has the nature of resolution, does not draw it? Because of the absence of the nature to give rebirth-linking. For this investigation, 'the strong draws, the weak does not draw,' applies only to those things having the nature to give rebirth-linking. But for that which lacks the nature of giving rebirth-linking, its strength is not a reason for drawing rebirth-linking.

Kathaṃ panetaṃ viññātabbaṃ “uddhaccasahagatassa paṭisandhidānasabhāvo natthī”ti? Dassanenapahātabbesu anāgatattā. Tividhā hi akusalā dassanenapahātabbā, bhāvanāyapahātabbā, siyā dassanenapahātabbā siyā bhāvanāyapahātabbāti. Tattha diṭṭhisampayuttavicikicchāsahagatacittuppādā dassanenapahātabbā nāma. Yathāha “katame dhammā dassanenapahātabbā? Cattāro diṭṭhigatasampayuttacittuppādā [V 2.0052] vicikicchāsahagato cittuppādo”ti (dha. sa. 1408). Te hi paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato “dassana”nti laddhanāmena sotāpattimaggeneva pahātabbattā “dassanenapahātabbā”ti vuccanti. Uddhaccasahagatacittuppādo [M 2.0070] bhāvanāyapahātabbo nāma. Yathāha “katame dhammā bhāvanāyapahātabbā? Uddhaccasahagato cittuppādo”ti. So hi aggamaggena pahātabbattā “bhāvanāyapahātabbo”ti vutto. Uparimaggattayañhi paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhasmiṃyeva bhāvanāvasena uppajjati, na adiṭṭhapubbaṃ kiñci passati, tasmā “bhāvanā”ti vuccati. Diṭṭhivippayuttadomanassasahagatacittuppādā pana siyā dassanenapahātabbā siyā bhāvanāyapahātabbā nāma. Yathāha “cattāro diṭṭhigatavippayuttā lobhasahagatacittuppādā dve domanassasahagatacittuppādā. Ime dhammā siyā dassanenapahātabbā siyā bhāvanāyapahātabbā”ti (dha. sa. 1409). Te hi apāyanibbattakāvatthāya paṭhamamaggena, sesāvatthāya uparimaggehi pahīyamānattā siyā dassanenapahātabbā siyā bhāvanāyapahātabbā nāma. Tattha siyā dassanenapahātabbampi dassanenapahātabbasāmaññena idha “dassanenapahātabbā”tveva voharanti. Yadi ca uddhaccasahagataṃ paṭisandhiṃ dadeyya, tadā akusalapaṭisandhiyā sugatiyaṃ asambhavato apāyesveva dadeyya, apāyagamanīyañca ekantena dassanenapahātabbā siyā, itarathā apāyagamanīyassa appahīnattā sekhānaṃ apāyuppatti āpajjati, na ca panetaṃ yuttaṃ, “catūhapāyehi ca vippamutto (khu. pā. 6.11; su. ni. 234), avinipātadhammo”tiādivacanehi saha virujjhanato, sati ca panetassa dassanenapahātabbabhāve “siyā dassanenapahātabbā”ti imassa vibhaṅge vattabbaṃ siyā, na ca panetaṃ vuttanti. Atha siyā “apāyagamanīyo rāgo doso moho tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesā”ti evaṃ dassanenapahātabbesu vuttattā uddhaccasahagatassāpi tattha saṅgaho sakkā kātunti? Taṃ na, tassa niyāmato bhāvanāyapahātabbabhāvena vuttattāti [M 2.0071] tasmā dassanenapahātabbesu avacanameva paṭisandhidānābhāvaṃ sādhetīti.

How then should this be understood: "There is no nature of giving rebirth-linking for that which is associated with restlessness"? Because it is not among those to be abandoned by insight. For unwholesome states are threefold: those to be abandoned by insight, those to be abandoned by development, and those that may be abandoned either by insight or by development. Among these, consciousnesses associated with views and the consciousness accompanied by doubt are called "to be abandoned by insight." As it is said: "Which states are to be abandoned by insight? The four consciousnesses associated with views and the consciousness accompanied by doubt." These are called "to be abandoned by insight" because they are to be abandoned solely by the path of stream-entry, which is named "insight" because it sees Nibbāna for the first time. The consciousness accompanied by restlessness is called "to be abandoned by development." As it is said: "Which states are to be abandoned by development? The consciousness accompanied by restlessness." This is said to be "to be abandoned by development" because it is to be abandoned by the highest path. For the three higher paths arise by way of developing that which has already been seen by the first path; they do not see anything previously unseen. Therefore, this is called "development." However, consciousnesses dissociated from views and those accompanied by displeasure are called "may be abandoned either by insight or by development." As it is said: "The four consciousnesses associated with greed, dissociated from views, and the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure—these states may be abandoned either by insight or by development." These are called "may be abandoned either by insight or by development" because, in the state of producing rebirth in the lower realms, they are abandoned by the first path, and in the remaining states, they are abandoned by the higher paths. Here, even those that 'may be abandoned by insight' are referred to simply as 'to be abandoned by insight' due to the general category. Now, if that which is associated with restlessness were to give rebirth, then, since an unwholesome rebirth-linking cannot occur in a happy destination, it would give rebirth only in the lower realms. And that which leads to the lower realms would invariably be abandoned by insight. Otherwise, if that which leads to the lower realms were not abandoned, rebirth in the lower realms would befall even trainees. But this is not proper, as it contradicts statements like "freed from the four lower realms" and "of a nature not to fall away." Moreover, if it were to be abandoned by insight, it should have been stated in the Vibhaṅga in the section on 'may be abandoned by insight,' but it is not stated. Then, could it be said: 'Since it is stated among those to be abandoned by insight that "lust, hatred, and delusion that lead to the lower realms, and the defilements associated with them," the consciousness accompanied by restlessness could also be included there'? That is not so, because it is stated as being invariably to be abandoned by development. Therefore, its not being mentioned among those to be abandoned by insight proves its absence of giving rebirth-linking.

Nanu ca paṭisambhidāvibhaṅge –

But surely, in the Paṭisambhidā Vibhaṅga:

“Yasmiṃ samaye akusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti upekkhāsahagataṃ uddhaccasampayuttaṃ, rūpārammaṇaṃ vā…pe… dhammārammaṇaṃ vā yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha, tasmiṃ samaye phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hoti, ime dhammā akusalā. Imesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā, tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 731) –

"At the time when an unwholesome consciousness arises, accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness, taking as its object a form... or a mental phenomenon... or whatever it may take as its object, at that time there is contact... non-distraction; these states are unwholesome. Knowledge of these states is the discrimination of states, and knowledge of their result is the discrimination of meaning."

Evaṃ [V 2.0053] uddhaccasahagatacittuppādaṃ uddharitvā tassa vipākopi uddhaṭoti kathamassa paṭisandhidānābhāvo sampaṭicchitabboti? Na idaṃ paṭisandhidānaṃ sandhāya uddhaṭaṃ, atha kho pavattivipākaṃ sandhāya. Paṭṭhāne pana –

Having thus cited the arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness, and also its result, how then should the absence of its giving rebirth-linking be accepted? This is not cited with reference to giving rebirth-linking, but rather with reference to resultant states in the course of life. However, in the Paṭṭhāna:

“Sahajātā dassanenapahātabbā cetanā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ kammapaccayena paccayo, nānakkhaṇikā dassanenapahātabbā cetanā vipākānaṃ khandhānaṃ kaṭattā ca rūpānaṃ kammapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.8.89) –

"Co-nascent volition to be abandoned by insight is a condition by way of kamma-condition for mind-originated material phenomena, and non-momentary volition to be abandoned by insight is a condition by way of kamma-condition for resultant aggregates and for kamma-produced materiality."

Dassanenapahātabbacetanāya eva sahajātanānakkhaṇikakammapaccayabhāvaṃ uddharitvāva “sahajātā bhāvanāyapahātabbā cetanā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ kammapaccayena paccayo”ti bhāvanāyapahātabbacetanāya sahajātakammapaccayabhāvova uddhaṭo, na pana nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayabhāvo. Tathā paccanīyanayepi –

Having cited only the co-nascent and non-momentary kamma-conditionality of volition to be abandoned by insight, and having stated, "co-nascent volition to be abandoned by development is a condition for mind-originated material phenomena by way of kamma-condition," only the co-nascent kamma-conditionality of volition to be abandoned by development is cited, but not its non-momentary kamma-conditionality. Similarly, in the negative method:

“Dassanenapahātabbo dhammo nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbassa dhammassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo, sahajāta… upanissaya…pe… pacchājāta… kammapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.8.98) –

"A state to be abandoned by insight is a condition for a state that is to be abandoned neither by insight nor by development through the object condition, co-nascence... decisive support... post-nascence... kamma condition."

Dassanenapahātabbasseva [M 2.0072] kammapaccayabhāvaṃ uddharitvā –

Having cited only the kamma-conditionality of that which is to be abandoned by insight:

“Bhāvanāyapahātabbo dhammo nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbassa dhammassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo, sahajāta… upanissaya… pacchājātapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.8.99) –

"A state to be abandoned by development is a condition for a state that is to be abandoned neither by insight nor by development through the object condition, co-nascence... decisive support... post-nascence condition."

Bhāvanāyapahātabbassa dhammassa sahajātādipaccayabhāvova vutto, na pana kammapaccayabhāvo, na ca nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayaṃ vinā paṭisandhiākaḍḍhanaṃ atthi, tasmā natthi tassa sabbathāpi paṭisandhidānaṃ. Pavattivipākaṃ panassa na sakkā nivāretuṃ paṭisambhidāvibhaṅge uddhaccasahagatānampi vipākassa uddhaṭattā, nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayassa ca paṭisandhivipākameva sandhāya anuddhaṭattā. Evañca pana katvā yadeke ācariyā vadanti “uddhaccacetanā ubhayavipākampi [V 2.0054] na deti paṭṭhāne nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayassa anuddhaṭattā”ti, taṃ tesaṃ abhinivesamattamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Only the co-nascent and other conditionality of the state to be abandoned by development is stated, but not its kamma-conditionality. Moreover, without the non-momentary kamma-condition, there is no drawing forth of rebirth-linking. Therefore, it does not give rebirth-linking in any way. However, its resultant states in the course of life cannot be prevented, because in the Paṭisambhidā Vibhaṅga, the result of even states accompanied by restlessness is cited, and because the non-citation of the non-momentary kamma-condition is only with reference to the rebirth-linking result. This being the case, when some teachers say, "A volition accompanied by restlessness does not give either kind of result because the non-momentary kamma-condition is not cited in the Paṭṭhāna," that should be seen as merely their own dogmatic adherence.

Yadi ca te vadeyyuṃ – yathā “vipākadhammadhammā”ti ettha vipāka-saddena vipākārahatā vuccati, evaṃ idhāpi uddhaccasahagatānaṃ vipākārahataṃ sandhāya “tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Yathā saddhindriyavinimuttassa adhimuccanaṭṭhassa abhāvepi saddhindriyassa adhimuccanasattivisesaṃ gahetvā saddhindriyadhammo adhimuccanaṭṭho atthoti vuccati, evamidhāpi dhammavinimuttassa vipākārahabhāvassa abhāvepi dhammānameva vipākārahasāmatthiyaṃ gahetvā tassa atthibhāvo vutto. Yadi ca te pavattivipākaṃ dadeyyuṃ, yathā –

And if they were to say: Just as in the phrase "states that are the nature of result," the term "result" refers to the potential for a result, so here too, regarding those accompanied by restlessness, the potential for a result is implied, hence it is said, "knowledge in their result." Just as, even in the absence of a function of resolution separate from the faculty of faith, by taking the distinctive power of resolution of the faculty of faith, it is said that the state of the faculty of faith has the function of resolution; so here too, even in the absence of a state of having the potential for a result separate from the states themselves, by taking the capability of the states themselves to have the potential for a result, its existence is stated. And if they were to give a resultant state in the course of life, as—

“Sukhāya vedanāya sampayutto dhammo dukkhāya vedanāya sampayuttassa dhammassa kammapaccayena paccayo, nānakkhaṇikā”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.2.57) –

"A state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with painful feeling by way of a non-momentary kamma-condition."

Pavattivipākassapi [M 2.0073] vasena nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayo vutto, evametthāpi nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayabhāvo vattabbo siyā. Na hi labbhamānassa avacane kāraṇaṃ atthīti tasmā yathādhammasāsane avacanampi abhāvameva dīpeti. Apica yadi uddhaccasahagatassa pavattivipākadānaṃ adhippetaṃ siyā, tadā “anupādinnupādāniyo dhammo upādinnupādāniyassa dhammassa na kammapaccayena paccayo”ti paṭisedho na kātabbo siyā. Na hi ṭhapetvā uddhaccaṃ añño koci anupādinnupādāniyo dhammo upādinnupādāniyassa dhammassa paccayo bhavituṃ asamattho atthīti, tayidametesaṃ abhilāpamattaṃ. Tathā hi yaṃ tāva vuttaṃ “vipākārahabhāvaṃ gahetvā tesaṃ vipāketi vutta”nti, tadeva tassa vipākasabbhāvaṃ dīpeti. Na hi vipākārahabhāve sati abhiññādīnaṃ viya tassa avipākatāya kāraṇaṃ atthīti. Yampi vuttaṃ “nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayassa avacanaṃ vipākabhāvaṃ dīpetī”ti, tampi na sundaraṃ, labbhamānassāpi katthaci kenaci adhippāyena avacanato. Tathā hi dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ labbhamānampi hadayavatthu na vuttaṃ. Tasmā yadi pavattivipākaṃ sandhāya nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayabhāvo vucceyya, tadā paṭisandhivipākadānampissa maññeyyunti labbhamānassapi pavattivipākassa vasena nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayabhāvo na vuttoti. Yaṃ pana anupādinnupādāniyassa upādinnupādāniyaṃ pati kammapaccayapaṭikkhepavacanaṃ, taṃ abhiññākusalādike sandhāyāti na ettāvatā uddhaccasahagatassa [V 2.0055] pavattivipākadānaṃ sabbathāpi paṭikkhipituṃ sakkāti. Yampi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “yathā ca abhiññācetanā, evamuddhaccacetanāpi ‘saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa’nti ettha apanetabbā”ti vuttaṃ, tampi uddhaccacetanāya tattha niddisiyamānāya yathā itarā paṭisandhipavattivasena duvidhassapi vipākaviññāṇassa paccayo, evamuddhaccacetanāpīti gaṇheyyunti vuttaṃ, na tassa pavattivipākābhāvatoti.

The kamma-condition with different moments is stated by way of the resultant process; thus, it might be said, here too the state of being a kamma-condition with different moments should be spoken of. For when something is available and not mentioned, there is no reason for its non-mention; thus, in accordance with the teaching of the Dhamma, even the absence of mention indicates its very absence. Furthermore, if the giving of a resultant process by that which is associated with restlessness were intended, then the prohibition stated as, “an unappropriated phenomenon is not a kamma-condition for an appropriated phenomenon,” should not have been made. For, apart from restlessness, there is no other unappropriated phenomenon that is incapable of being a condition for an appropriated phenomenon; this is merely their utterance. Indeed, as to what was said, “taking their worthiness to be a result, it is said of them that it is a result,” that very statement indicates its actual existence as a result. For when there is worthiness to be a result, there is no reason for its not being a result, unlike in the case of higher knowledges and so on. And as to what was said, “the absence of mention of the kamma-condition with different moments indicates its resultant nature,” that too is not well-founded, since even what is available is sometimes not mentioned due to some reason or intention. For example, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the heart-base, though available, is not mentioned. Therefore, if the kamma-condition with different moments were spoken of in relation to resultant processes, one might also assume it applies to rebirth-linking results; hence, the kamma-condition with different moments is not mentioned even for available resultant processes. As for the statement excluding an unappropriated phenomenon as a kamma-condition for an appropriated phenomenon, this refers to cases like wholesome deeds of higher knowledge; it does not entirely negate the possibility of resultant processes associated with restlessness. And what is said in the commentary—“just as the volition of higher knowledge, so too should the volition of restlessness be removed from ‘formations condition consciousness’”—that was said because if the volition of restlessness were indicated there, one might take it that just as the others are conditions for two kinds of resultant consciousness, by way of rebirth and process, so too is the volition of restlessness; it does not mean that there is no resultant process for it.

Ācariyabuddhamittādayo [M 2.0074] pana uddhaccasahagataṃ dvidhā vibhajitvā ekassa ubhayavipākadānaṃ, ekassa sabbathāpi vipākābhāvaṃ vaṇṇenti. Tesañhi ayaṃ vinicchayo – atthi uddhaccaṃ bhāvanāyapahātabbampi, atthi nabhāvanāyapahātabbampi. Tesu bhāvanāyapahātabbaṃ sekhasantānappavattaṃ, itaraṃ puthujjanasantānappavattaṃ. Phaladānañca puthujjanasantāne pavattasseva, netarassa. Tathā hi dassanabhāvanānaṃ abhāvepi yesaṃ puthujjanānaṃ, sekhānañca dassanabhāvanāhi bhavitabbaṃ, tesaṃ taduppattikāle tāhi pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā akusalā “dassanenapahātabbā, bhāvanāyapahātabbā”ti ca vuccanti. Puthujjanānaṃ pana bhāvanāya abhāvato bhāvanāyapahātabbacintā natthi, tena tesaṃ pavattamānā te dassanena pahātuṃ asakkuṇeyyāpi “bhāvanāyapahātabbā”ti na vuccanti. Yadi vucceyyuṃ, dassanenapahātabbā bhāvanāyapahātabbānaṃ kesañci keci kadāci ārammaṇārammaṇādhipatiupanissayapaccayehi paccayā bhaveyyuṃ. Sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgādīnañhi kesañci sakkāyadiṭṭhādayo keci atītādīsu kismiñci kāle ārammaṇādhipatiupanissayehi paccayā hontīti natthi, na ca paṭṭhāne “dassanenapahātabbā bhāvanāyapahātabbānaṃ kenaci paccayena paccayo”ti vuttā, tasmā natthi puthujjanesu pavattamānānamakusalānaṃ bhāvanāyapahātabbapariyāyo. Yadi tattha avacanameva pamāṇaṃ, evaṃ sati sekhasantānapavattānampi akusalānaṃ bhāvanāyapahātabbapariyāyo natthīti āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, sekhasantānappavattānaṃ bhāvanāya pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyattā. Teneva ca kiñci katvā sekhānaṃ dassanenapahātabbānaṃ akusalānaṃ pahīnabhāvena assādanābhinandanānaṃ vatthūni na honti. Pahīnatāya eva somanassassa hetubhūtā, avikkhepahetubhūtā ca na domanassaṃ, uddhaccañca uppādentīti na tesaṃ ārammaṇārammaṇādhipatipakatūpanissayabhāvaṃ [M 2.0075] gacchanti. Na hi pahīnakilese upanissāya ariyā rāgadosavikkhepe uppādenti. Vuttañca “sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti, na pacceti, na paccāgacchatīti sugato, sakadāgāmi…pe… arahattamaggena…pe… sugato”ti. Puthujjanānaṃ pana dassanena pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā [V 2.0056] dassanena pahātuṃ asakkuṇeyyānaṃ kenaci paccayena paccayā na hontīti na sakkā vattuṃ, “diṭṭhiṃ assādeti abhinandati, taṃ ārabbha rāgo uppajjati, diṭṭhi uppajjati, vicikicchā uppajjati, uddhaccaṃ uppajjati, vicikicchaṃ ārabbha vicikicchā uppajjati, diṭṭhi uppajjati, uddhaccaṃ uppajjatī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.407) diṭṭhivicikicchānaṃ uddhaccārammaṇabhāvassa vuttattā. Ettha hi uddhaccanti uddhaccasahagataṃ cittuppādaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na dassanenapahātabbesupi labbhamānacetasikaṃ uddhaccaṃ. Evañca katvā adhipatipaccayaniddese “diṭṭhiṃ garuṃ katvā assādeti abhinandati, taṃ garuṃ katvā rāgo uppajjati, diṭṭhi uppajjatī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.415) ettakameva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “uddhaccaṃ uppajjatī”ti, tasmā sekhasantānappavattānamakusalānaṃ dassanenapahātabbānaṃ kenaci paccayena paccayattābhāvato puthujjanānaṃ santāneva dassanenapahātabbānamakusalānaṃ paccayā na hontīti na sakkā vattunti paṭṭhāne dassanenapahātabbānaṃ bhāvanāyapahātabbassa ārammaṇārammaṇādhipatiupanissayapaccayattānuddharaṇaṃ sekhasantānappavattānaṃ bhāvanāyapahātabbapariyāyabhāvaṃ sādheti, puthujjanasantāneyeva nadassanenapahātabbānamakusalānaṃ bhāvanāyapahātabbapariyāyabhāvaṃ na sādheti, tasmā dassanabhāvanāhi pahātabbānaṃ atītādibhāvena navattabbattepi yādisānaṃ tāhi anuppattidhammatā āpādetabbā, te puthujjanesu pavattamānā [M 2.0076] dassanena pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā dassanamaggāpekkhāya tadappavattiyampi dassanenapahātabbā nāma. Sekhesu pavattamānā bhāvanāya pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā tadappavattiyampi tadapekkhāya bhāvanāyapahātabbā nāma. Dassanena pahātuṃ asakkuṇeyyā pana puthujjanesu pavattamānā heṭṭhā vuttanayena nevadassanenapahātabbā nabhāvanāyapahātabbā, tesu bhāvanāyapahātabbā sahāyavirahato vipākaṃ na janenti. Tathā hi tesaṃ dassanenapahātabbasaṅkhātaṃ sahakārīkāraṇaṃ sahāyabhūtaṃ natthīti bhāvanāyapahātabbacetanāya nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayabhāvo na vutto. Apekkhitabbadassanabhāvanārahitānaṃ pana puthujjanesu uppajjamānānaṃ sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgādīnaṃ, uddhaccasahagatacittuppādassa ca saṃyojanattayatadekaṭṭhakilesānaṃ anupacchinnatāya aparikkhīṇasahāyānaṃ vipākuppādanaṃ na sakkā paṭikkhipitunti uddhaccasahagatadhammānaṃ vipāko vibhaṅge vuttoti.

However, teachers such as Buddhamitta describe that which is accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca) by dividing it into two kinds: one that gives a twofold result, and one that gives no result whatsoever. For this is their determination: there is restlessness to be abandoned by development (bhāvanā), and there is restlessness not to be abandoned by development. Of these, that which is to be abandoned by development occurs in the mental continuum of a learner (sekha), while the other occurs in the mental continuum of an ordinary person (puthujjana). And the giving of fruit pertains only to that which occurs in the mental continuum of an ordinary person, not to the other. For thus, even in the absence of seeing (dassana) and development, for those ordinary persons and learners for whom there must be seeing and development, the unwholesome states that can be abandoned by these paths at the time of their arising are called 'to be abandoned by seeing' and 'to be abandoned by development.' But for ordinary persons, due to the absence of development, there is no consideration of what is 'to be abandoned by development'; therefore, those unwholesome states arising in them, even those that cannot be abandoned by seeing, are not called 'to be abandoned by development.' If they were so called, then some states to be abandoned by seeing would sometimes be conditions for some states to be abandoned by development by way of object, object-predominance, and strong support conditions. For it is not the case that some defilements such as identity-view are, at some time in the past, etc., conditions by way of object, predominance, or strong support for some other defilements such as desire and lust for one's own belongings; nor is it stated in the Paṭṭhāna that 'a state to be abandoned by seeing is a condition by some condition for a state to be abandoned by development.' Therefore, for unwholesome states arising in ordinary persons, there is no category of 'to be abandoned by development.' If the mere non-statement there is the authority, would it not then follow that there is no category of 'to be abandoned by development' even for unwholesome states arising in the mental continuum of a learner? It does not follow, because those arising in the mental continuum of a learner can be abandoned by development. And for that very reason, for learners, since the unwholesome states to be abandoned by seeing have been abandoned, they are no longer objects for savoring and delighting. Because of their very abandonment, they become a cause for joy and for non-distraction, and they do not produce displeasure and restlessness; thus, they do not become an object, object-predominance, or natural strong support condition for them. For noble ones do not generate lust, hatred, or restlessness by relying on abandoned defilements. And it is said: 'The Well-farer does not return to, does not relapse into, does not come back to those defilements that have been abandoned by the path of stream-entry; ... (and similarly for) the once-returner... by the path of arahantship... the Well-farer.' But for ordinary persons, it cannot be said that states that can be abandoned by seeing are not conditions by some condition for states that cannot be abandoned by seeing. For it is stated: 'One savors and delights in a view; taking that as an object, lust arises, a view arises, doubt arises, restlessness arises. Taking doubt as an object, doubt arises, a view arises, restlessness arises' (Paṭṭh. 1.1.407), since it has been stated that views and doubt have the nature of being an object for restlessness. Here, 'restlessness' is said referring to a mind-moment accompanied by restlessness, not the mental factor of restlessness which is also found in states to be abandoned by seeing. For this reason, in the explanation of the predominance condition, only this much is stated: 'Regarding a view as important, one savors and delights in it; regarding that as important, lust arises, a view arises' (Paṭṭh. 1.1.415); it is not stated 'restlessness arises.' Therefore—since it cannot be said that because unwholesome states to be abandoned by seeing in a learner's continuum are not a condition by any means, those in an ordinary person's continuum are likewise not conditions—the non-mention in the Paṭṭhāna of a state to be abandoned by seeing being an object, object-predominance, or strong support condition for a state to be abandoned by development establishes the existence of the category 'to be abandoned by development' for states arising in the continuum of a learner, but it does not establish the existence of this category for unwholesome states not to be abandoned by seeing, which are only in the continuum of an ordinary person. Therefore, even though states to be abandoned by seeing and development should not be spoken of in terms of past, etc., for those states for which a nature of non-arising must be brought about by these paths, those arising in ordinary persons that can be abandoned by seeing are, with respect to the path of seeing, called 'to be abandoned by seeing' even when that path does not occur. Those arising in learners that can be abandoned by development are, with respect to that development, called 'to be abandoned by development' even when it does not occur. But those states arising in ordinary persons that cannot be abandoned by seeing are, according to the method stated above, neither 'to be abandoned by seeing' nor 'to be abandoned by development.' Among these, those 'to be abandoned by development' do not generate a result due to the absence of an ally. For thus, since they lack the cooperative cause, which is an ally, designated as 'to be abandoned by seeing,' the state of being a different-moment kamma condition is not stated for the volition 'to be abandoned by development.' However, for desire, lust, etc., for one's own belongings, and for the mind-moment accompanied by restlessness, which arise in ordinary persons who are devoid of the required seeing and development—since for them the three fetters and the defilements of similar nature are not cut off and their allies are not exhausted—the production of a result cannot be rejected. Thus, the result of states accompanied by restlessness is stated in the Vibhaṅga.

Yadi evaṃ, apekkhitabbadassanabhāvanārahitānaṃ akusalānaṃ “nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbā”ti vattabbatā āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, appahātabbasabhāvānaṃ kusalādīnaṃ “nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbā”ti vuttattā, appahātabbaviruddhasabhāvattā ca akusalānaṃ[V 2.0057]. Yadi evaṃ te imasmiṃ tike navattabbāti vattabbā āpajjantīti? Nāpajjanti, cittuppādakaṇḍe dassitānaṃ dvādasākusalacittuppādānaṃ dvīhi padehi saṅgahitattā. Yathā hi uppannattike dhammavasena sabbesaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ saṅgahitattā kālavasena asaṅgahitāpi atītā “navattabbā”ti na [M 2.0077] vuttā cittuppādānurūpena saṅgahitesu navattabbassa abhāvā, evaṃ idhāpi cittuppādabhāvena saṅgahitesu navattabbassa abhāvā “navattabbā”ti na vuttā. Sabbena sabbañhi dhammavasena asaṅgahitassa tikadukesu navattabbatāpatti. Yattha hi cittuppādo koci niyogato navattabbo atthi, tattha tesaṃ catuttho koṭṭhāso atthīti yathāvuttapadesu viya tatthāpi bhinditvā bhājetabbe cittuppāde bhinditvā bhājeti “siyā navattabbāparittārammaṇā”tiādinā, tadabhāvā uppannattike, idha ca tathā na vuttanti.

If so, does it follow that for unwholesome states, which are devoid of the seeing and development to be undertaken, it should be said that they are 'to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development'? It does not follow, because wholesome states and others, which by nature are not to be abandoned, are described as 'to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development,' and because unwholesome states are by nature contrary to what is not to be abandoned. If so, does it follow that they should be said to be 'unclassifiable' in this triad? It does not follow, because the twelve unwholesome arisings of consciousness shown in the chapter on arisings of consciousness are included by two terms. For just as in the Triad of the Arisen, all conditioned phenomena are included by way of states, and past phenomena, though not included by way of time, are not called 'unclassifiable' because there is no 'unclassifiable' category among things grouped in accordance with arisings of consciousness; so too here, since they are grouped by way of being arisings of consciousness, they are not called 'unclassifiable' because there is no 'unclassifiable' category. For in every way, what is not included by way of states in the triads and dyads becomes designated as 'unclassifiable.' Wherever there is some arising of consciousness that is necessarily 'unclassifiable,' there a fourth category for them exists. Thus, just as in the aforementioned passages, in the case of an arising of consciousness that should be analyzed by breaking it down, one analyzes by breaking it down, saying, 'There might be unclassifiable states with limited objects,' and so on. Because this is absent in the Triad of the Arisen, and because it is not stated so here, this does not apply.

Atha vā yathā sappaṭighehi samānasabhāvattā rūpadhātuyaṃ “tayo mahābhūtā sappaṭighā”ti vuttā, yathāha “asaññasattānaṃ anidassanasappaṭighaṃ ekaṃ mahābhūta”nti, evaṃ puthujjanānaṃ pavattamānā bhāvanāyapahātabbasamānasabhāvā “bhāvanāyapahātabbā”ti vucceyyunti natthi navattabbatāpasaṅgo. Evañca sati puthujjanānaṃ pavattamānāpi bhāvanāyapahātabbā sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgādayo parabhaṇḍe chandarāgādīnaṃ upanissayapaccayo, rāgo ca rāgadiṭṭhīnaṃ adhipatipaccayoti ayamattho laddho hoti. Teneva hi –

Alternatively, just as in the form realm the three great elements are said to be 'resistant' because they have the same nature as resistant things—as it is said, 'For non-percipient beings, one great element is invisible and resistant'—so too, states occurring in worldlings that have the same nature as those to be abandoned by development could be called 'to be abandoned by development.' Thus there is no occasion for them to be designated 'unclassifiable.' And this being so, the meaning is obtained that even desire, lust, and so on for one's own belongings, which are to be abandoned by development and which occur in worldlings, are a decisive support condition for desire, lust, and so on for others' belongings; and that lust is a dominance condition for lust and wrong views. For this very reason—

“Bhāvanāyapahātabbo dhammo dassanenapahātabbassa dhammassa upanissayapaccayena paccayo, ārammaṇūpanissayo, pakatūpanissayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.8.84) –

“A state to be abandoned by development is a condition for a state to be abandoned by seeing by way of decisive support condition: object decisive support and natural decisive support.” (Paṭṭhāna 2.8.84)

Imissā niddese dassanenapahātabbānaṃ upanissayapaccayabhāvīdhamme niddisantena bhagavatā –

In this exposition, the Blessed One, indicating the states that become a decisive support condition for those to be abandoned by seeing, said:

“Pakatūpanissayo – patthanaṃ upanissāya pāṇaṃ hanati…pe… saṅghaṃ bhindati, bhāvanāyapahātabbo rāgo doso moho māno patthanā dassanenapahātabbassa rāgassa dosassa mohassa mānassa diṭṭhiyā patthanāya upanissayapaccayena paccayo[M 2.0078]. Sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgo parabhaṇḍe chandarāgassa upa…pe… sakapariggahe chandarāgo parapariggahe chandarāgassa upanissayapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.8.84) –

“Natural decisive support: Relying on yearning, one destroys life …pe… splits the Sangha. Lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and yearning that are to be abandoned by development are a condition for the lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, and yearning that are to be abandoned by seeing, by way of decisive support condition. Desire and lust for one's own goods are a condition for desire and lust for another's goods …pe… desire and lust for one's own retinue are a condition for desire and lust for another's retinue by way of decisive support condition.” (Paṭṭhāna 2.8.84)

Puthujjanasantāne [V 2.0058] patthanādayo niddiṭṭhā.

Yearning and so on are thus indicated in the mental continuum of a worldling.

Evampi yathā aphoṭṭhabbattā rūpadhātuyaṃ tayo mahābhūtā na paramatthato sappaṭighā, evaṃ apekkhitabbabhāvanārahitā puthujjanesu pavattamānā sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgādayo pana paramatthato bhāvanāya pahātabbāti bhāvanāyapahātabbānaṃ nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayatā na vuttā, na ca “dassanenapahātabbā bhāvanāyapahātabbānaṃ kenaci paccayena paccayo”ti vuttā. Ye hi dassanenapahātabbapaccayā kilesā, na te dassanato uddhaṃ pavattanti. Dassanenapahātabbapaccayassāpi pana uddhaccasahagatassa sahāyavekallamattameva dassanena kataṃ, na tassa koci bhāvo dassanena anuppattidhammataṃ āpāditoti tassa ekantabhāvanāyapahātabbatā vuttā, tasmā uddhaccabhāvena ekasabhāvasseva tassa sati sahāye vipākuppādanavacanaṃ, asati ca vipākānuppādanavacanaṃ na virujjhati. Tayidaṃ sabbametesaṃ ācariyānaṃ ahopurisikāramattaṃ. Kasmā? Uddhaccasahagatassa ekantabhāvanāyapahātabbabhāvena vuttattā. Evañhi vuttaṃ bhagavatā “katame dhammā bhāvanāyapahātabbā. Uddhaccasahagato cittuppādo”ti (dha. sa. 1406). Yadi ca uddhaccasahagataṃ nabhāvanāyapahātabbaṃ abhavissa, yathā atītārammaṇattike “niyogā anāgatārammaṇā natthī”ti (dha. sa. 1433) vatvā vibhajja vuttaṃ, evamidhāpi “niyogā bhāvanāyapahātabbā natthī”ti vatvā “uddhaccasahagato siyā bhāvanāyapahātabbo siyā navattabbo ‘dassanenapahātabbo’tipi ‘bhāvanāyapahātabbo’tipī”tiādi vattabbaṃ siyā[M 2.0079], na ca tathā vuttaṃ. Yā ca “tamatthaṃ paṭipādentehi yadi vucceyyu”ntiādinā yutti vuttā, sāpi ayutti. Kasmā? Dassanenapahātabbārammaṇānaṃ rāgadiṭṭhivicikicchāuddhaccānaṃ tena tena pahātabbabhāvavasena icchitattā. Yañca “uddhaccaṃ uppajjatī”ti uddhaccasahagatacittuppādo vuttoti dassetuṃ adhipatipaccayaniddese uddhaccassa anuddharaṇaṃ kāraṇavasena vuttaṃ, tampi akāraṇaṃ aññatthāpi sāvasesapāṭhānaṃ dassanato. Tathā hi “atīto dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassa, anāgato dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti etesaṃ vibhaṅge cetopariyañāṇaggahaṇaṃ katvā “paccuppanno dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassā”ti imassa vibhaṅge labbhamānampi cetopariyañāṇaṃ na gahitaṃ. Yampi bhāvanāyapahātabbassa vipākadānamhi dassanenapahātabbassa sahāyabhāvūpagamanaṃ vuttaṃ, tampi vicāretabbaṃ – kiṃ avijjādi viya dānasīlādīnaṃ upapattiyaṃyeva vipākadānasāmatthiyā ṭhānavasena dassanenapahātabbā bhāvanāyapahātabbānaṃ sahakārīkāraṇaṃ hoti, udāhu kileso viya kammassa paṭisandhidānamhīti[V 2.0059]? Kiñcettha – yadi tāva purimo nayo, sekhasantāne bhāvanāyapahātabbassa akiriyābhāvo āpajjati, pahīnāvijjāmānataṇhānusayasmiṃ santāne dānādi viya sahāyavekallena avipākasabhāvataṃ āpannattā. Atha dutiyo, bhāvanāyapahātabbattena abhimatassāpi dassanenapahātabbabhāvo āpajjati, paṭisandhidāne sati apāyagamanīyasabhāvānativattanato, tasmā amhehi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva uddhaccasahagatassa vipākadānaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, na yesaṃ kesañci vacanaṃ. Paṭṭhānānusārīhi bhavitabbanti.

Even so, just as the three great elements in the form realm are not ultimately resistant because they are intangible, so too desire, lust, and so on for one's own belongings, which occur in worldlings and are devoid of the development to be undertaken, are ultimately to be abandoned by development. However, it is not stated that states to be abandoned by development are conditioned by different-moment kamma, nor is it said that 'a state to be abandoned by seeing is a condition for states to be abandoned by development by way of any condition whatsoever.' For those defilements conditioned by what is to be abandoned by seeing do not occur beyond the path of seeing. For an arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness that has a condition to be abandoned by seeing, only the mere lack of an associate is effected by seeing; no state of it is brought to a nature of non-arising by seeing. Therefore, its quality of being exclusively abandoned by development is stated. Thus, for that which has the single nature of restlessness, the statement that it produces a result when it has an associate and does not produce a result when it does not, is not contradictory. All this is merely the personal conceit of those teachers. Why? Because what is accompanied by restlessness is said to be exclusively abandoned by development. For thus it was said by the Blessed One: 'What states are to be abandoned by development? The arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness.' (Dhs. §1406) If what is accompanied by restlessness were not to be abandoned by development, then just as in the Triad on Past Objects it is said, 'Necessarily, there are no states with future objects' (Dhs. §1433), and then an analysis is given, so here too it should have been said, 'Necessarily, there are no states to be abandoned by development,' and then it should be said, 'What is accompanied by restlessness might be abandoned by development, or it might be unclassifiable as “to be abandoned by seeing” or “to be abandoned by development,”' and so on. But it was not stated so. And the reasoning given, beginning, 'If those who are establishing that meaning should say…,' is also unsound. Why? Because it is intended that lust, wrong view, doubt, and restlessness—which have as their object what is to be abandoned by seeing—are to be abandoned by their respective means. And the non-mention of restlessness in the exposition of dominance condition, adduced to show that 'the arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness' is meant, is also not a valid reason, since texts with omissions are seen elsewhere. For example, in the analysis of 'a past state is a condition for a present state by way of object condition' and 'a future state is a condition for a present state by way of object condition,' the knowledge of others' minds is included; yet in the analysis of 'a present state is a condition for a present state,' the knowledge of others' minds is not included, though it can be obtained there. Further, the statement that what is to be abandoned by seeing assists in the giving of fruit by what is to be abandoned by development should be examined. Does what is to be abandoned by seeing act as a cooperative cause for what is to be abandoned by development—in the sense that it is a basis for the capacity of giving, virtue, etc., to give fruit in a future existence, like ignorance, etc.? Or is it like a defilement for kamma in giving rebirth-linking? Here, if the first alternative is taken, it would follow that in the continuum of a learner, what is to be abandoned by development would become functionally ineffective, for in a continuum where the latent tendencies of ignorance, conceit, and craving have been abandoned, it would, like giving, etc., assume a nature of not producing a result due to the lack of an associate. If the second alternative is taken, then even what is considered to be abandoned by development would become something to be abandoned by seeing, because when it gives rebirth-linking, it does not overcome its nature of leading to the plane of misery. Therefore, the giving of result by what is accompanied by restlessness should be accepted by us only in the way stated above, not according to the word of just anyone. One should be a follower of the Paṭṭhāna.

537-8. Yanti yaṃ āvajjanadvayaṃ. Karaṇamattattāti karaṇamattameva ṭhapetvā phaladānābhāvato. Vātapupphasamanti moghapupphasamaṃ, yathā taṃ paṭhamasañjātaṃ acchinnamūlepi rukkhe [M 2.0080] nibbattaṃ purimehi adinnaphalattā phalanibbattakaṃ na hoti, evamidaṃ anupacchinnabhavamūlepi santāne nibbattaṃ anāsevanabhāvena phaladāyakaṃ na hotīti adhippāyo. Javanattaṃ tu sampattanti aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ khīṇāsavāveṇikaṃ viññāṇamāha. Kiccasādhanatoti bhavataṇhāmūlassa avocchinnabhāve sati kusalākusalakammakiccassa sādhanato, dānāditaṃtaṃkiccasādhanavasena vā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā hi chinnamūlassa rukkhassa pupphaṃ pupphanamattaṃ ṭhapetvā aphalameva hoti, evametampi taṃtaṃkiccasādhanamattaṃ ṭhapetvā samucchinnabhavataṇhāmūle santāne pavattanato aphalamevāti.

537-8. The two advertences that pass away. Because it is merely an act: because, apart from being merely an act, it does not give fruit. Like a wind-flower: means like a barren flower. The meaning is that just as a flower that has first appeared, produced on a tree whose root is still uncut, does not produce fruit because the earlier ones did not give fruit, so this, though produced in a continuum where the root of existence is not cut off, is not fruit-giving because it is not repeatedly practiced. But has attained the state of impulsion: he speaks of the eighteen kinds of consciousness peculiar to one whose taints are destroyed. Because it accomplishes a function: because, when the root of craving for existence is not cut off, it accomplishes the function of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, or by way of accomplishing the particular functions of giving, and so on. This is what is meant: just as the flower of a tree with a cut root, apart from being merely a flower, is indeed fruitless, so this too, apart from being merely the accomplishment of this or that function, is indeed fruitless because it occurs in a continuum where the root of craving for existence has been utterly cut off.

539-40. Paṭiccāti hetudhammassa paṭimukhaṃ gantvā taṃ apaccakkhāya. Etīti pavattati, tiṭṭhati uppajjati vāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Etī”ti hi idaṃ uppattiṭṭhitīnaṃ sādhāraṇavasena pavattiparidīpakaṃ. Tenevāha “ṭhitiyuppattiyāpi vā”ti. Ekacco hi paccayo ṭhitiyā eva upakārako hoti yathā pacchājātapaccayo, ekacco uppattiyā eva yathā anantarādiko, ekacco ubhayassa yathā hetuādayo. Evaṃ paccaya-saddassa vacanatthaṃ dassetvā idāni paccayalakkhaṇaṃ dassento āha “yo dhammo”tiādi. Yoti hetudhammo. Yassāti yassa phaladhammassa. Ṭhitiyuppattiyāpi vāti ṭhititthaṃ, uppattitthaṃ vā. Ṭhitiyāti vā ṭhitikkhaṇe, uppattiyāti uppādakkhaṇe. Yassa dhammassa upakāro, yassa dhammassa ṭhitiyuppattiyāti vā sambandho. “Upakāro”ti iminā dhammena dhammasattiupakārakaṃ dasseti. “Sambhavo”tiādi paccayasseva pariyāyadassanaṃ. Sambhavati etasmāti sambhavo. Tathā pabhavo. Hinoti patiṭṭhāti etthāti hetu. Anekatthattā dhātusaddānaṃ hi-saddo mūla-saddo viya patiṭṭhattho veditabbo[V 2.0060]. Hinoti vā etena kammanidānabhūtena uddhaṃ ojaṃ abhiharantena mūlena [M 2.0081] viya pādapo tappaccayaṃ phalaṃ gacchati, vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ āpajjatīti hetu. Attano phalaṃ karotīti kāraṇaṃ. Paccayo matoti paccayova “sambhavo”tiādito mato. Atthato ete samānā, byañjanamattaṃyeva nesaṃ nānattanti vuttaṃ hoti.

539-40. Paṭicca means: having gone towards a causal state without rejecting it. Eti means: it proceeds, it persists, or it arises—this is what is said. For this word ‘eti’ is a common indicator of occurrence, illuminating both arising and persistence. Hence it is said, “or also for persistence and arising.” For one kind of condition is helpful only for persistence, like the postnascence condition; another is helpful only for arising, like the contiguity condition; and another is helpful for both, like the root condition and others. Having thus shown the verbal meaning of the word “condition,” now, to show the characteristic of a condition, he says, “whatever state,” etc. “Whatever” is the causal state. “Of which” is of which resultant state. “Or also for persistence and arising” means for the sake of persistence or for the sake of arising. Or “for persistence” means at the moment of persistence; “for arising” means at the moment of arising. The connection is: “is helpful to which state,” or “is helpful for the persistence or arising of which state.” By “is helpful,” it shows that this state is helpful by its intrinsic power as a state. “Origin,” etc., are synonyms shown for condition itself. It originates from this, thus it is an “origin” (sambhava). Similarly with “source” (pabhava). It is established herein, thus it is a “root” (hetu). Because verbal roots have many meanings, the root hi should be understood in the sense of establishing, like the word mūla (root). Or: by this, which is the basis of action, the fruit dependent on it goes, grows, and develops, just as a tree does by its root, which draws up sap; thus it is a “root” (hetu). It makes its own fruit, thus it is a “cause” (kāraṇa). “The condition is considered” means that the condition itself is considered to be “origin,” etc. In meaning they are the same; their difference is only in the letter—this is what is said.

541-5. Evaṃ paṭṭhāne āgatasabbapaccayānaṃ sādhāraṇavasena atthaṃ vatvā idhādhippetassa hetupaccayasseva sarūpaṃ dassetuṃ “lobhādi pana yo dhammo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Mūlaṭṭhenāti sampayuttānaṃ suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanasaṅkhātamūlaṭṭhena. Chaḷevāti mūlaṭṭhenūpakārakabhāvassa tesameva āveṇikabhāvena ete chaḷeva. Jātitoti kusalākusalābyākatajātito. Navadhāti tayo kusalahetū, tayo akusalahetū, tayo abyākatahetūti navadhā. Dhammānaṃ…pe… sādhakoti yathā sālivīhibījādīni sālivīhiādibhāvassa sādhakāni, maṇiādipabhāvatthūnañca nīlādivaṇṇāni nīlādimaṇipabhāya sādhakāni, evaṃ hetupaccayo yathārahaṃ attano sampayuttānaṃ kusalādittasādhakoti kusalākusalābyākatadhammānaṃ yathākkamaṃ kusalākusalābyākatabhāvasādhako mūlaṭṭhoti ayamettha attho. Eke ācariyāti revatācariyaṃ, tassa sissānusisse ca sandhāyāha. Atha vā garumhi bahuvacanampi yujjatīti revatācariyameva sandhāya “eke ācariyā”ti vuttaṃ.

541-5. Having thus spoken in a general way on the meaning of all the conditions that come in the Paṭṭhāna, in order to show the specific nature of just the root condition, which is intended here, it is said, “But whatever state, such as greed, etc.” By the meaning of root: by the meaning of root reckoned as the establishing of the well-founded state of associated states. Only six: because being helpful in the sense of a root is the unique characteristic of these six alone. By class: from the class of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. Ninefold: three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots, and three indeterminate roots—thus ninefold. Of states… accomplishes: just as rice seeds and so on accomplish the state of being rice plants and so on, and as the blue color and so on of gems and other lustrous things accomplish the blue lustre of the gem and so on, so the root condition appropriately accomplishes the wholesome, etc., nature of its own associated states. Thus, the meaning here is that the meaning of root is the accomplishment of the wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate nature of wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate states, respectively. Some teachers: this refers to the Elder Revata and his pupils and their pupils. Or, since the plural can be used for a respected person, “some teachers” is said referring only to the Elder Revata.

Evaṃ santeti yadi mūlaṭṭho kusalādibhāvasādhako, evaṃ sati. Yathā cittaṃ cittajarūpānaṃ paccayo hoti, evaṃ taṃsampayuttadhammāpīti āha “taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpisū”ti, hetusamuṭṭhānarūpesūti attho. Neva sampajjatīti na sijjhati, “hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena [M 2.0082] paccayo”ti vutto hetupaccayabhāvo na sampajjatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathā kusalākusalā hetū taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpassa kusalādibhāvāya na pariyattā, evaṃ abyākatopi hetu taṃsamuṭṭhānassa rūpassa abyākatabhāvāya na pariyatto. Sabhāvena hi taṃ abyākatanti āha “na hī”tiādi. Yadi kusalādibhāvaṃ na sādhenti, paccayāpi na hontīti vadeyyāti āha “na tesa”ntiādi. “Hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.1) vacanato te alobhādayo tesaṃ rūpānaṃ paccayā na na honti, bhavantevāti attho.

If this is so: if the meaning of root is the accomplishment of the wholesome, etc., nature, this being the case, just as consciousness is a condition for consciousness-originated matter, so too are the states associated with it. Thus he says, “for the material phenomena originated from them,” meaning, for the material phenomena originated from the roots. It is not established: it does not succeed. It is said that the state of being a root condition, stated as “Roots are a condition for states associated with the roots and for the material phenomena originated from them by root condition,” is not established. Just as wholesome and unwholesome roots are not adequate for the wholesome, etc., nature of the material phenomena originated from them, so too an indeterminate root is not adequate for the indeterminate nature of the material phenomena originated from it. For by its own nature it is indeterminate. Thus he says, “For not,” etc. If they do not accomplish the wholesome, etc., nature, one might say they are not conditions at all. Thus he says, “not of them,” etc. According to the text, “Roots are a condition for states associated with the roots and for the material phenomena originated from them by root condition” (Paṭṭh 1.1.1), those roots such as non-greed are indeed conditions for those material phenomena; it is not that they are not—this is the meaning.

546-7. Na [V 2.0061] gantabboti na paccetabbo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadi kusalādihetuyo attano viya attahetukānaṃ dhammānaṃ kusalādibhāvaṃ sādhenti, kusalākusalahetupaccayasambhūtā rūpadhammāpi te viya kusalādayo siyuṃ, hetuyo vā rūpānaṃ paccayā na siyuṃ, na ca panetaṃ ubhayampi atthi, tasmā kusalādīnaṃ kusalādibhāvasādhako mūlaṭṭhoti na viññātabbanti. Apica yadi hetupaṭibaddho kusalādibhāvo, tadā abyākatabhāvopi tappaṭibaddho siyā, ahetukānaṃ abyākatabhāvo na sijjhati. Yadi ca hetupaṭibaddho kusalādibhāvo, hetūnampi kusalādibhāvo appaṭibaddho siyā. Atha tesampi sesahetupaṭibaddho, evampi momūhacittasampayuttassa hetuno akusalabhāvo na sijjheyya. Atha tassa so aññahetuko siyā, evaṃ sati sesahetūnampi taṃhetukova siyā. Yathā ca sesahetūnaṃ, evaṃ avasesasampayuttadhammānampi taṃhetukova siyā. Atha siyā hetūnaṃ sabhāvatova kusalādibhāvo, sampayuttānaṃ pana [M 2.0083] hetupaṭibaddhoti, evaṃ sati alobho kusalo vā siyā abyākato vā. Yadi hi so sabhāvato kusalo, taṃsabhāvattā abyākato na siyā. Atha abyākato, taṃsabhāvattā kusalo na siyā alobhasabhāvassa adosattābhāvo viya. Yasmā pana ubhayathāpi hoti, tasmā yathā ubhayathā hontesu saddhādīsu sampayuttesu hetupaṭibaddhaṃ kusalādibhāvaṃ pariyesatha, na sabhāvato, evaṃ hetūsupi kusalāditā aññapaṭibaddhā pariyesitabbā, na sabhāvato. Sā pana pariyesiyamānā yonisomanasikārādipaṭibaddhā hotīti hetūsu viya hetusampayuttadhammesupi yonisomanasikārādipaṭibaddho kusalādibhāvo, na hetupaṭibaddhoti. Tenevāha –

546-7. Not to be accepted: not to be believed. This is what is said: If the wholesome, etc., roots accomplished the wholesome, etc., nature of the states rooted in them just as they do for themselves, then the material states produced by wholesome and unwholesome root conditions would also be wholesome, etc., like them; or the roots would not be conditions for the material states. But neither of these two is the case. Therefore, it should not be understood that the meaning of root is the accomplishment of the wholesome, etc., nature of wholesome, etc., states. Furthermore, if the wholesome, etc., nature were dependent on the roots, then the indeterminate nature would also be dependent on them, and the indeterminate nature of rootless states would not be established. And if the wholesome, etc., nature were dependent on the roots, then the wholesome, etc., nature of the roots themselves would have to be independent. But if their nature is dependent on the other roots, then the unwholesome nature of a root associated with a deluded consciousness would not be established. If that nature of it were caused by another root, then the nature of the other roots would also be caused by that one. And just as with the other roots, so too with the remaining associated states—their nature would be caused by that one. Now, it might be that the wholesome, etc., nature belongs to the roots by their own nature, but for the associated states it is dependent on the roots. In that case, non-greed could be either wholesome or indeterminate. For if it were wholesome by its own nature, because of that nature it could not be indeterminate. But if it were indeterminate, because of that nature it could not be wholesome, just as the nature of non-greed is not the state of non-hatred. But since it is both ways, therefore, just as in the case of associated states such as faith, etc., which can be both ways, you seek for a wholesome, etc., nature that is dependent on the roots, not on their own nature, so too in the case of the roots, their wholesomeness, etc., should be sought as dependent on something else, not on their own nature. And when it is sought, it is found to be dependent on wise attention, etc. Thus, just as in the case of the roots, so too in the case of the states associated with the roots, the wholesome, etc., nature is dependent on wise attention, etc., not on the roots. Therefore he said:

“Yoniso, bhikkhave, manasi karoto anuppannā ceva kusalā dhammā uppajjanti, uppannā ca kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhantī”tiādi (a. ni. 1.67).

“Bhikkhus, for one who attends wisely, unarisen wholesome states arise, and arisen wholesome states increase,” etc. (AN 1.67).

Samayaññunāti ābhidhammikamatavedinā. Suppatiṭṭhitabhāvassa sādhanenāti attahetukānaṃ dhammānaṃ sammā patiṭṭhitabhāvassa thirabhāvassa sādhanena. Laddhahetupaccayā hi dhammā viruḷhamūlā viya pādapā thirā honti suppatiṭṭhitā, ahetukā tilabījādisevālā viya na suppatiṭṭhitāti.

By one who knows the doctrine: by one who knows the view of the Abhidhammikas. By establishing the well-founded state: by establishing the well-founded state, the firm state, of states that have their own roots. For states that have obtained root-conditions are firm, well-established, like trees with developed roots; but rootless states are not well-established, like sesame seeds or duckweed.

548. Sabbasoti kāmāvacarādisabbabhāgena.

548. In all ways: in every portion, such as that of the sense sphere.

550-1. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe [V 2.0062] cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ abhāvato attanā sampayuttānaṃ, kaṭattārūpānameva ca paccayabhāvoti āha “attanā…pe… jātāna”nti. Kammassa katattā eva ca upacitattā ca na issarādihetuno sambhūtāni rūpāni kaṭattārūpāni, kammasamuṭṭhānarūpānīti attho[M 2.0084], kaṭattārūpāneva jātāni bhūtāni nibbattānīti kaṭattārūpajātāni. Tathevāti yathā paṭisandhiyaṃ kaṭattārūpānaṃ, evanti attho. Cittajānañcāti ca-saddena “attanā sampayuttāna”nti ākaḍḍhati.

550-1. At the moment of rebirth-linking, because of the absence of mind-originated matter, it is a condition only for the states associated with itself and for matter produced by kamma. Thus he says, “of those born… with itself.” Material phenomena produced because kamma has been done and accumulated, not produced from a cause such as a creator god, are ‘matter produced by kamma’ (kaṭattārūpāni); the meaning is kamma-originated matter. Born, become, generated only as matter produced by kamma, thus ‘born of matter produced by kamma’ (kaṭattārūpajātāni). Similarly: the meaning is, just as in the case of matter produced by kamma at rebirth-linking. And of mind-originated: by the word ‘and’ it draws in ‘associated with itself.’

553. Lokuttaravipākānaṃ paṭisandhivasena appavattanato natthi kammasamuṭṭhānassa paccayabhāvoti āha “cittajāna”ntiādi.

553. Because supramundane resultants do not occur by way of rebirth-linking, there is no conditionality for kamma-originated matter. Thus he says, “of mind-originated,” etc.

555. Hetupaccayasambhavoti hetupaccayasambhūtadhammo, hetupaccayato paccayuppannadhammānaṃ sambhavākāro vā. Sañjātasukhahetunāti sañjātañāṇena, sampajaññenāti attho. Ñāṇañhi “sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”tiādivacanato sukhaṃ hetu etassāti,

555. Arising from root condition: a state arisen from root condition, or the mode of arising of conditionally arisen states from a root condition. With the arisen cause of happiness: with arisen knowledge; the meaning is, with clear comprehension. For knowledge is the cause of happiness for this, on account of such sayings as: “The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated; one who is concentrated understands things as they really are,” etc.

“Diṭṭhe dhamme ca yo attho,

Yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro,

Paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.129) –

“The benefit in this very life

And the benefit in the life to come;

By comprehending the benefit, the steadfast one

Is called a ‘wise person.’” (SN 1.129)

Ādivacanato sukhassa hetūti vā “sukhahetū”ti vuccati.

Or, on account of the first saying, because it is a cause of happiness it is called ‘a cause of happiness’ (sukhahetu).

556. Lokassa adhipati lokādhipati, sakalalokanāyakenāti attho. Attādhīnānaṃ patinoti adhipatī. Chandaṃ tu jeṭṭhakaṃ katvāti “chandavato kiṃ nāma na sijjhatī”tiādikaṃ purimābhisaṅkhārūpanissayaṃ labhitvā uppajjamāne cittuppāde chando jeṭṭhakabhūto sampayuttadhamme vase vattamāno hutvā pavattati, sampayuttadhammā ca tassa vase pavattanti hīnādibhāvena tadanuvattanatoti āha “chandaṃ tu jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā”tiādi. Katvā dhuranti sahajātapubbaṅgamavasena [M 2.0085] pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā. Chandādhipati nāma so vā cittuppādo chandādhipati nāma “chando [V 2.0063] adhipati imassā”ti katvā. Esevāti “cittaṃ dhuraṃ katvā…pe… kālasmiṃ cittādhipati nāmā”tiādinā yathāvuttova nayo. Sesesūti cittādīsu. Ettha ca “chandaṃ…pe… kālasmi”ntiādinā kālassa niyamitattā cattāropete ekakkhaṇe adhipatī na hontīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañca katvā paṭṭhāne “chandādhipati chandasampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ adhipatipaccayena paccayo”tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.3) catunnampi adhipatīnaṃ paccayabhāvo visuṃ visuṃyeva uddhaṭo. Yadi hi te ekakkhaṇeyeva adhipatipaccayā siyuṃ, tadā yathā hetupaccayaniddese “hetū hetusampayuttakāna”ntiādinā avisesena vuttaṃ mūlaṭṭhena upakārakabhāvassa vijjamānena dvinnaṃ, tiṇṇampi hetūnaṃ ekakkhaṇe paccayabhāvūpagamanato, evaṃ ekakkhaṇeyeva bahūnaṃ jeṭṭhakabhāve sati adhipatipaccayaniddesepi “adhipatī adhipatisampayuttakāna”ntiādinā vattabbaṃ siyā. Yasmā pana evaṃ avatvā “chandādhipati chandasampayuttakāna”ntiādinā cattārova visesetvā vuttā, tasmā ekekadhammoyeva ekakkhaṇe adhipatipaccayo hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Jeṭṭhaṭṭhenāti pamukhabhāvena.

556. The lord of the world is the world’s lord (lokādhipati), meaning the leader of the entire world. A lord (adhipati) is a master of those dependent on him. 'Having made desire the foremost,' etc.: When a thought-moment arises, having obtained the support of a previous volitional formation, as in the saying, 'What is not accomplished for one with desire?', desire, having become the chief, proceeds by exercising control over the associated states, and the associated states proceed under its control, following it in a subordinate capacity. Hence, it is said, 'having made desire the foremost,' etc. 'Having made it the yoke' means having made it the forerunner by way of co-nascent precedence. That thought-moment is called 'desire-dominated' because 'desire is the lord of this.' This is the same method as stated above in the passage beginning: 'having made the mind the yoke... at the proper time, it is called mind-dominated.' 'In the rest' refers to mind, etc. Here, because time is specified by the passage beginning 'desire... at the proper time,' it should be understood that these four are not lords in a single moment. And so, in the Paṭṭhāna, the conditionality of each of the four lords is stated separately: 'Desire as lord is a condition for the states associated with desire and for the material forms originating from them by way of lord condition,' and so on (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.3). If they were lord-conditions in a single moment, then, just as in the exposition of the root-condition it is stated without distinction, 'roots for root-associated states,' etc.—because two or even three roots can be conditions in a single moment, their helpfulness existing by way of being a root—so too, if several could be chief in a single moment, in the exposition of the lord-condition it should have been stated, 'a lord for lord-associated states,' etc. But since it was not stated thus, and the four were specified distinctly as 'desire as lord for desire-associated states,' etc., it should be understood that only one single state is a lord-condition in a single moment. 'By the meaning of chief' means by way of being foremost.

Sobhanā mati, sobhanaṃ vā mataṃ etesaṃ atthīti sumatino, sammādiṭṭhikāti attho, tesaṃ matiṃ vibodheti pabodhetīti sumatimativibodhanaṃ. Kucchitā mati, kucchitaṃ vā mataṃ etesanti kumatino, micchādiṭṭhikā, tesaṃ matibhūtā matibhāvena parikappitattāti kumatimati, micchādiṭṭhi, sāyeva indhanasadisatāya indhanaṃ tassa pāvakaṃ aggi viyāti kumati…pe… pāvakaṃ. Atimadhuranti nipuṇagambhīrena attharasena [M 2.0086] ceva suvimalasakhilena byañjanarasena ca madhuraṃ. Avedīti ogāhetvā jānāti. Yo yoti theranavamajjhimesu yo koci. Jinavacanaṃ sakalaṃ avedīti tepiṭakassapi sakalajinavacanassa gahaṇasamatthatāpaṭilābhena taṃ avagacchati.

Those who have a beautiful thought or a beautiful view are the wise (sumatino); this means those of right view. It awakens and arouses their thought; thus it is 'the awakener of the thought of the wise' (sumatimativibodhanaṃ). Those who have a contemptible thought or a contemptible view are the unwise (kumatino), those of wrong view. Their thought, because it is conceived as a thought, is 'the thought of the unwise' (kumatimati), that is, wrong view. That very wrong view, being like fuel, is a fire for it; thus the text is a 'blaze for the thought of the unwise' (kumati…pāvakaṃ). 'Exceedingly sweet' means sweet with both the flavor of the meaning, which is subtle and profound, and the flavor of the phrasing, which is utterly pure and gentle. 'He understood' (avedī) means he knows by having penetrated it. 'Whoever' (yo yo) means any one among the elders, the newly ordained, and the middle-aged. 'He understood the entire word of the Victor' means he comprehends it by having attained the ability to grasp the entire word of the Victor, that is, the Tipiṭaka.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus the [commentary] named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī.

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Commentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma.

Pakiṇṇakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Miscellaneous Topics is finished.

9. Navamo paricchedo

9. The Ninth Chapter.

Puññavipākapaccayaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Condition for Meritorious Resultants.

560-1. Vaṭṭakathāya [V 2.0064] lokuttaravipākānaṃ alabbhanato “lokiyānevā”ti vuttaṃ. Puññāpuññādisaṅkhārāti puññābhisaṅkhāro apuññābhisaṅkhāro āneñjābhisaṅkhāroti tayo saṅkhārā. Tattha punāti attano santānaṃ apuññaphalato, dukkhasaṃkilesato ca sodheti, pujjaṃ bhavaphalaṃ nibbattetīti vā puññaṃ, attano phalassa abhisaṅkharaṇaṭṭhena abhisaṅkhāro cāti puññābhisaṅkhāro, puññapaṭipakkhato apuññaṃ, vuttanayena abhisaṅkhāro cāti apuññābhisaṅkhāro. Samādhipaccanīkānaṃ atidūratāya na iñjati na kampatīti āneñjaṃ, taṃ abhisaṅkharotīti āneñjābhisaṅkhāro. Tattha dānasīlādivasena pavattā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacetanā, bhāvanāvaseneva pavattā rūpāvacarakusalacetanā cāti terasa cetanā puññābhisaṅkhāro nāma. Pāṇātipātādivasena pavattā dvādasa akusalacetanā apuññābhisaṅkhāro nāma. Bhāvanāvaseneva pavattā catasso arūpāvacarakusalacetanā āneñjābhisaṅkhāro [M 2.0087] nāma. Bhavādīsu yathā paccayā, tathā yesañca vipākānaṃ paccayā, tepi viññātabbāti sambandho. Keci pana “tepīti saṅkhārānaṃ gahaṇa”nti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ, evaṃ sati “yesa”nti aniyamaniddesassa niyamakavacanābhāvato.

560-1. It is said 'mundane only' because supramundane resultants are unobtainable in the discourse on the round of existence. The 'formations of merit, demerit, etc.' are the three formations: the meritorious formation, the demeritorious formation, and the imperturbable formation. Herein, it purifies (punāti) one's own continuum from the fruit of demerit and from suffering and defilement, or it produces a desirable (pujjaṃ) fruit of existence; thus it is merit (puñña). And it is a formation (abhisaṅkhāra) in the sense of forming its own fruit; thus it is a meritorious formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra). Demerit (apuñña) is the opposite of merit, and it is a formation in the way stated; thus it is a demeritorious formation (apuññābhisaṅkhāra). Because it is very far from the opponents of concentration, it does not stir (iñjati), does not tremble (kampati); thus it is the imperturbable (āneñja). It forms that; thus it is the imperturbable formation (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra). Herein, the thirteen volitions—the eight sense-sphere wholesome volitions that proceed by way of giving, virtue, etc., and the five form-sphere wholesome volitions that proceed solely by way of mental development—are called the meritorious formation. The twelve unwholesome volitions that proceed by way of killing living beings, etc., are called the demeritorious formation. The four formless-sphere wholesome volitions that proceed solely by way of mental development are called the imperturbable formation. The connection is to be understood thus: just as they are conditions for existence, etc., so too are they conditions for those resultants 'of which' the text speaks. Some, however, say that 'those too' refers to the formations, but that is not correct; for if that were so, the indefinite reference with 'which' would have no restrictive term to qualify.

562. Katame pana te bhavādayoti āha “tayo bhavā”tiādi. Tattha kāmarūpārūpavasena tayo bhavā. Saññībhavaasaññībhavanevasaññīnāsaññībhavavasena, pana ekavokārabhavacatuvokārabhavapañcavokārabhavavasena ca tayo bhavā ettheva samodhānaṃ gacchanti. Catasso yoniyoti aṇḍajajalābujasaṃsedajaopapātikavasena cattāro sattanikāyā. Tattha bījakapāle nibbatto sattanikāyo aṇḍajayoni nāma. Mātugabbhe jalābuje nibbattasattanikāyo jalābujayoni nāma. Padumagabbhamānusakagabbhamalādisaṃsedūpanissayena uppajjanakasattanikāyo saṃsedajayoni nāma. Kutoci anuppajjitvā kevalaṃ tattha tattha paripuṇṇaṅgapaccaṅgo hutvā uppajjanakasattanikāyo opapātikayoni nāma. Gatipañcakaṃ heṭṭhā vibhāvitameva[V 2.0065]. Paṭisandhiviññāṇassa vatthubhūtā ca viññāṇakkhandhā cha viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo nāma. Tā pana nānattakāyādivasena sattavidhāti āha “viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo sattā”ti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

562.
