To the question, 'But what are these, existence, etc.?' he says, 'three kinds of existence,' etc. Herein, there are three kinds of existence by way of the sense-sphere, the form-sphere, and the formless-sphere. The three kinds of existence by way of existence with perception, existence without perception, and existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and also by way of one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, and five-constituent existence, are included right here. The four modes of generation are the four classes of beings by way of being egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneously born. Herein, the class of beings born from an egg is called the egg-born generation. The class of beings born in a mother's womb is called the womb-born generation. The class of beings that arises with moisture as support—in a lotus womb, a human womb, filth, etc.—is called the moisture-born generation. The class of beings that arises with fully formed major and minor limbs, not arising from anywhere but just there and then, is called the spontaneously born generation. The five destinations have already been explained above. The consciousness-aggregates that are the basis for rebirth-linking consciousness are called the six stations of consciousness. But these are sevenfold by way of 'diverse bodies,' etc., thus he says: 'There are seven stations of consciousness.' For it has been said:

“Sattimā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo. Katamā satta? Santi, bhikkhave, sattā nānattakāyā nānattasaññino. Seyyathāpi manussā ekacce ca devā ekacce ca vinipātikā, ayaṃ paṭhamā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santi, bhikkhave, sattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino. Seyyathāpi devā brahmakāyikā paṭhamābhinibbattā, ayaṃ dutiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santi, bhikkhave, sattā [M 2.0088] ekattakāyā nānattasaññino. Seyyathāpi devā ābhassarā, ayaṃ tatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santi, bhikkhave, sattā ekattakāyā ekattasaññino. Seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhā, ayaṃ catutthī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santi, bhikkhave, sattā sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā, ayaṃ pañcamī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santi, bhikkhave, sattā sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanūpagā, ayaṃ chaṭṭhī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santi, bhikkhave, sattā sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanūpagā, ayaṃ sattamī viññāṇaṭṭhitī”ti (dī. ni. 3.332; a. ni. 7.44).

“Bhikkhus, there are these seven stations of consciousness. What seven? There are, bhikkhus, beings diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as human beings, some devas, and some beings in the states of deprivation. This is the first station of consciousness. There are, bhikkhus, beings diverse in body and unified in perception, such as the devas of Brahmā’s Host at their first arising. This is the second station of consciousness. There are, bhikkhus, beings unified in body and diverse in perception, such as the devas of Streaming Radiance. This is the third station of consciousness. There are, bhikkhus, beings unified in body and unified in perception, such as the devas of Refulgent Glory. This is the fourth station of consciousness. There are, bhikkhus, beings who, with the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ have reached the base of the infinity of space. This is the fifth station of consciousness. There are, bhikkhus, beings who, with the complete transcendence of the base of the infinity of space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ have reached the base of the infinity of consciousness. This is the sixth station of consciousness. There are, bhikkhus, beings who, with the complete transcendence of the base of the infinity of consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ have reached the base of nothingness. This is the seventh station of consciousness.”

Ettha hi aparimāṇacakkavāḷavāsino manussā kāmāvacaradevā punabbasumātupiyaṅkaramātādayo vinipātikāsurā ca kusalavipākapaṭisandhikā vemānikapetā ceti ime dīgharassakisathūlakāḷaodātādivaṇṇasaṇṭhānavasena rūpakāyassa, ahetuduhetutihetuvasena paṭisandhisaññāya ca nānābhāvato nānattakāyanānattasaññino nāma, ayaṃ paṭhamā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Paṭhamajjhānatalavāsino pana tayo devā uparūparivāsīnaṃ vaṇṇādikamapekkhitvā attano vaṇṇādīnaṃ nihīnatāya rūpakāyassa nānābhāvato, paṭhamajjhānavipākaviññāṇavasena samānasaññitāya ca nānattakāyaekattasaññino nāma, ayaṃ dutiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti, caturāpāyavāsinopi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānavasena rūpakāyassa nānāsabhāvattā, akusalavipākasaññāvasena saññāya ekasabhāvattā ca dutiyaviññāṇaṭṭhitiyaṃyeva samodhānaṃ [M 2.0089] gacchantīti veditabbaṃ. Dutiyajjhānatalavāsino tayo devā vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena samānattā rūpakāyassa [V 2.0066] visesābhāvato pañcakanaye dutiyatatiyajjhānasaññāvasena paṭisandhisaññāya nānābhāvato ekattakāyanānattasaññino nāma, ayaṃ tatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Tatiyajjhānatalavāsino pana tayo devā rūpakāyavasena samānattā, pañcakanaye catutthajjhānavipākasaññāvasena paṭisandhisaññāya ca ekattā ekattakāyaekattasaññino nāma, ayaṃ catutthī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Vehapphalavāsino ceva pañca suddhāvāsavāsino ca vaṇṇasaṇṭhānavasena rūpakāyassa, pañcamajjhānavipākasaññāvasena paṭisandhisaññāya ca samānattā catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitimeva bhajanti. Ākāsānañcāyatanādayo tisso viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo pāḷivaseneva pākaṭā. Asaññasattā pana viññāṇābhāvena nevasaññānāsaññāyatanavāsino ca saññāya viya viññāṇassa sukhumabhāveneva viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu na gahitā, sattānaṃ nivāsatāya pana “sattāvāsā”ti vuccanti. Evañca katvā tehi satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo samodhānetvā nava sattāvāsā vuttā.

Here, the humans dwelling in countless world systems, the sense-sphere gods, Punabbasu's mother, Piyaṅkara's mother, and so forth, the fallen asuras, and the celestial ghosts with rebirth-linking as a result of wholesome kamma—these beings, due to the diversity in color, shape, and size (such as long, short, thin, stout, dark, and fair) of their material bodies, and due to the diversity in rebirth-linking perception (whether rootless, with two roots, or with three roots), are called 'diverse in body, diverse in perception.' This is the first station of consciousness. The gods dwelling in the first jhāna plane, upon observing the colors, etc., of those above them, perceive their own colors, etc., as inferior. Thus, due to the diversity in their material bodies and the sameness in their perception (by way of the first jhāna resultant consciousness), they are called 'diverse in body, one in perception.' This is the second station of consciousness. Beings in the four woeful states, due to the diversity in their bodily colors and shapes, and the sameness in their unwholesome-resultant perception, should be understood as included in this second station of consciousness. The gods dwelling in the second jhāna plane, due to the uniformity in their bodily colors and shapes, perceive no distinction in their material bodies. However, due to the diversity in their rebirth-linking perception (resulting from the second and third jhānas, according to the five-fold method), they are called 'one in body, diverse in perception.' This is the third station of consciousness. The gods dwelling in the third jhāna plane, due to the uniformity in their material bodies and the sameness in their rebirth-linking perception (resulting from the fourth jhāna, according to the five-fold method), are called 'one in body, one in perception.' This is the fourth station of consciousness. The gods of the Vehapphala realm and the five Pure Abodes, due to the uniformity in their bodily colors and shapes, and the sameness in their rebirth-linking perception (resulting from the fifth jhāna), also partake of this fourth station of consciousness. The three stations of consciousness, beginning with the base of infinite space, are evident from the Pāli text itself. Asaññasattā (non-percipient beings), due to the absence of consciousness, and those in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, due to the subtlety of their consciousness (which is like perception), are not included among the stations of consciousness. However, since they are abodes for beings, they are called 'abodes of beings.' Thus, by combining them with the seven stations of consciousness, nine abodes of beings are spoken of.

563-4. Idāni evaṃ vuttesu bhavādīsu dvattiṃsavipākānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ abhisaṅkhārānaṃ paccayabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “kāme puññābhisaṅkhārasaññitā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Navannaṃ pākacittānanti sahetukāhetukavasena navannaṃ sugatipaṭisandhivipākacittānaṃ. Nānakkhaṇika…pe… paccayehi cāti kusalākusalakammassa atītasseva attanā janetabbavipākānaṃ paccayabhāvato nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayena, tesameva balavakāraṇabhāvato upanissayapaccayena ca. Vuttañhi tassa upanissayattaṃ “kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ vipākassa upanissayapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.423). Sabbattha upanissayabhāvo balavakammavasena [M 2.0090] yojetabbo. Dubbalañhi kammaṃ upanissayo na hotīti paṭṭhānavaṇṇanāyaṃ dassitametaṃ.

Now, when these statements have been made regarding becoming and so on, to show the conditionality of the thirty-two results for the three types of formations, the phrase "associated with meritorious formations in the sense-sphere" and so on is begun. 'Of the nine resultant consciousnesses' refers to the nine fortunate-destination rebirth-linking resultant consciousnesses, classified as either with roots or without roots. 'By non-contemporaneous... and by conditions' means that past wholesome and unwholesome kammas serve as conditions for the resultant consciousnesses they generate, through the non-contemporaneous kamma condition. Moreover, because they are strong causal factors, they also serve as decisive support conditions. For their being a decisive support is stated thus: "Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is a condition for its result by way of decisive support condition" (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.423). In all cases, the nature of decisive support should be connected with strong kamma. For weak kamma does not serve as decisive support—this has been shown in the commentary on the Paṭṭhāna.

566-8. Pañcannanti kusalavipākacakkhusotaviññāṇasampaṭicchanasantīraṇadvayavasena pañcannaṃ. Duggatiyaṃ kusalavipākapaṭisandhiyā abhāvato āha “na honti paṭisandhiya”nti. Evaṃ paṭisandhipavattīnaṃ asaṅkaravasena paccayavidhiṃ dassetvā idāni samodhānetvā dassetuṃ “hontī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Soḷasannaṃ pavatte, paṭisandhiyaṃ navannanti yathālābhavasena yojetabbaṃ.

'Of the five' refers to the five: wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, receiving-consciousness, and the two investigating-consciousnesses. Because there is no wholesome-resultant rebirth-linking in a woeful destination, it is said, "They do not occur at rebirth-linking." Having thus explained the method of conditionality by distinguishing between rebirth-linking and the course of life, it is now stated by combining them: "They occur," etc. The sixteen in the course of life and the nine at rebirth-linking are to be connected according to availability.

569-74. Rūpe puññābhisaṅkhārāti abhiññāvajjitā pañca rūpāvacarapuññābhisaṅkhārā. Kasmā pana abhiññāya parivajjananti? Vipākadānābhāvato, tañca kho panassā vipākassa asambhavato[V 2.0067], na pana vipākuppādanasabhāvābhāvato. Yadi hi abhiññācetanā vipākaṃ uppādeyya, aññabhūmikakammassa aññabhūmikavipākuppādanāyogato sabhūmikameva uppādeyya. Taṃ pana kiṃ navattabbārammaṇaṃ vā uppādeyya parittādiārammaṇaṃ vā? Kiñcettha – yadi tāva navattabbārammaṇaṃ uppādeti, taṃ na yuttaṃ rūpāvacaravipākānaṃ ekantena kammasamānārammaṇatāya dassitattā, abhiññācetanāya ca sayaṃ parittādiārammaṇattā. Atha parittādiārammaṇaṃ uppādeti, tampi na yujjati rūpāvacaravipākānaṃ ekanteneva navattabbārammaṇabhāvato. Tathā hi vuttaṃ cittuppādakaṇḍe –

'Meritorious formations in the form realm' refers to the five meritorious form-realm formations, excluding supernormal knowledge. But why is supernormal knowledge excluded? Because it does not give a result; and that is because a result for it is impossible, not because it lacks the nature to produce a result. For if the volition associated with supernormal knowledge were to produce a result, then, since an action of one plane cannot produce a result on another plane, it would produce a result only on its own plane. Now, would it produce a result with a non-assertable object or with a limited, etc., object? In this regard, if it were to produce a result with a non-assertable object, that would not be fitting, because the results of the form realm are invariably shown to have the same object as the kamma, and the volition of supernormal knowledge itself has a limited, etc., object. But if it were to produce a result with a limited, etc., object, that too would not be suitable, because the results of the form realm invariably have a non-assertable object. Thus it is said in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness:

“Rūpāvacaratikacatukkajjhānā kusalato ca vipākato ca kiriyato ca catutthassa jhānassa vipāko ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ. Ime dhammā navattabbā ‘parittārammaṇā’tipi ‘mahaggatārammaṇā’tipi ‘appamāṇārammaṇā’tipī”ti (dha. sa. 1422).

"The form-sphere jhānas of the triad and tetrad, whether wholesome, resultant, or functional; the result of the fourth jhāna; the base of infinite space; the base of nothingness—these states are not to be designated as 'having limited objects,' 'having exalted objects,' or 'having immeasurable objects.'" (Dhs. 1422)

Apica [M 2.0091] samādhivijjāsambhārabhūtā abhiññā samādhissa ānisaṃsamattaṃ samādhiphalasadisā. Tassa tassa hi adhiṭṭhānavikubbanadibbasaddasavanādikassa yathicchitassa kiccassa nipphādanamattaphalā abhiññācetanā. Tenāha “so evaṃ samāhite citte”tiādi (pārā. 12-13) tasmā samādhissa phalasadisā abhiññācetanā na ca phalaṃ deti, dānasīlānisaṃsabhūto tasmiṃ bhave paccayalābho viya natthi tassa vipākuppādananti. Keci pana “samānabhūmikato āsevanalābhena balavantāni jhānāni vipākaṃ uppādenti samāpattibhāvato, abhiññā pana satipi jhānabhāve tadabhāvato tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ārammaṇe āgantukāyevāti dubbalā, tasmā vipākaṃ na detī”ti vadanti. Evañca katvā vuttaṃ anuruddhācariyena –

Moreover, supernormal knowledge (abhiññā), which constitutes the requisites of concentration and knowledge, is merely a benefit of concentration and is similar to the fruit of concentration. For the volition of supernormal knowledge has as its fruit merely the accomplishment of the desired task, such as determination, transformation, or hearing divine sounds. Hence, it is said, "When the mind is thus concentrated..." (Pārā. 12-13). Therefore, the volition of supernormal knowledge is similar to the fruit of concentration but does not yield a fruit; just as the obtaining of requisites in that existence, being a benefit of generosity and virtue, does not produce a result. Some, however, say: "The jhānas, being strong from obtaining repeated practice on the same plane, produce results because they are attainments. But supernormal knowledge, although it has the nature of jhāna, lacks that; being merely adventitious in regard to this or that object, it is weak; therefore, it does not give a result." And so it was said by the teacher Anuruddha—

“Samānāsevane laddhe, vijjamāne mahabbale;

Aladdhā tādisaṃ hetuṃ, abhiññā na vipaccatī”ti. (nāma. pari. 474);

"When repeated practice is obtained, and when great power is present, supernormal knowledge, not having obtained such a cause, does not ripen." (Nāmarūpapariccheda 474)

Tayidamakāraṇaṃ, parittajhānassa avisesena brahmapārisajjādīsu vipākadānavacanato. Na hi parittaṃ [V 2.0068] laddhāsevanameva tattha vipākaṃ detīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā samānāsevane laddheyeva jhānassa vipākadānaṃ na sakkā vattuṃ. Apica punappunaṃ parikammavasena abhiññāyapi vasibhāvasabbhāvā tassāpi ca balavabhāvo atthevāti vipākaṃ uppādeyya.

This is not a valid reason, because it is stated that the limited jhāna, without distinction, gives a result such as rebirth among Brahmā's retinue. For it is not said in the commentary that only a limited jhāna that has obtained repeated practice gives a result there. Therefore, it cannot be said that a jhāna gives a result only when repeated practice has been obtained. Moreover, through repeated preliminary practice, mastery over even supernormal knowledge is possible, and its strength also exists, thus it could produce a result.

Pañcannaṃ pākacittānanti pañcannaṃ rūpāvacaravipākacittānaṃ. Māpuññasaṅkhārāti apuññābhisaṅkhārā. “Ime apuññasaṅkhārā”ti vā padacchedo. Ekassāti ekassa akusalavipākasantīraṇassa. Channanti santīraṇavajjānaṃ channaṃ akusalavipākānaṃ. Pavatte paccayā honti aniṭṭharūpādiāpāthāgateti adhippāyo. Sugatiyaṃ akusalavipākapaṭisandhiyā abhāvato āha “na honti paṭisandhiya”nti. Catunnanti [M 2.0092] akusalavipākacakkhusotaviññāṇasampaṭicchanasantīraṇavasena catunnaṃ. Tāni pana ekantato aniṭṭhārammaṇāni. Rūpabhave ca kathaṃ aniṭṭhārammaṇasamāyogoti āha “so cā”tiādi. Soti so paccayabhāvo. “Kāmabhave”ti idaṃ aniṭṭharūpādīnaṃ visesanaṃ, na pana “upaladdhiya”nti imassa. Tenāha “aniṭṭha…pe… na vijjare”ti. Keci pana “upaladdhiyanti imasseva visesanabhāvena gahetvā brahmūnaṃ kāmabhavaṃ āgatakkhaṇe rūpādiupaladdhiya”nti vadanti. Aniṭṭha…pe… na vijjare ekantasukhavatthubhūte tattha vokiṇṇasukhadukkhakāraṇassa abhāvato.

Of the five resultant consciousnesses, this refers to the five resultant consciousnesses of the form sphere. 'Not meritorious formations' means unwholesome volitional formations. Alternatively, the phrase can be divided as 'these unwholesome volitional formations.' 'Of one' refers to one unwholesome resultant investigating-consciousness. 'Of six' refers to the six unwholesome resultant consciousnesses, excluding the investigating-consciousness. In the course of existence, they are conditions because disagreeable forms, etc., come into range; this is the meaning. Because there is no unwholesome resultant rebirth-linking in a happy destination, it is said, 'They do not occur at rebirth-linking.' 'Of four' refers to the four by way of unwholesome resultant eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, receiving-consciousness, and investigating-consciousness. Moreover, these invariably have disagreeable objects. And how is there an association with disagreeable objects in the form sphere? It is explained with the phrase 'so ca,' etc. 'So' refers to that state of being a condition. 'In the sense-sphere'—this qualifies disagreeable forms, etc., but not 'at the time of apprehension.' Therefore, it is said, 'disagreeable... are not found.' However, some say, taking this very phrase as a qualifier of 'at the time of apprehension,' that 'at the moment when Brahmās arrive in the sense-sphere, there is apprehension of forms, etc.' 'Disagreeable... are not found'—because in that state, which is a basis for exclusive pleasure, there is no cause for mingled pleasure and pain.

576. “Evaṃ tāvā”tiādi yathāvuttassevatthassa appanaṃ. Yathā cāti ca-saddena “yesañcā”ti saṅgaṇhāti. Tathāti etthāpi “te”ti saṅgaṇhitabbaṃ.

576. "So it is indeed," and so on, is an application of the meaning already stated. And by the word "ca" in "yathā ca," "yesañca" is included. Similarly, here too, "te" should be included.

577-81. Yattha vitthārappakāsanaṃ kataṃ, tato bhavato paṭṭhāya mukhamattappakāsanaṃ kātukāmo āha “tatrida”ntiādi. Tatrāti tesu bhavādīsu. Idanti nidassitabbabhāvena āsannapaccakkhamāha. Ādito pana paṭṭhāyāti bhavato paṭṭhāya. Avisesenāti kāmāvacararūpāvacaravasena visesābhāvena terasa puññābhisaṅkhārā. Dvibhavesūti kāmarūpabhavesu. Kesañci manussānaṃ, bhummadevānañca aṇḍajajalābujānampi sambhavato tadapekkhāya “catūsu…pe… yonisū”ti vuttaṃ. Nānatta…pe… ṭhitīsupīti aluttasamāsavasena vuttaṃ, nānattakāyanānattasaññādīsu catūsu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsūti attho. Vuttappakārasminti nānattakāyādike, puññābhisaṅkhārassa bhavādīsu ekavīsativipākānaṃ ekāvatthāya paccayo ahutvā duggatipariyāpannesu bhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu paṭisandhiṃ adatvā pavatteyeva aṭṭhannaṃ [V 2.0069] vipākānaṃ paccayabhāvato, kāmāvacarasugatipariyāpannesu paṭisandhiṃ datvā pavatte soḷasannaṃ vipākānaṃ [M 2.0093] paccayabhāvato, rūpāvacarabhūmipariyāpannesu paṭisandhiṃ datvā pavatte dasannaṃ vipākānaṃ paccayabhāvato vuttaṃ “yathāraha”nti.

577-81. Where a detailed explanation has been made, from that existence onwards, wishing to give a mere summary, he says, 'Herein,' etc. 'Herein' means among those beginning with existence. 'This' means he speaks of what is near and evident by way of indication. 'But from the beginning onwards' means starting from existence. 'Without distinction' means the thirteen meritorious formations, there being no distinction by way of the sense-sphere and form-sphere existences. 'In two existences' means in the sense-sphere and form-sphere existences. Because it is possible for some humans and earth-deities, and also for the egg-born and the womb-born, with reference to that it is said, 'in four... modes of birth.' 'Diversity... in stations' is said by way of an undeclined compound, meaning in the four stations of consciousness, such as diversity of body and diversity of perception. 'As stated' means in the diversity of body, etc. Because the meritorious formation is not a condition for the twenty-one resultants in a single state in existences, etc., and does not give rebirth-linking in the existences, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings included in an unhappy destination, but is a condition for eight resultants only in the course of existence; and because, having given rebirth-linking among those included in a sense-sphere happy destination, it is a condition for sixteen resultants in the course of existence; and because, having given rebirth-linking among those included in a form-sphere plane, it is a condition for ten resultants in the course of existence—for these reasons, it is said, 'as is fitting.'

582-3. Kāme bhave, rūpe bhaveti sambandho. Tīsu gatīsūti devamanussavajjesu tīsu gatīsu. Ekissāti nānattakāyaekattasaññīsaṅkhātāya ekissā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā. Ekasminti nānattakāyaekattasaññīsaṅkhāteyeva ekasmiṃ sattāvāse.

582-3. 'In the sense-sphere existence, in the form-sphere existence'—this is the connection. 'In three destinations' means in the three destinations excluding devas and humans. 'Of one' means of one station of consciousness known as having diversity of body and unity of perception. 'In one' means in one abode of beings known as having diversity of body and unity of perception.

584-6. Ekārūpabhaveti ekasmiṃ arūpabhave. Ekissā yoniyāti ekissāyeva opapātikayoniyā. Tīsu cittaṭṭhitīsūti ākāsānañcāyatanādīsu tīsu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu. Sattāvāse catubbidheti ākāsānañcāyatanādikeyeva catubbidhe sattāvāse. Vijānitabbā…pe… paccayāti saṅkhārā yathā paccayā yesañca paccayā, tathā tepi viññātabbāti attho.

584-6. 'In one formless existence' means in a single formless existence. 'In one mode of birth' means in one spontaneous mode of birth only. 'In three stations of consciousness' means in the three stations of consciousness beginning with the base of infinite space. 'The abode of beings is fourfold' means the fourfold abode of beings beginning with the base of infinite space only. 'To be understood... conditions' means: just as formations are conditions and of what they are conditions, so too should these be understood.

587-90. Nanu ca saṅkhārānaṃ paṭisandhipavattīsupi vipākānaṃ paccayabhāvo vutto. Tattha paṭisandhiyeva tāva na sakkā viññātuṃ. Yadi hi purimabhavato paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ idhāgacchatīti vucceyya, taṃ na yuttaṃ, rūpārūpadhammānaṃ kesaggamattampi desantarasaṅkamanābhāvato. Atha atītabhavanibbattasaṅkhārato na nibbattati, tampi na yujjati ahetukadosāpattitoti iminā adhippāyena codento āha “na rūpārūpadhammāna”ntiādi. Ācariyo tassādhippāyaṃ sampaṭicchitvā taṃ saññāpetukāmo āha “natthi cittassā”tiādi. Tato hetuṃ vināti tattha hetuṃ vinā, atītabhavanibbattakammasaṅkhāranikantiārammaṇaṃ vināti attho[M 2.0094]. Suladdhapaccayanti avijjādisahakārīkāraṇasahitassa saṅkhārassa vasena suṭṭhu avekallato paṭiladdhapaccayaṃ. Rūpārūpamattanti bāhirakaparikappitassa adhitiṭṭhanakassa sattajīvādino abhāvato rūpārūpadhammamattaṃ. Tenāha “na ca satto”tiādi. Bhavantara…pe… pavuccatīti vohāramattena bhavantaramupetīti pavuccati. Atthato pana paccayasāmaggiyā bhavantarabhāvena uppajjanamattanti adhippāyo.

587-90. But is it not said that formations are a condition for resultants in both rebirth-linking and the course of existence? There, to begin with, rebirth-linking itself cannot be understood. If it were said that the rebirth-linking consciousness from the previous existence comes here, that would not be proper, because material and immaterial phenomena lack the ability to transmigrate even a hair's breadth from one place to another. Alternatively, if it does not arise from formations produced in a past existence, that too is unacceptable due to incurring the fault of being causeless. With this intention, the one raising an objection says, 'Material and immaterial phenomena...' etc. The teacher, acknowledging his intention and wishing to make him understand, says, 'There is no...' etc. Then, 'without a cause' means without a cause there—that is, without the object of craving for kamma-formations produced in a past existence. 'Well-obtained condition' means a condition well-obtained, properly and completely, through the influence of formations accompanied by supporting factors like ignorance. 'Merely material and immaterial' means merely material and immaterial phenomena, because there is no externally imagined persisting entity like a self or vital principle. Therefore, it is said, 'Nor is there a being...' etc. 'Another existence... is spoken of' is merely a conventional expression, meaning 'goes to another existence.' But in essence, the meaning is merely arising as another existence due to the complete assemblage of conditions.

591. Idāni [V 2.0070] taṃ paṭisandhikkamaṃ pākaṭāya manussapaṭisandhiyā vasena pakāsetuṃ samārabhanto āha “tayida”ntiādi. Sudubbudhanti atidubbijāniyaṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā –

591. Now, beginning to explain that process of rebirth-linking by means of a clear human rebirth-linking, he says, 'This...' etc. 'Very hard to understand' means extremely difficult to understand. Thus the ancients said:

“Saccaṃ satto paṭisandhi, paccayākārameva ca;

Duddasā caturo dhammā, desetuñca sudukkarā”ti.

"Truth, a being, rebirth-linking, and the mode of conditionality—these four things are hard to see and very difficult to teach."

592-3. Āsannamaraṇassāti parūpakkamena vā āyukkhayādivasena vā samāsannamaraṇassa. Sussamāneti anukkamena upasussamāne. Gabbhaseyyakassa āyatanānaṃ anupubbuppatti viya nirodhopi anupubbato hotīti vuttaṃ “naṭṭhe cakkhundriyādike”ti. Keci pana “nānākammasamuṭṭhitesu cakkhundriyādīsu naṭṭhesū”ti vadanti. “Hadaya…pe… ke”ti iminā sesakāye kāyindriyassa niruddhabhāvo vuttoti ekakammasamuṭṭhitampi nassatevāti apare. Ānandācariyo pana “yamake” yassa cakkhāyatanaṃ nirujjhati, tassa manāyatanaṃ nirujjhatīti. Āmantā. Yassa vā pana manāyatanaṃ nirujjhati, tassa cakkhāyatanaṃ nirujjhatīti. Sacittakānaṃ acakkhukānaṃ cavantānaṃ tesaṃ manāyatanaṃ nirujjhati, no ca tesaṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ nirujjhati. Sacakkhukānaṃ cavantānaṃ tesaṃ manāyatanañca nirujjhati, cakkhāyatanañca nirujjhatī’tiādinā (yama. 1.āyatanayamaka.120) cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ [M 2.0095] cuticittena saha nirodho vuttoti cakkhundriyādīni cutito pubbe na nassanti. Atimandabhāvūpagamanaṃ pana sandhāya aṭṭhakathāya ‘niruddhesu indriyesū’ti vuttaṃ, na anavasesanirodhaṃ sandhāya. Pañcadvārikajavanānantarampi cuti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dassitā”ti vadati. Hadayavatthumattasminti hadayavatthupadesamatte. Na hi hadayavatthuṃ nissāya kāyindriyaṃ pavattati.

592-3. Āsannamaraṇassa means one who is near death, either due to external causes or due to the exhaustion of lifespan and so forth. Sussamāne refers to gradually drying up. Just as the sense bases of one in the womb arise sequentially, their cessation also occurs sequentially; thus it is said: 'When the eye faculty and so on are destroyed.' Some, however, say: 'When the eye faculty and other faculties, produced by diverse kamma, are destroyed.' By the phrase 'Hadaya…pe…ke,' the cessation of the body faculty in the remaining parts of the body is indicated. Thus, others say that even faculties arising from a single kamma perish. The teacher Ānanda, however, states in the Yamaka: 'For whom the eye-base ceases, for them does the mind-base cease? Indeed. Or, for whom the mind-base ceases, for them does the eye-base cease? For beings with consciousness but without eyes who are passing away, their mind-base ceases, but their eye-base does not cease. For beings with eyes who are passing away, both their mind-base and their eye-base cease,' and so on. By this, the cessation of the eye-base and other bases is said to occur together with the death-consciousness; therefore, the eye faculty and other faculties do not perish before death. However, with reference to their becoming extremely weak, the commentary states 'when the faculties have ceased,' not with reference to their complete cessation. He says that the commentary also shows that death can occur immediately after the five-door javana. Hadayavatthumattasminti means in the mere location of the heart-base, for the body faculty does not function by depending on the heart-base.

594-7. Vatthusannissitanti sesindriyānaṃ niruddhattā viññāṇassa nissayabhāvūpagamanasāmatthiyāyogena mandabhāvato vā hadayavatthumattasannissitaṃ. Cittanti tadā kammakammanimittādīni ārabbha pavattajavanaviññāṇaṃ. Taṃ pana sugatiyaṃ nibbattamānassa kusalaṃ hoti, duggatiyaṃ nibbattamānassa akusalaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

594-7. Vatthusannissitaṃ means that due to the cessation of the remaining faculties, and because of the weakness of consciousness or its incapacity to function as a support, it relies only on the heart-base. Cittaṃ refers to the javana-consciousness that arises at that time, taking as its object kamma, the sign of kamma, and so forth. For one being reborn in a happy destination, that consciousness is wholesome; for one being reborn in an unhappy destination, it is unwholesome. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Nimittassādagadhitaṃ vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭhati anubyañjanassādagadhitaṃ vā, tasmiṃ ce samaye kālaṃ karoti, ṭhānametaṃ vijjati, yaṃ dvinnaṃ [V 2.0071] gatīnaṃ aññataraṃ gatiṃ upapajjeyya nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 4.235).

‘Monks, consciousness that is greedy for the gratification in a sign, or greedy for the gratification in a secondary characteristic, remains established. If at that time one dies, this is possible: that one would be reborn in one of two destinations, either in hell or in the animal realm,’ and so on.

Yadi evaṃ –

If so—

“Gatisampattiyā ñāṇasampayutte katamesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hoti, kusalassa kammassa javanakkhaṇe tayo hetū kusalā tasmiṃ khaṇe jātacetanāya sahajātapaccayā honti, tena vuccati kusalamūlapaccayāpi saṅkhārā. Nikantikkhaṇe dve hetū akusalā tasmiṃ khaṇe jātacetanāya sahajātapaccayā honti, tena vuccati akusalamūlapaccayāpi saṅkhārā. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe tayo hetū abyākatā [M 2.0096] tasmiṃ khaṇe jātacetanāya sahajātapaccayā honti, tena vuccati nāmarūpapaccayāpi viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayāpi nāmarūpa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.232) –

‘In the case of rebirth in a good destination associated with knowledge, conditioned by which of the eight roots does that rebirth occur? At the moment of javana of wholesome kamma, three wholesome roots are co-arising conditions for the volition born at that moment; therefore it is said: “formations are also conditioned by wholesome roots.” At the moment of relishing, two unwholesome roots are co-arising conditions for the volition born at that moment; therefore it is said: “formations are also conditioned by unwholesome roots.” At the moment of rebirth-linking, three indeterminate roots are co-arising conditions for the volition born at that moment; therefore it is said: “consciousness is also conditioned by name-and-form, and name-and-form is also conditioned by consciousness.”’

Nikantikkhaṇe hetudvayapaccayāpi sugatipaṭisandhikassa kathaṃ dassitāti? Nayidaṃ maraṇāsannajavanasampayuttahetuyo sandhāya vuttaṃ, atha kho katakammassa taṃ kammaṃ ārabbha assādavasena pavattajavanasampayuttahetuyo sandhāya. Katūpacitampi hi kammaṃ taṇhāya assāditaṃ vipākābhinipphādane samatthanti. Keci pana “kammakaraṇakāle appahīnāvatthāya santāne anusayitahetuyo sandhāya nikantikkhaṇe dve hetuyoti vutta”nti vadanti, taṃ na yujjati, tesaṃ sahajātapaccayattāyogato. Pubbānusevitaṃ puññaṃ vā apuññameva vā kammaṃ, kammanimittaṃ vā ālambitvā cittaṃ pavattatīti sambandho. Pubbānusevitanti pubbe āsevitaṃ. “Katattā upacitattā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Taṇhāya anusevitabhāvaṃ sandhāya vā “pubbānusevita”nti vuttaṃ. “Anupubbasevita”ntipi pāṭhaṃ vadanti, paṭisandhivasena pubbe āsevitaṃ, pubbe dinnapaṭisandhikanti attho. Dinnapaṭisandhikampi pana aparajātīsu pavattivipākaṃ na nibbattetīti natthi. Puññāpuññaggahaṇena yathākammaṃ sugatiduggatipaṭisandhīnaṃ ārammaṇaṃ dasseti. Kammaṃ kammanimittaṃ vāti vā-saddena gatinimittaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha kammaṃ, gatinimittañca manodvāreyeva āpāthamāgacchati, kammanimittaṃ pana pañcadvārepi. Evañca katvā pañcadvāraggahitepi ārammaṇe paṭisandhi hoti. Apare pana gatinimittampi chadvāresu labbhatīti vaṇṇenti. Evañca katvā vuttaṃ saccasaṅkhepe –

At the moment of relishing, how are the two root conditions shown to be the cause for a happy rebirth? This is not said with reference to the roots associated with the death-proximate javana, but rather with reference to the roots associated with the javana that arises by way of relishing that past deed. For even a deed that has been done and accumulated, when relished by craving, is capable of producing its result. Some, however, say that the two roots at the moment of relishing refer to the latent roots present in the continuity of one who has not abandoned their basis. This is incorrect, because they are not suitable to be co-arising conditions. The connection is this: the mind arises taking as its object either a deed, meritorious or demeritorious, previously indulged in, or a sign of the deed. 'Previously indulged in' means indulged in before. For it is said, 'due to having been done and accumulated.' Or 'previously indulged in' is said with reference to its having been indulged in by craving. Some also read the text as 'repeatedly indulged in,' meaning previously indulged in by way of rebirth, or that which has given rebirth in the past. However, it is not the case that even that which has given rebirth in the past does not produce resultant consciousness in subsequent existences. By mentioning merit and demerit, it shows the object for happy or unhappy rebirths according to one's deeds. The word 'or' in 'a deed or a sign of a deed' includes the sign of destiny. Here, the deed and the sign of destiny appear only at the mind-door, while the sign of the deed can appear at the five sense-doors as well. Thus, even when the object is grasped at the five sense-doors, rebirth-linking occurs. Others, however, describe that the sign of destiny can also be obtained at the six doors. And so it is said in the Saccasaṅkhepa—

“Pañcadvāre [V 2.0072] siyā sandhi, vinā kammaṃ dvigocare”ti. (Sa. sa. 173).

‘Rebirth-linking may occur at the five doors; with two kinds of objects, excluding kamma.’

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ [M 2.0097] pana “gatinimittaṃ manodvāre āpāthamāgacchatī”ti vuttattā, tadārammaṇāya ca pañcadvārikapaṭisandhiyā adassitattā, mūlaṭīkādīsu ca “kammabalena upaṭṭhāpitaṃ vaṇṇāyatanaṃ supinaṃ passantassa viya, dibbacakkhukassa viya ca manodvāre eva gocarabhāvaṃ gacchatī”ti niyametvā vuttattā tesaṃ vacanaṃ na sampaṭicchanti ācariyā. Kammanimittañca panettha paccuppannaṃ pañcadvāre āpāthamāgacchantaṃ cutikālāsanne katakammassa ārammaṇasantāne uppannaṃ taṃsadisanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, itarathā tadeva paṭisandhiyā ārammaṇupaṭṭhāpakaṃ tadeva paṭisandhijanakaṃ bhaveyya, na ca paṭisandhiyā upacārabhūtāni viya, “etasmiṃ tayā pavattitabba”nti paṭisandhiyā ārammaṇaṃ anuppadentāni viya ca pavattāni cutiāsannajavanāni paṭisandhijanakāni bhaveyyuṃ. “Katattā upacitattā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Tadā ca paṭisandhiyā ekavīthiyaṃ viya pavattamānāni kathaṃ katūpacitāni siyuṃ, assādanabhūtāya taṇhāya aparāmaṭṭhāni kathaṃ paṭisandhinibbattakāni, na ca lokiyāni lokuttarāni viya samānavīthiphalāni hontīti. Taṃ viññāṇanti taṃ javanaviññāṇaṃ. Ekattanayena paṭisandhiviññāṇañca sandhāya vuttaṃ. Cutipaṭisandhitadāsannaviññāṇānañhi santativasena viññāṇanti upanītekattaṃ idha taṃ viññāṇanti adhippetaṃ.

However, in the commentary, it is stated, 'The sign of destiny appears at the mind-door.' Since five-door rebirth-linking that takes that as its object is not shown, and in the root subcommentaries and others, it is specifically stated, 'The visible object, established by the power of kamma, appears in the mind-door, like one seeing a dream, or like one with the divine eye,' therefore the teachers do not accept their statement. Here, the sign of kamma, appearing at the five doors as a present object, should be understood as similar to that which has arisen in the object-continuum of one near the time of death, who has performed the kamma. Otherwise, that very thing which presents the object for rebirth-linking would itself be the generator of rebirth-linking, and the death-proximate javanas, which are the generators of rebirth-linking, would not arise as if they were approaching rebirth-linking, nor would they arise presenting the object for rebirth-linking as if saying, 'You must proceed in this.' For it is said, 'Because it was done and accumulated.' At that time, how could those impulsions occurring as if in a single cognitive series with rebirth-linking be done and accumulated? How could they, untouched by craving, which is the nature of relishing, produce rebirth-linking? And mundane javanas are not like supramundane javanas in having results in the same cognitive series. 'That consciousness' refers to that javana-consciousness. It is also spoken of with reference to rebirth-linking consciousness by way of unity. For here, the oneness conveyed by 'consciousness' is intended to refer to 'that consciousness' by way of the continuity of the consciousnesses of death, rebirth-linking, and those near them.

Avijjāya paṭicchannādīnaveti anusayavasena pavattāya bhavataṇhāya, cittasampayuttāya vā avijjāya chāditadukkhādīnave. Tathābhūte pana kammādivisaye paṭisandhiviññāṇassa ārammaṇabhāvena uppattiṭṭhānabhūte. Taṇhāya appahīnattā eva purimuppannāya ca santatiyā tathāpariṇatattā paṭisandhiṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ viññāṇaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāraṃ hutvā pavattatīti āha “taṇhā nametī”ti. Sahajā pana saṅkhārāti cutiāsannajavanaviññāṇasahajātacetanā, sabbepi vā phassādayo. Khipantīti khipantā viya tasmiṃ visaye paṭisandhivasena viññāṇapatiṭṭhānassa [M 2.0098] hetubhāvena pavattanti. Tanti taṃ viññāṇaṃ. “Santativasā”ti vadanto tadeva viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsarati, na aññanti imañca micchāvādaṃ paṭikkhipati. Sati hi nānattanaye santativasena ekattanayo hotīti.

‘Dangers concealed by ignorance’ refers to the dangers of suffering concealed by craving for existence, which proceeds by way of latent tendencies, or by ignorance associated with the mind. In such a sphere of kamma and so on, which has become the place of origin for the rebirth-linking consciousness by serving as its object. Because craving has not been abandoned, and because the previously arisen continuum has been transformed in such a way, consciousness proceeds toward the place of rebirth-linking, having become inclined and tending downwards; thus it is said, ‘craving inclines it.’ ‘Co-arisen formations’ refer to the volition co-arisen with the death-proximate javana-consciousness, or all mental factors such as contact. ‘They propel’ means they proceed as a cause for the establishment of consciousness in that sphere by way of rebirth-linking, as if propelling it. ‘That’ refers to that consciousness. By saying ‘by way of continuity,’ he rejects the wrong view that it is that very same consciousness that runs on and transmigrates, not another. For when there is a principle of difference, the principle of oneness is established by way of continuity.

599. Ārammaṇādīhi…pe… pavattatīti ārammaṇanissayapaccayādīhi pavattati. Kathaṃ[V 2.0073]? Āsannamaraṇassa hi kammabalena manodvāre upaṭṭhāpitaṃ avijjāya paṭicchannādīnavaṃ kammādivisayaṃ ārabbha manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjati, tato maraṇāsannavīthiyā vatthudubbalabhāvena mandappavattiyā cattāri, pañca vā javanāni pavattanti, tadanantaraṃ tadārammaṇe sati, asati vā bhavaṅgavisayamālambitvā cuticittaṃ uppajjati. Bhavaṅgānantarampi cuti hotīti vadanti. Cuticitte pana niruddhe tadeva āpāthagataṃ kammakammanimittādiṃ ārabbha anupacchinnakilesabalavanimittaṃ sahajātasaṅkhārehi kammādiārammaṇe khipiyamānaṃ orimatīrarukkhavinibandhaṃ rajjuṃ ālambitvā mātikātikkāmako viya purimañca nissayaṃ jahati, aparañca kammasamuṭṭhitaṃ nissayaṃ assādayamānaṃ vā anassādayamānaṃ vā ārammaṇādīhi paccayehi pavattati. Ettha ca orimatīraṃ viya purimabhavo daṭṭhabbo, tattha ṭhitarukkho viya purimabhave pavattamānakkhandhā, rajju viya kammādiārammaṇaṃ. Keci pana “rajju viya hadayavatthū”ti vadanti, “rajju viya taṇhā”tipi apare. Puriso viya viññāṇaṃ, tassa rajjuggahaṇaṃ viya taṇhāya ārammaṇābhimukhanamanaṃ, payogo viya khipanakasaṅkhārā, mātikā viya cuticittaṃ, paratīraṃ viya paraloko.

599. ‘It proceeds by means of objects, etc.’… means it proceeds by means of conditions such as object, support, and so on. How? For one near death, due to the power of kamma, a mental object—a sphere of kamma and so on, whose danger is concealed by ignorance—is presented at the mind-door, and mind-door adverting arises taking that as its object. Then, in the near-death cognitive process, due to the weakness of the physical base, four or five impulsions proceed weakly. Immediately afterward, whether or not registering consciousness occurs, the death-consciousness arises, taking the object of the life-continuum. Some say that death occurs immediately after the life-continuum. When the death-consciousness has ceased, taking as its object that very kamma, sign of kamma, or sign of destiny that has come into range, propelled by the co-arisen formations towards the object of kamma and so on, by the strong sign of defilements that are not cut off, it abandons the previous support and proceeds by means of conditions such as the object, either relishing or not relishing the new support produced by kamma, like a man crossing a stream by grasping a rope tied to a tree on the near shore. Here, the near shore should be seen as the previous existence; the aggregates functioning in that existence, as the tree standing there; and the object of kamma, etc., as the rope. Some say the rope is like the heart-base, while others say it is like craving. Consciousness is like the man; his grasping the rope is like the inclining of craving toward the object; the propelling formations are like the effort; the stream is like the death-consciousness; and the far shore is like the next world.

600. Yathā puriso paratīre patiṭṭhahamāno paratīrarukkhavinibandhaṃ kiñci assādayamāno vā anassādayamāno vā kevalaṃ pathaviyaṃ sakabalappayogeheva patiṭṭhāti[M 2.0099], evamidampi bhavantarattabhāvavinibandhahadayavatthusaṅkhātaṃ nissayaṃ pañcavokārabhave assādayamānaṃ vā catuvokārabhave anassādayamānaṃ vā kevalaṃ ārammaṇanissayasampayuttadhammeheva pavattatīti taṃ viññāṇaṃ nāpi idhāgataṃ imasmiṃyeva bhave nibbattattā. Kammādinti atītabhavanibbattakammādiṃ. Ādi-saddena khipanakasaṅkhārānaṃ, namanavasena pavattataṇhāya, kammādivisayāya ādīnavapaṭicchādikāya ca avijjāya, daḷhaggāhādikarānaṃ upādānādīnañca gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha kammaṃ nāma upapajjavedanīyabhūtaṃ, aparāpariyavedanīyabhūtaṃ vā paṭisandhinibbattakakammaṃ. Khipanakasaṅkhārā nāma cutiāsannajavanasahajātasaṅkhārā, paṭisandhijanakakammasahagatasaṅkhārā vā, tato purimajavanasahagatasaṅkhārāti vā keci. Namanavasena pavattataṇhā nāma anusayāvatthāya pavattataṇhā. Esa nayo ādīnavapaṭicchādakaavijjāyapi. Kammādivisayā pubbe vuttāyeva. Daḷhaggāhakaraupādānā nāma maṇḍūkaṃ pannago viya upapattibhavassa daḷhaggahaṇavasena pavattā kāmupādānādayo.

600. Just as a person, while establishing himself on the far shore, whether relishing or not relishing anything tied to a tree on the far shore, stands on the ground solely by the application of his own strength; so too this consciousness, whether relishing the support called the heart-base (which is tied to the state of another existence) in the five-constituent existence, or not relishing it in the four-constituent existence, proceeds solely by means of phenomena associated with object and support. Therefore, that consciousness has not come here, because it is produced right within this very existence. ‘Kamma, etc.’ means kamma, etc., that produced the past existence. The term ‘etc.’ should be understood to include the propelling formations; craving that proceeds by way of inclining; ignorance that conceals the dangers of the sphere of kamma, etc.; and the clingings, etc., which cause firm grasping. Here, ‘kamma’ refers to the kamma that produces rebirth-linking, which is to be experienced either in this life or in a subsequent life. ‘Propelling formations’ are the formations co-arisen with the death-proximate javana, or the formations associated with the kamma that produces rebirth-linking, or, as some say, the formations associated with the preceding javanas. ‘Craving that proceeds by way of inclining’ is craving that proceeds in the state of a latent tendency. The same principle applies to ‘ignorance that conceals the dangers.’ The ‘spheres of kamma, etc.’ have been explained before. ‘Clinging that causes firm grasping,’ like a snake seizing a frog, refers to the clingings to sensual pleasures, etc., that proceed by way of firmly grasping the rebirth-existence.

601-5. Saddapaṭighosādīnaṃ [V 2.0074] satipi paccayapaccayuppannabhāve santānabandho na pākaṭoti tesaṃ ekattanānattabhāvaṃ anāmasitvā anāgatamatītahetusamuppādameva dassento “ettha cā”tiādimāha. Etthāti imasmiṃ cutipaṭisandhādhikāre. Paṭighosadīpamuddādīti ādi-saddena ādāsatalagatamukhanimittādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Aññattha agantvāti saddādipaccayadesaṃ anupagantvā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā saddādīnaṃ uppattipadesaṃ anupagantvā paṭighoso saddahetuko, padīpo padīpantarādihetuko, muddā lañchanahetuko, mukhanimittādikaṃ ādāsādiabhimukhādihetukaṃ hoti tato pubbe abhāvā, evamidampi paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ na [M 2.0100] hetudesaṃ gantvā taṃhetukaṃ hoti tato pubbe abhāvā, tasmā na idaṃ hetudesato purimabhavato idhāgataṃ paṭighosādayo viya saddādidesato, nāpi tato hetuṃ vinā uppannaṃ saddādīhi vinā paṭighosādayo viyāti. Atha vā aññatra agantvāti pubbe paccayapadese sannihitā hutvā tato aññatra gantvā tappaccayā na honti uppattito pubbe abhāvā, nāpi saddādipaccayā na honti, evaṃ idampīti vuttanayena yojetabbaṃ. Santānabandhato natthīti santānappabandhato natthi ekatā santānekattepi aññasseva viññāṇassa pātubhavanato, nāpi nānatā apubbānaṃ apubbānaṃ uppādepi paṭhamuppannaṃ dhammaṃ vinā pacchimassa anuppajjanato, padīpassa viya nānatā na siyā. Khaṇikāpi hi padīpajālā santānekattaṃ upādāya sā evāti vuccati, attakiccañca sādheti. “Sati santānabandhe”tiādinā santānabandhe ekantaṃ ekattāya ca nānattāya ca aggahetabbataṃ, gahaṇe ca dosaṃ dasseti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – santānabandhe sati yadi ekantena ekatā siyā, khīradadhīnampi anaññabhāvato, attatoyeva ca sayaṃ anuppajjanato khīrato dadhisambhūtaṃ na bhaveyya. Athāpi santānabandhe sati ekantaṃ nānatā bhaveyya, khīradadhīnampi nānattā, aññassa ca sāmibhāvamattena aparassa sāmibhāvāyogato khīrasāmi naro dadhisāmi na bhaveyya, na ca panevaṃ loke dissatīti.

601-5. Regarding sound, echoes, and the like, although there is a state of being a conditioned effect from a cause, the bond of continuity is not manifest. Therefore, without touching upon their oneness or otherness, and showing only the dependent arising from a past cause to a future effect, he says, “And here,” etc. “Here” refers to this section on death and rebirth-linking. “Echoes, lamps, seals, etc.”—the word “etc.” includes facial images in a mirror, and so on. “Not going elsewhere” means not going to the place of the conditions, such as sound. This means: Just as an echo is caused by sound without going to the place of the sound’s origin, a lamp is caused by another lamp, etc., a seal is caused by a stamp, and a facial image is caused by being opposite a mirror—none of these existed before—so too this rebirth-linking consciousness does not become conditioned by going to the place of its cause, having not existed before. Therefore, this consciousness does not come here from the place of its cause, from a previous existence, like echoes, etc., from sound, etc., nor does it arise without a cause, like echoes, etc., without sound, etc. Alternatively, “not going elsewhere” means that having been present in the place of the cause, they do not become its effects by going elsewhere, because they did not exist before their arising; nor are they without causes such as sound. In this way, this should be connected according to the stated principle. “There is no oneness from the bond of continuity” means that from the succession of the continuity, there is no oneness, because even when the continuity is one, it is another consciousness that appears. Nor is there otherness, because even with the arising of ever new phenomena, a later one does not arise without the first-arisen phenomenon; just as in the case of a lamp, there would not be otherness. For even a momentary lamp-flame, on account of the oneness of continuity, is said to be “the same one,” and it accomplishes its own task. The phrase, “When there is a bond of continuity,” etc., shows that in a bond of continuity, neither absolute oneness nor absolute otherness should be grasped, and it points out the fault in grasping either. This means: If there were absolute oneness in a bond of continuity, then because milk and curds would not be different, and because a thing does not arise from its very self, curds would not come into being from milk. If there were absolute otherness in a bond of continuity, then because milk and curds would be different, and because ownership of one thing does not entail ownership of another, the owner of the milk would not become the owner of the curds. Yet this is not seen in the world.

606. Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ lokavohāraparicchedo hoti, tasmā ekantaṃ ekatā, nānatāpi vā na ceva upagantabbā. Ekatte pana adhippete dhammato aggahetvā santānatova gahetabbaṃ, nānatte adhippete santānavasena aggahetvā dhammatova gahetabbanti adhippāyo. Tenāhu porāṇā –

606. Therefore, since the distinction in worldly usage is thus, one should not adhere to absolute unity or diversity. But when unity is intended, it should be grasped from the perspective of continuity, not from the perspective of ultimate reality; when diversity is intended, it should be grasped from the perspective of ultimate reality, not from the perspective of continuity. This is the meaning. Therefore the ancients said:

“Diṭṭhasantānabandhasmiṃ[M 2.0101], ekaññattavicāraṇe;

Sabhāguppattiyekatta-maññattaṃ khaṇabhedato”ti.

"In the connection of a perceived continuity, in the investigation of unity and diversity; unity is due to similar arising, diversity due to momentary destruction."

Ettha [V 2.0075] ca ekantaṃ ekatāpaṭisedhena “sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkha”nti imaṃ diṭṭhiṃ nivāreti, ekantaṃ nānatāpaṭisedhena “paraṃkataṃ sukhadukkha”nti.

Here, by rejecting absolute unity, the view "Pleasure and pain are self-made" is refuted; by rejecting absolute diversity, the view "Pleasure and pain are made by another" is refuted.

607-9. Nanu na sundaraṃ, nanu siyāti vā sambandho. Asaṅkantipātubhāveti saṅkantipātubhāvarahite, asaṅkantivasena vā pātubhāve, asaṅkamitvāva pātubhāveti attho. Khandhābhisambhavāti abhisambhūtakkhandhā, atha vā abhisambhavati kammaṃ etesūti abhisambhavā, khandhā, evaṃ abhisambhavā kammādhiṭṭhānabhūtā khandhāti attho. Idha niruddhattāti phalādhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ paralokaṃ agantvā idheva niruddhattā. Paratthāgamatoti paralokaṃ agamanato. Tassāti kammassa. Aññassāti yena taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, tato aññassa. Aññatoti yaṃ taṃ kammaṃ nibbattaṃ, tato aññato. Etaṃ vidhānanti idhalokato paralokaṃ gantvā natthi, tattha “aññeva khandhā nibbattantī”ti idaṃ sabbaṃ yathāvuttavidhānaṃ.

607-9. Is it not good? Or is there perhaps a connection? Asaṅkantipātubhāve means 'in the appearance without transition,' or 'in the appearance by way of non-transition,' or 'in appearing without having transitioned.' Khandhābhisambhava means 'the aggregates that have arisen,' or alternatively, 'the aggregates in which kamma arises,' thus, 'the aggregates that are the basis for kamma.' Idha niruddhattā means 'because of having ceased here,' that is, because of having ceased right here without going to the other world, which is the basis for the fruit. Paratthāgamato means 'from not going to the other world.' Tassa refers to that kamma. Aññassa means 'of another,' that is, of one other than the one who performed that kamma. Aññato means 'from another,' that is, from something other than what that kamma produced. Etaṃ vidhānaṃ means this arrangement: there is no going from this world to the other world; there, 'other aggregates arise'—all this is the arrangement as described.

611-4. “Santāne…pe… sādhako”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ pakāsetuṃ “ekasmiṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekasmiṃ santāneti yasmiṃ dhammapuñje kammaṃ nibbattaṃ, tasseva santāneti attho. Aññassātipi vā…pe… hoti. Tattha ekantaṃ ekattanānattānaṃ paṭisiddhattāti adhippāyo. Etassatthassāti hetuphalānaṃ atthato aññattepi teneva hetuphalabhāvena sambandhattā taṃ phalaṃ aññassa, aññatoti vā na vattabbanti etassa atthassa. Bījānanti ambamātuluṅgabījānaṃ. Abhisaṅkhāroti madhuādiparibhāvanaṃ. Madhuādināti [M 2.0102] madhucatumadhuraalattakarasādinā. Tassāti tassa paribhāvitabījassa. Paṭhamaṃ laddhapaccayoti madhurabhāvūpagamanato paṭhamameva laddhapaccayo. Kālantareti phalakāle. Evaṃ ñeyyamidampi cāti yathā etaṃ, evaṃ idampi ñātabbaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā hi ambabījādīsu madhunā, catumadhurena vā yojetvā ropitesu phalaraso madhuro hoti, mātuluṅgabīje ca alattakarasena rajitvā ropite ambilabhaṇḍo ratto hoti, na ca taṃ bījaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ vā phalaṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃ santepi kālantare phalaviseso na aññabījasantāne hoti, na ca aññasmiṃ bīje abhisaṅkhārapaccayato hoti, evameva ye idha loke nibbattakkhandhā, tesu nipphannaṃ kammaṃ vā paralokaṃ na gacchanti. Evampi kālantare vipākakkhandhā aññasmiṃ santāne na nibbattanti, na ca aññakammapaccayato hontīti.

611-4. To explain the meaning briefly stated as 'in the continuum... the doer,' the phrase 'in one continuum,' etc., is stated. Ekasmiṃ santāne means in the very continuum of that mass of phenomena in which the kamma was produced. Alternatively, 'of another,' etc., also... it is. Here, the intention is that absolute unity and diversity are refuted. For the purpose of this meaning: even though causes and results are distinct in reality, because they are connected by that very relationship of cause and effect, that result is not said to belong to another, nor to be from another—for this purpose. Bījānaṃ refers to the seeds of mango and citron. Abhisaṅkhāro means treatment with honey, etc. Madhuādinā means with honey, the four sweet substances, lac dye, etc. Tassa means of that treated seed. Paṭhamaṃ laddhapaccayoti means 'the first condition obtained' due to the attainment of sweetness. Kālantare means at the time of the fruit. Evaṃ ñeyyamidampi cāti means 'just as this is, so too should this be understood.' This is what is being said: Just as when mango seeds and the like are planted after being treated with honey or the four sweet substances, the flavor of the fruit becomes sweet, or when a citron seed is planted after being dyed with lac, the sour fruit becomes red—and yet neither that seed nor the treatment reaches the place of the fruit—even so, after a time, the special fruit does not arise in the continuum of another seed, nor does it arise from the condition of the treatment in another seed. In the same way, neither the aggregates that have arisen here in this world, nor the kamma produced in them, go to the other world. Even so, after a time, the resultant aggregates do not arise in another continuum, nor do they arise from the condition of another kamma.

Ettha [V 2.0076] hi abhisaṅkhataṃ bījaṃ viya kammaṃ vā satto, abhisaṅkhāro viya kammaṃ, bījassa aṅkurādippabandho viya sattassa paṭisandhiviññāṇādippabandho. Tatthuppannassa madhurarasassa ambilabhaṇḍe rattassa ca tasseva bījassa tato eva ca abhisaṅkhārato bhāvo viya kammakārakasseva sattassa tato eva ca abhisaṅkharaṇato bhāvo veditabbo.

Here, indeed, kamma or a being is like a treated seed; kamma is like the treatment; the series of sprout, etc., of a seed is like the series of rebirth-linking consciousness, etc., of a being. Just as the sweet taste that arises there, and the red color in the sour fruit, are due to that very seed and that very treatment, so should the state of the being, the doer of kamma, be understood as due to that very kamma.

615. Bālakāle…pe… phaladāyināti bālasarīre kataṃ vijjāpariyāpuṇanaṃ, sippasikkhanaṃ, osadhūpayogo ca na vuḍḍhasarīraṃ gacchati, atha ca tannimittaṃ vijjāpāṭavaṃ, sippajānanaṃ, anāmayatādi ca vuḍḍhasarīre honti, na ca tāni aññassa honti taṃsantatipariyāpanne eva sadise uppajjanato. Na ca yathā payuttena vijjāpariyāpuṇanādinā vinā tāni aññato honti tadabhāve abhāvato, evaṃ idhāpi santāne yaṃ phalaṃ, etaṃ nāññassa, na ca aññatoti [M 2.0103] yojetabbaṃ. Etena ca saṅkhārābhāve phalābhāvameva dasseti, na aññapaccayanivāraṇaṃ karoti.

615. In childhood... and so on... the fruit-giver: The learning of knowledge, the training in skills, and the application of medicines done in a young body do not go to an old body. Yet, because of that, proficiency in knowledge, skillfulness, and freedom from illness, etc., exist in the old body. These do not belong to another, because they arise similarly only within that continuity. Nor do they arise from another source without the applied learning of knowledge, etc., because in the absence of that, they are absent. Thus, here too, the fruit in the continuum, this is not another's, nor is it from another—this should be connected. By this, it shows only the absence of fruit in the absence of formations; it does not negate other conditions.

616-8. Evaṃ santepīti asaṅkantipātubhāve. Tattha ca yathāvuttadosapariharaṇe sati siddhepīti attho. Vijjamānanti padīpassa vaṭṭikāsneho viya vijjamānaṃ aniruddhanti attho. Avijjamānanti vaṭṭadukkhābhāvassa arahato cuticittaṃ viya avijjamānaṃ niruddhanti attho. Tappavattikkhaṇeti kammassa pavattamānakkhaṇeyeva. Tenāha “saddhimeva ca hetunā”ti. Avijjamānanti pavattikkhaṇato pubbe vijjamānataṃ asampattaṃ. Niruddhanti khaṇattayaṃ patvā niruddhaṃ. Tenāha –

616-8. Evaṃ santepi means 'even when this is so,' i.e., 'in the appearance without transition.' And there, when the aforementioned faults are avoided, it means that it is established. Vijjamānaṃ means 'existing,' like the wick and oil of a lamp, i.e., 'not ceased.' Avijjamānaṃ means 'non-existing,' like the passing away consciousness of an Arahant for whom the suffering of the round is absent, i.e., 'ceased.' Tappavattikkhaṇe means 'at the moment of its occurrence,' i.e., at the very moment when the kamma is occurring. Therefore it is said, 'with that very cause.' Avijjamānaṃ means 'non-existing,' i.e., not having attained existence before the moment of occurrence. Niruddhaṃ means 'ceased,' i.e., having reached the three moments and then ceased. Hence it is said:

“Pavattikkhaṇato pubbe, pacchā niccaphalaṃ siyā”ti.

"Before the moment of occurrence, and afterwards, there would be a permanent result."

Pubbeti kammāyūhanato pubbe. Avijjamānatāsāmaññena hetaṃ vuttaṃ. Pacchāti vipākappavattito pacchā ca.

Pubbe means 'before,' i.e., before the accumulation of kamma. This is said with reference to the general state of non-existence. Pacchā means 'afterward,' i.e., after the occurrence of the result.

619-20. Kaṭattāpaccayoti kaṭattā eva paccayo, na vijjamānatāya avijjamānatāya vāti attho. Tenāha “kāmāvacarassa kusalassa kammassa katattā upacitattā vipākaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppannaṃ hotī”tiādi (dha. sa. 431). Yadi evaṃ arahatā [V 2.0077] katakammampi kaṭattāpaccayo siyāti? Nayidamevaṃ. Yathā hi acchinnamūlasmiṃ rukkhe pupphitaṃ bījasamatthampi kusumaṃ mūle chinnamatte phaladāyakaṃ na hoti, evaṃ arahatopi kilesamūlassa abbocchinnakāle santāne pavattampi kammaṃ kilesamūlacchinnamatteyeva phaladāne asamatthabhāvaṃ āpannanti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

619-20. Condition by reason of having been done: The meaning is that it is a condition simply by reason of having been done, not by its existence or non-existence. Hence it is said: “On account of a wholesome kamma of the sense sphere having been done and accumulated, resultant eye-consciousness arises,” etc. (Dhs §431). If so, would kamma done by an arahant also be a condition by reason of having been done? No, it is not so. For just as on a tree whose root has not been cut, a flower that is capable of producing a seed does not become a fruit-giver as soon as the root is cut, so too, kamma that has occurred in the continuity of an arahant at a time when the root of defilements was not cut off becomes incapable of giving fruit as soon as the root of defilements is severed. Therefore the ancients said:

“Bālajanajjhāruḷho[M 2.0104],

Jātiratho kammakilesacakkoyaṃ;

Kilesacakkavidhamano,

Na yāti kammekacakkepī”ti.

“Mounted by foolish people, this chariot of birth has wheels of kamma and defilements; one who shatters the wheel of defilements does not proceed even on the single wheel of kamma.”

Kaṭattā ce paccayo, niccaphaladāyako vibandhoti āha “pāṭibhogādika”ntiādi. Pāṭibhogādikanti mūlabhāvūpagamanādikaṃ. Ādi-ggahaṇena “pacchā mūlaṃ dassāmī”ti bhaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ, iṇaggahaṇañca saṅgaṇhāti. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – pāṭibhogakiriyādīnaṃ vijjamānatā, avijjamānatā vā niyyātane, paṭibhaṇḍadāne, iṇadāne ca paccayo na hoti, atha kho karaṇamattaṃ, na ca taṃ niyyātanādīnaṃ niccameva paccayo hoti niyyātanādimhi kate paccayattābhāvato, evameva vipākuppādanepi kammassa vijjamānatā, avijjamānatā vā paccayo na hoti, atha kho karaṇamattameva, karaṇamatte ca sati vipakkavipākānaṃ paccayo na hotīti.

If it were a condition by reason of having been done, it would be a constant fruit-giver, which is an obstruction. Thus he said: “by way of guarantee, etc.” “By way of guarantee, etc.” means undertaking to be the principal, etc. By “etc.” is included taking goods on credit saying, “I will give the principal later,” and taking a loan. This is the intention here: The existence or non-existence of the act of guarantee, etc., is not a condition for repayment, giving substitute goods, or paying a debt; rather, the condition is the mere fact of having done it. And that is not always a condition for repayment, etc., because when repayment, etc., has been made, it ceases to be a condition. Similarly, in the production of a result, the existence or non-existence of the kamma is not the condition, but rather the mere fact of its having been done. And when there is only the fact of its having been done, it is not a condition for an unripe result.

621. Paramassa uttamassa atthassa pakāsanato paramatthappakāsano. Pītibuddhivivaḍḍhanoti pītiyā, ñāṇassa ca, pītisahagatassa vā ñāṇassa vivaḍḍhano.

621. Because it illuminates the highest, supreme meaning, it is the “Illumination of the Ultimate Meaning.” Increaser of joy and understanding: it is an increaser of joy and of understanding, or of understanding accompanied by joy.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

The Commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra,

Puññavipākapaccayaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the condition of the result of merit is completed.

10. Dasamo paricchedo

10. The Tenth Chapter

Rūpavibhāgavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Analysis of Materiality

622. Ādimhīti [M 2.0105][V 2.0078] uddesagāthāyaṃ. Idānīti cittacetasikavibhāvanānantaraṃ. Vibhāvananti niddesapaṭiniddesavasena sarūpato pakāsanaṃ.

622. “In the beginning” means in the verse of enumeration. “Now” means after the explanation of consciousness and mental factors. “Explanation” means the illumination of its own-nature by way of exposition and detailed exposition.

623. Ruppatīti sītuṇhādīhi vikāramāpajjati, āpādīyatīti vā attho. Vikārāpatti ca sītādivirodhipaccayasannidhāne visadisuppattiyeva. Na hi yathāsakaṃ paccayehi uppajjitvā ṭhitadhammānaṃ aññena kenaci vikārāpādanaṃ sakkā kātuṃ, tasmā purimuppannarūpasantati viya ahutvā pacchā uppajjamānānaṃ visabhāgapaccayasamavāyena visadisuppattiyeva idha “ruppana”nti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañca katvā saṅghiyānaṃ vipariṇāmavādo paccakkhato hoti. Nanu ca arūpadhammānampi virodhipaccayasamavāye visadisuppatti labbhatīti? Saccaṃ labbhati, na pana vibhūtatarā. Vibhūtatarā hettha visadisuppatti adhippetā ukkaṭṭhagativasena yathā “abhirūpassa kaññā dātabbā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.78).

623. “It is afflicted” (ruppati) means it undergoes alteration due to cold, heat, etc., or it is made to undergo it. And undergoing alteration is just the dissimilar arising in the presence of opposing conditions such as cold. For it is not possible for anything else to cause alteration in things that have arisen and stand by their respective conditions. Therefore, “affliction” (ruppana) should be understood here as just the dissimilar arising of what arises afterwards due to a combination of dissimilar conditions, not being like the previously arisen continuity of material form. And this being so, the Saṅghiyas’ doctrine of transformation is directly refuted. But is not dissimilar arising found also for immaterial phenomena in the combination of opposing conditions? True, it is found, but it is not so manifest. Here a more manifest dissimilar arising is intended, in the sense of the most excellent, as when it is said, “A maiden should be given to one of excellent form” (Saṃ. Ni. 3.78).

Kuto etaṃ viññāyatīti ce? Sītādiggahaṇato. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

If it is asked, “From where is this known?” From the inclusion of “cold,” etc. For thus it is said:

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ vadetha, ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā rūpanti vuccati. Kena ruppati? Sītenapi ruppati, uṇhenapi ruppati, jighacchāyapi ruppati, pipāsāyapi ruppati, ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassenapi ruppati, ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā rūpanti vuccatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.79).

“And what, bhikkhus, do you call material form? It is afflicted, bhikkhus, therefore it is called material form. By what is it afflicted? It is afflicted by cold, by heat, by hunger, by thirst, and by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and serpents. It is afflicted, bhikkhus, therefore it is called material form” (SN 22.79).

Ettha hi sītādiggahaṇaṃ sītādinā phuṭṭhassa ruppanaṃ vibhūtataraṃ, tasmā tadevettha gahitanti ñāpanatthaṃ. Itarathā ruppatīti sāmaññavacaneneva siddhe sītādiggahaṇaṃ niratthakaṃ siyāti.

Here, the inclusion of “cold,” etc., is for the purpose of showing that the affliction of one touched by cold, etc., is more manifest; therefore that alone is taken here. Otherwise, since it would be established by the general statement “it is afflicted,” the inclusion of “cold,” etc., would be meaningless.

Yadi [M 2.0106][V 2.0079] evaṃ, kathaṃ brahmaloke rūpasamaññā? Na hi tattha upaghātako sītādiphassaviseso labbhatīti? Saccaṃ, tatthāpi taṃsabhāvānativattanato. Aruppanassāpi hi ruppanasabhāvānativattanato rūpasamaññā hoti. Yathā aduddhampi khīraṃ taṃsabhāvānativattanato “duddha”nti vuccatīti. Atha vā kiñcāpi tattha upaghātako sītādiphassaviseso natthi, anuggāhako pana atthi. Tathā hi brahmānaṃ utujarūpaṃ atthi, tasmā attheva tattha ruppananti na koci tattha rūpasamaññāya vibandhoti.

If so, how is there the designation “material form” in the Brahma-world? For no specific kind of destructive contact with cold, etc., is found there. True, but even there, it is because of not transcending that nature. For even what is not being afflicted receives the designation “material form” because it does not transcend the nature of being afflicted, just as unmilked milk is called “milk” because it does not transcend its nature. Alternatively, although there is no specific kind of destructive contact with cold, etc., there, there is a supportive one. For the brahmās have materiality born of temperature. Therefore, there is indeed affliction there, so there is no obstacle to the designation “material form” there.

Rūpayatīti vāti sayaṃ vijjamānameva attano santānaṃ vikāramāpādayatīti attho. Iti purimaviggahena vikāruppatti “ruppana”nti dīpitaṃ. Iminā pana virodhipaccayasannipāte vijjamānasseva yo attano santāne visadisuppattihetubhāvo, taṃ ruppananti dīpitaṃ hoti. Imasmiṃ pakkhe arūpassa rūpasamaññāpasaṅgo eva natthi. Niruddhameva hi taṃ anantarādipaccayehi arūpaṃ uppādeti, na vijjamānanti. Ghaṭṭane vikārāpattiyaṃ rūpa-saddassa ruḷhī, tasmā arūpadhammānaṃ ghaṭṭanābhāvato na tesu rūpasamaññāti keci. Paṭighāto ruppananti apare, tesaṃ matena kiñcāpi sappaṭigharūpānameva rūpasamaññāpasaṅgo, atha kho avayavavohārena samudāyopi voharīyatīti sabbameva rūpaṃ rūpasamaññaṃ labhati. Keci panettha “rūpayatīti vaṇṇāyatanavasena vutta”nti vadanti. Tañhi vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ rūpayati, hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti. Tayidaṃ upari vaṇṇāyatananiddese visuṃyeva vuccatīti na tassa idha saṃvaṇṇane payojanaṃ atthi. Surūpoti dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasītianubyañjanabyāmappabhāketumālādīhi alaṅkatattā sobhanarūpakāyo, sabhāvattho vā rūpa-saddo “yaṃ loke [M 2.0107] piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa”ntiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.114) viya, tasmā surūpoti sobhanasabhāvo, tena dasabalacatuvesārajjādiasādhāraṇaguṇavisesasamāyogadīpanato satthu dhammakāyasampattiyāpi sobhanatā dassitā hoti.

Or, “it makes manifest” (rūpayati) means that, while existing, it itself causes alteration in its own continuity. Thus, by the former analysis, “affliction” was shown to be the arising of alteration. But by this analysis, it is shown that “affliction” is the state of being a cause for dissimilar arising in one's own continuity for what is existing when opposing conditions converge. In this view, there is no occasion for applying the designation “material form” to the formless. For it is only when it has ceased that it produces a formless state by way of proximity condition, etc., not while it is existing. Some say that the word “material form” is conventionally used for alteration upon impact; therefore, since formless phenomena lack impact, the designation “material form” does not apply to them. Others say “affliction” is impingement. According to their opinion, although the designation “material form” would apply only to material form with impingement, yet because the whole is designated by a term for a part, all material form receives the designation “material form.” Some here say that “it makes manifest” is stated in the sense of the visible-form base. For when undergoing alteration of color, it “makes manifest,” that is, it reveals that it has reached the heart. This will be stated separately below in the exposition of the visible-form base, so there is no purpose in commenting on it here. “Of beautiful form” means having a beautiful physical body, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide radiance, the flame-like protuberance, etc.; or the word “form” has the meaning of “nature,” as in “whatever in the world is of a dear form, of an agreeable form” (Pṭs I 114). Therefore, “of beautiful form” means of a beautiful nature. By this, in showing the combination of special, unique qualities such as the ten powers and the four kinds of fearlessness, the beauty of the Teacher's Dhamma-body is also shown.

624. Bhūtopādāyabhedatoti ettha tadadhīnavuttitāya bhavati ettha upādārūpanti bhūtaṃ. Atha vā mahābhūtāyeva idha purimapadalopavasena bhūta-saddena vuttā. Tenāha “catubbidhā mahābhūtā”ti. Bhūtāni upādiyateva, na pana sayaṃ tehi aññehi vā upādiyatīti upādāyaṃ. Evañca katvā catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ aññamaññaṃ nissāya pavattamānānampi upādāyarūpatāpasaṅgo natthi. Na hi te kevalaṃ aññamaññaṃ upādiyanteva, atha kho sayaṃ upādāyarūpehi [V 2.0080] upādiyanti, tasmā upādāya-saddaggahaṇasāmatthiyato na mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpatāpasaṅgoti. Atha vā “catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpa”nti (dha. sa. 584) vacanato catumahābhūtasannissitatāva upādāyarūpalakkhaṇaṃ, na bhūtattayādisannissitatāpīti na tesaṃ upādāyarūpatāti. Bhūtañca upādāyañca bhūtopādāyaṃ, tesaṃ vasena bhedatoti bhūtopādāyabhedato. Bhūtasaddassa ubhayaliṅgattā āha “mahābhūtā”ti. Upādāti upādāyarūpāni “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso”tiādīsu viya ettha ya-kāralopo daṭṭhabbo.

624. Regarding “by the distinction of primary and derived”: Here, because derived material form exists in dependence on them, they are “primary elements” (bhūta). Alternatively, the great primary elements themselves are here called “primary elements” by elision of the first word. Hence he said, “the four great primary elements.” What is “derived” (upādāya)? It is derived from the primary elements, but it is not itself that from which they or others are derived. This being so, there is no occasion for the four great primary elements to be considered derived material form, even though they occur in dependence on one another. For they are not merely derived from one another, but they are themselves that from which derived material form is derived. Therefore, by the force of the inclusion of the word “derived,” there is no occasion for the great primary elements to be considered derived material form. Alternatively, according to the passage “derived material form of the four great primary elements” (Dhs §584), the characteristic of derived material form is simply dependence on the four great primary elements, not on three or fewer primary elements; thus they are not derived material form. “Primary” (bhūta) and “derived” (upādāya) make “primary-and-derived” (bhūtopādāyaṃ); “by the distinction of” (bhedato) them is “by the distinction of primary and derived.” Since the word “bhūta” is of both genders, he says “great primary elements” (mahābhūtā, masc. pl.). “Derived” (upādā) means derived material forms (upādāyarūpāni); here the elision of the “ya” should be seen, as in “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso.”

625. Katame pana cattāro mahābhūtā, kathañca te mahābhūtasaññitā, kāni ca upādāyarūpāni, kathañca tāni “upādāyarūpānī”ti vuccantīti idaṃ codanaṃ hadaye katvā kamena sodhento āha “pathavīdhātū”tiādi. Cattārometi [M 2.0108] cattāro ime. Mahā ca so bhūto cāti mahābhūto, tena mahābhūtena sadevake loke mahantabhāvena pātubhūtena sammāsambuddhenāti attho. Atha vā –

625. Now, what are the four great primary elements, how are they designated as “great primary elements,” what are the derived material phenomena, and how are they called “derived material phenomena”? Holding this inquiry in mind and clarifying it step by step, he begins with “the earth element,” etc. “These four” (cattāro me) means “these four” (cattāro ime). “He is great (mahā) and he has become (bhūto),” thus “great-become” (mahābhūto). The meaning is: by that great-become one, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who has appeared with greatness in the world with its devas. Alternatively:

“Kālo ghasati bhūtāni,

Sabbāneva sahattanā;

Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto,

Sa bhūtapacaniṃ pacī”ti. (jā. 1.2.190) –

“Time devours beings,

All of them along with themselves;

But that being who devours time,

He cooks the cooker of beings.” (Ja I 260)

Ādīsu viya bhūta-saddassa sattesu, khīṇāsavesu ca pavattanato mahābhūtenāti mahatā sattena, mahākhīṇāsavenāti vā attho. Khīṇāsavopi hi parikkhīṇapaṭisandhikattā bhūtoyeva na bhavati, na ca bhavissatīti bhūtoti vuccati.

Just as in the preceding examples, the word bhūta is used for beings and for those whose taints are destroyed; thus, mahābhūtena means 'by a great being' or 'by a great one whose taints are destroyed.' For an Arahant, having exhausted rebirth, truly does not come to be and will not come to be, and so is called 'bhūta'.

626. Mahantā pātubhūtāti upādinnakasantānepi anupādinnakasantānepi sasambhāradhātuvasena mahantā hutvā bhūtā jātā nibbattāti attho. Tesaṃ anupādinnakasantāne –

626. ‘Greatly manifested’ (mahantā pātubhūtā) means that they have become, arisen, and been produced as great, by way of their constituent elements, in both appropriated and unappropriated continua. Regarding those in the unappropriated continuum:

“Duve satasahassāni, cattāri nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, saṅkhātāyaṃ vasundharā”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 584) –

“Two hundred thousand, and forty thousand;

By such a thickness, this earth is reckoned.” (Dhs.A. 584)

Ādinā [V 2.0081] nayena mahantapātubhūtatā vuttā. Upādinnakasantānepi anekayojanasatikamacchakacchapatigāvutappamāṇadevadānavādisarīravasena daṭṭhabbā. Vuttampi hetaṃ “santi, bhikkhave, mahāsamudde yojanasatikāpi attabhāvā”tiādi (a. ni. 8.20; cūḷava. 385; udā. 45).

In this way, their great manifestation is stated. Even in appropriated continua, they should be seen by way of the bodies of fish and turtles many hundreds of leagues in size, and of devas, dānavas, and others the size of three gāvutas. This too has been said: ‘Monks, there are beings in the great ocean with bodies a hundred leagues long,’ and so forth (A.N. 8.20; Cūḷava. 385; Udā. 45).

Mahābhūtasamāti [M 2.0109] anekabbhutavisesadassanena, anekabhūtadassanena ca mahantā bhūtā, mahantāni abbhutāni vā etesūti mahābhūtā, māyākārā, yakkhādayo vā jātivaseneva mahantā bhūtāti mahābhūtā, tehi ete samāti mahābhūtasamā. Ete hi yathā māyākārā amaṇiṃ eva udakaṃ maṇiṃ katvā dassenti, asuvaṇṇaṃyeva leḍḍuādikaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ katvā dassenti, yathā ca sayaṃ neva yakkhā na pakkhino samānā yakkhādibhāvampi dassenti, evamevaṃ sayaṃ anīlāneva hutvā nīlaṃ upādāyarūpaṃ dassenti, sayaṃ apītāyeva…pe… sayaṃ anodātāyeva hutvā odātaṃ upādāyarūpaṃ dassentīti māyākāramahābhūtasāmaññato mahābhūtā.

‘Similar to great beings’ (mahābhūtasamā) means that they are great beings (mahantā bhūtā) because they are seen with various extraordinary qualities and as many beings, or because there are great marvels in them, hence ‘great beings.’ Or, because magicians, Yakkhas, etc., are great beings by nature of their birth, hence ‘great beings.’ They are similar to these, hence ‘similar to great beings.’ For just as magicians make water that is not a gem appear as a gem, and a clod, etc., that is not gold appear as gold; and just as, though they are neither Yakkhas nor birds themselves, they display the state of Yakkhas, etc.; so too these, though not blue themselves, display blue derived form; though not yellow themselves... though not white themselves, display white derived form. Thus, by their commonality with the great beings who are magicians, they are called great elements.

Yathā ca yakkhā mahābhūtā yaṃ gaṇhanti, nevassa antosarīre ṭhānaṃ upalabbhati, na sarīrato bahi, na ca tassa aṅgamaṅgaṃ nissāya na tiṭṭhanti. Yadi hi sarīrassa anto ṭhitā, sakalasarīre byāpanaṃ na siyā. Atha bahi ṭhitā, yakkhaggahitakena katakusalākusalaṃ yakkhassa na siyā. Yadi cassa aṅgamaṅgaṃ nissāya na ṭhitā, yakkhaggahitake pahaṭe yakkhassa dukkhavedanuppatti na siyā, na ca sarīre rājiuṭṭhānaṃ bhaveyya. Yasmā panetaṃ sabbaṃ atthi, tasmā te aniddisitabbaṭṭhānā, evametepi na aññamaññassa anto na bahi ṭhitā upalabbhanti, na ca aññamaññaṃ nissāya na tiṭṭhanti. Yadi hi te aññamaññassa anto ṭhitā, na sakasakakiccakarā siyuṃ aññamaññaṃ anupavesanato. Atha aññamaññato bahi ṭhitā, vinibbhuttā siyuṃ, tathā ca sati avinibbhuttavādo parihāyeyya, tasmā aniddisitabbaṭṭhānāti. Yakkhamahābhūtasamānatāya mahābhūtasamā.
