Aniddisitabbaṭṭhānāpi cete patiṭṭhānādinā yathāsakakiccavisesena sesānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ upakārakā hontā sahajātādinā [M 2.0110] paccayena paccayo hutvā aññamaññaṃ nissāyeva tiṭṭhanti.

And just as Yakkhas, being great beings, seize someone—yet no place is found inside that person’s body, nor outside, nor do they stand without depending on the limbs. For if they were inside the body, there would be no pervasion of the entire body. If, however, they were outside, the wholesome and unwholesome deeds done by the one possessed would not belong to the Yakkha. And if they did not stand depending on the limbs, when the one possessed is struck, the Yakkha would not experience the arising of painful feeling, nor would lines appear on the body. But since all this does occur, their location is indeterminable. Similarly, these elements are not found standing inside or outside each other, nor do they stand without depending on one another. For if they were inside each other, they could not perform their respective functions due to mutual interpenetration. If, however, they were outside each other, they would be separate, and thus the doctrine of inseparability would fail. Therefore, their location is indeterminable. By their similarity to Yakkha great beings, they are called ‘similar to great beings.’ Though their location is indeterminable, they still support each other by their respective functions, such as providing a foundation, aiding the other three through conditions like co-nascence, and thus they stand depending on each other.

Vañcakattā abhūtenāti yakkhinīādayo viya abhūtena atacchena manāpavaṇṇasaṇṭhānādinā sattānaṃ vañcakattā mahantāni abhūtāni etesūti mahābhūtāti sammatā[V 2.0082]. Yathā hi yakkhinīādayo manāpehi kāḷasāmādivaṇṇehi, puthulapīvarakisādisaṇṭhānehi, hatthabhamuādivikkhepehi ca attano bhayānakabhāvaṃ paṭicchādetvā satte vañcenti, attano vasaṃ nenti, evametepi itthipurisādīsu manāpena chavivaṇṇena, manāpena aṅgapaccaṅgasaṇṭhānena, manāpena ca hatthapādaaṅgulibhamukavikkhepena attano kakkhaḷattādisarīralakkhaṇaṃ paṭicchādetvā bālajanaṃ vañcenti, attano sabhāvaṃ daṭṭhuṃ na dentā taṃ attano vasaṃ nenti.

‘By deceitfulness with the unreal’ (vañcakattā abhūtena) means that they are considered ‘great elements’ (mahābhūtā) because they are great in their deceitfulness of beings with unreal, untrue, pleasing colors, shapes, etc., just like female Yakkhas and others, and because there are great unrealities in them. For just as female Yakkhas and others conceal their terrifying nature by displaying pleasing colors like dark blue and dark, plump, stout, or thin shapes, and movements of hands, eyebrows, etc., thus deceiving beings and bringing them under their control; similarly, these elements conceal their own characteristics of harshness and so forth by displaying pleasing skin color, attractive limb shapes, and pleasing movements of hands, feet, fingers, and eyebrows, etc., in men and women, etc., deceiving foolish people and not allowing them to see their true nature, thereby bringing them under their control.

627-30. Cakkhusotantiādīsu rūpameva rūpatā. Hadayañca taṃ vatthu ca manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnanti hadayavatthu, hadayassa vā viññāṇassa vatthūti hadayavatthu, purimapadalopena pana “vatthu”nti vuttaṃ. Kabaḷīkāro āhāroyeva āhāratā. Kiñcāpi dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ rūpaniddese kabaḷīkāro āhāro osāne uddiṭṭho, idha pana nipphannarūpānaṃ ekaṭṭhāne dassanatthaṃ hadayavatthuanantaraṃ uddiṭṭhoti. Lahutā ādi yāsaṃ mudutākammaññatānanti lahutādayo, tāsaṃ tayaṃ lahutādittayaṃ, tattha lahubhāvo lahutā, tathā mudutāpi. Kammani sādhu kammaññaṃ, tassa bhāvo kammaññatā. Lahutādīnaṃ sayaṃ anipphannattā nipphannarūpavikārabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “rūpassā”ti visesanaṃ kataṃ. Catuvīsatīti gaṇanaparicchedo, balavarūpādīnaṃ nisedhanattho. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati[M 2.0111]. Nissāyāti nissāya eva, na pana nissayavasenapi. Catūhi upādānehi nimuttatāya nikkhantaṃ upādānato mānasaṃ etassāti nirupādānamānaso.

627-30. In the terms ‘eye, ear,’ etc., form is simply formness. The heart-base (hadayavatthu) is the basis for the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element. It is called ‘heart-base’ because it is the basis for the heart or for consciousness. But by eliding the first part of the compound, it is simply called ‘basis.’ Edible food is simply food-nature. Although in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī’s exposition of form, edible food is mentioned last, here it is mentioned immediately after the heart-base in order to show the grouping of produced forms in one place. ‘Lightness, etc.’ refers to lightness, softness, and wieldiness. These three—lightness, softness, and wieldiness—are called the triplet of lightness, etc. Among them, the state of being light is lightness, and similarly, softness. What is suitable for work is wieldiness, and its state is wieldiness. Since lightness, etc., are themselves unproduced, the qualification ‘of form’ is made to indicate that they are modifications of produced form. ‘Twenty-four’ is a numerical limit, intended to exclude strong form, etc. What needs to be said about that will become clear later. ‘Dependent’ means merely dependent, not even in the sense of a basis. ‘Free from grasping’ (nirupādānamānaso) means that the mind has emerged from the four kinds of grasping, therefore it is called ‘free from grasping.’

631-2. Patthaṭattāti puthuttā, tena puthubhāvato puthavī, puthavī eva pathavīti niruttinayena saddasiddhi dīpitā hoti. Ayaṃ pana sambhārapathaviyā vasena yujjati. Sā hi puthubhūtā patthaṭāti. Lakkhaṇapathaviyā vasena pana pathanaṭṭhena pathavī, sahajarūpānaṃ patiṭṭhābhāvena pakkhāyati upaṭṭhātīti attho. Purimopi vā attho lakkhaṇapathaviyā vasena labbhati. Vāyanatoti samudīraṇato, desantaruppattihetubhāvena bhūtasaṅghāṭassa pāpanatoti attho. Tejeti paripāceti, niseti vā, tikkhabhāvena sesabhūtattayaṃ usmāpetīti attho. Gāthābandhavasena cettha iti-saddalopato “tejeti”cceva vuttaṃ. Evaṃ “āpetī”ti etthāpi. Tasmā tejetīti tejo, āpetīti āpoti vuttaṃ hoti. Āpeti pālanāti anupāletabbarūpapariyosānaṃ āpeti pattharati. Tathā hetaṃ “ābandhanakicca”nti vuccati. Āpīyatīti āpo. Sosīyati pivīyatīti [V 2.0083] atthoti keci. Ayaṃ panattho sasambhārāpe yujjatīti vadanti, lakkhaṇāpepi yujjateva. Sopi hi pharusapācanavisosanākārena sesabhūtattayena pīyamāno viya pavattatīti. Āpāyatīti vā āpo, brūheti vaḍḍhetīti attho. Tathā hesa paribrūhanaraso. Tesanti yathāvuttānaṃ bhūtopādāyabhedānaṃ rūpānaṃ. Vakkhāmīti kathessāmi. Kiṃ kāraṇāti āha “lakkhaṇādīsū”tiādi. Hi-saddo hetuattho. Yasmā lakkhaṇādīsu ñātesu dhammā āvi bhavissanti, tasmā tesaṃ parato āvibhāvahetūti attho.

‘Because of being spread out’ (patthaṭattā) means because of its extensiveness. Hence, because of its extensive nature, it is called ‘earth’ (puthavī), and ‘puthavī’ itself is ‘pathavī’—thus, the derivation of the word is shown by way of etymology. This, however, is appropriate in the sense of earth as a composite (sambhārapathavī), for it is indeed extensive and spread out. In the sense of earth as a characteristic (lakkhaṇapathavī), however, it is ‘pathavī’ in the sense of extending, meaning it becomes manifest by serving as a foundation for co-arisen material phenomena. Alternatively, the former meaning is also obtained in the sense of earth as a characteristic. ‘Because of moving’ (vāyanato) means because of impelling, meaning it causes the aggregate of elements to reach other regions by being the cause of their arising there. ‘Tejeti’ means to mature or to sharpen; it means it heats the other three elements by its sharp nature. Here, due to the metrical structure, the word ‘iti’ is elided, so only ‘tejeti’ is stated. Likewise for ‘āpeti’. Therefore, it is said that ‘tejo’ (fire) is from ‘tejeti’ (it matures), and ‘āpo’ (water) is from ‘āpeti’ (it pervades). ‘Āpeti’ means to pervade; it pervades or spreads to the very limit of the material phenomena to be pervaded. Thus, it is called ‘the function of binding’ (ābandhanakicca). Some say ‘āpo’ is because ‘it is imbibed’ (āpīyati), meaning it is dried up or drunk. However, they say this meaning is appropriate for water as a composite (sasambhārāpo), but it is also appropriate for water as a characteristic (lakkhaṇāpo). For even that (characteristic water) proceeds as if being drunk by the other three elements in the manner of harsh ripening and desiccation. Alternatively, ‘āpo’ is because ‘it causes to increase’ (āpāyati), meaning it augments or increases. Thus, its characteristic function is augmenting. ‘Of these’ (tesaṃ) refers to the divisions of material phenomena, primary and derived, as previously described. ‘I will explain’ (vakkhāmi) means I will speak of. When asked, ‘For what reason?’ he said: ‘Because of characteristics, etc.’ Here, the word ‘hi’ has the meaning of cause. Since when the characteristics, etc., are known, the phenomena will become manifest, therefore, these are the causes for their subsequent manifestation—this is the meaning.

633-4. Kāni [M 2.0112] pana tāni lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni nāma, yesu ñātesu dhammā āvi bhavissantīti imaṃ codanaṃ sodhetuṃ lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni sarūpato kathento āha “sāmaññaṃ vā”tiādi. Sāmaññaṃ sādhāraṇo aniccādiko. Sabhāvo kakkhaḷādiphusanādiko asādhāraṇabhāvo. Kiccanti sandhāraṇādikiccaṃ. Sampattīti sampannabhāvo. “Suraso gandhabbo”tiādīsu hi gandhabbasampattiyā rasa-saddena vuccamānattā sampatti rasoti. Phalanti sahajātanānakkhaṇikavasena ṭhitaṃ phalaṃ. Upaṭṭhānanayoti gahetabbabhāvena ñāṇassa upaṭṭhānākāro. Āsannakāraṇanti padhānakāraṇaṃ.

What then are those characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes, by knowing which phenomena will become evident? To clarify this inquiry, explaining the characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes in their own nature, he says: ‘Generality or...’ etc. Generality (sāmañña) is what is common, such as impermanence, etc. Individual nature (sabhāva) is the particular nature, such as hardness, tangibility, etc. Function (kicca) is the activity, such as supporting, etc. Achievement (sampatti) is a state of accomplishment. For in phrases like ‘a Gandhabba of fine essence,’ because the accomplishment of the Gandhabba is expressed by the word ‘rasa’ (essence), accomplishment is ‘rasa’. Result (phala) is the result that exists by way of co-arising or of a different moment. The mode of manifestation (upaṭṭhānanaya) is the mode of its presentation to knowledge as something to be grasped. The proximate cause (āsannakāraṇa) is the principal cause.

Lakkhīyati etenāti lakkhaṇaṃ, kakkhaḷattaṃ lakkhaṇametissāti kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇā. Nanu ca kakkhaḷattameva pathavīdhātūti? Saccametaṃ. Tathā hi viññātāviññātasaddatthatāvasena asambhinnepi dhamme kappanāsiddhena bhedena evaṃ niddeso kato. Evañhi atthavisesāvabodho hotīti. Atha vā lakkhīyatīti lakkhaṇaṃ, kakkhaḷā hutvā lakkhiyamānā dhātu kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Sesāsupi eseva nayo. Patiṭṭhānarasāti sahajātadhammānaṃ patiṭṭhānabhāvakiccā. Asahajātānampi santativasena patiṭṭhānabhāvo hoteva. Tato eva nesaṃ sampaṭicchanākārena ñāṇassa paccupaṭṭhātīti sampaṭicchanapaccupaṭṭhānā. Iminā kiccavasenevettha “paccupaṭṭhāna”nti dasseti. Padaṭṭhānaṃ panettha catunnampi ekato katvā vakkhati.

‘It is marked by this,’ thus it is a characteristic; hardness is its characteristic, hence it has hardness as its characteristic. But is not hardness itself the earth element? This is true. For thus, even in a phenomenon that is not distinct, this description is made with a conceptually constructed distinction, by way of the known and unknown meaning of the word. For in this way an understanding of a specific meaning arises. Alternatively, ‘it is marked,’ thus it is a characteristic; the element that, being hard, is marked has hardness as its characteristic—this is how the meaning should be seen here. The same method applies to the remaining elements. Its characteristic function is to be a foundation for co-nascent phenomena. Even for non-co-nascent phenomena, it serves as a foundation by way of continuity. Therefore, it manifests to knowledge in the manner of receiving them; hence its manifestation is receiving. Hereby it is shown that ‘manifestation’ is in terms of its function. The proximate cause, however, he will speak of here collectively for all four.

Paggharaṇalakkhaṇāti dravatābhāvato vissandanalakkhaṇā. Brūhanarasāti sahajātadhammānaṃ milātabhāvūpagamanaṃ adatvā vaḍḍhanakiccā. Tathā hi sā tesaṃ pīṇitabhāvaṃ dassetīti vuccati. Saṅgahapaccupaṭṭhānāti bāhirakaudakaṃ [M 2.0113] viya nahāniyacuṇṇassa sahajātadhammānaṃ vippakirituṃ [V 2.0084] adatvā sampiṇḍanavasena saṅgaṇhanapaccupaṭṭhānā. Paripācanarasāti pariṇatabhāvakaraṇarasā. Maddavānuppadānapaccupaṭṭhānāti bāhiraggi viya jatulohādīnaṃ sahajātadhammānaṃ mudubhāvānuppadānapaccupaṭṭhānā. Vitthambhanalakkhaṇāti pūraṇalakkhaṇā. Samudīraṇarasāti kampanarasā. Abhinīhāro bhūtattayassa desantaruppattihetubhāvo, nīharaṇaṃ vā bījato aṅkurādikassa viya. Ekekā…pe… tabbāti pathavīdhātu āpādibhūtattayapadaṭṭhānā, āpodhātu pathavītejādibhūtattayapadaṭṭhānāti evaṃ ekekā dhātu avasiṭṭhabhūtattayapadaṭṭhānā.

Its characteristic is flowing, that is, streaming, due to its liquid state. Its characteristic function is augmenting, that is, the function of increasing co-nascent phenomena without allowing them to wither. Thus, it is said to show their thriving state. Its manifestation is cohesion; like external water binding bath powder, its manifestation is holding together co-nascent phenomena by way of binding, not allowing them to be scattered. Its characteristic function is maturing, that is, the function of causing a state of ripeness. Its manifestation is providing softness; like an external fire for lac, metal, and so on, its manifestation is providing softness to co-nascent phenomena. Its characteristic is distension, that is, filling. Its characteristic function is impelling, that is, agitating. Impulsion is the cause for the arising of the other three elements in another location, or it is the bringing forth, like that of a sprout from a seed. Each... and so on... Thus, the earth element has the other three elements, water and so on, as its proximate cause; the water element has the other three elements, earth, fire, and so on, as its proximate cause. In this way, each element has the remaining three elements as its proximate cause.

Ārohapariṇāhavasena hi majjhime imasmiṃ sarīre pariggayhamānā paramāṇubhedasañcuṇṇā sukhumarajabhūtā pathavīdhātu doṇamattā siyā. Sā ca tato upaḍḍhappamāṇāya āpodhātuyā yathā na vikirati, evaṃ ābandhanavasena saṅgahitā. Yathā pana paggharaṇasabhāvāya āpodhātuyā vasena kilinnabhāvaṃ picchalabhāvaṃ nāpajjati, evaṃ tejodhātuyā anupālitā. Yathā pana tassā vasena na vikirīyati, evaṃ vāyodhātuyā vitthambhitā saṅghātabhāvaṃ pāpitā. Evaṃ sukhumarajabhūtāpi ābandhanaparipācanasamudīraṇakiccāhi āpotejovāyodhātūhi laddhapaccayā sinehena temitā, tejasā paripakkā, vāyunā vitthambhitā piṭṭhacuṇṇāni viya na ito cito ca vikirīyati viddhaṃsīyati, avikiriyamānā aviddhaṃsiyamānā nānappakārakaṃ itthipurisaliṅgādibhāvavibhāgaṃ upagacchati, aṇuthūladīgharassathirakathinādibhāvañca pakāseti.

Indeed, the earth element in this average body, when considered in terms of its height and circumference, if broken down and crushed into fine dust of atomic particles, would be about a doṇa measure. And it is held together by the water element, which is about half that amount, so that it does not scatter, by way of binding. Just as it does not become wet or slimy through the water element, which has a flowing nature, so it is maintained by the fire element. And just as it does not scatter because of that, so it is supported by the air element and brought to a state of solidity. Thus, even as fine dust, having received conditions from the water, fire, and air elements through their functions of binding, maturing, and impelling, it is moistened by moisture, matured by heat, and supported by air. Like flour-dough, it does not scatter or disintegrate here and there; not scattering or disintegrating, it takes on various distinctions such as male and female characteristics and manifests qualities like smallness, largeness, length, shortness, stability, and hardness.

Yūsagatā ābandhanākārabhūtā panettha āpodhātu pathavīpatiṭṭhitā tejānupālitā vāyovitthambhitā na gaḷati[M 2.0114], na paggharati, na parissavati. Evaṃ tīhi dhātūhi anupālitā apaggharamānā aparissavamānā piṇḍitabhāvaṃ dasseti. Esā hi anubrūhanarasā.

Here, the water element, being in a fluid state and having the nature of binding, established on the earth element, maintained by the fire element, and supported by the air element, does not drip, does not flow, and does not leak out. Thus, being maintained by these three elements, not flowing or leaking out, it shows a state of cohesion. For its characteristic function is augmenting.

Asitapītādiparipācitā cettha usumākārabhūtā uṇhattalakkhaṇā tejodhātu pathavīpatiṭṭhitā āposaṅgahitā vāyovitthambhitā imaṃ kāyaṃ paripāceti, vaṇṇasampattiñcassa āvahati. Sā hi yathānubhuttassa āhārassa sammā pariṇāmanena rasādisampattiyā hetubhāvaṃ gacchantī imaṃ kāyaṃ paripāceti, vaṇṇasampattiñca āvahati. Kammūpanissayāya hi cittapasādahetukāya ca sarīre vaṇṇasampadāya tejodhātu visesapaccayo, pageva utuāhārasamuṭṭhānāya rūpasampattiyāti. Tāya ca pana paripācito ayaṃ kāyo na pūtibhāvaṃ gacchati.

Here, the fire element, which matures what is eaten, drunk, and so on, being of the nature of heat and characterized by warmth, established on the earth element, held together by the water element, and supported by the air element, matures this body and brings about its excellence of complexion. For by properly transforming the consumed food, it becomes the cause for the excellence of nutritive essence and other qualities, thus maturing this body and bringing about its excellence of complexion. Indeed, for the excellence of complexion in the body, which has kamma as its support and is caused by mental clarity, the fire element is a special condition; how much more so for the excellence of form arising from climate and food. And matured by it, this body does not become putrid.

Aṅgamaṅgānusaṭā [V 2.0085] cettha samudīraṇavitthambhanalakkhaṇā vāyodhātu pathavīdhātuyā attani patiṭṭhāpīyati. Yathā sahajātadhammehi visuṃ na hoti, evaṃ āpodhātuyā saṅgayhati. Yathā sahajātadhammā na parissavanti, evaṃ tejodhātuyā anupālīyati. Sā evaṃ tīhi dhātūhi yathārahaṃ anupāliyamānā imaṃ kāyaṃ vitthambheti. Tāya pana vitthambhito ayaṃ kāyo na paripatati, ujukaṃ tiṭṭhati, iccevaṃ ekekāya dhātuyā tissannaṃ dhātūnaṃ vaseneva pavattanato vuttaṃ “ekekā cettha sesabhūtattayapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā”ti.

Here, the air element, which pervades the major and minor limbs and is characterized by impulsion and distension, is established on the earth element. Just as it is not separate from its co-nascent phenomena, so it is held together by the water element. Just as co-nascent phenomena do not flow away, so it is sustained by the fire element. Thus, being appropriately sustained by these three elements, it supports this body. When this body is thus supported by it, it does not collapse but stands upright. Therefore, because each element functions by the influence of the other three elements, it is said, 'each one here should be understood as having the remaining three elements as its proximate cause.'

Evaṃ bhūtarūpānaṃ saddhiṃ vacanatthehi lakkhaṇādayo dassetvā idāni upādāyarūpāni dassento āha “cakkhatī”tiādi. Anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ cakkhati-saddassa vibhāvanatthatāpi sambhavatīti katvā vuttaṃ “vibhāvetīti attho”ti. Cakkhatīti pana viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ samavisamaṃ ācikkhantaṃ viya, abhibyattaṃ vadantaṃ viya hotīti attho. Atha [M 2.0115] vā cakkhatīti viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ rūpaṃ assādentaṃ viya hotīti attho. Cakkhatīti hi ayaṃ saddo “madhuṃ cakkhati, byañjanaṃ cakkhatī”tiādīsu viya assādattho. Vuttañhetaṃ – “cakkhuṃ kho, māgaṇḍiya, rūpārāmaṃ rūparataṃ rūpasamudita”nti (ma. ni. 2.209). Vakkhati ca “rūpesu āviñchanarasa”nti. Yadi evaṃ “sotaṃ kho, māgaṇḍiya, saddārāma”ntiādivacanato (ma. ni. 2.209) sotādīnampi saddādiassādakabhāvo atthīti tesampi cakkhusaddābhidheyyatā āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati niruḷhattā. Niruḷho hi esa cakkhu-saddo locaneyeva padumādīsu paṅkajādisaddā viyāti.

Having thus shown the characteristics and so forth of the primary material phenomena along with their verbal meanings, he now indicates the derived material phenomena, saying 'cakkhati,' and so on. Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the term 'cakkhati' (sees) can also have the meaning of 'vibhāveti' (makes clear); therefore it is said, 'it makes clear, that is the meaning.' Moreover, 'cakkhati' means that, supported by consciousness, it is as if declaring a form to be even or uneven, or as if speaking manifestly. Alternatively, 'cakkhati' means that, supported by consciousness, it is as if savoring a form. For this term 'cakkhati' has the sense of savoring, as in 'he savors honey,' 'he savors the seasoning,' and so on. As it is said: 'The eye, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in forms, takes pleasure in forms, is intoxicated with forms' (MN 2.209). And it will be said: 'Its function is to be drawn towards forms.' If so, then from statements like 'The ear, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in sounds' (MN 2.209), etc., does it follow that the ear and so on also have the nature of savoring sounds, etc., and thus come to be designated by the term 'eye'? It does not, because of established usage. For this term 'eye' is established as referring only to the visual organ, just as terms like 'mud-born' and so on refer to the lotus.

635-6. Cakkhurūpassa niddesappakaraṇepi cakkhu-saddasāmaññato āgataṃ sabbampi cakkhuṃ pabhedato dassetuṃ “tattha cakkhū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ cakkhuniddese. Paññāmaṃsappabhedatoti paññācakkhu maṃsacakkhūti evaṃ paññāmaṃsānaṃ vasena pabhedato. Tatthāti tasmiṃ duvidhe cakkhumhi. Paññāyeva paññāmayaṃ. Nāmatoti nāmehi pañcavidhanti sambandho. Katamehi nāmehīti āha “buddhadhammā”tiādi. Tattha buddhadhammasamantehīti buddhacakkhu dhammacakkhu samantacakkhūti imehi nāmehi. Ñāṇadibbehīti ñāṇacakkhu dibbacakkhūti ca nāmehi. Yathānukkamatoti yathāvuttaanukkamato. Nānattanti bhedaṃ. Meti mayhaṃ santikā, mayhaṃ vacanatoti vā attho. Nibodhatha jānātha.

635-6. Although this is the section explaining the eye as a material phenomenon, in order to show all kinds of 'eye' that come from the general term 'eye' by way of its divisions, the passage beginning 'Therein, the eye...' was stated. 'Therein' means in that explanation of the eye. 'By way of the division into wisdom and flesh' means the wisdom-eye and the flesh-eye; thus, the division is on the basis of wisdom and flesh. 'Therein' means in those two kinds of eyes. That which consists of wisdom is the wisdom-eye. 'By name' is to be connected with 'fivefold'; thus, 'fivefold by names.' By which names? He says, 'Buddha, Dhamma,' and so on. Therein, 'by Buddha, Dhamma, and Samanta' refers to these names: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, and the Samanta-eye. 'By Ñāṇa and divine' refers to the names: the knowledge-eye and the divine-eye. 'In due order' means according to the stated sequence. 'Diversity' means the distinction. 'From me' means from my presence, or from my words. 'Understand' means know.

637. Tattha [V 2.0086] “addasaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento satte apparajakkhe mahārajakkhe tikkhindriye”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.283) āgataṃ buddhacakkhu nāmāti dassento āha “āsayānusaye”tiādi. Tattha āsayānusayeti sattānaṃ āsaye ceva anusaye ca, tasmiṃ pavattanti attho[M 2.0116]. Tattha āgantvā seti cittaṃ etthāti āsayo. Byagghāsayo viya. Yathā hi byaggho gocaratthāya pakkantopi puna āgantvā vanagahaneyeva sayati, teneva ca taṃ tassa āsayoti vuccati, evaṃ aññatthāpi pavattaṃ cittaṃ āgantvā yattha sayati, taṃ tassa āsayoti veditabbaṃ. So pana sassatadassanādivasena catubbidho hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

637. Therein, showing what is called the Buddha-eye, which is mentioned in the passage beginning, 'I saw, bhikkhus, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, beings with little dust, beings with much dust, with keen faculties...' (MN 1.283), he says, 'in the inclinations and latent tendencies,' and so on. Therein, 'in the inclinations and latent tendencies' means that it functions with respect to the inclinations and latent tendencies of beings. Herein, an 'inclination' (āsaya) is so called because the mind, having come, lies down (seti) in it. It is like a tiger's lair (byagghāsaya). For just as a tiger, though it has gone away for the sake of prey, returns and lies down in the forest thicket, and for that reason this is called its lair, so too, wherever the mind, though it has been active elsewhere, comes and lies down, that should be understood as its inclination. This, however, is fourfold on the basis of views of eternalism and so on. For it has been said:

“Sassatucchedadiṭṭhī ca, khanti cevānulomikā;

Yathābhūtañca yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, etaṃ āsayasaññita”nti. (visuddhi. mahā. 1.136; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā; sārattha. ṭī. 1. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītivaṇṇanā; vi. vi. ṭī. 1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā)

The views of eternalism and annihilation, compliant acceptance, and the knowledge of things as they truly are—this is designated as inclination.

Anusayakathā upari āgamissati. Indriyānaṃ paropareti saddhāpañcamakānaṃ indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāve. Tikkhañhi indriyaṃ ukkaṭṭhagatattā paraṃ, mudu aparaṃ anukkaṭṭhagatattā. Idaṃ pana buddhacakkhu chasu asādhāraṇañāṇesu purimadvayanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The discourse on latent tendencies will come later. 'The superiority and inferiority of the faculties' refers to the sharpness and dullness of the five faculties beginning with faith. For a sharp faculty is 'superior' (para) because it has reached an excellent state, and a dull one is 'inferior' (apara) because it has not reached an excellent state. This Buddha-eye, however, should be understood as the first two of the six uncommon knowledges.

638. Heṭṭhā…pe… saññitanti “tasmiṃyeva āsane virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādī”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ heṭṭhā tīsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ dhammacakkhunti saññitaṃ. Ñāṇaṃ sabbaññutā panāti sabbaññubhāvasaṅkhātaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Tañhi sabbaññūti abhidhānassa, buddhiyā ca pavattinimittatāya sabbaññubhāvo nāma hoti. Ñeyyaṃ samantacakkhunti khandhādivasena samantato sabbaso dassanaṭṭhena samantacakkhunti ñeyyaṃ. Tenevāha –

638. The knowledge in the three lower paths, mentioned in the passage, 'On that very seat the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye arose,' is designated as the Dhamma-eye. The knowledge that is omniscience, however, is the knowledge designated as the state of being omniscient. For, because it is the cause for the designation 'omniscient one' and for the arising of the corresponding understanding, it is called the state of omniscience. It should be known as the all-around eye (samantacakkhu) because it has the characteristic of seeing everything from all sides in terms of the aggregates and so on. Therefore he said:

“Na tassa addiṭṭhamidhatthi kiñci,

Atho aviññātamajānitabbaṃ;

Sabbaṃ [V 2.0087] abhiññāsi yadatthi ñeyyaṃ,

Tathāgato tena samantacakkhū”ti. (cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85);

"Nothing here is unseen by him, nor anything unperceived or unknowable; he has directly known all that can be known, therefore the Tathāgata is the All-Around Eye."

639. Yaṃ cakkhuṃ udapādīti āgatanti yaṃ ñāṇaṃ “idaṃ dukkhanti, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ [M 2.0117] udapādī”ti (mahāva. 15) evaṃ tattha tattha suttesu āgataṃ, catūsu saccesu teparivaṭṭavasena “dukkhaṃ pariññeyyaṃ pariññāta”nti evamādinā dvādasavidhena ākārena pavattaṃ, idaṃ ñāṇacakkhu. Yā pana “addasaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, dibbena cakkhunā visuddhenā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.284) āgatā pañcamajjhānasaṅkhātaabhiññācittasampayuttā paññā, ayaṃ dibbacakkhūti dassetuṃ “abhiññācittajā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ca paṭhamatatiyañāṇāni kāmāvacarāniyeva. Catutthampi pana purimadvayamiva kāmāvacaranti ānandācariyena vuttaṃ. Ñāṇacakkhuṃ sahaariyamaggavipassanāñāṇantipi yujjatīti apare. Aggamaggena saha vipassanāpaccavekkhaṇañāṇanti pana yuttaṃ viya dissati.

639. That which is mentioned as 'the eye arose' refers to the knowledge that is mentioned in various suttas thus: 'Bhikkhus, concerning things not heard before, the eye arose, knowledge arose: "This is suffering"' (Mahāva. 15). This, which functions with regard to the four truths in twelve aspects by way of three rounds, such as 'suffering is to be fully understood, has been fully understood,' is the knowledge-eye. Furthermore, the wisdom associated with the mind of direct knowledge, which is designated as the fifth jhāna, and which is mentioned in the passage beginning, 'I saw, bhikkhus, with the divine eye, which is purified...' (MN 1.284), is the divine eye. To show this, the words 'born of the mind of direct knowledge' and so on were said. Herein, the first and third knowledges are exclusively of the sense-sphere. The fourth, too, is said by the teacher Ānanda to be of the sense-sphere, like the first two. Others hold that it is fitting for the knowledge-eye to be the knowledge of insight together with the noble path. However, it seems more fitting for it to be the knowledge of insight and reviewing, together with the supreme path.

640-4. Evaṃ paññācakkhussa pabhedaṃ dassetvā puna maṃsacakkhussāpi pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ “maṃsacakkhupī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sasambhārapasādatoti sasambhāracakkhu pasādacakkhūti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ vasena sambharīyati etehīti sambhārā, avayavā. Te pana upatthambhakabhūtā catusamuṭṭhānikarūpasantatiyo daṭṭhabbā. Saha sambhārehīti sasambhāraṃ. Sasambhārañca nāma maṃsapiṇḍo pavuccatīti sambandho. Akkhikūpaṭṭhinā heṭṭhāti heṭṭhāgataakkhikūpassa aṭṭhinā paricchinnoti sambandho. Uddhanti akkhikūpato uddhaṃ. Ubhato akkhikoṭīhīti akkhikūpassa ubhayabhāge akkhikoṭīhi. Matthaluṅgena antatoti akkhikūpassa abbhantare ṭhitena matthaluṅgena. Nhārusuttena ābandhoti nahārurajjūhi anto matthaluṅgena saha ābandho. Sakalopi ca lokoti sakalopi bālaputhujjanaloko. Yanti yaṃ maṃsapiṇḍaṃ. Kamalassa dalaṃ viyāti puthulavipulanīlatāya nīluppaladalaṃ viya. Jānātīti gaṇhāti. Cakkhu nāma na taṃ hotīti tathā gayhamānaṃ taṃ cakkhu nāma na hoti. Kiñcarahi tanti āha [M 2.0118] “vatthu tassāti vuccatī”ti. Tassāti tassa yathādhippetassa paramatthacakkhuno. Idaṃ panāti nigamanaṃ.

640-4. Having thus shown the divisions of the wisdom-eye, it is then said, 'the flesh-eye,' etc., to show the divisions of the flesh-eye. By 'sasambhāra' and 'pasāda' is meant the eye with its components and the sensitive eye; by means of these two, it is composed, hence they are called components, i.e., parts. These should be understood as the fourfold continuity of materiality that serves as support. 'With components' means together with its components. And 'sasambhāra' is called a lump of flesh—this is the connection. 'Below the eye socket bone' means bounded by the bone below the eye socket—this is the connection. 'Above' means above the eye socket. 'On both sides by the edges of the eye' means on both sides of the eye socket by the edges of the eye. 'Bounded inside by the brain' means inside the eye socket, bounded by the brain. 'Bound by sinews' means bound inside by sinews together with the brain. 'And all the world' means all the world of foolish ordinary people. 'That which' refers to that lump of flesh. 'Like a lotus petal' is like a blue lotus petal—broad, wide, and blue. 'They know it' means they grasp it. 'That is not called the eye' means what is grasped in that way is not called the eye. 'What then?'—thus it is said, 'the basis of that is called.' 'Of that' means of that ultimate eye as intended. 'This, however,' is the conclusion.

645-7. Taṃ [V 2.0088] pana sasambhāracakkhu yehi sambhārehi sambharīyati, te sarūpato, gaṇanato ca dassetuṃ “vaṇṇo gandho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhāvoti itthiyā itthibhāvo, purisassa pumbhāvoti labbhamānakabhāvo. Sambhavoti āpodhātumeva sambhavabhūtamāha. Saṇṭhānanti ca tena tenākārena sanniviṭṭhesu mahābhūtesu taṃtaṃsaṇṭhānavasena viññāyamānaṃ vaṇṇāyatanamāha. Āpodhātuvaṇṇāyatanehi ca anatthantarabhūtānampi sambhavasaṇṭhānānaṃ visuṃ vacanaṃ tathābhūtānaṃ, atathābhūtānañca āpādīnaṃ yathāvuttamaṃsapiṇḍe vijjamānattā. Āpodhātuvaṇṇāyatanānañhi santānavasena pavattamānānaṃ avatthāviseso sambhavo saṇṭhānañcāti. Daseteti catasso dhātuyo, tannissitā vaṇṇādayo cāti ime dasa. Catusamuṭṭhānāti antogatahetvatthamidaṃ visesanaṃ, catusamuṭṭhānikattāti vuttaṃ hoti.

645-7. That eye with its components, by which components it is composed, is described in terms of its own nature and enumeration as 'color, odor,' etc. 'Nature' means the woman's femaleness, the man's maleness—the state of being obtained. 'Origin' refers to the water element itself as the origin. And 'shape' refers to the visible form that is discerned according to various configurations when the great elements are arranged in certain ways. Though origin and shape are not essentially different from the water element and visible form, they are spoken of separately because such origins and shapes, both actual and potential, exist in the described lump of flesh. For the water element and visible form, the origin and shape are specific states of their uninterrupted continuity. 'Ten' refers to the four elements and the color, etc., dependent on them—these ten. 'Of fourfold origin' is a qualification that implies the underlying cause; it means 'having a fourfold origin.'

648. Cakkhu…pe… jīvitameva cāti imāni ekantakammasamuṭṭhānāni, purimāni ca catusamuṭṭhānānīti cattālīsañca cattāri ca rūpāni bhavanti, catucattālīsa rūpāni hontīti attho.

648. The eye…pe… and life itself—these are exclusively kamma-originated, while the former are of fourfold origin—thus there are forty and four materialities. The meaning is that there are forty-four materialities.

649-52. Imesaṃ pana rūpānaṃ vasenāti yathāvuttānaṃ saṅkhepato cuddasannaṃ, vitthārato catucattālīsānañca rūpānaṃ vasena. Paripiṇḍitanti samantato piṇḍitaṃ. Yattha setampi atthi, kaṇhampi lohitampi pathavīpi āpopi tejopi vāyopi, idaṃ pana semhussadattā setaṃ hoti, pittussadattā [M 2.0119] kaṇhaṃ, ruhirussadattā lohitakaṃ, pathavussadattā patthinaṃ hoti, āpussadattā paggharati, tejussadattā pariḍayhati, vāyussadattā sambhamati. Idaṃ sambhāravantatāya sambhāracakkhūti paṇḍitehi buddhādīhi pakāsitaṃ paridīpitaṃ. Ettha sitoti etaṃ sasambhāracakkhuṃ nissito tadāyattabhūto. Tenāha “ettha paṭibaddho”ti. Catunnaṃ pana bhūtānaṃ pasādoti catunnaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasannatāsabhāvo pasādo, “setena maṇḍalenassā”ti pāṭho yujjati. Potthakesu pana “sete tu maṇḍale tassā”ti likhanti. Kaṇhamaṇḍalamajjheti idhāpi “kaṇhamaṇḍalassa majjhe”ti vattabbe “catutthadū”tiādīsu viya chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ vibhattilopaṃ katvā “kaṇhamaṇḍalamajjhe”ti vuttaṃ. Evañhi attho ca yojanā ca suṭṭhu upapannā honti. Aṭṭhakathāyampi hi “setamaṇḍalaparikkhittassa kaṇhamaṇḍalassa majjhe”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 596) vuttaṃ. Apare pana yathāṭhitavaseneva pāṭhaṃ gahetvā “sabbaso parikkhittassa tassa sasambhārassa [V 2.0089] cakkhuno majjhe setamaṇḍale kaṇhamaṇḍale majjhe”ti yojenti. Diṭṭhamaṇḍaleti abhimukhe ṭhitānaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānuppattidesabhūte diṭṭhamaṇḍale.

649-52. Regarding these forms, it is by means of these forms as stated—briefly fourteen, and in detail forty-four—that they are explained. 'Paripiṇḍita' means completely gathered together. Wherever white exists, or black, red, earth, water, fire, or air—this, due to the predominance of phlegm, becomes white; due to bile, black; due to blood, red; due to the earth element, it becomes solid; due to the water element, it flows; due to the fire element, it burns; due to the air element, it moves. This is called the 'eye with its components' by the wise, such as the Buddhas, because it possesses components and is made clear and explained. Here, by 'sita' is meant that which is dependent on this eye with its components, being contingent upon it. Hence it is said, 'bound to this.' The clarity of the four elements refers to the nature of clarity of the four elements. The reading 'setena maṇḍalenassā' is appropriate. In manuscripts, however, it is written as 'sete tu maṇḍale tassā.' 'Kaṇhamaṇḍalamajjhe' here means 'in the middle of the black circle.' Though it should be expressed as 'kaṇhamaṇḍalassa majjhe,' for the sake of preserving meter, as in 'catutthadū' and similar cases, the inflection is dropped, and 'kaṇhamaṇḍalamajjhe' is used. This way, both the meaning and the construction are well established. In the commentary, it is also stated: 'in the middle of the black circle, surrounded by the white circle.' Others, however, take the text as it stands and explain: 'entirely surrounded, in the middle of the white circle, in the middle of the black circle of that eye with its components.' 'Diṭṭhamaṇḍala' refers to the visible circle, the sphere of perception for those standing in front, in the location where the bodily form arises.

653-5. Sandhāraṇā…pe… hutvānāti sandhāraṇanahāpanamaṇḍanabījanakiccāhi catūhi dhātīhi khattiyakumāro viya sandhāraṇābandhanaparipācanasamudīraṇakiccāhi attanissayabhūtāhi catūhi dhātūhi katūpakāraṃ hutvā. Utucittādināti tīhi santatisamuṭṭhāpakehi utucittāhārehi. Ettha ca kalāpantaragatā utuāhārā adhippetāti vadanti. Āyunā katapālananti catudhātunissiteneva jīvitindriyena rakkhiyamānaṃ. Tathā hetaṃ kammajarūpaparipālanalakkhaṇaṃ. Vaṇṇagandharasādīhīti ādi-ggahaṇena ojaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, “vaṇṇagandharasojāhī”ti [M 2.0120] vā pāṭho. Vatthudvārañca sādhayanti yathāyogaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ. Cakkhuviññāṇassa hi nissayabhāvato vatthubhāvaṃ, pavattimukhabhāvato dvārabhāvañca sādheti. Sampaṭicchanādīnaṃ pana tadārammaṇāvasānānaṃ aññanissitattā dvārabhāvameva sādheti, na vatthubhāvaṃ. Ūkāsirasamānena pamāṇenāti ūkāsirasamānena padesappamāṇena lakkhitaṃ hutvā ūkāsirasamānappamāṇe ṭhāneti vā attho. Tiṭṭhatīti satta akkhipaṭalāni byāpetvā sattasu picupaṭalesu āsittatelaṃ viya tiṭṭhati. Evañca katvā cakkhussa anekakalāpagatatā siddhā hoti. Upaddavānaṃ paṭalanirākaraṇepi hi cakkhu vijjatevāti. Yathā ca cakkhu, evamimassa nissayabhūtā catasso dhātuyo, āyuvaṇṇādīni ca satta akkhipaṭalāni byāpetvā ṭhitāneva avinibbhogavuttittāti gahetabbaṃ.

653-5. Supporting... and so on... "Having become" means that just as a young nobleman is supported by four nurses—bearing, bathing, adorning, and fanning—so too, the four elements, which are the basis of oneself, perform the functions of supporting, binding, maturing, and producing, thereby being of great assistance. "By climate, mind, etc." refers to climate, mind, and nutriment, the three causes that bring about continuity. Here, it is said that climate and nutriment, when included in other kalāpas, are intended. "Guarded by lifespan" means being protected by the life faculty, which itself depends on the four elements. For this is the characteristic of maintaining kamma-born materiality. "With color, odor, taste, etc."—the word "etc." includes nutritive essence. Alternatively, the reading may be "with color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence." "And they establish the base and door accordingly"—establishing their nature as base and door as is appropriate. For the eye-consciousness, it establishes both the state of being a base (as its support) and the state of being a door (as the avenue of arising). But for the receiving consciousness and others, which end with that object, because they depend on something else, it establishes only the state of being a door, not the state of being a base. "With a measure like the head of a louse"—it is marked by a measure comparable to the head of a louse, or the meaning is that it remains in a place of a measure the size of the head of a louse. "It stands"—having pervaded the seven layers of the eye, it remains like oil poured on seven layers of cotton cloth. Thus, by this explanation, the eye’s nature as consisting of multiple material groups is established. For even when the layers are removed due to disturbances, the eye still exists. And just as with the eye, so too the four elements that serve as its basis, along with lifespan, color, etc., should be understood to remain pervading the seven layers of the eye, inseparable in their nature.

656. Vuttanti dhammasenāpatinā vuttaṃ. Rūpāni manupassatīti ma-kāro padasandhikaro “aññamaññaṃ samaṇamacalo”tiādīsu viya. Atha vā manūti maccoti attho. Kiñcāpi cakkhu rūpaṃ na passati, kiñcarahi tannissitaṃ viññāṇameva. Tathā hi “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”tiādīsu viya nissitakiriyaṃ nissaye viya katvā vohārasambhavato “cakkhupasādena passatī”ti vuttaṃ. Ācariyajotipālattherenāpi hi imināva adhippāyena idaṃ vuttaṃ. Idamettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ, kiṃ cakkhu rūpaṃ passati, udāhu viññāṇanti, kiñcettha – yadi cakkhu passeyya, aññaviññāṇasamaṅginopi cakkhu passeyya. Atha viññāṇaṃ, kuṭṭādiantaritampi passeyya tassa appaṭighātattā? Nāyaṃ doso. Yassa “cakkhu passatī”ti mataṃ, tassāpi na sabbaṃ cakkhu passati, atha kho viññāṇādhiṭṭhitameva. Yassa pana viññāṇaṃ passatīti [V 2.0090] mataṃ, tassāpi na sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ [M 2.0121] passati, atha kho cakkhunissitameva, tañca antarite nuppajjati. Yattha ālokassa kuṭṭādīhi vinibandho, yattha pana so natthi phalikaabbhapaṭalādimhi, tattha antaritepi uppajjati eva, tasmā taṃ anuppannattā antaritaṃ na passati. Idameva ca sanniṭṭhānaṃ, yaṃ kho cakkhuviññāṇaṃ passatīti. Tañhi dassanakiccaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti. Tena dvārena karaṇabhūtenāti ayamettha abhisandhi. Atha vā nissitakiriyā nissayassa pavuccati yathā “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti. Ūkāsirasamūpamanti ūkāsirasamānūpamaṃ, ūkāsirappamāṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañcassa patiṭṭhānokāsavasena vuttaṃ, na pana attano pamāṇavasena. Tañhi paramāṇupariyantena pamāṇena atisukhumamevāti. Ūkāsirappamāṇe pana padese idaṃ pavattati. Na kevalañca idameva, sabbānipi sabbaṭṭhānikarūpāni tattha pavattanteva. Idañca tattha nibbattantaṃ taṃ padesaṃ pūretvā eva nibbattati. Ekūnapaṇṇāsakalāpavasena ca saheva pavattati, sattarasacittakkhaṇāyukattā rūpānaṃ, ekekassa ca cittassa tīsu tīsu khaṇesu kammajarūpānaṃ uppajjamānattā.

656. It is stated by the General of the Dhamma. In the phrase "rūpāni manupassati," the letter 'ma' is a conjunction between words, similar to phrases like "aññamaññaṃ samaṇamacalo"; alternatively, 'manu' means a mortal. Although the eye does not see forms, the consciousness dependent on it does. Just as in phrases like "mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī" (the beds are shouting), the action of the supported is attributed to the support for the sake of conventional usage; hence it is said, "one sees by means of eye-sensitivity." The Elder Ācariya Jotipāla also explained this with the same intention. Here is the conclusion: Does the eye see forms, or does consciousness? And what is the issue here? If the eye were to see, then the eye of one endowed with a different consciousness would also see. But if consciousness sees, could it see even through walls and so on, since it is unobstructed? This is not a flaw. For those who hold that "the eye sees," not every eye sees, but only that which is governed by consciousness. For those who hold that "consciousness sees," not all consciousness sees, but only that which is dependent on the eye, and that does not arise when obstructed. Where light is blocked by walls and so on, it does not arise; but where there is no such blockage, as in crystal, cloud, or a film, it arises even when there is an obstruction. Therefore, because it has not arisen, it does not see what is obstructed. And this is the conclusion: it is eye-consciousness that sees. For that is the function of seeing. If so, how is it said, "having seen forms with the eye"? The intention here is: through that door which serves as the instrument. Alternatively, the action of the supported is attributed to the support, as in "mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī." The phrase "ūkāsirasamūpama" means "comparable to a louse's head," that is to say, "the measure of a louse's head." This is stated in terms of its place of establishment, not in terms of its own size. For it is extremely subtle, with a measure down to an atom. However, it operates within the space of a louse's head. Not only this, but all material phenomena of every location are also present there. When it arises there, it arises filling that space completely. It exists together with forty-nine kalāpas, since material phenomena last for seventeen mind-moments, and for each mind, kamma-originated material phenomena arise in each of the three moments.

657. Suṇātīti sotanti ettha kiṃ sotaṃ suṇāti, udāhu viññāṇantiādinā heṭṭhā vuttanayena yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tanutambalomāciteti sasambhārasotabilassa anto sukhumehi tambavaṇṇalomehi sañcite. Aṅgulivedhakasaṇṭhāne padeseti aṅgulimuddikāsaṇṭhānamaṃsayutte padese. Vuttappakārāhīti sandhāraṇādikiccāhi. Āyunā paripāliyamānanti ettha vaṇṇādīhi parivāritanti sambandhitabbaṃ. Tiṭṭhatīti pubbe vuttanayena taṃ padesaṃ pūretvā tiṭṭhati. Sesaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Ghāyatīti gandhopādānaṃ karoti. Sāyatīti rasaṃ vindati. Jīvitamavhāyatīti ettha rasaggahaṇamūlakattā ajjhoharaṇassa jīvitanimittaṃ ajjhoharaṇaraso jīvitaṃ, taṃ [M 2.0122] avhāyati tasmiṃ ninnatāya avhāyantamiva hoti. Uppaladalaggasaṇṭhāne padeseti majjhe chinnassa uppaladalassa aggabhāgasaṇṭhāne padese. Malānanti kilesādimalānañceva malavisayānañca sāsavadhammānaṃ anuttariyabhāvaṃ gacchantesu kāmarāganidānakammajanitesu kāmarāgassa ca visesapaccayesu ghānajivhākāyesu kāyassa visesato sāsavapaccayattā soyeva tesaṃ āyoti vuccati. Tena hi phoṭṭhabbasukhaṃ assādentā sattā methunampi sevanti. Atha vā kāyindriyavatthukā cattāro khandhā balavakāmarāgādihetubhāvato visesato malā, tesamayaṃ āyo hetūti kāyoti vutto. Imasmiṃ kāyeti imasmiṃ sasambhārakāye. Sopi hi kucchitānaṃ kesādimalānaṃ āyabhāvato kāyoti vuccati. Yāvatā upādinnakaṃ atthīti iminā kesagganakhaggādīsu [V 2.0091] kāyapasādassa abhāvamāha. Kappāsapaṭale sneho viyāti imināssa nirantarabhāvaṃ. Ime ca pana cakkhādayo rūpādigocaraninnatāya vammikaudakaākāsagāmasivathikāsaṅkhātagocaraninnatāya ahisuṃsumārapakkhikukkurasigālā viya daṭṭhabbā. Visamajjhāsayatāya hi cakkhu vammikacchiddābhiratasappo viya, bilajjhāsayatāya sotaṃ udakabilābhiratasuṃsumāro viya, ākāsajjhāsayatāya ghānaṃ ajaṭākāsābhiratapakkhi viya, gāmajjhāsayatāya jivhā gāmābhiratakukkuro viya, upādinnakajjhāsayatāya kāyo āmakasusānābhiratasigālo viyāti. Visamajjhāsayatāyāti cakkhussa visamajjhāsayaṃ viya hotīti katvā vuttā. Cakkhumato vā puggalassa ajjhāsayavasena cakkhu visamajjhāsayaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi.

657. "Hears" means the ear—here, does the ear hear, or is it consciousness? The explanation should be connected as appropriate in the manner previously stated. "Filled with fine, tawny hairs" means the interior of the ear canal is filled with very fine, tawny-colored hairs. "Shaped like a finger-ring" refers to a place resembling the shape of a finger-ring, connected with flesh. "Of the aforementioned kinds" refers to functions such as supporting. "Maintained by life" here should be connected as surrounded by color, etc. "Stands" means it remains filling that place as previously described. The rest should be understood in the same way. "Smells" means it takes in odors. "Tastes" means it experiences flavor. "Invokes life" here, because the apprehension of flavor is the basis of swallowing, the flavor of swallowing is the condition for life—it "invokes" that, as if inclining towards it. "Shaped like the tip of a lotus petal" refers to a place resembling the tip of a severed lotus petal in the middle. "Of impurities" refers both to the impurities of defilements and to impure objects, as well as to phenomena connected with cankers. Among the nose, tongue, and body—which are unsurpassed, are special conditions for sensual desire, and are generated by kamma rooted in sensual desire—the body is particularly called their 'source' (āyo) because it is especially a condition for the cankers. Therefore beings experiencing tactile pleasure also engage in sexual intercourse. Alternatively, the four aggregates based on the body faculty are particularly called "impurities" because they are strong causes for sensual desire, etc. Their 'source' (āyo), their cause, is this; hence it is called the "body." "In this body" refers to this composite body. Indeed, it is called the "body" because it is the abode of foul things like hair, etc. "As far as the appropriated exists" indicates the absence of body-sensitivity in things like the tips of hairs, the tips of nails, etc. "Like oil on a cotton cloth" shows its continuous nature. And these, the eye and so on, inclined toward their objects like forms, etc., should be seen as inclined toward their respective domains—like snakes, crocodiles, birds, dogs, and jackals toward anthills, water, the sky, villages, and charnel grounds. For example, due to its crooked disposition, the eye is like a snake delighting in an anthill hole. Due to its disposition for holes, the ear is like a crocodile delighting in a water hole. Due to its disposition for space, the nose is like a bird delighting in the open sky. Due to its disposition for villages, the tongue is like a dog delighting in a village. Due to its disposition for what is appropriated, the body is like a jackal delighting in a fresh charnel ground. "Due to its crooked disposition" is said because the eye is considered to have a crooked disposition. Or, the eye has a crooked disposition in accordance with the disposition of the person who has an eye. The same applies to the rest.

Daṭṭhu…pe… lakkhaṇanti ettha daṭṭhuṃ kāmetīti daṭṭhukāmo tassa bhāvo daṭṭhukāmatā, rūpataṇhāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sā [M 2.0123] pana anāgate cakkhādīsu ādīnavapaṭicchādikāvijjāmūlapatthanāsabhāvā pākaṭā apākaṭāti duvidhā. Tattha yā ayaṃ “īdisaṃ īdisañca sukhumatamavisayaggahaṇasamatthaṃ cakkhu hotū”ti evaṃ kammāyūhanato pubbe, pacchā vā uppannā pākaṭā. Indriyavisesaṃ pana anāmasitvā avisesena paripuṇṇāyatanabhavasampattiṃ patthetvā, apatthetvā vā tattha avigatataṇhāvasena kammaṃ karontassa appahīnabhāvena anusayitā api kammasāmatthiyavicittahetubhūtā apākaṭā. Sā duvidhāpi nidānaṃ upanissayo yassa taṃ daṭṭhukāmatānidānaṃ, tadeva kammaṃ, taṃ samuṭṭhānametesanti daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānāni, evaṃvidhānaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādo daṭṭhukāmatā…pe… pasādo, taṃ lakkhaṇamassa, tathā hutvā lakkhīyatīti vā daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtapasādalakkhaṇaṃ.

To see… and so on… the characteristic: here, one who desires to see is a 'desirer-to-see'; the state of that is 'desire-to-see'—this is a designation for craving for forms. This craving, however, is twofold: evident and non-evident, having the nature of a longing rooted in ignorance that conceals the danger in the future regarding the eye and so forth. Here, what is evident is that which arises either before or after the accumulation of kamma, with the thought, "May I have an eye capable of grasping such and such extremely subtle objects." But what is non-evident is that which, in one who performs kamma by way of unabandoned craving—either longing or not longing, without distinction, for the perfection of an existence with complete sense-bases, without considering the specifics of the faculties—is latent due to not being abandoned, yet is a diverse cause for the efficacy of kamma. That kamma for which both these types of craving are the source and decisive support is 'that which has the desire-to-see as its source.' That very kamma is the origin of these primary elements; thus they are 'originated from kamma that has the desire-to-see as its source.' The sensitivity of primary elements of such a kind—the desire to see… and so on… the sensitivity—is its characteristic. Or, being thus, it is characterized; thus, it has as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements originated from kamma that has the desire-to-see as its source.

Ettha ca gabbhaseyyakānaṃ dinnapaṭisandhikaṃ, aññaṃ vā kammaṃ cakkhādīni nibbatteti. Opapātikānaṃ pana paṭisandhikkhaṇeva paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ nibbattamānānaṃ paṭisandhijanakameva kammaṃ paripuṇṇasakalamattabhāvaṃ nibbattetīti gahetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ pana ekakammunā nibbattamānānaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ visesoti? Kāraṇassa bhinnattā. Taṃtaṃbhavapatthanābhūtā hi taṇhā taṃtaṃbhavapariyāpannāyatanābhilāsatāya sayaṃ vicittarūpā upanissayabhāvena taṃtaṃbhavanibbattakakammassapi vicittabhedataṃ vidahati. Yato tadāhitavisesaṃ tathāvidhasamatthatāyogena anekarūpāpannaṃ viya anekavisiṭṭhasabhāvaṃ phalaṃ nibbatteti, na cettha samatthatāsamatthatāsabhāvato aññā [V 2.0092] veditabbā. Kāraṇavisesena āhitavisesassa visiṭṭhaphalanipphādanasamatthatābhāvato ekasseva kammassa soḷasādivipākanibbattanahetubhāvena ca ayamattho sampaṭicchitabbo. Lokepi ekasseva sālibījassa paripuṇṇāparipuṇṇataṇḍulaphalanibbattihetutā [M 2.0124] dissateva. Kiṃ vā etāya yutticintāya, na cintitabbamevetaṃ. Yato kammaphalaṃ cakkhādīni, kammavipāko ca sabbaso buddhānaṃyeva ñāṇassa visayo, na aññesaṃ atakkāvacarattā. Teneva bhagavatā “kammavipāko acinteyyo, na cintetabbo, yo cinteyya, ummādassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”tiādīnavaṃ (a. ni. 4.77) dassetvā paṭikkhittaṃ.

Here, for those born from a womb, the kamma that gives rebirth-linking, or other kamma, produces the eye and so forth. But for those born spontaneously, at the very moment of rebirth-linking, when they arise with complete sense-bases, it should be understood that only the kamma that generates rebirth produces them in a fully complete and entire existence. How then is there a difference in the eye and so forth produced by a single kamma? It is due to the diversity of conditions. For craving, which is the desire for existence in various realms, by desiring sense-bases pertaining to those realms, itself becomes varied in form. Through its role as a strong supporting condition, it imparts diverse distinctions even to the kamma that generates those existences. Since the kamma, influenced by such distinctions, produces a result of various distinct natures, as if having assumed many forms, through its capacity and connection to bring about such effects, and here, nothing else should be understood apart from the nature of capacity and its absence. Due to the distinction imparted by the diversity of conditions and the capacity to produce distinct results, and due to a single kamma being the cause for producing sixteen or more kinds of resultants, this meaning should be accepted. In the world too, it is seen that a single rice seed becomes the cause for producing fully or partially filled rice grains. Or why engage in such reasoning? This should not be pondered at all. For the results of kamma—the eye and so forth—and the maturation of kamma are entirely within the knowledge of the Buddhas alone, not others, because it is beyond the sphere of reasoning. Therefore, the Blessed One has discouraged such speculation, showing the danger: “The maturation of kamma is inconceivable; it should not be pondered. One who ponders it would partake of madness and distress” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.77).

Rūpesu āviñchanarasanti āviñchanaṃ puggalassa, āvajjanādiviññāṇassa vā tanninnabhāvappattiyā hetubhāvo. Ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānanti nissayapaccayabhāvato. Ālokādisannissayena kadāci uppajjamānānampi hi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppajjanakāle cakkhuṃ nissāya eva uppajjatīti. Etthāha – cakkhuviññāṇuppattisamaye sambhavantesu mandāmandamajjhimāyukesu ekūnapaṇṇāsacakkhūsu katamaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvaṃ paccanubhotīti? Vuccate –

Its function is drawing in with regard to forms, meaning that it is the cause for a person, or for the consciousness of adverting and so forth, to attain the state of being inclined towards them. Its manifestation is as a basis, due to its nature as a support condition. For even when eye-consciousness arises occasionally in dependence on light and other conditions, at the time of arising, it arises dependent only on the eye. Here it is said: At the time of the arising of eye-consciousness, among the forty-nine eyes—those of weak, strong, and moderate lifespan—which one experiences being the basis for eye-consciousness? It is said:—

“Paṭisandhicittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ ṭhānappattaṃ purejātaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya dutiyabhavaṅgaṃ uppajjati, tena saddhiṃ uppannaṃ ṭhānappattaṃ purejātaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya tatiyabhavaṅgaṃ uppajjati, iminā nayena yāvatāyukaṃ cittappavatti veditabbā”ti (visuddhi. 2.700) –

“Dependent on the pre-arisen base that has arisen at the moment of the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness and has reached its standing moment, the second life-continuum consciousness arises. Dependent on the pre-arisen base that has arisen together with that and reached its standing moment, the third life-continuum consciousness arises. In this manner, the continuity of consciousness should be understood as long as life lasts.” (Visuddhimagga 2.700)

Maggāmaggañāṇaniddese vuttanayena ekacittakkhaṇātītaṃ cakkhu rūpe ghaṭṭitvā viññāṇassa nissayo hoti, tasmā dvīsu bhavaṅgacalanesu purimassa anantarapaccayabhūtena bhavaṅgacittena saha uppannanti ayamattho idha sīhaḷasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ, visuddhimaggassa sīhaḷasaṃvaṇṇanāyañca vutto.

As described in the exposition of the knowledge of path and not-path, the eye, having passed one moment of consciousness and having struck a form, becomes the support for consciousness. Therefore, this meaning—that it arises together with the `bhavaṅga`-consciousness which is the immediately preceding condition for the first of the two `bhavaṅga` vibrations—is stated here in the Sinhalese commentary and also in the Sinhalese commentary on the Visuddhimagga.

Taḷākagāmamūlavāsidāṭhānāgattherena pana “āvajjanena, tassa anantarapaccayabhūtena bhavaṅgena vā saha uppannaṃ cakkhu”nti [M 2.0125] vuttaṃ, taṃ duvuttaṃ. Evañhi sati aññasmiṃ ghaṭṭite aññaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa nissayo hotīti vuttaṃ hoti, evañca bhavaṅgacalanato heṭṭhā tatiyacatutthehi yāva terasamacittena saha uppannampi nissayo hotīti āpajjeyya, na cetaṃ vattabbaṃ, tatiyacatutthacittato paṭṭhāya uppannaṃ kesañci vīthicittānaṃ dvārabhāvaṃ na gacchati niruddhattā[V 2.0093], manodvārassa niruddhasseva dvārabhāvassa dassanato. Yadi siyā “paṭisandhicittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya dutiyabhavaṅgaṃ uppajjatī”tiādivacanato “ekacittakkhaṇātītameva nissayoti adhippeta”nti idampi ekacittakkhaṇātītaṃ nissayoti yujjatīti, evaṃ sati “tassa anantarapaccayabhūtena bhavaṅgena vā”ti vacanaṃ yujjeyya, tena hi “cittakkhaṇadvayātītampi nissayo”ti paṭiññātaṃ siyā, tasmā nāyaṃ therassa adhippāyoti dissati. “Ekacittakkhaṇātikkamo”ti ca anatītekacittakkhaṇassa dubbalatāya ekacittakkhaṇātikkamena tassa balavabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuccati, na pana dviticatucittakkhaṇātītānaṃ nissayabhāvābhāvato. Evañca katvā vuttaṃ ācariyadhammapālattherena “sampaṭicchanādīni cutiāsannāni taduddhaṃ kammajarūpassa anuppattito ekasmiṃyeva hadayavatthusmiṃ vattantī”ti, tasmā taṃ therassa manorathamevāti na sārato paccetabbaṃ.

The elder Dāṭhānāga, a resident of Taḷākagāmamūla, however, said, “The eye arises together with adverting, or with the `bhavaṅga` that is its immediately preceding condition.” This is wrongly stated. For if this were so, it would mean that when one thing is struck, another becomes the basis for eye-consciousness. And thus, it would follow that what has arisen together with the third, fourth, up to the thirteenth consciousness before the `bhavaṅga` vibration could also become a basis. But this should not be said, for what has arisen from the third or fourth consciousness-moment onwards does not attain the state of being a door for any of the cognitive process consciousnesses, because it has ceased, as is seen from the mind-door being a door only when it has ceased. If it were said that, based on statements like, “The second `bhavaṅga` arises dependent on the base that arose at the moment of the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness,” the intended meaning is that only what has passed one consciousness-moment is the basis, this would be consistent. If so, the statement “or with the `bhavaṅga` that is its immediately preceding condition” would not be consistent, for then it would be claimed that what has passed two consciousness-moments is also a basis. Therefore, this does not appear to be the elder’s intended meaning. The phrase “the passing of one consciousness-moment” is said to indicate its strength after passing one moment, due to the weakness of what has not yet passed one moment, and not because of the absence of the state of being a basis for those that have passed two, three, or four consciousness-moments. And having considered this, the teacher, the elder Dhammapāla, said, “Receiving and the other processes, being near death, occur in one and the same heart-base, because kamma-born matter does not arise after that.” Therefore, that is merely the elder’s fancy and should not be accepted as substantial.

Sahajātesu bahūsu pasādesu kiṃ eko nissayo hoti, udāhu sabbeyevāti? Nanu vuttaṃ “pubbe ekampi cakkhu viññāṇassa paccayo hotī”ti, katamaṃ pana tanti? Yaṃ tattha visadaṃ hutvā rūpābhighaṭṭanārahaṃ. Visuddhimaggasīhaḷasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ pana “sabbeyeva nissayā hontī”ti vatvā “yadi evaṃ ‘cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa’nti ettha ‘rūpe cā’ti vacanaṃ viya ‘cakkhūnī’tipi bahuvacanaṃ kattabbanti [M 2.0126] anuyogaṃ katvā taṃvisodhanatthaṃ ‘sasambhāracakkhudvayanissitaṃ pasādadvayaṃ nissāya ekameva viññāṇaṃ uppajjatīti gaṇheyyu’nti imaṃ vippaṭipattiṃ nirākarontena bhagavatā bahuvacanamakatvā ‘rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo’tiādīsu (paṭṭhā. 1.1.2) viya sāmaññavasena ekavacanaṃ kata”nti vuttaṃ. Ācariyadhammapālattherena pana tadeva sīhaḷasaṃvaṇṇanāvacanaṃ anicchantena “ekampi cakkhu viññāṇassa paccayo hoti, rūpaṃ pana anekameva paccayabhāvavisesato”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā ceva amhehipi heṭṭhā vibhāvitanti. Yesaṃ bhūtānamayaṃ pasādo, teyeva imassa āsannakāraṇanti vuttaṃ “daṭṭhu…pe… padaṭṭhāna”nti. Sotapasādādīnampi lakkhaṇādiniddese vuttanayānusārena attho yojetabbo.

Among the many co-nascent sensitive faculties, is there one support, or are they all supports? Has it not been said, “Even one eye can be a condition for eye-consciousness”? But what is the principle there? That which is clear and capable of being struck by forms. However, in the Sinhalese commentary on the Visuddhimagga, having said “all are supports,” and then, having raised the objection that if so, in the phrase ‘eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and forms,’ just as ‘forms’ is plural, ‘eyes’ should also be plural, it is stated that to clarify that, the Blessed One, rejecting this misinterpretation (that they might take it as ‘dependent on two sensitive faculties, which are based on the two eyes with their components, only one consciousness arises’), used the singular form in a general sense, as in passages like ‘The form base is a condition for the eye-consciousness-element and its associated states by way of object condition’ (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.2). The teacher, the elder Dhammapāla, however, not accepting that wording of the Sinhalese commentary, stated, “Even one eye can be a condition for consciousness, but forms are many due to the distinction in their conditioning nature.” And this we have also explained below. Those primary elements of which this sensitivity is constituted are its proximate cause; thus it is said: “desire to see… proximate cause.” The meaning should be applied similarly in the description of characteristics and so forth regarding the ear faculty and others, following the method explained.

658. Kecīti mahāsaṅghiyesu ekacce. Cakkhādīsu tejādiadhikatā nāma tannissayabhūtānaṃ tadadhikatāyāti dassento “tejādhikāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha tejādhikānanti pamāṇavasena catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ samānabhāvepi kiccavasena tejodhātuadhikānaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Ākāsa [V 2.0094] …pe… sesakāti ākāsādhikānaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādo sotaṃ, vāyuadhikānaṃ ghānaṃ, toyādhikānaṃ jivhā, phoṭṭhabbasaṅkhātapathavādhikānaṃ kāyoti attho.

658. By “some” is meant some among the Mahāsaṅghikas. Indicating that the predominance of fire and so forth in the eye and so forth means the predominance of those elements in the primary matter that is their support, he said “of those in whom fire predominates,” and so on. Here, “of those in whom fire predominates” refers to those in whom the fire element predominates in terms of function, even though the four elements are in equal proportion in terms of measure. Thus it is for the rest as well. “Space… and so on… the remaining ones” means that the sensitivity of primary elements in which space predominates is the ear; of those in which the air element predominates, the nose; of those in which the water element predominates, the tongue; and of those in which the earth element, which constitutes the tangible, predominates, the body. This is the meaning.

659. Evaṃ pana vadantānaṃ kiṃ uttaranti āha “te panā”tiādi. Suttaṃ āharathāti na tumhākaṃ vacanamatteneva ayamattho sakkā saddhātuṃ, tassa pana paridīpakaṃ suttamāharatha. Sutte hi āhaṭe tassa neyyatthataṃ nītatthataṃ vicāretvā yadi tassa vasena ayamattho paññāyetha[M 2.0127], gaṇheyyāma nanti adhippāyo. Suttameva…pe… kiñcipīti ito cito ca suttaṃ gavesamānāpi addhā ekantena kiñcipi ekagāthāpadamattampi tadatthaparidīpakaṃ suttaṃ na dakkhissanteva tepiṭake buddhavacane tādisasseva suttantassa abhāvato.

659. What is the reply to those who speak thus? He says, 'But then...' and so on. 'Bring forth a sutta'—this matter cannot be believed merely on your word alone; therefore, bring forth a sutta that illuminates it. For when a sutta is brought forth, having investigated whether its meaning is one that requires interpretation or is definitive, if this matter were to be understood on that basis, we would accept it—this is the intention. 'Only the sutta... or anything...'—even searching here and there for a sutta, they will indeed certainly not find even so much as a single verse or phrase of a sutta that illuminates that meaning, because there is no such sutta in the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha.

660. Kiñcāpi suttantavasena ayamattho na dissati, yuttito pana dissatīti ce, tampi natthīti dassento āha “visese satī”tiādi. Bhūtānañhi visese sati pasādo kathaṃ bhave, neva bhaveyya, na ca bhaveyya, kiṃ kāraṇanti āha “samānānañhi bhūtānaṃ, pasādo paridīpito”ti. Yasmā samānānameva bhūtānaṃ pasādo porāṇehi paridīpito, na visamānānaṃ. Pathavīdhātuadhikakalāpassa hi kakkhaḷattā, āpodhātuadhikakalāpassa vissandanato, tejodhātuadhikakalāpassa pariggayhamānattā, vāyodhātuadhikakalāpassa ca vissaraṇato na tesu pasādo patiṭṭhātuṃ sakkoti, tasmā tesaṃ kiccato samānānaṃyeva pasādo uppajjeyya, na visamānānanti.

660. Although this meaning is not seen in the suttas, if it is argued that it is seen through reasoning, to show that this is not so, he said, "If there is a distinction," and so on. For how could sensitive matter arise if there is a distinction among the elements? It could not arise, nor would it arise. What is the reason? He said, "For sensitive matter is explained in relation to elements that are equal." Because sensitive matter has been explained by the ancients only in relation to elements that are equal, not those that are unequal. For because of the hardness of a kalāpa in which the earth element is dominant, the fluidity of a kalāpa in which the water element is dominant, the heat of a kalāpa in which the fire element is dominant, and the mobility of a kalāpa in which the air element is dominant, sensitive matter cannot be established in them. Therefore, sensitive matter would arise only in those that are equal in function, not in those that are unequal.

661-2. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ pasādānaṃ visesatāti āha “tasmā”tiādi. Yasmā vuttappakārena pasādavatthukānaṃ bhūtānaṃ visesena na bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā etesaṃ pasādanissayabhūtānaṃ idamūnaṃ, idamadhikanti etaṃ visesaparikappanaṃ sabbaso sabbākārena pahāya ñeyyā kammavisesena pasādānaṃ visesatā. Yathā avisesepi bhūtānaṃ rūpānaṃ rasādayo aññamaññavisadisā honti, evaṃ cakkhādayopi bhūtavisesābhāvepi aññamaññavisadisā honti. So panāyaṃ visiṭṭhabhāvo kammavisesena viññātabbo. Ekampi hi kammaṃ pañcāyatanikattabhāvapatthanānipphannaṃ cakkhādivisesahetutāya aññamaññassa asādhāraṇavisiṭṭhaṃ [M 2.0128] sāmatthiyavisesato. Na hi yena visesena cakkhussa paccayo, teneva sotassa hoti indriyantarabhāvappattito. “Paṭisandhikkhaṇe mahaggatā cetanā kaṭattārūpānaṃ kammapaccayena paccayo”ti vacanato paṭisandhikkhaṇe vijjamānānaṃ [V 2.0095] sabbesaṃyeva kaṭattārūpānaṃ ekā cetanā kammapaccayo hotīti viññāyati. Nānācetanāya hi tadā indriyuppattiyaṃ sati parittena ca mahaggatena ca kammena kaṭattārūpaṃ āpajjeyya, na cekā paṭisandhi anekakammanibbattā hotīti siddhamekena kammena anekindriyuppatti hotīti. “Na hi bhūtavisesena, hoti tesaṃ visesatā”ti idaṃ nigamanavasena vuttaṃ.

If this is so, how then is there a distinction among the sensitive faculties? It is said, "Therefore," etc. Because, in the manner stated, there should be no distinction among the elements that are the basis of the sensitive faculties, therefore, abandoning entirely and in every way this notion of distinction—such as "this is less, this is more"—among these elements that are the support of the sensitive faculties, the distinction among the sensitive faculties should be understood as arising from the diversity of kamma. Just as, even without any distinction among the material elements, flavors and so forth differ from one another, so too, even in the absence of any distinction among the material elements, the eye and other faculties differ from one another. However, this distinctive nature should be understood as due to the diversity of kamma. For even a single kamma, produced by the aspiration for the state of having five sense bases, becomes the cause of distinct faculties like the eye, etc., due to its unique capacity, making them uniquely distinct from one another. Indeed, the condition that serves as a cause for the eye does not serve as a cause for the ear, because they have attained the state of different faculties. From the statement, "At the moment of rebirth-linking, the developed volition is a condition for the kamma-originated material phenomena by way of kamma-condition," it is understood that at the moment of rebirth-linking, a single volition serves as the kamma-condition for all kamma-originated material phenomena. For if the faculties were to arise at that time from various volitions, kamma-originated matter would be produced by kamma that is both minor and developed; and a single rebirth-linking is not produced by multiple kammas. Thus, it is established that the arising of multiple faculties is by a single kamma. The statement, "It is not due to any distinction among the material elements that their distinction exists," is made by way of conclusion.

663. Evaṃ kammavisesato visiṭṭhesu ca etesu ārammaṇaggahaṇepi ayaṃ visesoti dassetuṃ “evametesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Appattagāhakanti asampattaggāhakaṃ attano nissayena saha anallīyananissaye eva rūpādivisaye viññāṇuppattihetubhāvato. Keci pana tampi “sampattaggāhakamevā”ti vadanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ sāntare adhike ca visaye viññāṇuppattihetubhāvato. Yadi hi cakkhusotāni sampattavisayameva gaṇhanti, cakkhupasādato vicchinnadese ṭhitesu tārakādīsu nissayavasena ca pamāṇato adhikesu candamaṇḍalādīsu rūpāyatanesu sotapasādato ca vicchinnadesasambhūtesu udaracammasandhicammādiantaritesu kucchisaddasandhisaddādīsu puthulesu ca samuddasaddādīsu saddāyatanesu viññāṇuppatti na siyā sampattaggāhakānaṃ kāyindriyādīnaṃ tathā adassanato.

663. Thus, to show that in these faculties, which are distinct due to the diversity of kamma, there is also this distinction in the apprehension of objects, it is said, 'Thus, in these...' and so on. 'Apprehending without contact' means grasping what is not arrived at, because it is a cause for the arising of consciousness with regard to an object, such as form, that does not adhere to its own support. Some, however, say that even that is "only apprehending by contact," but this is not well-founded, because it is a cause for the arising of consciousness in objects that are distant and large. For if the eye and ear were to grasp only what is in contact, then consciousness would not arise in the following cases: in relation to sense-objects of form like stars, which are situated in places disconnected from the eye's sensitive matter, or like the moon’s disk, which are large in measure in relation to the support; or in relation to sense-objects of sound like those in the belly or at the joints, which arise from disconnected places and are obstructed by things like the skin of the belly or the skin of the joints, or gross sounds like the sound of the ocean—since the body faculty and so on, which apprehend by contact, are not seen to perceive them in that way.

Ettha ca vadeyya – adhiṭṭhānato bahindriyassa pavatti hotīti sampattavisayameva yattakaṃ visayaṃ, tattakaṃ visayaṃ gahaṇākāraṃ pharitvā gaṇhāti, tasmā asiddhametaṃ “sāntare [M 2.0129] adhike ca visaye viññāṇuppattihetubhāvato”ti? Taṃ na, adhiṭṭhānato bahi indriyuppattiyā eva abhāvā. Adhiṭṭhānadese eva hi indriyaṃ pavattati tattha kiccādippayogadassanato. Sati ca etassa bahi pavattiyaṃ adhiṭṭhāne pihitepi visayaggahaṇaṃ siyā, tasmā adhiṭṭhānadese ṭhitānaṃyeva cakkhusotānaṃ asampattavisayasseva gahaṇato nāsiddhametaṃ “sāntare adhike ca viññāṇuppattihetubhāvato”ti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Here, one might say: “Because the faculty operates externally from its base, it grasps only the object that is in contact, encompassing that much of the object by pervading the mode of apprehension. Therefore, is it not unproven that it is ‘a cause for the arising of consciousness in a distant or large object’?” That is not so, because there is no arising of the faculty outside its base. For the faculty operates only in the location of its base, since its function and other applications are seen there. And if it operated externally, there could be apprehension of the object even if the location of its base were covered. Therefore, since the eye and ear, remaining in the location of their base, apprehend only an object not in contact, it is not unproven that it is "a cause for the arising of consciousness in a distant or large object." Hence, the ancients said—

“Sabbagocarayogepi, diṭṭhaṃ rūparavesu yaṃ;

Vicchinnaputhuviññāṇaṃ, sampattaggāhabādhaka”nti.

"Even when there is conjunction with all sense-objects, that which is seen in forms and sounds—consciousness of a separated and extensive object—is an obstruction to apprehension by contact."

Tassattho – sabbesaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ gocarena rūpādinā yoge ekakāriyasādhakattā sambandhe ghaṭṭane [V 2.0096] vā samāne sati rūparavesu rūpasaddāyatanesu visayabhūtesu cakkhādito dūrabhāvena ceva kenaci anantaritabhāvena ca vicchinnesu pamāṇato puthulesu ca visayesu uppajjamānaṃ yaṃ viññāṇaṃ, taṃ cakkhusotānaṃ sampattaggāhassa sampattaggahaṇassa bādhakanti.

The meaning of this is: when there is a conjunction—that is, a connection or collision—of all the faculties, such as the eye, with their objects, such as form, which accomplishes a single function, then the consciousness that arises in relation to objects that are the sense bases of form and sound—objects which are distant from the eye and so on, not obstructed by anything, separated, and extensive in measure—that consciousness is an obstruction to the apprehension by contact of the eye and ear.

Apica yadi cakkhu sampattaggāhakaṃ siyā, attano maṇḍale ṭhitaṃ vaṇṇampi passeyya. Tathā akkhipuṭe añjanaṃ pakhumamūle akkhivaṇṇaṃ pakhumamūle ghaṭṭiyamānaṃ añjanasalākampi passeyya, na ca panetaṃ dissati, tasmā tannissaye dese ṭhitameva visayaṃ gaṇhāti. Sotāyatanampi yadi sampattaggāhakaṃ abhavissa, cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ saddāyatanaṃ sotaviññāṇassa kadācipi ārammaṇapaccayo na siyā. Na hi bahiddhā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ uppatti atthi. Paṭṭhāne ca “saddāyatanaṃ sotaviññāṇadhātuyā ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.2) aviseseneva saddassa sotaviññāṇārammaṇabhāvo vutto[M 2.0130]. Kiñca yadi sotaṃ sampattaggāhakaṃ siyā, attano visayapadeseyeva gahetabbato gandhassa viya saddassāpi disādesavavatthānaṃ na siyā. Evañca saddānusārena kaṇḍaṃ pātentassa saddavedhino attano kaṇṇabileyeva sarapātanaṃ siyā, tasmā yattha uppanno saddo, tattheva ṭhito sotapathe āpāthamāgacchati.

Moreover, if the eye were to apprehend by contact, it would see the color within its own sphere. Similarly, it would see the collyrium on the eyelid, the color of the eye at the root of the eyelashes, and the collyrium stick striking the root of the eyelashes—but this is not seen. Therefore, it grasps the object while itself remaining situated in the place of its support. Likewise, if the ear were to apprehend by contact, the mind-originated sound base would never serve as an object condition for ear-consciousness. For mind-originated sounds do not arise externally. Yet, in the Paṭṭhāna, it is stated without distinction: "The sound base is a condition for the ear-consciousness element by way of object condition" (Paṭṭh. 1.1.2), which means that sound serves as an object for ear-consciousness. Moreover, if the ear were to apprehend by contact, then, like smell, there would be no determination of direction or location for sound, since it would have to be grasped only within its own location. Consequently, for one shooting an arrow guided by sound, the arrow would fall only into his own ear cavity. Therefore, sound, having arisen where it is, reaches the auditory path while remaining there.

Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ dūre ṭhitehi rajakādisaddā cirena suyyanti. Asampattaggāhakatte hi dūrāsannadesavattīnaṃ samakameva savanena bhavitabbanti? Nayidamevaṃ dūrāsannānaṃ yathāpākaṭe sadde gahaṇavisesato. Yathā hi dūrāsannānaṃ vacanasadde yathāpākaṭeva gahaṇavisesato akkharavisesanaṃ gahaṇaṃ, aggahaṇañca hoti, evaṃ rajakādisaddepi āsannassa ādito pabhuti yāva avasānā kamena pākaṭībhūte, dūrassa ca avasāne, majjhe vā piṇḍavasena pavattipākaṭībhūte yathāpākaṭaṃ nicchayaggāhakānaṃ sotaviññāṇavīthiyā parato pavattānaṃ manodvārikajavanānaṃ gahaṇavisesato lahukaṃ suto, cirena sutoti abhimāno hoti. Sotaviññāṇappavatti pana ubhayattha samānā saddassa uppannadese ṭhitassa attano vijjamānakkhaṇeyeva sotāpāthagamanato. Yadi saddassa bhūtaparamparāya samantato pavatti natthi, kathaṃ paṭighosuppattīti? Dūre ṭhitopi saddo aññattha paṭighosuppattiyā, bhājanādicalanassa ca paccayo hoti ayokanto viya ayocalanassāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

If that is so, how is it that the sounds of washermen and others, though distant, are heard after a long time? For if it is non-contact-apprehending, should there not be an identical hearing for those in distant and nearby places? This is not the case, because of the distinction in the apprehension of sound as it appears to those distant and near. Just as with the spoken words of those distant and near, there is a distinction in apprehension as it appears—the distinction of syllables is grasped, or it is not grasped—so too with the sounds of washermen and others. For one who is nearby, the sound gradually becomes clear from the beginning until the end. But for one who is far away, it becomes clear at the end, or in the middle, occurring as a conglomerate. Due to the distinction in apprehension by the mind-door impulsions that occur after the ear-consciousness process, which apprehend with certainty as it appears, the notion arises 'heard quickly' or 'heard after a long time'. However, the arising of ear-consciousness is the same in both cases, since the sound, remaining in the place where it arose, reaches the auditory path at the very moment of its existence. If sound does not propagate in all directions through a succession of elements, how does reverberation arise? It should be understood that even a sound from afar can be a condition for the arising of reverberation elsewhere, and for the movement of a container or something else, just as a magnet is for the movement of iron.

Sesaṃ…pe… gāhakanti yaṃ pana avasesaṃ ghānajivhākāyasaṅkhātaṃ pasādattayaṃ, taṃ sampattaggāhakaṃ [V 2.0097] hoti nissayavasena ceva sayañca attano nissaye allīneyeva visaye viññāṇuppattihetubhāvato.
