Gandharasānaṃ nissayesu ghānajivhānissayehi saha allīnāyeva gandharasā viññāyanti[M 2.0131]. Phoṭṭhabbañca bhūtattayarūpaṃ kāyanissayena allīnameva viññāyatīti.

The remainder… the apprehending faculty is that which remains, namely the triad of sensitive matter known as the nose, tongue, and body. It is contact-apprehending, both by way of support and because it itself, clinging to its own support, is the cause for the arising of consciousness in an object that is in contact. Scents and tastes are cognized only when they are in contact with their supports, the sensitive matter of the nose and tongue. And the tangible, which is the triad of primary elements, is cognized only when it is in contact with the bodily support.

Vaṇṇavikāramāpajjamānanti dosādīhi kāraṇehi amanāpavaṇṇassa uppattivasena vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ. Hadayaṅgatabhāvanti cittagataṃ ajjhāsayaṃ. Pakāsetīti rūpamiva pakāsaṃ karoti, saviggahamiva dassetīti attho. Anekatthattā hi dhātūnaṃ pakāsanattho eva rūpa-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Taṃ pana rūpanti sambandho. Cakkhumhi, cakkhussa vā paṭihananaṃ lakkhaṇametassāti cakkhupaṭihananalakkhaṇaṃ. Evaṃ sotapaṭihananalakkhaṇantiādīsupi. Paṭihananañcettha visayavisayīnaṃ aññamaññābhimukhabhāvo yogyadesāvaṭṭhānaṃ paṭighāto viyāti katvā. Yathā paṭighāte sati dubbalassa calanaṃ hoti, evaṃ visayābhimukhabhāve sati visayino taṃsambandhassa ca vatthurūpassa, tannissitassa ca bhavaṅgassa calanaṃ hoti. So rūpassa cakkhumhi, cakkhussa vā rūpe hoti. Tenāha “yamhi cakkhumhi anidassanamhi sappaṭighamhi rūpaṃ sanidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ paṭihaññi vā, yaṃ cakkhu anidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ rūpamhi sanidassanamhi sappaṭighamhi paṭihaññi vā”ti (dha. sa. 597) ca ādi. Visayabhāvo ārammaṇapaccayatā. Gocarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānanti ettha anaññathābhāvo visayatā, tabbahulatā gocarabhāvoti ayaṃ visayagocarānaṃ viseso. Saddāyatīti udāharīyati, sakehi vā paccayehi sotaviññeyyabhāvaṃ upanīyatīti attho. Attānaṃ gandhayatīti sugandhaṃ, duggandhanti vā attānaṃ pakāseti. Tenāha “sūcayatī”ti.

"Undergoing a change in appearance" means undergoing a change in appearance due to causes like defects, by way of the arising of an unpleasant appearance. "The state of having gone to the heart" means the disposition gone to the mind. "It makes clear" means it makes clear like a form, it shows distinctly; this is the meaning. Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word "rūpa" should be understood here as having the meaning of "making clear." The connection is "that form." Its characteristic is striking against the eye, or of the eye against it; hence it has the characteristic of striking against the eye. Similarly in the cases of "having the characteristic of striking against the ear," and so on. Here, "striking" is to be taken as the mutual facing of object and subject, their being situated in a suitable place, like a collision. Just as when there is a collision, the weaker one moves, so too when there is a facing of the object, there is a disturbance of the subject, of the material basis connected with it, and of the life-continuum dependent on it. That occurs of the form in the eye, or of the eye in the form. Hence it is said: "Wherein the invisible, resistant form strikes against the visible, resistant eye, or the invisible, resistant eye strikes against the visible, resistant form" (Dhs. 597), and so on. "The state of being an object" is the condition of being an objective support. In "being present as a sphere," "objectness" is its unchanging nature, while "the state of being a sphere" is its predominance; this is the distinction between object and sphere. "It sounds" means it is uttered, or it is brought to a state of being cognizable by ear-consciousness through its own conditions; this is the meaning. "It makes itself smelled" means it reveals itself as fragrant or foul-smelling. Hence it is said: "It indicates."

664. Itthiyā eva indriyaṃ itthindriyaṃ. Yathā cakkhādīni indriyāni purisassapi honti, nayidaṃ tathā. Idaṃ pana niyamena itthiyā eva hoti, tasmā “itthindriya”nti vuccati. Evaṃ purisindriyepi. Itthiyā bhāvo, itthīti bhavati etena cittaṃ[M 2.0132], abhidhānaṃ vāti itthibhāvo. Paṭisandhisamuṭṭhitoti paṭisandhiyaṃyeva samuṭṭhito, paṭisandhicittena saha ekakkhaṇe samuṭṭhito. Etena ṭhapetvā liṅgaparivattanaṃ cakkhundriyādīni viya imassa apātubhāvamāha. Yañcetaṃ itthiliṅgādīti yaṃ panetaṃ indriyaphalabhūtaṃ itthiliṅgādi. Ādi-ggahaṇena itthinimittaitthikuttaitthākappānaṃ saṅgaho. Tattha visadaavisadahatthapādāditā saṇṭhānaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ. Itthīnañhi hatthapādagīvāuraādisaṇṭhānaṃ na purisānaṃ viya hoti. Tathā hi [V 2.0098] tāsaṃ heṭṭhimakāyo visado, uparimakāyo avisado, hatthapādā khuddakā, mukhaṃ khuddakaṃ, thanamaṃsā avisadā, tā nimmassudāṭhikā. Kesabandhavatthaggahaṇañca itthinimittaṃ. Daharakālepi suppakamusalakādīhi kīḷā makacivākena suttakantananti ca evamādi itthikuttaṃ, itthikiriyāti attho. Avisadaṭṭhānagamanādiākāro itthākappo. Purisampi hi avisadaṃ disvā mātugāmo viya tiṭṭhati nipajjati nisīdati khādati bhuñjatīti vadanti. Idaṃ pana itthiliṅgādiparidīpanaṃ akusalanti vatvā aññathāpi vaṇṇenti ācariyā. Kathaṃ? Yonipadeso itthiliṅgaṃ, sarādhippāyā itthinimittaṃ, avisadaṭṭhānagamanādayo itthikuttaṃ, itthisaṇṭhānaṃ itthākappoti. Ettha ca adhippāyo nāma purisasmiṃ methunataṇhā. Sā hi tāsaṃ niccaṃ balavatarā pavattati, ato sāpi itthīti sañjānanassa nimittatāya “itthinimitta”nti vuccati. Kiñcāpi itthīti saññāṇassa nimittatāya kuttākappānampi nimitteyeva antogadhatā, tathāpi tesaṃ visuṃ gahaṇato sarādhippāyā eva nimittabhāvena adhippetā.

664. The faculty of a woman alone is the female faculty. Just as the faculties like the eye exist in a man as well, this is not so. This, however, belongs exclusively to a woman; therefore, it is called the "female faculty." The same applies to the male faculty. The state of being a woman, or the mind's becoming "woman" by means of this, or the designation "woman"—this is the female nature. "Originating at rebirth-linking" means it originates at the moment of rebirth-linking itself, arising in a single moment together with the rebirth-linking consciousness. By this, it is stated that, apart from a change of sex, this faculty does not appear, unlike the eye faculty and others. "And this female characteristic, etc." refers to the female characteristic, etc., which is the result of the faculty. The term "etc." includes the female mark, female behavior, and female deportment. Among these, the shape, being the distinctness and indistinctness of the hands, feet, etc., is the female characteristic. For women, the shape of their hands, feet, neck, chest, etc., is not like that of men. Specifically, their lower body is distinct, their upper body is indistinct, their hands and feet are small, their face is small, their breasts are indistinct, and they are without beards and large teeth. The tying of hair and the wearing of clothes are the female mark. Even in childhood, playing with winnowing baskets, toy mortars, etc., and spinning thread with a monkey's jawbone, and so on, is female behavior—meaning, female action. The manner of going to indistinct places, etc., is female deportment. Indeed, they say that even a man, when seen indistinctly, stands, lies down, sits, eats, and drinks like a woman. Having said that this explanation of female characteristics, etc., is unwholesome, the teachers also describe it differently. How? The genital region is the female characteristic; the voice and intention are the female mark; going to indistinct places, etc., is female behavior; the female form is female deportment. Here, "intention" refers to sexual desire for a man. For women, this desire is always stronger; therefore, because it is a mark for recognizing one as a woman, it is called the "female mark." Although female behavior and deportment are also included within the mark for recognizing one as a woman, nevertheless, because they are taken separately, only the voice and intention are intended as the mark.

665. Kiṃ panetaṃ itthiliṅgādi itthindriyaṃ viya paṭisandhisamuṭṭhitaṃ hotīti āha “itthindriyaṃ paṭiccevā”tiādi. Kiñcāpi hi itthiliṅgādīni yathāsakaṃ kammādinā paccayena samuṭṭhahanti[M 2.0133], yebhuyyena pana itthindriyasahiteyeva santāne taṃtadākārā hutvā sambhavanti, itarattha ca na bhavantīti tesaṃ tabbhāvabhāvitaṃ upādāya “itthindriyaṃ paṭicceva jāyantī”ti vuttāni. Evañca katvā vakkhati “itthi…pe… kāraṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāna”nti. Īdiseneva kāraṇabhāvasaṅkhātena adhipatibhāvena tassa indriyatā vuttā indriyasahite santāne itthiliṅgādiākārarūpapaccayānaṃ aññathā anuppādanato, na pana indriyādipaccayasambhavato. Tathā hetaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ viya ekakalāpagatānaṃ āhāro viya kalāpantararūpānaṃ upatthambhakamanupālakaṃ vā na hoti. Evañca katvā jīvitindriyaāhārānaṃ viya imassa indriyapaccayatā, atthiavigatapaccayatā ca pāḷiyaṃ na vuttā. Yasmā paccayantarādhīnāni itthiliṅgādīni, tasmā yatthassa ādhipaccaṃ, taṃsadisesu matacittakatarūpesupi taṃsaṇṭhānatā dissati. Yasmā panete itthindriyaṃ paṭicca jāyantāpi gabbhaseyyakānaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ na samuṭṭhahanti, pavatteyeva samuṭṭhahanti, tasmā āha “pavatte…pe… paṭisandhiya”nti.

665. But does this, the female characteristic and so on, arise at rebirth-linking like the female faculty? To this, it is said: 'Dependent on the female faculty,' and so on. For although female characteristics and so forth arise due to their respective causes such as kamma, they mostly appear in a continuum endowed with the female faculty, taking on those particular forms, and do not arise otherwise. Therefore, taking into account their being conditioned by that state, it is said that they arise 'dependent on the female faculty.' And thus it will be said: 'A female... has the state of being a cause as its manifestation.' It is precisely through such a state of dominance, designated as the state of being a cause, that its status as a faculty is stated—because the conditions for material phenomena in the form of female characteristics, etc., cannot otherwise arise in a continuum endowed with the faculty, and not because they arise from the faculty itself as a condition. Thus, this is not like the life faculty, which supports or maintains material phenomena belonging to a single cluster, nor like nutriment, which supports or maintains material phenomena in other clusters. And for this reason, its conditionality as a faculty, and its conditionality as presence and non-disappearance, like that of the life faculty and nutriment, are not stated in the Pāḷi. Because female characteristics, etc., are dependent on other conditions, wherever its dominance is present, that same configuration is seen even in matter in a dead body and in mind-produced matter. However, because these, though arising dependent on the female faculty, do not arise at rebirth-linking for those conceived in a womb but arise only during the course of existence, it is said: 'During the course... not at rebirth-linking.'

666-7. Saṃsedajaopapātikānaṃ pana kiñci itthindriyena saha paṭisandhiyameva nibbattati. Na cāti ca-kāro vacanīyantarasamuccaye. “Kiñcā”ti imassa atthe daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā [V 2.0099] liṅgādiākāresu rūpesu rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññeyyaṃ, tasmā āha “itthiliṅgādayo cakkhuviññeyyā hontī”ti. Yasmā pana tato aññāni yathāyogaṃ sotaviññeyyāni ceva manoviññeyyāni ca, tasmā vuttaṃ “na vā”ti. Yathāvutto papañco purisindriyepi yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabboti atidesaṃ karonto āha “esevā”tiādi. Sesepīti ettakeyeva vutte ito sesesu sabbesupīti kadāci koci cinteyyāti āha “purisindriye”ti[M 2.0134]. Paṭhamakappānanti paṭhamakappikanarānaṃ. Tesañhi ābhassaralokato cavitvā idhūpapannānaṃ dīghassa kālassa accayena oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āharataṃ muttakarīsesu sañjātesu tesaṃ nikkhamanatthāya vaṇamukhāni bhijjanti, purisassa purisabhāvo, itthiyā ca itthibhāvo pāturahosi. Tathā hi purimattabhāvesu pavattaupacārajhānānubhāvena yāva sattasantāne kāmarāgavikkhambhanavego na paṭipassambhati, na tāva balavakāmarāgūpanissayāni itthipurisindriyāni pāturahesuṃ. Yadā panassa vicchinnatāya balavakāmarāgo laddhāvasaro ahosi, tadā tadūpanissayāni tāni sattānaṃ santāne sañjāyanti.

However, for moisture-born and spontaneously-born beings, some are produced with the female faculty at rebirth-linking itself. The particle 'ca' in 'na ca' is for the inclusion of another statement; it should be understood here in the sense of 'although.' Because among material forms such as gender characteristics, the visible form is cognizable by the eye, it is said, 'female characteristics, etc., are cognizable by the eye.' However, since other forms are, as appropriate, cognizable by the ear and cognizable by the mind, it is stated, 'or not.' Making an application by extension to show that the aforesaid detailed explanation should be applied to the male faculty as well, as is suitable, he says, 'this very,' and so on. Lest someone might think, when only 'in the remaining' is said, that this applies to all the rest, he says, 'in the male faculty.' 'Of the first aeon' means of the people of the first aeon. For those who, having passed away from the Ābhassara world and arisen here, after a long time had passed and they were consuming coarse food, urine and feces were produced. For their exit, openings like wounds broke open, and the male state appeared for the male, and the female state appeared for the female. Indeed, by the power of access concentration that had occurred in previous existences, as long as the impetus of the suppression of sensual desire did not subside in a being's continuum, the female and male faculties, which have strong sensual desire as their support, did not appear. But when, due to the cutting off of that suppression, strong sensual desire found its opportunity, then those faculties, having that as their support, arose in the continuum of beings.

668. Paratoti paṭhamakappato aparabhāge. Pavatte…pe… parivattatīti yathā taṃ soreyyakaseṭṭhiputtassa viyāti adhippāyo. Api-saddena paṭhamapārājikāyaṃ vinītavatthupāḷiyaṃ āgatabhikkhussa, bhikkhuniyā viya ca paṭisandhiyaṃ samuṭṭhitassapi pavatte parivattanaṃ dīpeti. Yathāha –

668. 'Later' means in the period after the first aeon. 'During the course... it changes' means that it changes during the course of existence, as in the case of Soreyya, the merchant's son. With the word 'api,' he indicates the change during the course of existence even for one for whom the faculty arose at rebirth-linking, such as the monk who appears in the Pāḷi of the stories on what is decided in the first Pārājika, and likewise for the bhikkhunī. As it is said:

“Tena kho pana samayena aññatarassa bhikkhuno itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhūtaṃ hoti. Tena kho pana samayena aññatarissā bhikkhuniyā purisaliṅgaṃ pātubhūtaṃ hotī”ti (pārā. 69).

"Now at that time, the female characteristic had appeared in a certain monk. Now at that time, the male characteristic had appeared in a certain nun."

Yassa pana paṭisandhiyaṃ dvīsu ekampi na samuṭṭhitaṃ, so abhāvako nāma, tassa pavattiyampi indriyuppatti na hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

But for one for whom not even one of the two faculties has arisen at rebirth-linking, they are called 'one without the faculties,' and it should be understood that for such a one, the arising of a faculty does not occur even during the course of existence.

669. Kiṃ panetassa ubhayassapi nibbattiyā, vināsanassa ca kāraṇaṃ, yato idaṃ samuṭṭhāti, parivattatīti ca vuccatīti imaṃ anuyogaṃ manasi katvā āha “mahatā pāpakammenā”tiādi. Tattha mahatāti paradārikakammādinā mahābalena. Pāpakammena [M 2.0135] upanissayabhūtena[V 2.0100]. Mahatā kusalenevāti idaṃ sugatiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Duggatiyaṃ pana ubhayampi akusalakammeneva jāyati.

669. What then is the cause for both its arising and its destruction, on account of which it is said to 'originate' and 'transform'? Having kept this question in mind, he said: “By a great unwholesome kamma,” and so on. Here, “great” means powerful, as in the kamma of adultery and so on. “By unwholesome kamma” means that which serves as a supporting condition. “By great wholesome kamma indeed”—this is said with reference to a happy destination. In an unhappy destination, however, both arise solely from unwholesome kamma.

670. Indriye vinaṭṭhe ekanteneva liṅgampi vinassatevāti āha “itthiliṅgaṃ vinassatī”ti. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo daṭṭhabbo – imesu dvīsu purisindriyaṃ uttamaṃ, itthindriyaṃ hīnaṃ, purisindriyassa antaradhānaṃ mahantena akusalena kammena hoti, samuṭṭhānaṃ mahantena kusalakammena, itthindriyassa antaradhānaṃ dubbalākusalena, samuṭṭhānampi dubbalakusalena, duggatiyaṃ pana ubhayassāpi antaradhānaṃ, samuṭṭhānañca akusaleneva hotīti. Yadi sugatiyaṃ itthindriyampi kusaleneva nibbattati, kathañcarahi “paradārikakammaṃ katvā niraye paccitvā teneva pāpakammena pañcasatakkhattuṃ manussaloke itthī hutvā nibbattatī”tiādivacananti? Nāyaṃ virodho nissandaphalavasena vuttattā. Tathā hi paṭisandhiyaṃ tāva purisindriyanibbattanārahampi kammaṃ kadāci paradārikādinā balavapāpakammena paṭibāhitasāmatthiyaṃ assa, tadā attano purisindriyanibbattane asamatthatāya itthindriyameva nibbatteti. Pavattiyaṃ pana attano balavabhāvena itthindriyūpanissayaṃ paradārikamakusalakammaṃ paṭibāhitvā paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya purisindriyaṃ samuṭṭhāpentaṃ kadāci laddhasāmaggitāsañjātabalavisesena paradārikādinā kammena paṭibāhitasāmatthiyaṃ bhaveyya, tadā attano dubbalatāya purisindriyaṃ na nibbatteti[M 2.0136], itthindriyameva nibbatteti. Evaṃ paradārikādikammūpanissayena itthindriyassa nibbattanato taṃ tena nibbattitaṃ katvā vuccati.

670. When the faculty is destroyed, the characteristic is also entirely destroyed; hence it is said, 'the female characteristic is destroyed.' Here, the following meaning should be understood: among these two, the male faculty is superior, and the female faculty is inferior. The disappearance of the male faculty occurs due to a great unwholesome kamma, while its arising is due to a great wholesome kamma. The disappearance of the female faculty occurs due to a weak unwholesome kamma, and its arising also due to a weak wholesome kamma. In an unhappy destination, however, the disappearance and arising of both occur only through unwholesome kamma. If in a happy destination the female faculty also arises only through wholesome kamma, how then can there be statements such as, 'Having committed adultery, after being tormented in hell, due to that very evil kamma, one is reborn as a woman in the human world for five hundred existences'? There is no contradiction here, because this is stated by way of an outflowing result. For instance, at rebirth-linking, a kamma that is capable of producing the male faculty may sometimes have its capacity obstructed by a powerful unwholesome kamma such as adultery. Then, being unable to produce the male faculty, it produces only the female faculty. During the course of existence, however, a kamma that produces the male faculty from rebirth-linking onwards—having by its own power obstructed the unwholesome kamma of adultery which is a support for the female faculty—might sometimes have its own capacity obstructed by kamma such as adultery that has gained special strength due to a confluence of conditions. Then, due to its own weakness, it does not produce the male faculty, but produces only the female faculty. Thus, because the female faculty arises with kamma such as adultery as its supporting condition, it is said to be produced by that.

671-2. Yadā pana taṃ kammaṃ puna sāmaggipaṭilābhato, parikkhīṇapāpakammatāya vā balavappattaṃ abhavissa, tadā dinnavedhaṃ viya rukkhaṃ tadapagame attano balānurūpaṃ purisindriyaṃ nibbatteti, itthindriyaṃ pana attano kāraṇābhāvato nuppajjati. Ubhayassa pana nibbattiyampi visadisindriyanibbattanato pure sattarasamacittassa ṭhitikālamupādāya taṃtaṃsamuṭṭhāpakakammaṃ taṃ taṃ indriyaṃ na janeti. Sattarasamacittena saha uppannaṃ visadisindriyuppattito purimacittena saha nirujjhati. Yadi hi sattarasamacittuppādato parampi uppajjeyya, itaraṃ nuppajjati ekasmiṃ santāne dvinnaṃ sahuppattiyā anicchitattā. Teneva hi “yassa vā pana purisindriyaṃ uppajjati, tassa itthindriyaṃ uppajjatī”ti (yama. 3.indriyayamaka.188) imasmiṃ pañhe “no”ti (yama. 3.indriyayamaka.188) paṭikkhepo katoti. Evañca katvā vakkhati “ubhatobyañjanassāpī”tiādi[V 2.0101]. Ekasmiñca niruddhe tappaṭibaddhāni liṅgādīni katipayadivasehi nirujjhanti, tesu niruddhesu itarāni anukkamena jāyantīti ācariyā. Itthinimittuppādakakammato, purisanimittuppādakakammato vāti ubhato duvidhaṃ byañjanamassāti ubhatobyañjano. Tassāpīti yassa duvidhaṃ byañjanamatthi, tassāpi ekameva indriyaṃ siyā, kiṃ pana itarassāti dasseti.

But when that same kamma, either due to regaining favorable conditions or the exhaustion of unwholesome kamma, becomes strong, then—like a tree that has been pierced—it produces the male faculty in accordance with its own power upon the departure of that obstructing kamma, while the female faculty does not arise due to the absence of its own cause. However, even in the arising of both faculties, because of the arising of a dissimilar faculty, the kamma that generates each faculty does not produce that faculty, starting from the duration of the seventeen mind-moments prior to the arising of the dissimilar faculty. That previous faculty, having arisen together with the seventeenth mind-moment, ceases together with the mind-moment immediately preceding the arising of the dissimilar faculty. For if it were to arise even after the seventeenth mind-moment, the other faculty would not arise, since the simultaneous arising of two dissimilar faculties in a single continuum is not accepted. This is why, to the question, “When the male faculty arises, does the female faculty also arise?” (Yam. 3. Indriyayamaka. 188), the rejection “No” (Yam. 3. Indriyayamaka. 188) is given. And having established this, it will be said: “For one with both sets of characteristics as well…” and so on. Moreover, when one faculty ceases, the associated physical characteristics also cease within a few days, and when those have ceased, the other characteristics gradually arise—so say the teachers. One with both sets of characteristics (ubhatobyañjana) is one who has two kinds of characteristics, either from kamma producing female characteristics or from kamma producing male characteristics. “Of that one as well…” shows that even for one who has two kinds of characteristics, only one faculty would exist, let alone for another.

Nanu ca duvidhe byañjane sati indriyadvayenāpi bhavitabbaṃ, byañjanañhi taṃ taṃ indriyaṃ paṭicca jāyatīti? Saccaṃ jāyati, etthāpi itthiubhatobyañjanassa itthindriyaṃ paṭicca itthinimittameva yāvajīvaṃ pavattati, purisaubhatobyañjanassa purisindriyaṃ paṭicca purisanimittameva, itaraṃ pana na tassa itthindriyapurisindriyahetuto jāyati. Taṃ pana yena kāraṇena hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “evaṃ sante”ti anuyogaṃ katvā “na cābhāvo”tiādinā sodhanaṃ tu vuttaṃ. Evaṃ santeti ekasmiṃyeva indriye sati. Abhāvo cāti yaṃ paṭicca jāyati, tassa abhāvato purisaubhatobyañjanassa itthibyañjanābhāvo, itthiubhatobyañjanassa purisabyañjanābhāvoti attho[M 2.0137]. Na cābhāvo siyāti neva dutiyabyañjanassa abhāvo siyā. Na taṃ byañjanakāraṇanti taṃ indriyaṃ dutiyabyañjanakāraṇaṃ na hoti. Kasmā? Sadā abhāvato. Itthiubhatobyañjanassa hi yadā itthiyā rāgacittaṃ uppajjati, tadā purisabyañjanaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, itthibyañjanaṃ paṭicchannaṃ guḷhaṃ hoti, tathā itarassa itaraṃ. Yadi ca tesaṃ indriyaṃ dutiyabyañjanakāraṇaṃ bhaveyya, sadāpi byañjanadvayaṃ tiṭṭheyya, na pana tiṭṭhati, tasmā veditabbametaṃ “na tassa taṃ byañjanakāraṇa”nti. Kiñcarahi kāraṇanti ce? Āha “tassā…pe… kāraṇa”nti. Tattha kammasahāyanti purimabhavasiddhassa indriyanibbattakakammassa sahāyaṃ. Rāgacittanti itthiyā purisasmiṃ, purisassa itthiyaṃ vā uppannaṃ methunarāgacittaṃ. Tasmiñhi uppanne taṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ paṭippassaddhe paṭicchannaṃ hoti. Yasmā panimassa ekameva indriyaṃ hoti, tasmā itthiubhatobyañjanako sayampi paraṃ uddissa gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti, attānaṃ uddissa parampi gaṇhāpeti. So hi itthindriyavantatāya sayaṃ gaṇhāti, paresu upakkamakaraṇato paraṃ gaṇhāpeti. Purisaubhatobyañjanako paresu upakkamakaraṇato paraṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhāpeti, sayaṃ pana purisindriyavantatāya gabbhaṃ na gaṇhāti.

But is it not so that when there are two kinds of characteristics, there should also be two faculties? For a characteristic arises dependent on its respective faculty. It is true that it arises. In this case, for a female with both characteristics, the female characteristic itself persists for life dependent on the female faculty. Similarly, for a male with both characteristics, the male characteristic itself persists dependent on the male faculty. The other characteristic, however, does not arise from that one's female or male faculty as its cause. To explain the reason for this, the inquiry was made, “If that is so…” and then the clarification was stated with “there is no absence,” and so on. “If that is so” refers to when there is only one faculty. And “absence” means that due to the absence of that on which it depends to arise, for a male with both characteristics there is an absence of female characteristics, and for a female with both characteristics there is an absence of male characteristics. The phrase Na cābhāvo siyā means that there would not be an absence of the second characteristic. The phrase Na taṃ byañjanakāraṇaṃ means that the faculty is not the cause of the second characteristic. Why? Because of its constant absence. For instance, for a female with both characteristics, when a lustful thought arises, the male characteristic becomes manifest while the female characteristic remains hidden and concealed; the same applies vice versa for the other. If their faculty were the cause of the second characteristic, both characteristics would always be present. But since they are not, it should be understood that “that faculty is not the cause of that characteristic.” What, then, is the cause? The text states: “Its… cause…” Here, “assistant to kamma” refers to an assistant to the kamma that produced the faculty, established in a previous existence. “Lustful thought” means the thought of sexual lust that arises in a woman toward a man or in a man toward a woman. When such a thought arises, the corresponding characteristic becomes manifest; when it subsides, the characteristic becomes hidden. Moreover, since such a being possesses only one faculty, a female with both characteristics can both conceive by another and cause another to conceive. Due to possessing the female faculty, she can conceive herself; and by initiating action towards others, she can cause another to conceive. A male with both characteristics, by initiating action towards others, can cause another to conceive, but because he possesses the male faculty, he cannot conceive himself.

Yasmā itthindriye sati itthiliṅgādayo honti, tesu ca santesu itthīti pakāso hoti, tasmā [V 2.0102] taṃ tassa pakāsanakāraṇanti āha “itthīti pakāsanarasa”nti. Duvidhampi panetaṃ indriyaṃ kāyapasādo viya sakalasarīrabyāpakameva, na cassa kāyapasādena saṅkaro lakkhaṇabhedato, nissayabhedato ca.

Because when the female faculty exists, female characteristics and so forth exist, and when these exist, the designation ‘woman’ becomes manifest, therefore its function is said to be making manifest, with the words, ‘its function is to make manifest as a woman.’ Moreover, this faculty, in both its aspects, like body-sensitivity, pervades the entire body, yet there is no confusion with body-sensitivity due to differences in characteristic and differences in support.

673. Sahajarūpaparipālanalakkhaṇanti yathā attanā sahajātarūpāni tīsu khaṇesu pavattanti, evaṃ anupālanalakkhaṇaṃ. Jīvitindriyassa ekantakammajattā sahajaggahaṇeneva anupāletabbānampi [M 2.0138] kammajabhāvova siddhoti kammajaggahaṇaṃ na kataṃ. Yathāsakaṃ khaṇattayamattaṭṭhāyīnampi kammajarūpānaṃ pavattihetubhāveneva taṃ anupālakaṃ. Tenāha “tesaṃ pavattanarasa”nti. Pavattanañcettha vuttanayena tesaṃ yāpanaṃ ṭhapanaṃ ṭhitihetukatā. Na hi kammajānaṃ kammameva ṭhitihetu bhavituṃ sakkoti āhārajādīnaṃ āhārādi viya. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Taṅkhaṇābhāvato. Kammañhi niruddhaṃ rūpassa paccayo hoti, tato taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpāni matapitikā viya puttā cūḷapituādinissayena aññanissayeneva pavattanti, aññañca tesaṃ yāpanasamatthaṃ natthi aññatra jīvitindriyenāti tadeva tesaṃ pavattanarasaṃ. Āhārajādayo pana dharamānakapitikā viya puttā aññanirapekkhā sakasakapaccayavaseneva pavattanti. Āhārādayo hi attano atthikkhaṇeyeva rūpāni samuṭṭhāpetvā tesaṃ ṭhitipavattiyāva tiṭṭhanti, tato taṃsamuṭṭhānāni jīvitindriyanirapekkhāni. Sesānipi taṃtaṃpaccayavaseneva tiṭṭhantīti na aññaṃ ṭhapanakāraṇaṃ paccāsīsanti. Kammasamuṭṭhānampi cetaṃ uppādato paṭṭhāyeva anupālakaṃ. Yāpetabbāni pavattetabbāni sahajātabhūtāni padaṭṭhānametassāti yāpetabbabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

673. Its characteristic is the sustaining of co-nascent material phenomena, which means it sustains them so that they persist through the three moments. Because the life faculty is exclusively kamma-produced, by the inclusion of ‘co-nascent,’ the fact that those things to be sustained are also kamma-produced is established; thus, the inclusion of ‘kamma-produced’ is not made. Even for kamma-produced material phenomena that last for only their respective three moments, it is a sustainer by being the cause of their continuance. Hence it is said, “its function is causing them to continue.” Here, ‘causing to continue’ means, in the way described, their maintenance, preservation, and being the cause of their stability. For kamma alone cannot be the cause of stability for kamma-produced material phenomena, as nutriment and so on are for nutriment-produced phenomena. What is the reason? Because of its absence at that moment. For kamma, having ceased, is a condition for material phenomena. Thereafter, the material phenomena originated by it continue by relying on another support, like children whose parents have died relying on a paternal uncle or the like; there is nothing else capable of maintaining them besides the life faculty. Thus, that is its function of causing them to continue. Nutriment-produced phenomena and the rest, however, continue independently by means of their own respective conditions, like children whose parents are living. For nutriment and the like, having originated material phenomena while they themselves are present, also serve for their stability and continuance. Thereafter, the material phenomena originated by them are independent of the life faculty. The others, too, persist solely by their respective conditions, so they do not look for any other cause for their preservation. And this kamma-originated life faculty is a sustainer right from its arising. Its proximate cause is the co-nascent material phenomena that are to be maintained and made to continue.

674. Manoviññāṇadhātūti ṭhapetvā arūpāvacaravipākamanoviññāṇadhātuṃ avasesā manoviññāṇadhātu. Tenāha “pañcavokāre”ti. Pañcavokāre manodhātu, manoviññāṇadhātuyo ca yaṃ rūpaṃ nissāya pavattanti, taṃ “vatthū”ti pavuccatīti sambandho. Pañcavokāreti ca visesanaṃ manoviññāṇadhātuvasena kataṃ, manodhātu pana catuvokārabhave nattheva. Pāḷiyaṃ anāgatassāpi hadayavatthuno āgamato, yuttito ca atthibhāvo viññātabbo. Tattha āgamo tāva –

674. By ‘mind-consciousness element’ is meant the remaining mind-consciousness element, excluding the immaterial-sphere resultant mind-consciousness element. Hence it is said, “in the five-constituent existence.” The connection is that in the five-constituent existence, the material form on which the mind element and mind-consciousness elements dependently arise is called “the basis.” The specification “in the five-constituent existence” is made with reference to the mind-consciousness element, for the mind element does not exist in the four-constituent existence at all. The existence of the heart-basis, even if not mentioned in the Pāli Canon, should be understood from scripture and from reasoning. There, the scriptural reference is as follows:

“Yaṃ [M 2.0139] rūpaṃ nissāya manodhātu ca manoviññāṇadhātu ca pavattanti, taṃ rūpaṃ manodhātuyā ca manoviññāṇadhātuyā ca taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ nissayapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.8) –

“Whatever material form, dependent on which, the mind element and the mind-consciousness element occur, that material form is a condition by way of dependence for the mind element, the mind-consciousness element, and the states associated with them.”

Evamādi [V 2.0103] paṭṭhānavacanaṃ. Yutti pana evaṃ veditabbā – nipphannaupādāyarūpanissayaṃ dhātudvayaṃ pañcavokārabhave rūpapaṭibaddhavuttittā. Yaṃ yañhi rūpapaṭibaddhavutti, taṃ taṃ nipphannaupādāyarūpanissayaṃ dissati yathā cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Tattha na tāva rūpāyatanādīnaṃ, ojāya ca tannissayatā yujjati indriyapaṭibaddhato bahipi tesaṃ pavattidassanato, nāpi itthindriyapurisindriyānaṃ tadubhayavirahite abhāvakasantānepi dhātudvayadassanato. Jīvitindriyassāpi sahajaparipālanalakkhaṇakiccantaraṃ vijjatīti na tannissayatā yujjati. Tañhi kiccantare pasutaṃ na imāsaṃ nissayo bhavituṃ sakkoti, tasmā pārisesato tesaṃ nissayo hadayavatthu nāma atthīti viññātabbaṃ. Hotu tāva dhātudvayanissayo vatthu, upādāyarūpañca, taṃ panetaṃ kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ paṭiniyatakiccaṃ hadayappadese ṭhitamekanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kathametaṃ viññāyatīti? Vuccate – vatthurūpabhāvato kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ cakkhu viya. Yañhi viññāṇassa vatthubhūtaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ yathā cakkhupasādo, tato eva paṭiniyatakiccaṃ aṭṭhiṃ katvā manasi katvā sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā kiñci cintentassa hadayappadesassa khijjanato tatthedaṃ tiṭṭhatīti viññāyati. Yathāhu ācariyā –

Such is the exposition from the Paṭṭhāna. Reasoning, however, should be understood thus: the two elements depend on produced derived material phenomena in the five-constituent existence because their occurrence is connected with material phenomena. For whatever occurrence is connected with material phenomena is seen to depend on produced derived material phenomena, as in the case of the eye-consciousness element. Here, first of all, the dependence on the visible form base and others, as well as nutriment, is not suitable because their occurrence is seen even apart from their connection with faculties. Nor is it suitable for the femininity faculty and masculinity faculty, since the two elements are seen even in lineages where both are absent. As for the life faculty, it has another function—the characteristic of protecting what is co-nascent—so dependence on it is not suitable. For that which is engaged in another function cannot be the support for these elements. Therefore, it should be understood that, by elimination, their support is indeed the heart-basis. Let it be, then, that the basis for the two elements is a material phenomenon, and it is also derived material phenomenon. But this is kamma-originated, having a fixed function, and situated as a single entity in the region of the heart—it should be seen as such. How is this to be understood? It is said: because of its nature as a material basis, it is kamma-originated, like the eye. For whatever material form serves as the basis for consciousness, that is kamma-originated, just like the eye-sensitivity. From that very fact, having determined its fixed function, having paid close attention, having reflected with the whole mind, it is understood that when someone thinks something, agitation occurs in the region of the heart, and thus it stands there. As the teachers have said:

“Kammajaṃ vatthubhāvā taṃ, cakkhuṃva niyatakriyaṃ;

Cintāya ca urokhedā, tatra tiṭṭhanti vijāniya”nti.

“Being kamma-born and a basis, it has a fixed function like the eye; and from thought and the agitation of the chest, one should understand that they stand there.”

Yadi [M 2.0140] manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ nissayabhūtaṃ hadayavatthu nāma atthi, kasmā panetaṃ rūpakaṇḍe na vuttaṃ. Na hi labbhamānassa avacane kāraṇaṃ atthīti? No natthi kāraṇantarasambhavato. Kiṃ pana taṃ kāraṇaṃ? Desanābhedo. Yathā hi cakkhuviññāṇādīni ekantato cakkhādinissayāni, na evaṃ manoviññāṇaṃ ekantena hadayavatthunissitaṃ pañcavokārabhaveyeva tannissayattā, ekantena nissitavaseneva ca vatthudesanā pavattā. “Atthi rūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa vatthu, atthi rūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa na vatthū”tiādinā (dha. sa. 584) cakkhuviññāṇādīhi nissitehi visesitattā. Yampi ekantena hadayavatthunissayaṃ tassa vasena “atthi rūpaṃ manoviññāṇassa vatthū”tiādinā dukādīsu vuccamānesu na tadanuguṇā ārammaṇadukādayo sambhavanti. Na hi “atthi rūpaṃ manoviññāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ, atthi rūpaṃ na manoviññāṇassa ārammaṇa”nti sakkā vattunti vatthārammaṇadukā bhinnagatikā siyuṃ, na ekarasā desanā bhaveyya, ekarasañca desanaṃ desetuṃ tattha bhagavato ajjhāsayo, tasmā tattha hadayavatthu [V 2.0104] na vuttaṃ, na alabbhamānattā. Esā hi bhagavato pakati, yaṃ ekaraseneva desanaṃ desetuṃ labbhamānassāpi kassaci aggahaṇaṃ. Tathā hi nikkhepakaṇḍepi cittuppādavibhāgena avuccamānattā avitakkāvicārapadavisajjane vitakko vicāro cāti vattuṃ na sakkāti avitakkavicāramattapadavisajjane labbhamānopi vitakko na uddhaṭo, aññathā “vitakko cā”ti vattabbaṃ siyāti. Nissayabhāvato upari āropetvā vahantaṃ viya paccupaṭṭhātīti ubbāhanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

If there exists a heart-basis that serves as the foundation for the mind element and mind-consciousness element, why then is it not mentioned in the section on material phenomena? Is there no reason to omit what is available? No, there is a reason due to the possibility of another cause. What, then, is that reason? A difference in teaching. For instance, just as eye-consciousness and the like depend entirely on the eye and other sense bases, mind-consciousness does not exclusively rely on the heart-basis, because it depends on that basis only in the five-constituent existence, and the teaching of the basis is presented only in terms of exclusive dependence. Moreover, it is said in passages like, “There is material form that is a basis for eye-consciousness, and there is material form that is not a basis for eye-consciousness” (Dhs. 584), distinguishing what depends on eye-consciousness and the like as dependent. And even with respect to that which does rely exclusively on the heart-basis, when statements like “There is material form that is a basis for mind-consciousness” are made in the dyads and so on, corresponding dyads such as the object-dyad do not logically follow. For it cannot be said, “There is material form that is an object of mind-consciousness, and there is material form that is not an object of mind-consciousness.” If that were the case, the basis-object dyads would diverge in function, and the teaching would lack uniformity. But the Blessed One’s intention there was to teach a uniform teaching, so the heart-basis was not mentioned—not because it is unavailable. This is indeed the nature of the Blessed One: to teach a uniform teaching, even if it means omitting something available. For example, in the section on classification, because the analysis of thought-processes is not mentioned, one cannot say, “thought and examination” when explaining the term “without thought but with examination.” Though thought is available in the explanation of “without thought and with examination only,” it is not explicitly mentioned; otherwise, one would have to say, “and thought.” From its nature as a support, it manifests as if lifting up and carrying the dependent states; this is its manifestation as uplifting.

675. Catūsu āhāresu idha rūpādhikārato kabaḷīkāro āhāro gahetabboti āha “āhāratāti kabaḷīkāro āhāro”ti. Tattha kabaḷaṃ karīyatīti [M 2.0141] kabaḷīkāro. Āharīyatīti āhāro, kabaḷaṃ katvā ajjhoharīyatīti attho. Idañca savatthukaṃ katvā āhāraṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Kabaḷīkārāhārassa pana ojā idha āhāro nāma. Tenāha “yāya ojāyā”tiādi. So ca rūpāharaṇasabhāvo upatthambhanabalakaro aṅgamaṅgānusārīrasāharaṇabhūto bhūtanissito eko viseso. Bāhirāhārapaccayaṃ paṭilabhitvā eva ajjhattikāhāro rūpaṃ uppādetīti ayaṃ ajjhattikāhārassa upanissayabhāvenāpi rūpaṃ āharatīti āha “ojaṭṭhamakaṃ rūpaṃ āharatī”ti. Ojā aṭṭhamī yassa taṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ. Yāya ojāyāti attano udayānantaraṃ rūpajananato ojāsaṅkhātāya odanakummāsādivatthugatāya yāya pharaṇaojāya. Yattha yatthāti yamhi yamhi janapade, nagarādīsu ca. “Kabaḷīkāro āhāro”ti pavuccati tabbatthukattāti adhippāyo.

675. Regarding the four kinds of food, here, due to the section on material phenomena, edible food should be taken—thus it is said, “Food means edible food.” Herein, it is called edible food because it is made into a morsel. It is called food because it is consumed; the meaning is that it is made into a morsel and then swallowed. This is stated to show food along with its basis. However, the nutritive essence of edible food is here called food. Therefore, it is said, “By which nutritive essence,” etc. And that essence, having the nature of nourishing material phenomena, provides strength, pervades the limbs, sustains the body, and depends on the elements—it is a unique characteristic. The internal food generates material phenomena only after obtaining the external food as a condition. Thus, this external food also brings forth material phenomena by being a decisive support for the internal food, hence it is said, “It brings material phenomena consisting of the eightfold essence.” The essence is the eighth; that which has it is called “consisting of the eightfold essence.” “By which essence”—because immediately after its arising, it generates material phenomena, it is called essence, in the sense of nutritive essence. It exists within substances like rice and gruel as permeating essence. “Wherever”—in whatever country, city, and so on. “It is called edible food”—this is the meaning, because it serves as the physical basis for that nutriment.

676. Kiṃ pana vatthuno kiccaṃ, kiṃ ojāyāti ce? Parissayaharaṇaṃ vatthussa kiccaṃ, pālanaṃ ojāyāti dassento āha “annapānādika”ntiādi. Aggiṃ harati kammajanti kammajatejaṃ gaṇhāti. Antokucchiyañhi odanādivatthusmiṃ asati kammajatejo uṭṭhahitvā udarapaṭalasaṅkhātamupādinnarūpaṃ gaṇhāti, “chātomhi, āhāraṃ me dethā”ti vadāpeti, bhuttakāle udarapaṭalaṃ muñcitvā anupādinnakavatthuṃ gaṇhāti, atha satto ekaggo hoti. Yathā hi chāyārakkhaso chāyāpaviṭṭhaṃ disvā gahetvā devasaṅkhalikāya bandhitvā attano bhavane modanto chātakāle āgantvā sīse daṃsati, so daṭṭhattā viravati, taṃ viravaṃ sutvā sace aññepi manussā āgacchanti, so āgatāgate gahetvā khāditvā sakabhavane modati[M 2.0142], evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ annapānādikaṃ vatthu, taṃ taṃ kammajatejo gahetvā jīrāpetvā puna udarapaṭalaṃ gaṇhāti, tasmā annapānādikaṃ [V 2.0105] vatthu attano udarapaṭalaṃ paviṭṭhakāle upādinnakāyaṃ gahetvā ṭhitaṃ tato mocetvā attānaṃ gaṇhāpanavasena taṃ attano santikaṃ harati. Kevalanti ojāviyuttaṃ vatthu jīvitaṃ kammajabhūtaṃ taṃ pāletuṃ na sakkoti.

676. What then is the function of the physical basis, and what is the function of nutriment? The function of the physical basis is to remove dangers, and nutriment is for protection. To show this, it is said: "Food, drink, etc." It removes the kamma-born fire, meaning it takes up the heat generated by kamma. For when there is no food or similar substance in the stomach, the kamma-born heat arises and seizes the acquired material form known as the stomach lining. It makes one say, "I am hungry, give me food." At the time of eating, it releases the stomach lining and takes up the unacquired physical basis. Then the being becomes focused. Just as a shadow-demon, seeing someone who has stepped into a shadow, seizes them, binds them with celestial chains, and rejoices in its own abode. When hungry, it comes and bites the head. Being bitten, the person cries out. Hearing the cry, if other humans come, the demon seizes them as they arrive, devours them, and rejoices in its own dwelling. Similarly, whatever physical basis, such as food and drink, the kamma-born heat takes it, digests it, and then seizes the stomach lining again. Therefore, when the physical basis, such as food and drink, enters one's stomach lining, it releases the kamma-born heat that had seized the acquired body and remained there, and by allowing itself (the food/drink) to be taken hold of, it draws that (heat) to itself. The mere physical basis, devoid of nutriment, cannot sustain life and kamma-born materiality.

677. Ojā…pe… pācakanti ojā jīvitaṃ pāletuṃ sakkoti, kammajaṃ tejaṃ harituṃ na sakkoti āmāsayassa apuṇṇatoti adhippāyo. Upatthambhanapaccupaṭṭhānoti ojaṭṭhamakarūpaharaṇavaseneva imassa kāyassa upatthambhanavasena paccupaṭṭhāti. Kāyenāti rūpakāyena. Attano bhāvanti attano adhippāyaṃ. Viññāpentānanti paresaṃ saññāpentānaṃ. Kāyaggahaṇānusārenāti phandamānakāyagatavaṇṇassa gahaṇabhūtānaṃ cakkhudvārikajavanānantarappavattānaṃ nicchayaggahaṇasaṅkhātānaṃ manodvārikajavanānaṃ anussaraṇena tesaṃ anantaranti attho. Pañcadvāre hi rūpādiārammaṇe āpāthagate yathāpaccayaṃ kusalākusalajavane uppajjitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otiṇṇe manodvārikajavanaṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ katvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati, puna tasmiṃyeva dvāre visayaṃ vavatthāpetvā javanaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ otarati, tasmā cakkhudvārikajavanānantarappavattānaṃ dvinnaṃ javanavārānamanantaraṃ tatiyavāre pavattāya manodvārajavanavīthiyā eva gahitāya etāya karaṇabhūtāya catutthavāre manodvāre javaneneva bhāvo viññāyati. Etena viññatti-saddassa karaṇasādhanatā vuttā. Sayaṃ vātiādinā pana kammasādhanattamāha.

677. Ojā…pe… pācakanti: Nutriment can sustain life, but it cannot remove the kamma-generated heat, because the stomach is not full—this is the meaning. Upatthambhanapaccupaṭṭhānoti: It manifests as a support for this body by way of bearing the material octad with nutriment as the eighth. Kāyenāti: By the material body. Attano bhāvanti: One's own intention. Viññāpentānanti: Of those making known to others. Kāyaggahaṇānusārenāti: By recalling the mind-door impulsions, designated as 'decisive grasping,' which arise immediately after the eye-door impulsions that grasp the color of the vibrating body; the meaning is 'immediately after those.' For in the five sense-doors, when a visible form or other object comes into range, wholesome or unwholesome impulsions arise according to conditions and then subside into the life-continuum. Then, a mind-door impulsion, taking that same object, arises and subsides into the life-continuum. Again, after determining the object in that same door, an impulsion arises and subsides into the life-continuum. Therefore, immediately after the two rounds of impulsions that arise after the eye-door impulsions, the intention is made known in the fourth round by a mind-door impulsion, by means of this mind-door impulsion process which has occurred in the third round and has been grasped as the instrument. By this, the instrumental function of the word 'viññatti' is stated. But by 'sayaṃ vā,' etc., its function as an object is stated.

Evaṃ viññatti-saddassa kārakadvaye sambhavaṃ dassetvā idāni kāya-saddena saha kammadhārayasamāsaṃ dassetuṃ, “kāyo”ti vohārassa viññattiyampi ca pavattiṃ dassento “kāyena [M 2.0143] saṃvaro”tiādisuttamāha. Kāyavipphandanena adhippāyaviññāpanahetuttāti vipphandamānakāyena karaṇabhūtena adhippāyaviññāpanahetubhāvato kāyena viññattītipi kāyaviññattīti sambandho. Ayaṃ panettha attho – viññattiyā kāyavipphandanassa hetubhāvato taṃhetukaṃ kāyavipphandanasaṅkhātaṃ kāyaṃ gahetvā adhippāyajānanato viññatti adhippāyaviññāpanassa kāraṇabhāvena gayhatīti kāyena adhippāyaṃ viññāpetīti. Tathā kāyavipphandanaṃ gahetvā tassa kāraṇamettha atthīti viññattiyā gayhamānattā sayañca kāyena viññāyati, tasmā kāyena viññattītipi kāyaviññattīti.

Having thus shown the occurrence of the word 'viññatti' in two grammatical roles, now, in order to illustrate the kammadharaya compound with the word 'kāya,' and demonstrating the application of the term 'kāya' even to expression, he cites the sutta beginning, 'restraint by body.' 'Because it serves as a cause for making intention known through bodily movement' means: because of its being a cause for making intention known by means of the moving body acting as an instrument, the connection is that 'expression by the body' is also 'bodily expression.' Herein, this is the meaning: because expression is the cause of bodily movement, by grasping the 'body'—which is designated as bodily movement caused by that expression—in order to know the intention, 'viññatti' is apprehended as the instrumental cause for communicating intention; thus, 'one makes the intention known by means of the body.' Similarly, by grasping bodily movement, since its cause is present therein, and since it is apprehended by the expression, and also since it is itself known by the body, therefore 'expression by the body' is also 'bodily expression.'

678. Cittajāniladhātuyāti abhikkamādipavattakacittasamuṭṭhānavāyodhātuyā. Ākāravikāratāti [V 2.0106] ākārabhūto vikāro. Kassa pana sā ākāravikāratāti? Sāmatthiyato vāyodhātuadhikānaṃ cittajamahābhūtānaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ sāmatthiyaṃ? Calanahetutā, cittajatā, upādāyarūpatā ca. Atha vā cittajāniladhātuyā ekā ākāravikāratāti sambandho. Na kevalañhi sāmivacanaṃ calanasambandhāpekkhāya eva, atha kho ākāravikārasambandhāpekkhāyapīti.

678. 'Of the mind-born wind element' means of the wind element originated from the mind that causes forward movement and other activities. 'Alteration of mode' means an alteration that is a specific mode. But to what does that alteration of mode belong? By capacity, it belongs to the mind-born great elements in which the wind element is predominant. What is that capacity? Being the cause of motion, being mind-born, and being derived materiality. Alternatively, the connection is: the mind-born wind element has one alteration of mode. For the possessive case is used not only with reference to the connection with motion, but also with reference to the connection with the alteration of mode.

Yadi evaṃ, kathaṃ viññattiyā upādāyarūpattaṃ. “Cittajāniladhātuyā”ti hi vacanena vāyodhātuyāva ākāravikāratā viññatti āpajjati, na ca ekabhūtanissitaṃ upādāyarūpaṃ nāma atthi “catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpa”nti (dha. sa. 584) vacanatoti? Nāyaṃ doso, catunnaṃ vikāratā catūsu ekassapi hoti catusādhāraṇadhanaṃ viya. Aniladhātuadhikakalāpo vā idha “aniladhātū”ti vuccati, tadadhike taṃvohārato [M 2.0144] yathā sambhāradhātuyā adhikabhāvena pathavīvohāro, tasmā vāyodhātuadhikānaṃ cittajamahābhūtānaṃ ekā ākāravikāratā kāyaviññattīti na koci virodho. Adhikatā cassā sāmatthiyato daṭṭhabbā, na pamāṇato. Itarathā hi tesaṃ avinibbhogavuttitā na yujjeyya. Adhikatā hi attano adhikavasena itarehi vinibbhogappavattito hoti. Sāmatthiyādhikañca kāraṇānukāritāya. Kāraṇañhi abhikkamādipavattakaṃ cittaṃ, taṃ calanādhippāyasabhāvaṃ tato samuṭṭhite kalāpe anukaronte vāyodhātuyā eva adhikattaṃ yuttanti. Keci pana “vāyodhātuyā eva ākāravikāratā”ti gaṇhanti, tesaṃ matena upādārūpattaṃ durūpapannaṃ. Na hi ekassa vikāro catunnaṃ upādārūpanti sakkā vattuṃ.

If so, how can intimation be derived materiality? For by the statement 'of the mind-born air element,' intimation would become an alteration of the air element alone, and there is no such thing as derived materiality dependent on a single element, because of the statement: 'derived materiality is of the four great elements' (Dhs. 584). This is not a fault, for an alteration of the four can be of one among the four, like wealth common to four persons. Or here, an aggregate with a predominance of the air element is called 'the air element.' Due to that predominance, it is conventionally spoken of as such, just as there is the conventional usage 'earth' due to the predominance of the earth element in building materials. Therefore, there is no contradiction in saying that bodily intimation is a single alteration of mode in the mind-born great elements where the air element is predominant. And its predominance should be understood in terms of capacity, not quantity. Otherwise, their inseparability would not be tenable. For predominance occurs from functioning separately from the others by way of its own prevalence. And predominance of capacity is due to following the cause. For the cause—the mind that instigates forward movement, etc.—has the nature of intending motion. When the aggregate that arises from it follows this, the predominance of the air element is justified. Some, however, hold that 'it is an alteration of the air element alone.' According to their view, its status as derived materiality is difficult to establish. For one cannot say that the alteration of one is the derived materiality of the four.

Kīdisī panāyaṃ vikāratāti āha “sahajātassa rūpassa calane hetū”ti. Tattha sahajātassāti attanā sahajātassa. Yasmā utucittāhārajānaṃ calanaṃ cittajarūpasambandheneva hoti, nadīsotacalanena tattha pakkhittasukkhagomayapiṇḍādīnaṃ viya. Viññattivasena pana cittajānameva calanaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “sahajātassā”ti. Rūpassāti rūpakāyassa. Calaneti santhambhanasandhāraṇacalanasaṅkhāte calitabhāve. Santhambhanādikampi hi calanābhimukhatāya calananti yujjati. Hetūti hetubhūtā sahakārīkāraṇabhūtā. Ettāvatā ca kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Kāyaviññatti nāma neva phandamānarūpakāyo, na ca phandamānā vāyodhātu, atha kho mahantaṃ pāsāṇaṃ ukkhipantassa sabbathāmena gahaṇakāle sarīrassa ussāhanavikāro viya rūpakāyassa paripphandanapaccayabhāvena labbhamāno eko ākāravikāro kāyaviññatti nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti.

What kind of alteration is this? He says, 'a cause for the movement of co-nascent materiality.' Herein, 'of co-nascent' means of what is co-nascent with itself. Because the movement of materiality born of temperature, mind, and nutriment occurs only in connection with mind-born materiality, like the movement of lumps of dried cow-dung and so on thrown into a river's current. By way of intimation, however, the movement is only of what is mind-born; therefore, it is said, 'of co-nascent.' 'Of materiality' means of the material body. 'In movement' refers to the state of being moved, designated as stiffening, supporting, and moving. For even stiffening and so on may be called 'movement' because they are oriented towards movement. 'Cause' means being a cause, a cooperating cause. And by all this, what is stated? It is stated that what is called 'bodily intimation' is neither the vibrating material body nor the vibrating air element, but rather, like the alteration of exertion in the body of one lifting a large stone with all one's strength at the moment of grasping, it is a particular alteration of mode that is found as a condition for the vibration of the material body.

Nanu [M 2.0145][V 2.0107] ca phandamānavaṇṇādivinimutto koci vikāro atthi, tassa vaṇṇaggahaṇānantaraṃ gahaṇaṃ hotīti kathametaṃ viññāyatīti? Adhippāyaggahaṇato. Na hi viññattivikārarahitesu rukkhacalanādīsu adhippāyaggahaṇaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, hatthacalanādīsu pana diṭṭhaṃ, tasmā phandamānavaṇṇādivinimutto koci vikāro atthi adhippāyassa viññāpakoti sampaṭicchitabbametaṃ ekantena. Ñāpako ca hetu sayaṃ gahitoyeva attano ñāpetabbamatthaṃ ñāpeti, na vijjamānamattenāti. Ñāpetabbavaṇṇaggahaṇānantaraṃ vikāraggahaṇampi anumānato siddhaṃ. Tathā hi vadanti –

But is there some alteration distinct from the vibrating color and so on, the grasping of which occurs after the grasping of the color? How is this known? From the grasping of intention. For the grasping of intention is not seen in things devoid of the alteration of intimation, such as the shaking of trees, but it is seen in such things as the movement of hands. Therefore, it must be accepted without reservation that there is some alteration distinct from the vibrating color and so on that is an indicator of intention. And an indicative cause, only when it is itself grasped, makes known the meaning to be indicated, not by its mere existence. The grasping of the alteration after the grasping of the color to be indicated is also established by inference. For thus they say—

“Visayattamanāpannā,

Saddā nevatthabodhakā;

Na sattāmattato atthe,

Te aññātā pakāsakā”ti.

Sounds that have not become an object

Do not make the meaning known;

Not by mere existence, but when known,

Are they illuminators of the meaning.

Yadi vikāraggahaṇameva kāraṇamadhippāyaggahaṇassa, kasmā aggahitasaṅketānaṃ adhippāyaggahaṇaṃ na hotīti? Na kevalaṃ vikāraggahaṇameva adhippāyassa gahaṇassa kāraṇaṃ, atha kho purimasiddhasambandhaggahaṇañca imassa upanissayoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā hi araññe udakatitthe ussāpetvā ṭhapitagosīsādīni udakanimittāni disvā tadanantarappavattāya aviññāyamānantarāya manodvārajavanavīthiyā gosīsādīnaṃ udakasahacārīpakārasaññāṇākāraṃ gahetvā “udakamettha atthī”ti jānanaṃ, evaṃ phandamānavaṇṇaṃ gahetvā tadanantappavattāya aviññāyamānantarāya manodvāravīthiyā purimaggahitasambandhūpanissayasahitāya sādhippāyavikāraggahaṇaṃ hotīti.

If the mere grasping of alteration is the reason for grasping intention, why is there no grasping of intention for those who have not grasped the convention? It is not only the grasping of alteration that is the reason for grasping intention, but also the grasping of a previously established connection—this should be seen as its support. For example, just as when one sees signs of water like cow-hoof prints at a watering place in the forest, and immediately afterward, without a discernible interval, a mind-door impulsion process grasps the mode of perceiving the cow-hoof prints as being concomitant with water, leading to the knowledge, "There is water here," similarly, by grasping the flickering appearance and immediately afterward, without a discernible interval, the mind-door process—supported by the previously grasped connection—results in the grasping of the alteration together with the intention.

681-2. Sahajarūpacalanassa viññattivikārasahitāya vāyodhātuyā hetubhāvo yutto, kiṃ sabbā eva vāyodhātu [M 2.0146] sahajarūpaṃ cāletīti imaṃ codanaṃ sodhetuṃ “labhitvā panupatthambha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Upatthambhetīti upatthambhaṃ, upatthambhakapaccayanti attho. Ekāvajjanavīthiyanti manodvārikajavanavīthiṃ sandhāyāha pañcadvārikavīthiyā viññattisamuṭṭhāpakattābhāvato. Heṭṭhāhi chahi ca cittehīti sattasu javanesu heṭṭhimehi chahi javanehi samuṭṭhitaṃ vāyodhātuṃ upatthambhaṃ labhitvāti sambandho. Keci pana potthakesu “vāyodhātusamuṭṭhita”nti pāṭhaṃ disvā upatthambhanti bhāvasādhanavasena gahetvā heṭṭhā chahi cittehi uppannavāyodhātusamuṭṭhitaṃ [V 2.0108] upatthambhaṃ labhitvāti yojenti. Viññattisahitattanāti sayaṃ viññattisahitā attanā sahajātaṃ cittajarūpaṃ desantaruppattihetubhāvena calayati, na itarāti attho.

681-2. The causality for the movement of co-arisen materiality is fitting for the wind element accompanied by the alteration of intimation. But does every wind element move co-arisen materiality? To resolve this objection, it is said, 'having obtained support,' and so on. Upatthambha means 'that which supports,' i.e., a supporting condition. The phrase 'in one advertence process' refers to the mind-door impulsion process, as there is no production of intimation in the five-door process. The phrase 'by the lower six consciousnesses' is connected thus: having obtained as support the wind element arisen from the lower six impulsions among the seven impulsions. However, some, seeing the reading 'produced by the wind element' in manuscripts, interpret 'upatthambha' as a verbal noun, construing it as 'having obtained support that is produced by the wind element arisen from the lower six consciousnesses.' The phrase 'because it is accompanied by intimation' means that the wind element, being itself accompanied by intimation, moves the mind-produced materiality co-arisen with itself by being a cause for its arising in another region, not the other wind element. That is the meaning.

Ayaṃ panetthādhippāyo – yathā nāma sattahi yugehi ākaḍḍhitabbasakaṭe sattamayugayuttā eva goṇā heṭṭhā chasu yugesu yuttagoṇehi laddhupatthambhā sakaṭaṃ cālenti, paṭhamayugādiyuttā pana santhambhanasandhāraṇamattameva sādhentā tesaṃ upatthambhakā honti, evamevaṃ sattamajavanasamuṭṭhitā vāyodhātu heṭṭhā chahi javanehi samuṭṭhitavāyodhātuto laddhupatthambhā cittajarūpaṃ cāleti. Paṭhamajavanādisamuṭṭhitā pana santhambhanasandhāraṇamattaṃ sādhentā tassa upatthambhakā honti, desantaruppattiyeva cettha calanaṃ uppannadesato kesaggamattampi dhammānaṃ calanābhāvato, itarathā dhammānaṃ abyāpāratā, khaṇikatā ca na siyā. Kathaṃ panassa sahajarūpānaṃ desantaruppattiyā hetubhāvoti? Yathā attanā sahajarūpāni heṭṭhimajavanādisamuṭṭhitarūpehi patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānato aññattha uppajjanti, evaṃ tehi saha tattha uppattiyevassa desantaruppattihetubhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here is the intended meaning: Just as, in a cart that is to be drawn by seven yokes, the oxen yoked to the seventh yoke, supported by the oxen yoked to the six preceding yokes, move the cart, while those yoked to the first yoke and so on merely accomplish stiffening and sustaining, being supporters for them—in the same way, the wind element arising from the seventh impulsion, supported by the wind elements arising from the six preceding impulsions, moves the mind-produced materiality. The wind elements arising from the first impulsion and so on merely accomplish stiffening and sustaining, being supporters for it. Here, movement is simply arising in a different place, since there is no movement of phenomena even by a hair's breadth from the place where they arose. Otherwise, the non-operation of phenomena and their momentariness would not be possible. But how is it a cause for the arising of its co-arisen material phenomena in a different place? Just as the material phenomena co-arisen with it arise elsewhere than the place where they were established by the material phenomena arisen from the preceding impulsions and so on, so its being a cause for arising in a different place should be seen as simply its arising there together with them.

Atha [M 2.0147] phandamānavaṇṇaggahaṇānantaraṃ viññattiggahaṇassa vuttattā viññattisahitāti sattamajavanasamuṭṭhitāya eva ca visesitattā calanākārasahitāyeva vāyodhātu vikārasahitāti? Nayidamevaṃ desantaruppattihetubhāvena calayitumasakkontiyopi santhambhanasandhāraṇamattakaraṇena paṭhamajavanādisamuṭṭhānavāyodhātuyopi viññattivikārasahitā eva. Yena disābhāgena gantvā abhikkamādīni pavattetukāmo tadabhimukhabhāvavikārasambhavato. Adhippāyasahabhāvinañhi vikāraṃ viññattimācikkhanti. Teneva hi bhagavatā “katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ kāyaviññatti? Yā kusalacittassa vā…pe… abyākatacittassa vā abhikkamantassa vā…pe… pasārentassa vā kāyassa thambhanā santhambhanā santhambhitattaṃ viññatti viññāpanā viññāpitattaṃ. Idaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ kāyaviññattī”ti (dha. sa. 720) santhambhanasandhāraṇānampi paccayabhāvākāro kāyaviññattīti vutto. Evañca katvā manodvārāvajjanassāpi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakatāvacanaṃ suṭṭhu upapannaṃ hoti.

Then, since it is said that the grasping of intimation follows the grasping of the flickering appearance, and since only the wind element arisen from the seventh impulsion is specified as being 'accompanied by intimation', is the wind element accompanied by alteration only when it is accompanied by the mode of movement? It is not so. Even the wind element arising from the first impulsion and so on, although incapable of causing movement by being a cause for arising in another place, is still accompanied by the alteration of intimation by merely causing stiffening and supporting. This is because of the possibility of an alteration which is the state of facing the direction one intends to go to perform advancing, etc. For alteration that arises together with intention is indeed explained as intimation. Therefore, the Blessed One has said: 'What is that materiality which is bodily intimation? That which, for one advancing... or stretching out... with a wholesome mind... or an indeterminate mind, is the stiffening, supporting, or state of being sustained of the body; this is intimation, the act of intimating, the state of having intimated. This is that materiality which is bodily intimation.' (Dhs. 720) Thus, the mode of being a condition of even stiffening and supporting is described as bodily intimation. And this being so, the statement that mind-door adverting also produces intimation is well-founded.

683-4. Cittajātāya pathavīdhātuyā upādinnakaghaṭṭane paccayo yo ākāravikāro, ayaṃ vacīviññatti viññeyyāti sambandho. Tattha cittajātāyāti vacībhedappavattakacittasamuṭṭhānāya[V 2.0109]. Upādinnakaghaṭṭaneti upādinnakakalāpasaṅkhātassa akkharuppattiṭṭhānassa ghaṭṭanasaññite kicce ghaṭṭanassāti attho. Paccayoti tassa sahakārīkāraṇabhūto. Eko ākāravikāroti ghaṭṭiyamānaupādinnarūpato, ghaṭṭanti yā pathavīdhātuto ca vinivaṭṭo pathavīdhātuyā upādinnaghaṭṭanapaccayasabhāvarūpo eko ākāravikāravisesoti attho. Pathavidhātuyāti sāmivacanaṃ “ubhayasambandhāpekkha”ntiādi kāyaviññattiyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yathā tattha phandamānavaṇṇaggahaṇānantaraṃ [M 2.0148] gayhati, evamidha suyyamānasaddasavanānantaranti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idañca santhambhanādīnaṃ abhāvena ghaṭṭanena saddhiṃyeva saddassa uppajjanato “labhitvā panupatthambha”ntiādinayo na labbhati. Ghaṭṭanañhi paṭhamajavanādīsupi labbhateva. Tenāha “saddavasā”ti. Atha ghaṭṭanacalanānaṃ ko visesoti? Ghaṭṭanaṃ paccayavisesena bhūtakalāpānaṃ aññamaññaṃ āsannataruppādatā, calanaṃ ekassāpi desantaruppādanaparamparatāti ayametesaṃ viseso. Gosīsādiupamāpettha yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbā. Sāvāti sā eva sahasaddā viññatti. Sakyakulindunāti suparisuddhagaganatalassa sakkarājakulassa avabhāsakaṭṭhena tassa nisākarabhūtena. Atha vā indati paramissariyaṃ karotīti indu. Indu-saddassa uttamavācakattā sakkakuluttamenāti attho.

683-4. The connection is that the alteration in form, which is a condition for the striking of what is clung to by the mind-born earth element, is to be known as verbal intimation. Herein, 'born of mind' means arising from the mind that produces distinctions of speech. The phrase 'striking what is clung to' means the striking of the place of letter production, which is called the clung-to aggregate, in the function designated as striking. 'Condition' means being a co-operating cause for it. 'A single alteration in form' means a specific alteration in form that is distinct from the struck clung-to materiality and from the earth element that strikes, and which has the nature of a condition for the striking of what is clung to by the earth element. 'Of the earth element' is a genitive word, to be understood in the same way as explained regarding bodily intimation, considering mutual dependence, etc. The difference here is that just as there, the grasping follows immediately after the flickering form, so here, it follows immediately after hearing the sound. Moreover, because there is no stiffening, etc., and the sound arises simultaneously with the striking, the method beginning 'having obtained a support' does not apply here. For striking can occur even in the first impulsion, etc. Hence, it is said, 'by means of the sound.' Now, what is the difference between striking and movement? Striking is the closer mutual arising of material aggregates due to a specific condition, while movement is the successive arising of even a single one in a different location—this is their distinction. Similes like the cow-hoof prints, etc., should be applied here as appropriate. By 'that' (sā) is meant that very intimation, accompanied by sound. 'Of the Sakyan moon' means like the moon illuminating the perfectly pure sky, the illuminator of the Sakyan royal family who is like their moon. Alternatively, 'Indu' means 'he who exercises supreme sovereignty.' Due to the term 'Indu' signifying excellence, it means the supreme member of the Sakyan clan.

685. Atha viññatti tāva sahasaddāva, saddo pana cittajo aviññattiko atthīti ce? Natthīti dassento āha “saddo na cittajo”tiādi. Viññattighaṭṭananti viññattipaccayaṃ pathavīdhātuyā ghaṭṭanaṃ. Dhātusaṅghaṭṭanenevātiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ samattheti. Yasmā dhātusaṅghaṭṭaneneva saddo jāyati, na tena vinā, tasmāti attho. Anena ca ye vadanti “vitakkavipphārasaddo na sotaviññeyyoti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā cittasamuṭṭhāno vitakkavipphārasaddo viññattiyā vināpi uppajjati. ‘Yā tāya vācāya viññatti viññāpanā’ti (dha. sa. 636) hi vacanato asotaviññeyyena saddena saha viññatti na uppajjati, tatova cittajopi saddanavako atthī”ti, tesaṃ vādaṃ paṭikkhipati. Mahāaṭṭhakathāvādopi hi saddova hoti, na sotaviññeyyoti viruddhametanti maññamānehi saṅgahakārehi paṭikkhittova. Ānandācariyo pana mahāaṭṭhakathāvādaṃ [M 2.0149] appaṭikkhipitvāva tattha adhippāyaṃ vaṇṇeti. Kathaṃ? “Jivhātālucalanādikaravitakkasamuṭṭhitaṃ viññattisahajameva sukhumasaddaṃ dibbasotena sutvā ādisatī”ti sutte, paṭṭhāne ca oḷārikaṃ saddaṃ sandhāya sotaviññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayabhāvo [V 2.0110] vuttoti iminā adhippāyena vitakkavipphārasaddassa asotaviññeyyatā vuttāti.

685. Then, is intimation indeed accompanied by sound, but if it is said that there is a mind-born sound that is non-intimation? To show that there is not, it is said, 'Sound is not mind-born,' and so on. 'Striking of intimation' means the striking of the earth element which is a condition for intimation. 'By the mere collision of elements,' and so on, confirms the very meaning already stated. Because sound arises solely from the collision of elements and not without it, that is the meaning. And by this, the argument of those who say, 'The sound of thought-proliferation is not perceptible by the ear, as stated in the Great Commentary; therefore, the sound arising from thought-proliferation arises even without intimation. For, according to the statement, “whatever intimation, communication by that speech” (Dhs. 636), intimation does not arise together with sound not perceptible by the ear, and thus there is also a mind-born sound-nonad,' is refuted. For the view of the Great Commentary—that it is sound, but not perceptible by the ear—thinking this to be contradictory, has been refuted by the compilers. However, Ācariya Ānanda, without refuting the view of the Great Commentary, explains the intended meaning there. How? 'In the Sutta, [it is said that one] declares, having heard with the divine ear the subtle sound co-arisen with intimation, which arises from the initial thought that causes the movement of the tongue, palate, and so on,' and in the Paṭṭhāna, referring to gross sound, its being an object-condition for ear-consciousness is stated. By this intention, the imperceptibility by the ear of the sound of thought-proliferation is stated.

686-7. Viññāpanatoti vacīghosena adhippāyaviññāpanahetuttā. Sayaṃ viññeyyatoti gahaṇānusārena vacīghosena vā hetunā sayaṃ viññeyyattā. Tassāti viññattisaddassa. Sambhavo kārakadvayeti viññāpayatīti viññatti, viññāyatīti viññattīti evaṃ hetumhi, kammani vā tassa sambhavo nibbatti hotīti attho. Kiṃ panetaṃ viññattidvayaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, udāhu kammādisamuṭṭhānanti āha “na viññattidvaya”ntiādi. Aṭṭha rūpāni viyāti sakasakakalāpagataaṭṭharūpāni viya, viññattidvayassa ekato vuccamānattā kāyaviññattisahajakalāpe saddo na labbhatīti vacīviññattikalāpe labbhamānampi taṃ hitvā “aṭṭha”icceva vuttaṃ.

686-7. Because of communicating (viññāpanato) means because it is the cause of communicating intention through vocal sound. Because of being perceptible by itself (sayaṃ viññeyyato) means because it is perceptible by itself in accordance with apprehension or through vocal sound as a cause. 'Of that' refers to the word 'viññatti' (intimation). 'Its arising is in two agentive senses' means that its origination or production occurs either in the agentive sense (from 'viññāpayati,' one makes known) or in the objective sense (from 'viññāyati,' it is known). Now, is this pair of intimations mind-produced, or produced from kamma and so on? He said, 'Not the pair of intimations,' and so on. 'Like the eight material qualities' means like the eight material qualities belonging to their own respective kalāpas. Because the pair of intimations is spoken of together, and because sound is not found in the kalāpa co-arisen with bodily intimation, even though it is found in the kalāpa of verbal intimation, having omitted it, it is simply said, 'the eight.'

Yathāvuttavikāraggahaṇamukhena “ayaṃ idaṃ nāma kātukāmo”ti taṃsamaṅgino adhippāyo viññāyatīti āha “adhippāyappakāsanarasā”ti. Kāyavipphandanahetubhūtāya vāyodhātuyā vikārattā tassā kāyavipphandanassa hetubhāvākārena paccupaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ “kāya…pe… paccupaṭṭhānā”ti. Vāyodhātuyā kiccādhikatāya āha “cittasamuṭṭhānavāyodhātupadaṭṭhānā”ti. Vacīghosassa hetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhānāti vuttanayeneva vacīghosasaṅkhātassa cittajasaddassa hetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā.

Because the intention of one endowed with it—'this person desires to do this'—is understood by means of grasping the aforesaid modification, it is said, 'its function is to reveal intention.' Because it is a modification of the wind element which is the cause of bodily movement, its manifestation is in the form of being a cause for that bodily movement; thus it is said, 'its manifestation is as the cause of bodily movement.' Because of the predominance of the function of the wind element, it is said, 'its proximate cause is the mind-produced wind element.' By the same method as was stated for the manifestation of vocal sound as a cause, so too is the manifestation of the mind-produced sound, known as vocal utterance, as a cause.

Keci panettha “ghaṭṭane paccayoti vuttattā ghaṭṭanānantaraṃ saddassa uppatti hotīti gahetvā cittasamuṭṭhānapathavīdhātu upādinnaghaṭṭanamattaṃ [M 2.0150] karoti, ghaṭṭitakkhaṇe utusamuṭṭhānova saddo uppajjati, so pana cittapaccayattā pariyāyena cittasamuṭṭhānoti vuccatī”ti vadanti. Tesaṃ matena cittajasaddoyeva na labbhati, tasmā evaṃ aggahetvā udakatāpanakāle antoudakeyeva uppajjanakasaddo viya upādinne ghaṭṭetvā uppajjamānacittasamuṭṭhānapathavīdhātuyā uppattisamakālameva tasmiṃ kalāpe navamaṃ hutvā antoyeva bhūtikasaddo uppajjatīti gahetabbaṃ, tasmā cittasamuṭṭhānasaddopi vacīviññattivaseneva uppajjati, accharāpaharaṇādisaddo pana vacīviññattiyā abhāvato cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhānoyevāti.

Some here say: 'Because it is said, “striking is a condition,” taking it that the arising of sound occurs immediately after the striking, the mind-produced earth element merely performs the striking of what is appropriated. At the moment of striking, a sound produced by temperature arises, but because it is conditioned by mind, it is figuratively called “mind-produced.”' According to their view, a truly mind-produced sound is not obtained. Therefore, not accepting this, it should be understood that just as the bubbling sound arises within the water itself when water is heated, so too, having struck what is appropriated, a material sound arises internally within that kalāpa, becoming the ninth factor, simultaneously with the arising of the mind-produced earth element that is arising. Therefore, mind-produced sound also arises only by way of verbal intimation. However, sound such as the snapping of fingers, due to the absence of verbal intimation, is indeed produced by temperature conditioned by mind.

688. Viggahābhāvato [V 2.0111] na kassati, kasituṃ chindituṃ na sakkotīti akāso, soyeva ākāsoti āha “na kassatīti ākāso”ti, ko panesoti āha “rūpānaṃ vivaro”ti, kaṇṇacchiddādirūpānaṃ antaranti attho. Anena ajaṭākāsamāha. Yo…pe… paricchedoti pana iminā idhādhippetamākāsaṃ, so pana ruḷhīvasena ākāsoti pavuccati.

688. Because there is no conflict, it is not ploughed. Because one is unable to plough or cut it, it is 'akāsa'; that very thing is 'ākāsa'. Thus he says, 'It is not ploughed, therefore it is ākāsa.' What then is this? He says, 'It is the aperture of material forms,' meaning the interval between material forms such as the ear-hole. By this, he indicates unlimited space. But by this [phrase], 'That which... is the delimitation,' the space intended here is meant. This, however, is called 'ākāsa' by way of convention.

Rūpāni paricchindati, sayaṃ vā tehi paricchijjati, tesaṃ vā paricchedamattanti rūpaparicchedo, taṃ lakkhaṇametassāti rūpaparicchedalakkhaṇo. Ayañhi taṃ taṃ rūpakalāpaṃ paricchindanto viya hoti. Tenāha “rūpapariyantappakāsanaraso”ti. “Ayaṃ rūpānaṃ heṭṭhimo pariyanto, ayaṃ uparimo”ti evaṃ vibhāvanakiccoti attho. Atthato pana yasmā rūpānaṃ paricchedamattaṃ hutvā gayhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “rūpamariyādapaccupaṭṭhāno”ti. Etthāha – kiṃ panesa rūpe paricchindanto catusamuṭṭhānakalāpato paricchindati, atha ekasamuṭṭhānabahukalāpato, udāhu ekekasamuṭṭhānaekekakalāpato, ekekarūpato vāti? Ekekasamuṭṭhānaekekakalāpatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

It delimits material forms, or is itself delimited by them, or is merely the delimitation of them—this is the delimitation of material form; this is its characteristic. For it is as if delimiting each material kalāpa. Hence it is said, 'Its function is to reveal the limits of material form.' The meaning is: its task is to distinguish thus, 'This is the lower limit of material forms, this is the upper limit.' In essence, because it is grasped as merely the delimitation of material forms, it is said: 'It manifests as the boundary of material form.' Here it is asked: When it delimits material forms, does it delimit them from kalāpas of fourfold origin, or from many kalāpas of single origin, or from a single kalāpa of each single origin, or from each single material form? It should be understood as from a single kalāpa of each single origin.

Yadi [M 2.0151] hi catusamuṭṭhānakalāpato, ekasamuṭṭhānabahukalāpato vā paricchindati, evaṃ sati samphuṭṭhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno vā paricchindeyya, ekakalāpagatarūpānaṃ viya nānākalāpagatarūpānampi avinibbhogavuttitā vā āpajjeyya. Atha vā ekekarūpato paricchindati, evaṃ sati ekekakalāpagatarūpānampi nānākalāpagatarūpānaṃ viya aññamaññavinibbhogavuttitāpasaṅgo siyā, ubhayampi panetaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ, tasmā ekekasamuṭṭhānaekekakalāpato paricchindatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For if it were to delimit from kalāpas of fourfold origin, or from many kalāpas of single origin, then it would either delimit the manifestation as the state of being touched, or the state of being inseparable would apply even to material forms belonging to different kalāpas, just as it does to those belonging to a single kalāpa. Or, if it were to delimit from each single material form, then there would be the unwanted consequence of the state of being mutually separable even for material forms belonging to a single kalāpa, just as for those belonging to different kalāpas. But both of these are undesirable. Therefore, it should be understood that it delimits from a single kalāpa of each single origin.

Asamphuṭṭhabhāvachiddavivarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno vāti asamphuṭṭhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno vā chiddavivarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno vāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha yasmiṃ kalāpe bhūtānaṃ paricchedo, teheva asamphuṭṭhabhāvena paccupaṭṭhānato asamphuṭṭhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. Kiñcāpi hi kalāpantarabhūtā kalāpantarabhūtehi samphuṭṭhāva ekaghanapiṇḍabhāvena pavattattā, tathāpi dhammato aññamaññaṃ vivittattā asaṃkiṇṇā eva. Tesaṃ yā vivittatā aññamaññaṃ asaṃkiṇṇatā, ayaṃ paricchedo. Bhūtantarehi viya tehi so asamphuṭṭhova, itarathā paricchinnatā na siyā tesaṃ bhūtānaṃ byāpibhāvāpattito. Abyāpibhāvo hi asamphuṭṭhatā. Tenāha bhagavā imassa niddese “asamphuṭṭhaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehī”ti (dha. sa. 637).

'Or its manifestation is as the state of not being touched, or as the state of being a gap and an opening'—this is what is meant. Herein, in whatever kalāpa there is the delimitation of the primary elements, because it manifests through that very state of not being touched, its manifestation is as the state of not being touched. For although the primary elements of one kalāpa are indeed touched by the primary elements of another kalāpa, proceeding as a single solid mass, nevertheless, in reality, because of being separate from each other, they are indeed unmixed. Their separateness, their mutual unmixedness—this is the delimitation. That [delimitation] is untouched by them, just as by other primary elements; otherwise, there would be no delimitedness, due to those primary elements attaining a state of pervasiveness. For non-pervasiveness is the state of not being touched. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the analysis of this, 'Not touched by the four great elements' (Dhs. 637).
