Atha [V 2.0112] vā kalāpantarabhūtānaṃ aññamaññaṃ asaṃkiṇṇabhāvena paccupaṭṭhānato asamphuṭṭhatāpaccupaṭṭhānabhāvo vutto, kaṇṇacchiddamukhavivarādivasena chiddavivarabhāvassa paccupaṭṭhānato chiddavivarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānatā vuttā. Rūpaparicchede hi sati chiddavivarabhāvo hoti. Yesaṃ rūpānaṃ paricchedo, tattheva tesaṃ [M 2.0152] paricchedabhāvena labbhatīti vuttaṃ “paricchinnarūpapadaṭṭhāno”ti.

Or, because it manifests as the unmingled state of things that have become different groups, the state of having non-contact as its manifestation is stated. Because it manifests as the state of holes and openings, by way of the ear-hole, the mouth-opening, and so on, the state of having holes and openings as its manifestation is stated. For when there is a delimitation of matter, the state of holes and openings exists. For those material phenomena of which there is a delimitation, right there it is obtained as their state of being delimited; hence, it is said to have 'delimited matter as its proximate cause.'

689-91. Rūpassalahutādittayaniddeseti rūpassalahutā rūpassamudutā rūpassakammaññatāti imassa rūpalahutādittayassa niddese sampatte idaṃ vuccatīti adhippāyo. Heṭṭhā vuttanayenevāti arūpassa lahutādīsu “kāyalahubhāvo kāyalahutā”tiādinā vuttanayānusāreneva “rūpassa lahubhāvo lahutā”tiādinā rūpasambandhībhāvena rūpavikārāpi viññātabbā. Rūpassa lahubhāvo lahutā, sā rūpassa garubhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, garubhāvanimmaddanarasā, adandhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā, lahurūpapadaṭṭhānā. Rūpassa mudubhāvo mudutā, sā rūpassa thaddhabhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, thaddhabhāvanimmaddanarasā, sabbakiriyāsu avirodhitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, mudurūpapadaṭṭhānā. Rūpassa kammaññabhāvo kammaññatā, sā rūpassa akammaññabhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, akammaññabhāvanimmaddanarasā, sarīrakiriyāsu anukūlabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, kammaññarūpapadaṭṭhānāti. Attho panettha tattha tattha amhehi vuttānusārena veditabbo. Imā pana tisso rūpānaṃ vikārabhāvato “rūpavikārā”ti vuccantīti dassetuṃ “tisso…pe… vibhāvinā”ti vuttaṃ.

689-91. In 'the exposition of the triad of lightness of matter, etc.': when the exposition of this triad of lightness of matter, etc.—namely, lightness of matter, softness of matter, and wieldiness of matter—is reached, this is said; this is the intention. 'Just as in the method stated previously': just as in the method stated previously concerning lightness, etc., of the non-material, with the words, 'the state of lightness of the mental body is lightness of the mental body,' and so on, in the same way, by being related to matter, 'the state of lightness of matter is lightness,' etc., should also be understood as modifications of matter. The state of lightness of matter is lightness; its characteristic is the calming of the state of heaviness; its function is the subduing of heaviness; its manifestation is non-sluggishness; its proximate cause is light matter. The state of softness of matter is softness; its characteristic is the calming of the state of rigidity; its function is the subduing of rigidity; its manifestation is non-opposition in all activities; its proximate cause is soft matter. The state of wieldiness of matter is wieldiness; its characteristic is the calming of the state of unwieldiness; its function is the subduing of unwieldiness; its manifestation is a state of suitability for bodily actions; its proximate cause is wieldy matter. The meaning here should be understood in accordance with what we have stated in each respective case. But to show that these three are called 'modifications of matter' because they are a state of alteration of matter, it is said, 'the three... by the discerning one.'

Yathākkamaṃ panetā rūpassa dandhattakaradhātukkhobhapaṭipakkhapaccayasamuṭṭhānā, thaddhattakaradhātukkhobhapaṭipakkhapaccayasamuṭṭhānā, rūpānaṃ sarīrakiriyāsu ananukūlabhāvakaradhātukkhobhapaṭipakkhapaccayasamuṭṭhānāti veditabbaṃ. Tattha dhātukkhobhoti vātapittasemhapakopo, rasādidhātūnaṃ vā vikārāvatthā, dvidhā vuttāpi atthato pathavīdhātuādīnaṃyeva vikāroti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paṭipakkhapaccayā sappāyautuāhārāvikkhittacittatā, sā ca taṃtaṃvikārassa visesapaccayabhāvato vuttā, avisesena pana sabbesaṃ paccayā, tathā [M 2.0153] hi te kadācipi aññamaññaṃ na vijahanti. Tathā avijahantānaṃ pana dubbijānīyaṃ nānattanti taṃpakāsanatthaṃ “etāsa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Kamatova nidassananti sambandho. Lahutāya hi arogī nidassanaṃ, mudutāya madditacammaṃ, kammaññatāya sudhantasuvaṇṇaṃ.

Furthermore, these should be understood as arising, in sequence, from conditions that are the counterpart to a disturbance of the elements that causes sluggishness of matter; from conditions that are the counterpart to a disturbance of the elements that causes rigidity of matter; and from conditions that are the counterpart to a disturbance of the elements that causes the unsuitability of matter for bodily actions. Herein, 'disturbance of the elements' means the aggravation of wind, bile, and phlegm, or the state of alteration of the elements such as nutritive essence. Though spoken of in two ways, in meaning it should be seen as simply the alteration of the earth element and so on. The counterpart conditions are suitable climate, food, and undistractedness of mind. And this is stated because it is a specific condition for this or that alteration, but in general it is a condition for all of them, for they never abandon one another. However, since the diversity among things that do not abandon one another is difficult to discern, to make this clear it is said, 'of these,' and so on. The connection is by way of examples in order. For lightness, a healthy person is the example; for softness, softened leather; for wieldiness, well-refined gold.

Nanu cettha arogino tāva nidassanaṃ yuttaṃ tassa indriyabaddhasantānattā, suparimadditacammasudhantasuvaṇṇānaṃ [V 2.0113] pana kathaṃ. Na hi anindriyabaddharūpasantāne lahutādīni sambhavanti tathā dhātukkhobhapaṭipakkhapaccayābhāvato? Saccaṃ, mudukammaññasadisarūpanidassanamattametaṃ, na pana tattha idhādhippetamudutākammaññatāsabhāvato. Yadi evaṃ, kathaṃ tūlapicuādīsu lahubhāvādikanti? Na tattha paramatthato lahubhāvādikaṃ atthi, garubhāvādihetūnaṃ pana abhāvato tattha lahubhāvādivohāro.

Now, is not the example of a healthy person appropriate here, because that is a continuum bound with faculties? But what about well-softened leather and well-refined gold? For lightness and so on do not arise in a material continuum unbound with faculties, owing to the absence of conditions that are the counterpart to a disturbance of the elements. True, this is merely an example of matter that is similar to soft and wieldy, but it is not due to the intrinsic nature of softness and wieldiness intended here. If so, how can there be lightness and so on in cotton, wool, and the like? In an ultimate sense, there is no lightness and so on there; but because of the absence of causes for heaviness and so on, the designation 'lightness,' etc., is used there.

Kammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti ekantena tāsaṃ paccuppannapaccayāpekkhattā, itarathā sabbadābhāvinīhi lahutādīhi bhavitabbaṃ siyāti. Adandhatālakkhaṇāti agarubhāvalakkhaṇā. Garubhāvassa vinodanaṃ khipanaṃ apanayanaṃ kiccametissāti garubhāvavinodanarasā. Kiñcāpi hi ayaṃ rūpānaṃ garubhāvaṃ vinodetuṃ na sakkoti, garurūpapaṭipakkhānaṃ pana adandharūpānaṃ vikārattā “jāti naṃ uppādetī”tiādīsu viya pariyāyena garubhāvaṃ vinodeti nāma. Tassañhi vijjamānāyaṃ uppannarūpānaṃ agarubhāvoyevāti. Esa nayo mudutākammaññatāsu. Cetasikalahutādayo pana attano attano paccanīkānaṃ taṃtaṃakusaladhammānaṃ viddhaṃsakabhāvena pavattantīti vikāramattabhāvato nippariyāyeneva tāsaṃ taṃkiccatā labbhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Lahuparivattitapaccupaṭṭhānāti adandhassa arogīpurisassa aparāparaṃ saṅkanti parivattanaṃ viya adandhaparivattanaṃ hutvā paccupaṭṭhānāti attho. Yassa rūpassa lahutā, tattheva [M 2.0154] vikārabhāvena upalabbhanato lahurūpapadaṭṭhānā. Evamitarāsupi. Athaddhatāti akathinatā. Attano mudubhāveneva sabbakiriyāsu aviruddhā hutvā paccupaṭṭhātīti avirodhitāpaccupaṭṭhānā. Mudu hi katthaci na virujjhati. Tīsupi ṭhānesu paṭipakkhatthe a-kāro. Dandhatādihetūnaṃ paṭipakkhasamuṭṭhānattā lahutādīnanti keci. Apare pana sattāpaṭisedheti vadanti. Sarīrena kattabbakiriyānaṃ anukūlatāsaṅkhāto kammaññabhāvo lakkhaṇametissāti sarīrakiriyānukūlakammaññabhāvalakkhaṇā. Akammaññaṃ dubbalaṃ nāma hotīti kammaññatā adubbalabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vuttā.

One cannot act absolutely, because of their dependence on presently-arisen conditions; otherwise, lightness, etc., would have to be always present. 'Having non-sluggishness as its characteristic' means having non-heaviness as its characteristic. 'Having the removal of heaviness as its function' means its task is the dispelling, casting out, and removal of the state of heaviness. For although this cannot remove the heaviness of material phenomena, it is said to remove heaviness indirectly, because it is an alteration of non-sluggish material phenomena, which are the counterpart to heavy material phenomena, just as in such phrases as 'birth produces it.' For when it is present, arisen material phenomena are indeed non-heavy. This is the method for softness and wieldiness as well. Mental lightness and so on, however, proceed by destroying their respective opposing unwholesome states; thus, as they are not merely an alteration, it should be seen that their function is obtained without any indirectness. 'Having quick change as its manifestation' means: it manifests by being a non-sluggish change, like the successive movement and change of a healthy, non-sluggish person. Because lightness is found as an alteration right in that matter of which it is the lightness, it has light matter as its proximate cause. The same applies to the others. 'Non-rigidity' means non-hardness. Because of its own softness, it manifests as unopposed in all activities; thus, it has non-opposition as its manifestation. For what is soft is not opposed anywhere. In all three places, the 'a-' prefix is in the sense of a counterpart. Some say that lightness, etc., arise as counterparts to the causes of sluggishness, etc. Others, however, say it negates attachment. 'Having the state of wieldiness, which is suitability for actions to be done by the body, as its characteristic.' Because what is unwieldy is called 'weak,' wieldiness is said to have non-weakness as its manifestation.

692. Rūpānamācayo yotiādīsu yo nipphannarūpānaṃ ādito cayo, yathāpaccayaṃ tato tato āgatassa viya cayoti vā ācayasaṅkhāto rūpānaṃ paṭhamuppādo vaḍḍhi ca, so upacayoti uddese vutto “upaññattaṃ upasitta”ntiādīsu viya upa-saddassa paṭhamūpariatthadassanato. Yā pana tesaṃyeva rūpānaṃ anuppabandhatā anuppabandhavasena pavatti, sā santatīti pavuccati. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe hi rūpuppattiādicayabhāvato ācayo nāma, tato paraṃ yāva [V 2.0114] sattarasamacittuppādā vaḍḍhibhāvato upacayo nāma. Tadā hi rūpassa kammacittautūhi cayoyeva, na hāni. Atha vā yāva āhārasamuṭṭhāna rūpuppādo, cakkhādiuppādo vā, tāva upacayo nāma, tato paraṃ pana cutipariyosānaṃ santati nāma. Evañca katvā –

692. In such phrases as 'what is the accumulation of matter,' that which is the initial accumulation of produced matter—or the first arising and increase of matter, designated as 'ācaya' (accumulation), like an accumulation of what has come from here and there according to conditions—is called 'upacaya' (growth) in the enumeration, because the prefix 'upa-' is seen to have the meaning of 'first' and 'superior,' as in 'upaññattaṃ' and 'upasittaṃ.' But the uninterruptedness of those same material phenomena, their proceeding by way of an unbroken bond, is called 'santati' (continuity). For at the moment of rebirth-linking, because it is the initial accumulation of the arising of matter, it is called 'ācaya.' From then on, until the seventeenth mind-moment, because it is a state of increase, it is called 'upacaya.' For at that time there is only accumulation of matter from kamma, mind, and temperature, not decline. Or, until the arising of matter produced by nutriment, or the arising of the eye faculty, and so on, it is called 'upacaya.' But from then on until its ending at death, it is called 'santati.' And so it is said:

“Yo āyatanānaṃ ācayo, so rūpassa upacayo. Yo rūpassa upacayo, sā rūpassa santatī”ti (dha. sa. 641-642) –

“Whatever is the accumulation of the bases, that is the growth of matter. Whatever is the growth of matter, that is the continuity of matter.” (Dhs. 641–642)

Evaṃ [M 2.0155] upacayasantatīnaṃ atthato nānattābhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttāya pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

In the commentary to the Pāli passage stated thus for the purpose of showing the absence of difference in meaning between growth and continuity—

“Ācayo nāma nibbatti, upacayo nāma vaḍḍhi, santati nāma pavattī”ti vatvā “nadītīre khatakūpasmiñhi udakuggamanakālo viya ācayo nibbatti, paripuṇṇakālo viya upacayo vaḍḍhi, ajjhottharitvā gamanakālo viya santati pavattī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 641; visuddhi. 2.444) –

“Accumulation is called arising, growth is called increase, continuity is called occurrence.” Having said this, “Just as the time of water rising in a pit dug on the riverbank is like accumulation being arising, the time when it is full is like growth being increase, and the time when it overflows and flows away is like continuity being occurrence.” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Aṭṭhakathā 641; Visuddhimagga 2.444)

Upamā vuttā. “Rūpānamācayo”ti cettha bahuvacananiddesena uppādo nāma uppajjamānānaṃ vikāro. Vikāratte ca sati attano vikāravantadhammabhedabhinnattā ekakkhaṇepi uppajjamānānaṃ bahūnampi rūpānaṃ visuṃ visuṃyeva uppādavikārabhāvo, na piṇḍassevāti dīpitaṃ hoti. Na kevalañca rūpānameva uppatti īdisī, atha kho arūpadhammānampi uppādo rūpārūpadhammānaṃ jaratā, aniccatā, rūpassa lahumudukammaññatā cāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

A simile is stated. “The accumulation of forms”—here, by the designation in the plural, origination means the alteration of those that are arising. And because there is alteration, due to the fact that phenomena which are subject to alteration are distinct from each other by difference, even in a single moment, the origination and alteration of many forms occur distinctly, not of a mass—this is shown. Not only is the arising of forms like this, but it should be understood that so too are the arising of formless phenomena, the aging of phenomena both with and without form, their impermanence, and the lightness, softness, and workability of form.

693. Jātirūpanti dīpitaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu ubhayassapi rūpuppādasabhāvattāti adhippāyo. Yadi evaṃ, kasmā vibhajja vuttaṃ? Bhagavatā tatheva desitattā. Bhagavatāpi kasmā tathā desitanti āha “vuttamākāranānattā”tiādi. Ākāranānattaṃ heṭṭhā vibhāvitameva. Akkharassa paṭhamuppatti upacayo, punappunaṃ uppatti santati. Evaṃ tisamuṭṭhānarūpānampi daṭṭhabbanti evaṃ tesaṃ ākāranānattaṃ vaṇṇenti. Veneyyānaṃ vasena vāti tadā kira sotūnaṃ evaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ, ayaṃ jāti sabbesaṃ dhammānaṃ pabhavo, sayaṃ pana na kutoci jāyati, yathā taṃ “pakativādīnaṃ pakatī”ti. Tesaṃ micchāgāhaṃ vidhamento “jāti nāma na aññā, upacayasantativasena ṭhitā rūpuppattiyeva [V 2.0115] pana tathā vuccati, sā ca yassa uppādo[M 2.0156], tassa paccayeheva jātapariyāyaṃ labbhatī”ti dassanatthaṃ upacayo santatīti dvidhā bhinditvā desetīti ācariyā.

693. The meaning is that 'jātirūpa' is explained in the commentaries as the intrinsic nature of the arising of form, which comprises both. If so, why was it stated separately? Because the Blessed One taught it that way. And why did the Blessed One teach it thus? It is said, 'due to the variety of ways,' and so on. The variety of ways has already been explained below. The first arising of a syllable is growth, and its repeated arising is continuity. Thus, it should be seen also for material phenomena arisen from the three causes, and in this way their variety of ways is described. Or, it is for the sake of those to be trained—for at that time, the listeners thought, 'This birth is the origin of all phenomena, yet it itself is not born from anywhere,' just like the 'primal source of the naturalists.' To dispel their wrong view, the teachers say that 'birth is nothing else; it is merely the arising of material phenomena established through growth and continuity that is so called. And that arising, of whatever it is the arising, obtains the designation 'born' only from its own conditions'—to show this, they divided it into two, growth and continuity, and taught it accordingly.

Pubbantato pubbakoṭṭhāsato, anāgatabhāvatoti attho. Uppajjamāne rūpadhamme uppādo anāgatakkhaṇato ummujjāpento viya hotīti vuttaṃ “ummujjāpanaraso”ti. “Ime rūpadhammā sampaṭicchatha ne”ti niyyātento viya gayhatīti vuttaṃ “niyyātanapaccupaṭṭhāno”ti. Paripuṇṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānatā upari cayo upacayoti imassa atthassa vasena veditabbā. Yathā uppādakkhaṇappattaṃ uppannaṃ nāma hoti ādikamme tappaccayavasena, evaṃ uppādakkhaṇagataṃ upacitaṃ nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “upacitarūpapadaṭṭhāno”ti.

From the prior end, from the prior portion, meaning from the state of not yet having come into being. When a material phenomenon is arising, arising is as if causing it to emerge from the future moment—hence it is said, 'its characteristic function is to cause emergence.' It is grasped as if handing over, saying, “Accept these material phenomena!”—hence it is said, 'its manifestation is offering.' The manifestation as a state of completion should be understood according to the meaning of 'upacaya' as 'piling up upon.' Just as what has reached the moment of arising is called 'arisen' in the initial action due to its conditions, so what has reached the moment of arising is called 'accumulated'—hence it is said, 'its proximate cause is accumulated form.'

Pavattilakkhaṇāti anuppabandhato uppattivasena pavattamānarūpānaṃ pavattananti lakkhitabbā. Anuppabandhanarasāti pubbāparavasena anuppabandhanakiccā. Asati hi uppāde pubbāparavasena anuppabandho na siyā. Anuppabandharasattāyeva anupacchedavasena gahetabbato āha “anupacchedapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti. Pubbāparavasena ghaṭitarūpesu upalabbhanato vuttaṃ “anuppabandharūpapadaṭṭhānā”ti.

Having the characteristic of occurrence means it should be characterized as the occurrence of material phenomena that occur by way of arising as an unbroken series. Having the characteristic function of continuity means its function is continuity in terms of what precedes and what follows. For if there were no arising, there would be no continuity in terms of what precedes and what follows. Because its characteristic function is continuity, it should be grasped as non-severance—hence it is said, 'its manifestation is non-severance.' Since it is found in material phenomena connected in terms of what precedes and what follows, it is said, 'its proximate cause is continuous material phenomena.'

694. Jīraṇanti jiṇṇabhāvo, abhinavabhāvahānīti attho.

694. “Aging” means the state of being worn out, the loss of freshness—this is the meaning.

Pākaṭā rūpadhammesu khaṇḍiccādibhāvena dantādīsu vikāradassanato, itarā tadabhāvato apākaṭā. Kāmaṃ rūpadhammānampi khaṇikajarā paṭicchannā eva, yā “avīcijarā”ti vā vuccati. Arūpadhammānaṃ pana jarāya suṭṭhu paṭicchannabhāvadassanatthaṃ “pākaṭā rūpadhammesū”ti avisesena vuttaṃ. Khaṇḍiccādivikāro pana khaṇikajarāya natthi. Rūpaparipāko rūpadhammānaṃ jiṇṇatā, jaraṃ pattassa bhaṅgo avassaṃbhāvīti vuttaṃ [M 2.0157] “upanayanarasā”ti, bhaṅgūpanayanakiccāti attho. Sabhāvānapagamepītikakkhaḷattādisabhāvānapagamepi, ṭhitikkhaṇe hi jarā nāma, na ca tadā dhammasabhāvaṃ vijahati. Navabhāvo uppādāvatthā, tassā apagamabhāvena gayhatīti āha “navabhāvāpagamapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti. Vīhipurāṇabhāvo viyāti vīhibhāvānapagamepi abhinavabhāvāpagamanakaro vīhipurāṇabhāvo viya. Vīhipurāṇabhāvo sabbāvatthāni apaneti, ayaṃ pana kevalaṃ uppādāvatthameva apaneti. Parito sabbato bhijjananti lakkhitabbāti paribhedalakkhaṇā[V 2.0116]. Niccaṃ nāma dhuvaṃ, rūpaṃ pana khaṇabhaṅgitāya na niccanti aniccaṃ, tassa bhāvo aniccatā. Sā pana ṭhitippattarūpaṃ ṭhitiyameva vināsanabhāvena saṃsīdentī viya hotīti saṃsīdanarasā. Yasmā ca sā bhaṅgabhāvato khayavayākāreneva gayhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “khayavayabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti. Anukkamena vināso khayo nāma, dīpavaṭṭikāya saha telassa viya saha nirodho vayoti vadanti.

It is manifest in material phenomena through the state of brokenness and so on, due to seeing the alteration in teeth and the like; for the other (i.e., aging of immaterial phenomena), it is not manifest due to the absence of that. Indeed, even for material phenomena, momentary aging is concealed, which is also called “incessant aging.” But to show that the aging of immaterial phenomena is very well concealed, it was stated without distinction, “It is manifest in material phenomena.” However, the alteration such as brokenness does not exist for momentary aging. The ripening of material form is the aging of material phenomena. Because the destruction of that which has reached aging is inevitable, it is said, “its characteristic function is to lead towards,” meaning its function is to lead towards destruction. “Even when the intrinsic nature does not depart”—even when the intrinsic nature of hardness and so on does not depart. For aging occurs in the moment of presence, and at that time it does not abandon the intrinsic nature of the phenomenon. The new state is the state of arising; it is grasped as the state of the departure of that—hence it is said, “its manifestation is the departure of the new state.” It is like the oldness of rice: like the oldness of rice which causes the departure of the fresh state even while the nature of rice does not depart. The oldness of rice removes all states, but this (aging) only removes the state of arising. It should be characterized as breaking up all around—thus, it has the characteristic of disintegration. “Permanent” means fixed. But since material form is not permanent due to its momentary destruction, it is impermanent; its state is impermanence. And that, having reached the moment of presence, is as if it causes the material form to sink down with a state of destruction in its very presence—thus, its characteristic function is to cause sinking down. And because it is grasped in the manner of decay and vanishing, which is a state of destruction, it is said, “its manifestation is the state of decay and vanishing.” Destruction in sequence is called decay; cessation together, like that of a lamp’s wick along with the oil, is called vanishing, they say.

696-7. Samodhānatoti rāsito. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino. Middharūpassa vadanasīlā, middhavādo vā etesanti middhavādino. Middharūpaṃ nāmāti utucittāhāravasena tisamuṭṭhānaṃ middhaṃ nāma rūpaṃ. Te paṭikkhipitabbāti sambandho. Kathaṃ paṭikkhipitabbāti āha “munīsī”tiādi. Natthi nīvaraṇāti sotāpattimaggena vicikicchānīvaraṇassa, anāgāmimaggena kāmacchandabyāpādakukkuccanīvaraṇānaṃ, arahattamaggena thinamiddhanīvaraṇānañca pahīnattā. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – yadi middhaṃ rūpaṃ siyā, appahātabbaṃ bhaveyya. Rūpakkhandho abhiññeyyo pariññeyyo na pahātabbo na bhāvetabbo na sacchikātabbo. “Katame dhammā nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbā. Catūsu bhūmīsu kusalaṃ, catūsu bhūmīsu [M 2.0158] vipāko, tīsu bhūmīsu kiriyābyākataṃ, rūpañca nibbānañca, ime dhammā nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbā”ti (dha. sa. 1407) vacanena rūpadhammānaṃ pahānābhāvato. Evañca sati tassa nīvaraṇabhāvo virujjheyya nīvaraṇānaṃ pahātabbattā. Na hi nīvaraṇānaṃ appahātabbatte –

`Samodhānato` means from accumulation. `Kecīti` refers to the Abhayagiri residents. `Middharūpassa vadanasīlā`, they are prone to speaking about material drowsiness, or `middhavādo vā etesanti middhavādino`, they hold the doctrine of material drowsiness. `Middharūpaṃ nāmāti` refers to material drowsiness, which is so-called drowsiness arisen from the three causes of temperature, mind, and food. The connection is that they should be refuted. As to how they should be refuted, it is said, `munīsī`, etc. `There are no hindrances for you` means because the hindrance of doubt is abandoned by the path of stream-entry, the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, and remorse by the path of non-returning, and the hindrance of sloth and torpor by the path of arahantship. The meaning here is this: if drowsiness were a material phenomenon, it would be something not to be abandoned. The aggregate of material form is to be directly known and fully understood, not abandoned, not developed, not realized. By the statement, “Which things are not to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation? The wholesome in the four planes, the resultant in the four planes, the functional indeterminate in the three planes, and material form and Nibbāna—these things are not to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1407), it is shown that material phenomena are not to be abandoned. This being so, its nature as a hindrance would be contradicted, because hindrances are to be abandoned. For there is no state of hindrances not being things to be abandoned—

“Yā me kaṅkhā pure āsi, taṃ me akkhāsi cakkhumā;

Addhā munīsi sambuddho, natthi nīvaraṇā tavā”ti. (su. ni. 546) –

“The doubt that I had before, the one with the Eye has explained it to me. Truly, you are a sage, a fully awakened one; there are no hindrances for you.” (Suttanipāta 546)

Nīvaraṇappahānena bhagavato thomanaṃ yujjeyya. Yadi siyā, “rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahathātiādivacanato (ma. ni. 1.247; saṃ. ni. 3.33-34) rūpassa pahātabbatāpi paññāyatīti? Taṃ na, tabbisayachandarāgappahānassa tattha adhippetattā. Tenāha bhagavā “yo, bhikkhave, rūpe chandarāgavinayo, taṃ tattha pahāna”nti. Na ca panetaṃ na sakkā vattuṃ etthāpi “tabbisayachandarāgappahānavaseneva vutta”nti sādhakavacanabhāvato, kāmacchandādīnaṃ tattha pahānassa anadhippetattā ca, tasmā “natthi nīvaraṇā tavā”tiādivacanehi virujjhanato na middhaṃ rūpanti.

The abandonment of hindrances would be a fitting praise of the Blessed One. If it were said, “Monks, form is not yours, abandon it,” and so forth (Majjhima Nikāya 1.247; Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.33-34), would the abandonability of form also be understood? That is not so, because the intention there is the abandonment of desire and lust related to that object. Therefore, the Blessed One said, “Monks, whatever is the removal of desire and lust for form, that is its abandonment.” Nor can it be said that here also, “it is spoken of merely in terms of the abandonment of desire and lust related to that object,” because of the confirmatory nature of the statement, and because the abandonment of sensual desire and the like is not intended there; therefore, since it contradicts statements such as, “There are no hindrances for you,” torpor is not form.

Yadi [V 2.0117] pana paro daḷhamūḷhaggāhitāya taṃvisayachandarāgappahānavaseneva nīvaraṇappahānaṃ adhippetanti sakavādaṃ oḍḍeyya, tassa tannisedhanatthaṃ puna thinamiddhanīvaraṇassa avijjānīvaraṇena saha sampayogavacanañca āharanto āha “thinamiddhanīvaraṇa”ntiādi. Thinamiddhanīvaraṇañceva avijjānīvaraṇañca nīvaraṇena sampayuttanti sambandho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “catūhi sampayogo”ti (dhātu. 3) vacanato arūpadhammānameva aññamaññassa sampayogo labbhati, na rūpadhammānaṃ aññamaññaṃ arūpena vā, tasmā yadi middhaṃ rūpaṃ siyā, na taṃ sampayogavacanamarahatīti. Atha siyā – yathālābhavacanamettha sakkā [M 2.0159] viññātuṃ, “sakkharakathalampi macchagumbampi carantampi tiṭṭhantampī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.249) viya. Yathā hi “sakkharakathalikaṃ macchagumbampi carantampi tiṭṭhantampī”tiādīsu sakkharakathalikassa caraṇāyogato macchagumbāpekkhāya caraṇaṃ, ubhayāpekkhāya ṭhānanti evaṃ yathālābho yojīyati, evamidhāpi thināpekkhāya sampayogavacanaṃ, ubhayāpekkhāya nīvaraṇavacananti? Tampi na, rūpabhāvasseva asiddhattā. Siddhe hi rūpabhāve asambhavato yathālābhayojanā yujjeyyāti. Ettakeneva middhassa arūpabhāve siddhepi yathā dvikkhattuṃ bandhaṃ subandhaṃ hoti, evamanekasuttasādhitaṃ appadhaṃsiyaṃ hotīti paṭṭhānappakaraṇe “nīvaraṇaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca…pe… paccayā”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.8.8) imassa vibhaṅge “arūpe…pe… uppajjatī”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.8.8) vuttaṃ arūpabhavuppattimpi āharanto āha “mahāpakaraṇapaṭṭhāne”tiādi. Jhānanikantiādīnampi dhammato lobhādibhāvato kāmacchandanīvaraṇādīhi abhinnattā vuttaṃ “kāmacchandanīvaraṇa”ntiādi.

If another person, due to a firm and deluded grasp, were to advance their own theory that the abandonment of hindrances is intended only in the sense of relinquishing desire and lust concerning that object, then to refute that, the text brings forward the statement about the association of the hindrance of sloth and torpor with the hindrance of ignorance, saying, “the hindrance of sloth and torpor,” and so on. The connection is that the hindrance of sloth and torpor and the hindrance of ignorance are associated as hindrances. This is what is meant: according to the statement, “Association is of four kinds” (Dhātukathā 3), it is understood that only immaterial phenomena can be mutually associated, not material phenomena with each other or with immaterial phenomena. Therefore, if torpor were material, it would not be fit for the term “association.” Then it might be said that here the meaning can be understood distributively, as in such phrases as, “a gravel bank and a school of fish, whether moving or standing” (Dīgha Nikāya 1.249). For just as in “a gravel bank and a school of fish, whether moving or standing,” since a gravel bank cannot move, “moving” is applied with reference to the school of fish, and “standing” with reference to both, thus it is applied distributively; similarly, here too, could the term “association” be applied with reference to sloth, and the term “hindrance” with reference to both? But this too is not valid, because its material nature has not been established. For if its material nature were established, then due to the impossibility of association, a distributive application would be fitting. Although the immaterial nature of torpor is established by this much, just as a knot tied twice becomes very secure, so too a point established by many suttas becomes unassailable. Thus, citing the arising in the immaterial existence mentioned in the Paṭṭhāna, the great treatise, where in the analysis of the passage, “In dependence on a hindrance condition…” (Paṭṭhāna 3.8.8), it is said, “in the immaterial… it arises…” (Paṭṭhāna 3.8.8), the text says, “in the great treatise Paṭṭhāna,” and so on. Since delight in jhāna and so on are, by their nature, forms of greed and so on, they are not different from the hindrance of sensual desire and so on; hence it is said, “the hindrance of sensual desire,” and so on.

Ettha siyā – “pañcime, bhikkhave, āvaraṇā nīvaraṇā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.51) thinamiddhassa nīvaraṇabhāvena ekato āgatattā idhāpi “thinamiddhanīvaraṇa”nti ekato vuttaṃ, thinameva ca pana arūpabhave uppajjati thinamiddhanti? Tayidamasāraṃ, kukkuccassa na gahitattā. Yadi hi ekato gahitamatteneva idhāpi ekato gahaṇaṃ siyā, kukkuccassapi tattha ekato vuttassa idha gahaṇaṃ sambhaveyya, na ca panevaṃ atthi uddhaccanīvaraṇantveva vuttattā, tasmā na tassa arūpabhavuppattiṃ sakkā paṭibāhitunti. Ādi-saddena “kevalo hāyaṃ, bhikkhave, akusalarāsi, yadidaṃ pañca nīvaraṇā (a. ni. 5.52), ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya, vigatathinamiddhoti tassa thinamiddhassa cattattā [M 2.0160] vantattā muttattā pahīnattā paṭinissaṭṭhattā, tena vuccati vigatathinamiddhoti, idaṃ cittaṃ imamhā thinamiddhamhā [V 2.0118] sodheti visodheti parisodheti moceti vimoceti parimoceti vā”ti (vibha. 551) evamādiṃ pāḷiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

Here it might be said: In passages such as, “Monks, these five are coverings, hindrances…” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.51), since sloth and torpor are presented together as a hindrance, here too they are spoken of together as “the hindrance of sloth and torpor.” But is it only sloth that arises in the formless existence, referred to as “sloth-torpor”? This is unsound, because worry is not included. For if their being mentioned together there were sufficient reason for them to be mentioned together here, then worry, which is also mentioned together with restlessness there, would be included here. But this is not the case, as only the hindrance of restlessness is mentioned. Therefore, the arising of torpor in the formless existence cannot be blocked. The word “etc.” includes such Pāli passages as: “Monks, this is entirely a mass of the unwholesome, that is, the five hindrances” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.52); “Having abandoned these five hindrances, one is free from sloth and torpor”—because that sloth and torpor has been given up, relinquished, released, abandoned, and cast off, one is said to be free from sloth and torpor; “This mind is cleansed, purified, completely purified, freed, completely freed, and thoroughly freed from this sloth and torpor” (Vibhaṅga 551), and so on.

Yadipi siyā duvidhaṃ middhaṃ rūpaṃ, arūpañca. Tattha yaṃ arūpaṃ, taṃ nīvaraṇesu desitaṃ, na rūpanti? Tampi na, visesavacanābhāvato. Na hi visesetvā middhaṃ nīvaraṇesu desitaṃ “yadapi, bhikkhave, thinaṃ, tadapi nīvaraṇaṃ, yadapi middhaṃ, tadapi nīvaraṇaṃ, thinamiddhaṃ nīvaraṇanti iti hidaṃ uddesaṃ āgacchatī”ti avisesena vuttattā, tasmā middhassa duvidhataṃ parikappetvāpi na sakkā nīvaraṇabhāvaṃ nivattetuṃ. Sakkā hi vattuṃ yaṃ taṃ arūpato aññaṃ middhaṃ parikappitaṃ, tampi nīvaraṇaṃ middhasabhāvattā itaraṃ nīvaraṇaṃ viyāti. Yadi middhassa rūpabhāvaṃ na sampaṭicchatha, kathaṃ bhagavato niddā hoti, nanu middhassa “niddā pacalāyikā”tiādinā vibhaṅge vuttattā niddābhāvo siddhoti? Nayidamevaṃ, itthiliṅgādīsu viya niddāhetuno middhassa niddābhāvena vibhattattā. Evampi niddāhetuno middhassa abhāvato kathaṃ bhagavato niddāti ce? Sā bhagavato natthīti na sakkā vattuṃ “abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ aggivessana…pe… divā supitā”tiādivacanato (ma. ni. 1.387) na niddā bhagavato middhena, atha kho sarīragelaññena, tañca bhagavato natthīti na sakkā vattuṃ “piṭṭhi me āgilāyati, tamahaṃ āyamissāmī”ti (ma. ni. 2.22; saṃ. ni. 4.243) vacanato. Na cettha evamavadhāraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “middhameva niddāhetū”ti, tasmā aññopi atthi niddāhetu. Ko pana soti? Sarīragelaññaṃ, tasmā na bhagavato niddā middhahetukāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

What if torpor were twofold—material and immaterial—and the immaterial part is taught in the hindrances, but not the material part? That too is not so, because there is no distinguishing statement. For torpor is not taught in the hindrances with any specification, since it is stated without distinction: “Whatever, monks, is sloth, that too is a hindrance; whatever is torpor, that too is a hindrance; the hindrance of sloth and torpor—thus this comes into the summary.” Therefore, even by positing a twofold nature for torpor, its status as a hindrance cannot be averted. For it could be said that any other torpor conceived apart from the immaterial is also a hindrance because it has the nature of torpor, just like the other hindrance. If you do not accept the material nature of torpor, how then does the Blessed One sleep? Is it not established that torpor is the state of sleep, as stated in the Vibhaṅga: “Sleep is drowsiness”? This is not so, for sleep is analyzed as having torpor as its cause. If it is asked, “Even so, since the Blessed One is without torpor as a cause of sleep, how does he sleep?” It cannot be said that the Blessed One does not have sleep, because of the statement, “I recall, Aggivessana… having slept during the day.” The Blessed One’s sleep is not from torpor, but from bodily fatigue. And it cannot be said that the Blessed One did not have that, because of the statement, “My back is aching; I will stretch it.” And here it should not be understood as an exclusive statement that “torpor alone is the cause of sleep.” Therefore, there is another cause of sleep. What is it? Bodily fatigue. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One’s sleep is not caused by torpor.

698. Visuṃ visuṃ abhāvaṃ dassetvāti vāyodhātuādito visuṃ visuṃ natthibhāvaṃ dassetvā. Kathaṃ pana so dassitabboti [M 2.0161] āha “vāyodhātuyā”tiādi. Tattha kāyabalaṃ nāma atthato vāyodhātuyā pavattiākāraviseso tassā vipphārabhāvato. Yato bālānaṃ balanti vadantīti vuttaṃ “vāyodhātuyā gahitāya balarūpaṃ gahitamevā”ti. Sambhavo kāmadhātuyaṃ ekaccasattānaṃ indriyaparipākapaccayo āpodhātuyā pavattiākāravisesoti āha “āpodhātuyā sambhavarūpa”nti. Gahitāya gahitamevāti sambandho. Upacayasantativinimutto rūpuppādo natthi, uppādāvatthāya ca aññā jāti nāma natthevāti vuttaṃ “upacayasantatīhi jātirūpa”nti. Kammasamuṭṭhānassapi rogassa visabhāgapaccayasamuppanno dhātukkhobho āsannakāraṇaṃ[V 2.0119], pageva itarassa. So atthato rūpadhammānaṃ pākāvatthā ṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇesu eva siyāti vuttaṃ “jaratāaniccatādīhi rogarūpaṃ gahita”nti.

698. To show the non-existence of each individually—that is, to show the separate non-existence of each, beginning with the air element. But how should this be shown? It is explained with the phrase 'by the air element,' etc. Herein, bodily strength is, in essence, a particular mode of occurrence of the air element, due to its expansive nature. Since it is said that fools speak of strength, it is stated: 'When the air element is grasped, the form of strength is grasped.' Generation, the condition for the maturation of faculties in some beings of the sense-sphere, is a particular mode of occurrence of the water element—thus it is said: 'By the water element, the form of generation is grasped.' When it is grasped, it is indeed grasped—this is the connection. Without accumulation and continuity, the arising of form does not exist, and for the state of arising, there is no other birth—thus it is said: 'By accumulation and continuity, the form of birth is grasped.' For an illness produced by kamma, the disturbance of elements arising from incompatible conditions is a proximate cause, let alone for another kind of illness. In essence, this disturbance would be the state of ripening of material phenomena at the moments of stability and dissolution—thus it is said: 'By decay, impermanence, and so forth, the form of illness is grasped.'

699-704. Rūpāni samuṭṭhahanti jāyanti etehīti rūpasamuṭṭhānāni. Kāni pana tānīti āha “utucittāhārakammānī”ti.

699-704. Forms arise, are produced from these—thus they are the origins of form. But what are those? He says: 'Temperature, mind, nutriment, and kamma.'

Āhāro rūpahetuyoti ettha iti-saddo pakkhipitabbo, kammaṃ, utu ca cittañca āhāroti ime rūpahetuyoti. Rūpahetuyoti ca rūpassa janakapaccayāti attho. Tenāha “etehevā”tiādi. Ekamekaṃyeva samuṭṭhānaṃ etesanti ekasamuṭṭhānā. Nanu ekato eva paccayato paccayuppannassa uppatti natthīti? Saccaṃ natthi, rūpajanakapaccayesu ekatoti ayamettha abhisandhi. Aṭṭhindriyānīti cakkhādīni pañca, itthipurisindriyadvayaṃ, jīvitañcāti aṭṭhindriyāni. Kāyavacīviññattivasena viññattidvayaṃ.

In 'Nutriment is a cause of form,' the word 'iti' should be inserted, so that it reads: kamma, temperature, mind, and nutriment—these are the causes of form. 'Causes of form' means the generative conditions for form. Therefore, he says, 'By these alone,' etc. Their origin is each single one—thus they are single-origined. But is there not an arising of a conditionally arisen phenomenon from just a single condition? Truly, there is not. Here, the intention is that 'from one' refers to one among the generative conditions of form. The eight faculties are the five beginning with the eye, the two sex faculties, and the life faculty. The two intimations are bodily and verbal intimation.

Dvīhīti [M 2.0162] koci cittena, koci utunā cāti evaṃ dvīhi. Na hi ekasseva dve ekakkhaṇe paccayā honti. Evaṃ sesesupi. Utuāhāra…pe… katanti ekekaṃ utunā, āhārena, cittena cāti tīhi kataṃ. Catasso cāpi dhātuyoti cattāri mahābhūtāni. Tāni hi nissattanijjīvaṭṭhena dhātūti vuccanti. Kammādīhi catūhi bhavantīti catubbhavā. Dveti jaratā aniccatā.

By two—some by mind, some by temperature—thus by two. Indeed, two conditions do not occur for a single thing at one moment. Thus it is with the rest also. Temperature, nutriment... done—each done by temperature, by nutriment, and by mind—thus done by three. And the four elements—the four great elements. For these are called 'elements' in the sense of being without a living essence and without life. They arise from four things, such as kamma—thus having four origins. Two—decay and impermanence.

705-6. Idāni missakasamuṭṭhānānipi gahetvā taṃtaṃpaccayajātānaṃ gaṇanaparicchedaṃ dassetuṃ “kammenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha aṭṭhindriyāni vatthu suddhaṭṭhakaṃ santatyūpacayākāsāti vīsati kammajā. Viññattidvayaṃ saddo lahutādittayaṃ suddhaṭṭhakādayo ekādasāti sattarasa cetasā jāyare, cittajāti attho. Saddo lahutādittayaṃ suddhaṭṭhakādayo ekādasāti dasapañceva pannarasa utunā jāyare. Lahutādittayaṃ suddhaṭṭhakādayo ekādasāti cuddasa āhārato. Jaratāaniccatāhi te aṭṭhasaṭṭhi ca hontevāti sambandho.

705-6. Now, to show the numerical determination of phenomena arising from their respective conditions, having also included the mixed origins, the passage beginning with 'by kamma' is stated. Herein, the eight faculties, the base, the pure octad, continuity, accumulation, and space—these twenty are kamma-produced. The two kinds of intimation, sound, the triad beginning with lightness (lightness, pliancy, and adaptability), and the eleven comprising the pure octad and others—totaling seventeen—are born of mind; this is the meaning of 'cittaja'. Sound, the triad beginning with lightness, and the eleven comprising the pure octad and others—totaling fifteen—are born of temperature. The triad beginning with lightness, and the eleven comprising the pure octad and others—totaling fourteen—are from nutriment. With decay and impermanence, those phenomena become sixty-eight—this is the connection.

707-8. “Jaratā…pe… samuṭṭhitā”ti vatvā puna tattha kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “jātassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha jātassa pākabhedattāti jaratāya jātadhammassa pākattā, aniccatāya [V 2.0120] ca bhedattāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – jaratāaniccatā nāma uppannadhammassa honti, no uppajjamānassa. Yadi hi uppajjamānassa siyuṃ, tadā tāsampi jāyamānattapariyāyo yujjeyya. Uppannadhammassa pana jātito paraṃ imāsaṃ sambhavato na jāyantīti vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti. Yadi pana koci tesampi jātabhāve ko virodhoti paṭipajjeyya, tassa taṃ duggāhaṃ vidhamento āha “jāyeyyu”ntiādi. Hontu nāma tesampi pākabhedā[M 2.0163], tadāpi ko virodhoti āha “na hī”tiādi. Pāko na paripaccatīti sambandho, etena na bhijjatīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Pakkassa hi bhaṅgo niyato. Bhedo vā na ca bhijjatīti etthāpi pākabhāvopi vuttova. Na hi apakkaṃ bhijjatīti, aññathā uppādabhaṅgānaṃ anaññattappasaṅgato. Natthi tanti pākabhedānaṃ paccanaṃ bhijjanaṃ natthīti vuttamevatthaṃ saṅkhipitvā āha.

707-8. Having stated 'decay...arisen,' to further show the reason there, the passage beginning 'of what is born' was said. Here, 'due to the maturation and dissolution of what is born' means that decay is due to the maturation of a born phenomenon, and impermanence is due to its dissolution. This is what is meant: Decay and impermanence belong to a phenomenon that has arisen, not to one that is arising. If they belonged to what is arising, then the term 'arising' would also be applicable to them. But since these are possible for a phenomenon after it is born, it is proper to say they do not arise. If someone were to object, 'What contradiction is there if those also have the nature of being born?', countering that misunderstanding, he said 'They might arise...' Even if they were to have maturation and dissolution, what contradiction would there be? He said 'Not so...' 'Maturation does not ripen' is the connection; by this, 'it does not break' is explained. For the breaking of what is ripe is inevitable. Or, in 'dissolution, and it does not break,' here too, the state of maturation is already stated. For what is unripe does not break; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of the non-difference between arising and dissolution. 'There is not'—he states this, summarizing the meaning that there is no ripening or breaking of ripening and breaking themselves.

Ettāvatā ca kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yadi jaratāaniccatā kenaci paccayena jāyeyyuṃ, tadā uppannassa nāma jarāya, bhaṅgena ca bhavitabbanti tesaṃ jaratāaniccatāpi siyuṃ, na ca panetā upalabbhanti. Kasmā? Yasmā na jaratā aññajarāya jīrati, bhijjati vā, na ca bhaṅgo aññena bhaṅgena bhijjati, jīrati vā, itarathā sāpi jarā aparāya jarāya, bhaṅgena ca jīrati, bhijjati, so ca bhaṅgo aññāya jarāya, aññena bhaṅgena jīrati, bhijjatīti anavaṭṭhānappasaṅgatoti vuttaṃ hoti.

And what is said by this? If decay and impermanence were to arise from any condition, then since it is necessary for what has arisen to have decay and dissolution, those themselves would also have decay and impermanence—but these are not found. Why? Because decay does not decay or break by another decay, nor does dissolution break or decay by another dissolution. Otherwise, that decay would decay and break by another decay and dissolution, and that dissolution would decay and break by another decay and another dissolution—leading to the consequence of an infinite regress. Thus it is said.

709-10. “Jātassā”tiādi nigamanaṃ. Atha vā uttari vattabbacodanāya phalaṭhapanaṃ. “Siyā katthacī”tiādi paramatāsaṅkanaṃ. Etthāti etasmiṃ “jaratāaniccatādvayaṃ na paccati, na bhijjati vā”ti adhikāre. Rūpassūpacayotīti iti-saddo ādiattho, tena “rūpassa upacayo santatī”ti vacanenāti attho. Evaṃ pākopi paccatu, bhedopi paribhijjatūti sambandho. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – yathā kammādīhi uppajjanakarūpaniddese “katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ upādinnaṃ? Cakkhāyatanaṃ…pe… kāyāyatanaṃ itthindriyaṃ purisindriyaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi atthi rūpaṃ kammassa katattā rūpāyatanaṃ…pe… phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ ākāsadhātu rūpassa upacayo rūpassa santati kabaḷīkāro āhāro”tiādinā (dha. sa. 652) upacayasantatīnaṃ niddiṭṭhattā jāti [M 2.0164] jāyatīti dīpitaṃ hoti tassā aparajātiyā abhāvepi. Evaṃ jarābhaṅgānaṃ aparajarābhaṅgābhāvepi jīraṇaṃ, bhijjanañca sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, itarathā jātiyāpi bhedanā tadavatthāyevāti.

709-10. The passage beginning 'Of what is born' is the conclusion. Or, alternatively, it is the establishing of the result in response to further questioning. The passage beginning 'Could it be anywhere?' raises a doubt concerning another's view. 'Here' means in this context of 'the pair, decay and impermanence, does not ripen or break.' In the phrase `Rūpassūpacayoti` (the accumulation of form), the particle `iti` has the sense of 'etc.', by which the meaning is 'by the statement "the accumulation of form, the continuity of form."' Thus, 'let ripening also ripen, and let dissolution also break apart'—this is the connection. The intended meaning here is this: just as in the description of form arising from kamma and so on, it is said, 'What is that clung-to form? The eye-base… the body-base, the femininity faculty, the masculinity faculty, the life faculty, or whatever other form there is, produced by kamma… the tangible-base, the space element, the accumulation of form, the continuity of form, edible food,' and so on (Dhs. 652). Since accumulation and continuity are specified, it is shown that birth is born, even in the absence of a subsequent birth for it. Similarly, decaying and breaking should be accepted for decay and dissolution, even in the absence of subsequent decay and dissolution for them. Otherwise, since birth would also be a breaking, the situation would be the same.

711. “Na [V 2.0121] cevā”tiādi yathāsaṅkitaparamatassa paṭikkhipanaṃ. Yadi jāyatīti na viññātabbaṃ, evañca sati niddese kasmā vuttanti āha “jāyamānassā”tiādi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – asatipi jātiyā jāyamānatte jāyamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhinibbattibhāvato tassā tappaccayabhāvavohāro anumatoti tattha vuttā, na pana paramatthato jāyamānattā. Jāyamānassa hi abhinibbattimattaṃ jāti, tasmā asiddhena asiddhasādhanametanti.

711. The passage beginning 'Not indeed' is a refutation of the other's view as previously conjectured. If 'it is born' is not to be understood, then why is it stated in the exposition? He answers with the passage beginning 'of that which is being born.' This is what is meant: even though birth itself does not have the nature of being born, the conventional expression of its conditionality is permitted due to the manifestation of phenomena that are being born, and so it is stated there—but not because it is, in an ultimate sense, being born. For birth is merely the manifestation of what is being born; therefore, this is proving the unproven by means of the unproven.

712-7. “Tatthā”tiādinā punapi paramatāsaṅkaṃ katvā paṭikkhipati. Tattha yesaṃ dhammānaṃ yā jāti, sā tappaccayattavohāraṃ, abhinibbattisammutiñca labhatevāti sambandho. Tathāti yathā labhateva, tathā. Yaṃtaṃ-saddā hi abyabhicāritasambandhā. Tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paccayā etissāti tappaccayā, tassā bhāvo tappaccayattaṃ, tappaccayattena pavatto vohāro tappaccayattavohāro, taṃ kammapaccayabhāvādivohāranti attho. Abhinibbattisammutinti abhinibbattati jāyatīti evaṃ abhinibbattivasena pavattasammutiṃ. Kammādisambhavanti kammādicatupaccayasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Janakānaṃ paccayānaṃ ānubhāvakkhaṇuppāde abhāvatoti sambandho. Ayaṃ panettha attho – ye te rūpānaṃ janakapaccayā, tesaṃ taduppādanaṃ pati anuparatabyāpārānaṃ yo so paccayūpalakkhaṇiyo kiccānubhāvakkhaṇo, tadā jāyamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ vikārabhāvena labbhamānataṃ sandhāya vineyyapuggalavasena jātiyā paccayato jātattaṃ anuññātaṃ tato pure[M 2.0165], pacchā ca anupalabbhamānattā, evañca katvā vuttaṃ “jātiyā pana labbhatī”ti. Jarābhaṅgānaṃ pana paccayānubhāvakkhaṇato uttari ṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇesu labbhamānattā na evaṃ anuññātuṃ sakkāti, jātiyā pana labbhati so vohāroti adhippāyo. Tappaccayattavohārantiādigāthādvayaṃ nigamanavasena vuttaṃ.

By 'In that context,' and so on, he again refutes, having raised a doubt concerning another's view. There, whatever birth there is of those phenomena, that indeed obtains the conventional expression of conditionality and the conventional designation of manifestation—this is the connection. Thus: just as it is obtained, so it is. For the words 'that which' (yaṃ taṃ) indeed indicate an unfailing connection. For those phenomena, 'conditioned by that' means 'having that as condition'; the state of having that as condition is 'conditionality'; the conventional expression proceeding by way of conditionality is 'the conventional expression of conditionality.' This means the conventional expression of the state of being conditioned by kamma, and so on. 'Conventional designation of manifestation' means the conventional designation that proceeds by way of manifestation, i.e., 'it manifests, it arises.' 'Originating from kamma, etc.' means arising from the four conditions, such as kamma. The connection is: 'due to absence at the arising of the moment of the power of the generative conditions.' Here, the meaning is this: With reference to the generative conditions of material phenomena, the state of being born from conditions is permitted for the sake of teachable individuals, by taking into account the fact that phenomena which are being born are obtained as transformations at that moment—the moment of the influence of the function, which is characterized by the conditions, whose activity in producing those phenomena is unceasing. This is because these phenomena are unobservable before and after that moment; and thus it was stated: 'But it is obtained through birth.' However, for aging and dissolution, because they are obtained beyond the moment of the influence of conditions—during the moments of stability and dissolution—it is not possible to permit them in the same way. The intention is that that conventional expression is obtained through birth. The two verses beginning with 'the conventional expression of conditionality' are stated by way of conclusion.

718-9. Atha kiṃ imāya gīvākaṇḍūyāya, nanu vuttaṃ bhagavatā suttante “jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppanna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.20), tasmā kathametaṃ vuccati, jaratā aniccatā ceva na kehici samuṭṭhitāti yo vadeyya, tassa vitakkaṃ dassetvā paṭikkhipituṃ “anicca”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Kasmā na vattabbanti āha “sā hi pariyāyadesanā”ti. Pariyāyadesanattameva vibhāvetuṃ “aniccāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tathā-saddena “saṅkhatāna”nti saṅgaṇhāti.

Then what is this 'scratching of the neck' about? Has it not been said by the Blessed One in the discourse, "Monks, aging and death are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen" (Saṃ. Ni. 2.20)? Therefore, how can it be said that 'aging and impermanence are not produced by anyone'? To refute such a thought by showing its defect, "impermanent" and so on was stated. Why should it not be said? He says, "For that is a teaching by way of implication." To explain that it is indeed a teaching by way of implication, "impermanent" and so on was stated. By the word "thus," he includes "conditioned."

720-3. Aniccaṃ [V 2.0122] saṅkhatañcāti ca-saddena “paṭiccasamuppanna”nti saṅgaṇhāti. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – aniccasaṅkhatadhammānaṃ jarāmaraṇattā tesu santesu hoti, asantesu na hoti. Na hi ajātaṃ paripaccati, bhijjati vā, tasmā taṃ jātipaccayataṃ sandhāya “jarāmaraṇaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ, tatoyeva ca anicca”nti pariyāyena sutte āgataṃ. Yathā viññattiādīnaṃ nippariyāyato cittasamuṭṭhānatābhāvepi cittajānaṃ vikārattā cittasamuṭṭhānabhāvoti. Viññattiyo viyāti ca nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ lahutādīnampi cittajādibhāvassa pariyāyeneva icchitattā. Nippariyāyena aṭṭhāraseva nipphannarūpāni kammādisamuṭṭhānānīti. Tayanti jātijarābhaṅgasaṅkhātānaṃ lakkhaṇarūpattayaṃ.

"Impermanent and conditioned"—by the word 'ca' ('and'), it includes 'dependently arisen.' Here, the meaning is this: because aging and death are characteristics of impermanent, conditioned phenomena, they exist when these phenomena exist, and do not exist when they do not. For what is unborn does not ripen or break apart. Therefore, with reference to the state of having birth as a condition, it is stated in the sutta by way of implication: "Aging and death are conditioned, dependently arisen, and therefore impermanent." Just as, although intimations (viññatti) and the like are not directly mind-originated, they are still considered mind-originated because they are alterations of the mind-born phenomena. The example of intimations should be seen merely as an illustration, as lightness and other such qualities are also desired to be mind-originated only by way of implication. In the strict sense, only the eighteen concretely produced material phenomena are originated by kamma and other causes. "Taya" refers to the triad of characteristic forms, namely birth, aging, and dissolution.

Khaṃpupphaṃvāti [M 2.0166] ākāsakusumaṃ viya. Yathā ākāsakusumaṃ sabbaso ajātattā natthi, evamidampi natthīti attho. Niccaṃ vāsaṅkhataṃ viyāti yathā asaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ kenaci asaṅkhatattā niccaṃ dhuvaṃ, evamidampi kenaci asaṅkhatattā niccaṃ sassataṃ vāti attho. Nobhayaṃ panidanti idaṃ pana ubhayampi khaṃpupphaṃ viya no natthi, na ca nibbānaṃ viya asaṅkhataṃ vāti attho. Nissayāyattavuttitoti jāyamānaparipaccamānabhijjamānānaṃ jātiādimattabhāvena jāyamānādinissayapaṭibaddhavuttittā. Tameva nissayāyattavuttitaṃ samatthetuṃ “bhāve pathaviyādīna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – pathavīādīnaṃ nissayānaṃ bhāve jātiādittayaṃ paññāyati, tasmā no natthi, yasmā ca tesaṃ abhāve na paññāyati, tasmā na niccanti imameva ca abhinivesaṃ nisedhetuṃ bhagavatā jātiyā catujattaṃ, jarāmaraṇassa ca aniccādipariyāyo vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

"Like a sky-flower" means like a flower in the sky. Just as a sky-flower does not exist at all because it is unarisen, so too this does not exist—this is the meaning. "Or permanent like the unconditioned" means just as unconditioned Nibbāna is permanent and stable because it is unconditioned by anything, so too this would be permanent and eternal if it were unconditioned by anything—this is the meaning. "But this is neither" means this, however, is neither nonexistent like a sky-flower, nor is it unconditioned like Nibbāna—this is the meaning. "Because its occurrence is dependent on a support" means because its occurrence is bound to the support of things being born, and so on, by being merely the state of birth, and so on, of things that are being born, ripening, and breaking up. To establish this very dependence on a support, it is said: "in the existence of earth, etc." Here, the condensed meaning is this: in the existence of supports like earth, the triad of birth, etc., is evident; therefore, it is not nonexistent. And because in their absence it is not evident, it is not permanent. To refute this very adherence, it should be understood that the Blessed One spoke of the fourfold nature of birth and the discourse on the impermanence, etc., of aging and death.

724-5. Nipphannāni nāmāti “rūpassa paricchedo, rūpassa vikāro, rūpassa lakkhaṇa”ntiādinā paricchedādibhāvaṃ atikkamitvā attano kakkhaḷattādinā sabhāvena paricchijja gahetabbattā, apariyāyeneva kammādipaccayehi nipphannattā vā nipphannāni nāma. Tabbiparītato anipphannā.

"Concretely produced" means: because they are to be grasped, having been distinguished by their own nature of hardness, etc., transcending the state of being a delimitation, etc., such as 'the delimitation of form, the alteration of form, the characteristic of form'; or because they are produced directly by causes like kamma, they are called 'concretely produced.' Those that are the opposite of this are 'non-produced.'

Sesakā anipphannāti sutvā paro aniṭṭhaṃ āpādento āha “yadi hontī”tiādi. “Tesamevā”tiādinā pana taṃ paṭikkhipati. Kāyavikāro kāyaviññatti nāma, vacīvikāro vacīviññatti nāma, chiddaṃ vivaraṃ ākāsadhātu nāma, lahubhāvo lahutā nāma, mudubhāvo mudutā nāma[V 2.0123], kammaññabhāvo kammaññatā nāma, nibbatti upacayo nāma, pavatti santati nāma, jīraṇākāro jaratā nāma, hutvā abhāvākāro aniccatā nāmāti evaṃ tesaṃyeva aṭṭhārasannaṃ nipphannarūpānaṃ [M 2.0167] vikārabhūtattā nipphannā ceva saṅkhatā ca, tesaṃyeva ca rūpānaṃ vikārattā te asaṅkhatā nāma kathaṃ bhaveyyuṃ, nipphannā ceva saṅkhatāti sambandhaṃ katvā yadi anipphannarūpānaṃ nissayabhūtā nipphannarūpā saṅkhatā, tesaṃ pana vikārabhūtā kathaṃ asaṅkhatā nāma hontīti atthaṃ vaṇṇenti. Tesaṃ adhippāyena nipphannā cevāti va-kāro āgamasiddhoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Having heard that the remaining phenomena are non-produced, another, presenting an undesirable consequence, says, "If they exist," and so on. But with "of those very," and so on, he rejects that. Bodily alteration is called bodily intimation; verbal alteration is called verbal intimation; a hole or opening is called the space element; the state of lightness is called lightness; the state of softness is called pliancy; the state of adaptability is called wieldiness; production is called accumulation; progression is called continuity; the state of decay is called aging; the state of having been and then ceasing is called impermanence. Thus, because these are alterations of the very eighteen produced material phenomena, they are both produced and conditioned. And since they are alterations of those very material phenomena, how could they be called unconditioned? By establishing the connection that 'they are both produced and conditioned,' they explain the meaning thus: if the produced material phenomena, which serve as the basis for the non-produced material phenomena, are conditioned, then how could their alterations be called unconditioned? According to their intention, it should be understood that the 'va' particle in 'nipphannā ceva' is established by tradition.

726-7. Itthibhāvo…pe… vaṇṇitāti phalaṭhapanaṃ. “Evaṃ sante”tiādi codanā. “Aññaṃ panā”tiādi parihāro. Tattha cakkhukāyapasādānaṃ, ekattaṃ upapajjatīti cakkhupasāde kāyapasādabhāvassa, kāyapasāde cakkhupasādabhāvassa sabbhāvato purimassa phoṭṭhabbāvabhāsanaṃ, itarassa ca rūpāvabhāsanaṃ hotīti cakkhukāyapasādānaṃ ekībhāvo bhaveyyāti attho. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ. Sotakāyapasādādīnampi hi vuttanayena ekattaṃyevāti.

The state of being a woman...and so on...as described, is the establishing of the result. "If this is so," and so on, is the objection. "But another," and so on, is the resolution. Here, regarding the eye-sensitivity and body-sensitivity, "they become one" means that since the state of body-sensitivity exists in eye-sensitivity, and the state of eye-sensitivity exists in body-sensitivity, the former would have the illumination of tangible objects and the latter the illumination of visible forms; thus, the eye-sensitivity and body-sensitivity would become unified—this is the meaning. And this is merely an example. For the ear-sensitivity and body-sensitivity, etc., also become one in the way described.

728-30. Aññaṃ pana aññasmiṃ na catthīti ṭhapetvā aññamaññāvinibbhogavasena pavattiṃ aññaṃ rūpaṃ aññasmiṃ rūpe paramatthato nevatthi bhinnanissayabhāvena kalāpantaragatattā. Cakkhupasādo hi daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhitabhūtanissito, kāyapasādo phusitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtanissito. Asaṅkaranti asaṃkiṇṇaṃ. Yadi evaṃ, na sabbattha kāyāyatanādikanti? Tampi natthi paramatthato. Vinibbhujitvā hi nesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ paññāpetuṃ na sakkā, taṃ dassetuṃ “aññamaññāvinibbhogavasenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aññamaññā…pe… pavattitoti aññamaññaṃ santānato avinibbhujjanavasena avisaṃsaṭṭhavasena pavattanato. Avinibbhogarūpavasenāti pana attho na hoti. Na hi cakkhukāyapasādānaṃ ekakalāpagataavinibbhogarūpā ṭhānantaraṃ vattuṃ sakkāti[M 2.0168]. Yathā rūparasādīnaṃ vivecetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya aññamaññabyāpitā vuccati, na ca paramatthato rūpe raso atthi. Yadi siyā, rūpaggahaṇeneva rasaggahaṇaṃ gaccheyya. Evaṃ kāyāyatanādīnampi paramatthato na sabbattha atthitā, “idaṃ ettha, idaṃ etthā”ti ṭhānantaraṃ pana samayaññunā kenaci na sakkā vattunti. Atthi kāyapasādotīti itisaddo “tasmā”ti imassa atthe. Tenāha “tasmā”ti. Evamudīritanti sabbaṭṭhānikanti evamudīritaṃ.

728-30. "Another does not exist in another" means that, setting aside their occurrence by way of mutual inseparability, one form does not ultimately exist in another form, due to having distinct bases and being in different clusters. For example, the eye-sensitivity is based on the primary elements arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to see, while the body-sensitivity is based on the primary elements arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to touch. "Asaṅkara" means unmixed. If that is so, does the body-base, etc., not exist everywhere? That too does not exist in an ultimate sense. For it is impossible to separate them and make known their distinct characteristics. To illustrate this, it is said, "by way of mutual inseparability," etc. "By way of mutual inseparability... occurs" means they occur by way of not being separated from one another in the continuum, by way of not being intermingled. However, the meaning is not that they are inseparable forms. For it is impossible to say that the eye-sensitivity and body-sensitivity, being inseparable forms in the same cluster, have different locations. Just as color, taste, and so on are said to be mutually pervasive because of the impossibility of distinguishing them, yet in an ultimate sense, taste does not exist in color. If it did, grasping color would also mean grasping taste. Similarly, the body-base, etc., do not exist everywhere in an ultimate sense. However, no one who knows the convention can point out, "This is here, that is there." The word "iti" in "There is body-sensitivity" has the meaning of "therefore." Hence it is said, "therefore." "Thus declared" means "thus declared as pertaining to all locations."

731-2. Lakkhaṇādivasenāpīti yathāvuttalakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānavasenāpi. Dhajānaṃ [V 2.0124] …pe… gatāti pañcavaṇṇānaṃ nīlādipañcavaṇṇasuttamayānaṃ ekamekassa vā ekekavaṇṇavasena dhajānaṃ chāyā tesaṃ upamataṃ upamābhāvaṃ gatā sampattāti attho. Keci pana “chāyā upamā etesanti chāyāupamā, chāyāupamānaṃ bhāvo chāyāupamatā, taṃ gatā ete dhammā”ti vadanti. Taṃ pana tehi “chāyāupamataṃ gatā”ti ettha bahubbīhivaseneva rassattanti maññamānehi vuttaṃ bhaveyya. Gāthābandhatthaṃ pana rassattanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Catutthadū”tiādīsu hi vibhattilopampi katvā dassento ācariyo na īdisesu ṭhānesu byañjane ādaraṃ janeti. Yaṃ pana “tesa”nti heṭṭhāpadaṃ, “dhammāna”nti uparipadaṃ vā sambandhituṃ anicchantehi vuccati tattha “nānattaṃ samupāgata”nti. Taṃ ettha akāmāpi sambandhitabbameva. Na hi nānattaṃ samupāgataṃ tesanti nāpekkhatīti. Athāpi tattha “nānattaṃ samupāgatā”ti pāṭhaṃ parikappeyyuṃ, hotu tāva potthakesu adissamānampi pāṭhaṃ parikappetvā tesaṃ tuṭṭhi. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – yathā pañcavaṇṇānaṃ dhajānaṃ ekato katvā ussāpitānaṃ kiñcāpi chāyā ekābaddhā viya hoti, aññamaññaṃ pana asammissāva, evameva ime sabbaṭṭhānikarūpā [M 2.0169] kiñcāpi ekābaddhā viya honti, lakkhaṇato pana aññamaññaṃ bhinnasabhāvā asammissāyeva. Ekakalāpaṭṭhāpi hi lakkhaṇato bhinnasabhāvā, kiṃ pana nānākalāpaṭṭhāti.

731-2. "By way of characteristics, etc." means also by way of characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause as previously stated. "Of banners..." and so on means the shadows of banners made of threads of five colors—blue, etc.—either of each single banner or of banners according to each single color, have attained the state of being a simile for them. Some, however, say: "The shadow is the simile for these, thus 'shadow-simile'; the state of being a shadow-simile is 'shadow-similitude'; these phenomena have reached that." But that would be said by those who, in the phrase 'chāyāupamatāṃ gatā,' think that the shortening is due to a bahubbīhi compound. However, for the sake of the verse's structure, it should be seen as shortened. Indeed, the teacher, even showing the elision of inflections in cases like "the fourth or distant," does not pay attention to letters in such places. As for what is said by those unwilling to connect the word "tesaṃ" below or "dhammānaṃ" above—there "they have attained diversity"—that must be connected here, even if unwillingly. For 'attained diversity' surely requires 'of them.' Alternatively, they might propose the reading "they have attained diversity," but even if the reading is not found in the texts, let them be content with their conjecture. The meaning here is this: just as the shadows of five-colored banners, when raised together, appear as if bound together, yet are unmixed with one another, so too these material phenomena pertaining to all locations, though they appear as if bound together, are by their characteristics distinct in nature and unmixed. For even within a single cluster, they are distinct in nature by their characteristics—how much more so across different clusters!

733. Attano paccayehi loke niyuttaṃ, viditanti vā lokikaṃ, tassa bhāvo lokikattaṃ. Hinoti patiṭṭhahati sampayuttadhammarāsi etenāti hetu, mūlaṭṭhena upakārako lobhādiko ca alobhādiko ca, tādiso hetu na hotīti nahetu. Attano paccayehi saṅkhataṃ abhisaṅkhatanti saṅkhataṃ. Ābhavaggā, āgotrabhu vā savantīti āsavā, saha āsavehīti sāsavaṃ, āsavehi ālambitabbanti attho. Paccayāyattavuttitoti attano attano paccayādhīnappavattitāya sappaccayattāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nidassanamattametaṃ. Kāmāvacarattā ahetukattā hetuvippayuttattā saṃyojaniyattā ganthaniyattā upādāniyattā oghaniyattā yoganiyattā nīvaraṇiyattā saṃkilesikattā parāmaṭṭhattā acetasikattā cittavippayuttattā na rūpāvacarattā na arūpāvacarattā na apariyāpannattā aniyyānikattā aniccattāti evamādināpi kāraṇena ekavidhamevāti.

733. Engaged in the world by its own conditions, or known as worldly—its state is worldliness (lokikattaṃ). That by which a mass of associated states stands firm and is supported is a cause (hetu); in the sense of being a root, it is helpful, and is either greed and so on, or non-greed and so on. Where such a cause does not exist, that is a non-cause (nahetu). Conditioned by its own conditions, it is fabricated—thus it is conditioned (saṅkhataṃ). Flowing from the peak of existence or up to the change-of-lineage cognition are the taints (āsavā); together with the taints—thus, tainted (sāsavaṃ), meaning: it is to be taken as an object by the taints. "Because its occurrence is dependent on conditions" (paccayāyattavuttito) is said because it arises dependent on its own conditions; thus, it is with a condition (sappaccayattā). This is merely an illustration. Because it belongs to the sense-sphere, is without a root, is dissociated from roots, is to be bound by fetters, is to be tied by knots, is an object of clinging, is to be swept away by floods, is to be yoked by bonds, is to be obstructed by hindrances, is defiling, is grasped at, is non-mental, is dissociated from mind, does not belong to the form-sphere, does not belong to the formless-sphere, is not unincluded, does not lead out, is impermanent—and for such reasons, it is of one kind only.

734-8. Evaṃ ekavidhanayaṃ dassetvā idāni ādi-saddena saṅgahitaduvidhatādinayaṃ dassetuṃ “ajjhattikabahiddhā”tiādinā ajjhattikadukādayo āraddhā. Tattha ajjhattikaduke tāva āhito [V 2.0125] ahaṃ māno etthāti attā, attabhāvo, taṃ attānaṃ adhikicca uddissa pavattattā ajjhattā, indriyabaddhadhammā, tesu bhavāni, attani vā bhavāni ajjhattikāni. Kāmaṃ aññepi ajjhattasambhūtā atthi, ruḷhīvasena pana cakkhādīneva “ajjhattikānī”ti vuccanti. Atha vā “yadi mayaṃ na homa, tvaṃ kaṭṭhakaliṅgarūpamo bhavissasī”ti vadantā [M 2.0170] viya attabhāvassa sātisayaṃ upakārakānīti tāneva visesato ajjhattikanāmaṃ labhanti. Indriyānindriyāti ādhipaccaṭṭhena indriyāni, sesaṃ tadabhāvato anindriyaṃ. Tattha cakkhādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīsu adhipateyyaṃ tesaṃ paṭumandabhāvādianuvattanato, itthindriyapurisindriyadvayassa itthiliṅgādihetubhāve, jīvitindriyassa ca sahajarūpānupālaneti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Visayavisayībhāvato ghaṭṭanavasena gahetabbattā oḷārikaṃ, tabbiparītattā sukhumaṃ. Upādinnanti kammunā gahitaṃ. Kammanibbattañhi “mametaṃ phala”nti tena kammunā gahitaṃ viya hoti.

734-8. Having thus shown the single-fold method, now, to explain the twofold method and so on, which are included by the word "ādi," the internal dyad (ajjhattikaduka) and others are commenced, beginning with "internal and external." Herein, in the internal dyad: "Conceit is placed here" (āhito ahaṃ māno ettha) — thus, the self (attā), the individual existence (attabhāva). Because it occurs concerning that self, directed towards it, it is internal (ajjhattā). The phenomena bound to faculties, those that exist in them, or those that exist in the self, are internal (ajjhattikāni). Indeed, there are others born internally, but conventionally, only the eye and so on are called "internal." Alternatively, just as those saying, "If we were not, you would be like a log of wood," they specifically receive the name "internal" because they are of exceeding benefit to the individual existence. The faculties (indriyāni) and non-faculties (anindriyāni): by the meaning of dominance, they are faculties; the rest, due to the absence of that, are non-faculties. Herein, the dominance of the five, beginning with the eye, over eye-consciousness and so on should be seen as due to following their state of being sharp or dull. The two faculties, femininity and masculinity, should be seen in their being the cause of female characteristics and so on. And the life faculty should be seen in its maintenance of co-nascent materiality. By the nature of object and subject, because it is to be grasped by way of impact, it is gross (oḷārikaṃ); due to being the opposite of that, it is subtle (sukhumāṃ). Clung-to (upādinnaṃ) is what is grasped by kamma. For what is produced by kamma is as if grasped by that kamma, thinking, "This is my fruit."

Ekādasa…pe… sappaṭighanti cakkhuviññāṇāviññeyyattā sanidassanattābhāvato anidassanaṃ, aññamaññaṃ patanavasena pana paṭighasabbhāvato sappaṭighaṃ, ubhayapaṭikkhepena anidassanaappaṭighaṃ. Kammato jātanti ettha yaṃ ekantato kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ aṭṭhindriyāni, vatthu cāti navavidhaṃ rūpaṃ. Yañca ekādasavidhe catusamuṭṭhāne kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ ekādasavidhameva rūpanti evaṃ vīsatividhampi kammato uppajjanato kammajaṃ. Yañhi jātaṃ, yañca jāyati, yañca jāyissati, taṃ sabbampi “kammaja”nti vuccati yathā “duddha”nti. Kammato aññaṃ akammaṃ, akammato jātaṃ akammajaṃ. Aññatthe hi ayaṃ a-kāro. Tenāha “tadaññapaccayājāta”nti. Kammato aññapaccayato jātaṃ, utucittāhārajanti attho. Cittajattikādīni vuttānusārena yojetuṃ sakkāti na dassitāni.

Eleven...and so on... with impact (sappaṭighaṃ). "Invisible" (anidassanaṃ) is said because it is not cognizable by eye-consciousness and thus lacks visibility. However, due to the existence of impact by way of mutual striking, it is "with impact" (sappaṭighaṃ). By rejecting both, it is "invisible and without impact" (anidassanaappaṭighaṃ). "Born from kamma" (kammajaṃ) — here, that which is entirely produced by kamma includes the eight faculties and the physical base, making nine types of form. And among the elevenfold form that has four origins, the portion originated by kamma is also the elevenfold form. Thus, twenty types of form in total are called 'kamma-born' because they arise from kamma. Whatever has been born, whatever is being born, and whatever will be born, all that is called "kamma-born," just as "milk" is called "duddha." What is other than kamma is "non-kamma" (akammaṃ), and what is born from non-kamma is "non-kamma-born" (akammajaṃ). Here, the prefix "a-" has the meaning of 'other'. Therefore, it is said, "born from other conditions" (tadaññapaccayājātaṃ). This means born from conditions other than kamma, i.e., born from temperature, mind, and nutriment. The triads beginning with mind-born, etc., can be applied according to what has been stated, and so they are not shown.

Diṭṭhacatukke daṭṭhabbanti diṭṭhaṃ. Yaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ adakkhi, yañca dakkhissati, yañca dakkhati, yañca passeyya, taṃ sabbaṃ diṭṭhaṃ nāma taṃsabhāvānativattanato yathā “iṭṭha”nti. Esa nayo sutādīsupi. Diṭṭhaṃ nāma rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaviññeyyattā. Sutaṃ nāma saddāyatanaṃ sotaviññāṇaviññeyyattā. Mutaṃ nāma gandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanattayaṃ mutvā patvā gahetabbato[M 2.0171], pasādena saha sambandhanato vā. Tathā hetaṃ sampattaggāhakavisayaṃ vuttaṃ. Viññātaṃ nāma avasesaṃ kevalaṃ manoviññāṇaviññeyyattā.

In the tetrad of the seen, "seen" (diṭṭhaṃ) should be understood. Whatever form-base one has seen, whatever one will see, whatever one sees, and whatever one may see—all that is called "seen" because it does not transcend its own nature, just as "desired" (iṭṭha) does. This same method applies to the heard and so forth. "Seen" (diṭṭhaṃ) refers to the form-base, because it is cognizable by eye-consciousness. "Heard" (sutaṃ) refers to the sound-base, because it is cognizable by ear-consciousness. "Sensed" (mutaṃ) refers to the triad of bases—odor, taste, and tangible object—because they are to be sensed, reached, and grasped, or because of their connection with the sensitive faculty. Thus, this is said to be the object of a faculty that grasps upon contact. "Cognized" (viññātaṃ) refers to the remainder, solely because it is cognizable by mind-consciousness.

Dvārañceva [V 2.0126] vatthu cāti attanissitānaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ, aññanissitānaṃ sampaṭicchanādīnañca pavattimukhabhāvato dvārañceva attanissitānaṃ ādhārabhāvato vatthu ca. Dvārameva hutvā na vatthūti kevalaṃ kammadvārabhāvato dvārameva, tannissitassa cittuppādassa abhāvato na vatthu. Vatthumeva hutvā na dvāranti manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ nissayabhāvato vatthumeva, cakkhādayo viya saparanissitānaṃ pavattidvārābhāvato na dvāraṃ. Sesaṃ ekavīsatividhaṃ rūpaṃ vuttavipariyāyato neva dvāraṃ na vatthu ca. Catutthacatukketi vatthucatukke. Tatiyapadanti “vatthumeva hutvā nevindriya”nti padaṃ.

"Both door and basis": because they are the gateway for the occurrence of eye-consciousness and so forth, which are dependent on themselves, and of receiving-consciousness and so forth, which are dependent on another, they are a door; and because they are the support for those dependent on themselves, they are a basis. "Being only a door and not a basis": it is only a door because it is merely a kamma-door, but it is not a basis due to the absence of an arising of consciousness dependent on it. "Being only a basis and not a door": because it is the support for the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, it is only a basis; but unlike the eye and so forth, it is not a door because it is not a gateway for the occurrence of those dependent on themselves and on others. The remaining twenty-one kinds of material form, by the converse of what has been stated, are neither a door nor a basis. "The fourth tetrad" refers to the basis tetrad. "The third phrase" is the statement, "being only a basis and not a faculty."

739-40. Puna pañcavidhanti sambandho. Catujanti pakāsitaṃ catūhiyeva samuṭṭhānato.

739-40. Again, 'fivefold' is the connection. 'Fourfold' is explained as arising from just the four.

Cakkhuviññāṇaviññeyyaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ tena gahetabbato, na pana cakkhuviññāṇeneva viññeyyato. Tathā hetaṃ āvajjanādīhi ceva manodvārikajavanehi ca viññāyatīti. Esa nayo sotaviññeyyādīsupi. Manoviññāṇaviññeyyaṃ pana kevalaṃ manoviññāṇeneva viññātabbaṃ. Na hi rūpādito aññattha cakkhuviññāṇādīni pavattanti.

The form-base is termed 'cognizable by eye-consciousness' because it is to be grasped by it, not, however, because it is cognizable by eye-consciousness alone. For it is also cognized by adverting and so forth, and by mind-door impulsion. This same method applies to what is cognizable by ear-consciousness and the rest. But what is cognizable by mind-consciousness is to be cognized by mind-consciousness alone. For eye-consciousness and the rest do not occur with respect to anything other than form and so on.

Chavatthuavatthubhedatoti channaṃ vatthūnaṃ, avatthussa ca bhedato. Manodhātuviññeyyaṃ rūpādipañcakaṃ.

Chavatthuavatthubhedatoti: due to the division of the six bases and the non-basis. The pentad beginning with form is cognizable by the mind-element.

Manāyatanassa arūpattā, dhammāyatanassa ca ekadesato rūpattā āha “āyatanabhedato ekādasavidha”nti.

Due to the immateriality of the mind-base and the dhamma-base being partly material, it is said, "By the division of the bases, it is elevenfold."

743-5. Arūpabhave [M 2.0172] rūpuppattiyā abhāvato, asaññībhavassa ca rūpabhavapariyāpannattā vuttaṃ “kāmarūpabhavadvaye”ti. Bhummavajjesūti bhummadevānaṃ vajjanaṃ yonivibhāgaṃ patvā tesaṃ manussasadisattā. Purimā tissoti aṇḍajajalābujasaṃsedajayoniyo. Tā hi yathāvuttappabhedesu na labbhanti, tāsañca paṭikkhepena pacchimā opapātikayoni anuññātāti atthato āpannameva hotīti. Tattha nirayeti ussadānampi gahaṇato avīcimahāniraye kīṭapāṇakānampi sarīraṃ pacchā vaḍḍhanakaṃ hutvāva nibbattati, nijjhāmataṇhikapetānaṃ niccāturatāya kāmassa abhāvato gabbhaggahaṇaṃ na hoti, tasmā aṇḍajajalābujayoniyo tattha na [V 2.0127] santi, ādittattā kucchiyaṃ gabbhaṃ na patiṭṭhātīti keci. Nibbattamānānañca pāpakammānubhāvena mahādukkhassa pattabbatāya mahanteneva sarīrena bhavitabbanti saṃsedajayonipi tesaṃ na hoti, aggijālāya santappamānasarīrattā tesaṃ nibbattakāle allaṭṭhāne pupphādīsu sambhavābhāvato saṃsedajatā natthevātipi vadanti. Tena tesaṃ opapātikāva yonīti āha “nijjhāmataṇhike”ti. Atha saṃsedajaopapātikayonīnaṃ ko visesoti? Saṃsedajo tāva khuddakasarīro hutvā padumagabbhādiṃ nissāya nibbatto kamena vaḍḍhati. Itaro pana yattha yattha nibbattati, tattha tattha paricchinnappamāṇasarīrova soḷasavassuddesiko viya paripuṇṇaṅgapaccaṅgo pāturahosi.

743-5. In the formless existence, there is no arising of material form, and since the non-percipient existence is included in the form existence, it is said, "in the two existences of sensuality and form." "Excluding the earth-dwelling" (Bhummavajjesūti): this is the exclusion of earth-dwelling deities because, with regard to the division of origins, they are similar to humans. "The first three" (Purimā tisso): this refers to the egg-born, womb-born, and moisture-born origins. Indeed, these are not found in the classifications stated, and by their rejection, the last, the spontaneous origin, is permitted, so the meaning is naturally established. Therein, "in hell" (niraye): by including the minor hells, even in the great Avīci hell, the bodies of insects and creatures are produced, growing only afterwards.
