For the 'scorched by thirst' petas, due to their constant affliction and the absence of desire, there is no conception in a womb. Therefore, egg-born and womb-born origins do not exist there. Some say that because it is burning, a fetus cannot become established in the womb. Moreover, since beings being born there must experience great suffering due to the power of their evil kamma, they must have large bodies. Thus, the moisture-born origin is also not for them. Because their bodies are scorched by flames, and since at the time of their birth there is no possibility of arising in moist places like flowers, they have no moisture-born state, some say. Therefore, for them, the origin is only spontaneous; thus it is said, "for the 'scorched by thirst' petas." Now, what is the difference between the moisture-born and spontaneous origins? A moisture-born being, for one, is born with a small body, dependent on a lotus-womb or the like, and gradually grows. The other, however, wherever it is born, appears with a body of a definite size, like a sixteen-year-old, complete in all major and minor limbs.

Sese gatittayeti ṭhapetvā devagatiṃ, nirayagatiñca avasesamanussapetatiracchānasaññite gatittaye. Manussesu hi keci aṇḍajāpi honti kuntaputtadvebhātikattherā viya, keci saṃsedajāpi honti padumagabbhe nibbattapokkharasātibrāhmaṇādayo viya, keci opapātikāpi [M 2.0173] honti ambapāligaṇikādayo viya. Nijjhāmataṇhikāvasesapetā pana sabbacatuppadapakkhijātidīghajātiādayo sabbepi tiracchānā ca catuyonikāvāti.

"In the remaining three destinations": excluding the deva destination and the hell destination, in the remaining three destinations designated as human, peta, and animal. Indeed, among humans, some are egg-born, like the Elder Kuntaputta and his two brothers; some are moisture-born, like the Brahmin Pokkharasāti and others born in a lotus-womb; and some are spontaneously born, like the courtesan Ambapālī and others. But the petas other than the 'scorched by thirst' kind, and all animals—all quadrupeds, birds, long-bodied species, and so forth—are of the four origins.

746-7. Gabbhe mātukucchiyaṃ setīti gabbhaseyyako, soyeva rūpādīsu sattatāya gabbhaseyyakasatto. Tassa gabbhaseyyakasattassa. Tiṃsa rūpānīti kāyabhāvavatthudasakavasena samatiṃsa kammajarūpāniyeva. Tadā hi neva cittajarūpamatthi paṭisandhicittassa rūpasamuṭṭhāpakattābhāvato, nāpi utujaṃ purimuppannautuno abhāvā. Utu hi ṭhānappattaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, na ca āhārajaṃ tasmiṃ kāye ajjhohaṭassa abhāvato, tasmā kammasamuṭṭhānāniyeva tiṃsa rūpāni paṭisandhikkhaṇe nibbattanti, yānī “kalalarūpa”nti pavuccanti, paripiṇḍitāni ca tāni jātiuṇṇāya ekassa aṃsuno pasannatilatele pakkhipitvā uddhaṭassa paggharitvā agge ṭhitabindumattāni acchāni vippasannāni pasannatelabindusamānāni honti. Yathāhu –

746-7. 'One who lies in the womb' (gabbhe...seti) is a womb-dweller (gabbhaseyyako); that very being, due to attachment to forms and so forth, is a womb-dwelling being. For that womb-dwelling being, 'thirty forms' means precisely thirty kamma-born forms, by way of the body-decad, sex-decad, and basis-decad. At that time, there are no mind-born forms, because the rebirth-linking consciousness is not a producer of form, nor are there temperature-born forms, due to the absence of previously arisen temperature. For temperature produces form only when it has reached a stable condition. And there are no nutriment-born forms, due to the absence of anything ingested in that body. Therefore, at the moment of rebirth-linking, only the thirty kamma-produced forms arise, which are called 'kalala-form'. And these, gathered together, are the size of a drop remaining at the tip of a single strand of fine wool that has been dipped into clear sesame oil and withdrawn; they are clear, very limpid, resembling a drop of pure sesame oil. As it is said:

“Tilatelassa yathā bindu,

Sappimaṇḍo anāvilo;

Evaṃ vaṇṇapaṭibhāgaṃ,

Kalalanti pavuccatī”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 26);

"Just as a drop of sesame oil, or the clear surface of ghee, unclouded; so too, similar in appearance, it is called the kalala."

Sabhāvassevāti [V 2.0128] avadhāraṇena abhāvakassa bhāvadasakābhāvato tiṃsarūpānaṃ asambhavaṃ dīpeti. Tenāha “abhāva…pe… kāyavatthuvasena tū”ti. Abhāvagabbhaseyyānanti iminā abhāvaopapātikānaṃ na evanti dassetīti keci. Pubbe sabhāvakagabbhaseyyakassa pana vatvā tato nivattanatthaṃ “abhāvagabbhaseyyakasattāna”nti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pubbe gabbhaseyyaka-ggahaṇena aṇḍajānampi gahaṇe idha [M 2.0174] visuṃ vacanaṃ gobalībaddañāyavasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, na pana tesaṃ abhāvakabhāvanivattanatthanti. Itarathā hi vīsatirūpānaṃ vacanaṃ virujjhati. Abhāvakabhāvo panettha aṇḍajānaṃ pakaraṇato daṭṭhabbo. Na hi gabbhaseyyaka-saddena samāsabhūtaṃ abhāva-saddaṃ idha ānetuṃ sakkāti.

By the emphasis in 'sabhāvasseva' ('for one with sex'), it indicates the impossibility of thirty forms for one without sex (abhāvaka), due to the absence of the sex-decad. Therefore, it is said: "For one without sex... by way of the body and basis..." Some say that by this phrase "for womb-dwellers without sex," it is shown that it is not so for spontaneous beings without sex. But it should be understood that after speaking previously of the womb-dweller with sex, the phrase "for womb-dwelling beings without sex" is stated in order to distinguish from that. Previously, when egg-born beings were also included by the term 'womb-dweller,' the separate statement here should be understood by way of the 'cow and bull' maxim, and not, however, to negate their state of being without sex. Otherwise, the statement of twenty forms would be contradicted. Here, the state of being without sex should be understood from the context of egg-born beings. For it is not possible to bring the word 'abhāva' here as compounded with the word 'gabbhaseyyaka'.

748. Gahitāgahaṇenettha, ekādasa bhavanti teti ekasmiṃ kalāpe gahitarūpānaṃ aparakalāpe aggahaṇavasena suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, jīvitaṃ, kāyapasādo, vatthurūpanti abhāvakassa paṭisandhikkhaṇe ekādasa rūpāni bhavanti, sabhāvakassa pana dvīsu bhāvesu ekena saha dvādasa rūpāni honti. Eseva ca nayoti vuttesu, vakkhamānesu ca paṭisandhikkhaṇikakalāpesu aggahitaggahaṇena rūpaggahaṇe nayo eseva ñeyyo.

748. Here, by way of inclusion and non-inclusion, there are eleven. Thus, by including the forms in one group and not including them in another, the pure octad, the life faculty, body sensitivity, and the basis-form—these eleven forms arise at the moment of rebirth-linking for one who lacks the sex faculty. For one who possesses the sex faculty, however, with one of the two sex faculties, twelve forms arise. And this is the method: in the rebirth-linking groups that have been stated and will be stated, this same method should be understood for the grasping of forms by way of what is included and not included.

749. Nanu ca “sabbesu dasakesū”ti vuttaṃ, kathaṃ pana te dasakā jānitabbāti āha “jīvitenā”tiādi. Suddhakamaṭṭhakanti cattāri mahābhūtāni, tannissitā ca vaṇṇagandharasaojāti idaṃ jīvitādinā asammissaṃ suddhaṭṭhakaṃ. Imāniyeva hi aṭṭha katthaci avinibbhogavasenapi pavattito avinibbhogarūpāni avakaṃsato eko kalāpoti ca vuccati. Ācariyajotipālattherena pana “nipphannānipphannavasena dasa rūpāni avinibbhogavuttikāni eko kalāpo”ti vatvā puna taṃsamatthanatthaṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ –

749. But was it not said, 'In all the decades'? How then are these decades to be known? It is said, 'By life,' etc. The pure octad is the four great elements, and the color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence dependent on them—this is the pure octad, unmixed with life, etc. Indeed, these eight, because they occur inseparably in some cases, are called inseparable forms, and are also referred to as one group (kalāpa) at a minimum. However, the Elder Ācariya Jotipāla, having said, 'Ten forms, by way of produced and unproduced, are inseparable in function—one group,' then stated this to support that:

“Avinibbhogavuttīni, catujānekalakkhaṇā;

Nipphannānaṭṭha vā tesu, hitvāna kāyalakkhaṇe”ti.

Functioning inseparably, born of the four causes, with a single characteristic; or, among the produced forms, there are eight, excluding the two bodily characteristics.

750. Kāyadasakanti kāyo dasamo etthāti kāyadasakaṃ, asādhāraṇena vā kāyena lakkhitaṃ dasakaṃ kāyadasakaṃ. Esa nayo cakkhudasakādīsu. Pariyāpuṭaṃ ñātaṃ, kathitanti vā attho.

750. The body-decad (kāyadasaka) means that the body is the tenth herein, or it is a decad characterized by the body as its unique feature. This is the method for the eye-decad and so forth. The meaning is either 'known through thorough study' or 'explained'.

752-3. Kāmāvacaradevesu [M 2.0175][V 2.0129] sabbakālaṃ paṭisandhipavattīsu sattatiyā rūpānaṃ labbhanato vuttaṃ “niccaṃ rūpāni sattatī”ti. Na hi te kadācipi vikalindriyā, abhāvakā vā honti. “Manussesu opapātikasattāna”nti avisesena vuttepi ādikappikānaṃ bhāvadasakassa paṭisandhikkhaṇe abhāvato tesaṃ saṭṭhi rūpānīti veditabbaṃ. Jīvitanavakampi opapātikānaṃ, saṃsedajānañca kāmāvacarasattānaṃ pavatteyeva hoti tassa pācakagginā sahavuttittā, tassa ca ajjhohaṭāhārasannissayena sambhavato. Saṃsedajānampi paripuṇṇaṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ nibbattanato opapātikehi viseso natthīti tesaṃ visuṃ aggahaṇaṃ. Vibhaṅgepi hi –

752-3. Among the Kāmāvacara devas, since seventy-three forms are obtainable at all times, during rebirth-linking and continuity, it is said, 'Seventy-three forms are constant.' For they are never deficient in faculties or lacking the sex faculty. Although it is said generally, 'among humans and spontaneously arisen beings,' it should be understood that for those at the beginning of an aeon, there are sixty forms, due to the absence of the sex-decad at the moment of rebirth-linking. The life-nonad also occurs only in the continuity of spontaneously arisen and moisture-born beings among Kāmāvacara beings, due to its co-occurrence with the digestive fire and its arising dependent on ingested nutriment. Since moisture-born beings are produced with complete major and minor limbs, there is no difference from spontaneously arisen beings, hence they are not mentioned separately. For in the Vibhaṅga:

“Kāmadhātuyā upapattikkhaṇe kassaci ekādasāyatanāni pātubhavanti, kassaci dasāyatanāni, kassaci aparāni dasāyatanāni, kassaci navāyatanāni, kassaci sattāyatanāni pātubhavantī”ti (vibha. 1009) –

At the moment of arising in the sense-sphere realm, for some, eleven sense bases appear; for some, ten sense bases; for some, another ten sense bases; for some, nine sense bases; and for some, seven sense bases appear.

Imassa niddese “opapātikasattāna”ntiādinā opapātika-ggahaṇameva kataṃ, na saṃsedaja-ggahaṇaṃ. Tañca paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ saṃsedajānaṃ opapātikesu saṅgaṇhanato. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “saṃsedajayonikā paripuṇṇāyatanabhāvena opapātikasaṅgahaṃ katvā vuttā”ti. Padhānāya vā yoniyā sabbaparipuṇṇāyatanayoniṃ dassetuṃ “opapātikasattāna”nti vuttaṃ.

In this explanation, by the term 'spontaneously arisen beings,' etc., only the spontaneously arisen are mentioned, not the moisture-born. This is because moisture-born beings with complete sense bases are included among the spontaneously arisen. For so it is said in the commentary: 'Those of moisture-born origin are spoken of as included in the category of the spontaneously arisen, due to their state of having complete sense bases.' Or, to indicate the primary mode of birth—the mode of birth for all those with complete sense bases—the term 'spontaneously arisen beings' is used.

754-5. Cakkhusotavatthuvasāti cakkhudasakasotadasakavatthudasakavasā. Ānandācariyo panettha “rūpadhātuyaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇena saha cakkhusotavatthusattakānaṃ jīvitachakkassāti catunnaṃ kalāpānaṃ vasena sattavīsati [M 2.0176] rūpāni uppajjanti, tattha gandharasāhārānaṃ paṭikkhittattā”ti vatvā puna taṃ samatthento “pāḷiyañhi ‘rūpadhātuyā upapattikkhaṇe ṭhapetvā asaññasattānaṃ devānaṃ pañcāyatanāni pātubhavanti, pañca dhātuyo pātubhavantī’ti (vibha. 1015) vuttaṃ. Tathā ‘rūpadhātuyā cha āyatanāni nava dhātuyo’ti (vibha. 994) sabbasaṅgāhakavasena tattha vijjamānāyatanadhātuyo dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Kathāvatthumhi ca ghānāyatanādīnaṃ viya gandhāyatanādīnañca tattha bhāvo paṭikkhitto ‘atthi tattha ghānāyatananti? Āmantā. Atthi tattha gandhāyatananti? Na hevaṃ vattabbe’tiādinā (kathā. 520). Na ca aphoṭṭhabbāyatanānaṃ pathavīdhātuādīnaṃ viya agandharasāyatanānaṃ gandharasānaṃ tattha bhāvo sakkā vattuṃ phusituṃ sakkuṇeyyatāvinimuttassa pathavīādisabhāvassa viya gandharasāyatanabhāvavinimuttassa gandharasabhāvassa [V 2.0130] abhāvā. Yadi ca ghānasamphassādīnaṃ kāraṇabhāvo natthīti tāni āyatanānīti na vucceyyuṃ, dhātusaddo pana nissattanijjīvavibhāvakoti gandhadhāturasadhātūti avacane kāraṇaṃ natthi. Dhammasabhāvo ca nesaṃ ekantena icchitabbo sabhāvadhāraṇādilakkhaṇato aññassa abhāvā. Dhammānañca āyatanabhāvo ekantato yamake vutto ‘dhammo āyatananti? Āmantā’ti (yama. 1.āyatanayamaka.13), tasmā tesaṃ gandharasāyatanabhāvābhāvepi koci āyatanabhāvo vattabbo. Yadi ca phoṭṭhabbabhāvato añño pathavīādibhāvo viya gandharasabhāvato añño tesaṃ koci sabhāvo siyā, tesaṃ dhammāyatanasaṅgaho. Gandharasabhāve, pana āyatanabhāve ca sati gandho ca so āyatanañca gandhāyatanaṃ, raso ca so āyatanañca rasāyatananti idamāpannamevāti gandharasāyatanabhāvo ca na sakkā nivāretuṃ, ‘tayo āhārā’ti [M 2.0177] (vibha. 1015) vacanato kabaḷīkārāhārassa tattha abhāvo viññāyati, tasmā yathā pāḷiyā avirodho hoti, tathā gandharasojā hitvā rūpagaṇanā kātabbā. Evañhi dhammatā na vilomatā hotī”ti vadati.

754-5. By way of the eye, ear, and base, meaning by way of the eye-decad, ear-decad, and base-decad. Ānanda the Elder, however, states here: 'In the form realm, at the moment of rebirth-linking consciousness, twenty-seven material phenomena arise by way of four groups, namely, the eye-septad, ear-septad, base-septad, and the life-hexad, because odors, tastes, and nutriment are excluded there.' Then, further clarifying this, he says: 'For in the Pāli, it is said: "At the moment of arising in the form realm, except for non-percipient beings, five sense bases appear for the devas, and five elements appear" (Vibh. 1015). Likewise, "In the form realm, there are six sense bases and nine elements" (Vibh. 994). This is stated to show the sense bases and elements present there in an all-inclusive manner. In the Kathāvatthu, the existence of the nose sense base, etc., and the odor sense base, etc., is denied there, as in: "Is there the nose sense base there? Yes. Is there the odor sense base there? It should not be said thus," etc. (Kathā. 520). Nor can it be said that odors and tastes exist there as non-odor-and-taste-sense-bases, just as the earth element, etc., are not tangible-sense-bases. This is because there is no nature of odor and taste that is distinct from the state of being an odor-and-taste-sense-base, just as there is no nature of earth, etc., that is distinct from the ability to be touched. And if nose-contact, etc., have no causal basis, they would not be called sense bases. However, the term 'element' signifies the distinction between non-sentient and non-living, so there is no reason not to speak of the odor-element and taste-element. The intrinsic nature of these phenomena must be entirely accepted based on their characteristics of sustaining their own nature, etc., due to the absence of anything else. Furthermore, the state of being a sense base for phenomena is definitively stated in the Yamaka: "Is a phenomenon a sense base? Yes" (Yam. 1, Āyatanayamaka, 13). Therefore, even in the absence of their being odor and taste sense bases, some sense base nature should be acknowledged for them. And if, apart from their tangible nature, there were some other nature for them like the earth element, etc., or apart from their odor and taste nature, some other nature, then they would be included in the mental-phenomena-base. But if their odor and taste nature exists, and their sense base nature also exists, then that odor is also a sense base—the odor sense base—and that taste is also a sense base—the taste sense base. Thus, this is unavoidable, and their state as odor and taste sense bases cannot be prevented. From the statement "three nutriments" (Vibh. 1015), it is understood that physical food is absent there. Therefore, to avoid contradiction with the Pāli, the counting of material phenomena should be done excluding odor, taste, and nutritive essence. In this way, the natural order is not violated.' Thus he explains.

Ācariyajotipāladhammapālattherā pana taṃ paṭikkhipanti. Tathā ca vuttaṃ tehi “rūpāvacarasattānaṃ ghānajivhāyatanābhāvato vijjamānāpi gandharasā āyatanakiccaṃ na karontī”ti, te anāmasitvā pāḷiyaṃ “pañcāyatanāni pātubhavantī”ti “cha āyatanānī”ti (vibha. 993-994) ca ādi vuttaṃ. “Tayo āhārā”ti ca ajjhoharitabbassa āhārassa abhāvena ojaṭṭhamakarūpasamuṭṭhāpanasaṅkhātassa āhārakiccassa akaraṇato, na sabbena sabbaṃ gandharasānaṃ, ojāya ca abhāvato. Iti visayino kiccassa abhāvena visayo kiccabhāvadhammo na vutto. Yasmiñhi bhave visayī natthi, tasmiṃ taṃhetuko nippariyāyena visayassa āyatanabhāvo natthīti vijjamānassāpi avacanaṃ, yathā tattheva rūpabhave pathavītejovāyodhātūnaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanabhāvena. Yassa pana yattha vacanaṃ, tassa tattha visayīsabbhāvahetuko nippariyāyena āyatanabhāvo vutto, yathā tattheva rūpāyatanassa. Yadi visayīsabbhāvahetuko visayassa nippariyāyena āyatanabhāvo, kathamasaññasattānaṃ dve āyatanāni pātubhavanti. Asaññasattānañhi cakkhāyatanaṃ natthi. Atha tadabhāvena rūpāyatanaṃ aññesaṃ avisayoti? Nāyaṃ virodho. Yena adhippāyena rūpadhātuyaṃ saññīnaṃ gandhāyatanādīnaṃ avacanaṃ, tena na rūpāyatanassāpi avacananti asaññīnaṃ ekaṃ āyatanaṃ na vattabbaṃ. Yathāsakañhi indriyagocarabhāvāpekkhāya yesaṃ nippariyāyena āyatanabhāvo atthi, tesu [M 2.0178] niddisiyamānesu [V 2.0131] tadabhāvato rūpadhātuyaṃ saññīnaṃ gandhādike visuṃ āyatanabhāvena avatvā dhammasabhāvānativattanato, manoviññāṇassa ca visayabhāvūpagamanato dhammāyatanantogadhe katvā “pañcāyatanānī”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Etadatthañhi dhammāyatananti sāmaññato nāmakaraṇaṃ piṭṭhivaṭṭakāni vā tāni katvā “pañcāyatanānī”ti vuttaṃ. Yena ca pana adhippāyena asaññīnaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ vuttaṃ, tena saññīnaṃ, asaññīnampi gandhāyatanādīnaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ kātabbanti imassa nayassa dassanatthaṃ “asaññasattānaṃ devānaṃ dve āyatanāni pātubhavantī”ti (vibha. 1017) vuttaṃ.

The teachers, the elders Jotipāla and Dhammapāla, however, reject this. And so it has been stated by them: 'Although odors and tastes exist for beings in the form realm, they do not perform the function of a sense base due to the absence of the nose and tongue sense bases.' Without referring to them, it is said in the Pāli, 'Five sense bases appear' and 'Six sense bases,' etc. (Vibh. 993–994). Moreover, regarding the statement 'three kinds of nutriment,' because of the absence of nutriment to be ingested, the function of nutriment—which is defined as the production of materiality originating from nutritive essence—is not performed. This is not due to a complete absence of odors, tastes, and nutritive essence. Therefore, due to the absence of the function of the subject, the object is not spoken of as a phenomenon possessing the nature of a function. For in whatever existence the subject is absent, in that existence, for that reason, the object's nature as a sense base does not exist in a primary sense; hence, it is not mentioned even though it exists—just as in that same form realm, the earth, fire, and wind elements are not mentioned as the tangible sense base. But for whatever is mentioned in a certain place, its nature as a sense base is spoken of in a primary sense because of the existence of a subject there, just as in the case of the form sense base there. If an object's nature as a sense base exists in a primary sense because of the existence of a subject, how then do 'two sense bases appear' for non-percipient beings? For non-percipient beings lack the eye sense base. Is it then that, due to its absence, the form sense base is not an object for others? This is not a contradiction. For by the same intention that the odor sense base, etc., are not mentioned for percipient beings in the form realm, it is not that the form sense base is also unmentioned; hence, it should not be said that there is only one sense base for non-percipient beings. For, with respect to their being the domain of their respective faculties, when those things that have the nature of a sense base in a primary sense are being pointed out, due to the absence of that nature in the form realm for percipient beings, odors, etc., are not spoken of separately as sense bases. Since they do not transgress their nature as phenomena and because they come to be objects for mind-consciousness, having been included within the mind-object sense base, the Pāli states, 'Five sense bases.' For this purpose, the term 'mind-object sense base' is a general designation; or, having made them subsidiary, it is said, 'Five sense bases.' But by the same intention that the form sense base is stated for non-percipient beings, to show the principle that for both percipient and non-percipient beings the odor sense base, etc., should be taken separately, it is said, 'For non-percipient devas, two sense bases appear' (Vibh. 1017).

Asatipi hi tattha attano indriyesu rūpassa vaṇṇāyatanasabhāvātikkamo natthevāti taṃ rūpāyatanantveva vuccati. Iminā ca nayadassanena gandhādīni tīṇi pakkhipitvā saññīnaṃ aṭṭha āyatanāni, asaññīnaṃ pañcāti ayamattho dassito hoti. Evañcetaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, aññathā rūpaloke phusituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya pathavīādīnaṃ brahmūnaṃ vacīghoso eva ca na siyā. Na hi paṭighaṭṭananighaṃsanamantarena saddappavatti atthi, na ca phusanasabhāvānaṃ katthaci aphusanasabhāvatā sakkā viññātuṃ, phoṭṭhabbāyatanassa ca bhūtattayassa abhāve rūpabhave rūpāyatanādīnampi sambhavo eva na siyā, tasmā phusituṃ sakkuṇeyyatāyapi pathavīādīnaṃ tattha kāyindriyābhāvena tesaṃ phoṭṭhabbabhāvo na vutto. Evañca katvā rūpadhātuyaṃ tesaṃ sappaṭighatāvacanañca samatthitaṃ hoti. Vuttañhi “asaññasattānaṃ anidassanasappaṭighaṃ ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ paṭicca…pe… dve mahābhūtā”tiādi.

For even though one's own faculties are not present there, there is no transgression of the nature of form as the color sense base; hence, it is called simply the form sense base. By showing this method, and including the three—odor, etc.—it is demonstrated that there are eight sense bases for percipient beings and five for non-percipient beings. And this should be accepted thus; otherwise, due to the inability to touch in the form realm, the vocal utterances of the Brahmās of the earth-element sphere and so on would not exist. For there is no occurrence of sound without striking and friction, nor can a non-tangible nature be conceived anywhere for things that have a tangible nature. Moreover, in the absence of the tangible sense base of the three great elements, the arising of the form sense base, etc., in the form existence would not even be possible. Therefore, even though the earth element and so on are capable of being touched, their nature as tangible is not stated because the body faculty is absent there. And thus, the statement of their being with resistance in the form realm is also established. For it is said: 'For non-percipient beings, dependent on one invisible great element with resistance... (and so on)... two great elements,' etc.

Paṭigho ca nāma bhūtattayassa kāyapasādaṃ pati tannissayabhūtaghaṭṭanaṃ dvārena abhimukhabhāvo, idha pana taṃsabhāvatā, so ca phusituṃ asakkuṇeyyabhāvo ghaṭṭanāya [M 2.0179] abhāvato natthi. Yadi tattha asatipi visayimhi rūpāyatanampi gahetvā “dve āyatanānī”ti vuttaṃ, atha kasmā gandhāyatanādīni gahetvā “pañcāyatanānī”ti na vuttanti? Nayadassanavasena desanā pavattāti vuttovāyamattho. Atha vā tattha rūpāyatanasseva vacanaṃ kadāci aññabhūmikānaṃ pasādassa visayabhāvaṃ sandhāya, na pana itaresaṃ abhāvato, nāpi pariyāyena gandhāyatanādīnaṃ āyatanabhāvābhāvato.

Resistance, by name, is the confrontation of the three elements with the body sensitivity by means of striking its physical basis. Here, however, it is just their intrinsic nature. And that state of being unable to be touched is not due to the absence of striking. If, even when the subject is absent there, the form sense base is included and it is said, 'two sense bases,' then why are the odor sense base, etc., not included and it said, 'five sense bases'? This point has been explained: the teaching proceeds by way of presenting a method. Alternatively, the mention of only the form sense base there is sometimes with reference to its being an object for the sensitivity of beings of other planes, not because the others are absent, nor because the odor sense base, etc., lack the nature of a sense base in a secondary sense.

Asaññīnañhi rūpāyatanaṃ samānatalavāsīnaṃ vehapphalānaṃ, uparibhūmikānañca suddhāvāsānaṃ pasādassa [V 2.0132] visayabhāvaṃ gacchati, na pana gandharasāti tesaṃyeva tattha avacanaṃ yuttaṃ. Kathāvatthumhi ca nippariyāyena gandhāyatanādīnaṃ atthibhāvaṃ parijānantaṃ sandhāya paṭisedho kato. Yadipi cetaṃ vacanaṃ tattha gandhāyatanādīnaṃ abhāvavibhāvanaṃ na hoti, atthibhāvadīpanampi pana aññavacanaṃ natthevāti? Nayidamevaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu tattha tesaṃ atthibhāvassa niddhāretvā vuttattā. Yañhi aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ pāḷiyā na virujjhati, taṃ pāḷi viya pamāṇabhūtaṃ avigarahitāya ācariyaparamparāya yāvajjatanā āgatattā. Tattha siyā “yaṃ pāḷiyā na virujjhati aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ, taṃ pamāṇaṃ, idaṃ pana virujjhatī”ti? Nayidamevaṃ, yathā na virujjhati, tathā paṭipāditattā. Cakkhādīnaṃ āyatanānaṃ, tannissayānañca viññāṇānaṃ sattasuññatāsandassanatthaṃ bhagavato dhātudesanāti āyatanabhāvena vuttānaṃyeva dhātubhāvadīpanato dhātubhāvassāpi tesaṃ avacanaṃ yujjati eva, tasmā yathā pāḷiyā avirodho hoti, tathā cakkhudasakādivasena idha rūpagaṇanā katāti na ettha dhammatāvilomanāsaṅkāya okāsoti veditabbanti.

For the form sense base of non-percipient beings comes within the range of the sensitivity of the Vehapphala beings dwelling on the same plane, and of the Suddhāvāsa beings in the planes above; but odors and tastes do not. Therefore, it is appropriate that only these are not mentioned there. And in the Kathāvatthu, the refutation was made with reference to one who understands the existence of the odor sense base and so on in a primary sense. One might ask: Even if this statement does not clarify the non-existence of the odor sense base and so on there, is there then no other statement that indicates their existence? This is not so, because in the commentaries their existence there has been stated after having been determined. For a statement in the commentaries that does not contradict the Pāli is authoritative like the Pāli itself, having come down to the present day through an irreproachable lineage of teachers. Here one might say: 'A statement in the commentaries that does not contradict the Pāli is authoritative, but this one does contradict it.' This is not so, because it has been established in such a way that it does not contradict. The Blessed One's teaching of the elements is for showing the emptiness of a being with regard to the sense bases such as the eye and the consciousnesses dependent on them. Since the elemental nature is revealed only for those things spoken of as sense bases, it is indeed fitting that their elemental nature is also not mentioned. Therefore, just as there is no contradiction with the Pāli, so here the enumeration of material phenomena has been made by way of the eye-decad and so on. Thus, it should be understood that there is no occasion here for the suspicion of violating the natural order of things.

756. Jaccandhabadhirāti [M 2.0180] chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ dīghakaraṇaṃ. Na hi jaccandhabadhiraaghānarahite napuṃsake vatthukāyajivhādasakavasena idha tiṃsāti yujjati, idañca “opapātikassa jaccandhabadhiraghānarahite napuṃsake jivhākāyavatthudasakānaṃ vasena tiṃsa rūpāni uppajjantī”ti aṭṭhakathāvādaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Ānandācariyo pana taṃ “pāḷiyā na sametī”ti vatvā paṭikkhipati. Tathā cāha “netaṃ pāḷiyā sametī”ti. Na hi pāḷiyaṃ kāmāvacarānaṃ saṃsedajopapātikānaṃ aghānakānaṃ uppatti vuttā.

756. In 'jaccandhabadhira,' the lengthening is for the sake of preserving the meter. For it is not correct that here, for a sexless person who is congenitally blind, deaf, and without a nose, there are thirty material phenomena by way of the heart-base-decad, body-decad, and tongue-decad. And this is said having adopted the commentarial view that 'for a spontaneously born, sexless person who is congenitally blind, deaf, and without a nose, thirty material phenomena arise by way of the tongue-decad, body-decad, and heart-base-decad.' But the teacher Ānanda rejects this, saying, 'This does not accord with the Pāli.' And so he says, 'This does not accord with the Pāli.' For in the Pāli, the arising of moisture-born and spontaneously born beings of the sense-sphere who are without a nose is not mentioned.

Dhammahadayavibhaṅge hi –

For in the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga:

“Kāmadhātuyā upapattikkhaṇe kassaci ekādasāyatanāni pātubhavanti, kassaci dasāyatanāni, kassaci aparāni dasāyatanāni, kassaci navāyatanāni, kassaci sattāyatanāni pātubhavantī”ti (vibha. 1009) –

“At the moment of rebirth in the sensual realm, for some, eleven sense bases manifest; for some, ten sense bases; for some, another ten sense bases; for some, nine sense bases; and for some, seven sense bases manifest.”

Vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “aṭṭhāyatanāni pātubhavantī”ti. Yadi hi aghānakassāpi upapatti siyā, tikkhattuṃ “dasāyatanāni pātubhavantī”ti vattabbaṃ siyā, tikkhattuñca “navāyatanāni pātubhavantī”ti, na cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yamake ca ghānajivhānaṃ sahappavatti vuttāti taṃ upaparikkhitvā [V 2.0133] gahetabbanti. Ayañhettha ācariyassa adhippāyo – dhammahadayavibhaṅgapāḷiyañhi “ekādasā”ti paripuṇṇāyatanassa saddāyatanavajjāni ekādasāyatanāni vuttāni, “kassaci dasāyatanānī”ti andhassa cakkhāyatanavajjāni, “aparāni dasāyatanānī”ti badhirassa sotāyatanavajjāni, “navāyatanānī”ti andhabadhirassa cakkhusotavajjāni, “sattāyatanānī”ti gabbhaseyyakassa rūpagandharasakāyaphoṭṭhabbamanadhammāyatanavasena vuttaṃ. Yadi cakkhusotaghānavikalopi uppajjeyya, tassa aṭṭhevāyatanāni [M 2.0181] vattabbāni siyuṃ, na ca vuttaṃ “aṭṭhāyatanāni pātubhavantī”ti, tasmā nattheva cakkhusotaghānavikalo. Sati aghānakaupapattiyaṃ punapi “kassaci aparāni dasāyatanāni pātubhavantī”ti vattabbaṃ siyā. Tathā ca sati yathā andhabadhirassa vasena “kassaci navāyatanāni pātubhavantī”ti ekavāraṃ vuttaṃ, evaṃ andhāghānakassa, badhirāghānakassa ca vasena “kassaci aparāni navāyatanāni, kassaci aparāni navāyatanānī”ti vattabbaṃ siyā. Kāmabhave ajivhassa sattassābhāvato, ghānajivhāyatanānaṃ sahappavattivacanato ca tattheva kāmadhātuyaṃ aghānakassāsambhavoti.

It is stated thus, but it is not stated, “Eight sense bases manifest.” For if rebirth even for one without a nose were possible, it should be stated three times, “Ten sense bases manifest,” and three times, “Nine sense bases manifest,” but this is not stated. And in the Yamaka, it is stated that the nose and tongue arise together; this should be examined and understood. Herein lies the teacher’s intention: In the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga Pāḷi, “eleven” sense bases are stated for one with a complete set of sense bases, excluding the sound base; “for some, ten sense bases” excludes the eye base for the blind; “for others, ten sense bases” excludes the ear base for the deaf; “nine sense bases” excludes the eye and ear bases for the blind and deaf; and “seven sense bases” are stated in relation to one in the womb, by way of the form, smell, taste, body, tangible object, mind, and mental-object sense bases. If one lacking eyes, ears, and a nose were to arise, eight sense bases should be stated for that one, but it is not said, “Eight sense bases manifest.” Therefore, one lacking eyes, ears, and a nose does not exist. If rebirth without a nose were possible, then again it should be stated, “For some others, ten sense bases manifest.” And in that case, just as it is stated once regarding the blind and deaf, “For some, nine sense bases manifest,” so too regarding the blind without a nose and the deaf without a nose, it should be stated, “For some others, nine sense bases, and for some others, nine sense bases.” In the sensual realm, because there is no being without a tongue, and because of the statement that the nose and tongue bases arise together, rebirth without a nose is impossible in that same sensual realm.

Jotipālattherādayo pana “saṃsedajassa jaccandhabadhiraaghānakanapuṃsakassa jivhākāyavatthudasakānaṃ vasena tiṃsarūpāni uppajjantīti vuttaṃ, na opapātikassa. Dhammahadayavibhaṅgapāḷiyañca ‘upapattikkhaṇe’ti vuttattā opapātikasseva vasena nayo nīto. Yamakaṭṭhakathāyañca vuttaṃ ‘kāmadhātuyaṃ aghānako opapātiko natthi. Yadi bhaveyya, kassaci aṭṭhāyatanāni pātubhavantīti vadeyyā’ti, yampi dhammahadayavibhaṅge ‘kāmadhātuyā upapattikkhaṇe kassaci ekādasāyatanāni pātubhavantī’tiādīnaṃ niddese ‘opapātikānaṃ petāna’ntiādinā opapātika-ggahaṇameva kataṃ, na pana saṃsedaja-ggahaṇaṃ, taṃ paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃyeva saṃsedajānaṃ opapātikesu saṅgahavasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ ‘saṃsedajayonikā paripuṇṇāyatanabhāvena opapātikasaṅgahaṃ katvā vuttā’ti, padhānāya vā yoniyā sabbaṃ paripuṇṇāyatanaṃ yoniṃ saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ ‘opapātikāna’nti vuttanti ca, tasmā na koci pāḷivirodho”ti vadanti.

Jotipāla and other elders, however, say: “It is stated that for a moisture-born, congenitally blind, deaf, noseless, and sexless being, thirty types of form arise based on the tongue-decad, body-decad, and base-decad, but this is not so for one who is spontaneously born. And in the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga Pāḷi, since ‘at the moment of rebirth’ is stated, the reasoning is applied only with reference to the spontaneously born. And in the Yamaka commentary it is stated: ‘In the sensual realm, there is no spontaneously born being lacking a nose. If there were, one would say that eight sense bases manifest.’ Moreover, in the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga, in the explanation of passages such as ‘at the moment of rebirth in the sensual realm, eleven sense bases manifest for some,’ the term ‘spontaneously born’ is used specifically for ghosts and so on, and does not include the moisture-born. This should be understood as referring only to moisture-born beings with complete sense bases, who are included under the spontaneously born for the sake of classification. As the commentary states: ‘Those of moisture-born origin are spoken of as included with the spontaneously born on account of their having complete sense bases.’ Alternatively, to show that all types of birth with complete sense faculties are included under the primary type of birth, the term ‘spontaneously born’ is used. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Pāli texts.”

Apare panāhu – “kāmadhātuyaṃ aghānako opapātiko natthi. Yadi bhaveyya, kassaci aṭṭhāyatanāni pātubhavantīti [M 2.0182] vadeyyāti idaṃ manussesu saṃsedajopapātikānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, te paripuṇṇāyatanāva[V 2.0134]. Kesañci pana aghānakakīṭānaṃ atthibhāvato apāyesu saṃsedajopapātike sandhāyetaṃ vutta”nti vadanti. Taṃ ānandācariyādīnaṃ matena paṭikkhepārahamevāti.

Others, however, say: “In the sensual realm, there is no spontaneously born being lacking a nose. If there were, one would say that eight sense bases manifest.” This is said with reference to moisture-born and spontaneously born humans, who have complete sense bases. However, they say this is stated in reference to moisture-born and spontaneously born beings in the lower realms, because of the existence of some insects lacking a nose. This view, according to the opinion of the teacher Ānanda and others, is to be rejected.

757-8. Ukkaṃsassāvakaṃsassa antareti “sattatī”ti vuttaukkaṃsaparicchedassa, “tiṃsā”ti vuttaavakaṃsaparicchedassa ca majjhe. Anurūpato…pe… vibhāvināti jātiandhassa saṭṭhi rūpāni cakkhudasakābhāvato, tathā badhirassa sotadasakābhāvato, andhabadhirassa pana paṇṇāsa cakkhusotadasakābhāvatotiādinā nayena aññamaññāpekkhāya paripuṇṇā paripuṇṇānaṃ rūpānaṃ pāṇīnaṃ vasena rūpānaṃ samuppatti viññātabbāti attho. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ vuttamevāti.

757-8. “Between the higher and lower limits” means between the higher limit said to be “seventy” and the lower limit said to be “thirty.” “Appropriately… clearly…” means: For a person blind from birth, sixty forms arise due to the absence of the eye-decad; similarly, for a deaf person, due to the absence of the ear-decad; and for one both blind and deaf, fifty forms arise due to the absence of both the eye- and ear-decads. In this way, the arising of forms should be understood by way of beings with complete and incomplete forms, in relation to one another. Whatever needs to be said here has already been stated.

759-60. Evaṃ tīsu bhavesu paṭisandhiyaṃ rūpappavattiṃ dassetvā idāni pavattiyaṃ dassetuṃ “sattavīsati rūpānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kāmāvacarasattassa hi paripuṇṇāyatanassa asati andhabadhirādipasādavighāte yāva maraṇacittassa heṭṭhā sattarasamacittaṃ, tāva sattavīsati rūpāni pavattanti. Aparipuṇṇāyatanassa pana jaccandhādikassa heṭṭhā vuttanayena rūpānaṃ hāyanavaḍḍhanāni veditabbāni. Nanu aṭṭhavīsatiyeva rūpāni kāmabhave pavattantīti āha “appavattanato”tiādi.

759-60. Having thus shown the occurrence of form at rebirth-linking in the three planes of existence, to show its occurrence during the course of existence, it is now said, “twenty-seven forms,” and so on. For a being in the sensual realm with complete sense faculties, and without impairment of the sensitive faculties such as blindness or deafness, twenty-seven forms occur up to the seventeenth thought-moment before the death-consciousness. However, for one with incomplete sense faculties, such as one born blind, the decrease and increase of forms should be understood in the way previously stated. “But should it not be said that twenty-eight forms occur in the sensual realm?” To this, it is replied, “Due to non-occurrence,” and so on.

Ghānaṃ…pe… na vijjareti kāmavirāgabhāvanāvasena gandhādiggāhakesu pasādesu virattā hontīti ghānādittayaṃ natthi. Cakkhusotesu pana anuttaradassanādiatthaṃ virattā na hontīti tāni tesaṃ uppajjanti. Bhāvadvayaṃ kāmarāgūpanissayattā na uppajjati. Keci pana “lahutādittayampi rūpabhave [M 2.0183] natthi dandhattakarādidhātukkhobhābhāvato. Sati hi tādise dhātukkhobhe tappaṭipakkhehi lahutādīhi bhavitabba”nti vadanti, taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Na hi vūpasametabbapaccanīkāpekkho tabbirodhidhammuppādo. Tathā sati sahetukakiriyacittuppādesu kāyalahutādīnaṃ abhāvo eva siyā, tasmā pañceva rūpāni saññībrahmānaṃ na uppajjanti, avasesāni tevīsati rūpāni uppajjanti. Asaññībrahmānaṃ pana pañca pasādarūpāni, bhāvadvayaṃ, hadayavatthu, viññattidvayaṃ, lahutādittayanti terasa rūpāni vajjetvā avasesāni pannarasa uppajjanti.

“The nose... and so on ... does not exist” means that because, through the cultivation of dispassion towards sensual pleasures, they become dispassionate towards the sensitive faculties that grasp odors and so on, the triad beginning with the nose does not exist. However, in the case of the eye and ear, because they are not dispassionate for the sake of supreme vision and so on, those arise for them. The two material qualities of sex do not arise because they are a basis for sensual lust. Some, however, say: “Even the triad of lightness and so on does not exist in the fine-material existence because of the absence of elemental disturbances that cause sluggishness and so on. For if such elemental disturbances were present, there would have to be their counterparts, lightness and so on.” This is baseless. For the arising of a phenomenon that counteracts another does not depend on the presence of an opponent to be pacified. If that were the case, there would be an absence of bodily lightness and so on even in the arising of functional consciousness with roots. Therefore, only five material qualities do not arise for the Brahmās with perception, while the remaining twenty-three arise. For the Brahmās without perception, however, excluding the five sensitive material qualities, the two material qualities of sex, the heart-base, the two kinds of intimation, and the triad of lightness—thirteen material qualities in total—the remaining fifteen arise.

761. Catusantatīti [V 2.0135] catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ vasena catusantatirūpāni. Rūpe honti tisantatīti brahmānaṃ anāhārabhāvena āhārajarūpānaṃ abhāvato tisso santatiyo. Dvisantatīti cittajāhārajānaṃ abhāvato dve santatiyo. Bahiddhā ekasantatīti kammajādīnaṃ tissannampi abhāvato utujasantatiyeva.

761. “Four continuities” refers to the continuities of material qualities arising from four conditions. “In the fine-material realm, there are three continuities” means that for Brahmās, due to their not taking nutriment, there is an absence of nutriment-born material qualities; hence there are three continuities. “Two continuities” means that due to the absence of mind-born and nutriment-born material qualities, there are two continuities. “Externally, one continuity” means that due to the absence of the three beginning with kamma-born, only the temperature-born continuity remains.

762-4. Evaṃ paṭisandhipavattīsu rūpānaṃ gaṇanaparicchedaṃ vatvā idāni tattha nesaṃ uppattikkamaṃ dassetuṃ “rūpaṃ nibbattamāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbesanti kāmarūpabhavikānaṃ sabbasattānaṃ. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe panāti ettha dasakattayaṃ hotīti pāṭhaseso. Tenāha “yathevā”tiādi. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe dasakattayaṃ heṭṭhā vuttampi “tañca kho sandhicittassā”tiādikaṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ puna vuttaṃ. Cittassa tīsu khaṇesu kammajarūpānaṃ samuppattito āha “tathevā”tiādi. Tiṃsa tiṃsevāti tiṃsa tiṃseva kammajarūpāni.

762-4. Thus, having stated the enumeration and classification of material qualities in rebirth-linking and life-continuity, it is now said, 'Material quality arises,' and so on, to show their sequence of arising there. 'For all' means for all beings in the sense-sphere and fine-material existences. 'But at the moment of rebirth-linking'—here, the remaining text is 'the threefold decad arises.' Hence it is said, 'Just as...' and so on. The threefold decad at the moment of rebirth-linking, though stated previously, is mentioned again to show the distinction, 'That, however, is for the rebirth-linking consciousness,' and so on. Because kamma-born material qualities arise in the three moments of consciousness, it is said, 'Similarly...' and so on. 'Thirty each' means thirty kamma-born material qualities each.

Ānandācariyo pana “cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇameva natthi, bhaṅgakkhaṇe ca rūpuppādo natthīti catusamuṭṭhānikānipi rūpāni cittassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva hontī”ti āha. Vuttañhi tena [M 2.0184] – yo cettha cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇo vutto, so ca atthi natthīti vicāretabbo. Cittayamake hi “uppannaṃ uppajjamāna”nti (yama. 2.cittayamaka.81) etassa vibhaṅge “bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannaṃ no ca uppajjamāna”nti (yama. 2.cittayamaka.81) ettakameva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “ṭhitikkhaṇe bhaṅgakkhaṇe cā”ti. Tathā”na uppajjamānaṃ na uppanna”nti ettha “bhaṅgakkhaṇe na uppajjamānaṃ no ca na uppanna”nti ettakameva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “ṭhitikkhaṇe bhaṅgakkhaṇe cā”ti. Evaṃ “na niruddhaṃ na nirujjhamāna”nti etesaṃ paripuṇṇavissajjane “uppādakkhaṇe anāgatañcā”ti vatvā “ṭhitikkhaṇe”ti avacanaṃ, atikkantakālavāre ca “bhaṅgakkhaṇe cittaṃ uppādakkhaṇaṃ vītikkanta”nti (yama. 2.cittayamaka.83) vatvā “ṭhitikkhaṇe”ti avacanaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇābhāvaṃ cittassa dīpeti. Suttepi hi “ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ paññāyatī”ti (a. ni. 3.47) tasseva ekassa aññathattābhāvato yassā aññathattaṃ paññāyati, sā santatiṭṭhitīti na na sakkā vattuṃ. Vijjamānaṃ taṃkhaṇadvayasamaṅgī ṭhitanti. Yo cettha cittassa nirodhakkhaṇe rūpuppādo vutto, so ca vicāretabbo. Kasmā? “Yassa vā pana samudayasaccaṃ nirujjhati, tassa dukkhasaccaṃ uppajjatīti? No”ti (yama. 1.saccayamaka.136) vuttanti, na [V 2.0136] ca cittasamuṭṭhānarūpameva sandhāya paṭikkhepo katoti sakkā viññātuṃ cittasamuṭṭhānarūpādhikārassa abhāvāti.

Ānandācariya, however, says: 'There is no moment of presence for the mind, and at the moment of dissolution, the arising of material qualities does not occur. Therefore, even the fourfold-originated material qualities arise only at the moment of the mind's arising.' For it is said by him: 'What is here called the moment of presence for the mind, that should be investigated as to whether it exists or not.' For in the Cittayamaka, in the analysis of 'What has arisen is arising,' only this much is stated: 'At the moment of dissolution, what has arisen is not arising,' and it is not stated 'at the moment of presence and dissolution.' Similarly, in the statement 'What is not arising is not arisen,' only this much is stated: 'At the moment of dissolution, what is not arising is not arisen,' and it is not stated 'at the moment of presence and dissolution.' Thus, in the full explanation of 'not ceased and not ceasing,' after stating 'at the moment of arising and the future,' the non-mention of 'at the moment of presence,' and in the section on past time, after stating 'at the moment of dissolution, the mind has passed the moment of arising,' the non-mention of 'at the moment of presence' indicates the non-existence of a moment of presence for the mind. For in the Sutta too, it is said: 'Change is evident in what is present,' and since there is no change in that very single instance, it can indeed be said that what is evident as change is the presence of continuity. What exists, endowed with those two moments, is called 'present.' As for what is said here about the arising of material qualities at the moment of the mind's cessation, that too should be examined. Why? Because it is said: 'When the truth of arising ceases, does the truth of suffering arise for him? No.' And it cannot be understood that the denial was made with reference only to mind-originated material qualities, due to the absence of a discussion of mind-originated material qualities.

Ācariyassa hi ayamadhippāyo – uppannauppajjamānavārādīsu “ṭhitikkhaṇe”ti avacanaṃ “cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇaṃ nāma natthī”ti imamatthaṃ dīpeti. Na hi yathādhammasāsane abhidhamme labbhamānassa avacane kāraṇaṃ dissati. Na kevalaṃ abhidhamme avacanameva cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇabhāvajotakaṃ, apica kho “ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ paññāyatī”ti evamāgatā suttantapāḷipi. Aññathattaṃ nāma pubbāparaviseso. Apica yathā bhūto dhammo uppajjati, kiṃ tathā bhūtova bhijjati, udāhu [M 2.0185] aññathā bhūto. Yadi tathā bhūtova bhijjati, na jaratāya sambhavo. Aññathā bhūto, añño eva soti sabbathāpi ṭhitikkhaṇassa abhāvoyeva. Yadi ca cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe rūpaṃ uppajjeyya, taṃ dukkhasaccanti katvā “no”ti vattuṃ na sakkā, vuttañca, tasmā viññāyati “cittassa nirodhakkhaṇe rūpuppādo natthī”ti.

For the teacher's intention here is this: in the sections concerning 'what has arisen' and 'what is arising,' etc., the non-mention of 'moment of presence' indicates the meaning that 'there is no such thing as a moment of presence for the mind.' Indeed, in the true teaching of the Dhamma, in the Abhidhamma, no reason is seen for the non-mention of what is found. Not only is this non-mention in the Abhidhamma indicative of the non-existence of a moment of presence for the mind, but also the Suttanta passage that states, 'Change is evident in what is present,' and so on. Change means a difference between what precedes and what follows. Moreover, as a phenomenon arises in its true nature, does it cease in that same true nature, or does it cease in a different nature? If it ceases in that same true nature, decay is not possible. If it ceases in a different nature, then it is entirely different; thus, in every way, there is no moment of presence. And if material qualities were to arise at the moment of the mind's dissolution, having classified it as the truth of suffering, it would not be possible to say 'no,' but it has been said. Therefore, it is understood that 'there is no arising of material qualities at the moment of the mind's cessation.'

Ācariyajotipāladhammapālattherānaṃ panetaṃ nakkhamati. Tehi “ekadhammādhārabhāvepi uppādanirodhānaṃ añño uppādakkhaṇo, añño nirodhakkhaṇo. Uppādāvatthañhi upādāya uppādakkhaṇo, nirodhāvatthaṃ upādāya nirodhakkhaṇo. Uppādāvatthāya ca bhinnā nirodhāvatthāti ekasmiṃyeva ca sabhāvadhamme yathā icchitabbā, aññathā aññoyeva dhammo uppajjati, añño nirujjhatīti āpajjeyya, evaṃ nirodhāvatthāya viya nirodhābhimukhāvatthāyapi bhavitabbaṃ, sā ṭhiti jaratā cā”ti sampaṭicchitabbametaṃ.

However, this is not accepted by the venerable teachers Jotipāla and Dhammapāla. They say: 'Even when a single phenomenon is the basis, the moment of arising is distinct from the moment of cessation. For the moment of arising is designated in relation to the state of arising, and the moment of cessation in relation to the state of cessation. And since the state of arising is different from the state of cessation, they must be accepted as belonging to one and the same essential phenomenon; otherwise, it would follow that one phenomenon arises and another ceases. Thus, just as there is a state of cessation, so also there must be a state tending towards cessation—that is presence and aging.' This is to be accepted.

Yadi evaṃ, kasmā pāḷiyaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇo na vuttoti? Vineyyajjhāsayānurodhena nayadassanavasena pāḷigatīti veditabbāti. Abhidhammadesanāpi hi kadāci vineyyajjhāsayānurodhena pavattati, yathā rūpassa uppādo “upacayo santatī”ti bhinditvā desito. Hetusampayuttadukādidesanā cettha nidassitabbā. “Yassa vā panā”tiādipucchāya vissajjane ca arūpalokaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ vā sandhāya “no”ti sakkā vattuṃ. Ayañhi yamakadesanāya pakati, yadidaṃ yathāsambhavayojanāti. Atha vā paccāsattiñāyena yaṃ samudayasaccaṃ nirujjhati, tena yaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ uppādetabbaṃ cittacetasikatappaṭibaddharūpasaṅkhātaṃ, tassa [V 2.0137] tadā uppatti natthīti “no”ti vissajjanaṃ, na sabbassa vacanato, tasmā na [M 2.0186] sakkā cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe, bhaṅgakkhaṇe ca rūpuppādanaṃ paṭikkhipitunti vadanti.

If this is so, why is the moment of presence not mentioned in the Pāli canon? It should be understood that the Pāli canon proceeds by way of illustrating principles in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained. For even the Abhidhamma teachings sometimes proceed in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained, as when the arising of material qualities is explained by breaking it down into 'accumulation and continuity.' Here, teachings such as the 'root-associated dyads' should be exemplified. And in answering the question beginning with 'Or for whom,' it is possible to say 'no' with reference to the formless realm or to mind-originated material qualities. For this is the nature of the Yamaka teachings, namely, to connect things as they are possible. Alternatively, by the principle of proximity, when the truth of origin ceases, the truth of suffering—which is to be produced, defined as material qualities connected with mind and mental factors—does not arise at that time. Thus, the answer 'no' is given, not with respect to everything. Therefore, they say that it is not possible to deny the arising of material qualities at the moment of the mind's presence or at the moment of its dissolution.

Utujarūpāni pana paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitikkhaṇato paṭṭhāya aṭṭhakanavakavasena uppajjanti. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe hi uppannānaṃ kammajarūpānaṃ abbhantare sahuppādaekanirodhatejodhātu ṭhānaṃ patvā tassa ṭhitikkhaṇe aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti, tattha uppannā tejodhātu paṭisandhicittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe, tattha uppannā paṭhamabhavaṅgassa uppādakkhaṇeti evamādinā aṭṭhakaṃ, kadāci saddapātubhāvakāle tena saha saddanavakañca uppajjati. Cittajarūpāni ca paṭisandhito anantaraṃ paṭhamabhavaṅgato paṭṭhāya rūpajanakacittānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe aṭṭhakavasena, saddapātubhāvādikāle saddanavakādivasena ca pavattanti. Āhārajāni pana ekassa, dvinnaṃ vā sattāhānaṃ atikkamena nibbattanti. Nanu ca ajjhohaṭāhārapaccayena āhāro rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, gabbhe sayantassa ca kuto ajjhoharaṇāhāroti? Samātito. Mātarā hi bhuttaṃ kucchigatassa sarīre abbhañjanaṃ viya āhārakiccaṃ karoti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Moreover, temperature-born material qualities arise in sets of eight or nine from the moment of presence of the rebirth-linking consciousness onwards. For at the moment of rebirth-linking, the fire element that has arisen simultaneously and ceases together within the kamma-born material qualities, having reached its moment of presence, generates eight material qualities at that moment of presence. The fire element that arises there at the dissolution moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness, and the one that arises there at the arising moment of the first life-continuum, and so on—in this way an octad is generated; occasionally, at the time of the manifestation of sound, a nonad including sound also arises along with it. And mind-born material qualities proceed from immediately after rebirth-linking, beginning with the first life-continuum, in sets of eight at the arising moment of minds that generate material qualities, and in sets of nine including sound, etc., at the time of the manifestation of sound and so on. Now, nutriment-born material qualities arise after the lapse of one or two weeks. But does not ingested nutriment produce material qualities by way of condition? And how can there be ingested nutriment for one lying in the womb? From the mother. For the food eaten by the mother performs the function of nutriment for the body of the one in the womb, like an anointing. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Yañcassa bhuñjatī mātā,

Annaṃ pānañca bhojanaṃ;

Tena so tattha yāpeti,

Mātukucchigato naro”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.235);

“Whatever food, drink, and edibles his mother eats, By that the person dwelling in the mother's womb is maintained there.”

Tasmā mātarā ajjhohaṭāhārena anuggahite sarīre abbhantarikā ojā laddhappaccayā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, cakkhusotaghānajivhādasakā pana pañcapasādāvatthaṃ atikkamma pacchā sattame sattāhe uppajjanti, “ekādasame sattāhe”ti (yama. mūlaṭī. āyatanayamaka 22-254) ānandācariyo avoca. Ayamettha gabbhaseyyakānaṃ rūpappavattinayo.

Therefore, when the body is nourished by the food ingested by the mother, the internal nutritive essence, having obtained a condition, produces form. But the eye, ear, nose, and tongue decads arise in the seventh week, having passed beyond the stage of the five sense faculties. Ācariya Ānanda stated, 'In the eleventh week.' This is the way form arises for those lying in the womb.

Opapātikānampi [M 2.0187] paṭisandhicittassa uppādakkhaṇe kammasamuṭṭhānāni sattati rūpāni uppajjanti, tathevassa ṭhitikkhaṇe, bhaṅgakkhaṇe ca sattati sattatītiādinā vuttanayena ukkaṃsāvakaṃsato kāmabhavikasattānaṃ, rūpībrahmānañca yathāvuttanayeneva yathānurūpaṃ kammasamuṭṭhānānaṃ, utusamuṭṭhānānañca pavatti veditabbā. Āhārajarūpaṃ pana kāmāvacarānaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ [V 2.0138] attano mukhagatakheḷaṃ ajjhoharaṇakāle uppajjati. Saññībrahmānaṃ taṃ sabbena sabbaṃ natthi. Asaññīnañca cittajāhārajāni natthevāti ayaṃ viseso. Evaṃ uppajjamānesu ca panetesu rūpesu yaṃ cittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ, taṃ attanā sahuppannacittaṃ ādiṃ katvā sattarasamacittassa nirodhakkhaṇe nirujjhati, ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannaṃ aṭṭhārasamassa uppādakkhaṇe nirujjhati, bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannaṃ imassa ṭhitikkhaṇe nirujjhatīti evaṃ uppajjantaṃ, nirujjhantañca yāva maraṇacittassa heṭṭhā sattarasamacittaṃ, tāva yathārahaṃ catusantatiādivasena pavattatīti. Āsannamaraṇassa pana cutito sattarasamacittassa ṭhitikkhaṇamādiṃ katvā kammajarūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāti. Yadi samuṭṭhāti, maraṇaṃ na siyā anupacchinnattā kammajarūpānaṃ. Kammajarūpasamucchede hi “mato”ti vuccati. Vuttañhi –

For spontaneously born beings also, at the arising-moment of rebirth-consciousness, seventy kamma-produced material phenomena arise. Similarly, at the duration-moment and the dissolution-moment, seventy each arise, according to the method stated regarding increase and decrease. The occurrence of kamma-produced and temperature-produced material phenomena for beings in the desire realm and for form-realm Brahmās should be understood in accordance with the method stated and as appropriate. Nutriment-produced materiality, however, first arises for beings in the desire realm at the time of swallowing their own saliva. For perception-possessing Brahmās, that does not exist at all. And for non-percipient beings, mind-produced and nutriment-produced material phenomena do not exist—this is the distinction. Moreover, among these material phenomena that are arising, whatever arose at the arising-moment of the mind ceases at the dissolution-moment of the seventeenth mind-moment, counting the co-arisen mind as the first. What arose at the duration-moment ceases at the arising-moment of the eighteenth mind-moment. What arose at the dissolution-moment ceases at the duration-moment of this mind-moment. Thus, arising and ceasing continue in accordance with the fourfold continuity, etc., as appropriate, until the seventeenth mind-moment prior to the death-consciousness. However, for one nearing death, kamma-produced materiality does not arise starting from the duration-moment of the seventeenth consciousness before death. If it were to arise, death would not occur, because the continuity of kamma-produced material phenomena would not be broken. For it is when kamma-produced materiality is cut off that one is said to be 'dead.' For it was said:

“Āyu usmā ca viññāṇaṃ, yadā kāyaṃ jahantimaṃ;

Apaviddho tadā seti, niratthaṃva kaliṅgara”nti. (saṃ. ni. 3.95);

When life, heat, and consciousness abandon this body, then it lies discarded, like a useless log.

Sattarasamena saha uppannañca taṃ cuticittena saha nirujjhati, aparañca na uppajjati. Āyukkhayā, kammakkhayā, ubhayakkhayā, upakkamena vā kassacīti evaṃ kammajarūpasseva hi maraṇaṃ hoti satipi āhāraje, aṭṭhakathāmatena cittaje ca. Tampi apagatajīvassa na uppajjati. Utujarūpaṃ pana pavattati eva. Tathā saṃsedajānaṃ, opapātikānaṃ pana sarīranikkhepābhāvato tampi na pavattati.

That which arose with the seventeenth mind-moment before death ceases together with the death-consciousness, and no other kamma-born matter arises. Death occurs due to the exhaustion of lifespan, the exhaustion of kamma, the exhaustion of both, or by a destructive cause. Thus, death is indeed the cessation of kamma-born matter, even when nutriment-born matter is present, and, according to the commentaries, even when mind-born matter is present. That mind-born matter also does not arise for one whose life has ceased. Temperature-born matter, however, continues to occur. Similarly for moisture-born beings. But for spontaneously-born beings, since there is no casting off of the body, even that temperature-born matter does not continue.

765-6. Uppādavayavantatāya [M 2.0188] nicco dhuvo na hotīti anicco, niccakhaṇikatāya vā na icco sassatādivasena anupagantabboti anicco. Ayañhi vināso janakapaccayato aññahetunirapekkhatāya niccakhaṇikova hoti. Dhuvasāravirahitattā addhuvo. Avasavattanaṭṭhena anattā. Udayavayapaṭipīḷanena, dukkhavatthutāya ca dukkhānaṃ khandho samūhoti dukkhakkhandho. Evaṃvidho pana sukhehi asammissoyevāti āha “kevalo”ti. Kassacipi vā rūpassa sukhasabhāvassa abhāvato sakalopi dukkhakkhandhoti vuttaṃ “dukkhakkhandho ca kevalo”ti. Paccayayāpaniyatāya ca rogamūlatāya ca rogato. So hi yathārahaṃ paccayehi yāpetabbatāya yāpyarogo viyāti rogato daṭṭhabbo. Yāpyabyādhi hi rogo, itaro ābādho, mūlabyādhi viya cesa anubaddhabyādhīnaṃ kilesarogādīnaṃ mūlabhāvato rogato daṭṭhabbo. Dukkhatāsūlayogitāya, kilesāsucipaggharaṇatāya[V 2.0139], uppādajarābhaṅgehi uddhumātaparipakkapabhinnatāya ca gaṇḍato. So hi dukkhadukkhatā saṅkhāradukkhatā vipariṇāmadukkhatāti tividhadukkhatāsaṅkhātena rujjanena yuttatāya, yathārahamārammaṇavasena ca samannāgamavasena ca rāgādikilesāsucivissandanato, ahutvā sambhavanato, uppattiyā uddhumātattā jarābhaṅgehi ca yathākkamaṃ paripakkapabhinnabhāvato gaṇḍasadisoti gaṇḍato daṭṭhabbo. Avasavattanatāya, avidheyyatāya ca parato. Yathā hi paro patanto parassa vasaṃ na gacchati, evametaṃ subhasukhādibhāvena vase vattetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya avasavattanato “mā jīratha, mā marathā”tiādinā vidhātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya avidheyyabhāvato parato daṭṭhabbaṃ. Byādhijarāmaraṇehi palujjanato, ābyāsanato ca palokato. Idaṃ byādhiādīhi pakārehi [M 2.0189] bhijjanato, vinassanato, etehi eva vā ābyāsanato byasanatthassa loka-saddassa pavisiṭṭhassa ābyāsanatthatāya palokato daṭṭhabbaṃ. Chandanti rajjanavasena pavattaṃ chandaṃ.

765-6. Because it has arising and passing away, it is not permanent or stable—thus it is impermanent. Or because, being momentary, it is not to be regarded as eternal, and so forth—thus it is impermanent. For this very destruction occurs as a momentary event, independently of any cause other than the generative condition. Lacking any enduring essence, it is unstable. Due to its uncontrollable nature, it is non-self. Oppressed by arising and passing away, and being the basis for suffering, the aggregate is a mass of suffering—hence, the 'mass of suffering.' Such a state is entirely unmixed with happiness, which is why he says 'wholly.' Or, because there is no pleasant nature in any form, the entire mass is a mass of suffering—thus it is stated, 'the mass of suffering is wholly suffering.' Due to being maintained by conditions and being the root of disease, it is a disease. For it is to be seen as a disease, like a chronic disease, because it must be maintained by appropriate conditions. Indeed, a chronic illness is a disease; the other is an affliction. And like a root ailment, it is to be seen as a disease because it is the root of subsequent ailments such as the disease of defilements. Due to being connected with the dart of suffering, due to oozing with the impurities of defilements, and due to swelling, ripening, and bursting with arising, aging, and breaking up, it is a boil. For it is afflicted by the three kinds of suffering—namely, the suffering of suffering, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change; and due to the oozing of impurities of defilements like lust, in accordance with appropriate objects and in accordance with their arising; and because it comes into being from non-existence, swells up at its arising, and ripens and bursts in due course with aging and breaking up, it is like a boil, and thus it is to be seen as a boil. Because it cannot be controlled and is ungovernable, it belongs to another. Just as a falling object does not come under another's control, so too this, due to its inability to be controlled in terms of its nature as beautiful, pleasant, etc., and due to its ungovernable nature, as it cannot be commanded, 'Do not decay, do not die!'—thus it is to be seen as belonging to another. Because it crumbles and is afflicted by sickness, aging, and death, it is perishing. This should be understood as 'perishing' because it is broken and destroyed in various ways by sickness and so on, or because it is afflicted by these very things, and because the word 'loka', meaning 'ruin', has the specific meaning of 'affliction'. The word 'chanda' refers to the desire that arises through attachment.

767. Dhammasenāpatināti dhammasenāya pati nāyakoti dhammasenāpati, sāriputtatthero, tena. Hitasaṅkhāto attho etassāti hitatthi, tena. Sakkaccāti uggahaṇadhāraṇādīsu atandito hutvā.

767. By 'Dhammasenāpati' is meant the lord, the leader of the army of Dhamma, thus Dhammasenāpati, the Elder Sāriputta; by him. By 'hitatthi' is meant one whose aim is benefit; by that one. By 'sakkacca' is meant being diligent in learning, memorizing, and so forth.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus is named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

in the Commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Rūpavibhāgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of Form is completed.

11. Ekādasamo paricchedo

11. The Eleventh Chapter

Nibbānaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Nibbāna

768-9. Ādito [V 2.0140] rūpānantaramuddiṭṭhaṃ yaṃ nibbānanti sambandho. Tassa vibhāvanaṃ yathābalaṃ pavakkhāmīti sambandho.

768-9. The connection is: that which is called Nibbāna was indicated from the beginning, immediately after form. The connection is: I will explain its analysis according to my ability.

Bhavābhavanti bhavato bhavaṃ, khuddakaṃ, mahantaṃ vā bhavaṃ. Vinanatoti saṃsibbanato. Taṇhā hi saṃsāranāyikabhāvena bhavato bhavaṃ, sugatiduggativasena khuddakamahantaṃ bhavaṃ vā aparāparabhāvāya saṃsibbati, tunnakaraṇaṃ viya karoti. Nikkhantattāti visaṃyogavasena nissaṭattā. Maraṇapaṭipakkhatāya, amatasadisatāya vā amataṃ. Sabbadukkhanissaṭattā paramaṃ sukhaṃ. Sabbepi saṅkhārā samanti upasamanti anuppattidhammataṃ āpajjanti etenāti sabbasaṅkhārasamatho. Khandhūpadhiādayo sabbepi upadhī upaddavā paṭinissajjīyanti etenāti sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo. Yasmā taṃ āgamma kāmataṇhādibhedā taṇhā sabbaso khayaṃ gacchati, virajjati, nirujjhati [M 2.0190] ca, tasmā taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodhoti ca vuccati. Apica rujjhanti ettha sattā kilesanigaḷabandhāti rodho, saṃsārassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tato nikkhantoti nirodho.

‘From existence to existence’ means existence from existence, whether small or great existence. The component 'vāna' is called ‘weaving’ because it means stitching together. For craving, by being the guide of saṃsāra, stitches together existence from existence—whether small or great existence in terms of good or bad destinations—for repeated becoming, just as a tailor does. The component 'ni' is called ‘release’ because of its complete separation by way of disjunction. It is called ‘the Deathless’ because it is opposed to death or because it resembles the deathless. Since it is the complete release from all suffering, it is the ultimate happiness. All formations cease, subside, and attain the state of non-origination through this; thus it is called ‘the calming of all formations’. The aggregates, substrates of existence, and all other afflictions are relinquished through this; thus it is called ‘the relinquishment of all substrates of existence’. Since, by realizing this, craving in all its forms, such as sensual craving, completely decays, fades away, and ceases, therefore it is called ‘the destruction of craving’, ‘dispassion’, and ‘cessation’. Furthermore, beings are obstructed here by the fetters of defilements; this is called ‘obstruction’ (rodha), a designation for saṃsāra. Emerging from that is ‘cessation’ (nirodha).

770. Adhigamāti tadanurūpāya paṭipattiyā ariyamaggena paṭivijjhanena.

770. Attainment is by means of penetration with the Noble Path through practice conforming to it.

Rāgakkhayādibhāvena sabbadukkhasantiyā paccayatāya, kilesasantāpābhāvena ca santilakkhaṇaṃ. Accutirasanti sabhāvāpariccajanato acavanasampattikaṃ. Assāsakaraṇarasanti assāsakaraṇakiccaṃ. Tañhi pānabhojanādisuññe sabhayakantāre paribbhamanena parissantassa addhikapurisassa assāsajanakabhāvena upaṭṭhitaṃ vanantodakaṃ viya sabbaññubuddhānampi vacanapathātikkantamahādukkhabherave saṃsārakantāre paribbhamanena parissantassa yathānurūpaṃ paṭipattimaggaṃ paṭipannassa yogāvacarassa anādimati saṃsāre supinantenapi adiṭṭhapubbatāya dassanasamakālameva [V 2.0141] paramassāsaṃ janeti. Khandhanimittavicittatāya aviggahaṃ hutvā gayhatīti animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Sabbasaṅkhatanissaraṇupāyabhāvato nissaraṇaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetīti nissaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

By way of the destruction of lust and so forth, by being the cause for the pacification of all suffering, and by the absence of the torment of defilements, it has the characteristic of peace. It has the function of being unshaken because it does not abandon its intrinsic nature, being the attainment of the unmoving. It has the function of providing relief because it accomplishes the task of giving solace. For just as water in the forest, appearing as a source of relief, provides relief to a weary traveler wandering in a fearful wilderness devoid of drink and food, so too, for the meditator who has entered the appropriate path of practice, weary from wandering in the terrifying wilderness of great suffering that is saṃsāra, which transcends even the speech of the Omniscient Buddhas, and which has never been seen even in a dream throughout beginningless saṃsāra, it generates the highest solace at the very moment of seeing. Because it is grasped as being devoid of the various signs of the aggregates, it is manifested as signless. Since it is the means of escape from all conditioned things, it is manifested as escape.

Evaṃ nibbānassa lakkhaṇādikaṃ dassetvā idāni vitaṇḍavādipakkhaṃ dassetvā pariharanto āha “etthāhā”tiādi, na paramatthato atthi aññatra paññattimattatoti adhippāyo. Kuto panāyamabhinivesoti āha “titthiyānaṃ…pe… nīyato”ti. Yathānurūpāya paṭipattiyāti sīlasamādhipaññāsaṅkhātaṃ sammāpaṭipattiyā. Yathā hi cetoñāṇalābhino eva ariyā paresaṃ lokuttaracittaṃ jānanti, tatthāpi ca arahā eva sabbesaṃ cittaṃ jānāti, evaṃ [M 2.0191] nibbānampi sīlādisammāpaṭipattibhūtena upāyeneva upalabbhatīti “natthī”ti na vattabbaṃ ariyehi upalabbhanīyato. Yathā hi jaccandhatemirikādīnaṃ adassanena “sūriyādayo natthī”ti na vattabbā cakkhumantānaṃ gocarabhāvena atthevāti siddhattā, evametampi bālaputhujjanassa adassanamattena “natthī”ti na vattabbaṃ. Ariyānaṃ pana paññācakkhuno padeseneva upaṭṭhānato ekantena sampaṭicchitabbaṃ “atthi nibbāna”nti. Ayamettha adhippāyo. Atha rāgādīnaṃ khayamattameva nibbānanti ceti sambandho. Āyasmatā…pe… therena dassitoti sambandho. Rāgakkhayādidīpakaṃ suttaṃ neyyatthanti adhippāyena “taṃ na”iti paṭikkhepaṃ katvā ekaṃsena cetaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, itarathā yathārutavasena pāḷiyā atthe gayhamāne bahudosā āpajjantīti te dassetuṃ “arahattassāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Arahattaṃ puṭṭhena tenevāyasmatā sāriputtattherenāti adhippāyo. Tava matenāti sāsanayuttiṃ avicāretvā pāḷidassanamatteneva vippalapato tavajjhāsayena. Na ca panetaṃ yuttaṃ, tathāpīti adhippāyo. Lokuttaraphalacittassa rāgādīnaṃ khayamattatāpajjanaṃ na yuttaṃ tassa aggaphalassa catukkhandhabhāvena pāḷiyaṃ āgatattā. Tasmāti yuttiṃ avicāretvā pāḷidassanamatteneva voharantassa aniṭṭhappasaṅgato. Byañjanacchāyāyāti vimaddāsahabhūtāya saddatthamattacchāyāya. Ubhinnanti nibbānavasena, arahattavasena ca āgatānaṃ ubhinnaṃ suttānaṃ. Atthoti adhippāyattho.

Having thus shown the characteristics and so forth of Nibbāna, now, while refuting the opponent’s side of the argument, he says, ‘Here, indeed,’ etc., intending to convey that ultimately it does not exist except as a mere concept. But how does this insistence arise? He says, ‘Of the sectarians...is led.’ ‘By the appropriate practice’ means by the right practice consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Just as the noble ones, who possess the knowledge of others’ minds, know the supramundane minds of others, and yet only the Arahant knows all minds, so too Nibbāna is apprehended only by the means of right practice consisting of virtue, etc. Therefore, it should not be said, ‘It does not exist,’ since it is apprehendable by the noble ones. Just as it cannot be said, ‘The sun and the like do not exist,’ due to the non-seeing of those born blind or with eye-diseases, because it is established that they exist as objects for those with eyes, so too this should not be said, ‘It does not exist,’ merely because ordinary fools do not see it. But since it appears partially to the noble ones through the eye of wisdom, it should be absolutely accepted that ‘Nibbāna exists.’ This is the meaning here. Then, the connection is made that ‘the mere destruction of lust, etc., is Nibbāna,’ as shown by the venerable elder... The sutta illustrating the destruction of lust, etc., is of interpretable meaning—with this intention, having rejected it by saying, ‘That is not,’ one should accept this unequivocally. Otherwise, if the meaning of the text is taken literally, many faults arise. To show this, it is said, ‘Even of Arahantship...’ When asked about Arahantship, it is intended that the venerable elder Sāriputta himself... ‘By your opinion’ means according to your own inclination, merely babbling based on seeing only the text, without considering what is suitable to the Dispensation. And yet this is not proper, but still...—this is the intention. It is not proper to attribute the mere destruction of lust, etc., to the supramundane fruition consciousness, because in the texts, that highest fruit is described as consisting of four aggregates. Therefore, undesirable consequences follow for one who speaks merely based on the appearance of the text, without considering what is proper. ‘By the shadow of the expression’ means by the mere shadow of the literal meaning, which cannot withstand scrutiny. ‘Of both’ means of both suttas that come by way of Nibbāna and Arahantship. ‘The meaning’ means the intended meaning.

Ko pana so atthoti āha “yassa panā”tiādi. Rāgādīnaṃ khayoti rāgādīnaṃ anuppādanirodho. So dhammo akkhayopi samāno rāgādīnaṃ khayassa upanissayattā khayopacārena “rāgādīnaṃ khayo nibbāna”nti vutto [M 2.0192] “tipusaṃ jaro, guḷo semho”tiādīsu phalūpacārena [V 2.0142] vuttaṃ viyāti sambandho. Kilesānaṃ anuppattinirodhakkhayassa maggassa ārammaṇabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ atthato “khayassa upanissayo”ti vattabbataṃ labbhatīti āha “khayassa upanissayattā”ti. Khayopacārenāti attano kāriyabhūtassa khayassa attani upacārena tassa nāmavasenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Jarakāraṇaṃ tipusaṃ jaroti vutto, semhakāraṇaṃ guḷo semhoti vutto. Khayanteti rāgādīnaṃ parikkhayāvasāne. Khayoti vā maggo vuccati “khaye ñāṇa”ntiādīsu (dha. sa. dukamātikā 142) viya, tassa ante nirodhāvasāne uppannattā khayoti vuttaṃ phalūpacārena, samīpūpacārena vā.

But what is that meaning? He says, ‘For that which is...’ etc. ‘The destruction of lust and so forth’ means the cessation without arising of lust and so forth. That Dhamma, though itself unceasing, is called ‘the destruction of lust, etc., is Nibbāna’ by figurative speech of destruction, because it is the proximate condition for the destruction of lust and so forth, just as in the examples ‘ginger is old age, molasses is phlegm,’ etc., where it is spoken of by figurative speech of the effect—this is the connection. He says, ‘because it serves as the proximate condition of destruction,’ meaning that Nibbāna, being the object of the path that brings about the non-arising, cessation, and destruction of the defilements, is in reality spoken of as ‘the proximate condition of destruction’. ‘By figurative speech of destruction’ means that it is called so by applying the name of its effect, the destruction, to itself. Ginger, which causes aging, is called ‘old age’; molasses, which causes phlegm, is called ‘phlegm’. ‘At the end of destruction’ here refers to the complete ending of lust and so forth. Alternatively, the path itself is called ‘destruction,’ as in phrases like ‘knowledge of destruction’ (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Duka-mātikā 142). Since it arises at the end of cessation, it is called ‘destruction’ by figurative speech of the effect or by proximity.

Sabbe bālaputhujjanāpīti soṇasigālādayo sabbepi bālaputhujjanā samadhigata…pe… bhaveyyuṃ khaṇavasena rāgādīnaṃ khayassa tesampi atthitāya. Tathā ca sati paṭipattiyā niratthakabhāvo āpajjeyyāti adhippāyo. Rāgādikkhayānaṃ bahubhāvatoti rāgādīnaṃ viya tesaṃ khayānampi tabbikārabhāvena bahubhāvato. Evañhi sati rāgassa khayo rāgakkhayo, na dosādīnaṃ, tathā dosakkhayopīti añño rāgakkhayo, añño dosakkhayo, añño mohakkhayoti tiṇṇaṃ akusalamūlānaṃ khayabhūtāni tīṇi nibbānāni, catunnaṃ upādānānaṃ khayabhūtāni cattārītiādinā bahūni nibbānāni nāma honti. Idāni ādi-saddasaṅgahite dose dassetuṃ “saṅkhatalakkhaṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. “Tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, saṅkhatassa saṅkhatalakkhaṇāni, uppādo paññāyati, vayo paññāyati, ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ paññāyatī”ti (a. ni. 3.47) vacanato vayasaṅkhāto khayo saṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “saṅkhatalakkhaṇañca nibbānaṃ bhaveyyā”ti. “Jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppanna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.20) vacanato āha “saṅkhatapariyāpanna”nti[M 2.0193]. Yaṃ pana saṅkhatapariyāpannaṃ, taṃ itarasaṅkhatadhammo viya aniccaṃ hoti paccayādhīnavuttitoti āha “saṅkhatapariyāpannattā anicca”nti. “Aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti (dī. ni. 2.221) hi vuttaṃ. Ettāvatā ca kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yadi bhavato manorathaparipūraṇatthaṃ khayaṃ nibbānanti vadāma, asaṅkhatassa saṅkhatalakkhaṇattā, saṅkhatapaṭipakkhassa saṅkhatapariyāpannattā sabbakālikabhāvena niccassa aniccatā, tato ca paramasukhassa dukkhatā ca āpajjeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘All foolish ordinary beings’ means even dogs, jackals, and the like—all foolish ordinary beings—could attain... because the destruction of lust and so on exists for them too in a momentary way. If this were the case, the practice would become meaningless—this is the intended meaning. ‘Because the destruction of lust and so on is abundant’ means because their destructions are abundant by way of their modifications, just as lust and so on are. Thus, if that were the case, the destruction of lust would be the destruction of lust alone, not of hatred and so on. Likewise for the destruction of hatred. Thus, there would be a separate destruction of lust, a separate destruction of hatred, and a separate destruction of delusion. The destructions of the three unwholesome roots would constitute three Nibbānas, and the destructions of the four kinds of clinging would constitute four, and so on—there would be many so-called Nibbānas. Now, to point out the faults implied by the word ‘etc.’ (ādi-sadda), it is said: ‘the characteristics of the conditioned,’ etc. From the statement, ‘Monks, these three are the characteristics of the conditioned: arising is apparent, vanishing is apparent, and the alteration of what persists is apparent’ (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.47), it is said that destruction, called ‘vanishing,’ is a characteristic of the conditioned. Thus, it is said, ‘Nibbāna would have the characteristic of the conditioned.’ From the statement, ‘Monks, aging and death are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.20), he says: ‘included within the conditioned.’ Whatever is included within the conditioned is impermanent, like other conditioned phenomena, because its nature depends on conditions—hence he says: ‘Because it is included within the conditioned, it is impermanent.’ For it is said: ‘Conditioned things are indeed impermanent’ (Dīgha Nikāya 2.221). And what is meant by this? If, to fulfill the desire of the proponents, we were to say that destruction is Nibbāna, then because the unconditioned would have the characteristics of the conditioned, and because what opposes the conditioned would be included within the conditioned, the eternally unchanging would become impermanent, and the highest bliss would become suffering—this is what is being said.

Ettāvatā bhaṅgakkhayassa nibbānadosaṃ dassetvā idāni anuppādakkhayassa tabbhāvaṃ nisedhetuṃ “yadi khayo nibbānaṃ bhaveyyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Paṭhamamaggassa anantarapaccayabhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ gotrabhu [V 2.0143] nāma. Sesamaggapurecaraṃ vodānaṃ nāma. Phalasamāpattipurecaraṃ anulomaṃ nāma. Taṃ pana saṅkhārārammaṇamevāti idha na gahitaṃ. Bhadramukhāti parassa anunayavacanaṃ. “Khīyantī”ti vattamānaniddesena idāni khīyamānataṃ pucchati. Esa nayo sesesupi. Upadhāretvāti upaparikkhitvā. “Gotrabhu…pe… mukhā”ti pucchāya “rāgādīnaṃ khayameva vadāmī”ti tayā dinnapaṭivacanassa avirujjhanavasena satipurekkhāraṃ kathehīti adhippāyo. Gotrabhucittādīnaṃ gotrabhuvodānamaggānaṃ. Gotrabhukkhaṇe kilesānaṃ anuppādanirodhassa abhāvato āha “rāgādayo khīyissantī”ti. Phalamevāti kilesānaṃ khīṇakāle uppajjamānaṃ phalacittameva. Ārammaṇaṃ apassantoti gotrabhuādīnaṃ vattabbārammaṇaṃ apassanto. Atha vā itaresaṃ ārammaṇabhāve sati gahetabbapaccayaṃ apassanto.

Having thus shown the fault of Nibbāna being cessation through destruction, now, to refute its being cessation through non-arising, it is said: “If destruction were Nibbāna…” The knowledge that is the immediate condition for the first path is called ‘gotrabhū.’ That which precedes the remaining paths is called ‘vodāna.’ That which precedes fruition attainment is called ‘anuloma.’ However, since that takes only formations as its object, it is not included here. ‘Bhadramukha’ is a conciliatory term of address for another. By the present tense indication “are being destroyed,” he asks about the state of being destroyed now.
