This method applies to the rest as well. ‘Upadhāretvā’ means ‘having investigated.’ Regarding the question, “Gotrabhū… mukhā,” the intended meaning is: “Speak with mindfulness at the forefront, in a way that does not contradict the reply you gave, namely, ‘I declare only the destruction of lust, etc.’” Of the gotrabhū-consciousness, etc.—that is, of gotrabhū, vodāna, and the paths—since at the moment of gotrabhū there is no cessation through non-arising of the defilements, it is said: “Lust, etc., will be destroyed.” ‘Phalameva’ means ‘only the fruition consciousness that arises when the defilements have been destroyed.’ ‘Ārammaṇaṃ apassanto’ means ‘not seeing the object that should be spoken of for gotrabhū, etc.’ Alternatively, it means not seeing the condition to be grasped when others have the state of being an object.

“Apicā”tiādi pariyāyantarenapi anuppādanirodhassa nibbānabhāvanisedhanaṃ. “Uppādīyatīti attho”ti pana [M 2.0194] maggassa uppattiyā kilesakkhayopi uppādito nāma hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Na hi itarathā khayassa uppādo nāma atthi. Atha vā “addhā so…pe… niruttaro bhavissatī”ti ettakena ganthena khaṇanirodhassa ceva anuppādanirodhassa ca nibbānabhāve dosaṃ dassetvā idāni “khaye ñāṇa”ntiādīsu (dha. sa. dukamātikā 142) viya maggassāpi khayapariyāyattā “rāgakkhayo”tiādivacanamatteyeva samānabhāvena gahite maggassāpi nibbānabhāvappasaṅgaṃ, tathā ca sati aniṭṭhāpattiṃ sambhāvento āha “apicā”tiādi. Evañhi sati “uppādīyatī”ti maggameva sandhāya tiṭṭhati. Yadi maggassa nibbānabhāvappasaṅgo idha sambhāvito, evaṃ sati gotrabhussa maggārammaṇatādidosā vattabbāti? Saccaṃ vattabbā, ettakenāpi pana parassa vacanapaṭibāhanaṃ sakkā kātunti parihārantaradassane byāpāro katoti. Yathānurūpāya paṭipattiyāti chavisuddhiparamparāsaṅkhātāya yathānulomapaṭipattiyā.

By another expression, beginning with ‘Apicā,’ the refutation of non-arising cessation as Nibbāna is stated. However, it is said, “It arises, meaning,” because with the arising of the path, the destruction of defilements is also said to have arisen. For otherwise, there is no such thing as the arising of destruction. Alternatively, having shown with this much text the fault in momentary cessation and non-arising cessation being Nibbāna, now, just as in phrases like “knowledge of destruction” and so on (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, du. mā. 142), since the path is also synonymous with destruction, if it is taken as being equally implied in expressions like “the destruction of lust” and so on, then the path too would be implied to have the nature of Nibbāna. And anticipating an undesired consequence in such a case, it is said, “Apicā” and so on. For in this way, “it arises” refers only to the path. If the implication of the path being Nibbāna is considered here, then should faults like the gotrabhū’s object being the path also be stated? Indeed, they should be stated. But since with this much another’s argument can be refuted, the effort is made to show another explanation. ‘Yathānurūpāya paṭipattiyā’ means by the practice that is in conformity, which is described as the sequence of purification of virtue.

771. Assaddhoti pabuddhasaddho, maggāgatāya acalasaddhāya samannāgato, maggāgatasaddhāya hi samannāgato ākāse buddhavesaṃ māpetvāpi “niccaṃ sukhaṃ attā”ti vadantassa na saddahati seyyathāpi sūrambaṭṭhoti (a. ni. 1.255). Akataññūti akataṃ nibbānaṃ jānātīti akataññū. Sandhicchedoti bhavasandhānakarassa taṇhāpāpassa chindanena puna bhavapaṭisandhiyāpi chinnatāya paṭisandhiṃ khepetvā ṭhito. Hatāvakāsoti khīṇapaṭisandhikattāyeva āyatiṃ katthaci okāsaloke adissamānattā vihatāvakāso. Vantāsoti katthaci abhisaṅgābhāvato [V 2.0144] chaḍḍitataṇhoti attho. Uttamaporisoti sadevaloke aggadakkhiṇeyyatāya visiṭṭho poriso.

771. ‘Assaddho’ (literally ‘faithless’) here means ‘one with awakened faith,’ endowed with unwavering faith that has reached the path. For one endowed with faith that has reached the path would not believe someone who, even having conjured up a Buddha-image in the sky, says, “The self is permanent, happy,” just like a brave warrior (A.N. 1.255). ‘Akataññū’ means ‘one who knows the unmade,’ because he knows Nibbāna, which is unmade. ‘Sandhicchedo’ means ‘one who has cut off the connection,’ because by severing the evil of craving that causes connection to existence, and because rebirth-linking is also severed, he stands having exhausted rebirth. ‘Hatāvakāso’ means ‘one whose opportunity is destroyed,’ because since rebirth-linking is exhausted, he is no longer seen in any realm of existence in the future, thus his opportunity is abolished. ‘Vantāso’ means ‘one who has vomited out,’ meaning he has discarded craving, as there is no attachment anywhere. ‘Uttamaporiso’ means ‘the supreme person,’ because he is a distinguished person in the world with its devas, worthy of the highest offerings.

Duppaṭividdhāti [M 2.0195] paṭivijjhituṃ, paṭilabhituñca dukkarā. Kāmādīnaṃ nissaraṇīyatāya nissaraṇīyā, yadidaṃ nekkhammaṃ, etaṃ kāmānaṃ nissaraṇanti sambandho. Tattha kāmānaṃ nissaraṇanti kāmehi niggamanaṃ, atha vā nissaranti niggacchanti ettha etenāti vā nissaraṇaṃ, kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ, nissaraṇupāyanti attho. Nekkhammanti paṭhamajjhānaṃ. Tañhi kāmehi nikkhantanti “nekkhamma”nti idha gahitaṃ, aññattha pana pabbajjādayopi “nekkhamma”nti pavuccanti. Vuttañhi –

‘Duppaṭividdhā’ means ‘hard to penetrate,’ because it is difficult to penetrate and to attain. It is an escape because it is the means of escape from sensual pleasures and so on; the connection is that this renunciation is the escape from sensual pleasures. Here, ‘the escape from sensual pleasures’ means departure from sensual pleasures; or alternatively, it is an ‘escape’ because one departs or escapes from this place or by this means—thus, the meaning is the place of escape from sensual pleasures, or the means of escape. ‘Nekkhamma’ means the first jhāna. For it is taken here as ‘nekkhamma’ because it is a departure from sensual pleasures. Elsewhere, however, going forth and other practices are also called ‘nekkhamma.’ For it is said—

“Pabbajjā paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, nibbānañca vipassanā;

Sabbepi kusalā dhammā, ‘nekkhamma’nti pavuccare”ti. (itivu. aṭṭha. 109; dī. ni. ṭī. 2.360; a. ni. ṭī. 2.3.66; visuddhi. mahā. 1.56; netti. ṭī. 76 missakahārasampātavaṇṇanā);

“Going forth, the first jhāna, Nibbāna, and insight; all wholesome states are called ‘Renunciation’.”

Arūpaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ. Bhūtanti vijjamānaṃ, khandhapañcakanti attho. “Bhūtamidanti, sāriputta, samanupassāmī”tiādīsu khandhapañcakaṃ “bhūta”nti vuccati. Attano kāraṇaṃ paṭicca samaṃ, sammā ca uppannanti paṭiccasamuppannaṃ. Paṭhama…pe… bhaveyyāti saṅkhatanissaraṇabhāvena vuttassa nibbānassa abhāvappattiyā ca tadekayoganiddiṭṭhānaṃ yathākkamaṃ kāmarūpanissaraṇānaṃ paṭhamajjhānākāsānañcāyatanānampi abhāvoyeva āpajjeyya. Idāni yathādhippetamatthaṃ āgamena dassetuṃ “na tu khayo”tiādi vuttaṃ.

‘Arūpa’ means the base of infinite space. ‘Bhūta’ means ‘existing,’ that is, the five aggregates. In passages such as “I perceive this as existing, Sāriputta,” the five aggregates are called ‘bhūta.’ ‘Paṭiccasamuppanna’ means ‘dependently arisen,’ because it arises equally and rightly in dependence on its own cause. If it were as stated in “first… etc… it would be,” then, with the attainment of absence by Nibbāna, which is described as the escape from the conditioned, it would follow that the first jhāna and the base of infinite space—pointed out as being uniquely connected with it as the respective escapes from the sensual realm and the form realm—would also become absent. Now, to show the intended meaning through scripture, it is said, “but not destruction,” etc.

“Atthi…pe… suphusitanti cā”ti natthi nissaraṇaṃ loke, kiṃ vivekena kāmāpīti evaṃ mārena paṭibāhite. “Atthi…pe… suphusita”nti nibbānaṃ patiṭṭhapentena āḷavakattherena vuttaṃ. Suphusitanti suṭṭhu phusitaṃ, sacchikatanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ajātantiādīni cattāri padāni aññamaññavevacanāni. Atha vā vedanādayo viya hetupaccayasamavāyasaṅkhātāya kāraṇasāmaggiyā na jātaṃ na nibbattanti ajātaṃ[M 2.0196]. Kāraṇena vinā sayameva ca na bhūtaṃ na pātubhūtaṃ na uppannanti abhūtaṃ. Evaṃ ajātattā abhūtattā yena kenaci kāraṇena na katanti [V 2.0145] akataṃ. Jātabhūtakatabhāvo ca nāma rūpādīnaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ hoti, na asaṅkhatasabhāvassa nibbānassāti dassanatthaṃ asaṅkhatanti vuttaṃ. Paṭilomato vā samecca sambhūya paccayehi katanti saṅkhataṃ, na tathā saṅkhataṃ, saṅkhatalakkhaṇarahitanti ca asaṅkhatanti. Evaṃ anekehi kāraṇehi nibbattitabhāve paṭisiddhe pakativādīnaṃ pakati viya siyā nu kho, ekeneva kāraṇena etaṃ katanti āsaṅkāya na kenaci katanti dassanatthaṃ “akata”nti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ apaccayampi samānaṃ sayameva nu kho idaṃ bhūtaṃ pātubhūtanti āsaṅkāya tannivattanatthaṃ “abhūta”nti vuttaṃ. Ayañcetassa asaṅkhatākatābhūtabhāvo sabbena sabbaṃ ajātadhammattāti dassetuṃ “ajāta”nti vuttaṃ.

When Māra thus repelled it, saying, “There is no escape in the world; what use is dispassion from sensual pleasures?” the words “There is… well touched” were spoken by the Elder Āḷavaka to establish Nibbāna. ‘Suphusitaṃ’ means ‘thoroughly touched,’ which is to say ‘directly experienced.’ The four terms beginning with ‘unborn’ are synonyms for one another. Alternatively, ‘ajāta’ (unborn) means ‘not born, not arisen’ from the assemblage of causes, which is described as the combination of causes and conditions, just like feelings and so on. ‘Abhūta’ (unbecome) means ‘not become, not manifested, not arisen’ by itself without a cause. Thus, because it is unborn and unbecome, ‘akata’ (unmade) means ‘not made by any cause whatsoever.’ The state of being born, become, and made belongs to conditioned phenomena like form, etc., not to Nibbāna, which is unconditioned in nature; to show this, it is called ‘asaṅkhata’ (unconditioned). Conversely, ‘saṅkhata’ (conditioned) means ‘made by causes, having come together and arisen’; ‘asaṅkhata’ (unconditioned) means ‘not so conditioned,’ and ‘devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned.’ Thus, having refuted the possibility of being produced by many causes, to dispel the doubt that it might be like the ‘nature’ of the proponents of inherent nature, or that it might be made by a single cause, it is said ‘akata’ (unmade) to show that it is not made by anyone. Similarly, even though it is without conditions, to dispel the doubt that it might have become or manifested by itself, it is said ‘abhūta’ (unbecome). And to show that this very state of being unconditioned, unmade, and unbecome is entirely due to its nature of being unborn, it is said ‘ajāta’ (unborn).

Asaṅkhatantīti iti-saddo ādiattho. Tena –

In the phrase ‘Asaṅkhataṃ’ti,’ the word ‘iti’ has the meaning of ‘and so on.’ By that—

“No cetaṃ, bhikkhave, abhavissa ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhataṃ. Nayidha jātassa bhūtassa katassa saṅkhatassa nissaraṇaṃ paññāyetha. Yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, atthi ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhataṃ, tasmā jātassa bhūtassa katassa saṅkhatassa nissaraṇaṃ paññāyatī”ti (udā. 73) –

“Bhikkhus, if there were not this unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, no escape would be discerned here from what is born, become, made, conditioned. But since, bhikkhus, there is the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, therefore an escape is discerned from what is born, become, made, conditioned.” (Udāna 73)

Evamādisuttapadaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tenāha “anekesu suttantesū”ti. Dhammena sadevakassa lokassa sāmī, dhammassa vā yathicchitaṃ desanato sāmī issaroti dhammasāmī. Tathāgata-saddassa attho heṭṭhā kathitova. Sammā sāmaṃ sabbadhamme abhisambuddho, sammā sayameva sammohaniddāvigamena paṭibuddho, buddhiyā vikasitavāti vā sammāsambuddho.

It includes such passages from the suttas. Therefore, it is said, “in many suttas.” Dhammasāmī means ‘lord of the Dhamma,’ because by the Dhamma he is the lord of the world with its devas, or because he is the lord and master by teaching the Dhamma as he wishes. The meaning of the word ‘Tathāgata’ has already been explained previously. Sammāsambuddho means ‘perfectly self-enlightened,’ because he is rightly and by himself fully enlightened to all phenomena, or because he is rightly and by himself awakened through the removal of the sleep of delusion, or because his wisdom has blossomed.

Parittattiketi [M 2.0197] “parittā dhammā, mahaggatā dhammā, appamāṇā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 12) evaṃ parittādidhammavasena āgate parittattike.

In the Parittattika: this refers to the limited triad, which is presented by way of limited phenomena and so forth, as in “limited phenomena, exalted phenomena, immeasurable phenomena” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, triadic matrix 12).

Navattabbārammaṇattāti navattabbārammaṇattappasaṅgato. Tenāha “navattabbārammaṇapakkhaṃ bhajeyyu”nti. Rūpāvacarattikacatukkajjhānāti catukkanayena tikajjhānā, pañcakanayena catukkajjhānā. Kusalakiriyānaṃ abhiññābhāvappattiyā parittādikepi ārabbha pavattanato “catutthassa jhānassa vipāko”ti āha. Tasmāti yathāvuttayuttito ceva pāḷito ca. Kiñca bhiyyo [V 2.0146] – saṅkhatadhammārammaṇaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ, apica anulomabhāvappattaṃ kilese tadaṅgavasena pajahati, samucchedavasena pajahituṃ na sakkoti, tathā sammutisaccārammaṇaṃ paṭhamajjhānādikusalañāṇaṃ vikkhambhanavaseneva kilese pajahati, na samucchedavasena. Iti saṅkhatadhammārammaṇassa, sammutisaccārammaṇassa ca ñāṇassa kilesānaṃ samucchedappahāne asamatthabhāvato tesaṃ samucchedappahānakarassa ariyamaggañāṇassa tadubhayaviparītabhāvena ārammaṇena bhavitabbaṃ, tañca nibbānameva. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Because of the implication of its being an object that cannot be designated. Hence it is said, “They should resort to the side of what cannot be designated as an object.” The triad of form-sphere jhānas and the tetrad of jhānas means the triad of jhānas according to the fourfold method, and the tetrad of jhānas according to the fivefold method. Regarding the wholesome and functional states, because they arise by taking limited objects, etc., as their basis for the attainment of the state of higher knowledges, it is said, “The result of the fourth jhāna.” Therefore: from the reasoning as stated and from the Pāli text. What is more? Insight knowledge, which has conditioned phenomena as its object and has reached the state of conformity, abandons defilements by way of substitution, but it cannot abandon them by way of eradication. Similarly, the wholesome knowledge of the first jhāna, etc., which has conventional truth as its object, abandons defilements only by way of suppression, not by way of eradication. Thus, because the knowledge that has conditioned phenomena as its object and the knowledge that has conventional truth as its object are incapable of eradicating defilements, the noble path knowledge, which accomplishes their eradication, must have an object that is the opposite of both of these. And that is Nibbāna itself. Therefore, the ancients said—

“Ñāṇaṃ yaṃ saṅkhatālambaṃ, paññattālambameva vā;

Pāpe hanti na taṃ vatthuṃ, tadaññaṃ sampaṭicchiya”nti.

“That knowledge which is supported by the conditioned, or which is supported by a concept, does not destroy evils, having accepted a different basis.”

Rūpasabhāvābhāvatoti etena yathā rūpadhammānaṃ ruppanasabhāvo, paṭighātavantatā kalāpato vuttiyā padesasambandho sabhāvo, evaṃ nibbānassa katthaci paṭighāto, sappadesatā ca natthīti dasseti. Na hi nibbānaṃ “asukadisāya, asukapadese”ti vā niddisīyati. Papañcābhāvatoti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhipapañcehi saha avaṭṭhānavasena abhāvato, tesaṃ abhāvapaccayatāya ca. Taṇhādiṭṭhimānā [M 2.0198] hi saṃsāre satte papañcentīti papañcā nāma.

Because of the absence of the nature of matter: by this it is shown that just as material phenomena have the nature of being afflicted, have resistance, and have a nature of connection to a location by way of groups and occurrence, so Nibbāna has no resistance or locality anywhere. Indeed, Nibbāna is not designated as being “in such a direction” or “in such a place.” Because of the absence of proliferation: this is because of its non-coexistence with the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views, and because it is the condition for their absence. For craving, views, and conceit, since they cause beings to proliferate in saṃsāra, are called “proliferations.”

772-5. Evaṃ nibbānaṃ yuttito, suttato ca sādhetvā idāni tassa pariyāyasandassanatthaṃ “accantamananta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha saṃsārappavattiyā pariyosānabhūtattā antaṃ. Iminā anupādisesanibbānadhātu kathitāti vadanti, sopādisesanibbānadhātupi vaṭṭati, akatantipi paṭhanti. So heṭṭhā vuttatthova. Sauppādavayantābhāvena anantaṃ. Kilesapariḷāhābhāvena, kilesakkhobhābhāvena ca santaṃ. Palokitābhāvena apalokitaṃ. Atittikarabhāvena paṇītaṃ. Sabbadukkhahananato saraṇaṃ. Kilesacorehi anupaddutattā nibbhayatāya khemaṃ. Sabbupaddavanivāraṇato tāṇaṃ. Jātiādidukkhehi anubandhassa allīyituṃ yuttaṭṭhānatāya leṇaṃ. Yathāpaṭipannassa santidāyakattena paraṃ patiṭṭhābhāvato parāyaṇaṃ.

772-5. Thus, having established Nibbāna through reasoning and from the suttas, now to show its synonyms, the words “the ultimate, the endless,” etc., are stated. Herein, it is the “end” because it is the conclusion of the continuation of saṃsāra. By this, they say, the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining is spoken of. The Nibbāna-element with residue remaining is also applicable, and some read “unmade.” That has the meaning as stated previously. It is “endless” because of the absence of arising and passing away. It is “peaceful” because of the absence of the fever of defilements and the absence of the agitation of defilements. It is “undecaying” because of the absence of decay. It is “excellent” because of its nature of not causing dissatisfaction. It is “refuge” because it destroys all suffering. It is “safe” because of fearlessness, since it is unassailed by the thieves of the defilements. It is “protection” because it wards off all calamities. It is “shelter” because it is a suitable place to retreat for one who is pursued by the suffering of birth and so on. It is the “final goal” because it gives peace to one who has practiced accordingly and because there is no further resort.

Sabbapīḷāvimuttatāya sivaṃ. Upanissayahīnānaṃ sabbaññumukhato sutvāpi ṭhapetvā guṇavasena sabhāvato paṭivijjhituṃ dukkaratāya nipuṇaṃ. Aviparītatāya saccaṃ. Sabbadukkhaparikkhayakarattā dukkhakkhayaṃ. Tejussadatāya santattaayoguḷe makkhikāhi viya catūhi [V 2.0147] āsavehi ārammaṇakaraṇavasena pavattituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya anāsavaṃ. Mahākāruṇikassāpi dhammadesanāya appossukkabhāvāpādanena paṭivijjhituṃ dukkaratāya sududdasaṃ. Lokuttaradhammesupi asaṅkhataguṇena visiṭṭhatāya paraṃ. Saṃsāramahāsamuddassa tīrabhūtattā pāraṃ. Maṃsacakkhuno, dibbacakkhuno vā agocaratāya anidassanaṃ. Nidassanasaṅkhātāya upamāya abhāvato vā anidassanaṃ.

It is “auspicious” because it is free from all affliction. It is “subtle” because it is difficult for those who lack supporting conditions to penetrate it in its intrinsic nature, as opposed to by way of its qualities, even after hearing of it from the mouth of the Omniscient One. It is “truth” because it is not distorted. It is “the destruction of suffering” because it brings about the complete destruction of all suffering. It is “taintless” because it is impossible for the four taints to arise taking it as an object, just as it is impossible for flies to alight on a red-hot iron ball. It is “very hard to see” because of the difficulty in penetrating it, which brings about a lack of eagerness for teaching the Dhamma even in the Greatly Compassionate One. It is “supreme” because it is distinguished by its unconditioned quality even among supramundane phenomena. It is “the far shore” because it is the shore of the great ocean of saṃsāra. It is “unmanifest” because it is beyond the range of the physical eye or the divine eye; or because of the absence of a simile, which is called a likeness.

Avipariṇāmadhammattā [M 2.0199] dhuvaṃ. Tatoyeva paramapatiṭṭhābhāvato dīpaṃ. Rogādipīḷābhāvato abyāpajjhaṃ. Tatoyeva anītikaṃ. Taṇhālayābhāvato anālayaṃ. Saṅkhatāsaṅkhatesu asaṅkhatakoṭṭhāsabhūtattā, paramapatiṭṭhābhāvato vā padaṃ. Avināsabhāvena accutaṃ. Akkharaṇato avinassanato akkharaṃ.

It is “permanent” because its nature is not to change. It is “an island” for that very reason, and because it is the ultimate resort. It is “unafflicted” because of the absence of the affliction of disease and so on. For that very reason, it is “free from calamities.” It is “without abode” because of the absence of the abode of craving. It is “the state” because it constitutes the unconditioned part among the conditioned and the unconditioned, or because it is the ultimate resort. It is “imperishable” because of its indestructible nature. It is “the unperishing” because it does not perish and is not destroyed.

Saṅkhatanissaṭattā vimutti. Bhavabandhanavimuttihetutāya mokkhaṃ.

Because it is an escape from the conditioned, it is liberation. Because it is the cause of liberation from the bondage of existence, it is deliverance.

776-7. Evanti yathāvuttanayena. Viññāyāti uggahaparipucchāvasena jānitvā. Adhigamūpāyoti paṭivijjhanūpāyabhūtā tisso sikkhā. Kātabboti paṭipajjitabbo.

776-7. Thus means in the way stated. Having understood means having known by way of learning and questioning. The means of attainment means the three trainings, which are the means of penetration. To be done means to be practiced.

Saddhaṃ, buddhiñca karoti vaḍḍhetīti saddhābuddhikaraṃ. Tathāgatamateti tipiṭakabuddhavacane, catūsu saccesu vā. Paññāya sambhūtaṃ, paññāya vā sambhavo etassāti paññāsambhavaṃ, tadeva sampasādanaṃ buddhādīsu adhimuccanaṃ, taṃ karotīti paññāsambhavasampasādanakaraṃ. Atthabyañjanasālinanti atimadhurehi atthabyañjanehi samannāgataṃ, atthabyañjanasāravantanti vā attho ra-kārassa la-kāraṃ katvā. Sāraṃ jānantīti sāraññū, te vimhāpetīti sāraññuvimhāpanaṃ. Niṭṭhanti pariyosānaṃ, sutamayamūlakaṃ anupādāparinibbānanti adhippāyo.

It makes and increases faith and wisdom; thus, it is a producer of faith and wisdom. The teaching of the Tathāgata means the word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka, or the four truths. Born of wisdom, or that which has its origin in wisdom, is wisdom-born. That very thing is confidence, which is conviction in the Buddha and so on. That which produces confidence born of wisdom is a producer of wisdom-born confidence. Rich in meaning and letter means endowed with very sweet meaning and letter; or, changing the ‘r’ to an ‘l’, the meaning is possessing the essence of meaning and letter. Those who know the essence are knowers of the essence; that which astonishes them is the astonishing of the knowers of the essence. Conclusion means the end; the intention is the final Nibbāna without clinging, which is rooted in what is learned.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra,

Nibbānaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Exposition of Nibbāna is concluded.

12. Dvādasamo paricchedo

12. The Twelfth Chapter

Paññattiniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of Concepts

Etthāti [M 2.0200][V 2.0148] yathāuddiṭṭhadhammānaṃ niddesapariyosāne. Ettakamevāti cittacetasikarūpanibbānamattameva. Paññāpetabbatoti paramatthadhammā viya sakasakasabhāvavasena apaññāyamānā hutvā lokasaṅketavasena paññāpiyamānattā. Paññāpanatoti paramatthavasena vijjamānāvijjamānadhammānaṃ pakāsanavasena paññāpanato. Tattha “paññāpetabbato”ti iminā paññāpīyati pakārena ñāpīyatīti paññattīti evaṃ kammasādhanavasena atthapaññattibhūtā upādāpaññatti vuttā. “Paññāpanato”ti iminā paññāpeti pakārena ñāpetīti paññattīti evaṃ kattusādhanavasena tassā abhidhāyakabhūtā nāmapaññattīti veditabbaṃ. Paṇṇattidukaniddese “saṅkhā…pe… vohāro”ti (dha. sa. 1313-1314) catūhi padehi upādāpaññatti vuttā. “Nāmaṃ…pe… abhilāpo”ti (dha. sa. 1313-1314) chahi padehi nāmapaññatti kathitāti ācariyānaṃ icchitattā vuttaṃ “tenevāhā”tiādi. Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānanti heṭṭhā abhidhammamātikāya vuttānaṃ kusalākusalādidhammānaṃ. Saṅkhāti “ahaṃ mamā”tiādinā saṅkhāyamānatā. Samaññāti saṅketavasena ñāyamānatā. Paññattīti asaṅkaravasena anekadhā vibhajitvā paññāpiyamānatā. Vohāroti pākaṭaṃ katvā vuccamānatā, kathanavasena upayujjamānatā vā. Atthābhimukhaṃ namatīti nāmaṃ. Taṃ pana anvattharuḷhīvasena duvidhaṃ, sāmaññaguṇakittimaopapātikanāmavasena catubbidhaṃ. Nāmakammanti nāmakaraṇaṃ. Nāmadheyyanti nāmaṭhapanaṃ, nāmadheyyanti vā seṭṭhānaṃ nāmaṃ. Akkharadvārena atthaṃ nīharitvā utti kathanaṃ nirutti. Byañjananti pākaṭakaraṇaṃ. Abhilāpoti abhilāpanaṃ.

Herein, at the conclusion of the exposition of the phenomena as enumerated. Only this much: just mind, mental factors, form, and Nibbāna. ‘To be designated’ (paññāpetabba) is so called because, unlike ultimate phenomena, they are not apprehended in terms of their own intrinsic nature but are designated by way of worldly convention. ‘Designation’ (paññāpana) means the act of designating by way of making known phenomena that exist or do not exist in the ultimate sense. Here, by ‘to be designated’ (paññāpetabbato), it is said that ‘that which is designated or made known is a designation’ (paññāpīyati pakārena ñāpīyatīti paññatti); thus, by way of the passive derivation, the dependent designation (upādāpaññatti), which is a designation of meaning, is stated. By ‘designation’ (paññāpanato), it is said that ‘that which designates or makes known is a designation’ (paññāpeti pakārena ñāpetīti paññatti); thus, by way of the active derivation, the name-designation (nāmapaññatti), which is the expresser of that, should be understood. In the exposition of the pair of designations, the dependent designation is stated by four terms: ‘reckoning… utterance’ (Dhs. 1313–1314). The name-designation is spoken of by six terms: ‘name… expression’ (Dhs. 1313–1314). Because this was desired by the teachers, it is said, ‘Therefore, indeed, he said,’ and so forth. ‘Of those various phenomena’ refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, and other phenomena mentioned in the Abhidhamma matrix. ‘Reckoning’ (saṅkhā) means being reckoned as ‘I’ or ‘mine,’ and so on. ‘Designation’ (samaññā) means being known by way of convention. ‘Concept’ (paññatti) means being designated in various ways by being divided without confusion. ‘Utterance’ (vohāra) means being spoken of by making it manifest, or being used by way of speaking. ‘Name’ (nāma) means that which bends towards meaning. That, however, is twofold by way of etymological usage and conventional usage; it is fourfold by way of generic names, quality names, coined names, and adventitious names. ‘Naming’ (nāmakamma) is the act of naming. ‘Appellation’ (nāmadheyya) is the establishment of a name, or ‘appellation’ is the name of the noble ones. ‘Etymology’ (nirutti) is the explanation of meaning by drawing out the meaning through letters. ‘Expression’ (byañjana) is the act of making manifest. ‘Verbalization’ (abhilāpa) is the act of verbalizing.

Ahanti [M 2.0201] rūpādivinimuttaṃ ahaṃkārabuddhivisayabhūtaṃ attano khandhasamūhasantānamupādāya paññattaṃ tadaññānaññabhāvena anibbacanīyaṃ upādāpaññattiṃ vadati. Tenāha “ahanti hī”tiādi. “Ahanti…pe… katvā”ti upādāpaññattiyā uppattiṃ dassetvā yathātiādinā taṃ pakāseti.

‘I’ (ahaṃ) refers to a dependent designation (upādāpaññatti) that is designated by taking as its basis the continuity of one’s own aggregate-group, being free from form and so forth, being the object of the notion of ‘I,’ and being indefinable as either the same as or different from that. Therefore it is said, ‘For ‘I’…’ and so forth. Having shown the arising of dependent designation with ‘Having made ‘I’…’ and so forth, he then explains it with ‘as…’ and so forth.

Yasmā [V 2.0149] “samaññā paññatti vohāro”ti “evaṃ saṅkhā”ti imasseva vevacanaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “idāni paññāpanato paññatti”ntiādi.

Since ‘designation, concept, utterance’ is simply a synonym for ‘reckoning,’ therefore it is said, ‘Now, designation is so called because of the act of designating,’ and so forth.

Tadanurūpā jātāti tajjā, avijjamānapaññatti viya kevalaṃ lokasaṅketavaseneva ahutvā dhammasabhāvassa anurūpavasena pavattā paññattīti attho. Nāmapaññattipi vacanatthasaṅkhātakāraṇaṃ upādāya paṭicca pavattanato upādāpaññattivohāraṃ labhatīti tassāpi upādāpaññattipariyāyo vutto. Gaṇṭhipadakārenāpi hi imināva adhippāyena upādāpaññattīti upādānavatī paññatti kāraṇavatiṃ kāraṇabhūtamatthamupādāya gahetvā tannissayena paññāpīyati, sabbopi paññattibhedo anena lakkhaṇena upādāpaññattimeva bhajati. Anupādāya hi paññatti natthīti vuttaṃ. Upanidhāpaññattīti paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ ekapaññattiṃ upanidhāya apekkhitvā pavattā paññatti. Cakkhusota-ggahaṇena ajjhattikāyatanāni dasseti, rūpasadda-ggahaṇena bāhirāyatanāni. Pathavītejovāyu-ggahaṇena phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ pabhedato dasseti. Eteneva dhammāyatanepi labbhamānabhedo dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

‘Born in accordance with that’ (tajjā) means that it is a designation that functions in accordance with the nature of phenomena, not being merely by way of worldly convention like a non-existent designation. The name-designation, too, because it functions dependently by taking as its basis a cause consisting of verbal meaning, obtains the designation ‘dependent designation’; thus, a synonym for dependent designation is stated for it as well. Indeed, even by the author of the Gaṇṭhipada, with this very intention, it is said that ‘dependent designation’ (upādāpaññatti) means a designation possessing a basis (upādāna), which is designated in dependence on a causal object, taking up that causal object; and all kinds of designations partake of this characteristic, becoming dependent designations. For it is said, ‘Without a basis, there is no designation.’ ‘Comparative designation’ (upanidhāpaññatti) is a designation that functions by comparing or considering a single designation that is its opposite. By the inclusion of ‘eye’ and ‘ear,’ the internal sense bases are shown; by the inclusion of ‘form’ and ‘sound,’ the external sense bases. By the inclusion of ‘earth, fire, and wind,’ the tangible sense base is shown in its varieties. In this same way, the variety that can be obtained in the mind-object sense base should be regarded as shown.

Yasmā pathavādikā paññatti sasambhārapathaviyaṃ ekassa nāmaṃ gahetvā samūhamevopādāya paññāpīyati, ghaṭādikā ca paññatti dhammasamūhesu sabbesameva nāmaṃ gahetvā samūhamevopādāya paññāpīyati, tasmā vuttaṃ “ekassa vā”tiādi[M 2.0202]. Tattha ekassa nāmaṃ gahetvā samūhamupādāya paññāpiyamānāya pathavādivasena pākaṭabhāvato taṃ ṭhapetvā itaraṃ dassetuṃ “katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ samūhapaññatti nāma samūhassa paññāpanato. Disākāsādīsu disā-ggahaṇena candasūriyāvattanamupādāya paññāpiyamānaṃ puratthimādidisāpaññattiṃ dasseti. Ākāsa-ggahaṇena asamphuṭṭhadhamme upādāya paññāpiyamānaṃ kūpaguhādiākāsapaññattiṃ dasseti. Kāla-ggahaṇena candāvattanādikamupādāya paññāpiyamānaṃ pubbaṇhādikālapaññattiṃ dasseti. Nimitta-ggahaṇena bahiddhā pathavīmaṇḍalādikaṃ, ajjhattikañca bhāvanāvisesaṃ upādāya paññāpiyamānaṃ kasiṇanimittādikaṃ dasseti. Abhāva-ggahaṇena bhāvanābalena appavattanasabhāvaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanajhānaṃ upādāya pavattaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanajhānārammaṇaṃ abhāvapaññattiṃ dasseti. Nirodha-ggahaṇena bhāvanābalena niruddhaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ nissāya paññattaṃ nirodhapaññattiṃ dasseti. Ādi-ggahaṇena khayādisabhāvaṃ taṃ taṃ dhammamupādāya paññāpiyamānaṃ aniccalakkhaṇādikaṃ [V 2.0150] saṅgaṇhāti. Sāpi hi disākāsādikā viya dhammasamūhamupādāya apaññattabhāvato asamūhapaññattiyevāti.

Since the designation of earth and so forth is designated by taking the name of one element in the earth with its constituents and taking the collection as its basis, and the designation of a pot and so forth is designated by taking the name of all its components in the collection of phenomena and taking the collection as its basis, therefore it is said, ‘of one or many,’ and so forth. Herein, to show the other kind of designation, setting aside that which is designated by taking the name of one and taking the collection as its basis—because it is evident by way of earth and so forth—it is said, ‘how,’ and so forth. This is called a collective designation because it designates a collection. Among directions, space, and so forth, by the inclusion of ‘direction,’ he shows the designation of the eastern direction and so forth, which is designated by taking the revolution of the moon and sun as its basis. By the inclusion of ‘space,’ he shows the designation of space in a well, cave, and so forth, which is designated by taking uncontacted phenomena as its basis. By the inclusion of ‘time,’ he shows the designation of morning time and so forth, which is designated by taking the revolution of the moon and so forth as its basis. By the inclusion of ‘sign,’ he shows the kasiṇa sign and so forth, which is designated by taking an external earth-disk and so forth, and an internal special meditation state as its basis. By the inclusion of ‘non-existence,’ he shows the designation of non-existence, which is the object of the sphere of nothingness jhāna, arising by taking as its basis the sphere of infinite space jhāna, whose nature is non-arising due to the power of meditation. By the inclusion of ‘cessation,’ he shows the designation of cessation, which is designated by relying on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which has ceased due to the power of meditation. By the inclusion of ‘and so forth,’ he includes characteristics such as impermanence and so forth, which are designated by taking as their basis the nature of destruction and so forth in those respective phenomena. Indeed, that too, like directions, space, and so forth, is a non-collective designation because it is not designated by taking a collection of phenomena as its basis.

Sāti ayaṃ dvidhā upādāpaññatti. Tajjāpaññatti vacanatthaṃ amuñcitvā pavattito upādāpaññattiyaṃyeva saṅgayhatīti vuttaṃ “vijjamānaṃ paramatthaṃ jotayatī”ti. Evañca katvā upari “cha paññattiyopi ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchantī”ti vuttaṃ. Vijjamānanti sabhāvena upalabbhamānaṃ. Avijjamānanti ṭhapetvā lokasaṅketaṃ sabhāvavasena anupalabbhamānaṃ. Nāmamattanti nāmamattavantaṃ. Sotadvārajavanānantaranti paccuppannasaddārammaṇāya sotadvārajavanavīthiyā, tadanusārappavattāya atītasaddārammaṇāya manodvārajavanavīthiyā ca anantarappavattena[M 2.0203]. Manodvārajavanavīthipi hi sotadvārajavanānantarappavattā taggahaṇeneva idha gahitā. Gahitapubbasaṅketenāti “ayaṃ imassa attho, idamimassa vācaka”nti evaṃ vacanavacanatthasambandhaggahaṇavasena gahitapubbabhāvasaṅketena. Yāyāti yāya nāmapaññattiyā karaṇabhūtāya. Manodvārajavanaviññāṇena kattubhūtena. Manodvārajavanaviññāṇena vā karaṇabhūtena, yāya nāmapaññattiyā kattubhūtāyāti attho. Paññāpīyatīti sammutiparamatthavasena pana duvidhaṃ atthajātaṃ paññāpīyati viññāpīyatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

That is, this dependent designation is twofold. Because the designation ‘born in accordance with that’ functions without abandoning the verbal meaning, it is included within dependent designation itself; therefore, it is said, ‘It illuminates existing ultimate reality.’ And so, it is stated further on, ‘Even the six designations are included here.’ ‘Existing’ (vijjamāna) means what is apprehended by intrinsic nature. ‘Non-existing’ (avijjamāna) means what is not apprehended by intrinsic nature, apart from worldly convention. ‘Merely name’ (nāmamatta) means possessing merely a name. ‘Immediately following the ear-door javana’ refers to that which arises immediately following the ear-door javana process, which has a present sound-object, and the mind-door javana process, which has a past sound-object and functions in accordance with it. For the mind-door javana process, too, because it functions immediately following the ear-door javana, is included here by that very reference. ‘By previously grasped convention’ means by a convention that has been previously grasped by way of grasping the relationship between word and meaning, as in ‘This is the meaning of this, this is the expresser of this.’ ‘By which’ (yāya) means by which name-designation, acting as the instrument, or by the mind-door javana consciousness, acting as the agent; or by the mind-door javana consciousness, acting as the instrument, and by which name-designation, acting as the agent—this is the meaning. ‘It is designated’ (paññāpīyati) means that the twofold class of meanings, by way of conventional and ultimate reality, is designated or made known—this is what is said. Therefore, the ancients said—

“Atthā yassānusārena, viññāyanti tato paraṃ;

Sāyaṃ paññatti viññeyyā, lokasaṅketanimmitā”ti.

“That by which meanings are subsequently understood, this designation should be known as fashioned by worldly convention.”

Katarajavanavīthiyaṃ panāyaṃ viññāyatīti? “Ghaṭo”tiādisaddaṃ suṇantassa ekamekaṃ saddaṃ ārabbha paccuppannātītārammaṇavasena dve dve javanavārā honti, tato saddasamudāyamārabbha eko, tato nāmapaññattimārabbha ekoti evaṃ saddasamudāyārammaṇāya javanavīthiyā anantaraṃ nāmapaññatti pākaṭā hoti, tato paraṃ atthāvabodhoti ācariyā.

But in which javana process is this known? When one hears a sound such as ‘pot,’ two javana-courses occur for each individual sound, taking present and past objects as their basis; then one arises taking the collection of sounds as its basis; then one arises taking the name-designation as its basis. Thus, immediately after the javana process with the collection of sounds as its object, the name-designation becomes manifest; after that is the understanding of the meaning, say the teachers.

Yaṃ sandhāya chakkanayo vuttoti sambandho. Tathā avijjamānānanti paramatthato avijjamānānaṃ. Kenaci ākārenāti paramatthato, lokasaṅketato vā kenaci pakārena. Anupalabbhamānānaṃ pañcamasaccādīnanti ākāsādipañcamasaccādīnaṃ. Ādi-ggahaṇena aṭṭhamabojjhaṅgādike saṅgaṇhāti. Pakatipurisādīnanti satvarajatamānaṃ samānāvatthā pakatiaṅguṭṭhādiparimāṇo [V 2.0151] kārako vedako attā purisotiādinā parikappitānaṃ pakatipurisādīnaṃ. Ādi-ggahaṇena ākāsakusumādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Vijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti paramatthato vijjamānāhi vijjādīhi [M 2.0204] avijjamānassa puggalassa paññattattā. Sesesupi imināva nayānusārena attho veditabbo. Etthevāti upādāpaññattiyameva.

The connection is: it is stated with reference to the sixfold method. Similarly, ‘of non-existent things’ refers to those that do not exist in the ultimate sense. ‘In any way’ means in any mode, either in the ultimate sense or according to worldly convention. ‘Of the unapprehendable fifth truth, etc.’ refers to the fifth truth, etc., such as space. By the inclusion of ‘etc.,’ it encompasses the eighth factor of enlightenment, etc. ‘Of pakati, purisa, etc.’ refers to those conceptually contrived as pakati—the state of equilibrium of sattva, rajas, and tamas—and purisa—the self, the doer, the experiencer, of the size of a thumb, etc. By the inclusion of ‘etc.,’ it also encompasses a flower in the sky, etc. ‘A designation of the non-existent by means of the existent’ is because the non-existent person is designated by means of existent things like knowledge, etc., which exist in the ultimate sense. The meaning of the remaining terms should also be understood according to this same method. ‘Just here’ refers only to the designation based on what is clung to.

“Kusaggenudakamādāya, samudde udakaṃ mine;

Evaṃ mānusakā kāmā, dibbakāmāna santike”ti. (jā. 2.21.389) –

“Just as one might measure the water of the ocean by taking it up on the tip of a blade of grass, so are human pleasures in comparison to divine pleasures.”

Vacanato manussaloke cakkavattisampattidibbasampattiṃ upanidhāya nihīnāyevāti vuttaṃ “kapaṇaṃ…pe… nidhāyā”ti. Mānusakanti manussaloke bhavaṃ. Paramattho ca vijjatīti pāṭhaseso.

According to the saying, it is stated ‘miserable… laid aside’ that in the human world, even the attainment of a wheel-turning monarch is indeed inferior when compared to divine attainment. ‘Human’ means that which exists in the human world. ‘And the ultimate meaning exists’ is the remainder of the text.

778. Tatiyā koṭi na vijjati anupalabbhamānattā. Vuttañhetaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

778. A third category does not exist, because of being unapprehendable. And this has been stated in the Great Commentary:

“Duve saccāni akkhāsi, sambuddho vadataṃ varo;

Sammutiṃ paramatthañca, tatiyaṃ nopalabbhatī”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.439-443);

“The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, declared two truths: conventional truth and ultimate truth—a third is not found.”

Paravādesu na kampatīti pakatipurisantarādivādīnaṃ paresaṃ titthiyānaṃ vādesu sampattesu, nimittabhūtesu vā na kampati na pavedhati na calatīti attho.

‘He does not waver in the doctrines of others’ means that he does not waver, tremble, or become unsettled when the doctrines of others—such as the sectarians who are proponents of pakati, purisa, an inner self, and so on—are encountered or become manifest. This is the meaning.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus, in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra,

Paññattiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the exposition of designations is concluded.

13. Terasamo paricchedo

13. The Thirteenth Chapter

Kārakapaṭivedhavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Penetration of the Agent

Niddiṭṭhāti [V 2.0152] uddesaniddesādivasena dassitā. Kusalādayoti kusalākusalā. Etesaṃ pana na niddiṭṭhoti sambandho[M 2.0205]. Pubbe “kārako”ti vacanaṃ viya “vedako”ti avuttepi “attā kārako vedako”ti attano laddhitāya “tassa hi kārakassa vedakassā”ti vuttaṃ. Kusalākusalānamabhāvopi siyā, itarathā ahetukadosāpattitoti adhippāyo. Tesaṃ kusalākusalānaṃ āyattā vutti etesanti tadāyattavuttino. Tesanti kusalākusalādīnaṃ. Tasmāti kārakābhāve kusalākusalānaṃ, tabbipākānañca abhāvato. Niratthikāti desetvāpi bodhetabbābhāvato niratthikā. “Nāyaṃ niratthikā”ti vatvāpi “sātthikā”ti vacanaṃ pana parassa daḷhaggāhatthaṃ. Lokepi hi evaṃ vohāraṃ voharanti, evameva bhavati, nāññathātiādi. Tatthāti kārakābhāvepi attā atthīti gahaṇe. Anurodhoti anukūlapakkhapātoti attho. Idhāti kārakābhāvepi kusalādayo atthīti gahaṇe. Virodhoti paṭigho.

‘It has been explained’ means it has been shown by way of summaries, detailed explanations, and so forth. ‘Wholesome, etc.’ refers to the wholesome and unwholesome. The connection, however, is ‘has not been explained of these’. Previously, although ‘experiencer’ was not stated like the word ‘doer’, it was said ‘for that doer and experiencer’ because of their own doctrine that ‘the self is the doer and experiencer’. The meaning is that there might also be an absence of wholesome and unwholesome states; otherwise, the fault of causelessness would be incurred. ‘Those whose living depends on them’ means those whose existence depends on these wholesome and unwholesome states. ‘Of them’ refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, etc. ‘Therefore’ means because of the absence of a doer, and consequently the absence of wholesome and unwholesome states and their results. ‘Useless’ means useless because there is no one to be enlightened even after teaching. However, the statement ‘it is meaningful’, even after saying ‘this is not useless’, is for the sake of the other's firm grasping. For in the world, people also use such expressions as, ‘it is just so, and not otherwise,’ etc. ‘There’ means in the view that the self exists even in the absence of a doer. ‘Agreement’ means partiality to a favorable side; this is the meaning. ‘Here’ means in the view that wholesome states, etc., exist even in the absence of a doer. ‘Opposition’ means resistance.

Evaṃ kārakābhāvepi kusalādīnaṃ sabbhāvaṃ yuttito sādhetvā idāni lokasiddhena nidassanena sādhetuṃ “athāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Athāpīti kārakābhāvepi. Pathavi-ggahaṇena pathavojaṃ dasseti. Tathā āpa-ggahaṇena āpojaṃ. Tejoti sītuṇhavasena duvidhā tejodhātu. Utūti hemantādiutu. Ādi-ggahaṇena bījādike saṅgaṇhāti. Janakapaccayo hetu, anupālanakapaccayo paccayo nāmāti āha “hetupaccayasāmaggiyā”ti. “Phalanibbattako hetu, paccayo anupālanako”ti hi vuttaṃ.

Thus, having established through reasoning the existence of wholesome states, etc., even in the absence of a doer, now, in order to establish it with a well-known worldly example, ‘Moreover,’ etc., is stated. ‘Moreover’ means even in the absence of a doer. By the mention of ‘earth,’ it indicates the nutritive essence of earth. Similarly, by the mention of ‘water,’ the nutritive essence of water. ‘Fire’ is the fire element, twofold by way of cold and heat. ‘Season’ means the seasons such as winter, etc. By the inclusion of ‘etc.,’ it includes seeds and the like. The generating condition is the cause; the supporting condition is called condition—thus, it says ‘through the combination of cause and condition.’ For it is said, ‘The cause is the producer of the fruit; the condition is the supporter.’

Evaṃ kārakābhāvepi kusalākusalappavattiṃ sādhetvā idāni paraparikappitaṃ attānameva tāva paṭikkhipituṃ “athāpi cetthā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Kāmaṃ paññāparibāhiradiṭṭhiyā eva attā parikappīyati, paro pana “paññāya parikappemī”ti maññatīti [M 2.0206] tassa laddhivasena “paññāya parikappito”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ upaparikkhissāma tāvāti tiṭṭhatu tāva cesā kārakābhāvepi kusalādīnaṃ [V 2.0153] bhāvābhāvavicāraṇā paṭhamaṃ tameva attānaṃ upaparikkhissāmāti attho. Dosamettha vattukāmo pucchatīti adhippāyena paṭiññaṃ adatvāva pucchanto āha “kiñcetthā”ti. Sacetano vā udāhu acetano vāti ettha ko dosoti attho. Itaro ubhayathāpi dosoyeva. Yañhi acetanaṃ attānaṃ, na taṃ kārakaṃ, vedakañca, yathā taṃ pākārataruādayo. “Acetanovāyaṃ attā”ti anumānena kārakavedakattābhāvasiddhitoti dassetuṃ “yadi acetano”tiādi vuttaṃ. Anaññoti avinibbhogavasena anañño. Itarathā “sacetano”ti vacanameva na upapajjeyya. Sahabhāvī nāma añño na hotīti. Attanopi nāso siyāti avinibbhogavuttirūpesu ekassa nāse itarassāpi vināso viya. Cetanāyapi nāso na bhavati avinibbhogarūpesu ekassa avināse itarassāpi avināso viyāti adhippāyo.

Having thus established the occurrence of wholesome and unwholesome states even in the absence of a doer, now, in order to refute the self as conceived by others, the passage beginning with ‘athāpi cetthā’ is introduced. Indeed, although the self is conceived only by views that are external to wisdom, another might think, ‘I conceive it through wisdom.’ Thus, based on their doctrine, it is said to be ‘conceived by wisdom.’ ‘Let us investigate that first’ means: let this discussion about the presence or absence of wholesome states, etc., even in the absence of a doer, stand for now; first we will investigate that self itself. Intending to state a fault here, he asks ‘What then?’ without first admitting the proposition. The meaning is: ‘Is it conscious or unconscious? What fault is there in this?’ The other replies: In either case, there is a fault. For if the self is unconscious, it is neither a doer nor an experiencer, like a wall or a tree. To show that the absence of agency and experience is established by the inference, ‘This self is unconscious,’ the passage ‘if it is unconscious,’ etc., is stated. ‘Not other’ means not distinct, in the sense of being inseparable. Otherwise, the statement ‘it is conscious’ would not be tenable. ‘That which co-exists’ is not another. The destruction of the self would also occur, just as in the case of inseparable things, the destruction of one entails the destruction of the other. The meaning is that there would be no destruction of consciousness either, just as among inseparable things, when one is not destroyed, the other is also not destroyed.

“Cetanāya anaññattā”ti kāraṇaṃ vatvā tameva samatthetuṃ “cetanattāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. “Attano anāse sati cetanāyapi vināso na bhavatī”ti sutvāpi parassa niruttarabhāvo, cetanāya nāse visesakāraṇābhāvatoti adhippāyenāha “atha cetanāyayevā”tiādi. Attāva nassatu, tiṭṭhatu cetanā. Ko hi visesakāraṇābhāve attani anurodho, cetanāya virodhoti adhippāyo. Paṭiññā hīnāti pubbe dinnapaṭiññā parihīnā. Atha na bhavati, “paṭiññā hīnā”ti yadi attano vināse cetanāya avināso na bhavati. Cetanattānaṃ anaññabhāvena cetanāya nāse attanopi vināsappasaṅgato [M 2.0207] attā na nassatīti tava paṭiññā hīnā. Vuttappakārato viparītaṃ vāti yathāvuttappakārato viparītaṃ. Cetanāya vināsepi attā na nassati, attano pana avināsepi cetanā nassatīti evaṃ vā tava adhippāyo siyāti attho. Attā nassatu, cetanā tiṭṭhatu aññabhāve ubhinnaṃ samānayogakkhamatāya bhavitabbatoti adhippāyo. Paṭiññāhīno bhavasīti cetanāyeva nassati, attā na nassati paṭiññāya hīno bhavasi.

'Because of the non-otherness of volition'—having stated this reason, to support it, 'volition and self,' etc., is stated. Even having heard, 'When the self is not destroyed, the destruction of volition also does not occur,' the opponent is left without a reply, due to the absence of a specific reason for the destruction of volition. With this intention, he says, 'But if it is by volition alone,' and so on. Let the self be destroyed, but let volition remain. For what attachment is there to the self, and what opposition to volition, when there is no specific reason? This is the intention. 'The proposition is deficient' means the previously given proposition is abandoned. Or, if it is not so, 'the proposition is deficient' applies if, upon the destruction of the self, the non-destruction of volition does not occur. Due to the non-otherness of volition and self, from the consequence of the self's destruction upon the destruction of volition, your proposition that 'the self is not destroyed' is deficient. 'Or contrary to what was stated' means contrary to the way it was stated. The meaning is: or could this be your intention, that 'even with the destruction of volition, the self is not destroyed, but even with the non-destruction of the self, volition is destroyed'? Let the self be destroyed, let volition remain—the intention is that if they were other, both should have an equal standing. 'You become one with a deficient proposition' means: if volition alone is destroyed and the self is not destroyed, you become one whose proposition is deficient.

Idhāti aññattha pakkhe. Lakkhaṇakatanti aññamaññavisadisehi bhinnalakkhaṇehi kataṃ. Desantarakatanti bhinnadesakataṃ. Jāto vedīyati ñāyatīti jātavedo, aggissetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ḍayhamāneti uddhane pakkhipitvā paccamāne. Eko pavattipadeso imesanti ekadesā, tesaṃ bhāvoti ekadesattaṃ.

'Here' means in another case. 'Made with characteristics' means made with distinct characteristics, dissimilar from each other. 'Made in another place' means made in a different place. 'He is known when born, thus Jātaveda'; this is a designation for fire. 'Being burned' means being cooked after placing it in an oven. 'Those who have one region of occurrence are of one region'; their state is 'being of one region'.

Avinibbhogatoti lakkhaṇato bhedepi ṭhānavasena avinibbhujjanato avisaṃsaṭṭhattā “ekadesatte”tiimasseva [V 2.0154] vevacanavasena “avinibbhogabhāvepī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ ayuttanti taṃ “ubhinnaṃ ekadesatā natthī”ti iminā saha na yujjati. Paṭiññā hīnāti yadi pubbapaṭiññā pamāṇaṃ, ayaṃ paṭiññā hīnā. Yadi vā pana ayaṃ pamāṇaṃ, itarā hīnāti attho. Atha vā cetanāya attano padesavasena nānatte attano acetanattabhāvappattito “sacetano attā”ti heṭṭhā tayā dinnapaṭiññā parihīnāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

'Due to inseparability': even though there is a distinction in characteristics, because it is not separated by way of location and is not unmixed, 'even in the state of inseparability' is stated as a synonym for 'being of one region.' 'That is inappropriate' means it does not accord with the statement, 'There is no state of being of one region for both.' 'The proposition is deficient' means: if the prior proposition is the standard, then this proposition is deficient. Or, if this one is the standard, then the other is deficient—that is the meaning. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus: because volition has diversity according to its own regions, leading to the self's attainment of a state of being without volition, the proposition you gave before—'the self has volition'—is abandoned.

Acetano attāti attā acetanoti katvā. Pubbe vuttadosatoti “yadi acetano siyā”tiādinā ādito vuttadosato. Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ upaparikkhiyamāne vimaddanasaho hoti, tasmā.

'The self is without volition' means taking it that the self is without volition. 'From the previously stated fault' means from the fault stated at the beginning with, 'If it were without volition,' and so on. 'Therefore' means: because, when examined in this way, it is subject to refutation, therefore.

779. Yadi [M 2.0208] evanti yadi paramatthato kusalākusalānaṃ kārako, tabbipākānañca vedako natthi, evaṃ sante atha kasmā bhagavatā vuttanti sambandho.

779. 'If it is so' means: if ultimately there is no doer of wholesome and unwholesome actions, nor an experiencer of their results, then, this being so, why was it stated by the Blessed One? This is the connection.

Sandhāvatīti saṃsarati. Attanā katakusalākusalakammapaccayattā vipākabhūtaṃ sukhadukkhampi attanā katameva nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “sukhadukkhaṃ sayaṃkata”nti.

'It runs on' means 'it transmigrates.' Because pleasure and pain, which are the result, are conditioned by the wholesome and unwholesome kamma done by oneself, they are indeed made by oneself; hence it is said, 'Pleasure and pain are self-made.'

780. Saṃsāramāpannoti –

780. 'Having fallen into saṃsāra'—

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, ‘saṃsāro’ti pavuccatī”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; visuddhi. 2.619) –

"The continuous succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases, proceeding unbroken, is called 'saṃsāra.'"

Evaṃ vuttakhandhapaṭipāṭiādivasappavattaṃ saṃsāraṃ punappunaṃ pavattivasena paṭipanno. Dukkhamassa mahabbhayanti assa saṃsārāpannassa sattassa jātiādidukkhaṃ mahabbhayaṃ mahābhayasaṃvattanakanti attho. Opapātikoti uppajjamāno.

He has entered, by way of repeated occurrence, the saṃsāra that proceeds by way of the continuous succession of aggregates and so forth as stated. 'Suffering is a great terror for him' means: for that being who has fallen into saṃsāra, the suffering of birth and so forth is a great terror, conducive to great fear. This is the meaning. 'Spontaneously arisen' means arising.

781. Bhārā have pañcakkhandhāti rūpādayo pañcakkhandhā bhārabhūtā, sīse nikkhittabhārasadisāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhārahāro ca puggalo tassa pañcakkhandhabhārassa hārako. Bhārādānanti [V 2.0155] paṭisandhivasena pañcakkhandhabhāraggahaṇaṃ. Bhāranikkhepananti puna aggahetabbatāpādanena anupādāparinibbānavasena bhārassa nikkhipanaṃ.

781. 'The five aggregates are indeed a burden' means that the five aggregates—form and so forth—are a burden; it is said they are like a load placed on the head. And the person is the bearer, the carrier of that burden of the five aggregates. 'Taking up the burden' means the grasping of the burden of the five aggregates by way of rebirth-linking. 'Laying down the burden' means the laying down of the burden by way of final Nibbāna without clinging, by bringing it to a state where it cannot be taken up again.

782. Yanti kusalākusalakammaṃ. Sakanti āyattaṃ.

782. 'They go' refers to wholesome and unwholesome kamma. 'One's own' means dependent.

783. Ekassa puggalassāti sambandho. Ekena kappenāti ekasmiṃ kappe.

783. 'Of one person' is the connection. 'In one eon' means in one eon.

784. Assaddhotiādi heṭṭhā vuttatthaṃ.

784. 'Faithless,' and so on, has the meaning stated below.

“Tañca [M 2.0209] kho sammutivasena, na paramatthato”ti vatvā tadeva patiṭṭhāpetuṃ “nanu bhagavatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Kiṃ nu satto”ti gāthā vajirāya theriyā vuttāpi bhagavato adhippāyavaseneva vuttattā bhagavatā vuttā nāma hotīti katvā vuttaṃ “bhagavatā idampi vutta”nti.

Having stated, 'And that is by way of convention, not in an ultimate sense,' to establish that very point, 'Was it not by the Blessed One,' etc., is said. Although the verse 'What now is a being?' was spoken by the elder nun Vajirā, since it was spoken in accordance with the Blessed One’s intention, it is considered to have been spoken by the Blessed One; hence it is said, 'This too was spoken by the Blessed One.'

785. Kiṃ nu sattoti paccesīti rūpavedanādīsu kiṃ nāma satto puggaloti gaṇhāsi.

785. 'What now is a being that you believe in?' means: Among form, feeling, and so on, what do you take to be a being or a person?

786. Aṅgasambhārāti cakkādiavayavasambhāresu, cakkādiavayavānaṃ samodhānevāti attho. Saddoti vohāro.

786. 'On the collection of parts' means on the assembly of components such as wheels; this is the meaning. 'Sound' means designation.

Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ paramatthato sattassa abhāvo bhagavatā vutto, tasmā. Na vacanamattameva ālambitabbaṃ adhippāyaṃ pahāyāti attho. Daḷhamūḷhova hutvā gaṇhātīti daḷhamūḷhaggāhī, kāraṇe dassitepi apariccajanavasena gahaṇaṃ daḷhaggahaṇaṃ. Kāraṇasseva daṭṭhumasamatthatāvasena gahaṇaṃ mūḷhaggahaṇaṃ. Tādisena na bhavitabbanti āha “na ca…pe… bhavitabba”nti. Suttapadānanti neyyatthanītatthavasena ubhayathā ṭhitānaṃ suttantānaṃ.

'Therefore' means: because the absence of a being in an ultimate sense has been stated by the Blessed One, therefore. The meaning is that one should not rely merely on the words, abandoning the intention. 'One who grasps, having become firmly deluded' is a 'firmly deluded grasper.' Grasping without relinquishing, even when the reason is shown, is firm grasping. Grasping due to the inability to see the reason itself is deluded grasping. One should not be like that—thus he says: 'And one should not be…' 'Of the words of the suttas' means of the suttas which stand in two ways: as having a meaning that needs to be inferred and a meaning that is explicit.

Dve saccāni vuttāni tathā tathā vinetabbānaṃ puggalānaṃ vasenāti adhippāyo. Yesañhi sammutidesanāya visesādhigamo hoti, tesaṃ sammutisaccavasena deseti. Yesañca paramatthadesanāya, tesaṃ paramatthavasena deseti. Desabhāsākusalo viya ācariyo taṃtaṃdesavāsimāṇavānaṃ tāya tāya bhāsāya. Sammutisaccaṃ paramatthasaccañcāti ettha “puggalo satto [V 2.0156] itthī puriso khattiyo brāhmaṇo devo”tievamādi paramatthato avijjamānampi loke katasaṅketavasena tathattā sammutisaccaṃ[M 2.0210]. Khandhadhātuāyatanāni satipaṭṭhānātievamādi paramatthavaseneva tathatthā paramatthasaccaṃ. Tenāhu aṭṭhakathācariyā –

The intention is that two truths are spoken according to the individuals to be trained in various ways. For those for whom the attainment of distinction comes through conventional teaching, he teaches in terms of conventional truth. And for those for whom it comes through ultimate teaching, he teaches in terms of ultimate truth, like a teacher skilled in regional languages teaching students residing in various regions in their respective languages. Here, regarding conventional truth and ultimate truth: terms such as 'person, being, woman, man, noble, brahmin, god,' and so forth, though non-existent in an ultimate sense, are conventional truth because they are so by way of established convention in the world. The aggregates, elements, sense-bases, foundations of mindfulness, and so on, are ultimate truth because they are so in an ultimate sense. Therefore, the commentary masters said:

“Saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇaṃ;

Paramatthavacanaṃ saccaṃ, dhammānaṃ bhūtakāraṇaṃ. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.439-443);

"A statement by convention is true, by reason of worldly convention; an ultimate statement is true, by reason of the real nature of phenomena."

“Tasmā vohārakusalassa, lokanāthassa satthuno;

Sammutiṃ voharantassa, musāvādo na jāyatī”ti.

"Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World, who is skilled in expression, false speech does not arise when he is using conventional terms."

787-8. Yo so imaṃ ganthaṃ accantaṃ satatampi cinteti, tassa tato siddhā paramā paññā vepullabhāvaṃ gacchati. Adhiṃ cittasantāpaṃ nīharati apanetīti adhinīharaṃ. Vimatiyā vicikicchāya, mohassa vā vināsaṃ karoti upanissayabhāvatoti vimativināsakaraṃ. Atthabyañjanasampadāya manavaḍḍhanato piyakaraṃ. Vikasatīti dibbati. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane, abhidhamme vā.

787-8. Whoever constantly and thoroughly reflects upon this text, for them the highest wisdom, having arisen from that, attains abundance. It removes and dispels the mental fever of distress, thus it is 'the remover of distress'. It destroys doubt, uncertainty, or delusion by being a decisive support for their destruction, thus it is 'the destroyer of doubt'. Because it increases the mind through the perfection of meaning and expression, it is 'heart-pleasing'. It blossoms forth, thus it shines. 'Here' means in this Dispensation, or in the Abhidhamma.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus, in the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra,

Kārakapaṭivedhavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the discernment of factors is completed.

14. Cuddasamo paricchedo

14. The Fourteenth Chapter

Rūpāvacarasamādhibhāvanāniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition on the Development of Form-Sphere Concentration

789. Evaṃ [V 2.0157] paramatthasammutivasena ubhayathāpi sabbadhamme saṅkhepato dassetvā idāni yasmā tesu uggahaṇaparicchedādivasena kataparicayena atthakāmena kulaputtena ekaṃsato bhāvanāya abhiyogo kātabbo, tasmā bhāvanānayaṃ saṅkhepato dassetumārabhanto āha “bhāvanānaya”ntiādi. Tattha bhāvanānayanti [M 2.0211] lokiyalokuttarabhāvanānayaṃ, kusaladhammānaṃ vaḍḍhanakkamanti attho. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ hitaṃ ānayati upanetīti hitānayo, taṃ hitānayaṃ. Mānayanti mānento. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthehi anusāsanato sattānaṃ sukhaṃ ānetīti sukhānayo, taṃ sukhānayaṃ. Paramaṃ byākaromi, paramaṃ bhāvanānayanti vā yojanā.

789. Having thus briefly shown all phenomena in both ultimate and conventional terms, now, since a noble son who desires the goal and has become familiar with them by way of learning, delimitation, and so forth, should apply himself definitively to development, therefore, beginning to briefly show the method of development, he says 'the method of development' and so on. Herein, 'the method of development' means the method of mundane and supramundane development, that is, the order of progressive development of wholesome states. It brings and conveys welfare in this life and the next—thus, it is 'the bringer of welfare'; that is, the bringer of welfare. Esteeming, that is, honoring. Through instruction regarding benefits in this life and the next, it brings happiness to beings—thus, it is 'the bringer of happiness'; that is, the bringer of happiness. 'I declare the highest'—or, the interpretation is, 'the highest method of development'.

790. Manussānaṃ dhammato uttaraṃ ñāṇadassananti sambandho. Tattha manussānaṃ dhammā nāma manussānaṃ pakatidhammabhūtā dasa kusalakammapathā, tato uttaraṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ nāma mahaggatalokuttaradhammā. Te hi jānanaṭṭhena ñāṇaṃ, paccakkhato viya dassanaṭṭhena ca dassananti adhippetā. “Uttarimanussāna”nti vā yathāṭhitavaseneva sambandho. Bālamanussādito uttarimanussānaṃ jhāyīnañceva ariyānañcāti attho.

790. The connection is: 'knowledge and vision higher than the Dhamma of humans.' Herein, 'the Dhamma of humans' refers to the ten wholesome courses of action, which are the natural principles of humans. And 'the higher knowledge and vision' refers to the exalted and supramundane Dhammas. Indeed, these are intended as knowledge in the sense of knowing, and vision in the sense of seeing as if directly. Alternatively, the connection is 'of higher humans,' as it stands. The meaning is: of higher humans than foolish humans, namely, of meditators and noble ones.

791. Saṅkassarasamācāretiādīhi sīlavisuddhiyā payojanadassanaṃ. Tattha saṅkāya saritabbo samācāro assāti saṅkassarasamācāro. Yaṃ kiñci lāmakakammaṃ disvā “idaṃ asukena kataṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ pavattetabbāya saṅkāya attano vā pare yaṃkiñci mantente disvā “mama idañcidañca asāruppaṃ jānitvā mantetī”ti evaṃ pavattasaṅkāya upagantabbasamācāroti attho. Dussīleti etadeva vibhāvetuṃ “sīlavajjite”ti vuttaṃ. Dussīleti vā dūsitasīle khaṇḍādibhāvaṃ upagatasīle. Sīlavajjiteti sabbena sabbaṃ sīlavirahite. Natthi jhānanti lokiyajjhānampi tāva natthi. Kuto maggoti lokuttaramaggo kuto, kena kāraṇena lokuttaradhammānaṃ hetuyeva vijjatīti attho.

791. The purpose of virtue purification is shown by 'conduct that gives rise to doubt' and so on. Herein, 'saṅkassarasamācāra' means conduct that should be remembered with doubt. The meaning is: conduct that should be approached with doubt that arises thus: upon seeing any trivial deed, one thinks, 'This must have been done by so-and-so'; or upon seeing others deliberating about something, one thinks, 'They must be deliberating, knowing this or that is unsuitable for me.' To clarify this very point about 'immoral', 'devoid of virtue' is said. Or, 'immoral' means one whose virtue is corrupted, whose virtue has reached a state of being broken, etc. 'Devoid of virtue' means entirely lacking virtue. 'There is no jhāna' means there is not even mundane jhāna. The meaning of 'How much less the path?' is: how could there be the supramundane path, for what reason could the cause for supramundane states exist?

792. Caranti [M 2.0212][V 2.0158] tasmiṃ sīle paripūrakāritāya pavattantīti cārittaṃ. Vāritaṃ tāyanti rakkhanti tena, vāritato vā attānaṃ tāyatīti vārittaṃ. Yaṃ bhagavatā “idaṃ kātabba”nti paññattisikkhāpadapūraṇaṃ, idaṃ cārittaṃ nāma. Yaṃ “na kātabba”nti paṭikkhittaṃ, tassa akaraṇaṃ vārittaṃ nāma. Acchiddantiādīsu yassa sattasu āpattikkhandhesu majjhe sikkhāpadaṃ bhinnaṃ, tassa sīlaṃ chiddasāṭako viya chiddaṃ nāma hoti, tabbiparītaṃ acchiddaṃ. Yassa ādimhi vā ante vā bhinnaṃ, tassa pariyante chinnasāṭako viya khaṇḍaṃ nāma hoti, tadaññaṃ akkhaṇḍaṃ. Kamassa ādarakaraṇavasena akkhaṇḍanti, kamavilaṅghanavasena “akkhaṇḍamacchidda”nti vā pāṭho. Akammāsa-ggahaṇena asabalattampi vuttaṃ, sabalakammāsānaṃ bhedassa appamattakabhāvato. Ettako hi tesaṃ viseso. Yassa paṭipāṭiyā dve tīṇi sikkhāpadāni bhinnāni, tassa piṭṭhiyā, kucchiyā vā uṭṭhitena visabhāgavaṇṇena kāḷarattādīnaṃ aññatarena sabalavaṇṇā gāvī viya sabalaṃ nāma hoti. Yassa antarantarā bhinnāni, tassa antarantarā visabhāgavaṇṇabinducitragāvī viya kammāsaṃ nāma hoti. Yaṃ pana tathāvidhaṃ na hoti, taṃ “asabalaṃ akammāsa”nti vuccati. Aninditanti iminā bhujissaviññuppasatthaaparāmaṭṭhasamādhisaṃvattanikabhāve saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha “imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā”ti evaṃ taṇhāya aparāmaṭṭhaṃ taṇhādāsabyato mocitattā bhujissaṃ nāma. Adāsañhi loke bhujissoti vadanti. Yathāvuttaguṇapāripūriyā buddhādīhi viññūhi pasaṃsitabbanti viññuppasatthaṃ. Taṇhādiṭṭhīhi aparāmaṭṭhaṃ ṭhitibhāgiyaṃ aparāmaṭṭhaṃ nāma. Jhānādīnaṃ paccayo bhavituṃ samatthaṃ visesabhāgiyaṃ samādhisaṃvattanikaṃ nāma.

792. They conduct themselves in that virtue, acting to fulfill it—this is called cāritta. They protect themselves from what is prohibited, or they protect themselves by means of what is prohibited—this is called vāritta. What the Blessed One has declared as "This should be done" as the fulfillment of the training rules—this is called cāritta. What has been prohibited as "This should not be done," abstaining from that is called vāritta. In terms like "unperforated": for one whose training rule is broken in the middle among the seven classes of offenses, their virtue is called "perforated," like a perforated cloth; the opposite is "unperforated." For one whose training rule is broken at the beginning or end, their virtue is called "fragmented," like a cloth torn at the edges; the opposite is "unfragmented." It is called "unfragmented" due to the care taken in observance, or the reading "unfragmented and unperforated" is due to not violating the observance. By the inclusion of "unblemished," "unstainedness" is also stated, because the difference between the stained and the blemished is insignificant. This is indeed their distinction. For one whose training rules are broken in sequence, two or three at a time, their virtue is called "stained," like a cow with patches of a different color on its back or belly. For one whose training rules are broken intermittently, their virtue is called "speckled," like a cow with spots of a different color scattered throughout. What is not like that is called "unstained and unblemished." By "unblamed" it is included in the state of being free, praised by the wise, unclung to, and conducive to concentration. Here, "free" means being unclung to by craving, released from the slavery of craving, not thinking, "By this virtue, or practice, or holy life, I will become a god or some divine being." For in the world, they call one who is not a slave "free." It is "praised by the wise" because it is worthy of praise by the wise, such as the Buddhas, due to the complete fulfillment of the aforementioned qualities. It is "unclung to" because it is untouched by craving and wrong views, belonging to the state of stability. It is "conducive to concentration" because it is capable of being a condition for jhāna and the like, belonging to the state of distinction.

793-7. Vivekasukhanti [M 2.0213] kāyacittūpadhivivekasukhaṃ. Kāyavivekasukhampi hi sampannasīlasseva dussīlassa suññāgārādīsu vasatopi bheravārammaṇādiāpāthagamanena dukkhasseva visesato sampajjanato. Alaṅkāro anuttaroti devabrahmarājarājamahāmattādīnaṃ majjhe anaññasādhāraṇasobhāpaṭilābhahetutāya niruttaro alaṅkāraviseso. Ratananti cakkavattīnaṃ cakkaratanāditopi savisesaṃ ratijananato anuttaraṃ ratanaṃ. Cakkaratanādikañhi vaṭṭanissitameva ratiṃ janeti, idaṃ pana vivaṭṭanissitampi janetīti visesato ratijanakaṃ hoti. Icchiticchitassa sampattivisesassa nipphādanato cintāmaṇisamanti cintāmaṇi. Yānanti saṃsārakantārataraṇe yānaṃ. Sītalanti cittasītibhāvakaraṇena sītalaṃ. Kilesamaladhovananti gaṅgāyamunādīhipi [V 2.0159] dubbisodhanīyassa kilesakālusiyassa dhovanaṃ. Guṇānaṃ mūlabhūtanti sabbesampi lokiyalokuttaraguṇānaṃ mūlabhūtaṃ. “Sīle patiṭṭhāya (saṃ. ni. 1.23), ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ, sīlañca suvisuddha”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.369) ca ādivacanañhettha nidassanaṃ. Dosānaṃ vītikkamavatthubhūtassa balassa vināsanato dosānaṃ balaghāti.

793-7. The happiness of seclusion is the happiness of seclusion of body, mind, and the substrata of existence. For the happiness of bodily seclusion is only for one endowed with virtue; for an immoral person dwelling in empty houses and the like, it is distinctly realized as suffering due to the encountering of frightening objects and so forth. The unsurpassed ornament is the supreme ornament because it causes the attainment of unparalleled splendor among gods, Brahmās, kings, great ministers, and the like, a splendor not shared with others. The jewel is the supreme jewel because it generates joy surpassing even the wheel-treasure and other treasures of a universal monarch. For the wheel-treasure and the like generate delight dependent on the cycle of existence alone, but this generates delight even dependent on that which is beyond the cycle—thus it is especially joy-producing. Like the wish-fulfilling gem, because it accomplishes the attainment of special accomplishments that are desired. The vehicle is the means of crossing the wilderness of saṃsāra. Cooling, because it brings about the cooling of the mind. Washing away the stains of defilements, because it cleanses the blackness of defilements, which is difficult to purify even by the Ganges and Yamunā rivers. The root of all virtues, because it is the foundation of all mundane and supramundane virtues. Here, passages such as 'Established in virtue...' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.23), 'What is the origin of wholesome qualities...' and 'Virtue is perfectly purified' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.369) serve as illustrations. The destroyer of the power of faults, because it destroys the strength of faults, which are the basis for transgressions.

Tasmāti yasmā evaṃvidhānisaṃsasampannaṃ sīlaṃ, tasmā. Duvidhalakkhaṇanti okkhittacakkhuappasaddādivasena kāyakammādīnaṃ avippakiṇṇatāsādhanato samādhānalakkhaṇaṃ, kusaladhammānaṃ mūlabhāvato patiṭṭhānalakkhaṇanti evaṃ duvidhalakkhaṇaṃ, cārittavārittavasena vā duvidhasabhāvanti attho. Atthānaṃ kāmeti tassa hitāsīsanavasenāti atthakāmo. Piyaṃ sīlamassāti piyasīlo.

Therefore: because virtue is thus endowed with such benefits, therefore. 'The twofold characteristic': through keeping the eyes downcast, speaking little, and so on, it has the characteristic of composure by accomplishing the non-scatteredness of bodily action and so forth; and, being the root of wholesome qualities, it has the characteristic of being a foundation—thus, it has a twofold characteristic. Alternatively, it has a twofold nature by way of conduct and restraint—this is the meaning. 'He desires their welfare': in the manner of wishing for their good—thus, he is one who desires welfare. 'Virtue is dear to him': thus, he is one who loves virtue.

798-9. Kātabbo palibodhassupacchedoti sambandho. Katividho panāyaṃ palibodho, kiṃ sarūpo cāti āha “palibodhā [M 2.0214] dasā”tiādi, “āha mahāaṭṭhakathāya”nti adhippāyo. Tattha āvāsoti ekampi ovarakaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva sakalopi saṅghārāmo, so tattha paṭibaddhacittassa palibodho, na itarassa. Kulanti ñātikulaṃ vā upaṭṭhākakulaṃ vā, taṃ tehi saṃsaṭṭhaviharatova palibodho. Lābhoti cattāro paccayā, tepi tattha sāpekkhasseva palibodhā. Gaṇoti suttantikagaṇo vā ābhidhammikagaṇo vā. So uddesaparipucchādānena samaṇadhammassa okāsālābhino palibodho. Kammanti navakammaṃ, taṃ karontena vaḍḍhakiādīhi laddhāladdhaṃ jānitabbaṃ, katākate ussukkaṃ āpajjitabbanti sabbathāpi palibodho. Addhānanti maggagamanacittassa dubbinodanīyatāya taṃ samaṇadhammassa palibodho. Ñātīti ettha kula-ggahaṇena ñātikulassapi gahitattā ekekā ñāti idha gahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Ye pana vihāre ācariyupajjhāyādayo, ghare mātādayo, te gilānā palibodhā. Ābādhoti yo koci rogo, so bādhayamāno palibodho. Ganthoti pariyattipariharaṇaṃ, taṃ sajjhāyādīhi niccabyāvaṭasseva palibodho. Iddhīti pothujjanikaiddhi. Sā hi dupparihārā appamattakeneva bhijjati, ayaṃ pana vipassanāya palibodho, na samādhissa samādhiṃ patvā paṭilabhitabbattā. Teti te palibodhā.

798-9. The connection is: the cutting off of obstacles should be done. Now, how many kinds of obstacles are there, and what are their characteristics? It is said: 'There are ten obstacles,' and so on, the meaning being 'as said in the Great Commentary.' Therein, 'dwelling' means anything from a single cell onwards up to an entire monastery; this is an obstacle for one whose mind is attached to it, not for others. 'Family' refers to either a family of relatives or a family of supporters; it is an obstacle only for one who lives mingling closely with them. 'Gain' refers to the four requisites; these too are obstacles only for one who is dependent on them. 'Group' means a group studying the Suttas or the Abhidhamma; this is an obstacle for one who does not find opportunity for the ascetic's practice due to giving instruction, questioning, and teaching. 'Work' refers to new construction; this is an obstacle, for while doing it, one must know what has been obtained or not obtained by carpenters and others, and be zealous about what has been done or not done; thus, it is an obstacle in every way. 'Travel' is an obstacle to the ascetic's practice because the mind concerned with going on a journey is hard to divert. 'Relatives': here, since the family of relatives has already been included by the term 'family,' individual relatives should be understood. Those in the monastery like teachers and preceptors, or at home like one's mother and others, are obstacles when they are sick. 'Illness' means any disease; when it afflicts, it is an obstacle. 'Study' means learning and maintaining the scriptures; this is an obstacle only for one constantly occupied with recitation and similar activities. 'Supernormal power' refers to the supernormal power of an ordinary person; this is hard to maintain and is destroyed by even a little carelessness. This, however, is an obstacle to insight, not to concentration, because it is to be obtained only after having attained concentration. These are the obstacles.

800-2. Palibodhassupacchedaṃ katvāti ettha paṭhamo tattha nirapekkhacittatāya, dutiyo asaṃsaggena, tatiyo lābhasakkāruppattiṭṭhānaṃ pahāya aññattha gamanena, catuttho yathāraddhaganthasamāpanena[V 2.0160], aññassa saṅgāhaṇena vā, pañcamo yathāraddhakammassa niṭṭhāpanena, saṅghādīnaṃ niyyātanena vā, chaṭṭho gantvā kiccatīraṇena, sattamo upaṭṭhahitvā [M 2.0215] ñātīnaṃ pākatikakaraṇena, aṭṭhamo bhesajjakaraṇena, vīriyādhiṭṭhānena vā, navamadasamā tattha abyāvaṭatāya upacchinditabbā. Upasaṅkamitabboti yattha so vasati, tattha upasaṅkamanavidhiñceva upasaṅkamantena paṭipajjitabbavidhānañca visuddhimagge vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Ito parañhi ganthavitthārapariharaṇatthaṃ visuddhimagge āgatavitthāraṃ pahāya padatthavaṇṇanamattaṃ karissāma. Kammaṭṭhānassāti ettha yogakammassa pavattiṭṭhānatāya, uparūparibhāvanākammassa kāraṇabhāvato ca kammaṭṭhānaṃ. Taṃ pana sabbatthakapārihāriyavasena duvidhaṃ. Tattha mettā, maraṇassati, asubhasaññā ca sabbattha atthayitabbato icchitabbato sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Cariyānukūlaṃ pana yaṃ kiñci kammaṭṭhānaṃ niccaṃ pariharitabbattā pārihāriyakammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Imaṃ duvidhaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ yo deti, ayaṃ kammaṭṭhānassa dāyako, sopi īdiso pariyesitabboti dassetuṃ “piyo garū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Piyoti sīlasampadādīhi sattānaṃ piyāyitabbo. Garūti tatoyeva garukātabbo pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garuṃ katvā daṭṭhabbo. Bhāvanīyoti sambhāvanīyo. Vattāti kiñci ālasiyampi disvā codetvā ovādavasena vadanasīlo. Vacanakkhamoti paṭipucchakkhamo, paṭipucchito asaṃhīro hutvā sambhāsanakkhamoti vuttaṃ hoti. Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattāti tiracchānakathaṃ akathetvā dasakathāvatthupaṭisaṃyuttaṃ gambhīrameva kathaṃ kattā. No caṭṭhāne niyojakoti appavattitabbaṭṭhānabhūte ahite na niyojako. Evamādiguṇopetanti ādi-saddena saddhāsampadādiguṇayogaṃ dasseti. Kālenāti attano, ācariyassa ca sappāyakālena.

800-2. 'Having cut off the obstacles': here, the first is to be cut off by indifference of mind towards it; the second by non-association; the third by abandoning places where gain and honor arise and going elsewhere; the fourth by completing the study as begun, or by having another take it up; the fifth by completing the work as begun, or by entrusting it to the Sangha and others; the sixth by going and settling the matter; the seventh by attending to relatives and restoring them to their normal state; the eighth by preparing medicine, or by a determination of energy; the ninth and tenth are to be cut off by non-engagement in them. 'Should be approached': where he dwells, the method of approaching and the manner of conduct when approaching should be understood according to the way stated in the Visuddhimagga. From here onward, to avoid elaborating the text, we will only give the explanation of the meaning of the words, leaving aside the detailed exposition found in the Visuddhimagga. 'Of the meditation subject': here, it is called a meditation subject because it is the basis for the practice of yoga and because it is the cause for higher and higher development. It is of two kinds: universal and to be constantly practiced. Among them, loving-kindness, mindfulness of death, and perception of the foul are called universal meditation subjects because they are to be sought and are desirable everywhere. But any meditation subject suitable to one's temperament, which should be constantly practiced, is called a meditation subject to be constantly practiced. The one who gives this twofold meditation subject is the giver of the meditation subject, and such a one should be sought. To show this, it is said: 'dear, revered,' etc. 'Dear': he should be endeared to beings through virtues like moral perfection. 'Revered': he should be revered for that very reason, regarded as weighty, like a stone umbrella. 'To be cultivated': worthy of esteem. 'A speaker': one who is in the habit of speaking by way of urging and advising, even when seeing some laziness.
