'Patient in speech': able to endure questioning; it is said that, when questioned, he is not timid and is able to engage in conversation. 'A speaker of deep talk': one who does not speak frivolous talk but only deep talk connected with the ten topics of discussion. 'Not one who directs wrongly': not one who directs to what is unbeneficial, to a place where one should not proceed. 'Endowed with such qualities and so on': by the word 'and so on' (`ādi`), it indicates the possession of qualities like the perfection of faith. 'At the right time': at a time suitable for oneself and the teacher.

803. Vattaṃ katvāti ācariyassa navakamahallakabhāvānurūpena khandhake āgataṃ ācariyavattaṃ katvā. Idāni ācariyena [M 2.0216] paṭipajjitabbavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “tenāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenāpīti kammaṭṭhānadāyakenapi. Caritaṃ ñatvā dātabbanti cetopariyañāṇalābhinā tassa cittācāraṃ, hadayalohitaṃ vā passitvā itarena “tvaṃ kiṃcaritosi, ke vā pana te dhammā bahulaṃ samudācarantī”tiādinā paṭipucchitvā tassa caritaṃ jānitvā tadanurūpena dātabbaṃ.

803. “Having performed the duties” means having performed the duties towards one's teacher, as laid out in the Khandhaka, in accordance with the teacher's status as new or senior. Now, to explain the procedure the teacher should follow, it is said, “Even by him,” and so forth. “Even by him” means even by the giver of the meditation subject. “Knowing the temperament, it should be given” means that one who has attained knowledge of others’ minds should observe his mental conduct or his heart's blood, while another should inquire, “What is your temperament? What qualities frequently arise in you?” and so on, and having understood his temperament, give accordingly.

804. Iriyāpathāditopi kesañci caritaṃ jānituṃ sakkā, taṃ pana na ekantikaṃ, “caritaṃ ñatvā”ti vuttaṃ, katamaṃ pana taṃ, katividhā vāti āha “caritaṃ panidaṃ rāgadosamohavasenā”tiādi[V 2.0161]. Ussannabhāvena santāne caratīti caritaṃ, asati paṭipakkhabhāvanāyaṃ santāne pavattanārahā rāgādayo.

804. It is also possible to know someone’s temperament from their postures and so on, but that is not definitive. “Having known the temperament” is stated. What is that, and of what kinds is it? It is said, “Now, this temperament is by way of lust, hatred, and delusion,” and so forth. “Temperament” (`carita`) is so called because it moves (`carati`) in the mental continuum with predominance; lust, etc., are liable to occur in the mental continuum in the absence of the development of opposing qualities.

805. Vomissakanayāti sampayogavasena, ekasantatipariyāpannatāvasena ca nesaṃ saṃsaggabhedā. Catusaṭṭhi bhavantīti –

805. By the mixed method: their distinctions of association are by way of combination and by way of inclusion in a single continuum. They become sixty-four, thus:

“Rāgādike tike satta, satta saddhādike tike;

Ekadvitikamūlamhi, missato sattasattaka”nti –

“Seven in the triad beginning with lust, seven in the triad beginning with faith; in single, dual, and triple roots, a mixture of seven sevens.”

Evaṃ vuttehi navahi sattakehi yathārahaṃ vibhajiyamānā tesaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ catusaṭṭhi bhavanti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ upanandattherena –

Thus, when divided appropriately by the nine sevens so described, there are sixty-three, which together with wrong view, become sixty-four. For so it was stated by the Elder Upananda:

“Rāgo doso ca moho ca, rāgena paṭighopi ca;

Saddhiṃ rāgena moho ca, mohopi paṭighena ca.

“Lust, hatred, and delusion; lust also with aversion; delusion with lust; and delusion with aversion.

“Rāgādittayamekanti, satta rāgādike tike;

Saddhā buddhi ca takko ca, saddhiṃ saddhāya buddhi ca.

“The triad beginning with lust as one—seven in the triad beginning with lust. Faith, understanding, and reasoning; and understanding with faith.

“Saddhāya takkanañceva, buddhiyā takkanampi ca;

Saddhādittayamekanti, satta saddhādike tike.

“Reasoning with faith, and reasoning with understanding; the triad beginning with faith as one—seven in the triad beginning with faith.

“Rāgādikaṃ [M 2.0217] tikañceka-mekadvitikabhedato;

Saddhābuddhivitakkehi, yathāyogaṃ vimissiya.

“The triad beginning with lust, by division into single, dual, and triple, having mixed them as is fitting with faith, understanding, and reasoning.

“Ekamūle dvimūle ca, paccekaṃ sattakattayaṃ;

Timūle sattakañcekaṃ, ñeyyaṃ taṃ sattasattakaṃ.

“With the single-rooted and the double-rooted, there are three sets of seven each; with the triple-rooted, there is one set of seven—know that as the seven sevens.

“Saddhiṃ [V 2.0162] rāgena saddhā ca, saddhiṃ teneva buddhi ca;

Teneva takkanaṃ tena, saddhābuddhi ca tena ca.

“Faith together with lust; understanding together with that; reasoning with that; and faith and understanding with that.

“Saddhāsaṅkappanaṃ tena, buddhisaṅkappanampi ca;

Vimissetvāna teneva, saddhābuddhivitakkanaṃ.

“Faith-resolve through that, and understanding-resolve also; having mingled with that, faith, understanding, and reasoning.

“Rāgamūlanaye ceva-mekaṃ sattakamuddise;

Saddhiṃ dosena saddhā ca, saddhiṃ teneva buddhi ca.

“In the method rooted in lust, one set of seven should be declared; faith together with hatred, and understanding together with that.

“Teneva takkanaṃ tena, saddhābuddhi ca tena ca;

Saddhāsaṅkappanaṃ tena, buddhisaṅkappanampi ca.

“Reasoning together with that, faith and understanding together with that; faith-resolve through that, and understanding-resolve also.

“Vimissetvāna teneva, saddhābuddhivitakkanaṃ;

Dosamūlanaye ceva-mekaṃ sattakamuddise.

“Having mingled with that, faith, understanding, and reasoning; in the method rooted in hatred, one set of seven should be declared.

“Saddhiṃ mohena saddhā ca, saddhiṃ teneva buddhi ca;

Teneva takkanaṃ tena, saddhābuddhi ca tena ca.

“Faith together with delusion, and understanding together with that; reasoning together with that, faith and understanding together with that.

“Saddhāsaṅkappanaṃ tena, buddhisaṅkappanampi ca;

Vimissetvāna teneva, saddhābuddhivitakkanaṃ.

“Faith-resolve through that, and understanding-resolve also; having mingled with that, faith, understanding, and reasoning.

“Mohamūlanaye ceva-mekaṃ sattakamuddise;

Ekamūle naye cevaṃ, ñeyyaṃ taṃ sattakattayaṃ.

“In the method rooted in delusion, one set of seven should be declared; in the single-rooted method, thus, that triad of sevens should be understood.

“Missetvā rāgadosehi, saddhā teheva buddhi ca;

Tehi saṅkappanaṃ tehi, saddhābuddhi ca tehi ca.

“Having mingled with lust and hatred, faith together with those, and understanding also with those; resolve together with those, and faith and understanding together with those.

“Saddhāsaṅkappanaṃ [V 2.0163] tehi, buddhisaṅkappanampi ca;

Tehi dvīheva missetvā, saddhābuddhivitakkanaṃ.

“Faith-resolve together with those, and understanding-resolve also; having mingled with those two, faith, understanding, and reasoning.

“Rāgadosanaye ceva-mekaṃ sattakamuddise;

Missetvā rāgamohehi, saddhā teheva buddhi ca.

“In the method of lust and hatred, one set of seven should be declared; having mingled with lust and delusion, faith together with those, and understanding also with those.

“Tehi [M 2.0218] saṅkappanaṃ tehi, saddhābuddhi ca tehi ca;

Saddhāsaṅkappanaṃ tehi, buddhisaṅkappanampi ca.

“Resolve together with those, and faith and understanding together with those; faith-resolve together with those, and understanding-resolve also.

“Tehi dvīheva missetvā, saddhābuddhivitakkanaṃ;

Rāgamohanaye ceva-mekaṃ sattakamuddise.

“Having mingled with those two, faith, understanding, and reasoning; in the method of lust and delusion, one set of seven should be declared.

“Missetvā dosamohehi, saddhā teheva buddhi ca;

Tehi saṅkappanaṃ tehi, saddhābuddhi ca tehi ca.

“Having mingled with hatred and delusion, faith together with those, and understanding also with those; resolve together with those, and faith and understanding together with those.

“Saddhāsaṅkappanaṃ tehi, buddhisaṅkappanampi ca;

Tehi dvīheva missetvā, saddhābuddhivitakkanaṃ.

“Faith-resolve together with those, and understanding-resolve also; having mingled with those two, faith, understanding, and reasoning.

“Dosamohanaye ceva-mekaṃ sattakamuddise;

Dvimūlamhi naye cevaṃ, ñeyyaṃ taṃ sattakattayaṃ.

“In the method of hatred and delusion, one set of seven should be declared; in the two-rooted method, thus, that triad of sevens should be understood.

“Rāgappaṭighamohehi, saddhā teheva buddhi ca;

Tehi saṅkappanaṃ tehi, saddhābuddhi ca tehi ca.

“With lust, aversion, and delusion, faith together with those, and understanding also with those; resolve together with those, and faith and understanding together with those.

“Saddhāsaṅkappanaṃ tehi, buddhisaṅkappanampi ca;

Tehi tīheva missetvā, saddhābuddhivitakkanaṃ.

“Faith-resolve together with those, and understanding-resolve also; having mingled with those three, faith, understanding, and reasoning.

“Timūlamhi naye ceva-mekaṃ sattakamuddise;

Evaṃ tesaṭṭhi hotīti, viññeyyaṃ navasattakaṃ;

Diṭṭhiyāpi ca hoteva, catusaṭṭhīti kecanā”ti.

“In the three-rooted method, one set of seven should be declared; thus there are sixty-three, so the nine sevens should be understood. And with view, it becomes sixty-four, according to some.”

806-7. Nanu ca “caritaṃ ñatvā dātabba”nti vuttaṃ, kiṃcaritassa pana kiṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ anukūlanti [V 2.0164] imaṃ anuyogaṃ sandhāya taṃtaṃcaritānukūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā puna tassa gaṇanato appanāvahato jhānappabhedato samatikkamato vaḍḍhanāvaḍḍhanato ārammaṇato bhūmito gahaṇato paccayato bhedaṃ dassetuṃ “asubhā cā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha dasa asubhāti uddhumātakaṃ vinīlakaṃ vipubbakaṃ vicchiddakaṃ vikkhāyitakaṃ vikkhittakaṃ hatavikkhittakaṃ lohitakaṃ puḷavakaṃ aṭṭhikanti ime dasa. Tathā kāyagatāsati cāti ime [M 2.0219] ekādasa rāgavikkhambhanassa upāyabhāvato rāgacaritassa anukūlā. Asubha-ggahaṇena cettha tadārammaṇasamādhipubbaṅgamaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahitaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi yathārahaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Appamāṇasattārammaṇattā appamaññā, mettā karuṇā muditā upekkhāti catunnaṃ brahmavihārānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Te pana savaṇṇakasiṇā nīlakasiṇaṃ pītakasiṇaṃ lohitakasiṇaṃ odātakasiṇanti imehi catūhi vaṇṇakasiṇehi sahitā aṭṭha dosavikkhambhanupāyabhāvato, appaṭighātavisayattā ca dosacaritassa anukūlā.

806-7. Was it not said, “One should give having known the temperament”? But what meditation subject is suitable for what temperament? To address this inquiry, having shown the meditation subjects suitable for each temperament, and then to show the distinction—from its enumeration, from its leading to absorption, from its types of jhāna, from its transcending, from its increase and decrease, from its object, from its ground, from its mode of apprehension, and from its conditions—the section beginning with “the foul things,” and so forth, was begun. Here, the ten foul things are: the bloated, the livid, the festering, the split open, the gnawed, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the bloody, the worm-infested, and the skeleton. Likewise, mindfulness of the body—these eleven are suitable for one of lustful temperament because they are the means of suppressing lust. By the term “foul things” here, the meditation subject preceded by concentration on that object is meant. The same should be understood for the rest accordingly. Due to having immeasurable beings as their object, they are called the immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity—this is the designation for the four divine abidings. These, together with the four color kasiṇas—the blue, yellow, red, and white kasiṇas—making eight in total, are suitable for one of hateful temperament because they are the means of suppressing hatred and because their objects are non-repugnant.

808. Taṃ…pe… panekakanti ettha ekakanti idaṃ anussatiapekkhaṃ, anussatīsu ekanti attho, na mohacaritavitakkacaritāpekkhaṃ tesaṃ aññassāpi anukūlassa labbhanato. Taṃ pana mohacaritassa, vitakkacaritassa ca gaṇanabalena cittassa patiṭṭhānato anukūlaṃ.

808. That…etc. Here, the word “one” is with reference to the recollections, meaning “one among the recollections,” not with reference to those of deluded or speculative temperament, since for them another suitable subject can also be found. But that is suitable for those of deluded and speculative temperament because it serves as a foundation for the mind through the power of counting.

809-11. Purimā…pe… dehinoti “buddhānussati dhammānussati saṅghānussati sīlānussati cāgānussati devatānussatī”ti idaṃ pāḷikkamena purimaṃ anussatichakkaṃ saddhācaritassa atisappāyavasena anukūlaṃ. Maraṇūpasamāyuttā satīti maraṇe, upasame ca yuttā sati, maraṇānussati, upasamānussati cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Āhāranissitā saññāti āhāre paṭikkūlasaññā. Dhātuvavatthānanti catudhātuvavatthānaṃ. Buddhippakatijantunoti buddhicaritassa sattassa. Sesāni kasiṇānīti dosacaritassa anukūlesu vuttehi catūhi vaṇṇakasiṇehi avasesāni pathavīāpotejovāyoālokākāsakasiṇāni, evaṃ purimāni cattāri, imāni chāti dasa imasseva ujuvipaccanīkā, imassa asappāyanti gahetabbavisesassa abhāvato rāgādisabbacaritānaṃ anukūlāti vaṇṇitā.

809-11. The section beginning with “the previous…for the embodied one,” that is, “recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities”—this first set of six recollections, according to the textual order, is suitable for one of faithful temperament by way of being extremely favorable. “Recollection associated with death and peace” means recollection associated with death and with peace; thus, it is called recollection of death and recollection of peace. “Perception based on food” refers to perception of repulsiveness in food. “The analysis of the elements” is the four-element analysis. “For a being of intelligent nature” means for a being of intellectual temperament. “The remaining kasiṇas” refers to the earth, water, fire, air, light, and space kasiṇas, which are the ones remaining after the four color kasiṇas mentioned as suitable for one of hateful temperament. Thus, the previous four and these six make ten. Because they lack a specific feature to be grasped that is directly opposite or unsuitable to any particular temperament, they are described as suitable for all temperaments, such as those of lust and so on.

812. Ekantavipaccanīkabhāvatoti [M 2.0220] rāgacaritādīnaṃ asubhādikammaṭṭhānassa ujuvipaccanīkatāya. Atisappāyatoti saddhācaritādīnaṃ buddhānussatiādikammaṭṭhānassa atisappāyato. Evaṃ ujuvipaccanīkavasena, atisappāyavasena ca idaṃ sabbaṃ visuṃ visuṃ tesaṃ anukūlanti [V 2.0165] vuttaṃ, na pana itarassa ananukūlabhāvato. Na hi rāgādīnaṃ avikkhambhikā, saddhādīnaṃ vā anupakārikā kusalabhāvanā nāma atthi. Tathā hi meghiyasutte –

812. “By way of being directly opposite” refers to the direct opposition of meditation subjects like foulness to those of lustful temperament, and so forth. “By way of extreme suitability” means the extreme suitability of meditation subjects like recollection of the Buddha to those of faithful temperament, and so forth. Thus, it is said that all these are individually suitable for them by way of direct opposition and by way of extreme suitability, but not because they are unsuitable for others. For there is no wholesome development that does not suppress lust and so forth, or that does not assist faith and so forth. For thus it is stated in the Meghiya Sutta:

“Cattāro dhammā uttari bhāvetabbā, asubhā bhāvetabbā rāgassa pahānāya, mettā bhāvetabbā byāpādassa pahānāya, ānāpānassati bhāvetabbā vitakkupacchedāya, aniccasaññā bhāvetabbā asmimānasamugghātāyā”ti (a. ni. 9.3; udā. 31) –

“Four things should be further developed: foulness should be developed for the abandonment of lust, loving-kindness should be developed for the abandonment of ill will, mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of discursive thought, and the perception of impermanence should be developed for the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am.’” (AN 9.3; Ud 4.1)

Ekasseva cattāro dhammā bhāvetabbāti vuttā. Tathā rāhulovādasuttepi “mettaṃ, rāhula, bhāvanaṃ bhāvehī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 2.120) satta kammaṭṭhānāni vuttāni, na cāyasmato meghiyassa cattāripi caritāni santi, nāpi rāhulattherassa sabbacaritāni, tasmā vacanamatte abhinivesaṃ akatvā sabbattha adhippāyo pariyesitabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

It is said that four qualities should be developed by a single person. Similarly, in the Advice to Rāhula Sutta, seven meditation subjects are mentioned, beginning with, “Develop the meditation of loving-kindness, Rāhula” (MN 62). Yet, the Venerable Meghiya did not have all four temperaments, nor did the Elder Rāhula have all temperaments. Therefore, it is said that one should not fixate on the mere words but should seek the underlying intention in all cases.

813-4. Kiñcāpi vuttanayena kammaṭṭhānānaṃ gaṇanaparicchedopi sakkā ñātuṃ, saṅkarattā pana sukhena viññātuṃ na sakkāti tesaṃ sāmaññato, visuṃ visuṃ jātito ca gaṇanaparicchedaṃ dassetuṃ “kammaṭṭhānāni sabbānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Cattālīsāti niddiseti pāḷito, aṭṭhakathāto ca samodhānetvā “samacattālīsā”ti niddiseyya. Kathaṃ? Kasiṇāni dasa…pe… saññā cāhāratā iti. Asubhānussatī dasāti dasa-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo “dasa asubhā[M 2.0221], dasa anussatī”ti. Dasa asubhā heṭṭhā kathitāva. “Purimānussatichakka”nti ettha vuttā cha, maraṇānussati kāyagatāsati ānāpānassati upasamānussatīti imā dasa anussatiyo. Catudhātuvavatthānanti pathavādīnaṃ catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ vavatthānaṃ. Saññā cāhāratāti gāthābandhavasena ga-kārassa lopaṃ katvā āhāragatā saññā “āhāratā saññā”ti vuttā. Āhāroyeva vā āhāratā, taggatā ca saññā upacārato “āhāratā”ti vuttā, āhāre paṭikkūlasaññāti attho.

813-4. Although it is possible to know the enumeration and classification of meditation subjects in the way described, yet due to their complexity, they cannot be easily comprehended. Thus, to show their enumeration and classification generally, individually, and by nature, it is said, “All meditation subjects,” and so on. Forty is indicated from the Pāli text, and combining this with the commentaries, it should be indicated as “exactly forty.” How? The ten kasiṇas... and so on... up to the perception regarding food. Regarding 'ten foulnesses and recollections,' the word 'ten' should be applied to each separately: 'ten foulnesses, ten recollections.' The ten foulnesses have already been explained below. The six mentioned in 'the first six recollections,' along with recollection of death, mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of breathing, and recollection of peace—these are the ten recollections. Analysis of the four elements is the determination of the four elements: earth, and so on. As for 'perception regarding food,' due to the constraints of verse, the syllable 'ga' is elided, and āhāragatā saññā, the perception directed towards food, is called 'āhāratā saññā.' Alternatively, food itself is āhāratā, and the perception directed toward it is metaphorically called 'āhāratā'; the meaning is the perception of repulsiveness in food.

815-6. Kiṃ imesu sabbesuyeva kammaṭṭhānesu jhānaṃ nibbattatīti? Āma, nibbattati sabbesveva upacārajjhānaṃ, appanājhānaṃ pana kesuci na nibbattati, tasmā kānici upacārameva nibbattenti, kānici appanampi. Kathaṃ panetaṃ daṭṭhabbanti āha “etesū”tiādi. Upacārameva [V 2.0166] āvahantīti upacārāvahā “apekkho”tiādīsu viya hettha avadhāraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha ānāpānassatiṃ, kāyagatāsatiñca hitvā sesā buddhānussatiādayo aṭṭha anussatiyo, saññā, vavatthānañcāti ete dasa nānappakārakattā, gambhīrattā, sabhāvadhammattā ca asati bhāvanāvisese upacārāvahā vuttā.

815-6. Does jhāna arise in all these meditation subjects? Yes, access jhāna arises in all of them, but absorption jhāna does not arise in some. Therefore, some produce only access concentration, while others produce absorption as well. But how is this to be understood? It is said, “In these…” and so on. Those that bring only access are 'access-bringing.' Just as in cases like 'the hopeful one,' here too, the exclusive sense should be understood. Among these, apart from mindfulness of breathing and mindfulness of the body, the remaining eight recollections—such as recollection of the Buddha—the perception of repulsiveness in food, and the analysis of the four elements, these ten are called 'access-bringing' because of their diverse nature, profundity, and their character as intrinsic phenomena, in the absence of a special development of the practice.

817-8. Evaṃ upacārappanāvahato dassetvā idāni jhānappabhedato dassetuṃ “appanāyāvahesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Catukkajjhānikāti catukkanayavasena catubbidharūpāvacarajjhānavanto, tesaṃ ekekasseva ārammaṇabhūtāti attho. Pañcakanayavasena pana “pañcakajjhānikā”ti veditabbā. Paṭhamajjhānikāti paṭhamajjhānasseva ārammaṇabhūtā, paṭikkūlabhāvato pana itaresaṃ ārammaṇāni na honti. Paṭikkūlepi hi visaye vitakkabalena paṭhamajjhānaṃ appeti caṇḍasotanadiyaṃ arittabalena nāvā viya. Sesāni pana tadabhāvato na tesu appenti.

817-8. Having thus shown them from the perspective of bringing access and absorption, now to show them from the perspective of the distinction of jhāna, it is said, “Among those that bring absorption,” and so on. 'Pertaining to the four jhānas' means that they are objects for the four types of form-sphere jhānas according to the fourfold method; this is the meaning. According to the fivefold method, however, they should be understood as 'pertaining to the five jhānas.' 'Pertaining to the first jhāna' means they serve as objects only for the first jhāna. Due to their repulsive nature, they do not serve as objects for the other jhānas. For even with a repulsive object, the first jhāna reaches absorption through the power of applied thought, like a boat in a swift-flowing river by the power of an oar. The remaining jhānas, however, due to the absence of that, do not reach absorption in those objects.

819. Tikajjhānavahāti [M 2.0222] catukkanayena tikajjhānavahā, pañcakanayena pana catukkajjhānavahā, mettākaruṇāmuditā hi mettādīnaṃ somanassasahagatānameva ārammaṇattā pañcamajjhānikā na honti. Appanappattā hi mettādayo somanassena vinā nappavattanti. Catutthopi brahmavihāroti sambandho. Brahmānaṃ uttamānaṃ vihāro, brahmabhūto vā vihāroti brahmavihāro, so upekkhābhāvanāvasena catutthajjhāniko. Tatthāpi mettādivasena paṭiladdhajjhānacatukkassevetaṃ appeti, netarassa. Kasmā? Mettādīnaṃ nissandattā. Yathā hi kasiṇānaṃ nissandā āruppā, yathā ca samathavipassanānissandā nirodhasamāpatti, evaṃ mettādinissandā upekkhā. Āruppā catutthajjhānikāti aṅgasamatāvasena āruppāpi catutthajjhānasseva pabhedāti katvā vuttaṃ.

819. 'Bringing the three jhānas' means that according to the fourfold method, they bring three jhānas, but according to the fivefold method, they bring four jhānas. For loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, since they have as their objects only those accompanied by joy, are not 'pertaining to the fifth jhāna.' Indeed, loving-kindness and so on, having reached absorption, do not proceed without joy. The connection is also with the fourth divine abode. A divine abode is the dwelling of supreme Brahmās, or a dwelling that has become sublime; this is a divine abode. And this, by way of the development of equanimity, pertains to the fourth jhāna. Here too, it leads to absorption only for one who has obtained the four jhānas by way of loving-kindness and so on, not for another. Why? Because it is the outflow of loving-kindness and so on. Just as the formless attainments are the outflow of the kasiṇas, and just as the attainment of cessation is the outflow of serenity and insight, so too is equanimity the outflow of loving-kindness and so on. The statement 'the formless attainments pertain to the fourth jhāna' is made because, due to the equality of their factors, the formless attainments are considered a subdivision of the fourth jhāna.

820. Evaṃ jhānabhedato dassetvā puna samatikkamato dassetuṃ “vasenārammaṇaṅgāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ārammaṇasamatikkamo aṅgasamatikkamoti atikkamitabbānaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ, aṅgānañca vasena samatikkamo duvidho. Kiṃ sabbesveva duvidho labbhati, noti āha “gocarā…pe… tikkamo”ti. Catūsu hi āruppesu ārammaṇasamatikkamova hoti ākāsakasiṇavajjitesu navasu ārammaṇesu aññataraṃ samatikkamitvā [V 2.0167] ākāsānañcāyatanassa, ākāsānañcāyatanādīni ca samatikkamitvā viññāṇañcāyatanādīnaṃ pattabbattā, aṅgātikkamo pana arūpe natthi catunnañcāpi aṅgānaṃ vasena samānattā. Rūpe jhānaṅgatikkamoti rūpāvacarikakammaṭṭhānesu vitakkādīnaṃ jhānaṅgānaṃ atikkamo, idañca labbhamānakavasena vuttaṃ. Paṭhamajjhānikesu duvidhopi samatikkamo natthi, nīvaraṇasamatikkamo idha aṭṭhannampi samāpattīnaṃ sādhāraṇattā na gahito.

820. Having thus shown them from the perspective of the distinction of jhānas, to show them again from the perspective of surpassing, it is said, “by way of the object and the factors,” and so on. The surpassing of the object and the surpassing of the factors—thus, the surpassing by way of the objects to be surpassed and the factors is twofold. Is this twofold surpassing obtained in all cases? No, it is said, “in the sphere... surpassing.” For in the four formless attainments, there is only the surpassing of the object. This is because the base of infinite space is to be attained by surpassing one of the nine objects excluding the space kasiṇa, and the base of infinite consciousness and so on are to be attained by surpassing the base of infinite space and so on. But there is no surpassing of factors in the formless realm, due to the sameness of their four factors. 'The surpassing of jhāna factors in the form realm' is the surpassing of the jhāna factors such as applied thought and so on, in the form-sphere meditation subjects. And this is said by way of what is attainable. In the meditation subjects pertaining to the first jhāna, neither type of surpassing exists. The surpassing of the hindrances is not taken up here because it is common to all eight attainments.

821. Evaṃ [M 2.0223] samatikkamavasena dassetvā puna vaḍḍhanāvaḍḍhanavasena dassetuṃ “daseva kasiṇānī”tiādimāha. Imesu cattālīsāya kammaṭṭhānesu dasa kasiṇāneva vaḍḍhetabbāni. Na ca…pe… asubhādayoti sesā asubhādayo pana neva vaḍḍhetabbā. Kasmā? Paricchinnākāreneva upaṭṭhānato, ānisaṃsābhāvato ca. Tathā hi dasa asubhāni, kāyagatāsati ca attano ṭhitokāsena paricchinnattā paricchinnākāreneva upaṭṭhahanti. Vaḍḍhitesupi kuṇaparāsi eva upaṭṭhātīti na koci ānisaṃso atthi. Avaḍḍhitesupi hi tesu kāmarāgavikkhambhanā hotiyeva. Yadi evaṃ, asubhajjhānānaṃ appamāṇārammaṇatāvacanaṃ virujjhatīti? Na virujjhati. Ekacco hi uddhumātake vā aṭṭhike vā mahante nimittaṃ gaṇhāti, ekacco appaketi iminā pariyāyena ekaccassa parittārammaṇajjhānaṃ hoti, ekaccassa appamāṇārammaṇaṃ. Yo vā etaṃ ānisaṃsābhāvaṃ apassanto vaḍḍheyya, tassa vasena appamāṇārammaṇatā vuttā. Ānāpānanimittampi nāsikaggamukhanimittādiparicchinnaṃ upaṭṭhāti, vaḍḍhayatopi ca vātarāsiyeva vaḍḍhati. Picupiṇḍādivasena upaṭṭhahantampi hi nimittaṃ vātasaṅghāṭamattameva, tathā brahmavihāranimittampi vaḍḍhentassa sattarāsiyeva vaḍḍheyya, na ca tena koci attho hoti, tasmā tadubhayampi na vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādi (vibha. 663), tampi pariggahavasena vuttaṃ, na nimittavaḍḍhanavasena. Kiñci brahmavihāre paṭibhāganimittameva natthi, kimayaṃ vaḍḍheyya, appamāṇārammaṇatā panettha pariggahitamattavasena veditabbā. Āruppārammaṇesu ākāsaṃ kasiṇugghāṭamattattā kasiṇāpagamavaseneva manasi kātabbaṃ, tato paraṃ vaḍḍhayato na kiñci hoti, viññāṇaṃ sabhāvadhammattā na sakkā [M 2.0224] vaḍḍhetuṃ, parikammameva hi vaḍḍhetuṃ sakkā, viññāṇāpagamo tassa abhāvamattattā, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanārammaṇampi sabhāvadhammattāyeva na sakkā vaḍḍhetuṃ, tasmā tānipi na vaḍḍhetabbāni. Appamāṇārammaṇatā āruppānaṃ vipulakasiṇugghāṭimākāse pavattiyā veditabbā. Buddhānussatiādayo ca animittattā na vaḍḍhetabbā[V 2.0168]. Paṭibhāganimittañhi ayaṃ vaḍḍheyya, tañca nesaṃ natthi, tasmā ime asubhādayo tiṃsa kammaṭṭhānāni paricchinnokāsattā, payojanābhāvato, avaḍḍhanato ca na vaḍḍhetabbāni.

821. Having thus shown it by way of transcending, he then explains it by way of expanding and not expanding, saying, 'Only the ten kasiṇas,' and so on. Among these forty meditation subjects, only the ten kasiṇas should be expanded. And not... the foulness meditations, etc.; the remaining foulness meditations, etc., however, should not be expanded. Why? Because they appear with a limited form and because there is no benefit. For instance, the ten foulness meditations and mindfulness of the body appear with a limited form due to their confined location. Even if one expands them, only a heap of corpses appears—there is no benefit. Even without expanding them, the suppression of sensual desire still occurs. If this is so, does it contradict the statement that the foulness jhānas have an immeasurable object? It does not. Some take a large sign from a bloated corpse or a skeleton, while others take a small one. Thus, in this way, for some, the jhāna has a limited object, while for others, it has an immeasurable object. Or, for one who expands it without seeing this lack of benefit, the immeasurability of the object is spoken of in reference to him. The sign of breathing also appears limited, such as at the tip of the nose or the mouth. Even if one expands it, only a mass of air increases. For even if the sign appears as a lump of cotton or the like, it is merely an aggregate of air. Likewise, if one expands the sign of the divine abodes, only a mass of beings increases, but there is no benefit in doing so. Therefore, both should not be expanded. As for what is said, 'With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, one dwells pervading one direction,' etc. (Vb. 663), this is stated in terms of encompassing, not in terms of expanding the sign. Moreover, in the divine abodes, there is no counterpart sign at all—what would one expand? The immeasurability of the object here should be understood merely in terms of encompassing. Among the objects of the formless attainments, space—since it is merely the removal of the kasiṇa—should be attended to by way of the kasiṇa's removal. Beyond that, expanding it yields nothing. Consciousness, being a natural phenomenon, cannot be expanded—only the preliminary meditation can be expanded. The passing away of consciousness is merely its absence. The object of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, being a natural phenomenon, also cannot be expanded. Therefore, these too should not be expanded. The immeasurability of the objects of the formless attainments should be understood as their occurring in the space made vast by the removal of the kasiṇa. The recollection of the Buddha and the others, being signless, should not be expanded. For one would expand the counterpart sign, but they lack it. Thus, these thirty meditation subjects—the foulness meditations and the rest—should not be expanded due to their confined location, lack of purpose, and because they are not for expansion.

822-3. Evaṃ vaḍḍhanāvaḍḍhanato dassetvā puna ārammaṇato dassetuṃ “daseva kasiṇānī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Paṭibhāganimittāni honti ārammaṇānīti imāni dvāvīsa paṭibhāganimittabhūtāni ārammaṇāni honti. Sesāti avasesā aṭṭhārasa neva paṭibhāganimittārammaṇā siyuṃ.

822-3. Having thus shown it by way of expanding and not expanding, the passage beginning 'Only the ten kasiṇas' was commenced to show it again by way of the object. The counterpart signs are objects. Thus, these twenty-two are objects that are counterpart signs. The remaining eighteen are not objects that are counterpart signs.

824-5. Idāni bhūmito dassetuṃ “asubhānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Devesu nappavattanti tattha asubhānaṃ, paṭikkūlassa ca āhārassa abhāvato. Tacapañcakampi hi tattha pavattamānaṃ dibbānubhāvena paṭikkūlākārena nopaṭṭhāti. Assāsapassāsānaṃ brahmaloke abhāvato “ānāpānassati cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Jhānānubhāvanibbattānañhi atthassa abhāvato natthi brahmaloke assāsapassāsā.

824-5. Now, to show it by way of the plane of existence, the passage beginning 'The foulness meditations' was stated. The foulness meditations do not occur among the devas because of the absence there of the foul and of repulsive food. For even the five parts ending with skin, though present there, do not appear in a repulsive aspect due to divine power. Since there is no in-and-out breathing in the Brahmā world, the passage beginning 'And mindfulness of breathing' was stated. For in the Brahmā world, there is no in-and-out breathing because there is no need for them, they being produced by the power of jhāna.

827. Idāni gahaṇato dassetuṃ “catuttha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha catutthaṃ…pe… diṭṭheneva gahetabbāti vāyokasiṇaṃ vajjetvā sesā nava kasiṇā, dasa asubhānīti imāni [M 2.0225] ekūnavīsati diṭṭheneva vatthunā karaṇabhūtena gahetabbāni uggahetabbāni. Tathā ca vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “diṭṭhena gahetabbāni, pubbabhāge cakkhunā oloketvā nimittaṃ nesaṃ gahetabbanti attho”ti (visuddhi. 1.47).

827. Now, to show it by way of grasping, the passage beginning 'The fourth' was stated. There, the fourth (and so on) should be taken by sight alone—excluding the air kasiṇa, the remaining nine kasiṇas and the ten foulness meditations: these nineteen should be taken and apprehended by means of the visible object as the instrument. Thus, it is said in the commentary: 'They should be taken by sight; in the preliminary stage, having looked at them with the eye, their sign should be taken—this is the meaning' (Visuddhi. 1.47).

828-31. Satiyampi ca kāyamhīti kāyagatāsatiyampi. Diṭṭhena tacapañcakanti tacapañcakamattameva diṭṭhena gahetabbaṃ. Sesamettha sutenevāti ettha kāyagatāsatiyaṃ sesaṃ vakkapañcakādi suteneva gahetabbaṃ. Iti kāyagatāsati diṭṭhasutena gahetabbā. Uttaroṭṭhanāsikaggesu phuṭṭhassa assāsapassāsassa gahetabbato vuttaṃ “ānāpānassati ettha, phuṭṭhena paridīpitā”ti. Ucchusassādīnaṃ pattesu calamānavaṇṇaggahaṇamukhena, sarīrasamphassavasena ca vātassa gahetabbattā vuttaṃ “vāyokasiṇamevettha, diṭṭhaphuṭṭhena gayhatī”ti. Āditova gahetabbā na hontītiādikammikena bhāvanārambhavasena na paṭṭhapetabbāni, heṭṭhime tayo brahmavihāre, kasiṇesu rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānañca anadhigantvā sampādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā.

828-31. And 'in the body, with mindfulness' means in mindfulness directed to the body. 'By sight, the five parts ending with skin' means only the five parts ending with skin should be taken by sight. 'The remainder here by hearing' means that in mindfulness directed to the body, the remainder, such as the five parts beginning with the kidneys, should be taken only by hearing. Thus, mindfulness directed to the body should be taken by sight and hearing. Because the in-and-out breath that touches the upper lip or the tip of the nose is to be taken, it is said, 'Mindfulness of breathing here is clarified by contact.' Because the wind is to be taken by way of grasping the appearance of the movement in the leaves of sugarcane and so on, and by way of bodily contact, it is said, 'The air kasiṇa here is taken by sight and contact.' 'They are not to be taken from the very beginning' means they should not be established by a beginner at the start of the development, because it is impossible to accomplish them without having first attained the lower three divine abodes and the fourth form-realm jhāna among the kasiṇas.

832-5. Evaṃ [V 2.0169] gahaṇavasena dassetvā idāni paccayato dassetuṃ “kammaṭṭhānesu hetesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha etesu kammaṭṭhānesūti ettha yathārahaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ, jhānānañca gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ākāsakasiṇassa ugghāṭetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā vuttaṃ “ākāsakasiṇaṃ vinā”ti. Mettādiekekasmiṃ brahmavihāre tīṇi tīṇi jhānāni paṭilabhitvā ṭhitasseva upekkhābrahmavihāravasena pañcamajjhānaṃ uppajjatīti vuttaṃ “tayo brahmavihārā”tiādi. Dvinnaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanajavanānaṃ samanantarā nirodhaṃ phusatīti katvā vuttaṃ “catutthamāruppa”ntiādi. Vipassanābhavasampattisukhānaṃ [M 2.0226] paccayāti vipassanāya, bhavasampattiyā, diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārassa ca paccayā hontīti attho.

832-5. Having thus shown it by way of grasping, now to show it by way of conditions, the passage beginning 'Among these meditation subjects' was stated. Here, in 'among these meditation subjects,' the grasping of the objects and the jhānas should be understood as is appropriate. Because the space kasiṇa cannot be removed, it is said, 'except for the space kasiṇa.' Because the fifth jhāna arises by way of the divine abode of equanimity only for one who stands having attained three jhānas in each of the divine abodes such as loving-kindness, it is said, 'the three divine abodes,' etc. Because one touches cessation immediately after two javanas of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is said, 'the fourth formless attainment,' etc. 'As conditions for insight, attainment of existence, and happiness' means they are conditions for insight, for the attainment of existence, and for abiding in bliss in this very life.

836-9. Evaṃ pasaṅgena āgataṃ kammaṭṭhānavibhāgaṃ dassetvā puna ācariyena paṭipajjitabbavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Santike vasantassāti ācariyena saddhiṃ ekagehe, ekavihāre vā vasantassa. Kathetabbanti pavattiṃ sutvā sutvā kathetabbaṃ. Āgatassāgatakkhaṇeti sa-kāro padasandhimattakaro, āgatāgatakkhaṇeti attho. Atha vā āgatassa āgatakkhaṇe kathetabbaṃ. Īdisesu hi ṭhānesu āmeḍitasāmatthiyatova labbhati. Na hi ekavārameva āgatassa tasmiṃ khaṇe kathetabbaṃ, tato paraṃ na kathetabbanti yujjati.

836-9. Having thus shown the classification of meditation subjects by way of incidental mention, now, to show the method to be followed by the teacher, the passage beginning 'Having taken up a meditation subject' was stated. For one dwelling nearby: this means for one dwelling in the same house or monastery with the teacher. It should be spoken of: this means it should be spoken of repeatedly after hearing the progress. At the moment of arrival: the 'sa-' here merely facilitates the joining of words, meaning 'at each moment of arrival.' Alternatively, it should be spoken of at the moment of arrival. For in such cases, it is obtained only by the power of repetition. For it is not reasonable to say that it should be spoken of only once at the moment of arrival and not afterward.

Nātisaṅkhepavitthāranti atisaṃkhittaṃ, ativitthārañca akatvā tassa sukhena uggaṇhanappamāṇaṃ kathetabbaṃ. Sace pana so pakatiyāva uggahitakammaṭṭhāno hoti, sajjhāyavasena vā manasikāravasena vā kataparicayo, tassa ekaṃ, dve vā nisajjā attano sammukhāva sajjhāyaṃ kāretvā dātabbaṃ. Evaṃ ācariyena paṭipajjitabbavidhiṃ dassetvā puna gahitakammaṭṭhānena tena yoginā uttari kātabbavidhānaṃ dassento āha “tenapī”tiādi. Sammaṭṭhānanti yattha pahaṭo samati, taṃ sammaṭṭhānaṃ, idaṃ sammaṭṭhānaṃ viyāti sammaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā hi sammaṭṭhāne gahite puggalaṃ attano verī abhibhavituṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ kammaṭṭhāne gahite manobhusaṅkhāto kāmarāgo taṃsamaṅgipuggalaṃ abhibhavitvā attano vase kātuṃ na sakkoti[M 2.0227]. Tena vuttaṃ “sammaṭṭhānaṃ viyāti sammaṭṭhāna”nti. Mano abhibhavatīti manobhū, tassa manobhuno. Aṭṭhārasahi…pe… vivajjiteti –

Not too brief or too detailed: this means it should be explained to the extent that it can be easily learned, without being overly condensed or overly elaborate. However, if that person has naturally already grasped the meditation subject, or is familiar with it through recitation or mental attention, then after one or two sittings, it should be given to him after having him recite it in one's own presence. Having thus shown the method to be followed by the teacher, now, to show the further procedure to be undertaken by the meditator with the grasped meditation subject, he said the passage beginning 'By him also.' A stronghold (sammaṭṭhāna): that place where one is struck and stands firm, that is a stronghold. It is a stronghold in the sense of 'like a stronghold.' Just as when a stronghold is secured, one's enemy cannot overcome a person, so too when a meditation subject is grasped, sensual desire, which is called 'mind-born,' cannot overcome that person who possesses it and bring him under its control. Therefore, it is said, 'It is a stronghold in the sense of being like a stronghold.' 'Mind-overcoming' (mano abhibhavatīti) means 'mind-born' (manobhū), and 'of that mind-born' (tassa manobhuno). By the eighteen... should be avoided:

“Mahāvāsaṃ [V 2.0170] navāvāsaṃ, jarāvāsañca panthaniṃ;

Soṇḍiṃ paṇṇañca pupphañca, phalaṃ patthitameva ca.

A large dwelling, a new dwelling, an old dwelling, and a roadside one; one with a pond, and with leaves, and flowers, and fruits, and that which is sought after.

“Nagaraṃ dārunā khettaṃ, visabhāgena paṭṭanaṃ;

Paccantasīmāsappāyaṃ, yattha mitto na labbhati.

A town, a place with timber, a field, a port with incompatible people; a border region, an unsuitable place, and where a friend is not found.

“Aṭṭhārasetāni ṭhānāni, iti viññāya paṇḍito;

Ārakā parivajjeyya, maggaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ yathā”ti. (visuddhi. 1.52) –

Knowing these eighteen places, the wise person should avoid them from afar, just as one avoids a perilous path.

Evaṃ vuttehi aṭṭhārasahi vihāradosehi sabbakālaviyutte. Anurūpeti imesu aṭṭhārasasu dosesu aññatarenapi samannāgato ananurūpo nāma, tadabhāvena attano yogakammassa anukūle. Mahāvihārādayo hi yogakammassa anukūlā na honti, tasmā mahāvihāre tāva vattakaraṇādinā palibodho hoti. Yattha pana sabbaṃ katameva, avasesāpi saṅghaṭṭanā natthi, evarūpo mahāvihāropi anurūpova. Navavihāre bahuṃ navakammaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti, tasmā so asati aññasmiṃ anukūle kāraṇe ananurūpo hoti. Tathā jiṇṇavihāropi bahupaṭijaggitabbatāya kammaṭṭhānantarāyiko. Panthanissitako āgantukehi rattindivaṃ samokiṇṇatāya. Yattha soṇḍī nāma pāsāṇapokkharaṇī hoti, so soṇḍivihāro. Tattha bahū pānīyatthāya samosaranti, tathā paṇṇapupphaphalavati vihāre taṃtadatthāya. Patthanīye lokasammate vihāre viharantaṃ “arahā”ti sambhāventā bahū āgacchanti. Nagarasannissitepi vihāre visabhāgārammaṇāpāthagamanādīni honti. Dārusannissite kaṭṭhahārikādīhi [M 2.0228] aphāsu hoti. Khettasannissite vihāramajjheyeva khalamaṇḍalakaraṇādinā aphāsu hoti. Visabhāgapuggalādhivutthepi kalahanivāraṇādīsu te upavadanti. Paṭṭanasannissite abhiṇhaṃ nāvāsatthehi āgatamanussehi aphāsu hoti. Paccantanissite manussā buddhādīsu appasannā honti. Rajjasīmasannissite dvinnaṃ rājūnaṃ kalahe sati dvinnaṃ vijitesu piṇḍāya vicarantaṃ bhikkhuṃ “ayaṃ carapuriso”ti gahetvā bandhanādikaṃ pāpeyyuṃ, asappāye amanussādiupaddavā honti. Kalyāṇamittānadhivutthe uppannakaṅkhāya vinodake asati mahādosoyevāti etepi vihārā ananurūpā, tasmā tādise vihāre parivajjetvā vuttadosavirahite anurūpe vihāre vihātabbaṃ.

When it is entirely free from these eighteen faults of a dwelling just stated, it is suitable. If it is endowed with even one of these eighteen faults, it is called unsuitable; by the absence of these, it is conducive to one's meditation practice. Indeed, great monasteries and the like are not conducive to meditation practice, because in a great monastery, there are obstacles such as the performance of duties. However, if everything is already done and there is no remaining disturbance from crowds, even such a great monastery is suitable. In a new monastery, much new construction work must be done; therefore, if there is no other conducive reason, it is unsuitable. Similarly, an old monastery is an obstacle to the meditation subject because it requires much maintenance. A roadside dwelling is unsuitable because it is crowded day and night with visitors. Where there is a stone pond called a soṇḍī, that is a soṇḍī monastery. Many people gather there for water. Likewise, in a monastery abundant with leaves, flowers, and fruits, people gather for those very things. In a monastery that is desirable and esteemed by the world, many visitors come, supposing the resident to be an Arahant. Even in a monastery near a city, there is coming into range of unsuitable objects and so on. A monastery near timber is inconvenient due to wood-gatherers and others. A monastery near fields is inconvenient due to activities like making threshing floors right in the middle of the monastery. Even in a monastery inhabited by incompatible individuals, they find fault when one tries to prevent disputes and so on. A monastery near a port is frequently inconvenient due to people arriving on ships for trade. In a monastery in a border region, people have little faith in the Buddha and so on. In a monastery near a kingdom’s border, if two kings quarrel, they may seize a monk wandering for alms in their respective territories, thinking, 'This is a spy,' and inflict imprisonment or worse. In unsuitable places, there are dangers from non-human beings and so on. A monastery not inhabited by good friends is a great fault, as there is no one to dispel arising doubts. Therefore, these monasteries are unsuitable. One should avoid such monasteries and dwell in a suitable monastery free from the aforementioned faults.

Tassa [V 2.0171] pana vihārassa anurūpabhāvo evaṃ veditabboti dassetuṃ “gāmato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gāmatoti gocaragāmato. Nātidūreti gocaragāmassa aḍḍhagāvutato orabhāgatāya na atidūre. Naccāsanneti pacchimena pamāṇena gocaragāmato pañcadhanusatikatāya na atisanne. Iminā gamanāgamanasampannataṃ dasseti. Gocaragāmassa pana uttaradisāya vā dakkhiṇadisāya vā nātidūraṃ naccāsannaṃ senāsanaṃ visesena gamanāgamanasampannaṃ hoti, nātidūranaccāsannatā cettha nidassanamattaṃ. Pañcaṅgasaṃyuteti pana vuttattā nātidūranaccāsannatāya saha divā appakiṇṇatādīni cattāri samodhānetvā pañcaṅgasaṃyuttatā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

To show that the suitability of that monastery should be understood in this way, the passage beginning 'from the village' was stated. 'From the village' means from the alms-round village. 'Not too far' means not excessively distant, being on this side of half a gāvuta from the alms-round village. 'Not too close' means not excessively near, being five hundred bow-lengths from the alms-round village by the final measure. This indicates that it is suitable for coming and going. A lodging that is neither too far nor too close to the alms-round village, whether to the north or the south, is especially suitable for coming and going. Here, 'not too far' and 'not too close' are merely an illustration. However, since it is stated to be 'endowed with five factors,' the endowment with five factors should be understood by combining the quality of being neither too far nor too close with the four qualities beginning with being uncrowded during the day. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ nātidūraṃ hoti naccāsannaṃ gamanāgamanasampannaṃ divā appakiṇṇaṃ rattiṃ [M 2.0229] appasaddaṃ appanigghosaṃ appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassaṃ, tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane viharantassa appakasireneva uppajjanti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārā, tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane therā bhikkhū viharanti bahussutā āgatāgamā dhammadharā vinayadharā mātikādharā, te kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paripucchati pañhaṃ ‘idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ; imassa ko atthoti. Tassa te āyasmanto avivaṭañceva vivaranti, anuttānīkatañca uttāniṃ karonti, anekavihitesu ca kaṅkhāṭṭhāniyesu dhammesu kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 10.11).

And how, monks, is a lodging endowed with five factors? Here, monks, a lodging is not too far nor too near, suitable for coming and going; by day it is uncrowded, by night it is quiet and with little noise; it has little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. While dwelling in that lodging, robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick arise for one with little difficulty. Moreover, in that lodging, elder monks dwell—learned, versed in the traditions, holders of the Dhamma, holders of the Vinaya, holders of the Mātikās. From time to time, one approaches and questions them: ‘How is this, venerable sirs? What is the meaning of this?’ Then those venerable ones reveal what has not been revealed, make plain what has not been made plain, and dispel doubt regarding various matters that are grounds for doubt. Thus, monks, a lodging is endowed with five factors.

Ettha ca nātidūranaccāsannabhāvena gamanāgamanasampannatā paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ, divā mahājanasaṃkiṇṇatābhāvena, rattiyaṃ janālāpasaddābhāvena, sabbadāpi janasannipātanigghosābhāvena appakiṇṇaappasaddaappanigghosabhāvo dutiyaṃ, ḍaṃsamakasādiparissayābhāvo tatiyaṃ, appakasirena cīvarapiṇḍapātādipaccayalābho catutthaṃ, bahussutatādiguṇasamannāgatānaṃ therānaṃ vasanabhāvo pañcamanti imehi pañcahi aṅgehi saṃyutte samannāgate vihārasmiṃ vihātabbaṃ.

Here, suitability for coming and going by virtue of being neither too far nor too near is the first factor. The state of being uncrowded, quiet, and with little noise—by virtue of being uncrowded by many people during the day, free from the sound of people's talk at night, and always free from the clamor of people's gatherings—is the second. The absence of dangers such as gadflies and mosquitoes is the third. Obtaining requisites such as robes and almsfood with little difficulty is the fourth. The fact that elders endowed with qualities such as being well-learned are dwelling there is the fifth. One should dwell in a monastery that is endowed with and possessed of these five factors.

840-1. Paṭhamaṃ vuttaāvāsādimahāpalibodhe upādāya khuddakapalibodho, idāni taṃ palibodhaṃ sarūpato dassetvā tassa upacchindanākāraṃ āvi kātuṃ “dīghā kesā”tiādi vuttaṃ. So patto suṭṭhu pacitabboti yojanā.

840-1. The minor obstacles are mentioned in relation to the great obstacles beginning with residence, which were mentioned first. Now, to show that obstacle in its true form and to make clear the way to cut it off, the passage beginning 'long hair' is stated. The construction is: 'That bowl should be well fired.'

842-5. Pavivitteti [V 2.0172] janavivitte okāse. Vajjetvā…pe… lohitanti ime cattāro kasiṇadosā, tasmā [M 2.0230] evarūpā mattikā vajjetvā. Saṇhāyāti apanītatiṇamūlasakkharavālukāya sumadditāya sukhumāya. Aruṇavaṇṇāyāti aruṇanibhāya, aruṇavaṇṇappabhāyāti attho. Bahiddhā vāpi tādiseti bahiddhāpi vihārapaccante paṭicchannaṭṭhāne. Saṃhārimanti saṃharitabbaṃ gahetvā caraṇayogyaṃ. Tatraṭṭhakanti yattha kataṃ, tattheva tiṭṭhanakaṃ.

"Secluded" means in a place remote from people. "Avoiding... blood"—these are the four faults of the kasiṇa; therefore, such clay should be avoided. "Smooth" means free from grass, roots, gravel, and sand, well-kneaded, and fine. "Of dawn color" means resembling the hue of dawn; the meaning is having the radiance of dawn color. "Even outside" means even in a concealed place outside the monastery enclosure. "Portable" means it should be collected and is suitable for carrying. "Fixed in place" means remaining right where it was made.

847-50. Pamāṇatoti vakkhamānappamāṇato. Vaṭṭaṃ ākoṭetvāti parimaṇḍalaṃ katvā ākoṭetvā. Tanti taṃ cammaṃ vā kaṭasāraṃ vā dussapaṭṭaṃ vā. Kaṇṇikanti kaṇṇikāsadisaṃ, parimaṇḍalato padumakaṇṇikākāranti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “sama”nti. “Kaṇṇikāsama”nti vā pāṭho. Vidatthicaturaṅgulanti caturaṅgulādhikavidatthippamāṇaṃ. Etadeva hi pamāṇaṃ sandhāya aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “suppamatte vā sarāvamatte vā”ti (visuddhi. 1.55) vuttaṃ. Vivaṭṭanti nibbānaṃ. Kasiṇaparikammaṃ karontopi hi ettakeyeva aṭṭhatvā nibbānatthāyeva vāyamati. Bherītalasamaṃ katvāti pāṇikāya ghaṃsetvā ninnatunnataṭṭhānābhāvena bherītalaṃ viya samaṃ katvā. Sammajjitvāna taṃ ṭhānanti yasmiṃ ṭhāne nisīditvā taṃ kasiṇaṃ oloketi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ sace uklāpaṃ hoti, sammajjitvā. Nhatvāti sarīradarathavinodanatthaṃ nhatvā.

"According to measure" means according to the measure about to be described. "Beating into a circle" means making it round by beating it. "That" refers to the leather, mat of reeds, or cloth. "Like the pericarp of a lotus" means resembling the pericarp of a lotus; it is said to be shaped like the pericarp of a lotus. Hence it is called "even." Alternatively, the reading is "like the pericarp of a lotus." "Four fingers beyond a span" means a span plus four fingers in measure. This is indeed the measure referred to in the commentary as "of the size of a winnowing basket or a bowl" (Visuddhimagga 1.55). "Turning away" means Nibbāna. Even while performing the kasiṇa preparation, one confines oneself to just that and strives for the sake of Nibbāna. "Making it level like a drumhead" means smoothing it with a trowel to make it even like a drumhead, without depressions or elevations. "Having swept that place" means if the place where one sits to observe the kasiṇa is covered with rubbish, it should be swept. "Having bathed" means bathing to remove bodily weariness.

851-2. Tamhā kasiṇamaṇḍalā hatthapāsappamāṇasmiṃ padeseti tamhā kasiṇamaṇḍalassa, ṭhapitaṭṭhānamhā aḍḍhateyyahatthantare padese, kasiṇamaṇḍalassa, pīṭhassa ca majjhaṃ hatthapāsappamāṇaṃ katvā paññatteti vuttaṃ hoti. Vidatthicaturaṅgule ucceti vidatthicaturaṅgulaṃ hutvā ucce, vidatthicaturaṅgulapādaketi vuttaṃ hoti. Dūre nisinnassa hi kasiṇaṃ na [M 2.0231] upaṭṭhāti, āsannatare nisinnassa hatthapāṇikāpadādayo kasiṇadosā paññāyanti. Uccatare nisinnena ca gīvaṃ paṇāmetvā oloketabbaṃ hoti, nīcatare jaṇṇukāni rujjanti, tasmā hatthapāsappamāṇe padese vidatthicaturaṅgulapādake pīṭhe nisīditabbaṃ. Yasmā catūsu iriyāpathesu sayanaṃ kosajjapakkhiyaṃ, ṭhānacaṅkamanāni uddhaccapakkhiyāni, nisajjā pana alīnuddhaccapakkhiyā, santo iriyāpatho, tasmā vuttaṃ “nisīditvā”ti, samantato ūrubaddhāsanaṃ pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvāti attho. Yenākārena nisīdantassa nisajjā sukhā hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyā”ti. Uparimaṃ sarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā aṭṭhārasapiṭṭhikaṇṭake koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādetvāti attho. Evañhi nisinnassa cammamaṃsanahārūni na oṇamanti, athassa yā tesaṃ oṇamanapaccayā khaṇe khaṇe [V 2.0173] vedanā uppajjeyyuṃ, tā na uppajjanti. Tāsu anuppannāsu cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ na paripatati. Tato ca pubbenāparaṃ visesappattiyā vuddhiṃ phātiṃ upagacchati. Idāni ārammaṇapariggahupāyaṃ dassento āha “katvā parimukhaṃ sati”nti, kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ satiṃ ṭhapetvāti attho. Abhi-saddena hi samānattho idha pari-saddo, atha vā samīpatthena pari-saddena mukhassa samīpe satiṃ katvāti attho. Yathāha – “ayaṃ sati upaṭṭhitā hoti supaṭṭhitā nāsikagge vā mukhanimitte vā. Tena vuccati parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti (vibha. 537). Atha vā “parīti pariggahaṭṭho, mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho, satīti upaṭṭhānaṭṭho. Tena vuccati ‘parimukhaṃ sati”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.164) vacanato “pariṇāyikā”tiādīsu viya pari-saddo pariggahaṭṭho, “suññatavimokkhamukha”ntiādīsu viya mukha-saddo niyyānaṭṭhoti katvā pariggahitaniyyānasatiṃ katvā sabbathā gahitāsammosaṃ [M 2.0232] pariccattasammosaṃ satinepakkaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

"From that kasiṇa circle, in a place at a distance of a hand's reach" means: from the established position of the kasiṇa circle, in a place at a distance of two and a half cubits; it is said that the space between the kasiṇa circle and the seat is prepared with the measure of a hand's reach. "High by a span and four fingers" means: being high by a span and four fingers; it is said that the seat has legs a span and four fingers high. For one sitting too far away, the kasiṇa does not appear clearly. For one sitting too close, flaws in the kasiṇa, such as the appearance of one's hand, palm, or foot, become evident. If one sits too high, one must bend the neck to look down, and if too low, the knees ache. Therefore, one should sit on a seat at a distance of a hand's reach, with legs a span and four fingers high. Among the four postures, lying down is associated with laziness, while standing and walking are associated with restlessness. Sitting, however, is free from both laziness and restlessness—a peaceful posture. Hence, it is said, "having sat down." The meaning is: having folded the legs into the lotus posture, binding the thighs firmly. To indicate the posture in which sitting is comfortable, it is said, "setting the body upright." The upper body should be kept straight, aligning the eighteen spinal bones one after another. For one sitting thus, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not sag. If they were to sag, momentary pains would arise, but since they do not, the mind becomes unified, and the meditation subject does not falter. Moreover, through successive distinctions, it grows and flourishes. Now, to explain the method of grasping the object, it is said: "having established mindfulness in front." The meaning is: setting mindfulness facing the meditation subject. Here, the prefix "pari-" conveys the same meaning as "abhi-" or, alternatively, "pari-" in the sense of proximity—establishing mindfulness near the face. As it is said: "This mindfulness is well-established at the tip of the nose or the sign of the mouth. Therefore, it is called 'establishing mindfulness in front.'" Or, as stated in another text: "'Pari' signifies grasping, 'mukha' signifies the means of deliverance, and 'sati' signifies establishment. Hence, it is called 'parimukhaṃ sati.'" Just as in "pariṇāyikā," the prefix "pari" conveys the sense of grasping, and in phrases such as "suññatavimokkhamukha," "mukha" signifies the means of deliverance—thus, it is said that one establishes mindfulness that is grasped as a means of deliverance, and which is completely unconfused and free from forgetfulness, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.

853-5. Kāmesvādīnavaṃ disvāti “kāmā nāmete aṭṭhikaṅkhalikūpamā nirassādaṭṭhenā”tiādinā vatthukāmakilesakāmesu ādīnavaṃ paccavekkhitvā. Nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khematoti nekkhammaṃ khemato disvā kāmanissaraṇaṃ sabbadukkhasamatikkamassa upāyabhūtaṃ nekkhammanti evaṃ nekkhammasaṅkhātaṃ saupacārajjhānaṃ, nibbānaṃ, vipassanaṃ, sabbepi vā kusaladhamme khemato nibbhayato disvā, tattha jātābhilāso hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Paramaṃ…pe… ratanattayeti buddhādiratanattaye ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇena balavapītipāmojjaṃ janayitvā. Bhāgī…pe… muttamanti “ahaṃ imāya sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhaariyasāvakehi paṭipannāya nekkhammapaṭipattiyā cittavivekādippavivekajassa sukhassa addhā ekantena bhāgī assaṃ, lābhī bhaveyya”nti evaṃ paṭipattiyaṃ ānisaṃsadassanena tabbisayaṃ uttamaṃ mahantaṃ ussāhaṃ katvā. Ākārena samenevāti atiummīlitaatimandālocanāni vajjetvā nātiummīlitanātimandālocanasaṅkhātena samena ālocanākārena. Atiummīlayato hi atisukhumaṃ, avibhūtañca rūpagataṃ upanijjhāyato viya cakkhu kilamati, attano sabhāvavibhāvanato ca maṇḍalaṃ ativibhūtaṃ hoti, tathā vaṇṇato, lakkhaṇato vā upatiṭṭheyya, tenassa nimittaṃ nuppajjati. Atimandaṃ ummīlayato ca gajanimīlakena pekkhantassa viya rūpagataṃ maṇḍalaṃ avibhūtaṃ hoti. Dassane mandabyāpāratāya kosajjapātato cittañca līnaṃ hoti, evampi nimittaṃ nuppajjati, tasmā yathā nāma ādāsatale mukhanimittaṃ gaṇhanto na tattha [V 2.0174] atigāḷhaṃ ummīlati, na atimandaṃ, atha kho samena ākārena gaṇhāti, evameva nātiummīlanādinā samena [M 2.0233] ākārena gaṇhantena bhāvetabbanti. Nimittaṃ gaṇhatāti pathavīkasiṇe cakkhunā gahitaṃ nimittaṃ manasā gaṇhantena.

"Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures" means having reflected on the danger in both sense objects and the defilements of sensuality, as in the statement, "These sensual pleasures are like a skeleton, devoid of essence," and so on. "Seeing renunciation as safety" means having seen renunciation as safety, that renunciation is the escape from sensual desires, the means to transcend all suffering. Thus, renunciation here refers to access jhāna, Nibbāna, insight, or indeed all wholesome qualities, seen as safety and freedom from fear. Having developed a longing for it, it is said. "The supreme... the Triple Gem" means by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem—the Buddha and so on—one generates strong joy and delight. "A partaker... liberated" means this refers to the thought, "May I, through this path of renunciation practiced by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples, certainly and surely become a partaker and recipient of the happiness born of mental seclusion and other forms of detachment." Thus, seeing the benefits in this practice, one exerts supreme and great effort in that regard. "With a balanced manner of looking" means avoiding looking with eyes either too wide open or too slightly open; one should look in a balanced manner. For if one opens the eyes too wide, the object appears overly subtle and indistinct, like straining to see something too fine, and the eyes grow tired. Also, the circle becomes excessively distinct, revealing its physical nature, so that its color or characteristics appear too clearly; for that reason, the sign does not arise. If one opens the eyes too little, like an elephant half-closing its eyes, the object becomes indistinct. Due to sluggishness in perception and laziness, the mind becomes dull, and again, the sign does not arise. Therefore, just as one who takes a reflection in a mirror does not open the eyes too wide or too little but perceives with a balanced manner, so too should one develop it with a balanced manner—neither too wide open nor too slightly open. "Taking up the sign" means, in the case of the earth kasiṇa, taking up with the mind the sign perceived by the eye.

856-7. Idāni nimittaggahaṇopāyaṃ dassetuṃ “na vaṇṇo pekkhitabbo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na vaṇṇo pekkhitabbo soti yo tattha pathavīkasiṇe aruṇavaṇṇo, so na cintetabbo vaṇṇavasena manasikaroto vaṇṇakasiṇabhāvūpagamanato. Cakkhuviññāṇena pana gahitaggahaṇaṃ na sakkā vāretuṃ, tenevettha “na oloketabbo”ti avatvā “manasānupekkhitā hotī”tiādīsu viya manasā cintanavasena pekkhanaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Daṭṭhabbaṃ na ca lakkhaṇanti yaṃ tattha pathavīdhātuyā thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ na manasikātabbaṃ tassa manasikāre dhātukammaṭṭhānassa gahitattā. Vaṇṇaṃ pana amuñcitvāti disvā gahetabbattā pana vaṇṇaṃ amuñcitvā. Ussadassa vasena hi cittaṃ paṇṇattidhammasminti pathavīdhātuyā sattito adhikabhāvena sasambhārapathaviyā “pathavī”ti vohāro, tasmiṃ sasambhārapathaviṃ upādāya paññatte paṇṇattidhamme ādāsatalagatamukhanimitte viya cittaṃ ṭhapetvā. Ekaggamānasoti puna nānārammaṇe cittaṃ avisāretvā ekaggamānaso hutvā. Pathavī pathaviccevaṃ vatvāti ettha paṭhamasamannāhāre kassaci vacībhedopi siyāti vuttanti ācariyadhammapālatthero āha.

856-7. Now, to explain the method of grasping the sign, it is said: "One should not look at the color," etc. "One should not look at the color" means that in the earth-kasiṇa, the reddish color should not be contemplated; for by attending to it by way of its color, one arrives at the state of the color-kasiṇa. However, it is impossible to prevent eye-consciousness from grasping what has been apprehended, which is why instead of saying "one should not look," the grasping of looking is taken in the sense of mental contemplation, as in such passages as "one should observe with the mind." "And the characteristic should not be seen" means that the characteristic of rigidity in the earth element should not be attended to, because by attending to it, the element itself would be grasped as the meditation subject. "But not abandoning the color" means that since it must be grasped after having been seen, one does so without abandoning the color. "For the mind is established in the conceptual dhamma through prominence" refers to the designation "earth" applied to composite earth due to the prominence of the earth element over its essence, with its constituent parts. Here, the mind is fixed on the conceptual dhamma, which is a concept based on the composite earth, like the reflection of a face in the surface of a mirror. "With a one-pointed mind" means not letting the mind wander to various objects but remaining with a one-pointed mind. "Saying 'earth, earth'"—here, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla says that in the initial application of mind, some may also have a verbal utterance.

858. Yadi vohāramatte cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ, nāmantaravasena pathavī manasikātabbā bhaveyyāti hotu, ko dosoti dassento āha “pathavī medanī”tiādi. Atha vā kiṃ pathavīnāmeyeva vutte bhāvanā hoti, udāhu aññasmimpīti āha “pathavī medanī”tiādi. Ekaṃ vattumpi vaṭṭatīti etesu yaṃ icchati, taṃ attano paguṇatāya vā pacuratāya vā āgacchantaṃ ekaṃ vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Kiñcāpi [M 2.0234] evaṃ vaṭṭati, apica “pathavī”ti etadeva nāmaṃ pākaṭaṃ, tasmā pākaṭavaseneva “pathavī pathavī”ti bhāvetabbanti ācariyā.

858. If the mind is to be established merely in a conventional term, one might think, 'Let the earth be attended to by means of another name. What is the fault in that?' To show this, it is said, 'The earth, the ground,' and so on. Alternatively, one might ask, 'Does the development of meditation occur only when the name 'earth' is said, or also with another?' To address this, it is said, 'The earth, the ground,' and so on. It is permissible to say just one of these terms; one may say whichever one comes to mind due to one's own familiarity or its common usage. Although this is permissible, the name 'earth' is the most evident. Therefore, the teachers say that one should develop the meditation by way of the evident term, repeating, 'Earth, earth.'

859-60. Ummīlitvā…pe… tāva soti yāva vakkhamānākārena uggahanimittaṃ nuppajjati, tāva kiñci kālaṃ cakkhuṃ ummīlitvā nimittaggahaṇavasena pathavīmaṇḍalaṃ oloketvā puna kiñci kālaṃ cakkhūni nimīlitvāti evaṃ vārasatampi vārasahassampi tato bhiyyopi [V 2.0175] ummīlitvā so yogī āvajjeyya, yenākārena oloketvā gahitaṃ, tenākārena taṃ samannāhareyyāti attho.

859-60. 'Having opened... and so on... so long as': This means that as long as the learning sign has not arisen in the manner to be described, for some time he should open his eyes and look at the earth circle by way of grasping the sign, then for some time close his eyes. Thus, a hundred times or a thousand times or even more, that yogi should reflect. In whatever manner he has looked and grasped it, in that same manner he should bring it to mind—this is the meaning.

861-3. Āpāthaṃ tu yāti ceti yadi manodvārikajavanānaṃ gocarabhāvaṃ upagacchati, taṃ uggahanimittaṃ tadā uppannanti pavuccatīti yojanā. Yadi uggahanimittepi pathavīmaṇḍalaṃ oloketvā bhāveti, paṭibhāganimittuppatti na siyā. Samīpaṭṭhena ca na sakkā anoloketunti vuttaṃ “nisīditabbaṃ no ceva”ntiādi. Yathāsukhaṃ nisinnena, yathāsukhaṃ vā bhāvetabbanti sambandho.

861-3. 'If it comes into range': if it enters the sphere of the mind-door impulsion-moments, then it is said that the learning sign has arisen. This is the connection. If one develops it by looking at the earth-kasiṇa disk even when the learning sign has arisen, the counterpart sign would not arise. And because one is sitting near it, it is not possible not to look at it, hence it is said: "One should sit, and not otherwise," etc. The connection is that one should sit comfortably, or develop it comfortably.

864-5. Papañca…pe… dhovaneti passāvādinā kenaci karaṇīyena nisinnaṭṭhānato aññattha gantvā puna āgamma nisīdantena pādā dhovitabbā honti. Adhotapādena hi senāsanaṃ akkamato āpatti hoti, khaṇe khaṇe pādadhovane ca papañco hoti, tasmā tassa parihāratthaṃ dve upāhanāyeva icchitabbā. Tāva bahutalikā saddampi janeyyuṃ, saddo ca jhānakaṇṭako, tasmā vuttaṃ “ekatalikā”ti. Tathā “parissayavinodanatthaṃ kattaradaṇḍo ca icchitabbo”ti (visuddhi. 1.57) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Asappāyena kenacīti vakkhamānena āvāsādiasappāyesu kenacideva asappāyena[M 2.0235]. Taṃ ṭhānanti kasiṇamaṇḍalassa ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ. Ādāya taṃ punāti yathājātaṃ uggahanimittaṃ puna gahetvā, puna uppādetvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

864-5. 'Elaboration... washing': This means that on account of urination or some other necessary task, having gone elsewhere from the place of sitting and then having returned to sit again, the feet should be washed. For by treading upon the lodging with unwashed feet, an offense is incurred, and washing the feet again and again is an elaboration. Therefore, to avoid this, a pair of sandals is desirable. But thick-soled sandals would make noise, and noise is a thorn to jhāna. Hence, it is said: "single-soled." Similarly, it is stated in the commentary: "A staff for warding off dangers should also be desired" (Visuddhimagga 1.57). 'By anything unsuitable': This refers to any of the unsuitable things to be mentioned, such as an unsuitable dwelling. 'That place': This refers to the location where the kasiṇa disk is placed. 'Taking it again': This means taking up the learning sign again as it had arisen, which is to say, generating it again.

866-7. Pīṭhe sukhanisinnenāti puna vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā vuttaniyāmena pīṭhe sukhanisinnena. Bhāvetabbanti taṃ nimittaṃ manasikāravasena vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Samannāharitabbanti sammā āvajjitabbaṃ, sammā vā anu āharitabbaṃ. Takkāhatanti “takkanato takko”ti evaṃ laddhanāmena bhāvanācittasampayuttena sammāsaṅkappena āhananapariyāhananakiccena aparāparaṃ pavattanena kammaṭṭhānaṃ āhataṃ, pariyāhatañca kātabbaṃ, balappattavitakko manasikāro bahulaṃ pavattetabboti attho.

866-7. 'Comfortably seated on a seat': This means having returned to the dwelling place and, in the manner described, being comfortably seated on a seat. 'It should be developed': That sign should be expanded by way of attention. 'It should be properly brought to mind': It should be properly attended to, or properly brought near. 'Struck by applied thought': This means that the meditation subject should be struck and thoroughly worked upon by right thought (sammāsaṅkappa) in the form of applied thought (takka)—so called because it thinks—which is associated with the meditative mind and performs the function of striking and thoroughly striking through repeated application. The meaning is that strong applied thought and attention should be frequently exercised.

868-70. Taṃ icchatīti taṃ nimittaṃ manasikātuṃ icchati. Evaṃ karontassāti evaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ takkāhataṃ karontassa. Yathā bhāvanā pubbenāparaṃ visesaṃ āvahati, evaṃ anuyuñjantassa, evaṃ karoto pana yadā saddhādīni indriyāni suvisadāni tikkhāni pavattanti[V 2.0176], tadā assaddhiyādīnaṃ dūrībhāvena sātisayaṃ thāmappattehi sattahi balehi laddhupatthambhāni vitakkādīni kāmāvacarāneva jhānaṅgāni bahūni hutvā pātubhavanti. Tato ca tesaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhūtā kāmacchandādayo saddhiṃ tadekaṭṭhehi pāpadhammehi dūrībhavanti. Tena vuttaṃ “vikkhambhanti…pe… pañca nīvaraṇānipī”ti. Samādhiyati…pe… yoginoti tassa yogino paṭibhāganimittaṃ ārabbha uppannaupacārasamādhinā upacārajjhānena cittampi samādhiyati, paṭibhāganimittampi uppajjati upacārajjhānassa tena vinā abhāvato.

868-70. 'He desires it' means he desires to attend to that sign. 'For one who does so' means for one who makes the meditation subject struck by applied thought in this way. Just as the development brings successive distinctions, so for one who applies himself thus, when the faculties of faith and so forth proceed in a very clear and sharp way, then, due to the removal of lack of faith and so forth, the jhāna factors of applied thought and so on, which are merely of the sense-sphere, having obtained support from the seven powers that have attained exceeding strength, become numerous and manifest. And then, sensual desire and so forth, which are their direct opponents, along with the unwholesome states associated with them, are far removed. Hence it is said: 'They suppress... the five hindrances.' 'Is concentrated... for the yogi' means that for that yogi, the mind becomes concentrated through access concentration, which is access jhāna that has arisen taking the counterpart sign as its object; and the counterpart sign also arises, because access jhāna does not exist without it.

871-4. Imassāti paṭibhāganimittassa. Purimassāti uggahanimittassa. Thavikāti ādāsathavikato. Balākā viya [M 2.0236] toyadeti meghasamīpe balākā viya. Sā hi meghassa nīlattā sayaṃ atiparisuddhā upaṭṭhāti, tadā taṃ upaṭṭhātīti sambandho. Evaṃ ādāsamaṇḍalūpamādīhi uggahanimittato paṭibhāganimittassa suvisuddhataṃ, saṇhasukhumatañca dasseti. Tenāha “tatodhikatara”nti. Uggahanimitte aṅgulipadapāṇikāpadādayo kasiṇadosā paññāyanti, idaṃ pana vuttanayena tatopi sataguṇaṃ sahassaguṇaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhātīti attho. Tanusaṇṭhānavantantiādi aparamatthasabhāvattā vuttaṃ. Yadi hi taṃ edisaṃ bhaveyya, cakkhuviññeyyaṃ siyā, oḷārikaṃ sammasanūpagaṃ tilakkhaṇāhaṭaṃ, na panetaṃ tādisanti. Yadi panetaṃ na saṇṭhānādivantaṃ, kathaṃ jhānassa ārammaṇabhāvoti āha “upaṭṭhā…pe… maya”nti. Tattha paññajanti bhāvanāmayaṃ paññājanitaṃ, bhāvanāpaññāya sañjānanamattanti vuttaṃ hoti. Na hi asabhāvadhammassa kutocisamuṭṭhānaṃ atthi. Tenāha “bhāvanāmayaṃ upaṭṭhānākāramatta”nti, kevalaṃ samādhilābhino bhāvanāvisesajanitaṃ tammayaṃ upaṭṭhānākāramattameva bhāvanāvisesānubhāvena upaṭṭhātīti attho.

871-4. By 'this' (imassa) is meant the counterpart sign. By 'the former' (purimassa) is meant the learning sign. By 'thavikā' is meant 'from a mirror case.' By 'like a crane in a cloud' (balākā viya toyadeti) is meant 'like a crane near a rain cloud.' For it appears extremely pure due to the blueness of the cloud; thus the connection is that it appears at that time. In this way, through similes like the mirror disk, the counterpart sign is shown to be far clearer, and more refined and subtle, than the learning sign. Hence it is said: 'more than that.' In the learning sign, flaws of the kasina such as finger marks and hand marks are evident, but this, in the manner described, appears a hundred or a thousand times purer than that. The phrase 'having a subtle form, etc.' is said because it has no ultimate reality. For if it were such, it would be perceptible by the eye, gross, accessible to comprehension, and subject to the three characteristics—but it is not so. But if it has no form, etc., how can it be the object of jhāna? He says: 'It appears... as if.' There, 'born of wisdom' (paññajaṃ) means produced by development, generated by wisdom; it is said to be merely a recognition by the wisdom of development. For there is no arising from anywhere for a phenomenon without intrinsic nature. Hence he says: 'merely a mode of appearance produced by development,' meaning that for one who has attained samādhi, it appears solely as a mere mode of appearance, consisting of that, generated by the excellence of development, through the power of the excellence of development.

875-8. Vikkhambhitāneva sannisinnāneva na puna tadatthaṃ ussāho kātabboti adhippāyo. Paṭibhāganimitte hi uppajjamāneyeva taṃvisayaṃ upacārajjhānaṃ nīvaraṇe vikkhambhentameva uppajjati. Kilesā sannisinnāvāti avasesā tadekaṭṭhakilesā ca sammadeva nisinnā, upasantāti attho. “Upacārasamādhinā”ti vutte itaropi samādhi atthīti atthato āpannanti tampi dassetuṃ “ākārehi pana dvīhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dvīhi ākārehīti jhānadhammānaṃ paṭipakkhadūrībhāvo, thirabhāvappatti cāti imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi. Idāni tāni kāraṇāni samādhiavatthāmukhena dassetuṃ “upacārakkhaṇe”tiādi vuttaṃ. Upacārakkhaṇeti upacārabhūmiyaṃ [V 2.0177] upacārāvatthāyaṃ[M 2.0237]. Tassa paṭilābheti yadatthāya ayaṃ paṭipanno, tassa appanāsamādhissa paṭilābhe adhigamāvatthāyaṃ. Kathaṃ upacārabhūmiyaṃ samādhiyati, kathañca appanābhūmiyanti āha “nīvāraṇappahānenā”tiādi. Upacārakkhaṇe yadipi jhānaṅgāni paṭutarāni mahaggatabhāvappattāni na honti, tesaṃ paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ vikkhambhanena cittaṃ samādhiyati, paṭilābhabhūmiyampi appanāpattānaṃ jhānaṅgānaṃ pātubhāvena samādhiyatīti attho.

875-8. The meaning is that when the hindrances are merely suppressed or fully settled, no further effort should be made for that purpose. For when the counterpart sign arises, access jhāna arises in that very domain by merely suppressing the hindrances. By 'the defilements are fully settled' is meant that the remaining defilements and those associated with that object are properly subdued, i.e., pacified. When 'by access concentration' is said, it is implied in meaning that there is also another concentration. To show that too, 'but by two aspects,' etc., is said. By 'by two aspects' is meant by these two reasons: the distancing from the opponents of the jhāna factors, and the attainment of stability. Now, to explain those reasons through the state of concentration, 'at the moment of access,' etc., is said. By 'at the moment of access' is meant on the access level, at the stage of access. By 'for its attainment' is meant at the stage of realization, for the attainment of absorption concentration, for the purpose for which this practitioner strives. How is concentration achieved on the access level, and how on the absorption level? He says: 'By abandoning the hindrances,' etc. At the access stage, even though the jhāna factors are not yet fully distinct or have not reached the elevated state, the mind becomes concentrated through the suppression of their opposing states. At the attainment stage, concentration occurs through the manifestation of the jhāna factors that have reached absorption. That is the meaning.

879-80. Aṅgāni…pe… na cāti upacārakkhaṇe aṅgāni na ca thāmajātāni neva bhāvanābalappattāni hontīti attho. Appanāyāti appanakkhaṇe. Tasmāti yasmā aṅgāni thāmajātāni jāyare, tasmā. Appanācittaṃ divasampi pavattatīti yathā nāma balavā puriso āsanā vuṭṭhāya divasampi tiṭṭheyya, evamevaṃ appanāsamādhimhi uppanne jhānacittaṃ sakiṃ bhavaṅgavāraṃ chinditvā uppannaṃ kevalaṃ rattimpi divasampi kusalajavanapaṭipāṭivaseneva pavattatīti attho. “Appanāpattaṃ divasampi pavattatī”ti vadatā upacārakkhaṇe na tathāti dassitaṃ hoti. Tattha hi aṅgānaṃ athāmajātattā yathā nāma daharo kumāro ukkhipitvā ṭhapiyamāno punappunaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patati, evamevaṃ cittaṃ kālena nimittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, kālena bhavaṅgaṃ otarati.

879-80. By 'the factors... and so on... are not' is meant that at the access moment, the factors are not strong, nor have they attained the power of development. By 'at absorption' (appanāya) is meant at the moment of absorption. By 'therefore' (tasmā) is meant because the factors become strong, therefore. By 'absorption consciousness may continue for a whole day' is meant that just as a strong man, having risen from his seat, might stand for a whole day, in the same way, when absorption concentration arises, the jhāna consciousness, having cut off the bhavaṅga stream once, arises and continues solely through a sequence of wholesome javanas for the entire night and day. By saying 'what has attained absorption may continue for a whole day,' it is shown that it is not so at the access moment. For there, due to the factors being not strong, just as a young boy, when lifted and placed down, repeatedly falls to the ground, so too the mind sometimes takes the sign as its object and sometimes sinks back into bhavaṅga.

881-4. Teneva pallaṅkenāti yasmiṃ nisinno paṭibhāganimittaṃ adhigacchi, teneva pallaṅkena karaṇabhūtena, hetubhūtena vā taṃ nimittaṃ vaḍḍhetvā. Upacārabhūmiyañhi nimittavaḍḍhanaṃ yuttaṃ. Cakkavattiyagabbhovāti cakkavatti bhavituṃ puññavā gabbho viya. Parihāni na vijjatīti laddhūpacārajjhānassa parihāni na vijjati. Nimitte hi aparihīne tadārammaṇaṃ jhānaṃ aparihīnameva hoti, nimitte pana ārakkhābhāvena vinaṭṭhe laddhajjhānampi vinassati tadāyattavuttittā. Tenāha “ārakkhaṇe”tiādi.

881-4. By 'with that same cross-legged posture' (teneva pallaṅkena) is meant having developed that sign with that same cross-legged posture in which one was seated when the counterpart sign was attained, either as the instrument or as the cause. For the development of the sign is suitable in the access stage. By 'like a wheel-turning monarch's womb' (cakkavattiyagabbho) is meant like a womb possessed of merit, fit to produce a wheel-turning monarch. By 'there is no decline' (parihāni na vijjati) is meant there is no decline for one who has attained access jhāna. For if the sign does not decline, the jhāna with that as its object also does not decline; but if the sign is destroyed through lack of guarding, even the attained jhāna is destroyed since its mode of being depends on that. Hence he said, 'in protecting,' etc.

885.
