Āvāsoti [M 2.0238] yasmiṃ āvāse vasantassa anuppannaṃ nimittaṃ nuppajjati, uppannaṃ vā vinassati, anupaṭṭhitā ca sati na upaṭṭhāti, asamāhitañca cittaṃ na samādhiyati, ayaṃ asappāyo āvāso, tasmā yasmiṃ vihāre bahū āvāsā honti, tattha ekekasmiṃ tīṇi tīṇi divasāni vasitvā yattha cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na hoti, taṃ pahāya tabbiparīte vasitabbaṃ. Gocaroti gocaragāmo, so senāsanato atidūre accāsanne pubbadisāya vā pacchimadisāya vā asulabhabhikkho asappāyo. Bhassanti dvattiṃsatiracchānakathāpariyāpannā asappāyakathā. Sā hissa [V 2.0178] nimittantaradhānāya saṃvattati. Puggaloti tiracchānakathiko, sīlādiguṇavirahito puggalo, yaṃ nissāya asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ na samādhiyati, samāhitaṃ vā thiraṃ na hoti, evarūpo. So hi taṃ kaddamodakamiva acchaṃ udakaṃ malīnameva karoti. Bhojanaṃ pana kassaci ambilaṃ, kassaci madhuraṃ asappāyaṃ hoti. Utupi kassaci sīto, kassaci uṇho. Tasmā yaṃ bhojanaṃ vā utuṃ vā sevantassa phāsu na hoti, taṃ bhojanaṃ so ca utu asappāyo. Iriyāpathoti ṭhānacaṅkamanādīsu yo imassa asamāhitacittassa samādhānāya, samāhitacittassa ca thirabhāvāya na hoti, ayaṃ asappāyo iriyāpatho, tasmā tampi āvāsaṃ viya tīṇi divasāni upaparikkhitvā vajjetabbaṃ.

885. By 'dwelling' (āvāsa) is meant a residence where, for one staying there, the unarisen sign does not arise, or the arisen sign vanishes, mindfulness is not established, and the mind does not become concentrated. Such a dwelling is unsuitable. Therefore, in a monastery where there are many dwellings, one should stay in each for three days. If the mind does not become unified there, one should abandon it and stay in one of the opposite kind. By 'alms resort' (gocara) is meant the alms-gathering village. If it is too far or too close, or in the eastern or western direction, or if alms are hard to obtain, it is unsuitable. By 'talk' (bhassa) is meant unsuitable conversation included within the thirty-two types of base topics of discussion. Such talk leads to the disappearance of the sign. By 'person' (puggala) is meant a person who engages in base talk or lacks virtues like morality—a person due to whom an unconcentrated mind does not become concentrated, or a concentrated mind does not become steady. Such a person muddies clear water like a mud ball. Food, however, may be unsuitable for some if it is sour, for others if it is sweet. Climate, too, may be cold for some, hot for others. Thus, whatever food or climate does not bring comfort when used is unsuitable. By 'posture' (iriyāpatha) is meant standing, walking, etc., which do not help an unconcentrated mind to concentrate or a concentrated mind to stabilize. Such a posture is unsuitable. Therefore, one should examine it for three days, like a dwelling, and then avoid it.

886. Sappāye satta seveyyāti vuttaviparītavasena sappāye āvāsādike satta seveyya. Tattha bhassasappāyaṃ nāma dasakathāvatthusannissitaṃ, tampi mattāya bhāsitabbaṃ. Evañhi paṭipajjatoti evaṃ vuttappakārena satta asappāye vajjetvā satta sappāye sevanavasena paṭipajjantassa nimittāsevanabahulassa.

886. By 'one should cultivate association with the suitable seven' (sappāye satta seveyya) is meant one should associate with the seven suitable things, such as a suitable dwelling, etc., in a way contrary to what was stated. Here, 'suitable talk' means talk relating to the ten grounds for discussion, and even that should be spoken in moderation. By 'practicing thus' (evaṃ hi paṭipajjati) is meant for one who practices by avoiding the seven unsuitable things and associating with the seven suitable things in the way described, while frequently attending to the sign.

888-9. Yena [M 2.0239] vinā appanāya kusalo na hoti, so dasavidho vidhi, appanākosallaṃ, tannibbattaṃ vā ñāṇaṃ ganthavitthārabhayena idha na dassitaṃ, atthikena pana visuddhimaggato (visuddhi. 1.60) gahetabbanti adhippāyo. Paṭiladdhe nimittasmiṃ, evañhi sampādayato appanākosallaṃ appanā sampavattatīti sambandho.

Without which one is not skilled in absorption, that tenfold method, the skill in absorption itself, or the knowledge produced thereby is not shown here for fear of prolixity. But the intent is that one who desires it should take it from the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga 1.60). Having obtained the sign, for one who thus accomplishes skill in absorption, absorption occurs—this is the connection.

890-2. Sāti appanā. Evañhīti hi-saddo hetuattho, yasmā ṭhānametaṃ na vijjati, tasmā cittappavattiākāraṃ bhāvanācittassa līnuddhatādivasena pavattiākāraṃ sallakkhayaṃ upadhārento samataṃ vīriyasseva vīriyassa samādhinā samataṃyeva yojayetha, kathaṃ pana yojayethāti āha “īsakampī”tiādi. Tattha layanti līnabhāvaṃ, saṅkocanti attho. Yantanti gacchantaṃ, paggaṇhetheva samabhāvāyāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “accāraddhaṃ nisedhetvā samameva pavattaye”ti. Taṃ mānasanti sambandho.

By 'that' (sā) is meant absorption. By 'thus indeed' (evaṃ hi), the word 'hi' has the meaning of a reason, because such a state does not exist; therefore, observing and considering the manner of the mind's activity—the manner of activity of the meditative mind due to sluggishness, restlessness, and so forth—one should yoke the balance of energy with the balance of concentration. But how should one yoke it? He says: 'even slightly,' and so on. Therein, 'laya' means a state of sluggishness; 'saṅkoca' signifies contraction. By 'going' (yanta) is meant 'moving forward'; the intention is: one should indeed arouse it for the sake of balance. Hence he says: 'having restrained what is excessively exerted, one should proceed evenly.' That is mental—this is the connection.

894-9. Evanti vuttappakārena vīriyasamatāyojanavasena, paṭipannabhāvanāmānasaṃ paṭibhāganimitteyeva ṭhapanavasena nimittābhimukhaṃ paṭipādayato tassa yogino. Samijjhissatīti uppajjissati[V 2.0179]. Pathavīkasiṇanti pathavīti bhāvanāvasena upaṭṭhitaṃ tadeva paṭibhāganimittaṃ. Javanānīti kāmarūpāvacarajavanāni. Tenāha “ekaṃ tu rūpāvacarikaṃ bhave”ti. Aññehīti pākatikehi kāmāvacaracittehi. Balavatarāti bhāvanābalena paṭutarabhāvappattiyā accantabalavanto. Parikammopacāratoti parikammattā, upacārattā ca. Tattha parikammattāti paṭisaṅkharaṇattā. Upacārattāti yathā gāmādīnaṃ āsannadeso “gāmūpacāro, nagarūpacāro”ti vuccati, evaṃ appanāya āsannattā samīpacārittā. Upacārāni [M 2.0240] appanaṃ upecca carantīti katvā. Appanāyānulomattāti nānāvajjanavīthiyaṃ parikammatopi lahukaṃ appanānipphādakavasena, guṇavasena vā appanāya anukūlattā. Etthāti etesu parikammopacārānulomasaññitesu. Sabbantimaṃ tatiyaṃ, catutthaṃ vā gotrabhūti pavuccati parittagottassa abhibhavanato, mahaggatagottassa bhāvanato ca.

'Thus' means: of that yogi engaged in development who directs the mind towards the counterpart sign by applying balanced energy as described and by establishing it right on the counterpart sign. 'It will succeed' means it will arise. 'Earth kasiṇa' means that very counterpart sign which has arisen through the development of 'earth'. 'Javanas' means the javanas of the sense-sphere and form-sphere. Therefore it is said: 'Only one is of the form-sphere.' 'By others' means by ordinary sense-sphere consciousnesses. 'Stronger' means exceedingly powerful due to having attained a state of greater proficiency through the power of development. 'Because of preliminary and access' means because of being preliminary and because of being access. Herein, 'because of being preliminary' means because of being preparatory. 'Because of being access' means that just as the vicinity of a village or town is called 'the access to the village' or 'the access to the city,' so too, because of being near to absorption, because of moving in its vicinity, it is called 'access'. They are called 'access' because they move toward absorption. 'Because of conformity to absorption' means because of being favorable to absorption, either by way of producing absorption or by way of its qualities. 'Herein' means among these, which are termed preliminary, access, and conformity. 'The very last, the third or fourth,' is called change-of-lineage, because of overcoming the limited lineage and because of developing the exalted lineage.

900-3. Avisesena sabbesaṃ sabbā samaññāti paṭhame naye gahitāgahaṇaṃ hotīti āha “gahitāgahaṇenā”tiādi. Ekekassa gahitanāmaṃ itaresaṃ aggahaṇato, ekekanāmavasena gahitassa itaranāmavasena aggahaṇato vā nānāvajjanaparikammameva parikammanti adhippāyena “paṭhamaṃ upacāraṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vāti vā-saddo aniyamo, so pana khippābhiññadandhābhiññavasena veditabbo. Khippābhiññassa hi catutthaṃ appeti, dandhābhiññassa pañcamaṃ. Tato paranti pañcamato paraṃ. Tenāha “chaṭṭhe vā”tiādi. Kasmā na jāyatīti āha “āsannattā bhavaṅgassā”ti. Cittaniyāmavasena hi uppajjitabbesu sattasu javanesu chaṭṭhasattamajavanavāragaḷanaṭṭhānabhūtattā bhavaṅgassa āsannaṃ javanaṃ patati. Tāvadeti tāvadeva. Chaṭṭhaṃ, sattamaṃ vā javanaṃ patantaṃ viya hoti parikkhīṇajavanattāti adhippāyo.

'By way of non-distinction, all designations are common to all' means that in the first method, there is inclusion and exclusion; thus it is said, 'by inclusion and exclusion,' and so on. Because the name of one is taken while that of others is not, or because what is taken by way of one name is not taken by way of another, with the intention that preliminary work is just preliminary work, it is said, 'the first, or access,' and so on. 'The fourth or fifth'—the word 'or' indicates no fixed rule, but it should be understood according to whether one has quick or slow direct knowledge. For one with quick direct knowledge, the fourth attains absorption; for one with slow direct knowledge, the fifth. 'Beyond that' means beyond the fifth. Therefore it is said, 'or in the sixth,' and so on. Why does it not arise? It is said, 'because of its proximity to the life-continuum.' For, according to the fixed order of consciousness, among the seven impulsions that are to arise, an impulsion near the life-continuum falls, because the sixth and seventh impulsions are the place where the sequence overflows. 'Just then' means just then. The intention is that the sixth or seventh impulsion is as if falling, because of the exhaustion of the impulsion.

904-6. Atha kimetaṃ vuccati “chaṭṭhe sattame vāpi appanā na jāyatī”ti? Ābhidhammikagodattatthero hi “purimā purimā kusalā dhammā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ āsevanapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.12) imaṃ suttaṃ vatvā yathā aladdhāsevanaṃ paṭhamajavanaṃ gotrabhuṃ na uppādeti, laddhāsevanaṃ [M 2.0241] pana balavabhāvato dutiyaṃ, tatiyaṃ vā gotrabhuṃ uppādeti, evaṃ laddhāsevanatāya balavabhāvato chaṭṭhaṃ, sattamampi vā appetīti chaṭṭhaṃ, sattamampi vā appanā hotīti vadatī”ti imaṃ codanaṃ manasi nidhāya therassa taṃ mataṃ paṭikkhipitvā yathāvuttamatameva patiṭṭhāpetuṃ “purimehī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Now, what is meant by this: 'even in the sixth or seventh, absorption does not arise'? For the Elder Godatta, the Abhidhammika, having cited this passage, 'Preceding wholesome states are a condition for subsequent wholesome states by way of the repetition condition' (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.12), says that just as the first impulsion, not having gained repetition, does not produce change-of-lineage, but the second or third, having gained repetition, produces change-of-lineage due to its strength, so too, due to having gained repetition and its strength, the sixth or even the seventh attains absorption—thus, he says, absorption occurs in the sixth or even the seventh. Bearing this objection in mind, in order to reject that Elder's view and to establish only what has been stated, it is said, 'by the preceding,' and so on.

Pariyante [V 2.0180] ṭhātuṃ neva sakkotīti papāte eva patatīti adhippāyo. Appetuṃ na sakkotīti patiṭṭhātuṃ appanāvasena uppajjituṃ na sakkoti. Na cettha “purimā purimā”tiādisuttapadaṃ sādhakaṃ āsevanapaccayalābhassa balavabhāve anekantikattā. Tathā hi aladdhāsevanāpi paṭhamacetanā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyā hoti, laddhāsevanā dutiyacetanā yāva chaṭṭhacetanā aparāpariyavedanīyā, tasmā laddhāsevanepi chaṭṭhasattame appanā na hoti āsannabhavaṅgatāya dubbalattāti adhippāyo. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ sattamajavanacetanā upapajjavedanīyā ānantariyā hoti? Nāyaṃ viseso, āsevanapaccayalābhena balavappattiyā, kiñcarahi kiriyāvatthāvisesato. Kiriyāvatthā hi ārambhamajjhapariyosānavasena tividhā. Tattha pariyosānāvatthāya sanniṭṭhāpakacetanābhāvena upapajjavedanīyāditā hoti, na balavabhāvenāti ācariyā.

'He is unable to stand at the edge' means he falls right into the abyss—this is the intention. 'He cannot attain absorption' means he cannot arise by way of absorption, that is, he cannot be established. And here, the textual phrase 'preceding, preceding,' and so on, is not proof, because the strength gained from the repetition condition is not certain. For indeed, even the first volition, without having gained repetition, is to be experienced in this very life, while the second volition up to the sixth volition, having gained repetition, are to be experienced in a subsequent life. Therefore, even when repetition has been gained, absorption does not occur in the sixth or seventh because of its weakness due to proximity to the life-continuum—this is the intention. If so, how is it that the seventh impulsion-volition is an immediately effective kamma to be experienced at rebirth? This distinction is not due to the attainment of strength through gaining the repetition condition; rather, it is due to a specific functional state. For the functional state is threefold: initial, middle, and concluding. Therein, in the concluding state, due to its nature as a conclusive volition, it comes to be experienceable at rebirth, and so on, not because of its strength—so say the teachers.

907. Eka…pe… panāti ayaṃ appanā ekacittakkhaṇāyeva ekavārameva uppajjitvā nirujjhati, na samāpattivīthiyaṃ viya yathicchakaṃ pavattati. Sattasu hi ṭhānesu kālaparicchedo nāma natthi, paṭhamappanāyaṃ, lokiyābhiññāsu, catūsu maggesu, maggānantare phale, rūpārūpabhavesu bhavaṅgaṭṭhāne nirodhassa paccaye nevasaññānāsaññāyatane nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa phalasamāpattiyanti. Etesu hi katthaci atiittarā, katthaci appamāṇā cittakkhaṇā honti, katthaci sampuṇṇajavanavīthi [M 2.0242] addhā labbhati. Tathā hi maggānantaraṃ phalaṃ tiṇṇaṃ upari na hoti, nirodhassa paccayo nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ dvinnaṃ upari na hoti, rūpārūpabhavesu bhavaṅgassa parimāṇaṃ natthi, sesesu pana catūsu ṭhānesu ekameva cittanti tasmā ekacittakkhaṇikāyeva appanā hotīti veditabbā.

907. 'One... but...' means this absorption, arising only once, ceases in a single moment of consciousness; it does not continue as desired, as in an attainment process. For in seven instances there is no fixed duration: in the first absorption; in the mundane higher knowledges; in the four paths; in the fruition immediately following a path; in the state of the life-continuum in the form and formless existences; in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception as a condition for cessation; and in the attainment of fruition for one emerging from cessation. For in these, sometimes the moments of consciousness are extremely brief, sometimes they are immeasurable, and sometimes a full impulsion-process is obtained for a long duration. For example, the fruition immediately following a path does not occur for more than three moments; the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception as a condition for cessation does not occur for more than two; and in the form and formless existences, the life-continuum has no fixed measure. But in the remaining four instances, there is only a single consciousness. Therefore, it should be understood that the first absorption is of a single moment of consciousness.

908. Paccavekkhaṇahetukanti paccavekkhaṇahetuṃ katvā. Nanu ca paccavekkhaṇaṃ āvajjanādīhi, na pana tena āvajjanādi, tasmā kathaṃ paccavekkhaṇahetukaṃ hotīti yujjati? Nāyaṃ doso bhavanakiriyāya paccavekkhaṇahetukattā. Na hi asati paccavekkhaṇe sā hoti nirodhassa paccayabhūtajhānantaramiva, sati pana paccavekkhaṇe sā hoti, tasmā anvayabyatirekavasena labbhati. Tassā paccavekkhaṇahetukatāti na na yujjati “paccavekkhaṇahetuka”nti vacanaṃ. Paccavekkhaṇahetukaṃ āvajjananti vā sambandho. Āvajjanañhi paccavekkhaṇañāṇānaṃ anantarapaccayabhāvena kāraṇaṃ hoti.

908. "Paccavekkhaṇahetuka" means having made reflection its cause. But is not reflection accomplished through attention and so on, and not attention and so on through it? Therefore, how is it reasonable to say that something is caused by reflection? This is not a fault, because the act of development is caused by reflection. For without reflection, it does not occur, as is the case immediately after the jhāna that is a condition for cessation. But when reflection is present, it occurs. Therefore, this is established by way of presence and absence. Because it is caused by reflection, the statement "caused by reflection" is not unreasonable. Or the connection is: "attention is caused by reflection." For attention is a cause for the knowledges of reflection by way of being an immediate condition.

911-3. Nānāvisayaluddhassa[V 2.0181], ito cito ca bhamantassa cetasoti sambandho. Samādhānevāti samādhānā eva, samādhānakaraṇatoti attho. Pāmojjabhāvatoti pāmojjena samānayogakkhamatāya tassā tabbhāvavuttittā. Atha vā byāpādena ghaṭṭiyamānassa cittassa pamuditabhāvakaraṇato pītiyeva “pāmojja”nti vuccati, tassa bhāvo, tasmā pāmojjasabhāvattāti attho. Sītalattasabhāvatoti byāpādagginā santāpiyamānassa cittassa nibbāpanavasena sītalattasabhāvattā.

911–913. The connection is with the mind (cetasā) that is "greedy for various objects" (nānāvisayaluddhassa) and "wandering here and there" (ito cito ca bhamantassa). "Samādhāneva" means simply for concentration; the meaning is "because it causes concentration." "Pāmojjabhāvato" means because it is said to have the nature of joy (pāmojja) due to its capacity for the same application as joy. Or alternatively, because joy (pīti) itself is called "pāmojja" since it causes a state of delight in a mind afflicted by ill will; its nature is that, so the meaning is "due to having the nature of joy." "Sītalattasabhāvato" means because of having the nature of coolness, by way of extinguishing the mind that is being scorched by the fire of ill will.

914-6. Savipphārikabhāvenāti yoniso saṅkappavasena kāmavitakkādiṃ madditvā pavattanato savipphārikasabhāvena. Nekkhammādipavattitoti ettha nekkhamma-ggahaṇena brahmavihāravajjaṃ [M 2.0243] paṭhamajjhānaṃ gahitaṃ. Ādi-saddena tīsu brahmavihāresu paṭhamajjhānaṃ gahitanti vadanti. Avūpasantabhāvassāti uddhaccassa sarūpakathanena taṃsahavattino anutāpasabhāvassa kukkuccassāpi sarūpaṃ kathitamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā sayañcevātisantatoti uddhaccapaṭipakkhasabhāvavacanena kukkuccapaṭipakkho pītibhāvopi. Tenāha “sukhaṃ uddhaccakukkuccadvayassā”ti. Matiyā anurūpattāti paññāya anurūpattā. Tathā ca vuttaṃ ācariyadhammapālattherena “vicāro vicikicchāya paṭipakkho ārammaṇe anumajjanavasena paññāpatirūpakasabhāvattā”ti. Potthakesu pana “pītiyā anurūpattā”ti pāṭho dissati, tassa ca vicāro anumajjanasabhāvavantatāya pīti viya ārammaṇe anivattanto ogāhetvā pavattatīti pītiyā anurūpattā sandehasabhāvattā ārammaṇaṃ anajjhogāhetvā pavattamānāya vicikicchāya paṭipakkhoti atthaṃ vadanti.

914–916. "Savipphārikabhāvena" means by having an expansive nature, because it proceeds by crushing sensual thoughts and the like through wise intention. "Nekkhammādipavattito": here, by the taking of "nekkhamma" (renunciation), the first jhāna, excluding the brahmavihāras, is taken. They say that by the word "ādi" (and so on), the first jhāna in the three brahmavihāras is taken. "Avūpasantabhāvassa": it should be understood that by describing the nature of restlessness, the nature of remorse, which has the nature of regret and accompanies it, is also described. Similarly, by "sayañcevātisantato" (being very tranquil by itself), with the word for the nature of the counterpart to restlessness, the counterpart to remorse—the state of joy—is also implied. Therefore it is said, "happiness is for the pair of restlessness and remorse." "Matiyā anurūpattā" means because of being in accordance with wisdom (paññā). And thus it was said by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla: "Investigation (vicāra) is the counterpart to doubt because it has the nature of a semblance of wisdom, by way of repeatedly examining the object." In some books, however, the reading "pītiyā anurūpattā" (being in accordance with joy) is seen. And they state its meaning thus: investigation, due to its nature of repeatedly examining, proceeds by plunging into the object without turning back, like joy; thus, being in accordance with joy, it is the counterpart to doubt, which, due to its nature of uncertainty, proceeds without fully plunging into the object.

917. Tividhakalyāṇanti ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇatāsaṅkhātāhi paṭipadāvisuddhiādīhi tividhakalyāṇatāhi yuttaṃ. Yathāha “paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi, upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, sampahaṃsanā pariyosāna”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.158). Tattha pubbabhāgapaṭipadāvasena jhānassa paripanthato visujjhanaṃ paṭipadāvisuddhi nāma, sā pana yasmā jhānassa uppādakkhaṇe labbhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “paṭipadāvisuddhi ādī”ti. Visodhetabbatādīnaṃ abhāvato jhānapariyāpannāya tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccanipphattiyā anubrūhanā upekkhānubrūhanā nāma. Sā panāyaṃ visesato jhānassa ṭhitikkhaṇe labbhati. Tena vuttaṃ “upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe”ti. Tattha [M 2.0244] dhammānaṃ anativattanādisādhakassa ñāṇassa kiccanipphattivasena pariyodapanā sampahaṃsanā [V 2.0182] nāma. Sā jhānassa osānakkhaṇe pākaṭā hotīti vuttaṃ “sampahaṃsanā pariyosāna”nti.

917. "Threefold excellence" means endowed with the threefold excellence designated as excellence in the beginning, middle, and end, which are the purity of the path and so on. As it is said: "For the first jhāna, the purity of the path is the beginning, the cultivation of equanimity is the middle, and thorough delighting is the end" (Paṭis I 158). Herein, the purification from the obstacles to jhāna by way of the preliminary path is called "purity of the path." Since this is obtained at the moment of the jhāna's arising, it is said, "purity of the path is the beginning." The cultivation by means of accomplishing the function of specific neutrality, which is included in the jhāna, due to the absence of things to be purified, is called "the cultivation of equanimity." This is specifically obtained at the moment of the jhāna's duration. Therefore, it is said, "the cultivation of equanimity is the middle." Herein, the purification by way of accomplishing the function of the knowledge that establishes the non-transgression of states and so on is called "thorough delighting." This becomes manifest at the concluding moment of the jhāna, hence it is said, "thorough delighting is the end."

Abhayagirivāsino “paṭipadāvisuddhi nāma sasambhāriko upacāro, upekkhānubrūhanā nāma appanā, sampahaṃsanā nāma paccavekkhaṇā”ti (visuddhi. 1.75) evaṃ paṭipadāvisuddhiādike vaṇṇenti, taṃ ayuttaṃ. Evañhi sati ajhānadhammehi jhānadhammassa guṇasaṃkittanaṃ nāma kataṃ hoti. Na hi bhūmantaraṃ bhūmantarapariyāpannaṃ hoti, antoappanāyameva āgamanavasena paṭipadāvisuddhi, tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccanipphattiādīhi upekkhānubrūhanādayo ca veditabbā. Evañca katvā vuttaṃ bhagavatā “ekattagataṃ cittaṃ paṭipadāvisuddhipakkhantarañceva hoti upekkhānubrūhitañca ñāṇena sampahaṃsita”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.158). Ettha hi ekattagataṃ cittanti indriyānaṃ ekarasabhāvena, ekaggatāya ca sikhappattiyā tadanuguṇaekattagataṃ sasampayuttamappanācittaṃ, tasseva paṭipadāvisuddhipakkhandanādi pakkhantaraṃ vuccati.

The Abhayagiri residents describe the purity of the path and so on thus: "The purity of the path is access concentration with its requisites, the cultivation of equanimity is absorption, and thorough delighting is reviewing" (cf. Vism I 75); but that is incorrect. For if this were so, it would be an enumeration of the qualities of a jhāna factor by means of non-jhāna factors. Indeed, one plane is not included in another plane. The purity of the path should be understood as the coming to be within absorption itself, while the cultivation of equanimity and so on should be understood through the accomplishment of the function of specific neutrality, and so on. And having understood it thus, the Blessed One said: "The mind that has attained unification is both inclined towards the purity of the path, cultivated by equanimity, and thoroughly gladdened by knowledge" (Paṭis I 158). Herein, "the mind that has attained unification" is the absorption consciousness with its associated states, which has attained unification in conformity with that, due to the faculties having a single function and due to one-pointedness having reached its peak. Its very leaping into the purity of the path, and so on, is called its aspect (pakkhantara).

Dasalakkhaṇasaṃyutanti “ādimhi tīṇi lakkhaṇāni, majjhe tīṇi, pariyosāne cattārī”ti evaṃ dasaparimāṇehi appanāya lakkhitabbabhāvena lakkhaṇasaṅkhātehi paripanthato visuddhijhānādīhi saṃyuttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

"Endowed with ten characteristics" means endowed with the jhāna factors purified from obstacles and so on, which are designated as characteristics because they are to be marked by absorption, and which number ten thus: "three characteristics at the beginning, three in the middle, and four at the end." For this was said:

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi. Ādissa kati lakkhaṇāni? Ādissa tīṇi lakkhaṇāni. Yo tassa paripantho, tato cittaṃ visujjhati, visuddhattā cittaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati, paṭipannattā [M 2.0245] tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati, yañca paripanthato cittaṃ visujjhati, yañca visuddhattā cittaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati, yañca paṭipannattā tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati, paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi, ādissa imāni tīṇi lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ ādikalyāṇañceva hoti lakkhaṇasampannañca.

"The purity of the path is the beginning for the first jhāna. How many characteristics does the beginning have? The beginning has three characteristics. Whatever is an obstacle to it, from that the mind is purified; being purified, the mind enters upon the middle sign of serenity; having entered upon it, the mind leaps into it. And that the mind is purified from the obstacle, and that being purified the mind enters upon the middle sign of serenity, and that having entered upon it the mind leaps into it—these are the three characteristics of the beginning, which is the purity of the path for the first jhāna. Therefore, it is said that the first jhāna is excellent in the beginning and endowed with characteristics."

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, majjhassa kati lakkhaṇāni? Majjhassa tīṇi lakkhaṇāni. Visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati, samathapaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati[V 2.0183], ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati, yañca visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati, yañca samathapaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati, yañca ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati, paṭhamassa jhānassa upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, majjhassa imāni tīṇi lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ majjhekalyāṇañceva hoti lakkhaṇasampannañca.

"The cultivation of equanimity is the middle of the first jhāna. How many characteristics does the middle have? The middle has three characteristics. One observes the purified mind with equanimity; one observes the mind that has entered upon serenity with equanimity; one observes the establishment of unification with equanimity. And that one observes the purified mind with equanimity, and that one observes the mind that has entered upon serenity with equanimity, and that one observes the establishment of unification with equanimity—these are the three characteristics of the middle, which is the cultivation of equanimity for the first jhāna. Therefore, it is said that the first jhāna is excellent in the middle and endowed with characteristics."

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ. Pariyosānassa kati lakkhaṇāni? Pariyosānassa cattāri lakkhaṇāni. Tattha jātānaṃ dhammānaṃ anativattanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, indriyānaṃ ekarasaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, tadupagavīriyavāhanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, āsevanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, paṭhamassa jhānassa sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ, pariyosānassa imāni cattāri lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇañceva hoti lakkhaṇasampannañcā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.158).

“Thorough delighting is the conclusion of the first jhāna. How many characteristics does the conclusion have? The conclusion has four characteristics: thorough delighting in the sense of not transgressing the states that have arisen in it; thorough delighting in the sense of the faculties being of a single essence; thorough delighting in the sense of sustaining the effort conducive to it; and thorough delighting in the sense of cultivation. Thorough delighting is the conclusion of the first jhāna, and the conclusion has these four characteristics. Therefore it is said, ‘The first jhāna is excellent in its conclusion and endowed with characteristics.’” (Paṭis. I 158)

Ettha ca gotrabhucittassa nānāvajjanavīthiyaṃ uppajjanārahaparipanthato visujjhanato tadāgamanavasena jhānacittassa visujjhanākāraṃ sandhāya “yo tassa paripantho, tato cittaṃ visujjhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Gotrabhucittasseva tathā visuddhattā [M 2.0246] āvaraṇavirahitaṃ hutvā ekattanayena majjhimasamathanimittasaṅkhātaṃ samappavattaṃ appanāsamādhipaṭipajjanaṃ sandhāya “visuddhattā cittaṃ majjhimasamathanimittaṃ paṭipajjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi khīrasseva dadhibhāvābhāvepi tadeva khīraṃ dadhisampannantiādīsu viya gotrabhucittassa appanābhāvābhāvepi ekasantatipariṇāmūpagamanavasena taṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ līnuddhaccasaṅkhātaantadvayānupagamanena majjhimaṃ paccanīkavūpasamanato yathā samathasaṅkhātaṃ yogino sukhavisesānaṃ kāraṇabhāvato nimittabhūtaṃ appanāsamādhiṃ paṭipajjati nāma, tathā paṭipannattā pana samāhitabhāvūpagamanena ekattanayavaseneva tattha pakkhandanaṃ sandhāya “paṭipannattā tattha cittaṃ pakkhandatī”ti vuttaṃ. Ekattanayañhi vinā gotrabhussa appanāpakkhandanaṃ natthi. Evaṃ tāva purimacitte vijjamānākārassa idha nibbattiyā jhānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe tividhalakkhaṇasampannaṃ nāma. Yathā hi lokiyavipassanāya kiccanipphattiyā lokuttaramaggo “vipassanā”ti vuccati, evaṃ visuddhassa pana tassa puna visodhane byāpārākaraṇato tatramajjhattupekkhākiccavasena puggalassa ajjhupekkhanato vuttaṃ “visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhatī”ti. Appanāsamādhibhāvūpagamanena samathavippaṭipannassa puna samādhāne byāpārākaraṇato vuttaṃ “samathapaṭipannaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhatī”ti.

Here, referring to the manner of purification of the jhāna-consciousness by way of its arrival, due to its purification from the obstacles fit to arise in the various adverting processes of the gotrabhū consciousness, it is said, “Whatever is an obstacle to it, from that the mind is purified.” Because the gotrabhū consciousness itself is thus purified, being free from obstructions, it is said, “the mind enters upon the middle sign of serenity,” referring to the entering upon absorption concentration, which is called the middle sign of serenity, proceeding uniformly by way of unification. For just as in phrases like “that very milk is endowed with curd” even when milk has not yet become curd, so too, even though the gotrabhū consciousness has not yet become absorption, by way of undergoing transformation into a single continuity, it is said to enter upon absorption concentration, which is the middle sign of serenity—middle, by not approaching the two extremes called sluggishness and restlessness; serenity, by pacifying opposing factors; and a sign, because it is the cause of the yogi's special happiness. Because it has entered upon it in this way, it is said, “the mind leaps into it,” referring to the leaping into it by way of unification, by undergoing the state of being concentrated. For without the way of unification, there is no leaping of the gotrabhū consciousness into absorption. Thus, by the manifestation here of the characteristics existing in the preceding consciousness, the jhāna is said to be endowed with threefold characteristics at the moment of its arising. Just as the supramundane path is called “insight” by the accomplishment of its function through mundane insight, so too, because one does not engage in further purifying that which is already purified, and because the person observes impartially by way of the function of equanimity towards that, it is said, “one observes impartially the purified mind.” By undergoing the state of absorption concentration, and because one does not engage in re-establishing concentration for one who has strayed from serenity, it is said, “one observes impartially the mind that has entered upon serenity.”

Evaṃ [V 2.0184] samathapaṭipannabhāvatoyeva pubbe “kathaṃ nu kho kilesasaṃsaggaṃ pajaheyya”nti paṭipannassa idāni samathapaṭipattiyā tassa pahīnattā pāpamittasaṃsaggaṃ pahāya ekassa viharato sappurisassa viya ekattena upaṭṭhitassa jhānacittassa puna ekattupaṭṭhāne byāpārākaraṇaṃ sandhāya “ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccavasena jhānaṃ majjhe tividhalakkhaṇasampannaṃ nāma hoti. Pubbabhāgappavattapārihāriyañāṇena cittassa saṃkilesavodānakaradhammesu [M 2.0247] ādīnavānisaṃsaṃ disvā yathā tattha jātānaṃ dhammānaṃ aññamaññānativattanaṃ hoti, tathā bhāvanāya sampahaṃsitattā visodhitattā tatramajjhattupekkhāya vasena anubrūhite citte samādhipaññāsaṅkhātayuganaddhadhammānaṃ aññamaññānativattiyā pavattanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “tattha jātānaṃ dhammānaṃ anativattanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā”ti. Saddhāpañcamakānaṃ indriyānaṃ nānākilesehi vimuttattā vimuttivasena ekarasataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “indriyānaṃ ekarasaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā”ti. Tesaṃ anativattanasampahaṃsanānaṃ anurūpavasena alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ hutvā vīriyassa pavattiṃ sandhāya “tadupagavīriyavāhanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā”ti vuttaṃ. Yā panassa tasmiṃ khaṇe pavattā āsevanā, uppādato paṭṭhāya ṭhitipariyosānānaṃ āsevanapaccayabhāvavasena pavattākāro, taṃ sandhāya “āsevanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ dhammānaṃ anativattanādibhāvasādhanena pariyodāpakassa ñāṇassa kiccavasena jhānapariyosāne catūhi lakkhaṇehi sampannaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, by the very fact of having entered upon serenity, for one who previously practiced thinking, “How indeed might one abandon association with defilements?” that is now abandoned through the practice of serenity. Referring to the non-engagement in re-establishing one-pointedness for the jhāna-consciousness—which is established in one-pointedness like a virtuous person who, having abandoned association with evil friends, dwells alone—it is said, “One observes impartially the establishment of one-pointedness.” In this way, by way of the function of equanimity towards that, the jhāna in its middle phase is said to be endowed with three characteristics. By the preliminary knowledge, having seen the danger and benefit in states that defile and states that purify the mind, and because the mind is thoroughly delighted and purified through development and strengthened by equanimity, the text states that the yoked qualities of concentration and wisdom proceed without transgressing each other, referring to ‘thorough delighting in the sense of not transgressing the states that have arisen in it.’ Because the five faculties, with faith as the fifth, are freed from various defilements and have a single essence by way of liberation, it is said, ‘thorough delighting in the sense of the faculties being of a single essence.’ In accordance with their non-transgression and thorough delighting, and because energy proceeds without slackness or agitation, it is said, ‘thorough delighting in the sense of sustaining the effort conducive to it.’ And the cultivation that occurs at that moment, the manner of its proceeding by way of being a condition for cultivation from its arising to its stability and culmination, is referred to by ‘thorough delighting in the sense of cultivation.’ Thus, by way of the function of the purifying knowledge that establishes the non-transgression and other qualities of phenomena, it should be understood that at the culmination of jhāna, it is endowed with four characteristics.

919-20. Visodhetvāna pāpaketi pāripanthike dhamme visesena sodhetvā sayaṃ pahānamatte aṭṭhatvā atisayappahānavasena puna sodhetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Cittabhāvanavepullanti samādhibhāvanāya vipulabhāvaṃ. Yathā hi bhāvanāvasena nimittassa uppatti, evamassa bhāvanāvasena vaḍḍhanampi, tasmā ekaṅgulādivasena nimittaṃ vaḍḍhayantassa punappunaṃ bahulīkārena jhānabhāvanāpi vuḍḍhiṃ viruḷhiṃ, abhiññāvasena ca vepullaṃ āpajjati. Tena vuttaṃ “cittabhāvanavepullaṃ…pe… vaḍḍhetabba”nti.

919-20. ‘Having purified the evil’ means having especially purified the obstructive states, not having merely stood at the point of abandoning them oneself, but having purified them again by way of surpassing abandonment—thus it is said. ‘The abundance of mind-development’ refers to the abundant state of concentration development. Just as the sign arises through development, so too does its growth through development. Therefore, for one who increases the sign by a finger’s breadth and so on through frequent and repeated practice, the development of jhāna also attains growth, increase, and abundance by way of higher knowledge. Hence it is said, ‘The abundance of mind-development... should be cultivated.’

921-3. Vaḍḍhanābhūmiyo dvevāti vaḍḍhanaṭṭhānāni dveyeva. Dvīsu ṭhānesu avassaṃ ekattaṃ vaḍḍhetabbanti ācariyā. Tatrāti sāmiatthe bhummavacanaṃ, tassāti attho. Tatrāti [M 2.0248] vā dvīsu bhūmīsu. Kasitabbaṃ…pe… yathicchakanti yathā nāma kassako kasitabbaṭṭhānaṃ naṅgalena paricchinditvā paricchedabbhantaraṃ kasituṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ paricchindati, evamevaṃ ekaṅguladvaṅgulativaṅgulacaturaṅgulamattaṃ [V 2.0185] manasā paricchinditvā paricchinditvā yathāparicchedaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Tato vidatthiratanappamukhapariveṇavihārasīmānaṃ, gāmanigamajanapadarajjasamuddasīmānañca paricchedavasena vaḍḍhayantena cakkavāḷaparicchedaṃ katvā vā tato vāpi uttari paricchinditvā vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “yathicchakaṃ vaḍḍhetabba”nti. Aparicchinditvā pana na vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Na hi aparicchede bhāvanā pavattati. Tathā ca vuttaṃ “santake no anantake”ti. Evaṃ vaḍḍhitañca taṃ nimittaṃ vaḍḍhitavaḍḍhitaṭṭhāne pathaviyā ukkūlavikūlanadīviduggapabbatavisamesu saṅkusatasamabbhāhataṃ usabhacammaṃ viya hoti.

921-3. ‘There are two grounds for expansion’ means there are only two places for expansion. The teachers say that one-pointedness must be expanded in these two places without fail. Here, ‘tatrāti’ is a locative case in the sense of possession, meaning ‘its.’ Alternatively, ‘tatrāti’ can mean ‘in those two grounds.’ ‘One should cultivate... as desired’ means that just as a farmer, after marking the area to be plowed with a plow, defines the area within which to plow, so too should one mentally delineate the area—whether one finger, two fingers, three fingers, or four fingers in size—and expand it repeatedly according to the defined boundaries. From there, one should expand by defining the boundaries of the monastery precincts, starting with a span or a cubit, as well as the boundaries of villages, towns, districts, kingdoms, and oceans. One may even define and extend it to the limits of the world-system or further beyond. Thus it is said, ‘One should expand as desired.’ However, one should not expand without defining boundaries, for meditation does not proceed in an undefined space. As it is said, ‘Within limits, not without.’ When expanded in this way, that sign—repeatedly expanded in its designated place—on the earth becomes like a bull's hide struck a hundred times with a stake, free from high and low places, rivers, difficult passages, and uneven mountains.

924-6. Tasmiṃ pana nimitte pattapaṭhamajjhānena ādikammikena idāneva dutiyajjhānādiadhigamāya ussāhaṃ akatvā tasmiṃyeva paṭhamajjhāne pañcahākārehi suciṇṇavasinā bhavitabbanti dassetuṃ “pattepī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Suciṇṇo vaso vasibhāvo etenāti suciṇṇavasinā, suṭṭhu āsevitavasināti attho. Katamā tā vasiyo, yāsaṃ vasenāyaṃ pañcahākārehi suciṇṇavasīti āha “āvajjana”ntiādi. Tattha āvajjananti na āvajjanamattameva adhippetaṃ āvajjanavasitāya adhippetattā. Āvajjanāya pana uppannāya javanehipi bhavitabbaṃ. Tāni ca kho āvajjanakapparatāya cittābhinīhārassa yathāvajjitavasena honti. Adhigamena samaṃ, sasampayuttassa jhānassa sammā āpajjanaṃ paṭipajjanaṃ samāpatti. Abhibhuyya ṭhapanaṃ, adhiṭṭhānaṃ viyāti vā adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Vasitāti etesu āvajjanādīsu yathāruci pavattiyo[M 2.0249], yatthicchakaṃ, yadicchakaṃ, yāvaticchakaṃ pavattituṃ samatthabhāvo.

924-6. However, to show that a beginner, who has attained the first jhāna through that sign, should become well-practiced and masterful in that very first jhāna through five aspects, without making an effort at that moment to achieve the second jhāna and beyond, it is said, 'even when attained,' etc. 'Suciṇṇavasinā' means one who has thoroughly practiced mastery; the meaning is, one whose mastery is well-cultivated. What are those masteries by which one is said to be well-practiced and masterful in five ways? He says, 'adverting,' etc. Here, 'adverting' is not meant as mere adverting, because mastery of adverting is intended. However, when adverting has arisen, there must also be impulsions. And those impulsions occur according to how one directs the mind, in accordance with being intent on adverting. Samāpatti is the correct entering into and practice of the jhāna together with its associated factors, on a par with its attainment. Adhiṭṭhāna is establishing after having overcome; or it is like a determination. 'Mastery' is the ability to proceed as one likes in these aspects, such as adverting, wherever one wishes, as one wishes, and for as long as one wishes.

Tattha paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhāya paṭhamaṃ vitakkaṃ āvajjayato bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā uppannāvajjanānantaraṃ vitakkārammaṇāneva cattāri, pañca vā javanāni javanti, tato dve bhavaṅgāni, tato puna vicārārammaṇaṃ āvajjanaṃ vuttanayeneva javanānīti evaṃ pañcasu jhānaṅgesu paṭipāṭiyā nirantaraṃ cittaṃ pesetuṃ samatthabhāvo, tattha adandhāyitattaṃ āvajjanavasitā nāma. Samāpajjitukāmatānantaraṃ dvīsu bhavaṅgesu uppannesu bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā uppannāvajjanānantaraṃ samāpajjituṃ samatthatā samāpajjanavasitā nāma. Ayañca matthakappattā āvajjanasamāpajjanā satthu yamakapāṭihāriyakāladhammadesanādīsu labbhati. Dhammasenāpatissa yakkhena sīse pahāradānasamaye, mahāmoggallānattherassa nandopanandadamanasamaye vā labbhati, aññattha pana tato dandhāyeva, setu viya sīghasotāya nadiyā oghaṃ bhavaṅgavegaṃ upacchinditvā yathāparicchinnakālaṃ [V 2.0186] jhānaṃ ṭhapetuṃ samatthatā, bhavaṅgapātato rakkhaṇayogyatā adhiṭṭhānavasitā nāma. Yathāparicchinnakālaṃ atikkamituṃ adatvā jhānato vuṭṭhānasamatthatā vuṭṭhānavasitā nāma.

Here, emerging from the first jhāna, when one adverts to applied thought, the bhavaṅga is interrupted, and immediately after the arising of adverting, four or five impulsions occur with applied thought as their object; then two bhavaṅga moments follow, after which adverting occurs again with sustained thought as its object, and impulsions proceed in the same manner. Thus, the ability to send the mind uninterruptedly in sequence through the five jhāna factors, without sluggishness, is called mastery in adverting. The ability to interrupt the bhavaṅga immediately after two bhavaṅga moments have arisen when one wishes to enter absorption, and then to enter absorption right after the arising of adverting, is called mastery in entering. This mastery in adverting and entering, having reached its peak, is found in the Teacher during the Twin Miracle, teaching the Dhamma, etc. It is also found in the Elder Dhammasenāpati when the yakkha struck his head, or in the Elder Mahāmoggallāna when subduing Nandopananda. Elsewhere, however, it is slower. Just as a dam blocks the current of a swift-flowing river, the ability to establish the jhāna for a predetermined time by cutting off the impetus of bhavaṅga, and the suitability for protecting the mind from falling into bhavaṅga, is called mastery in resolve. The ability to emerge from jhāna without allowing the predetermined time to be exceeded is called mastery in emerging.

Atha vā yathāparicchinnakālato upari gantuṃ adatvā ṭhapanasamatthatā adhiṭṭhānavasitā nāma. Paricchinnakālato anto avuṭṭhahitvā yathākālavaseneva vuṭṭhānasamatthatā vuṭṭhānavasitā nāma. Atha vā vuttanayeneva paricchinnakālato anūnaṃ katvā samāpattiṃ ṭhapetuṃ samatthatāva adhiṭṭhānavasitā nāma. Kālaparicchedaṃ atikkamitvā vuṭṭhitassapi niddālukassa paṭibujjhitvā punappunaṃ niddokkamanaṃ viya vuṭṭhitasamāpattimeva punappunaṃ asamāpajjitvā vuṭṭhānasamatthatā, tattha ālayākaraṇayogyatā ca vuṭṭhānavasitā nāma.

Or, the ability to establish the jhāna without allowing it to go beyond the predetermined time is called mastery in resolve. The ability to emerge from the jhāna precisely at the predetermined time, without emerging earlier, is called mastery in emerging. Or, in the same way as stated before, the ability to establish the attainment for no less than the predetermined time is called mastery in resolve. Even for one who has emerged after exceeding the predetermined time, like a sleepy person who, having woken up, repeatedly inclines to sleep, the ability to stay emerged without re-entering again and again the very attainment from which one has emerged, and the suitability for making no attachment to it, is called mastery in emerging.

Paccavekkhaṇavasitā [M 2.0250] pana āvajjanavasitāya eva saṅgahitā. Paccavekkhaṇajavanāneva hi tesaṃ tesaṃ jhānaṅgānaṃ āvajjanānantaraṃ pavattāni, tasmā yadaggena āvajjanavasiyā siddhi, tadaggena paccavekkhaṇavasitā siddhāti veditabbaṃ. Keci pana jhānaṅgānaṃ apākaṭabhāvepi tesu nirantaraṃ āvajjanāya pavattanasamatthatā āvajjanavasitā nāma, tesaṃ yathāsabhāvapaccavekkhaṇavasena javanappavattanasamatthatā paccavekkhaṇavasitā nāma. Atha vā satipi sattannaṃ javanānaṃ pavattiyaṃ nirantaraṃ āvajjanasamatthatā āvajjanavasitā nāma, vasitābalena sattamajavanaṃ appatvā catupañcajavaneheva paccavekkhaṇasamatthatā paccavekkhaṇavasitā nāma. Atha vā ñāṇavippayuttacittehi paccavekkhituṃ asamatthabhāvepi “paccavekkhissāmī”ti uppannaāvajjanānantarameva bhavaṅgesu kālaṃ avītināmetvā sīghameva āvajjituṃ samatthatā āvajjanavasitā nāma, vasitābalena, paccavekkhaṇabalena ñāṇavippayuttacittehipi paccavekkhituṃ samatthatā paccavekkhaṇavasitā nāmāti vadanti. Yasmā panetā yathāvuttaniyāmena punappunaṃ āvajjanādinā sādhetabbā, tasmā vuttaṃ “āvajjitvā”tiādi.

The mastery of reviewing, however, is included within the mastery of adverting. For the reviewing javanas occur immediately after the adverting to each of the jhāna factors; therefore, it should be understood that the mastery of reviewing is achieved to the same extent as the mastery of adverting. Some, however, say that even when the jhāna factors are not clearly apparent, the ability to cause adverting to occur continuously in them is called the mastery of adverting, and the ability to cause javanas to occur by reviewing them according to their own nature is called the mastery of reviewing. Alternatively, the ability to continuously advert even during the occurrence of the seven javanas is called the mastery of adverting, and the ability to review with just four or five javanas, without reaching the seventh javana, due to the power of mastery, is called the mastery of reviewing. Or, even when one is unable to review with consciousness dissociated from knowledge, the ability to quickly advert without passing time in the bhavaṅga moments immediately after the adverting 'I will review' has arisen is called the mastery of adverting. The ability, through the power of mastery and the power of reviewing, to review even with consciousness dissociated from knowledge is called the mastery of reviewing, they say. Since these must be repeatedly achieved through adverting and so on in the manner described, it is said: 'Having adverted,' etc.

927. Imesu pana ādikammikena samāpajjanabahuleneva bhavitabbaṃ, na paccavekkhaṇabahulena. Paccavekkhaṇabahulassa hi jhānaṅgāni thūlāni dubbalāni hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, athassa tāni eva upaṭṭhitattā upari ussukkanāya paccayataṃ nāpajjanti, so appaguṇe jhāne ussukkamāno paṭhamajjhānāva parihāyati, na ca sakkoti dutiyaṃ adhigantuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “paṭhame [V 2.0187] avasippatte”tiādi. Ubhato bhaṭṭhoti puna paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjituṃ na sakkotīti adhippāyo. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

927. Now, among these, a beginner should be one who frequently enters jhāna, not one who frequently reviews. For one who reviews frequently, the jhāna factors appear coarse and weak. Because they appear in this way, they do not become a condition for striving for what is higher. Thus, zealously striving after a jhāna of little quality, one falls away from the first jhāna and is unable to attain the second. Therefore, it is said: 'When the first is not mastered,' etc. 'Lost on both sides' means that one is unable to enter the first jhāna again. Such is the meaning. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Idhekacco [M 2.0251] bhikkhu bālo abyatto akhettaññū akusalo vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, so taṃ nimittaṃ nāsevati, na bhāveti, na bahuliṃ karoti, na svādhiṭṭhitaṃ adhiṭṭhāti. Tassa evaṃ hoti ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, so na sakkoti vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, so na sakkoti vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ubhato bhaṭṭho ubhato parihīno”ti (a. ni. 9.35).

Here, a certain monk—foolish, inexpert, unacquainted with the field, unskillful—quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is born of seclusion, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure. He does not cultivate that sign, does not develop it, does not practice it frequently, does not firmly establish it. It occurs to him, ‘What if I, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought… were to enter and dwell in the second jhāna?’ But he is unable, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought… to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. It occurs to him, ‘What if I, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… were to enter and dwell in the first jhāna?’ But he is unable, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… to enter and dwell in the first jhāna. This, monks, is called a monk who is lost to both, who has fallen away from both.

928-31. Kāmassahagatā…pe… carantīti ārammaṇavasena kāmasahagatā hutvā saññā ceva manasikārā ca samudācaranti. Saññāsīsena cettha taṃsahagato cittuppādo gahito, manakkāra-ggahaṇena āvajjananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāmānupakkhandānaṃ saññāmanasikārānaṃ vasena hānaṃ parihāniṃ bhajatīti hānabhāgiyaṃ. Keci pana “saṃkilesanti hānabhāgiyo dhammo’ti (vibha. 828) vacanato hānabhāgiyā kāmasaññādikāti tehi parihāpiyamānaṃ jhānampi kāraṇūpacārena hānabhāgiyaṃ nāmā”ti vadanti. Tadanudhammatā satīti tasseva jhānassa anudhammatā ārammaṇavasena tadanugatā satipatirūpakā nikanti. Atakkasahitāti avitakkaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ pattukāmassa taṃ santato, manasi karoto ārammaṇavasena taṃsahagatā. Visesabhāgiyanti visesabhūtassa dutiyajjhānassa padaṭṭhānatāya taṃ bhajatīti [M 2.0252] visesabhāgiyaṃ. Nibbidāsaṃyutāti vipassanārammaṇā.

928-31. 'Associated with sensual pleasures… they occur' means that perception and attention, having become associated with sensual pleasures by way of object, arise. Herein, by the heading of perception, the consciousness associated therewith is taken; by the taking of attention, it should be understood as adverting. By means of perceptions and attentions that are constituents of sensual pleasure, one partakes of decline and deterioration; thus, it is the decline-portion. Some, however, say: 'According to the text, “a defiling state is partaking of decline” (Vibh. 828), the things partaking of decline are sensual perceptions, etc., and even the jhāna that is made to decline by them is called the decline-portion by a figurative use of the cause.' 'Mindfulness that is a conformity to that' means the conformity to that jhāna, a longing resembling mindfulness that follows it by way of object. 'Accompanied by non-applied thought' means: for one desiring to attain the second jhāna, which is without applied thought, and who attends to it as peaceful, these are associated with that by way of object. 'Partaking of distinction' means: because it serves as a proximate cause for the distinguished second jhāna, it partakes of it; thus it is 'partaking of distinction.' 'Connected with disenchantment' means having insight as its object.

932-5. Paguṇatoti vasitappattato. Āsannākusalārikāti nīvaraṇappahānassa taṃpaṭhamatāya āsannanīvaraṇapaccatthikā. Thūlaṃ nāma vipulampi pheggu viya sukhabhañjanīyanti āha “thūlattā…pe… dubbalā”ti. Tatoti dutiyajjhānato. Dubbalāni aṅgāni imissāti aṅgadubbalā. Santato cintayitvāti paṭhamajjhāne viya oḷārikaṅgānaṃ abhāvato, santadhammasamaṅgitāya [V 2.0188] ca santanti evaṃ santavasena manasi katvā. Kiñcāpi hi ye dhammā dutiyajjhāne pītisukhādayo, te paṭhamajjhānepi santi, tehi pana te santatarā, paṇītatarā ca honti. Nikantinti nikāmanaṃ apekkhanti attho. Pariyādāyāti khepetvā, vikkhambhetvāti attho.

932-5. 'From being proficient' means from having attained mastery. 'Near to the unwholesome enemies' means being the immediate adversary of the hindrances because their abandonment is the very first step. 'Coarse' means that although extensive, it is like sapwood, easily broken—hence it is said, 'Because of coarseness… weak.' 'From that' means from the second jhāna. 'It has weak factors' means having weak factors. 'Having considered it as tranquil' means attending to it as tranquil because of the absence of gross factors, unlike in the first jhāna, and because it is endowed with tranquil states. For although the factors in the second jhāna—such as rapture and bliss—also exist in the first jhāna, here they are more tranquil and more sublime. 'Longing for' means desiring, expecting. 'Having encompassed' means having exhausted, that is, having suppressed.

943-4. Sampasādananti sampasādanasaṅkhātāya saddhāya yogato jhānampi sampasādanaṃ nīlavaṇṇayogato nīlavatthaṃ viya. Nanu cāyaṃ saddhā paṭhamajjhānepi atthi, kasmā idameva “sampasādana”nti vuttanti? Vuccate – paṭhamajjhānaṃ vitakkavicārakkhobhena vīcitaraṅgasamākulamiva jalaṃ na suppasannaṃ hoti, tasmā satipi saddhāya taṃ sampasādananti na vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana vitakkavicārakkhobhābhāvena laddhokāsā balavatī saddhā, tasmā balavasaddhāya samannāgatattā idameva “sampasādana”nti vuttaṃ. Ajjhattanti niyakajjhattaṃ, attani jātaṃ, attano santāne nibbattanti attho. Tīṇi aṅgāni imassāti tivaṅgikaṃ. Sesanti pītiādīnaṃ aññehi balavabhāvo, tiṇṇaṃ catunnaṃ vā javanānaṃ parikammopacārānulomagotrabhubhāvo, chaṭṭhe sattame vā appanāyānuppatti ekacittakkhaṇatā, tato bhavaṅgapāto, puna bhavaṅgaṃ vicchinditvā paccavekkhaṇatthāya āvajjanaṃ, tato jhānapaccavekkhaṇanti idaṃ sabbaṃ [M 2.0253] vuttāvasesaṃ heṭṭhā paṭhamajjhāne vuttanayeneva samupalakkhitabbaṃ.

943-4. 'Tranquil-faith' refers to the jhāna itself, by virtue of its connection with faith, which is called 'tranquil-faith,' just as a blue cloth is called blue due to its association with the color blue. But is not this confidence also present in the first jhāna? Why is this one alone called 'tranquil-faith'? It is said: The first jhāna, disturbed by applied and sustained thought, is like water agitated by waves—not perfectly serene. Therefore, even though confidence exists there, it is not called 'tranquil-faith.' In this second jhāna, however, because the disturbance of applied and sustained thought is absent, confidence finds its opportunity and becomes strong. Thus, because it is endowed with strong confidence, this one alone is called 'tranquil-faith.' 'Internal' means one’s own internal state—what has arisen within oneself, what has been produced in one’s own mental continuum. 'It has three factors' means it is threefold. The rest—the greater strength of rapture and the other factors, the phases of preliminary work, access, conformity, and change-of-lineage occurring within three or four javanas, the arising of absorption in the sixth or seventh moment, the single moment of consciousness, the lapse into the life-continuum, the interruption of the life-continuum again for the purpose of reviewing, the adverting to review the jhāna—all this remaining explanation should be understood in the same way as described for the first jhāna.

948-9. Piyatoti kāmayato. Uppilāpananti kāmañcāyaṃ pariggahesu apariccattapemassa anādīnavadassino taṇhāsahagatāya pītiyā pavattiākāro, idha ca dutiyajjhānapīti adhippetā, tathāpi sabbaso pītiyaṃ avirattassāpi anubandheyyāti uppilāpanaṃ idha ādīnavavasena vuttaṃ. Atha vā dutiyajjhānasseva tatiyajjhānaṃ viya ahutvā uppilāpanākārena pavatti uppilāpanaṃ viyāti uppilāpananti vuttaṃ. Tatiyaṃ santato disvāti sambandho.

948-9. 'From being dear' means for one who desires. 'Uplifting' refers to the manner in which rapture, accompanied by craving, arises in one who has not abandoned affection for possessions and who does not see the danger in sensual pleasures. Here, specifically, the rapture of the second jhāna is intended. Nevertheless, because it would persist even for one not entirely dispassionate towards rapture, 'uplifting' is here spoken of in terms of its danger. Alternatively, because the second jhāna itself occurs in an uplifting manner, unlike the third jhāna, it is as if floating; thus it is called 'uplifting.' 'Having seen the third as peaceful'—this is the connection.

957-8. Satiyā sampajaññena sampannanti saraṇalakkhaṇāya satiyā, asammohalakkhaṇena sampajaññena ca sampannaṃ. Kāmaṃ purimajjhānesupi satisampajaññaṃ atthi, na hi muṭṭhassatissa, asampajānato ca upacāramattampi sampajjati, pageva appanā, yebhuyyena pana avippayogībhāvena pavattamānesu pītisukhesu pītisaṅkhātassa oḷārikaṅgassa pahāne sukhumatāya idha sātisayo satisampajaññabyāpāroti idheva satisampajaññasampannatā vuttāti veditabbā. Ekaṅgahīnanti [V 2.0189] pītiyā pahīnabhāvena ekaṅgavippahīnaṃ. Sā panesā dutiyajjhānassa vitakkavicārā viya appanākkhaṇeyeva pahīyati. Tenassa sā “pahānaṅga”nti vuccati.

957-8. 'Endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension' means endowed with mindfulness characterized by recollection, and clear comprehension characterized by non-delusion. Granted, mindfulness and clear comprehension exist even in the earlier jhānas, for one with lapsed mindfulness or lacking clear comprehension cannot achieve even access concentration, let alone absorption. However, it should be understood that being 'endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension' is spoken of specifically here because, with the abandoning of the gross factor known as rapture from amidst the rapture and bliss that for the most part proceed in a state of non-disassociation, there is an exceptional function of mindfulness and clear comprehension here due to the resulting subtlety. 'Lacking one factor' means lacking one factor because of the abandonment of rapture. Now, this rapture is abandoned at the very moment of absorption, just as applied and sustained thought are for the second jhāna. Therefore, that rapture is called a 'factor of abandonment.'

972. Somanassassa pahīnattā āha “ekaṅgavippahīna”nti. Tañca pana somanassaṃ ekavīthiyaṃ purimajavanesuyeva pahīyati.

972. Because of the abandoning of gladness, it is said to be 'devoid of one factor.' And that gladness is abandoned in the very first javanas in a single cognitive series.

974. Purimajjhānesu parikammādivasena pavattānaṃ kāmāvacarajavanānaṃ ekasadisattā idha labbhamānaṃ kañci visesaṃ dassetuṃ “yasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Āsevanaṃ na hotīti āsevanapaccayena paccayo na hoti. Ayañhettha adhippāyo [M 2.0254] – yasmā padantarasaṅgahitassa attano sabhāvaggāhāpanasaṅkhātaāsevanapaccayattābhāvato sukhavedanā upekkhāvedanāya āsevanapaccayena paccayo na hoti, catutthajjhāneva upekkhāvedanāya bhavitabbaṃ sātisayaṃ sukhavirāgabhāvanattā, tasmā idha appanāvīthiyaṃ upekkhāsampayuttajavaneheva bhavitabbanti.

974. Since the sense-sphere javanas that arise in the earlier jhānas by way of preparatory work and so forth are similar, the phrase 'since...' and so forth is stated to show some distinction obtainable here. 'There is no repetition' means there is no condition by way of the repetition condition. The intention here is this: Since pleasant feeling is not a condition for equanimous feeling by way of the repetition condition—due to the absence of the repetition condition, which consists in causing the grasping of the own-nature of what is included in a different factor—equanimity must occur in the fourth jhāna because of the cultivation of a superior dispassion towards pleasure. Therefore, in the absorption process here, only javanas accompanied by equanimity should occur.

976. Evaṃ catukkanayavasena jhānappabhedaṃ dassetvā idāni pañcakanayampi dassetuṃ “yaṃ catukkanaye”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dvidhā pana katvānāti vitakkavicārānaṃ visuṃ visuṃ pahānaṅgavasena gaṇanato dvidhā katvā. Dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ katanti avitakkavicāramattaṃ avitakkaavicāranti evaṃ dutiyajjhānañceva tatiyajjhānañca kataṃ abhidhammeti adhippāyo. Suttantesu hi pañcakanayo sarūpato na gahito, kasmā pana abhidhamme gahitoti? Puggalajjhāsayato, sannisinnadevaparisāya hi yesaṃ paṭhamajjhāne vitakko eva oḷārikato upaṭṭhāti, itare santato, tesaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ avitakkavicāramattaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ katvā pañcakanayena desesi. Yesaṃ vitakkavicārā oḷārikato upaṭṭhitā, tato tesaṃ avitakkaavicāraṃ tivaṅgikaṃ katvā catukkanayena desesi. Yesaṃ vitakkova oḷārikato upaṭṭhāti, tehi taṃ atikkamitvā caturaṅgikaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ uppādetuṃ sakkā. Yesaṃ vitakkavicārā, tehi dvepi ekato atikkamitvā tivaṅgikaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ uppādetuṃ sakkā.

976. Having thus shown the classification of jhānas by the fourfold method, now, to present the fivefold method as well, the phrase 'that which in the fourfold method' and so forth is stated. 'Having divided it into two' means dividing it by counting the abandoning of applied thought and sustained thought as separate factors. 'The second is made the third' means that 'without applied thought, with only sustained thought' and 'without applied thought and without sustained thought' are thus made the second and third jhānas respectively in the Abhidhamma—this is the intention. For in the Suttas, the fivefold method is not taken in its own form. Why then is it taken in the Abhidhamma? Due to the disposition of individuals. For in an assembly of devas seated together, to those for whom in the first jhāna only applied thought appears as gross, while the other factor is subtle, for them, the second jhāna was taught by the fivefold method, making it four-factored: 'without applied thought, with only sustained thought.' To those for whom both applied thought and sustained thought appear as gross, the second jhāna was taught by the fourfold method, making it three-factored: 'without applied thought and without sustained thought.' Those for whom only applied thought appears as gross are able to transcend it and produce the second jhāna with four factors. Those for whom both applied thought and sustained thought appear as gross are able to transcend both at once and produce the second jhāna with three factors.

979. Atthabyañjanavasena suṭṭhu madhuraṃ, tatoyeva varataraṃ vacanaṃ yassa soyaṃ sumadhuravarataravacano. Kaṃ nu janaṃ neva rañjayati, na hi ekampi na rañjayati. Atinisita [V 2.0190] …pe… nīyoyanti [M 2.0255] atitikhiṇabuddhippasādehi janehi vedanīyo ayaṃ gantho, paricchedoti vā adhippāyo.

979. He whose speech is exceedingly sweet and even more excellent by way of meaning and expression is 'one whose speech is exceedingly sweet and more excellent'. What person indeed does it not delight? Indeed, it delights every single one. This text is to be understood by people with extremely keen and clear intellect; or the meaning is 'definition'.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus is named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī.

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

The Commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Rūpāvacarasamādhibhāvanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the description of the development of form-sphere concentration is concluded.

15. Pannarasamo paricchedo

15. The Fifteenth Chapter

Arūpāvacarasamādhibhāvanāniddesavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Description of the Development of Formless-Sphere Concentration.

980. Evaṃ pathavīkasiṇavasena catukkapañcakajjhānāni dassetvā yasmā sesakasiṇavasena niddisiyamāne ganthagāravo hoti, tasmā taṃ sabbaṃ ṭhapetvā arūpāvacaraṃ vibhāvetuṃ “rūpārūpa”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Rūpārūpamatītenāti rūpārūpabhavaṃ atikkantena, punānūpapattivasena rūpārūpabhavaṃ atikkantena, pageva kāmāvacarabhavaṃ. Rūpārūpādivedināti rūpārūpādibhūmantaravedinā.

980. Thus, having shown the fourfold and fivefold jhānas by way of the earth kasiṇa, because there would be textual prolixity in specifying by way of the remaining kasiṇas, all that is set aside, and the phrase 'form and formless' and so forth is commenced in order to explain the formless sphere. By 'one who has transcended form and formless' is meant one who has transcended the form and formless existence, one who has transcended the form and formless existence by way of no renewed arising, let alone the sense-sphere existence. By 'one who knows the beginning of form and formless' is meant one who knows the beginning of the form and formless realms and so forth.

982-4. Yasmā ayaṃ arūpāvacarasamādhi nāma rūpavirāgabhāvanā rūpavirāgavaseneva abhinipphādetabbāva, tasmā taṃ uppādetukāmassa rūpe virajjanākāraṃ, virattamānasena ca tadatthāya paṭipajjanavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “rūpe kho”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Daṇḍanaṭṭhena daṇḍo, muggarādi, parapīḷanādhippāyena tassa ādānaṃ daṇḍādānaṃ. Ādi-saddena satthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññādīnaṃ, adinnādānādīnañca gahaṇaṃ. Cakkhurogādayoti ādi-saddena sotarogādīnaṃ. Rūpe ādīnavaṃ disvāti karajarūpādioḷārikarūpe tannidānaṃ dosaṃ disvā. Nibbindamānasoti virattamānaso. Arūpanti arūpāvacarabhāvanaṃ. Tamhā kasiṇarūpāti tamhā paṭibhāganimittasaṅkhātā kasiṇarūpā. Nanu cāyaṃ rūpe ādīnavaṃ disvā taṃ [M 2.0256] samatikkamatthāya paṭipajjati[V 2.0191], paṭibhāganimittañca arūpaṃ paṇṇattimattattāti kathaṃ tasmā nibbijjatīti anuyogaṃ sandhāya opammavasena tamatthaṃ dassento āha “sūkarābhihatova sā”ti. Yathā hi vane sūkarena pahatamatto sunakho tato bhīto rūpadassanavelāyaṃ bhattapacanaukkhaliṃ dūrato disvā sūkarapaṭibhāgatāya tassaṃ sūkarāsaṅkaṃ uppādetvā utrasto palāyateva, evameva rūpe nibbindamānaso taṃ atikkamitukāmo tappaṭibhāge kasiṇarūpepi nibbijjati, samatikkamitukāmoti adhippāyo.

982-4. Since this formless concentration, which is the development of dispassion towards form, must be brought about only by way of dispassion towards form, therefore, to show the manner of becoming dispassionate towards form for one who desires to produce it, and the method of practice for that purpose by one whose mind is dispassionate, the phrase 'in form, indeed' and so forth is commenced. A stick, in the sense of a means of punishment, is a club and so forth; taking it up with the intention of harming others is 'taking up a stick'. By the word 'and so forth' is meant the taking up of knives, quarrels, disputes, conflicts, abusive speech, slander, and so on, as well as taking what is not given, and so forth. By 'eye diseases and so forth' is meant ear diseases and so forth by the word 'and so forth'. By 'seeing the danger in form' is meant seeing the fault, which is its cause, in gross form such as the physical body. By 'one with a disenchanted mind' is meant one with a dispassionate mind. By 'the formless' is meant the development of the formless sphere. By 'from that kasiṇa form' is meant from that kasiṇa form, which is designated as the counterpart sign. Now, since one sees the danger in form and practices to transcend it, and since the counterpart sign is formless, being merely a concept, how does one become disenchanted with that? In response to this inquiry, illustrating that meaning by way of a simile, he said, 'like a dog struck by a boar'. Just as a dog in the forest, having been struck by a boar, becomes frightened and, upon seeing a cooking pot from a distance at a time when form is visible, and due to its resemblance to a boar, conceives the notion of a boar and flees in terror, so too, one who is disenchanted with form and seeks to transcend it becomes disenchanted even with the kasiṇa form, which is its counterpart, desiring to go beyond it—this is the meaning.

985-6. Catutthe pana jhānasminti ṭhapetvā paricchinnākāsakasiṇaṃ navasu pathavīkasiṇādīsu aññatarasmiṃ paṭiladdhacatutthajjhāne. Keci pana ālokakasiṇampi ṭhapetvā aṭṭhasūti vadanti. Tassa pana ṭhapane kāraṇaṃ na dissati. Suṭṭhu ciṇṇo carito atippaguṇikato āvajjanādilakkhaṇo vasībhāvo etenāti suciṇṇavasī. Karoti…pe… yatoti yasmā idaṃ catutthajjhānacittaṃ mayā nibbindakasiṇarūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti. Āsannasomanassañcāti yato tatiyajjhānassa āsannatāya āsannasomanassapaccatthikañca. Thūlasantavimokkhatoti santavimokkhasaṅkhātaarūpajjhānato etaṃ yato thūlaṃ oḷārikaṃ. Arūpajjhānañhi ye te santā vimokkhā atikkamma rūpe āruppantiādīsu “santavimokkha”nti vuccati, santatāsiddhi cassa anussatito daṭṭhabbā.

985-6. By 'in the fourth jhāna,' however, is meant the fourth jhāna attained in any one of the nine kasiṇas, beginning with the earth kasiṇa, excluding the limited space kasiṇa. Some, however, say in eight, excluding the light kasiṇa as well, but no reason is seen for its exclusion. By 'one with well-practiced mastery' is meant one by whom mastery, characterized by adverting and so forth, has been well-practiced, well-conducted, and made highly proficient. By 'it makes... because' is meant: because this fourth jhāna consciousness makes the kasiṇa form, from which one is disenchanted, its object. By 'and has joy nearby' is meant that because of its nearness to the third jhāna, it has joy as a nearby adversary. By 'from the gross peaceful liberation' is meant that this is gross, that is, coarse, compared to the formless jhāna, which is designated as 'peaceful liberation'. For the formless jhāna is called 'peaceful liberation' in such passages as, 'those peaceful liberations which, having transcended form, are the formless states,' and the accomplishment of its peaceful nature is to be understood from recollection.

987-91. Catuttheti catutthajjhāne. Paṭhamāruppañca santato disvāti sambandho, santavasena manasi karitvāti attho. Santato manasikaraṇeneva cettha paṇītato, sukhumato [M 2.0257] ca manasikāro siddhova hotīti na te visuṃ gahitā. Pattharitvānāti pageva vaḍḍhitaṃ, tadā vaḍḍhanavasena vā pattharitvā. Pubbakālavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena naṃ ugghāṭetvā pacchā na vaḍḍhitabbanti dasseti. Na hi taṃ pacchā vaḍḍhanatthāya vāyamiyamānampi vaḍḍhatīti. Tenāti kasiṇarūpena.

987-91. By 'in the fourth' is meant in the fourth jhāna. And 'seeing the first formless state as peaceful' is the connection; the meaning is having attended to it as peaceful. By attending to it as peaceful, the attention here as refined and subtle is accomplished, so they are not taken separately. By 'having spread out' is meant having already expanded it, or having spread it out in the manner of expansion at that time. This is said with reference to the earlier time. Thus, it shows that after opening it up, it should not be expanded later. For even when one strives to expand it afterward, it does not grow. By 'that' is meant by means of the kasiṇa form.

Idānissa ugghāṭanākāraṃ dassetuṃ “ākāso iti vā”tiādiṃ vatvā puna taṃ samatthetuṃ “ugghāṭento hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Udayavasena, paricchedapharaṇavasena ca antābhāvato ananto. Na saṃvelletīti kaṭasārakakilañjādayo viya na paṭisaṃharati. Nāvajjanto na pekkhantoti anāvajjanto anapekkhanto. Aññadatthu tena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ vuttanayena manasikarontoyevāti adhippāyo[V 2.0192]. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānassa ārammaṇabhūtaṃ kasiṇarūpaṃ sabbena sabbaṃ amanasikaroto, tena ca phuṭṭhokāsaṃ “ākāso ākāso”ti manasikaroto yadā taṃ bhāvanānubhāvena ākāsaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti, tadā so kasiṇaṃ ugghāṭeti nāmāti.

Now, to show its method of opening up, after saying 'space, or' and so forth, then to substantiate it again, 'when opening up, indeed' and so forth is stated. It is boundless because there is no end due to the manner of arising and the pervading of the boundaries. 'It does not roll up' means it does not retract like a mat of reeds or a bundle of twigs. By 'not adverting to or looking at' is meant not turning the mind towards or looking at. Indeed, the intention is that one only attends to the space pervaded by it in the stated way. For this is what is said: When, for one who does not attend at all to the kasiṇa form, which is the object of the fourth jhāna of the form sphere, and who instead attends to the space pervaded by it as 'space, space,' that appears as space through the power of development—then one is said to have opened up that kasiṇa.

992-5. Evaṃ kasiṇugghāṭanavasena paṭiladdhe ākāsanimitte puna paṭipajjanavidhiṃ, yassatthāya yesaṃ paṭipajjati, tadatthasiddhañca dassetuṃ “kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ nimitta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ākāsassa animittabhāvepi nimittena phuṭṭhokāsabhāvato “nimitta”nti vuttaṃ. Pañca…pe… vikkhambhantīti nanu rūpāvacarapaṭhamajjhānassa upacārakkhaṇeyeva nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhitāni, tato paṭṭhāya ca na tesaṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṃ atthi. Yadi siyā, jhānato parihāyeyyāti? Saccametaṃ, imassa pana jhānassa vaṇṇabhaṇanavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ yathā aññatthāpi heṭṭhā pahīnānaṃ upari pahānavacananti. Ye pana “sabbe kusalā dhammā sabbesaṃ akusalānaṃ paṭipakkhāti katvā evaṃ vutta”nti vadanti, tehi dutiyajjhānūpacārādīsu nīvaraṇavikkhambhanāvacanassa [M 2.0258] kāraṇaṃ vattabbaṃ hoti. Yampi ceke vadanti “santeva sukhumāni rūpāvacaraavikkhambhanīyāni, tāni sandhāyetaṃ vutta”nti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ. Na hi mahaggatakusalesu lokuttarakusalaṃ viya odhiso pahānaṃ nāma atthi. Yo pana rūpāvacarehi arūpānaṃ uḷāraphalatādiviseso, so bhāvanāvisesena santatarappaṇītatarabhāvena tesuyeva purimapurimehi pacchimapacchimānaṃ viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idhāpīti na kevalaṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhāne, “sesāni kāmāvacarānī”tiādīsu pana idha yaṃ vattabbaṃ avuttaṃ, taṃ rūpāvacarajjhānaniddese vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ.

992-5. Thus, after having obtained the space-sign by opening up the kasiṇa, to show the method of practicing further, for whose purpose and for whom one practices, and the accomplishment of that purpose, it is stated: “The space-sign from the opened-up kasiṇa,” and so on. Even though space itself is not a sign, it is called a “sign” because it is the space pervaded by the sign. “The five hindrances… suppress”—indeed, at the moment of access concentration of the first form-sphere jhāna, the hindrances are suppressed, and from that point onward, there is no re-arising of them. If there were, one would fall from the jhāna. This is true, but this is stated by way of describing this jhāna, just as elsewhere the abandoning of what has already been abandoned is mentioned at a higher stage. Those who say, “All wholesome states are the opponents of all unwholesome states,” should explain the reason for the statement about the suppression of hindrances in the access to the second jhāna and so on. Some say, “There exist subtle hindrances not suppressed by the form-sphere attainments, and this is said with reference to them.” That is merely their opinion. For in the exalted wholesome states, there is no abandoning by stages as there is in the supramundane wholesome states. The superiority of the formless attainments over the form-realm attainments, such as their loftier fruits, should be understood as a distinction due to the refinement of meditation, whereby the later attainments are more peaceful and more sublime than the earlier ones, just as each succeeding stage is more so than the preceding one within those very formless attainments. Here too—not only in the fourth form-sphere jhāna—but also in statements like “the remaining are of the sense-sphere,” what is to be said but has not been said here should be understood according to the method explained in the exposition of the form-sphere jhānas.

997-1001. “Puna bhāvetukāmenā”ti vutte paṭhamameva paṭhamāruppassa bhāvitattā kiṃ bhāvetukāmenāti anuyoge “dutiyāruppamānasa”nti vuttaṃ, na pana “dutiyāruppamānasaṃ bhāvetukāmenā”ti iminā ajjhāsayena. Na hi paṭhamaṃ dutiyāruppaṃ bhāvitanti. Rūpāvacarajjhānaṃ anatikkamitvā anadhigantabbato taṃ manasikārasamudācārassa hānabhāgiyabhāvāvahanato rūpāvacarajjhānametassa paccatthikanti katvā vuttaṃ “āsanna…pe… paccatthikanti cā”ti. Vīthipaṭipannāya bhāvanāya uparūparivisesāvahabhāvato, paṇītabhāvasiddhito ca paṭhamāruppato dutiyāruppaṃ santatarasabhāvanti āha “dutiyāruppa…pe… panā”ti. Vakkhati hi “supaṇītatarā honti, pacchimā pacchimā idhā”ti [V 2.0193] (abhidha. 1040). Viññāṇamiccevaṃ manasā kātabbanti viññāṇaṃ viññāṇaṃ iccevaṃ manasā kātabbaṃ, kevalaṃ anantaṃ anantanti na manasi kātabbaṃ. Tenāha “anantanti…pe… manasā nidhā”ti. Anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ anantaṃ viññāṇanti pana manasi kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

997-1001. When it is said, 'wishing to develop further,' since the first immaterial attainment has already been developed, in response to the question 'wishing to develop what?', it is stated 'the mind of the second immaterial attainment,' but not with the intention of saying 'wishing to develop the mind of the second immaterial attainment.' For the second immaterial attainment is not developed first. Because it is unattainable without having transcended the form-sphere jhāna, and because the practice of attending to that jhāna leads to a state of decline, the form-sphere jhāna is its adversary, and so it is said, 'proximate... and an adversary.' Because the meditation that has entered upon the path brings about progressively higher distinctions, and because of its accomplished sublimity, the second immaterial attainment is of a more serene nature than the first; thus it is said, 'the second immaterial... and so on.' For it will be said, 'The later ones here are increasingly more refined.' 'Consciousness should thus be attended to in the mind' means that one should attend to 'consciousness, consciousness' in the mind; one should not attend merely to 'infinite, infinite.' Therefore, it is said, 'infinite... should not be placed in the mind.' However, it is permissible to attend to 'infinite consciousness, infinite consciousness' in the mind.

1002-6. Tasmiṃ [M 2.0259] pana nimittasminti tasmiṃ paṭhamāruppaviññāṇasaṅkhāte viññāṇanimitte. Vicārentassa mānasanti bhāvanācittaṃ pavattentassa. Ākāsaphuṭaviññāṇeti kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ pharitvā pavatte paṭhamāruppaviññāṇe ārammaṇabhūte. Appetīti appanāvasena pavattati. Sabhāvadhammepi ārammaṇasamatikkamabhāvanāvisesabhāvato idaṃ appanāpattaṃ hoti catutthāruppaṃ viya. Appanā…pe… nayovāti dutiyāruppajjhāne purimabhāge tīṇi, cattāri vā javanāni kāmāvacarāni upekkhāvedanāsampayuttāneva honti. Catutthaṃ, pañcamaṃ vā āruppamānasantiādinā appanānayo paṭhamāruppajjhāne vuttanayova. Pharitvā pavattaviññāṇanti paṭhamāruppaviññāṇaṃ viññāṇañcanti vuccatīti ruḷhīsaddavasena vuttabhāvameva pakāsetuṃ “viññāṇā…pe… siyā”ti vuttaṃ. Pubbe anantassa ākāsassa ārammaṇakaraṇavasena anantatāya “viññāṇañca”nti vuttanti. Puna manasikāravasena vā anantatāya tathā vuttanti dassetuṃ “manakkāravasenāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dutiyāruppaṃ bhāvento hi paṭhamāruppaṃ anantato anavasesato manasi karonto anantanti manasi karoti.

1002-6. 'In that sign, however' refers to the sign of consciousness, designated as the first immaterial consciousness. 'For one whose mind is investigating' means for one who is causing the meditation-mind to proceed. 'In the consciousness that has pervaded space' refers to the first immaterial consciousness, which has become the object, having arisen by pervading the space from which the kasiṇa was removed. 'It attains' means it proceeds by way of absorption.
