Even though its object is a real phenomenon, this attains absorption, like the fourth immaterial attainment, because of the special nature of the development which consists in transcending the object. 'The method of absorption... and so on' means that in the second immaterial jhāna, in the preliminary phase, three or four impulsions occur which are of the sense-sphere and associated only with equanimous feeling. By 'the fourth or fifth is the immaterial mind,' and so on, the method of absorption is the same as that described for the first immaterial jhāna. To clarify that 'the consciousness that arose by pervading,' meaning the first immaterial consciousness, is called 'infinite consciousness' by way of a conventional term, it is said, 'consciousness... and so on.' It was called 'infinite consciousness' because of its infinitude, which comes from having previously made infinite space its object. Or, to show that it was so called because of its infinitude by way of attention, it is said, 'also by way of attention,' and so on. For one who is developing the second immaterial attainment, by attending to the first immaterial attainment as infinite and without remainder, attends to it as 'infinite.'

1010. Paṭhamāruppaviññāṇābhāvoti kasiṇaṃ ugghāṭetvā ākāso viya ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ pahāya tassa abhāvo manasi kātabbo. Kasmā panettha dutiyāruppaviññāṇābhāvaṃ amanasikatvā paṭhamāruppaviññāṇābhāvo manasi kātabboti? Vuccate – tayidaṃ ārammaṇātikkamanavasena pattabbaṃ, na pana aṅgātikkamanavasena. Tathā ca sati ārammaṇeyeva sātisayaṃ dosadassanena taṃ samatikkamitabbaṃ, ārammaṇañca dutiyāruppassa paṭhamāruppameva, tasmā kasiṇe ādīnavaṃ disvā taṃ ugghāṭetvā tabbivittākāsassa viya paṭhamāruppaviññāṇe ādīnavaṃ disvā taṃ pahāya [M 2.0260] tadabhāvasseva manasikaraṇaṃ yuttanti. Abhayagirivāsino pana “viññāṇañcāyatanābhāvoyeva manasi kātabbo”ti vadanti, te pana imesaṃ ārammaṇātikkamanavasena pattabbabhāvaṃ asallakkhetvā kathenti. Yadi sallakkhenti, aññattha dosaṃ disvā aññassa samatikkame atippasaṅgadosato na muccanti.

1010. 'The absence of the first immaterial consciousness' means: just as space is attended to after removing the kasiṇa, so too, having abandoned the base of the infinity of space, its absence should be attended to in the mind. Why, then, should the absence of the first immaterial consciousness be attended to here, and not the absence of the second immaterial consciousness? It is said: This is to be attained by way of transcending the object, not by way of transcending the factors. And that being the case, it is by seeing an exceeding fault in the object itself that it is to be transcended. And the object of the second immaterial attainment is precisely the first immaterial attainment. Therefore, just as one sees the danger in the kasiṇa, removes it, and attends to the space devoid of it, so too, it is fitting that one sees the danger in the first immaterial consciousness, abandons it, and attends only to its absence. The Abhayagirivāsins, however, say, 'The absence of the base of the infinity of consciousness itself should be attended to.' But they say this without having marked that these attainments are to be reached by way of transcending the object. If they had marked this, they would not be free from the fault of undue extension, which consists in seeing a fault in one thing and transcending another.

Athāpi [V 2.0194] vadeyyuṃ – “viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ sato samāpajjati, sato samāpajjitvā sato vuṭṭhāti, sato vuṭṭhahitvā taññeva viññāṇaṃ bhāvetī’ti vacanato viññāṇañcāyatanābhāvoyeva manasi kātabbo”ti, tayidaṃ pāḷiatthaṃ virujjhitvā gahaṇavasena cintitaṃ. Na hettha taññeva viññāṇanti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Yadi hi taṃ adhippetaṃ siyā, viññāṇañcāyatananti tassa padhānabhāvena niddiṭṭhattā taññevāti vacaneneva pariyattaṃ, kiṃ viññāṇanti vacanena. Atha sarūpaniddesatthaṃ viññāṇavacanaṃ, evaṃ sati taññeva viññāṇañcāyatananti vuttaṃ siyā, tasmā viññāṇanti vacanena yaṃ ārabbha viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ pavattaṃ, tasseva ākāsānañcāyatanassa gahaṇaṃ, na itarassāti suṭṭhu vuttaṃ.

Furthermore, they might say: 'Because of the statement, "One mindfully enters the base of the infinity of consciousness; having mindfully entered, one mindfully emerges; having mindfully emerged, one develops that very consciousness," the absence of the base of the infinity of consciousness itself should be attended to.' But this is a view conceived through misapprehension, which contradicts the meaning of the Pāli text. For here, by 'that very consciousness,' the base of the infinity of consciousness is not intended. If it were intended, since that has been designated as primary by the term 'base of the infinity of consciousness,' the words 'that very' would have been sufficient; what need for the word 'consciousness'? If the word 'consciousness' were for the purpose of designating its nature, then it would have been said, 'that very base of the infinity of consciousness.' Therefore, by the word 'consciousness,' what is taken is that very base of the infinity of space, taking which as object the base of the infinity of consciousness proceeded, not the other. Thus, it is well said.

1011-2. Paṭhamāruppaviññāṇābhāvomanasikātabboti vatvā manasikāravidhiṃ dassetuṃ “taṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Akatvā manasāti manasā ārammaṇaṃ akatvā sabbena sabbaṃ taṃ acintetvā. “Ākāsaṃ ākāsa”nti manasi karontassa kasiṇavivittākāsaṃ viya “natthi natthī”ti, “suññaṃ suñña”nti vā manasi karontassa viññāṇavivittaṃ abhāvamattameva upaṭṭhātīti āha “natthī”tiādi. Vā-saddo aniyamattho, tena dvīsu pakāresu ekenapi atthasiddhi hotīti dasseti. Avuttavikappanattho vā vā-saddo, tena “vivittaṃ vivitta”nti [M 2.0261] imassapi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Aniyamo panettha tiṇṇampi visuṃ visuṃ pariyāyabhāvatova siddho. Pariyāyasaddā hi visuṃ visuṃyeva atthaṃ sādhentā pariyāyāti loke niruḷhā. Yathāhu –

1011-2. Having said, 'The absence of the first immaterial consciousness should be attended to,' in order to show the method of attention, 'But that...' and so on was said. 'Without making it an object of mind' means not making it an object with the mind, not thinking of it at all in any way. Just as for one attending 'space, space,' the space devoid of the kasiṇa appears, so for one attending 'there is not, there is not,' or 'void, void,' only the mere absence, devoid of consciousness, presents itself; thus it is said, 'there is not,' and so on. The word 'or' has the meaning of indeterminacy; thereby it shows that the purpose is accomplished by even one of the two methods. Or the word 'or' has the meaning of including unstated alternatives; thereby, the inclusion of 'secluded, secluded' should also be understood. The indeterminacy here is established simply from the fact that all three are separately synonyms. For words that are synonyms are established in the world as 'synonyms' because they accomplish the meaning separately. As it is said:

“Pariyāyeneva te yasmā, vadantatthaṃ na saṃhatā;

Pariyāyatthaṃ tato sabbaṃ, pariyāyesu vavatthita”nti.

'Since they express the meaning only by way of synonyms, not collectively; therefore, all synonymous meaning is established in the synonyms.'

1013-6. Tasmiṃ nimitteti paṭhamāruppaviññāṇassa abhāvasaṅkhāte jhānuppattikāraṇabhūte nimitte. Sati santiṭṭhatīti abhāvanimittārammaṇā sati sammā suppatiṭṭhitā hutvā tiṭṭhati. Satisīsena cettha upacārajjhānānuguṇānaṃ saddhāpañcamānaṃ indriyānaṃ sakiccayogaṃ dasseti. Upacārajjhānaṃ pana “bhiyyopi samādhiyati mānasa”nti iminā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasiṇugghāṭimā…pe… abhāvaketi evaṃ pavattaviññāṇassa natthibhāvasaṅkhāte vināsābhāvake na pure abhāvādike. Appanānayo panettha pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayānusārena veditabboti āha “appanāya nayo”tiādi.

1013-6. 'On that sign' means on the sign which has become the cause for the arising of the jhāna, designated as the absence of the first immaterial consciousness. 'Mindfulness is established' means that mindfulness, having the sign of absence as its object, stands well and truly established. And here, with mindfulness as the leader, it shows the application to their own functions of the five faculties, with faith as the fifth, which are conducive to access concentration. It should be understood that access concentration, however, is stated by this: 'the mind is further concentrated.' '...in the absence' means in the absence which is destruction, designated as the non-existence of the consciousness that was thus occurring; not in a primordial absence or the like. The method of absorption here should be known in accordance with the method described for the earth kasiṇa; thus it is said, 'the method of absorption,' and so on.

1017-9. Evaṃ [V 2.0195] yaṃ tattha avasiṭṭhaṃ, taṃ atidisitvā idāni visesaṃ dassetuṃ “ākāsagataviññāṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Parikammamanakkāre tasmiṃ antarahiteti “natthi natthī”ti pavattaparikammamanasikāre amanasikaraṇena asmiṃ paṭhamāruppaviññāṇe antarahite, na pana khaṇabhaṅgavasena, jhānaparihānivasena vā antarahite. Khaṇabhaṅgavasena hi antaradhānaṃ khaṇe khaṇe upalabbhati. Parihānivasena ca antaradhāne puna taṃ anuppādetvā uttari ñāṇādhigamoyeva natthīti. Tassāpagamamattaṃva passanto vasatīti tassa paṭhamāruppassa abhāvamattaṃ passanto so yogāvacaro viharati. Yathā kathaṃ viyāti āha “sannipāta”ntiādi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā nāma koci puriso maṇḍalamāḷādīsu [M 2.0262] katthaci kenacideva karaṇīyena sannipatitaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ disvā katthaci gantvā sannipātakiccāvasāne uṭṭhāya pakkantesu bhikkhūsu puna taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā olokento suññameva passati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbanti. Tatridaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – yathā so puriso sannipatitaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ disvā gato, tato sabbesu bhikkhūsu apagatesu taṃ ṭhānaṃ tehi suññameva passati, na pana tesaṃ kutoci apagatakāraṇaṃ, evamayaṃ yogāvacaro pubbe viññāṇañcāyatanajjhānacakkhunā paṭhamāruppaviññāṇaṃ disvā natthīti manasikārena tasmiṃ apagate tatiyāruppacakkhunā tassa natthibhāvameva passati, na tassa apagatakāraṇaṃ vīmaṃsati jhānassa tādisābhogābhāvatoti.

Thus, what remained there has been referred to; now, to show the distinction, the words beginning with “consciousness gone to space” were stated. When that has disappeared in the preliminary attention: when this consciousness of the first immaterial attainment has disappeared through not attending to it during the preliminary attention that proceeds as “there is not, there is not”—not, however, due to momentary dissolution or due to the decline of jhāna. For disappearance due to momentary dissolution is found from moment to moment. And when there is disappearance due to the decline of jhāna, without producing that jhāna again, there is no further attainment of higher knowledge at all. He dwells seeing only its mere passing away: that yogin abides seeing merely the absence of that first immaterial attainment. To what is this similar? He says: “assembly,” and so on. This is what is meant: just as a certain person, having seen a community of bhikkhus assembled in a circular hall or elsewhere for some duty, goes somewhere, and when the business of the assembly is concluded and the bhikkhus have risen and departed, returns to that place and, looking, sees it as merely empty—so should this matter be understood. Herein is the application of the simile: just as that person, having seen the assembled community of bhikkhus, went away, and after all the bhikkhus have departed, sees that place as merely empty of them, but does not consider the reason for their departure; so too this yogin, having previously seen the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment with the eye of the jhāna of the base of infinite consciousness, when that has disappeared due to the attention “there is not,” sees only its state of absence with the eye of the third immaterial jhāna, without investigating the reason for its disappearance, because the jhāna lacks such advertence.

1020-4. Catutthā…pe… na ca santanti yathā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanacittaṃ saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattiyā savisesaṃ santaṃ, evamayaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpatti na ca santā tadabhāvatoti adhippāyo. Ca-saddo panettha avuttasamuccayattho. Tena “saññā rogo, saññā gaṇḍo, saññā sallaṃ, etaṃ santaṃ, etaṃ paṇītaṃ, yadidaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatana”nti imassapi saṅgaho veditabbo. Catutthaṃ santatoti saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāveneva savisesaṃ santatāya, asantabhāvakararogādisarikkhakasaññāvirahato ca santato disvā. “Santaṃ santamidaṃ citta”nti iminā bhāvanākāraṃ dasseti. Vibhaṅgepi hi taṃyeva ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ santato manasi karotīti ayameva bhāvanākāro gahito. Apare pana “pāḷiyaṃ imassa bhāvanākāro na gahito”ti vatvā tattha kāraṇaṃ vadanti, tattha vattabbaṃ visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanādito gahetabbaṃ.

Fourth... and not peaceful: the meaning is that just as the consciousness of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is especially peaceful due to reaching the subtle state of residual formations, so this attainment of the base of nothingness is not peaceful due to the absence of that. Here, the word 'ca' has the meaning of collecting what is unstated. By it, the inclusion of this statement should be understood: 'Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a dart. This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' Having seen the fourth as peaceful: because of its being especially peaceful due to the very subtlety of residual formations, and due to the absence of perception, which is like diseases and so on that cause a state of non-peace. By 'Peaceful, peaceful is this mind,' he shows the mode of development. For in the Vibhaṅga as well, this very mode of development is adopted: 'he attends to that very base of nothingness as peaceful.' But others, saying, 'This mode of development is not adopted in the Pāli Canon,' state a reason for that. What should be said in that regard should be taken from the commentary on the Visuddhimagga and so on.

1027. Tatiyāruppasaṅkhātakkhandhesu ca catūsupi ārammaṇabhūtesūti adhippāyo.

1027. The meaning is that it is also in all four aggregates, which are reckoned as the third immaterial attainment and serve as its object.

1029-31. Abhāvamattampīti [M 2.0263][V 2.0196] suññatamattampi evaṃ sukhumampīti adhippāyo. Santārammaṇatāyāti santaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etassāti santārammaṇā, tabbhāvo santārammaṇatā, tāya, na jhānasantatāya. Na hi tatiyāruppasamāpatti catutthāruppato santatarā. Codako yaṃ santato manasi karoti, na tattha ādīnavadassanaṃ bhaveyya. Asati ca ādīnavadassane na samatikkamo eva siyāti “santato ce manakkāro kathañca samatikkamo”ti āha. Itaro “anāpajjitukāmattā”tiādinā parihāramāha. Tena ādīnavadassanampi atthevāti dasseti. Yasmiñhi jhāne abhirati, tattha āvajjanasamāpajjanādipaṭipattiyā bhavitabbaṃ. Sā panassa tatiyāruppe sabbasova natthi, kevalaṃ suññabhāvato ārammaṇakaraṇamattameva. Tathā hesa kiñcāpi taṃ santato manasi karoti, atha khvassa “ahametaṃ āvajjissāmi, samāpajjissāmī”ti ābhogo samannāhāro na hoti. Kasmā? Ākiñcaññāyatanato nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā paṇītataratāya. Yathā hi rājā mahatā rājānubhāvena nagaravīthiyaṃ caranto dantakārādayo kammakāre cheke anekāni dantavikatiādīni sippāni karonte disvā “aho vata re chekā ācariyā, īdisāni sippāni karissantī”ti evaṃ tesaṃ chekatāya tussati, na cassa evaṃ hoti “aho vatāhampi rajjaṃ pahāya evarūpo sippiko bhaveyya”nti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Rajjasiriyā mahānisaṃsatāya, so tesaṃ jīvitaṃ tiṇāyapi amaññamāno te samatikkamitvā gacchati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Even mere absence: the meaning is even mere voidness, thus 'even so subtle.' Because of having a peaceful object: it has a peaceful object, thus it has a peaceful object; the state of that is having a peaceful object. It is by this, not by the peacefulness of the jhāna. For the third immaterial attainment is not more peaceful than the fourth immaterial attainment. The questioner says, 'If one attends to it as peaceful, there would be no seeing of danger in it. And when there is no seeing of danger, there would be no transcendence at all.' Thus he says, 'If the attention is as peaceful, how then is there transcendence?' The other states the solution with the words beginning, 'due to the desire not to enter into it.' By this, he shows that there is indeed seeing of danger. For in whichever jhāna one delights, there must be the practice of adverting, attaining, and so on. But for him, in the third immaterial attainment, there is none of that at all; there is only the mere making of the state of voidness an object. Thus, although he attends to it as peaceful, still there is no bending of the mind or application for him, such as, 'I will advert to this, I will attain this.' Why? Because the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is more sublime than the base of nothingness. For it is like a king, moving through the city streets with great royal majesty, who sees skilled workers like ivory-carvers and others practicing various crafts such as carving ivory and thinks, 'Oh, what skilled masters, to create such crafts!' He is pleased by their skill, but it does not occur to him, 'Oh, that I too might give up kingship and become such a craftsman!' What is the reason for that? Because of the great benefit of royal splendor. Regarding their livelihood as not even worth a blade of grass, he transcends them and goes on his way. This matter should be seen thus.

1032. Sukhumaṃ paranti ukkaṃsato sukhumaṃ, paṭhamajjhānūpacārato paṭṭhāya hi tacchentiyā viya pavattamānāya bhāvanāya [M 2.0264] anukkamena saṅkhārā tattha antimakoṭṭhāsataṃ pāpitāti. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ bhāvanā attano kiccaṃ sādheti, nanu cesā tadavatthaṃ pāpitā ārammaṇaṃ na sammā upanijjhāyatīti? Nayidameva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bhāvanābalena sukhumabhāvaṃ pāpitāpi cesā attano kicce dubbalattaṃ na pāpitā, atha kho vipphārikatābhāvaṃ gamitā, tena tathā sukhumāpi attano kicce na dubbalā evāti na tattha tassā asāmatthiyaṃ hoti.

1032. ‘Subtle beyond’ means subtle in the highest degree. For starting from the access concentration of the first jhāna, by means of the development that proceeds gradually like one who chisels, the formations are brought to the state of being the final portion. If so, how does the development accomplish its own task? Surely, having reached that state, it does not properly contemplate the object? This should not be seen thus. For although it has reached a state of subtlety by the power of development, it has not been brought to a state of weakness in its own function; rather, it has been made to reach a state of non-diffuseness. Therefore, though it is so subtle, it is not at all weak in its own task, so there is no incapability for it in that regard.

1033-4. Yāya saññāyāti yādisāya saññāya saddappavattihetubhūtāya. So nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamaṅgī puggalo. Nevasaññī ca nāsaññī hoti nevasaññānāsaññāsamaṅgī hoti. Na kevalaṃ tu saññāva edisī sukhumā nevasaññānāsaññā hoti, atha kho pana vedanādayopi sukhumā, vedanāpi nevavedanānāvedanā, cittampi nevacittaṃnācittaṃ, phassopi nevaphassonāphasso[V 2.0197]. Esa nayo sesasampayuttadhammesu. Saññāsīsena pana “nevasaññānāsaññāyatana”nti vuttaṃ “nānattakāyā nānattasaññino”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.332, 341, 357, 359; a. ni. 7.44; 9.24) viya. Nanu cettha yadi saññā atthi, kathaṃ nevasaññāti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Yadi natthi, kathaṃ nāsaññāti anuyogaṃ sandhāya imamatthaṃ upamāhi sādhetuṃ “pattamakkhanatelenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pattamakkhaṇatelenāti antovutthatāya yāguyā saddhiṃ akappiyaṭṭhena telaṃ atthīti, nāḷipūrādīnaṃ vasena natthīti ca vattabbena patte makkhitatelena. Maggasmiṃ udakena cāti upāhanatemanamattaṭṭhena udakaṃ atthīti, nahānavasena natthīti ca vattabbena maggasmiṃ udakena.

By which perception: by whatever kind of perception that is the cause for the currency of the term. That person is one endowed with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He is neither one with perception nor one without perception; he is one endowed with neither-perception-nor-non-perception. And not only is perception of such a subtle kind that it is neither perception nor non-perception, but feeling and the other states are also subtle. Feeling is neither feeling nor non-feeling; consciousness is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness; contact is neither contact nor non-contact. This is the method for the remaining associated states. But it is called 'the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception' with perception as the principal factor, as in such passages as 'beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions.' Now, with reference to the objection, 'If perception exists here, how can it rightly be called "neither perception"? If it does not exist, how can it be called "nor non-perception"?', in order to establish this meaning with similes, the words beginning 'with oil for smearing a bowl' were stated. Therein, 'with oil for smearing a bowl' means with oil smeared on a bowl, which can be said to exist in the sense of being unsuitable together with gruel placed inside, and not to exist in the sense of a full measure and so on. And 'with water on a path' means with water on a path, which can be said to exist in the sense of being just enough to moisten footwear, and not to exist in the sense of being enough for bathing.

1035-7. Ayaṃ atthoti kiñci visesaṃ upādāya sabhāvato atthīti vattabbasseva dhammassa kiñci visesaṃ upādāya [M 2.0265] natthīti vattabbatāsaṅkhāto ayamattho. Paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya hi nevasaññatā, saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvena nāsaññatā ca hoti. Tenāha “paṭusaññāya kiccassā”tiādi. Ārammaṇasañjānanañceva vipassanāya visayabhāvaṃ upagantvā nibbidājananañca paṭusaññākiccaṃ kathamayaṃ saññāva samānā saññākiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotīti āha “yathā dahanakicca”ntiādi. Nhātukāmassa uṇhasītabhāvaṃ akatvā sukhajananatāya sukhodakaṃ, tasmiṃ. Tejodhātu yathā dahanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, evamesā atisantārammaṇe pavattattā ārammaṇasañjānanaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, paramasukhumattaṃ gatāva. Teneva hesā akatābhinivesassa vipassanāñāṇena sukhaggayhā na hotīti sesasamāpattīsu saññā viya vipassanāya visayabhāvaṃ upagantvā nibbidājananampi kātuṃ na sakkoti, aññesu hi khandhesu akatavipassanābhiniveso bhikkhu nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakkhandhe sammasitvā nibbidaṃ pattuṃ samattho nāma natthi, api āyasmā sāriputto. Pakativipassako pana sāriputtasadiso bhikkhu khandhādimukhena vipassanaṃ abhinivisitvā dvārārammaṇehi saddhiṃ dvārappavattadhammānaṃ vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā ṭhito sakkuṇeyya tabbisayaṃ udayabbayañāṇaṃ uppādetuṃ, sopi kalāpasammasanavaseneva, no anupadadhammavipassanāvasena. Na hi sāriputtasadiso bhikkhu catutthāruppapariyāpannesu phassādidhammesu vinibbhujitvā visuṃ visuṃ sarūpato gahetvā aniccādivasena sammasituṃ sakkoti. Kevalaṃ pana avinibbhujja ekato gahetvā kalāpato samūhatoyeva sammasituṃ samattho hoti, evaṃ sukhumattenesā vijjati.

1035-7. 'This meaning' refers to the fact that, when considering any particular aspect, a phenomenon that can be said to exist by nature can also be said not to exist when considering another aspect. Due to the inability to perform the function of sharp perception, there is 'neither perception'; and due to the extreme subtlety of the remaining formations, there is 'nor non-perception'. Hence it is said, 'the function of sharp perception,' etc. Since the function of sharp perception is both the recognition of an object and the generation of disenchantment by becoming an object for insight, how can this perception, being perception itself, fail to perform this function? Thus it is said, 'just as the function of burning,' etc. Just as in pleasant water, which generates comfort for one desiring to bathe without being hot or cold, the fire element cannot perform its burning function; similarly, this perception, operating on an excessively subtle object, cannot perform its function of recognizing the object, for it has become extremely subtle. Therefore, for one who has not established the application of insight, this perception is not easily grasped by the knowledge of insight. Like perception in other attainments, it cannot serve as an object for insight or generate disenchantment. Indeed, a monk who has not established the application of insight into the other aggregates cannot attain disenchantment by contemplating the aggregates of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—not even the Venerable Sāriputta. However, a natural insight meditator like the Venerable Sāriputta, having established insight by way of the aggregates, etc., and having begun insight into phenomena occurring at the sense-doors along with their objects, might be able to arouse knowledge of arising and passing away in that sphere—but only through the method of contemplating groups, not through the method of insight into individual phenomena. For not even a monk like the Venerable Sāriputta can separate and individually grasp the phenomena of contact, etc., included in the fourth immaterial attainment, and contemplate them as impermanent, etc. He can only contemplate them collectively, as a whole, in groups, without separating them. Thus, it exists in this extremely subtle way.

1038-40. Rūpanti [V 2.0198] kasiṇarūpasaṅkhātaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ. Ākāsanti kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ. Viññāṇanti ākāse pavattaviññāṇaṃ[M 2.0266]. Tadabhāvakanti tassa ākāse pavattaviññāṇassa abhāvakaṃ. Kamatoti paṭhamāruppaṃ samatikkamitvā hotītiādinā anukkamato. Attanā vuttamatthaṃ aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ āharitvā sādhento “āha cā”tiādimāha. Idhāti imāsu catūsu arūpasamāpattīsu. Pacchimā pacchimā samāpattiyo hi purimāpurimāhi samāpattīhi supaṇītatarā suṭṭhu paṇītatarā, sundarapaṇītatarāti vā attho. Pāsādatalasāṭikāti catubhūmakapāsādassa heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimato uparūpari savisesā pañca kāmaguṇā, cattāro pāsādatalā ca thūlasaṇhasaṇhatarasaṇhatamasuttehi vihitā āyāmavitthārato samappamāṇā sāṭikā ca.

1038-40. 'Form' refers to the counterpart sign, known as the kasiṇa form. 'Space' refers to the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa. 'Consciousness' refers to the consciousness occurring in relation to that space. 'The absence of that' means the absence of that consciousness occurring in relation to that space. 'Gradually' means in sequence, by transcending the first immaterial attainment, and so on. To establish the meaning he himself has stated, he introduces the commentary’s words, saying, 'And it is said,' and so on. 'Here' refers to these four immaterial attainments. The later attainments are more sublime, more exceedingly sublime, or more beautifully sublime than the earlier attainments; this is the meaning. 'Like the silken cloths on a palace floor' refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure, which are increasingly distinguished from the lowest to the highest of a four-storied palace, and the four palace floors, and cloths of equal length and width, made of coarse, fine, finer, and finest threads.

1042. Rūpārūpabhavaṃ abhibhuyya nibbānaṃ yāti, atha vā nīvaraṇe abhibhuyya rūpārūpabhavaṃ yātīti attho.

1042. Having overcome existence in the form and formless realms, one goes to Nibbāna; or, having overcome the hindrances, one goes to existence in the form and formless realms—this is the meaning.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus is the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī.

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Arūpāvacarasamādhibhāvanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the development of concentration in the formless sphere is concluded.

16. Soḷasamo paricchedo

16. The Sixteenth Chapter.

Abhiññāniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Higher Knowledges.

1043-7. Paranti visiṭṭhaṃ katvā, visesatoti attho. Catutthajjhānamattepīti rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānamattepi, nāvassaṃ arūpajjhānehīti adhippāyo. Arūpāvacarajjhānaṃ appaṭiladdhopi hi katādhikāro bhikkhu abhiññā sampādetuṃ samattho hoti. Ettha catutthajjhānaggahaṇeneva heṭṭhā tīṇi jhānāni gahitāni. Tesu hi aciṇṇavasī catutthajjhānaṃ uppādetumpi na sakkoti. Abhiññāsu anuyogaṃ [M 2.0267] kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti vatvā tattha payojanaṃ dassetuṃ “abhiññā [V 2.0199] nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Niṭṭhaṅgatāti adhigatānisaṃsatāya ceva bhāvanāsukhatāya ca niṭṭhaṃ nipphattiṃ gatā. Samādhibhāvanāya hi lokiyābhiññā udayaphalabhāvena pākaṭā. So abhiññāya ca samādhinā ca samannāgato sukheneva paññābhāvanaṃ sampādessati.

1043-7. 'Superior' means 'as a distinction,' having made it distinguished. 'Even with just the fourth jhāna' means even with just the fourth jhāna of the form realm; the intention is that this is not necessarily by means of the formless jhānas. For even a monk who has not attained the formless jhānas, if he has made the necessary preparations, is capable of achieving the higher knowledges. Here, by the mention of the fourth jhāna, the three lower jhānas are also included. For without having practiced and gained mastery in them, one is not able to even produce the fourth jhāna. Having said that it is fitting to apply oneself to the higher knowledges, to show the purpose therein, it is said, 'Higher knowledges, indeed,' and so on. 'Accomplished' means having reached completion, both because the benefits have been attained and because of the bliss of development. For mundane higher knowledges are manifest as the fruit that arises from the development of concentration. Endowed with both higher knowledge and concentration, he will easily accomplish the development of wisdom.

1048-9. Dibbānītiādi lokiyābhiññānaṃ sarūpato uddisanaṃ. Dibbāni cakkhusotānīti dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ, dibbasotañāṇañcāti dasseti. Iddhīti iddhividhañāṇaṃ. Imā pana abhiññāyo pattukāmena ādikammikena yoginā yasmā odātakasiṇapariyantesu aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu catutthajjhānaṃ, tabbasena ca arūpasamāpattiyo nibbattetvā vā na vā kasiṇānulomatādīhi cuddasahi ākārehi cittaṃ dametabbaṃ. Na hi evaṃ adametvā pubbe abhāvitabhāvano ādikammiko yogāvacaro pañca abhiññāyo nipphādessatīti tasmā taṃ cittaparidamanaṃ avassaṃ kātabbanti dassetuṃ “kasiṇānulomatādīhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kasiṇānulomatādīhīti kasiṇānulomatā kasiṇapaṭilomatā kasiṇānulomapaṭilomatā jhānānulomatā jhānapaṭilomatā jhānānulomapaṭilomatā jhānukkantikatā kasiṇukkantikatā jhānakasiṇukkantikatā aṅgasaṅkantikatā ārammaṇasaṅkantikatā aṅgārammaṇasaṅkantikatā aṅgavavatthāpanatā ārammaṇavavatthāpanatāti imehi cuddasahi ākārehi.

1048-9. 'Divine,' and so forth, is an indication of the mundane higher knowledges according to their nature. 'Divine eyes and ears' indicates the knowledge of the divine eye and the knowledge of the divine ear. 'Psychic power' indicates the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power. Now, a beginner yogi who wishes to attain these higher knowledges must tame the mind through fourteen modes, beginning with adapting to the kasiṇas. This is done after having developed the fourth jhāna in the eight kasiṇas ending with the white kasiṇa, and, based on that, the formless attainments (or without having developed them). For without taming the mind in this way, a beginner yogāvacara whose practice is undeveloped will not produce the five higher knowledges. Therefore, to show that this taming of the mind must certainly be done, it is said, 'through adapting to the kasiṇas, etc.' 'Through adapting to the kasiṇas, etc.' means: adapting to the kasiṇas, reversing the kasiṇas, adapting and reversing the kasiṇas, adapting to the jhānas, reversing the jhānas, adapting and reversing the jhānas, transcending the jhānas, transcending the kasiṇas, transcending the jhānas and kasiṇas, shifting the factors, shifting the object, shifting the factors and object, determining the factors, and determining the object—by these fourteen modes.

Tattha aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu paṭipāṭiyā satakkhattuṃ sahassakkhattumpi samāpajjanaṃ, tatheva uppaṭipāṭiyā, paṭipāṭiuppaṭipāṭivasena ca samāpajjananti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ākārānaṃ vasena kasiṇānulomatādayo vuttā. Paṭhamajjhānato [M 2.0268] paṭṭhāya yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ, ayaṃ jhānānulomatā nāma. Tesaṃ paṭilomato jhānapaṭilomatā nāma. Anulomapaṭilomato jhānaanulomapaṭilomatā nāma.

Therein, with regard to the eight kasiṇas: entering absorption in forward order a hundred or even a thousand times; likewise, entering in reverse order; and entering by way of both forward and reverse order—by means of these three modes, the practices beginning with 'adapting to the kasiṇas' are explained. Starting from the first jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the forward sequence of jhānas. Their reverse order is called the backward sequence of jhānas. The combination of forward and backward sequences is called the forward-and-backward sequence of jhānas.

Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tattheva tatiyaṃ samāpajjati, tato tadeva ugghāṭetvā ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, tato ākiñcaññāyatananti evaṃ kasiṇaṃ anokkamitvā jhānasseva ekantarikabhāvena ukkamanaṃ jhānukkantikatā nāma. Evaṃ āpokasiṇādimūlikāpi yojanā kātabbā. Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā puna tadeva tejokasiṇe, tato nīlakasiṇe, tato lohitakasiṇeti jhānaṃ anukkamitvā kasiṇasseva ekantarikabhāvena ukkamanaṃ kasiṇukkantikatā nāma. Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā, tejokasiṇe tatiyaṃ[V 2.0200], nīlakasiṇaṃ ugghāṭetvā ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, lohitakasiṇato ākiñcaññāyatananti iminā nayena jhānassa ceva kasiṇassa ca ukkamanaṃ jhānakasiṇukkantikatā nāma.

Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, one then attains the third jhāna right there. After that, having removed that very kasiṇa, one attains the base of infinite space, and then the base of nothingness. In this way, without leaving the kasiṇa, the transcending by skipping one level of jhāna is called 'the skipping of jhāna' (jhānukkantikatā). Similarly, this method should be applied based on the water kasiṇa and others. Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, one then attains the same jhāna in the fire kasiṇa, next in the blue kasiṇa, and then in the red kasiṇa. Without skipping the jhāna, the transcending by skipping one kasiṇa at a time is called 'the skipping of kasiṇa' (kasiṇukkantikatā). Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, then the third jhāna in the fire kasiṇa, removing the blue kasiṇa to attain the base of infinite space, and from the red kasiṇa attaining the base of nothingness—in this manner, the transcending of both the jhāna and the kasiṇa is called 'the skipping of jhāna and kasiṇa' (jhānakasiṇukkantikatā).

Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tattheva itaresampi samāpajjanaṃ aṅgasaṅkantikatā nāma. Sabbakasiṇesu ekekasseva samāpajjanaṃ ārammaṇasaṅkantikatā nāma. Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā, āpokasiṇe dutiyaṃ, tejokasiṇe tatiyaṃ, vāyokasiṇe catutthaṃ, nīlakasiṇaṃ ugghāṭetvā ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, pītakasiṇato viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ, lohitakasiṇato ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ, odātakasiṇato nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti evaṃ aṅgānaṃ, ārammaṇānañca samatikkamanaṃ aṅgārammaṇasaṅkantikatā nāma.

Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, then attaining the other jhānas right there as well, is called 'the transition of factors' (aṅgasaṅkantikatā). In all kasiṇas, attaining only one jhāna at a time is called 'the transition of the object' (ārammaṇasaṅkantikatā). Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, the second in the water kasiṇa, the third in the fire kasiṇa, the fourth in the air kasiṇa; then, having removed the blue kasiṇa, one attains the base of infinite space; from the yellow kasiṇa, the base of infinite consciousness; from the red kasiṇa, the base of nothingness; and from the white kasiṇa, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—thus, the surpassing of both factors and objects is called 'the surpassing of factors and objects' (aṅgārammaṇasaṅkantikatā).

Paṭhamajjhānaṃ nāma pañcaṅgikanti vavatthapetvā dutiyaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ, tatiyaṃ tivaṅgikaṃ, catutthaṃ duvaṅgikaṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti [M 2.0269] evaṃ jhānaṅgamattasseva vavatthāpanaṃ aṅgavavatthāpanaṃ nāma. Tathā “idaṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ, idaṃ āpokasiṇa”ntiādinā ārammaṇamattasseva vavatthāpanaṃ ārammaṇavavatthāpanaṃ nāma. Aṅgārammaṇavavatthāpanampi eke icchantīti. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana anāgatattā addhā taṃ bhāvanāsukhaṃ na hoti. Imehi pana cuddasahi ākārehi cittaparidamanaṃ kātuṃ aṭṭhasamāpattilābhīnaṃ satesu, sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti.

Having determined that the first jhāna is five-factored, the second four-factored, the third three-factored, the fourth two-factored, and so on for the base of infinite space up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—thus, the determination of the jhāna factors alone is called 'the determination of factors' (aṅgavavatthāpanaṃ). Similarly, the determination of the object alone, by thinking, “This is the earth kasiṇa, this is the water kasiṇa,” and so on, is called 'the determination of the object' (ārammaṇavavatthāpanaṃ). Some also accept 'the determination of both factors and objects' (aṅgārammaṇavavatthāpanaṃ). However, since this is not found in the commentaries, that bliss of development certainly does not arise from it. Yet, among hundreds or thousands of those who have attained the eight attainments, only one is able to tame the mind in these fourteen ways.

1050-1. Danteti cuddasahi ākārehi dante. Samāhiteti catutthajjhānasamādhinā samāhite. Suddheti nīvaraṇadūrībhāvena, paccanīkasamanepi abyāvaṭāya tatramajjhattupekkhāya sampāditasatipārisuddhiyā sabbhāvena vā suparisuddhe. Pariyodāteti sudhantasuvaṇṇassa nighaṃsanena viya parisuddhattāyeva pariyodāte, pabhassareti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā vitakkavicārakkhobhavirahavasena pariyodāteti vuttaṃ hoti. Anaṅgaṇeti “mādisassa samādhisampannassa īdisena bhavitabba”nti evaṃ jhānapaṭilābhapaccayānaṃ “aho vata mameva satthā paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvā bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyā”tiādinayappavattānaṃ pāpakānaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ abhāvena anaṅgaṇe. Anupakkileseti upagantvā kilissanaṭṭhena upakkilesasaṅkhātānaṃ rāgādīnaṃ, “abhijjhā cittassa upakkileso, byāpādo, kodho”tiādinā āgatānaṃ cittupakkilesānaṃ vā vigatattā vigatupakkilese. Mudubhūteti paguṇabhāvāpādanena [V 2.0201] subhāvitattā mudubhūte, vasibhāvappatteti vuttaṃ hoti. Vasibhāvappattañhi cittaṃ suparimadditaṃ viya cammaṃ suparikammakatā viya ca lākhā mudūti vuccati. Kammanīyeti muduttāyeva iddhipādabhāvūpagamanena kammakkhame, vikubbanādiiddhikammayogyeti vuttaṃ hoti. Mudujātañhi cittaṃ kammakkhamaṃ hoti, sudhantamiva suvaṇṇaṃ, ubhayampi [M 2.0270] cetaṃ subhāvitattāyeva hoti. Yathāha – “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ bhāvitaṃ bahulīkataṃ muduñca hoti kammaniyañca, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, citta”nti (a. ni. 1.47). Ṭhiteti etesu parisuddhabhāvādīsu niccalaṃ avaṭṭhite, bhāvanāpāripūriyā vā paṇītabhāvaṃ sammasitvā ṭhite. Acaleti ṭhitattāyeva akampe, āneñjappatteti vuttaṃ hoti. Mudukammaññabhāvehi vā attano vase ṭhitattā ṭhite, saddhādīhi pariggahitattā assaddhiyādīhi akampanato acale.

1050-1. “Danta” (tamed): tamed in fourteen ways. “Samāhita” (composed): composed by the concentration of the fourth jhāna. “Suddha” (pure): pure by the removal of hindrances, or by the complete purity of mindfulness achieved through impartial equanimity that is not involved even when faced with opposition—thus, thoroughly purified. “Pariyodāta” (cleansed): thoroughly cleansed, like refined gold that has been polished to perfect purity—hence, it is called radiant; or, it is called “pariyodāta” because it is free from the agitation of initial thought and sustained thought. “Anaṅgaṇa” (unblemished): unblemished by the absence of evil desires conditioned by the attainment of jhāna, which arise in the manner of “one endowed with such concentration as I am should be like this,” or “Oh, if only the Teacher would question me again and again and teach the Dhamma to the monks,” and so on. “Anupakkilesa” (undefiled): free from defilements, such as lust and so on, which are called defilements because they cling and corrupt, or free from the mental defilements mentioned in the texts, such as “covetousness is a defilement of the mind, ill will, anger,” and so on. “Mudubhūta” (pliant): made pliant through thorough cultivation, well-developed—thus, it is said to have attained mastery. For a mind that has attained mastery is called pliant, like well-tanned leather or well-prepared lac. “Kammanīya” (workable): capable of work due to its pliancy, fit for performing psychic powers such as transformation. For a mind that has become pliant is workable, like well-refined gold; both of these are so due to thorough cultivation. As it is said: “Monks, I do not perceive even one other thing that, when developed and cultivated, becomes so pliant and workable as the mind” (A. Ni. 1.47). “Ṭhita” (steady): steady and unshaken in these states of purity, etc., or established in a sublime state through the perfection of development. “Acala” (immovable): unshaken due to its steadiness—thus, it is said to have attained imperturbability. Or, it is steady because it remains under its own control due to its pliancy and workability, and immovable because it is guarded by faith and so on, and not disturbed by lack of faith and so on.

Aṭṭhaṅgasampanneti ṭhitiacalatānaṃ visuṃ visuṃ aggahaṇena samāhiteti visuṃ ekaṅgaṃ katvā. Tāsaṃ pana visuṃ visuṃ gahaṇe suvisuddhatādīnaṃ samāhitacittassa aṅgabhūtattā samāhiteti imaṃ aṅgabhāvena aggahetvā suvisuddhatādīhi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi sampannatā veditabbā. Iddhividhāyāti iddhikoṭṭhāsatthāya, iddhippabhedāya vā. Atthato pana iddhividhā nāma ekassa bahubhāvādianekavidhānapaccayabhūtaṃ abhiññāñāṇaṃ. Abhinīharatīti abhiññādhigamatthāya parikammacittaṃ kasiṇārammaṇato apanetvā abhiññābhimukhaṃ peseti. Iddhivikubbananti ettha ijjhatīti iddhi, nipphajjati paṭilabbhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yañhi nipphajjati, paṭilabbhati ca, taṃ ijjhatīti vuccati. Yathāha –

“Aṭṭhaṅgasampanna” (endowed with eight constituents): this is understood by not taking ‘steadiness’ and ‘immovability’ separately, but by making ‘composed’ a single constituent separately. However, if those are taken separately, then, since purity and so on are constituents of the composed mind, the state of being endowed with eight constituents, such as purity and so on, should be understood without taking ‘composed’ as a constituent. “Iddhividhāya” (for the varieties of psychic power): for the sake of the division of psychic powers, or for the distinction of psychic powers. In meaning, however, ‘varieties of psychic power’ refers to the knowledge of direct knowing, which is the condition for various manifestations, such as becoming many from one. “Abhinīharati” (he directs): for the sake of attaining direct knowing, he directs the preparatory mind towards direct knowing, removing it from the kasiṇa object. “Iddhivikubbana” (psychic transformation): here, ‘it succeeds’ means psychic power; ‘it is accomplished, it is attained’—thus it is said. For whatever is accomplished and attained, that is called ‘succeeding’. As it is said—

“Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa, tassa cetaṃ samijjhatī”tiādi; (Su. ni. 772; mahāni. 1; netti. 5,44);

“For one who desires a desire, that succeeds for him,” and so forth; (Su. ni. 772; mahāni. 1; netti. 5,44);

Iddhiyeva vikubbanaṃ pakativaṇṇavijahanakiriyanti iddhivikubbanaṃ, idaṃ iddhīsu vikubbaniddhiyā padhānabhāvato vuttaṃ, iddhi ca vikubbanañcāti vā iddhivikubbanaṃ. Visuṃ gahaṇampi vuttakāraṇeneva daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Transformation that is psychic power, the act of abandoning one’s natural appearance, is 'psychic transformation'. This is stated because of the prominence of the transformation psychic power among the psychic powers. Alternatively, ‘psychic power and transformation’ is 'psychic transformation'. The separate mention should also be understood for the reason stated.

1052-4. Yathā pana taṃ nipphādetabbaṃ, taṃ vidhiṃ dassetuṃ “abhiññāpādakajjhāna”ntiādi [V 2.0202] vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “anupubbena cattāri [M 2.0271] jhānāni samāpajjitvā catutthajjhānato vuṭṭhāyā”ti keci, taṃ ayuttaṃ. Yadicchakaṃ samāpajjanatthañhi cittaparidamanaṃ, catutthajjhānameva ca abhiññāpādakaṃ, na itarāni. Sataṃ…pe… mānasanti sace sataṃ icchati, “sataṃ homi, sataṃ homī”ti, sace sahassaṃ icchati, “sahassaṃ homi, sahassaṃ homī”ti evaṃ parikammamānasaṃ katvā. “Parikammamānasa”nti ca pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya “sataṃ homī”tiādinā pavattitakāmāvacaracittaṃ, pādakajjhānañca. Abhi…pe… punāti ettha pubbe abhiññāpādakajjhānasamāpajjanaṃ parikammacittassa samādhānatthaṃ, puna samāpajjanaṃ adhiṭṭhānacittassa balaggāhatthaṃ. Adhiṭṭhātīti sataṃ āvajjetvā tato paraṃ pavattānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ, catunnaṃ vā pubbabhāgacittānaṃ anantarā uppannena sanniṭṭhāpanavasena adhiṭṭhānanti laddhanāmena abhiññāñāṇena sanniṭṭhānaṃ karoti, sataṃ nipphādetīti attho. “Adhiṭṭhāna”nti hi sabbattha abhiññāñāṇaṃ vuccati.

1052-4. To show the method by which it should be accomplished, the phrase “the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge,” and so forth, is stated. Here, some say, “having successively attained the four jhānas and emerged from the fourth jhāna,” but that is incorrect. For the taming of the mind is for the purpose of attaining as desired, and only the fourth jhāna is the basis for direct knowledge, not the others. “A hundred… and so forth… mind”: if one wishes for a hundred, one thinks, “May I be a hundred, may I be a hundred”; if one wishes for a thousand, one thinks, “May I be a thousand, may I be a thousand,” thus forming the preparatory mind. And “preparatory mind” refers to the sense-sphere consciousness that arises after emerging from the basis-jhāna with thoughts like “May I be a hundred,” and so forth, and also the basis-jhāna itself. “Direct… and so forth… again”: here, the prior attainment of the basis-jhāna for direct knowledge is for the purpose of concentrating the preparatory mind, and the subsequent attainment is for strengthening the determining mind. “He determines”: after adverting to a hundred, he makes a determination by means of the direct knowledge that has arisen immediately after three or four subsequent preliminary consciousness-moments; this direct knowledge is called “determination” by way of its function of settling. The meaning is that he produces a hundred. For “determination” in all cases refers to direct knowledge.

1055-7. Nimittārammaṇanti paṭibhāganimittārammaṇaṃ. Parikammamanānettha satārammaṇikānīti ettha etesu parikammādhiṭṭhānesu parikammamānasāni “sataṃ homī”ti pavattāni kāmāvacaramānasāni satārammaṇikāni ekekassa cittassa vasena satārammaṇikāni honti paccekaṃ “sataṃ homī”ti pavattanato. Sahassārammaṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Tadādhiṭṭhānacittampīti tassa satādikassa adhiṭṭhānacittampi. Satārammaṇikatā ca pana nesaṃ vaṇṇavasena, no sattapaññattivasena. Rūpañhi sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā katvā dassetabbaṃ, na paññatti. Ettha ca yadi nīlavaṇṇameva sataṃ abhinipphādeti, vaṇṇassa taṃtaṃsantānavasena nānattepi nīlavasena ekattā ekamekaṃ parikammacittaṃ sabbaṃ nīlajātaṃ ālambati.

1055-7. “Nimittārammaṇa” (object of the sign) means the object that is the counterpart sign. Here, regarding the phrase 'the preparatory minds here have a hundred objects': in these preparatory and determining stages, the preparatory minds—which are sense-sphere minds proceeding with 'May I be a hundred'—have a hundred objects. With respect to each single mind, they have a hundred objects, because each one proceeds with 'May I be a hundred.' The same method applies to a thousand objects and so on. “Also the determining mind of that” means also the determining mind of that hundred, etc. Moreover, their having a hundred objects is in terms of color, not in terms of the concept of a being. For it is form that should be made and shown as a hundred or a thousand, not a concept. And in this case, if one produces just a hundred blue colors, even though the colors differ due to their respective continua, nevertheless, because of the oneness of their blueness, each preparatory mind takes as its object all that has arisen as blue.

Yadi pana nānāvaṇṇanānākiriyaparikammacittānampi bahubhāvo hoti, ekamekaṃ ekekavaṇṇaṃ, ekekavaṇṇesu ca nānākiriyaṃ [M 2.0272] ārammaṇaṃ karoti. Adhiṭṭhānacittaṃ pana vaṇṇasāmaññaṃ gahetvāpi parikammārammaṇaṃ nānāvaṇṇavantaṃ abhinipphādeti acinteyyānubhāvattā iddhivisayassa. Appanācittaṃ viyāti viya-ggahaṇaṃ abhiññācittassa, jhānacittassa ca paṭhamuppattiyaṃ sadisabhāvato vuttaṃ, na tassa appanābhāvato. Teneva hi pubbe vuttaggahaṇena visesitanti. Catutthajjhānikanti rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānavantaṃ, tena sampayuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ catutthajjhānassa, imassa ca ko visesoti āha “parikammavisesovā”ti. Na hettha parikammavisesaṃ [V 2.0203] vinā añño viseso atthi. Appanāya pubbabhāgappavattānipi tīṇi cattāri javanāni gahitaggahaṇena, aggahitaggahaṇena vā parikammopacārānulomāni sabbapacchimaṃ gotrabhunāmakantiādi sesaṃ samānameva. Tenāha “sesaṃ pubbasamaṃ idhā”ti. Iddhividhañāṇavaṇṇanā.

But if there are many preparatory minds with various colors and various actions, each one takes a single color as its object, and within each color, various actions as its object. The determining mind, however, even while grasping the general aspect of color, produces an object of preparation endowed with various colors, due to the inconceivable power of the domain of psychic power. “Like the absorption mind”: the word “like” is stated because of the similarity between the direct knowledge mind and the jhāna mind in their first arising, not because the former is an absorption. For that very reason, it is distinguished by the term mentioned previously. “Pertaining to the fourth jhāna” means possessing the fourth jhāna of the form sphere, or associated with it. If so, what is the difference between the fourth jhāna and this? He says, “Or the difference lies in the special preliminary work.” For here, there is no other difference apart from the special preliminary work. The three or four impulsions that occur in the preliminary part before absorption—whether taking a previously grasped object or not—are preparation, access, and adaptation, with the very last one being called ‘change-of-lineage,’ and so forth; the rest is the same. Hence it is said, “The rest is the same as before here.” This is the explanation of the Knowledge of the Kinds of Psychic Power.

1058. Dibbasotanti devatānaṃ pittasemhādīhi apalibuddhehi dūrepi ārammaṇaggahaṇasamatthehi dibbasotapasādehi samānattā, dibbavihāravasena paṭiladdhattā, attanā ca dibbavihārasannissitattā dibbaṃ, savanaṭṭhena sotakiccakaraṇato, taṃsadisatāya ca sotaṃ. Idanti yaṃ uddese “dibbāni cakkhusotānī”ti (abhidha. 1048) dibbasotaṃ uddiṭṭhaṃ, taṃ idanti attho.

1058. The Divine Ear (dibbasota) is called 'divine' (dibba) because of its similarity to the divine ear-sensitivity of deities, which is unobstructed by bile, phlegm, and so forth, and is capable of grasping objects even at a distance; and because it is obtained by means of divine abiding; and because it is itself dependent on divine abiding. It is called 'ear' (sota) because it performs the function of an ear in the sense of hearing, and because of its similarity to one. “Idaṃ” ('this') refers to the divine ear that was indicated in the summary statement, 'the divine eye and ear' (Abhidh. 1048).

1059-64. Paṭhamaṃ oḷārikasaddaṃ āvajjetvā pacchā sukhumasaddassa āvajjitabbato āha “mahanto sukhumopi cā”ti. Paricayakaraṇatthañhi paṭhamaṃ araññe sīhādīnaṃ sadde ādiṃ katvā sabbe oḷārikato paṭṭhāya yathānukkamena sukhumasaddā āvajjitabbā, tathā puratthimādīsu disāsu oḷārikānampi sukhumānampi saddānaṃ saddanimittaṃ manasi [M 2.0273] kātabbaṃ. Tassa te saddā pakaticittassapi pākaṭā honti, parikammacittassa pana ativiya pākaṭā. Tassāti tassa yogino. Saddassa nimittanti oḷārikassa, sukhumassa vā saddassa yathāvuttaṃ upādāyupādāya labbhamānaoḷārikasukhumākāraṃ. Manasi kubbatoti “imissā disāya ayaṃ saddo oḷāriko, sukhumo vā”ti evaṃ parikammacittena manasi karontassa. Saddesūti ye parikammacittassa visayabhūtā oḷārikā, sukhumā vā saddā, tesu. Aññataranti yattha parikammakaraṇavasena abhiṇhaṃ manasikāro pavatto, taṃ ekaṃ saddaṃ. Yadi abhiññācittampi parikammena gahitameva ārammaṇaṃ karoti, ko pana tassa, imassa vā visesoti? Vuccate – parikammacittaṃ asutassa gahaṇato saddamattaṃ gaṇhāti, abhiññācittaṃ pana asutampi gaṇhantaṃ savanākārena gahaṇato atthāvabodhassa paccayabhāveneva gaṇhātīti ayametesaṃ viseso. Sutakovidāti pariyattiyaṃ chekā.

1059-64. Because one should first advert to the gross sound and afterwards to the subtle sound, it is said, “both the great and the subtle.” For the purpose of familiarization, one should first advert to all gross sounds, beginning with those of lions and other creatures in the forest, and then in due order to the subtle sounds. Similarly, in the eastern and other directions, one should fix in mind the sign of sounds, both gross and subtle. For that meditator, those sounds become evident even to the natural mind, but they are exceedingly evident to the preparatory mind. “His” refers to that meditator. “The sign of sound” refers to the gross or subtle aspect of the sound, which is obtained by repeatedly taking up the sound as described. “Fixing it in mind” refers to the meditator who, with the preparatory mind, attends thus: “In this direction, this sound is gross or subtle.” “Among sounds” refers to those gross or subtle sounds that have become the object of the preparatory mind. “Any one” refers to a single sound on which frequent attention has been applied by way of the preparatory practice. If the direct-knowledge mind also takes as its object that which was grasped by the preparation, what then is the difference between them? It is said: the preparatory mind, in grasping what is unheard, grasps merely the sound; but the direct-knowledge mind, while also grasping what is unheard, grasps it in the manner of hearing, precisely as a condition for understanding the meaning—this is the distinction between them. “Skilled in what is heard” means skilled in the scriptural teachings.

1065-6. Thāmajātanti jātathāmaṃ, daḷhabhāvappattanti attho. Vaḍḍhetabbaṃ pādakajjhānārammaṇaṃ kittakanti āha “etthantaragata”ntiādi. Pādakajjhānassa hi ārammaṇabhūtaṃ [V 2.0204] kasiṇanimittaṃ “ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ pharatū”ti manasi karitvā pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjantassa kasiṇanimittaṃ tattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati. So samāpattito vuṭṭhāya puna pādakajjhānaṃ asamāpajjitvāpi anekappabhedepi sadde āvajjati subhāvitabhāvanattā. Tattha aññataraṃ saddaṃ ārabbha uppannāvajjanānantaraṃ cattāri, pañca vā javanāni uppajjanti, tesu pacchimaṃ iddhicittaṃ hoti. Evaṃ yattakaṃ saddaṃ icchati, tattakaṃ tattha gataṃ āvajjitvā abhiññāñāṇena jānāti. Yena pana evaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ avaḍḍhitaṃ, tena punapi pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitabbameva. So hi taṃ ṭhānagatasaddaṃ pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvāva tato [M 2.0274] vuṭṭhāya abhiññācittena suṇāti. Tato eva hi “pādakārammaṇena…pe… suṇātīti sāsaṅkaṃ vadatī”ti (visuddhi. mahā. 2.400) vuttaṃ. Iddhividhalābhī pana sesābhiññalābhino viya vijjamānasaddādiārammaṇamattameva akatvā āgantukarūpanimmāpanato sabbathāpi dvikkhattuṃ pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvāva taṃ nipphādeti. Ekaṅguladvaṅgula-ggahaṇañcettha sukhumasaddāpekkhāya kataṃ.

1065-6. "Thāmajāta" means one in whom strength has arisen, that is, one who has attained a state of firmness. Regarding how much the object of the base jhāna should be expanded, it is said, "gone within this extent," and so on. For one entering the base jhāna, having made the mental resolve, "May the kasiṇa sign, which is the object of the base jhāna, pervade this much space," the kasiṇa sign pervades that much space and remains. Having emerged from that attainment, even without re-entering the base jhāna, one attends to sounds of various kinds because the meditation is well-developed. There, taking a certain sound as object, after the arising of adverting, four or five impulsions arise, of which the last is the mind of psychic power. Thus, whatever sound one wishes, having attended to it as it has gone there, one knows it with the knowledge of direct knowledge. However, for one by whom the kasiṇa sign has not been thus expanded, it is necessary to enter the base jhāna again. For only by entering the base jhāna and emerging from it can one hear that sound which has gone to that place with the mind of direct knowledge. Hence, it is said, "with the base as object... one hears," which is stated with reservation. One who has attained the various psychic powers, however, unlike those who have attained the other direct knowledges, does not merely take existing sounds and so on as their object; rather, on account of creating an adventitious form, they accomplish it only after entering the base jhāna twice in every case. And the taking of one or two finger-breadths here is done with respect to subtle sounds.

1068. Suṇantoti evaṃ paricchinditvā paricchinditvā savanena vasikatābhiñño hutvā yathāvajjite suṇanto. Pāṭiyekkampīti ekajjhaṃ pavattamānepi yāva brahmalokā ekakolāhalaṃ katvā uṭṭhite saṅkhabherīpaṇavādisadde paccekaṃ vatthubhedena vavatthāpetukāmatāya sati “ayaṃ saṅkhasaddo, ayaṃ bherīsaddo, ayaṃ paṇavasaddo”tiādinā paccekaṃyeva vavatthāpetuṃ sakkotiyevāti. Dibbasotañāṇavaṇṇanā.

1068. "Suṇanto" means: having become one whose direct knowledge is mastered in hearing by thus defining and defining, one hears as one has attended. "Pāṭiyekkaṃ" means: even when sounds of conches, drums, tambourines, and so on arise simultaneously, making a single great noise up to the Brahmā world, if there is a desire to determine each individually according to the difference in their source, one is indeed able to determine each one separately, thinking, "this is the sound of a conch, this is the sound of a drum, this is the sound of a tambourine," and so on. This is the description of the knowledge of the divine ear.

1069-73. Cetopariyamānasanti pariyātīti pariyaṃ, sarāgādivasena paricchijja jānātīti attho. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gati attho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho hotīti. Cetaso pariyaṃ cetopariyaṃ, manasi bhavanti mānasaṃ, ñāṇaṃ, cetopariyañca taṃ mānasañcāti cetopariyamānasaṃ. Dibbacakkhuvasenevāti dibbacakkhuupanissayeneva. Tañhi etassa uppādane parikammaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā idaṃ dibbacakkhuvaseneva pavattati, tasmā. Dibbena cakkhunāti dibbasadisatādīhi “dibbacakkhū”ti laddhavohārena dibbacakkhuñāṇena disvāti sambandho. Hadayanti na hadayavatthu, atha kho hadayamaṃsapesi. Yaṃ bahi kamalamakuḷasaṇṭhānaṃ anto kosātakīphalasadisanti vuccati. Tañhi nissāya idāni [M 2.0275] vuccamānaṃ lohitaṃ tiṭṭhati. Hadayavatthu pana imaṃ lohitaṃ nissāya pavattati. Lohitaṃ disvāti lohitassa vaṇṇaṃ disvā. Dibbacakkhunopi hi vaṇṇameva dissati. Teneva [V 2.0205] hi taṃ cakkhusadisattā “cakkhū”ti vuccati. Parassāti aññassa. Yathā hi yo paro na hoti, so attā, evaṃ yo attā na hoti, so paro. Kathaṃ pana dibbacakkhunā lohitassa vaṇṇadassanena paracittaṃ viññeyyanti āha “somanassayute”tiādi. Lohitanti rattaṃ nigrodhaphalasamānavaṇṇaṃ. Kāḷakanti jambusadisavaṇṇaṃ. Tilatelūpamanti anena pasannabhāvamāha.

1069-73. The term "cetopariya" means "knowing the range of the mind," that is, discerning it by distinguishing states such as lust, etc.; for of those roots (`dhātu`) of which 'going' (gati) is the meaning, 'understanding' (buddhi) is also their meaning. "Cetopariyaṃ" refers to the range of the mind, while "mānasaṃ" means "mental," "knowledge," and thus "cetopariyamānasaṃ" combines both—knowledge of the range of the mind. "By means of the divine eye" refers to the support of the divine eye alone, for this is its preparatory work. "Therefore" means: because this proceeds by means of the divine eye alone, therefore... "With the divine eye" is connected with "having seen with the knowledge of the divine eye," which has obtained the designation "divine eye" because of its similarity to the divine, and so on. "Heart" here does not mean the heart-base, but rather the piece of heart-flesh—described externally as shaped like a lotus bud and internally resembling a kosātakī fruit. For depending on this, the blood now being spoken of is established. The heart-base, however, proceeds in dependence on this blood. "Having seen the blood" means having perceived the color of the blood, for the divine eye, too, sees only color. It is precisely because of this similarity to the eye that it is called an "eye." "Of another" means of someone else. For just as one who is not another is self, so one who is not self is another. But how can one discern another’s mind by seeing the color of the blood with the divine eye? This is explained: "accompanied by joy," etc. "Red" refers to a color resembling a banyan fruit. "Dark" refers to a color like a jambu fruit. "Like sesame oil" indicates its clear nature.

Kathaṃ pana citte somanassa sahagatādimhi sati kammajassa lohitassa vividhavaṇṇabhāvāpattīti? Kiñcāpi hadayavatthusannissitabhūtāni kammajāneva, taṃ pana lohitaṃ kammajamevāti natthi catusantatirūpassapi tattha labbhamānattā. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “idaṃ rūpaṃ somanassindriyasamuṭṭhānaṃ, idaṃ domanassindriyasamuṭṭhānaṃ, idaṃ upekkhindriyasamuṭṭhānanti parassa hadayalohitavaṇṇaṃ passitvā”ti (visuddhi. 2.401) vuttaṃ. Evampi yaṃ tattha acittajaṃ, tassa yathāvuttavaṇṇabhedena na bhavitabbanti? Bhavitabbaṃ sesasantatirūpānaṃ tadanuvattanato. Yathā hi gamanādīsu cittajarūpāni utujakammajāhārajarūpehi anuvattīyanti, aññathā kāyassa desantarappattiyeva na siyāti, evamidhāpi cittajarūpaṃ sesasantatirūpehi anuvattīyati, pasādakodhavelāsu ca cakkhussa vaṇṇabhedāpattiyeva tassatthassa nidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tasmā somanassādiyuttacittānurūpaṃ uppannacittasamuṭṭhānarūpavasena sesatisamuṭṭhānarūpānampi nānāvaṇṇatā hotiyevāti suṭṭhu vuttaṃ “lohitaṃ lohitaṃ siyā”tiādi. Disvā hadayalohitanti paṭhamaṃ tāva anumānañāṇena [M 2.0276] lohitaṃ disvā. Kātabbaṃ thāmataṃ gatanti uppādetvā thāmabhāvaṃ gataṃ kātabbaṃ.

But how, when the mind is accompanied by joy and so on, does the kamma-born blood attain a state of various colors? Although the elements dependent on the heart-base are indeed kamma-born, it is not that the blood is only kamma-born, because the material form of the four continuities is also found there. For this very reason, it is said in the commentary: "This material form arises from the joy faculty, this from the displeasure faculty, this from the equanimity faculty—having seen the color of another’s heart-blood" (Visuddhimagga 2.401). Even so, should that which is not mind-born there not have the aforementioned color-distinctions? It should be so, because the remaining continuities of material form follow that. Just as in actions like walking, the mind-born material forms are followed by material forms born of temperature, kamma, and nutriment—otherwise the body’s movement from one place to another would not be possible—so too here, the mind-born material form is followed by the remaining continuities of material form. And at times of serenity or anger, the variation in the eye’s color should be seen as an illustration of this matter. Therefore, it is well said, "The blood may be red," and so on, because in accordance with a mind associated with joy, etc., by means of the arisen mind-originated matter, the matter originated from the other three sources also indeed comes to have various colors. "Having seen the heart-blood" means: first, having seen the blood with inferential knowledge. "To be made to have attained strength" means: having produced it, it should be brought to a state of strength.

Cetopariyañāṇañhi uppādetukāmena yoginā dibbacakkhulābhinā eva satā heṭṭhā vuttanayena rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ abhinīhārakkhamaṃ katvā ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbena cakkhunā parassa hadayamaṃsapesiṃ nissāya vattamānassa lohitassa vaṇṇadassanena idāni imassa cittaṃ “somanassasahagata”nti vā “domanassasahagata”nti vā “upekkhāsahagata”nti vā nayaggāhavasena vavatthāpetvā pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya “imassa cittaṃ jānāmī”ti parikammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Kālasatampi kālasahassampi punappunaṃ pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tatheva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Tassevaṃ dibbena cakkhunā hadayalohitavaṇṇadassanādividhinā paṭipajjantassa “idāni cetopariyañāṇaṃ uppajjissatī”ti yaṃ tadā pavattatīti vavatthāpitaṃ cittaṃ, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjanaṃ tīṇi cattāri vā javanāni kāmāvacarāni javanti. Catutthaṃ, pañcamaṃ vā abhiññācittaṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānikaṃ[V 2.0206]. Tattha yaṃ tena appanācittena sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ, idaṃ cetopariyañāṇaṃ. Tañhi yattha anena parikammaṃ kataṃ, taṃ parassa cittaṃ paccakkhato paṭivijjhantaṃ vibhāventameva hutvā pavattati, rūpaṃ viya ca dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ, saddaṃ viya ca dibbasotañāṇaṃ. Tato paraṃ pana kāmāvacaracittehi sarāgādivavatthāpanaṃ hoti nīlādivavatthāpanaṃ viya.

To develop the knowledge of encompassing minds, a yogī who has attained the divine eye should, while being such, make the fourth jhāna of the form realm, endowed with eight factors and capable of being directed, according to the method stated below. Then, by expanding the light and seeing with the divine eye the color of the blood present in dependence on another's piece of heart-flesh, they should determine by way of grasping the method whether that person's mind is now accompanied by joy, displeasure, or equanimity. After determining this, they should enter the base jhāna and emerge, performing the preparatory work, "I will know this one's mind." This should be practiced a hundred or a thousand times, entering and emerging from the base jhāna again and again, and one should proceed thus. As they proceed in this way—by the method of observing the color of the heart's blood with the divine eye, and so on—taking as its object the mind that was determined as, "now the knowledge of encompassing minds will arise," a mind-door adverting occurs, and three or four sense-sphere impulsions run. The fourth or fifth is the direct-knowledge mind, belonging to the fourth jhāna of the form realm. The knowledge associated with that absorption mind is the knowledge of encompassing minds. For it proceeds by directly penetrating and clarifying the other's mind that was the object of the preparatory work, just as the knowledge of the divine eye does with forms and the knowledge of the divine ear does with sounds. Thereafter, the determination of 'with lust,' and so on, occurs by means of sense-sphere minds, just as one determines colors like 'blue,' and so on.

1074-5. Evamadhigatassa pana cetopariyañāṇassa thāmagamanavidhānampi adhigamavidhānasadisameva, tadevettha ācariyena dassitaṃ. Evaṃ thāmagatetiādi thāmagamanānisaṃsadassanaṃ. Sabbamevāti idaṃ “kāmāvacaracittaṃ, rūpārūpesu [M 2.0277] mānasa”nti ubhayapadenapi sambandhitabbaṃ, catupaṇṇāsavidhaṃ kāmāvacaracittaṃ, pañcadasarūpāvacaracittaṃ, dvādasaarūpāvacaracittanti sabbameva, paccekaṃ sarāgādippabhedakaṃ vijānātīti attho. Puthujjanassa vasenāyaṃ abhiññākathāti lokuttaracittaṃ idha anuddhaṭaṃ. Tampi hi uparimo, sadiso vā ariyo heṭṭhimassa, sadisassa ca cittaṃ jānāti, heṭṭhimo pana uparimassa cittaṃ na jānāti. Yathā cetaṃ, evaṃ arūpāvacarajjhāne akatābhiniveso puthujjano, sekhopi vā arūpāvacaracittaṃ na jānāti. Aṭṭhasamāpattikassa pana vasena idhārūpāvacaracittassāpi jānanaṃ vuttaṃ. Arahā pana āruppe akatābhinivesopi tappaṭicchādakaavijjāya vihatattā tampi jānātiyeva. Cetopariyañāṇavaṇṇanā.

1074-5. For one who has attained the knowledge of the penetration of minds in this way, the method of establishing its stability is similar to the method of attainment. This is what the teacher has shown here. Thus, the phrase 'thus having attained stability' and so forth, indicates the benefit of attaining stability. The phrase 'all indeed' should be connected with both clauses: 'sense-sphere mind' and 'mind in the form and formless realms.' It refers to all fifty-four types of sense-sphere mind, fifteen types of form-sphere mind, and twelve types of formless-sphere mind—all of which are known individually as with lust and so forth. This is the meaning. This discussion of supernormal knowledge is from the perspective of an ordinary person, so the supramundane mind is not included here. For a superior noble one, or one of equal attainment, knows the mind of an inferior one and of one of equal attainment, but an inferior one does not know the mind of a superior one. Similarly, an ordinary person who has not made application to the formless jhānas—or even a trainee—does not know formless-sphere mind. However, with regard to one who has attained the eight attainments, the knowledge of formless-sphere mind is also mentioned here. But an arahant, even if not having made application to the formless attainments, still knows them because the ignorance that conceals them has been destroyed. This is the exposition of the knowledge of the penetration of minds.

1076-7. Pubbe atītajātīsu nivāsā nivutthā attano santāne pavattā, saparaviññāṇehi gocarāsevanāya āsevitā ca khandhā pubbenivāsā. Paraviññāṇaviññātāpi hi pubbe nivasiṃsu etthāti pubbenivāsāti vuccanti, te pana chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇādīsu buddhānaṃyeva visayā, pubbe nivāsesu sarūpavibhāvakaṃ ñāṇaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ. Tena. Tadanussatīti tesaṃ pubbenivāsānaṃ anussati. Heṭṭhā tīsu jhānesu yathārahaṃ pītisukhehi kāyacittānaṃ sampīṇanāya cattāri jhānāni samāpajjitabbānīti āha “jhānāni panā”tiādi. Aññathā pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvāyevāti vuttaṃ siyā. Yāya nisajjāya nisinnassa anussaraṇārambho, sā idha sabbapacchimā nisajjā.

1076-7. In past, previous births, the abodes where one dwelt and passed through in one's own continuum, and the aggregates that were frequented by seeking objects with one's own and others' consciousness—these are called past abodes. For even the aggregates cognized by others' consciousness dwelt there in the past; hence they are called past abodes. However, these are only within the domain of the Buddhas, such as in recalling broken lineages, etc. The knowledge that reveals the nature of past abodes is the knowledge of past abodes. By that, the recollection of those past abodes is called 'recollection of that'. Below, it is said, beginning with 'the jhānas, however,' that the four jhānas should be attained as appropriate for the exhilaration of body and mind with joy and happiness in the three lower jhānas. Otherwise, it might be said that one must first attain the base jhāna. The sitting posture in which one is seated when the recollection begins is here the very last sitting posture.

1078-80. Tato pabhuti…pe… kkamāti tasmiṃ bhave purimabhavādīsu kataṃ sabbampi saṅgahetvā sabbamāvajjitabbantiādinā visuṃ visuṃ rattindivādivasena dasseti. Divase [M 2.0278] rattiyaṃ katanti sabbapacchimanisajjāto paṭṭhāya āsanapaññāpanaṃ senāsanappavesananti paṭilomena [V 2.0207] sakalaṃ rattindivaṃ katakiccaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ. Katamāvajjitabbanti yaṃ etthantare katakiccaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ paṭilomakkameneva āvajjitabbanti attho. Ettakaṃ pana pakaticittassapi pākaṭaṃ, parikammacittassa pana atipākaṭameva. Sace panettha kiñci na pākaṭaṃ hoti, puna pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya āvajjitabbaṃ, ettakena dīpe jalite viya pākaṭaṃ hoti. Pādakajjhānasamāpajjanañhi satthakassa viya nisānasilā satipaññānaṃ nisitabhāvāvahaṃ, tasmā tā taṃsamāpajjanena paramanepakkappattā honti. Purimasmiṃ bhaveti imamhā bhavā anantare purimasmiṃ bhave.

1078-80. From that time onward... and so on... It shows, beginning with 'all should be adverted to, having gathered all that was done in that existence, in previous existences, and so forth,' separately, by day and night, and so on. The phrase 'what was done during the day and night' means that all actions performed throughout the day and night, from the very last sitting posture onwards—such as arranging seats and entering lodgings—should be adverted to in reverse order. The meaning of 'what is to be adverted to' is that whatever was done in between should all be adverted to in reverse sequence. However, this much is clear even to the ordinary mind, but for the preparatory mind, it is exceedingly clear. If anything here remains unclear, one should re-enter the base jhāna, emerge, and then advert to it. By this means, it becomes as clear as a lighted lamp. For entering the base jhāna is like a whetstone for a knife, bringing sharpness to mindfulness and wisdom; therefore, through this attainment, they reach supreme dexterity. The phrase 'in the previous existence' means the existence immediately preceding this one.

1081. Nibbattaṃ nāmarūpañcāti attano paccayehi nibbattanāmarūpaṃ. Sādhukanti suṭṭhu aparihāpetvā āvajjitabbaṃ. Pahoti hi imissā abhiññāya katādhikāro bhikkhu paṭhamavāreneva paṭisandhiṃ ugghāṭetvā cutikkhaṇe nāmarūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ kātuṃ, tathā asakkontenāpi dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā pādakajjhānameva punappunaṃ samāpajjitabbaṃ, tato ca vuṭṭhāya punappunaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ. Āvajjantena ca pana paṭhamaṃ rūpaṃ āvajjitvā pacchā nāmaṃ āvajjitabbanti ācariyā. Apare pana vipariyāyena vadanti.

1081. The phrase 'and the arisen name-and-form' means the name-and-form that arises because of its own conditions. The phrase 'thoroughly' means it should be well adverted to without neglecting it. For a monk who has made the necessary preparations for this supernormal knowledge, it is possible to uncover rebirth-linking in the first attempt and make the name-and-form at the moment of death the object. Even if one cannot do so, without abandoning the endeavor, one should repeatedly attain the base jhāna and, upon emerging, advert again and again. When adverting, some teachers say one should first advert to form and then to name. Others, however, teach the opposite order.

Tattha pacchimanisajjāto pabhuti yāva paṭisandhito ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattañāṇaṃ atītajātīsu nivutthadhammārammaṇābhāvato pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ nāma na hoti, taṃ pana parikammañāṇameva. Yadā panassa paṭisandhiṃ atikkamma cutikkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāmarūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjati, tasmiṃ niruddhe vuttanayena appanācittaṃ [M 2.0279] uppajjati, tena sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ nāma. Tenāha “yadā panā”tiādi.

There, the knowledge that arises from the time of the last sitting until rebirth-linking, taking that as its object, is not called knowledge of the recollection of past abodes, because there is no object of phenomena dwelt in in past lives; it is, however, only preparatory knowledge. But when, having passed beyond rebirth-linking, mind-door adverting arises taking as object the name-and-form that arose at the moment of death, and upon its cessation, absorption mind arises in the manner described, the knowledge associated with it is called knowledge of the recollection of past abodes. Therefore, it is said, beginning with 'but when,' and so forth.

Etthāha – kiṃ ekeneva abhiññācittena cutikkhaṇe pavattanāmarūpaṃ sabbampi ārammaṇaṃ karoti, udāhu aññena aññenāti. Kiñcettha yadi ekeneva, dūrato cittapaṭaṃ pekkhantassa viya anirūpitarūpena vavatthānaṃ hoti. Yadi ca aññena aññena, visuṃ visuṃ pādakajjhānasamāpajjanādinā bhavitabbanti? Ubhayathāpi na doso. Iddhivisayassa hi acinteyyattā ekenapi abhiññācittena nāmarūpe passanto nirūpitarūpeneva passati, na anirūpitarūpeneva passati, aññenapi vā paṭhamameva pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya samāhitacittena [V 2.0208] kataparikammassa pavattitattā puna samāpajjanaṃ vinā āvajjitvā ārammaṇaṃ karotiyevāti. Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇavaṇṇanā.

Here it is asked: Does it make all the name-and-form occurring at the moment of death its object with just one supernormal knowledge mind, or with separate ones? And if with just one, then the determination would be like someone looking at a painted cloth from a distance—its form unclear. And if with separate ones, would one have to attain the base jhāna and so forth separately for each? In either case, there is no fault. For due to the inconceivability of the sphere of psychic power, even seeing name-and-form with a single supernormal knowledge mind, one sees it with its form determined, not undetermined. Alternatively, having first attained the base jhāna and emerged, one whose mind is concentrated because preparatory work has already been performed can take the object simply by adverting to it without needing to re-enter the jhāna. Exposition of the Knowledge of the Recollection of Past Abodes.

1086-8. Dibbacakkhunāti dibbasadisattā, dibbavihāravasena paṭilabhitabbattā, attanā ca dibbavihārasannissitattā mahājutikatādīhi vā dibbaṃ, rūpadassanaṭṭhena cakkhumivāti cakkhu. Yathā hi maṃsacakkhu viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ samavisamaṃ ācikkhantaṃ viya pavattati, idaṃ pana tato sātisayaṃ cakkhukiccakārīti dibbañca taṃ cakkhu cāti dibbacakkhu, tena dibbacakkhunā. Kasiṇārammaṇanti aṭṭhannampi kasiṇānaṃ vasena kasiṇārammaṇaṃ. Abhinīhārakkhamaṃ katvāti cuddasavidhena cittaparidamanena aṭṭhaṅgasampannatākaraṇena abhinīhārakkhamaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇābhimukhaṃ pesanārahaṃ pesanayogyaṃ katvā. “Tejo…pe… kasiṇampi vā āsannaṃ kātabba”nti pāṭhaseso. Āsannaṃ kātabbanti dibbacakkhuñāṇuppattiyā samīpabhūtaṃ kāraṇabhūtaṃ kātabbaṃ, tattha upacārajjhānaṃ paguṇataraṃ katvā [M 2.0280] taṃ vaḍḍhetvā icchitakkhaṇe upaṭṭhānayogyaṃ katvā ṭhapetabbanti vuttaṃ hoti. Etthāti imasmiṃ dibbacakkhunā rūpadassanavisaye. Seṭṭhanti paridīpitanti ālokakasiṇasseva pabhāvissajjanasabhāvena ālokakaraṇena itarehi visiṭṭhattā visiṭṭhanti paridīpitaṃ.

1086-8. “With the divine eye”—because it is similar to the divine, because it is obtainable through the power of divine abiding, and because one depends on divine abiding oneself; or because it is divine due to great radiance and so on, and because it is like an eye in the sense of seeing forms. Just as the fleshly eye, based on consciousness, functions as if reporting what is even and uneven, this surpasses that and performs the function of an eye more excellently—thus it is both divine and an eye, hence “divine eye,” and the text says “with the divine eye.” “With a kasiṇa as object”—the object is a kasiṇa by means of any of the eight kasiṇas. “Having made it suitable for directing”—having made it suitable for directing, worthy of being directed toward divine eye knowledge, by subduing the mind in fourteen ways and fulfilling the eight factors. “The fire...pe...or the kasiṇa should be brought near”—this is the rest of the passage. “Should be brought near”—it should be made proximate, a cause for the arising of divine eye knowledge. There, having made the access jhāna more familiar, having developed it, one should establish it so that it is ready to appear at the desired moment—this is what is meant. “Here”—in this matter of seeing forms with the divine eye. “Best”—this is explained as 'distinguished'; the light kasiṇa is so described because, by its nature of emitting radiance and producing illumination, it is superior to the others.

1089-90. Uppādetvāti paṭhamajjhānaniddese vuttanayena upacārajjhānuppādanena uppādetvā. Upacārajjhānuppattiyā hi saddhiṃ paṭibhāganimittuppatti. Yasmā pādakajjhānaṃ vijjamāneyeva āloke appanāvasena pavattimattaṃ vinā attano balena ālokaṃ pharituṃ na sakkoti, nāpi yathāpatthaṭaṃ thāvaraṃ kātuṃ, parikammaṃ pana tadubhayampi kātuṃ samatthaṃ, tasmā upacārabhūmiyaṃyeva taṃ vaḍḍhetabbanti āha “upacārabhūmiya”ntiādi. Upacārabhūmīti cettha ālokassa thāvarakaraṇavasappavattaṃ parikammacittamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Appananti jhānavasena appanaṃ. Na hi akataparikammassa abhiññāvasena appanā sijjhati. Tenāha “pādakajjhānanissita”nti. Pādakajjhānanissitanti pādakajjhānārammaṇaṃ hoti, na dibbacakkhussa parikammanissitaṃ parikammārammaṇaṃ hoti, tathā ca sati ālokavaḍḍhanābhāvato rūpadassanaṃ na siyāti adhippāyo.

“Having generated”: As explained in the method for the first jhāna, it means generating by means of generating access jhāna. For with the arising of access jhāna comes the arising of the counterpart sign. Since the base jhāna, although existing, is unable by its own power to pervade with light, apart from its mere occurrence by way of absorption, nor to make it stable as spread, whereas the preliminary work is capable of doing both, therefore it should be developed only in the access stage—thus it is said, “in the access stage,” etc. Here, “access stage” should be understood as precisely the preliminary consciousness that proceeds by way of making the light stable. “Absorption”: It is absorption by way of jhāna. For one who has not done the preliminary work, absorption by way of direct knowledge does not succeed. Therefore it is said, “dependent on the base jhāna.” “Dependent on the base jhāna”: It has the base jhāna as its object; it does not have as its object the object of the preliminary work for the divine eye.
