That being so, because there would be no increase of light, the seeing of forms would not occur—this is the meaning.

1091-3. Anto…pe… bhaveti antogatameva rūpagataṃ passitabbaṃ bhave, na bahiddhā vikkhepuppattihetubhāvato [V 2.0209] passitabbaṃ dibbacakkhunāti adhippāyo. Na hi āloke pharitepi maṃsacakkhussa āpāthaṃ hoti. Parikammassa vāro hi atikkamati tāvadeti idha parikammaṃ nāma yathāvuttakasiṇārammaṇaṃ upacārajjhānaṃ, taṃ rūpagataṃ passato na pavattati, kasiṇālokavasena ca rūpagatadassanaṃ kasiṇāloko ca parikammavasenāti tadubhayampi parikammassa [M 2.0281] appavattiyā na hoti. Tenāha “ālokopī”tiādi. Tasmiṃ antarahite rūpagatampi na ca dissati, rūpagataṃ passato parikammassa vāro atikkamati, parikammapasutassa kasiṇārammaṇañāṇaṃ hotīti rūpagataṃ dissati, kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti āha “tenā”tiādi.

“Internally...should be”: The form that has become internal should be seen, not one that is external, because it is a cause for the arising of distraction, and thus should not be seen with the divine eye—this is the meaning. For indeed, even when light is pervaded, it does not come within the range of the fleshly eye. “The turn of the preliminary work passes at that point”: Here, preliminary work means the access jhāna with the kasiṇa as its object, as previously described. For one who sees the form, it (the preliminary work) does not proceed; and the seeing of forms by means of the kasiṇa-light, and the kasiṇa-light itself by means of preliminary work—both of these do not occur due to the non-proceeding of the preliminary work. Therefore, it is said, “Even the light...” and so on. When that (light) disappears, the form is also not seen. When one is seeing the form, the turn of the preliminary work passes. For one devoted to preliminary work, knowledge with the kasiṇa as its object arises, and thus the form is seen. As for how one should proceed, it is said, “Therefore...” and so on.

1094-9. Evaṃ anukkamenāti punappunaṃ pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tato vuṭṭhāya abhiṇhaṃ ālokapharaṇena. Āloko thāmavāti ālokagato ciraṭṭhāyī siyā, tathā ca sati tattha sucirampi rūpagataṃ passateva. Tena vuttaṃ “āloko etthā”tiādi. Svāyamattho tiṇukkūpamāya vibhāvetabboti dassento āha “tiṇukkāyā”tiādi. Eko kira rattiyaṃ tiṇukkāya maggaṃ paṭipajji, tassa sā tiṇukkā vijjhāyi, athassa samavisamāni na paññāyiṃsu, so taṃ tiṇukkaṃ bhūmiyaṃ ghaṃsitvā puna ujjālesi, sā pajjalitvā purimālokato mahantaramālokaṃ akāsi, evaṃ punappunaṃ vijjhātaṃ ujjālayato kamena sūriyo uṭṭhāsi, sūriye uṭṭhite “ukkāya kammaṃ natthī”ti taṃ chaḍḍetvā divasampi agamāsi. Tattha ukkāloko viya parikammakāle kasiṇāloko, ukkāya vijjhātāya samavisamānaṃ adassanaṃ viya rūpagataṃ passato parikammassa vārātikkamena āloke antarahite rūpagatānaṃ adassanaṃ, ukkāya ghaṃsanaṃ viya punappunaṃ pādakajjhānasamāpajjanaṃ, ukkāya purimālokato mahantatarālokakaraṇaṃ viya puna parikammaṃ karoto balavatarālokapharaṇaṃ, sūriyuṭṭhānaṃ viya thāmagatālokassa yathāvaḍḍhitaparicchedaṃ pharitvā avaṭṭhānaṃ, tiṇukkaṃ chaḍḍetvā divasampi gamanaṃ viya padittālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā thāmagatenālokena divasampi rūpadassanaṃ. Ettāvatā ca dibbacakkhussa nānāvajjanaparikammañceva dibbacakkhuñāṇañca dassitaṃ, na tassa uppattikkamoti [M 2.0282] taṃ dassetuṃ “uppādanakkamopī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā suviññeyyameva. Tāni cattāri pañca vāti potthakesu likhanti. “Tīṇi cattāri vā panā”ti pāṭho.

“Thus gradually” means by repeatedly entering and emerging from the base jhāna, then continuously pervading with light. “The light becomes strong” means the light should persist for a long time, and with that, one can see forms there for a very long time. Hence it is said, “The light is here,” etc. This meaning should be illustrated by the simile of the grass torch, as shown by the phrase “like a grass torch,” etc. It is said that once a man walked a path at night with a grass torch. When his torch was extinguished, he could no longer discern the even and uneven ground. So he rubbed the torch against the ground and relit it. When it flared up, it produced a much brighter light than before. By repeatedly relighting it as it was extinguished, gradually the sun rose. When the sun rose, thinking, “There is no more need for the torch,” he discarded it and continued his journey even during the day. Here, the light of the torch is like the light of the kasiṇa during the preliminary stage. The inability to see the even and uneven ground when the torch is extinguished is like the non-seeing of forms when the light disappears because the turn of the preliminary work has passed. Rubbing the torch is like repeatedly entering the base jhāna. The torch producing a brighter light than before is like the stronger pervasion of light when the preliminary work is done again. The rising of the sun is like the firmly established light pervading its range as developed and remaining established. Discarding the torch and continuing by day is like seeing forms throughout the day with the firmly established light after having developed the radiant light. By this much, both the varied preliminary work of the divine eye and the knowledge of the divine eye are shown, but not its process of arising. To explain that, it is said, “The process of arising, too,” etc. This is easily understood by the method explained below. “Four or five” are written in the texts. The reading “three or four, or alternatively” is also found.

1100. Tattha atthasādhakacittanti yadatthāyesa paṭipanno, tassa tadatthasādhanato atthasādhakabhūtaṃ [V 2.0210] cittaṃ. Tasmiñhi uppanne maṃsacakkhussa anāpāthayogyaṃ antokucchigataṃ hadayavatthunissitaṃ heṭṭhāpathavītalanissitaṃ tirokuṭṭapabbatapākāragataṃ paracakkavāḷagatanti idaṃ rūpaṃ āpāthaṃ āgacchati, maṃsacakkhunā dissamānaṃ viya hoti. Tadeva cettha rūpaṃ sarūpato vibhāvanasamatthaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ viya. Na pana āvajjanaparikammavasena pavattāni pubbabhāgacittāni. Tāni hi ārammaṇaṃ karontānipi na yāthāvato taṃ vibhāvetvā pavattanti āvajjanasampaṭicchanādicittāni viyāti.

1100. Herein, “the mind accomplishing the purpose” is that mind which, for the purpose for which one is practicing, accomplishes that purpose. When it arises, a form not within the range of the physical eye—such as one inside the belly, based on the heart-base, resting beneath the earth’s surface, concealed by walls, mountains, or ramparts, or in another world-system—comes into range. It appears as if visible to the physical eye. That very mind here is capable of discerning the form in its true nature, like eye-consciousness. But the preceding mind-moments that occur through the preliminary work of adverting are not so. For even though they take it as an object, they do not proceed having discerned it as it really is, like the mind-moments of adverting, receiving, and so on.

1101-2. Nanu ca anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ yathākammūpagañāṇanti dve abhiññāñāṇāni atthi, kasmā tāni idha na dassitānīti āha “anāgataṃsañāṇassā”tiādi. Ijjhanti dibbacakkhunāti visuṃ parikammassa abhāvato dibbacakkhuñāṇapaṭilābheneva tassa parivārāni hutvā paṭiladdhāni honti. Tatoyeva hi tāni tassa paribhaṇḍañāṇānīti vuccanti. Yathā hi sinerussa parivāraṭṭhāniyāni taṃsiddhiyā siddhāni mekhalaṭṭhānāni paribhaṇḍānīti vuccanti, evaṃ imānipi dibbacakkhusiddhiyā siddhāni tassa paribhaṇḍānīti veditabbāni.

But are there not two direct knowledges, namely, the knowledge of the future and the knowledge of how beings fare according to their deeds? Why are these not shown here? He said, “Of the knowledge of the future,” etc. “They succeed through the divine eye”: because there is no separate preliminary work for them, they are attained by the very attainment of the divine eye knowledge, having become its retinue. For this very reason, they are called its accessory knowledges. Just as the mekhala regions (girdles) of Mount Sineru, which stand in the place of its retinue and are accomplished through its accomplishment, are called its accessories, so too these knowledges, accomplished through the accomplishment of the divine eye, should be understood as its accessories.

Hotu tāva evametaṃ, cutūpapātañāṇaṃ pana kiṃ na dassitanti āha “cutūpapātañāṇampī”tiādi. Dibbacakkhuñāṇameva hi cutiyaṃ, upapattiyañca rūpaṃ vibhāventaṃ cutūpapāte pavattattā “cutūpapātañāṇa”nti vuccati, avasesarūpavibhāvanakāle [M 2.0283] “dibbacakkhū”ti vuccati, tasmā paramatthato nāmadvayena āgataṃ ekameva ñāṇaṃ, dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ cutūpapātañāṇanti pana byañjanatoyeva nānanti. Katthaci manomayañāṇantipi visuṃ abhiññāñāṇaṃ āgataṃ, taṃ atthato iddhividhañāṇameva. Dibbacakkhuñāṇavaṇṇanā.

Let that be so for now. But why was the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings not shown? He said, “The knowledge of the passing away and reappearance as well.” Indeed, the divine eye knowledge itself, when discerning forms in passing away and reappearance, is called “knowledge of passing away and reappearance” because it occurs with respect to passing away and reappearance. When discerning the remaining forms, it is called “divine eye.” Therefore, in the ultimate sense, it is a single knowledge that has come with two names. However, “divine eye knowledge” and “knowledge of passing away and reappearance” are different only in phrasing. In some places, the knowledge of the mind-made body is also mentioned as a separate direct knowledge, but in meaning, it is the same as the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power. The explanation of the divine eye knowledge.

1103. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Anena tarenāti anena abhidhammāvatāranāmakena tarena.

1103. “Here”: in this Dispensation. “By this means”: that is, by this means called the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus is named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī.

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

The Commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Abhiññāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Exposition of Direct Knowledge is finished.

17. Sattarasamo paricchedo

17. The Seventeenth Chapter.

Abhiññārammaṇaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Objects of Direct Knowledge.

1104-5. Pañca [V 2.0211] iddhividhādīnīti –

The five, beginning with the kinds of psychic power –

“Iddhividhaṃ dibbasotaṃ, paracittavijānanā;

Pubbenivāsānussati, dibbacakkhūti pañcadhā”ti. –

“The kinds of psychic power, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of past lives, and the divine eye—thus are they fivefold.” –

Evamāgatā pañca. Sattābhiññā imā panāti atītaṃsañāṇassa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇe, manomayañāṇassa ca iddhividhañāṇe antogadhattā vuttaṃ. Atītaṃsañāṇaṃ nāma paresaṃ paccuppannabhave yāva paṭisandhipariyosānaṃ pavattacittārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Manomayañāṇampi nāma manomayakāyābhinimmānādivasappavattaṃ iddhividhañāṇaṃ.

Thus, five are arrived at. But these are called seven abhiññās because it is said that the knowledge of the past is included in the knowledge of recollection of past lives, and the mind-made knowledge is included in the knowledge of psychic power. The knowledge of the past is the knowledge that has as its object the consciousness of others occurring in the present existence, up to the limit of rebirth-linking. And the mind-made knowledge is the knowledge of psychic power that occurs by way of creating a mind-made body and so forth.

1106. Idāni imesaṃ abhiññāñāṇānaṃ ārammaṇavinicchaye asammohatthaṃ taṃ dassetumārabhanto āha “sattanna”ntiādi[M 2.0284]. Cattāro ārammaṇattikāti parittārammaṇattiko maggārammaṇattiko atītārammaṇattiko ajjhattārammaṇattikoti ime cattāro ārammaṇattikā. Etthāti idaṃ paccāmasanaṃ kiṃ tikānaṃ, udāhu ārammaṇānanti, kiñcettha – yadi tikānaṃ, tadayuttaṃ. Na hi tikesu abhiññāñāṇāni pavattanti. Atha ārammaṇānaṃ, tampi ayuttaṃ. Na hi aññaṃ uddisitvā aññassa paccāmasanaṃ yuttanti. Yathā icchasi, tathā hotu. Bhavatu tāva tikānaṃ, nanu vuttaṃ “tikesu abhiññāñāṇāni nappavattantī”ti? Nāyaṃ virodho tikavohārena ārammaṇānaṃyeva gayhamānattā. Atha vā pana hotu ārammaṇānaṃ, nanu vuttaṃ “aññaṃ uddisitvā aññassa paccāmasanaṃ ayutta”nti. Ayampi na doso yathāvuttakāraṇenevāti.

1106. Now, to prevent confusion in determining the objects of these abhiññā knowledges, beginning to show that, he says, “of the seven,” and so on. The four triads of objects are: the limited-object triad, the path-object triad, the past-object triad, and the internal-object triad. Here, the reflection arises: does this reference concern the triads, or the objects? What is the case here? If it concerns the triads, that is unsuitable, for abhiññā knowledges do not occur in the triads. But if it concerns the objects, that too is unsuitable, for it is not fitting to refer to something else after having stated something else. Let it be as you wish. Let it be about the triads for now. But was it not said, “Abhiññā knowledges do not occur in the triads”? This is not a contradiction, because the objects themselves are grasped through the expression ‘triads’. Or else, let it be about the objects. But was it not said, “It is unsuitable to refer to something different from what was initially referred to”? This also is not a fault, for the very reason already stated.

1107-10. Parittādīsu sattasūti asatipi vatthubhede bhūmikālasantānabhedavasena bhinnesu [V 2.0212] parittamahaggataatītānāgatapaccuppannaajjhattabahiddhārammaṇavasena sattasu parittādiārammaṇavibhāgesu. Iddhividhañāṇassa maggārammaṇatāya abhāvato idha maggārammaṇattiko na labbhati. Kāyaṃ cittasannissitaṃ katvā adissamānena kāyena gantukāmoti sambandho. Cittasannissitakaraṇañca taṃ viya kāyassa adissamānasīghagatikatāvasena taggatikatāpādanaṃ. Yathā cittaṃ na dissati sīghagamanañca, evaṃ kāyampi adissamānaṃ, sīghagamanañca katvā yathicchitaṭṭhānaṃ gantukāmoti ayañhettha attho. Cittavasenāti mahaggatacittavasena pariṇāmetīti pāṭhaseso. Tenāha “taṃ mahaggate ca cittasmiṃ samāropetī”ti. Pādakajjhānañhi samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya “ayaṃ kāyo idaṃ cittaṃ viya adissamāno, sīghagamano ca hotū”ti parikammaṃ karoti, parikammaṃ pana katvā puna samāpajjitvā [M 2.0285] vuṭṭhāya tatheva parikammaṃ karonto kāyaṃ gahetvā mahaggate pādakacitte samāropeti, taggatikaṃ karoti viya, adissamānaṃ, sīghagamanañca karoti. Taṃ pana sīghagamanatthaṃ abhāvitiddhipādānaṃ viya dandhaṃ appavattitvā katipayacittavāreheva icchitaṭṭhānappattivasena daṭṭhabbaṃ, na ekacittakkhaṇeneva. “Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, citta”nti (a. ni. 1.48) hi ettha añña-ggahaṇeneva rūpadhammānaṃ gahitattā cittakkhaṇavasena rūpappavatti na yuttā. Yattha yattha ca dhammā uppajjanti, tattha tattheva bhijjanti ca, na ca iddhibalena dhammānaṃ kenaci lakkhaṇaññathattaṃ sakkā kātunti. Cittavasena rūpakāyaṃ pādakajjhāne samāropentassa kāyameva ārammaṇanti āha “kāyārammaṇato”ti, kāye vaṇṇārammaṇatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāyasannissitaṃ katvā cittanti ettha na cittaṃ kāyaṃ viya dandhaṃ dissamānaṃ karoti, kintu dandhadissamānagatikaraṇamattamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

1107-10. “Among the seven beginning with the limited”—this refers to the seven divisions of objects beginning with the limited, namely, limited, exalted, past, future, present, internal, and external objects, which are differentiated by way of difference in plane, time, and continuum, even though there is no difference in the object-base. Here, the path-object triad is not obtained because the knowledge of psychic power does not have the path as its object. The connection is: desiring to go with an invisible body, having made the body dependent on the mind. And making it dependent on the mind means producing in the body a state of swift, invisible movement like that of the mind, thus establishing its swift movement. Just as the mind is invisible and swiftly moving, so too, having made the body invisible and swiftly moving, one desires to go to any desired place; this is the meaning here. “By means of the mind” means transforming it by means of the exalted mind; this is the remainder of the text. Therefore, he said, “He focuses it on that exalted mind.” For having attained the preliminary jhāna and risen from it, one performs the preliminary work, thinking, “May this body become invisible and swift-moving like this mind.” Having done the preliminary work, one attains it again and rises, and while doing the preliminary work in the same way, one takes the body and focuses it on the exalted preliminary consciousness, making it of like movement, as it were, invisible and swift-moving. However, that swift movement should be understood as achieving the desired place over several turns of consciousness, not proceeding slowly like those with undeveloped psychic powers, and not in a single thought-moment. For it is said, “Monks, I do not see any other single thing that changes as quickly as the mind.” (AN 1.48) Here, by the inclusion of “other,” material phenomena are included, so the occurrence of form in a single thought-moment is not suitable. Wherever phenomena arise, there they also cease, and it is not possible for anyone to alter the characteristics of phenomena by psychic power. When one focuses the material body on the preliminary jhāna by means of the mind, he says that the body itself is the object, thus “from the object of the body,” which means the object is the color appearance of the body. In the phrase “having made the mind dependent on the body,” it should be understood that one does not make the mind slow and visible like the body, but merely makes its movement slow and visible.

1112-3. Anāgatamatītañca karoti visayaṃ yadāti mahādhātunidhāne mahākassapattherādīnaṃ viya anāgataṃ adhiṭṭhahantānaṃ anāgataṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, kāyavasena cittapariṇāmanakāle tadeva ciraniruddhaṃ pādakajjhānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karontānaṃ atītaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, tadā atītārammaṇaṃ, anāgatagocarañca hoti, paccuppanno gocaro paccuppannassa rūpakāyassa ārammaṇakaraṇato. Hatthiādayo abhinimminantassāpi hi kiñcāpi parikammaṃ anāgatārammaṇaṃ hoti, adhiṭṭhānacittaṃ pana paccuppannārammaṇameva. Upacārārammaṇaṃ viya hi paṭibhāganimittaṃ tena saha pātubhūtameva tassārammaṇaṃ hoti.

1112-3. When one makes the future and past an object, as in the great element-store meditation, like the great elder Mahākassapa and others who resolve upon the future, making the future their object, or when, at the time of transforming the mind by means of the body, they make the long-ceased foundational jhāna their object, thus making the past their object—then it has a past object and a future range, while the present range is due to making the present material body its object. For even when creating elephants and the like, though the preliminary work has a future object, the resolving mind has only a present object. Like the access object, the counterpart sign that has arisen together with it is its object.

1114-5. Kāyaṃ [V 2.0213] …pe… [M 2.0286] siyāti attano kāyaṃ cittavasena pariṇāmanakāle ajjhattassa kāyassa ārammaṇakaraṇato, attano cittaṃ kāyavasena pariṇāmanakāle cittassa ārammaṇakaraṇato. Vā-saddena avuttasamuccayatthena gahite attano kumāravaṇṇādiabhinimmānakāle kāyassa ārammaṇakaraṇato ca ajjhattārammaṇaṃ siyā. Bahiddhā rūpadassaneti bahiddhā hatthiassādirūpadassanakāle.

1114-5. “The body... may be”: when transforming one’s own body through the power of the mind, it makes the internal body its object; when transforming one’s own mind through the power of the body, it makes the mind its object. And when the word “or” is taken in the sense of implied combination, it may also have an internal object when creating an appearance of a young boy, etc., making the body its object. “Seeing external forms” refers to the time of seeing external forms like elephants and horses.

1116-8. Paccuppanne paritte cāti sarūpavibhāvanametaṃ. Dibbasotassa hi paccuppannova saddo ārammaṇaṃ hoti, so ca sabhāvato parittova. Kucchisaddassāti kucchiyaṃ vātasaddassa. Tattha pāṇakasaddassa pana savane bahiddhārammaṇameva. Vasitāpattassa attano vitakkavipphārasaddasavanepi ajjhattārammaṇanti vadanti, taṃ pana ekādasabhavaṅgacittato upari bhavaṅgaṃ pavattitumadatvā bhavaṅgato vuṭṭhāya āvajjanasamatthatāvasena vasitāpattasseva yujjati. “Parassa ca saddassā”ti sambandhitabbaṃ. Na hi parassa kucchisaddasavaneyeva bahiddhārammaṇaṃ hoti, atha kho parassa cittasamuṭṭhānasaddasavanepīti.

1116-8. “In the present and limited”—this is an explanation of its intrinsic nature. For the divine ear, only a present sound is an object, and that is naturally limited. “The sound of the belly” means the sound of wind in the belly. But hearing the sound of beings therein has only an external object. Some say that for one who has attained mastery, hearing the sound of one’s own thought-expansion is an internal object; however, this is fitting only for one who has attained mastery, by virtue of the capacity to advert after rising from the life-continuum, without allowing the life-continuum to proceed beyond the eleventh life-continuum consciousness. “And the sound of another” should be connected. For it is not only hearing another’s belly sound that has an external object, but also hearing a sound produced by another’s mind.

1119-22. Parittādīsūti parittamahaggataappamāṇamaggaatītānāgatapaccuppannabahiddhārammaṇesu. Parittānanti kāmāvacaracittānaṃ. Majjhimānanti parittaappamāṇānaṃ majjhe bhavattā majjhimasaṅkhātānaṃ rūpārūpāvacaracittānaṃ. Majjhebhavatā ca desanāvasena, na sabhāvavasena. Cetopariyañāṇaṃ parassa cittameva jānāti, avasesakkhandhattayaṃ pana na jānātīti imaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathāvādaṃ sandhāyāha “maggacittassa jānane”tiādi. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – yasmā cetopariyañāṇaṃ cittameva jānāti, tasmā taṃ maggārammaṇaṃ na hoti[M 2.0287], maggasampayuttacittajānanato pana pariyāyena maggārammaṇatā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ anuññātāti. Paṭṭhāne pana –

1119-22. “In the limited, etc.” means in the limited, exalted, immeasurable, path, past, future, present, and external objects. “Limited” refers to sense-sphere consciousnesses. “Middling” refers to form and formless-sphere consciousnesses, which are called “middling” because they exist between the limited and the immeasurable. This is based on the way of teaching, not on their intrinsic nature. The knowledge of others’ minds knows only the mind of another, but it does not know the remaining three aggregates. Referring to this view of the Great Commentary, he says, “In knowing the path-consciousness,” etc. The meaning here is this: because the knowledge of others’ minds knows only the mind, it does not have the path as its object. However, since it knows the mind associated with the path, the commentary acknowledges indirectly that it can have the path as an object. But in the Paṭṭhāna—

“Kusalā khandhā iddhividhañāṇassa cetopariyañāṇassa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa yathākammūpagañāṇassa anāgataṃsañāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.404) –

“Wholesome aggregates are a condition by way of object condition for the knowledge of psychic powers, the knowledge of mind-penetration, the knowledge of the recollection of past lives, the knowledge of the destiny of beings according to their actions, and the knowledge of the future.” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.404)

Vuttattā [V 2.0214] cattāropi khandhā cetopariyañāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ honti, tasmā nippariyāyeneva maggārammaṇatā labbhatīti idamettha saṅgahakārānaṃ sanniṭṭhānaṃ.

Because it is stated that the four aggregates are the object of the knowledge of mind-penetration, therefore the state of having the path as an object is obtained directly. This is the conclusion of the compilers on this matter.

1123-5. Atītasattadivasabbhantare, anāgatasattadivasabbhantareyeva ca pavattaṃ paracittaṃ cetopariyañāṇaṃ jānāti, tato paṭṭhāya pana paṭisandhipariyosānaṃ, cutipariyosānañca pavattaṃ atītaṃsañāṇassa, anāgataṃsañāṇassa ca gocaranti adhippāyenāha “atīte”tiādi. Atītassa, anāgatassa ca paracittassa jānanaṃ sambhavati, paccuppannassa pana na sambhavatīti pucchati “kathañca panā”tiādi. Itaro yattha sambhavati, taṃ dassetuṃ paccuppannaṃ tāva vibhajitvā dassento “paccuppannaṃ tidhā vutta”ntiādimāha. Khaṇasantatiaddhatoti khaṇapaccuppannaṃ santatipaccuppannaṃ addhāpaccuppannanti evaṃ khaṇasantatiaddhāvasena tidhā vuttaṃ.

1123-5. The knowledge of penetrating others' minds knows the mind of another occurring within the past seven days and precisely within the future seven days. However, with the intention of showing that from that point onward, what has occurred up to the limit of rebirth-linking and the limit of death is the domain of the knowledge of the past and the knowledge of the future, he said, 'in the past,' etc. It is possible to know the mind of another in the past and future, but not in the present. Thus, the question is asked, 'But how then?' To show where it is possible, the other, first distinguishing the present, said, beginning with 'the present is spoken of in three ways,' etc. 'By moment, continuity, and duration' means the momentary present, the continuous present, and the durational present; thus, it is spoken of in three ways: by way of moment, continuity, and duration.

1126. Tikkhaṇasampattanti uppādaṭṭhitibhaṅgavasena khaṇattayapariyāpannaṃ. Paccuppannakhaṇādikanti khaṇa-saddādikaṃ paccuppannaṃ khaṇapaccuppannanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekadvesantativārapariyāpannanti ettha andhakāre nisīditvā ālokaṭṭhānaṃ gatassa na ca tāva ārammaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, yāva pana taṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, etthantare pavattā rūpasantati, arūpasantati vā “ekadvesantativārā”ti [M 2.0288] veditabbā. “Ālokaṭṭhāne vicaritvā ovarakaṃ paviṭṭhassāpi na tāva sahasā rūpaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, yāva taṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, pubbeva tattha nisinnassa viya etthantare ekadvesantativārā veditabbā. Dūre ṭhatvā pana rajakādīnaṃ hatthavikāraṃ, ghaṇṭibherīādiākoṭanahatthavikārañca disvā na pana tāva saddaṃ suṇāti, yāva pana taṃ suṇāti, etthantare ekadvesantativārā veditabbā”ti (visuddhi. 2.416) evaṃ tāva majjhimabhāṇakattherā vadanti.

1126. 'Comprised of three moments' means that which is included in the three moments of arising, presence, and dissolution. 'The present beginning with moment' means that the present, beginning with the word 'khaṇa' (moment), is called the momentary present. 'Included in one or two continuity-occasions': Here, for one who sits in darkness and then goes to a lighted place, the object does not become apparent immediately. Until it becomes apparent, the continuity of form or the formless continuity that occurs in this interval is to be understood as 'one or two continuity-occasions.' Similarly, for one who has wandered in a lighted area and entered a room, the form does not become apparent immediately. The interval until it becomes apparent is also to be understood as one or two continuity-occasions, just as for someone who had been sitting there previously. Furthermore, when standing at a distance and seeing the hand movement of washermen and others, or the hand movement of striking a bell or drum, the sound is not heard immediately. The interval until it is heard is also to be understood as one or two continuity-occasions (Visuddhimagga 2.416). This is what the Majjhimabhāṇaka elders say.

Saṃyuttabhāṇakā pana “rūpasantati arūpasantatīti dve santatiyo vatvā udakaṃ akkamitvā gatassa yāva tīre akkantaudakalekhā na vippasīdati, addhānato āgatassa yāva kāye usumabhāvo na vūpasammati, ātapā āgantvā gabbhaṃ paviṭṭhassa yāva andhakārabhāvo na vigacchati, antogabbhe kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikatvā divā vātapānaṃ vivaritvā olokentassa yāva akkhīnaṃ phandanabhāvo na vūpasammati, ayaṃ rūpasantati nāma. Dve tayo javanavārā arūpasantati nāmāti vatvā tadubhayampi santatipaccuppannaṃ nāmā”ti (visuddhi. 2.416) evaṃ [V 2.0215] ekameva santativāraṃ vadanti. Tattha majjhimabhāṇakavāde ekaccassa sīghampi pākaṭaṃ hotīti ekadvesantativārāti eka-ggahaṇampi kataṃ. Ācariyadhammapālatthero pana “atiparittasabhāvautuādisamuṭṭhānā vā ekadvesantativārā veditabbā”tipi (visuddhi. mahā. 2.416) āha.

The Saṃyuttabhāṇakas, however, having stated 'material continuity and immaterial continuity' as two continuities, say: 'For one who steps into water and goes, the line of disturbed water does not immediately become clear upon reaching the shore; for one who has traveled a long distance, the bodily heat does not immediately subside; for one who enters a room after being in the sun, the state of darkness does not immediately vanish; for one who, while meditating inside a room, opens a window during the day and looks out, the flickering of the eyes does not immediately subside. This is called the material continuity. Two or three impulsion-moments are called the immaterial continuity.' They say that both of these are called the continuous present (Visuddhimagga 2.416). Thus they speak of only a single continuity-occasion. Therein, in the view of the Majjhimabhāṇakas, because for some it becomes clear quickly, the inclusion of 'one' was made in 'one or two moments of continuity.' The elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, however, also says that 'one or two moments of continuity should be understood as arising from extremely subtle natures, conditions, etc.' (Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā 2.416).

1127-8. Ekabbhavaparicchinnanti ekasmiṃ bhave paṭisandhicutivasena paricchinnaṃ ekabhavapariyāpannaṃ dhammajātaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “yo cāvuso mano, ye ca dhammā, ubhayametaṃ paccuppannaṃ, tasmiṃ ce paccuppanne chandarāgapaṭibaddhaṃ hoti viññāṇa”ntiādi, santatipaccuppannañcettha abhidhammaṭṭhakathāsu āgataṃ, addhāpaccuppannaṃ sutte. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino.

1127-8. 'Limited to a single existence' means the class of phenomena limited to a single existence, bounded by way of rebirth-linking and death, and included within one existence. This refers to what was said: 'Friend, whatever the mind, and whatever the mental phenomena, both are present; and if, in that present, consciousness is bound by desire and lust...' etc. Here, the continuous present is mentioned in the Abhidhamma commentaries, while the durational present is in the suttas. 'Some' refers to the Abhayagirivāsins.

1129-30. Yathā [M 2.0289] cātiādi ettha tesaṃ opammadassanaṃ. Ekapupphaṃ attano vaṇṭena ekassa vaṇṭaṃ vijjhatīti sambandho. Mahājanassāpi…pe… vijjhatīti “atītaṃ cittaṃ, anāgataṃ cittaṃ, imassa cittaṃ, asukassa citta”nti evaṃ vibhāgaṃ akatvā parassa cittaṃ jānāmicceva rāsivasena mahājanassa citte āvajjite ekassa cittaṃ ekena cittena uppādakkhaṇe vā ṭhitikkhaṇe vā bhaṅgakkhaṇe vā ekantena paṭivijjhatīti attho.

1129-30. 'Just as,' etc. Here, their simile is shown. A single flower, with its own stalk, pierces the stalk of another—this is the connection. 'Even for a great multitude... it pierces' means that without making distinctions such as 'past mind, future mind, this one's mind, that one's mind,' but simply knowing another's mind in a mass-like way, when the mind of a great multitude is attended to, one person's mind is entirely penetrated by one mind, whether at the moment of arising, presence, or dissolution—this is the meaning.

1131-2. Taṃ pana tesaṃ vacanaṃ ayuttanti dassetuṃ “yenāvajjatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vassasahassampi hi evaṃ āvajjayato āvajjanajavanānaṃ ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe ṭhānaṃ natthi, abhiññācittañca sace khaṇapaccuppannaṃ jānāti, āvajjanena saha ekārammaṇe vattamānameva jānāti, no aññathā, tasmā tesaṃ āvajjanajavanānaṃ dvinnaṃ saha ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe aṭṭhānābhāvato taṃ na yujjati. Bhavatu tāva ko ettha dosoti ce āha “āvajjanajavanāna”ntiādi. Tattha maggaphalavīthito aññaṃ aniṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. Maggaphalavīthiyañhi āvajjanādīnaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇattā, gotrabhuādīnañca nibbānārammaṇattā nānārammaṇatā iṭṭhā, aññattha pana aniṭṭhā, tasmā aniṭṭhe ṭhāne javanāvajjanānaṃ nānārammaṇatāpattidoso ayuttoti taṃ tesaṃ vacanaṃ ayuttanti pakāsitaṃ aṭṭhakathāsūti adhippāyo.

1131-2. To show that their statement is incorrect, it is said, 'by which one attends,' etc. For even if one were to attend thus for a thousand years, there is no standing together of attention and impulsion moments on a single object. And if the supernormal knowledge mind knows the momentary present, it knows only what is occurring simultaneously with attention on a single object, not otherwise. Therefore, since there is no standing together of both attention and impulsion moments on a single object, their claim is untenable. If one asks, 'What fault is there here?' it is said, 'attention and impulsion moments,' etc. Here, a situation other than the path and fruition process is an undesirable state. In the path and fruition process, because attention and so forth have formations as their object, and because the change-of-lineage and others have Nibbāna as their object, the multiplicity of objects is desirable. Elsewhere, however, it is undesirable. Therefore, because the fault of the arising of a multiplicity of objects for impulsions and attentions in an undesirable situation is untenable, their statement is untenable—this is the meaning clarified in the commentaries.

1133-4. Yadi evaṃ, kathaṃ cetopariyañāṇaṃ paccuppannārammaṇaṃ hotīti āha “tasmā”tiādi. Yasmā evaṃ ayuttanti pakāsitaṃ, tasmā. Javanavāratoti ekajavanavāravasena[V 2.0216]. Idaṃ pana khaṇapaccuppannānantaraṃ lahukaṃ katvā paccuppannadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, yaṃ pana vattamānajavanavīthito atītānāgatavasena dvitijavanavīthiparimāṇakāle pavattaṃ paracittaṃ[M 2.0290], taṃ sabbampi “santatipaccuppannaṃ nāmā”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 2.416) vuttaṃ, tasmā javanavāratoti dvitijavanavāravasena dīpetabbaṃ, na sakalena paccuppannaddhunāti adhippāyo. Niddiṭṭhaṃ saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ dīpanātiādi javanavārassa addhāpaccuppannabhāvadīpanamukhena iddhicittassa pavattiākāradīpanaṃ.

1133-4. If so, how does the knowledge of penetration of others' minds have a present object? It is said, 'therefore,' etc. Because it has been shown to be incorrect, therefore. 'By the impulsion-occasion' means by way of a single impulsion-occasion. But this is said for the purpose of easily showing the present by making it immediately follow the momentary present. However, another's mind, which occurs in the time span of a second impulsion process, extending from the current impulsion process into past and future, is all called 'continuous present,' as stated in the commentary (Visuddhimagga 2.416). Therefore, 'by the impulsion-occasion' should be explained as by way of a second impulsion-occasion, not the entire present duration—this is the intended meaning. It is explained in the Saṃyutta Commentary. Here, 'this explanation,' etc., through clarifying the durational present nature of the impulsion-occasion, elucidates the mode of operation of the psychic power mind.

1139-41. Santatipaccuppannampi addhāpaccuppanneneva saṅgahetvā āha “addhāvasā…pe… panā”ti. Ānandācariyo panettha abhidhammamātikāya āgatassa paccuppannapadassa addhāsantatipaccuppannapadatthatā na katthaci pāḷiyaṃ vuttā, tasmā cittasāmaññena cittaṃ āvajjayamānaṃ abhimukhībhūtaṃ vijjamānacittaṃ āvajjeti, parikammāni ca taṃ taṃ vijjamānacittaṃ cittasāmaññeneva ārammaṇaṃ katvā cittajānanaparikammāni hutvā pavattanti. Cetopariyañāṇaṃ pana vijjamānacittaṃ paṭivijjhantaṃ tena saha ekakkhaṇe uppajjati. Tattha yasmā santānaggahaṇato ekattavasena āvajjanādīni cittanteva pavattāni, tañca cittameva, yaṃ cetopariyañāṇena vibhāvitaṃ, tasmā samānākārappavattito na aniṭṭhe ṭhāne nānārammaṇatā hotīti khaṇapaccuppannavaseneva imassa paccuppannārammaṇataṃ icchati. Itarānīti āvajjanaparikammacittāni. Cakkhudvāre viññāṇanti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ.

1139-41. Even the continuous present is included under the durational present, hence it is said: 'the duration...' etc. Ānanda the Teacher, however, says that nowhere in the Pāli texts is it stated that the meaning of the term 'present' found in the Abhidhamma matrix is the durational or continuous present. Therefore, when one attends to the mind through the general characteristic of mind, one attends to a presently existing mind that has become manifest; and preliminary acts, taking that presently existing mind as their object through the general characteristic of mind, proceed as preliminary acts of knowing the mind. The knowledge of others' minds, however, penetrating the presently existing mind, arises simultaneously with it in a single moment. Herein, because the acts of attending, etc., occur in the mind alone, taking the continuity as a unity, and that mind itself is what is discerned by the knowledge of others' minds, there is no diversity of objects in an undesirable state due to the uniformity of their occurrence. Thus, he holds that its object is present only in the sense of a momentary present. 'The others' means the attending and preliminary minds. 'Consciousness at the eye-door' means eye-consciousness.

1143-7. Parittādīsu aṭṭhasūti cetopariyañāṇassa vuttesu paccuppannārammaṇaṃ hitvā navattabbārammaṇañca pakkhipitvā aṭṭhasu parittādīsu. Atīte…pe… phalampi vāti ettha attanāti nidassanamattaṃ. Parehipi bhāvitamaggaṃ, sacchikataphalañca pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena samanussarati. Vā-saddena vā avuttasamuccayatthena attanā bhāvitaṃ maggaṃ, phalampi vā parehi bhāvitaṃ maggaṃ, phalampi vāti evamattho gahetabbo. Tathā [M 2.0291] ca vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “attanā, parehi bhāvitamaggaṃ, sacchikataphalañca anussaraṇakāle”ti (visuddhi. 2.417). Eva-kāraṃ pana padapūraṇamattameva. Phalampi vāti ettha “bhāvita”nti na sambandhitabbaṃ. Na hi phalaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ hoti, atha kho sacchikātabbamevāti. Samanussarato magganti etthāpi “attanā, parehi vā bhāvita”nti sambandhitabbaṃ. Ekantatoti niyamato.

1143-7. 'Among the eight, such as the limited, etc.' means: among the eight categories stated for the knowledge of others' minds, having set aside the present object and included the 'not-to-be-stated' object. 'The past... etc. ...or the fruit'—here, 'by oneself' is merely for the purpose of indication. One also recollects the path developed by others and the fruit realized by them through the knowledge of recollection of past lives. The word 'or' has the meaning of including what has not been stated; thus, the meaning should be understood as: the path developed by oneself, or the fruit; or the path developed by others, or the fruit. And so it is said in the commentary: 'At the time of recollection, the path developed by oneself or by others, and the fruit realized' (Visuddhimagga 2.417). The particle 'eva' here is merely a phrase-filler. In 'or the fruit,' the word 'developed' should not be connected, for the fruit is not to be developed but rather is to be realized. In 'recollecting the path,' 'developed by oneself or by others' should also be connected. 'Absolutely' means invariably.

1148-50. Nanu [V 2.0217] ca cetopariyañāṇayathākammūpagañāṇānipi atītārammaṇāneva, kiṃ pana tesaṃ, imassa ca ārammaṇe nānākaraṇanti āha “cetopariyañāṇampī”tiādi. Kiñcāpīti ayaṃ nipātasamudāyo, eko vā nipāto visesānabhidhānanimitte upagamane daṭṭhabbo. Atha khoti visesābhidhānasamārambhe. Cittamevāti idaṃ pubbe vicāritameva. Atīte cetanāmattanti idampi pubbe viya mahāaṭṭhakathāvādaṃ sandhāyeva vuttaṃ. Tattha hi yathākammūpagañāṇassa cetanāmattameva ārammaṇaṃ hoti, na cittaṃ, nāpi itare dhammā, yato taṃ yathākammūpaganti vuccatīti iminā adhippāyena yathākammūpagañāṇaṃ atītacetanāmattameva ārammaṇaṃ karotīti vuttaṃ, heṭṭhā dassitapāḷivasena sabbe cattāropi khandhā yathākammūpagañāṇassa ārammaṇanti saṅgahakārānaṃ sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Natthi kiñci agocaranti kiñci khandhaṃ vā khandhapaṭibaddhaṃ nāmagottādiṃ vā agocaraṃ nāma natthi. Tañhi atītakkhandhakhandhapaṭibaddhesu dhammesu sabbaññutaññāṇasamānagatikamevāti adhippāyo.

1148-50. But are not the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of beings' rebirth according to their deeds also past-objected? So what is the difference in their objects compared to this knowledge of past lives? To this, it is said, 'the knowledge of others' minds also...' and so on. 'Although' is a collection of particles, or a single particle, to be understood as indicating an approach to a reason for not stating a distinction. 'But' introduces the commencement of stating a distinction. 'Only the mind' refers to what has already been discussed earlier. 'Only volition in the past' is also, as before, stated with reference to the teaching of the Great Commentary. There, it is explained that for the knowledge of rebirth according to deeds, only volition is the object, not the mind nor other phenomena—because it is called 'knowledge of rebirth according to deeds.' With this meaning, it is said that the knowledge of rebirth according to deeds takes only past volition as its object. However, according to the Pāli passage cited earlier, all four aggregates are the object of the knowledge of rebirth according to deeds—this is the conclusion of the compilers. 'There is nothing beyond its scope' means there is no aggregate, nothing connected to aggregates, no name, clan, etc., that is beyond its scope. For it has the same range as the knowledge of omniscience regarding past aggregates and phenomena connected to aggregates—this is the intended meaning.

1151-2. Attakkhandhānussaraṇeti attano khandhānussaraṇakāle. Saraṇe…pe… gocaranti “atīte vipassī bhagavā ahosi, tassa mātā bandhumatī, pitā bandhumā”tiādinā nayena nāmagottādiṃ, pathavīnimittādiñca anussaraṇakāle [M 2.0292] navattabbārammaṇaṃ hoti. Navattabbagocaranti hi parittārammaṇaatītārammaṇattikavasena vuttaṃ, ajjhattārammaṇattikavasena pana ākiñcaññāyatanajjhānassa ārammaṇabhūtadhammārammaṇakāle navattabbārammaṇaṃ hoti, avasesapaññattārammaṇakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ hoti. Nāmagottanti cettha khandhapaṭibaddho sammutisiddho byañjanattho, na byañjanaṃ. Byañjanañhi saddāyatanasaṅgahitattā parittaṃ hoti. Yathāha “niruttipaṭisambhidā parittārammaṇā”ti (vibha. 749).

1151-2. 'Recollection of one’s own aggregates' refers to the time of recollecting one's own aggregates. 'In recollection... etc. ...its range': at the time of recollecting, by the method of 'In the past, there was the Blessed One Vipassī, his mother was Bandhumatī, his father was Bandhumā,' and so on—names, clans, etc., and the earth-kasiṇa and so on—the object is 'not-to-be-stated'. The range of the 'not-to-be-stated' is said in terms of the triad of limited objects, past objects, etc. But in terms of the triad of internal objects, at the time when the mental object that is the object of the jhāna of the base of nothingness is the object, the object is 'not-to-be-stated'. At the time when the object is the remaining concepts, it is an external object. Here, 'names and clans' refer to the meaning of the expression connected with the aggregates, established by convention, not the expression itself. For the expression, being included in the sound-base, is limited. As it is said: 'The discrimination of language has a limited object' (Vibh. 749).

1154. Dibbasotasamanti yasmā paccuppannaṃ, parittañca rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, tasmā paccuppannārammaṇaṃ, parittārammaṇañca hoti, attano kucchigatarūpadassane, parassa hadayanissitalohitadassanādīsu ca ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, bahiddhārammaṇañca hoti.

1154. The divine eye, because it takes present and limited form as its object, therefore has a present object and a limited object. When seeing forms within one's own belly, and when seeing blood based in another's heart, etc., it has an internal object and an external object.

1155-6. Parittādīsu aṭṭhasūti pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa vuttesu atītārammaṇaṃ vajjetvā anāgatārammaṇaṃ pakkhipitvā aṭṭhasu. Nibbattissati…pe… pajānatoti iminā nibbattakkhandhajānanamāha[V 2.0218]. Anāgataṃsañāṇassa anāgatamagocaraṃ natthi. Tampi hi anāgatakkhandhakhandhapaṭibaddhesu dhammesu sabbaññutaññāṇasamānagatikameva.

1155-6. 'Among the eight, such as the limited, etc.' means: among the eight stated for the knowledge of recollection of past lives, having excluded the past object and included the future object. 'He will be reborn… he understands' – with this, he speaks of knowing the aggregates that will arise. For the knowledge of the future, there is no future that is beyond its scope. That too, in regard to phenomena connected to future aggregates, has a range similar to the knowledge of omniscience.

1163. Jānane nāmagottassāti “anāgate metteyyo nāma sammāsambuddho uppajjissati, tassa subrahmā nāma pitā bhavissati, brahmavatī nāma mātā”tiādinā nayena nāmagottādijānanakāle.

1163. In knowing the name and clan: 'In the future, a Fully Enlightened One named Metteyya will arise. His father will be named Subrahma, and his mother will be named Brahmavatī'—in this way, at the time of knowing the name, clan, etc.

1164-5. Parittādīsu pañcasūti parittamahaggataatītaajjhattabahiddhārammaṇavasena pañcasu. Kāmakammassāti kāmāvacarakammassa.

1164-5. 'In the five, such as the limited, etc.' means: in the five by way of limited, sublime, past, internal, and external objects. 'Of sense-sphere kamma' means of kamma belonging to the sense-sphere.

1169. Vividhatthavaṇṇapadanti [M 2.0293] nānappakāraatthapadehi, byañjanapadehi ca sampannaṃ. Madhuratthamatinīharanti madhuratthaṃ atinīharañcāti padacchedo.

1169. 'Having various meaningful and descriptive words' means endowed with words of various meanings and with words of expression. The word-division of 'Madhuratthamatinīharanti' is 'madhuratthaṃ atinīharañca iti'.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the Commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra,

Abhiññārammaṇaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the exposition on the objects of direct knowledge is completed.

18. Aṭṭhārasamo paricchedo

18. The Eighteenth Chapter

Diṭṭhivisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Purification of View

1170-2. Idāni yasmā evaṃ abhiññāvasena adhigatānisaṃsāya thiratarāya samādhibhāvanāya samannāgatena bhikkhunā paññā bhāvetabbā hoti. Evañhi sā sabbākārena thiratarā sikhappattā ca hoti, tasmā tassā bhāvanānayavibhāvanatthamārabhanto āha “samādhiṃ panā”tiādi[V 2.0219]. Kā paññāti sarūpapucchā. Ko catthoti imissā ko attho. Paññāti padaṃ kaṃ abhidheyyatthaṃ nissāya vattatīti adhippāyo.

1170-2. Now, since wisdom should be developed by a monk who is endowed with a very stable development of concentration, the benefits of which have been attained by way of direct knowledge. For in this way, wisdom becomes in every way more stable and has reached its peak. Therefore, beginning in order to explain the method of its development, he says, 'But concentration...' and so on. 'What is wisdom?' is a question about its nature. 'And what is its meaning?' means 'what is the meaning of this?' The intention is: depending on what denotative meaning does the word 'wisdom' proceed?

1173-4. Paññā vipassanāpaññāti idhādhippetameva paññaṃ dasseti, aññattha pana bahuvidho paññāpabhedo hoti. Puññacittasamāyutāti kusalacittasampayuttā. Ettha ca puñña-ggahaṇena duvidhampi abyākataṃ nivatteti, tathā “atthi saṃkiliṭṭhā”ti evaṃ pavattaṃ micchāvādaṃ paṭisedheti. Vipassanā-ggahaṇena kammassakatādivasappavattaṃ sesakusalapaññaṃ. Jānanā vā pakāratoti vutte “kimidaṃ pakārato jānanaṃ nāmā”ti anuyogaṃ manasi nidhāya sañjānanavijānanākāravisiṭṭhaṃ nānappakārato jānananti dassetuṃ “saññāviññāṇapaññānaṃ, ko viseso kimantara”nti kathetukamyatāpucchaṃ [M 2.0294] katvā vissajjanamāha “saññāviññāṇapaññāna”ntiādinā. Jānanatte samepi cāti visayavijānanākāre samānepi.

1173-4. 'Wisdom is insight-wisdom'—here, this specifically indicates the intended wisdom, but elsewhere, there are many kinds of wisdom. 'Associated with meritorious consciousness' means associated with wholesome consciousness. Here, the term 'merit' excludes both kinds of indeterminate states, and it refutes the false view that holds, 'There is a defiled one.' The term 'insight' excludes the remaining wholesome wisdom that occurs based on the ownership of deeds, etc. When it is said, 'or knowing in various ways,' keeping in mind the inquiry, 'What is this knowing in various ways?', to show that it is distinguished by the modes of recognition and discernment, knowing in diverse ways, having posed the question that one intends to answer in order to clarify the difference: 'What is the distinction, what is the difference, between perception, consciousness, and wisdom?', the answer is given: 'Perception, consciousness, and wisdom...' and so on. 'Even when the act of knowing is the same' means even when the manner of knowing the object is similar.

1175. Sañjānanamattaṃvāti “nīlapīta”ntiādikaṃ ārammaṇe vijjamānaṃ, avijjamānaṃ vā saññānimittaṃ katvā jānanaṃ. Tathā hesā puna sañjānanapaccayakaraṇarasā. Matta-saddena visesanivattiatthena vijānanappajānanākāre nivatteti, eva-kārena kadācipi imissā te visesā na santiyevāti avadhāreti. Tenāha “lakkhaṇappaṭivedha”ntiādi. “Aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ kātuṃ neva sakkoti, viññāṇakiccampi kātuṃ na sakkoti, saññā kuto paññākiccaṃ kareyyāti lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoticceva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “maggaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkotī”ti.

1175. 'Merely perceiving' means knowing by forming a perception-sign of what exists or does not exist in the object, such as 'blue, yellow,' etc. Likewise, this perception has the characteristic of being a condition for repeated recognition. The word 'merely' prevents distinguishing and understanding, indicating with certainty that these distinctions never exist in it. Hence it is said, 'penetrating the characteristics,' etc. It cannot penetrate the characteristics such as 'impermanent, suffering, non-self,' nor can it perform the function of consciousness—how then could perception perform the function of wisdom? Thus, it is said that it cannot penetrate the characteristics, but it is not said that it cannot lead to the path.

1176. Viññāṇaṃ pana ārammaṇe pavattamānaṃ na tattha saññā viya nīlapītādikassa sañjānanavaseneva pavattati, atha kho taṃ tattha aniccatādivisesaṃ, aññañca tādisaṃ visesaṃ jānantameva pavattatīti āha “viññāṇaṃ panā”tiādi. Kathaṃ pana viññāṇaṃ lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ karotīti? Paññāya dassitamaggena. Lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāya hi anekavāraṃ lakkhaṇāni paṭivijjhitvā pavattamānāya paguṇabhāvato paricayavasena ñāṇavippayuttacittenapi vipassanā sambhavati, yathā taṃ paguṇassa ganthassa sajjhāyane ñāyāgatāpi vārā na viññāyanti. Lakkhaṇaṃ paṭivijjhitunti ca lakkhaṇānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na paṭivijjhanaṃ.

1176. However, consciousness, when arising in relation to an object, does not operate merely through the mode of recognizing blue, yellow, etc., as perception does. Instead, it operates knowing the specific characteristics such as impermanence and other such distinctions. Hence it is said, 'But consciousness,' etc. How then does consciousness accomplish penetration of characteristics? Through the path shown by wisdom. For, through repeatedly penetrating the characteristics with insight meditation that takes characteristics as its object, fluency arises, and thus insight occurs even with consciousness disjoined from knowledge—just as, in the recitation of a well-mastered text, even phrases that have come in proper sequence are not consciously noticed. And 'penetrating the characteristics' is said with reference to making the characteristics the object, not the penetration itself.

1177. Ussakkitvāti 220 udayabbayādiñāṇapaṭipāṭiyā ārabhitvā maggaṃ pāpetumeva taṃ viññāṇaṃ na sakkoti asambodhasabhāvattā. Vuttanayanti viññāṇe vuttanayaṃ. Sā hi ārammaṇañca jānāti, lakkhaṇañca paṭivijjhati. Attano pana [M 2.0295] anaññasādhāraṇena ānubhāvena maggaṃ pāpetuñca sakkoti. Bālagāmikaheraññikānaṃ kahāpaṇajānanamiva ca nesaṃ ārammaṇajānanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yathā hi heraññikaphalake ṭhapitaṃ kahāpaṇarāsiṃ eko asañjātavohārabuddhi bāladārako, eko gāmikapuriso, eko heraññikoti tīsu janesu passamānesu bāladārako kahāpaṇānaṃ cittavicittadīgharassacaturassaparimaṇḍalabhāvamattameva jānāti, “idaṃ manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogāvahaṃ ratanasammata”nti na jānāti. Gāmikapuriso tadubhayaṃ jānāti, “ayaṃ cheko mahāsāro, ayaṃ kūṭo, ayaṃ aḍḍhasāro, ayaṃ pādasāro”tiādikaṃ pana vibhāgaṃ na jānāti. Heraññiko sabbepi te pakāre jānāti, jānanto ca oloketvāpi jānāti, ākoṭitasaddaṃ sutvāpi jānāti, gandhaṃ ghāyitvāpi rasaṃ sāyitvāpi hatthena dhārayitvāpi “asukasmiṃ gāme vā nigame vā nagare vā pabbate vā nadītīre vā kato”tipi “asukaācariyena kato”tipi jānāti. Tattha saññā asañjātavohārabuddhino bāladārakassa kahāpaṇadassanaṃ viya vibhāgaṃ akatvā piṇḍavaseneva ārammaṇaṃ gaṇhāti nīlādivasena ārammaṇassa upaṭṭhānākāraggahaṇato, viññāṇaṃ gāmikapurisassa kahāpaṇadassanamiva ekaccavisesaggahaṇasamatthatāya, paññā anavasesaggahaṇasamatthatāya heraññikassa kahāpaṇadassanamiva daṭṭhabbāti.

1177. 'Ussakkitvāti' means that consciousness, having begun with the sequence of knowledge regarding arising and passing away, etc., is unable to lead to the path, because it is not inherently capable of awakening. 'Vuttanayaṃ' refers to the way stated regarding consciousness. But wisdom knows its object and penetrates its characteristics, and by its own unique power, it is able to lead to the path. The knowledge of objects by these three should be understood like the knowledge of coins by a child, a villager, and a goldsmith. Just as, when a pile of coins is placed on a goldsmith’s board, three people observe it: a child whose practical understanding has not arisen, a villager, and a goldsmith. The child knows only the varied colors, lengths, shapes, and roundness of the coins but does not understand that 'this is considered a jewel that brings enjoyment and use to people.' The villager knows both aspects but does not distinguish details like 'this is genuine, this is counterfeit, this is half-value, this is quarter-value,' etc. The goldsmith, however, knows all these distinctions. Moreover, by merely looking, he knows; by hearing the sound when struck, he knows; by smelling the scent, tasting the flavor, or holding it in his hand, he knows. He even knows 'this was made in such-and-such village, town, city, mountain, or riverbank' or 'this was made by such-and-such craftsman.' Here, perception, like the seeing of coins by the child whose practical understanding has not arisen, grasps the object as a mere lump without distinguishing it, by taking the mode of appearance of the object as blue, etc. Consciousness, like the villager’s seeing of coins, is capable of grasping some distinctions. Wisdom, like the goldsmith’s seeing of coins, should be regarded as capable of grasping all distinctions without omission.

1178-80. Sabhāvapaṭivedhananti sako bhāvo, samāno vā bhāvo sabhāvo, tassa paṭivedhanaṃ ñātapariññātīraṇapariññāvasena sabhāvasāmaññalakkhaṇapaṭivedhanaṃ. Ghaṭapaṭādipaṭicchādakassa bāhirandhakārassa dīpāloko viya yathāvuttadhammasabhāvapaṭicchādakassa viddhaṃsanarasā. Uppajjamānoyeva hi ñāṇāloko hadayandhakāraṃ vidhamento [M 2.0296] uppajjatīti āha “sammohanandhakārassa, viddhaṃsanarasā matā”ti. Tatoyeva sabbadhammesu asammuyhanākārena paccupatiṭṭhati, kāraṇabhūtā vā sayaṃ phalabhūtaṃ asammohaṃ paccupatiṭṭhāpetīti āha “asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti. Vipassanāpaññāya idhādhippetattā samādhi tassā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tathā hi “samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 4.99; 5.1071; a. ni. 11.2) suttapadanti āha “samādhāsannakāraṇā”ti.

1178-80. 'Penetration of intrinsic nature' (sabhāvapaṭivedhana) means one’s own nature, or common nature, is intrinsic nature. The penetration of that is the penetration of intrinsic and universal characteristics by way of the full understanding of knowing and comprehending. Just as the light of a lamp dispels the external darkness covering a pot or a cloth, so too is its function of dispelling the darkness that conceals the intrinsic nature of phenomena as described. For the light of knowledge arises dispelling the darkness of the heart as it arises. Thus it is said: 'It is considered to have the function of dispelling the darkness of delusion.' Therefore, it stands forth in all phenomena as non-confusion, or being the cause, it itself establishes non-confusion as its result. Thus it is said: 'It is manifested as non-confusion.' Since insight wisdom is intended here, concentration is its proximate cause. For it is said in the sutta: 'One who is concentrated understands things as they really are.' Hence, it is said: 'Having concentration as its proximate cause.'

1181-2. Dhammasabhāvapaṭivedho [V 2.0221] nāma paññāya āveṇiko sabhāvo, na tenassā koci vibhāgo labbhatīti āha “lakkhaṇenekadhā vuttā”ti. Lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko vuccati vaṭṭaṃ, tappariyāpannatāya loke niyuttā, tattha vā viditāti lokikā. Tattha apariyāpannattā alokikā. Katamā panettha lokiyā, katamā lokuttarā cāti āha “lokiyenā”tiādi. Lokiyakusalacittuppādesu maggasampayuttā lokiyena maggena yuttā. Visesato pana diṭṭhivisuddhiādivisuddhicatukkasaṅgahitamaggasaṃyuttā samudāye pavattā paññā tadekadesesupi pavattatīti magga-ggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, paccekampi vā sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ maggasamaññāti katvā. Lokato uttarā uttiṇṇāti lokuttarā. Lokuttarāpi hi maggasampayuttā bhāvetabbā, vipassanāpariyosāne labbhatevāti lokuttara-ggahaṇaṃ na virujjhati. Tenāha “lokuttarenā”tiādi. Sutamayāditotiādiggahaṇena bhāvanāmayaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

1181-2. The penetration of the intrinsic nature of phenomena is the unique intrinsic nature of wisdom, and no distinction can be made in it by that; hence it is said, 'stated as one by its characteristic.' The world (loka) is so called in the sense of breaking up and crumbling; it is the round of existence. Those included in the world, or known in it, are called mundane. Those not included in it are called supramundane. But here, what is mundane and what is supramundane? It is said, 'by the mundane,' etc. In the arising of mundane wholesome states of consciousness, wisdom associated with the path is connected with the mundane path. Specifically, wisdom arises in the aggregate connected with the path, which includes the four kinds of purification such as purification of view, even though it may also arise in individual aspects of the path. The term 'path' is used here comprehensively, or alternatively, the term 'path' can be assigned to each of right view, etc. That which has gone beyond the world, transcended it, is called supramundane. For the supramundane, too, is associated with the path and is to be developed—it is certainly attained at the conclusion of insight. Thus, the inclusion of the supramundane is not contradicted. Hence it is said, 'by the supramundane,' etc. By the phrase 'arising from learning,' etc., wisdom born of development is included.

1183-5. Attanova cintāyāti tassa tassa anavajjassa atthassa sādhane paropadesena vinā attano upāyacintāvaseneva[M 2.0297]. Bhūripaññenāti mahāpaññena, patthaṭatāya pathavīsamānapaññena vāti attho. Parato pana sutvānāti parato upadesaṃ sutvā. Suteneva ca nipphannāti antogatahetvatthamidaṃ visesanaṃ, suteneva nipphannattāti attho. “Nipphannattā sutena vā”ti vā pāṭho. Yathā vāpi tathā vāti parato sutvā vā asutvā vā. Appanāpattāti idaṃ sikhāpattaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ, na pana appanāpattāva bhāvanāmayāti. Tissopi panetā paññā pāḷivasena evaṃ veditabbā –

1183-5. “By one’s own thinking” means by thinking about one’s own means alone, without relying on others’ advice, in order to accomplish that which is blameless. “Of vast wisdom” means of great wisdom, or of wisdom as expansive as the earth—this is the meaning. “But having heard from another” means having heard instruction from another. “And accomplished through hearing”—this is an adjective implying an inherent causal meaning; it means that it is accomplished through hearing. Alternatively, the reading is “or because it is accomplished through hearing.” “Whether thus or otherwise” means whether having heard from another or not. “Through attainment of absorption” is said to show that this is culminating wisdom born of development, but it is not only born of attainment of absorption. Moreover, these three kinds of wisdom should be understood thus, according to the wording of the Pali text –

“Tattha katamā cintāmayā paññā? Yogavihitesu vā kammāyatanesu yogavihitesu vā sippāyatanesu yogavihitesu vā vijjāṭhānesu kammassakataṃ vā saccānulomikaṃ vā rūpaṃ aniccanti vā, vedanā, saññā, saṅkhārā, viññāṇaṃ aniccanti vā, yaṃ evarūpaṃ anulomikaṃ khantiṃ diṭṭhiṃ ruciṃ mudiṃ pekkhaṃ dhammanijjhānakkhantiṃ parato asutvā paṭilabhati, ayaṃ vuccati cintāmayā paññā. Tattha katamā sutamayā paññā…pe… sutvā paṭilabhati, ayaṃ vuccati sutamayā paññā. Sabbāpi samāpannassa paññā bhāvanāmayā paññā”ti (vibha. 768).

“Herein, what is wisdom born of reflection? In fields of work conducive to spiritual practice, or in fields of crafts conducive to spiritual practice, or in spheres of knowledge conducive to spiritual practice, or in the realization that actions are one’s own, or in conformity with truth, [reflecting that] form is impermanent, or feeling, perception, formations, [or] consciousness [is] impermanent—whatever such conformity, acceptance, view, inclination, delight, consideration, acceptance of the scrutiny of the Dhamma one attains without hearing it from another, this is called wisdom born of reflection. Herein, what is wisdom born of learning?... Whatever one attains by hearing, this is called wisdom born of learning. All wisdom of one who has attained [samāpatti] is wisdom born of development.” (Vibh. 768).

Ettha ca kiñcāpi kammāyatanādivasena cintāmayasutamayapaññā mahaggatalokuttaravasena bhāvanāmayapaññā [V 2.0222] ca vuttā, idha pana antimabhavikānaṃ dvinnaṃ bodhisattānameva labbhamānā cintāmayabhūtā saccānulomikā paññā, pūritapāramīnaṃ avasesamahāpaññānaṃ labbhamānā sutamayā saccānulomikā paññā, lokuttarappanāpattāpi bhāvanāmayapaññāva adhippetā.

Here, although wisdom born of reflection, wisdom born of learning, and wisdom born of development are mentioned in terms of the bases of action and so forth, and also in terms of the exalted and supramundane, in this context, the wisdom conforming to truth that is born of reflection is attainable only by the two Bodhisattas of the last existence. For those who have fulfilled the perfections, the wisdom conforming to truth that is born of learning is attainable by the remaining great knowers. Even the supramundane wisdom that has attained absorption is intended as wisdom born of development.

1186. [M 2.0298] Paṭisambhidācatukkassāti atthadhammaniruttipaṭibhānasaṅkhātassa paṭisambhidācatukkassa vasena. Nanu cettha vipassanāpaññā adhippetā, kasmā paṭisambhidā āhaṭāti? Vipassakānaṃ ñāṇapāṭavatthaṃ paññāppabhede niddisiyamāne paṭisambhidāpaññāpi vattukāmatāya, paṭisambhidāpaññāya vā vipassanāphalabhūtattā lokiyalokuttarapaññādhikāre vā lokuttarapaññāya saha pāpuṇitabbaṃ paṭisambhidāpaññampi vattukāmatāya idheva vuttāti. Atthadhammaniruttīsu ñāṇanti “atthe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā, dhamme ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā, tatra dhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 718) evamāgataṃ atthādīsu tīsu pabhedagataṃ ñāṇattayaṃ. Tīsupīti yathāvuttesu tīsupi paṭisambhidāñāṇesu gocarakiccalakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānabhūmiādivasena te ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa imāni ñāṇāni idamatthajotakānīti evaṃ pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ, parittamahaggataappamāṇavasena vā tīsu ñāṇesu ñāṇaṃ. Paṭisambhidārammaṇampi hi paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā hoti. Teneva ca suttantabhājanīyapāḷiyaṃ “ñāṇesu ñāṇa”nti, aṭṭhakathāya ca “sabbatthakañāṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā ñāṇaṃ paccavekkhantassa pabhedagataṃ ñāṇa”nti (vibha. aṭṭha. 718) avisesena vuttaṃ. Evañca katvā mahaggatapaṭisambhidāñāṇassa abhāvepi niruttipaṭisambhidā parittārammaṇā, tisso paṭisambhidā siyā parittārammaṇā, siyā mahaggatārammaṇā, siyā appamāṇārammaṇāti paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāya mahaggatārammaṇatāpi pañhāpucchakapāḷiyaṃ vuttā.

1186. “The fourfold analytical knowledge” refers to the fourfold analytical knowledge, namely, the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of sagacity. But is not insight wisdom intended here? Why is analytical knowledge brought in? Because when classifying the types of wisdom for the purpose of showing the proficiency of knowledge of insight meditators, the wisdom of analytical knowledge is also intended to be spoken of; or because the wisdom of analytical knowledge is the fruit of insight; or because in the context of mundane and supramundane wisdom, the wisdom of analytical knowledge, which should be attained along with supramundane wisdom, is also intended to be spoken of, therefore it is mentioned here. “Knowledge in meaning, phenomena, and language”: “Knowledge about meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning, knowledge about phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena, knowledge about the expression and language regarding those phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language” (Vibhaṅga 718). Thus comes the threefold knowledge classified in meaning and so forth. “In the three as well”: In the three analytical knowledges as mentioned, the knowledge that reviews them, taking their object, function, characteristic, essence, manifestation, proximate cause, base, etc., as its object, saying, “These knowledges illuminate such meanings,” is the classified knowledge. Or, knowledge in the three knowledges may be in terms of limited, exalted, or immeasurable. Indeed, the analytical knowledge of sagacity can also have analytical knowledge as its object. Therefore, in the Suttanta Bhājanīya text, it is said, “knowledge in knowledges,” and in the commentary, “the classified knowledge that reviews knowledge by taking all-pervading knowledge as its object” (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 718) is stated without distinction. Thus, even though there is no exalted analytical knowledge, the analytical knowledge of language has a limited object. The three analytical knowledges may have a limited object, an exalted object, or an immeasurable object. The exalted object of the analytical knowledge of sagacity is also mentioned in the question-and-answer recitation.

Abhidhammabhājanīye pana –

In the Abhidhamma classification –

“Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ vā…pe… dhammārammaṇaṃ vā, yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha, tasmiṃ [M 2.0299] samaye phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hoti. Ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye aññepi atthi arūpino dhammā, ime dhammā kusalā. Tesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Yāya niruttiyā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paññatti hoti, tatra dhammaniruttābhilāpe [V 2.0223] ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā. Yena ñāṇena tāni ñāṇāni jānāti ‘imāni ñāṇāni idamatthajotakānī’ti, tesu ñāṇesu ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 725) –

‘At the time when a sense-sphere wholesome consciousness arises, accompanied by gladness, associated with knowledge, having a form as its object…or…having a mental phenomenon as its object, or having whatever it may take as its object, at that time there is contact…and non-distraction. And whatever other immaterial phenomena there are at that time, these phenomena are wholesome. Knowledge of these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena. Knowledge of their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning. The knowledge concerning the designation of these phenomena by whatever expression, the knowledge concerning the verbal expression of those phenomena, is the analytical knowledge of language. The knowledge by which one knows those knowledges, ‘These knowledges illuminate this meaning,’ knowledge concerning those knowledges is the analytical knowledge of sagacity.’

Cittuppādakkamena desanāya pavattattā sāvaseso pāṭho kato. Cittuppādasaṅgahite atthe asesetvā desanā hi abhidhammabhājanīye pavattā, na sabbañeyyeti yathādassitavisayavacanavasena “yena ñāṇena tāni ñāṇāni jānātī”ti vuttaṃ, na taṃ aññārammaṇataṃ paṭisedheti desanāya atapparabhāvato. Evañca katvā tattha nibbāne, anāgatepi atthapaṭisambhidā siyā na vattabbā atītārammaṇātipi anāgatārammaṇātipi paccuppannārammaṇātipīti atthapaṭisambhidāya nibbānārammaṇatā vuttā. Ettha ca atthoti saṅkhepato hetuphalassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Hetuphalañhi yasmā hetuanusārena arīyati adhigamīyati sampāpuṇīyati, tasmā atthoti vuccati. Dhammotipi saṅkhepato paccayassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. So hi yasmā taṃ taṃ dahati pavatteti, sampāpuṇituṃ vā dhāreti, tasmā dhammoti vuccati. Niruttīti sattānaṃ mūlabhāsābhūtā māgadhikabhāsā, yāya buddhānaṃ desanā hoti. Paṭibhānanti heṭṭhā vuttaṃ ñāṇattayameva. Vuttañhetaṃ abhidhamme “dukkhe ñāṇaṃ…pe… tassa vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”tiādi.

The teaching proceeds by way of the arising of consciousness; hence, the text is made with a remainder (i.e., it is not exhaustive). For the teaching in the Abhidhamma classification proceeds by exhaustively encompassing the meaning included in the arising of consciousness, not by encompassing all knowables, in accordance with the statement concerning the object as shown: “by that knowledge one knows those knowledges.” This does not deny that it has another object, because that is not the primary purpose of the teaching. And having done so, it should not be said that the analytical knowledge of meaning regarding Nibbāna, even in the future, is exclusively past-objected, or future-objected, or present-objected. Thus, the analytical knowledge of meaning is said to have Nibbāna as its object. Here, “meaning” (attha) is, in brief, a designation for cause and effect. For cause and effect, because they are approached, attained, and reached in accordance with the cause, therefore they are called “meaning.” “Dhamma” is also, in brief, a designation for condition. For because it bears, produces, or maintains that which is to be attained, therefore it is called “dhamma.” “Nirutti” (language) is the Magadhi language, which is the root language of beings, by which the teaching of the Buddhas takes place. “Paṭibhāna” (analytical knowledge of sagacity) is simply the three knowledges mentioned previously. For it is said in the Abhidhamma: “Knowledge of suffering… (and so on)… knowledge of its result is the analytical knowledge of meaning,” and so on.

1187. Yasmā [M 2.0300] panāyaṃ saṅkhepatthova, pabhedavasena ca vuccamāno pākaṭo hoti, tasmā taṃ saṅgahetvā pabhedatova atthādike dassetuṃ “yaṃ kiñci paccayuppanna”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci paccayuppannanti yaṃ kiñci hetādipaccayato samuppannaṃ. Taṃ pana “idaṃ ito nibbatta”nti evaṃ hetuanusārena viññāyamānameva idha adhippetaṃ, tathā kusalākusalaphalabhūtā vipākā abyāpārasantivasena viññāyamānā, sesā abyāpārabhūtā kiriyā dhammā avipākasantivasena, asaṅkhataṃ nissaraṇabhūto nirodho nibbutisantivasena, buddhavacanatthabhūto khandhādiparamatthadhammo imāya ayaṃ dīpitoti evaṃ pāḷianusārena viññāyamānova atthasamaññaṃ labhatīti āha “yaṃ kiñci paccayuppanna”ntiādi. Tattha hetuphalaṃ, bhāsitattho ca sakasakahetupaṭibaddho, bhāsitapaṭibaddho ca viññāyatīti pariyāyato, sesaṃ sakasakabhāvavaseneva viññāyatīti nippariyāyatova attho nāma. Tattha pariyāyattho suttantabhājanīyavasena vutto, nippariyāyattho abhidhammabhājanīyavasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bhāsitanti pāḷidhammamāha. Sesaṃ atthapañcakesu vuttanayena yathārahaṃ yojetvā veditabbaṃ.

1187. However, since this is only a brief meaning, and it becomes clear when explained by way of divisions, therefore, having summarized it, the explanation of meaning and so on is commenced from the divisions, with “Whatever is dependently arisen,” and so forth. “Whatever is dependently arisen” means whatever has arisen from conditions such as causes. But here, it is intended that it be understood as “this is produced from that,” in accordance with the cause. Similarly, the results that are the fruit of wholesome or unwholesome actions are understood as a state of non-activity; the remaining functional phenomena, being inactive, are understood as a state of non-result; the unconditioned, which is liberation, cessation, is understood as a state of extinguishment; the ultimate realities, such as the aggregates, which constitute the meaning of the Buddha’s words, obtain the designation 'meaning' only when understood in accordance with the Pāli, as has been explained. Therefore, it is said, “Whatever is dependently arisen,” and so forth. Herein, cause and effect, and the meaning of what is spoken, are understood as connected to their respective causes and connected to what is spoken, respectively, by way of interpretation. The rest is understood according to its own individual nature, and thus is meaning in a direct sense. Herein, the meaning by way of interpretation is stated in the manner of the Suttanta classification, while the direct meaning is to be seen in the manner of the Abhidhamma classification. “What is spoken” refers to the Dhamma in the Pāli. The rest should be understood by applying it appropriately according to the method stated in the five aspects of meaning.

Ettha [V 2.0224] ca nibbānaṃ pattabbo attho, bhāsitattho ñāpetabbo attho, itaro nibbattetabbo atthoti tividho hoti attho. Maggo sampāpako hetu, bhāsitaṃ ñāpako hetu, itaraṃ nibbattako hetūti evaṃ tividho hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiriyādhammānañcettha avipākatāya dhammabhāvo na vutto. Yadi evaṃ vipākā na hontīti atthabhāvo na vattabbo? Na, paccayuppannabhāvato. Evaṃ sati kusalākusalānampi paccayuppannattā atthabhāvo āpajjati? Nāyaṃ doso appaṭisiddhattā. Vipākassa pana padhānahetutāya [M 2.0301] pākaṭabhāvato dhammabhāvo eva tesaṃ vutto, kiriyānaṃ paccayabhāvā dhammabhāvo āpajjatīti ce? Nāyaṃ doso appaṭisiddhattā. Kammaphalasambandhassa pana hetubhāvābhāvato dhammabhāvo na yuttoti. Apica “ayaṃ imassa paccayo, ayaṃ paccayuppanno”ti evaṃ bhedamakatvā kevalaṃ kusalākusale vipākakiriyadhamme ca paccavekkhantassa dhammatthapaṭisambhidā na hontīti tesaṃ atthadhammatā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, meaning is threefold: Nibbāna is the meaning to be attained; the meaning of what is spoken is the meaning to be made known; and the other is the meaning to be produced. The path is the cause that leads to attainment; what is spoken is the cause that makes known; and the other is the cause that produces—thus, it should be seen that the cause is threefold. And herein, for functional phenomena, their nature as a cause (dhamma) is not stated due to their non-resultant nature. If so, should it not be said that they do not have the nature of an effect (attha) because they are not results? No, because they are dependently arisen. This being so, since wholesome and unwholesome states are also dependently arisen, would they too acquire the nature of an effect? This is not a fault, as it is not disallowed. However, for results, their nature as a cause is stated because they are evident as being a principal cause. If it is said that for functional phenomena, the nature of a cause arises from their being a condition? This is not a fault, as it is not disallowed. But since the relationship between kamma and its fruit lacks the nature of a cause, its nature as a cause is not fitting. Furthermore, for one who examines merely wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional phenomena without making the distinction, ‘This is the condition for this; this is conditioned by it,’ the analytical knowledges of cause and effect do not arise. Therefore, their nature as cause and effect is stated—this should be seen.

1189. Sabhāvaniruttīti aviparītanirutti, aviparītaniruttīti tassa tassa atthassa bodhane sabbakālaṃ paṭiniyatasambandho abyabhicāravohāro māgadhabhāsāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sā hi sabbakālaṃ paṭiniyatasambandho, itarā bhāsā pana kālantarena parivattanti. Atthato panesā nāmapaññattīti ācariyā. Yathāhu –

1189. Sabhāvanirutti (inherent expression) means undistorted expression. Undistorted expression is said to be the Magadhi language, which is an unfailing usage, always having a fixed connection in conveying the meaning of each thing. For it always has a fixed connection, whereas other languages change over time. But in terms of meaning, this is a designation of a name, say the teachers. As they said:

“Nirutti māgadhā bhāsā, atthato nāmasammutī”ti.

“Nirutti is the Magadhi language; in terms of meaning, it is a conventional designation of a name.”

Apare pana – yadi sabhāvanirutti paññattisabhāvā, evaṃ sati paññatti abhilapitabbā, na vacananti āpajjati, evañca sati “tatra dhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā”ti idaṃ na sakkā vattuṃ, abhilapitabboti abhilāpo. Na hi vacanato aññaṃ abhilapitabbaṃ uccāretabbaṃ atthi, atha phassādivacanehi bodhetabbaṃ abhilapitabbaṃ, evañca sati atthadhammānampi bodhetabbattā tesampi niruttibhāvo āpajjati, apica aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “phassoti ca sabhāvanirutti, phassā phassanti na sabhāvaniruttī”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 718) vacanato viññattivikārasahito saddo niruttīti dassitameva, “taṃ sabhāvaniruttisaddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ sabhāvaniruttābhilāpe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā, evamayaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā [M 2.0302] saddārammaṇā nāma jātā, na paññattiārammaṇā”ti [V 2.0225] ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 718) vuttattā niruttisaddārammaṇāya sotaviññāṇavīthiyā parato manodvāre niruttipaṭisambhidā pavattati, evañca katvā “niruttipaṭisambhidā parittārammaṇā”ti vacanaṃ upapannaṃ hotīti vadanti. Ācariyajotipālattherādayo panāhu – “niruttipaṭisambhidā paccuppannārammaṇā”ti vacanaṃ paccuppannaṃ saddaṃ gahetvā pacchājānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, evañca sati aññasmiṃ paccuppannārammaṇe aññaṃ paccuppannārammaṇanti vuttanti āpajjati, yathā pana dibbasotañāṇaṃ manussādisaddabhedanicchayassa paccayabhūtaṃ taṃtaṃsaddavibhāvakaṃ, evaṃ sabhāvāsabhāvaniruttinicchayassa paccayabhūtaṃ paccuppannasabhāvaniruttisaddārammaṇaṃ taṃvibhāvakaṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidāti vuccamāne na koci pāḷivirodho, taṃ sabhāvaniruttisaddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassāti ca paccuppannasaddārammaṇapaccavekkhaṇaṃ pavattentassāti na na sakkā vattuṃ. Tampi hi ñāṇaṃ sabhāvaniruttiṃ vibhāventameva taṃtaṃsaddapaccavekkhaṇānantaraṃ taṃtaṃpabhedanicchayassa hetubhāvato niruttiṃ bhindantaṃ paṭivijjhantameva uppajjatīti ca pabhedagatampi hotīti.

Others, however, say: If inherent expression is of the nature of a designation, then it follows that the designation would be what is to be expressed, not the speech. In that case, the statement, “Knowledge in the utterance of the expression of phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language,” cannot be made, for what is to be expressed is the expression. For there is nothing else to be expressed or uttered apart from speech. Rather, what is to be expressed is that which is to be made known by words such as “contact.” If this is so, then since meanings and causes must also be made known, it would follow that they too have the nature of expression. Moreover, in the commentary, according to the statement, “The term ‘contact’ (phasso) is an inherent expression, but ‘contacts’ (phassā, phassanti) is not an inherent expression” (Vibh-a 718), it is indeed shown that sound accompanied by modifications of communication is expression. The commentary also states: “For one who reflects, taking that sound of inherent expression as the object, the knowledge that has gone into the distinctions concerning that utterance of inherent expression is the analytical knowledge of language. Thus, this analytical knowledge of language is said to have arisen with sound as its object, not with designation as its object” (Vibh-a 718). Therefore, the analytical knowledge of language arises at the mind-door after the ear-consciousness process, which has the sound of the expression as its object. And this being so, the statement “the analytical knowledge of language has a limited object” becomes justified, they say. However, teachers like the Elder Jotipāla say: “The statement ‘the analytical knowledge of language has a present object’ is said with reference to taking a present sound and subsequently knowing it.” If this is so, then it would follow that one present object is said to be another present object. Just as the divine ear-knowledge, which is the condition for determining the distinctions of human and other sounds, makes those particular sounds clear, so too, if the knowledge that is the condition for determining inherent and non-inherent expressions, which has the present sound of inherent expression as its object and makes it clear, is called the analytical knowledge of language, there is no contradiction with the Pāli.
