And it is indeed not impossible to say that “for one who reflects, taking that sound of inherent expression as the object” means “for one who engages in reflection with a present sound as object.” For that knowledge, too, arises precisely while discerning the inherent expression, immediately after reflecting on that particular sound, because it serves as the cause for determining those particular distinctions; and thus it arises penetrating and breaking down the expression, and is also one that has gone into the distinctions.

1190. Tividhanti idaṃ heṭṭhā vibhāvitanayamevāti. Paccavekkhatoti imāni ñāṇāni idamatthajotakānīti asammohavasena paccavekkhantassa. Nanu ca tīṇi ñāṇānipi atthadhammasabhāvaṃ nātivattantīti ñāṇesu ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā, dhammapaṭisambhidā ca hoti, kasmā pana “tesu…pe… mata”nti visuṃ vuttanti? Sārammaṇesu tīsu ñāṇesu pavattañāṇassa adhippetattā. Yañhi ñāṇārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ tassa ārammaṇampi asammohavasena paṭivijjhantameva pavattati, taṃ idha paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā nāma. Evañca katvā vuttaṃ “imāni ñāṇāni [M 2.0303] idamatthajotakānī”ti. Ñāṇamattārammaṇaṃ pana ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidāyeva. Ettha ca kiñcāpi ayaṃ paṭisambhidā sārammaṇesu ñāṇesu pavattati, ārammaṇānaṃ pana pabhedaṃ heṭṭhā ñāṇattayameva vibhāveti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā dhammadesanāya asamattho bahussuto kiñcāpi dhammakathikena kathetabbaṃ dhammaṃ jānāti, desanā pana dhammakathikasseva visayoti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Imāsu pana pacchimānaṃ tissannaṃ sekhāsekhamaggakkhaṇe asammohavasena paṭivedho hoti, atthapaṭisambhidāya ārammaṇakaraṇavasenapi. Tathā hi sā maggaphalasabhāvāpi hoti. Evañca katvā sā lokiyalokuttarā, sesā tisso lokiyāva. Tenāhu porāṇā –

1190. “Threefold” refers to the method explained below. “Reflecting” means for one who reflects without delusion that “these knowledges illuminate this meaning.” Now, since the three knowledges do not transcend the nature of meaning and phenomena, the knowledge about these knowledges is the analytical knowledge of meaning and the analytical knowledge of phenomena. Why then is it stated separately, “in these... it is considered”? Because what is intended is the knowledge that occurs in regard to the three knowledges that have objects. For the knowledge that has knowledge as its object proceeds by penetrating its object without delusion; this is here called the analytical knowledge of perspicuity. And so it was said: “these knowledges illuminate this meaning.” However, knowledge that has only knowledge as its object is just the analytical knowledge of meaning. And here, although this analytical knowledge occurs in regard to knowledges that have objects, it is the triad of knowledges below that explains the distinction of the objects. To what is this comparable? Just as one who is learned but incapable of teaching the Dhamma may know the Dhamma that should be taught by a Dhamma teacher, yet the teaching itself is the domain of the Dhamma teacher alone—so should this be understood. Moreover, for the last three of these analytical knowledges, penetration without delusion occurs at the path moment of the trainee and the adept, also by way of making them an object for the analytical knowledge of meaning. For that analytical knowledge of meaning also has the nature of path and fruit. Thus, it is both mundane and supramundane, while the remaining three are purely mundane. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Lābho [V 2.0226] tāsamasammohā, sekhāsekhapathakkhaṇe;

Atthapaññā yathālambā, sā dvidhāññā tu sāsavā”ti.

“Their gain is non-delusion at the path moment of the trainee and adept. The wisdom of meaning is according to its object; it is twofold, but the others are with taints.”

1191. Imā pana catasso paṭisambhidā pañcahi ākārehi visadabhāvaṃ gacchantīti dassetuṃ “pariyattī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha pariyatti nāma buddhavacanassa pariyāpuṇanaṃ, pāḷiaṭṭhakathāsu gaṇṭhipadaatthapadavinicchayakathā paripucchā parito sabbato ñātuṃ pucchāti katvā. Savanaṃ sakkaccaṃ aṭṭhiṃ katvā sotaviññāṇavasena gahaṇaṃ, adhigamo magguppatti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “adhigamo nāma arahattamagguppattī”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 718) vuttaṃ. Taṃ sekhabhūmiyaṃ pabhedagamanaṃ appavisayaṃ, asekhabhūmiyaṃ bahuvisayanti katvā vuttaṃ. Sātisayaṃ vā adhigamanaṃ sandhāyeva vuttaṃ. Sekhena pattānampi hi imāsaṃ arahattappattiyā visadabhāvādhigamoti. Pubbayogo viya pana arahattappatti arahatopi paṭisambhidāvisadatāya paccayo na na hotīti pañcannampi yathāyogaṃ sekkhāsekkhapaṭisambhidāvisadatāya kāraṇatā yojetabbā. Pubbayogo nāma pubbabuddhānaṃ [M 2.0304] sāsane gatapaccāgatikabhāvena yāva anulomagotrabhusamīpaṃ, tāva vipassanābhiyogo. Adhigamapubbayogā cettha anuppannaṃ uppādenti, uppannañca visadaṃ karonti, sesāni pana suvisadabhāvasseva paccayāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

1191. Now, to show how these four analytical knowledges become clear in five ways, the passage beginning “mastery of the texts” was stated. Herein, “mastery of the texts” means the learning of the Buddha's word; this is done by questioning in order to know completely from all sides the discussion on the decision of the meaning of difficult terms in the Pāli and the commentaries. “Hearing” is grasping through ear-consciousness, having paid careful and earnest attention. “Attainment” is the arising of the path. But in the commentary it is said: “Attainment means the arising of the path to arahantship.” This was said because its scope is small on the trainee's plane and large on the adept's plane. Or it was said with reference to a superior attainment. For even for those who have attained them as trainees, the attainment of the clarity of these analytical knowledges comes with the attainment of arahantship. And just as prior effort, the attainment of arahantship is also a condition for the clarity of the analytical knowledges even for an arahant. Thus the five should be connected as appropriate as causes for the clarity of the analytical knowledges of both trainees and adepts. “Prior effort” means the practice of insight in the dispensation of previous Buddhas, by way of having gone forth and come back, up to the proximity of conformity knowledge and change-of-lineage knowledge. Herein, attainment and prior effort generate what has not yet arisen and clarify what has arisen, while the remaining factors should be seen as conditions for its complete clarity.

1192-4. Evaṃ ekavidhādivasena paññāya pabhedaṃ dassetvā idāni bhāvanāvidhānaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kathaṃ bhāvetabbā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yasmā imāya paññāya khandhādayo dhammā bhūmi, sīlavisuddhi ceva cittavisuddhi cāti imā dve visuddhiyo mūlaṃ, diṭṭhivisuddhi kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi ñāṇadassanavisuddhīti imā pañca visuddhiyo sarīraṃ, tasmā tesu bhūmibhūtesu dhammesu uggahaparipucchāvasena ñāṇaparicayaṃ katvā mūlabhūtā dve visuddhiyo sampādetvā sarīrabhūtā pañca visuddhiyo sampādentena bhāvetabbāti dassetuṃ “khandhādīsū”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Khandhādīsūti khandhāyatanadhātuindriyapaṭiccasamuppādādibhedesu. Bhūmibhūtesu cāti lakkhaṇādiggahaṇavasena ñāṇassa pavattiṭṭhānabhūtesu. Sīlaṃ cittavisuddhinti mūlabhūtaṃ sīlavisuddhiṃ, cittavisuddhiñca. Sati hi sīlavisuddhiyaṃ, cittavisuddhiyañca ayaṃ paññā mūlajātā nāma hoti, nāsatīti. Diṭṭhivisuddhādayo pañcāti upabrūhetabbattā sarīrabhūtā diṭṭhivisuddhiādayo pañca. Imissā hi paññāya santānavasena pavattamānāya pādapāṇisīsaṭṭhāniyā [V 2.0227] diṭṭhivisuddhiādayo imā pañca visuddhiyo avayavena samudāyūpalakkhaṇanayena sarīranti veditabbā. Tāya paññāyāti uggahaparipucchādivasena khandhādīsu dhammesu pavattapaññāya. Jananāditoti jātijarāmaraṇādīhi.

Having thus shown the classification of wisdom in terms of its singlefold and other aspects, the passage beginning, “How should it be developed?” is now stated to explain the method of cultivation. Herein, for this wisdom, the aggregates and other phenomena are the ground; the two purifications, purification of virtue and purification of mind, are the root; and the five purifications—purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision—are the body. Therefore, to show that it should be developed by one who has cultivated familiarity with knowledge regarding these ground-phenomena through study and questioning, and who has accomplished the two root-purifications and is accomplishing the five body-purifications, the passage beginning, “in the aggregates, etc.” is stated. “In the aggregates, etc.” means in the divisions such as aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, dependent origination, and so on. “And in the ground-phenomena” means in those phenomena that serve as the ground for the occurrence of knowledge through grasping their characteristics and so on. “Purification of virtue and purification of mind” refers to the root-purification of virtue and purification of mind. For when purification of virtue and purification of mind are present, this wisdom is called “root-born,” but not when they are absent. “The five beginning with purification of view” are the five purifications that constitute the body because they are to be augmented. For when this wisdom proceeds as a continuity, these five purifications beginning with purification of view are like the feet, hands, and head, and thus should be understood as the body by the method of indicating a whole by its parts. “By that wisdom” means by the wisdom that occurs regarding the phenomena of the aggregates and so on through study and questioning. “From generation, etc.” means from birth, aging, death, and so on.

1195-6. “Bhāvetabbā”ti vatvā idāni yasmā khandhādibhūmīsu sīlavisuddhicittavisuddhisaṅkhātehi mūlehi suppatiṭṭhitena pañcavisuddhisaṅkhātasarīrassa vaḍḍhaneneva paññāvaḍḍhanā nāma [M 2.0305] hoti, tasmā vipassanāpaññāya bhūmibhūtesu khandhādīsu ekadesadassanatthaṃ “rūpañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu pañcasu khandhesu. Yaṃ kiñcīti anavasesapariyādānaṃ. Atītānāgatādikantiādinā pana tadeva ekādasasu okāsesu pakkhipitvā dasseti. Ādi-ggahaṇena paccuppannassa gahaṇaṃ.

Having said, “Should be developed,” now, because the growth of wisdom comes about precisely through the growth of the body consisting of the five purifications, for one who is well-established on the roots—purification of virtue and purification of mind—in the ground of the aggregates, etc., therefore, in order to show a part of the aggregates, etc., which are the ground for insight wisdom, it is said, “form and so on.” “Therein” means in these five aggregates. “Whatever” means including everything without remainder. And with “past, future, and so on,” it shows that same thing placed in eleven instances. The word “and so on” includes the present.

1197-1200. Hīnantiādīsu akusalakammasamuṭṭhānatāya hīnaṃ, kusalakammasamuṭṭhānatāya paṇītaṃ. Akusalavipākuppattihetubhūtatāya vā hīnaṃ, vipariyāyena paṇītaṃ. Duppariggahabhūtasukhumarūpādivasena dūraṃ, itaravasena santikantiādinā attho veditabbo. Sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvāti atītādivibhāgabhinnaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ rūparāsivasena buddhiyā ekajjhaṃ gahetvā “mahāudakakkhandho”tiādīsu viya “rāsaṭṭhena rūpakkhandho”ti vuccati. Suttepi hi vuttaṃ “tadekajjhaṃ abhisaṃyūhitvā abhisaṅkhipitvā”ti. Vedanākkhandhotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ekekesu pana vedanādīsu “samuddo mayā diṭṭho”tiādīsu viya samudāyavohārassa avayavepi dissanato khandha-saddo ruḷhīvasena pavattatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ taṃ kiñci vedayitalakkhaṇanti sambandho. Vedanākkhandhoyeva vedanākkhandhatā. Vedanāya atītādivibhāge vitthārakathā visuddhimaggato (visuddhi. 2.497 ādayo) gahetabbā. Abhisaṅkhāralakkhaṇanti saṅkhārakkhandhassa cetanāpadhānatāya evaṃ vuttaṃ, sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇe rāsikaraṇalakkhaṇaṃ sampiṇḍanalakkhaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā “saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.79) vuttattā yathā attano phalasaṅkhataṃ sammadeva nipphannaṃ hoti, evaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇasabhāvanti attho. Ayaṃ pana kusalākusalacetanāya vasena vaṭṭati.

1197-1200. In the passage beginning 'Inferior,' form is 'inferior' because it originates from unwholesome kamma; it is 'superior' because it originates from wholesome kamma. Or it is 'inferior' because it is a cause for the arising of unwholesome results, and 'superior' for the opposite reason. The meaning should be understood such that it is 'distant' by way of being subtle form, etc., that is difficult to comprehend, and 'near' in the opposite way. 'Having made it all one' means: having mentally taken all that which is divided by way of past, etc., together as a single heap of form, it is called 'the aggregate of form' in the sense of a heap, as in such phrases as 'a great mass of water.' For it is also said in a sutta: 'having amassed it, having compacted it.' This same method applies to the aggregate of feeling, etc. However, in the case of each one, feeling, etc., the word 'aggregate' should be seen as functioning by conventional usage, since the designation for a whole is also seen applied to a part, as in 'I have seen the ocean.' The connection is: 'whatever has the characteristic of being felt.' The state of being the aggregate of feeling is just the aggregate of feeling. The detailed discussion on the division of feeling into past, etc., should be taken from the Visuddhimagga (Vism 14.129ff). 'Having the characteristic of forming': this is said because the aggregate of formations has volition as its chief; it means it has the characteristic of massing, the characteristic of compacting, associated phenomena in an object. Alternatively, because it is said, 'they form the formed' (SN 22.79), the meaning is that it has the nature of forming in such a way that its own resultant 'formed thing' is properly produced. This operates by way of wholesome and unwholesome volition.

1202-5. Evaṃ [M 2.0306] vipassanāpaññāya bhūmibhūte dhamme ekadesato dassetvā idāni sīlacittavisuddhīnaṃ heṭṭhā vuttattā tā avatvā idaṃ paññābhāvanāya ādibhūtaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhiṃ dassetuṃ [V 2.0228] “cattāro ca mahābhūtā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Taṃ sampādetukāmena ca yogāvacarena catudhātuvavatthānavasena vā dvādasāyatanavasena vā pañcakkhandhavasena vā ubhinnaṃ saṅkhepakoṭṭhāsānaṃ vasena vā paṭiladdhajjhānavasena vā nāmarūpassa vavatthāpetabbabhāvepi tena tena mukhena vavatthānappakāsanassa atipapañcāvahattā yathādhigatakkhandhavaseneva idha vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ. Ekāsītiyā cittenāti ekāsītiyā lokiyacittena. Lokuttaracittāni pana neva sukkhavipassakassa, na samathayānikassa pariggahaṃ gacchanti anadhigatattā. Cattārorūpino khandheti cattāro arūpino khandhe. Sītuṇhādivirodhipaccayasamavāye vikārāpajjanato rūpaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ. Ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ namanato nāmaṃ namanalakkhaṇaṃ. Parigaṇhatīti paricchedakārikāya paññāya paricchinditvā gaṇhāti.

1202-5. Having thus shown in part the phenomena that are the foundation for insight wisdom, now, without mentioning the purification of virtue and mind since they have been stated earlier, this is begun with “the four great elements,” etc., to show the purification of view, which is the initial foundation for the development of wisdom. For the meditator who wishes to accomplish this, although the discernment of name-and-form should be done either through analysis of the four elements, the twelve sense bases, the five aggregates, the two summary portions, or the attainment of jhāna, due to the excessive proliferation that would arise from explaining the method of discernment through each of these approaches, the discernment here is shown only according to the aggregates as they have been understood. “By eighty-one types of consciousness” means by the eighty-one types of mundane consciousness. The supramundane consciousnesses, however, are not included within the scope of either the dry-insight practitioner or the serenity practitioner, as they have not been attained. “The four formless aggregates” refers to the four immaterial aggregates. Form has the characteristic of being afflicted because it is subject to alteration on the concurrence of opposing conditions like cold and heat. Name has the characteristic of inclining towards an object. “Comprehends” means one grasps by defining with the wisdom that delimits.

1206-9. Tālassa kandaṃ tu yamakanti dvīhi bījehi nibbattitaṃ ekībhūtaṃ yamakatālakandaṃ. Tañhi yamakaṃ bhinnasantānampi abhinnaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti, evaṃ rūpārūpadhammāti. Nāmañca rūpañcāti eteneva tassa duvidhabhāve siddhe “dvidhā vavatthapetī”ti idaṃ nāmarūpavinimuttassa aññassa abhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tenevāha “nāmato rūpato”tiādi. Nāmarūpamattatāya avinicchitattā, santānādighanabhedassa ca akatattā abhinivesena vinā samūhekattaggahaṇavasena “satto”ti pavatto sammoho sattasammoho, tassa ghātatthaṃ vikkhambhanatthaṃ. Bahusuttavasenāti “yathā hī”tiādinā idha dassitānaṃ, aññesañca “rūpañca hidaṃ, mahāli, attā abhavissa[M 2.0307], nayidaṃ rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvatteyyā”ti (mahāva. 20; saṃ. ni. 3.59) evamādīnaṃ sambahulānaṃ suttantānaṃ vasena. Tanti taṃ nāmarūpaṃ.

1206-9. The trunk of the tāla tree, known as yamaka, arises from two seeds and becomes unified as the yamaka tāla trunk. Though its continuity is split, it appears undivided—just so are form and formless phenomena. The phrase “name and form” itself establishes their dual nature; hence, “analyses into two” is to show the absence of anything else apart from name and form. Therefore, it is said: “from name, from form,” etc. Because its nature as merely name-and-form has not been determined, and because the compactness of continuity and so on has not been broken up, the delusion “a being” that proceeds by way of grasping it as a single mass is the delusion about a being; this is for the purpose of destroying and suppressing it. “By way of many suttas” means by way of the many suttas shown here with “just as,” etc., and others such as: “Mahāli, if this form were self, then this form would not lead to affliction” (Mahāvagga 20; SN 22.59). “That” refers to that name-and-form.

1210-2. Aṅgasambhārāti aṅgasambhārahetu tannimittaṃ amuñcitvā sati eva tasminti attho. Saddoti vohāro. Khandhesūti pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu santesu te amuñcitvāva sattoti sammuti vohāro. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā akkhacakkapañjaraīsādīsu aṅgasambhāresu ekenākārena ekajjhaṃ rāsi hutvā saṇṭhitesu “ratho”ti vohāramattaṃ hoti, paramatthato pana ekekasmiṃ aṅge upaparikkhiyamāne ratho nāma natthi, evameva upādānakkhandhasaṅkhātesu rūpārūpadhammesu santānavasena pavattamānesu “satto”ti vā “puggalo”ti vā “jīvo”ti vā vohāramattaṃ, paramatthato pana ekekasmiṃ dhamme upaparikkhiyamāne “asmī”ti vā “aha”nti vā gāhassa vatthubhūto satto nāma natthi, kevalaṃ nāmarūpamattameva atthīti. Evaṃ passato hi dassanaṃ [V 2.0229] yathābhūtadassanaṃ nāma hoti, yaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhīti vuccati. Sace koci satto nāma natthi, kathañcarahi nāmarūpamatte gamanādiatthakiccasiddhatā hotīti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “yathāpī”tiādi. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – yathā dārumayaṃ yantaṃ nijjīvaṃ jīvavirahitaṃ abbhantare vattamānassa jīvassa abhāvato tatoyeva nirīhakaṃ nibyāpāraṃ, atha ca pana dārurajjusamāyoge paccayavisesavasena taṃ dāruyantaṃ gacchatipi tiṭṭhatipi, sajīvaṃ sabyāpāraṃ viya gamanādikiccaṃ sādhentamiva khāyati, tathā idaṃ nāmarūpampi kiñcāpi nijjīvaṃ nirīhakañca, atha ca pana aññamaññasaṅkhatapaccayavisesassa samāyoge sajīvaṃ sabyāpāraṃ gacchantaṃ tiṭṭhantañca khāyatīti.

1210-2. “On the assembly of parts” means: on account of the assembly of parts, when it exists, without leaving its characteristic appearance aside. “Word” means designation. “On the aggregates” means: when the five aggregates of clinging exist, without leaving them aside, the designation “being” is a convention. This is what is said: Just as when the parts of a chariot—such as the axle, wheel, frame, and pole—are assembled in a certain way and arranged together in a heap, they are conventionally called a “chariot,” but in the ultimate sense, when each part is examined, there is no such thing as a chariot. Similarly, with the form and formless phenomena designated as the aggregates of clinging that proceed by way of continuity, terms like “being,” “person,” or “living soul” are merely a convention. In the ultimate sense, when each phenomenon is examined, there is no being that is the basis for the grasp “I am” or “I”; there is only mere name-and-form. For one who sees thus, the vision is called “seeing things as they really are,” which is known as the purification of view. If someone should ask, “If there is no such thing as a being, how then can mere name-and-form accomplish such tasks as going?”—this is addressed with the example beginning “Just as….” Here is the condensed meaning: Just as a wooden machine, being lifeless, devoid of a living soul, and thus inert and inactive because of the absence of an inner living being, yet due to the combination of wood and ropes—through specific conditions—that wooden machine appears to move or stand, as if it were alive and active, accomplishing tasks like movement; so too this name-and-form, though lifeless and inert, appears to move and stand as if alive and active due to the combination of specific, mutually formed conditions.

1213. Saccatoti [M 2.0308] bhūtato, paramatthatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ abhisaṅkhataṃ yantamiva suññaṃ jīvādinā. Paccayehi abhisaṅkhataṃ idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ yantamiva suññanti vā sambandho. Dukkhassa puñjoti niccāturatāya dukkhassa rāsi. Tiṇakaṭṭhasādisoti attasuññatāya tiṇakaṭṭhasamo.

1213. “Truly” means actually; that is to say, in the ultimate sense. This name-and-form is conditioned, empty like a machine of a living soul and so on. Or the connection is: this name-and-form, conditioned by causes, is empty like a machine. “A heap of suffering” means a mass of suffering due to constant affliction. “Like grass and sticks” means it is like grass and sticks on account of its emptiness of self.

1215. Yamakanti yugaḷaṃ. So ca yamakabhāvo aññamaññanissitabhāvenāti āha “ubho aññoññanissitā”ti. Tato eva ekasmiṃ bhijjamānasmiṃ ubho bhijjanti. Na hi kadāci pañcavokārabhave maraṇavasena rūpe nirujjhante arūpaṃ anirujjhantaṃ, arūpe vā nirujjhante rūpaṃ anirujjhantaṃ atthi. Ekavokārabhavacatuvokārabhavesu pana tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ anissāya pavattiyā kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttamevāti. So panāyaṃ bhaṅgo paccayavaseneva, paccayanirodheneva nāmarūpanirodhoti attho. Paccayāti paccayabhūtā, aññamaññassa paccayā hontāpi ekasmiṃ bhijjamānasmiṃ ubho bhijjantiyevāti attho.

1215. “Yamaka” means a pair. And that twin nature is due to mutual dependence, as stated: “Both depend on each other.” Therefore, when one breaks, both break. For it never happens that in five-constituent existence, when form ceases by way of death, the formless does not cease, or when the formless ceases, form does not cease. However, in one-constituent and four-constituent existences, the reason for their functioning without mutual dependence has been explained above. But this breaking occurs only through the power of conditions; that is, the cessation of name-and-form is only due to the cessation of conditions. “Conditions” means being causal; even while being conditions for each other, when one breaks, both break—this is the meaning.

1216-9. Nittejanti tejahīnaṃ ānubhāvavirahitaṃ. Yattha pana taṃ nittejaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “na byāharatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na hi aññathā saddahanussāhanādīsu nāmaṃ nittejanti sakkā vattuṃ, nāpi rūpaṃ sandhāraṇābandhanādīsu. Teneva hi “tathā rūpampi nitteja”nti vatvā “bhuñjāmīti…pe… na vijjatī”ti vuttaṃ.

1216-9. “Powerless” means devoid of potency, lacking influence. To illustrate wherein it is powerless, it is said: “It does not speak,” etc. For otherwise it could not be said that name is powerless in matters like faith and effort, nor that form is powerless in maintaining and binding. Therefore, after saying, “Thus form too is powerless,” it is stated: “I eat… it is not found,” etc.

1220-1. Nāmaṃ nissāyātiādinā byatirekavasenapi nāmarūpānaṃ nittejataṃyeva vibhāveti[V 2.0230]. Rūpañhi gamanādikiriyāsu nāmaṃ nissāya pavattati, nāmaṃ dassanādikiriyāsu rūpaṃ nissāya. Aññamaññaṃ sannissāya cassa attakiccasiddhipi paccekaṃ asamatthataṃ vibhāveti. Tathā hi nāmarūpassa attasuññatā, nibyāpāratā ca suṭṭhutaraṃ pākaṭā hontīti. Kathaṃ [M 2.0309] pana paccekaṃ asamatthānaṃ samuditabhāve sati samatthatā hoti asāmaggiyaṃ ahetūnaṃ sāmaggiyampi ahetukabhāvāpattito. Na hi paccekaṃ daṭṭhuṃ asakkontānaṃ satampi sahassampi samuditaṃ daṭṭhuṃ sakkotīti codanaṃ hadaye katvā āha “imassa panā”tiādi. Upamāyapi hi asiddho attho sādhetabbo. Tenevāha “upamaṃ te karissāmi, upamāyapi idhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ jānantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.258; a. ni. 8.8; 10.95; jā. 2.19.24). Ayaṃ panettha jaccandhapīṭhasappīnaṃ upamā – yathā jaccandho ca pīṭhasappī ca disā pakkamitukāmā assu. Jaccandho pīṭhasappiṃ evamāha “ahaṃ kho, bhaṇe, sakkomi pādehi pādakaraṇīyaṃ kātuṃ, natthi ca me cakkhūni, yehi samaṃ visamaṃ passeyya”nti. Pīṭhasappī jaccandhaṃ evamāha “ahaṃ kho, bhaṇe, sakkomi cakkhunā cakkhukaraṇīyaṃ kātuṃ, natthi ca me pādā, yehi abhikkameyyaṃ paṭikkameyyaṃ vā”ti. So tuṭṭhahaṭṭho jaccandho pīṭhasappiṃ aṃsakūṭaṃ āropesi, pīṭhasappī jaccandhassa aṃsakūṭe nisīditvā evamāha “vāmaṃ muñca, dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇha, dakkhiṇaṃ muñca, vāmaṃ gaṇhā”ti. Tattha jaccandhopi nittejo dubbalo na sakena balena gacchati, tatheva pīṭhasappī na sakena balena gacchati, na ca tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ nissāya gamanaṃ na pavattati, evameva nāmampi nittejaṃ na sakena tejena uppajjati, na tāsu tāsu kiriyāsu pavattati, rūpampi nittejaṃ na sakena tejena uppajjati, na tāsu tāsu kiriyāsu pavattati, na ca tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ nissāya uppatti vā pavatti vā na hotīti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

1220-1. By stating “dependent on name,” etc., it further clarifies the powerless nature of name-and-form by way of contrast. For form, dependent on name, operates in actions like walking; and name, dependent on form, operates in actions like seeing. By their mutual dependence, the accomplishment of its own function reveals their individual inability. Thus, the emptiness of self and inactivity of name-and-form become very clearly evident. But how can things that are individually incapable become capable when combined? For it would follow that things that are not causes when they are separate would also be non-causes when they are combined. Keeping in mind the objection that just as a hundred or a thousand individuals unable to see cannot see even when gathered together, he says, “But in this case,” etc. For even an unproven meaning must be established through a simile. Hence it is said: “I will give you a simile, for by a simile some wise persons here understand the meaning of what is said” (MN 29; AN 8:8; 10:95; Ja 24). Here is the simile of the man born blind and the cripple: Suppose a man born blind and a cripple wished to travel. The man born blind would say to the cripple, “Friend, I can do with my feet what needs to be done with feet, but I have no eyes with which to see the even and uneven.” The cripple would say to the man born blind, “Friend, I can do with my eyes what needs to be done with eyes, but I have no feet with which to go forward or back.” Pleased and delighted, the man born blind lifted the cripple onto his shoulders. Seated on the blind man’s shoulders, the cripple said, “Avoid the left, take the right; avoid the right, take the left.” In this case, the man born blind, being powerless and weak, does not go by his own strength; similarly, the cripple does not go by his own strength. Yet their going does not fail to proceed by depending on each other. So too, name, being powerless, does not arise by its own potency, nor does it operate in those various actions; and form, being powerless, does not arise by its own potency, nor does it operate in those various actions. Yet their arising or operating does not fail to occur by depending on each other. Therefore, the ancients said—

“Na sakena balena jāyare,

Nopi sakena balena tiṭṭhare;

Paradhammavasānuvattino,

Jāyare saṅkhatā attadubbalā.

“Not by their own power are they born, nor by their own power do they endure; following the sway of other phenomena, they are born, conditioned, and weak in themselves.

“Parapaccayato [M 2.0310][V 2.0231] ca jāyare, paraārammaṇato samuṭṭhitā;

Ārammaṇapaccayehi ca, paradhammehi cime pabhāvitā”ti. (visuddhi. 2.677);

“Born from other conditions, arisen from an external object; by object-conditions and by other phenomena, these are produced.”

1222-3. Idāni nāvāyantikūpamāyapi nāmarūpānaṃ avasavattitaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādigāthādvayaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha nissāyāti patiṭṭhāya. Yantīti gacchanti. Manusse nissāyāti netubhūte niyāmakakammakarādimanusse apassāya. Na hi tesaṃ araṇaggahaṇalaṅkārasaṇṭhāpanaudakasiñcanādikiriyāya vinā nāvā icchitadesaṃ pāpuṇāti, yathā pana ubhopi aññamaññaṃ nissāya aṇṇave gacchanti, evaṃ nāmañca rūpañca ubho aññamaññaṃ nissitā pavattantīti adhippāyo.

1222-3. Now, to clarify the non-subservience of name-and-form by means of the simile of the ship and the mariners, the two verses beginning with “Just as…” have been stated. Herein, “depending on” means relying upon. “They go” means they proceed. “Depending on people” means relying on people who are guides, such as the helmsman and workers. For without their actions—such as taking the rudder, setting up the rigging, and bailing water—the ship cannot reach its desired destination. Just as both travel on the ocean in dependence on each other, so too name and form both proceed in dependence on each other—this is the meaning.

1224. Sattasaññaṃ vinodetvāti yathāvuttanayehi anādikālabhāvitaṃ khandhapañcake sattaggāhaṃ vikkhambhetvā. Nāma…pe… vuccatīti “idaṃ nāmaṃ, ettakaṃ nāmaṃ, na ito bhiyyo. Idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti ca evaṃ sabbākārena tesaṃ lakkhaṇasallakkhaṇamukhena tamatthabhāvadassanaṃ etaṃ attadiṭṭhimalavisodhanato diṭṭhivisuddhīti vuccati buddhādīhīti attho. Na kevalañcetaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhiyeva vuccati, nāmarūpavavatthāpanantipi etasseva adhivacananti veditabbaṃ. Jātiāditoti jātijarābyādhiādito dukkhato. Yathāha “jātipi dukkhā, jarāpi dukkhā, byādhipi dukkho, maraṇampi dukkhaṃ, yampicchaṃ na labhati, tampi dukkhaṃ, saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti (mahāva. 14; saṃ. ni. 5.1081; paṭi. ma. 2.30). Antadvayanti sassatucchedasaṅkhātaṃ antadvayaṃ. Atha vā sattassa accantaṃ atthibhāvasaṅkhātaṃ, tassa natthibhāvasaṅkhātañca antadvayaṃ. Paramatthato anupalabbhanato hi satto [M 2.0311] atthīti vajjitabbameva, lokasaṅketatova upalabbhanato natthītipi vajjitabbamevāti. Suṭṭhutaraṃ parisuddhaṃ karotīti sambandho. Diṭṭhigatāni malānīti diṭṭhigatasaṅkhātāni malāni. Asesaṃ nissesato nāsaṃ vināsaṃ vikkhambhanaṃ upenti. Tathā hetaṃ diṭṭhimalavisodhanato diṭṭhivisuddhīti vuccati.

1224. “To dispel the perception of a being” means: having suppressed, in the manner already stated, the grasping at a being in the five aggregates, which has been cultivated since beginningless time. “Name… is said…” thus: “This is name, this much is name, no more than this. This is form, this much is form, no more than this.” And in this way, seeing the true nature of these things in all aspects by means of discerning their general and specific characteristics—this, because it cleanses the stain of the view of self, is called “purification of view” by the Buddhas and others; this is the meaning. Not only is this called purification of view, but it should be understood that “the determination of name-and-form” is also a designation for this very thing. “From birth, etc.” means from the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and so on. As it is said: “Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, not getting what one wants is also suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.” “The two extremes” means the two extremes designated as eternalism and annihilationism. Or else, it means the two extremes: the one designated as the absolute existence of a being, and the one designated as its non-existence. For since a being is not found in an ultimate sense, one should not say “it exists”; and since it is found by way of worldly convention, one should not say “it does not exist.” The connection is with the words: “It purifies very thoroughly.” “The stains of wrong views” means the stains designated as wrong views. They come to destruction, ruin, and suppression completely, without remainder. Thus, because it cleanses the stain of wrong view, it is called “purification of view”.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus it is in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the commentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma,

Diṭṭhivisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the commentary on the exposition of the purification of view.

19. Ekūnavīsatimo paricchedo

19. The Nineteenth Chapter.

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt.

1227. Anantaraṃ [V 2.0232] niddiṭṭhāya diṭṭhivisuddhiyā visayabhāvena dassitattā “etassā”ti vuttaṃ, na tadaññato visesanatthaṃ tadaññassa ca abhāvato. Ajjhattaṃ vā hi vipassanābhiniveso hotu bahiddhā vā, atthasiddhiyaṃ pana lakkhaṇato sabbampi nāmarūpaṃ anavasesato pariggahitameva hotīti. Jānitvā hetupaccayeti hetupaccaye pariggaṇhitvā, hetupaccaye pariggaṇhanahetūti vuttaṃ hoti. Paccayapariggahaṇahetu hissa addhattaye kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ hotīti. Vitaritvāti atikkamitvā, vikkhambhetvāti attho. Taṃ pana ñāṇaṃ tathāvigataṃ vasibhāvappattaṃ jhānaṃ viya yogino santāne pabandhavasena pavattatīti katvā vuttaṃ “ṭhita”nti.

1227. 'Of this' is stated because the purification of view, which was expounded immediately before, has been shown as its object; it is not for the purpose of distinguishing it from something else, since there is nothing else. For whether the adherence to insight is internal or external, in the accomplishment of the goal, all name-and-form is indeed comprehended without remainder by way of its characteristic. 'Having known the cause and condition' means having comprehended the cause and condition; it is said to be for the sake of comprehending the cause and condition. For the reason for comprehending the conditions is that it leads to the overcoming of his doubt concerning the three periods of time. 'Having overcome' means having transcended; the meaning is having suppressed. And because that knowledge, being such and having reached mastery, proceeds in the yogi's mental continuum by way of an uninterrupted sequence, like a jhāna, the word 'established' is stated.

1229-30. Nāmarūpassa…pe… āvajjitvāti yathā nāma kusalo bhisakko rogaṃ disvā tassa samuṭṭhānaṃ pariyesati, yathā vā pana anukampako puriso kumāraṃ uttānaseyyaṃ [M 2.0312] rathikāya nipannaṃ disvā “kassa nu kho ayaṃ puttako”ti tassa mātāpitaro āvajjati, evamevaṃ nāmarūpassa ko hetu, ko vā paccayo bhave. Na tāvetaṃ ahetukaṃ sabbattha, sabbadā, sabbesañca ekasadisabhāvāpattito, na issarādihetukaṃ nāmarūpato uddhaṃ issarādīnaṃ abhāvato. Yepi nāmarūpamattameva issarādayoti vadanti tesaṃ issarādisaṅkhātanāmarūpassa ahetubhāvāpattito, tasmā bhavitabbamassa hetupaccayehi, “ko nu kho”ti nāmarūpassa hetupaccaye āvajjitvāti attho. Evaṃ tāva katvā imassa nāmarūpassa hetupaccaye pariggaṇhantena oḷārikattā, supākaṭattā ca rūpassa paccayapariggaho sukaroti paṭhamaṃ tassa paccayapariggaho kātabboti dassento āha “rūpakāyassā”tiādi. Tattha yathā nāmarūpassa paccayapariggaho ahetuvisamahetuvādanivattiyā hoti, evaṃ nibbidāvirāgāvahabhāvena tattha tattha abhiratinivattiyāpi icchitabboti taṃ dvattiṃsākāravasena dassetuṃ “kesā lomā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Having reflected on name-and-form...' means: just as a skilled physician, seeing a disease, seeks its origin, or as a compassionate person, seeing a child lying face up in the street, reflects, 'Whose child might this be?' and thinks of its parents, in the same way one reflects on the cause and condition of name-and-form, thinking: 'What could be the cause, what the condition?' It is not, in the first place, without a cause, for that would entail that it would have to be the same everywhere, always, and for everyone. Nor is it caused by a creator, etc., because there are no such creators, etc., apart from name-and-form. As for those who say that a creator, etc., is just name-and-form, for them it would follow that the name-and-form designated as a creator, etc., would be causeless. Therefore, it must have causes and conditions. The meaning is that one reflects on the cause and condition of name-and-form, thinking, 'What, indeed...?'. Having done so, for one comprehending the cause and condition of this name-and-form, because form is gross and very evident, the comprehension of its conditions is easy. Indicating that, for this reason, the comprehension of its conditions should be done first, he says, 'of the physical body...' etc. Herein, just as the comprehension of the conditions for name-and-form serves to remove the theories of causelessness and inappropriate cause, so too it is desirable that it serves to remove delight in this or that by leading to disenchantment and dispassion. To show this by way of the thirty-two parts, the words 'head hair, body hair...' etc., are stated.

1232-3. Avijjā…pe… matoti avijjā taṇhā upādānaṃ kammanti idaṃ catubbidhaṃ [V 2.0233] dhammajātaṃ etassa yathāvuttassa rūpakāyassa hetu, catubbidho āhāro paccayoti attho. Kasmā pana purimaṃ hetu, itaro paccayoti codanaṃ sandhāya “janako”tiādiṃ vatvā taṃ lokavasena samatthetuṃ “hetvaṅkurassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha janakoti, anupālakoti ca antogatahetvatthamidaṃ visesanaṃ, janakattā, anupālakattāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha janakattāti nibbattakattā. Iminā bījaṃ viya aṅkurassa avijjādayo rūpakāyassa asādhāraṇakāraṇatāya hetūti dassitaṃ. Anupālakattāti upatthambhakattā. Iminā pana aṅkurassa pathavīsalilādayo [M 2.0313] viya āhāro sādhāraṇakāraṇatāya paccayoti dassitanti veditabbaṃ.

'Ignorance... etc... is considered' means: ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma—this fourfold set of phenomena is the cause of this aforesaid physical body, and the four kinds of nutriment are its condition; this is the meaning. But why is the former the cause and the other the condition? In reference to this objection, having stated 'the producer,' etc., in order to support this by way of worldly convention, the words 'the cause of the sprout,' etc., were stated. Herein, 'producer' and 'sustainer' are adjectives that include the meaning of cause; that is, it is said 'because of being a producer' and 'because of being a sustainer.' Herein, 'because of being a producer' means because of being a generator. By this it is shown that ignorance and so on are the cause of the physical body by being its specific condition, like the seed for a sprout. 'Because of being a sustainer' means because of being a supporter. By this it should be known that it is shown that nutriment is the condition by being its general condition, like earth and water for a sprout.

1234-7. Itime…pe… gatāti evamete avijjādayo pañca dhammā yathārahaṃ hetubhāvaṃ, paccayabhāvañca gatā. Mātāva upanissayāti avijjā bhavesu vijjamānadosapaṭicchādanabhāvena, taṇhā patthanābhāvena, upādānaṃ daḷhaggāhabhāvenāti evaṃ saṅkhārabhavānaṃ hetubhūtā janakasahāyatāya bhavanikantitaṃsahajātaāsannakāraṇattā abhisaṅkhārikā, apassayabhūtā vāti mātā viya upanissayā honti. Yathā pitujanitasukke puttassa uppattīti pitā janako, evaṃ kammaṃ sattassa uppādakattā janakanti āha. Yathā dhātī jātassa kumārassa vaḍḍhitā sandhārikā, evaṃ āhāro uppannassa kāyassa brūhetā, sandhārako cāti vuttaṃ “dhātī…pe… bhave”ti. Kāmañcettha avijjādayo nāmakāyassāpi paccayo, pakārantarena pana tassa pākaṭaṃ paccayapariggahavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “cakkhuñcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha cakkhuñcāti ca-saddo samuccayattho, tena cakkhuviññāṇassa āvajjanādiṃ ajjhattaṃ sabbaṃ paccayajātaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Rūpamālokameva cāti pana ca-saddena yathā bāhirarūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayo, yathā ca āloko upanissayapaccayo, evaṃ aññampi bāhiraṃ paccayajātaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Paṭiccāti paccayabhūtaṃ laddhāti attho. Tena cakkhussa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena, rūpālokānañca yathāsambhavaṃ ārammaṇaupanissayapurejātaatthiavigatavasena, itaresañca saddasaṅgahitānaṃ anantarādisahajātādivasena paccayabhāvaṃ dasseti. Ādi-saddena phassādīnaṃ viya saha paccayehi sotaviññāṇādīnaṃ saṅgaho veditabbo. Evaṃ sammasanūpagaṃ sabbaṃ nāmaṃ saha paccayena saṅgahitaṃ hoti. Tenāha “nāmakāyassa paccayaṃ parigaṇhatī”ti.

'These... have become' means: in this way these five phenomena beginning with ignorance have become, respectively, cause and condition. 'Like a mother as support' means: ignorance by concealing the dangers in existences, craving by aspiring, and clinging by firm grasping—thus, being causes of kamma-process existence, they are formational by being an aid to the generator (kamma), by being the co-nascent and proximate cause for delight in existence, or they are a support; thus they are a decisive support condition like a mother. Just as a father is the generator because a son is produced from the semen generated by the father, so he says that kamma is the generator because it produces a being. Just as a wet-nurse is the developer and sustainer of a born child, so nutriment is the developer and sustainer of the arisen body; thus it is said, 'a wet-nurse... becomes.' Although here ignorance and so on are also conditions for the mental body, in order to show the method for comprehending its conditions in another, more evident way, the words 'the eye and...' etc., are stated. Herein, in 'the eye and,' the particle 'ca' has a collective sense; by it, he includes the entire set of internal conditions for eye-consciousness, beginning with adverting. And in 'form and light,' by the particle 'ca,' just as external form is the object condition for eye-consciousness and light is the decisive support condition, so he includes the other set of external conditions. 'Depending on' means having obtained the state of being a condition. By this he shows the conditionality of the eye by way of dependence, pre-nascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance; of form and light, as is possible, by way of object, decisive support, pre-nascence, presence, and non-disappearance; and of the others included by the word 'etc.,' by way of contiguity, co-nascence, etc. By the word 'etc.' the inclusion of ear-consciousness, etc., along with their conditions, such as contact, should be understood. In this way, all mentality that is subject to comprehension is included along with its conditions. Hence he says: 'he comprehends the conditions for the mental body.'

1238-40. Disvānāti [M 2.0314] etarahi pavattiṃ disvā. Tathevidanti iminā na kevalaṃ sappaccayatāmattameva [V 2.0234] paccāmaṭṭhaṃ, atha kho yādisehi etarahi pavattati, tādisehi avijjādipaccayeheva atītepi pavattitthāti paccayasahitatāpi paccāmaṭṭhāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pubbanteti atītakhandhappabandhakoṭṭhāse. Pañcadhāgatāti –

'Having seen' means having seen the present occurrence. 'Just so': by this, not only is the mere fact of its being conditioned grasped, but it should be understood that just as it occurs now with such conditions as ignorance and so on, so too in the past it occurred with the very same conditions. Thus its being accompanied by conditions is also grasped. 'The past' means in the section concerning the continuum of past aggregates. 'Gone in five ways:'

“Ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhānaṃ, na nu kho ahosiṃ ahamatītamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ nu kho ahosiṃ ahamatītamaddhānaṃ, kathaṃ nu kho ahosiṃ ahamatītamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20; mahāni. 174) –

“Was I in the past? Or was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past?”

Pañcahi ākārehi āgatā, pavattā vā. Aparanteti anāgate khandhappabandhakoṭṭhāse. Pañcadhā samudīritāti –

They have come, or have occurred, in five ways. 'The future' means in the section concerning the continuum of future aggregates. 'Declared in five ways:'

“Bhavissāmi nu kho ahamanāgatamaddhānaṃ, na nu kho bhavissāmi ahamanāgatamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ nu kho bhavissāmi ahamanāgatamaddhānaṃ, kathaṃ nu kho bhavissāmi ahamanāgatamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ bhavissāmi nu kho ahamanāgatamaddhāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20; mahāni. 174) –

“Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I become in the future?”

Evaṃ pañcadhā kathitā.

Thus they are stated in five ways.

1241. Paccuppannepi addhāneti etarahi paṭisandhiṃ ādiṃ katvā cutipariyante addhānepi. Addhāna-ggahaṇena cettha paccuppannakhandhakoṭṭhāsameva vadati. Na hi tabbinimutto añño koci kālo nāma atthīti. Chabbidhā parikittitāti –

1241. 'In the present time-period' means in the present time-period that has rebirth-linking for its beginning and death for its end. And here by the term ‘time-period,’ it refers only to the section of present aggregates, for there is indeed no time separate from that. 'Declared in six ways:'

“Ahaṃ nu khosmi, no nu khosmi, kiṃ nu khosmi, kathaṃ nu khosmi, ayaṃ nu kho satto kuto āgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī ca bhavissatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20; mahāni. 174) –

“Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? From where has this being come? Where will this being go?”

Evaṃ [M 2.0315] chabbidhā vuttā. “Sabbe tasanti daṇḍassā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 129-130) viya padesepi [V 2.0235] sabba-saddassa pavattanato “sabbā”ti vatvāpi “anavasesā”ti vuttaṃ. Natthi etissā avaseso avasiṭṭhoti anavasesā, soḷasavidhāpi cesā ekakaṅkhāvasenāpi anavasiṭṭhā hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pahiyyatīti vikkhambhanavasena pahiyyati. Kāmaṃ nāmarūpamattaṃ vinā sattassa adassanena diṭṭhivisuddhiyāva paccuppanne kaṅkhā pahīnā, atītānāgate kaṅkhānaṃ pahānena pana paccuppanne kaṅkhāya atisayappahānaṃ dassetuṃ idheva sā vuttā. Atha vā paccuppanne nissattanāmarūpassa paccayesu pavattakaṅkhāya idheva tīraṇato sā idha vuttā. Vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ vā etaṃ idha paccuppannakaṅkhāya pahānavacanaṃ yathā taṃ sotāpattimaggādīsu pahīnānampi ca pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānātiādinā anāgāmimaggādīsu vacananti.

Thus they are stated in six ways. Just as in such verses as ‘All tremble at the rod,’ the word ‘all’ is used to refer to a part, so too here, although it says ‘all,’ it is also said to be ‘without remainder.’ There is no remainder or residue for this; thus it is called ‘without remainder.’ It is said that even this sixteenfold doubt is without remainder when considered as a single doubt. It is abandoned: it is abandoned by way of suppression. Granted, since a being is not seen apart from mere name-and-form, doubt about the present is abandoned by the purification of view itself; however, it is mentioned here in order to show the surpassing abandonment of doubt in the present through the abandonment of doubts about the past and future. Alternatively, it is stated here because the doubt that occurs concerning the conditions of selfless name-and-form in the present is resolved right here. Or else, this statement here about the abandonment of doubt in the present is a matter of embellishment, just as the abandonment of the five lower fetters, though they are abandoned at the path of stream-entry, is spoken of at the path of the non-returner and so on.

1242. Kammavipākānaṃ vasenāpīti purimakammabhavasmiṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanaṃ saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanaṃ upādānaṃ, cetanā bhavo iti ime pañca dhammā purimakammabhavasmiṃ idha paṭisandhiyā paccayā, idha paṭisandhi viññāṇaṃ, okkanti nāmarūpaṃ, pasādo āyatanaṃ, phuṭṭho phasso, vedayitaṃ vedanā iti ime pañca dhammā idhūpapattibhavasmiṃ pure katassa kammassa paccayā, idha paripakkattā āyatanānaṃ moho avijjā…pe… cetanā bhavo iti ime pañca dhammā kammabhavasmiṃ āyatiṃ paṭisandhiyā paccayāti evaṃ vuttānaṃ kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭānaṃ vasena. Kilesavaṭṭopi cettha kammasahāyatāya kammavaṭṭeneva saṅgahitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

1242. By way of kamma and its results: In the previous kamma-existence, delusion is ignorance, accumulation is formations, delight is craving, approaching is clinging, and volition is existence. These five states in the previous kamma-existence are the conditions for rebirth-linking here. Here, rebirth-linking is consciousness, descent is name-and-form, sensitivity is the sense base, the touched is contact, and the felt is feeling. These five states in this rebirth-existence are the result of kamma done previously. Here, owing to the maturing of the sense bases, delusion is ignorance… volition is existence. These five states in the kamma-existence are the conditions for future rebirth-linking. This is by way of the round of kamma and the round of results, which have been described thus. It should be understood that the round of defilements is included here within the round of kamma because it assists kamma.

1243. Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyanti ettha diṭṭhadhammo vuccati paccakkhabhūto paccuppanno attabhāvo, tattha veditabbaphalaṃ kammaṃ [M 2.0316] diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ. Upapajjāparāpariyāhosikammavasā panāti upapajjavedanīyaaparāpariyavedanīyaahosikammavasena. Uttarapadalopavasena hi “upapajjāparāpariya”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha paccuppannabhavato anantaraṃ upapajjitvā veditabbaphalaṃ kammaṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ. Apare apare diṭṭhadhammato aññasmiṃ aññasmiṃ yatthakatthaci attabhāve veditabbaphalaṃ kammaṃ aparāpariyavedanīyaṃ. Ahosi eva kammaṃ, na tassa vipāko ahosi, atthi, bhavissati cāti evaṃ vattabbakammaṃ ahosikammaṃ.

1243. To be experienced in this very life: Here, ‘this very life’ refers to the directly perceived, present existence. Kamma whose result is to be experienced therein is called ‘to be experienced in this very life.’ But by way of kamma to be experienced upon rebirth, in subsequent lives, or that is defunct: this means by way of kamma to be experienced upon rebirth, kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives, and defunct kamma. For ‘upon rebirth and in subsequent lives’ is stated by way of elision of the final term. Therein, kamma whose result is to be experienced after one has arisen immediately after the present existence is called ‘to be experienced upon rebirth.’ Kamma whose result is to be experienced in other and further existences, in whatever place, different from this very life, is called ‘to be experienced in subsequent lives.’ Kamma that merely was, of which it can be said, ‘its result has not been, is not, and will not be,’ is defunct kamma.

Paṭipakkhehi anabhibhūtatāya, paccayavisesena paṭiladdhavisesatāya ca balavabhāvappattā tādisassa pubbābhisaṅkhārassa vasena sātisayā hutvā pavattā paṭhamajavanacetanā tasmiṃyeva attabhāve [V 2.0236] phaladāyinī diṭṭhadhammavedanīyā nāma. Sā hi vuttākārena balavati javanasantāne guṇavisesayuttesu upakārānupakāravasappavattiyā, āsevanālābhena appavipākatāya ca itaradvayaṃ viya pavattasantānuparamāpekkhaṃ, okāsalābhāpekkhañca kammaṃ na hotīti idheva pupphamattaṃ viya pavattivipākamattaṃ ahetukaphalaṃ deti, sahetukaphaladāne pana paṭisandhiākaḍḍhanampi āpajjeyya. Tathā asakkontanti kammassa vipākadānaṃ nāma upadhippayogādipaccayantarasamavāyeneva hotīti tadabhāvato tasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākaṃ dātuṃ asakkontaṃ. Ahosikammaṃ…pe… vipākoti ettha “ahosi kamma”nti padaṃ visuṃ visuṃ yojetabbaṃ “ahosi kammaṃ nāhosi kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.234). Tattha sakasakakālātikkantassa upapajjavedanīyassa, diṭṭhadhammavedanīyassa ca vasena purimaṃ vuttaṃ. Tañhi kammassa[M 2.0317], vipākakālassa ca atītattā tathā vattabbattaṃ labhati, dutiyaṃ anāgate arahattaṃ pāpuṇantassa purimabhavesu kataṃ adinnavipākaṃ aparāpariyavedanīyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tatiyaṃ pana anantarabhave kataṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ, arahato atītabhavesu kataṃ aparāpariyavedanīyañca sandhāya vuttaṃ. Apare pana “ekameva atītaṃ kammaṃ addhattaye vipākābhāvaṃ sandhāya tidhā vibhajitvā vutta”nti vadanti.

The first javana-volition—which has become powerful by not being overcome by opposing factors and by having gained distinction through special conditions, and which has become pre-eminent by the power of such a prior volitional formation—is called ‘to be experienced in this very life’ because it gives its fruit in that very existence. For that volition, being powerful in the aforesaid manner in the javana-continuum, endowed with special qualities, occurring by way of helpful and unhelpful conditions, and having little result due to not obtaining repetition, is not kamma that awaits the cessation of the process of existence or awaits the obtaining of an opportunity, like the other two. Thus it gives right here a rootless fruit, which is merely a result in the course of life, like a mere flower; but in giving a fruit with roots, it might even draw in a rebirth-linking. Thus ‘being unable’ means being unable to give a result in that very existence due to the absence of such factors, since the giving of a kamma-result occurs only through the combination of other conditions such as the substrate, effort, and so on. Defunct kamma… its result: here the words ‘there was kamma’ should be construed separately with each phrase: ‘There was kamma, its result was not; there was kamma, its result will not be; there was kamma, its result is not.’ Therein, the first statement is made with reference to kamma to be experienced upon rebirth and kamma to be experienced in this very life that have passed beyond their respective times. For that kamma obtains such a designation because both the kamma and the time for its result have passed. The second is stated with reference to kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives, which was performed in former existences by one who will attain arahantship in the future and has not yet given its result. The third is stated with reference to kamma to be experienced upon rebirth that was performed in the immediately preceding existence, and with reference to kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives that was performed in past existences by an arahant. Others, however, say: ‘A single past kamma is spoken of as divided into three with reference to the absence of a result in the three periods of time.’

Atthasādhikāti dānādipāṇātipātādiatthassa nipphādikā. Kā pana sāti āha “sattamajavanacetanā”ti. Sā hi sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā vuttanayena paṭiladdhavisesā, paṭisandhiyā anantarapaccayabhāvino vipākasantānassa anantarapaccayabhāvena vā tathā abhisaṅkhatā samānā anantarattabhāve vipākadāyinī upapajjavedanīyaṃ nāma. Yebhuyyavuttiyā cettha “sattamajavanacetanā”ti vuttaṃ. Paccavekkhaṇavasitādipavattiyaṃ pana pañcamādikāpi hoti. Vipākaṃ detīti paṭisandhiṃ datvā pavattivipākaṃ deti, adinnapaṭisandhikaṃ pana pavattivipākaṃ detīti natthi. Cutianantarañhi upapajjavedanīyassa okāsoti ācariyā. Paṭisandhiyā pana dinnāya jātisatepi pavattivipākaṃ deti. Tenāha bhagavā “tiracchānagate dānaṃ datvā sataguṇā pāṭikaṅkhitabbā”ti (ma. ni. 3.379). Ubhinna…pe… detīti yathāvuttakāraṇavirahato diṭṭhadhammūpapajjavedanīyabhāvaṃ asampattā pañca cetanā vipākadānasabhāvassa anupacchinnattā yadā okāsaṃ labhati, tadā paṭisandhivipākaṃ, pavattivipākaṃ vā deti. Sati saṃsārappavattiyāti iminā [V 2.0237] asati saṃsārappavattiyaṃ ahosikammapakkhe tiṭṭhati vipaccanokāsassa abhāvatoti dīpeti.

Accomplishing the purpose: this means accomplishing the purpose of such acts as giving or taking life, etc. But what is that? It is said: ‘the seventh javana-volition.’ For that, the concluding volition, having gained distinction in the way described, and having been formed in such a way as to be the immediate condition for the resultant continuum that is the immediate condition for rebirth-linking, or being similarly formed, gives its result in the immediately following existence and is called ‘to be experienced upon rebirth.’ Here, ‘the seventh javana-volition’ is stated by way of general rule. But in the case of such attainments as reviewing and mastery, it can also be the fifth and so on. It yields a result: having given rebirth-linking, it yields a result in the course of life. But there is no case of its yielding a result in the course of life without having given rebirth-linking. For the teachers say that the opportunity for kamma to be experienced upon rebirth is immediately after death. But once rebirth-linking has been given, it yields a result in the course of life even for a hundred births. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Having given a gift to one in the animal realm, a hundredfold return is to be expected.” It yields a result for both…: The five volitions, which have not attained the state of being experienced in this very life or upon rebirth due to the absence of the aforesaid reasons, give either a rebirth-linking result or a result in the course of life when they get an opportunity, since their nature of giving a result has not been cut off. When there is a continuation of saṃsāra: by this it is shown that when there is no continuation of saṃsāra, it falls into the category of defunct kamma because of the absence of an opportunity to ripen.

1244. Evaṃ [M 2.0318] tāva vipākadānakālavasena catubbidhaṃ dassetvā idāni vipākadānapariyāyato, kiccato ca catubbidhataṃ dassetuṃ “garuka”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha garukanti mahāsāvajjaṃ, mahānubhāvañca aññena kammena paṭibāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyakammaṃ. Bahulanti abhiṇhaso kataṃ, ekavāraṃ katvāpi abhiṇhasamāsevitañca. Āsannanti maraṇāsannakāle anussaritaṃ, tadā katañca. Kaṭattākammanti garukādibhāvaṃ asampattaṃ katamattatoyeva kammanti vattabbakammaṃ. Tattha kusalaṃ vā hotu akusalaṃ vā, garukāgarukesu yaṃ garukaṃ mātughātakādikammaṃ vā mahaggatakammaṃ vā, tadeva paṭhamaṃ vipaccati. Tathā bahulābahulesu yaṃ bahulaṃ susīlyaṃ dussīlyaṃ vā, tadeva paṭhamaṃ vipaccati. Dūrāsannesu yaṃ āsannaṃ maraṇakāle anussaritaṃ, teneva upapajjati. Āsannakāle kate ca vattabbameva natthīti. Kaṭattā pana kammaṃ punappunaṃ laddhāsevanaṃ purimānaṃ abhāve paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati. Iti garukaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ vipaccati. Tathā hi taṃ “garuka”nti vuttaṃ. Garuke asati bahulīkataṃ, tasmimpi asati āsannaṃ, tasmimpi asati kaṭattākammanti vuttaṃ “purimajātīsu katakammaṃ vipaccatī”ti.

1244. Having thus shown the fourfold classification in terms of the time of yielding results, now, to show the fourfold classification in terms of the manner of yielding results and their function, the terms “weighty,” etc., are used. Herein, “weighty” (garuka) means a kamma that is greatly blameworthy or of great power, which cannot be obstructed by any other kamma. “Habitual” (bahula) means kamma frequently done, or even if done only once, frequently resorted to. “Proximate” (āsanna) means kamma remembered at the time of death, or done at that time. “Reserve kamma” (kaṭattā kamma) refers to a kamma that has not attained the status of weighty, etc., and is called a kamma merely by virtue of being done. Herein, whether wholesome or unwholesome, among weighty and non-weighty kammas, that which is weighty—such as matricide or a sublime kamma—ripens first. Similarly, among habitual and non-habitual kammas, that which is habitual—whether good conduct or misconduct—ripens first. Among distant and proximate kammas, that which is proximate—remembered at the time of death—leads to rebirth. And if it is done at the time of death, there is no need to speak of it. But reserve kamma, when repeatedly cultivated, draws rebirth in the absence of the former types of kamma. Thus, the weighty kamma ripens first of all. That is why it is called “weighty.” If there is no weighty kamma, the habitual ripens; if there is no habitual, the proximate ripens; if there is no proximate, the reserve kamma ripens. Hence it is said, “The kamma done in past lives ripens.”

1245. Paṭisandhidānādivasena vipākasantānassa nibbattakaṃ janakaṃ. Sukhadukkhasantānassa, nāmarūpappabandhassa vā ciratarappattihetubhūtaṃ upatthambhakaṃ. Tenāha “sukhadukkhaṃ upatthambheti, addhānaṃ pavattetī”ti. Sukhadukkhe pavattamāne bavhābādhatādipaccayūpanipātanena saṇikaṃ saṇikaṃ tassa vibādhakaṃ upapīḷakaṃ. Tenāha “sukhadukkhaṃ pīḷeti bādhati, addhānaṃ pavattituṃ na detī”ti. Tathā paṭipakkhakammavipākassa appavattikaraṇavasena upacchedakaṃ paṭibāhakaṃ upaghātakaṃ. Tenāha “tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā”ti.

1245. It is generative (janaka) of the resultant continuity by means of rebirth-linking and so forth. It is supportive (upatthambhaka) of the continuity of pleasure and pain, or of the series of mind-and-matter, serving as a cause for their prolonged occurrence. Hence it is said: “It supports pleasure and pain and prolongs the duration.” While pleasure and pain are occurring, it is oppressive (upapīḷaka), gradually afflicting them through the arising of many ailments and other conditions. Hence it is said: “It oppresses and afflicts pleasure and pain, not allowing the duration to continue.” Similarly, it is destructive (upaghātaka) by preventing the fruition of an opposing kamma-result, thereby cutting off and obstructing it. Hence it is said: “Having obstructed its result.”

Rūpañca [M 2.0319] arūpavipākakkhandho cāti rūpārūpavipākakkhandho, kammajarūpassāpi vipākapariyāyo atthīti “rūpārūpavipākakkhandhe”ti vuttaṃ. Aññena kammenāti kusalena vā akusalena vā aññena kammena kattubhūtena dinnāya paṭisandhiyā vipāke janite. Tenāha “janite vipāke”ti. Pavattivipākaṃ sandhāya “janite vipāke”ti vadanti. Uppajjanakasukhadukkhaṃ [V 2.0238] upatthambhetīti upatthambhakakammaṃ kusalaṃ samānaṃ aññenapi kusalakammena uppajjamānakaṃ sukhaṃ tassa paṭipakkhavibādhanavasena upatthambheti. Akusalaṃ aññena akusalakammena upapajjamānaṃ dukkhaṃ tatheva upatthambheti. Evañca upatthambhentaṃ taṃ dīghakālaṃ pavatteti nāmāti āha “addhānaṃ pavattetī”ti. Uppajjanakasukhadukkhaṃ pīḷetīti upapīḷakaṃ akusalaṃ samānaṃ sukhitassa rogādiantarāyakāraṇasampādakabhāvena sukhasantānaṃ upacchindantaṃ pīḷeti, kusalañca rogādinā dukkhitassa bhesajjādisukhādikāraṇasampādakabhāvena dukkhasantānaṃ vicchindantaṃ pīḷeti. Keci pana “sukhadukkhassa kāraṇaṃ asampādentampi paṭisandhidāyakakammassa pavattivipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā sayaṃ vipākadāyakakammaṃ upapīḷakakamma”nti vadanti. Evaṃ sante pana paṭisandhidāyakameva janakakammanti vuttaṃ siyā.

Materiality and the immaterial resultant aggregates are the material-immaterial resultant aggregates; for even materiality born of kamma has a resultant aspect, thus it is said, “the material and immaterial resultant aggregates.” By another kamma—that is, when a result has been generated by another kamma, whether wholesome or unwholesome, which has served as the agent giving rebirth-linking. Hence it is said, “when a result has been generated.” They say “when a result has been generated” with reference to the result during the course of existence. It supports the arising pleasure and pain—that is, supportive kamma, being wholesome, supports the arising pleasure produced by another wholesome kamma by obstructing its opposite. Similarly, unwholesome kamma supports the arising pain produced by another unwholesome kamma in the same way. And by supporting in this way, it is said to prolong it for a long time; thus it is said, “it prolongs the duration.” It oppresses the arising pleasure and pain—that is, oppressive kamma, being unwholesome, oppresses the continuity of pleasure for a happy person by bringing about causes for diseases and other obstacles, thereby cutting it off. And wholesome kamma oppresses the continuity of pain for a suffering person by providing causes for medicine and other forms of happiness, thereby cutting it off. Some, however, say, “Oppressive kamma is that which, even without producing the cause of pleasure and pain, obstructs the result that arises during the course of existence from the rebirth-giving kamma and is itself the kamma that gives the result.” If this is so, then it would mean that only the rebirth-giving kamma is the generative kamma.

Apica upaghātakena saha imassa visesabhāvo āpajjati, taṃ paṭisandhivipākassa paṭibāhakanti ce? Taṃ na, avisesena vuttattāti. “Dubbalaṃ kammaṃ ghātetvā”ti vutte “nanu tassa pubbeyeva siddhattā, niruddhattā ca kathamidaṃ tadupaghātakaṃ hotī”ti āpannaṃ codanaṃ sandhāya kammassa ghātanaṃ nāma tassa vipākapaṭibāhanamevāti dassento āha “tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā”ti. Taṃpaṭibāhanañca attano vipākuppattiyā okāsakaraṇanti vuttaṃ “attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karotī”ti. Vipaccanāya katokāsaṃ kammaṃ [M 2.0320] vipakkameva nāma hotīti āha “evaṃ…pe… uppannaṃ nāma hotī”ti.

Furthermore, does a special characteristic arise for this oppressive kamma in association with destructive kamma? Is that destructive kamma an obstructer of the rebirth-result? No, because it is stated without distinction. When it is said, “Having destroyed a weak kamma,” the objection that arises is: “But since that kamma was already accomplished and has ceased, how can this be its destroyer?” To show that the destruction of kamma means precisely the obstruction of its result, the text says, “Having obstructed its result.” And that obstruction is said to create an opportunity for the arising of one’s own result, as stated: “It makes an opportunity for its own result.” A kamma for which an opportunity has been made to ripen is indeed called “ripened”; hence it is said: “Thus... it is called arisen.”

Upapīḷakaṃ aññassa vipākaṃ upacchindati, na sayaṃ attano vipākaṃ deti, upaghātakaṃ pana dubbalakammaṃ upacchinditvā attano vipākaṃ uppādetīti ayametesaṃ viseso. Keci pana ācariyā aparenāpi nayena janakādikammaṃ icchanti. Kathaṃ? Yasmiṃ kamme kate paṭisandhiyaṃ, pavatte ca vipākakaṭattārūpānaṃ uppatti hoti, taṃ janakaṃ. Yasmiṃ pana kate aññena janitassa iṭṭhassa vā aniṭṭhassa vā phalassa vibādhakavicchedakapaccayānuppattiyā, upabrūhakapaccayuppattiyā ca janakānubhāvānurūpaṃ pariposakaciratarappabandhā honti, taṃ upatthambhakaṃ. Janakena nibbattitaṃ kusalaphalaṃ, akusalaphalaṃ vā yena paccanīkabhūtena rogadhātuvisamatādinimittatāya bādhīyati, taṃ upapīḷakaṃ. Yena pana kammunā janakasāmatthiyavasena ciratarappabandhārahampi samānaṃ phalavicchedakapaccayuppattiyā upahaññati vicchijjati, taṃ upaghātakanti.

Oppressive kamma obstructs the result of another but does not give its own result; destructive kamma, however, obstructs a weak kamma and then produces its own result—this is their distinction. Some teachers, however, understand the generative kamma and other types according to another method. How? That is generative (janaka) kamma due to which, when it is performed, there is the arising of resultant kamma-born materiality at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. That is supportive (upatthambhaka) kamma due to which, when it is performed, through the non-arising of conditions that obstruct or sever a desirable or undesirable fruit produced by another, and through the arising of supportive conditions, that fruit is nourished and its continuity is prolonged in accordance with the power of the generative kamma. That is oppressive (upapīḷaka) kamma which, being an opposing factor, afflicts the wholesome or unwholesome fruit produced by the generative kamma on account of signs such as disease and imbalance of elements. And that is destructive (upaghātaka) kamma by which a fruit, though capable of a long-lasting continuity by the power of the generative kamma, is harmed and cut off due to the arising of conditions that sever it.

Ettha [V 2.0239] ca keci appābādhadīghāyukatāsaṃvattanavasena dutiyassa kusalabhāvaṃ, bavhābādhaappāyukatāsaṃvattanavasena pacchimānaṃ dvinnaṃ akusalabhāvañca vaṇṇenti, bhūridattādīnaṃ pana nāgādīnaṃ, ito anuppadinnayāpanakapetānañca apāyesu akusalavipākassa upatthambhanūpapīḷanūpaghātakāni kammāni santīti catunnampi kusalākusalabhāvo na virujjhati. Kiñcāpi kammānaṃ kammantarañceva vipākantarañca buddhānaṃ kammavipākañāṇasseva yāthāvasarasato pākaṭaṃ hoti. Buddhāveṇikañhetaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ sāvakehi, vipassakena pana ekadesato jānitabbaṃ. Na hi sabbena sabbaṃ ajānantassa paccayapariggaho paripūrati, tasmā tādisaṃ pariggahaṃ sandhāya “iti ima”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Yādisehi paccayehi paccuppanne addhāne [M 2.0321] nāmarūpassa pavatti, tādiseheva itarasmimpi addhadvayeti evaṃ yathā atītānāgate nayaṃ neti, taṃ dassetuṃ “yathā ida”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Addhattayepi kiriyākiriyāphalamattatādassanaparattā codanāya. Itī kammañcevātiādinā vuttassevatthassa nigamanavasena vuttaṃ. Tassevaṃ…pe… pahiyyatīti tassevaṃ samanupassato yā sā pubbantādayo ārabbha “ahosiṃ nu kho aha”ntiādinā nayena pavattā vicikicchā pahiyyati.

Here, some describe the second (type of kamma) as wholesome, as it is conducive to health and long life, and the last two as unwholesome, as they lead to much illness and a short life. However, for beings like Bhūridatta and other nāgas, as well as for those petas in the lower realms who sustain themselves on what is not given from this world, there exist kammas that support, oppress, or destroy the unwholesome result. Thus, the wholesome and unwholesome nature of all four is not contradicted. Although the specific workings of kamma and its result are fully clear only to the Buddhas through their knowledge of kamma and its fruit—this being a knowledge unique to the Buddhas and not shared with the disciples—it should be known in part by an insight meditator. For one who does not know everything in every way, the grasp of conditions is not completed. Therefore, with reference to such a grasp, it is said, “Thus, this…” and so on. To show how one applies the method to the past and future, it is said, “Just as this…” and so on; this means that the conditions by which mind and matter proceed in the present time are similar to those in the other two time periods. In all three periods of time, the exhortation is concerned with seeing things as merely action, its absence, and its fruit. Thus, with the statement “kamma indeed…” and so on, what has been said is stated by way of conclusion. “For one who thus… it is abandoned” means that for one who contemplates in this way, the doubt that arises concerning the past, etc., in the manner of “Did I exist?” and so on, is abandoned.

1246-8. Pahīnāya pana tāya sabbabhavayonigatiṭhitisattāvāsesu hetuphalasambandhavaseneva pavattanāmarūpamattameva khāyati. Tenevāha “hetuphalassa sambandhavasenevā”tiādi. Kāraṇasāmaggiyaṃ dānādīhi sādhitakiriyāya pavattamānāya kāraṇamatte kattuvohāroti āha “kāraṇato uddhaṃ kāraṇaṃ na ca passatī”ti. Pāka…pe… paṭivedakaṃ na passatīti sambandho. Pākapaṭivedakanti vipākavindakaṃ. Evaṃ apassanto pana kāraṇe sati kārakoti, vipākappavattiyā sati paṭisaṃvedakoti samaññāmatteneva paṇḍitā voharanti. Iccevaṃ sammappaññāya passati. Suddhadhammāti kenaci sattena vā puggalena vā amissadhammā. Evetanti evaṃvidhaṃ etaṃ dassanaṃ sammadassanaṃ, aviparītadassananti attho.

1246-8. When that doubt is abandoned, only mind-and-matter, proceeding through the connection of cause and effect, appears in all realms of existence, origins of birth, destinations, stations, and abodes of beings. Therefore, he said: “Through the connection of cause and effect,” and so on. When an action accomplished through giving and so on proceeds from a causal assemblage, the designation ‘doer’ is applied to the mere cause; hence he said: “He sees no doer beyond the cause.” The connection is that he does not see the ripening… nor the one who experiences it. The experiencer of the ripening means the one who finds the result. Thus, not seeing in this way, the wise use mere designations, speaking of a ‘doer’ when a cause exists, and of an ‘experiencer’ when the result proceeds. In this way, one sees with right wisdom. “Pure phenomena” means phenomena unmixed with any being or person. “Thus this” means this kind of vision is right vision; the meaning is non-perverted vision.

1249. Bījarukkhādikānaṃ vāti yathā bījato rukkho, rukkhato bījanti evaṃ kāraṇaparamparagavesane anādikālikattā bījarukkhasantānassa pubbā koṭi natthi, evaṃ kammapaccayā vipāko, vipākapaccayā kammanti pariyesane anādikālikattā kammavipākasantānassa pubbā koṭi na paññāyati. Ādi-saddena “kukkuṭiyā aṇḍaṃ, aṇḍato kukkuṭī, punapi kukkuṭiyā aṇḍa”nti evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

1249. “As with seeds, trees, etc.” means: just as a tree comes from a seed and a seed from a tree, so when investigating the sequence of causes, because of its beginninglessness, no first point of the continuum of seeds and trees is found. Similarly, when one examines how result is conditioned by kamma and kamma by result, because of its beginninglessness, no first point of the continuum of kamma and result is discerned. By the word “etc.” is included such things as: “from a hen an egg, from an egg a hen, and again from a hen an egg.”

1250-3. Anāgatepi [M 2.0322][V 2.0240] saṃsāreti yathā atīte, evaṃ anāgatepi addhāne khandhānaṃ paṭipāṭītiādinā vuttasaṃsāre sati. Appavatti na dissatīti kammato vipāko bhavissati, vipākato kammanti anāgate kāriyaparamparāya gavesiyamānāya aparikkhīṇasaṃyojanassa kammavipākānaṃ appavattanaṃ na dissati, pavattati evāti attho. Hetuphalasambandhavasena pavattamāne saṃsāre “pubbā koṭi na paññāyatī”ti vacanena kāraṇe ādissa abhāvo vutto, “appavatti na dissatī”ti vacanena phalassa avasānābhāvo vuttoti. Etamatthanti “kammassa kārako natthī”tiādinā vuttamatthaṃ. Asayaṃvasīti na sayaṃvasino, micchābhinivesaparavasāti attho. Aññamaññavirodhinoti itarītaraviruddhā diṭṭhiyo vā diṭṭhiyā vā aññamaññena saha virodhino. Gambhīrañāṇagocaratāya gambhīraṃ. Tathā nipuṇaṃ. Sattasuññatāya, aññamaññasabhāvasuññatāya ca suññaṃ. Paccayanti nāmarūpassa paccayaṃ, tappaccayapaṭivedheneva ca sabbaṃ paṭividdhaṃ hotīti.

1250-3. “It transmigrates in the future just as in the past” means that in the future, just as in the past, the sequence of aggregates continues in the cycle of existence as described. “No cessation is seen” means that for one with unexhausted fetters, when investigating the future sequence of effects—that from kamma there will be a result, and from a result, kamma—no cessation of kamma and its result is seen; it simply continues. By the statement “no first point is discerned” in the saṃsāra that proceeds through the connection of cause and effect, the absence of an initial cause is stated; and by the statement “no cessation is seen,” the absence of a final effect is stated. “This meaning” refers to the meaning conveyed by such statements as “There is no doer of the kamma.” “Not self-controlled” means not being one's own master, that is, being under the sway of wrong adherence. “Mutually contradictory” means that views are opposed to one another, or that those holding the views are in opposition to one another. “Profound” because it is the domain of profound knowledge. Likewise, “subtle.” “Empty” because of the emptiness of a being and the emptiness of mutual inherent nature. “Condition” means the condition for name-and-form, and by penetrating that very condition, everything is penetrated.

1254-6. Kammaṃ natthi vipākamhīti kuṭṭādīsu rajādi viya vipāke santiṭṭhamānaṃ kammaṃ natthi. Pāko kamme na vijjatīti tathā kamme santiṭṭhamāno vipāko natthi. Yathāvuttamevatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā na sūriye”tiādi vuttaṃ. Maṇimhīti sūriyakantamaṇimhi. Na tesaṃ bahi so atthīti te muñcitvā tehi bahi so aggi natthi. Sambhārehīti samaṅgībhūtehi ātapādīhi tīhi kāraṇehi. Na anto kammassātiādi atthato heṭṭhā vuttampi upamānigamanatthaṃ punapi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

1254-6. “There is no kamma in the result”: there is no kamma abiding in the result in the way that dust and so on abides in a heap and so on. “The result does not exist in the kamma”: similarly, there is no result abiding in the kamma. To clarify this same meaning with a simile, the passage beginning “Just as not in the sun…” was stated. “In the gem” means in the sunstone. “It is not outside of them” means that apart from them, that fire does not exist. “By the conditions” means by the three causes—sunlight, etc.—having come together. The passage beginning “Not within the kamma…” should be seen as stated again for the purpose of concluding the simile, though its meaning was already stated before.

1257-8. Yadi hetu, phalañca aññamaññarahitaṃ, kathaṃ hetuto phalaṃ nibbattatīti āha “kammañca kho upādāyā”ti. Na kevalaṃ kammaphalameva suññaṃ katturahitaṃ, sabbampi dhammajātaṃ kārakarahitanti [M 2.0323] dassetuṃ “na hettha devo”tiādigāthā vuttā. Hetusambhārapaccayāti ekena hetunā ekassa, anekassa vā phalassa anibbattito hetusamūhanimittaṃ, sambhāroti vā paccayādhivacananti hetupaccayanimittanti attho.

1257-8. If cause and effect were devoid of one another, how would an effect be produced from a cause? To answer this, he said: “But depending on kamma…” To show that not only are kamma and its fruit empty and devoid of a doer, but that the entire class of phenomena is devoid of a maker, the verse beginning “Here there is no deva…” was stated. Regarding ‘cause-aggregate-condition’: since a single effect or multiple effects are not produced from a single cause, this term indicates a collection of causes. Or, since ‘aggregate’ is a term for ‘condition,’ the meaning is that it indicates a cause and a condition.

1259. Addhāsu taritvā kaṅkhanti tīsu addhāsu soḷasavidhaṃ kaṅkhaṃ vitaritvā. Na kevalametaṃ soḷasavidhameva kaṅkhaṃ vitarati, atha kho “satthari kaṅkhatī”tiādinayappavattaṃ (dha. sa. 1123; vibha. 915) aṭṭhavidhaṃ kaṅkhampi pajahati. Tathā hettha buddho dhammo saṅgho sikkhāti [V 2.0241] kaṅkhāya gocarabhūtā lokiyā dhammā adhippetā. Na hi lokuttaradhamme ārabbha kilesā pavattituṃ sakkonti. Pubbantoti atītā khandhāyatanadhātuyo, aparantoti anāgatā, pubbantāparantoti tadubhayaṃ, addhāpaccuppannaṃ vā tadubhayabhāgayuttattā. Paṭiccasamuppannadhammaggahaṇena gahito aṭṭhamo kaṅkhāvisayo nāmarūpamattaṃ, idappaccayatā-ggahaṇena pana tassa paccayo gahito, tasmā soḷasavatthukāya pahīnāya aṭṭhavatthukā kaṅkhā appatiṭṭhāva hotīti. Etāsañca pahānena dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatānipi vikkhambhanti diṭṭhekaṭṭhattā vicikicchāya. Yathā hi diṭṭhi samucchijjamānā vicikicchāya saddhiṃyeva samucchijjati, evaṃ vicikicchā vikkhambhiyamānā diṭṭhiyā saddhiṃyeva vikkhambhīyati. Attābhinivesūpanissayā hi “ahosiṃ nu kho aha”ntiādinayappavattā (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20; mahāni. 174) soḷasavatthukā kaṅkhā, sā eva ca pubbantādivatthubhāvena vuttā, attābhinivesavatthukāni dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni, buddhādivatthukā ca tadekaṭṭhāti. Uṭṭhitanti uppajjitvā ṭhitaṃ.

1259. “Having crossed over doubt concerning the periods” means having overcome the sixteenfold doubt concerning the three periods. He does not only overcome this sixteenfold doubt, but he also abandons the eightfold doubt that proceeds in the manner of “he doubts about the Teacher,” etc. (Dhs §1123; Vibh 915). Here, the worldly phenomena that are the objects of doubt—the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, and the training—are intended. For defilements cannot arise in relation to the supramundane states. “The past end” means the past aggregates, sense bases, and elements; “the future end” means the future ones; “the past and future end” means both, or the present time because it is connected with both parts. The eighth object of doubt, which is grasped by apprehending dependently arisen phenomena, is mere name-and-form; but by apprehending specific conditionality, its condition is also grasped. Therefore, when the doubt concerning sixteen objects is abandoned, the doubt concerning eight objects has no footing. By the abandonment of these, the sixty-two kinds of views are also suppressed, because they have the same foundation as doubt. For just as a view, when being eradicated, is eradicated together with doubt, so too doubt, when being suppressed, is suppressed together with views. The doubt concerning sixteen objects has clinging to self as its basis and proceeds in the manner of “Was I indeed in the past?” etc. (MN 2; SN 12.20); this is what is spoken of in terms of the past end, etc., as its objects. The sixty-two views have clinging to self as their object, and those concerning the Buddha, etc., have that same foundation. “Arisen” (uṭṭhitaṃ) means having arisen and become established.

1260-2. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ [M 2.0324] nāmāti yathāvuttakaṅkhāvitaraṇato kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ nāma. Na kevalaṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ nāma, dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇantipi yathābhūtañāṇantipi sammādassanantipi idaṃ samudīritaṃ. Ettha ca dharīyanti attano paccayehīti dhammā, tiṭṭhati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti ṭhiti, dhammānaṃ ṭhiti dhammaṭṭhiti, paccayadhammā.
