Atha vā dhammoti kāraṇaṃ “dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 718-721) viya, dhammassa ṭhitisabhāvo, dhammato ca añño sabhāvo natthīti paccayadhammānaṃ paccayabhāvo, dhammaṭṭhitiyaṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ. Saṅkhārānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ aniccatādi yathābhūtaṃ, tattha ñāṇanti yathābhūtañāṇaṃ. Sammā passatīti sammādassanaṃ. Laddhappatiṭṭhoti sāsane patiṭṭhā nāma ariyamaggo. Ayaṃ pana taṃ anadhigatopi tadadhigamupāyapaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhitattā laddhappatiṭṭho viya hotīti “laddhappatiṭṭho”ti vutto. Tatoyeva cūḷako sotāpanno, lokiyāhi sīlasamādhipaññāhi samannāgatattā uttari appaṭivijjhanto sotāpanno viya niyato, sugatiparāyaṇo ca hotīti cūḷasotāpanno. Sotāpanno hi khīṇāpāyaduggativinipātoti. Atha vā laddhappatiṭṭho kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhisamadhigamena. Sappaccayanāmarūpadassanena hi sammadditadiṭṭhikaṇṭako viniddhutaahetukavisamahetuvādo yathāsakapaccayeheva dhammappavattiṃ ñatvā sāsane patiṭṭhitasaddho laddhappatiṭṭho nāma hotīti. Nāmarūpavavatthānena dukkhasaccaṃ, dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇena samudayasaccaṃ, tasseva aparabhāge aniccato manasikārādividhinā maggasaccañca abhiññāya pavattiyā dukkhabhāvaṃ disvā tassa appavatte nirodhe [V 2.0242] ekaṃseneva ninnajjhāsayatāya lokiyeneva ñāṇena catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ adhigatattā apāyesu abhabbuppattiko, sotāpannabhūmiyañca bhabbuppattiko hotīti cūḷasotāpanno nāmāti vuttaṃ “sotāpanno [M 2.0325] hi cūḷako”ti. Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ mahānisaṃsametaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tasmā sapañño attano hitānupekkhanapaññāya samannāgato. Tenāha “atthakāmo”ti.

1260-2. “It is called the overcoming of doubt” (kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ) because it is an overcoming of doubt as was described. This is not only called “the overcoming of doubt,” but it is also spoken of as “knowledge of the stability of phenomena” (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa), “knowledge of things as they are” (yathābhūtañāṇa), and “right view” (sammādassana). Herein, “phenomena” (dhammā) are so called because they are borne (dharīyanti) by their own conditions. “Stability” (ṭhiti) is so called because the fruit stands (tiṭṭhati) therein, its occurrence being dependent on that. The stability of phenomena is dhammaṭṭhiti; this means conditioned phenomena. Alternatively, “dhamma” means cause, as in “the discrimination of dhammas” (dhammapaṭisambhidā), etc. (Vibh 718-21). The stable nature of a dhamma is its own-nature of stability, and there is no other own-nature apart from that dhamma; thus it is the nature of being a condition for conditioned phenomena. Knowledge in the stability of phenomena is “knowledge of the stability of phenomena” (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa). “As they are” (yathābhūtaṃ) refers to the true nature of formations, such as impermanence; knowledge therein is “knowledge of things as they are” (yathābhūtañāṇa). “Right view” (sammādassana) is so called because it sees rightly. “One who has gained a footing” (laddhappatiṭṭho): in the Dispensation, the “footing” (patiṭṭhā) is the noble path. But this person, though not having attained it, is called “one who has gained a footing” because he is established in the practice that is the means for its attainment. For that reason, he is a “lesser stream-enterer” (cūḷasotāpanno). Because he is endowed with mundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom, but has not yet penetrated to what is higher, he is like a stream-enterer, certain, and bound for a good destination; thus he is a “lesser stream-enterer.” For a stream-enterer has destroyed rebirth in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world. Alternatively, he has “gained a footing” by attaining the purification by overcoming doubt. For by seeing name-and-form with its conditions, he has crushed the thorn of views, dispelled the doctrines of causelessness and dissimilar causes, and, having known that phenomena proceed from their respective conditions, he has established faith in the Dispensation and is thus called “one who has gained a footing.” By determining name-and-form, he understands the truth of suffering; by knowledge of the stability of phenomena, the truth of the origin; and in the subsequent stage, by the method of attending to impermanence, etc., the truth of the path. Having seen the suffering nature of existence, and with an inclination bent exclusively on its non-occurrence, that is, on cessation, he has, even with mundane knowledge, attained the four noble truths. Thus he becomes one incapable of arising in the planes of misery and capable of arising on the plane of a stream-enterer. Therefore he is called a “lesser stream-enterer,” as it is said: “For he is a lesser stream-enterer.” “Therefore” (tasmā): because this knowledge has such great benefit, a “wise person” (sapañño) is one endowed with the wisdom that looks to one's own welfare. Hence He said: “one who desires his own good” (atthakāmo).

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus in the so-named Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra,

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the exposition of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt is finished.

20. Vīsatimo paricchedo

20. The Twentieth Chapter

Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is the Path and What Is Not the Path

1263. Idāni kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyā anantaraṃ uddiṭṭhāya maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiyā niddesakkamo anuppatto, sā pana yasmā obhāsādiupakkilesasambhave sati hoti, obhāsādayo ca udayabbayañāṇe sambhavanti, udayabbayañāṇañca tilakkhaṇavipassanāya sati uppajjati, tassa ca kalāpasammasanaṃ ādi. Tañhi atītādibhedabhinnānaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhipitvā vavatthānavasena pavattanato ādikammikassa sukarasammasanaṃ, tasmā paṭhamaṃ tattheva abhiyogaṃ karontena kamato taṃ sampādetabbanti dassetuṃ “kalāpasammasanenevā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Atha vā dvinnaṃ visuddhīnamantare kalāpasammasanaṃ hoti, tañca kho dvīsu ekāya visuddhiyā saṅgahetabbaṃ, maggāmaggañāṇassa ca ādibhūtattā tatthevassa saṅgaho yuttoti ettheva naṃ saṅgahitukāmatāya vuttaṃ “kalāpasammasanenevā”tiādi. Keci pana kalāpasammasanaṃ nāma ekavisuddhiyampi na antogadhanti taṃ anāmasitvāva vipassanācāraṃ vaṇṇenti. Kalāpasammasanenevāti atītādibhedabhinnānaṃ [M 2.0326] dhammānaṃ saṅkhipitvā vavatthānavasena kalāpato, kalāpānaṃ vā sammasanena maggāmaggañāṇadassanavipassanāya yogo karaṇīyo. Atha vā [V 2.0243] bhummatthe karaṇaniddesavasena kalāpasammasane yogo karaṇīyoti attho. “Kalāpasammasaneneva yogo karaṇīyo”ti vatvāpi taṃ pana visuddhimaggato (visuddhi. 2.692) gahetabbanti ganthavitthāraparihāratthaṃ idha na dassitanti.

1263. Now, after the Purification by Overcoming Doubt, the turn has come for the exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is the Path and What Is Not the Path. This purification arises when there are corruptions of insight such as illumination. These corruptions arise in the knowledge of arising and passing away, and the knowledge of arising and passing away arises when there is insight into the three characteristics, of which the comprehension of groups is the beginning. Since this comprehension of groups—which proceeds by way of defining through summarizing phenomena divided into past, etc.—is easy for a beginner to grasp, therefore, to show that one should accomplish this in sequence by first applying oneself right there, the passage beginning 'by the comprehension of groups alone' was stated. Alternatively, the comprehension of groups occurs between the two purifications, and it must be included in one of them. Since it is the beginning of the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path, it is proper to include it right there. It is with the intention of including it here that the passage beginning 'by the comprehension of groups alone' was stated. Some, however, hold that the comprehension of groups is not included in any single purification, and they describe the practice of insight without mentioning it. 'By the comprehension of groups alone' means that the practice of insight into the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path should be undertaken by way of groups—that is, by summarizing and defining phenomena divided into past, etc.—or by the comprehension of groups. Alternatively, the meaning is that the practice should be undertaken in the comprehension of groups, with the instrumental case used in the sense of the locative. Although it is said, 'The practice should be undertaken by the comprehension of groups alone,' it is not shown here in order to avoid prolixity, as this should be understood from the Visuddhimagga (Vism 692).

1264. Paccuppannassa dhammassāti santatipaccuppannassa, khaṇapaccuppannassa vā. Ādito pana khaṇapaccuppannassa udayavayaṃ duppariggahaṃ, tasmā santatipaccuppannavasena paṭhamaṃ udayabbayānupassanaṃ kātabbaṃ. Nibbattīti dvinnaṃ paccuppannānaṃ vasena paṭhamābhinibbatti ca khaṇanibbatti ca. Vipariṇāmoti vināso.

1264. “Of a present phenomenon” means of the continuity-present or of the moment-present. But at the beginning, the arising and passing away of the moment-present is difficult to grasp; therefore, contemplation of arising and passing away should first be done by way of the continuity-present. “Production” means both the initial production and the momentary production, corresponding to the two kinds of the present. “Change” means destruction.

1265. Anupassanāpi ñāṇanti yā udayassa ca vayassa ca anupassanā, sā ñāṇanti varañāṇena sammāsambuddhena desitaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

1265. “Contemplation is also knowledge”: The contemplation of arising and of passing away is knowledge. This was taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One with his supreme knowledge. Here is the Pāli:

“Kathaṃ paccuppannānaṃ dhammānaṃ vipariṇāmānupassane paññā udayabbayānupassane ñāṇaṃ? Jātaṃ rūpaṃ paccuppannaṃ, tassa nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ udayo. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ vayo. Anupassanā ñāṇaṃ. Jātā vedanā…pe… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ… jātaṃ cakkhuṃ…pe… jāto bhavo paccuppanno, tassa nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ udayo. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ vayo. Anupassanā ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.49).

“How is there wisdom in contemplating the change of present phenomena, and knowledge in contemplating arising and passing away? Arisen form is present; its characteristic of production is arising, its characteristic of change is passing away. Contemplation is knowledge. Arisen feeling… perception… formations… consciousness… arisen eye… arisen existence is present; its characteristic of production is arising, its characteristic of change is passing away. Contemplation is knowledge” (Ps I 49).

Ettha pana udayadassanaṃ yāvadeva khayadassananti vayadassanassa padhānataṃ dassetuṃ “vipariṇāmānupassane paññā”ti vatvā taṃ pana vayadassanaṃ udayadassanapubbakanti vuttaṃ “udayabbayānupassane ñāṇa”nti.

Here, to show the predominance of the vision of passing away, it is said, ‘wisdom in contemplating change,’ for the vision of arising is only for the sake of the vision of destruction. But since that vision of passing away is preceded by the vision of arising, it is said, ‘knowledge in contemplating arising and passing away.’

1266-8. Pubbe [M 2.0327] uppattitoti jananato pubbe anuppannassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nicayo rāsi vā natthi, yato āgaccheyya uppajjamānaṃ aladdhattabhāvassa sabbena sabbaṃ avijjamānattā. Tenāha “tathā uppajjato”tiādi. Yathā anāgate addhāne ime dhammā sabbena sabbaṃ natthi, evaṃ atītepi addhānanti dassento “tathā nirujjhamānassā”tiādiṃ vatvā avijjamānānaṃyeva rūpārūpadhammānaṃ hetupaccayasamavāye uppādo, uppajjitvā ca sabbaso abhāvūpagamoti imamatthaṃ samudāyagataṃ tadekadesabhūtāya upamāya vibhāvetuṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne aṭṭhakathāya [V 2.0244] (visuddhi. 2.723) vīṇūpamā āgatā. Sā idhāpi āharitvā vattabbāti adhippāyena “ettha vīṇūpamā”tiādimāha. Etassatthassāti avijjamānānaṃyeva uppādo, uppannānañca parato abhāvoti imassa atthassa pakāsane. Vīṇūpamāti vīṇāvasena āgatā upamā. Sā panevaṃ daṭṭhabbā – yathā vīṇāya vādiyamānāya uppannassa saddassa neva uppattito pubbe sannicayo atthi, na uppajjamāno sannicayato āgato. Na nirujjhamānassa disāvidisāgamanaṃ atthi, na niruddho katthaci sannicito tiṭṭhati, atha kho vīṇañca vīṇavādanañca purisassa ca tajjaṃ vāyāmaṃ paṭicca ahutvā sambhoti, hutvā paṭiveti, evaṃ sabbepi rūpārūpadhammā ahutvā sambhonti, hutvā paṭiventīti.

1266-8. ‘Before its production’: this means it is said that before its generation it was unproduced. There is no accumulation or heap from which an arising phenomenon might come, because what has not yet acquired existence is entirely non-existent. Therefore it is said, ‘so from arising,’ etc. To show that just as these phenomena are entirely non-existent in the future, so too were they in the past, it is said, ‘so of the ceasing,’ etc. To clarify this meaning in its entirety—that there is the production of non-existent material and immaterial phenomena through a conjunction of causes and conditions, and that having been produced they pass into complete non-existence—and by means of a partial simile, the simile of the lute is introduced here in the commentary (Vism 723). With the intention that it should be brought in and stated here too, it is said, ‘Here the simile of the lute,’ etc. This is for the clarification of this meaning: the production of what is non-existent, and the subsequent non-existence of what has been produced. ‘The simile of the lute’ means the simile that comes by way of the lute. It should be seen thus: Just as, when a lute is being played, the sound that is produced has no prior accumulation, nor does it come from an accumulation when it is being produced; and when it is ceasing, it does not go to any direction or intermediate direction, nor does the ceased sound remain accumulated anywhere; rather, dependent on the lute, the plectrum, and the person’s corresponding effort, it comes to be without having been, and having been, it vanishes—so too all material and immaterial phenomena come to be without having been, and having been, they vanish.

1269-70. Evaṃ saṅkhepato udayabbayamanasikāravidhiṃ dassetvā puna yāni etasseva udayabbayañāṇassa vibhaṅge “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) paccayasamudayaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati, “taṇhāsamudayā…pe… kammasamudayā…pe… [M 2.0328] āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) paccayasamudayaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati, nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati, rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passanto imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passati. “Avijjānirodhā rūpanirodho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) paccayanirodhaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati, “taṇhānirodhā…pe… kammanirodhā…pe… āhāranirodhā rūpanirodho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) paccayanirodhaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati, vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati, rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passanto imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passati. Tathā “avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) paccayasamudayaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati, “taṇhāsamudayā…pe… kammasamudayā…pe… phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) paccayasamudayaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati, nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passanto vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati, vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passanto imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passati. “Avijjānirodhā…pe… taṇhānirodhā…pe… kammanirodhā…pe… phassanirodhā vedanānirodho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) paccayanirodhaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passati, vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passati, vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passanto imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passati, vedanākkhandhassa viya saññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇakkhandhānaṃ[V 2.0245]. Ayaṃ pana viseso – viññāṇakkhandhassa phassaṭṭhāne “nāmarūpasamudayā nāmarūpanirodhā”ti.

1269-70. Having thus briefly shown the method of attending to arising and passing away, again, in the analysis of this very knowledge of arising and passing away it is said: ‘With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form’ (Ps I 50); thus one sees the arising of the form aggregate in the sense of the arising of conditions. ‘With the arising of craving… with the arising of kamma… with the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form’ (Ps I 50); thus one sees the arising of the form aggregate in the sense of the arising of conditions. Seeing the characteristic of production, too, one sees the arising of the form aggregate. Seeing the arising of the form aggregate, one sees these five characteristics. ‘With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form’ (Ps I 50); thus one sees the passing away of the form aggregate in the sense of the cessation of conditions. ‘With the cessation of craving… with the cessation of kamma… with the cessation of nutriment, there is the cessation of form’ (Ps I 50); thus one sees the passing away of the form aggregate in the sense of the cessation of conditions. Seeing the characteristic of change, too, one sees the passing away of the form aggregate. Seeing the passing away of the form aggregate, one sees these five characteristics. Similarly: ‘With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling’ (Ps I 50); thus one sees the arising of the feeling aggregate in the sense of the arising of conditions. ‘With the arising of craving… with the arising of kamma… with the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling’ (Ps I 50); thus one sees the arising of the feeling aggregate in the sense of the arising of conditions. Seeing the characteristic of production, too, one sees the arising of the feeling aggregate. Seeing the arising of the feeling aggregate, one sees these five characteristics. ‘With the cessation of ignorance… with the cessation of craving… with the cessation of kamma… with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling’ (Ps I 50); thus one sees the passing away of the feeling aggregate in the sense of the cessation of conditions. Seeing the characteristic of change, too, one sees the passing away of the feeling aggregate. Seeing the passing away of the feeling aggregate, one sees these five characteristics. This is similar for the aggregates of perception, formations, and consciousness. This, however, is the difference: for the consciousness aggregate, in place of contact, it is ‘from the arising of name-and-form… from the cessation of name-and-form.’

Evaṃ ekekassa khandhassa udayabbayadassane dasa dasa katvā samapaññāsa lakkhaṇāni vuttāni, tesaṃ vasenapi “evampi rūpasamudayo, evampi rūpavayo, evampi rūpaṃ udeti, evampi rūpaṃ vetī”ti paccayato ceva khaṇato ca vitthārena ca manasikāravidhiṃ dassetuṃ “tasseva ñāṇassā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha avijjāsamudayāti avijjāya uppādā[M 2.0329], atthibhāvāti attho. Nirodhaviruddho hi uppādo atthibhāvo hoti, tasmā purimabhavasiddhāya avijjāya sati imasmiṃ bhave rūpasamudayo rūpassa uppādo hotīti attho. Ādi-saddasaṅgahitesu “taṇhāsamudayā rūpasamudayo, kammasamudayā rūpasamudayo, āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayo”ti ca, tathā vayadassane “avijjānirodhā rūpanirodho, taṇhānirodhā… kammanirodhā… āhāranirodhā rūpanirodho”ti ca ādīsu avijjādīhi tīhi atītakālikāni tesaṃ sahakārīkāraṇabhūtāni upādānādīnipi gahitānevāti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, in the contemplation of the arising and passing away of each aggregate, fifty characteristics are stated, ten for each. By means of these, in order to show in detail the method of attention both from the side of conditions and from the side of moments—‘Thus is the arising of form, thus the passing away of form; thus form arises, thus form passes away’—the passage beginning ‘Of that same knowledge’ was started. Here, ‘with the arising of ignorance’ means with the production of ignorance, that is, with its existence. For production, which is the opposite of cessation, is existence. Therefore, the meaning is that when there is ignorance established in a previous existence, the arising of form, the production of form, occurs in this existence. In the passages beginning ‘with the arising of craving, the arising of form; with the arising of kamma, the arising of form; with the arising of nutriment, the arising of form,’ and similarly in the contemplation of passing away, ‘with the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of form; with the cessation of craving… with the cessation of kamma… with the cessation of nutriment, the cessation of form,’ it should be understood that by the three past factors beginning with ignorance, their ancillary causes such as clinging are also included.

Pavattipaccayesu kabaḷīkārāhārassa balavatāya so eva gahito “āhārasamudayā”ti. Tasmiṃ pana gahite pavattipaccayatāsāmaññena utucittānipi gahitāneva hontīti catusamuṭṭhānikarūpassa paccayato udayadassanaṃ vibhāvitamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avijjātaṇhūpanissayasahiteneva kammunā rūpakāyassa nibbatti, asati ca avijjūpanissayāya bhavanikantiyā jātiyā asambhavoyevāti. Yathā rūpassa avijjātaṇhūpanissayatā, evaṃ vedanādīnampi daṭṭhabbā. Āhāro pana uppannassa rūpassa posako kabaḷīkārāhārassa adhippetattā, kāmaṃ yathādhiṭṭhānattā vā desanāya. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesena vā āhāraggahaṇaṃ. Avijjānirodhāti aggamaggañāṇena avijjāya anuppādanirodhato anāgatassa rūpassa anuppādanirodho hoti paccayābhāve abhāvato. “Taṇhānirodhā kammanirodho”ti etthāpi eseva nayo. Āhāranirodhāti pavattipaccayassa kabaḷīkārāhārassa abhāve. Rūpanirodhoti taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpassa abhāvo hotīti. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ[M 2.0330]. Ayaṃ pana viseso – “phuṭṭho vedeti, phuṭṭho sañjānāti, phuṭṭho cetetīti (saṃ. ni. 4.93), phassapaccayā vedanā, cakkhusamphassajā vedanā, saññā cetanā”ti vacanato phasso vedanāsaññāsaṅkhārakkhandhānaṃ pavattipaccayo, tannirodhā ca tesaṃ nirodho, mahāpadānamahānidānasuttesu[V 2.0246], abhidhamme ca aññamaññapaccayavāre “nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇa”nti (dī. ni. 2.57, 97; kathā. 719) vacanato nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇassa pavattipaccayo, tannirodhā ca tassa nirodhoti vuttaṃ “phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo”tiādi.

Because of the strength of physical food among the conditions for continuance, it alone is taken up with the words 'from the arising of nutriment.' When this is taken, however, temperature and mind are also included by the common characteristic of being conditions for continuance. Thus, it should be understood that the arising of material form with four origins is clearly shown through its conditions. The material body is produced only by kamma accompanied by ignorance and craving as its decisive support. For if there were no delight in existence with ignorance as its decisive support, there would be no possibility of birth. Just as material form has ignorance and craving as its decisive support, so too should feeling and the other aggregates be understood. Nutriment, however, nourishes already arisen material form, since physical food is intended; or, if you like, this is according to the determination in the teaching. Or the taking up of nutriment is by way of an emphatic statement. 'With the cessation of ignorance': through the supreme path-knowledge, with the non-arising cessation of ignorance, the non-arising cessation of future material form occurs, because in the absence of the condition, there is an absence of the result. 'With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of kamma': here too, the same method applies. 'With the cessation of nutriment': in the absence of physical food, the condition for continuance. 'There is the cessation of material form': there is the absence of the material form that originates from it. The rest should be understood in accordance with the method stated below. This, however, is the distinction: 'Having been touched, one feels; having been touched, one perceives; having been touched, one intends' (SN 4.93). According to the statements 'with contact as condition, feeling,' 'feeling born of eye-contact,' 'perception,' and 'volition,' contact is a condition for the continuance of the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, and with its cessation, they too cease. In the Mahāpadāna and Mahānidāna Suttas, and in the Abhidhamma in the section on mutual conditionality, it is said: 'with name-and-form as condition, consciousness' (DN 2.57, 97; Kv 719). Thus, name-and-form is a condition for the continuance of consciousness, and with its cessation, consciousness also ceases. This is what is meant by 'with the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling,' and so on.

1271. Dasa dasāti rūpakkhandhassa udayadassane avijjā taṇhā kammaṃ āhāroti imesaṃ paccayānaṃ atthitāsaṅkhatalakkhaṇāni ceva rūpassa nibbattilakkhaṇañcāti imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni, vayadassane avijjādīnaṃ catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ anuppādanirodho, rūpassa khaṇanirodho cāti imāni pañca lakkhaṇānīti rūpakkhandhassa dasa lakkhaṇāni, tathā vedanākkhandhādīnaṃ catunnaṃ cattālīsa lakkhaṇānīti evaṃ samapaññāsa lakkhaṇāni honti. Tenāha “paññāsa lakkhaṇānī”ti. Lakkhaṇaṭṭho pana tesaṃ catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ atthitā, anuppādanirodho cāti aṭṭha lakkhīyati etehi rūpādīnaṃ udayo ca vayo cāti lakkhaṇāni. Catunnañhi paccayānaṃ atthitāhi rūpādiudayo lakkhīyati, anuppādanirodhaaccantanirodhehi vayo, nibbattivipariṇāmāni pana saṅkhatalakkhaṇānevāti. Dhamme samanupassatīti rūpādike dhamme udayabbayavante samanupassati. Ettha ca keci tāva āhu “arūpakkhandhānaṃ udayabbayadassanaṃ addhāsantativasena, na khaṇavasenā”ti, tesaṃ matena khaṇato udayabbayadassanameva na siyā. Apare panāhu “paccayato udayabbayadassanena atītādivibhāgaṃ anāmasitvā sabbasādhāraṇato [M 2.0331] avijjādipaccayā vedanāya sambhavaṃ labbhamānataṃ passati, na uppādaṃ. Avijjādiabhāve ca tassā asambhavaṃ alabbhamānataṃ passati, na bhaṅgakkhaṇato. Udayabbayassa dassane paccuppannānaṃ uppādaṃ, bhaṅgañca passatī”ti, taṃ ayuttaṃ. Santativasena hi rūpārūpadhamme udayabbayato manasi karontassa anukkamena bhāvanāya balappattakāle ñāṇassa tikkhavisadabhāvappattiyā khaṇato udayabbayā upaṭṭhahantīti.

1271. Ten by ten: In seeing the arising of the material aggregate, there are these five characteristics: the characteristic called the existence of these conditions—ignorance, craving, kamma, and nutriment—and the characteristic of the production of material form. In seeing its passing away, there are these five characteristics: the non-arising cessation of the four conditions, ignorance and so on, and the momentary cessation of material form. Thus there are ten characteristics for the material aggregate. Similarly, for the four other aggregates beginning with the feeling aggregate, there are forty characteristics. Thus there are fifty characteristics in all. That is why it is said, 'fifty characteristics.' The meaning of 'characteristic' here is that the existence and the non-arising cessation of those four conditions are eight things by which the arising and passing away of material form and so on are marked; thus they are characteristics. For the arising of material form and so on is marked by the existence of the four conditions, and their passing away by their non-arising cessation and final cessation. Production and change, however, are simply characteristics of the conditioned. 'He contemplates phenomena': he contemplates phenomena such as material form as being subject to arising and passing away. Here, some say: 'The seeing of the arising and passing away of the immaterial aggregates is by way of temporal continuity, not by way of the moment.' According to their opinion, there would be no seeing of arising and passing away from moment to moment. But others say: 'By seeing arising and passing away from a condition, without considering the division into past, etc., one sees universally the possibility of the occurrence of feeling from conditions such as ignorance, its obtainability, but not its arising. And in the absence of ignorance, etc., one sees its impossibility, its non-obtainability, but not its moment of dissolution. In seeing arising and passing away, one sees the arising and dissolution of present phenomena.' This is incorrect. For when one attends to the arising and passing away of material and immaterial phenomena by way of continuity, as the development of meditation gradually gains power and his knowledge attains a state of sharpness and clarity, arising and passing away from moment to moment become manifest.

1272-5. Ayañhi paṭhamaṃ paccayato udayabbayaṃ manasi karonto pacchā avijjādike paccayadhamme vissajjetvā udayabbayavante khandhe gahetvā tesaṃ paccayato udayabbayadassanamukhena khaṇatopi udayabbayaṃ manasi karoti. Tassa yadā ñāṇaṃ tikkhaṃ visadaṃ hutvā pavattati, tadā rūpārūpadhammā khaṇe khaṇe uppajjantā, bhijjantā ca hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Tena vuttaṃ “evaṃ rūpudayo hotī”tiādi. Tattha evaṃ rūpudayoti evaṃ vuttanayena avijjāsamudayā…pe… taṇhāsamudayā…pe… kamma…pe… āhārasamudayāpi rūpassa sambhavo[V 2.0247]. Evamassa vayoti evaṃ vuttanayeneva avijjānirodhā…pe… taṇhānirodhā…pe… kamma…pe… āhāranirodhā rūpassa vayo anuppādoti ayaṃ paccayato vitthārena manasikāro. Udeti evaṃ rūpampīti evaṃ samudayato kammasamuṭṭhānarūpampi āhārautucittasamuṭṭhānarūpampi udeti uppajjati nibbattati. Evaṃ rūpaṃ tu vetīti kammasamuṭṭhānarūpampi āhārautucittasamuṭṭhānarūpampi evaṃ veti nirujjhatīti ayaṃ khaṇato vitthārena manasikāro. Tena vuttaṃ “evaṃ paccayatopettha khaṇato udayabbaya”nti. Sabbadhammā pākaṭā hontīti iti ime dhammā ahutvā sambhonti, hutvā paṭiventi. Yathā paccuppanne, evaṃ atītānāgatepīti nayavasena atītādidhammānaṃ dvedhā udayabbayaṃ passato saccapaṭiccasamuppādanayalakkhaṇabhedā [M 2.0332] pākaṭā honti. Tassevaṃ pākaṭībhūtasabbadhammasabhāvassa “evaṃ kira nāmime dhammā anuppannapubbā uppajjanti, uppannā nirujjhantī”ti niccanavāva hutvā saṅkhārā upaṭṭhahanti. Na kevalañca niccanavāva, udake daṇḍakena katalekhā viya, āragge ṭhapitasāsapo viya, vijjusañcāro viya ca parittakālaṭṭhāyino upaṭṭhahanti. Tenāha “udake daṇḍarājīvā”tiādi. Udake daṇḍarājiādayova kiñcāpi uttaruttari atiparittaṭṭhāyibhāvanidassanatthaṃ dassitā, tathāpi dandhanirodhā eva nidassitā, tatopi lahutaranirodhattā saṅkhārānaṃ. Tathā hi gamanassādānaṃ devaputtānaṃ heṭṭhupariyena parimukhaṃ dhāvantānaṃ sirasi, pāde ca baddhakhuradhārāsannipātatopi sīghataro rūpanirodho vutto, pageva arūpadhammānaṃ. Na kevalaṃ parittatarakālaṭṭhāyinova upaṭṭhahanti, atha kho asārāpi khāyantīti āha “kadalī”tiādi. Tattha maṇḍalākārena āvijjhiyamānaṃ alātameva alātacakkaṃ. Mantosadhappabhāvitā indajālādikā māyā.

1272-5. For this person first attends to arising and passing away in terms of conditions, and afterwards, having set aside the conditional phenomena such as ignorance, he takes up the aggregates that are subject to arising and passing away and attends to their arising and passing away also moment by moment, by way of seeing their arising and passing away from conditions. When his knowledge proceeds, having become sharp and clear, material and immaterial phenomena present themselves as arising and breaking up from moment to moment. Therefore it is said: 'Thus is the arising of material form,' and so on. Herein, 'thus is the arising of material form' means that in the way stated, there is the occurrence of material form from the arising of ignorance… from the arising of craving… from kamma… from the arising of nutriment. 'Thus is its passing away' means that in the very same way stated, with the cessation of ignorance… with the cessation of craving… with kamma… with the cessation of nutriment, the passing away of material form is its non-arising. This is the detailed attention in terms of conditions. 'Thus material form also arises': in this way, from this arising, kamma-born material form and also material form born of nutriment, temperature, and mind arise, are produced, come to be. 'But thus material form passes away': kamma-born material form and also material form born of nutriment, temperature, and mind thus pass away, cease. This is the detailed attention moment by moment. Therefore it is said: 'Thus here arising and passing away are from a condition and moment by moment.' 'All phenomena become manifest': thus these phenomena, not having been, come to be; having been, they pass away. Just as in the present, so too in the past and future—for one who sees in this way the twofold arising and passing away of past and other phenomena, the different characteristics of the methods of the truths and of dependent origination become manifest. For one to whom the nature of all phenomena has thus become manifest, the formations present themselves as if ever new, with the thought: 'So it seems these phenomena, not having arisen before, arise; and having arisen, they cease.' And not only as if ever new, but they also present themselves as lasting for a very short time, like a line drawn on water with a stick, like a mustard seed placed on the point of an awl, like a flash of lightning. Therefore it is said: 'Like a line of a stick on water,' and so on. Although the examples of the line of a stick on water and so on are shown to illustrate a progressively shorter duration, they are nevertheless shown as examples of slow cessation, because formations cease even more quickly than that. For the cessation of material form is said to be swifter than the impact of razor blades tied to the head and feet of deities as they rush past each other up and down—how much more so the cessation of immaterial phenomena. Not only do they present themselves as lasting for a very short time, but they also appear as being without substance. Therefore it is said: 'Like a plantain trunk,' and so on. Herein, a firebrand whirled in a circle is a 'fire-wheel.' Magic such as the conjuror's art is produced by means of chants and herbs.

1276-7. Ettāvatāti yvāyaṃ kalāpasammasananiyojanato paṭṭhāya yāva udayabbayapaṭivedhāya bhāvanā vidhi āraddho, ettāvatā bhāvanāvidhānena kalāpasammasanampi udayabbayañāṇuppādasseva parikammanti. Udayabbayadassanaṃ ñāṇanti sambandho. Lakkhaṇāni ca…pe… ṭhitanti vayadhammameva uppajjati, uppannañca vayaṃ upetīti iminā ākārena samapaññāsa lakkhaṇāni paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitaṃ. Adhunā uppannaṃ na tāva balappattanti āha “taruṇa”nti. Kalāpasammasanādivasena pavattasammasanaṃ nippariyāyena vipassanāsamaññaṃ labhati. Udayabbayānupassanādivasena pavattameva labhatīti āha “yassa cā”tiādi.

1276-7. 'Up to this point': This refers to the method of development that has been undertaken, beginning from the application to the comprehension of groups up to the penetration of arising and passing away. By this method of development up to this point, the comprehension of groups is the preliminary work for the arising of the knowledge of arising and passing away. The connection is: 'The seeing of arising and passing away is knowledge.' 'And the characteristics... established': having penetrated the fifty characteristics in this manner—'what has the nature of passing away arises, and what has arisen undergoes passing away'—it is established. Because what has just arisen has not yet gained strength, it is now called 'immature.' The comprehension that proceeds by way of the comprehension of groups, etc., directly obtains the name 'insight.' That which proceeds by way of the contemplation of arising and passing away, etc., also obtains it. Therefore it is said, 'And for whom,' and so on.

1278-80. Athassa [V 2.0248] imāya taruṇavipassanāya vipassantassa dasa vipassanupakkilesā uppajjantīti dassento āha [M 2.0333] “vipassanāyā”tiādi. Etāyāti udayabbayānupassanāsaṅkhātāya taruṇavipassanāya, na bhaṅgānupassanādisaṅkhātāya taruṇavipassanāya, nāpi nibbidānupassanādisaṅkhātāya balavavipassanāyāti attho. Na hi tadā vipassanupakkilesā uppajjantīti. Vipassakassāti ca vipassakassevāti eva-kāro luttaniddiṭṭho. Teneva vakkhati “sampattapaṭivedhassā”tiādi. Diṭṭhiggāhādivatthubhāvena vipassanaṃ upakkilesantīti upakkilesā. Sampatto catusaccaphalapaṭivedho yena so sampattapaṭivedho, so ca sotāpannādīnaṃ aññataro hotīti āha “sotāpannādino”ti. Apicāti ayaṃ vakkhamānasamuccayattho. Idañca ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena vuttaṃ balavavipassanāpattassāpi anuppajjanato. Sampattapaṭivedhassāti vā balavipassanāpattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sopi hi paṭivedhappattiyā āsannārahadese ṭhitattā sampattapaṭivedho nāma hoti. Evañca sati apicāti vuttasamuccayattho hoti. Atha vā api-saddo vuttasamuccayattho. Ca-saddo avuttasamuccayattho. Tena nikkhittakammaṭṭhānaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā antarā vosānaṃ āpannassāpi vipassanupakkilesā na uppajjanti. Vippaṭipannassāti sīlavipattiādivasena yathā tathā vippaṭipannakassa, garahitabbapaṭipannassāti attho. Atha vā vippaṭipannassāti vipassanābhāvanāsaṅkhātāya sammāpaṭipattiyā abhāvena virahitapaṭipattikassa.

1278–80. Now, to show that for one practicing with this tender insight, ten imperfections of insight arise, it is said, “of insight,” and so on. “By this” means by the tender insight known as the contemplation of arising and passing away, not by the tender insight known as the contemplation of dissolution and so on, nor by the strong insight known as the contemplation of disenchantment and so on. For at that time, the imperfections of insight do not arise. “For the insight practitioner” means specifically for the insight practitioner; the particle eva is elided. Therefore, it will be said, “for one who has attained penetration,” and so on. Because they defile insight by being a basis for grasping at views and so on, they are called imperfections. One by whom the penetration to the fruit of the four truths has been attained is “one who has attained penetration,” and such a one is a stream-enterer or another, hence it is said, “of a stream-enterer, and so on.” The word “Moreover” (apica) serves to conjoin what will be said. And this is stated by way of the supreme designation, because they do not arise even for one who has attained strong insight. Alternatively, “for one who has attained penetration” is said in reference to one who has reached strong insight. For such a person, being established in a region near to and worthy of the attainment of penetration, is called “one who has attained penetration.” In this way, “Moreover” serves to conjoin what has been stated. Alternatively, the word api conjoins what has been stated, while the word ca conjoins what has not been stated. Thus, it includes one who has laid aside the meditation subject. Even for one who has begun insight practice but stopped midway, the imperfections of insight do not arise. “For one who has practiced wrongly” means one who has practiced wrongly by way of a corruption of virtue or the like; the meaning is, one whose practice is blameworthy. Alternatively, “for one who has practiced wrongly” means one who is devoid of the practice, being without the right practice designated as the development of insight.

1281. Vipassanāpaṭipattiyeva hi sasambhārā pubbabhāge sammāpaṭipatti, tadaññā vippaṭipatti, tenevassa visuddhipakkhe “sammāva paṭipannassā”ti vuttaṃ. Sā ca nikkhittadhurassāpi hotīti imasmiṃ pakkhe nikkhittakammaṭṭhānopi imināva saṅgahito hotīti. Sammāva paṭipannassāti heṭṭhā vuttavidhānena sammā eva paṭipannassa, na vippaṭipannassa vā nikkhittadhurassa [M 2.0334] vā. Yuttayogassāti yuttena yogena, ñāṇena vā bhāvanamanuyuñjanasīlassa. Sā pana yuttayogitā samathavasenāpi hotīti tannivattanatthamāha “sadā vipassakassevā”ti. Uppajjantīti etthāpi eva-kāro sambandhitabbo, tena na nuppajjantīti attho. Aññathā maggāmaggañāṇasseva asambhavato. Kirāti anussutiyaṃ. Sā panesā anussuti pāḷivaseneva āgatāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathāha –

1281. For the practice of insight itself, together with its requisites in the preliminary part, is the right practice; any other is wrong practice. Therefore, in the section on purification, it is said, “for one who is rightly practicing.” And since this can also be the case for one who has laid down the burden, in this alternative one who has laid aside the meditation subject is also included by this. “For one who is rightly practicing” means for one who is practicing rightly in the way explained previously, not for one who has practiced wrongly or has laid down the burden. “For one who is suitably yoked” means for one who is devoted to the practice of development with a suitable application, that is, with knowledge. But since that suitable application can also occur by way of serenity, to exclude that he said, “always for the insight meditator alone.” With “they arise,” too, the particle eva should be connected, so the meaning is that they certainly do arise; otherwise, the knowledge of path and not-path would be impossible. The word kirā indicates a traditional teaching. And it should be understood that this traditional teaching has come down by way of the Pāli Canon. As it is said:

“Kathaṃ dhammuddhaccaviggahitaṃ mānasaṃ hoti? Aniccato manasikaroto obhāso uppajjati[V 2.0249], obhāso dhammoti obhāsaṃ āvajjeti, tato vikkhepo uddhaccaṃ, tena uddhaccena viggahitamānaso aniccato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Dukkhato…pe… anattato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tathā aniccato manasikaroto ñāṇaṃ uppajjati…pe… pīti passaddhi sukhaṃ adhimokkho paggaho upaṭṭhānaṃ upekkhā nikanti uppajjati, nikanti dhammoti nikantiṃ āvajjeti, tato vikkhepo uddhaccaṃ, tena uddhaccena viggahitamānaso aniccato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Dukkhato…pe… anattato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.6).

“How is the mind seized by excitement over phenomena? When one is attending to impermanence, an illumination arises. Thinking, ‘The illumination is the Dhamma,’ one adverts to the illumination. From that comes distraction, which is excitement. With a mind seized by that excitement, one does not understand the contemplation of impermanence as it really is. … of suffering … one does not understand the contemplation of non-self as it really is. Similarly, when one is attending to impermanence, knowledge arises … joy, tranquility, happiness, resolution, exertion, mindfulness, equanimity, and attachment arise. Thinking, ‘Attachment is the Dhamma,’ one adverts to attachment. From that comes distraction, which is excitement. With a mind seized by that excitement, one does not understand the contemplation of impermanence as it really is. … of suffering … one does not understand the contemplation of non-self as it really is.” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.6)

1282. Idāni tesaṃ obhāsādīnaṃ sarūpavibhāvanatthaṃ tesu uppannesu vipassanāya upakkilissanākārañca dassetuṃ “vipassanāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vipassanāya obhāsoti vipassanācittasamuṭṭhitaṃ, sasantatipatitautusamuṭṭhānañca bhāsuraṃ rūpaṃ. Tattha vipassanācittasamuṭṭhānaṃ yogino sarīraṭṭhameva pabhassaraṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati, itaraṃ sarīraṃ muñcitvā ñāṇānubhāvānurūpaṃ [M 2.0335] samantato pharati, taṃ tasseva paññāyati, tena phuṭṭhokāse rūpagatampi passati. Passanto ca cakkhuviññāṇena passati, udāhu manoviññāṇenāti vīmaṃsitabbametanti vadanti. Ācariyadhammapālattherena pana “dibbacakkhulābhino viya taṃ manoviññāṇaviññeyyamevāti yuttaṃ viya dissatī”ti (visuddhi. mahā. 2.733) vuttaṃ.

1282. Now, to explain the nature of the illumination and the other imperfections, and to show the way insight is defiled when they arise, the passage beginning “of insight” was stated. The illumination of insight is a radiant material form produced by the insight-consciousness and by temperature falling within one’s own continuity. Among these, that produced by the insight-consciousness remains luminous only within the yogi’s body. The other, leaving the body, spreads all around in accordance with the power of the knowledge. It is discerned only by the yogi himself, and in the space pervaded by it he also sees material forms. And they say that this should be investigated: whether, when seeing, he sees with eye-consciousness or with mind-consciousness. But the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has said: “It seems proper that, like for one who has obtained the divine eye, it is cognizable only by mind-consciousness” (Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā 2.733).

1283-4. Maggappatto phalappatto, ahamasmīti gaṇhatīti “na vata me ito pubbe evarūpo obhāso uppannapubbo, addhā ariyamaggaṃ pattosmi, phalaṃ sacchākāsi”nti amaggaṃyeva “maggo”ti gaṇhāti. Tassevaṃ pana gaṇhatoti tassa amaggaṃyeva “maggo”ti gaṇhantassa. Vipassanāvīthīti paṭipāṭiyā pavattamānā vipassanāva ukkantā nāma hoti, yogino “maggaṃ pattosmī”ti adhimānena vissaṭṭhattā. Vipassanāvīthintipi pāṭho, tassevaṃ gaṇhato vipassanā tatoyeva vīthiṃ ukkantā nāma hotīti attho. Obhāsameva so bhikkhu, assādento nisīdatīti so bhikkhu attanā āraddhaṃ vipassanaṃ vissajjetvā obhāsameva lobhavasena vā diṭṭhivasena vā assādento nisīdati. So kho panāyaṃ obhāso kassaci bhikkhuno pallaṅkaṭṭhānamattameva obhāsento uppajjati, kassaci antogabbhaṃ, kassaci bahigabbhaṃ, kassaci sakalavihāraṃ gāvutaṃ aḍḍhayojanaṃ yojanaṃ dviyojanaṃ tiyojanaṃ, kassaci pathavītalato [V 2.0250] paṭṭhāya yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmalokā ekālokaṃ kurumāno, yathā samuddamhi yojanamatte macchakacchapā paññāyanti, evaṃ uppajjanti. Bhagavato pana dasasahassilokadhātuṃ obhāsento udapādi.

1283–4. He grasps, ‘I have attained the path, I have attained the fruit,’ thinking: ‘Surely, such an illumination has never arisen in me before! I have certainly attained the noble path, I have realized the fruit.’ Thus he grasps what is not the path as the path. For him grasping in this way: that is, for him who grasps what is not the path as the path. The course of insight: the insight that was proceeding in sequence is said to have ‘deviated,’ because it has been abandoned by the yogi through the conceit, ‘I have attained the path.’ There is also the reading vipassanāvīthinti, the meaning of which is that for one who grasps in this way, the insight has thereby deviated from its course. That bhikkhu, delighting in the illumination, sits down: having given up the insight he had undertaken, that bhikkhu sits delighting in the illumination alone, either through greed or through wrong view. Now, for some bhikkhus this illumination arises illuminating only the place of their seat; for some, the interior of their cell; for some, the exterior of their cell; for some, the entire monastery, a league, half a yojana, a yojana, two yojanas, three yojanas; for some, it arises making everything a single light from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma world, just as in the ocean fish and turtles are visible for a yojana. For the Blessed One, however, it arose illuminating the ten-thousand-world-system.

1285. Vipassanāpītīti vipassanācittasampayuttā pīti. Khuddikādikā heṭṭhā vaṇṇitāyeva, ayañca pañcavidhā pīti udayabbayānupassanāya [M 2.0336] vīthipaṭipannāya anukkamena uppajjati. Matthakappattena pana udayabbayañāṇena saddhiṃ pharaṇāpītiyeva hoti. Upacārappanakkhaṇato aññadāpi hi pharaṇāpīti hotiyevāti. Tena vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sakalasarīraṃ pūrayamānā uppajjatī”ti (visuddhi. 2.734; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1.dhammuddesavāra jhānaṅgarāsivaṇṇanā).

1285. The joy of insight is the joy associated with the insight-consciousness. The minor joy and the others have been described below. And this fivefold joy arises in sequence for one who has entered upon the course of the contemplation of arising and passing away. But with the knowledge of arising and passing away that has reached its peak, there is only transportive joy. For transportive joy occurs even at times other than the moment of access and absorption. Thus it is said in the Commentary: “It arises filling the entire body” (Visuddhimagga 2.734; Dhammasaṅgaṇī Aṭṭhakathā 1, Dhammuddesavāra, Jhānaṅgarāsivaṇṇanā).

1286-7. Yogino…pe… honti hīti yassāyaṃ passaddhi uppannā, tassa yogino rattiṭṭhāne vā divāṭṭhāne vā nisinnassa kāyacittāni passaddhāneva honti, neva daratho hotīti attho. Passaddhiādīni cha yugaḷāni aññamaññayogīnīti passaddhiyā uppannāya itarāpi uppannāyeva hontīti kiccadassanamukhena tā sabbāpi dassento “lahūni cā”tiādimāha. Ettha ca kāya-ggahaṇena rūpakāyassāpi gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, na vedanādikkhandhattayasseva. Kāyapassaddhiādayo hi rūpakāyassāpi darathādinimmaddakāti. Kammaññāneva hontīti na kevalaṃ kammaññāneva suvisadāni ujukāniyeva honti, avinābhāvitāya pana tadubhayaṃ visuṃ na vuttaṃ. Kāyacittānaṃ passaddhādibhāvo ca tesaṃ apassaddhādihetubhūtānaṃ uddhaccādithinamiddhādidiṭṭhimānādisesanīvaraṇādiassaddhiyādimāyāsāṭheyyādisaṃkilesadhammānaṃ viddhaṃsanavaseneva tadā vipassanācittuppādassa pavattanato.

1286–7. The phrase ‘For the yogi … they are indeed’ means that when this tranquility has arisen for that yogi, whether he is seated in his nighttime or daytime dwelling, his body and mind are tranquil; there is no distress. Since the six pairs beginning with tranquility are mutually connected, when tranquility has arisen the others also arise. Showing them all by way of displaying their function, he said, “and lightness,” etc. And here, by the taking up of ‘body,’ the taking up of the material body should be understood, not only that of the three aggregates beginning with feeling. For bodily tranquility and the others crush the distress, etc., of the material body as well. They become workable: they become not only workable but also very pure and straight; but because of their inseparability, these two are not stated separately. The state of tranquility, etc., of body and mind occurs because at that time the arising of the insight-consciousness proceeds only by way of the demolition of those defiling states that are the cause of their lack of tranquility, etc., such as restlessness, sloth and torpor, wrong views, conceit, the remaining hindrances, lack of faith, deceit, hypocrisy, and other defilements.

1288-90. Manussānaṃ ayanti mānusī, manussayogyakāmasukharati. Tādisehi manussavisesehi anubhavitabbatānativattanato dibbaratipi saṅgahitā, mānusīsadisatāya, kāmasukhabhāvena dibbā rati vā mānusī, tassā atikkantatāya na mānusīti amānusī, taṃ amānusiṃ. Suññāgāranti yaṃ kiñci vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ, vipassanaṃ eva vā, sāpi hi [M 2.0337] niccabhāvādisuññatāya, yogino sukhasannissayatāya ca “suññāgāra”nti vattabbataṃ labhati. Cittassa anupasamakarānaṃ kilesānaṃ vigamena santacittassa saṃsāre bhayassa ikkhanena bhikkhuno sammā [V 2.0251] ñāyena rūpārūpadhammānaṃ udayabbayānupassanādivasena te vipassato sammasato sammāraddhavipassanānaṃ manussānaṃ visayatāya amānusī vipassanāpītisukhasaññitā rati hotīti ayamettha gāthāya saṅkhepattho. Dutiyagāthā pana udayabbayañāṇameva sandhāya vuttā. Tattha yato yatoti rūpato, arūpato vā.

1288–90. Human delight is what pertains to humans, the pleasure and joy of sensual bliss suitable for humans. Because it is not surpassed by what can be experienced by such exceptional humans, even divine delight is included. Due to its similarity to human delight and its nature as a sensual pleasure, divine delight is also human. Because it surpasses this, it is not human, thus it is superhuman. A 'secluded dwelling' refers to any secluded lodging, or even insight meditation itself. For it is also called a 'secluded dwelling' because of its emptiness of permanence and so on, and because it is a basis of happiness for the yogi. For a bhikkhu whose mind is peaceful through the removal of defilements that disturb its tranquility, who sees the danger in saṃsāra, and who rightly observes material and immaterial phenomena in terms of their arising and passing away—for those who have rightly undertaken insight, there arises a superhuman delight, known as the rapture and happiness of insight. This is the condensed meaning of the verse. The second verse, however, refers specifically to the knowledge of arising and passing away. In that context, 'from whatever' means from form or from the formless.

1291. Ñāṇādayoti ñāṇasaddhādayo satta. Vuttanayenāti “ñāṇanti vipassanāñāṇaṃ, saddhāti vipassanācittasampayuttā saddhā”tiādinā vuttanayānusārena vipassanāvaseneva ñeyyā. Tattha ñāṇaṃ rūpārūpadhamme udayabbayānupassanāvasena tulayantassa tīrentassa vissaṭṭhaindavajiramiva avigatavegaṃ tikhiṇaṃ sūraṃ ativisadaṃ uppajjati. Tathā hi tena yogī “maggaṃ pattosmī”ti maññati. Saddhāti kilesakālusiyāpagamena cittacetasikānaṃ atisayapasādabhūtā balavatī saddhā, na pana kammaphalaṃ, ratanattayaṃ vā saddahanavasena pavattā. Satipi sūpaṭṭhitā acalā pabbatarājasadisā uppajjati. Imissā ca uppannāya so yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ paccavekkhati, taṃ taṃ ṭhānamassa anupavisitvā okkhanditvā pakkhanditvā paribhaṇḍabhūtassa yathākammūpagañāṇassa upaṭṭhahante paralokavisayattā vaṇṇāyatanavisayamatītanti dibbacakkhuno paraloko viya satiyā upaṭṭhāti. Sukhaṃ pana sakalasarīraṃ abhisandamānaṃ atipaṇītaṃ uppajjati. Tasmiñhi uppanne taṃsamuṭṭhitehi atipaṇītehi rūpehi sabbo kāyo pariphuṭo, paribrūhito ca hoti. Upekkhā pana vipassanupekkhā [M 2.0338] ceva āvajjanupekkhā ca. Tattha vicinitavicayattā saṅkhārānaṃ vicinane majjhattabhāvena ṭhitā vipassanupekkhā. Sā pana atthato tathāpavattā tatramajjhattupekkhāva. Manodvārāvajjanacittasampayuttā vedanā āvajjane ajjhupekkhanavasena pavattiyā āvajjanupekkhāti vuccati. Duvidhā panesā tadā uppajjati. Tathā hi tasmiṃ samaye sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ udayabbaye majjhattabhūtā vipassanupekkhā balavatī uppajjati, manodvāre āvajjanupekkhāpi. Sā hissa taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ āvajjantassa vissaṭṭhaindavajiramiva, pattapuṭe pakkhandatattanārāco viya ca sūrā tikhiṇā hutvā pavattati. Vīriyampi asithilamanaccāraddhaṃ sampayuttadhamme kilesapakkhato kosajjapakkhato paggaṇhantaṃ supaggahitamuppajjati, nikanti ca obhāsādipaṭimaṇḍitāya vipassanāya ālayaṃ kurumānā bhāvanāya sātisayappavattiyā sukhumā santākārā uppajjati. Yā kilesoti pariggahitumpi na yuttā. Yathā ca obhāse, evaṃ etesupi aññasmiṃ uppanne yogāvacaro “na vata me ito pubbe evarūpā pīti uppannapubbā, evarūpā passaddhi ñāṇaṃ saddhā sati sukhaṃ upekkhā vīriyaṃ nikanti uppannapubbā, addhā maggaphalappattosmī”ti gaṇhāti, tassevaṃ gaṇhato vipassanā vīthiukkantā nāma hoti. So teyeva [V 2.0252] assādento nisīdati. Ime ca pana vipassanupakkilesā yebhuyyena samathavipassanālābhino uppajjanti. So samāpattivikkhambhitānaṃ kilesānaṃ asamudācārato “arahā aha”nti cittaṃ uppādetīti.

1291. “Knowledge and the others” refers to the seven factors beginning with knowledge and faith. “In the way stated” means they are to be understood only through insight meditation, according to the way explained: “Knowledge refers to insight knowledge, faith refers to faith associated with the mind engaged in insight,” and so on. Here, knowledge arises sharp, swift, vigorous, and exceedingly clear—like a released thunderbolt—as the meditator observes the arising and passing away of material and immaterial phenomena, weighing and discerning them. Indeed, the yogi thinks, “I have attained the path.” Faith here is strong faith, being a great serenity of mind and mental factors due to the removal of the stain of the defilements—not faith proceeding by way of believing in kamma and its results or in the Triple Gem. Mindfulness arises very well established, unshakable like a king of mountains. When this mindfulness arises, whatever the yogi reviews, that object appears to him as if it has been entered into and plunged into, just as the next world appears to the divine eye of one for whom the fully-equipped knowledge of the ripening of kamma is present. Happiness arises, exceedingly sublime, suffusing the entire body. When this happiness arises, the entire body is permeated and augmented by the accompanying exceedingly sublime material phenomena. Equanimity here is both insight-equanimity and adverting-equanimity. Insight-equanimity is that which stands with neutrality in investigating formations, since the investigation has been completed. In reality, it is just equanimity-as-neutrality that is proceeding in that way. The feeling associated with mind-door adverting consciousness is called adverting-equanimity, because it functions by looking on with equanimity in adverting. At this time, both kinds arise: strong insight-equanimity, which is neutral toward the arising and passing away of all formations, and also adverting-equanimity at the mind-door. The latter operates swiftly and sharply for him as he adverts to that object, like a released thunderbolt and like a hot iron arrow dropped into a leaf-cup. Energy arises well-exerted, neither too slack nor too strained, upholding the associated states against defilements and laziness. Attachment (nikanti) arises subtly and with a peaceful appearance, taking a liking to the insight adorned with radiance and other qualities, and proceeding with the exceedingly developed meditation. It is so subtle that it is not even fit to be recognized as a defilement. Just as with radiance, when any of these others arise, the meditator thinks: “Never before has such rapture, tranquility, knowledge, faith, mindfulness, happiness, equanimity, energy, or attachment arisen in me. Surely, I have attained the path and fruition!” When he grasps it thus, his insight is said to have overshot the path. He sits down, savoring just those states. These corruptions of insight mostly arise in those who have gained serenity and insight. Because his defilements are suppressed by the attainment and do not arise, he generates the thought, “I am an arahant.”

1292-3. Upaklesassa vatthutoti nippariyāyato diṭṭhimānataṇhā idha upakkilesā tesaṃ vatthuto uppattiṭṭhānatāya, na sabhāvato akusalattā. Yathā pana obhāsādayo, evaṃ nikantipi diṭṭhiggāhādīnaṃ ṭhānaṃ hotīti [M 2.0339] vatthubhāvopissā yujjateva. Taṃtamāvajjamānassa, bhāvanā parihāyatīti taṃ taṃ obhāsādikaṃ āvajjamānassa diṭṭhimānataṇhāvasena “mama obhāso”tiādiggāhaṃ pavattentassa bhāvanā vīthiṃ okkamitvā parivaṭṭati. Appaṃ sutametassāti appassuto.

1292–3. The basis of the corruption: Here, view, conceit, and craving are the corruptions in a direct sense. The radiance and so on are called 'corruptions' because they are the basis—the place of origin—for these, not because they are unwholesome by nature. Just as with radiance and the others, so too attachment becomes a place for grasping at views and the like; thus its nature as a basis is indeed appropriate. For one who adverts to such things, meditation declines: that is, for one who adverts to that radiance and so on, and who, influenced by view, conceit, and craving, gives rise to the grasp 'this radiance is mine,' and so on, the meditation deviates from the path and deteriorates. 'He has heard little' means one of little learning.

1294-7. Bahussuto pana obhāsādīsu uppannesu “ayaṃ kho me obhāso uppanno, so kho panāyaṃ anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno khayadhammo vayadhammo virāgadhammo nirodhadhammo”ti vā, sace obhāso attā bhaveyya, attāti gahetuṃ vaṭṭeyya, anattā ca panāyaṃ attāti gahito, tasmā “so avasavattanaṭṭhena anattā, hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena anicco, udayabbayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkho”tiādinā samanupassati, so evaṃ samanupassanto upakkilesajaṭaṃ vijaṭetvā obhāsādayo dhammā na maggo, upakkilesavinimuttaṃ pana vīthipaṭipannaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ maggoti maggañca amaggañca vavatthapeti. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbobhāsādayo”tiādi. Maggāmaggesu ñāṇanti maggāmaggañāṇaṃ, maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhipattiyā ca tena yoginā tiṇṇaṃ saccānañca vavatthānaṃ kataṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? Diṭṭhivisuddhiyā tāva nāmarūpavavatthāpanena dukkhasaccavavatthānaṃ kataṃ hoti, kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyā paccayapariggahena samudayasaccassa vavatthānaṃ. Abhidhammanayasmiñhi sabbakilesā, kammañca samudayasaccaṃ, imissaṃ maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiyaṃ sammā maggassa avadhāraṇena maggasaccaṃ. Tadupāyabhūtassa hi maggassa avadhāraṇena taṃ avadhāritamevāti evaṃ lokiyeneva tāva ñāṇena tiṇṇaṃ saccānaṃ vavatthānaṃ kataṃ hoti.

1294-7. A learned person, however, when radiance and other phenomena arise, reflects: "This radiance has arisen in me, but it is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, vanishing, fading away, and cessation." Or, if the radiance were the self, it would be appropriate to grasp it as self. But since this is not-self and yet it is grasped as self, therefore, he contemplates thus: "It is not-self in the sense of being without control; it is impermanent in the sense of becoming non-existent after having been; it is suffering in the sense of being oppressed by rise and fall," and so on. By contemplating in this way, he disentangles the tangle of corruptions. The phenomena of radiance and the like are not the path, but the insight knowledge that is free from corruptions and proceeds along the path is the path. Thus, he distinguishes between the path and the non-path. Hence it is said, "All radiance and the like," etc. Knowledge of the path and the non-path is the knowledge of path and non-path; this is said to be the purification of knowledge and vision of the path and non-path. By attaining the purification of knowledge and vision of the path and non-path, the yogi has also determined the three truths. How? First, through the purification of view, the determination of name-and-form constitutes the determination of the truth of suffering. Through the purification by overcoming doubt, the discernment of conditions constitutes the determination of the truth of the origin. In the Abhidhamma method, all defilements and kamma are the truth of the origin. In this purification of knowledge and vision of the path and non-path, the truth of the path is determined by the correct determination of the path. For by determining the path, which serves as the means, that itself is determined. Thus, for the time being, the three truths are determined even with mundane knowledge.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus in the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the Commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra,

Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the exposition on the purification of knowledge and vision of the path and non-path is finished.

21. Ekavīsatimo paricchedo

21. The Twenty-first Chapter

Paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition on the Purification of Knowledge and Vision of the Way

1298. Aṭṭhañāṇavasenevāti [M 2.0340][V 2.0253] udayabbayañāṇādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ ñāṇānaṃ vasena. Vipassanācārassa matthakappattiyā saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ sikhāpattā vipassanā. Sikhāpatti panassā udayabbayañāṇādīnaṃ aṭṭhañāṇānaṃ vasenāti āha “aṭṭhañāṇavasenā”ti. Navamanti saccānulomikañāṇaṃ. Iti udayabbayādīni aṭṭha, idañca navamañāṇaṃ paṭipadāñāṇadassananti pavuccati. Paṭipajjati etāya ariyamaggoti paṭipadā, udayabbayādīnaṃ jānanaṭṭhena, paccakkhato dassanaṭṭhena ñāṇadassanañcāti katvā.

1298. “By way of the eight knowledges” means by way of the eight knowledges beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away. For the practice of insight, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations is insight that has attained its peak. But this attainment of the peak is by way of the eight knowledges beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away; thus he said, “by way of the eight knowledges.” The ninth is the knowledge of conformity to truth. Thus, the eight, beginning with arising and passing away, and this ninth knowledge, are called the knowledge and vision of the way. Because one proceeds on the noble path by this, it is the way; and since it knows arising and passing away, etc., and sees them directly, it is knowledge and vision.

1299. Tāni pana ñāṇāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “aṭṭha ñāṇānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha udayabbayānupassanāñāṇaṃ kiñcāpi tīraṇapariññāya patiṭṭhaṃ, tathāpi yathāvuttaṭṭhena paṭipadāñāṇadassanampi hotiyevāti tampi idha vuttaṃ. Itarattha pana uppannamattaṃ appaguṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Appaguṇañhi niccasaññādipahānasiddhiyā pahānapariññāya adhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Yato tadadhigamena aṭṭhārasasu mahāvipassanāsu ekaccā adhigatāva honti. Na hi udayabbayānaṃ paccakkhato paṭivedhena vinā sāmaññākārānaṃ tīraṇamattena sātisayaṃ paṭipakkhappahānaṃ sambhavati. Asati ca paṭipakkhappahāne kuto ñāṇādīnaṃ vajiramiva avihatavegatā tikhiṇavisadāditā vā, tasmā paguṇabhāvappattaṃ udayabbayañāṇaṃ pahānapariññāpakkhiyameva daṭṭhabbaṃ.

1299. To present these knowledges according to their own individual nature, it is said, “the eight knowledges,” etc. Herein, although the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away is established in comprehension by judging, it is also included here as the knowledge and vision of the way in the aforementioned sense. In the other context, however, it was mentioned with reference to its mere arising and its immature state. For that immature state is the basis for comprehension by abandoning, which accomplishes the abandoning of perceptions of permanence, etc. Indeed, by its attainment some of the eighteen great insights are attained. For without directly penetrating arising and passing away, a mere judging of general characteristics cannot possibly overcome the opposing factors to a significant degree. And without the abandonment of opposing factors, how can the unthwarted momentum, sharpness, clarity, etc., of knowledges, like a diamond, arise? Therefore, the knowledge of arising and passing away, when it has attained a state of proficiency, should be regarded as belonging to the side of comprehension by abandoning.

1300-2. Bhaṅgeti saṅkhārānaṃ bhaṅge. Yathābhūtadassāvī bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ, tebhūmakadhammā, tesu bhayato [M 2.0341] upatiṭṭhantesu bhāyitabbākāraggāhiñāṇaṃ bhayeñāṇaṃ. Tathā hetaṃ “bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇa”nti vuccati. Muccituṃ icchatīti muccitukamyaṃ, cittaṃ, puggalo vā, tassa bhāvo muccitukamyatā, taṃ pana ñāṇamevāti āha “ñāṇaṃ muccitukamyatā”ti. Puna paṭisaṅkhānākārena pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ. Nirapekkhatāya saṅkhārānaṃ upekkhanavasena pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ. Gāthābandhatthaṃ pana visandhiniddeso. Oḷārikoḷārikassa saccapaṭicchādakatamassa [V 2.0254] vigamanena saccapaṭivedhānukūlattā saccānulomikaṃ. Taṃ pana idanti āha “saccānulomañāṇanti, anulomaṃ pavuccatī”ti.

1300-2. “Destruction” means the destruction of formations. “Fear” is so called because one who sees things as they truly are fears it; this refers to the phenomena of the three realms. When they appear as fearful, the knowledge that apprehends the aspect to be feared is the knowledge of fear. Thus, it is called “the knowledge of the appearance of terror.” “Desirous of deliverance” refers to one who desires to be freed—be it the mind or the person—and the state of that is the “desire for deliverance.” That, however, is simply knowledge; hence it is said, “the knowledge is the desire for deliverance.” Again, the knowledge that occurs in the mode of reflection is the knowledge of reflective contemplation. The knowledge that occurs with equanimity toward formations due to a sense of indifference is the knowledge of equanimity toward formations. However, for the purpose of composing the verse, the explanation is given without euphonic conjunction. “Conformity to truth” is so called because it is favorable to the penetration of truth by dispelling the grossest of things that conceal the truth. This is stated here: “the knowledge of conformity to truth is called conformity.”

1303. Nanu ca udayabbayañāṇassa pageva siddhattā kimatthaṃ puna tatthāpi abhiyogoti ce? Aniccādilakkhaṇasallakkhaṇatthaṃ. Udayabbayañāṇañhi heṭṭhā dasahi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭhaṃ hutvā yāthāvasarasato tilakkhaṇaṃ sallakkhetuṃ nāsakkhi, upakkilesavinimuttaṃ pana sakkoti, tasmā lakkhaṇasallakkhaṇatthaṃ puna tattheva yogo kātabbo. Lakkhaṇāni cassa udayabbayādīnaṃ amanasikārā, santatiiriyāpathaghanachannatāya ca nopaṭṭhahanti, tasmā udayabbayaṃ manasi katvā santatiṃ ugghāṭetvā aniccalakkhaṇaṃ, abhiṇhapīḷanaṃ pariggahetvā iriyāpathaṃ ugghāṭetvā dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ, dhātuyo vinibbhujitvā ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā anattalakkhaṇañca sallakkhetvā “aniccā dukkhā anattā”ti saṅkhārā punappunaṃ sammasitabbā. Tassevaṃ tulayato tīrayato yadā saṅkhāragataṃ attano lahuupaṭṭhānena, ñāṇassa ca tikkhatāya tirohituppādādibhedaṃ bhijjamānameva upaṭṭhāti, bhaṅgeyeva tassa ñāṇaṃ santiṭṭhati, tadā bhaṅgānupassanā nāma vipassanāñāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti. Tassa tadeva saṅkhāranirodhārammaṇabhaṅgānupassanaṃ āsevantassa yadā [M 2.0342] sabbabhavayonigatiṭṭhitinivāsesu saṅkhārā bhijjanasabhāvatāya yakkharakkhasādayo viya mahābhayaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, tadāssa bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti. Kiṃ panidaṃ ñāṇaṃ bhāyatīti? Na bhāyati. Tañhi “atītā saṅkhārā niruddhā, paccuppannā nirujjhanti, anāgatā nirujjhissantī”ti tīraṇamattameva hoti, byasanāpannānaṃ pana sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ bhayato upaṭṭhitānaṃ gahaṇena bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇanti vuccatīti.

1303. If it is asked, “But isn’t the knowledge of arising and passing away already established? What then is the purpose of further effort there?” It is for the discernment of the characteristics of impermanence, etc. For the knowledge of arising and passing away, being previously defiled by the ten imperfections, was unable to thoroughly discern the three characteristics as they truly are. But when freed from the imperfections, it can. Therefore, for the purpose of discerning the characteristics, further effort should be made right there. The characteristics do not appear due to not attending to arising and passing away, and because they are concealed by continuity, posture, and compactness. Thus, one should focus on arising and passing away, break up the continuity, and discern the characteristic of impermanence. One should grasp the constant oppression, break up the posture, and discern the characteristic of suffering. One should analyze the elements, dissolve the compactness, and discern the characteristic of not-self. Then, one should repeatedly contemplate the formations as “impermanent, suffering, not-self.” As one weighs and examines in this way, when the formations—due to their swift manifestation and the sharpness of knowledge—appear as simply breaking up, with the distinction of their disappearance and appearance ceasing, the knowledge settles only on their dissolution. At that time, the insight knowledge called “contemplation of dissolution” is attained. As one continues to cultivate this contemplation of dissolution, which takes the cessation of formations as its object, when all formations in all existences, wombs, destinations, stations, and abodes appear as a great terror, like ogres and demons, due to their nature of breaking up, then the knowledge of the appearance of terror is attained. But does this knowledge actually experience terror? No, it does not. It merely judges thus: “Past formations have ceased, present ones are ceasing, future ones will cease.” However, because it apprehends all formations as appearing as a terror, like those who are stricken by calamity, it is called the “knowledge of the appearance of terror.”

Tassa taṃ bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ āsevantassa yadā sabbabhavagatesu saṅkhāresu tāṇaṃ vā leṇaṃ vā parāyaṇaṃ vā na paññāyati, ukkhittāsiko viya paccāmitto sādīnavā eva saṅkhārā upaṭṭhahanti, tassa saṅkhārānaṃ ādīnavameva passantassa ādīnavañāṇaṃ nāma uppannaṃ hoti. Tassevaṃ sabbasaṅkhāre ādīnavato passantassa yadā tibhavapariyāpannesu nibbedo uppajjati, ukkaṇṭhā saṇṭhahanti, sabbasaṅkhāravisaṃyutte santipade abhiratiṃ paṭilabhati, tadāssa nibbidānupassanaṃ nāma ñāṇaṃ uppannaṃ hoti. Tassa yadā iminā nibbidāñāṇena sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindantassa ekasaṅkhārepi cittaṃ na sajjati, sabbasmā saṅkhārato sappamukhagatassa viya maṇḍūkassa muccitukāmatā uppajjati, tadā muccitukamyatāñāṇaṃ nāma uppannaṃ hoti. Tassevaṃ sabbasaṅkhārehi muccitukāmassa niccasukhasubhaattākārena pana upaṭṭhituṃ asamatthataṃ pāpetvā muccanassa [V 2.0255] upāyasampādanatthaṃ aniccantikatādīhi aniccalakkhaṇaṃ, abhiṇhapaṭipīḷanatādīhi dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ, ajaññakatādīhi paṭikkūlataṃ, tucchatādīhi anattalakkhaṇañca āropetvā sabbasaṅkhāragataṃ pariggaṇhantassa paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ nāma uppannaṃ hoti. Tena panevaṃ pariggahitasaṅkhārena yā sā “suññamidaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā”tiādinā dvikoṭikādibhedā suññatā vuttā, sā [M 2.0343] pariggahetabbā. Tassevaṃ suññato disvā tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā sammasantassa yadā bhayañca nandiñca vippahāya vissaṭṭhabhariyassa viya saṅkhāragatesu upekkhā santiṭṭhati, tīsu bhavesu cittaṃ na sampasāriyati, tadāssa saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ nāma uppannaṃ hoti. Taṃ panetaṃ yāva nibbānaṃ na passati, tāva disākāko viya kūpakayaṭṭhiṃ punappunaṃ saṅkhārameva anabhimatampi nissāya saṅkhāravicinanepi majjhattameva hutvā tiṭṭhati. Tena vuttaṃ “etesu pana ñāṇesū”tiādi.

When that knowledge of the appearance of terror is cultivated by him, and when in all formations belonging to existence no protection, shelter, or ultimate refuge is discerned, formations appear as fraught with danger, like an enemy with upraised sword. For him who sees only the danger in formations, the knowledge of danger arises. When he thus sees all formations as fraught with danger, and when revulsion arises regarding what is included in the three realms of existence, weariness becomes established, and he gains delight in the peaceful state disjoined from all formations, then the knowledge of contemplation of revulsion arises in him. When, through this knowledge of revulsion, he becomes repulsed by all formations, and his mind does not cling even to a single formation, but there arises in him a desire to be freed from all formations, like a frog that has entered a snake’s mouth and wishes to escape, then the knowledge of desire for deliverance arises. For him who thus desires to be freed from all formations, having been brought to a state of inability to perceive them in the mode of permanence, pleasure, beauty, or self, and who instead, in order to accomplish the means of deliverance, attributes to them the characteristic of impermanence—through their impermanent nature and so forth; the characteristic of suffering—through their continually oppressive nature and so forth; repulsiveness—through their not being one's own and so forth; and the characteristic of non-self—through their emptiness and so forth, thus comprehensively grasping all formations, the knowledge of reflective contemplation arises. Then, by him who has thus grasped formations, that emptiness which is described as “This is empty of self or anything belonging to self,” with its twofold division and so forth, must be comprehended. When, having seen them thus as empty and attributed the three characteristics to them, he contemplates them, and when, having abandoned both fear and delight, his equanimity toward formations is established—like one who has laid down a burden—and his mind no longer extends among the three realms of existence, then the knowledge of equanimity toward formations arises in him. But this knowledge persists until he sees Nibbāna. Like a direction-crow on a ship's mast, again and again relying on formations even though they are not desired, he remains neutral while investigating formations. Hence it is said, “Among these knowledges,” and so on.

1306. Vipassanā…pe… vuṭṭhānagāminīti sikhaṃ uttamabhāvaṃ pattattā sikhāpattā. Vuṭṭhānaṃ gacchatīti vuṭṭhānagāminī. “Vuṭṭhāna”nti hi bahiddhā nimittabhūtā abhiniviṭṭhavatthuto ceva ajjhattappavattato ca vuṭṭhahanato maggo vuccati, taṃ gacchatīti vuṭṭhānagāminī, maggena saddhiṃ ghaṭīyatīti attho.

1306. Insight... and so forth... is called 'peak-attained' because it has attained the peak, the highest state. It is called 'leading to emergence' because it goes to emergence. For 'emergence' refers to the path because of the emergence from both the external object of adherence which has become a sign and from the internal process. It goes to that, thus it is 'leading to emergence'; the meaning is that it is connected with the path.

1307. Tanti yaṃ sikhāpattā vipassanā saccānulomañāṇanti ca vuccati, taṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ. Āsevantassāti punappunaṃ sammasanavasena sevantassa bhāventassa bahulīkarontassa. Tassa hi adhimokkhasaddhā bhāvanāvasena balavatarā nibbattissati, vīriyaṃ supaggahitaṃ paṭipakkhavidhamanasamatthaṃ hoti, ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvena sati supatiṭṭhitā hoti, passaddhisukhānaṃ sātisayatāya cittaṃ susamāhitaṃ, tatova anulomañāṇuppattiyā paccayo bhavituṃ samatthā tikkhatamā saṅkhārupekkhā uppajjati.

1307. That which is called insight that has attained the peak, and also the knowledge of conformity with the truths, is the knowledge of equanimity toward formations. For one who cultivates it—that is, for one who cultivates it repeatedly by way of reviewing, develops it, and makes it abundant—indeed, faith as determination will become stronger through cultivation, energy will be well-exerted and capable of destroying opposition, mindfulness will be well-established due to facing the object, the mind will be well-concentrated due to the excellence of tranquility and happiness, and from that, capable of being a condition for the arising of the knowledge of conformity, the sharpest knowledge of equanimity toward formations arises.

1308-12. Aniccā…pe… votarateva sāti aniccādīsu ekena ākārena sammasantī sattakkhattuṃ pavattitvā bhijjantī bhavaṅgaṃ otiṇṇā nāma hoti, tato paraṃ bhavaṅgavāroti katvā[M 2.0344]. Saṅkhārupekkhākatanayenāti aniccādinā ārammaṇakaraṇavaseneva saṅkhārupekkhāya katanayena, na sammasitanayena. Tenāha “aniccādi…pe… kurumāna”nti. Bhavaṅgāvaṭṭanaṃ katvāti bhavaṅgassa nivattanaṃ katvā cittassa bhavaṅgavasena pavattituṃ adatvā. Parikammanti maggassa [V 2.0256] parikammattā paṭisaṅkhārakattā. Upacāranti maggassa āsannattā, samīpacārittā vā.

1308-12. Impermanent... and so on... Contemplating with one aspect among impermanence and so on, having occurred seven times and then broken, it is said to have descended into the life-continuum; after that is the life-continuum phase. By the method of equanimity toward formations means: by the method done by equanimity toward formations solely by way of taking impermanence and so on as the object, not by the method of contemplation. Therefore, it is said, 'Impermanent, etc.... doing.' Having caused the life-continuum to revert means: having caused the life-continuum to turn back, not allowing the mind to proceed by way of the life-continuum. Preparation: because it is preparation for the path, because it performs reconditioning. Access: because it is near the path, or because it moves in proximity.

1313-6. Anulomattaṃ sayameva vadati “purimāna”ntiādinā. Idañhi aniccalakkhaṇādivasena saṅkhāre ārabbha pavattattā, “udayabbayavantānaṃyeva vata dhammānaṃ udayabbayañāṇaṃ uppādavaye addasā”ti ca “bhaṅgavantānaṃyeva vata bhaṅgānupassanaṃ bhaṅgamaddasā”ti ca “sabhayaṃyeva vata bhayatupaṭṭhānassa bhayato upaṭṭhita”nti ca “sādīnaveyeva vata ādīnavānupassanaṃ ādīnavamaddasā”ti ca “nibbinditabbeyeva vata nibbidāñāṇaṃ nibbinda”nti ca “muccitabbamhiyeva vata muccitukamyatāñāṇaṃ muccitukāmaṃ jāta”nti ca “paṭisaṅkhātabbameva vata paṭisaṅkhāñāṇena paṭisaṅkhāta”nti ca “upekkhitabbaṃyeva vata saṅkhārupekkhāya upekkhita”nti ca atthato vadamānaṃ viya imesañca aṭṭhannaṃ ñāṇānaṃ katakiccatāya anulometi sabbāsaṃyeva vipassanānaṃ lakkhaṇattayasammasanakiccattā, tathā upari ca ariyamagge sattatiṃsāya bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ tāya paṭipadāya pattabbatāya. Na hi anulomañāṇe thūlathūlasaccapaṭicchādakasaṃkilesavikkhambhanavasena appavattante gotrabhuñāṇaṃ uppajjati, gotrabhuñāṇe ca anuppanne maggañāṇaṃ na uppajjati, tasmā purimapacchimānaṃ bhāgānaṃ anulomattā “anulomanti saññita”nti. Tenevāti heṭṭhimañāṇānaṃ anulomamukhena, upari bodhipakkhiyānaṃ anulomanato ca. Saccānulomañāṇanti pavuccati maggasaccassa anulomikattā. Vuṭṭhānagāminiyāti saṅkhārārammaṇāya vuṭṭhānagāminiyā [M 2.0345] vipassanāya. Pariyosānanti purimā koṭi. Saṅkhārārammaṇavipassanāsu hi ayaṃ visesato vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāti. Asaṅkhatārammaṇaṃ pana sabbena sabbaṃ ariyamaggasaṅkhātaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ gacchati upetīti. Tatopi hi visesato “vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā”ti vattabbataṃ labhatīti āha “ñeyyaṃ sabbappakārenā”tiādi.

1313-6. It speaks of its own conformity by means of 'of the former,' and so on.
