For this arises in relation to formations by way of the characteristic of impermanence, etc., and thus, as if speaking in meaning, it conforms to the accomplished function of these eight knowledges: 'Indeed, the knowledge of rise and fall saw the rise and fall of things that are subject to rise and fall;' 'Indeed, the contemplation of dissolution saw the dissolution of things that are subject to dissolution;' 'Indeed, the knowledge of appearance as terror appeared as terror in what is fearful;' 'Indeed, the contemplation of danger saw the danger in what is dangerous;' 'Indeed, the knowledge of revulsion was revulsed by what is to be revulsed by;' 'Indeed, the knowledge of desire for deliverance desired deliverance from what is to be delivered from;' 'Indeed, the knowledge of reflection reflected on what is to be reflected upon;' and 'Indeed, equanimity toward formations was equanimous toward what is to be regarded with equanimity.' It also conforms because the function of all insights is the contemplation of the three characteristics, and likewise because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are to be attained by that path above. For if the knowledge of conformity does not proceed by way of suppressing the gross defilements that cover the truths, the knowledge of change-of-lineage does not arise; and if the knowledge of change-of-lineage does not arise, the knowledge of the path does not arise. Therefore, because of its conformity to the preceding and succeeding parts, it is called 'conformity.' For that very reason, by way of conforming to the lower knowledges and conforming to the factors of enlightenment above, it is called the knowledge of conformity with the truths, because it conforms to the truth of the path. 'Leading to emergence' refers to the insight leading to emergence that has formations as its object. 'Culmination' means the foremost limit. For among insights that have formations as their object, this is specifically the insight leading to emergence. But as for the unconditioned object, it goes to and approaches the emergence which is designated the noble path in its entirety. From that, too, it especially obtains the designation 'insight leading to emergence.' Hence it is said: 'to be known in every way,' etc.

1317-8. Kittitāti thomitā, ariyamaggādhiṭṭhānatāya mahantānaṃ sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ esanato gavesanato mahesinā sammāsambuddhena. Santakilesatāya santā. Yoganti bhāvanaṃ, bhāvanābhiyogaṃ vā.

1317-8. 'Praised' means extolled by the Great Seeker, the Perfectly Enlightened One—so-called from seeking and searching for the great aggregates of virtue and so on—because it is the foundation of the noble path. 'Peaceful' because defilements are pacified. 'Yoke' means development, or application to development.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus is named the Abhidhammattha-vikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

in the Commentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma.

Paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Purification of Knowledge and Vision of the Way is concluded.

22. Bāvīsatimo paricchedo

22. The Twenty-Second Chapter

Ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Purification of Knowledge and Vision

1319-21. Idāni [V 2.0257] ñāṇadassanavisuddhiyā niddese anuppatte sā yassa ñāṇassa anantaraṃ uppajjati, taṃ tāva dassento “ito para”ntiādimāha. Ito paranti ito anulomañāṇato upari. Āvajjaniyaṭhānattāti āvajjanakiccaṃ karontaṃ kiriyamanodhātu viya maggassa āvajjanaṭṭhāne ṭhitattā abbohārikameva ubhayavisuddhilakkhaṇābhāvato. Kiñcāpi evaṃ, tathāpi vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāya pariyosānattā vipassanāpakkhiyamevāti āha “vipassanāya sotasmiṃ, patitattā vipassanā”ti. Etenassa paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhibhajanaṃ dasseti.

1319-21. Now, when the exposition of the purification of knowledge and vision has been reached, showing first the knowledge immediately after which it arises, he says, “From here onward,” etc. “From here onward” means above the knowledge of adaptation. “Because it is a place for adverting”—just as the functional mind-element, which performs the function of adverting, is merely nominal because it stands in the place of adverting for the path, lacking the characteristics of both purifications. Although this is so, nevertheless, because it is the culmination of the insight that leads to emergence, it is indeed on the side of insight. Hence, he said: “Because it has fallen into the stream of insight, it is insight.” By this, he shows that it partakes of the purification of knowledge and vision of the path.

1322. Puthujjanesu [M 2.0346] bhavaṃ pothujjanikaṃ, tadeva gottaṃ ariyehi asammissā puthujjanasamaññāti pothujjanikagottaṃ. Ekavaṃsajānañhi samānā samaññā “gotta”nti vuccati, gaṃ tāyati buddhiṃ, abhidhānañca ekaṃsikavisayatāya rakkhatīti katvā. Vā-saddo vakkhamānatthavikappane. Abhibhuyya pavattito gotrabhūti sambandho. Gottaṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ “ariyo”ti buddhiyā, abhidhānassa ca tāyanato pavattanatoti adhippāyo. Tato bhavatīti tato gottato ārammaṇapaccayato bhavati. Iti-saddo cettha hetuttho daṭṭhabbo. Tena yasmā tato bhavati, tasmā gotrabhūti attho.

1322. What pertains to ordinary people is 'of ordinary people,' and that very lineage, unmixed with the noble ones, is the designation 'ordinary person,' hence 'lineage of ordinary people.' For those born of the same family, the common designation is called 'lineage,' because it protects understanding and the designation by being of a single subject. The word 'vā' indicates an alternative meaning that will be explained. The connection is that it is 'gotrabhū' because it arises by overcoming. 'Lineage' refers to Nibbāna, on account of the understanding 'noble,' and because it protects and promotes that designation; that is the intended meaning. 'It arises from that' means it arises from that lineage as its object-condition. Here, the word 'iti' should be understood in the sense of reason. Therefore, because it arises from that, the meaning is 'gotrabhū.'

1323-5. Ñāṇadassanavisuddhi eva ñāṇadassanasuddhikaṃ. Taṃ sampādetuṃ panicchatā tena bhikkhunā yaṃ aññaṃ kiñcipi kātabbaṃ, taṃ natthīti sambandho. Kasmā natthīti ce āha “yaṃ hī”tiādi. “Katamevā”ti vutte “katha”nti anuyogassa upaṭṭhitattā “anulomāvasānaṃ hī”tiādinā taṃ samattheti.

1323-5. The purification of knowledge and vision is itself the purification of knowledge and vision. To accomplish that, there is nothing else whatsoever that the monk needs to do—this is the connection. If asked why there is nothing else, he says: “Because...” and so on. When asked, “What exactly?”—because the question “how?” arises—he supports that with “the conclusion of adaptation,” and so on.

1326-7. Evaṃ uppannaanulomañāṇassa panassa etehi tīhipi anulomañāṇehi attano balānurūpena thūlathūle saccapaṭicchādakatamamhi antaradhāpite sabbasaṅkhāragate cittaṃ na pakkhandati[V 2.0258], na laggati, padumapalāsato udakaṃ viya patikuṭati pativaṭṭati, sabbaṃ nimittārammaṇampi sabbaṃ pavattārammaṇampi palibodhato upaṭṭhāti, athassa sabbasmiṃ nimittappavattārammaṇe palibodhato upaṭṭhite dutiyassa vā tatiyassa vā anulomañāṇassa anantaraṃ gotrabhuñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Tenāha “tassā”tiādi. Paṭhamāvajjanañceva paṭhamābhogatāpi cāti paṭhamāvajjanaṃ paṭhamābhogabhūtaṃ. Sakatthe hi ayaṃ tā-paccayoti. Tattha āvajjanaṃ cittasantānassa pariṇāmanavasena, ābhogo attano ābhujanavasena daṭṭhabbo.

1326-7. When the knowledge of adaptation has thus arisen for him, and when the grossest concealer of truth has been dispelled by these three knowledges of adaptation according to their strength, the mind does not rush toward or cling to any formation. Like water on a lotus leaf, it recoils and turns back. All sign-objects and all process-objects present themselves as an obstruction. When all sign-objects and process-objects present themselves as an obstruction to him, immediately after the second or third knowledge of adaptation, the knowledge of change-of-lineage arises. Therefore, he said, “of that,” and so on. The first advertence and the first application are the first advertence which is the state of first application. This tā-suffix is used in its own sense. Herein, advertence should be seen as the transformation of the mind-continuum, and application as the way of bending towards.

1328-33. Anantarādīhīti [M 2.0347] anantarasamanantaraāsevanaupanissayanatthivigatavasena chahi paccayehi. Muddhanti muddhabhūtaṃ. Ekantikatāya ekavārameva ca uppajjanato punarāvattābhāvena pana anāvattaṃ. Anāvajjanampi cāti anāvajjanampisamānaṃ. Saññaṃ datvā viyāti “evaṃ uppajjāhī”ti saññaṃ datvā viya. Anibbiddhapubbanti apadālitapubbaṃ. Viddhaṃsentovāti vināsento eva. Jāyatīti nibbattati. Ettha ca imaṃ upamaṃ āharanti – eko kira issāso aṭṭhausabhamatte padese phalakasataṃ ṭhapāpetvā vatthena mukhaṃ veṭhetvā saraṃ sannayhitvā cakkayante aṭṭhāsi, añño puriso cakkayantaṃ āvijjhitvā yadā issāsassa phalakaṃ abhimukhaṃ hoti, tadā tattha daṇḍakena saññaṃ deti. Issāso daṇḍakasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva saraṃ khipitvā phalakasatanibbijjhati. Tattha daṇḍakasaññaṃ dento viya gotrabhuñāṇaṃ, issāso viya maggañāṇaṃ, daṇḍakasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva phalakasataṃ nibbijjhanaṃ viya maggañāṇassa gotrabhuñāṇena dinnasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā anibbiddhapubbānaṃ apadālitapubbānaṃ lobhadosamohakkhandhānaṃ nibbijjhananti.

1328-33. 'By immediacy, etc.' means through six conditions: immediacy, contiguity, repetition, decisive support, absence, and disappearance. 'Foremost' means having become the foremost. Due to its absoluteness, it arises only once and does not recur; hence, it is non-returning. 'And also non-adverting' means it is similar to non-adverting. 'As if giving a sign' means as if giving a sign, saying, “May you arise thus.” 'Never before pierced' means never before split. 'Destroying' means utterly destroying. 'Is born' means it arises. Here, they give this simile: It is said that once an archer, in a space of about eight usabhas, had a hundred planks set up. He covered his face with a cloth, nocked an arrow, and stood at a revolving machine. Another man, after setting the revolving machine in motion, when the planks were directly in front of the archer, gave him a signal with a stick. The archer, without missing the stick signal, shot the arrow and pierced all hundred planks. In this simile, the giving of the stick signal is like the change-of-lineage knowledge. The archer is like the path knowledge. The piercing of the hundred planks without missing the stick signal is like the path knowledge, without missing the sign given by the change-of-lineage knowledge, making Nibbāna its object and piercing the previously unpierced, undestroyed aggregates of greed, hatred, and delusion.

1335-8. Anāmatagga…pe… mahodadhinti aṭṭhamabhavato paṭṭhāya nibbattakaṃ aññātakoṭiṃ saṃsāravaṭṭadukkhamahāsamuddaṃ. Pāṇātipātādipañcaverāni ceva pañcavīsati mahābhayāni cāti sabbaverabhayāni. Anekepi ānisaṃseti ratanattaye niviṭṭhasaddhādike ānisaṃse. Ādimaggenāti sotāpattimaggasaṅkhātena paṭhamamaggena. Paṭhamamaggañāṇavaṇṇanā.

1335-8. 'With undiscoverable beginning... the great ocean' means the great ocean of the suffering of the cycle of existence, which has an unknown end and entails rebirth from an eighth existence onwards. 'The five enmities beginning with the destruction of life, and the twenty-five great fears' means all enmities and fears. 'Many benefits' refers to the benefits, such as steadfast faith and so on established in the Triple Gem. 'By the initial path' means by the first path, designated as the path of stream-entry. The explanation of the knowledge of the first path.

1339. Tassevānantaranti tassa anantaraṃyeva. Dvepi tīṇi vāti nātitikkhapaññassa dve, tikkhapaññassa tīṇi phalacittāni.

1339. 'Immediately after that' means immediately after that, indeed. 'Two or three' means two fruition-consciousnesses for one with not-so-sharp wisdom, and three for one with sharp wisdom.

1340-3. “Ajānitvā [M 2.0348][V 2.0259] vadanti te”ti vatvā tattha kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “ekassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pañcamaṃ maggacittanti imināva chaṭṭhassa abhāvadīpanena “ekaṃ phalacitta”nti vadato godattattherassa vādopi paṭikkhitto.

1340-3. Having said, “They speak without knowing,” to show the reason for that, the passage beginning with “for one” was stated. By this very statement, “the fifth path-consciousness,” which shows the absence of a sixth, the view of the Elder Godatta, who says “one fruition-consciousness,” is also refuted.

1344. “Ettāvatā”ti paṭhamamaggassa uppattianantaraṃ phalassa uppattimattena. Sotāpannoti vuccatīti sotāpanno nāma dutiyo ariyapuggaloti vuccati. So devarajjacakkavattirajjādipamādaṭṭhānaṃ āgamma bhusaṃ pamattopi hutvā kāmasugatiyaṃ sattakkhattumeva sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantakaraṇasamattho hoti. Yathāha –

1344. “By this much” means merely by the arising of the fruit immediately after the arising of the first path. “One is called a stream-enterer” means the second noble person is called a stream-enterer. Even if such a one, having come to a basis for heedlessness such as sovereignty over the devas or universal sovereignty, becomes greatly heedless, after wandering and transmigrating at most seven times in the sensual happy destinations, he is capable of making an end of suffering. As it is said:

“Kiñcāpi te honti bhusaṃ pamattā,

Na te bhavaṃ aṭṭhamamādiyantī”ti. (khu. pā. 6.9; su. ni. 232; netti. 115);

“Though they might be exceedingly heedless, they do not take up an eighth existence.”

Rūpārūpalokesu pana na tathā niyamoti ācariyā.

However, the teachers say that there is no such fixed rule in the form and formless worlds.

1347. Phalādīnanti ādi-saddena pahīnakilesādike saṅgaṇhāti. Tathā ca “iminā vatāhaṃ maggena āgato”ti paṭhamaṃ maggaṃ paccavekkhati, tato “ayaṃ me ānisaṃso laddho”ti phalaṃ paccavekkhati, tato “ime nāma me kilesā pahīnā”ti pahīnakilese paccavekkhati, tato “ime nāma me kilesā avasiṭṭhā”ti uparimaggattayavajjhe kilese paccavekkhati, avasāne “ayaṃ me dhammo ārammaṇato paṭividdho”ti amataṃ nibbānaṃ paccavekkhati. Iti sotāpannassa pañca paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni honti. Yathā ca sotāpannassa, evaṃ sakadāgāmianāgāmīnampi. Arahato pana avasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇaṃ nāma natthi. Evaṃ sabbānipi ekūnavīsati paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni. Tenāha “paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni, bhavantekūnavīsatī”ti.

1347. “Of fruition, etc.”: by the word “etc.” it includes the abandoned defilements and the like. Thus, first, one reviews the path, thinking, “By this path I have come.” Then, one reviews the fruition, thinking, “This benefit I have obtained.” Then, one reviews the abandoned defilements, thinking, “These defilements have been abandoned by me.” Then, one reviews the defilements to be destroyed by the three higher paths, thinking, “These defilements of mine remain.” Finally, one reviews the deathless Nibbāna, thinking, “This Dhamma has been penetrated by me as its object.” Thus, a stream-enterer has five kinds of reviewing knowledge. As it is for the stream-enterer, so it is for the once-returner and the non-returner. But for an Arahant, there is no reviewing of remaining defilements. Thus, in all, there are nineteen reviewing knowledges. Hence it is said: “The reviewing knowledges are nineteen.”

1348-50. Yāsaṃ [M 2.0349] paccavekkhaṇavasena imāni ñāṇāni pavattanti, tā dassetuṃ “maggo phalañcā”tiādimāha. Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedoyeva ceso. Pahīnāvasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇañhi sekhānampi hoti vā na vā. Na hi sabbeva tattha samatthā honti. Teneva hi mahānāmo [V 2.0260] bhagavantaṃ pucchi “ko su nāma me dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīno, yena me ekadā lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.175). Yogamārabhateti tasmiṃyeva vā āsane nisinno, aparena vā samayena kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ tanubhāvakarāya sakadāgāmimaggasaṅkhātāya dutiyāya bhūmiyā adhigamatthāya vipassanāyogaṃ karoti, dutiyabhāvo cassa desanāvasena, uppattivasena ca veditabbo. Sampayuttānaṃ pana nissayabhāvena te dhammā bhavanti etthāti bhūmi, yasmā vā samānepi lokuttarabhāve sayampi bhavati, na nibbānaṃ viya apātubhūtaṃ, tasmāpi “bhūmī”ti vuccati. Ñāṇena parimajjatīti tena tenākārena indriyānaṃ tikkhatarataṃ sampādetvā, balabojjhaṅgānañca paṭutarabhāvaṃ sādhetvā lakkhaṇattayaṃ tīraṇavasena parimajjati.

To show those things on the basis of which these reviewing knowledges proceed, he said, "the path and the fruit," and so on. And this is the supreme instance. For even for trainees, the reviewing of abandoned and remaining defilements may or may not occur, for not all are capable in that regard. For this reason Mahānāma asked the Blessed One: "What quality, sir, remains unabandoned in me, on account of which states of lust sometimes invade my mind and remain?" and so on. He undertakes the practice: either while sitting on that very seat or at another time, he undertakes the practice of insight for the purpose of attaining the second stage, called the path of the once-returner, which makes sensual lust and ill will tenuous. And this second state should be understood in terms of the teaching and in terms of its arising. Because the associated states exist here as a support, it is called a "stage." Or, because, although it shares the supramundane nature, it itself comes to be, not unmanifested like Nibbāna, it is also called a "stage." He polishes with knowledge: having brought the faculties to a sharper state in this way or that, and having effected a more acute state for the powers and the enlightenment factors, he polishes by discerning the three characteristics.

1351-2. Tattha aparāparaṃ ñāṇaṃ cārento parivatteti. Tenāha “vipassanāvīthiṃ ogāhatī”ti. Heṭṭhā vuttanayenāti udayabbayañāṇādīnaṃ uppādane vuttanayeneva. Gotrabhussa anantaranti ettha gotrabhu viya gotrabhu. Paṭhamamaggapurecārikañāṇañhi puthujjanagottābhibhavanato, ariyagottabhavanato ca nippariyāyato “gotrabhū”ti vuccati, idaṃ pana taṃsadisatāya pariyāyato gotrabhu. Ekaccasaṃkilesavisuddhiyā, pana accantavisuddhiyā ārammaṇakaraṇato ca “vodāna”nti vuccati. Tenāha paṭṭhāne “anulomaṃ vodānassa anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417). Yasmā [M 2.0350] pana paṭisambhidāmagge “uppādādiabhibhavanaṭṭhaṃ upādāya aṭṭha gotrabhudhammā samādhivasena uppajjanti, dasa gotrabhudhammā vipassanāvasena uppajjantī”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.60) gotrabhunāmavaseneva āgataṃ, tasmā idhāpi “gotrabhussa anantara”nti vuttaṃ gottasaṅkhātanibbānato bhūtanti katvā. Dutiyamaggañāṇavaṇṇanā.

There, applying knowledge again and again, one turns it over. Hence, it is said, "he plunges into the course of insight." "In the manner stated above" means in the very manner stated for the arising of the knowledge of arising and passing away, etc. "Immediately following the change-of-lineage": here, it is like the actual change-of-lineage. For the knowledge preceding the first path is called 'change-of-lineage' in the primary sense, because it overcomes the lineage of the worldling and establishes the noble lineage; but this knowledge, because of its similarity to that, is 'change-of-lineage' in a figurative sense. It is called 'purification' (vodāna) because it makes Nibbāna its object for the purification of some defilements and for ultimate purification. Hence, it is said in the Paṭṭhāna: "Conformity is a condition for purification by way of proximity condition." Since, however, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga it is designated by the name 'change-of-lineage' in such passages as, "Eight change-of-lineage states arise by way of concentration for the purpose of overcoming origination, etc., and ten change-of-lineage states arise by way of insight," therefore, here too, "immediately following the change-of-lineage" is said, taking it as that which has arisen from Nibbāna, which is reckoned as the lineage. The Explanation of the Knowledge of the Second Path.

1355-7. Yanti yasmā. Sakidevāti ekavārameva. Imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvāti iminā pañcasu sakadāgāmīsu cattāro vajjetvā ekova gahito. Ekacco hi idha sakadāgāmiphalaṃ patvā idheva parinibbāyati, ekacco idha patvā devaloke parinibbāyati, ekacco devaloke patvā tattheva parinibbāyati, ekacco devaloke patvā idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāyatīti ime cattāropi idha na gahitā. Yo pana idha patvā devaloke yāvatāyukaṃ vasitvā idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāyati, ayamekova idha gahitoti. Antakaro bhaveti dukkhassantakaro bhaveyya, bhave vā antakaro bhavassa antakaroti attho. Tatiyāya bhūmiyā pattiyāti sambandho. Byāpādakāmarāgānaṃ [V 2.0261] pahānāyāti tesaṃyeva sakadāgāmimaggena tanukarānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ niravasesappahānāya. Tatiyamaggañāṇavaṇṇanā.

"They go" means because. "Only once" means just one time. "Having come to this world": by this, only one among the five kinds of once-returners is taken, excluding four. For one person, having attained the fruit of once-returning here, attains final Nibbāna right here. Another, having attained it here, attains final Nibbāna in the deva world. Another, having attained it in the deva world, attains final Nibbāna right there. Another, having attained it in the deva world, is reborn here and attains final Nibbāna. These four are not included here. But the one who, having attained it here, lives out their lifespan in the deva world, is reborn here, and then attains final Nibbāna—this one alone is included here. "He becomes an end-maker" means he would become a maker of an end of suffering, or an end-maker of existence; the meaning is a maker of an end to existence. The connection is with the attainment of the third stage. "For the abandoning of ill will and sensual lust" means for the abandoning without remainder of those same fetters that were attenuated by the path of the once-returner. The Explanation of the Knowledge of the Third Path.

1363-7. Paṭisandhivasena kāmabhavassa anāgamanato anāgāmī. Tenāha “tattheva parinibbāyī”ti. Tatthevāti suddhāvāse vā aññattha vā yattha uppanno, tattheva parinibbāyi. Anāvattisabhāvoti tasmā lokā idha paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena imaṃ lokaṃ punarāgamanābhāvato anāvattanasabhāvo, buddhadassanatheradassanadhammassavanānaṃ panatthāya āgamanaṃ hotiyeva. Rūparāgādipahānāyāti [M 2.0351] rūparāgaarūparāgamānauddhaccaavijjāsaṅkhātānaṃ pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanānaṃ niravasesappahānāya. Viddhaṃsāyāti vināsāya. Catutthamaggañāṇavaṇṇanā.

Because of not returning to sense-sphere existence by way of rebirth-linking, he is a non-returner. Therefore, it is said, "he attains final Nibbāna right there." "Right there" means wherever he is reborn, whether in the Pure Abodes or elsewhere, he attains final Nibbāna right there. He is of a non-returning nature because he does not come back to this world by way of taking a new rebirth-linking; however, his return for the purpose of seeing the Buddha, seeing the elders, or hearing the Dhamma does indeed occur. "For the abandoning of lust for form, etc." means for the abandoning without remainder of the five higher fetters, namely, lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. "For destruction" means for annihilation. The Explanation of the Knowledge of the Fourth Path.

1371-4. Mahākhīṇāsavoti mahānubhāvato nibaddhapūjāvacanametaṃ, na upādāyavacanaṃ “yathā mahāmoggallāno”ti. Na hi cūḷakhīṇāsavo nāma atthi. Anuppatto sadattho sakattho, pūjattho vā etenāti anuppattasadattho, sadatthoti ca arahattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tañhi attupanibandhanaṭṭhena, attānaṃ avijahanaṭṭhena, attano paramatthaṭṭhena ca attano atthattā “sadattho”ti vuccati. Khīṇāni dasapi bhavasaṃyojanāni etassāti khīṇasaṃyojano. Dakkhiṇaṃ arahatīti dakkhiṇeyyo. Catassopīti sotāpattimaggo sakadāgāmimaggo anāgāmimaggo arahattamaggoti catassopi. Visuddhikāmenāti attano visuddhiṃ icchantena. Tapoyeva dhanamassāti tapodhano, tena.

"Great one with taints destroyed": on account of his great power, this is a fixed term of veneration, not a comparative term as in "like Mahāmoggallāna." For there is no such thing as a "lesser one with taints destroyed." "One who has attained his own goal": one who has attained his own true goal, or the goal worthy of veneration. Here, "one's own goal" should be understood as Arahantship. For it is called "one's own goal" because it is bound to oneself, because it does not forsake oneself, and because it is one's own ultimate good. "One with fetters destroyed": one for whom the ten fetters of existence have been destroyed. "Worthy of offerings": he is worthy of a gift. "All four": this refers to all four paths: the path of stream-entry, the path of the once-returner, the path of the non-returner, and the path of Arahantship. "By one who desires purity": by one who wishes for his own purity. "One whose wealth is austerity": by him whose wealth is the practice of austerity.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra,

Ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Exposition of the Purification of Knowledge and Vision is finished.

23. Tevīsatimo paricchedo

23. The Twenty-Third Chapter

Kilesappahānakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Abandonment of Defilements

1375. Idāni [V 2.0262] imissāyeva catutthañāṇāya ñāṇadassanavisuddhiyā ānubhāvavijānanatthaṃ yena ye dhammā pahātabbā, tesaṃ pahānañca abhisamayakāle pariññādikiccāni ca dassetuṃ “etesu yena ye dhammā”tiādi āraddhaṃ[M 2.0352]. Ye dhammāti ye saṃkilesadhammā. Saṃyojanādīsu khandhehi khandhānaṃ, phalena kammassa, dukkhena vā sattānaṃ saṃyojanaṭṭhena bandhanaṭṭhena saṃyojanāni. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ vibādhanaṭṭhena, upatāpanaṭṭhena, saṃkiliṭṭhatāya ca kilesā. Abhinivesādivasena micchāviparītaṃ pavattanato micchāsabhāvāti micchattā. Loke dhammā, lokapariyāpannā dhammā, lokappavattiyaṃ sati anuparamadhammattā vāti lokadhammā. Maccherassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vāti macchariyaṃ. Viparītaṭṭhena vipallāsā. Nāmakāyassa ca rūpakāyassa ca ganthanato ganthā. Ariyehi agantabbā, ayuttā gatīti vā agati. Āsavantīti āsavā, ābhavaggato sabbamokāsalokaṃ, āgotrabhuto sabbe dhamme byāpetvā pavattantīti attho, āsavanti saṃsāradukkhanti vā āsavā, cakkhādīhi vā saṃvarāsaṃvaradvārehi sattasantāne āsavanti vaṇato yūsāni sandanti viyāti āsavā, āsavanti vā etehi cittāni visayesūti āsavā. Saṃsāramahāsāgarappattihananato oghā viyāti oghā. Heṭṭhā vuttanayena yojanato yogā. Nivārenti lokiyalokuttaraguṇavisesādhigamanti nīvaraṇāni. Aniccādidhammasabhāvaṃ atikkamma parato asabhāvato āmasantīti parāmāsā. Maṇḍūkaṃ pannago viya ārammaṇaṃ bhusaṃ ādiyantīti upādānāni. Appahīnabhāvena sattasantāne anusenti mūsikavisaṃ viya anurūpakāraṇaṃ labhitvā uppajjantīti anusayā. Cittassa malīnabhāvakaraṇaṭṭhena malā. Akusalakammāni ca tāni duggatīnaṃ pathā cāti akusalakammapathā. Idha pana kammapathabhāvaṃ appattānaṃ taṃsabhāvato gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Cittaṃ uppajjati etthāti cittuppādo, cetasikarāsi, akusalo ca so cittuppādo cāti akusalacittuppādo.

1375. Now, to make known the power of this very fourth knowledge, the purification by knowledge and vision, and to show which states are to be abandoned by which path, their abandonment, and the functions of full understanding, etc., at the time of realization, the passage beginning 'By which path are what states...' is introduced. 'What states' means the defiled states. The fetters are so called in the sense that they fetter and bind aggregates with aggregates, kamma with its fruit, or beings with suffering. The defilements are so called because they afflict, torment, and defile associated states. Wrongnesses are wrong states because they proceed in a wrong and perverted way through adherence and so on. Worldly states are phenomena included in the world; or, when the world process continues, they are states that do not cease. Stinginess is the state of being a miser, or the act itself. Perversions are so called in the sense of being distorted. The knots are so called because they bind the mental body and the physical body. A wrong course is a path not to be taken by the noble ones, or an improper course. The taints are so called because they flow, meaning they proceed pervading all phenomena from the change-of-lineage consciousness up to the peak of existence; or they make saṃsāric suffering flow; or they flow into a being’s mental continuum through the doors of the sense faculties, whether restrained or unrestrained, like juices oozing from a sore; or because of them, minds flow out to objects. The floods are so called because they are like a flood, striking one down into the great ocean of saṃsāra. The yokes are so called because they yoke, in the way explained above. The hindrances are so called because they hinder the attainment of special worldly and supramundane qualities. Adherences are so called because they grasp things wrongly, transgressing the true nature of phenomena such as impermanence. Clinging is seizing objects intensely, like a snake seizing a frog. The latent tendencies are so called because they lie latent in a being’s mental continuum in their unabandoned state, arising when a suitable cause is found, like rat poison. Stains are so called because they cause the mind to be stained. Unwholesome courses of action are unwholesome actions and they are paths to a bad destination. Here, however, it should be understood that states are included by their nature even when they have not reached the status of a course of action. An arising of consciousness is that wherein consciousness arises, a collection of mental factors; and since that arising of consciousness is unwholesome, it is an unwholesome arising of consciousness.

Kāmabhavato [M 2.0353] uparikoṭṭhāsabhāvato tatiyamaggappattiyā uddhaṃ bhajitabbato, sevitabbato cāti [V 2.0263] uddhambhāgā, rūpārūpabhavā, tesaṃ hitāni tatthuppajjanakhandhādiyojanatoti uddhambhāgiyāni, tāniyeva saṃyojanānīti uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni. Rūpārūpabhavato heṭṭhimakoṭṭhāsabhāvato tatthuppādakilesānaṃ appahīnabhāvena tatiyamaggappattiyā heṭṭhā bhajitabbato vā adhobhāgā, kāmabhavā, tesaṃ hitāni saṃyojanānīti adhobhāgiyasaṃyojanānīti.

Because they constitute the portion above the sense-sphere existence, and because they are to be dealt with above the attainment of the third path, the form and formless existences are the 'higher parts.' The fetters connected with them, which yoke the aggregates, etc., that arise there, are the 'higher fetters.' These are the fetters called the higher fetters. Because they constitute the portion below the form and formless existences, or because they are to be dealt with below the attainment of the third path as the defilements that produce them are still unabandoned, the sense-sphere existence is the 'lower part.' The fetters connected with it are the 'lower fetters.'

Imesu pana dasasu rūpabhavasaṃyojanaṃ, arūpabhavasaṃyojanaṃ, kāmabhavasaṃyojanañca atthato lobhova, sakkāyadiṭṭhisīlabbataparāmāsāpi diṭṭhiyeva, tasmā dhammato satta saṃyojanāni.

Among these ten, the fetter of existence in the form realm, the fetter of existence in the formless realm, and the fetter of existence in the sense-sphere are in substance greed. Identity view and adherence to rules and observances are also just view. Therefore, in terms of their intrinsic nature, there are seven fetters.

Micchāsaṅkappo micchāvāyāmo micchāsamādhīti tathā pavattānaṃ vitakkavīriyasamādhīnamadhivacanaṃ. Micchāvācādayo tayo tathā pavattā cetanā. Micchāsati pana cittuppādo. Micchāñāṇaṃ tathā pavatto moho. Micchāvimutti lokathūpikādīsu mokkhoti pavattamicchāgāho.

Wrong thought, wrong effort, and wrong concentration—these are terms for thought, energy, and concentration that proceed wrongly. Wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood are volitions that proceed similarly. Wrong mindfulness, however, is an arising of consciousness. Wrong knowledge is delusion that proceeds wrongly. Wrong liberation is the wrong grasp that proceeds as 'liberation' in regard to worldly stupas and the like.

Kāraṇūpacārenāti lābhahetuko lābho, alābhahetuko alābhotiādinā kāriyassa kāraṇavasena upacaraṇena. Lokadhammaggahaṇanti lokadhammaggahaṇena gahaṇaṃ.

'By way of causal metaphor' means by the figurative use of the cause for the effect, as in 'the cause of gain is called gain,' 'the cause of loss is called loss,' and so on. 'Grasping worldly states' means the act of grasping by means of the grasping of worldly states.

Āvāse macchariyaṃ, āvāsahetukaṃ vā macchariyanti āvāsamacchariyaṃ. Evaṃ kulamacchariyādīnipi. Tattha āvāsoti vihārādi. Kulanti upaṭṭhākakulaṃ, ñātikulañca. Lābhoti paccayalābhoyeva. Vaṇṇoti sarīravaṇṇo ca guṇavaṇṇo ca. Dhammoti āgamo, adhigamo ca.

Stinginess concerning a dwelling, or stinginess caused by a dwelling, is dwelling-stinginess. Similarly with stinginess concerning family, and so on. Here, 'dwelling' means a monastery and so on. 'Family' means a supporting family and a family of relatives. 'Gain' means only gain of requisites. 'Complexion/praise' means bodily appearance and praise of virtues. 'Dhamma' means the scriptures and realization.

“Tayo”ti [M 2.0354] vatthuṃ abhinditvā vuttaṃ, bhinditvā ca pana vuccamāne dvādasa honti.

'Three' is said without analyzing the subject matter. But when it is spoken of after analyzing it, there are twelve.

Abhisajjanūpanayhanavasena pavattanato abhijjhābyāpādānaṃ kāyaganthatā daṭṭhabbā. “Idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti evaṃ avatthumhi pavatto abhiniveso idaṃsaccābhiniveso. Sīlabbataparāmāsaidaṃsaccābhinivesakāyaganthā cettha atthato diṭṭhiyeva, tasmā dhammato tayo kāyaganthā.

The nature of being bodily knots for covetousness and ill will should be seen from their proceeding by way of attachment and resentment. The adherence that proceeds regarding a groundless matter as 'This alone is true, all else is false' is the adherence that 'this alone is true.' Here, the bodily knots of adherence to rules and observances and the adherence that 'this alone is true' are in substance merely view, and so, in terms of their intrinsic nature, there are three bodily knots.

“Chandadosamohabhayānī”ti [V 2.0264] agatikāraṇattā vuttaṃ, chandādīhi pana akattabbakaraṇaṃ, kattabbākaraṇañca agati nāma.

'Desire, hatred, delusion, and fear' are mentioned because they are the causes of wrong courses. Furthermore, doing what should not be done and not doing what should be done, on account of desire and the like, is called a 'wrong course.'

Āsavesu kāmarāgabhavarāgā atthato lobhoti dhammato tayo āsavā.

Among the taints, the taint of sensual lust and the taint of lust for existence are in substance greed. Thus, in terms of their intrinsic nature, there are three taints.

Tesamevāti kāmarāgādīnameva. Te hi ogho viya attani patite apāyasamuddaṃ pāpenti, saṃsāradukkhato ca sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na denti, khandhādīni ca khandhādīhi yojenti.

The same refers to sensual lust and the like. For they, like a flood, cause those who have fallen into them to reach the ocean of the plane of misery, do not allow one to lift one’s head from the suffering of saṃsāra, and yoke aggregates with aggregates.

Kāmupādānādīnīti kāmupādānadiṭṭhupādānasīlabbatupādānaattavādupādānāni. Diṭṭhupādānādīni cettha tathā pavattā diṭṭhiyeva, kāmupādānaṃ lobhoti dhammato dve upādānāni.

The clingings beginning with sensual clinging are: sensual clinging, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self. Here, clinging to views and the other two are essentially wrong view, while sensual clinging is greed. Thus, in terms of their intrinsic nature, there are two kinds of clinging.

Sattānusayāti ettha yadi appahīnaṭṭhena sattasantāne anusentīti anusayā. Kasmā satteva vuttā, nanu aññesampi kilesānaṃ appahīnabhāvo vijjatīti? Na mayaṃ appahīnamattena anusayaṃ vadāma, kintu appahīnabhāvena thāmagatakilesā anusayāti, thāmagamanañca nesaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇo sabhāvo daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi dhammasabhāvavedinā tathāgatena imeyeva anusayā vuttā, kāmarāgoyeva anusayo kāmarāgānusayo. Evaṃ [M 2.0355] sesesupi. Apare pana “kāmarāgassa anusayo”tiādinibbacanaṃ vatvā kāmarāgādīnaṃ bījabhūtā attabhāvassa kilesasambhūtā kilesuppādanasatti anusayāti vaṇṇenti, tesaṃ matapaṭikkhepo idha papañcāvahattā anāhaṭo.

Regarding the seven latent tendencies: they are called latent tendencies because they lie latent in a being's mental continuum in the sense of not being abandoned. Why, then, are only seven mentioned, since other defilements also exist in an unabandoned state? We do not define a latent tendency merely by its unabandoned state, but as a defilement that has become strong through being unabandoned. Their distinctive nature of becoming strong should be understood as unique to them. Indeed, the Tathāgata, who knows the true nature of phenomena, has declared these very seven as latent tendencies. For example, sensual lust itself is the latent tendency, hence 'the latent tendency of sensual lust.' The same applies to the rest. Others, however, explain this by deriving it as 'the latent tendency of sensual lust,' and they describe a latent tendency as a potency for producing defilements, which is born of defilements and is the seed-state of sensual lust and so on, and of individual existence. The refutation of their view is not presented here as it would lead to proliferation.

Pāṇassa atipāto pāṇātipāto, pāṇoti vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ. Tasmiṃ pāṇe pāṇasaññino jīvitindriyupacchedakappayogasamuṭṭhāpikā vadhakacetanā pāṇātipāto. Parabhaṇḍe tathāsaññino tadādāyakappayogasamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā adinnādānaṃ. Asaddhammakāmatāya kāyadvārappavattā agantabbaṭṭhānavītikkamacetanā kāmesumicchācāro. Abhūtaṃ vatthuṃ bhūtato paraṃ viññāpetukāmassa tathā viññāpanappayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. So pana parassa atthabhedakarova kammapatho, itaro kammameva. Saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa parabhedanakāmatāya, attapiyakamyatāya vā parabhedakappayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā pisuṇavācā. Sāpi dvīsu bhinnesuyeva kammapatho. Paramammacchedakappayogasamuṭṭhāpikā ekantapharusacetanā pharusavācā. Anatthaviññāpanappayogasamuṭṭhāpikā [V 2.0265] saṃkiliṭṭhacetanā samphappalāpo nāma. So pana parehi gahiteyeva kammapatho hoti. “Aho vatedaṃ mama hotū”ti evaṃ parabhaṇḍābhijjhāyanalakkhaṇā abhijjhā. “Aho vatāyaṃ satto vinasseyyā”ti evaṃ manopadosalakkhaṇo byāpādo. “Natthi dinna”ntiādinā nayena viparītadassanalakkhaṇā micchādiṭṭhi. Ettha ca natthikaahetukaakiriyadiṭṭhīhiyeva kammapathabhedo.

The destruction of a living being is pāṇātipāta. 'Living being' (pāṇa) by convention is a being; in the ultimate sense, it is the life faculty. The volition to kill, which initiates an effort to cut off the life faculty of one perceived as a living being, is destruction of life. The volition to steal, which initiates an effort to take another's property, perceived as such, is taking what is not given. The volition to transgress in a place one should not go, proceeding through the body door out of illicit sensual desire, is sexual misconduct. The volition of one who wishes to make another know as true what is untrue, which initiates an effort to make it known thus, is false speech. This becomes a course of action only when it damages another's welfare; otherwise, it is merely an action. The volition that initiates an effort to cause division in another, arising from a defiled mind with the wish to divide others or from a wish to make oneself dear, is slanderous speech. This too becomes a course of action only when two people are divided. The volition that is entirely harsh, which initiates an effort to cut another to the quick, is harsh speech. The defiled volition that initiates an effort to make known what is unbeneficial is called idle chatter. This becomes a course of action only when it is accepted by others. Covetousness is characterized by coveting another's property thus: 'Oh, that this were mine!' Ill will is characterized by mental corruption thus: 'Oh, that this being would perish!' Wrong view is characterized by perverted seeing in the way of 'There is nothing given,' etc. Here, the distinction as a course of action is made specifically by the nihilistic view, the view of non-causality, and the view of inefficacy of action.

Imesu ca pāṇātipātādi tividhaṃ kāyakammameva. Taṃ kāyavacīdvāresuyeva uppajjati, na manodvāre. Tathā musāvādādi [M 2.0356] catubbidhaṃ vacīkammameva. Abhijjhādikaṃ pana tividhaṃ manokammameva. Taṃ tīsupi dvāresu pavattati. Dvārantaresupi pavattamānassa sakasakanāmāpariccāgo vuttoyeva. Dhammato cettha ādito satta cetanāsabhāvā, itare tayo cetanāsampayuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Mahāsāvajjaappasāvajjappayogādibhedo pana tattha tattha vuttanayena veditabbo.

Among these, the three types of action beginning with the destruction of life are bodily kamma only. They arise only through the body and speech doors, not through the mind door. Similarly, the four types of action beginning with false speech are verbal kamma only. However, the three types of action beginning with covetousness are mental kamma only. They operate through all three doors. The non-abandonment of their respective names even when they operate through other doors has already been stated. Here, it should be understood that, in terms of their intrinsic nature, the first seven are of the nature of volition, while the remaining three are associated with volition. The distinction between greatly blameworthy, slightly blameworthy, by way of application, etc., should be understood according to the method explained in the respective cases.

Etānīti imāni maggañāṇāni. Yathāsambhavanti taṃtaṃmaggānurūpaṃ.

`These` means these path-knowledges. `As is appropriate` means in accordance with their respective paths.

Apāyaṃ gacchanti etehīti apāyagamanīyā. Sesāti na apāyagamanīyā. Oḷārikāti tatiyamaggena pahātabbāvatthaṃ upādāya oḷārikā. Tenāha “sukhumā tatiyamaggañāṇavajjhā”ti. Sukhumā kāmarāgapaṭighāti sambandho. Catutthamaggañāṇavajjhā evāti avadhāraṇena paṭhamamaggādivajjhataṃ nivatteti. Na hi rūparāgādīnaṃ apāyagāminiyāvatthāpi atthi, yato te paṭhamañāṇavajjhāpi siyunti.

They go to the plane of misery on account of these, hence they are 'leading to the plane of misery.' `The rest` means not leading to the plane of misery. `Coarse` means coarse with reference to the state of being abandonable by the third path. Therefore he said: “Subtle, to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path.” The connection is: `subtle` refers to sensual desire and aversion. By the emphasis 'to be abandoned only by the knowledge of the fourth path,' it excludes their being abandoned by the knowledge of the first path and so on. For there is no state of leading to the plane of misery for form-desire and so on, on account of which they could also be abandoned by the first knowledge.

Yattha yattha pana eva-saddena avadhāraṇaṃ akatvā yaṃ yaṃ dutiyañāṇavajjhanti vā tatiyañāṇavajjhanti vā catutthañāṇavajjhanti vā vakkhati, tattha tattha so so purimañāṇehi hatāpāyagamanīyādibhāvova hutvā upariñāṇavajjho hotīti veditabbo. Tena lobha…pe… catutthañāṇavajjhānīti ettha lobhādayo heṭṭhimamaggavajjhāpi honteva.

But wherever, without making an emphasis with the word 'eva,' it is said that something is to be abandoned by the second knowledge, or the third knowledge, or the fourth knowledge, there it should be understood that this thing—its nature of leading to the plane of misery and so on having been destroyed by the preceding knowledges—becomes abandonable by a higher knowledge. Therefore, when it is said 'greed...pe...are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge,' here greed and so on are indeed also abandonable by the lower paths.

Yaseti parivāre.

`Fame` means in the sense of retinue.

Dukkhe sukhanti saññācittavipallāsāti sambandho.

The connection is: 'happiness in suffering' is a perversion of perception and of mind.

Agatiyo [V 2.0266] paṭhamamaggañāṇavajjhāti kiñcāpi chandādayo taṇhādisabhāvā uparimaggavajjhā, tathāpi tammūlakassa akattabbakaraṇassa, kattabbākaraṇassa ca apāyagamanīyatāya paṭhamamaggañāṇavajjhā.

The wrong courses of action are abandonable by the knowledge of the first path. Although desire and so on, which have the nature of craving and so on, are abandonable by the higher paths, nevertheless, because their root—the doing of what should not be done and the not doing of what should be done—leads to the plane of misery, they are abandonable by the knowledge of the first path.

Katākatakusalākusalavisayaṃ [M 2.0357] yaṃ vippaṭisārabhūtaṃ kukkuccaṃ, taṃ idha tatiyañāṇavajjhaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana “kukkuccapakatatāya āpattiṃ āpajjatī”ti vuttaṃ kukkuccaṃ, taṃ sandhāya “kukkuccavicikicchā sotāpattimaggena pahīyantī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1176) dhammasaṅgaṇīaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā dvinnaṃ vacanānaṃ ayaṃ adhippāyo veditabbo. Aññesupi edisesu ṭhānesu adhippāyova pariyesitabbo, na virodhato paccetabbaṃ. Oḷārikānavasesappahānaṃ vā sandhāya kukkuccassa paṭhamatatiyañāṇavajjhatā vuttā. Yaṃ pana arahato uppajjamānaṃ “bhagavatā paṭikkhittaṃ anuvasitvā anuvasitvā āvasathapiṇḍaṃ bhuñjitunti kukkuccāyanto na paṭiggahesī”ti (pāci. 204) āgataṃ kukkuccaṃ, na taṃ nīvaraṇaṃ. Na hi nīvaraṇaṃ arahato uppajjati, nīvaraṇapatirūpakaṃ pana kappatīti vīmaṃsanabhūtaṃ vinayakukkuccaṃ nāma, taṃ tathāpavattacittuppādova.

That worry which is remorse concerning the domain of skillful and unskillful things done and not done, that is here said to be abandonable by the third knowledge. But with reference to the worry mentioned as 'one falls into an offense because of a tendency to worry,' it is said in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary: 'Worry and doubt are abandoned by the path of stream-entry' (Dhs-A. 1176). Therefore, the intention of these two statements should be understood. In other such cases, too, the intention should be sought; a contradiction should not be assumed. Or, the fact that worry is abandonable by the first and third knowledges is stated with reference to the abandonment of the gross portion and the remainderless abandonment. But the worry that arises in an arahant—as seen in the passage, 'becoming worried, thinking, “I have eaten almsfood from a residence forbidden by the Blessed One,” he did not accept it' (Pāc. 204)—that is not a hindrance. For a hindrance does not arise in an arahant. Rather, what is called 'disciplinary worry' (vinayakukkucca), which is a form of investigation into what is a semblance of a hindrance and what is allowable, is just such an arising of a state of mind.

Kāmarāgapaṭighānusayā anusahagatā tatiyañāṇavajjhā, oḷārikānaṃ pana dutiyañāṇavajjhatā heṭṭhā vuttanayāva.

The underlying tendencies of sensual desire and aversion, along with their concomitants, are abandonable by the third knowledge; but the fact that the gross ones are abandonable by the second knowledge is in the way already stated above.

Akusalacittuppāda-ggahaṇena cettha makkhapalāsamāyāsāṭheyyathambhasārambhādīnaṃ saṅgaho katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

And here, by the mention of the arising of unwholesome consciousness, it should be seen that an inclusion has been made of hypocrisy, contempt, deceit, craftiness, obstinacy, impetuosity, and so on.

1376. Tena tenāti tena tena ghātakena saddhiṃ. Kiṃ panetāni ete dhamme ghātentāni atītānāgate ghātenti, udāhu paccuppanneti. Kiṃ panettha, yadi tāva atītānāgate, aphalo vāyāmo āpajjati. Kasmā? Pahātabbānaṃ tadā natthitāya. Atha paccuppanne, tathāpi aphalo vāyāmena saddhiṃ pahātabbānaṃ atthitāya. Athāpi kathañci pahānaṃ siyā, saṃkilesikā maggabhāvanā āpajjati [M 2.0358] pahātabbappahāyakānaṃ sahāvaṭṭhānato? Saccametaṃ, ye pana maggena asamugghāṭitattā kāraṇalābhe sati avassaṃ uppajjanārahā kilesā, te attano uppattiyā anuppattidhammataṃ āpādentāni etāni te anāgate ghātenti nāma.

1376. 'By that, by that' means together with that, that destroyer. But do these things, while destroying those states, destroy past and future ones, or present ones? What of it? If they destroy past and future ones, the effort is fruitless. Why? Because what is to be abandoned does not exist then. If they destroy present ones, the effort is still fruitless, because what is to be abandoned exists together with the effort. And even if abandonment could somehow occur, would the development of the path become defiled, due to the co-existence of what is to be abandoned and what abandons? This is true. However, as for those defilements that, not having been uprooted by the path, are sure to arise when a cause is obtained, these path factors, by bringing those defilements to a state where they cannot arise in the future, are said to destroy them.

1377-82. Pariññādīni [V 2.0267] kiccānīti pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāvasena cattāri kiccāni. Vuttānīti “dukkhaṃ pariññeyya”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1099), “yo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) ca vuttāni. Saccābhisamayeti catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ paṭivijjhanakkhaṇe.

1377-82. `The functions beginning with full understanding` means the four functions: full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development. `Stated` means stated in such texts as: “Suffering is to be fully understood” (SN 56.11), and “Bhikkhus, one who sees suffering…” (SN 56.12). `At the time of the comprehension of the truths` means at the moment of penetrating the four noble truths.

Yathāsabhāvatoti aviparītasabhāvena. “Jānitabbānī”ti vatvā kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ, kathaṃ nāma ekekassa ñāṇassa ekakkhaṇe cattāri kiccāni sambhavanti. Na hi tādisaṃ kiñci loke diṭṭhaṃ atthi, na ca vacanaṃ labbhatīti codanaṃ manasi nidhāya tesaṃ jānanavidhiṃ upamāvasena tāva dassetuṃ “padīpo hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vidaṃsetīti dasseti. Pariyādiyatīti khepeti.

`According to its true nature` means with an unperverted nature. Having said 'they are to be known,' [an objection is raised]: 'But how is this to be known? How indeed can four functions for a single knowledge occur in a single moment? For nothing like this is seen in the world, nor is such a statement found.' Keeping this objection in mind, in order to show the method of knowing them by way of a simile, the passage beginning 'For a lamp...' was stated. `It illuminates` means it shows. `It consumes` means it exhausts.

1383-4. Pariññābhisamayenāti anavasesato paricchijja jānanasaṅkhātena paṭivijjhanena. Abhisametīti asammohavasena paṭivijjhati. Pahānābhisamayenevāti samucchedappahānasaṅkhātena paṭivijjhanena asammohatova abhisameti. Bhāvanāvidhināti sahajātādipaccayatāvasena bhāvanābhisamayavidhinā. Maggañāṇañhi sammāsaṅkappādivasena maggapubbabhāgabhāvanāsambhūtena ariyamaggabhāvanāsaṅkhātena paṭivijjhanena abhisametīti aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ asammohato paṭivijjhati. Tañhi sampayuttadhammesu sammohaṃ viddhaṃsentaṃ attanipi sammohaṃ viddhaṃsetiyeva. Nirodhanti [M 2.0359] nibbānaṃ. Sacchikarotīti paccakkhakaraṇavasena paṭivijjhati. “Nirodhaṃ sacchikarotī”ti nirodhasaccamekaṃ ārammaṇapaṭivedhena cattāripi saccāni asammohapaṭivedhena maggañāṇaṃ paṭivijjhati.

1383-4. 'By the comprehension of full understanding' means by the penetration that is characterized as knowing through having defined without remainder. 'He comprehends' means he penetrates by way of non-delusion. 'By the comprehension of abandonment' means he comprehends by way of non-delusion through the penetration that is characterized as abandonment by cutting off. 'By the method of development' means by the method of the comprehension of development by way of the condition of co-nascence and so on. For path-knowledge—by means of the penetration characterized as the development of the noble path, which is produced by the development of the preliminary part of the path by way of right intention and so on—comprehends, that is, it penetrates the Noble Eightfold Path without delusion. For while destroying delusion in associated states, it also destroys delusion in itself. 'Cessation' means Nibbāna. 'He realizes' means he penetrates by way of making it directly present. When it is said 'He realizes cessation,' it means that path-knowledge penetrates the one truth, the truth of cessation, by way of object-penetration, and it penetrates all four truths by way of penetration without delusion.

Evaṃ yuttivasena vibhāvitaṃ ekapaṭivedhaṃ āgamenapi sādhetuṃ “vuttampi ceta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Maggasamaṅgissa ñāṇanti hi “yo nu kho, āvuso, dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi so passati, dukkhanirodhampi, dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadampi so passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) ekasaccadassanasamaṅgino aññasaccadassanasamaṅgibhāvavicāraṇāyaṃ tamatthaṃ sādhetuṃ āyasmatā gavampatittherena vuttaṃ. Aññathā kamābhisamaye sati purimadiṭṭhassa puna adassanato samudayādipassato dukkhādidassanaṃ puna avattabbaṃ siyā. Idāni panettha upamāsaṃsandanaṃ karonto āha “padīpo”tiādi. Nissayābhāvahetutāya dukkhapariññāya vaṭṭijjhāpanasadisatā, paṭipakkhaviddhaṃsanatāya samudayappahānassa andhakāravināsanasadisatā, ñāṇālokaparibrūhanatāya maggabhāvanāya [V 2.0268] ālokavidaṃsanasadisatā, tena tena maggena yathā yathā nirodhassa sacchikiriyā, tathā tathā kilesasnehapariyādānaṃ hotīti nirodhasacchikiriyāya snehapariyādānasadisatā kāraṇūpacārena vuttā.

In order to establish by scripture as well this single penetration that has been explained by way of reasoning, the passage beginning 'And this was said...' was stated. For this was said by the Venerable Gavampati Thera to establish the meaning in the context of investigating how one endowed with the vision of one truth is endowed with the vision of the other truths: 'The knowledge of one endowed with the path is this: “Friend, one who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering”' (SN 56.30). Otherwise, if there were a sequential comprehension, since what was seen before would not be seen again, it would not be necessary to state again the seeing of suffering and so on for one who sees the origin and so on. Now, making a connection with the simile here, he says: 'A lamp...' and so on. The full understanding of suffering is like the burning up of the wick because it is the cause for the absence of a support; the abandoning of the origin is like the destruction of darkness because it destroys the opponent; the development of the path is like the illuminating of light because it augments the light of knowledge; because the exhaustion of the 'oil' of the defilements occurs in whatever way the realization of cessation occurs by means of each path, the realization of cessation is said to be like the exhaustion of the oil by a metaphor based on the cause.

1385-6. Aparāyapi upamāya tamatthaṃ dassento āha “uggacchanto”tiādi. Obhāsetīti pakāseti. Paṭihaññatīti paṭippassambheti. Etthāpi yathā sūriyo rūpagatāni obhāseti, evaṃ maggañāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ parijānāti. Yathā andhakāraṃ vināseti, evaṃ samudayaṃ pajahati. Yathā ālokaṃ dasseti, evaṃ sahajātādipaccayatāya maggaṃ bhāveti[M 2.0360]. Yathā sītaṃ paṭippassambheti, evaṃ sabbakilesadarathapariḷāhapaṭippassaddhibhūtaṃ nirodhaṃ sacchikarotīti upamāsaṃsandanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

1385-6. Showing this meaning with another simile, he said, 'The rising...' and so on. 'It illuminates' means it makes manifest. 'It strikes down' means it pacifies. Here too, the connection of the simile should be seen in this way: just as the sun illuminates forms, so path-knowledge fully understands suffering. Just as it destroys darkness, so it abandons the origin. Just as it reveals light, so it develops the path by way of the condition of co-nascence and so on. Just as it allays the cold, so it realizes cessation, which is the pacification of all defilements, distress, and burning.

1388. Appetīti pappoti. Dukkhapariññāya sakkāyatīrasamatikkamabhāvato orimatīrappajahanasadisatā, maggabhāvanāya sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammavahanatāya bhaṇḍavahanasadisatā, ettāvatā paññābhāvanāya nānākilesaviddhaṃsanavasappavatto ānisaṃso dassito hotīti.

1388. 'He applies' means he attains. Because the full understanding of suffering is the transcending of the near shore of identity, it is like abandoning the near shore. Because the development of the path is the carrying of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, it is like carrying goods. By this much, the benefit of the development of wisdom is shown, which is that it proceeds with the power to destroy the various defilements.

Ariyaphalasamāpattinirodhasamāpattiyopi panassā ānisaṃsāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tā pana saṅkhepato evaṃ daṭṭhabbā – “ariyaphalasamāpattī”ti hi catunnampi phalaṭṭhānaṃ attano attano ariyaphalassa diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthaṃ nirodhe appanā. Cattāropi hi ariyapuggalā sakaṃ sakaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjanti. Keci pana “anāgāmiarahantova samāpajjanti samādhismiṃ paripūrakāritāyā”ti vadanti, taṃ akāraṇaṃ attanā paṭiladdhasamāpattisamāpajjane samādhismiṃ paripūrakāritāya kātabbābhāvato. Sabbaso asamucchinnakilesassa hi puthujjanassāpi attanā paṭiladdhalokiyasamāpattisamāpajjanaṃ labbhati, kimaṅgaṃ pana samucchinnekaccakilesānaṃ ariyānaṃ. Uparimā pana heṭṭhimaṃ pubbe paṭiladdhampi na samāpajjanti puggalantarabhāvaṃ upagatattā. Samugghāṭitakammakilesanirodhanena hi puthujjanehi viya sotāpannassa, sotāpannādīhi sakadāgāmiādīnaṃ puggalantarabhāvūpagamanaṃ atthi, anantaraphalattā ca lokuttarakusalānaṃ heṭṭhimato uparimo bhavantaragato viya hotīti tassa tassa ariyassa taṃ taṃ phalaṃ bhavaṅgasadisaṃ hoti, tasmā puggalantarabhāvūpagamanena [M 2.0361] paṭippassaddhattā natthi uparimassa heṭṭhimaphalasamāpattiyā [V 2.0269] samāpajjanaṃ, heṭṭhimo pana uparimaṃ na samāpajjati anadhigatattāti cattāropi puggalā sakasakaphalameva samāpajjanti. Taṃ pana samāpajjitukāmena ariyasāvakena rahogatena paṭisallīnena udayabbayādivasena saṅkhārā vipassitabbā. Tassa pavattānupubbavipassanassa saṅkhārārammaṇagotrabhuñāṇānantaraṃ phalasamāpattivasena nirodhe cittaṃ appeti. Phalasamāpattininnacittatāya cettha sekhassa phalameva uppajjati, na maggo. Añño eva hi vipassanācāro ariyamaggāvaho, añño phalasamāpattiāvaho.

Furthermore, the benefits of fruition attainment and cessation attainment should also be seen. These should be briefly understood as follows: "Fruition attainment" refers to the application to cessation for the sake of experiencing the blissful dwelling in this very life, which is the noble fruition for each of the four noble individuals. Indeed, all four noble individuals attain their respective fruition attainments. Some, however, say that only non-returners and arahants attain it due to their having perfected concentration. This is unfounded, because there is no need to have perfected concentration to enter an attainment that one has already personally achieved. Even an ordinary person, whose defilements are not entirely uprooted, can achieve and enter mundane attainments—how much more so for the noble ones, who have uprooted some defilements. Moreover, those of higher stages do not enter the attainments of lower stages that they had previously attained because they have attained a different individual state. Just as there is a progression to another individual state for a stream-enterer from an ordinary person through the eradication of defilements and kamma, and similarly, for a once-returner, etc., from a stream-enterer, etc., and because the supramundane wholesome states have immediate fruition, the higher individual is like one who has passed to another state of existence from the lower. Thus, for each noble one, their respective fruition becomes like the life-continuum. Therefore, due to the subsiding brought about by the attainment of another individual state, there is no entering of a lower fruition attainment by one of a higher level; however, one of a lower level does not enter one of a higher level because it has not been attained. Hence, all four individuals enter only their own respective fruitions. A noble disciple who wishes to attain this should go into solitude, withdraw, and contemplate the formations by way of arising and passing away, etc. For one with such progressive insight, immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge with formations as its object, the mind becomes absorbed in cessation by way of fruition attainment. Here, due to the mind’s inclination toward fruition attainment, only the fruition arises in a trainee, not the path. For the course of insight leading to the noble path is one thing, and the course leading to fruition attainment is another.

Tathā hi ariyamaggavīthiyaṃ anulomañāṇāni anibbiddhapubbānaṃ thūlathūlalobhakkhandhādīnaṃ sātisayaṃ padālanena lokiyañāṇesu ukkaṃsapāramippattāni maggānukūlāni hutvā uppajjanti, phalasamāpattivīthiyaṃ pana tāni tena tena maggena tesaṃ tesaṃ kilesānaṃ samucchinnattā kilesavikkhambhane nirussukkāni kevalaṃ ariyānaṃ phalasamāpattisukhasamaṅgibhāvassa parikammappattāni hutvā uppajjantīti na tesaṃ kutoci vuṭṭhānasambhavo. Yato nesaṃ pacchimo saṅkhāranimittato vuṭṭhahitvā maggassa anantarapaccayo bhaveyya, teneva ca phalasamāpattiyā anantarapaccayabhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇameva hoti, na nibbānārammaṇanti veditabbaṃ. Pubbābhisaṅkhāravasena cassā pabandhavasena pavattiparicchinnakālāpagame bhavaṅgavasena tato vuṭṭhānañca veditabbaṃ.

For in the noble path process, conformity knowledge arises by greatly shattering the previously unbroken gross defilements like greed and so forth, having attained the highest excellence among mundane knowledges and being conducive to the path. But in the fruition attainment process, that same knowledge, because those defilements have been eradicated by the respective path and because it is without effort in suppressing defilements, arises solely as a preliminary act for the noble ones’ enjoyment of the bliss of fruition attainment. Thus, there is no possibility of their emergence from any source. For the last of them cannot emerge from the sign of formations to become an immediate condition for the path; for that very reason, it should be understood that the knowledge which is the immediate condition for fruition attainment has formations as its object, not Nibbāna. Moreover, it should be understood that emergence from it occurs due to the force of previous volitional formations, upon the passing of the period determined by the continuity of the process, and then by way of the life-continuum.

Nirodhasamāpatti pana tatiyacatutthaphalaṭṭhānaṃ anupubbanirodhavasena cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ appavatti. Anāgāmiarahantoyeva hi kāmacchandādisamucchindanena samādhismiṃ paripūrakāritāya samathaphalasamannāgatattā nirodhaṃ samāpajjanti. Tathā hetaṃ samathavipassanānaṃ yuganandhabhāvappavattanavasena dvīhi balehi samannāgatasseva sambhavati, tasmā taṃ samāpajjitukāmena [M 2.0362] anāgāminā, khīṇāsavena vā aṭṭhasamāpattilābhinā rahogatena paṭisallīnena paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tattha saṅkhārā aniccato dukkhato anattato vipassitabbā, tato dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ catutthaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tatheva tattha saṅkhārā sammasitabbā, atha ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya nānābaddhāvikopanaṃ saṅghapaṭimānanaṃ satthupakkosanaṃ addhānaparicchedoti catubbidhaṃ pubbakiccaṃ kātabbaṃ.

The attainment of cessation, however, is the non-occurrence of mental phenomena and their concomitants by way of successive cessation for one established in the third and fourth fruitions. For only non-returners and arahants attain cessation, due to having eradicated sensual desire and the like, being perfected in concentration, and being endowed with the fruit of serenity. Indeed, this is possible only for one endowed with the two powers, by way of the balanced development of serenity and insight. Therefore, a non-returner or an arahant who has obtained the eight attainments and wishes to enter that attainment, having gone into solitude and seclusion, should enter the first jhāna. Having emerged from it, the formations therein should be seen with insight as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Then, having entered the second, third, and fourth jhānas, the base of infinite space, and the base of infinite consciousness and emerged from them, the formations therein should be contemplated in the same way. Then, having entered the base of nothingness and emerged from it, the fourfold preliminary duty should be performed: determination regarding unconnected belongings, awaiting a summons from the Saṅgha, awaiting a summons from the Teacher, and the determination of the duration.

Tattha [V 2.0270] sarīrato visaṃyuttā mañcapīṭhādayo sattāhabbhantare yathā na nassanti, tathā adhiṭṭhānaṃ nānābaddhāvikopanaṃ. Sarīrasaṃyutte visuṃ adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthi. Saṅgho pana ñattikammādīsu kiñcideva kammaṃ kattukāmo “yāva maṃ na pakkosati, tāvadeva vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti pubbābhogakaraṇaṃ saṅghapaṭimānanaṃ. Satthā ca “sikkhāpadapaññāpanādīsu yāva maṃ na pakkosati, tāvadeva vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti pubbābhogakaraṇaṃ satthupakkosanaṃ. Sattāhabbhantare attano āyusaṅkhārassa pavattanasamatthatāvalokanaṃ addhānaparicchedo. Evaṃ katapubbakiccena nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjitabbaṃ. Athekaṃ vā dve vā cittavāre atikkamitvā acittako hoti, nirodhaṃ phusati, tato yathāparicchedaṃ tatiyacatutthaphalānaṃ aññatarena nirodhā vuṭṭhahissatīti. Evamayaṃ duvidhā samāpatti lokuttarapaññāya ānisaṃso.

Herein, 'determination regarding unconnected belongings' is the determination that items disconnected from the body, such as a bed or a chair, should not perish within seven days. For things connected to the body, there is no need for a separate determination. When the Saṅgha intends to perform some formal act, such as a motion, the preliminary attention, 'I will arise only when the Saṅgha summons me,' is 'awaiting a summons from the Saṅgha'. And when the Teacher is about to lay down a training rule or the like, the preliminary attention, 'I will arise only when the Teacher summons me,' is 'awaiting a summons from the Teacher'. Examining one's own capacity for the continuation of the life-faculty within seven days is 'the determination of the duration'. Having performed these preliminary duties, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception should be attained. Then, after one or two mind-moments have passed, one becomes devoid of mind and touches cessation. Thereafter, according to the determined limit, one will emerge from cessation with either the third or the fourth fruition. Thus, this twofold attainment is a benefit of supramundane wisdom.

1392-4. Sadevakalokato uttiṇṇena, uttaritarena vāti lokuttarena sammāsambuddhena. Paññāya bhāvananti sambandho. Hitabhāvananti idhalokaparalokahitavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ paññābhāvanaṃ. Sukhasaṃhitanti siniddhacchāyudakavantatādinā sukhasahitaṃ. Hitanti yogakammassa hitaṃ[M 2.0363]. Uttamanti uggatatamaṃ, accuggataṃ balavantampīti adhippāyo. Aviggahakampadanti viggahañca kampañca na detīti aviggahakampadanti attho.

1392-4. By the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One who has crossed over, who has gone beyond the world with its gods, that is, by the supramundane one. The connection is 'the development of wisdom'. 'Development for welfare' means this development of wisdom, which makes manifest the welfare in this world and the next. 'Conducive to happiness' means accompanied by happiness, due to such things as pleasant shade and water. 'Welfare' means the welfare of the yogic practice. 'Supreme' means most eminent, exceedingly elevated, and also powerful—this is the intention. 'Not giving rise to strife or agitation' means it does not give rise to strife and agitation—this is the meaning.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus, in the work named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī,

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

the commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra,

Kilesappahānakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the discourse on the abandonment of defilements is concluded.

24. Catuvīsatimo paricchedo

24. The Twenty-Fourth Chapter

Paccayaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of Conditions

1395. Idāni nesaṃ paccayavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “yesa”ntiādi āraddhaṃ.

1395. Now, in order to show their mode of conditioning, the passage beginning with “yesaṃ” is commenced.

Paṭicca [V 2.0271] enaṃ phalameti pavattati, tiṭṭhati, uppajjati vāti paccayo, hinoti patiṭṭhāti etthāti hetu, anekatthattā dhātusaddānaṃ hi-saddo mūla-saddo viya patiṭṭhattho veditabbo, hinoti vā etena kammanidānabhūtena uddhaṃ ojaṃ atiharantena mūlena viya pādapo tappaccayaṃ phalaṃ gacchati viruḷhiṃ āpajjatīti hetu, hetu ca so mūlaṭṭhena, paccayo ca upakārakaṭṭhenāti hetupaccayo, hetu hutvā paccayo hetubhāvena paccayoti attho.

A condition (paccaya) is that depending on which a result comes to be, proceeds, endures, or arises. It is a root (hetu) because a result is sent forth (hinoti) by it, or is established (patiṭṭhāti) in it. Because verbal roots have many meanings, the sound ‘hi’ should be understood in the sense of establishment, like the word ‘root’ (mūla). Or, it is a root (hetu) because by means of it a result is sent forth (hinoti) and attains growth, just as a tree, by means of its root—which is the basis of its function and which draws nutritive sap upwards—goes to its fruit dependent on that condition. It is a root in the sense of being a foundation, and a condition in the sense of being an accessory factor; thus it is a root-condition (hetupaccaya). The meaning is: being a root, it is a condition; it is a condition by way of being a root.

Evaṃ ārammaṇapaccayādīsu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Svāyaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ kammasamuṭṭhānānaṃ, pavattiyaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ, ubhayattha sahajātanāmadhammānañca paccayo. Sabbalokiyalokuttaranti iminā paññattiyāpi loke viditabhāvena lokiyapadena saṅgahitattā rūpādibhedesu chabbidhesu saṅkhatāsaṅkhatapaññattidhammesu na koci dhammo ārammaṇapaccayo na hotīti dasseti. Teneva “yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ ārabbhā”ti aniyato [M 2.0364] katoti. Nanu ca “yaṃ yaṃ dhamma”nti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.2-3) vuttattā paññattiyā gahaṇaṃ na hotīti? Nāyaṃ doso dhammasaddassa ñeyyavacanattā. Ārabbhāti ālambitvā, gahetvāti attho. Uppajjantīti idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ. Te pana taṃ ārabbha uppajjanti ceva tiṭṭhanti ca. Yathā hi dubbalo puriso daṇḍaṃ vā rajjuṃ vā ālambitvā uṭṭhahati ceva tiṭṭhati ca, evaṃ cittacetasikā dhammā rūpādiārammaṇaṃ ālambitvā uppajjanti ceva tiṭṭhanti cāti.

This same method should be understood in the case of the object condition and so on. This root-condition is a condition for kamma-produced material phenomena at rebirth-linking, for mind-produced material phenomena during the course of existence, and for conascent mental phenomena in both cases. By the phrase “all mundane and supramundane,” it is shown that among the six types of objects—which are categorized as conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena, and concepts—there is no phenomenon that is not an object condition, because even a concept, by virtue of being known in the world, is included under the term “mundane.” For that reason, it is stated indefinitely: “depending on whatever phenomenon.” But is it not so that because it is said “whatever phenomenon,” a concept is not included? This is not a fault, because the word “phenomenon” (dhamma) denotes that which is knowable. ‘Having taken as object’ (ārabbha) means having depended on, having grasped. The word ‘arise’ is merely an illustration. For depending on that object, they both arise and persist. Just as a weak person, relying on a staff or a rope, both rises and stands, so too mental phenomena and their concomitants, relying on an object such as a material form, both arise and persist.

Jeṭṭhakaṭṭhena upakārako dhammo adhipatipaccayo. Jeṭṭhakaṭṭhenāti ca pamukhabhāvena. Attādhīnānañhi patibhūto dhammo adhipatīti so tesaṃ pamukhabhāvena pavattati. “Chandādhipati chandasampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ adhipatipaccayena paccayo”tiādivacanato chandādayo cattāro dhammā sahajātanāmarūpānaṃ sahajātādhipatīti dassento āha “tattha sahajātādhipatī”tiādi. “Chandavato kiṃ nāma kammaṃ na sijjhatī”tiādikaṃ purimābhisaṅkhārūpanissayaṃ labhitvā uppajjamāne cittuppāde chandādayo dhurabhūtā jeṭṭhakabhūtā sampayuttadhamme, taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpe ca sādhayamānā vase vattayamānā hutvā pavattanti, te ca tesaṃ vasena vattanti hīnādibhāvena tadanuvattanato. Tena te adhipatipaccayā honti, no ca kho ekato. Yadā hi chandaṃ dhuraṃ chandaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā cittaṃ pavattati, tadā chandova adhipati, na itare. Esa nayo sesesupi. Adhipatibhāvopi hi nesaṃ attano pavattinivārake abhibhuyya pavattanato hoti. Avasesanti yathāvuttānaṃ tesaṃ garukātabbatābhāvato, garukatasseva ca [V 2.0272] ārammaṇādhipatibhāvavacanato. Vuttañhetaṃ “yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ garuṃ katvā ye ye dhammā uppajjanti [M 2.0365] cittacetasikā dhammā, te te dhammā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ adhipatipaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.3). Tattha garuṃ katvāti garukāracittīkāravasena vā assādanavasena vā garuṃ bhārikaṃ laddhabbaṃ anavaññātaṃ katvā. Garukātabbañhi ārammaṇaṃ tanninnapoṇapabbhārānaṃ assādanapaccavekkhaṇamaggaphalānaṃ attano vase vattayamānaṃ viya paccayo hoti, tasmā ayaṃ attādhīnānaṃ patibhāvena upakārakattā adhipatipaccayo daṭṭhabbo.

A phenomenon that assists by way of being foremost is a dominance condition (adhipatipaccaya). ‘By way of being foremost’ means by way of being principal. For a phenomenon that is a guarantor for those dependent on it is a dominant (adhipati); thus it proceeds as their principal. From such statements as, ‘Desire as a dominant is a condition by way of dominance condition for phenomena associated with desire and for the material phenomena originating therefrom,’ he shows that the four phenomena beginning with desire are conascence-dominants for conascent mentality-materiality, saying, ‘Therein, the conascence-dominant,’ and so on. When a mind-moment arises having obtained the support of a prior resolve such as, ‘What deed can one with desire not accomplish?’, desire and the like, being the yoke and being foremost, proceed accomplishing and exercising control over the associated phenomena and the material phenomena originating therefrom. And those phenomena proceed under their control, following them by being subordinate, and so on. Thus they are dominance conditions, but not simultaneously. For when the mind proceeds having made desire the yoke, having made desire foremost, then desire alone is the dominant, not the others. This is the method in the remaining cases as well. For their state of dominance comes about by proceeding having overcome their own obstacles. ‘The remaining’ is said because the aforementioned phenomena are not worthy of being made weighty, and because it is said that only what is made weighty has the nature of object-dominance. For it is said: ‘Whatever phenomena, that is, mental phenomena and their concomitants, arise making a certain phenomenon weighty, that phenomenon is a condition for those phenomena by way of dominance condition.’ Herein, ‘making weighty’ means making it weighty, heavy, something to be attained, and not to be slighted, either by way of respect and reverence or by way of enjoying it. For a weighty object is a condition for those states that are inclined, sloped, and bent towards it—such as the reviewing of gratification, path, and fruit—as if bringing them under its own control. Therefore, this should be understood as a dominance condition because it assists by being a guarantor for those dependent on it.

Antarayatīti antaraṃ, byavadhāyakanti attho, nāssa antaraṃ vijjatīti anantaro, soyeva paccayoti anantarapaccayo, anantarabhāvena upakārako dhammoti adhippāyo. Anantaraniruddhāti attano nirodhānantaraṃ anurūpacittuppādassa uppattipaccayabhāvena tassa uppattiyā purimabhāge anantaraṃ hutvā niruddhā, rūpadhammā pana anantarapaccayā natthi.

It makes an interval, thus it is an interval (antara), meaning it is a separator. There is no interval for it, thus it is uninterrupted (anantara). That very condition is the proximity condition (anantarapaccayo). The meaning is that it is a state that assists by way of being uninterrupted. ‘Immediately ceased’ (anantaraniruddhā) means: having ceased immediately after their own cessation, having been uninterrupted in the preceding phase for the arising of a subsequent suitable consciousness, by way of being a condition for its arising. Material phenomena, however, are not proximity conditions.

Samanantarabhāvena upakārako dhammo samanantarapaccayo, tathā samanantarapaccayopīti ṭhapetvā upasaggamattaṃ na ettha koci viseso. Yo hi anantarapaccayo, sova samanantarapaccayoti. Purimapacchimānañhi anantaruppādabhāvato nirantaruppādanasamatthatā anantarapaccayatā, rūpakalāpānaṃ viya saṇṭhānābhāvato paccayapaccayuppannānaṃ sahaṭṭhānābhāvato ca “idamito uddhaṃ heṭṭhā tiriya”nti vibhāgābhāvā attano ekattamiva upanetvā suṭṭhu anantarabhāvena uppādetuṃ samatthatā samanantarapaccayatā, tasmā dhammato avisesepi vineyyavasena byañjanatthamattato visesaṃ gahetvā tesaṃ visuṃ desanā katā. Yampi “atthānantaratāya anantarapaccayo, kālānantaratāya samanantarapaccayo”ti ācariyānaṃ mataṃ, taṃ “nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa [M 2.0366] nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ kusalaṃ phalasamāpattiyā samanantarapaccayena paccayo”tiādīhi (paṭṭhā. 1.1.418) virujjhatītiādinā paṭikkhittaṃ.

A state that assists by way of immediate contiguity is the contiguity condition (samanantarapaccayo). Thus, for the contiguity condition as well, apart from the mere prefix, there is no difference here. For what is the proximity condition is also the contiguity condition. Because preceding and succeeding states arise without an interval, the ability to cause an uninterrupted arising is the nature of the proximity condition. And because, unlike material groups, there is no shape, and because the condition and the conditioned do not share a location, there is no division such as ‘this is above, below, or across from that’—thus, by bringing them to a state of oneness, as it were, the ability to cause arising well and without interval is the nature of the contiguity condition. Therefore, although there is no difference in the phenomena themselves, a distinction is made for the sake of the trainees and for the mere purpose of the letter, and thus they are taught separately. Moreover, the view of the teachers that ‘the proximity condition is due to the immediacy of meaning, and the contiguity condition is due to the immediacy of time’ is refuted by such passages as, ‘For one emerging from the attainment of cessation, the wholesome state of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of the contiguity condition,’ and so on, because it is contradicted.

Uppajjamānova sahuppādanavasena upakārako dhammo sahajātapaccayo pakāsassa padīpo viya, so panāyaṃ “cittacetasikā dhammā aññamaññaṃ, sahajātarūpānañca, mahābhūtā aññamaññaṃ, upādārūpānañca, paṭisandhikkhaṇe vatthuvipākā aññamañña”nti ca tividho hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “cittacetasikā”tiādi. Yampi hi pāḷiyaṃ arūpakkhandhādivasenassa chabbidhataṃ vuttaṃ, tampi ettheva saṅgahitaṃ. Yo panettha sesarūpadhammānaṃ, ubhayattha vatthuno ca pavattiyā [V 2.0273] arūpadhammānaṃ, upādārūpānañca aññamaññaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ sahajātapaccayattābhāvo, so paccayabhāvasāmatthiyavisesāyogatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

A state that, while itself arising, assists by way of co-arising is a conascence condition (sahajātapaccayo), like a lamp for light. This, however, is threefold: ‘consciousness and mental factors mutually, and for conascent matter; the great elements mutually, and for derived matter; and at the moment of rebirth-linking, the physical base and resultant states mutually.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘consciousness and mental factors,’ etc. Indeed, what is stated in the Pāli canon as being sixfold by way of the immaterial aggregates, etc., is also included here. The absence of conascence conditionality here—of the remaining material phenomena for one another, of the physical base for the immaterial phenomena that arise during life, and of derived matter and the great elements for one another—should be understood as due to the unsuitability of a special capacity for being a condition.

Aññamaññaṃ uppādanupatthambhanabhāvena attano upakārakassa upakārako dhammo aññamaññapaccayo. Aññamaññupatthambhakatidaṇḍakaṃ viya upakārakatā ca aññamaññatāvaseneva daṭṭhabbā, na sahajātādivasena. Sahajātādipaccayo hontoyeva hi koci kassaci aññamaññapaccayo na hoti cittacetasikānaṃ cittajarūpe sati, mahābhūtānaṃ upādārūpe sati aññamaññapaccayattābhāvato. Yathāha “cattāro khandhā arūpino aññamaññapaccayena paccayo, cattāro mahābhūtā…pe… okkantikkhaṇe nāmarūpaṃ aññamaññapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.7).
