Ācariyena pana paccayuppannadhamme aparāmasitvā vuccamānattā avisesena vuttaṃ “tathā aññamaññapaccayo”ti.

A state that assists its own assistant by way of mutual generation and support is a mutuality condition (aññamaññapaccayo). Its assistance should be understood solely in terms of mutuality, like a tripod of sticks supporting one another, not in terms of conascence and so on. For although something may be a conascence condition, etc., it is not necessarily a mutuality condition for something else, because there is an absence of mutuality conditionality in the case of consciousness and mental factors with consciousness-born matter, and in the case of the great elements with derived matter. As it is said: ‘The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of the mutuality condition; the four great elements... at the moment of conception, mentality-materiality is a condition for itself by way of the mutuality condition’ (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.7). However, because the teacher speaks without referring to the conditioned phenomena, it is stated without distinction: ‘Thus, the mutuality condition.’

Taruādīnaṃ pathavī viya adhiṭṭhānākārena, cittakammādīnaṃ paṭādayo viya ca nissayākārena upakārako dhammo [M 2.0367] nissayapaccayo. Vatthurūpānīti sattannaṃ viññāṇadhātūnaṃ adhiṭṭhānākārena nissayapaccayabhūtāni vatthurūpāni. Mahābhūtā cittacetasikā cāti aññamaññaṃ, upādārūpānañca tatheva nissayabhūtāni mahābhūtāni aññamaññaṃ, sahajātarūpānañca nissayākārena paccayāni cittacetasikāni, tadadhīnavuttitāya attano phalena nissito na paṭikkhittoti nissayo.

A state that assists in the manner of a foundation, like the earth for trees and so on, and in the manner of a support, like a cloth for a painting and so on, is a dependence condition (nissayapaccayo). ‘Physical bases’ (vatthurūpāni) are the physical bases that have become dependence conditions for the seven consciousness-elements in the manner of a foundation. The great elements are a dependence for one another; consciousness and mental factors are a dependence for one another; likewise, the great elements are a dependence for derived matter; and consciousness and mental factors are conditions for conascent matter in the manner of dependence. Because its occurrence is dependent on that, and its fruit is supported by it, it is not rejected; thus, it is a dependence (nissaya).

Yathā pana bhuso āyāso upāyāso, evaṃ bhuso nissayo upanissayo, balavakāraṇanti attho, tasmā balavakāraṇabhāvena upakārako dhammo upanissayapaccayoti veditabbo. So ārammaṇūpanissayo anantarūpanissayo pakatūpanissayoti tividhoti āha “ārammaṇā”tiādi. Tattha –

Just as great effort is ‘endeavor’ (upāyāso), so a strong dependence is ‘decisive support’ (upanissayo), meaning a powerful cause. Therefore, a state that assists by way of being a powerful cause should be understood as the decisive support condition (upanissayapaccaya). It is threefold—object decisive support, proximity decisive support, and natural decisive support—as stated: ‘by way of object,’ etc. Therein—

“Dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā uposathakammaṃ katvā taṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhati, pubbe suciṇṇāni garuṃ katvā paccavekkhati, jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā jhānaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhati, sekhā gotrabhuṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhanti, vodānaṃ garuṃ katvā [V 2.0274] paccavekkhanti, sekhā maggā vuṭṭhahitvā maggaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhantī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.423) –

“Having given a gift, undertaken virtue, and performed the Uposatha observance, one reviews it, esteeming it. One reviews previously well-practiced deeds, esteeming them. Having emerged from jhāna, one reviews the jhāna, esteeming it. Trainees review the change-of-lineage, esteeming it. They review purification, esteeming it. Trainees, having emerged from the path, review the path, esteeming it” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.423).

Evamādinā nayena ārammaṇūpanissayo tāva ārammaṇādhipatinā saddhiṃ nānattaṃ akatvāva vibhatto. Tenāha “ārammaṇūpanissayo ārammaṇādhipatiyevā”ti. Kiñcāpi nānattaṃ akatvā vibhatto, tathāpi ayaṃ tesaṃ viseso – yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ garuṃ katvā cittacetasikā uppajjanti, taṃ niyamato tesaṃ ārammaṇesu balavārammaṇaṃ hoti. Iti garukātabbamattaṭṭhena ārammaṇādhipati, balavakāraṇaṭṭhena ārammaṇūpanissayoti ca evametesaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In this and other ways, the object decisive support condition is analyzed without making a distinction from the object predominance condition. Hence it is said: ‘The object decisive support condition is just the object predominance condition.’ Although it is analyzed without making a distinction, still this is their difference: whatever object is esteemed when consciousness and mental factors arise, that is invariably a powerful object among their objects. Thus, object predominance is in the sense of being what is to be esteemed, while object decisive support is in the sense of being a powerful cause. In this way, their distinction should be understood.

Anantarūpanissayopi [M 2.0368] “purimā purimā kusalā khandhā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ kusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ upanissayapaccayena paccayo”tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.423) nayena anantarapaccayena saddhiṃ nānattaṃ akatvāva vibhattoti āha “anantarūpanissayo pana anantarapaccayovā”ti. Evaṃ santepi attano anantarā anurūpacittuppādavasena anantarapaccayo, balavakāraṇavasena anantarūpanissayapaccayoti evametesaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The proximity decisive support condition has also been analyzed without making a distinction from the proximity condition, according to the method beginning, “Preceding wholesome aggregates are a condition for succeeding wholesome aggregates by way of the decisive support condition,” etc. (Paṭṭh. 1.1.423). Therefore, he said: “The proximity decisive support condition, however, is just the proximity condition.” Even so, their distinction should be understood thus: the proximity condition is so by way of the arising of a suitable consciousness immediately after itself, whereas the proximity decisive support condition is so by way of being a powerful cause.

Pakatiyā eva paccayantararahitena attano sabhāveneva upanissayo pakatūpanissayo, ārammaṇaanantarehi amissova puthageva koci upanissayoti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā pakato upanissayo pakatūpanissayo. Pakatoti cettha pa-kāro upasaggo, so attano phalassa uppādanasamatthabhāvena santāne nipphāditabhāvaṃ, upasevitabhāvañca dīpeti, tasmā attano santāne nipphanno vā kāyikasukhadukkhasaddhāsīlādi upasevito vā utubhojanādi pakatūpanissayoti attho. Upasevanañcettha duvidhaṃ upayogopasevanaṃ ārammaṇūpasevanañca. Evañca katvā anāgatassāpi upanissayapaccayatā laddhā hoti. Kāyikasukha…pe… yo cāti ettha kāyikasukhadukkhāni rāgasaddhādīnaṃ, utubhojanādayo cittasamādhānādīnaṃ, saddhāsīlādayo saddhāsīlādīnañca upanissayā honti. Ādi-saddena yaṃ yaṃ upanissāya yassa yassa sambhavo, taṃ taṃ tassa tassa upanissayapaccayabhūtaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Paccayamahāpadeso hesa, yadidaṃ upanissayapaccayoti.

A natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya) is a decisive support by its own inherent nature alone, devoid of other conditions. It is said to be a distinct decisive support, unmixed with object or contiguity. Alternatively, a prominent decisive support is a natural decisive support. Herein, the prefix ‘pa-’ indicates its capacity to produce its own result, its state of having been produced in the continuity, and its state of having been resorted to. Therefore, the meaning is that bodily pleasure and pain, faith, virtue, and so on, produced in one’s own continuity, or climate, food, and so on, that are resorted to, are ‘natural decisive support.’ Resorting here is twofold: resorting by way of utilization and resorting by way of object. By this means, the state of being a decisive support condition is established even for the future. Herein, bodily pleasure and pain are decisive supports for lust, faith, and so on; climate, food, and so on, for mental concentration, and so on; and faith, virtue, and so on, for faith, virtue, and so on. By the word ‘etc.’ (ādi) is included whatsoever, in dependence upon which there is the arising of whatsoever; that becomes a decisive support condition for this. For this is a great domain of conditions, namely, the decisive support condition.

Paccayuppannato paṭhamataraṃ uppajjitvā vattamānabhāvena upakārako dhammo purejātapaccayo. So [V 2.0275] ca rūpadhammova samāno arūpadhammasseva hoti. Tenāha “vatthupurejāto [M 2.0369] nāmā”tiādi. Yathā cettha “vatthurūpānī”ti hadayavatthunopi gahaṇaṃ, evaṃ “rūpādīnī”tiādi-ggahaṇena dhammārammaṇassāpi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nanu ca pañcārammaṇāneva ārammaṇapurejātabhāvena āgatānīti? Saccaṃ āgatāni, pañhāvāre pana “sekhā vā puthujjanā vā cakkhuṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato vipassantī”tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.424) avisesena paccuppannacakkhādīnampi gahitattā dhammārammaṇassa ārammaṇapurejātabhāvo na sakkā paṭibāhituṃ. Atthatopi hetaṃ siddhaṃ “yaṃ yaṃ paccuppannaṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā manodvāre cittaṃ pavattati, taṃ tassa ārammaṇapurejātaṃ hotī”ti. Ettha ca nissayārammaṇākārādīhi visiṭṭhā purejātabhāvena vinā upakārabhāvaṃ agacchantānaṃ vatthārammaṇānaṃ purejātākārena upakārakatā purejātapaccayatāti ayamassa nissayārammaṇapaccayatāhi viseso.

A phenomenon that, having arisen earlier than the conditioned phenomenon and being present, is of assistance, is the prenascent condition. And it, being a material phenomenon, is a condition only for an immaterial phenomenon. Hence it is said: “The base is prenascent,” and so on. Herein, just as by the phrase “material bases” the heart-base is also included, so too by the phrase “forms, etc.,” the inclusion of the mental object should be understood. Is it not so that only the five sense-objects are included by way of being prenascent objects? Indeed they are, but in the section of questions, because it is stated without distinction, “Whether trainees or ordinary people, contemplating the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self,” etc. (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.424), where the present eye and so on are also included, the state of the mental object as a prenascent object cannot be denied. Moreover, this is established by the meaning: “Whatever present object is taken up, and consciousness proceeds at the mind-door, that is its prenascent object.” Herein, the assistance in the mode of prenascence of base-objects—which are distinguished by modes such as support and object and do not come to be of assistance without the prenascent state—is the prenascent condition. This is its distinction from the support and object conditions.

Gijjhapotakasarīrānaṃ āhārāsā cetanā viya purejātānaṃ rūpānaṃ upatthambhakabhāvena upakārako dhammo pacchājātapaccayo. Manosañcetanāhāravasena hi pacchājātacittacetasikehi vinā santānaṭṭhitihetubhāvaṃ agacchantānaṃ pacchājātākārena cittacetasikānaṃ upakārakatā vippayuttākārādīhi visiṭṭhā pacchājātapaccayatāti evaṃ sabbapaccayānaṃ paccayantarākāravisiṭṭhā upakārakatā daṭṭhabbā. So pana “pacchājātā cittacetasikā dhammā purejātassa imassa kāyassa pacchājātapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.11) āgatattā ekavidhoti āha “cittacetasikāvā”ti.

A phenomenon that is of assistance by way of supporting pre-arisen material phenomena, like the volition that is the desire for food for the bodies of vulture chicks, is the postnascent condition. For, by way of mental volition as nutriment, the assistance of postnascent consciousness and mental factors in the postnascent mode—for those material phenomena that would not attain the state of being a cause for the continuity’s persistence without them—is the postnascent condition, distinguished by modes such as dissociation. Thus, the assistance of all conditions should be understood as distinguished by modes from other conditions. Since it is stated, “Postnascent consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this pre-arisen body by way of postnascent condition” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.11), it is said to be of one kind: 'consciousness and mental factors'.

Purimapurimaparicitagantho viya uttaruttarassa ganthassa kusalādibhāvena attasadisapaguṇabalavabhāvavisiṭṭhaṃ attasajātiyatāgāhakaṃ [M 2.0370] āsevanaṃ, tena paccayā sajātiyadhammāva āsevanapaccayo. Bhinnajātikā hi bhinnajātikānaṃ āsevanaguṇena paguṇabalavabhāvavisiṭṭhaṃ kusalādibhāvasaṅkhātaṃ attano gatiṃ gāhāpetuṃ na sakkonti, na ca sayaṃ tato gaṇhanti. Te pana anantarātītāni lokiyakusalākusalāni ceva anāvajjanakiriyājavanāni cāti āha “ṭhapetvā āvajjanadvaya”ntiādi. “Na maggapaccayā āsevane eka”nti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.221) vacanato ahetukakiriyāsu hasituppādasseva āsevanabhāvena, āvajjanadvayaṃ āsevanapaccayo na hoti, lokuttarampi kusalaṃ bhinnajātikasseva phalassa purecarattā na tena, āsevanaguṇaṃ gaṇhāpeti, vipākābyākatampi kammavasena[V 2.0276]. Vipākabhāvappattaṃ kammapariṇāmitaṃ kammavegakkhittaṃ patitaṃ viya hutvā pavattamānaṃ attano sabhāvaṃ gāhetvā paribhāvetvā neva aññavipākaṃ pavatteti, na ca purimavipākānubhāvaṃ gahetvā uppajjati. Lokuttaravipākampi hi kiñcāpi javanavasena uppajjati, āsevanaguṇaṃ pana gaṇhāti, na ca aññaṃ gāhāpeti. Yampi “āsevanavinimuttaṃ javanaṃ natthī”ti ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ, tampi “yebhuyyavasena vutta”nti viññāyati, itarathā pana ācariyassa asamapekkhitāvidhāyakattappasaṅgato. Tathā hi vuttaṃ paṭṭhānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “lokuttaro pana āsevanapaccayo nāma natthī”ti (paṭṭhā. aṭṭha. 1.12). Maggo pana gotrabhuto āsevanaṃ na gaṇhātīti natthi bhūmiādivasena nānājātikatāya anadhippetattā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ paṭṭhāne “gotrabhu maggassa āsevanapaccayena paccayo, vodānaṃ maggassa āsevanapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.426).

Just as a preceding text that has been repeatedly studied imparts proficiency and strength to a subsequent text, so repetition is the acquisition of a similar nature, distinguished by a proficient and strong nature in terms of skillfulness and so on. By that condition, only phenomena of the same kind are the repetition condition. For things of a different kind cannot, through the quality of repetition, cause things of a different kind to acquire their own course—that is, the state of being skillful and so on, distinguished by a proficient and strong nature—nor do they themselves acquire it from them. These, however, are the immediately past mundane wholesome and unwholesome states, and the functional impulsions excluding adverting; thus it is said, “excluding the two advertings,” and so on. According to the statement, “The path is not a condition as one in repetition” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.221), among the rootless functional states, only the smile-producing consciousness has the nature of repetition; the two advertings are not a repetition condition. Moreover, the supramundane wholesome state, being a forerunner to a result of a different kind, does not cause it to acquire the quality of repetition; and so with the resultant-indeterminate, due to kamma. A resultant state, having reached its resultant state through the maturation of kamma, like something fallen, thrown by the force of kamma, proceeds having grasped and imbued its own nature; it neither causes another resultant to proceed, nor does it arise having grasped the power of a previous resultant. For although the supramundane resultant also arises by way of impulsion, it acquires the quality of repetition but does not cause another to acquire it. And that which was said by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, “There is no impulsion devoid of repetition,” is understood as “said as a general rule”; otherwise, it would follow that the teacher made a statement without considering exceptions. For thus it is said in the Paṭṭhāna commentary: “There is no such thing as a supramundane repetition condition” (Paṭṭhāna Aṭṭha. 1.12). However, it is not that the path does not acquire repetition from the change-of-lineage, because a diversity of kinds by way of stage, etc., is not intended. For thus it is said in the Paṭṭhāna: “Change-of-lineage is a condition for the path by way of repetition condition; purification is a condition for the path by way of repetition condition” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.426).

Cittappayogasaṅkhātaāyūhanakiriyābhāvena sahajātānaṃ, nānakkhaṇikānañca upakārako dhammo kammapaccayo[M 2.0371]. Kammanti hi cetanā vuccati, sā ca āyūhanabyāpārā. Paccayuppannena saha uppannā sahajātā, paccayuppannato nānakkhaṇe bhavā nānakkhaṇikā. Sahajātā lokiyalokuttarā cetanāti sambandho. Sā sahajātanāmānaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ paccayo, itarā pana vipākakaṭattārūpānanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sāsavakusalākusalacetanāti attano uppādavisiṭṭhe santāne sesapaccayasamāgame pavattamānānaṃ vipākakaṭattārūpānaṃ santānavisesanakiriyābhāvena upakārikā kāmarūpārūpakusalacetanā, akusalacetanā ca. Tassā hi tathā kiriyābhāvena pavattattā tesaṃ pavatti, na aññathā. Itarā pana sahajātānaṃ āyūhanakiriyābhāvena pavattamānā upakārikāti vattabbaṃ. Avadhāraṇena panettha cetanāsampayuttaṃ abhijjhādikammaṃ paṭikkhipati satipi vipākadhammasabhāve cetanāvajjānaṃ ataṃsabhāvattā. Anāsava…pe… paccayoti iminā lokiyakusalacetanāya visesamattaṃ dasseti, na nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayatābhāvaṃ. Evañca katvā vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “arūpāvacaracetanā, pana lokuttaracetanā ca uppajjitvā niruddhā attano attano vipākakkhandhānaṃ nānakkhaṇikakammapaccayena paccayo”ti.

The kamma condition is a phenomenon helpful to co-arisen states and to those occurring at different moments, by way of the action of exertion called mental application. For 'kamma' is called volition, and that has the function of exertion. Those arisen together with the conditioned phenomenon are co-arisen; those existing at a different moment from the conditioned phenomenon are of a different moment. The connection is that co-arisen volition is mundane and supramundane. That volition is a condition for co-arisen mental phenomena and for material phenomena originated by them. The other, however, should be understood as a condition for resultant and kamma-produced material phenomena. Wholesome and unwholesome volitions associated with taints—that is, wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere, form-sphere, and formless-sphere, and unwholesome volitions—are helpful by the action of particularizing the continuity of resultant and kamma-produced material phenomena that occur in their own continuity, distinguished by their arising, when other conditions converge. For their occurrence happens because that volition functions in such a way, and not otherwise. But the other—the co-arisen volition—should be said to be helpful to co-arisen states by functioning as an action of exertion. Here, by this specification, it excludes kamma such as covetousness, even when conjoined with volition, because although there is the nature of resultant phenomena, those things devoid of volition do not have that nature. By 'untainted... and so on... condition,' it shows only a special characteristic of mundane wholesome volition, not the absence of the different-moment kamma conditionship. Thus it is said in the commentary: 'But formless-sphere volition and supramundane volition, having arisen and ceased, are a condition by way of different-moment kamma for their respective resultant aggregates.'

Attano nirussāhasantabhāvena sahajātanāmarūpānaṃ nirussāhasantabhāvāya upakārakā arūpadhammāva vipākapaccayo. Tenāha “vipākacittacetasikā”ti. Te hi payogena asādhetabbatāya kammassa katattā nipphajjanamattato nirussāhasantabhāvā honti, na kilesavūpasamasantabhāvā[V 2.0277]. Nirussāhasantabhāvato eva hi bhavaṅgādayo duviññeyyā. Pañcadvārepi hi javanappavattiyāva rūpādīnaṃ gahitatā viññāyati. Abhinipātasampaṭicchanasantīraṇamattā pana vipākā duviññeyyā eva.

The result condition consists of immaterial phenomena which, by their own effortless and peaceful nature, are helpful for the effortless and peaceful state of co-arisen name-and-form. Therefore, it is said: 'resultant consciousness and mental factors.' For they are effortless and peaceful merely by being produced from the performance of kamma, not needing to be accomplished by exertion, and not because their peaceful nature comes from the pacification of defilements. Indeed, it is due to their effortless and peaceful nature that the life-continuum and other states are difficult to discern. Even in the five-door process, the grasping of forms and so on is discerned only during the occurrence of impulsion. But the resultant moments, which are merely the impact, receiving, and investigating, are indeed difficult to discern.

Rūpārūpānaṃ [M 2.0372] upatthambhakaṭṭhena upakāro āhārapaccayo. Satipi hi janakabhāve upatthambhakattameva āhārassa padhānakiccaṃ, janayantopi ca āhāro avicchedavasena upatthambhentova janetīti upatthambhanabhāvova āhārabhāvoti. Tattha kabaḷīkāro āhāro rūpakāyasseva upatthambhako, sesā tayo rūpārūpakāyassa. Na kevalañhi te nāmadhammānameva avicchedahetukā, atha kho paṭisandhiyaṃ kaṭattārūpānaṃ, pavatte cittajarūpānampi.

The nutriment condition is helpfulness to material and immaterial phenomena by way of supporting them. For even when it has a generative function, the primary function of nutriment is precisely to support. And although nutriment generates, it generates only by supporting through non-interruption; thus, the nature of supporting is indeed the nature of nutriment. Herein, edible food supports only the material body, while the remaining three support both the material and immaterial body. For they are not only the cause for the non-interruption of mental phenomena alone, but also for kamma-produced material phenomena at rebirth-linking and for mind-produced material phenomena during the course of existence.

Tesu tesu kiccesu paccayuppannadhammehi attānaṃ anuvattāpanakasaṅkhātaādhipaccaṭṭhena paccayo indriyapaccayo. Adhipatipaccayadhammānañhi pavattivinivārake abhibhavitvā pavattanena garubhāvo adhipatiyaṭṭho, indriyānaṃ pana dassanādikiccesu cakkhuviññāṇādīhi, jīvane kammajarūpehi, arūpadhammehi ca jīvantehi sukhitādibhāvesu sukhitādīhi adhimokkhapaggahaupaṭṭhānāvikkhepappajānanesu “anaññātaṃ ñassāmī”ti pavattiyaṃ ājānane, aññātāvibhāve ca saddhādisahajātehīti evaṃ taṃtaṃkiccesu cakkhādipaccayehi dhammehi cakkhādīnaṃ anuvattaniyatāmattaṃ indriyānaṃ ādhipaccaṭṭhoti ayameva tesaṃ viseso. Rūpasattaka-ggahaṇena cakkhādīni pañca, itthipurisindriyadvayañca dasseti. Jīvitindriyaṃ pana arūpajīvitindriyena saddhiṃ ekato katvā jīvita-ggahaṇena gahitaṃ. Evañhi dvāvīsati indriyāni honti. “Anādimati saṃsāre anaññātaṃ asacchikataṃ catusaccadhammaṃ, nibbānameva vā ñassāmī”ti pavattassa indriyaṃ anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ, paṭhamamaggañāṇaṃ. Ājānato paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhamariyādaṃ anatikkamitvā jānato indriyaṃ aññindriyaṃ, sotāpattiphalato yāva arahattamaggā chasu ñāṇaṃ, aññātāvino catūsu saccesu pariniṭṭhitakiccassa indriyaṃ aññātāvindriyaṃ, arahattaphalañāṇaṃ[M 2.0373]. Paṭhamaṃ pariyāyato indriyattaṃ sandhāya rūpasattaka-ggahaṇena gahetvāpi puna kathañci upakārakattābhāvato itthipurisindriyānaṃ ettha aggahaṇaṃ dassetuṃ “tesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tāni hi yebhuyyena liṅgādīhi anuvattiyamānānipi paccayabhāvato nānuvattīyantīti vuttovāyamattho.

The faculty condition is a condition in the sense of dominance, characterized by making conditioned phenomena conform to itself in their respective functions. For the dominance of the phenomena of the dominant condition is their weighty state, occurring by overpowering obstacles to their arising. For the faculties, however, their dominance is simply this: in their respective functions, it is merely the fact that the eye faculty and so on are to be followed by their conditioned phenomena—for instance, in the function of seeing, by eye-consciousness and so on; in the function of living, by kamma-produced matter and by living immaterial phenomena; in states of being happy, etc., by happiness, etc.; in the functions of resolution, exertion, mindfulness, non-distraction, and understanding, and in the occurrence of the thought 'I will know the unknown,' in knowing, and in the manifestation of what has been known, by faith and other co-arisen factors. This is their distinguishing feature. By the phrase 'the sevenfold material group,' the five faculties of the eye, etc., and the two faculties of femininity and masculinity are indicated. The material life faculty, however, is included with the immaterial life faculty under the single term 'life.' Thus, there are twenty-two faculties. The faculty of one for whom there occurs the thought, 'In beginningless saṃsāra, I will know the fourfold noble truth, or Nibbāna itself, which is unknown and unrealized,' is the faculty of 'I will know the unknown,' which is the knowledge of the first path. The faculty of one who knows, knowing without transgressing the limit seen by the first path, is the faculty of knowing, which is the six kinds of knowledge from the fruition of stream-entry up to the path of arahantship. The faculty of one who has known, who has completed the task regarding the four truths, is the faculty of one who has known, which is the fruition-knowledge of arahantship. Although they were initially included by the phrase 'the sevenfold material group' to indicate the nature of faculties in a general way, the phrase 'in their respective functions' is stated here to show that the faculties of femininity and masculinity are not included, because they have no way of being helpful. For although they are generally followed in matters of gender and so on, from the standpoint of being a condition, they are not followed; this is the meaning that has been stated.

Ārammaṇūpanijjhānalakkhaṇūpanijjhānavasena [V 2.0278] upagantvā ārammaṇanijjhānaṃ jhānapaccayatā, so ca vitakkādīnameva āveṇiko sabhāvoti āha “jhānapaccayo”tiādi. Te pana paṭisandhiyaṃ kaṭattārūpānaṃ, pavatte cittajarūpānaṃ, ubhayattha nāmadhammānañca paccayāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The jhāna condition is the focusing on an object, approached by way of focusing on the object and focusing on characteristics. And since that is the unique nature of vitakka and the others, he said, 'jhāna condition,' etc. These, however, should be understood as conditions for kamma-produced material phenomena at rebirth-linking, for mind-produced material phenomena during the course of existence, and for mental phenomena in both instances.

Sugatito, duggatito, kusalato, akusalato vā niyyānaṭṭhena sahajātānaṃ upakārakatā maggapaccayatā, sā ca sammādiṭṭhādīnanti āha “maggapaccayo”tiādi. Saṅkappa-ggahaṇena sammāsaṅkappaṃ, micchāsaṅkappañca dasseti. Evaṃ sesesupi. Micchāsaṅkappādayo hi apāyamaggaṅgā, micchāsatimicchāvācādayo cettha tathāpavattacittuppādā, cetanā ca, ayampi jhānapaccaye vuttānameva paccayuppannānaṃ paccayoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The path condition is helpfulness to co-arisen states in the sense of leading forth from a good destination, from a bad destination, from the wholesome, or from the unwholesome. And that belongs to right view and so on; therefore, he said, 'path condition,' etc. By the term 'thought,' it indicates both right thought and wrong thought. Likewise for the remaining factors. For wrong thought and the others are factors of the path to the plane of misery. Herein, wrong mindfulness, wrong speech, and the others, and volition, are the arisings of consciousness that occur in that way. This should also be understood as a condition for the very same conditioned phenomena mentioned under the jhāna condition.

Paramatthena bhinnānampi ekībhāvagatānaṃ viya ekuppādādibhāvasaṅkhātasampayogalakkhaṇena upakārakatā sampayuttapaccayatā, sā ca nāmadhammānameva, na rūpadhammānanti āha “sampayuttapaccayo”tiādi.

The association condition is helpfulness characterized by conjunction—defined as the state of having a single arising and so on—for phenomena which, though distinct in an ultimate sense, are as if they had attained a state of oneness. And that applies only to mental phenomena, not to material phenomena; therefore, he said, 'association condition,' and so on.

Aññamaññasambandhatāya yuttānampi samānānaṃ vippayuttabhāvena visaṃsaṭṭhatāya nānattūpagamanena upakārakatā vippayuttapaccayatā, sā ca vatthūnaṃ, cittacetasikānameva vāti āha “vippayuttapaccayo”tiādi. Cha vatthūni hi sattannaṃ [M 2.0374] viññāṇānaṃ yathārahaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ, pavatte, cittacetasikā paṭisandhiyaṃ kaṭattārūpānaṃ, pavattiyaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānānañca vippayuttapaccayo. Vatthupurejātānīti idaṃ cakkhādivatthuvaseneva vuttaṃ, hadayavatthu pana paṭisandhiyampi paccayabhāvato sahajātampi labbhati. Vuttampi hetaṃ abyākatapadassa sahajātavibhaṅge “paṭisandhikkhaṇe vipākābyākatā khandhā kaṭattārūpānaṃ, khandhā vatthussa, vatthu khandhānaṃ vippayuttapaccayena paccayo”ti. Tathā pacchājātā cittacetasikāti ca cakkhuviññāṇādivaseneva vuttaṃ, “sahajātā kusalā khandhā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ vippayuttapaccayena paccayo”tiādivacanato (paṭṭhā. 1.1.434) pana sahajātāpi labbhanti. Evañca katvā vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “vippayuttapaccayo sahajātapurejātapacchājātavasena tividho”ti. Ayaṃ pana rūpadhammo samāno rūpadhammassa paccayo na hoti sampayogāsaṅkāya abhāvato.

The condition of dissociation is the helpfulness, even for those connected by mutual relationship, by being dissociated, by being unmixed, and by entering into diversity. And that is for the physical bases and for consciousness and mental factors; therefore, he said, 'vippayuttapaccayo,' and so on. For the six bases are conditions of dissociation for the seven kinds of consciousness, appropriately at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence; and consciousness and mental factors are conditions of dissociation for kamma-produced material phenomena at rebirth-linking, and for mind-produced material phenomena during the course of existence. 'Preceding physical bases' is said with reference to the eye-base and so on; but the heart-base is also obtained as co-arisen, because it is a condition even at rebirth-linking. It is also said in the analysis of the indeterminate section on co-arisen states: 'At the moment of rebirth-linking, the indeterminate resultant aggregates are a condition for kamma-produced material phenomena; the aggregates are a condition for the base, and the base is a condition for the aggregates by way of dissociation.' Similarly, 'subsequent consciousness and mental factors' is said with reference to eye-consciousness and so on. But from statements like, 'The co-arisen wholesome aggregates are a condition for mind-produced material phenomena by way of dissociation,' co-arisen ones are also obtained. Thus, it is said in the commentary: 'The condition of dissociation is threefold: co-arisen, preceding, and subsequent.' However, a material phenomenon is not a condition for another material phenomenon due to the absence of the possibility of association.

Yesañhi nāmānaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ abbhantarato nikkhamantānaṃ viya pavatti, rūpānañca nāmasannissayeneva [V 2.0279] uppajjamānānaṃ sampayogāsaṅkā hoti, tesameva vippayuttapaccayatā vuttā. Rūpānaṃ pana rūpehi sāsaṅkā natthi, vatthusannissayeneva ca jāyantānaṃ nāmānaṃ visayamattaṃ ārammaṇanti tenāpi tesaṃ sampayogāsaṅkā natthi. Paccuppannasabhāvena atthibhāvena tādisasseva dhammassa upatthambhakattena upakārakatā atthipaccayatā. Satipi hi janakatte ṭhitiyaṃyeva sātisayo atthipaccayānaṃ byāpāroti upatthambhakatā tesaṃ gahitā, te ca rūpajīvitindriyādīnevāti āha “atthipaccayo”tiādi. Rūpajīvitindriyañhi kaṭattārūpānaṃ, kabaḷīkārāhāro imassa kāyassa[M 2.0375], ārammaṇapurejātāni cittacetasikānaṃ nissayapaccaye vuttadhammā, tattheva vuttapaccayuppannañca atthipaccayo. Nissayapaccaye vuttadhammāti ca vatthurūpamahābhūtacittacetasikānaṃ dhammasāmaññeneva gahaṇaṃ, na nissayapaccayabhāvīnaṃyeva. Pacchājātānampi cittacetasikānaṃ purejātassa kāyassa pañhāvāre paccayabhāvena niddiṭṭhattā. Ettha ca atthibhāvābhāvena anupakārakānameva atthibhāvena upakārakatāya atthipaccayatābhāvato natthi nibbānassa sabbadā bhāvino atthipaccayatā, uppādādiyuttānaṃ vā natthibhāvopakāratāviruddho upakārakabhāvo atthipaccayatāti na tassa tappaccayattappasaṅgo.

For those mental phenomena, such as eye-consciousness and so forth, whose functioning is like emerging from within, and for material phenomena arising solely dependent on mental phenomena, there is a possibility of association. For these very same phenomena, the condition of dissociation is stated. However, for material phenomena, there is no such possibility of association with other material phenomena. And for mental phenomena that arise solely dependent on a physical basis, their object is merely a sense-field, so for them too there is no possibility of association. The presence condition is the helpfulness by way of upholding such a phenomenon through its present nature and existence. Even when there is a generative function, the activity of presence conditions is especially in upholding; thus, their role of upholding is understood, and these are the material life faculty and so forth. Hence, it is said, 'The presence condition,' etc. Indeed, the material life faculty is a presence condition for kamma-born material phenomena; physical nutriment for this body; pre-arisen objects for mind and mental factors; and the phenomena mentioned in the support condition and the dependently arisen mentioned therein are also presence conditions. And 'the phenomena mentioned in the support condition' refers to the physical basis, the great elements, and mind and mental factors, taken generally as phenomena, not merely those that function as support conditions. This is because even subsequently arisen mind and mental factors are designated as conditions for the pre-existent body in the section on questions. Here, since the presence condition is helpfulness by way of existence for those that are not helpful by way of non-existence, there is no presence condition for Nibbāna, which always exists. Or, for phenomena connected with arising, the presence condition is a helpful state that is contrary to helpfulness by way of non-existence; therefore, there is no implication that Nibbāna is a condition in that way.

Natthipaccayotiādīsu anantaratāmattena, cittaniyāmakabhāvena vā upakārakatā anantarapaccayatā. Ekasmiṃ phassādidhammasamudāye pavattamāne dutiyassa abhāvato attano ṭhitiyā okāsamalabhantānaṃ anantaraṃ uppajjamānakacittacetasikānaṃ okāsadānavasena upakārakatā natthipaccayatā. Attano sabhāvāvigamena appavattamānānaṃ vigatabhāvena upakārakatā vigatapaccayatā. Atthato pana dvinnampi anantarapaccayabhāvīdhammattā aviseso vutto. Sabhāvatāmattena upakārakatā atthipaccayatā, nirodhānupagamanavasena upakārakatā avigatapaccayatāti paccayaviseso tesaṃ dhammāvisesepi veditabbo. Dhammānañhi samatthatāvisesaṃ sabbākārena ñatvā bhagavatā catuvīsatipaccayā desitāti bhagavati saddhāya “evaṃ visesā ete dhammā”ti sutamayañāṇaṃ uppādetvā cintābhāvanāmayañāṇehi tadabhisamayāya yogo karaṇīyo. Avisesepi dhammasāmatthiyassa tathā tathā vinetabbapuggalānaṃ vasena heṭṭhā vuttopi paccayo puna pakārantarena vuccati yathā ahetukadukaṃ vatvāpi hetuvippayuttadukaṃ viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In the section on the absence condition and so forth, helpfulness by way of mere immediacy or by way of determining the mind is the contiguity condition. When one group of phenomena such as contact is occurring, the helpfulness of the absence condition is by providing an opportunity for the immediately arising mind and mental factors which, due to the absence of a second group, would not obtain an opportunity for their own existence. The helpfulness by way of disappearance is for phenomena that do not occur due to the non-disappearance of their intrinsic nature, being helpful by their having disappeared. In essence, however, no distinction is stated, as both are phenomena having the nature of the contiguity condition. Helpfulness by way of mere intrinsic nature is the presence condition; helpfulness by way of not having gone to cessation is the non-disappearance condition. Thus, the distinction among these conditions should be understood based on the distinctions in the nature of the phenomena, even when the phenomena themselves are not distinct. Indeed, having fully comprehended the varying capacities of phenomena in every way, the Blessed One taught the twenty-four conditions. Therefore, one should develop faith in the Blessed One, generate knowledge based on hearing—‘These phenomena indeed have such distinctions’—and then make an effort to realize this through knowledge based on reflection and meditation. Even when the capability of phenomena is not distinct, a condition, even one mentioned before, is stated again in a different way for the sake of individuals to be trained in that way, just as, after stating the rootless dyad, the dyad dissociated from roots is explained—this should be understood.

Yasmā [M 2.0376] mahābhūtā aññamaññaṃ, upādārūpānañca sahajātapaccayā, mahābhūtā aññamaññaṃ aññamaññanissayapaccayā, upādārūpānaṃ nissayapaccayāva, kabaḷīkāro āhāro imassa kāyassa [V 2.0280] āhārapaccayo, mahābhūtā aññamaññaṃ, upādārūpānañca jīvitindriyaṃ kaṭattārūpānañca atthiavigataindriyapaccayā, tasmā vuttaṃ “rūpaṃ rūpassa…pe… sattadhā paccayo hotī”ti.

Because the great elements are co-nascence conditions for each other and for derived material phenomena; the great elements are mutual support conditions for each other, and are support conditions for derived material phenomena; edible food is a nutriment condition for this body; and the great elements for each other and for derived material phenomena, and the life faculty for kamma-born material phenomena, are presence, non-disappearance, and faculty conditions; therefore it is said: “Form is a condition for form... in seven ways.”

Rūpaṃ arūpassātiādīsupi heṭṭhā vuttapaccayuppannadhamme suṭṭhu upalakkhetvā paccayo yojetabbo. Rūpaṃ rūpārūpassāti natthīti idaṃ sahajātapaccayabhūtampi rūpaṃ rūpārūpadvayassa paccayabhāvena anāgatanti katvā vuttaṃ.

In the sections on ‘Form for the formless,’ etc., one should carefully discern the dependently arisen phenomena mentioned therein and apply the condition. The statement ‘Form is not a condition for both form and the formless’ is made considering that even form, though being a co-nascence condition, does not function as a condition for the pair of form and the formless.

Sabbesaṃ paccayānaṃ ārammaṇapaccaye upanissayapaccaye, sahajātanānakkhaṇikacetanāya kammapaccaye, sahajātapurejātapacchājātādibhedassa atthipaccaye ca samodhānato sabbepi paccayā saṅkhepato catubbidhāyevāti dassento āha “sabbe panime”tiādi.

Showing that all conditions, due to their inclusion in the object condition, the decisive support condition, the kamma condition with its co-arisen and asynchronous volition, and the presence condition with its various types such as co-arisen, pre-arisen, and post-arisen, are in brief only of four kinds, he says ‘all these’ and so on.

Iti abhidhammatthavikāsiniyā nāma

Thus is named the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī.

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Paccayaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of conditions is completed.

Nigamanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Concluding Section

1400-2. Sabbadhammesu appaṭihatagatitāya sundarā mati imassāti sumati, tassa sumatissa bhagavato mativicāraṃ ñāṇacāraṃ bodhetīti sumatimativicārabodhano. Viruddhā mati yesaṃ te vimatino, viruddhā matīti ca viruddhadassananti attho. Tesaṃ vimohaṃ vināsetīti [M 2.0377] vimativimohavināsano. Yato yasmā nāmato sumatinā bhikkhunā mānato bahumānena āyācitasammānato āyācito hutvā sammā avanato sadāyeva mato ayaṃ, tato tasmā mayā racito abhidhammāvatāro. Tathā hi bhāvanā sādhūnaṃ sambhāvanā hitavibhāvanā hitappakāsanato sadā tosadāti yojanā.

Because his mind is beautiful, with unobstructed progress in all dhammas, he is called Sumati. Sumatimativicārabodhano signifies that he awakens the investigation of the mind and the course of knowledge of that Blessed One, Sumati. Those who have opposing views are called Vimatino, and 'opposing view' means 'wrong view.' Vimativimohavināsano signifies that he destroys their delusion. Since this Abhidhammāvatāra was composed by me, having been requested with great respect and honor by the monk named Sumati, and this work was always properly esteemed and approved, therefore, indeed, the cultivation of this work is for the esteem of the virtuous, and by manifesting and proclaiming benefit, it always brings joy—this is the connection.

1403-14. Ayuttaṃ [V 2.0281] vā viruddhaṃ vāti ettha “aṭṭhakathāya vimukhabhūtaṃ ayuttaṃ nāma, pāḷiyā vimukhabhūtaṃ viruddha”nti vadanti. Byappathānanti ca vācanāmaggānanti attho. Tividhāti eko byappatho saddasampanno, na atthasampanno, eko atthasampanno, na saddasampanno, eko ubhayasampannoti tippakārāti attho. Hitameva atthoti hitattho, taṃ attano kāmetīti hitatthakāmo. Asaṃkiṇṇakulākulehi asambhinnakulehi saṃkiṇṇe. Kelāsoyeva sikharoti kelāsasikharo, so hi himavato caturāsītiyā kūṭasahassānaṃ pāmokkho rajatamayo mahāsikharo. Tadākārehi sabbasetehi pāsādehi paṭimaṇḍitattā kelāsa…pe… maṇḍito. Kaṇhadāsenāti evaṃnāmakena upāsakena. Pācīnapāsādeti pācīnadisābhāgasannissite pāsāde. Ayanti ayamabhidhammāvatāro.

“Unconnected or contradictory”—here, they say that “what is inconsistent with the commentary is called ‘unconnected,’ and what is inconsistent with the Pāli is called ‘contradictory.’” And “byappathāna” means ‘paths of recitation,’ that is, ‘methods of expression.’ “Threefold”—one mode of expression is complete in sound but not in meaning, another is complete in meaning but not in sound, and a third is complete in both. Thus, it is of three kinds—this is the meaning. ‘Hitattho’ means ‘beneficial meaning’; ‘hitatthakāmo’ means ‘one desiring what is beneficial for oneself.’ “With unmixed families” means with families that are not intermingled. “Kelāsa alone is the peak”—‘kelāsasikharo’ means ‘Kelāsa peak,’ for it is the foremost among the eighty-four thousand peaks of the Himalayas, a great silver peak. Because it is adorned with all-white palaces of that form, it is described as Kelāsa... adorned. “By Kaṇhadāsa” means by a lay disciple so named. “In the eastern palace” means in a palace situated in the eastern quarter. “This” means this Abhidhammāvatāra.

Niṭṭhitāyaṃ abhidhammatthavikāsinī nāma

Herein is completed the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī.

Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Nigamanakathā

The Conclusion

1.

1.

Ramme [M 2.0378] pulatthinagare nagarādhirāje,

Raññā parakkamabhujena mahābhujena;

Kārāpite vasati jetavane vihāre,

Yo rammahammiyavarūpavanābhirāme.

He dwells in the Jetavana monastery, which was caused to be built by King Parakkamabhuja, the mighty-armed, in the delightful city of Pulatthi, the chief of cities; it is delightful with its lovely mansions and excellent groves.

2.

2.

Sampannasīladamasaṃyamatositehi,

Sammānito vasigaṇehi guṇākarehi;

Patto munindavacanādisu nekagantha-

Jātesu cācariyataṃ mahitaṃ vidūhi.

He, honored by groups of ascetics who are treasuries of virtues, complete in virtue, self-control, and restraint, and content, attained revered mastership among the learned in the words of the Sage-King and in various kinds of texts.

3..

3..

Ñāṇānubhāvamiha [V 2.0282] yassa ca sūcayantī,

Saṃvaṇṇanā ca vinayaṭṭhakathādikānaṃ;

Sāratthadīpanimukhā madhuratthasāra-

Sandīpanena sujanaṃ paritosayantī.

And here, indicating whose power of wisdom, is the commentary on the Vinaya commentary and others, with the Sāratthadīpanī as its head, delighting the good by illuminating the sweet essence of the meaning.

4.

4.

Tassānukampamavalambiya sāriputta-

Ttherassa thāmagatasāraguṇākarassa;

Yo sāsane jinavarassa ratiṃ uḷāraṃ,

Pappoti nandipariveṇanivāsavāsī.

By relying on the compassion of that Elder Sāriputta, an abode of unwavering strength and essential virtues, he, dwelling in Nandana Monastery, attains great delight in the teaching of the Supreme Conqueror.

5.

5.

Sa sādhayaṃ sotuhitaṃ anappakaṃ,

Sumaṅgalodīritanāmavissuto;

Akābhidhammatthavikāsiniṃ imaṃ,

Pakāsayantiṃ madhuratthasampadanti.

He, accomplishing much that is beneficial to the listener, renowned by the name Sumaṅgala, made this Abhidhammatthavikāsinī, which reveals the prosperity of its sweet meaning.

Abhidhammāvatāraṭīkā samattā.

The Sub-commentary on the Abhidhammāvatāra is completed.
